stem: A 72-year-old woman tripped at home and landed on her outstretched left arm. An X-ray in the emergency department shows a fracture through the surgical neck of the humerus. Pinprick sensation is reduced over a small patch on the outer aspect of the upper arm just below the point of the shoulder. Sensation in the forearm and hand is normal, and she can extend her wrist and fingers. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
why_correct: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, so it is vulnerable in fractures here and in anterior shoulder dislocation. It supplies deltoid and teres minor and gives sensation to the regimental badge area over the lateral upper arm. Reduced sensation in exactly this patch after a surgical neck fracture points to axillary nerve injury.
why_wrong: A. Radial nerve injury follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop, but her wrist extension is intact. B. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus and has no cutaneous area on the lateral arm. C. Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula without arm numbness. D. Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion and numbs the lateral forearm, not the shoulder.
pearl: Always test and document regimental badge sensation in surgical neck fractures and shoulder dislocations, both before and after any manipulation.
thinking: Fall onto outstretched arm ↓ Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus ↓ Nerve that wraps around the surgical neck ↓ Numb patch over lateral upper arm: regimental badge area ↓ Axillary nerve
exam_trap: A, radial nerve — the best-known nerve injury with humeral fractures, but it follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop; her wrist extension is normal.
takeaway: Surgical neck fracture with a numb regimental badge area: axillary nerve injury.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 9 Oct 2026 (held pack H01). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Peak flow variability and reversibility — asthma
stem: A 23-year-old woman sees her GP with several months of night-time cough, chest tightness and wheeze, worse in cold air. Her twice-daily home peak flow diary shows wide swings, with the lowest readings on waking. Spirometry shows a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio, and repeat spirometry 15 minutes after inhaled salbutamol shows a substantial rise in FEV1. What do these findings indicate?
why_correct: Marked variability in peak flow, worst in the morning, together with obstructive spirometry that improves substantially after a bronchodilator, shows airflow obstruction that varies and reverses. This is the physiological hallmark of asthma and, with a typical history, supports the diagnosis. UK guidance confirms asthma with objective tests such as FeNO, spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility and peak flow variability, rather than relying on symptoms alone.
why_wrong: A. Fixed obstruction, as in established COPD, shows little change after a bronchodilator and little day-to-day variation. B. A restrictive defect reduces FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio. D. Upper airway obstruction produces a flattened flow–volume loop and stridor rather than bronchodilator reversibility. E. Normal diurnal variation is small and does not produce obstructive spirometry.
pearl: Asthma is variable and reversible; COPD is persistent and largely fixed. A reduced FEV1/FVC that improves significantly with salbutamol, with early-morning dips in peak flow, points to asthma.
thinking: Nocturnal cough and wheeze, cold-air trigger ↓ Peak flow swings, lowest on waking ↓ Obstructive spirometry ↓ Large improvement after salbutamol ↓ Variable, reversible airflow obstruction
exam_trap: A, fixed airflow obstruction — the reduced FEV1/FVC ratio shows obstruction, which tempts this answer, but the substantial bronchodilator response and diurnal swings show it is reversible, not fixed.
takeaway: Morning peak flow dips plus bronchodilator reversibility mean reversible obstruction, the signature of asthma.

presentation: Dyspepsia with alarm features — urgent endoscopy
stem: A 64-year-old man sees his GP with 6 weeks of gnawing upper abdominal discomfort after meals. He has never had indigestion before. He has had to tighten his belt by two notches without trying, and his wife thinks he looks pale. He takes no regular medicines. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Carbon-13 urea breath test for H. pylori
options.B: Full-dose proton pump inhibitor for 4 weeks, then review
options.D: Routine referral to the gastroenterology clinic

correct_answer: E. Urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
why_correct: New dyspepsia in an older man with unexplained weight loss raises concern about oesophageal or gastric cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance recommends urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in this situation, so that any lesion can be seen and biopsied. Starting empirical treatment or testing for H. pylori first would delay the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features. B. An empirical PPI trial may mask symptoms and delay the diagnosis of a cancer. C. Ultrasound does not assess the gastric or oesophageal mucosa. D. A routine referral is too slow when cancer is suspected.
pearl: Upper GI red flags: dysphagia at any age, or age 55 and over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. These need urgent direct-access endoscopy, not a PPI trial.
thinking: New-onset dyspepsia in an older adult ↓ Unexplained weight loss and pallor ↓ Alarm features for upper GI cancer ↓ Tissue diagnosis needed quickly ↓ Urgent direct-access endoscopy
exam_trap: B, full-dose PPI for 4 weeks — it is the usual first step for dyspepsia, but alarm features change the pathway, and a PPI may heal the surface of a cancer and delay its diagnosis.
takeaway: New dyspepsia with weight loss in an older adult needs urgent endoscopy, not a PPI trial.

stem: A 47-year-old woman who has had several admissions with alcohol-related pancreatitis attends clinic. Over the last few months her stools have become pale, bulky and oily; they are difficult to flush and smell very offensive. She has lost weight despite a good appetite and has recently been diagnosed with diabetes. She is not jaundiced. What is the most likely cause of the change in her stools?

options.C: Obstruction of the common bile duct

why_correct: Repeated pancreatitis has progressed to chronic pancreatitis, destroying acinar tissue and reducing lipase secretion. Undigested fat then reaches the colon, producing pale, bulky, oily, offensive stools that are hard to flush, with weight loss. New diabetes reflects loss of islet tissue as well. Treatment is pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals, alongside stopping alcohol.
why_wrong: B. Coeliac disease can cause steatorrhoea but does not fit the history of recurrent alcohol-related pancreatitis. C. Bile duct obstruction causes pale stools with jaundice and dark urine, which she does not have. D. Bacterial overgrowth can coexist with chronic pancreatitis but is not the primary explanation. E. Bile acid diarrhoea causes watery stools, typically after ileal disease or resection, rather than fatty ones.
pearl: Chronic pancreatitis gives pain, steatorrhoea and diabetes as exocrine and endocrine tissue are lost. Treat malabsorption with pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with food, and check fat-soluble vitamins.
thinking: Recurrent alcohol-related pancreatitis ↓ Pale, bulky, oily stools that are hard to flush ↓ Weight loss and new diabetes ↓ Loss of acinar and islet tissue ↓ Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
exam_trap: C, common bile duct obstruction — pale stools tempt this answer, but obstruction comes with jaundice and dark urine, whereas oily, hard-to-flush stools point to fat maldigestion.
takeaway: Steatorrhoea after recurrent pancreatitis means exocrine insufficiency; treat with enzyme replacement.

stem: A 51-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a weekend of heavy drinking with 12 hours of constant, severe upper abdominal pain boring through to his back, and repeated vomiting. His heart rate is 108/min and blood pressure 128/80 mmHg. His epigastrium is tender with guarding and bowel sounds are reduced. An erect chest X-ray shows no free air under the diaphragm. Serum lipase is many times the upper limit of normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed from typical pain (constant, severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, often with vomiting) together with a markedly raised serum lipase or amylase. Alcohol and gallstones are the commonest causes in the UK. Management is supportive with IV fluids, analgesia and severity assessment, with ultrasound to look for gallstones.
why_wrong: A. A perforated ulcer usually causes sudden generalised peritonitis with free air under the diaphragm, which is absent here. B. Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain with fever and a positive Murphy's sign, without a markedly raised lipase. C. An inferior myocardial infarction can cause epigastric pain, so an ECG is essential, but it does not raise lipase. E. Biliary colic is self-limiting pain with normal pancreatic enzymes.
pearl: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed with two of three: typical pain, lipase or amylase at least three times normal, and imaging features. Gallstones and alcohol are the leading UK causes; always perform an ECG in epigastric pain.
thinking: Constant epigastric pain radiating to the back ↓ Vomiting after heavy alcohol intake ↓ No free air on erect film ↓ Lipase markedly raised ↓ Acute pancreatitis
exam_trap: A, perforated duodenal ulcer — epigastric pain with guarding fits, and amylase can rise modestly in perforation, but the absence of free air and a markedly raised lipase point to pancreatitis.
takeaway: Back-radiating epigastric pain with a markedly raised lipase is acute pancreatitis.

presentation: Stable upper GI bleed — timing of endoscopy
stem: A 72-year-old woman who takes aspirin and has been buying ibuprofen for knee pain presents to the emergency department after passing two black, tarry stools. She feels a little light-headed on standing but is alert. Her heart rate is 88/min and blood pressure 132/78 mmHg. Her haemoglobin is lower than on her previous blood test. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Immediate endoscopy before IV access or blood tests
options.B: Admit, resuscitate as needed, calculate a risk score and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours
options.C: Discharge with an oral PPI and an outpatient endoscopy
options.D: Start an IV PPI infusion and defer endoscopy for a week

correct_answer: B. Admit, resuscitate as needed, calculate a risk score and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours
why_correct: This is an acute upper GI bleed from a probable aspirin- and NSAID-related ulcer in a patient who is currently haemodynamically stable. NICE advises resuscitation as needed, formal risk assessment with the Glasgow–Blatchford score before endoscopy, and endoscopy within 24 hours of admission for stable patients. Endoscopy immediately after resuscitation is reserved for unstable patients with severe bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Endoscopy never precedes basic assessment and resuscitation, and immediate endoscopy is for unstable patients. C. Melaena with a falling haemoglobin in an older patient on aspirin is not a low-risk bleed suitable for discharge. D. NICE advises against starting acid suppression before endoscopy in non-variceal bleeding, and delaying endoscopy is unsafe. E. Terlipressin and antibiotics are for suspected variceal bleeding, for which there are no features here.
pearl: Upper GI bleed: unstable means resuscitate then endoscope immediately; stable means risk-score and endoscope within 24 hours. Only very low-risk patients (Glasgow–Blatchford score of 0) may be considered for early discharge.
thinking: Melaena on aspirin and an NSAID ↓ Probable peptic ulcer bleed ↓ Currently haemodynamically stable ↓ Resuscitate as needed and risk-score ↓ Endoscopy within 24 hours
exam_trap: A, immediate endoscopy — urgency feels right in any GI bleed, but immediate endoscopy is for unstable patients after resuscitation; a stable patient needs endoscopy within 24 hours.
takeaway: Stable upper GI bleed: resuscitate as needed, risk-score and endoscope within 24 hours.

stem: A 31-year-old man with terminal ileal Crohn's disease, treated with azathioprine, is seen in the emergency department with 5 days of worsening right lower abdominal pain and swinging fevers. His bowels are opening normally and there is no blood in his stool. His temperature is 38.9°C. There is a tender, fixed fullness in the right iliac fossa without generalised peritonism. CRP and white cell count are raised. What is the most likely complication?

options.B: Small bowel obstruction from a stricture

why_correct: Crohn's disease is transmural, so inflamed bowel can penetrate and form a contained collection. Swinging fevers, focal pain and a tender mass in the right iliac fossa with raised inflammatory markers point to an ileocaecal abscess. Contrast CT or MRI confirms it, and treatment is antibiotics with percutaneous drainage where feasible; immunosuppression should not be escalated until sepsis is controlled.
why_wrong: A. Toxic megacolon involves colonic dilatation with systemic toxicity, usually in severe colitis. B. Obstruction would cause colicky pain, vomiting and distension, and his bowels are working normally. D. A perianal abscess causes perianal pain and swelling, not a right iliac fossa mass. E. Carcinoma would not explain swinging fevers and a tender mass developing over days.
pearl: Swinging fever plus a tender right iliac fossa mass in Crohn's disease is an abscess until proven otherwise. Image first, drain and give antibiotics, and avoid escalating immunosuppression until sepsis is controlled.
thinking: Known ileal Crohn's on immunosuppression ↓ Swinging fevers and raised inflammatory markers ↓ Tender fixed right iliac fossa mass ↓ Transmural penetrating disease ↓ Intra-abdominal abscess
exam_trap: B, small bowel obstruction from a stricture — strictures are common in ileal Crohn's disease, but obstruction causes vomiting and distension, not swinging fevers with a tender mass.
takeaway: Crohn's disease with swinging fever and a tender RIF mass: think abscess, image and drain.

stem: A 27-year-old man with stricturing terminal ileal Crohn's disease presents with 24 hours of colicky central abdominal pain, green vomiting and abdominal distension. He has not passed flatus since the morning. He is afebrile and his observations are stable. The abdomen is distended and mildly tender without guarding. CT shows dilated small bowel loops down to a narrowed segment of terminal ileum, with no perforation, abscess or features of ischaemia. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.B: Nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and close monitoring
options.C: Oral budesonide and a low-residue diet at home
options.D: A stimulant laxative to relieve the obstruction

correct_answer: B. Nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and close monitoring
why_correct: Small bowel obstruction from a Crohn's stricture, without signs of strangulation, perforation or sepsis, is managed conservatively first: nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids with electrolyte correction and regular reassessment. Many episodes settle, particularly when there is an inflammatory component, after which the IBD and surgical teams plan definitive treatment. Surgery is reserved for failure to settle or signs of bowel compromise.
why_wrong: A. Emergency surgery is reserved for peritonitis, ischaemia or failure of conservative management. C. Oral treatment at home is unsafe in a patient who is vomiting and obstructed. D. Stimulant laxatives are contraindicated in mechanical obstruction. E. Endoscopic dilatation is a planned procedure for selected short strictures, not an emergency treatment for acute obstruction.
pearl: Bowel obstruction without peritonism, sepsis or ischaemia: drip and suck first. Features of strangulation, such as constant pain, fever, tachycardia or peritonism, demand urgent surgical review.
thinking: Known stricturing ileal Crohn's disease ↓ Colicky pain, bilious vomiting, distension ↓ CT: obstruction at the stricture ↓ No perforation, abscess or ischaemia ↓ Conservative drip and suck first
exam_trap: A, emergency laparotomy — obstruction feels surgical, but without strangulation or peritonism, Crohn's-related obstruction is first managed conservatively and bowel is preserved where possible.
takeaway: Uncomplicated Crohn's stricture obstruction: nil by mouth, NG tube, IV fluids and review.

presentation: Lower GI symptoms — FIT to guide referral
stem: A 56-year-old woman sees her GP with 2 months of looser, more frequent stools, with occasional dark blood mixed in. She has no abdominal pain and her weight is stable. Abdominal examination is normal and digital rectal examination reveals no mass. Her full blood count is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent suspected cancer referral for colonoscopy without further testing
options.D: Routine referral to the gastroenterology clinic

why_correct: NICE suspected cancer guidance uses a quantitative faecal immunochemical test to guide referral for most adults with lower GI symptoms, including a change in bowel habit or unexplained rectal bleeding. A result above the referral threshold triggers a suspected cancer pathway referral. If the result is negative but symptoms persist or concern remains, she should still be safety-netted and reassessed. Direct referral without FIT is kept for findings such as a rectal or anal mass.
why_wrong: A. Referral without FIT is not the standard route when examination is normal. B. Calprotectin helps separate inflammatory bowel disease from functional symptoms in younger adults and is not used for cancer triage at this age. D. A routine referral would be too slow if this is cancer. E. Treating symptoms without investigation risks missing colorectal cancer.
pearl: Lower GI symptoms in primary care: FIT first to guide referral, and a positive result means a suspected cancer pathway referral. A rectal or anal mass needs referral regardless, and a negative FIT never overrides ongoing clinical concern.
thinking: Woman in her fifties with a change in bowel habit ↓ Blood mixed with the stool ↓ Normal abdominal and rectal examination ↓ NICE uses FIT to guide referral ↓ Quantitative FIT
exam_trap: A, urgent referral without testing — red-flag symptoms make immediate referral feel safest, but current UK guidance uses FIT to guide referral unless there is a rectal or anal mass.
takeaway: Change in bowel habit with a normal rectal examination: request a FIT to guide urgent referral.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to her GP by her mother with 3 months of intermittent crampy right-sided abdominal pain and loose stools without visible blood. She has lost weight and keeps getting painful mouth ulcers. For the past week she has had tender, raised, dusky red lumps on both shins. There is a fleshy skin tag at the anal margin. Faecal calprotectin is raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic right-sided pain, non-bloody diarrhoea and weight loss in a teenager, with mouth ulcers, a perianal skin tag and erythema nodosum, point to Crohn's disease. Crohn's can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus, and erythema nodosum often parallels disease activity. The raised faecal calprotectin confirms intestinal inflammation, and she needs specialist referral for endoscopy and imaging.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease causes diarrhoea and weight loss but not erythema nodosum, perianal tags or a raised calprotectin. B. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause weight loss, raised inflammatory markers or extra-intestinal signs. C. Ulcerative colitis typically causes bloody diarrhoea and does not involve the mouth or cause perianal skin tags. D. Sarcoidosis causes erythema nodosum but not chronic diarrhoea with perianal disease.
pearl: Crohn's disease: mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural inflammation, often non-bloody diarrhoea and perianal disease. Erythema nodosum, mouth ulcers and peripheral arthritis tend to flare with bowel activity.
thinking: Teenager with weight loss and non-bloody diarrhoea ↓ Right-sided pain, mouth ulcers, perianal skin tag ↓ Erythema nodosum on the shins ↓ Raised faecal calprotectin ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: C, ulcerative colitis — it can also cause erythema nodosum and a raised calprotectin, but the absence of blood, right-sided pain, mouth ulcers and perianal disease point to Crohn's.
takeaway: Non-bloody diarrhoea with mouth ulcers, perianal tags and erythema nodosum suggests Crohn's disease.

presentation: Painless obstructive jaundice — pancreatic head cancer
stem: A 70-year-old man sees his GP because his wife noticed that his eyes have turned yellow. He has had generalised itching for 3 weeks, with dark urine and pale stools. He has no abdominal pain but has lost weight, and he was diagnosed with diabetes 4 months ago. He is jaundiced, and there is a smooth, non-tender mass below the right costal margin that moves with respiration. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Gallstone in the common bile duct
options.B: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas

correct_answer: B. Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
why_correct: Painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable, non-tender gallbladder suggests malignant obstruction of the distal common bile duct, most often from a carcinoma of the head of the pancreas (Courvoisier's law). Weight loss and new-onset diabetes in later life add to the suspicion. NICE advises an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for older adults with jaundice, and urgent pancreatic imaging.
why_wrong: A. Gallstone obstruction is usually painful, and chronic inflammation leaves a fibrosed gallbladder that rarely distends. C. Viral hepatitis gives a hepatitic picture without a palpable gallbladder or progressive weight loss. D. An empyema is acutely tender with fever and systemic upset. E. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is usually associated with ulcerative colitis and does not cause a distended gallbladder.
pearl: Courvoisier's law: in a jaundiced patient, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to stones. Painless jaundice, weight loss and new diabetes in an older adult should prompt urgent pancreatic imaging.
thinking: Painless obstructive jaundice: itch, dark urine, pale stools ↓ Weight loss and new diabetes ↓ Palpable non-tender gallbladder ↓ Malignant distal bile duct obstruction ↓ Pancreatic head carcinoma
exam_trap: A, common bile duct stone — it is the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice, but stones usually cause pain and a shrunken fibrotic gallbladder, so a painless palpable gallbladder points to cancer.
takeaway: Painless jaundice with a palpable non-tender gallbladder suggests carcinoma of the pancreatic head.

stem: A 33-year-old woman sees her GP with 10 days of loose stools containing blood and mucus. She is opening her bowels several times a day with urgency and crampy lower abdominal pain. She has never had bowel problems before. She is eating and drinking, her temperature is 37.6°C and she is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.C: Stool microscopy and culture with C. difficile testing
options.D: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

correct_answer: C. Stool microscopy and culture with C. difficile testing
why_correct: New bloody diarrhoea may be infective or the first presentation of inflammatory bowel disease, and the two can look identical. Stool microscopy and culture (for organisms such as Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella and E. coli O157) with C. difficile testing should be sent first, because infection must be excluded before a diagnosis of colitis is made. Endoscopy and further tests follow if stool tests are negative and symptoms persist.
why_wrong: A. Calprotectin is raised in both infective and inflammatory colitis, so it cannot separate them. B. Endoscopy is used once infection has been excluded, unless she is acutely unwell. D. CT is not a first-line test in a clinically stable patient. E. Coeliac disease does not cause bloody diarrhoea.
pearl: Bloody diarrhoea: send stool culture and C. difficile testing before labelling it inflammatory bowel disease. Remember E. coli O157 and haemolytic uraemic syndrome, and avoid antimotility drugs in suspected infective colitis.
thinking: First episode of bloody diarrhoea with urgency ↓ Infection and new IBD can look identical ↓ Infection must be excluded first ↓ Stool tests are quick and non-invasive ↓ Stool culture with C. difficile testing
exam_trap: B, flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsies — it is the key test for suspected colitis, but infection must be excluded first, as infective colitis can mimic IBD endoscopically.
takeaway: New bloody diarrhoea: send stool culture and C. difficile testing before investigating for IBD.

presentation: Unstable upper GI bleed — resuscitation and endoscopy
stem: A 58-year-old woman with a known duodenal ulcer collapses at home after vomiting a large amount of fresh blood. In the emergency department she is pale and clammy, with a heart rate of 128/min and blood pressure of 82/48 mmHg. She has no history of liver disease and rarely drinks alcohol. Two large-bore cannulas are in place. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Resuscitate, including blood transfusion, then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
options.B: IV PPI infusion and endoscopy on the next day's list
options.C: CT angiography before any fluid or blood is given
options.D: Terlipressin and antibiotics with endoscopy within 24 hours

correct_answer: A. Resuscitate, including blood transfusion, then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
why_correct: She has a severe upper GI bleed with shock. Resuscitation comes first, including blood transfusion and activation of the major haemorrhage protocol if needed, with blood tests, crossmatch and senior and critical care involvement. NICE advises endoscopy immediately after resuscitation for unstable patients with severe acute upper GI bleeding, so that the bleeding ulcer can be treated endoscopically. Interventional radiology or surgery is used if endoscopic treatment fails.
why_wrong: B. Waiting until the next day is unsafe in a shocked patient, and acid suppression does not replace endoscopic haemostasis. C. Imaging before resuscitation delays life-saving treatment. D. Terlipressin and antibiotics are for suspected variceal bleeding, and a 24-hour window is for stable patients. E. Surgery is reserved for failure of endoscopic and radiological control.
pearl: Unstable upper GI bleed: ABCDE, two large-bore cannulas, transfuse blood (major haemorrhage protocol if needed), then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation; interventional radiology or surgery if endoscopy fails.
thinking: Large haematemesis with shock ↓ Known ulcer, no liver disease ↓ Resuscitate with blood first ↓ Unstable severe bleed ↓ Endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
exam_trap: D, terlipressin and antibiotics — they are often reached for in haematemesis, but without features of liver disease this is a peptic ulcer bleed, and a 24-hour endoscopy window is too slow for an unstable patient.
takeaway: Unstable upper GI bleed: resuscitate with blood, then endoscope immediately after resuscitation.

stem: A 24-year-old man is referred to the gastroenterology clinic with 8 months of bringing food back into his mouth during or soon after most meals. It happens without effort, nausea or retching. The food tastes as it did when eaten, not sour, and he often re-chews and swallows it. He has no concerns about his weight or shape and no difficulty swallowing. Gastroscopy is normal and oesophageal manometry shows no motility disorder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rumination syndrome is the effortless regurgitation of recently eaten food during or shortly after meals, without nausea or retching, often re-chewed and re-swallowed or spat out. The food is undigested and not sour, which distinguishes it from reflux, and tests for structural or motility disease are normal. It is a functional disorder driven by unconscious contraction of the abdominal wall and is treated with diaphragmatic breathing and behavioural therapy rather than acid suppression.
why_wrong: B. Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia, and manometry would be abnormal. C. Reflux causes heartburn and sour regurgitation, not effortless return of food that tastes as eaten. D. Bulimia involves deliberate self-induced vomiting with concerns about weight or shape. E. Gastroparesis causes nausea, early satiety and vomiting of food hours after eating.
pearl: Rumination: effortless regurgitation within minutes of eating, no nausea, food tastes as eaten, normal investigations. Treat with diaphragmatic breathing techniques and behavioural therapy, not PPIs.
thinking: Effortless return of food during or soon after meals ↓ No nausea or retching, not sour ↓ Re-chewed and swallowed ↓ Normal endoscopy and manometry ↓ Rumination syndrome
exam_trap: C, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — regurgitation sounds like reflux, but reflux is sour and associated with heartburn, whereas here food returns unchanged, effortlessly and repeatedly.
takeaway: Effortless regurgitation of unchanged food soon after meals with normal tests is rumination syndrome.

stem: A 49-year-old woman with a long history of alcohol-related pancreatitis is reviewed in clinic with oily, offensive stools and weight loss. A recent CT scan shows an atrophic pancreas with scattered calcification. She has not yet started any enzyme supplements and her stools are soft but formed. Which test is most appropriate to confirm reduced pancreatic exocrine function?
why_correct: Faecal elastase is a simple, non-invasive test of pancreatic exocrine function: elastase is secreted by the pancreas and survives intestinal transit, so a low stool level indicates exocrine insufficiency. It is not affected by pancreatic enzyme replacement, because supplements are of porcine origin and the assay measures human elastase. A formed stool is needed, as watery diarrhoea can dilute the sample and give a falsely low result.
why_wrong: A. Serum lipase is used to diagnose acute pancreatitis and is often normal in chronic disease. B. Serum amylase is similarly unhelpful in chronic pancreatitis. D. Calprotectin detects intestinal mucosal inflammation, not pancreatic function. E. HbA1c assesses endocrine failure (diabetes), not exocrine function.
pearl: Acute pancreatitis: serum lipase or amylase. Chronic pancreatitis: CT for structure and calcification, faecal elastase for exocrine function, and HbA1c or glucose for endocrine function.
thinking: Chronic pancreatitis with calcification on CT ↓ Steatorrhoea and weight loss ↓ Need to confirm exocrine failure ↓ Non-invasive stool marker of pancreatic secretion ↓ Faecal elastase
exam_trap: A, serum lipase — it is the pancreatic blood test everyone remembers, but it diagnoses acute inflammation; a burnt-out pancreas may have normal or low serum enzymes despite severe insufficiency.
takeaway: Confirm pancreatic exocrine insufficiency with faecal elastase on a formed stool.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with colonic Crohn's disease has had recurrent perianal swelling and intermittent purulent discharge for 3 months. On examination there is a small external opening with granulation tissue to one side of the anus, and an indurated track can be felt running towards the anal canal. She has no abdominal symptoms. Which imaging is most appropriate to define the anatomy of this lesion?
why_correct: This is a perianal fistula complicating Crohn's disease. Pelvic MRI is the preferred imaging because it shows the course of the primary tract in relation to the sphincters, any secondary extensions and any associated abscess, which together determine surgical and medical management. Any abscess is drained, often with a seton, before anti-TNF therapy is started.
why_wrong: A. CT gives poor soft-tissue detail of the sphincter complex. B. Sigmoidoscopy assesses rectal inflammation but cannot map a fistula tract. C. Fistulography is uncomfortable, inaccurate and largely obsolete. D. Endoanal ultrasound is a reasonable alternative in expert hands but is less accurate than MRI for complex or high fistulas.
pearl: Perianal Crohn's disease: MRI pelvis to map the fistula, examination under anaesthesia with drainage and seton placement for sepsis, then anti-TNF therapy once sepsis is controlled.
thinking: Crohn's disease with recurrent perianal swelling and discharge ↓ External opening beside the anus ↓ Perianal fistula ↓ Need to map the tract relative to the sphincters ↓ MRI pelvis
exam_trap: D, endoanal ultrasound — it is a genuine option for perianal fistulas, but MRI is more accurate for the complex tracts and abscesses typical of Crohn's disease and is the preferred first test.
takeaway: Map a Crohn's perianal fistula with pelvic MRI before planning treatment.

stem: A 41-year-old man with coeliac disease, who admits he follows his diet poorly, has a gastroscopy for persistent upper abdominal discomfort. He takes no regular medicines. The gastric body shows thickened folds studded with small raised nodules, each with a central erosion. Gastric biopsies show a marked increase in lymphocytes within the surface and pit epithelium, without gland destruction or atrophy. H. pylori is not seen and other testing for it is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Lymphocytic gastritis is defined by a dense infiltrate of intraepithelial lymphocytes in the surface and pit epithelium of the stomach and often appears endoscopically as varioliform gastritis: raised nodules with central erosions. It is strongly associated with coeliac disease and frequently improves on a strict gluten-free diet. The absence of H. pylori, atrophy and gland destruction helps exclude the alternatives.
why_wrong: B. Autoimmune gastritis causes body atrophy with loss of parietal cells, often with pernicious anaemia, not an intraepithelial lymphocytosis. C. H. pylori gastritis is excluded by negative histology and testing. D. MALT lymphoma shows a dense lamina propria infiltrate with lymphoepithelial lesions destroying glands, usually with H. pylori. E. NSAID gastropathy shows reactive changes with few inflammatory cells, and he takes no NSAIDs.
pearl: Lymphocytic gastritis is the gastric counterpart of coeliac enteropathy: intraepithelial lymphocytosis with varioliform erosions. Strict gluten avoidance usually helps; consider it in coeliac patients with ongoing dyspepsia.
thinking: Coeliac disease with poor dietary adherence ↓ Varioliform nodules with central erosions ↓ Intraepithelial lymphocytosis without gland destruction ↓ H. pylori negative, no atrophy ↓ Lymphocytic gastritis
exam_trap: D, gastric MALT lymphoma — lymphocyte-rich gastric biopsies suggest lymphoma, but lymphoma destroys glands with lymphoepithelial lesions, whereas here the lymphocytes sit within intact epithelium.
takeaway: Coeliac disease plus intraepithelial lymphocytes in gastric biopsies points to lymphocytic gastritis.

presentation: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction — failed conservative treatment
stem: An 81-year-old man is on the orthopaedic ward 5 days after a hip hemiarthroplasty. His abdomen has become hugely distended, though only mildly tender, and he is passing little flatus. CT shows marked dilatation of the right and transverse colon with a very dilated caecum and no mechanical obstruction. For 48 hours he has been managed with nil by mouth, a nasogastric tube, IV fluids, electrolyte correction and withdrawal of opioids, without improvement. There is no peritonism, and his heart rate is 80/min in sinus rhythm. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: IV neostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.D: Continue the same conservative management for another week

correct_answer: A. IV neostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring
why_correct: This is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome), a functional colonic dilatation that is common after orthopaedic surgery. When conservative treatment fails and the caecum is markedly dilated, IV neostigmine is the next step, as it increases parasympathetic tone and colonic motility. It can cause profound bradycardia, so it is given with continuous cardiac monitoring and atropine immediately available. Colonoscopic decompression is used if neostigmine fails or is contraindicated, and surgery is reserved for perforation or ischaemia.
why_wrong: B. Colonoscopic decompression is second-line after failed or contraindicated neostigmine. C. Surgery is reserved for perforation, ischaemia or failure of other measures. D. Prolonged waiting with a markedly dilated caecum risks ischaemia and perforation. E. Metoclopramide acts mainly on the upper gut and has no proven role in colonic pseudo-obstruction.
pearl: Ogilvie's syndrome: exclude mechanical obstruction, correct electrolytes and stop opioids and anticholinergics. If there is no improvement, give IV neostigmine with cardiac monitoring; colonoscopic decompression next; surgery for perforation.
thinking: Elderly patient after orthopaedic surgery ↓ Massive colonic dilatation without mechanical cause ↓ Failed conservative management ↓ No peritonism, no bradycardia ↓ IV neostigmine with cardiac monitoring
exam_trap: B, colonoscopic decompression — it seems a direct way to deflate the colon, but it is technically difficult, often needs repeating and is used after neostigmine fails or cannot be given.
takeaway: Ogilvie's syndrome failing conservative care: IV neostigmine with cardiac monitoring.

presentation: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth — breath test
stem: A 64-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis attends the gastroenterology clinic with a year of bloating, abdominal distension and loose, offensive stools, with weight loss. Blood tests show a low vitamin B12 with a high serum folate. Coeliac serology, faecal elastase and colonoscopy are all normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
why_correct: Systemic sclerosis impairs small bowel motility, allowing colonic-type bacteria to overgrow in the small intestine. The bacteria consume vitamin B12 and synthesise folate, so a low B12 with a high folate is a useful clue alongside bloating and malabsorptive diarrhoea. The glucose hydrogen breath test detects an early rise in exhaled hydrogen from bacterial fermentation and is the usual non-invasive test; treatment is a course of antibiotics plus attention to the underlying cause.
why_wrong: A. SeHCAT diagnoses bile acid diarrhoea, which does not explain a high folate with a low B12. C. CT colonography images the colon, which is already normal on colonoscopy. D. Gastrin testing is for suspected Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, which causes peptic ulceration with diarrhoea, not this picture. E. Capsule endoscopy looks for mucosal lesions and does not detect bacterial overgrowth.
pearl: Suspect bacterial overgrowth where there is stasis: systemic sclerosis, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, blind loops or strictures. A low B12 with a high folate is a clue; confirm with a glucose hydrogen breath test.
thinking: Systemic sclerosis with poor gut motility ↓ Bloating, offensive loose stools, weight loss ↓ Low B12 with high folate ↓ Coeliac, pancreatic and colonic causes excluded ↓ Glucose hydrogen breath test for bacterial overgrowth
exam_trap: A, SeHCAT scan — bile acid diarrhoea is a common hidden cause of chronic diarrhoea, but it does not explain the bloating with low B12 and high folate that point to bacterial overgrowth.
takeaway: Gut dysmotility with low B12 and high folate: test for bacterial overgrowth with a hydrogen breath test.

presentation: Rheumatoid arthritis — escalation to biological therapy
stem: A 49-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis attends the rheumatology clinic. Despite 6 months of combination treatment with methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine at optimal doses, he has multiple swollen, tender joints, persistently raised inflammatory markers and new erosions on hand X-rays. His disease activity score remains in the severe range. Tuberculosis screening is negative and he has no history of cancer or heart failure. What is the most appropriate next step?
correct_answer: D. A TNF inhibitor with methotrexate
why_correct: Severe active rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded to intensive combination conventional DMARDs is an indication for advanced therapy under NICE technology appraisal guidance. In a patient who has not previously had a biological drug, a TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab or etanercept, given with methotrexate, is the usual first choice. Screening for tuberculosis and other infections is completed beforehand, as here.
why_wrong: A. Rituximab is generally used after an inadequate response to, or intolerance of, a TNF inhibitor, or when TNF inhibitors cannot be used. B. Long-term steroids cause significant harm and do not adequately control erosive disease. C. Swapping one conventional DMARD for another is unlikely to help once combination therapy has failed. E. Joint injections relieve individual joints but do not control systemic erosive disease.
pearl: RA ladder: conventional DMARD (usually methotrexate) started early, short-term steroid bridging, then combination therapy, then a biological or targeted synthetic DMARD if disease stays active. Screen for TB and hepatitis before biologics.
thinking: Seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Failed intensive combination conventional DMARDs ↓ Disease remains severely active ↓ Eligible for advanced therapy, TB screen negative ↓ TNF inhibitor with methotrexate
exam_trap: A, rituximab — it is a licensed biological drug for rheumatoid arthritis, so it tempts, but it is usually reserved for after a TNF inhibitor has failed or cannot be used.
takeaway: RA still severe after combination DMARDs: add a TNF inhibitor to methotrexate.

stem: A 54-year-old woman calls an ambulance with 1 hour of heavy central chest pain and sweating. The paramedic's ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF with ST depression in aVL. She has been given aspirin. The regional heart attack centre, with a 24-hour catheter laboratory, is 30 minutes away by ambulance, and she has no contraindications to any treatment. What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.A: Thrombolysis in the nearest emergency department
options.B: Wait for a high-sensitivity troponin result before deciding
options.C: Direct transfer for primary percutaneous coronary intervention
options.D: Admit to the coronary care unit for IV heparin and medical therapy

correct_answer: C. Direct transfer for primary percutaneous coronary intervention
why_correct: This is an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction presenting well within 12 hours of symptom onset. NICE recommends primary PCI as the reperfusion strategy when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given, which is easily achievable here. She should be taken directly to the heart attack centre, as every delay to reperfusion increases the loss of myocardium.
why_wrong: A. Fibrinolysis is used when primary PCI cannot be delivered in time, which is not the case here. B. Troponin is not needed to diagnose STEMI and waiting for it delays reperfusion. D. Anticoagulation and medical therapy alone do not reopen the artery. E. CT coronary angiography is used to investigate stable chest pain, not acute STEMI.
pearl: STEMI within 12 hours: primary PCI if it can be delivered within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could be given; otherwise fibrinolysis, then transfer. ST elevation alone justifies reperfusion; never wait for troponin.
thinking: Ischaemic chest pain for 1 hour ↓ Inferior ST elevation with reciprocal change ↓ STEMI within the reperfusion window ↓ PCI centre close by ↓ Direct transfer for primary PCI
exam_trap: B, wait for troponin — troponin is central to diagnosing NSTEMI, but in STEMI the ECG is enough and waiting only delays reperfusion.
takeaway: STEMI with a PCI centre reachable in time: transfer directly for primary PCI.

stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 5 am with severe pain in the right lower abdomen and groin that woke him 2 hours ago, and he has vomited twice. He was reluctant to mention any scrotal symptoms. On examination the right testis is very tender, lies higher than the left with a horizontal lie, and the right cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Urgent scrotal exploration by the surgical team
options.D: Observe for appendicitis with serial abdominal examination
options.E: Analgesia, scrotal support and review later in the day

correct_answer: B. Urgent scrotal exploration by the surgical team
why_correct: A suddenly painful, high-riding testis with a horizontal lie and an absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. It is a surgical emergency because testicular viability falls rapidly over hours, so urgent scrotal exploration with detorsion and bilateral fixation is needed. Imaging should not delay surgery when the clinical picture is typical.
why_wrong: A. Doppler ultrasound can be falsely reassuring and delays definitive treatment. C. Epididymo-orchitis has a more gradual onset and is unusual at this age without sexual activity or urinary symptoms. D. Testicular pain is often referred to the lower abdomen, and the scrotal findings make torsion the diagnosis. E. Any delay risks loss of the testis.
pearl: Always examine the testes in a boy with lower abdominal pain. Suspected torsion means urgent exploration; salvage rates are highest within about 6 hours, and both testes are fixed at surgery.
thinking: Adolescent with sudden pain and vomiting ↓ Pain felt in the groin and lower abdomen ↓ Tender high-riding testis with a horizontal lie ↓ Absent cremasteric reflex ↓ Torsion: urgent exploration
exam_trap: A, Doppler ultrasound — imaging feels like a safe confirmatory step, but it delays surgery and can show apparently preserved flow in partial torsion.
takeaway: Suspected testicular torsion: urgent surgical exploration without waiting for imaging.

stem: A 42-year-old woman on a day-case ward develops widespread urticaria, a hoarse voice and wheeze within minutes of starting an IV co-amoxiclav infusion. Her heart rate is 128/min, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% on air. The infusion has been stopped and help has been called. What is the most appropriate first drug treatment?

options.A: IM adrenaline 500 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh

correct_answer: A. IM adrenaline 500 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh
why_correct: This is anaphylaxis, with airway, breathing and circulation problems after exposure to a likely trigger. Resuscitation Council UK guidance is intramuscular adrenaline, 500 micrograms for an adult, into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement, alongside high-flow oxygen, an IV fluid bolus and lying her flat. IV adrenaline is reserved for experienced specialists, and antihistamines and steroids are not first-line treatments.
why_wrong: B. Antihistamines treat skin features only and do not reverse airway or circulatory compromise. C. Steroids act slowly and are no longer routinely advised in the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis. D. A 1 mg IV bolus is the cardiac arrest dose and can cause fatal arrhythmias in a patient with a pulse. E. Salbutamol may help persisting bronchospasm but does not treat shock or airway swelling.
pearl: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline first (adult 500 micrograms, child 6–12 years 300 micrograms, under 6 years 150 micrograms), repeated after 5 minutes. No improvement after two doses means refractory anaphylaxis needing an adrenaline infusion.
thinking: Sudden urticaria, hoarseness and wheeze after an IV antibiotic ↓ Hypotension and hypoxia ↓ Anaphylaxis ↓ Adrenaline is the first-line drug ↓ IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
exam_trap: D, IV adrenaline 1 mg bolus — she has IV access and is very unwell, which tempts IV use, but 1 mg is the cardiac arrest dose and in a patient with a pulse it can cause dangerous arrhythmias.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 500 micrograms into the thigh first, repeated after 5 minutes if needed.

stem: A 38-year-old man fell through a glass door and has a deep forearm laceration with pulsatile bleeding, now controlled with a tourniquet. Paramedics gave him 1 litre of crystalloid. In the emergency department he is anxious, cool and pale, with a heart rate of 135/min and blood pressure of 82/56 mmHg. What is the most appropriate resuscitation?

options.A: A further 2 litres of crystalloid to restore a normal blood pressure
options.C: Activate the major haemorrhage protocol and transfuse blood products
options.E: Await a laboratory haemoglobin before giving blood

correct_answer: C. Activate the major haemorrhage protocol and transfuse blood products
why_correct: He is in haemorrhagic shock after major blood loss. With the bleeding controlled, the priority is to restore circulating volume with blood, so the major haemorrhage protocol should be activated to deliver red cells with plasma and platelets, alongside tranexamic acid in trauma. Large volumes of crystalloid dilute clotting factors, worsen acidosis and hypothermia, and increase bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Large-volume crystalloid causes dilutional coagulopathy and carries no oxygen. B. Vasopressors do not replace lost volume and can worsen tissue perfusion in hypovolaemia. D. Synthetic colloids offer no benefit and are associated with kidney injury. E. Haemoglobin may be near normal early in acute bleeding, and waiting delays transfusion.
pearl: Haemorrhagic shock: stop the bleeding, give blood rather than crystalloid, activate the major haemorrhage protocol, give tranexamic acid early in trauma, and prevent the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy.
thinking: Major arterial bleeding after injury ↓ Tachycardia, hypotension, cool and pale ↓ Haemorrhagic shock with significant blood loss ↓ Lost volume must be replaced with blood ↓ Activate the major haemorrhage protocol
exam_trap: A, further crystalloid — fluid feels like the natural treatment for hypotension, but in haemorrhage it dilutes clotting factors and worsens bleeding; blood is the fluid of choice.
takeaway: Haemorrhagic shock: activate the major haemorrhage protocol and give blood, not more crystalloid.

stem: A 34-year-old woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill presents to the emergency department with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness and a small amount of haemoptysis. Her heart rate is 108/min, blood pressure 126/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% on air. A chest X-ray is normal. The two-level Wells score places her in the 'PE likely' group. She is not pregnant, has normal renal function and no bleeding risk factors. The CT scanner will be unavailable for the next 6 hours. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Start interim therapeutic anticoagulation and arrange CTPA
options.B: Request a D-dimer and decide on imaging after the result
options.C: Withhold anticoagulation until CTPA confirms the diagnosis
options.E: Arrange a leg vein ultrasound instead of CTPA

correct_answer: A. Start interim therapeutic anticoagulation and arrange CTPA
why_correct: In suspected PE classed as 'likely', NICE recommends CT pulmonary angiography and, if it cannot be done immediately, interim therapeutic anticoagulation while awaiting the scan. A DOAC such as apixaban or rivaroxaban is usually suitable, with the decision reviewed once imaging is available. Delaying anticoagulation in a likely PE risks clot propagation and further emboli; her combined pill should also be stopped.
why_wrong: B. D-dimer is not used to exclude PE in the 'likely' group. C. Withholding treatment for several hours exposes her to the risk of further emboli. D. Thrombolysis is for PE causing haemodynamic instability, and her blood pressure is normal. E. Leg ultrasound may help when CTPA is unsuitable or there are leg symptoms, but it does not replace CTPA here.
pearl: PE likely: CTPA, with interim anticoagulation (usually apixaban or rivaroxaban) if there is any delay. PE unlikely: D-dimer first. Thrombolysis only for PE with haemodynamic instability. Stop oestrogen-containing contraception.
thinking: Pleuritic pain and haemoptysis on the combined pill ↓ Stable, PE likely on Wells ↓ CTPA needed but delayed ↓ Untreated PE risks further emboli ↓ Interim anticoagulation while awaiting CTPA
exam_trap: C, withhold anticoagulation until CTPA confirms — waiting for proof feels safer, but in a likely PE an unavoidable delay to imaging should be covered with interim anticoagulation.
takeaway: Likely PE with delayed CTPA: start interim anticoagulation while waiting for the scan.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is admitted with a closed fracture of both forearm bones, now in an above-elbow backslab. Six hours later she is distressed by increasing forearm pain despite IV morphine. Passive extension of her fingers causes severe pain. The forearm feels tense, the radial pulse is palpable and capillary refill in the fingers is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Elevate the arm high on pillows and review in 4 hours
options.B: Split the backslab and dressings down to skin and arrange urgent fasciotomy
options.C: Doppler the radial artery and reassure if flow is normal
options.D: Increase the opioid dose and reassess in the morning
options.E: Repeat the forearm X-ray to check the fracture position

correct_answer: B. Split the backslab and dressings down to skin and arrange urgent fasciotomy
why_correct: Pain out of proportion to the injury, escalating despite strong opioids and severe on passive stretch of the muscles in a tense compartment, is acute compartment syndrome. All circumferential dressings and casts should be released down to skin, the limb kept at heart level, and the orthopaedic team should perform urgent fasciotomy once the diagnosis is made. A palpable pulse and normal capillary refill do not exclude it, because raised compartment pressure compromises muscle perfusion long before it occludes large arteries.
why_wrong: A. High elevation reduces arterial inflow and can worsen compartment ischaemia; the limb should be kept at heart level. C. Normal arterial flow does not exclude compartment syndrome. D. Escalating analgesia masks the key symptom and delays surgery. E. Fracture position does not explain the clinical picture, and delay risks muscle necrosis.
pearl: Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs; pulses are often present until late. Split casts to skin, keep the limb at heart level and proceed to urgent fasciotomy.
thinking: Forearm fracture in a backslab ↓ Escalating pain despite opioids ↓ Severe pain on passive finger extension, tense forearm ↓ Palpable pulse does not reassure ↓ Release dressings and urgent fasciotomy
exam_trap: C, Doppler and reassure — a normal pulse feels reassuring, but compartment syndrome is a tissue perfusion problem and arterial flow is usually preserved until it is too late.
takeaway: Pain on passive stretch after a fracture: release dressings to skin and arrange urgent fasciotomy.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with Graves' disease, who stopped taking carbimazole several months ago, is on the surgical ward the day after an emergency appendicectomy. She has become agitated and confused, with a temperature of 39.8°C, profuse sweating, vomiting and diarrhoea. Her pulse is 160/min and irregularly irregular, and her blood pressure is 142/70 mmHg. There are no signs of heart failure. In addition to supportive care and treating any infection, which treatment combination is most appropriate?

options.A: Lugol's iodine as the first drug, followed by an antithyroid drug
options.C: Paracetamol, cooling and IV fluids only
options.E: Propranolol and propylthiouracil, then iodine, with IV hydrocortisone

correct_answer: E. Propranolol and propylthiouracil, then iodine, with IV hydrocortisone
why_correct: This is thyroid storm, a life-threatening decompensation of thyrotoxicosis, precipitated here by surgery and a stopped antithyroid drug. Treatment combines a beta-blocker such as propranolol to control adrenergic effects, a thionamide (propylthiouracil is often preferred as it also reduces peripheral conversion of T4 to T3) to block new hormone synthesis, iodine given after the thionamide to block hormone release, and hydrocortisone, with supportive care in a high-dependency setting.
why_wrong: A. Iodine given before a thionamide can provide substrate for further hormone synthesis and worsen thyrotoxicosis. B. Radioactive iodine takes weeks to work and is not used in an acute storm. C. Supportive measures alone do not treat the underlying hormone excess. D. Surgery in an uncontrolled thyrotoxic patient carries high risk and is not first-line treatment for a storm.
pearl: Thyroid storm order: beta-blocker, thionamide, then iodine at least an hour later, plus steroid, cooling and fluids. Avoid aspirin for the fever because it displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins.
thinking: Known Graves' disease off treatment ↓ Postoperative fever, agitation, vomiting and fast AF ↓ Thyroid storm ↓ Block effects, then synthesis, then release ↓ Beta-blocker, thionamide, iodine and steroid
exam_trap: A, Lugol's iodine first — iodine rapidly blocks hormone release, which makes it attractive, but given before a thionamide it can fuel further hormone synthesis.
takeaway: Thyroid storm: beta-blocker and thionamide first, iodine afterwards, plus steroid and supportive care.

stem: A 79-year-old man is found at home in winter, drowsy and confused. His daughter says he stopped taking his levothyroxine several months ago. His temperature is 31.8°C, pulse 44/min and respiratory rate 8/min. He has a puffy face, dry skin and slow-relaxing reflexes. His sodium is low and his glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral levothyroxine 25 micrograms daily and discharge with GP follow-up
options.B: Rapid active external rewarming with forced warm air as the priority
options.C: IV thyroid hormone and IV hydrocortisone, slow rewarming and critical care support
options.D: IV atropine and external pacing as the first treatment
options.E: High-dose IV thyroid hormone alone, without corticosteroid

correct_answer: C. IV thyroid hormone and IV hydrocortisone, slow rewarming and critical care support
why_correct: Severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation and reduced consciousness is myxoedema coma, a medical emergency. Treatment is IV thyroid hormone replacement with IV hydrocortisone, given until coexisting adrenal insufficiency has been excluded, together with slow passive rewarming, ventilatory support if needed, correction of hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia, and treatment of any precipitant in a critical care setting.
why_wrong: A. Low-dose oral treatment is far too slow, and absorption is unreliable in a drowsy, unwell patient. B. Rapid active external rewarming causes peripheral vasodilatation and can precipitate cardiovascular collapse. D. The bradycardia is due to hypothyroidism and hypothermia and improves as they are treated. E. Giving thyroid hormone without steroid can precipitate an adrenal crisis if adrenal insufficiency coexists.
pearl: Myxoedema coma: IV thyroid hormone plus IV hydrocortisone (steroid before or with thyroid hormone), slow passive rewarming, ventilatory support and correction of sodium and glucose, in critical care.
thinking: Stopped levothyroxine, cold exposure ↓ Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, drowsiness ↓ Myxoedema coma ↓ Possible coexisting adrenal insufficiency ↓ IV thyroid hormone, hydrocortisone and slow rewarming
exam_trap: E, high-dose IV thyroid hormone alone — replacing the missing hormone seems logical, but without hydrocortisone the rising metabolic demand can unmask adrenal insufficiency and cause an adrenal crisis.
takeaway: Myxoedema coma: IV thyroid hormone with IV hydrocortisone, slow rewarming and critical care.

stem: A 66-year-old man on the coronary care unit, 2 days after an anterior myocardial infarction, suddenly becomes unresponsive. He has no pulse and is not breathing normally. The cardiac monitor shows a chaotic, irregular waveform with no identifiable QRS complexes. Defibrillator pads are already attached and chest compressions have started. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.C: IV adrenaline 1 mg before any shock
options.D: IV amiodarone 300 mg before any shock

why_correct: A pulseless patient with a chaotic waveform has ventricular fibrillation, a shockable rhythm. Resuscitation Council UK guidance is immediate unsynchronised defibrillation with minimal interruption to chest compressions, and in a witnessed, monitored arrest with pads already attached up to three quick successive shocks may be given. Adrenaline and amiodarone are given after the third shock if the rhythm remains shockable.
why_wrong: A. Synchronised shocks need an identifiable QRS to time against and are used for tachyarrhythmias with a pulse. C. Adrenaline is not given before defibrillation in a shockable arrest. D. Amiodarone follows the third shock, not the first. E. Atropine has no role in the cardiac arrest algorithm.
pearl: Shockable arrest (VF or pulseless VT): shock, then 2 minutes of CPR, with adrenaline and amiodarone after the third shock. In a witnessed, monitored arrest with pads on, up to three stacked shocks are allowed.
thinking: Unresponsive, pulseless, not breathing normally ↓ Chaotic waveform with no QRS ↓ Ventricular fibrillation ↓ Shockable rhythm ↓ Immediate unsynchronised defibrillation
exam_trap: A, synchronised cardioversion — cardioversion is the familiar treatment for unstable tachyarrhythmias, but synchronisation needs an organised QRS and a pulse; VF needs an unsynchronised shock.
takeaway: VF or pulseless VT: defibrillate immediately with an unsynchronised shock.

stem: A 34-year-old hillwalker is brought in by mountain rescue after being found in the snow. He is in cardiac arrest in ventricular fibrillation, and his core temperature is 26°C. CPR is in progress and three shocks have been given without success. A team able to provide extracorporeal rewarming is available. What is the most appropriate next step in his resuscitation?

options.A: Continue shocks every 2 minutes and give adrenaline after alternate cycles
options.B: Stop resuscitation, as survival at this temperature is unlikely
options.C: Delay further shocks and withhold adrenaline until he is warmer, continuing CPR with active rewarming
options.D: Give adrenaline at double the usual frequency to overcome the cold
options.E: Increase the shock energy and give amiodarone after each shock

correct_answer: C. Delay further shocks and withhold adrenaline until he is warmer, continuing CPR with active rewarming
why_correct: The severely hypothermic heart responds poorly to defibrillation and drugs, and drugs accumulate because metabolism is slowed. Resuscitation guidance is to give up to three shocks, then delay further attempts and withhold adrenaline until the core temperature rises above 30°C, while continuing high-quality CPR and active rewarming, ideally extracorporeal. Hypothermia protects the brain, so prolonged resuscitation can succeed.
why_wrong: A. Standard shock and drug intervals are ineffective and drugs accumulate at this temperature. B. Hypothermia is protective, and death should not be confirmed until the patient has been rewarmed. D. More frequent adrenaline increases the risk of toxicity once circulation and metabolism recover. E. Escalating shocks and repeated amiodarone are unlikely to work until he is rewarmed.
pearl: Hypothermic arrest: up to three shocks, then hold further shocks and adrenaline until above 30°C; between 30 and 35°C double the drug intervals. Rewarm actively, ideally extracorporeally. Not dead until warm and dead.
thinking: Cardiac arrest after cold exposure ↓ Severe hypothermia ↓ Heart resistant to shocks and drugs ↓ Drugs accumulate, brain protected by cold ↓ Delay shocks and adrenaline, continue CPR and rewarm
exam_trap: B, stop resuscitation — prolonged arrest seems futile, but hypothermia protects the brain and good outcomes occur after prolonged CPR with rewarming.
takeaway: Hypothermic arrest: limit shocks, withhold adrenaline until warmer and rewarm during CPR.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is on the trauma ward after a motorcycle collision in which she fractured her left femur and tibia; she is awaiting fixation. About 36 hours after admission she becomes restless and confused and is breathing rapidly, with an oxygen saturation of 86% on air. There are fine petechiae in her axillae and on the conjunctivae. Her temperature is 38.0°C. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis

why_correct: Respiratory distress, neurological dysfunction and a petechial rash appearing 1 to 3 days after long-bone fractures is fat embolism syndrome. Fat globules from the marrow reach the lungs and systemic circulation, causing hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae, typically in the axillae, upper trunk and conjunctivae. Management is supportive with oxygen and organ support, and early fracture stabilisation reduces the risk.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary embolism causes hypoxia but not a petechial rash, and typically occurs later. C. Pneumonia would not explain petechiae and confusion this early. D. Meningococcal sepsis causes a non-blanching rash and confusion, but the timing after long-bone fractures and the axillary and conjunctival petechiae point to fat embolism. E. Opioid toxicity causes slow breathing and pinpoint pupils, not tachypnoea and petechiae.
pearl: Fat embolism triad: hypoxia, confusion and petechiae (axillae, upper chest, conjunctivae), 24–72 hours after long-bone or pelvic fractures. Early fixation reduces the risk; treatment is supportive.
thinking: Long-bone fractures awaiting fixation ↓ Onset after 1 to 2 days ↓ Hypoxia and tachypnoea ↓ Confusion with axillary and conjunctival petechiae ↓ Fat embolism syndrome
exam_trap: A, pulmonary embolism — trauma and immobility raise the risk of VTE and hypoxia fits, but PE does not produce petechiae or such early confusion; the triad points to fat embolism.
takeaway: Hypoxia, confusion and petechiae a day or two after long-bone fractures is fat embolism syndrome.

stem: A 45-year-old man falls from scaffolding and arrives in the emergency department 40 minutes later with an unstable pelvic fracture, now in a pelvic binder. He is pale and drowsy, with a heart rate of 140/min and blood pressure of 72/40 mmHg. The major haemorrhage protocol has been activated and he is being prepared for interventional radiology. Which transfusion strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: Crystalloid until haemoglobin falls below a set threshold
options.B: Group O red cells alone until coagulation results are available
options.C: Wait for fully crossmatched blood before transfusing
options.D: Platelets and plasma first, adding red cells later
options.E: Red cells with plasma in a balanced ratio, early platelets and tranexamic acid

correct_answer: E. Red cells with plasma in a balanced ratio, early platelets and tranexamic acid
why_correct: In major traumatic haemorrhage, blood components are given early in balanced ratios, red cells with plasma and platelets, to prevent the dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy that worsens bleeding. Tranexamic acid given as early as possible after injury reduces death from bleeding. Further products are then guided by laboratory or point-of-care tests, alongside control of the bleeding source, warming and correction of calcium.
why_wrong: A. Crystalloid worsens coagulopathy, and haemoglobin lags behind blood loss. B. Red cells alone cause dilutional coagulopathy, and waiting for clotting results delays plasma. C. Waiting for crossmatched blood delays life-saving transfusion; group O or group-specific blood is used initially. D. Red cells are needed immediately to restore oxygen-carrying capacity.
pearl: Major haemorrhage: activate the protocol, give red cells and plasma in a balanced ratio with early platelets, tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury, keep the patient warm, check calcium and control the source.
thinking: High-energy pelvic fracture ↓ Profound shock despite a pelvic binder ↓ Major haemorrhage protocol activated ↓ Prevent trauma-induced coagulopathy ↓ Balanced components plus early tranexamic acid
exam_trap: B, red cells alone until coagulation results — red cells restore oxygen delivery, but transfusing them alone dilutes clotting factors and worsens bleeding; plasma should be given from the start.
takeaway: Major traumatic haemorrhage: balanced red cells, plasma and platelets with early tranexamic acid.

stem: A 63-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden, severe pain between his shoulder blades, which he describes as ripping. His left radial pulse is weaker than the right, and there is a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. His blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg in the right arm. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy without ST elevation. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
correct_answer: D. CT angiography of the aorta
why_correct: Sudden, severe ripping pain radiating to the back, a pulse deficit and a new aortic regurgitation murmur in a hypertensive man point to acute aortic dissection. CT angiography of the whole aorta is the rapid, widely available test that confirms the diagnosis and shows its extent, which determines whether urgent surgery is needed. In a patient too unstable for the scanner, transoesophageal echocardiography is an alternative.
why_wrong: A. Troponin may be normal or raised and neither confirms nor excludes dissection. B. D-dimer is non-specific and cannot confirm the diagnosis. C. Coronary angiography is for acute coronary syndromes and can be dangerous in dissection. E. Exercise testing is contraindicated in acute chest pain and would not show a dissection.
pearl: Suspect dissection with tearing pain radiating to the back, a pulse or blood pressure difference between the arms, new aortic regurgitation or neurological signs. Confirm with CT aortic angiography; type A needs urgent surgery.
thinking: Hypertensive man with sudden ripping interscapular pain ↓ Weaker left radial pulse ↓ New early diastolic murmur ↓ Suspected acute aortic dissection ↓ CT angiography of the aorta
exam_trap: A, serial troponin — chest pain triggers the acute coronary syndrome pathway, but waiting for troponin wastes time, and treating presumed ACS with antithrombotics can be catastrophic in dissection.
takeaway: Ripping back pain with a pulse deficit: confirm aortic dissection with CT aortic angiography.

stem: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, who stopped his anticoagulant a month ago because of nosebleeds, presents with 4 hours of sudden, severe central abdominal pain and vomiting. He is writhing in pain, yet his abdomen is soft with only mild tenderness. His lactate is raised and a blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis. What is the most appropriate investigation?
correct_answer: A. CT angiography of the abdomen
why_correct: Sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination findings, in a patient with atrial fibrillation who is not anticoagulated, with a raised lactate and acidosis, suggests embolic acute mesenteric ischaemia. CT angiography is the investigation of choice because it shows the vascular occlusion and the state of the bowel. It should not be delayed over concerns about renal function, as the condition is rapidly fatal without revascularisation or resection.
why_wrong: B. An erect chest X-ray looks for perforation and is usually normal in early ischaemia. C. Ultrasound is limited by gas-filled bowel and cannot reliably assess the mesenteric arteries. D. Laparoscopy may follow imaging but can miss early ischaemia and does not show the vessels. E. Amylase may be mildly raised in ischaemia and is non-specific.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to the signs, atrial fibrillation and a raised lactate: think acute mesenteric ischaemia, though a normal lactate does not exclude it. Request CT angiography urgently and involve the vascular and general surgeons.
thinking: AF without anticoagulation ↓ Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ Soft abdomen with minimal tenderness ↓ Raised lactate and acidosis ↓ CT angiography for mesenteric ischaemia
exam_trap: E, serum amylase — severe abdominal pain in an older patient prompts a pancreatitis screen, but amylase is non-specific and can rise modestly in ischaemia, delaying the CT angiography he needs.
takeaway: Abdominal pain out of proportion to signs with AF: urgent CT angiography for mesenteric ischaemia.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer presents with a week of increasing breathlessness and now feels light-headed. Her heart rate is 124/min and blood pressure 84/60 mmHg, falling noticeably during inspiration. Her neck veins are distended, her heart sounds are quiet and her chest is clear. Bedside echocardiography shows a large pericardial effusion with collapse of the right heart chambers in diastole. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
why_correct: Hypotension, raised venous pressure, quiet heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus with a large effusion and diastolic collapse of the right heart are cardiac tamponade. The pericardial fluid is preventing the heart from filling, so urgent echocardiography-guided pericardiocentesis is life-saving. In malignant effusion, recurrence is common, and a pericardial window or extended drainage may be needed later.
why_wrong: A. Diuretics reduce preload and worsen hypotension in tamponade. B. Vasodilators lower filling pressures and can precipitate collapse. C. The echo shows tamponade, not pulmonary embolism, and thrombolysis could cause bleeding into the pericardium. D. A chest drain treats pleural, not pericardial, fluid.
pearl: Beck's triad: hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds, often with pulsus paradoxus. Tamponade is preload-dependent: give fluid if needed while arranging drainage, and avoid diuretics and vasodilators.
thinking: Malignancy with progressive breathlessness ↓ Hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds ↓ Pulsus paradoxus ↓ Large effusion with diastolic right heart collapse ↓ Urgent pericardiocentesis
exam_trap: A, high-dose IV furosemide — breathlessness with distended neck veins suggests heart failure, but in tamponade reducing preload worsens filling and can precipitate cardiac arrest.
takeaway: Tamponade with hypotension needs urgent pericardiocentesis; avoid diuretics and vasodilators.

stem: A 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his wife found him at home beside empty blister packs of the dosulepin he takes for chronic back pain. He is drowsy but protecting his airway. His pupils are dilated and his skin is warm and dry. Pulse 128/min, regular; blood pressure 88/54 mmHg. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with broad QRS complexes, and a venous blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
why_correct: Dosulepin is a tricyclic antidepressant, and broad QRS complexes with hypotension and acidosis reflect cardiac sodium-channel blockade. IV sodium bicarbonate provides a sodium load and alkalinisation, which narrows the QRS, reduces the risk of arrhythmia and improves blood pressure. It is given alongside airway support and senior and poisons-service (TOXBASE) advice.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil does not reverse tricyclic toxicity and can provoke seizures in a mixed or tricyclic overdose. B. Amiodarone has sodium-channel and QT-prolonging effects and can worsen tricyclic cardiotoxicity. D. Gastric lavage is not recommended routinely and risks aspiration in a drowsy patient. E. Naloxone reverses opioids and will not correct sodium-channel blockade.
pearl: Anticholinergic features plus a broad QRS after an overdose should make you think tricyclic. The QRS is the danger marker, and bicarbonate is the drug that treats it.
thinking: Overdose of dosulepin, a tricyclic ↓ Dilated pupils, dry skin, tachycardia: anticholinergic picture ↓ Broad QRS, hypotension and acidosis: sodium-channel blockade ↓ Needs sodium load and alkalinisation ↓ IV sodium bicarbonate
exam_trap: B, IV amiodarone — a broad-complex ECG tempts you to reach for an antiarrhythmic, but amiodarone adds further sodium-channel and QT effects and can precipitate arrhythmia in tricyclic poisoning.
takeaway: Tricyclic overdose with a broad QRS or hypotension: give IV sodium bicarbonate.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is having an emergency laparoscopic appendicectomy. Anaesthesia was induced with a rapid sequence induction using suxamethonium and is maintained with desflurane. Thirty minutes into the operation the anaesthetist notices that the end-tidal carbon dioxide keeps climbing despite increased ventilation. Her jaw and limbs have become stiff, her heart rate is 142/min and her core temperature is rising steadily. The volatile agent has been switched off. What is the most appropriate specific treatment?
why_correct: Rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, muscle rigidity, tachycardia and a climbing temperature after suxamethonium and a volatile agent is malignant hyperthermia, an inherited disorder of skeletal muscle calcium release. Dantrolene reduces calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is the specific treatment, given once the trigger has been stopped. Cooling, correction of acidosis and hyperkalaemia, and critical care support accompany it.
why_wrong: A. Cooling is supportive, and paracetamol does not act on this non-infective hypermetabolic process. C. A beta-blocker slows the heart rate but does not stop the muscle hypermetabolism. D. Ondansetron is an antiemetic and has no role in malignant hyperthermia. E. A non-depolarising relaxant does not stop the intracellular calcium release driving the crisis.
pearl: The earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia is often an unexplained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide; temperature rise can come later. Stop the trigger, call for help and give dantrolene.
thinking: Suxamethonium and a volatile agent given ↓ Rising end-tidal carbon dioxide despite more ventilation ↓ Rigidity, tachycardia and rising temperature ↓ Malignant hyperthermia ↓ IV dantrolene
exam_trap: A, cooling blankets and IV paracetamol — the rising temperature draws attention to cooling, but cooling alone does not halt the runaway muscle metabolism and the patient will continue to deteriorate without dantrolene.
takeaway: Hypermetabolic crisis under anaesthesia with rising CO2 and rigidity is malignant hyperthermia: give dantrolene.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with an anxiety disorder is brought to the emergency department three hours after swallowing a large quantity of her propranolol tablets. She is drowsy and cool peripherally. Her pulse is 38/min and blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, and her capillary glucose is at the lower limit of normal.
