Her ECG shows sinus rhythm with a normal QRS duration, very large-amplitude QRS complexes across the chest leads, and asymmetrical, down-sloping ST depression with T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. A troponin is not raised. What is the most likely explanation for the ECG?

options.C: Left ventricular hypertrophy with a strain pattern

correct_answer: C. Left ventricular hypertrophy with a strain pattern
why_correct: Aortic stenosis imposes a chronic pressure load on the left ventricle, which thickens. On the ECG this produces increased QRS voltages in the chest leads, and the secondary repolarisation changes in the lateral leads (asymmetrical ST depression and T-wave inversion) are called a strain pattern. With no chest pain, a normal troponin and a normal QRS width, this is hypertrophy rather than infarction or a conduction block.
why_wrong: A. Lateral ST changes can mimic ischaemia, but she is pain-free with a normal troponin and the voltages are markedly increased. B. Left bundle branch block needs a broad QRS, and her QRS duration is normal. D. Right ventricular hypertrophy gives right axis deviation and a dominant R wave in V1, with changes in the right-sided chest leads. E. Digoxin causes a scooped ST segment but does not increase QRS voltage, and she takes no medicines.
pearl: Large chest-lead voltages plus lateral asymmetrical ST depression and T inversion in a patient with hypertension or aortic stenosis is LVH with strain, not acute ischaemia.
thinking: Pressure-loaded left ventricle from aortic stenosis ↓ ECG shows very large QRS voltages with a normal QRS width ↓ Lateral asymmetrical ST depression and T inversion, troponin normal ↓ Secondary repolarisation change of a thick ventricle ↓ Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain
exam_trap: A, Acute lateral non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction — lateral ST depression and T inversion look ischaemic, but the huge voltages, absence of pain and a normal troponin point to hypertrophy with strain.
takeaway: High chest-lead voltage plus lateral strain changes in aortic stenosis or hypertension means LVH, not acute MI.

stem: A 58-year-old man who smokes attends the emergency department the morning after a 40-minute episode of central chest tightness at home. He is now completely comfortable and his observations are normal. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with symmetrical, deep T-wave inversion in V1 to V4, preserved R-wave progression, no Q waves and an isoelectric ST segment. His first high-sensitivity troponin is within the normal range. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge with an outpatient exercise tolerance test
options.B: Discharge with reassurance that this is a normal T-wave variant
options.C: Start an NSAID and colchicine for pericarditis
options.D: Admit under cardiology for early coronary angiography

correct_answer: D. Admit under cardiology for early coronary angiography
why_correct: Deep symmetrical (or biphasic) T-wave inversion in the anterior chest leads after an episode of chest pain, in a patient now pain-free with preserved R waves and little or no troponin rise, is the Wellens pattern. It indicates a critical stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery and a high risk of an extensive anterior infarction within days. He should be admitted and managed as an acute coronary syndrome with early angiography.
why_wrong: A. Exercise testing can provoke infarction in a critical LAD lesion and is contraindicated. B. Deep new anterior T inversion after typical chest pain must not be dismissed as a normal variant. C. Pericarditis gives widespread saddle ST elevation and PR depression, not localised anterior T inversion. E. Thrombolysis is only for ST-elevation infarction and has no role here.
pearl: Wellens: pain-free patient, recent angina, deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3, preserved R waves, normal or slightly raised troponin. Think proximal LAD — angiography, never a stress test.
thinking: Typical ischaemic pain that has resolved ↓ Deep symmetrical anterior T inversion, no Q waves, isoelectric ST ↓ A normal troponin does not exclude a high-risk lesion ↓ Wellens pattern = critical proximal LAD stenosis ↓ Admit for early coronary angiography
exam_trap: A, Discharge with an outpatient exercise tolerance test — a pain-free patient with a normal troponin seems low risk, but stressing a critical LAD stenosis can precipitate a large anterior infarct.
takeaway: Deep anterior T inversion after chest pain, now pain-free: think Wellens and arrange angiography, not a stress test.

stem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with an hour of crushing central chest pain. He is sweaty and pale with cool peripheries, a pulse of 112/min and a blood pressure of 84/52 mmHg. His ECG shows horizontal ST depression in leads I, II, aVL and V3 to V6, with ST elevation confined to lead aVR, which is greater than any ST elevation in V1. What is the most likely underlying cause?

options.B: Left main stem or severe three-vessel coronary disease
options.E: Pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain

correct_answer: B. Left main stem or severe three-vessel coronary disease
why_correct: Widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR reflects diffuse subendocardial ischaemia, which occurs when a very large territory of myocardium is underperfused. In a patient with ongoing ischaemic pain and cardiogenic shock this pattern suggests left main stem occlusion or severe three-vessel disease, and needs immediate senior and interventional cardiology input.
why_wrong: A. Posterior infarction causes ST depression localised to V1–V3 with tall R waves, not widespread depression with aVR elevation. C. Pericarditis gives widespread saddle ST elevation with PR depression, and PR elevation in aVR. D. Takotsubo usually produces anterior ST elevation or deep T inversion, often after emotional stress, without this global ischaemic pattern. E. Pulmonary embolism may cause right heart strain changes such as T inversion in V1–V4, not this picture with crushing pain and widespread ST depression.
pearl: ST elevation in aVR plus widespread ST depression in a shocked patient with chest pain = global subendocardial ischaemia: think left main stem or triple-vessel disease and escalate immediately.
thinking: Crushing ischaemic chest pain with shock ↓ Widespread ST depression across limb and chest leads ↓ ST elevation only in aVR ↓ Diffuse subendocardial ischaemia over a large territory ↓ Left main stem or three-vessel disease
exam_trap: A, Isolated posterior myocardial infarction — ST depression is also its main ECG sign, but posterior MI changes are confined to V1–V3 with dominant R waves, not widespread with aVR elevation.
takeaway: aVR elevation with widespread ST depression in a shocked patient suggests left main or three-vessel disease.

stem: An 81-year-old man who lives alone is found by a neighbour lying on his kitchen floor on a winter morning, having fallen during the night. He is drowsy and no longer shivering. A low-reading thermometer confirms a markedly reduced core temperature. His ECG shows a slow regular rhythm, prolonged intervals and a dome-shaped positive hump immediately after each QRS complex, at the point where the ST segment begins, most obvious in the chest leads. What is this ECG feature?
why_correct: A positive deflection at the junction of the QRS complex and the ST segment (the J point) is the Osborn or J wave, the classic ECG sign of hypothermia. It becomes more prominent as temperature falls and resolves with rewarming. Bradycardia and prolonged PR, QRS and QT intervals commonly accompany it.
why_wrong: A. A delta wave is a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS in pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White), not at its end. B. A U wave follows the T wave and is typical of hypokalaemia. C. An epsilon wave is a small notch after the QRS in V1–V3 in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, not a feature of cold exposure. E. Brugada pattern is coved ST elevation in V1–V2 in an inherited channelopathy, not a J-point dome in a cold patient.
pearl: A hump at the J point in a cold, bradycardic patient is an Osborn wave; it resolves with rewarming. Handle hypothermic patients gently, as the cold myocardium is prone to ventricular fibrillation.
thinking: Prolonged exposure after a fall, markedly low core temperature ↓ Bradycardia with prolonged intervals ↓ Extra positive deflection at the QRS–ST junction ↓ Classic hypothermia sign ↓ Osborn (J) wave
exam_trap: C, Epsilon wave — it is also a small extra deflection just after the QRS, but it occurs in right ventricular cardiomyopathy in V1–V3, not as a J-point hump in hypothermia.
takeaway: A J-point hump in a cold, bradycardic patient is an Osborn wave of hypothermia.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is reviewed on the oncology ward because of increasing breathlessness over a week. Her pulse is 118/min, blood pressure 96/64 mmHg, and her jugular venous pressure is raised. Her chest is clear on auscultation. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with small QRS complexes in all leads, and the height of the QRS alternates between consecutive beats. What is the most likely cause of these ECG findings?
why_correct: Low-voltage QRS complexes whose amplitude alternates from beat to beat (electrical alternans) occur when the heart swings within a large pericardial effusion. Malignancy, particularly breast and lung cancer, is a common cause. With tachycardia, hypotension and a raised JVP, tamponade must be suspected and urgent echocardiography arranged, with pericardiocentesis if confirmed.
why_wrong: B. Massive pulmonary embolism causes tachycardia and right heart strain but not beat-to-beat QRS alternation. C. Hypothyroidism causes low-voltage complexes with bradycardia, not tachycardia with alternans. D. Dilated cardiomyopathy gives broad complexes and conduction abnormalities rather than alternating low voltages. E. A large pleural effusion can reduce voltages but does not cause alternans and would give dullness and reduced breath sounds.
pearl: Electrical alternans with low voltages = swinging heart in a large pericardial effusion. Add hypotension, tachycardia and a raised JVP and it is tamponade until proven otherwise.
thinking: Breathless patient with cancer, tachycardic, hypotensive, raised JVP ↓ ECG: small complexes in all leads ↓ QRS height alternates beat to beat ↓ Heart swinging in fluid ↓ Large pericardial effusion
exam_trap: B, Massive pulmonary embolism — breathlessness, tachycardia, hypotension and a raised JVP fit, and cancer raises clot risk, but PE does not produce alternating low-voltage QRS complexes.
takeaway: Low voltage plus electrical alternans means a large pericardial effusion; consider tamponade.

stem: A 44-year-old woman who grew up in Bangladesh attends her GP with breathlessness on exertion and occasional palpitations. As a child she had a prolonged illness with fever and painful, swollen joints. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm with a P wave in lead II that is wide and has two humps, and a P wave in V1 with a large, deep negative terminal portion. Echocardiography is arranged. Which valve lesion is most likely to be found?
why_correct: A broad, notched (bifid) P wave in lead II with a prominent negative terminal component in V1 indicates left atrial enlargement, the P mitrale pattern. The classic cause is mitral stenosis, which obstructs left atrial emptying, and her childhood illness suggests rheumatic fever, the commonest cause of mitral stenosis worldwide. She is also at risk of atrial fibrillation as the atrium dilates.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatic aortic regurgitation dilates the left ventricle rather than producing isolated left atrial enlargement. B. Pulmonary stenosis loads the right heart and gives right ventricular hypertrophy, not P mitrale. C. Tricuspid disease enlarges the right atrium, giving tall peaked P waves (P pulmonale). E. Aortic stenosis causes left ventricular hypertrophy; the dominant ECG change is increased voltage and strain rather than a bifid P wave.
pearl: Big left atrium = broad bifid P in II (P mitrale), classically mitral stenosis. Big right atrium = tall peaked P in II (P pulmonale), from lung disease or tricuspid lesions.
thinking: Childhood rheumatic illness, now breathless with palpitations ↓ P wave broad and bifid in II, deep terminal negativity in V1 ↓ Left atrial enlargement ↓ Lesion obstructing left atrial emptying ↓ Mitral stenosis
exam_trap: C, Tricuspid regurgitation — an abnormal P wave suggests an atrial problem, but right atrial enlargement gives tall peaked P waves, not the broad bifid shape of left atrial enlargement.
takeaway: A broad bifid P wave in lead II is P mitrale, classically from mitral stenosis.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is seen in a falls clinic after several episodes of light-headedness, two of which ended in a fall. Between episodes she feels well and her examination is normal. A 72-hour ambulatory ECG shows periods of slow sinus rhythm with pauses lasting several seconds, which coincide with her symptoms, and separate runs of a fast, irregularly irregular rhythm. Carotid sinus massage produces no significant pause. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sinus node dysfunction producing symptomatic bradycardia and sinus pauses alternating with paroxysmal atrial tachyarrhythmias (often atrial fibrillation) is sick sinus syndrome, also called tachy-brady syndrome. It is commonest in older people due to degeneration of the conducting tissue. Symptomatic patients usually need a permanent pacemaker, which then allows rate-control drugs to be used safely, and anticoagulation is considered for the atrial fibrillation.
why_wrong: A. Mobitz II shows dropped QRS complexes after P waves with a constant PR, not sinus pauses without P waves. C. Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is made unlikely by the negative carotid sinus massage and does not explain the tachyarrhythmia. D. Vasovagal syncope has a trigger and prodrome and does not produce runs of atrial fibrillation. E. Complete heart block shows P waves and QRS complexes dissociated at a slow ventricular rate, not intermittent pauses with bursts of fast irregular rhythm.
pearl: Tachy-brady on a Holter (sinus pauses plus paroxysmal AF) = sick sinus syndrome. Rate-slowing drugs worsen the pauses, so pacing usually comes first.
thinking: Older woman with intermittent light-headedness and falls ↓ Holter: sinus bradycardia and pauses matching symptoms ↓ Separate runs of irregular tachyarrhythmia ↓ Sinus node failing in both directions ↓ Sick sinus syndrome
exam_trap: C, Carotid sinus hypersensitivity — common in older fallers, but carotid sinus massage was negative and it does not cause runs of atrial tachyarrhythmia.
takeaway: Alternating sinus pauses and paroxysmal AF in an older patient indicate sick sinus syndrome.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with Crohn's disease, who had an extensive small-bowel resection two years ago, presents to the emergency department with numbness around her mouth and painful cramping of both hands. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm with a prolonged QT interval; the ST segment is long and flat, and the T wave itself is of normal shape and width. Which electrolyte disturbance best explains her presentation?
why_correct: Low ionised calcium lengthens the ST segment, so the QT interval is prolonged while the T wave keeps its normal shape. Neuromuscular irritability causes perioral paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm. Malabsorption after small-bowel resection (vitamin D deficiency, often with low magnesium) is a recognised cause, and symptomatic hypocalcaemia is treated with intravenous calcium gluconate with cardiac monitoring.
why_wrong: A. Hypokalaemia flattens T waves and produces U waves, giving an apparently long QT, but does not cause perioral numbness and tetany. B. Hypercalcaemia shortens the ST segment and QT interval. D. Raised magnesium causes weakness, loss of reflexes and conduction delay, not tetany. E. Hypernatraemia causes thirst and confusion and has no characteristic effect on the ST segment.
pearl: Calcium moves the ST segment: low calcium = long ST and long QT; high calcium = short QT. Tetany plus a long QT means check calcium and magnesium.
thinking: Perioral numbness and hand cramps = neuromuscular irritability ↓ Malabsorption after bowel resection ↓ ECG: long QT due to a long ST segment, normal T wave ↓ Selective ST lengthening is a calcium effect ↓ Hypocalcaemia
exam_trap: A, Hypokalaemia — common in Crohn's disease and also linked to an apparently long QT, but through flat T waves and U waves rather than a long ST segment, and it does not cause tetany.
takeaway: Tetany with a long QT from a lengthened ST segment indicates hypocalcaemia.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who rows competitively for her university attends her GP surgery for travel vaccinations. The practice nurse notes a regular pulse of 46/min and books a GP review. She has no dizziness, blackouts, chest pain or breathlessness and trains twice daily without difficulty. Her blood pressure and examination are normal, and there is no family history of sudden death. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with normal intervals and no other abnormality. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Refer to cardiology for pacemaker assessment
options.C: Advise her to stop training until an echocardiogram is done
options.D: Explain that this is a normal effect of endurance training and no action is needed
options.E: Advise her to reduce training intensity until her heart rate rises

correct_answer: D. Explain that this is a normal effect of endurance training and no action is needed
why_correct: Endurance training increases resting vagal tone and stroke volume, so a slow resting sinus rate is a normal physiological adaptation. In an asymptomatic athlete with a normal examination, no worrying family history and an otherwise normal ECG, no investigation or treatment is needed and she can be reassured.
why_wrong: A. Ambulatory monitoring is for symptoms such as syncope or palpitations, which she does not have. B. Pacing is for symptomatic or pathological bradycardia, not physiological sinus bradycardia. C. Stopping training is unnecessary without symptoms, a murmur or an abnormal ECG. E. Her heart rate is a healthy adaptation and does not need to be raised.
pearl: Athletic heart: resting sinus bradycardia, and sometimes first-degree or Mobitz I block, are normal in trained athletes. Red flags are exertional syncope, chest pain, a murmur or family history of sudden death.
thinking: Young endurance athlete with a slow pulse ↓ No syncope, chest pain or exercise limitation ↓ Normal examination, family history and ECG apart from rate ↓ High vagal tone from training ↓ Reassure: physiological bradycardia
exam_trap: A, Arrange an urgent 24-hour ambulatory ECG — a rate in the 40s looks abnormal, but investigation is driven by symptoms or red flags, and she has none.
takeaway: Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia in a trained athlete with a normal ECG needs only reassurance.

stem: An 83-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a mechanical trip. He has no chest pain or palpitations and his observations are normal. There is a well-healed scar below his left clavicle. A junior colleague is concerned because his ECG shows a regular broad-complex rhythm at 60/min. On closer inspection, each broad QRS complex, which resembles left bundle branch block, is immediately preceded by a very narrow vertical spike. What does this ECG show?

options.C: New left bundle branch block from acute infarction

why_correct: The scar below the clavicle suggests a permanent pacemaker. A sharp spike immediately before every broad QRS shows that each beat is initiated by a pacing lead in the right ventricle. Because the impulse spreads from the right ventricle through muscle rather than the conducting system, the QRS is broad with a left bundle branch block-like shape, which is the expected appearance of ventricular pacing.
why_wrong: B. Ventricular tachycardia is faster and is not preceded by pacing spikes, and he is well. C. A paced QRS normally looks like LBBB and is not by itself a sign of infarction, especially without chest pain. D. Hyperkalaemia gives peaked T waves and broad complexes without pacing spikes. E. Artefact is irregular and does not sit consistently before every QRS at a fixed rate.
pearl: Spike then broad LBBB-like QRS at a regular set rate = ventricular pacing. Look for a pacemaker scar before calling a broad-complex rhythm dangerous.
thinking: Well older man with an infraclavicular scar ↓ Regular broad complexes at a fixed rate ↓ Narrow spike before every QRS ↓ Beats initiated by a right ventricular lead ↓ Ventricular paced rhythm
exam_trap: C, New left bundle branch block from acute infarction — the QRS does look like LBBB, but the pacing spikes and lack of symptoms show it is simply the expected morphology of ventricular pacing.
takeaway: A spike before every broad LBBB-like QRS means a ventricular paced rhythm.

stem: A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with three hours of central chest heaviness spreading to her jaw, which eased partly with sublingual GTN. Her observations are stable. Her ECG shows horizontal ST depression in V4 to V6 with no ST elevation, and her high-sensitivity troponin is raised and rising on repeat testing. She has no history of bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Activation of the primary PCI pathway
options.C: Discharge with outpatient CT coronary angiography
options.E: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, with risk-score-guided timing of coronary angiography

correct_answer: E. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, with risk-score-guided timing of coronary angiography
why_correct: Ischaemic chest pain with ST depression and a rising troponin is a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Management is antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a second antiplatelet agent according to local protocol) and an anticoagulant such as fondaparinux, with a formal risk score such as GRACE used to decide how soon coronary angiography is done. Higher-risk patients have angiography early in the admission.
why_wrong: A. Thrombolysis gives no benefit in NSTEMI and only increases bleeding. B. The primary PCI pathway is for ST-elevation infarction or its equivalents. C. A raised, rising troponin with ischaemic ECG changes is an acute infarction needing admission, not outpatient imaging. D. NSAIDs and colchicine treat pericarditis, which gives saddle ST elevation and pleuritic pain.
pearl: NSTEMI: antiplatelets plus an anticoagulant, then risk-score-guided timing of angiography. Fibrinolysis has no place without ST elevation.
thinking: Typical ischaemic chest pain ↓ ST depression, no ST elevation ↓ Troponin raised and rising = infarction ↓ NSTEMI ↓ Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy with risk-guided angiography
exam_trap: A, Immediate thrombolysis — it is a reflex for myocardial infarction, but fibrinolysis is only for ST-elevation infarction and causes harm in NSTEMI.
takeaway: NSTEMI is treated with antiplatelets and anticoagulation, with angiography timed by risk, never thrombolysis.

stem: A 70-year-old man attends a pre-operative assessment clinic before an elective inguinal hernia repair. He feels well, has never fainted and has no breathlessness. He takes atenolol for hypertension. His pulse is 62/min and regular. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 260 ms that does not vary from beat to beat, and no P waves are dropped. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Refer for a permanent pacemaker before surgery
options.B: Postpone surgery and arrange an urgent 24-hour ambulatory ECG
options.C: No specific treatment; proceed with surgery and review his rate-slowing medication
options.E: Insert a temporary pacing wire before anaesthesia

correct_answer: C. No specific treatment; proceed with surgery and review his rate-slowing medication
why_correct: A prolonged PR interval that is constant, with every atrial impulse conducted, is first-degree atrioventricular block. In an asymptomatic patient it is usually benign, needs no treatment and is not a reason to delay surgery. Rate-slowing drugs such as beta-blockers can lengthen AV conduction, so his atenolol should be reviewed and the anaesthetist made aware.
why_wrong: A. Pacing is not indicated for asymptomatic first-degree block. B. Ambulatory monitoring is not needed without symptoms or higher-grade block. D. Admission for monitoring is unnecessary in a well patient with a stable, benign conduction delay. E. Temporary pacing is for unstable bradycardia or high-grade block, not first-degree block.
pearl: First-degree AV block: long but constant PR, every P conducted. Usually benign; look for AV-nodal blocking drugs and electrolyte problems rather than pacing.
thinking: Asymptomatic man at pre-operative assessment ↓ PR long but constant, every P conducted ↓ First-degree AV block ↓ Benign; beta-blocker may contribute ↓ No treatment, proceed, review medication
exam_trap: B, Postpone surgery and arrange an urgent 24-hour ambulatory ECG — any heart block sounds worrying before an operation, but isolated asymptomatic first-degree block does not need further tests or delay.
takeaway: Asymptomatic first-degree AV block needs no treatment beyond reviewing AV-nodal blocking drugs.

stem: A 63-year-old woman had a myocardial infarction treated with a coronary stent two years ago. She has now been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, and despite three months of dietary changes and increased activity her HbA1c remains above target. Her BMI is 29 kg/m2 and her renal function is normal. What is the most appropriate drug treatment?

options.B: Metformin alone, reviewing in three months

correct_answer: A. Metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor
why_correct: Metformin remains the foundation of drug treatment for type 2 diabetes. In a person with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, NICE recommends adding an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit to metformin. Of the options, metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor gives the best protection against further cardiovascular events as well as lowering glucose.
why_wrong: B. Metformin alone misses the cardiovascular benefit recommended for patients with established cardiovascular disease. C. Gliclazide lowers glucose but adds hypoglycaemia and weight gain without cardiovascular benefit. D. DPP-4 inhibitors lower glucose but are cardiovascular-neutral. E. Insulin is not first-line in a newly diagnosed patient without symptomatic hyperglycaemia.
pearl: Type 2 diabetes plus established cardiovascular disease: metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit. Counsel about genital infections and sick-day rules for ketoacidosis.
thinking: New type 2 diabetes above target after lifestyle measures ↓ Metformin is first-line ↓ Previous MI = established cardiovascular disease ↓ Add an agent with proven cardiovascular benefit ↓ Metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_trap: B, Metformin alone, reviewing in three months — classic stepwise teaching suggests one drug first, but established cardiovascular disease changes the plan to include an SGLT2 inhibitor.
takeaway: In type 2 diabetes with cardiovascular disease, combine metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has an X-ray for back pain that began after lifting a bag of shopping. It shows a new wedge compression fracture of a thoracic vertebra, and a DXA scan confirms osteoporosis. Her calcium and renal function are normal, she has no swallowing difficulty and she can sit upright after taking tablets. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.C: Weekly oral alendronic acid with calcium and vitamin D

correct_answer: C. Weekly oral alendronic acid with calcium and vitamin D
why_correct: A vertebral fragility fracture with osteoporosis on DXA needs bone-protective treatment to reduce further fractures. An oral bisphosphonate such as weekly alendronic acid is first-line, provided she can follow the administration instructions (taken fasting with a full glass of water, staying upright for 30 minutes). Calcium and vitamin D are given alongside unless dietary intake and vitamin D status are adequate.
why_wrong: A. Denosumab is an option when bisphosphonates are unsuitable or not tolerated. B. Raloxifene is not first-line and increases the risk of venous thromboembolism. D. Teriparatide is a specialist treatment for severe osteoporosis, for example with multiple vertebral fractures. E. Calcium and vitamin D alone do not adequately reduce fracture risk after a fragility fracture.
pearl: Fragility fracture plus osteoporosis: oral bisphosphonate first, with calcium and vitamin D. Check the patient can take it fasting and upright, and consider dental health before starting.
thinking: Low-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ DXA confirms osteoporosis ↓ Needs drug treatment to cut future fracture risk ↓ No barriers to oral therapy ↓ Weekly alendronic acid with calcium and vitamin D
exam_trap: A, Six-monthly subcutaneous denosumab — it is effective and convenient, but it is used when oral bisphosphonates cannot be taken or tolerated.
takeaway: First-line treatment after a fragility fracture with osteoporosis is an oral bisphosphonate.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with antiphospholipid syndrome, diagnosed after two late miscarriages, stopped her warfarin a month ago. Over three days she develops abdominal pain, falling urine output with a rapidly rising creatinine, mottled skin over her legs, painful dusky fingertips and new weakness of her right arm. Imaging shows renal infarcts and a small cerebral infarct. Her platelet count is mildly low, her clotting screen and fibrinogen are normal, and the blood film shows no significant red-cell fragmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Thrombosis developing in three or more organs over a few days, in a patient with known antiphospholipid syndrome (here after stopping anticoagulation), is catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome. It is a rare but frequently fatal emergency caused by widespread small-vessel occlusion. Management is in critical care with anticoagulation, high-dose corticosteroids and often plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin.
why_wrong: A. TTP causes a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with many red-cell fragments on the film, which are absent. B. DIC prolongs clotting times and consumes fibrinogen, but these are normal. C. HUS is usually diarrhoea-associated and features fragmentation haemolysis with renal failure. E. Vasculitis inflames rather than thromboses vessels and does not fit known antiphospholipid syndrome with multiple infarcts.
pearl: Antiphospholipid syndrome plus multi-organ thrombosis evolving over days = catastrophic APS. Treat aggressively in critical care: anticoagulation, steroids, and plasma exchange or IVIG.
thinking: Known antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulation stopped ↓ Rapid thrombosis in kidney, brain, skin and digits ↓ Normal clotting and no film fragments ↓ Not DIC or TTP ↓ Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome
exam_trap: A, Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura — low platelets, renal impairment and neurological signs fit, but TTP requires a haemolytic anaemia with red-cell fragments, which this film lacks.
takeaway: Multi-organ thrombosis over days in antiphospholipid syndrome is catastrophic APS, a medical emergency.

presentation: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
stem: A 58-year-old woman with vitiligo and hypothyroidism has had numb feet for several months and now falls when walking in the dark. She has reduced vibration and joint position sense in the feet, a positive Romberg test, absent ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses. Her full blood count shows a macrocytic anaemia, her serum B12 is low and her folate is also low. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: Oral folic acid alone, rechecking blood tests in four weeks
options.B: Red-cell transfusion to correct the anaemia
options.C: Oral folic acid now, adding B12 injections once haemoglobin improves
options.D: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin first, adding folic acid once B12 replacement has started
options.E: MRI of the spine before any replacement is given

correct_answer: D. Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin first, adding folic acid once B12 replacement has started
why_correct: Dorsal column loss combined with pyramidal signs and absent ankle jerks in a patient with low B12 is subacute combined degeneration of the cord, probably due to pernicious anaemia given her autoimmune history. Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin must be started promptly, using the intensive regimen for neurological involvement, with specialist advice. Folic acid may also be needed but should not be given before B12 replacement, because it can correct the blood count while the neurological damage progresses.
why_wrong: A. Folic acid alone leaves the B12 deficiency untreated and may worsen the cord damage. B. Transfusion is not needed for a chronic, compensated anaemia and does not treat the cause. C. Giving folate first risks precipitating or accelerating neurological deterioration. E. Imaging should not delay treatment of a clear, reversible cause of a progressing myelopathy.
pearl: Low B12 and low folate together: always start B12 first (or at least at the same time), never folate alone. Neurological involvement needs prompt, intensive intramuscular hydroxocobalamin.
thinking: Autoimmune background, sensory ataxia, extensor plantars, absent ankle jerks ↓ Macrocytic anaemia with low B12 ↓ Subacute combined degeneration of the cord ↓ Folate first can worsen the neurology ↓ IM hydroxocobalamin first, folate after
exam_trap: C, Oral folic acid now, adding B12 injections once haemoglobin improves — correcting both deficiencies seems logical, but folate before B12 can precipitate irreversible cord damage.
takeaway: With B12 deficiency and neurological signs, replace B12 before folate, promptly and intramuscularly.

stem: A 16-year-old girl attends her GP with her mother because her periods have been very heavy since they started, often flooding through protection at night. She has frequent nosebleeds that take a long time to stop and bled heavily after a tooth extraction. Her mother needed a blood transfusion after giving birth. Examination is normal apart from pallor. Her platelet count is normal, prothrombin time is normal and APTT is slightly prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding (heavy menstrual bleeding, nosebleeds, bleeding after dental work) with an affected mother suggests an autosomal dominant bleeding disorder. Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder; platelets are normal, and the APTT may be mildly prolonged because von Willebrand factor carries and protects factor VIII. Diagnosis is confirmed with von Willebrand factor antigen and activity and factor VIII levels, and tranexamic acid or desmopressin may be used.
why_wrong: A. Immune thrombocytopenia causes a low platelet count, which is normal here. B. Haemophilia B is X-linked, mainly affects males and causes joint and muscle bleeds rather than mucosal bleeding. C. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a rare autosomal recessive platelet defect with a normal APTT. E. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time first and is neither lifelong nor familial.
pearl: Mucosal bleeding (heavy periods, nosebleeds, dental bleeding) in a woman with a family history and normal platelets: think von Willebrand disease. Joint and muscle bleeds in boys: think haemophilia.
thinking: Heavy periods from menarche, nosebleeds, dental bleeding ↓ Mother affected = autosomal pattern ↓ Normal platelets and PT, slightly long APTT ↓ Mucocutaneous bleeding with reduced factor VIII carrier ↓ Von Willebrand disease
exam_trap: B, Haemophilia B — the prolonged APTT suggests a factor deficiency, but haemophilia is X-linked, rare in girls and causes deep rather than mucosal bleeding.
takeaway: Familial mucosal bleeding with normal platelets and a mildly long APTT suggests von Willebrand disease.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the GP because his mother noticed tiny red spots on his legs and several bruises over two days. He had chickenpox two weeks ago and is otherwise well, afebrile and playing normally. There is no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, and his joints are normal. A same-day full blood count shows a platelet count of 9 × 10⁹/L with normal haemoglobin and white cell count, and the blood film shows no abnormal cells apart from some large platelets. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An isolated, severe thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal blood count and film, in a well child a few weeks after a viral infection, is immune thrombocytopenia. Antibodies against platelets lead to their destruction, and the marrow responds by releasing large young platelets. In children it is usually self-limiting; management is often observation with advice to avoid contact sports, with treatment reserved for significant bleeding, under specialist guidance.
why_wrong: A. IgA vasculitis causes purpura with a normal platelet count, typically over the buttocks and legs with joint or abdominal pain. B. Leukaemia usually affects more than one cell line, with blasts, lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. C. Non-accidental injury does not cause a very low platelet count, although it should always be considered with bruising. D. Meningococcal disease produces a febrile, unwell child.
pearl: Well child, recent viral illness, petechiae, isolated low platelets, normal film: ITP. Any other abnormal cell line, organomegaly or an unwell child: think leukaemia or sepsis.
thinking: Well child with petechiae and bruising after a viral illness ↓ Platelets very low ↓ Haemoglobin, white cells and film otherwise normal ↓ Isolated antibody-mediated platelet destruction ↓ Immune thrombocytopenia
exam_trap: B, Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia — bruising in a child rightly raises concern, but leukaemia rarely spares the other cell lines, and the film shows no blasts.
takeaway: Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal film in a well child after a viral illness is ITP.

stem: A 24-year-old woman develops a deep vein thrombosis three months after starting a combined oral contraceptive pill. Her brother had a pulmonary embolism at the age of 30. She is seen in the haematology clinic after completing anticoagulation. In a clotting assay, adding activated protein C to her plasma fails to lengthen the clotting time as much as expected. What is the most likely inherited abnormality?
why_correct: Failure of activated protein C to prolong the clotting time is activated protein C resistance. In the great majority of cases this is due to the factor V Leiden mutation, which makes factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C. It is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry, and its risk is multiplied by oestrogen-containing contraception, which she should now avoid.
why_wrong: B. Protein S deficiency reduces the cofactor for protein C, but resistance to added activated protein C classically reflects an abnormal factor V. C. Antithrombin deficiency is rarer and is identified by low antithrombin activity. D. The prothrombin mutation raises prothrombin levels and is detected by genetic testing, not by this assay. E. Antiphospholipid syndrome is acquired, not inherited, and is diagnosed by lupus anticoagulant and antiphospholipid antibodies.
pearl: Activated protein C resistance = factor V Leiden in the vast majority. Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated once a thrombophilia and previous VTE are known.
thinking: Young woman with DVT on the combined pill ↓ First-degree relative with early PE ↓ Plasma resistant to activated protein C ↓ Factor V not inactivated by protein C ↓ Factor V Leiden mutation
exam_trap: B, Protein S deficiency — it is part of the protein C pathway, so it seems to fit, but resistance to added activated protein C points to an abnormal factor V.
takeaway: Activated protein C resistance is almost always due to factor V Leiden.

stem: A 66-year-old man sees his GP with three months of tiredness. He has no abdominal pain, change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding or indigestion, and does not take anti-inflammatory drugs. He eats a varied diet including meat. Blood tests show a low haemoglobin with a low MCV and a low ferritin. Coeliac serology is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Oral iron, investigating only if the haemoglobin fails to improve
options.B: Urgent referral for upper and lower gastrointestinal investigation, starting oral iron
options.D: Repeat the full blood count in three months
options.E: Check vitamin B12 and folate levels

correct_answer: B. Urgent referral for upper and lower gastrointestinal investigation, starting oral iron
why_correct: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man, or a postmenopausal woman, without an obvious cause is presumed to be due to gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and colorectal or gastric cancer must be excluded. He should be referred urgently for investigation of both the upper and lower gastrointestinal tract, and oral iron is started at the same time to replenish stores.
why_wrong: A. Treating with iron and waiting for a response delays the diagnosis of a possible cancer. C. Upper endoscopy alone may miss a colonic source; both ends need examining because lesions can coexist. D. Repeating the count only delays investigation of unexplained iron deficiency. E. B12 and folate deficiency cause macrocytosis, and the cause here is already established as iron deficiency.
pearl: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in a man or postmenopausal woman: test for coeliac disease and investigate both upper and lower GI tracts, while replacing iron.
thinking: Older man with microcytic anaemia ↓ Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency ↓ Diet adequate, no NSAIDs, coeliac negative ↓ Occult GI blood loss, possibly malignant ↓ Upper and lower GI investigation with oral iron
exam_trap: A, Oral iron, investigating only if the haemoglobin fails to improve — it treats the anaemia, but anaemia from a bleeding cancer can also respond to iron, so the cause must be found regardless.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older man needs urgent upper and lower GI investigation, not just iron.

stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted with severe mid-back pain after bending to pick something up, and an X-ray shows a vertebral collapse. Over recent weeks she has been thirsty, constipated and increasingly tired. Blood tests show a raised calcium, a creatinine much higher than her previous result, a normocytic anaemia and a very high ESR. Her alkaline phosphatase is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and a bone lesion together (the CRAB features), with a very high ESR, strongly suggest multiple myeloma. Myeloma bone disease is purely lytic because osteoblast activity is suppressed, so the alkaline phosphatase is typically normal despite fractures. The next tests are serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains and urine for Bence Jones protein, with urgent haematology referral.
why_wrong: A. Hyperparathyroidism raises calcium but does not explain anaemia, a very high ESR or rapid renal decline. B. Bone metastases usually raise the alkaline phosphatase, which is normal here. C. Osteoporosis does not cause hypercalcaemia, anaemia or a very high ESR. E. Paget's disease causes a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase with a normal calcium.
pearl: CRAB (calcium, renal, anaemia, bone) with a high ESR and normal alkaline phosphatase is myeloma until proven otherwise; request electrophoresis, free light chains and urine Bence Jones protein.
thinking: Older woman with a vertebral collapse ↓ Hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and anaemia ↓ Very high ESR suggests a paraprotein ↓ Normal ALP fits purely lytic bone disease ↓ Multiple myeloma
exam_trap: B, Metastatic breast cancer — a common cause of hypercalcaemia and vertebral collapse in older women, but metastases usually raise the ALP, and the high ESR with renal failure fits myeloma better.
takeaway: CRAB features with a high ESR and normal ALP point to multiple myeloma.

stem: A 55-year-old woman on a surgical ward is receiving her first unit of red cells after a bowel resection. About ten minutes after it starts, the nurse calls because the patient feels hot and restless, has severe pain in her lower back and says she feels something terrible is happening. Her blood pressure has fallen from 128/76 to 82/48 mmHg and red-brown urine is draining into her catheter bag. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Slow the transfusion and give paracetamol
options.B: Give IV chlorphenamine and continue the transfusion
options.C: Stop the transfusion, keep the line open with saline through a new giving set and begin resuscitation
options.D: Continue the transfusion and give IV furosemide
options.E: Complete the unit, then send a direct antiglobulin test

correct_answer: C. Stop the transfusion, keep the line open with saline through a new giving set and begin resuscitation
why_correct: Fever, back pain, haemoglobinuria, hypotension and a sense of doom within minutes of starting a transfusion indicate an acute haemolytic reaction, most often from ABO incompatibility due to an identification error. The transfusion must be stopped at once, venous access maintained with saline through a new giving set, and the patient resuscitated with senior help. Her identity is rechecked against the unit, the unit and giving set are returned to the laboratory, and bloods are sent for haemolysis, DAT, renal function and coagulation.
why_wrong: A. Slowing and giving paracetamol is for an isolated mild fever, not shock with haemoglobinuria. B. Antihistamines treat mild allergic reactions, and continuing gives more incompatible blood. D. Continuing the unit worsens haemolysis; furosemide is for fluid overload. E. Completing the unit delivers more incompatible cells and could be fatal.
pearl: Any severe transfusion reaction (shock, pain, haemoglobinuria, breathing difficulty): stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with saline, resuscitate, then recheck identity and return the unit.
thinking: Symptoms within minutes of starting blood ↓ Fever, back pain, hypotension, dark urine, sense of doom ↓ Intravascular haemolysis, likely ABO incompatibility ↓ Every further millilitre worsens it ↓ Stop the transfusion and resuscitate
exam_trap: A, Slow the transfusion and give paracetamol — fever during a transfusion is often mild, but fever with shock, pain and haemoglobinuria means haemolysis and the unit must be stopped completely.
takeaway: Shock, back pain and dark urine early in a transfusion: stop it immediately and resuscitate.

stem: A 52-year-old man sees his GP with a dragging discomfort in the left upper abdomen, feeling full after small meals, night sweats and weight loss. His spleen is palpable well below the left costal margin, extending towards the umbilicus. His white cell count is very high, and the film shows neutrophils with many myelocytes and metamyelocytes and increased basophils. Cytogenetics show a t(9;22) translocation. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.D: An oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib

correct_answer: D. An oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib
why_correct: A very high white count with granulocytes at every stage of maturation, basophilia, massive splenomegaly and the t(9;22) Philadelphia translocation is chronic myeloid leukaemia in chronic phase. The translocation creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, which encodes a constantly active tyrosine kinase. Oral tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib block this kinase, give deep and durable responses in most patients and are first-line treatment under haematology care.
why_wrong: A. Hydroxycarbamide may briefly lower the white count but does not target the BCR-ABL1 abnormality. B. Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells and is used in lymphomas and CLL. C. All-trans retinoic acid treats acute promyelocytic leukaemia. E. Splenectomy does not treat the leukaemia and is not used first-line.
pearl: CML: massive splenomegaly, very high WCC with the full granulocyte spectrum and basophilia, Philadelphia chromosome. Treat with a BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
thinking: Massive splenomegaly with sweats and weight loss ↓ Very high WCC, all stages of granulocytes, basophilia ↓ t(9;22) = Philadelphia chromosome ↓ BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase drives the disease ↓ Tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib
exam_trap: A, Long-term hydroxycarbamide as definitive therapy — it lowers the white count and is sometimes used briefly, but only a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targets BCR-ABL1 and controls the disease.
takeaway: Philadelphia-positive CML is treated first-line with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib.

stem: A 30-year-old man of Middle Eastern origin is seen in the infectious diseases clinic. While working in Pakistan he was treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria and then started a course of primaquine, without any prior blood test. Since returning to the UK two days ago he has noticed dark urine, yellow eyes and breathlessness on exertion. His haemoglobin has fallen sharply, and his reticulocytes and unconjugated bilirubin are raised. Repeat malaria films are negative. The blood film shows red cells that look as if pieces have been removed from their edges, and a supravital stain shows small inclusions within red cells. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute haemolysis shortly after an oxidant drug such as primaquine, with bite cells and Heinz bodies on the film and a negative direct antiglobulin test, is typical of G6PD deficiency. Without the enzyme, red cells cannot withstand oxidative stress, so haemoglobin denatures into Heinz bodies, which the spleen removes, leaving bite cells. It is X-linked and common in people of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, African and Asian origin; management is stopping the trigger and supportive care, with transfusion if severe.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary spherocytosis gives spherocytes rather than bite cells and is not triggered by drugs. B. Malaria can cause haemolysis, but repeat films are negative. D. Warm autoimmune haemolysis is DAT-positive. E. Sickle cell disease shows sickled cells and causes painful crises, not drug-triggered oxidative haemolysis.
pearl: Oxidant trigger (primaquine, dapsone, fava beans, infection) plus bite cells and Heinz bodies with a negative DAT = G6PD deficiency. Always check G6PD status before giving primaquine.
thinking: Man of Middle Eastern origin with haemolysis after primaquine ↓ DAT negative, malaria films negative ↓ Bite cells and Heinz bodies = oxidative damage ↓ Red cells lack protection against oxidants ↓ G6PD deficiency
exam_trap: B, Recrudescent malaria — haemolysis in a recently treated malaria patient tempts this, but repeat films are negative and bite cells with Heinz bodies indicate oxidative damage.
takeaway: Haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies after an oxidant drug indicates G6PD deficiency.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is admitted to a medical ward with community-acquired pneumonia and is expected to spend most of the next few days in bed. She has no history of bleeding, her platelets and renal function are normal, and she takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs. As the admitting doctor, what is the most appropriate approach to preventing venous thromboembolism?

options.C: Treatment-dose apixaban until she is mobile
options.D: Document a VTE and bleeding risk assessment, offering prophylactic low molecular weight heparin if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk
options.E: No prophylaxis, as she has no surgical risk factors

correct_answer: D. Document a VTE and bleeding risk assessment, offering prophylactic low molecular weight heparin if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk
why_correct: Every adult admitted to hospital should have a documented assessment of their risk of venous thromboembolism and of bleeding, using a recognised tool, as soon as possible after admission. An acutely ill medical patient with significantly reduced mobility is at increased risk, so if her VTE risk outweighs her bleeding risk she should be offered pharmacological prophylaxis, usually low molecular weight heparin, with reassessment as her condition changes.
why_wrong: A. Mechanical prophylaxis is considered in medical patients only when drug prophylaxis is contraindicated, which is not the case here. B. Aspirin is not used for VTE prophylaxis in medical inpatients. C. Treatment-dose anticoagulation is for established thrombosis, not prevention. E. Medical patients with reduced mobility carry a substantial VTE risk, so surgery is not needed to justify prophylaxis.
pearl: Every admission: documented VTE and bleeding risk assessment. Medical patients at risk get prophylactic LMWH if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk; reassess at consultant review and whenever the picture changes.
thinking: Acutely ill medical patient with reduced mobility ↓ All admissions need risk assessment ↓ Balance VTE risk against bleeding risk ↓ No bleeding risk factors identified ↓ Document assessment and offer prophylactic LMWH
exam_trap: A, Anti-embolism stockings alone — they feel safe because they avoid bleeding, but in medical patients mechanical methods are reserved for when drug prophylaxis is contraindicated.
takeaway: Assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and offer LMWH when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.

stem: A 26-year-old woman of Pakistani origin attends her booking appointment at the antenatal clinic at 10 weeks of pregnancy. She feels well. Her full blood count shows a haemoglobin just below the normal range but a very low MCV and MCH, with a red cell count at the upper end of normal. Her ferritin is normal. She mentions that a previous course of iron tablets did not change her blood count. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Start oral iron and recheck the blood count in four weeks
options.B: Haemoglobin analysis by HPLC or electrophoresis, and offer testing to her partner
options.D: Bone marrow examination with iron staining
options.E: Repeat the full blood count at 28 weeks

correct_answer: B. Haemoglobin analysis by HPLC or electrophoresis, and offer testing to her partner
why_correct: A microcytosis that is disproportionate to a mild anaemia, with a preserved red cell count, normal ferritin and no response to iron, suggests thalassaemia trait. Haemoglobin analysis by HPLC or electrophoresis confirms it, for example a raised HbA2 in beta-thalassaemia trait. In pregnancy this matters urgently, because if her partner is also a carrier the baby may have a serious haemoglobinopathy, so partner testing and counselling are offered through the antenatal screening programme.
why_wrong: A. Ferritin is normal and iron has already failed, so more iron is inappropriate and risks overload. C. Intravenous iron is for proven iron deficiency, which she does not have. D. Bone marrow examination is not needed for a typical trait picture. E. Waiting until 28 weeks wastes the time needed for partner testing and prenatal diagnosis if required.
pearl: Very low MCV with only mild anaemia, preserved red cell count and normal ferritin: think thalassaemia trait and confirm with HPLC. In pregnancy, test the partner promptly.
thinking: Mild anaemia but very low MCV and MCH ↓ Red cell count preserved, ferritin normal ↓ No response to previous iron ↓ Thalassaemia trait in a higher-prevalence group ↓ Haemoglobin HPLC and partner testing
exam_trap: A, Start oral iron and recheck the blood count in four weeks — microcytic anaemia in pregnancy is usually iron deficiency, but a normal ferritin and previous failure of iron point away from it.
takeaway: Disproportionate microcytosis with normal ferritin suggests thalassaemia trait; confirm with HPLC and test the partner in pregnancy.

stem: A 23-year-old man sees his GP with a painless lump in his neck that has grown over six weeks. He has generalised itching, drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. There is a firm, rubbery, non-tender lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa and smaller nodes in the neck. A chest X-ray shows mediastinal widening. He is referred urgently to haematology. Which investigation is most appropriate to establish the diagnosis and its subtype?

options.A: Excision biopsy of a lymph node
options.C: Monospot test and review in two weeks
options.D: CT of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis alone
options.E: A two-week course of antibiotics and review

correct_answer: A. Excision biopsy of a lymph node
why_correct: Persistent painless lymphadenopathy with B symptoms, itch and mediastinal widening in a young adult strongly suggests lymphoma, probably Hodgkin lymphoma. Diagnosis and subtyping need tissue that preserves the lymph node architecture and allows immunohistochemistry, best provided by excision biopsy of a whole node (an adequate core biopsy is sometimes used when excision is not feasible). Imaging follows for staging.
why_wrong: B. Fine-needle aspiration gives only scattered cells and cannot reliably diagnose or subtype lymphoma. C. Glandular fever is unlikely with this persistent, progressive picture and should not delay biopsy. D. CT stages the disease but cannot provide the histological diagnosis. E. Antibiotics only delay diagnosis in painless nodes with systemic symptoms.
pearl: Suspected lymphoma: tissue is the issue. Excision node biopsy (or an adequate core) gives architecture and immunohistochemistry; FNA is not enough. Stage with imaging afterwards.
thinking: Young adult with painless rubbery nodes ↓ Night sweats, weight loss, itch, mediastinal mass ↓ Suspect lymphoma ↓ Diagnosis needs node architecture and immunohistochemistry ↓ Excision lymph node biopsy
exam_trap: B, Fine-needle aspiration cytology — it is quick and minimally invasive, but it cannot show nodal architecture or allow reliable lymphoma subtyping.
takeaway: Suspected lymphoma is diagnosed by excision lymph node biopsy, not fine-needle aspiration.

stem: A 58-year-old man attends his GP with several months of tiredness. He has no bleeding or weight loss, and examination is unremarkable. His full blood count shows a mildly low haemoglobin and large red cells (high MCV); white cells and platelets are normal. What is the most appropriate initial approach to finding the cause?

options.A: Check ferritin and start a trial of oral iron
options.B: Check B12, folate, thyroid function and liver function, and take an alcohol and medication history
options.E: Request a faecal immunochemical test and refer for colonoscopy

correct_answer: B. Check B12, folate, thyroid function and liver function, and take an alcohol and medication history
why_correct: Macrocytic anaemia has megaloblastic causes (vitamin B12 or folate deficiency) and non-megaloblastic causes such as alcohol excess, liver disease, hypothyroidism, certain drugs (for example methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide and some antiepileptics) and myelodysplasia. The first step is therefore B12, folate, thyroid and liver tests with a careful alcohol and drug history, plus a blood film and reticulocyte count. Marrow examination is reserved for unexplained cases.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency causes a low, not raised, MCV. C. Bone marrow examination is considered only if simple tests do not explain the macrocytosis or other cell lines are abnormal. D. Haemoglobin electrophoresis investigates microcytosis due to haemoglobinopathies. E. FIT and colonoscopy investigate iron deficiency from occult bowel bleeding, not macrocytosis.
pearl: Macrocytosis: B12, folate, TFTs, LFTs, alcohol, drugs and reticulocytes (haemolysis), then consider myelodysplasia. Microcytosis: iron studies and haemoglobinopathy screen.
thinking: Tired man with anaemia ↓ MCV raised = macrocytic ↓ Common causes: B12, folate, alcohol, liver, thyroid, drugs ↓ Simple first-line tests cover these ↓ B12, folate, TFTs, LFTs plus alcohol and drug history
exam_trap: E, Request a faecal immunochemical test and refer for colonoscopy — unexplained anaemia in an older man rightly prompts thoughts of bowel cancer, but that pathway applies to iron deficiency with a low MCV.
takeaway: Investigate macrocytic anaemia with B12, folate, thyroid and liver tests plus an alcohol and drug history.

stem: An 11-month-old boy who has just started pulling himself up to stand is brought to the emergency department with a hot, swollen right knee after a minor tumble. He is afebrile and otherwise well. His mother says a large lump appeared at the site of his last immunisation, and her brother had a bleeding problem as a child. His platelet count and prothrombin time are normal, and his APTT is prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bleeding into a joint after minimal trauma, a large haematoma after an intramuscular injection and an affected maternal uncle suggest an X-linked inherited bleeding disorder. A prolonged APTT with normal platelets and prothrombin time fits a deficiency of factor VIII (haemophilia A) or factor IX (haemophilia B), confirmed by factor assays. Joint bleeds often first appear as the child becomes mobile; treatment is factor replacement through a haemophilia centre, avoiding intramuscular injections and NSAIDs.
why_wrong: A. Non-accidental injury must be considered with unexplained bleeding, but it does not prolong the APTT, and the family history points to an inherited cause. B. Septic arthritis usually causes fever and an unwell child and does not explain the abnormal APTT. C. Von Willebrand disease usually causes mucosal bleeding with an autosomal pattern; haemarthroses are uncommon. D. Immune thrombocytopenia lowers the platelet count, which is normal.
pearl: Haemarthrosis plus prolonged APTT with normal PT and platelets, in a boy with an affected maternal relative = haemophilia. Mucosal bleeding with an autosomal pattern = von Willebrand disease.
thinking: Infant boy with a joint bleed after minimal trauma ↓ Large haematoma after an IM injection ↓ Maternal uncle affected = X-linked ↓ Isolated prolonged APTT ↓ Haemophilia A or B
exam_trap: A, Non-accidental injury — unexplained bleeding in an infant must raise safeguarding concerns, but the isolated prolonged APTT and family history indicate a clotting factor deficiency.
takeaway: Haemarthrosis with an isolated prolonged APTT in a boy indicates haemophilia.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with long-standing coeliac disease, who finds it hard to keep to her gluten-free diet, is found to have Howell–Jolly bodies and target cells on her blood film. An abdominal ultrasound shows a small spleen. Her full blood count is otherwise normal. Which measure is most important to reduce her risk of serious harm?

options.B: Vaccination against encapsulated bacteria and annual influenza vaccination, with advice to seek urgent treatment for fever and consideration of antibiotic prophylaxis
options.D: An annual blood film to monitor splenic function
options.E: Oral iron and folic acid supplements

correct_answer: B. Vaccination against encapsulated bacteria and annual influenza vaccination, with advice to seek urgent treatment for fever and consideration of antibiotic prophylaxis
why_correct: Howell–Jolly bodies show that the spleen is not clearing red-cell remnants, so she has functional hyposplenism, a recognised complication of coeliac disease. Hyposplenic patients are at risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcus. As after splenectomy, they should be vaccinated against these organisms, offered annual influenza vaccination, told to seek urgent care for fever and assessed for antibiotic prophylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin does not address the main danger, which is infection. C. Hyposplenism alone is not a reason to avoid live vaccines in an otherwise immunocompetent person. D. Repeating the film monitors but does not reduce her risk. E. Iron and folate may correct deficiencies from malabsorption but do not prevent overwhelming sepsis.
pearl: Howell–Jolly bodies = absent or non-functioning spleen (splenectomy, sickle cell disease, coeliac disease). Protect against encapsulated bacteria with vaccines, consider prophylactic antibiotics and treat fever urgently.
thinking: Howell–Jolly bodies and a small spleen ↓ Functional hyposplenism linked to coeliac disease ↓ The spleen normally clears encapsulated bacteria ↓ Risk of overwhelming sepsis ↓ Vaccinate, educate about fever, consider prophylaxis
exam_trap: C, Avoidance of all live vaccines — it sounds protective in someone with impaired immunity, but hyposplenism alone does not contraindicate live vaccines, and missed vaccination is the real danger.
takeaway: Howell–Jolly bodies mean hyposplenism; vaccinate against encapsulated bacteria and treat fever urgently.

stem: A 77-year-old man has routine blood tests at his annual GP review and feels well. His white cell count is raised because of a lymphocytosis, which persists on a repeat test six weeks later; haemoglobin and platelets are normal. The blood film shows numerous small, mature-looking lymphocytes and many smudge cells. He has a few small, painless, rubbery nodes in both axillae and no hepatosplenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A persistent lymphocytosis of small, mature lymphocytes with smudge cells in an older adult, often found incidentally, is typical of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry (immunophenotyping) of peripheral blood. Early-stage, asymptomatic disease is usually monitored without treatment (watch and wait), with treatment started for progressive disease, cytopenias or symptoms.
why_wrong: B. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia shows immature blasts and marrow failure and is mainly a disease of children. C. Chronic myeloid leukaemia causes a granulocytosis with splenomegaly rather than mature lymphocytes. D. Infectious mononucleosis causes atypical reactive lymphocytes in a younger, symptomatic patient and resolves. E. Hodgkin lymphoma does not cause a circulating lymphocytosis with smudge cells.
pearl: Older adult, incidental persistent lymphocytosis of small mature cells with smudge cells: CLL. Confirm with peripheral blood flow cytometry; many patients need only monitoring.
thinking: Older well man, incidental finding ↓ Persistent lymphocytosis on repeat ↓ Small mature lymphocytes with smudge cells ↓ Painless lymphadenopathy ↓ Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
exam_trap: D, Infectious mononucleosis — lymphocytosis with nodes suggests a viral cause, but it is transient, affects younger symptomatic patients and produces atypical rather than small mature lymphocytes.
takeaway: Persistent mature lymphocytosis with smudge cells in an older adult is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with three weeks of increasing tiredness, a fever and swollen, bleeding gums. She has scattered bruises. Her full blood count shows a low haemoglobin, a low platelet count and a raised white cell count. The blood film shows large immature cells with prominent nucleoli, some containing fine, needle-shaped pink inclusions in their cytoplasm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Symptoms of marrow failure (anaemia, bleeding, infection) with circulating blasts indicate an acute leukaemia. Auer rods, the needle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions, are found only in myeloid blasts, and gum infiltration is typical of monocytic subtypes, so this is acute myeloid leukaemia, the commonest acute leukaemia in adults. She needs same-day haematology referral.
why_wrong: A. Lymphoblasts do not contain Auer rods, and ALL is mainly a disease of children. B. CLL shows small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells, not blasts. D. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia with no blasts. E. Myelofibrosis gives teardrop cells and a leucoerythroblastic film with massive splenomegaly.
pearl: Auer rods = myeloid blasts = AML. Gum hypertrophy suggests a monocytic subtype; DIC with bundles of Auer rods suggests acute promyelocytic leukaemia. Refer the same day.
thinking: Tiredness, fever, bruising, gum bleeding = marrow failure ↓ Blasts on the film = acute leukaemia ↓ Needle-shaped pink inclusions = Auer rods ↓ Auer rods are myeloid ↓ Acute myeloid leukaemia
exam_trap: A, Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia — blasts with marrow failure fit any acute leukaemia, but Auer rods are found only in myeloid blasts.
takeaway: Blasts containing Auer rods indicate acute myeloid leukaemia.

stem: A 79-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with black, tarry stools. He is confused and cannot list his medicines, and his family cannot yet be contacted. His platelet count is normal. His clotting screen shows a markedly prolonged prothrombin time with a raised INR, a normal or only slightly prolonged APTT, and a normal fibrinogen. Which of the following medicines is most likely to explain this clotting pattern?
why_correct: Warfarin blocks the vitamin K-dependent production of functional factors II, VII, IX and X. Factor VII has the shortest half-life and belongs to the extrinsic pathway, so the prothrombin time (expressed as the INR) lengthens first and most, which is why it is used for monitoring. A markedly prolonged PT with normal platelets and fibrinogen in a bleeding patient therefore suggests warfarin, which may need urgent reversal with vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate.
why_wrong: A. Unfractionated heparin mainly prolongs the APTT. B. Clopidogrel impairs platelet function without altering the PT or APTT. D. Aspirin also affects platelets only, leaving the clotting screen normal. E. Low molecular weight heparin has little effect on routine clotting tests and is monitored, when needed, by anti-Xa levels.
pearl: Prolonged PT/INR: warfarin, vitamin K deficiency or liver disease. Prolonged APTT: heparin, haemophilia or lupus anticoagulant. Antiplatelet drugs leave the clotting screen normal.
thinking: GI bleed with unknown medicines ↓ Platelets and fibrinogen normal ↓ PT/INR markedly prolonged, APTT normal or slightly long ↓ Reduced vitamin K-dependent factors, factor VII first ↓ Warfarin
exam_trap: A, Unfractionated heparin — it is also an anticoagulant that deranges the clotting screen, but it prolongs the APTT rather than the PT.
takeaway: A prolonged PT/INR with a normal APTT and platelets fits warfarin effect.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with myelodysplasia attends the haematology day unit for her regular red-cell transfusion. Forty minutes into the unit, she starts shivering and develops a new low-grade fever. Her pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation are unchanged from baseline. She has no rash, wheeze, breathlessness or back pain, and the bedside identity check was correct. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline
options.B: Stop the transfusion and give IV furosemide
options.C: Stop the transfusion permanently and manage as an acute haemolytic reaction
options.D: Temporarily stop or slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and continue with closer observation if no other features develop
options.E: Continue at the same rate and recheck observations at the end of the unit

correct_answer: D. Temporarily stop or slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and continue with closer observation if no other features develop
why_correct: An isolated rise in temperature with chills, without hypotension, breathlessness, pain, rash or signs of haemolysis, is most consistent with a febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction, caused by cytokines or recipient antibodies to donor white cells. People who receive regular transfusions are particularly prone. The transfusion is paused or slowed and paracetamol given; if she remains otherwise well it can continue with more frequent observations, but any deterioration means stopping and treating as a severe reaction.
why_wrong: A. Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, and she has no airway, breathing or circulatory compromise. B. Furosemide treats transfusion-associated circulatory overload, which causes breathlessness and raised blood pressure, not isolated fever. C. There are no features of haemolysis such as hypotension, pain or dark urine. E. A new fever needs action and closer, not less frequent, monitoring.
pearl: Isolated mild fever with chills and stable observations during a transfusion = febrile non-haemolytic reaction: pause or slow, paracetamol, observe closely. Fever plus any other feature = stop and escalate.
thinking: Fever with chills during a regular transfusion ↓ Observations otherwise stable ↓ No rash, wheeze, pain or haemoglobinuria; ID check correct ↓ Febrile non-haemolytic reaction ↓ Pause or slow, paracetamol, continue with closer observation
exam_trap: C, Stop the transfusion permanently and manage as an acute haemolytic reaction — fever can herald haemolysis, but with no hypotension, pain or dark urine and a correct ID check, a mild febrile reaction is far more likely.
takeaway: Isolated mild fever during a transfusion: pause or slow, give paracetamol and observe closely.

stem: A 30-year-old man with coeliac disease and a history of recurrent sinus infections is receiving fresh frozen plasma before a procedure. Within a few minutes he develops itchy wheals, swelling of his lips, a hoarse voice and wheeze. His blood pressure falls to 78/40 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Slow the transfusion and give oral paracetamol
options.B: Give IV chlorphenamine and continue the transfusion more slowly
options.C: Stop the transfusion and give IV furosemide
options.D: Stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline, managing as anaphylaxis
options.E: Give IV hydrocortisone and restart the transfusion once the wheeze settles

correct_answer: D. Stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline, managing as anaphylaxis
why_correct: Urticaria, angioedema, airway involvement, wheeze and hypotension soon after starting a blood product indicate an anaphylactic transfusion reaction. Recurrent sinus infections and coeliac disease suggest IgA deficiency, in which anti-IgA antibodies can react with IgA in donor plasma. The transfusion is stopped and anaphylaxis treated according to Resuscitation Council UK guidance with intramuscular adrenaline, oxygen and IV fluids, repeating adrenaline if needed. Future products may need to come from IgA-deficient donors or be washed, on haematology advice.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol treats fever and does nothing for airway or circulatory compromise. B. Antihistamines are not first-line in anaphylaxis, and continuing the product sustains the reaction. C. Furosemide treats circulatory overload, not anaphylaxis, and would worsen hypotension. E. Steroids act too slowly, are not first-line, and restarting the product is dangerous.
pearl: Transfusion reaction with urticaria plus airway, breathing or circulation problems = anaphylaxis: stop and give IM adrenaline. Think IgA deficiency, especially with coeliac disease or recurrent infections.
thinking: Reaction within minutes of a plasma product ↓ Urticaria, lip swelling, hoarse voice, wheeze, hypotension ↓ Life-threatening airway and circulation features ↓ Anaphylaxis, possibly from IgA deficiency ↓ Stop the product and give IM adrenaline
exam_trap: B, Give IV chlorphenamine and continue the transfusion more slowly — appropriate for mild urticaria alone, but airway swelling and hypotension mean anaphylaxis, which needs adrenaline and stopping the product.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis during a transfusion: stop the product and give IM adrenaline; consider IgA deficiency.

stem: An 81-year-old woman is on the orthopaedic ward two days after a hip hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. Her haemoglobin has drifted down since surgery, but she is comfortable, not breathless and her observations are stable. She has no history of heart disease and there is no sign of ongoing bleeding. A nurse asks whether she should be transfused. Which approach to red-cell transfusion is most appropriate?

options.A: A restrictive, individualised approach, transfusing below a threshold of around 70 g/L or for symptoms, one unit at a time with reassessment
options.B: A liberal threshold of 100 g/L to help her rehabilitation
options.C: Two units whenever her haemoglobin falls after surgery
options.D: No transfusion under any circumstances, using oral iron alone
options.E: Transfusion to keep her haemoglobin above 120 g/L because of her age

correct_answer: A. A restrictive, individualised approach, transfusing below a threshold of around 70 g/L or for symptoms, one unit at a time with reassessment
why_correct: For stable patients without active bleeding or acute coronary syndrome, NICE recommends a restrictive transfusion strategy, with a threshold of around 70 g/L; restrictive strategies are at least as safe as liberal ones and reduce transfusion-related harm. Patients who are not bleeding should usually receive a single unit followed by clinical review and a repeat haemoglobin. The decision is individualised to symptoms and comorbidity rather than a number alone.
why_wrong: B. Liberal thresholds increase transfusion without improving outcomes for most stable patients. C. Routine two-unit transfusion ignores the benefit of single units with reassessment. D. Transfusion may still be needed if her haemoglobin falls very low or she becomes symptomatic. E. Age alone does not justify a high target, which exposes her to circulatory overload and other risks.
pearl: Stable, not bleeding, no acute coronary syndrome: restrictive threshold, one unit at a time, then reassess. Different thresholds apply in acute coronary syndrome, major haemorrhage and chronic transfusion dependence.
thinking: Stable post-operative patient, no bleeding ↓ No acute coronary syndrome ↓ Restrictive strategies are as safe and reduce harm ↓ Single units with reassessment ↓ Restrictive, individualised transfusion
exam_trap: B, A liberal threshold of 100 g/L to help her rehabilitation — a higher haemoglobin seems helpful for mobilising older patients, but liberal strategies have not shown benefit and add transfusion risks.
takeaway: In stable non-bleeding patients without ACS, transfuse restrictively and one unit at a time.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis, who takes methotrexate and regular naproxen, is found to have a microcytic anaemia on her monitoring blood tests. Her CRP is mildly raised. Iron studies show a low serum ferritin, a low transferrin saturation and a raised total iron-binding capacity. What is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
why_correct: A low ferritin is the most specific single test for iron deficiency, and because ferritin rises with inflammation, a low value despite active arthritis is even more convincing. A low transferrin saturation with a raised total iron-binding capacity completes the iron-deficient picture. In this patient, gastrointestinal blood loss from an NSAID is a likely cause and should be considered.
why_wrong: A. Anaemia of chronic disease gives a normal or raised ferritin with a low or normal total iron-binding capacity. C. Thalassaemia trait has normal iron studies. D.
