HELLP causes hypertension, haemolysis and low platelets.
pearl: Itching on the palms and soles without a rash in the third trimester: check bile acids. Cholestasis of pregnancy is mostly a risk to the fetus, and the timing of birth depends on the bile acid level.
thinking: Third-trimester itch ↓ Worst on hands and feet ↓ No primary rash ↓ Raised bile acids, normal platelets and glucose ↓ Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
exam_trap: A, Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy — it is the commonest itchy condition of late pregnancy. But it causes a visible rash, whereas cholestasis causes itch with normal skin and raised bile acids.
takeaway: Itchy palms and soles with no rash and raised bile acids in late pregnancy: obstetric cholestasis.

stem: A 19-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy unit at 11 weeks with dark brown vaginal spotting and frequent vomiting. Her uterus is palpable well above the pubic symphysis, larger than expected for her dates. Her blood pressure is raised, and her serum hCG is far higher than expected for her gestation. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous intrauterine mass with many small cystic spaces and no fetal pole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bleeding, exaggerated vomiting, a uterus large for dates, very high hCG and early hypertension, with an intrauterine mass of multiple cystic spaces and no fetus, indicate a molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease). Management is surgical evacuation with histology, followed by registration with a specialist trophoblastic screening centre for hCG follow-up, because a minority develop persistent disease.
why_wrong: A. Twins can raise hCG and enlarge the uterus but would show two gestational sacs or fetuses on ultrasound. B. A missed miscarriage does not produce very high hCG or a cystic mass. C. Hyperemesis does not explain the ultrasound appearance or the large uterus. D. The pregnancy is intrauterine.
pearl: Molar pregnancy: very high hCG, large-for-dates uterus, severe vomiting and sometimes early hypertension or hyperthyroidism, with a snowstorm-like cystic mass on scan. Evacuate, then follow up hCG.
thinking: Early pregnancy bleeding and severe vomiting ↓ Uterus larger than dates ↓ hCG far above expected, early hypertension ↓ Cystic intrauterine mass, no fetus ↓ Molar pregnancy
exam_trap: A, Twin pregnancy — it also gives a large uterus, high hCG and more severe vomiting. But ultrasound would show two sacs or fetuses, not a cystic mass with no fetal pole.
takeaway: Very high hCG, large-for-dates uterus and a cystic mass without a fetus mean molar pregnancy.

stem: A 44-year-old woman tells her GP about two months of bleeding after intercourse and an offensive, bloodstained vaginal discharge. She has not attended her last two cervical screening invitations. On speculum examination there is an irregular, ulcerated area on the cervix that bleeds readily on contact. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Take a cervical screening sample today and act on the result
options.B: Make an urgent suspected cancer referral to gynaecology
options.C: Take swabs and start doxycycline for presumed cervicitis
options.E: Treat as ectropion and review in three months

correct_answer: B. Make an urgent suspected cancer referral to gynaecology
why_correct: An irregular, ulcerated cervix that bleeds on contact, with post-coital bleeding and offensive discharge, is suspicious for cervical cancer. NICE recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral when the appearance of the cervix is consistent with cancer, for colposcopy and biopsy. A screening test is not appropriate for a woman with symptoms and a visible lesion.
why_wrong: A. Screening is for women without symptoms, and a result could falsely reassure and delay diagnosis. C. Infection does not explain an ulcerated, irregular lesion and treating it would delay referral. D. A suspicious cervix needs the urgent pathway, not a routine appointment. E. An ectropion is smooth and regular, not ulcerated and irregular.
pearl: A visibly abnormal cervix needs urgent referral, whatever the screening history. Never use a screening test to investigate symptoms or a visible lesion.
thinking: Post-coital bleeding and offensive discharge ↓ Missed screening ↓ Irregular, ulcerated, contact-bleeding cervix ↓ Appearance consistent with cancer ↓ Urgent suspected cancer referral
exam_trap: A, Take a cervical screening sample today and act on the result — she is overdue for screening, so catching up seems efficient. But screening is designed for well women, and a visible suspicious lesion needs urgent referral regardless of any sample.
takeaway: A cervix that looks suspicious for cancer needs urgent referral, not a screening test.

presentation: Tubal ectopic pregnancy suitable for methotrexate
stem: A 27-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy unit at six weeks of amenorrhoea with light spotting and only mild, intermittent pelvic discomfort. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a small adnexal mass consistent with a tubal ectopic pregnancy, with no fetal heartbeat and no free fluid. Her serum hCG is modestly raised and has risen on a repeat sample 48 hours later. She is haemodynamically stable, can attend follow-up reliably, and would prefer to avoid an operation. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: A stable woman with a small, unruptured tubal ectopic, no heartbeat, no significant pain and a modest hCG is suitable for medical management with a single dose of intramuscular methotrexate, provided she can attend follow-up for serial hCG. This avoids surgery, which matches her preference. Expectant management is suitable only when hCG is low and falling.
why_wrong: B. Her hCG is rising, which shows the pregnancy is still active and makes expectant management unsuitable. C. Salpingectomy is appropriate for rupture, significant pain, a larger mass or a visible heartbeat, or if she chooses it, but she prefers to avoid surgery and is a good candidate for medical treatment. D. Mifepristone with misoprostol is used for miscarriage and termination, not ectopic pregnancy. E. Salpingotomy is a surgical option mainly for women with fertility risk factors, and she wishes to avoid surgery.
pearl: Methotrexate suits a stable, pain-free woman with a small unruptured tubal ectopic, no heartbeat, a modest hCG and reliable follow-up. A rising hCG rules out expectant management.
thinking: Tubal ectopic, haemodynamically stable ↓ Small mass, no heartbeat, no free fluid, minimal pain ↓ hCG modest but rising, so not expectant ↓ Wants to avoid surgery and can attend follow-up ↓ Intramuscular methotrexate
exam_trap: B, Expectant management with repeat hCG — she is well with a small ectopic, so a watch-and-wait approach seems least invasive. But a rising hCG shows active trophoblast, and expectant management is reserved for a low and falling hCG.
takeaway: Small unruptured ectopic, stable, rising but modest hCG and wants no surgery: single-dose methotrexate.

stem: A 36-year-old woman at 32 weeks attends maternity triage with severe epigastric pain going through to her back, vomiting and feeling generally unwell. Her blood pressure is raised and urine dipstick shows proteinuria. Blood tests show a low platelet count, a markedly raised ALT, a raised LDH and fragmented red cells on the blood film. Amylase, glucose and clotting are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Haemolysis (fragmented red cells, raised LDH), elevated liver enzymes and low platelets in a hypertensive woman with proteinuria in the third trimester is HELLP syndrome, a severe form of pre-eclampsia. Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain is typical and can be mistaken for gastrointestinal disease. It is an obstetric emergency requiring stabilisation, magnesium sulfate, blood pressure control and delivery.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis is unlikely with a normal amylase and does not explain haemolysis or low platelets. B. Biliary colic does not cause haemolysis, thrombocytopenia or hypertension. C. Fatty liver of pregnancy typically causes hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy, which are absent. D. Reflux does not cause abnormal blood tests or hypertension.
pearl: Epigastric pain in late pregnancy is pre-eclampsia or HELLP until proven otherwise. Check blood pressure, urine, platelets, liver enzymes and a blood film before calling it reflux or gallstones.
thinking: Third trimester epigastric pain ↓ Hypertension and proteinuria ↓ Low platelets, raised ALT, haemolysis ↓ Normal glucose and clotting argue against fatty liver ↓ HELLP syndrome
exam_trap: A, Acute pancreatitis — severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting is its textbook description. But the amylase is normal, and haemolysis with low platelets in a hypertensive woman points to HELLP.
takeaway: Late-pregnancy epigastric pain with hypertension, haemolysis, high liver enzymes and low platelets is HELLP.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after waking with sudden, severe right lower abdominal pain that comes in waves. She has vomited three times. She is afebrile. There is marked tenderness in the right iliac fossa and right adnexa. A urine pregnancy test is negative and urine dipstick is normal. Ultrasound shows an enlarged right ovary containing a large cyst. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden onset of severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting, in a girl with an enlarged ovary containing a cyst, is ovarian torsion until proven otherwise. A cyst or mass makes the ovary prone to twisting on its pedicle, cutting off its blood supply. It needs urgent gynaecological review and laparoscopy to untwist and preserve the ovary; a normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis usually develops gradually, with central pain moving to the right iliac fossa and fever, not sudden onset on waking. B. PID causes gradual bilateral pain with fever and discharge, usually in sexually active women. C. The pregnancy test is negative. E. A normal urine dipstick and the ovarian cyst make ureteric colic unlikely.
pearl: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting and an ovarian cyst is torsion. Go to laparoscopy on clinical suspicion; Doppler flow can be normal, and delay costs the ovary.
thinking: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain ↓ Vomiting, afebrile ↓ Pregnancy test negative, urine normal ↓ Enlarged ovary with a cyst ↓ Ovarian torsion
exam_trap: A, Acute appendicitis — right iliac fossa pain and vomiting in a teenager is the classic appendicitis presentation. But the sudden onset, lack of fever and the ovarian cyst point to torsion.
takeaway: Sudden pelvic pain with vomiting and an ovarian cyst is torsion: urgent laparoscopy to save the ovary.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped taking apixaban a month ago because of nosebleeds. Four hours ago her right foot and calf suddenly became painful. On examination the leg is pale and cold below the knee, with no popliteal or foot pulses; the femoral pulse is present. She has reduced sensation in her toes but can move them. The calf is soft. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Restart apixaban and arrange an outpatient arterial duplex scan
options.B: Aspirin and clopidogrel with a vascular clinic appointment
options.C: Intravenous unfractionated heparin and urgent vascular surgical review
options.E: Elevate the leg and apply compression bandaging

correct_answer: C. Intravenous unfractionated heparin and urgent vascular surgical review
why_correct: Sudden pain, pallor, coldness and pulselessness in a patient with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation is acute limb ischaemia, most likely embolic. The limb is threatened but salvageable, with sensory loss but preserved movement and a soft calf. Immediate intravenous heparin limits clot propagation while urgent vascular surgical assessment arranges revascularisation, such as embolectomy.
why_wrong: A. This is a limb-threatening emergency that cannot wait for outpatient tests. B. Antiplatelets do not treat an acute embolus, and a clinic appointment is far too slow. D. Movement is preserved and the calf is soft, so the limb is salvageable. E. Elevation and compression reduce arterial flow further and worsen ischaemia.
pearl: The six Ps of acute limb ischaemia are pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishingly cold, paraesthesia and paralysis. Sensory or motor loss means a threatened limb: heparin and urgent revascularisation.
thinking: Sudden painful, pale, cold, pulseless leg ↓ AF off anticoagulation: embolus ↓ Sensory loss, movement preserved ↓ Threatened but salvageable limb ↓ IV heparin and urgent vascular review
exam_trap: A, Restart apixaban and arrange an outpatient arterial duplex scan — she clearly needs anticoagulation for her AF, so restarting it looks logical. But an acutely ischaemic limb needs immediate heparin and revascularisation, not outpatient care.
takeaway: Acute limb ischaemia: immediate IV heparin and urgent vascular surgery to save the limb.

stem: A 58-year-old man who smokes sees his GP with three months of tiredness, night sweats and weight loss. He mentions one episode of blood in his urine that he did not report. On examination there is a left-sided scrotal swelling feeling like a bag of worms, which does not empty when he lies down. His full blood count shows a raised haemoglobin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Visible haematuria, systemic symptoms and a new left varicocele that does not empty on lying down suggest renal cell carcinoma: a left renal tumour can obstruct the left renal vein, into which the left testicular vein drains. Some kidney cancers secrete erythropoietin, causing a raised haemoglobin. Smoking is a risk factor, and he needs an urgent suspected cancer referral.
why_wrong: A. The swelling is a varicocele of the veins, not a testicular mass, and testicular tumours do not cause haematuria or polycythaemia. B. Bladder cancer causes haematuria but would not explain the varicocele or raised haemoglobin. C. Polycythaemia vera does not cause haematuria or a varicocele. E. Stones cause pain, not systemic symptoms, polycythaemia or a varicocele.
pearl: A new left varicocele that does not empty on lying down suggests renal vein obstruction, so examine and image the left kidney. Kidney cancer can also cause polycythaemia, fever and hypercalcaemia.
thinking: Haematuria in a smoker with systemic symptoms ↓ Left varicocele that stays full when lying down ↓ Left renal vein obstruction ↓ Raised haemoglobin from erythropoietin ↓ Renal cell carcinoma
exam_trap: B, Bladder cancer — visible haematuria in a smoker is its classic presentation. But bladder cancer cannot explain a non-emptying left varicocele or a raised haemoglobin, which both point to the kidney.
takeaway: Haematuria plus a new non-emptying left varicocele suggests a left renal cell carcinoma.

stem: A 30-year-old man attends the emergency department with 18 hours of abdominal pain that started around his umbilicus and has settled in the right lower abdomen. He has no appetite, his temperature is 37.9°C, and he winced at every bump on the drive in. Pressing in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa, and there is guarding over the right iliac fossa. Urine dipstick is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Discharge with oral antibiotics and safety-netting advice
options.B: Surgical review for appendicectomy, with IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics
options.E: Analgesia and discharge with GP follow-up

correct_answer: B. Surgical review for appendicectomy, with IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics
why_correct: Pain moving from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, low-grade fever, pain on movement, Rovsing's sign and localised guarding make acute appendicitis highly likely. It is a clinical diagnosis in a young man and needs urgent surgical review, keeping him nil by mouth with IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics, and laparoscopic appendicectomy to prevent perforation.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotic-only treatment is not the standard of care for a man with peritonism and needs specialist decision, not discharge. C. Colonoscopy has no role and could risk perforation. D. Delaying assessment for a week risks perforation. E. Discharging a patient with localised peritonism is unsafe.
pearl: Pain moving from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa, anorexia and localised peritonism make appendicitis a clinical diagnosis in young men. Imaging is more useful in women, children and older adults.
thinking: Periumbilical pain moving to the right iliac fossa ↓ Anorexia, low-grade fever ↓ Rovsing's sign and guarding ↓ Acute appendicitis ↓ Surgical review for appendicectomy
exam_trap: A, Discharge with oral antibiotics and safety-netting advice — antibiotic treatment of uncomplicated appendicitis is discussed widely. But it is not standard care in UK practice, and a patient with peritonism should be assessed by surgeons, not sent home.
takeaway: Migratory right iliac fossa pain with peritonism: urgent surgical review for appendicectomy.

stem: A 48-year-old woman was admitted two days ago with constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and a positive Murphy's sign. Ultrasound showed gallstones with a thickened gallbladder wall and no bile duct dilatation. She is improving on intravenous antibiotics, her liver tests are normal, and she is otherwise fit and well. On the ward round, she asks when she should have her gallbladder removed. What is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Discharge and add her to the waiting list for surgery in 6 to 8 weeks
options.B: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission, within a week of diagnosis
options.C: Percutaneous cholecystostomy now, with surgery later
options.D: No surgery unless she has another attack

correct_answer: B. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission, within a week of diagnosis
why_correct: NICE recommends early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, within a week of diagnosis, for people with acute cholecystitis who are fit for surgery. Early surgery is as safe as delayed surgery, shortens the total length of illness and hospital stay, and avoids readmissions with recurrent attacks while waiting.
why_wrong: A. Delayed interval surgery was traditional practice but leads to more recurrent attacks and readmissions. C. Cholecystostomy is for patients too unwell or frail for surgery. D. Gallstone cholecystitis commonly recurs, so surgery is advised in fit patients. E. ERCP treats bile duct stones, and her liver tests and bile duct are normal.
pearl: Acute cholecystitis in a fit patient: laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week of diagnosis. Cholecystostomy is for patients too unwell for surgery.
thinking: Acute calculous cholecystitis ↓ Responding to antibiotics ↓ Fit for surgery ↓ Early surgery shortens illness and avoids readmission ↓ Laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week
exam_trap: A, Discharge and add her to the waiting list for surgery in 6 to 8 weeks — this cooling-off approach was standard teaching for years. But current evidence and NICE favour early surgery, which reduces recurrent attacks and overall time in hospital.
takeaway: Fit patient with acute cholecystitis: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week of diagnosis.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a right inguinoscrotal hernia that he has always been able to push back attends the emergency department. For eight hours the lump has been painful and he has been unable to reduce it. He has vomited several times and has not passed wind since the morning. The lump is tense, very tender and the overlying skin is red and warm. He is tachycardic. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Attempt manual reduction and discharge if successful
options.B: Refer to the routine hernia clinic
options.C: Fit a truss and review in six weeks
options.E: Admit for analgesia and observation overnight

correct_answer: D. Resuscitate and arrange emergency surgery
why_correct: A previously reducible hernia that has become painful, tense and irreducible, with vomiting, absent flatus, red overlying skin and tachycardia, is obstructed and strangulated, meaning the blood supply to its contents is compromised. He needs resuscitation with IV fluids, analgesia, a nasogastric tube and emergency surgery to assess bowel viability, resect any dead bowel and repair the hernia.
why_wrong: A. Forcing reduction of a strangulated hernia can push dead bowel back into the abdomen. B. A routine clinic is far too slow for a surgical emergency. C. A truss has no role in an irreducible or strangulated hernia. E. Observation delays surgery and allows bowel to infarct and perforate.
pearl: Painful, tense, irreducible hernia with obstruction or skin changes means strangulation: no forceful reduction, but resuscitation and emergency surgery. Red skin and tachycardia suggest ischaemic bowel.
thinking: Known hernia, now irreducible and painful ↓ Vomiting and no flatus: obstruction ↓ Tender, red overlying skin and tachycardia ↓ Strangulation with threatened bowel ↓ Resuscitation and emergency surgery
exam_trap: A, Attempt manual reduction and discharge if successful — reduction can work for a recently incarcerated hernia without obstruction. But with red skin, obstruction and tachycardia the bowel may be ischaemic, and reducing it hides the problem.
takeaway: Irreducible, tender hernia with obstruction or skin changes: resuscitate and operate urgently.

stem: A 54-year-old woman tells her GP that over the past two months her right nipple has become pulled inwards, and she can feel a firm area beneath it. On examination there is a hard, irregular mass behind the right nipple, fixed to the overlying tissue, and a firm node in the right axilla. She had a normal screening mammogram two years ago. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Wait for her next screening mammogram
options.B: Review after her next period to see whether it changes
options.C: Urgent suspected cancer referral to a breast clinic for triple assessment
options.D: Prescribe antibiotics for presumed duct ectasia
options.E: Request a breast ultrasound from primary care and act on the result

correct_answer: C. Urgent suspected cancer referral to a breast clinic for triple assessment
why_correct: A new hard, irregular, fixed breast mass with nipple retraction and an axillary node is highly suspicious for breast cancer. NICE recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 30 and over with an unexplained breast lump. The breast clinic performs triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (mammography and ultrasound) and core biopsy.
why_wrong: A. Screening is for women without symptoms, and waiting would delay diagnosis. B. A hard, fixed lump with nipple retraction should not be observed through a cycle. D. Duct ectasia does not explain a hard, fixed mass with an axillary node, and antibiotics delay diagnosis. E. Imaging is arranged as part of triple assessment at the breast clinic, not by the GP.
pearl: Hard, fixed, irregular breast lump with skin or nipple changes or an axillary node needs urgent referral for triple assessment. A recent normal mammogram does not exclude cancer.
thinking: New breast mass in a woman over 30 ↓ Hard, irregular and fixed ↓ Nipple retraction and axillary node ↓ Highly suspicious for cancer ↓ Urgent referral for triple assessment
exam_trap: A, Wait for her next screening mammogram — she is within the screening programme and had a normal mammogram recently. But screening is for women without symptoms; a symptomatic lump needs urgent referral regardless.
takeaway: Suspicious breast lump: urgent referral for triple assessment, regardless of recent screening.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who tends to be constipated has had two months of tearing pain when she opens her bowels, followed by a burning ache lasting about an hour. She has noticed streaks of bright red blood on the toilet paper. When the buttocks are gently parted, there is a linear split at the posterior midline of the anal verge with a small skin tag at its outer end. Digital rectal examination is deferred because of pain. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Topical glyceryl trinitrate with dietary fibre, fluids and a bulk-forming laxative
options.E: Oral metronidazole and referral to exclude a fistula

correct_answer: A. Topical glyceryl trinitrate with dietary fibre, fluids and a bulk-forming laxative
why_correct: Severe pain on defecation with bright red bleeding and a posterior midline tear is an anal fissure; symptoms for more than six weeks and a sentinel skin tag show it is chronic. First-line treatment is softening the stool (fibre, fluids, laxatives) with a topical agent that relaxes the internal sphincter, such as glyceryl trinitrate ointment, or diltiazem as an alternative. Surgery is considered only if this fails.
why_wrong: B. Sphincterotomy is reserved for fissures that do not heal with medical treatment, because of the risk of incontinence. C. Banding treats internal haemorrhoids, which are painless. D. Topical steroids do not help a fissure to heal. E. There is no abscess or fistula, and metronidazole is not standard treatment.
pearl: Anal fissure: pain on defecation with bright red blood, usually posterior midline. Off-midline or multiple fissures should prompt a search for Crohn's disease, infection or malignancy.
thinking: Tearing pain on defecation and bright red blood ↓ Posterior midline split ↓ Over six weeks with a sentinel tag: chronic fissure ↓ Relax the sphincter and soften the stool ↓ Topical GTN with fibre and laxatives
exam_trap: B, Referral for lateral internal sphincterotomy — it heals most chronic fissures and the fissure here is chronic. But medical treatment comes first, and surgery carries a risk of incontinence.
takeaway: Chronic anal fissure: topical GTN or diltiazem with stool softening first; surgery only if it fails.

stem: A 21-year-old woman found a lump in her left breast while showering three weeks ago. It has not changed through her menstrual cycle. On examination there is a 2 cm smooth, rubbery, well-defined lump that moves freely under the fingers and is not tender. There are no skin or nipple changes and no axillary nodes. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Reassure that it is a fibroadenoma and discharge without referral
options.B: Prescribe antibiotics and review in two weeks
options.C: Probable fibroadenoma — refer to a breast clinic for triple assessment
options.D: Aspirate the lump in the surgery

correct_answer: C. Probable fibroadenoma — refer to a breast clinic for triple assessment
why_correct: A smooth, rubbery, well-defined and highly mobile painless lump in a young woman is most likely a fibroadenoma. However, a new discrete lump should still be assessed in a breast clinic, where triple assessment (examination, ultrasound and biopsy if needed) confirms the diagnosis. Once confirmed, most fibroadenomas can be left alone, with excision offered if large, growing or troublesome.
why_wrong: A. A clinical diagnosis alone is not enough; a discrete lump needs specialist assessment to confirm it. B. There are no signs of infection. D. Aspiration in primary care is not appropriate for a solid lump and is not part of GP management. E. Wide excision is for phyllodes tumours or cancer, not a presumed fibroadenoma.
pearl: A smooth, mobile, rubbery lump in a young woman is usually a fibroadenoma, but it should be confirmed by triple assessment before reassurance. Most can then be left alone.
thinking: Young woman with a discrete breast lump ↓ Smooth, rubbery, very mobile, painless ↓ Probable fibroadenoma ↓ Diagnosis still needs confirming ↓ Breast clinic for triple assessment
exam_trap: A, Reassure that it is a fibroadenoma and discharge without referral — the features are classic, and cancer is rare at 21. But a new discrete lump still needs triple assessment to confirm the diagnosis before she is reassured.
takeaway: Probable fibroadenoma still needs triple assessment; once confirmed, it can usually be observed.

stem: An 82-year-old man with Parkinson's disease and long-standing constipation is on a medical ward. Over two days his abdomen has become hugely distended and drum-like, he has passed no stool or wind, and he has started to vomit. His abdomen is not peritonitic, his lactate is normal and he is haemodynamically stable. An abdominal X-ray shows a massively dilated loop of bowel arising from the left side of the pelvis and extending towards the right upper quadrant, shaped like a coffee bean. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Phosphate enema and regular oral laxatives
options.E: Endoscopic decompression with a flexible sigmoidoscope and a flatus tube

correct_answer: E. Endoscopic decompression with a flexible sigmoidoscope and a flatus tube
why_correct: A massively dilated, coffee bean-shaped loop arising from the pelvis in an elderly, constipated man with neurological disease is sigmoid volvulus. Without peritonitis or signs of ischaemia, first-line management is endoscopic decompression with a flexible sigmoidoscope, leaving a flatus tube in place. Emergency surgery is needed if decompression fails or bowel ischaemia or perforation is suspected, and recurrence is common.
why_wrong: A. Enemas and laxatives do not untwist a volvulus and laxatives can worsen obstruction. B. Right hemicolectomy is for caecal volvulus, which arises on the right. C. Neostigmine treats colonic pseudo-obstruction, where there is no twist. D. This is an acute obstruction that needs decompression now, not elective investigation.
pearl: Sigmoid volvulus: elderly, constipated, often with neurological or psychiatric illness; coffee bean sign from the pelvis. Decompress with a flexible sigmoidoscope unless there is peritonitis.
thinking: Elderly, constipated, Parkinson's disease ↓ Massive distension with no stool or flatus ↓ Coffee bean loop from the left pelvis ↓ No peritonitis or ischaemia ↓ Endoscopic decompression
exam_trap: C, Intravenous neostigmine — colonic pseudo-obstruction also causes massive distension in frail elderly inpatients. But the coffee bean loop shows a twist, which neostigmine cannot correct and which needs decompression.
takeaway: Sigmoid volvulus without peritonitis: endoscopic decompression with a flatus tube first.

stem: A 68-year-old woman tells her GP about a small, painless swelling in her right groin that she noticed three weeks ago. On examination there is a soft, non-tender lump below the inguinal ligament, inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It does not disappear when she lies down and is not reducible. There is no thrill on coughing and no varicose veins. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.A: Direct inguinal hernia — watchful waiting as it is painless
options.C: Femoral hernia — prompt surgical referral for repair
options.D: Inguinal lymph node — observe and review in six weeks
options.E: Indirect inguinal hernia — fit a truss

correct_answer: C. Femoral hernia — prompt surgical referral for repair
why_correct: A groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, in an older woman, is a femoral hernia; inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the tubercle. Femoral hernias pass through a narrow, rigid femoral canal, are often irreducible and carry a high risk of strangulation. They should be referred promptly for repair even when painless.
why_wrong: A. An inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle, and watchful waiting is unsafe for a femoral hernia. B. A saphena varix disappears on lying down, has a cough thrill and usually accompanies varicose veins. D. A lymph node is usually firm and may be multiple; this is a hernia in a typical position and should not be observed. E. The lump is not inguinal, and trusses have no role.
pearl: Femoral hernia: below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, commonest in older women, often irreducible and at high risk of strangulation. Refer for repair even if painless.
thinking: Groin lump in an older woman ↓ Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle ↓ Irreducible, no thrill, no varicose veins ↓ Femoral hernia with high strangulation risk ↓ Prompt surgical repair
exam_trap: A, Direct inguinal hernia — watchful waiting as it is painless — watchful waiting is acceptable for small, painless inguinal hernias. But the position below and lateral to the pubic tubercle makes this femoral, where strangulation risk makes repair essential.
takeaway: Lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral: refer for repair even if painless.

stem: A 42-year-old woman attends the emergency department with sudden, severe right loin pain that comes in waves and spreads to her groin. She cannot keep still and has vomited. She is afebrile, her urine dipstick shows blood, and a pregnancy test is negative. Her kidney function is normal and she has no history of peptic ulcer, asthma or heart disease. What is the most appropriate analgesia and imaging?

options.A: Intravenous morphine and a renal ultrasound
options.C: Oral paracetamol and a plain KUB X-ray
options.D: Intravenous paracetamol and contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen
options.E: Intramuscular or rectal diclofenac and non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder

correct_answer: E. Intramuscular or rectal diclofenac and non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder
why_correct: Loin-to-groin colicky pain, restlessness and haematuria indicate renal colic. NICE recommends an NSAID by any route as first-line analgesia, with paracetamol if NSAIDs are unsuitable and opioids only if both are contraindicated or ineffective. Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder is the imaging of choice in adults, ideally within 24 hours, and ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy and children.
why_wrong: A. Opioids are not first-line, and ultrasound is less accurate than CT for ureteric stones in non-pregnant adults. B. Nephrostomy is for an obstructed, infected kidney, and she is afebrile. C. Plain X-ray misses many stones and oral paracetamol alone is inadequate here. D. Contrast is not needed to detect stones and can obscure them.
pearl: Renal colic: NSAID first, opioid only if NSAIDs and paracetamol are unsuitable or ineffective; non-contrast CT KUB for adults. Fever with obstruction is an emergency needing drainage.
thinking: Loin-to-groin colicky pain, restless ↓ Haematuria, afebrile, not pregnant ↓ Renal colic ↓ NSAID is most effective first-line analgesia ↓ NSAID plus non-contrast CT KUB
exam_trap: A, Intravenous morphine and a renal ultrasound — the pain is severe, and ultrasound avoids radiation. But NSAIDs are more effective for renal colic than opioids, and non-contrast CT is the most accurate test in non-pregnant adults.
takeaway: Renal colic: NSAID first-line analgesia and non-contrast CT KUB in non-pregnant adults.

stem: A 76-year-old man attends the emergency department because he has not passed urine for ten hours and has severe lower abdominal pain. For a year he has had hesitancy and a weak stream, and two days ago he started a cold remedy containing an antihistamine and a decongestant. There is a tender, dull swelling above the pubis, and a bladder scan shows a large volume of urine. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.B: Start tamsulosin and arrange urology clinic review
options.D: Book for transurethral resection of the prostate
options.E: Encourage him to try passing urine in a warm bath and rescan in four hours

why_correct: Painful inability to pass urine with a palpable, dull bladder and a large volume on scanning is acute urinary retention, here likely triggered by an anticholinergic and decongestant on a background of benign prostatic enlargement. Immediate urethral catheterisation relieves pain and decompresses the bladder; the residual volume is recorded and kidney function checked. The cold remedy is stopped, and an alpha-blocker is started before a trial without catheter.
why_wrong: B. Tamsulosin helps before a trial without catheter but does not relieve retention now. C. Suprapubic catheterisation is used when urethral catheterisation fails or is contraindicated. D. TURP may be needed later but is not an emergency treatment. E. He is in pain with a large bladder volume, and delaying drainage is inappropriate.
pearl: Acute urinary retention: catheterise urethrally first, record the residual volume, check kidney function, stop drugs that cause retention, start an alpha-blocker and arrange a trial without catheter.
thinking: Painful inability to pass urine ↓ Distended bladder confirmed on scan ↓ Prostate symptoms plus a new anticholinergic decongestant ↓ Acute urinary retention ↓ Urethral catheterisation
exam_trap: B, Start tamsulosin and arrange urology clinic review — alpha-blockers are the treatment for the underlying prostatic obstruction. But they take time to work and do not empty a painfully distended bladder now.
takeaway: Acute urinary retention: urethral catheter first, then an alpha-blocker before a trial without catheter.

stem: A 74-year-old retired lorry driver attends his GP surgery to discuss a blood test arranged by a locum, which showed a raised PSA. For several months he has been getting up three times a night to pass urine. Rectal examination reveals an asymmetrical prostate with a firm, craggy left lobe; it is not tender and he is afebrile. Urine dipstick is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Recheck the PSA in two months to see whether it is rising
options.B: Prescribe an alpha-blocker and review his nocturia in three months
options.C: Refer on the urology suspected cancer pathway
options.D: Start a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor to shrink the gland
options.E: Prescribe a quinolone for presumed chronic prostatitis

correct_answer: C. Refer on the urology suspected cancer pathway
why_correct: A prostate that feels hard, irregular or craggy on rectal examination is suspicious of cancer, and together with a raised PSA it needs referral on the suspected cancer pathway. In secondary care he will usually have multiparametric MRI followed by biopsy if indicated. An abnormal examination alone justifies referral, whatever the PSA.
why_wrong: A. Repeating the PSA only delays assessment of a gland that already feels malignant. B. An alpha-blocker may help his urinary symptoms but does nothing about suspected cancer. D. A 5-alpha reductase inhibitor lowers PSA and can mask cancer, and the gland needs assessment first. E. He has no pain, fever or tenderness, and antibiotics would delay diagnosis.
pearl: Never let urinary symptoms distract you: the rectal examination finding drives the decision. A craggy, asymmetrical prostate is a reason for suspected cancer referral on its own.
thinking: Older man with nocturia and raised PSA ↓ Rectal examination: hard, craggy, asymmetrical lobe ↓ No features of infection ↓ Suspected prostate cancer ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: A, recheck the PSA — PSA does fluctuate, so a repeat test feels careful. But the abnormal rectal examination is itself a referral criterion, and waiting for a second result only delays diagnosis.
takeaway: A hard or craggy prostate on examination needs suspected cancer referral, whatever the PSA does next.

stem: A 63-year-old woman telephones her GP practice because she passed bright red urine once yesterday morning. She has had no burning, frequency or loin pain. A urine sample she drops off later is positive for blood only, with no nitrites or leucocytes. She has smoked about 20 cigarettes a day for most of her adult life and takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Refer on the urology suspected cancer pathway
options.B: Send the urine for culture and start trimethoprim
options.C: Arrange a renal ultrasound and refer only if it is abnormal
options.D: Repeat the dipstick in a month and refer if blood persists
options.E: Offer a routine urology appointment if the bleeding recurs

correct_answer: A. Refer on the urology suspected cancer pathway
why_correct: Unexplained visible haematuria in an older adult, with no evidence of infection, must be treated as possible urothelial cancer until proven otherwise. Smoking is the main risk factor for bladder cancer. She needs a suspected cancer referral for cystoscopy and imaging of the upper urinary tract.
why_wrong: B. There are no urinary symptoms or nitrites to suggest infection, and treating one would delay diagnosis. C. A normal ultrasound does not exclude bladder cancer, which needs cystoscopy. D. A single episode of visible haematuria is enough to refer, and waiting delays diagnosis. E. Bladder cancer often bleeds intermittently, so waiting for a second episode is unsafe.
pearl: Bladder cancer classically bleeds painlessly and intermittently, so one episode that has stopped is still a red flag. The bleeding stopping is not reassurance.
thinking: Single episode of frank haematuria ↓ No pain, no infection on dipstick ↓ Older smoker ↓ Possible urothelial cancer ↓ Suspected cancer referral for cystoscopy and imaging
exam_trap: E, routine referral if it recurs — the bleeding has stopped and she feels well, so waiting seems reasonable. But bladder tumours bleed intermittently, and one episode of unexplained visible haematuria at this age warrants urgent referral now.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria in an older adult without infection means urgent cystoscopy referral.

stem: A 31-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic worried about an infection because his right testis feels heavier than the left. He has no pain, urethral discharge or dysuria. On examination there is a firm, irregular, non-tender area that cannot be separated from the body of the right testis. The epididymis feels normal, and a torch held against the scrotum does not light up the swelling. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: First-void urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, then review
options.B: Fine-needle aspiration of the swelling in clinic
options.C: Repeat examination after a course of doxycycline
options.E: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis

why_correct: A firm, painless swelling arising from the body of the testis in a young man is a testicular tumour until proven otherwise. Urgent scrotal ultrasound is the first investigation, with serum tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG and LDH) taken alongside. Testicular cancer is highly curable when diagnosed early.
why_wrong: A. He has no features of infection, and screening for STIs would delay assessment of a probable tumour. B. Needling a suspected testicular tumour through the scrotum is avoided because it risks tumour seeding. C. A painless intratesticular mass is not epididymitis, and antibiotics delay diagnosis. E. CT is used for staging once a tumour is confirmed, not as the first test.
pearl: Location is the key: lumps you can separate from the testis are usually benign, but a lump within the body of the testis needs urgent ultrasound.
thinking: Young man with a heavy testis ↓ Firm, painless lump inseparable from the testis ↓ Does not transilluminate, epididymis normal ↓ Probable testicular tumour ↓ Urgent scrotal ultrasound
exam_trap: A, NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea — the setting is a sexual health clinic and he is worried about infection, so testing feels natural. But there is no pain or discharge, and an intratesticular mass needs imaging first.
takeaway: A painless lump within the body of the testis needs urgent scrotal ultrasound and tumour markers.

stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the emergency department. Two days ago she developed burning on passing urine, and since last night she has had shivering attacks, vomiting and an ache in her right flank. Her temperature is 38.9°C and a pregnancy test is negative. She is markedly tender when the right costovertebral angle is percussed, but the abdomen is otherwise soft. Urinalysis shows leucocytes and nitrites. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Lower urinary tract infection — three days of nitrofurantoin
options.B: Acute pyelonephritis — antibiotics for upper urinary tract infection, IV if she cannot tolerate oral
options.C: Renal colic — NSAID analgesia and CT KUB
options.E: Pelvic inflammatory disease — ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazole

correct_answer: B. Acute pyelonephritis — antibiotics for upper urinary tract infection, IV if she cannot tolerate oral
why_correct: Lower urinary symptoms followed by fever, rigors, vomiting and loin tenderness indicate infection that has ascended to the kidney. Acute pyelonephritis needs an antibiotic that achieves good renal tissue levels, guided by local policy and urine culture. Because she is vomiting, intravenous treatment and admission are appropriate until she can take oral therapy.
why_wrong: A. Fever, rigors and loin tenderness mean upper-tract infection, and nitrofurantoin does not reach adequate kidney levels. C. Renal colic causes severe colicky pain radiating to the groin, not fever with nitrite-positive urine. D. Appendicitis causes right iliac fossa pain and would not explain dysuria with nitrites and loin tenderness. E. Pelvic inflammatory disease causes lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness, not loin pain with infected urine.
pearl: Ask yourself whether the infection is in the bladder or the kidney: fever, rigors and loin tenderness move you away from nitrofurantoin to an antibiotic that treats the kidney.
thinking: Dysuria followed by fever and rigors ↓ Vomiting and right loin pain ↓ Renal angle tenderness with nitrites and leucocytes ↓ Upper urinary tract infection ↓ Acute pyelonephritis treated with appropriate antibiotics, IV if vomiting
exam_trap: A, three days of nitrofurantoin — dysuria with nitrites looks like a simple cystitis. But systemic features and loin tenderness mean pyelonephritis, where nitrofurantoin is ineffective and a short course is inadequate.
takeaway: Dysuria plus fever, rigors and loin tenderness is pyelonephritis: avoid nitrofurantoin, treat the kidney.

stem: A 55-year-old man who smokes and has raised cholesterol sees his GP. Over the past 18 months he has found it progressively harder to achieve an erection firm enough for intercourse. His libido is normal and his relationship is good. He takes atorvastatin and no other medication. Examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Assess his cardiovascular risk and offer a PDE5 inhibitor such as sildenafil
options.C: Psychosexual counselling as his only treatment
options.D: Referral to urology for a penile prosthesis
options.E: Sildenafil, advising that GTN spray can be used safely alongside it

correct_answer: B. Assess his cardiovascular risk and offer a PDE5 inhibitor such as sildenafil
why_correct: Gradual-onset erectile dysfunction with preserved libido in a man with vascular risk factors is usually vasculogenic and can be an early marker of cardiovascular disease. He should have his cardiovascular risk assessed (blood pressure, lipids, glucose or HbA1c) and be offered a PDE5 inhibitor first-line. PDE5 inhibitors must not be taken with nitrates because the combination can cause profound hypotension.
why_wrong: A. Testosterone is for confirmed hypogonadism, and his normal libido makes that unlikely. C. A gradual, organic-sounding picture with vascular risk factors is not purely psychogenic. D. A prosthesis is reserved for failure of medical treatment. E. Nitrates such as GTN are contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors because of the risk of severe hypotension.
pearl: Erectile dysfunction can precede a coronary event by years: treat the symptom and look for vascular disease. Always ask about nitrates before prescribing sildenafil.
thinking: Gradual erectile dysfunction, libido preserved ↓ Smoker with raised cholesterol ↓ Likely vascular cause and marker of cardiovascular risk ↓ Assess cardiovascular risk ↓ First-line PDE5 inhibitor, never with nitrates
exam_trap: E, sildenafil with GTN allowed — sildenafil is the right drug, so this option looks correct at first glance. But nitrates with a PDE5 inhibitor can cause profound hypotension, so the safety advice is dangerously wrong.
takeaway: Erectile dysfunction is a vascular warning sign: check cardiovascular risk, offer a PDE5 inhibitor, never with nitrates.

stem: A 24-year-old man attends the emergency department with a two-day history of a steadily worsening ache in his left testis, now with redness and swelling of the scrotum and some stinging when he passes urine. He has a new sexual partner. His temperature is 37.9°C. The left epididymis is thickened and tender, the testis lies in a normal position, lifting the scrotum eases his pain, and the cremasteric reflex is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Epididymo-orchitis — testicular torsion must still be considered
options.D: Testicular tumour — urgent ultrasound and tumour markers

correct_answer: A. Epididymo-orchitis — testicular torsion must still be considered
why_correct: A gradual onset of testicular pain with epididymal tenderness, urinary symptoms, low-grade fever, pain relieved by elevation and a preserved cremasteric reflex points to epididymo-orchitis, most often due to chlamydia or gonorrhoea in a sexually active young man. No single sign reliably excludes torsion, so if there is any doubt urgent urological review is needed. Once torsion is excluded, he needs STI testing and antibiotics.
why_wrong: B. Torsion is usually sudden and severe with a high-riding testis and an absent cremasteric reflex, unlike this gradual picture. C. Appendix testis torsion mainly affects prepubertal boys and causes a small tender nodule at the upper pole. D. Tumours usually present as a painless lump rather than painful, inflamed swelling with urinary symptoms. E. A hernia arises from the groin, and there is no groin swelling or obstruction described.
pearl: Epididymo-orchitis is a diagnosis made only once torsion has been confidently excluded. When in doubt, the surgeon explores.
thinking: Gradual scrotal pain over two days ↓ Dysuria, new partner, low-grade fever ↓ Tender epididymis, relief on elevation, cremasteric reflex present ↓ Epididymo-orchitis ↓ Keep torsion in mind until excluded
exam_trap: B, testicular torsion — every acute scrotum should make you think of torsion, so it is tempting to choose exploration. But the slow onset, urinary symptoms, epididymal tenderness and preserved reflex favour infection, while torsion is still kept in mind.
takeaway: Gradual scrotal pain with urinary symptoms suggests epididymo-orchitis, but always consider torsion first.

stem: A 79-year-old man on the orthopaedic ward had a urinary catheter inserted after repair of a hip fracture. The nurse calls you because the end of his penis has become swollen and painful over the past few hours. The foreskin is retracted behind the glans and forms a tight, oedematous ring, and the nurse has been unable to pull it forward. The glans is swollen but pink. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Add him to a routine circumcision list
options.B: Apply a topical steroid cream and review tomorrow
options.C: Start oral flucloxacillin for cellulitis of the foreskin
options.D: Remove the catheter and wait for the swelling to settle
options.E: Prompt manual reduction with analgesia, escalating to urology if it fails

correct_answer: E. Prompt manual reduction with analgesia, escalating to urology if it fails
why_correct: This is paraphimosis: the retracted foreskin has become trapped behind the glans and acts as a constricting band. It is a urological emergency because worsening oedema can compromise blood supply to the glans. Treatment is prompt manual reduction with good analgesia and measures to reduce the swelling, with urgent urology input for a dorsal slit if reduction fails.
why_wrong: A. Circumcision may be considered later, but the constriction needs relieving now. B. Topical steroids are used for phimosis and do not release a tight band behind the glans. C. There is no infection, and antibiotics do not relieve the constriction. D. Paraphimosis does not reliably resolve on its own, and waiting risks ischaemia of the glans.
pearl: After catheterisation or penile examination, always return the foreskin to its normal position. A forgotten retracted foreskin is the classic cause of paraphimosis in hospital.
thinking: Recent catheterisation ↓ Foreskin retracted and stuck behind the glans ↓ Tight oedematous ring with swollen glans ↓ Paraphimosis, risk of ischaemia ↓ Urgent manual reduction with analgesia
exam_trap: D, remove the catheter and wait — the catheter seems to be the cause, so removing it feels logical. But the trapped foreskin will not reduce by itself, and delay risks loss of blood supply to the glans.
takeaway: Paraphimosis is an emergency: reduce the foreskin promptly and call urology if you cannot.

stem: A 34-year-old woman attends her 8-week postnatal check at the GP surgery. For the past month she has felt low and tearful on most days, no longer enjoys anything, feels she is failing as a mother and is struggling to concentrate. She wakes early even when her baby is asleep. She has no thoughts of harming herself or the baby and no psychotic symptoms. She is exclusively breastfeeding and wants to continue. Guided self-help has not helped, and she asks about medication. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure her that this is the baby blues
options.B: Advise her to stop breastfeeding before she starts an antidepressant
options.C: Arrange same-day admission to a mother-and-baby unit
options.E: Start sertraline while she continues to breastfeed, with regular review and psychological support

correct_answer: E. Start sertraline while she continues to breastfeed, with regular review and psychological support
why_correct: Persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, poor concentration and early waking for a month after delivery are postnatal depression, not baby blues. She has not improved with self-help and wants medication, so an antidepressant is appropriate alongside psychological therapy. Sertraline is a suitable choice because it passes into breast milk in only small amounts, and she should be reviewed regularly, with referral to specialist perinatal services if symptoms are severe or worsen.
why_wrong: A. Baby blues start in the first week and settle within about two weeks; her symptoms are persistent and more severe. B. Sertraline is compatible with breastfeeding, so she does not need to stop. C. Mother-and-baby unit admission is for severe illness, psychosis or high risk, which she does not have. D. St John's wort is not recommended because its safety and drug interactions are uncertain.
pearl: Ask about thoughts of self-harm and harm to the baby at every perinatal mental health assessment. Breastfeeding is not a reason to withhold appropriate treatment.
thinking: Eight weeks postpartum ↓ A month of low mood, anhedonia, guilt and early waking ↓ No risk or psychosis, self-help failed ↓ Postnatal depression ↓ Sertraline while breastfeeding, plus support and review
exam_trap: B, stop breastfeeding first — many mothers and clinicians worry about medicines in breast milk. But sertraline is considered compatible with breastfeeding, and stopping removes a benefit she values.
takeaway: Postnatal depression can be treated with sertraline while the mother continues to breastfeed.

stem: A 46-year-old man was admitted to the surgical ward three days ago with acute pancreatitis. He drinks heavily every day. Tonight the nurses find him shaking, sweating and frightened, picking at insects he believes are crawling on the bed sheets, and he does not know where he is. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse 118/min and blood pressure 158/94 mmHg. Capillary glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Intramuscular haloperidol as the main treatment
options.C: Oral thiamine with zopiclone at night
options.D: A benzodiazepine (parenterally if he cannot take oral) plus intravenous thiamine

correct_answer: D. A benzodiazepine (parenterally if he cannot take oral) plus intravenous thiamine
why_correct: Confusion, visual hallucinations, tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension and fever around three days after stopping alcohol are delirium tremens. It is a medical emergency, treated with a benzodiazepine such as chlordiazepoxide or lorazepam, which reduces the risk of seizures and death. High-dose intravenous thiamine is also given to prevent or treat Wernicke's encephalopathy, and he needs close monitoring and supportive care.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotics do not treat withdrawal and can lower the seizure threshold; they are only adjuncts. B. Glucose before thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy, and fluids alone do not treat withdrawal. C. Zopiclone does not treat delirium tremens, and oral thiamine is inadequate in this situation. E. Acamprosate helps maintain abstinence later and has no role in acute withdrawal.
pearl: Patients admitted for other reasons often go into alcohol withdrawal on day 2 or 3 of their stay. Ask about alcohol on admission and plan ahead.
thinking: Heavy drinker admitted three days ago ↓ Confusion with visual hallucinations ↓ Tremor, sweating, tachycardia, fever ↓ Delirium tremens ↓ Benzodiazepine plus IV thiamine
exam_trap: A, IM haloperidol — an agitated, hallucinating patient seems to need an antipsychotic. But it does not treat alcohol withdrawal and can lower the seizure threshold, while benzodiazepines treat the cause.
takeaway: Delirium tremens is treated with benzodiazepines plus parenteral thiamine, not antipsychotics.

stem: A 47-year-old woman is admitted to the surgical ward with gallstone pancreatitis. On her second morning the nurse reports that she is shaky, sweating and restless, and keeps asking to go home. Her pulse is 108/min and blood pressure 152/94 mmHg. She is orientated in time and place and is not seeing or hearing things that are not there. Her partner mentions that she usually drinks a bottle of wine every evening. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: A reducing course of chlordiazepoxide plus thiamine
options.C: Acamprosate to reduce craving, plus thiamine
options.D: Promethazine at night and reassess in the morning
options.E: Supportive care only, as she is not confused

correct_answer: B. A reducing course of chlordiazepoxide plus thiamine
why_correct: These are features of early alcohol withdrawal in a dependent drinker who stopped abruptly on admission. A reducing benzodiazepine regimen such as chlordiazepoxide prevents progression to withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens, and thiamine is given to protect against Wernicke's encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and does nothing for the underlying withdrawal. C. Acamprosate supports abstinence once withdrawal is complete; it does not treat acute withdrawal. D. A sedating antihistamine will not prevent withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. E. Absence of confusion does not mean she is safe; untreated withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens.
pearl: Any dependent drinker admitted to hospital stops drinking abruptly, and withdrawal usually begins within the first day, so ask about alcohol on admission and anticipate it.
thinking: Daily heavy drinking, admitted and stopped abruptly ↓ Tremor, sweating, restlessness, tachycardia; orientated, no hallucinations ↓ Early alcohol withdrawal ↓ Prevent seizures and delirium tremens; protect against Wernicke's ↓ Reducing chlordiazepoxide plus thiamine
exam_trap: A, haloperidol — her restlessness and requests to leave invite sedation with an antipsychotic. But antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not correct the withdrawal state; a benzodiazepine is the treatment.
takeaway: Alcohol withdrawal: reducing benzodiazepine plus thiamine; antipsychotics are not the treatment.

stem: A 31-year-old accountant sees her GP because she keeps turning down promotions that would involve presenting to clients. For years she has dreaded meetings and eating in front of colleagues, fearing she will say something foolish and be judged; her face flushes and her hands tremble in these situations, and she now avoids work social events. She has had a course of individual CBT with partial benefit and would now like to add medication. Which drug is the most appropriate to offer?
why_correct: This is social anxiety disorder: persistent fear of scrutiny and negative evaluation, with avoidance and functional impairment. Individual CBT is the first-line psychological treatment, and when medication is wanted an SSRI such as escitalopram or sertraline is the first-line drug.
why_wrong: B. Benzodiazepines carry a risk of dependence and are not recommended for routine treatment of social anxiety disorder. C. Propranolol may blunt tremor and flushing but does not treat the disorder and is not recommended for routine use. D. Antipsychotics are not used to treat social anxiety disorder. E. Buspirone is not a recommended treatment for social anxiety disorder.
pearl: Social anxiety disorder is fear of being judged, not ordinary shyness; treat with individual CBT and, if medication is wanted, an SSRI rather than beta-blockers or benzodiazepines.
thinking: Long-standing fear of scrutiny and embarrassment ↓ Avoidance with work impairment, autonomic symptoms in social situations ↓ Social anxiety disorder ↓ CBT first; SSRI when medication is chosen ↓ Escitalopram
exam_trap: C, propranolol — the flushing and trembling make a beta-blocker look sensible, and it is sometimes used for occasional performance nerves. But it only masks physical symptoms and is not a recommended treatment for social anxiety disorder.
takeaway: Social anxiety disorder: CBT first; if medication is needed, an SSRI such as escitalopram or sertraline.

stem: A 23-year-old man is seen by the early intervention in psychosis team after his sister becomes worried about him. Over the past five months he has stopped going to college, believes his neighbours have hidden cameras in his flat to monitor him, and hears two voices discussing what he is doing. A urine drug screen, blood tests and physical examination are unremarkable. He agrees to try medication alongside psychological therapy. What is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?

options.C: An oral second-generation antipsychotic such as aripiprazole

correct_answer: C. An oral second-generation antipsychotic such as aripiprazole
why_correct: This is a first episode of psychosis with persecutory delusions and third-person auditory hallucinations, without an organic or substance cause. First-line drug treatment is an oral antipsychotic chosen with the patient after discussing side effects, combined with CBT for psychosis and family intervention; an oral second-generation agent is a common first choice.
why_wrong: A. Lithium is a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder, not first-line treatment for psychosis. B. An antidepressant does not treat psychotic symptoms. D. Clozapine is reserved for schizophrenia that has not responded to adequate trials of two different antipsychotics. E. Long-acting injections are an option later for adherence or patient preference, not the routine starting treatment.
pearl: Clozapine is never first-line: it is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after adequate trials of two different antipsychotics, because of its blood monitoring and serious adverse effects.
thinking: Months of persecutory beliefs, voices discussing him, functional decline ↓ Normal organic and drug screen ↓ First-episode psychosis ↓ Oral antipsychotic plus psychological therapy ↓ Oral second-generation antipsychotic
exam_trap: D, clozapine — it is the most effective antipsychotic and is well known to examiners. But it is reserved for treatment resistance because of agranulocytosis risk and the monitoring burden.
takeaway: First-episode psychosis: oral antipsychotic with CBTp and family intervention; clozapine only for treatment resistance.

stem: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted to a medical ward after several weeks of eating almost nothing. Nasogastric feeding is started. On the third day she complains of muscle weakness and breathlessness, and the cardiac monitor shows new runs of irregular beats. Which blood abnormality is the hallmark of the complication she has most likely developed?
why_correct: Feeding after prolonged starvation triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome and can cause muscle and respiratory weakness, arrhythmias, heart failure and confusion. High-risk patients are fed cautiously with close electrolyte monitoring, replacement and thiamine.
why_wrong: A. Potassium moves into cells during refeeding, so it falls rather than rises. B. Calcium is not the characteristic disturbance of refeeding. C. Refeeding tends to cause sodium and fluid retention rather than hypernatraemia. D. Amylase is not part of the refeeding picture.
pearl: Check phosphate, potassium and magnesium before feeding a malnourished patient and daily in the first days; start feeding slowly and give thiamine before feeding begins.
thinking: Prolonged starvation, then feeding restarted ↓ New weakness, breathlessness and arrhythmias within days ↓ Refeeding syndrome ↓ Insulin drives phosphate into cells ↓ Hypophosphataemia
exam_trap: A, hyperkalaemia — arrhythmias immediately suggest a high potassium. But in refeeding potassium shifts into cells and falls; the defining abnormality is low phosphate.
takeaway: Refeeding syndrome is defined by hypophosphataemia; feed slowly and monitor electrolytes closely.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder was started on citalopram by an out-of-hours doctor three weeks ago for low mood. She takes no mood stabiliser. Her husband phones the community mental health team because she has been spending large sums online, sleeping about two hours a night without feeling tired, and talking rapidly about a business idea that will make her famous. What is the most appropriate change to her medication?

options.A: Continue citalopram and add zopiclone at night
options.B: Increase citalopram to treat residual low mood
options.D: Stop citalopram and start an antipsychotic such as olanzapine

correct_answer: D. Stop citalopram and start an antipsychotic such as olanzapine
why_correct: She has developed a manic episode while taking an antidepressant without mood-stabiliser cover. Antidepressants can precipitate or worsen mania, so citalopram should be stopped and an antimanic drug started; an antipsychotic such as olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone or haloperidol is first-line, with lithium or valproate as alternatives or additions.
why_wrong: A. A hypnotic leaves the antidepressant in place and does not treat the mania. B. Increasing the antidepressant could worsen the manic episode. C. Lamotrigine is used for bipolar depression and does not treat acute mania. E. Swapping one SSRI for another still exposes her to an antidepressant during mania.
pearl: When a patient with bipolar disorder becomes manic, check the drug chart: an antidepressant without mood-stabiliser cover is a common trigger.
thinking: Bipolar disorder, recently started on an SSRI without a mood stabiliser ↓ Reduced need for sleep, overspending, pressured speech, grandiosity ↓ Antidepressant-associated mania ↓ Remove the trigger and treat the mania ↓ Stop citalopram and start an antipsychotic
exam_trap: A, adding zopiclone — sleep loss is prominent and a hypnotic feels practical. But it leaves the antidepressant fuelling the episode and does not treat the mania.
takeaway: Mania while on an antidepressant: stop the antidepressant and start an antimanic drug.

stem: A 28-year-old man tells his GP that he is late for work most days because he must check that the cooker, taps and door locks are off, repeating the sequence until it feels right, often for over an hour. He has recurring unwanted images of his flat catching fire, which he knows are irrational but cannot dismiss. His mood is otherwise normal. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: Lorazepam when the urges are strong
options.B: CBT including exposure and response prevention

correct_answer: B. CBT including exposure and response prevention
why_correct: Intrusive, unwanted images that he recognises as his own and irrational, neutralised by repetitive checking that consumes time and impairs function, is obsessive-compulsive disorder. First-line treatment is CBT incorporating exposure and response prevention, with an SSRI as an alternative or addition depending on severity and preference.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines may ease anxiety briefly but do not treat OCD and risk dependence. C. Antipsychotics are only used by specialists as augmentation, never as monotherapy. D. Psychodynamic therapy is not an evidence-based first-line treatment for OCD. E. Pregabalin is not a treatment for OCD.
pearl: In OCD the patient recognises the obsessions as products of their own mind; if the thoughts are believed to be inserted from outside, consider psychosis instead.
thinking: Recurrent intrusive images he knows are irrational ↓ Repeated checking to relieve anxiety, consuming time and impairing work ↓ Obsessive-compulsive disorder ↓ First-line: CBT with ERP and/or an SSRI ↓ CBT including exposure and response prevention
exam_trap: A, a benzodiazepine — the distress and urgency suggest an anxiolytic. But benzodiazepines do not reduce obsessions or compulsions and carry a risk of dependence.
takeaway: OCD: CBT with exposure and response prevention and/or an SSRI.

stem: A 41-year-old bus driver sees his GP four months after his bus was involved in a fatal collision. He wakes most nights from vivid dreams of the crash, sometimes feels he is back at the scene when he hears brakes screech, is constantly on edge, and has refused to drive since. He is struggling at home and has not returned to work. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.B: A single session of psychological debriefing
options.C: Watchful waiting for a further three months

why_correct: Re-experiencing (nightmares and flashbacks), avoidance and hyperarousal persisting for months after a traumatic event, with impairment, is post-traumatic stress disorder. First-line treatment is a trauma-focused psychological therapy: individual trauma-focused CBT, or EMDR for non-combat trauma.
why_wrong: A. A hypnotic does not treat PTSD and risks dependence. B. Psychological debriefing is not recommended and may worsen outcomes. C. Symptoms are established and impairing months after the event, so active treatment is needed rather than waiting. D. Antipsychotics are not first-line and are only considered by specialists for disabling symptoms that have not responded to other treatment.
pearl: Do not offer psychological debriefing after trauma; watchful waiting may suit mild symptoms in the first weeks, but established PTSD needs trauma-focused therapy.
thinking: Fatal crash months ago ↓ Nightmares and flashbacks, avoidance of driving, hypervigilance ↓ Persistent impairment ↓ Post-traumatic stress disorder ↓ Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR
exam_trap: A, zopiclone — disturbed sleep is the most tangible complaint. But a hypnotic does not treat the disorder and risks dependence; trauma-focused therapy addresses the nightmares and the rest.
takeaway: PTSD: trauma-focused CBT or EMDR first; no debriefing and no routine first-line drugs.

stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia that has not responded to two different antipsychotics is to start clozapine. The ward pharmacist explains that he must be registered with a monitoring service and attend for regular blood tests, weekly at first. What is the main serious adverse effect these blood tests are designed to detect?
why_correct: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia and agranulocytosis, which may be fatal through overwhelming infection. It is supplied only with mandatory registered full blood count monitoring, most frequent in the early months, and is stopped if the neutrophil count falls significantly. Patients are told to report sore throat, fever or flu-like symptoms promptly.
why_wrong: A. Hypothyroidism is a recognised effect of lithium rather than the reason for clozapine blood monitoring. B. Clozapine causes little rise in prolactin compared with many antipsychotics. D. Kidney injury is not the target of clozapine monitoring. E. Hyponatraemia is not the dangerous effect that clozapine monitoring is designed to detect.
pearl: Other serious clozapine effects are myocarditis early in treatment, severe constipation with risk of ileus, hypersalivation and seizures at higher doses.
thinking: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia starting clozapine ↓ Mandatory registered blood monitoring, most frequent early ↓ Risk of neutropenia leading to fatal sepsis ↓ Full blood count tracks neutrophils ↓ Agranulocytosis
exam_trap: B, hyperprolactinaemia — antipsychotics as a group are linked to raised prolactin. But clozapine has little prolactin effect, and its blood monitoring targets neutrophils.
takeaway: Clozapine: mandatory FBC monitoring for agranulocytosis; also watch for myocarditis and constipation.

stem: A community midwife visits a 29-year-old woman eight days after an uncomplicated delivery. Her partner says she has hardly slept for three nights, is pacing and talking rapidly, and switches between laughter and tears. She tells the midwife that the baby was swapped at the hospital and is not really hers, and at times she seems unsure where she is. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Same-day psychiatric assessment with admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit
options.B: Reassure that this is the baby blues and review in a week
options.C: Start sertraline and arrange GP review
options.D: Routine referral to the perinatal mental health team
options.E: Sleep hygiene advice and promethazine at night

correct_answer: A. Same-day psychiatric assessment with admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit
why_correct: Rapid onset of mood instability, sleeplessness, confusion and delusions about the baby in the first weeks after birth is postpartum (puerperal) psychosis. It is a psychiatric emergency with risk of suicide and harm to the infant, needing same-day specialist assessment and usually admission to a mother-and-baby unit.
why_wrong: B. Baby blues causes mild tearfulness in the first days after birth without psychotic features or confusion. C. Treating this as postnatal depression misses an emergency, and an antidepressant could worsen a mood-driven psychosis. D. A routine referral is far too slow for a condition that can deteriorate within hours. E. Sedation and sleep advice do not address the psychosis or the risk.
pearl: Pre-existing bipolar disorder or a previous puerperal psychosis are the strongest risk factors; these women need a perinatal mental health plan before delivery.
thinking: Days after delivery ↓ Insomnia, labile mood, confusion, delusion about the baby ↓ Postpartum psychosis ↓ Psychiatric emergency with risk to mother and baby ↓ Same-day assessment and admission to a mother-and-baby unit
exam_trap: B, baby blues — the timing in the first week and the tearfulness fit. But baby blues never involves delusions or confusion; those features mean psychosis.
takeaway: Delusions or confusion after childbirth mean postpartum psychosis: same-day psychiatric admission.

stem: A 2-year-old girl is admitted to the paediatric ward for the fourth time in six months with reported episodes of going floppy and blue at home. Every episode has been described only by her mother. EEG, cardiac investigations, a metabolic screen and overnight oximetry have all been normal, and no episode has occurred in hospital. The mother is now asking for further specialist referrals and tests. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange a sleep study and an MRI brain
options.B: Discuss with the named safeguarding lead and follow child-protection procedures
options.D: Tell the mother you believe she is inventing the episodes
options.E: Discharge home with an apnoea monitor and open access

correct_answer: B. Discuss with the named safeguarding lead and follow child-protection procedures
why_correct: Repeated events reported by only one carer, never observed by staff, with normal extensive investigation and carer pressure for more tests, should raise concern about fabricated or induced illness. This is a safeguarding issue: discuss with the named or designated safeguarding professional and follow local child-protection procedures rather than subjecting the child to further invasive tests.
why_wrong: A. More investigations expose the child to further potential harm and are driven only by the reported history. C. Starting medication for an unconfirmed diagnosis may itself harm the child. D. Confronting the carer before a safeguarding plan is agreed can increase the risk to the child. E. Discharge with a monitor ignores the safeguarding concern.
pearl: In suspected fabricated or induced illness, the harm to the child comes from unnecessary tests and treatment; share concerns with safeguarding leads early.
thinking: Recurrent events reported only by one carer ↓ Never witnessed, all investigations normal ↓ Carer seeking more tests ↓ Possible fabricated or induced illness ↓ Escalate through safeguarding procedures
exam_trap: A, more tests — excluding rare organic causes feels thorough. But repeated investigation itself harms the child; this pattern demands a safeguarding referral.
takeaway: Events only one carer ever sees, with normal tests: think fabricated or induced illness and escalate.

stem: A 44-year-old man sees his GP with three months of low mood, loss of interest in his usual hobbies, early morning waking and poor appetite. He has been signed off work because he cannot concentrate and is struggling to look after himself. He denies thoughts of suicide or self-harm and has no psychotic symptoms or history of mania. He would like treatment. What is the most appropriate first-line option?

options.B: Watchful waiting with review in a month
options.C: An SSRI such as sertraline, with individual CBT

correct_answer: C. An SSRI such as sertraline, with individual CBT
why_correct: He has depression causing marked functional impairment without risk or psychotic features. First-line treatment, chosen with the patient, is an SSRI such as sertraline and/or a high-intensity psychological therapy such as individual CBT; combining the two is particularly effective for more severe depression.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines are not a treatment for depression and risk dependence. B. Watchful waiting is not appropriate when depression is already causing significant impairment. D. Antipsychotics are not first-line for non-psychotic depression. E. St John's wort is not recommended because of variable potency and drug interactions.
pearl: When starting an SSRI, warn about early side effects and delayed benefit, and review within a couple of weeks; sooner in those under 25 or at increased risk.
thinking: Low mood, anhedonia, biological symptoms for months ↓ Off work, struggling with self-care ↓ No suicidal ideation or psychosis ↓ Depression with significant impairment ↓ SSRI with individual CBT
exam_trap: B, watchful waiting — useful for very mild or recent symptoms. But he has established depression with major functional loss, so active treatment is indicated.
