stem: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing COPD is reviewed on the respiratory ward because she has become more drowsy since admission with an infective exacerbation. An arterial blood gas on room air shows: pH 7.30, PaO2 7.2 kPa, PaCO2 8.6 kPa, bicarbonate 31 mmol/L. How should this result be interpreted?

options.B: Chronic type 2 respiratory failure with full compensation
options.C: Primary metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
options.E: Acute type 2 respiratory failure with no chronic component

why_correct: She is hypoxaemic with a raised PaCO2, which is type 2 respiratory failure. The raised bicarbonate shows longstanding renal compensation for chronic carbon dioxide retention, but the pH is still low, so there has been an acute rise in carbon dioxide on top of chronic retention. This pattern is typical of an exacerbation in COPD and is a common indication to consider non-invasive ventilation.
why_wrong: A. Type 1 failure has a normal or low PaCO2. B. Full compensation would bring the pH back into the normal range. C. In a primary metabolic alkalosis the pH would be high, not low. E. A purely acute rise in carbon dioxide would not yet have produced a raised bicarbonate.
pearl: Read the gas in order: pH, then PaCO2, then bicarbonate. Low pH plus high PaCO2 plus high bicarbonate means chronic retention with a fresh acute rise.
thinking: Low PaO2 and high PaCO2 ↓ Type 2 respiratory failure ↓ Raised bicarbonate means chronic retention ↓ pH still acidaemic ↓ Acute-on-chronic type 2 failure
exam_trap: B, chronic compensated type 2 failure — the raised bicarbonate draws you to chronicity, but compensation is only complete when the pH is normal; this pH is still acidaemic.
takeaway: High CO2, high bicarbonate and low pH means acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sharp left-sided chest pain that started suddenly while he was sitting at his desk this morning. He becomes slightly breathless only on climbing stairs. He has no previous lung disease. Pulse is 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute and oxygen saturation 98% on air. Chest X-ray shows a left pneumothorax with a visible rim of about 2.5 cm at the level of the hilum. He would prefer to go home. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Needle aspiration in the emergency department
options.B: Insertion of a small-bore chest drain and admission
options.C: Admission for high-flow oxygen and repeat chest X-ray
options.D: Conservative management with safety-net advice and outpatient review
options.E: Referral for surgical pleurodesis during this admission

correct_answer: D. Conservative management with safety-net advice and outpatient review
why_correct: This is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a young man who is stable and has minimal symptoms. Current British Thoracic Society guidance bases management on symptoms, high-risk features and patient preference rather than size alone, so conservative management with clear return advice and planned follow-up is appropriate. He should avoid flying until resolution is confirmed and should be advised never to scuba dive unless he has had definitive surgery.
why_wrong: A. Aspiration is for patients who are significantly breathless, have high-risk features or choose intervention. B. A chest drain is not needed in a stable patient with minimal symptoms. C. Admission for oxygen is unnecessary when he is suitable for ambulatory management. E. Surgery is reserved for recurrence, persistent air leak or failure of other measures.
pearl: In a stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax, ask how the patient is rather than how big the rim is. Breathlessness, instability and high-risk features drive intervention.
thinking: Young, no lung disease ↓ Primary spontaneous pneumothorax ↓ Stable, minimal breathlessness, no high-risk features ↓ Symptoms guide treatment, not size ↓ Conservative with follow-up
exam_trap: A, needle aspiration — older algorithms tied a rim of 2 cm or more to aspiration, but current guidance lets a stable, minimally breathless patient be managed conservatively.
takeaway: Stable, minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax can be managed conservatively whatever the rim size.

stem: A 55-year-old man develops pleuritic right-sided chest pain and breathlessness 10 days after an open inguinal hernia repair. Pulse is 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% on air. CT pulmonary angiography shows segmental pulmonary emboli in the right lower lobe. Renal and liver function are normal and he has no history of cancer or bleeding. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: He has a confirmed pulmonary embolism with stable blood pressure. NICE recommends a direct oral anticoagulant, apixaban or rivaroxaban, as first-line treatment, and these can be started without initial parenteral anticoagulation. As the clot was provoked by surgery, around 3 months of treatment is usually enough.
why_wrong: A. Thrombolysis is for pulmonary embolism with haemodynamic instability. B. Unfractionated heparin is reserved for situations such as instability, possible thrombolysis or severe renal impairment. C. Aspirin is not adequate treatment for venous thromboembolism. D. Warfarin needs parenteral anticoagulant cover until the INR is in range and is no longer first-line.
pearl: Apixaban and rivaroxaban need no heparin lead-in; dabigatran and edoxaban do need at least 5 days of parenteral anticoagulation first.
thinking: Post-operative pleuritic pain and breathlessness ↓ CTPA confirms PE ↓ Blood pressure stable ↓ No renal or cancer issues ↓ DOAC such as apixaban
exam_trap: B, unfractionated heparin — tachycardia and hypoxia make him seem sick, but he is normotensive, so the DOAC pathway applies and heparin infusion adds nothing.
takeaway: Stable pulmonary embolism: start a DOAC such as apixaban; save thrombolysis for instability.

stem: A 71-year-old woman who smoked for 40 years is seen in the respiratory clinic. She has had a cough for 2 months, has lost 6 kg and has new finger clubbing. Her GP arranged a chest X-ray, which shows a left hilar mass with widening of the mediastinum. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.C: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest including the liver and adrenal glands
options.E: A course of antibiotics and repeat chest X-ray in 6 weeks

correct_answer: C. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest including the liver and adrenal glands
why_correct: NICE advises a contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, extending to include the liver and adrenal glands, for people whose chest X-ray suggests lung cancer. This both stages the disease and shows the safest and most informative site for tissue sampling, so it comes before bronchoscopy or PET-CT.
why_wrong: A. PET-CT is used after CT to stage patients who may be suitable for curative treatment. B. Bronchoscopy follows CT, which guides the choice of biopsy route. D. Sputum cytology is insensitive and gives no staging information. E. Waiting and repeating the film delays diagnosis in a high-risk woman with a suspicious mass.
pearl: In suspected lung cancer the order is chest X-ray, contrast CT chest and upper abdomen, then the biopsy that gives both diagnosis and the highest stage.
thinking: Heavy smoker with weight loss and clubbing ↓ Chest X-ray shows hilar mass ↓ Suspected lung cancer ↓ Stage first to plan biopsy ↓ Contrast CT chest with liver and adrenals
exam_trap: B, bronchoscopy with biopsy — getting tissue feels like the priority, but CT first shows whether a lymph node or metastasis gives a better, single diagnostic and staging biopsy.
takeaway: Chest X-ray suggesting lung cancer: next is contrast CT of chest including liver and adrenals.

presentation: Pleural fluid analysis using Light's criteria
stem: A 63-year-old woman is seen on the medical ward with a moderate left pleural effusion. A diagnostic tap produces straw-coloured fluid. Results: pleural fluid protein 28 g/L, serum protein 50 g/L, pleural fluid LDH 260 U/L, serum LDH 300 U/L. How should this fluid be classified?
why_correct: When pleural protein is borderline, Light's criteria are applied. The fluid is an exudate if the pleural to serum protein ratio is above 0.5, the pleural to serum LDH ratio is above 0.6, or pleural LDH is more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum. Here the protein ratio is 0.56 and the LDH ratio is 0.87, so this is an exudate despite the low absolute protein.
why_wrong: A. The protein looks low, but both ratios meet Light's criteria for an exudate. C. Empyema is frankly purulent or turbid fluid, often with a low pH. D. Chylothorax is milky fluid with high triglycerides. E. Haemothorax is blood-stained fluid with a high haematocrit.
pearl: An absolute protein under 30 g/L does not guarantee a transudate. If protein is borderline, calculate Light's ratios; meeting any one criterion means exudate.
thinking: Borderline pleural protein ↓ Apply Light's criteria ↓ Protein ratio 0.56, LDH ratio 0.87 ↓ At least one criterion met ↓ Exudate
exam_trap: A, transudate — a protein below 30 g/L looks transudative at first glance, but the ratios to serum values decide and both point to an exudate.
takeaway: Light's criteria: meeting any one ratio criterion makes the fluid an exudate.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with a 10-day history of fever, painful swollen ankles and tender red lumps on both shins. A chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. He has no cough, eye symptoms or weight loss. Serum calcium, renal function and liver tests are normal, and respiratory review finds normal lung function. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral prednisolone with a slow taper
options.B: NSAIDs for symptoms and clinical review; spontaneous resolution is expected
options.C: Endobronchial ultrasound-guided biopsy of a hilar lymph node
options.D: Start methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent

correct_answer: B. NSAIDs for symptoms and clinical review; spontaneous resolution is expected
why_correct: Fever, ankle periarthritis, erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy form Löfgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis. It has an excellent prognosis and usually resolves without specific treatment, so management is symptom relief with NSAIDs and monitoring. The classic combination is specific enough that tissue diagnosis is not usually required.
why_wrong: A. Steroids are kept for significant organ involvement such as hypercalcaemia or impaired lung function. C. A biopsy is unnecessary in the typical Löfgren picture. D. Methotrexate is for chronic sarcoidosis needing long-term treatment. E. There are no features of tuberculosis.
pearl: Löfgren syndrome carries the best prognosis of all sarcoidosis presentations; most patients recover fully within months to 2 years.
thinking: Erythema nodosum plus ankle arthritis plus fever ↓ Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy ↓ Löfgren syndrome ↓ No organ-threatening disease ↓ NSAIDs and observe
exam_trap: A, oral prednisolone — sarcoidosis is classically steroid-responsive, but Löfgren syndrome is self-limiting and steroids are only for significant organ involvement.
takeaway: Löfgren syndrome usually settles on its own: NSAIDs and observation.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with COPD confirmed on spirometry attends her annual review at the GP surgery. She stopped smoking last year, has completed pulmonary rehabilitation and is up to date with vaccinations. She uses a salbutamol inhaler several times a day and is still breathless when walking to the shops. She has had no exacerbations in the past year. There is no history of atopy, no variation in symptoms during the day and her blood eosinophil count is normal. What is the most appropriate change to her treatment?

options.A: Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist with a long-acting beta-2 agonist
options.B: Add a long-acting beta-2 agonist with an inhaled corticosteroid
options.C: Start triple therapy with an inhaled corticosteroid, LABA and LAMA

correct_answer: A. Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist with a long-acting beta-2 agonist
why_correct: NICE advises that people with COPD who remain limited by breathlessness despite non-drug measures and a short-acting bronchodilator, and who have no asthmatic features or features suggesting steroid responsiveness, are offered a LAMA plus a LABA. Dual long-acting bronchodilation improves breathlessness without the pneumonia risk of inhaled steroids.
why_wrong: B. LABA with an inhaled corticosteroid is for patients with asthmatic features or features suggesting steroid responsiveness. C. Triple therapy is for continued exacerbations or symptoms despite dual therapy. D. Theophylline is used only after inhaled therapy has been optimised. E. Long-term oral steroids are rarely used and are not a routine step.
pearl: In COPD, the presence or absence of asthmatic or steroid-responsive features (atopy, raised eosinophils, diurnal or marked variability) decides between LAMA plus LABA and LABA plus ICS.
thinking: COPD, still breathless on short-acting bronchodilator ↓ Non-drug measures done ↓ No asthmatic or steroid-responsive features ↓ No inhaled steroid needed ↓ LAMA plus LABA
exam_trap: B, LABA with inhaled corticosteroid — many patients are on this combination, but without asthmatic features an inhaled steroid adds pneumonia risk without benefit at this stage.
takeaway: COPD without asthmatic features, still breathless: add LAMA plus LABA.

stem: A 34-year-old woman recently recruited from a country with a high incidence of tuberculosis attends occupational health before starting work as a nurse on a UK ward. She feels well, with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. An interferon-gamma release assay is positive and her chest X-ray is normal. HIV test and liver function tests are normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Three months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin
options.B: Six months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol
options.D: No treatment and discharge from follow-up
options.E: Repeat interferon-gamma release assay in 12 months

correct_answer: A. Three months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin
why_correct: A positive IGRA with a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms indicates latent tuberculosis infection. NICE recommends treating latent infection in eligible adults, including recent arrivals from high-incidence countries, with either 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin or 6 months of isoniazid, both given with pyridoxine. Treatment greatly reduces the lifetime risk of reactivation.
why_wrong: B. Four-drug therapy is for active tuberculosis, which has been excluded here. C. BCG does not treat existing infection and offers little benefit to infected adults. D. Leaving latent infection untreated leaves a lifetime risk of reactivation. E. A repeat test does not change the diagnosis or reduce the risk.
pearl: Rifampicin induces liver enzymes and makes hormonal contraception unreliable; advise women of reproductive age to use another method during treatment. It also turns urine and tears orange.
thinking: Positive IGRA ↓ No symptoms and normal chest X-ray ↓ Latent TB, not active disease ↓ Eligible adult from high-incidence country ↓ 3 months isoniazid plus rifampicin
exam_trap: B, standard four-drug therapy — a positive TB test prompts thoughts of full treatment, but with no symptoms and a normal X-ray this is latent infection, which needs a shorter, simpler regimen.
takeaway: Latent TB in an eligible adult: treat with 3 months isoniazid plus rifampicin or 6 months isoniazid.

stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed in the sleep clinic. His wife reports loud snoring and pauses in his breathing at night, and he has fallen asleep in afternoon meetings at work. He has a BMI of 36 kg/m2 and treated hypertension. An overnight sleep study confirms moderate obstructive sleep apnoea. He has already been referred to a weight management service. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: NICE recommends continuous positive airway pressure for adults with moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea. CPAP splints the upper airway open during sleep, abolishing obstructive events and improving daytime sleepiness. Weight loss is encouraged alongside, and he should be advised about his duty to inform the DVLA if sleepiness affects his driving.
why_wrong: A. A mandibular advancement device is an option for mild disease or for people who cannot tolerate CPAP. C. Oxygen does not prevent the airway collapse that causes the apnoeas. D. Modafinil does not treat the airway obstruction and is not a primary treatment. E. Upper airway surgery is not a first-line treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea in adults.
pearl: Excessive sleepiness from OSA that affects driving must be reported to the DVLA; drivers can usually resume once symptoms are controlled on treatment.
thinking: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness ↓ Sleep study confirms moderate OSA ↓ Airway collapses during sleep ↓ Keep it open mechanically ↓ CPAP
exam_trap: A, mandibular advancement device — it is less intrusive and does treat OSA, but it is for mild disease or CPAP intolerance, not first choice in moderate disease.
takeaway: Moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea: CPAP is first-line, with weight loss alongside.

stem: A 76-year-old man who spent 30 years fitting pipe lagging in power stations sees his GP with 3 months of a dull, constant right chest ache, worsening breathlessness and a 7 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a large right pleural effusion. CT shows nodular, irregular pleural thickening encasing the right lung and extending onto the mediastinal pleura. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pipe lagging is a classic source of asbestos exposure. Decades later, persistent chest wall pain, breathlessness, weight loss and a unilateral effusion with nodular, circumferential pleural thickening are typical of malignant pleural mesothelioma. Diagnosis is confirmed by pleural biopsy, and the patient may be entitled to industrial injuries compensation.
why_wrong: B. Tuberculous pleurisy usually presents with fever and night sweats and lacks this encasing nodular thickening. C. Heart failure typically causes bilateral effusions without pleural thickening or chest pain. D. Pleural plaques are asymptomatic, discrete and calcified, and do not cause effusions or weight loss. E. A parapneumonic effusion follows a pneumonia with fever and productive cough.
pearl: Mesothelioma usually appears 30 to 40 or more years after asbestos exposure. Chest wall pain and weight loss with nodular pleural thickening should raise concern.
thinking: Occupational asbestos exposure ↓ Chest pain, breathlessness and weight loss ↓ Unilateral effusion ↓ Nodular pleural thickening encasing the lung ↓ Mesothelioma
exam_trap: D, benign pleural plaques — they are the commonest asbestos-related finding, but they are asymptomatic and never cause a large effusion or weight loss.
takeaway: Asbestos exposure plus chest pain, effusion and nodular pleural thickening suggests mesothelioma.

stem: A 71-year-old retired accountant who has never smoked and has no occupational dust exposure sees his GP with 9 months of gradually worsening breathlessness on exertion and a persistent dry cough. He has finger clubbing and fine, velcro-like crackles at both lung bases. There is no ankle swelling and his JVP is not raised. Spirometry shows a reduced FVC with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio, and his gas transfer is reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Progressive exertional breathlessness, dry cough, clubbing and fine bibasal inspiratory crackles in an older adult, with a restrictive pattern and reduced gas transfer, are typical of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. With no relevant exposure, an idiopathic cause is most likely. High-resolution CT is the key next test and usually shows basal, subpleural reticulation and honeycombing.
why_wrong: A. COPD gives an obstructive pattern and is usually smoking-related. C. Asbestosis would look similar but needs significant asbestos exposure, which he does not have. D. Bronchiectasis causes a chronic productive cough with coarse crackles. E. Heart failure can cause basal crackles, but not clubbing, and there are no signs of fluid overload.
pearl: Fine end-inspiratory velcro crackles plus clubbing in an older patient with a restrictive pattern should prompt high-resolution CT for pulmonary fibrosis.
thinking: Slowly progressive breathlessness and dry cough ↓ Clubbing and fine bibasal crackles ↓ Restrictive spirometry, low gas transfer ↓ No exposure to explain it ↓ Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
exam_trap: C, asbestosis — it gives an identical clinical picture, but the question deliberately removes any occupational exposure, leaving an idiopathic cause.
takeaway: Clubbing, fine bibasal crackles and restrictive spirometry without exposure suggest IPF.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter after 3 days of cough, fever and increasing drowsiness. She is newly confused about the date and place. Respiratory rate is 32 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, pulse 112 beats per minute and oxygen saturation 90% on air. Urea is raised. Chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral amoxicillin and discharge home with her daughter
options.B: Oral doxycycline at home with GP review in 48 hours
options.D: Admission, withholding antibiotics until sputum culture results are available
options.E: Admission, oxygen and IV antibiotics for high-severity pneumonia

correct_answer: E. Admission, oxygen and IV antibiotics for high-severity pneumonia
why_correct: New confusion, raised urea, tachypnoea, low blood pressure and age over 65 give a high CURB-65 score, indicating high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with a high risk of death. She needs admission, controlled oxygen, fluids and prompt antibiotics for high-severity pneumonia, usually a beta-lactam such as co-amoxiclav with a macrolide, given IV because of the severity, following local policy.
why_wrong: A. Oral amoxicillin at home is only for low-severity pneumonia. B. Home treatment is unsafe for a confused, hypotensive, hypoxic patient. C. Amoxicillin alone does not give the broader cover needed for high-severity disease. D. Antibiotics should start promptly; delay worsens outcomes.
pearl: CURB-65 = Confusion, Urea raised, Respiratory rate 30 or more, Blood pressure low, age 65 or over. Use it alongside clinical judgement, not instead of it.
thinking: Cough, fever and consolidation ↓ Confusion, raised urea, tachypnoea, low BP, age over 65 ↓ High-severity pneumonia ↓ Needs hospital care ↓ Admit, oxygen and IV antibiotics
exam_trap: C, admission with oral amoxicillin — admitting feels like the key decision, but high-severity pneumonia needs broader cover, given IV in a patient this unwell.
takeaway: High-severity pneumonia: admit, give oxygen and start broad IV antibiotics promptly.

stem: A 52-year-old man on the surgical ward becomes acutely breathless 20 minutes after a right subclavian central venous catheter was inserted. He is agitated, oxygen saturation is 84% on high-flow oxygen, pulse 138 beats per minute and blood pressure 76/40 mmHg. His neck veins are distended, the trachea is deviated to the left, and the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Immediate needle decompression of the right hemithorax
options.B: Urgent portable chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis
options.C: Formal insertion of a right-sided chest drain as the first step
options.D: Rapid IV fluid bolus and reassess

correct_answer: A. Immediate needle decompression of the right hemithorax
why_correct: A pneumothorax after central line insertion, with hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side and a silent, hyper-resonant hemithorax is a tension pneumothorax. This is a clinical diagnosis and needs immediate decompression on the affected side without waiting for imaging, followed by a chest drain.
why_wrong: B. Waiting for an X-ray delays life-saving treatment in obstructive shock. C. A chest drain follows decompression and takes too long as the first step in a peri-arrest patient. D. Fluids do not relieve the obstruction to venous return. E. CT is unsafe in an unstable patient, and pulmonary embolism does not explain the chest signs.
pearl: Tension pneumothorax pushes the trachea away from the affected side. Hypotension plus a silent, hyper-resonant hemithorax means decompress first, image later.
thinking: Sudden collapse after subclavian line ↓ Hypotension, raised JVP, tracheal deviation away ↓ Hyper-resonant silent right chest ↓ Tension pneumothorax ↓ Immediate decompression
exam_trap: B, urgent portable chest X-ray — confirmation feels responsible, but tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and the patient may arrest while waiting for the film.
takeaway: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: decompress immediately, image afterwards.

presentation: Acute upper GI bleed with shock
stem: A 66-year-old woman who takes naproxen for knee osteoarthritis is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. She has vomited coffee-ground material twice and passed black, tarry stools. She is pale with cool peripheries, pulse 118 beats per minute and blood pressure 88/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: IV proton pump inhibitor and IV tranexamic acid, then endoscopy on the next routine list
options.B: Oral proton pump inhibitor and outpatient endoscopy within 2 weeks
options.C: Resuscitation with fluids and blood, then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
options.D: Transfuse to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L and repeat bloods the next day
options.E: CT angiography as the first-line investigation

correct_answer: C. Resuscitation with fluids and blood, then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
why_correct: She has an upper gastrointestinal bleed with shock, most likely from an NSAID-related peptic ulcer. NICE advises resuscitation with IV access, fluids and blood, and endoscopy immediately after resuscitation in unstable patients (within 24 hours for everyone else) so that the bleeding point can be treated. Naproxen should be stopped.
why_wrong: A. NICE advises against giving a PPI before endoscopy, tranexamic acid does not improve outcomes, and waiting for a routine list is unsafe. B. Outpatient management is dangerous in a shocked patient. D. A restrictive transfusion target is preferred and transfusion alone does not stop the bleeding. E. CT angiography is for when endoscopy cannot locate or control the bleeding.
pearl: Use the Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment and the full Rockall score after endoscopy. Give PPI after endoscopy, not before.
thinking: Coffee-ground vomit and melaena on an NSAID ↓ Upper GI bleed ↓ Hypotensive, tachycardic and cool ↓ Haemodynamically unstable ↓ Resuscitate, then endoscopy immediately
exam_trap: A, IV PPI and tranexamic acid — both feel like active treatments for bleeding, but neither is recommended before endoscopy, and they delay the endoscopy that actually treats the source.
takeaway: Unstable upper GI bleed: resuscitate, then endoscopy immediately after resuscitation.

stem: A 33-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes sees her GP with several months of bloating, intermittent loose pale stools and tiredness. Her periods are light. Blood tests show a mild anaemia with a low ferritin. She eats a normal diet that includes bread and pasta every day. What is the most appropriate first investigation?

options.A: Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody with total IgA
options.C: A trial of a gluten-free diet and review in 6 weeks

correct_answer: A. Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody with total IgA
why_correct: Unexplained iron deficiency, bloating and loose stools in someone with type 1 diabetes make coeliac disease likely. NICE recommends tissue transglutaminase IgA as the first test, with total IgA to exclude IgA deficiency, while the patient is still eating gluten. Positive serology leads to referral to gastroenterology for confirmation.
why_wrong: B. Colonoscopy does not examine the duodenum and is not the first test for suspected coeliac disease. C. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing can give false-negative serology and biopsy. D. HLA typing is mainly useful to rule out coeliac disease and is not a first-line test. E. Calprotectin is used to distinguish inflammatory bowel disease from IBS, not to diagnose coeliac disease.
pearl: People with type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease, and first-degree relatives of people with coeliac disease, should have a low threshold for coeliac serology.
thinking: Bloating, loose stools, iron deficiency ↓ Autoimmune background of type 1 diabetes ↓ Suspect coeliac disease ↓ Still eating gluten ↓ tTG IgA with total IgA
exam_trap: C, gluten-free diet trial — symptom improvement seems a quick answer, but removing gluten before testing makes the serology and biopsy falsely negative.
takeaway: Suspected coeliac disease: tTG IgA with total IgA while still eating gluten.

stem: A 32-year-old woman, who stopped smoking 6 months ago, is reviewed in clinic with 6 weeks of bloody diarrhoea with mucus, rectal urgency and a feeling of incomplete emptying. Stool cultures are negative. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows inflamed, friable mucosa with loss of the vascular pattern, beginning at the anal verge and continuing without interruption to the limit of the examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bloody diarrhoea with urgency and tenesmus, negative stool cultures and continuous mucosal inflammation starting at the rectum are typical of ulcerative colitis. Onset or flare after stopping smoking is a recognised feature, because smoking appears to be protective in ulcerative colitis.
why_wrong: A. Crohn's disease typically shows skip lesions, often spares the rectum and is worsened by smoking. B. Infective colitis is usually short-lived and stool cultures here are negative. D. Microscopic colitis causes watery, non-bloody diarrhoea with normal-looking mucosa. E. IBS does not cause bleeding or visible inflammation.
pearl: Ulcerative colitis always starts at the rectum and spreads continuously proximally. Smoking protects against ulcerative colitis but worsens Crohn's disease.
thinking: Bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus ↓ Infection excluded ↓ Continuous inflammation from rectum ↓ Onset after stopping smoking ↓ Ulcerative colitis
exam_trap: A, Crohn's disease — both cause bloody diarrhoea in young adults, but rectal involvement with continuous inflammation and onset after stopping smoking point firmly to ulcerative colitis.
takeaway: Continuous inflammation spreading up from the rectum indicates ulcerative colitis.

stem: A 61-year-old woman with cirrhosis due to fatty liver disease and known ascites is reviewed on the gastroenterology ward because she has a temperature of 37.9 degrees C, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and new mild confusion. A diagnostic ascitic tap shows a neutrophil count of 420 cells/mm3; culture is pending. An erect chest X-ray shows no free air. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Increase the dose of spironolactone and restrict salt
options.D: IV antibiotics and IV human albumin solution
options.E: Withhold antibiotics until the ascitic culture result is available

correct_answer: D. IV antibiotics and IV human albumin solution
why_correct: In a patient with cirrhosis and ascites, an ascitic neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or more confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, even before culture results. Treatment is prompt IV antibiotics, such as a third-generation cephalosporin or as per local policy, together with IV albumin, which reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome and death.
why_wrong: A. Increasing diuretics does not treat infection and may worsen kidney function. B. Removing fluid does not treat the infection. C. Laparotomy is for secondary peritonitis from a surgical cause, such as perforation, which is not suggested here. E. Culture is often negative in SBP, and delaying antibiotics increases mortality.
pearl: Tap the ascites in every patient with cirrhosis admitted to hospital, and in anyone with ascites who has fever, abdominal pain, confusion or worsening kidney function.
thinking: Cirrhosis with ascites ↓ Fever, tenderness, new confusion ↓ Ascitic neutrophils clearly raised ↓ Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis ↓ IV antibiotics and IV albumin
exam_trap: E, waiting for culture — it seems logical to confirm infection, but the neutrophil count makes the diagnosis and cultures are often negative; delay is dangerous.
takeaway: Raised ascitic neutrophils in cirrhosis means SBP: start IV antibiotics and give albumin.

stem: A 57-year-old woman undergoes gastroscopy for persistent dyspepsia that has not settled with lifestyle advice. She takes no NSAIDs or aspirin and has no drug allergies. Gastroscopy shows a clean-based duodenal ulcer, and a rapid urease test on a gastric biopsy is positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Full-dose proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks with no other treatment
options.B: Seven days of a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and either clarithromycin or metronidazole
options.E: Repeat gastroscopy after 8 weeks of PPI before deciding on further treatment

correct_answer: B. Seven days of a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and either clarithromycin or metronidazole
why_correct: A duodenal ulcer with a positive urease test is H. pylori-associated. NICE recommends eradication with 7 days of a proton pump inhibitor plus amoxicillin and either clarithromycin or metronidazole for people without penicillin allergy. Eradication heals the ulcer and greatly reduces the chance of it coming back.
why_wrong: A. Acid suppression alone heals the ulcer but leaves H. pylori in place, so it is likely to recur. C. H2-receptor antagonists do not eradicate H. pylori. D. Surgery is not used for uncomplicated peptic ulcer disease. E. Delaying eradication offers no benefit, and routine repeat gastroscopy is not needed for a duodenal ulcer.
pearl: In penicillin allergy, use a PPI with clarithromycin and metronidazole. A gastric ulcer, unlike a duodenal ulcer, needs repeat endoscopy to confirm healing and exclude cancer.
thinking: Duodenal ulcer on gastroscopy ↓ Positive urease test ↓ H. pylori is the driver ↓ No penicillin allergy ↓ 7-day PPI-based triple therapy
exam_trap: A, 8 weeks of PPI alone — it heals the ulcer, so it seems sufficient, but without eradication the ulcer is very likely to return.
takeaway: H. pylori-positive peptic ulcer: give 7-day PPI-based triple eradication therapy.

stem: A 44-year-old woman who drinks about half a bottle of vodka a day is admitted with 3 weeks of worsening jaundice, low-grade fever and a tender, enlarged liver. Bilirubin is markedly raised, the prothrombin time is prolonged and AST is about twice ALT. White cell count is raised, but a full septic screen including ascitic tap and chest X-ray is negative, and there is no gastrointestinal bleeding. Her Maddrey discriminant function indicates severe disease. Which treatment is most likely to improve her short-term survival?
why_correct: Jaundice, fever and a tender liver in a heavy drinker, with AST more raised than ALT, suggest alcohol-related hepatitis, and the Maddrey score shows severe disease. Once infection and bleeding have been excluded, prednisolone for 4 weeks is the treatment with evidence of short-term survival benefit. Response is reviewed after a week, and steroids are stopped early if there is no improvement.
why_wrong: A. Pentoxifylline did not improve survival in a large UK trial. B. N-acetylcysteine alone has no proven survival benefit. C. Ursodeoxycholic acid is used in primary biliary cholangitis. D. Transplantation is not usually offered during acute alcohol-related hepatitis and requires assessment of abstinence.
pearl: Exclude infection and gastrointestinal bleeding before starting steroids in alcohol-related hepatitis. Lasting survival depends on stopping drinking.
thinking: Heavy drinker with jaundice, fever and tender liver ↓ AST more than ALT ↓ Alcohol-related hepatitis ↓ Severe on Maddrey score, infection excluded ↓ Prednisolone
exam_trap: A, pentoxifylline — it was once an accepted alternative, but a large UK trial showed no survival benefit, so it is no longer recommended.
takeaway: Severe alcohol-related hepatitis without infection or bleeding: consider prednisolone for 4 weeks.

stem: A 26-year-old man is admitted to the acute medical unit after taking extra paracetamol tablets over 3 days for toothache. He is now drowsy and disorientated, with a flapping tremor and yellow sclerae. His INR is 6.2 and creatinine is rising. Arterial pH remains low despite IV fluid resuscitation. Acetylcysteine has been started. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent discussion with and transfer to a specialist liver unit
options.B: Give fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR
options.D: Stop acetylcysteine as it is too late to help
options.E: Continue acetylcysteine on the general ward with daily INR checks

correct_answer: A. Urgent discussion with and transfer to a specialist liver unit
why_correct: This staggered paracetamol overdose has caused acute liver failure, with encephalopathy, severe coagulopathy, acidosis and kidney injury. He needs urgent discussion with a specialist liver unit for intensive care and transplant assessment, without waiting for all prognostic criteria to be met. Acetylcysteine should continue.
why_wrong: B. Clotting factors should not be given without active bleeding, because the INR is a key marker of severity. C. Dialysis may support kidney function but does not treat liver failure, and little paracetamol remains to remove. D. Acetylcysteine still helps in established liver failure and should be continued. E. A general ward cannot provide the care or transplant assessment he may need.
pearl: Staggered paracetamol overdoses cannot be plotted on the treatment nomogram; treat with acetylcysteine regardless of the level.
thinking: Staggered paracetamol overdose ↓ Encephalopathy, high INR, acidosis, rising creatinine ↓ Acute liver failure ↓ May need transplant ↓ Urgent specialist liver unit referral
exam_trap: B, fresh frozen plasma — a very high INR looks like something to fix, but correcting it without bleeding hides the main prognostic marker used to decide on transplantation.
takeaway: Paracetamol-induced acute liver failure: continue acetylcysteine and refer urgently to a liver unit.

stem: A 59-year-old woman with years of heartburn sees her GP because food has been sticking behind her breastbone for 6 weeks. It started with meat and now happens with bread. She has lost 5 kg without trying. Examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.B: CT of the chest and abdomen
options.D: Trial of high-dose PPI for 8 weeks then review
options.E: Urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy

correct_answer: E. Urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia to solids with weight loss suggests oesophageal cancer, possibly from Barrett's oesophagus after longstanding reflux. NICE advises an urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for anyone with dysphagia, whatever their age. Endoscopy allows direct inspection and biopsy, with CT staging afterwards.
why_wrong: A. A barium swallow may show a stricture but cannot provide tissue. B. CT is used for staging once a diagnosis has been made. C. Manometry is for motility disorders such as achalasia after obstruction has been excluded. D. A PPI trial delays diagnosis of a possible cancer.
pearl: Dysphagia is a red flag at any age. Progression from solids to softer foods suggests a mechanical narrowing such as a cancer or stricture.
thinking: Food sticking behind sternum ↓ Progressive, solids first ↓ Weight loss and longstanding reflux ↓ Possible oesophageal cancer ↓ Urgent endoscopy with biopsy
exam_trap: D, PPI trial — her long reflux history makes a peptic stricture tempting, but dysphagia with weight loss needs urgent endoscopy, not empirical treatment.
takeaway: Dysphagia at any age needs urgent direct-access endoscopy.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought in by her daughter, who says she has been sleepy in the day and awake at night for 2 days and is now muddled. She has not opened her bowels for 4 days. She has a coarse flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. She is afebrile, an ascitic tap is not suggestive of infection and there is no sign of bleeding. What is the most appropriate first-line drug treatment?

options.D: Lactulose titrated to two to three soft stools a day
options.E: Oral lorazepam to settle her confusion

correct_answer: D. Lactulose titrated to two to three soft stools a day
why_correct: Altered sleep pattern, confusion and asterixis in cirrhosis indicate hepatic encephalopathy, here likely precipitated by constipation. Lactulose is first-line: it speeds gut transit and reduces ammonia production and absorption. The dose is adjusted to achieve two to three soft stools a day, and any other precipitants are sought and treated.
why_wrong: A. Rifaximin is added to lactulose to prevent recurrence, not used alone first-line. B. Protein restriction worsens malnutrition and is no longer advised. C. Mannitol is for raised intracranial pressure in acute liver failure. E. Benzodiazepines can worsen or precipitate encephalopathy.
pearl: Common triggers for hepatic encephalopathy are constipation, infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and sedatives.
thinking: Cirrhosis with confusion and day-night reversal ↓ Flapping tremor ↓ Hepatic encephalopathy, constipation as trigger ↓ Reduce gut ammonia ↓ Lactulose
exam_trap: A, rifaximin — it is a recognised treatment, but it is added to lactulose for secondary prevention rather than used alone first-line.
takeaway: Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose first-line and treat the precipitant.

presentation: Acute ischaemic stroke within the thrombolysis window
stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly develops left facial droop, left arm weakness and slurred speech while shopping at 10:15. She arrives in the emergency department at 11:30. She ignores her left side and has a moderately severe deficit on stroke scoring. She takes no anticoagulants. Blood glucose is normal and blood pressure is 172/94 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Aspirin 300 mg now and admission to the stroke unit
options.C: MRI brain before deciding on any treatment
options.D: IV thrombolysis and CT angiography to assess for thrombectomy

correct_answer: D. IV thrombolysis and CT angiography to assess for thrombectomy
why_correct: She has an acute ischaemic stroke with a clear onset well within 4.5 hours, no haemorrhage on CT and no contraindications. NICE recommends IV thrombolysis, and CT angiography should be done straight away to look for a large vessel occlusion suitable for mechanical thrombectomy. Neglect suggests a cortical stroke, which raises the likelihood of a proximal occlusion.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin is for patients not having thrombolysis, or is started 24 hours after thrombolysis once haemorrhage is excluded. B. Anticoagulation does not help acute ischaemic stroke and increases bleeding risk. C. Waiting for MRI delays reperfusion; non-contrast CT is enough to proceed. E. Decompressive surgery is for malignant swelling of a large infarct, not for initial treatment.
pearl: Time is brain. Check glucose, do non-contrast CT, and if there is no bleed and the patient is eligible, thrombolyse and image the vessels for thrombectomy at the same time.
thinking: Sudden focal deficit with known onset ↓ Within thrombolysis window ↓ CT excludes haemorrhage, no contraindications ↓ Possible large vessel occlusion ↓ Thrombolysis and CT angiography
exam_trap: A, aspirin 300 mg — it is correct for many strokes, but when the patient is eligible for thrombolysis, giving aspirin first misses the chance of reperfusion.
takeaway: Eligible ischaemic stroke in the window: thrombolyse and assess for thrombectomy together.

presentation: Suspected meningococcal septicaemia in primary care
stem: A GP is called to see a 19-year-old woman in her shared university accommodation. She has had a fever and vomiting since last night, aching legs, and her hands and feet are cold. Her neck is not stiff. On her thighs there are several purple spots that do not fade when a glass is pressed on them. She is drowsy but responsive. An ambulance has been called. She has no known drug allergies. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Oral amoxicillin and review in 4 hours
options.B: IM or IV benzylpenicillin now, without delaying transfer
options.C: Give no treatment and let the hospital take blood cultures first
options.E: Take blood cultures in the community before any antibiotic

correct_answer: B. IM or IV benzylpenicillin now, without delaying transfer
why_correct: Fever, vomiting, leg pain, cold peripheries and a non-blanching rash suggest meningococcal septicaemia, which can occur without neck stiffness. In primary care, a single dose of IM or IV benzylpenicillin should be given as soon as possible, provided this does not delay emergency transfer to hospital.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics are inadequate in suspected meningococcal disease. C. Withholding antibiotics in the community risks rapid deterioration. D. A non-blanching rash with fever must be treated as meningococcal disease, not managed at home. E. Taking cultures should not delay antibiotics or transfer.
pearl: Leg pain, cold hands and feet and abnormal skin colour are early signs of meningococcal sepsis and can come before the rash or any neck stiffness.
thinking: Fever and vomiting ↓ Cold peripheries and leg pain ↓ Non-blanching rash ↓ Meningococcal septicaemia ↓ Benzylpenicillin now, transfer urgently
exam_trap: C, leave it for the hospital — doctors worry about spoiling cultures, but in suspected meningococcal disease immediate antibiotics in the community save lives.
takeaway: Suspected meningococcal disease in the community: give benzylpenicillin and transfer without delay.

stem: A 59-year-old woman sees her GP the morning after a 20-minute episode the previous evening when the left side of her face drooped and her left hand felt clumsy. Her symptoms resolved completely and examination is now normal. She takes no anticoagulants, has no bleeding disorder and no aspirin allergy. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Clopidogrel 75 mg daily and routine neurology referral
options.B: Aspirin 75 mg daily and TIA clinic review within a week
options.C: Send her to the emergency department for a CT head before any antiplatelet
options.D: Start apixaban and refer to the TIA clinic
options.E: Aspirin 300 mg now and specialist assessment within 24 hours

correct_answer: E. Aspirin 300 mg now and specialist assessment within 24 hours
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological symptoms that resolve completely suggest a transient ischaemic attack, which carries a high early risk of stroke. NICE advises giving aspirin 300 mg immediately, unless contraindicated, and referring for specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset. Risk scores are no longer used to decide urgency.
why_wrong: A. A routine referral is too slow for a suspected TIA. B. A low dose and a one-week wait do not match current advice for a recent TIA. C. Brain imaging is not needed before aspirin unless bleeding is suspected, for example in someone taking an anticoagulant. D. Anticoagulation is only started once a cardioembolic source such as atrial fibrillation is confirmed and haemorrhage excluded.
pearl: Suspected TIA in the last 7 days: aspirin 300 mg and specialist review within 24 hours. TIA more than 7 days ago: specialist review within 7 days.
thinking: Sudden focal deficit ↓ Complete resolution within an hour ↓ Suspected TIA within last 7 days ↓ High early stroke risk ↓ Aspirin 300 mg and specialist review within 24 hours
exam_trap: C, CT before antiplatelet — imaging before aspirin feels safe, but in a patient not on anticoagulants it only delays prevention; specialist imaging follows later.
takeaway: Suspected TIA: aspirin 300 mg now and specialist assessment within 24 hours.

stem: A 27-year-old man is seen in the neurology clinic with 5 days of numbness spreading up from his feet to his waist and new urinary urgency. Last year he had 3 weeks of double vision that recovered completely without treatment. Examination shows brisk reflexes in the legs and upgoing plantars. MRI shows several periventricular and juxtacortical white matter lesions and a short lesion in the cervical spinal cord. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord

why_correct: Two separate episodes affecting different parts of the nervous system (brainstem and spinal cord) months apart, with recovery from the first, show dissemination in time and space. Typical periventricular, juxtacortical and short spinal cord lesions on MRI support relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
why_wrong: A. Neuromyelitis optica usually causes severe optic neuritis and long spinal cord lesions over three or more segments. B. Guillain-Barré syndrome causes reduced or absent reflexes, not upper motor neurone signs. C. Subacute combined degeneration is gradual, symmetrical and not relapsing. D. Primary progressive disease causes steady worsening from onset without distinct relapses.
pearl: Multiple sclerosis needs lesions separated in time and in space. Common first presentations are optic neuritis, a brainstem syndrome or a partial spinal cord syndrome.
thinking: Double vision that resolved ↓ New spinal cord syndrome months later ↓ Separate episodes in different places ↓ Typical white matter lesions on MRI ↓ Relapsing-remitting MS
exam_trap: A, neuromyelitis optica — it also causes relapses with spinal cord involvement, but it typically produces long cord lesions and severe optic neuritis rather than short lesions with periventricular changes.
takeaway: Separate neurological episodes in time and space with typical MRI lesions mean relapsing-remitting MS.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease by a specialist. Over the past year her handwriting has become small, she has a tremor of her left hand at rest, and she now takes a long time to dress and has difficulty turning over in bed. Examination shows asymmetrical rigidity and slow, small movements. She lives alone and wants treatment to stay independent. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.D: Levodopa combined with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor

correct_answer: D. Levodopa combined with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor
why_correct: When motor symptoms are affecting quality of life, NICE recommends levodopa, given with carbidopa or benserazide, as first-line treatment for Parkinson's disease. It gives the greatest improvement in motor symptoms, and its side-effect profile is better suited to an older person than the alternatives.
why_wrong: A. Dopamine agonists are less effective and carry risks of impulse-control disorders, hallucinations and daytime sleepiness, particularly in older people. B. Anticholinergics cause confusion and are avoided in older people. C. MAO-B inhibitors have a modest effect, so are an option only when motor symptoms are not affecting quality of life. E. Amantadine is mainly used for levodopa-induced dyskinesias.
pearl: Parkinson's disease medicines must never be stopped suddenly, for example when a patient is nil by mouth, because of the risk of acute akinesia or neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome.
thinking: Rest tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity ↓ Parkinson's disease ↓ Motor symptoms affecting daily life ↓ Older patient ↓ Levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor
exam_trap: A, ropinirole — dopamine agonists were once used to delay levodopa, but in an older patient with impaired function levodopa works better and is better tolerated.
takeaway: Parkinson's disease affecting quality of life: start levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor.

stem: A 33-year-old man sees his GP about headaches he has had two or three times a month for a year. Each attack is a throbbing pain on one side of his head with vomiting, and he has to lie in a dark room for most of the day. Ibuprofen alone takes the edge off but he still misses work. He has no aura, no other medical problems and neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate acute treatment to offer?

options.B: An oral triptan combined with an NSAID
options.C: Daily propranolol only, with no change to acute treatment
options.E: Regular daily co-codamol to prevent attacks

correct_answer: B. An oral triptan combined with an NSAID
why_correct: This is migraine without aura that is not adequately controlled by a simple analgesic. NICE recommends offering a triptan combined with an NSAID or paracetamol for acute treatment. The combination works better than either drug alone and should be taken early in the headache phase.
why_wrong: A. Opioids are not recommended for migraine and risk medication overuse headache. C. Prevention does not replace effective acute treatment, and attacks of this frequency do not automatically need it. D. Ergotamine has been replaced by triptans because of side effects. E. Regular daily analgesics cause medication overuse headache.
pearl: Using triptans or opioids on 10 or more days a month, or simple analgesics on 15 or more days, can cause medication overuse headache.
thinking: Recurrent unilateral throbbing headache ↓ Vomiting, needs dark room ↓ Migraine without aura ↓ Simple analgesia not enough ↓ Triptan plus NSAID
exam_trap: C, propranolol — prevention is tempting because attacks are frequent, but the question asks about acute treatment, and a triptan plus NSAID is the step needed now.
takeaway: Migraine not controlled by simple analgesia: offer a triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is admitted with 5 days of tingling in her feet and increasing weakness, first in her legs and now in her arms. She had a flu-like illness 10 days ago. She now needs a walking frame. Reflexes are absent in all four limbs and she has mild bilateral facial weakness. Forced vital capacity is being monitored and is currently stable. Lumbar puncture shows a raised protein with a normal white cell count. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: Ascending weakness with areflexia after an infection, with a raised CSF protein and normal cell count, indicates Guillain-Barré syndrome. Patients who cannot walk unaided should be treated with IV immunoglobulin, or plasma exchange, which are equally effective. Forced vital capacity and autonomic function must be monitored closely because respiratory failure can develop quickly.
why_wrong: B. Oral steroids are ineffective in Guillain-Barré syndrome. C. IV steroids do not improve outcome. D. Observation alone is only appropriate in mild disease when the patient can still walk unaided. E. There is no evidence of viral encephalitis or meningitis.
pearl: Monitor forced vital capacity regularly in Guillain-Barré syndrome; oxygen saturation falls late. A falling FVC needs early intensive care review.
thinking: Ascending weakness after infection ↓ Areflexia and facial weakness ↓ High CSF protein, normal cells ↓ Guillain-Barré syndrome, cannot walk unaided ↓ IV immunoglobulin
exam_trap: C, IV methylprednisolone — it is used in many inflammatory neurological conditions, but steroids do not help Guillain-Barré syndrome.
takeaway: Guillain-Barré syndrome with loss of independent walking: give IV immunoglobulin and monitor FVC.

stem: A 52-year-old man sees his GP because he woke yesterday with the left side of his face drooping. He dribbles when drinking, cannot wrinkle his left forehead or fully close his left eye, and sounds seem uncomfortably loud in his left ear. There are no vesicles in the ear or mouth, the ear canal and drum look normal, and there is no limb weakness or other neurological sign. What is the most appropriate management?

options.C: Reassurance only, as most cases recover
options.D: Oral prednisolone now, with eye lubricants and taping the eye closed at night
options.E: Same-day referral for IV antivirals and IV steroids

correct_answer: D. Oral prednisolone now, with eye lubricants and taping the eye closed at night
why_correct: A sudden unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness involving the forehead, with no other neurological signs or ear vesicles, is Bell's palsy. Oral prednisolone started within 72 hours of onset improves the chance of full recovery. Because he cannot close his eye, eye protection with lubricants and taping at night is essential to prevent corneal damage.
why_wrong: A. Antivirals alone are not effective and are not recommended. B. Imaging is not needed for a typical Bell's palsy with no other neurological signs. C. Reassurance alone misses the benefit of early steroids and the need for eye protection. E. IV treatment and hospital referral are not needed for uncomplicated Bell's palsy.
pearl: Forehead involvement suggests a lower motor neurone lesion. Forehead sparing suggests an upper motor neurone lesion such as a stroke.
thinking: Sudden one-sided facial weakness ↓ Forehead involved, so lower motor neurone ↓ No vesicles or other neurological signs ↓ Bell's palsy within 72 hours ↓ Prednisolone and eye protection
exam_trap: A, oral aciclovir alone — a viral cause is suspected, but antivirals alone do not improve recovery; steroids are the key treatment.
takeaway: Bell's palsy within 72 hours: oral prednisolone plus eye protection.

presentation: Prolonged convulsive seizure without IV access
stem: A 32-year-old woman with epilepsy and a learning disability lives in a supported living home. Staff call for help because she has been having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure for 6 minutes. She is lying on her side, her airway is clear and she is not cyanosed. No one present can insert a cannula. Her care plan includes emergency medication. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.E: No medication until the seizure has lasted 10 minutes

why_correct: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more needs treatment because it may not stop by itself. Without IV access, NICE recommends buccal midazolam as first-line treatment in the community, given by trained carers following the person's care plan. It acts quickly, is easy to give and is more dignified than rectal medication.
why_wrong: A. IV lorazepam is first-line once IV access is available, which it is not here. B. Rectal diazepam works but is now second choice to buccal midazolam when there is no IV access. D. Levetiracetam is a second-line treatment after benzodiazepines have failed. E. Treatment should start at 5 minutes, not 10.
pearl: Benzodiazepines can be given up to two doses in total, including any pre-hospital dose; if seizures continue, move to a second-line drug such as levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate.
thinking: Generalised seizure over 5 minutes ↓ Needs treatment now ↓ No IV access ↓ Community setting with care plan ↓ Buccal midazolam
exam_trap: B, rectal diazepam — it is effective and was the traditional choice, but buccal midazolam is now preferred because it is faster, easier and more dignified.
takeaway: Prolonged convulsive seizure without IV access: buccal midazolam first.

presentation: Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with normal CT
stem: A 38-year-old man was lifting weights at the gym when he felt a sudden, severe pain at the back of his head, reaching its worst within a few seconds. He vomited and went home to rest, coming to the emergency department the following morning. A non-contrast CT head performed 14 hours after the onset of the headache is normal. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge with analgesia and GP follow-up
options.C: Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
options.E: Start IV antibiotics for possible meningitis

correct_answer: C. Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
why_correct: A thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds must be investigated for subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT is less sensitive when it is performed more than 6 hours after onset, so a normal scan does not exclude bleeding. NICE advises considering lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset to look for xanthochromia, so it can be done now.
why_wrong: A. Discharge before subarachnoid haemorrhage has been excluded is unsafe. B. MRI is not the standard next test for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage after a normal CT. D. Repeating the CT does not improve sensitivity as blood is cleared and becomes harder to see. E. There is no fever or other feature to suggest meningitis.
pearl: Xanthochromia takes about 12 hours to develop, so lumbar puncture is timed for at least 12 hours after headache onset; earlier samples can be falsely reassuring.
thinking: Sudden severe headache peaking in seconds ↓ Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage ↓ CT done late is normal ↓ Late CT can miss blood ↓ Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
exam_trap: A, discharge — a normal CT and normal examination feel reassuring, but a late CT can miss subarachnoid haemorrhage and a missed bleed can be fatal.
takeaway: Thunderclap headache with a normal late CT: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia.

presentation: Horner's syndrome from an apical lung tumour
stem: A 62-year-old woman who smoked for 35 years sees her GP with 3 months of severe pain in her left shoulder that spreads down the inner side of her arm to her little finger. She has noticed weakness and wasting of the small muscles of her left hand. Her left upper eyelid droops slightly and her left pupil is smaller than the right, with no difference in eye movements. What is the most likely cause?

options.E: C8 nerve root compression from cervical spondylosis

why_correct: Shoulder and inner arm pain, small hand muscle wasting and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (ptosis and a small pupil) in a long-term smoker suggest an apical lung tumour (Pancoast tumour). It invades the lower brachial plexus and the sympathetic chain. She needs an urgent chest X-ray under the suspected cancer pathway.
why_wrong: A. A cervical rib can compress the lower brachial plexus but does not usually cause Horner's syndrome. C. A third nerve palsy causes ptosis with a dilated pupil and abnormal eye movements. D. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ptosis without pupil changes or hand wasting. E. Root compression from spondylosis does not cause Horner's syndrome.
pearl: Horner's syndrome plus arm pain and small hand muscle wasting in a smoker is a Pancoast tumour until proven otherwise.
thinking: Shoulder pain spreading to inner arm ↓ Small hand muscle wasting, lower brachial plexus ↓ Ptosis with small pupil, Horner's ↓ Long-term smoker ↓ Apical lung tumour
exam_trap: E, C8 root compression — it explains the arm pain and hand weakness, but it cannot explain the Horner's syndrome, which needs a lesion of the sympathetic chain.
takeaway: Horner's syndrome with lower brachial plexus signs in a smoker: think Pancoast tumour.

stem: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes attends the emergency department with a day of vomiting and abdominal pain. He has not taken his insulin since the vomiting began. He is breathing deeply and rapidly. Capillary glucose is 17 mmol/L and blood ketones are 5.2 mmol/L. Venous pH is 7.14 and bicarbonate is 9 mmol/L. Lactate is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Diabetic ketoacidosis is defined by the combination of diabetes or hyperglycaemia, a high blood ketone level and a metabolic acidosis (low pH or low bicarbonate). He meets all three, and missed insulin during illness is a common trigger. The glucose does not have to be very high: ketoacidosis can occur with only moderately raised or even normal glucose.
why_wrong: A. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state usually has very high glucose and osmolality without significant ketosis or acidosis. C. Alcoholic ketoacidosis occurs after heavy drinking, usually with normal or low glucose. D. Starvation ketosis causes mild ketosis without significant acidosis. E. A normal lactate makes lactic acidosis unlikely.
pearl: Never rule out DKA because the glucose is only moderately raised; check ketones and blood gases in any unwell person with diabetes, particularly those taking SGLT2 inhibitors.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes, missed insulin, vomiting ↓ Raised glucose ↓ High ketones ↓ Acidosis with low bicarbonate ↓ Diabetic ketoacidosis
exam_trap: A, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — any hyperglycaemic emergency may come to mind, but HHS lacks marked ketosis and acidosis, and this glucose is too low for it.
takeaway: DKA = diabetes or hyperglycaemia plus ketonaemia plus acidosis; glucose need not be very high.

stem: A 38-year-old woman sees her GP with 4 months of tiredness, dry skin, constipation, weight gain and heavier periods. She has no heart disease and is not pregnant. Blood tests show a markedly raised TSH, a low free T4 and positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.D: No treatment, with repeat thyroid function tests in 6 months

why_correct: A raised TSH with a low free T4 and positive peroxidase antibodies indicates overt primary hypothyroidism due to autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis. NICE recommends levothyroxine. In adults under 65 without cardiovascular disease, a full replacement dose based on body weight can be considered from the start, and TSH is checked after a few weeks to adjust the dose.
why_wrong: B. Liothyronine is not recommended for routine treatment of primary hypothyroidism. C. Carbimazole treats hyperthyroidism. D. Watching and waiting is for some cases of subclinical hypothyroidism, not overt disease with symptoms. E. Hydrocortisone is for adrenal insufficiency, not thyroid hormone deficiency.
pearl: Start levothyroxine at a low dose and increase slowly in older people and those with heart disease, to avoid provoking angina or arrhythmia.
thinking: Tiredness, weight gain, constipation, menorrhagia ↓ High TSH, low free T4 ↓ Overt primary hypothyroidism ↓ Autoimmune cause ↓ Levothyroxine
exam_trap: D, repeat tests in 6 months — this is used for mild subclinical hypothyroidism, but a low free T4 with symptoms is overt disease that needs treatment.
takeaway: Overt primary hypothyroidism: treat with levothyroxine and titrate to TSH.

stem: A 36-year-old woman sees her GP with 3 months of weight loss despite a good appetite, sweating, a fine tremor and palpitations. Her eyes feel gritty and her partner says they look more prominent. She has a smooth, diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid with a soft bruit over it. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is raised. Her youngest child is 4 years old. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hyperthyroidism with a smooth, diffuse goitre, a thyroid bruit and eye signs is typical of Graves' disease. Thyroid eye disease is specific to Graves' disease, caused by antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor. TSH receptor antibody testing confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Toxic multinodular goitre has an irregular, nodular gland and occurs in older people without eye disease. C. Subacute thyroiditis causes a painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness. D. A toxic adenoma is a single palpable nodule. E. Factitious thyrotoxicosis causes a small or impalpable thyroid.
pearl: Smoking increases the risk and severity of thyroid eye disease; advising patients to stop is part of management.
thinking: Weight loss, tremor, palpitations ↓ Suppressed TSH, high free T4 ↓ Smooth goitre with bruit ↓ Eye signs ↓ Graves' disease
exam_trap: A, toxic multinodular goitre — it is a common cause of hyperthyroidism, but the gland is nodular, patients are older, and there is no eye disease.
takeaway: Hyperthyroidism with diffuse goitre and eye disease is Graves' disease.

stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed in the endocrine clinic with easy bruising, thin skin, difficulty climbing stairs, newly diagnosed diabetes and hypertension. He takes no steroid medicines in any form. An overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows failure of cortisol suppression, and a late-night salivary cortisol is raised, confirming hypercortisolism. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
why_correct: Once Cushing's syndrome has been confirmed biochemically, the next step is to find the cause. Plasma ACTH separates ACTH-independent disease (low ACTH, usually an adrenal tumour) from ACTH-dependent disease (normal or high ACTH, from a pituitary or ectopic source). This result decides which imaging and further tests are needed.
why_wrong: A. Adrenal imaging is appropriate only once ACTH is shown to be suppressed. B. Pituitary MRI follows confirmation of ACTH-dependent disease, and small incidental pituitary lesions are common. C. Hypercortisolism is already confirmed, so further screening tests add nothing. D. Petrosal sinus sampling is a specialised test used later to distinguish pituitary from ectopic ACTH.
pearl: Order in Cushing's: exclude steroid use, confirm excess cortisol, measure ACTH, then image the right place.
thinking: Features of cortisol excess ↓ No exogenous steroids ↓ Hypercortisolism confirmed ↓ Next, localise: ACTH-dependent or not ↓ Plasma ACTH
exam_trap: B, pituitary MRI — Cushing's disease is the commonest endogenous cause, but imaging before measuring ACTH risks chasing an incidental finding.
takeaway: Confirmed Cushing's syndrome: measure plasma ACTH before any imaging.

presentation: Primary adrenal insufficiency — confirming the diagnosis
stem: A 28-year-old man with vitiligo sees his GP with 3 months of tiredness, weight loss, dizziness on standing and a craving for salty food. His palmar creases and gums look darker than usual. His blood pressure falls on standing. Blood tests show a low sodium and a raised potassium. He is not acutely unwell. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
why_correct: Fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension, salt craving and pigmentation with low sodium and high potassium, in someone with another autoimmune condition, suggest primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). The short Synacthen test confirms it: cortisol fails to rise adequately after synthetic ACTH. A high plasma ACTH shows the cause is in the adrenal glands.
why_wrong: A. A single random cortisol is unreliable for confirming or excluding adrenal insufficiency. C. Dexamethasone suppression tests look for cortisol excess, not deficiency. D. The aldosterone to renin ratio screens for primary hyperaldosteronism. E. Imaging is not used to make the diagnosis, and autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest UK cause.
pearl: If adrenal crisis is suspected, give IV or IM hydrocortisone straight away after taking blood; do not delay treatment for a Synacthen test.
thinking: Fatigue, weight loss, pigmentation ↓ Low sodium, high potassium, postural drop ↓ Suspected Addison's disease ↓ Needs dynamic test of adrenal reserve ↓ Short Synacthen test
exam_trap: A, random cortisol — it is quick and often done first, but a single value cannot confirm adrenal insufficiency; a stimulation test is needed.
takeaway: Suspected Addison's disease is confirmed with a short Synacthen test.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes after two raised HbA1c results. She has a BMI of 31 kg/m2 and has started making changes to her diet and activity. She has no history of cardiovascular disease or heart failure, and her renal function and urine albumin to creatinine ratio are normal. She has no contraindications to any diabetes medicines. According to current NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?

options.A: Metformin alone, adding a second drug later if HbA1c rises
options.C: Modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor

correct_answer: C. Modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor
why_correct: NICE now recommends offering modified-release metformin together with an SGLT2 inhibitor as initial treatment for adults with type 2 diabetes, including those without cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease. The combination improves glucose control and weight and reduces cardiovascular events compared with metformin alone. If metformin is not tolerated or is contraindicated, an SGLT2 inhibitor is offered alone.
why_wrong: A. Metformin alone with later step-up was the previous pathway and has been replaced. B. Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain and are not first-line. D. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not recommended as initial treatment for this group. E. Insulin is not first-line for a well patient with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes.
pearl: Before starting an SGLT2 inhibitor, warn about genital fungal infections, dehydration and the rare risk of ketoacidosis, including during acute illness, when the drug should be paused.
thinking: New type 2 diabetes ↓ No cardiovascular, heart failure or kidney disease ↓ Not early-onset ↓ Current NICE initial treatment ↓ MR metformin plus SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_trap: A, metformin alone — this was standard practice for years and appears in many older resources, but NICE now offers an SGLT2 inhibitor with metformin from the start.
takeaway: Type 2 diabetes initial drug treatment: modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with a history of two kidney stones has routine blood tests at her GP surgery. Adjusted calcium is raised at 2.85 mmol/L. Parathyroid hormone is 5.9 pmol/L (reference range 1.6 to 6.9). Renal function and vitamin D are normal. She takes no regular medicines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: When calcium is high, PTH should be suppressed. A PTH in the upper half of the reference range is therefore inappropriately normal and indicates primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a single parathyroid adenoma. Kidney stones are a typical complication.
why_wrong: B. Malignancy raises calcium through PTH-related peptide or bone metastases, with suppressed PTH. C. Sarcoidosis raises calcium through excess activated vitamin D, which suppresses PTH. D. Vitamin D toxicity also suppresses PTH, and her vitamin D is normal. E. She takes no diuretics; thiazides cause only mild hypercalcaemia and often unmask underlying primary hyperparathyroidism rather than explaining it.
pearl: A high calcium with a normal PTH is not reassuring. Any PTH that is not suppressed in hypercalcaemia points to the parathyroid glands.
thinking: Raised calcium ↓ PTH should be suppressed ↓ PTH in normal range, so inappropriately normal ↓ History of kidney stones ↓ Primary hyperparathyroidism
exam_trap: B, malignancy — it is a common and serious cause of hypercalcaemia, but it suppresses PTH; an unsuppressed PTH points to the parathyroid glands.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia with an unsuppressed PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A 44-year-old man sees his GP with several months of sudden episodes of pounding headache, palpitations, drenching sweats and pallor, each lasting 10 to 20 minutes. A pharmacist measured his blood pressure during one attack at 210/120 mmHg, but readings in the surgery between attacks are normal. Recent bloods showed impaired fasting glucose. Thyroid function is normal. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.D: Start propranolol and review in 4 weeks

why_correct: Episodes of headache, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal severe hypertension and normal readings in between suggest a phaeochromocytoma. The first step is biochemical confirmation, with plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines. Imaging is arranged only after the biochemistry is positive.
why_wrong: B. Imaging comes after biochemical confirmation, as incidental adrenal lesions are common. C. Urinary 5-HIAA is for carcinoid syndrome, which typically causes flushing and diarrhoea rather than hypertensive episodes. D. A beta-blocker without prior alpha-blockade can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure in phaeochromocytoma. E. Ambulatory monitoring confirms hypertension but cannot diagnose the cause.
pearl: In phaeochromocytoma, alpha-blockade (for example phenoxybenzamine) is always started before any beta-blocker, both medically and before surgery.
thinking: Episodes of headache, palpitations and sweating ↓ Paroxysmal severe hypertension ↓ Suspect catecholamine excess ↓ Confirm biochemically first ↓ Plasma free metanephrines
exam_trap: D, propranolol — palpitations and anxiety-like attacks make a beta-blocker tempting, but unopposed beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma can cause a hypertensive crisis.
takeaway: Suspected phaeochromocytoma: plasma free metanephrines first, imaging second.

stem: A 71-year-old woman on the medical ward is being treated for community-acquired pneumonia. Her sodium has fallen to 122 mmol/L. She takes no diuretics and has not been vomiting. She has moist mucous membranes, no postural drop in blood pressure, a normal JVP and no oedema. Serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is inappropriately high and urine sodium is raised. Thyroid function and a morning cortisol are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: B. Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion
why_correct: Hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and a raised urine sodium in a euvolaemic patient, with thyroid and adrenal disease excluded and no diuretics, meets the criteria for SIADH. Pneumonia is a recognised cause. Fluid restriction and treatment of the pneumonia are the usual first steps.
why_wrong: A. She is clinically euvolaemic, with no history of fluid loss. C. Primary polydipsia produces very dilute urine, not concentrated urine. D. A normal morning cortisol makes adrenal insufficiency unlikely. E. She is not taking a diuretic.
pearl: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion: check volume status, exclude diuretics, hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before making it.
thinking: Low sodium and low serum osmolality ↓ Concentrated urine with high urine sodium ↓ Clinically euvolaemic ↓ Thyroid, adrenal and diuretics excluded ↓ SIADH due to pneumonia
exam_trap: D, adrenal insufficiency — it can produce an identical biochemical picture, but a normal morning cortisol makes it unlikely here.
takeaway: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine, after exclusions, is SIADH.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with Graves' disease, who stopped taking carbimazole 2 months ago, is brought to the emergency department with a chest infection. She is agitated and confused, with a temperature of 40.1 degrees C, vomiting and diarrhoea. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 156 beats per minute. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is very high. Which treatment approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Lugol's iodine first, then propylthiouracil an hour later, with propranolol and hydrocortisone
options.B: Propylthiouracil first, then Lugol's iodine at least an hour later, with propranolol and hydrocortisone
options.C: Radioactive iodine once the infection has been treated

correct_answer: B. Propylthiouracil first, then Lugol's iodine at least an hour later, with propranolol and hydrocortisone
