why_wrong: B. Body dysmorphic disorder involves preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance, not distress about sexed characteristics relieved by gender recognition. C. Delusional disorder involves a fixed false belief, and there are no psychotic features here. D. Depression would cause pervasive low mood, whereas their mood lifts when they are recognised as a woman. E. The identity disturbance of borderline personality disorder is unstable and shifting, whereas this sense of identity has been consistent for years.
pearl: Gender incongruence is not a mental illness in itself; the distress it causes is what brings people to doctors. Respectful language and timely referral matter most.
thinking: Long-standing sense of being a different gender from that assigned at birth ↓ Distress focused on sexed features such as facial hair and voice ↓ Relief when recognised in the experienced gender ↓ No perceived defect, psychosis or unstable identity ↓ Gender dysphoria
exam_trap: B, body dysmorphic disorder — distress about appearance and repeated grooming can look similar, but BDD centres on a perceived flaw, whereas this distress is about sexed characteristics and eases with gender recognition.
takeaway: Persistent distress at the mismatch between experienced gender and sexed characteristics is gender dysphoria.

stem: A 36-year-old woman attends her GP surgery in December with headaches, nausea and tiredness for two weeks. The headaches are worse in the mornings and ease when she spends the day at work. Her two children have also been complaining of headaches and feeling sick, and she mentions that the family's elderly gas boiler has been making a strange noise. She has no fever, the neurological examination is normal, and her oxygen saturation is 98% on air. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
why_correct: Several members of the same household with headache, nausea and fatigue that improve away from home, in winter, with a faulty gas appliance, strongly suggests chronic carbon monoxide exposure. Pulse oximetry is unreliable because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a normal reading is expected. She needs urgent assessment with a carboxyhaemoglobin level on co-oximetry, high-flow oxygen started as soon as poisoning is suspected, and the household must not return until the appliance is made safe.
why_wrong: A. Influenza causes fever and myalgia and would not improve each day she leaves the house. B. Tension-type headache would not explain nausea in several family members linked to the home. D. Medication-overuse headache needs regular analgesic use and does not affect the whole household. E. Gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea over days, not morning headaches that resolve away from home.
pearl: Think carbon monoxide when several people or pets in one home have headaches that improve away from it. Normal saturations do not exclude it; ask for co-oximetry.
thinking: Headache, nausea and fatigue ↓ Several household members affected ↓ Symptoms ease away from home, faulty gas boiler in winter ↓ Normal oximetry does not reassure ↓ Carbon monoxide poisoning
exam_trap: A, influenza — a winter illness affecting a whole family sounds infectious, but there is no fever and symptoms ease whenever she leaves the house, which points to an environmental exposure.
takeaway: Household clusters of headache that improve away from home suggest carbon monoxide; oximetry reads falsely normal.

stem: A 52-year-old farm labourer is brought to the emergency department after spending the morning spraying crops in hot weather without a mask. He is drooling, has a wheeze with copious bronchial secretions, and has had diarrhoea and urinary incontinence. His pupils are very small, his pulse is 46/min, and fine twitching is visible in the muscles of his arms and chest. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Organophosphate pesticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates. Muscarinic effects cause salivation, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, diarrhoea, urinary incontinence, miosis and bradycardia, and nicotinic effects cause fasciculations and later weakness. Treatment includes decontamination with protective equipment, airway support and atropine titrated to dry the chest secretions.
why_wrong: A. Opioids cause small pupils and respiratory depression but a dry chest without secretions or fasciculations. C. Anticholinergic toxicity causes the opposite picture: dry skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia and urinary retention. D. Serotonin syndrome causes hyperthermia, clonus, tachycardia and dilated pupils. E. Beta-blocker overdose causes bradycardia and hypotension but not secretions, diarrhoea or fasciculations.
pearl: Cholinergic toxicity drowns the patient in secretions: the killer is the wet chest. Atropine is titrated until secretions dry, not to the pupil size.
thinking: Agricultural pesticide exposure ↓ Drooling, bronchorrhoea, diarrhoea and incontinence ↓ Miosis and bradycardia ↓ Fasciculations from nicotinic excess ↓ Organophosphate poisoning
exam_trap: A, opioid toxicity — pinpoint pupils strongly suggest opioids, but opioids do not cause profuse secretions, diarrhoea and fasciculations, which define a cholinergic toxidrome.
takeaway: Pinpoint pupils with secretions, bradycardia and fasciculations after pesticide exposure suggest organophosphate poisoning.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after her flatmate found her beside several empty boxes of amitriptyline. She is drowsy and agitated, with dry flushed skin and dilated pupils. Her pulse is 128/min and her blood pressure is low. Her ECG shows a sinus tachycardia with a broad QRS complex, and shortly after arrival she has a brief generalised seizure. Her airway is being managed. What is the most appropriate specific treatment?
why_correct: Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac sodium channels, widening the QRS and causing arrhythmias, hypotension and seizures, alongside anticholinergic features. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate provides a sodium load and alkalinises the blood, which reduces drug binding to sodium channels, narrows the QRS and improves blood pressure. It is indicated when there is QRS widening, arrhythmia, hypotension or acidosis.
why_wrong: B. Flumazenil can precipitate seizures, particularly when a tricyclic has been taken, and is contraindicated. C. Amiodarone can worsen conduction problems and is not used for tricyclic cardiotoxicity. D. Calcium is used for calcium channel blocker toxicity and hyperkalaemia, not tricyclic sodium channel blockade. E. Naloxone reverses opioids and does not affect tricyclic toxicity.
pearl: Tricyclic overdose: anticholinergic signs plus a broad QRS, hypotension and seizures. Sodium bicarbonate is the antidote of choice for the cardiac effects.
thinking: Tricyclic overdose ↓ Anticholinergic features: dry skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia ↓ Broad QRS, hypotension and seizure ↓ Sodium channel blockade ↓ Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
exam_trap: C, amiodarone — a broad-complex ECG suggests an antiarrhythmic, but the QRS widening is due to sodium channel blockade, which amiodarone can worsen; sodium bicarbonate treats the cause.
takeaway: Tricyclic overdose with a broad QRS or hypotension is treated with intravenous sodium bicarbonate.

stem: A 64-year-old man tells his GP that for two months food has been sticking behind his breastbone. It started with bread and meat, and in the last few weeks even soup has been hard to get down. His trousers have become loose. He has smoked for 40 years and has had heartburn on and off for many years. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor and review in 8 weeks
options.C: Urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway

correct_answer: C. Urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia, first for solids and then liquids, with weight loss in an older smoker with long-standing reflux is an alarm presentation for oesophageal cancer. Dysphagia alone warrants an urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway, which allows direct inspection and biopsy. Weight loss and his risk factors only add to the urgency.
why_wrong: A. An empirical acid suppression trial delays diagnosis and can mask symptoms. B. A barium swallow cannot provide tissue and is not the first-line urgent test. D. Routine referral is too slow for a suspected cancer. E. H. pylori testing is for uncomplicated dyspepsia, not dysphagia.
pearl: Dysphagia is always a red flag, regardless of age. Progression from solids to liquids suggests a mechanical, often malignant, obstruction.
thinking: Food sticking behind the sternum ↓ Progressing from solids to liquids ↓ Weight loss, smoking and long-standing reflux ↓ Suspected oesophageal cancer ↓ Urgent direct-access endoscopy
exam_trap: A, proton pump inhibitor trial — his long history of heartburn suggests reflux and a peptic stricture, but dysphagia with weight loss is an alarm feature that must not be treated empirically.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss needs urgent endoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway, not a PPI trial.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes sees her GP because she feels exhausted all the time. She has iron deficiency anaemia despite light periods and a normal diet, and she has noticed intermittent loose, pale stools that are hard to flush, recurrent mouth ulcers, and an intensely itchy rash of small blisters on her elbows and knees. Her blood glucose control has recently become erratic, with several unexplained hypoglycaemic episodes. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Unexplained iron deficiency, steatorrhoea, mouth ulcers, an itchy blistering rash on extensor surfaces typical of dermatitis herpetiformis and erratic glucose control from malabsorption, in a woman with type 1 diabetes, point to coeliac disease. Autoimmune conditions such as type 1 diabetes increase its risk. Serology with tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA should be checked while she is still eating gluten.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause iron deficiency, steatorrhoea or a blistering rash. B. Crohn's disease can cause malabsorption and ulcers, but not dermatitis herpetiformis. C. Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea after dairy, without malabsorption of iron or a rash. E. Pernicious anaemia causes B12 deficiency, not iron deficiency, steatorrhoea or a blistering rash.
pearl: Dermatitis herpetiformis is essentially pathognomonic of coeliac disease. Test anyone with unexplained iron deficiency or type 1 diabetes with new gastrointestinal symptoms.
thinking: Iron deficiency without blood loss ↓ Steatorrhoea, mouth ulcers and erratic glucose from malabsorption ↓ Itchy blistering rash on extensor surfaces ↓ Background type 1 diabetes ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: B, Crohn's disease — mouth ulcers, diarrhoea and iron deficiency fit inflammatory bowel disease, but the itchy blistering extensor rash is dermatitis herpetiformis, which points to coeliac disease.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency, malabsorption and dermatitis herpetiformis suggest coeliac disease; test on a gluten diet.

stem: A 46-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the emergency department after sudden-onset severe pain between his shoulder blades while lifting a heavy box. He describes it as ripping and maximal from the start. He is sweaty and distressed. The left radial pulse is noticeably weaker than the right. The ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy without ST elevation, and the chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden, severe, ripping interscapular pain at maximum intensity from onset in a hypertensive man, with a pulse deficit and a widened mediastinum, indicates acute aortic dissection. The pulse deficit reflects the dissection flap compromising a branch vessel. He needs urgent CT angiography, blood pressure and heart rate control, and early specialist referral; thrombolysis and anticoagulation must be avoided.
why_wrong: A. Myocardial infarction builds up over minutes and does not cause a pulse deficit or a widened mediastinum, and there is no ST elevation. C. Oesophageal rupture follows vomiting and causes surgical emphysema or pneumomediastinum. D. Tension pneumothorax causes respiratory distress, absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation. E. Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting, not pulse asymmetry.
pearl: Pain that is maximal at onset, a pulse or blood pressure difference between arms and a wide mediastinum point to dissection. Always consider it before giving thrombolysis.
thinking: Hypertensive man with sudden severe interscapular pain ↓ Ripping and maximal from onset ↓ Unequal radial pulses ↓ Widened mediastinum, no ST elevation ↓ Acute aortic dissection
exam_trap: A, inferior myocardial infarction — severe chest or back pain with sweating suggests an infarct, but pain that peaks instantly, a pulse deficit and a widened mediastinum are features of dissection.
takeaway: Sudden ripping pain to the back with a pulse deficit and wide mediastinum is aortic dissection until proven otherwise.

stem: A 63-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who noticed at breakfast that the right side of his face had dropped. He understands what is said to him but his speech is halting and effortful, and he cannot find the words he wants. His right arm is markedly weak, while his right leg is only mildly affected. He has no double vision, vertigo or difficulty swallowing. Which arterial territory is most likely to be involved?
why_correct: Right-sided face and arm weakness greater than leg weakness, with expressive aphasia in a right-handed man, localises to the dominant left hemisphere in the middle cerebral artery territory. The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral motor cortex representing the face and arm, and the frontal language area. He needs urgent brain imaging to guide reperfusion therapy.
why_wrong: B. Anterior cerebral artery strokes affect the leg more than the arm and face. C. A right middle cerebral artery stroke would cause left-sided weakness and typically neglect rather than aphasia. D. Posterior cerebral artery strokes cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia rather than marked motor and language deficits. E. Vertebrobasilar strokes cause brainstem or cerebellar signs such as diplopia, vertigo and dysphagia.
pearl: Face and arm worse than leg means middle cerebral artery; leg worse than arm means anterior cerebral artery. Aphasia localises to the dominant hemisphere.
thinking: Sudden right face and arm weakness ↓ Leg relatively spared ↓ Expressive aphasia in a right-handed man ↓ Lateral cortex of the dominant hemisphere ↓ Left middle cerebral artery
exam_trap: B, left anterior cerebral artery — it is also a left-sided anterior circulation territory, but it mainly affects the leg; marked face and arm weakness with aphasia points to the middle cerebral artery.
takeaway: Contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia localises to the dominant middle cerebral artery territory.

stem: An 84-year-old man is on the orthopaedic ward two days after surgery for a hip fracture. The night nurse reports that although he was calm and chatty during the morning, he has since been pulling at his cannula, talking about insects on the wall and dozing off mid-sentence before becoming agitated again. He cannot keep track of a simple conversation or name the months of the year backwards. His daughter says that before the fall he lived alone and managed his own shopping and finances. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An acute onset of inattention, fluctuating alertness and visual hallucinations after surgery, in a man who was cognitively independent beforehand, is delirium. The key features are acute onset, fluctuation and impaired attention. Common precipitants after hip fracture include pain, infection, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and drugs such as opioids, all of which should be sought and treated.
why_wrong: A. Alzheimer's disease causes gradual decline over months to years, and he was independent before the fall. C. Dementia with Lewy bodies does cause visual hallucinations and fluctuation, but develops gradually, not abruptly after an operation. D. Late-onset schizophrenia does not cause impaired attention or altered alertness. E. Psychotic depression would be preceded by persistent low mood and would not explain the fluctuating alertness.
pearl: Delirium is defined by acute onset, fluctuation and inattention. Always collect a collateral history of baseline function to separate it from dementia.
thinking: Older man after hip surgery ↓ Abrupt change within a day ↓ Fluctuating alertness and inattention ↓ Visual hallucinations, previously independent ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: C, dementia with Lewy bodies — fluctuating cognition and vivid visual hallucinations are its hallmarks, but onset was abrupt after surgery in a man who was previously independent, which is delirium.
takeaway: Acute fluctuating inattention after surgery or illness is delirium; find and treat the cause.

stem: A 24-year-old man tells his GP that he is repeatedly troubled by images of his flat burning down because he left the cooker on, or of burglars harming his partner because he left the door unlocked. He recognises these fears are excessive and come from his own mind, but he cannot dismiss them. He checks the cooker and locks many times before leaving home, often returning to check again, and is now regularly late for work. He feels temporary relief after checking, but the doubt returns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Intrusive, unwanted thoughts and images of harm that he recognises as products of his own mind (obsessions), with repeated checking that briefly relieves the anxiety (compulsions) and causes functional impairment, are obsessive-compulsive disorder. The relief is short-lived, which maintains the cycle. First-line treatment is CBT including exposure and response prevention, with an SSRI for more severe symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Generalised anxiety disorder involves broad worry about everyday matters without repetitive rituals. B. In psychosis the belief is held as true and externally caused, whereas he recognises these thoughts as his own and excessive. D. Anankastic personality disorder is a pervasive trait of perfectionism and rigidity, without distressing intrusive thoughts driving rituals. E. Panic disorder causes discrete episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms.
pearl: In OCD the patient recognises the thoughts as their own and resists them. Rituals give brief relief, which reinforces the cycle; exposure and response prevention breaks it.
thinking: Intrusive images of harm ↓ Recognised as excessive and from his own mind ↓ Repetitive checking giving brief relief ↓ Significant functional impairment ↓ Obsessive-compulsive disorder
exam_trap: D, anankastic personality disorder — the obsessive-compulsive name is similar, but that is a pervasive style of perfectionism and control, not intrusive unwanted thoughts with neutralising rituals.
takeaway: Intrusive unwanted thoughts with anxiety-relieving rituals that impair function mean obsessive-compulsive disorder.

stem: The mother of a 29-year-old woman with schizophrenia telephones the GP surgery. Her daughter has missed her last two depot antipsychotic injections. Over the past fortnight she has barely slept, has locked herself in her flat and believes the neighbours are watching her through the television. She is eating very little and has stopped answering most calls. She has not threatened anyone and has not mentioned self-harm. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure the mother and review at the next routine appointment in 3 months
options.B: Prescribe sertraline and review in 4 weeks
options.C: Prescribe a hypnotic for sleep and review in a month
options.D: Arrange urgent assessment by her community mental health or crisis team, including a risk assessment
options.E: Ask the police to detain her under section 136 of the Mental Health Act

correct_answer: D. Arrange urgent assessment by her community mental health or crisis team, including a risk assessment
why_correct: Missed depot medication followed by insomnia, social withdrawal, poor self-care and persecutory beliefs indicates relapse of schizophrenia. She needs urgent assessment by the mental health team who know her, including assessment of risk to herself through self-neglect and of risk to others. Early intervention can restore treatment and may avoid admission.
why_wrong: A. Waiting three months risks further deterioration, self-neglect and harm. B. An antidepressant does not treat a psychotic relapse. C. A hypnotic treats a symptom and leaves the relapse unaddressed. E. Section 136 applies to people in a public place, and an urgent mental health assessment is the proportionate first step.
pearl: Missed depots plus reduced sleep are the classic early warning signs of relapse. Act early through the team that knows the patient, and always assess risk.
thinking: Known schizophrenia ↓ Missed depot antipsychotic ↓ Insomnia, withdrawal, self-neglect and paranoid beliefs ↓ Psychotic relapse ↓ Urgent mental health team assessment with risk assessment
exam_trap: E, police detention under section 136 — urgent action is needed, but section 136 applies to people in public places and there is no immediate danger; the right step is urgent assessment by her mental health team.
takeaway: Psychotic relapse after stopping antipsychotics needs urgent mental health assessment including risk.

stem: A 77-year-old woman taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation fell at home yesterday and struck her head. Today her family find her increasingly drowsy and confused. A CT head shows an acute subdural haematoma, and her INR is well above her target range. Neurosurgical advice is being sought. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment for her anticoagulation?

options.B: Withhold warfarin and recheck the INR tomorrow
options.C: Intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate

correct_answer: C. Intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
why_correct: An intracranial bleed in a patient taking warfarin is a major, life-threatening haemorrhage requiring immediate full reversal. Prothrombin complex concentrate replaces the vitamin K dependent clotting factors within minutes, and intravenous vitamin K sustains the correction once the concentrate wears off. Warfarin is stopped, and the INR is rechecked after treatment.
why_wrong: A. Fresh frozen plasma is slower, needs large volumes and corrects less completely; it is used only if PCC is unavailable. B. Simply withholding warfarin takes days to correct the INR, which is far too slow for an intracranial bleed. D. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin. E. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin.
pearl: Major bleeding on warfarin needs both parts: PCC for speed and IV vitamin K for durability. Match the reversal agent to the drug.
thinking: Warfarin with a raised INR ↓ Intracranial haemorrhage after a fall ↓ Major, life-threatening bleed ↓ Need rapid and sustained factor replacement ↓ PCC plus intravenous vitamin K
exam_trap: E, idarucizumab — it is a specific anticoagulant reversal agent, so it feels targeted, but it only reverses dabigatran; warfarin needs prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K.
takeaway: Major bleeding on warfarin: give prothrombin complex concentrate with intravenous vitamin K immediately.

presentation: Lithium toxicity risk during intercurrent illness
stem: A 47-year-old man with bipolar disorder, stable for years on lithium, telephones the GP practice. For the past two days he has had diarrhoea and vomiting after a family meal, and he is struggling to keep fluids down. He feels weak and a little shaky. He asks whether he should carry on with his tablets as usual. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Arrange same-day medical review with an urgent lithium level and kidney function
options.B: Continue lithium as normal and take loperamide
options.C: Take ibuprofen regularly for the abdominal cramps
options.D: Take an extra dose of lithium to replace tablets lost through vomiting
options.E: Reduce fluid intake until the vomiting settles

correct_answer: A. Arrange same-day medical review with an urgent lithium level and kidney function
why_correct: Vomiting and diarrhoea cause dehydration and sodium loss, which reduce renal lithium clearance, so the lithium level can climb into the toxic range quickly. Shakiness and weakness may be early signs of toxicity. He needs same-day assessment with a lithium level, renal function and electrolytes, and advice on whether to withhold lithium while he is unable to keep fluids down.
why_wrong: B. Carrying on unchanged ignores the risk of a rapidly rising lithium level during fluid loss. C. NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance and can themselves precipitate toxicity. D. Extra doses risk serious toxicity, as lithium has a narrow therapeutic range. E. Reducing fluids worsens dehydration and lithium accumulation.
pearl: Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics all raise lithium levels. Coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, ataxia and confusion suggest toxicity.
thinking: Patient on lithium ↓ Vomiting and diarrhoea causing fluid and sodium loss ↓ Reduced renal lithium clearance ↓ Shakiness may signal early toxicity ↓ Same-day review with lithium level and renal function
exam_trap: B, continue as normal with loperamide — it seems sensible for simple gastroenteritis, but it ignores the danger that fluid loss poses to lithium clearance and the hint of early toxicity.
takeaway: Vomiting or diarrhoea on lithium needs urgent review with a lithium level, as toxicity can develop quickly.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and persistent albumin in her urine started ramipril three months ago. Since then she has had an irritating, tickly dry cough that disturbs her sleep. She has no breathlessness, fever or sputum, her chest is clear and a chest radiograph is normal. Her blood pressure is now at target. She asks whether her medication could be changed. What is the most appropriate option?

options.D: Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan

correct_answer: D. Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan
why_correct: A persistent dry cough beginning after starting an ACE inhibitor, with a clear chest and normal radiograph, is most likely due to accumulation of bradykinin. An angiotensin receptor blocker blocks the same pathway without affecting bradykinin, so it rarely causes cough. It also preserves the renal protection she needs for diabetic kidney disease with albuminuria.
why_wrong: A. Another ACE inhibitor will cause the same class-effect cough. B. Suppressing the cough with codeine leaves the cause in place and adds side effects. C. Amlodipine controls blood pressure but loses the protection against progression of albuminuric kidney disease. E. An inhaled corticosteroid treats airway inflammation, which is not the cause here.
pearl: ACE inhibitor cough is a class effect and can start weeks or months after starting. An ARB is the natural substitute when renin-angiotensin blockade is needed.
thinking: New dry cough after starting ramipril ↓ Clear chest and normal radiograph ↓ Bradykinin-mediated class effect ↓ Diabetes with albuminuria needs renin-angiotensin blockade ↓ Switch to an ARB
exam_trap: C, amlodipine — it is a reasonable antihypertensive and would stop the cough, but with diabetic albuminuria she needs the kidney protection that renin-angiotensin blockade provides.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough: switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker, especially when renal protection is needed.

stem: A 39-year-old woman who takes the combined oral contraceptive pill attends her GP surgery five days after returning from a 14-hour coach journey. Her left calf has ached and felt tight for two days. The whole left lower leg is swollen, with pitting oedema to mid-shin, and the calf is tender along the deep veins. A few superficial veins are more prominent than on the right. There is no erythema or warmth, and she is afebrile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Unilateral calf pain and swelling with pitting oedema, tenderness along the deep venous system and collateral superficial veins, after prolonged immobility in a woman taking an oestrogen-containing pill, is deep vein thrombosis. She should be assessed with the two-level Wells score and proximal leg vein ultrasound or D-dimer as appropriate. Interim anticoagulation is given if the scan cannot be done promptly.
why_wrong: A. A ruptured Baker's cyst causes sudden calf pain in someone with knee disease, often with a bruise at the ankle, and has no venous risk factors here. C. A muscle strain follows exertion and does not cause pitting oedema of the whole lower leg. D. Superficial thrombophlebitis produces a tender, red, cord-like superficial vein rather than diffuse swelling. E. Cellulitis causes warmth, erythema and often fever, which are absent.
pearl: Long travel, oestrogen, surgery, pregnancy and cancer are key DVT risk factors. Use the Wells score to decide between immediate ultrasound and D-dimer.
thinking: Unilateral calf pain and swelling ↓ Pitting oedema and deep venous tenderness ↓ Long journey and combined pill ↓ No warmth, redness or fever ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: A, ruptured Baker's cyst — it is the classic DVT mimic causing calf pain and swelling, but she has no knee disease and has clear thrombotic risk factors.
takeaway: Unilateral calf swelling after prolonged immobility on oestrogen suggests DVT; assess with Wells and imaging.

stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and long-standing athlete's foot attends the emergency department. Over two days, redness has spread from his left ankle up his shin. The skin is hot, swollen and tender, with poorly defined edges, and there are cracked, macerated areas between his toes. His temperature is 38.2 degrees C and he has had shivers, but his blood pressure is normal and his pain is in keeping with the appearance. There is no crepitus, and foot pulses are present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute, unilateral, spreading, hot, tender erythema with poorly defined margins, fever and rigors, with a portal of entry from fissured tinea pedis, is cellulitis. It is a bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually streptococcal or staphylococcal. Treatment is with an appropriate antibiotic such as flucloxacillin, plus treatment of the athlete's foot to reduce recurrence.
why_wrong: B. Venous eczema is usually bilateral, itchy and scaly, with no fever. C. DVT causes swelling and pain but not spreading hot erythema with fever and rigors. D. Necrotising fasciitis causes severe pain out of proportion to the skin changes, rapid deterioration and sometimes crepitus, which are absent. E. Gout affects a joint, not a spreading area of shin skin.
pearl: Look for a portal of entry, such as tinea pedis or a wound, and treat it. Pain out of proportion, crepitus or rapid systemic decline suggests necrotising fasciitis.
thinking: Spreading, hot, tender redness of one shin ↓ Poorly defined edge with fever and rigors ↓ Portal of entry from tinea pedis ↓ No features of necrotising infection ↓ Cellulitis
exam_trap: D, necrotising fasciitis — a febrile diabetic with a spreading red leg must prompt the thought, but there is no disproportionate pain, crepitus or haemodynamic compromise.
takeaway: Spreading hot, tender erythema with fever and a portal of entry is cellulitis; look for red flags of necrotising infection.

stem: A 55-year-old man who takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension wakes at 3 am with excruciating pain at the base of his right big toe. By morning the joint is swollen and the overlying skin is red and shiny, and he cannot bear even the bedsheet touching it. A year ago he had a similar episode in the same toe that settled by itself within a week. His temperature is 37.4 degrees C and he otherwise feels well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A sudden, intensely painful, red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint, peaking within hours, in a man taking a thiazide diuretic, with a previous self-limiting attack in the same joint, is acute gout. Thiazides reduce urate excretion. Treatment of the flare is with an NSAID, colchicine or a short course of steroid, and urate-lowering therapy is discussed once he has had recurrent attacks.
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis must always be considered in a hot joint, but recurrent self-limiting attacks in the big toe without systemic illness favour gout. B. Pseudogout mainly affects the knees and wrists of older people. C. Cellulitis affects skin and soft tissue rather than producing exquisite joint tenderness with recurrent episodes. D. Reactive arthritis follows infection and usually affects large lower-limb joints with eye or urinary features.
pearl: Podagra plus a thiazide or loop diuretic is a classic gout combination. If there is doubt about infection, aspirate the joint before treating.
thinking: Sudden severe pain at the base of the big toe ↓ Red, shiny, exquisitely tender joint ↓ Previous self-limiting attack in the same joint ↓ Thiazide diuretic reducing urate excretion ↓ Acute gout
exam_trap: A, septic arthritis — any hot swollen joint must raise this, but he is systemically well and has had a previous attack that resolved by itself, which favours gout.
takeaway: Recurrent acute attacks at the first MTP joint, especially on a thiazide, suggest gout.

stem: A 37-year-old man attends his GP with three months of feeling on edge, palpitations, loose stools and intolerance of warm rooms. He has lost weight despite eating more than usual. He has a fine tremor of his outstretched hands, warm moist palms, lid lag and a regular pulse of 112/min. Blood tests show an undetectable TSH and a raised free T4. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Weight loss with increased appetite, heat intolerance, frequent stools, tremor, tachycardia and lid lag, with a suppressed TSH and raised free T4, is primary hyperthyroidism. The thyroid is producing excess hormone, which suppresses pituitary TSH through negative feedback. The commonest cause is Graves' disease, and TSH receptor antibodies help confirm it.
why_wrong: A. A TSH-secreting adenoma causes raised thyroid hormones with a normal or raised TSH, not a suppressed TSH. B. Primary hypothyroidism causes a raised TSH with low free T4. C. Subclinical hyperthyroidism has a low TSH with normal free thyroid hormones. E. Anxiety can cause palpitations and tremor but not abnormal thyroid function, weight loss with increased appetite or lid lag.
pearl: Read TSH and free T4 together: low TSH with high T4 means primary hyperthyroidism; a normal or high TSH with high T4 suggests a pituitary cause or assay problem.
thinking: Weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance ↓ Tremor, tachycardia, lid lag ↓ Suppressed TSH ↓ Raised free T4 ↓ Primary hyperthyroidism
exam_trap: C, subclinical hyperthyroidism — a low TSH is common to both, but subclinical disease has normal free thyroid hormones, whereas here the free T4 is raised.
takeaway: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and thyrotoxic features means primary hyperthyroidism.

stem: A 41-year-old woman has been seen twice in the emergency department with episodes in which her heart pounds, she becomes pale and drenched in sweat, and she has a severe throbbing headache. Each lasts about 20 minutes and often occurs when she bends forward or strains. During one episode, her blood pressure was markedly raised, and between episodes it is only mildly elevated. She does not feel a sense of impending doom beforehand, and there is no flushing or diarrhoea. Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Paroxysms of headache, sweating, palpitations and pallor with marked hypertension during attacks, sometimes provoked by abdominal pressure or straining, suggest episodic catecholamine release from a phaeochromocytoma. The first investigation is plasma free or urinary metanephrines. If confirmed, alpha-blockade must be established before any beta-blocker and before surgery.
why_wrong: A. Panic attacks are usually preceded by fear or a sense of impending doom and do not cause severe hypertensive surges. B. Carcinoid syndrome causes flushing and diarrhoea rather than pallor and hypertension. C. Thyrotoxicosis causes continuous rather than episodic symptoms, with weight loss and heat intolerance. E. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes sustained hypertension, often with low potassium, without paroxysms.
pearl: The triad of headache, sweating and palpitations with high blood pressure during attacks suggests phaeochromocytoma. Never start a beta-blocker before alpha-blockade.
thinking: Paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations ↓ Pallor with marked hypertension during attacks ↓ Triggered by straining or bending ↓ No fear prodrome, no flushing ↓ Phaeochromocytoma
exam_trap: A, panic disorder — palpitations, sweating and recurrent short episodes are typical of panic, but the documented severe hypertension and mechanical triggers point to catecholamine surges.
takeaway: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with very high blood pressure during attacks suggests phaeochromocytoma.

stem: A 26-year-old man with vitiligo attends his GP with six months of increasing tiredness, nausea, vague abdominal pain and weight loss. He has started craving salty food and feels light-headed when he stands up. His palmar creases and the inside of his cheeks look darker than before. His blood pressure falls significantly on standing. Blood tests show a low sodium and a high potassium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fatigue, weight loss, gastrointestinal symptoms, salt craving, postural hypotension, pigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, in a man with another autoimmune condition, are typical of primary adrenal insufficiency. Loss of cortisol and aldosterone explains the electrolyte disturbance and hypotension, and high ACTH causes the pigmentation. He needs urgent assessment with a 9 am cortisol and ACTH, and emergency hydrocortisone if he becomes unwell.
why_wrong: A. Hypothyroidism causes weight gain and cold intolerance, not pigmentation and hyperkalaemia. B. Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low ACTH, so there is no pigmentation, and aldosterone is preserved, so potassium is normal. C. Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension with low potassium, the opposite picture. D. Anorexia nervosa causes weight loss but not pigmentation, salt craving or hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Pigmentation plus hyperkalaemia points to a primary adrenal cause. Never delay hydrocortisone in a suspected adrenal crisis while waiting for results.
thinking: Fatigue, weight loss and gastrointestinal symptoms ↓ Salt craving and postural hypotension ↓ Buccal and palmar crease pigmentation ↓ Low sodium with high potassium, background autoimmunity ↓ Primary adrenal insufficiency
exam_trap: B, secondary adrenal insufficiency — it also causes fatigue and hypotension, but the pigmentation from high ACTH and the raised potassium from aldosterone loss show the problem is in the adrenal gland.
takeaway: Hyperpigmentation, postural hypotension, low sodium and high potassium suggest Addison's disease.

stem: A 45-year-old man is reviewed in clinic three weeks after a serious head injury in a road traffic collision. Since leaving hospital he has been getting up five or six times a night to pass large amounts of pale urine and has been drinking iced water constantly, even waking to drink. His capillary glucose, calcium and potassium are normal, his serum sodium is at the upper end of normal and his urine is very dilute. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Large volumes of dilute urine day and night with intense thirst, starting after a head injury, with normal glucose and calcium and a high-normal sodium, suggest cranial diabetes insipidus (now also termed arginine vasopressin deficiency). Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary reduces ADH release, so the kidneys cannot concentrate urine. A water deprivation test with a desmopressin response confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong: B. Primary polydipsia also causes dilute polyuria, but the sodium tends to be low-normal because water intake drives the urine output. C. Diabetes mellitus causes osmotic polyuria with hyperglycaemia, and glucose is normal. D. Hypercalcaemia can cause polyuria, but calcium is normal. E. Prostatic enlargement causes frequent small voids, not large volumes of dilute urine.
pearl: In polyuria with dilute urine, the serum sodium is a clue: high-normal suggests diabetes insipidus, low-normal suggests primary polydipsia. Exclude glucose, calcium and potassium causes first.
thinking: Polyuria and polydipsia day and night ↓ Started after a head injury ↓ Glucose, calcium and potassium normal ↓ Dilute urine with high-normal sodium ↓ Cranial diabetes insipidus
exam_trap: B, primary polydipsia — constant drinking with dilute urine fits it too, but the onset after head injury, waking at night to drink and a high-normal sodium favour ADH deficiency.
takeaway: Dilute polyuria with thirst after head injury and normal glucose suggests cranial diabetes insipidus.

stem: A 72-year-old woman was started on carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia a month ago. She is brought to the emergency department with nausea, headache and new confusion. Her serum sodium is markedly low. She has moist mucous membranes, normal skin turgor, no peripheral oedema and no postural drop in blood pressure. She takes no diuretics. Her urine is concentrated with a high urinary sodium, and her thyroid function and morning cortisol are normal. Which diagnosis best explains her hyponatraemia?
correct_answer: D. Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH)
why_correct: Hyponatraemia in a clinically euvolaemic patient with inappropriately concentrated urine and a high urinary sodium, normal thyroid and adrenal function and no diuretic use, fits SIADH. Carbamazepine is a recognised cause, as are SSRIs, lung disease, malignancy and intracranial pathology. Management includes stopping the culprit drug and fluid restriction, with specialist input for severe or symptomatic hyponatraemia because correcting sodium too fast risks osmotic demyelination.
why_wrong: A. Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia would show dry mucous membranes, postural hypotension and usually a low urinary sodium. B. Addison's disease is excluded by the normal morning cortisol. C. Heart failure causes oedema and fluid overload, which are absent. E. Diabetes insipidus causes dilute urine and tends towards high sodium.
pearl: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion: euvolaemia, concentrated urine, high urinary sodium, normal thyroid and adrenal function, no diuretics. Always review the drug chart.
thinking: Low sodium with confusion ↓ Clinically euvolaemic ↓ Concentrated urine and high urinary sodium ↓ Normal thyroid and cortisol, no diuretics, new carbamazepine ↓ SIADH
exam_trap: B, Addison's disease — it causes hyponatraemia with a high urinary sodium and can mimic SIADH, but her morning cortisol is normal and she has no postural hypotension.
takeaway: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and normal thyroid and adrenal function is SIADH; check drugs.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted for the third time in a year with severe, poorly localised abdominal pain and vomiting. Previous scans and an appendicectomy found no cause. This episode began a few days after she started a progestogen-only pill. Her abdomen is soft with little tenderness despite her distress, she is constipated, anxious and agitated, her pulse is 118/min and her blood pressure is raised. Her sodium is low, and she has new weakness of both upper arms. A urine sample left on the windowsill has turned a dark reddish-brown. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent attacks of severe abdominal pain with few abdominal signs, autonomic features such as tachycardia, hypertension and constipation, psychiatric disturbance, hyponatraemia, proximal motor weakness and urine that darkens on standing are characteristic of acute intermittent porphyria. Attacks are precipitated by hormones such as progestogens, many drugs, fasting, alcohol and infection. A raised urinary porphobilinogen confirms an attack, and treatment includes stopping triggers, carbohydrate and haem arginate.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes epigastric tenderness and a raised amylase or lipase, not neuropathy and dark urine. B. Lead poisoning can cause abdominal pain and neuropathy, but there is no exposure and it is associated with anaemia and basophilic stippling. D. Somatic symptom disorder does not explain objective hyponatraemia, hypertension, weakness and urine colour change. E. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, without neuropsychiatric features.
pearl: Think porphyria when abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric features and hyponatraemia recur together, especially after a new drug or hormone. Check urinary porphobilinogen during the attack.
thinking: Recurrent severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen ↓ Tachycardia, hypertension, constipation and agitation ↓ Hyponatraemia and proximal weakness ↓ Dark urine, trigger from a progestogen ↓ Acute intermittent porphyria
exam_trap: D, somatic symptom disorder — repeated admissions with pain out of proportion to examination invite this label, but objective hyponatraemia, hypertension, neuropathy and urine change point to an organic cause.
takeaway: Recurrent abdominal pain with neuropathy, hyponatraemia and darkening urine suggests acute intermittent porphyria.

stem: A 32-year-old woman sees her GP because her hearing has slowly worsened over two years, and it became more noticeable during her recent pregnancy. Her mother needed a hearing aid in her forties. She has no ear pain, discharge or dizziness. Both tympanic membranes look normal and move normally. Rinne test is negative on the left and Weber lateralises to the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradual conductive hearing loss (negative Rinne, Weber to the affected side) with a normal, mobile tympanic membrane in a young adult with a family history fits otosclerosis. Abnormal bone remodelling fixes the stapes footplate, and pregnancy classically accelerates it. Management is referral to ENT for audiology, hearing aids or stapes surgery.
why_wrong: A. Vestibular schwannoma causes unilateral sensorineural loss, often with tinnitus, so Weber would lateralise away from the affected ear. B. Otitis media with effusion gives a dull, retracted or poorly mobile drum, not a normal one. C. Presbycusis is bilateral, sensorineural and age-related, not conductive in a 32-year-old. E. Cholesteatoma causes foul discharge and a visible retraction pocket or debris on otoscopy.
pearl: Conductive hearing loss with a completely normal-looking drum narrows the field quickly: think otosclerosis, especially in a young woman with a family history and worsening in pregnancy.
thinking: Slowly progressive hearing loss in a young woman ↓ Rinne negative and Weber to the same side = conductive loss ↓ normal mobile drum excludes effusion and cholesteatoma ↓ family history and pregnancy-related worsening ↓ Otosclerosis
exam_trap: B, Otitis media with effusion — it is the commonest cause of conductive loss and tempts on that basis, but it produces an abnormal, poorly mobile drum, whereas here the drum looks and moves normally.
takeaway: Conductive loss plus a normal, mobile eardrum in a young adult points to otosclerosis.

stem: A 19-year-old university student attends her GP with three months of a dry cough that wakes her most nights. She becomes wheezy and tight-chested when cycling in cold air, and the symptoms ease completely over a few days at a time. She had eczema as a child. Examination today is normal and she has never smoked. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Variable wheeze, chest tightness and nocturnal cough triggered by exercise and cold air, with symptom-free spells and a personal history of atopy, is the typical pattern of asthma. A normal examination between episodes does not exclude it. The diagnosis should then be supported with objective testing before starting treatment, in line with current UK guidance.
why_wrong: A. Reflux can cause nocturnal cough but does not cause exercise-induced wheeze and chest tightness. B. Bronchiectasis produces a chronic productive cough with daily sputum, not intermittent dry symptoms. D. Postnasal drip causes cough and throat clearing but not wheeze or chest tightness. E. COPD is a disease of older smokers with persistent, progressive symptoms rather than variable ones.
pearl: Variability is the signature of asthma: symptoms that come and go, worsen at night or with exercise and cold air, and settle completely in between, often with atopy in the background.
thinking: Young non-smoker with nocturnal cough ↓ wheeze and chest tightness with exercise and cold air ↓ symptom-free between episodes and childhood eczema ↓ variable airflow obstruction with atopy ↓ Asthma
exam_trap: A, Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — night-time cough tempts towards reflux, but reflux does not explain wheeze and chest tightness brought on by exercise and cold air.
takeaway: Episodic wheeze, night cough and exercise triggers with normal periods between suggest asthma.

stem: A 19-year-old woman attends her GP three days after being given amoxicillin at a walk-in centre for a sore throat. She has a week of fever, marked fatigue and tender swollen glands at the back of her neck, and a palpable spleen tip. Since yesterday she has had a widespread itchy, flat and slightly raised red (maculopapular) rash on her trunk and limbs, with no wheals. Her lips, mouth and eyes are unaffected and she has no breathing difficulty. What is the most likely explanation for the rash?

options.D: Aminopenicillin rash in Epstein–Barr virus infection

correct_answer: D. Aminopenicillin rash in Epstein–Barr virus infection
why_correct: Fever, fatigue, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly in a young adult point to glandular fever, and a widespread maculopapular rash after amoxicillin is a well-recognised drug-virus interaction rather than true penicillin allergy. Amoxicillin should be stopped and the rash managed symptomatically. She should also be advised to avoid contact sports for several weeks because of splenic enlargement.
why_wrong: A. Stevens–Johnson syndrome involves mucosal surfaces with blistering and skin pain, which she does not have. B. Scarlet fever produces a fine sandpaper rash with a strawberry tongue, not this picture with splenomegaly. C. An IgE-mediated allergy causes urticaria or angioedema within minutes to hours of a dose, and this rash does not imply lifelong penicillin avoidance. E. Measles presents with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis before the rash.
pearl: Amoxicillin given during glandular fever commonly causes a maculopapular rash; it is not a true allergy, so do not label the patient penicillin-allergic without specialist assessment.
thinking: Young adult with prolonged sore throat and fatigue ↓ posterior cervical nodes and palpable spleen = glandular fever ↓ amoxicillin given, maculopapular rash days later without mucosal involvement ↓ drug-virus interaction ↓ Aminopenicillin rash in Epstein–Barr virus infection
exam_trap: C, IgE-mediated penicillin allergy — a rash after amoxicillin tempts towards allergy, but the timing and maculopapular pattern in glandular fever indicate a non-allergic interaction, and mislabelling closes off useful antibiotics for life.
takeaway: Rash after amoxicillin in glandular fever is a drug-virus interaction, not a true penicillin allergy.

stem: A 27-year-old woman attends the emergency department with a painful, swollen left calf for two days. She started a combined oral contraceptive pill two months ago and returned from a long-haul flight four days ago. There is no history of injury and she is afebrile. The left calf is tender along the deep veins, there is pitting oedema to the ankle, and the calf is visibly larger than the right. What diagnosis should be investigated first?
why_correct: Unilateral calf swelling, pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep venous system in a woman taking a combined oral contraceptive pill, with a recent long-haul flight, strongly suggests deep vein thrombosis. Oestrogen-containing contraception increases venous thromboembolism risk. Assess with the Wells score and arrange proximal leg vein ultrasound and/or D-dimer as appropriate, with interim anticoagulation if imaging is delayed.
why_wrong: A. A ruptured Baker's cyst usually follows knee pathology and causes sudden posterior knee pain spreading down the calf. B. Cellulitis causes a hot, red, spreading area of skin, usually with fever. C. Superficial thrombophlebitis causes a tender, red, cord-like superficial vein without generalised calf swelling. E. Muscle strain follows exertion or injury and does not cause pitting oedema.
pearl: Combined hormonal contraception plus another provoking factor such as long-haul travel stacks VTE risk. A swollen, tender calf in this setting needs formal DVT assessment, not reassurance.
thinking: Young woman on the combined pill and recently flown ↓ unilateral swollen tender calf with pitting oedema ↓ no trauma or fever ↓ provoked venous thrombosis risk ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: B, Cellulitis — a swollen painful leg often tempts towards cellulitis, but there is no fever or spreading erythema, and the oestrogen exposure and recent flight are clear thrombotic risk factors.
takeaway: A swollen tender calf in a woman on the combined pill needs assessment for deep vein thrombosis.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after suddenly becoming breathless at work. She describes a sharp pain on the right side of her chest that catches on deep breathing. She has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill for several years and has no past medical history. Heart rate is 112/min, oxygen saturation is 93% on air and temperature is normal. Breath sounds are equal and the chest is clear. What diagnosis must be urgently excluded?
why_correct: Sudden breathlessness with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and low oxygen saturation but a clear chest, in a woman taking oestrogen-containing contraception, must be treated as pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise. Assess with the two-level Wells score and arrange CT pulmonary angiography or D-dimer accordingly, giving interim anticoagulation if imaging is delayed.
why_wrong: A. A panic attack does not cause hypoxia and should only be considered once serious causes are excluded. B. Pneumonia typically causes fever, productive cough and focal chest signs. C. A pneumothorax would usually reduce breath sounds on the affected side, but here they are equal. D. Pericarditis causes central chest pain that eases on sitting forward, not sudden breathlessness with hypoxia.
pearl: Hypoxia with a clear chest is a red flag for pulmonary embolism. Pleuritic pain and tachycardia in a woman on oestrogen-containing contraception should trigger Wells scoring, not reassurance.
thinking: Sudden breathlessness with pleuritic chest pain ↓ tachycardia and low saturations but clear chest and equal breath sounds ↓ oestrogen-containing contraception = VTE risk ↓ perfusion problem rather than airway or lung parenchyma ↓ Pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: A, Panic attack — a young, anxious, tachycardic woman tempts towards panic, but panic does not cause hypoxia, and missing a pulmonary embolism can be fatal.
takeaway: Sudden pleuritic pain with hypoxia and a clear chest on the combined pill means pulmonary embolism.

stem: An 81-year-old woman who had a myocardial infarction five years ago attends her GP with two months of worsening breathlessness. She now sleeps on three pillows and wakes at night gasping, needing to sit on the edge of the bed. Her shoes no longer fit. There is pitting oedema to both knees, fine crackles at both lung bases and the jugular venous pulse is visible at the angle of the jaw. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, bilateral pitting oedema, bibasal crackles and a raised jugular venous pressure after a previous myocardial infarction are classic features of heart failure with fluid overload. The next step in primary care is an NT-proBNP test, with echocardiography and specialist assessment as indicated.
why_wrong: B. COPD exacerbations cause wheeze and sputum, and do not raise the JVP with bibasal crackles in this way. C. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema from low albumin but does not cause orthopnoea or a raised JVP. D. Pneumonia causes fever, cough and focal chest signs over days. E. Venous insufficiency causes ankle oedema without breathlessness or a raised JVP.
pearl: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea are the most specific symptoms of heart failure; a raised JVP confirms the oedema is from right-sided pressure rather than low albumin or venous disease.
thinking: Previous myocardial infarction ↓ orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea ↓ bilateral oedema, bibasal crackles and raised JVP ↓ systemic and pulmonary fluid overload ↓ Heart failure
exam_trap: C, Nephrotic syndrome — marked bilateral oedema can tempt towards a low-albumin cause, but nephrotic syndrome does not raise the JVP or cause orthopnoea and nocturnal breathlessness.
takeaway: Orthopnoea, nocturnal breathlessness, oedema and a raised JVP after an MI mean heart failure.

stem: A 66-year-old man who has smoked for 45 years attends the practice nurse with a painful ulcer over the outer aspect of his right ankle that has not healed for six weeks. For years he has had calf cramps after walking a short distance. The pain is worst at night and eases if he hangs his leg over the side of the bed. The ulcer is small, deep and punched-out with a pale base. The skin of the foot is shiny and hairless, and foot pulses are very weak. What type of ulcer is most likely?
why_correct: A painful, punched-out ulcer with a pale base on the lateral ankle, in a smoker with intermittent claudication, night pain relieved by dependency, hairless shiny skin and weak pulses, reflects critical limb ischaemia with an arterial ulcer. An ankle brachial pressure index should be measured and he needs urgent vascular referral. Compression bandaging must not be applied.
why_wrong: A. Venous ulcers are shallow, sloughy and usually over the medial malleolus with surrounding varicose eczema and haemosiderin staining. B. Neuropathic ulcers are painless and occur over pressure points on the sole in patients with sensory loss. C. Pressure ulcers occur over bony prominences in immobile patients. E. A Marjolin ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a long-standing scar or chronic wound.
pearl: Rest pain relieved by hanging the leg down plus a painful punched-out ulcer means critical arterial insufficiency. Check the ABPI and never compress an ischaemic leg.
thinking: Long-term smoker with claudication ↓ night pain eased by dependency = rest pain ↓ painful punched-out lateral ankle ulcer, hairless skin, weak pulses ↓ inadequate arterial perfusion ↓ Arterial ulcer
exam_trap: A, Venous ulcer — venous ulcers are the most common leg ulcers and tempt by frequency, but they are shallow, medial and relatively painless, and compression for a venous ulcer would harm this ischaemic limb.
takeaway: A painful punched-out ulcer with rest pain and weak pulses is arterial: check ABPI, refer vascular.

stem: A 55-year-old man with three previous attacks of gout started allopurinol two weeks ago. He now telephones his GP because his left first metatarsophalangeal joint has again become red, hot and very painful over 24 hours. He is afebrile, otherwise well and can bear weight. He asks whether the new tablet has caused this. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Allopurinol has failed and should be stopped
options.B: Starting urate-lowering therapy can trigger a flare as crystal deposits are mobilised
options.C: This is an allopurinol hypersensitivity reaction
options.D: Allopurinol raises serum urate during the first weeks of treatment
options.E: The new pain indicates septic arthritis caused by allopurinol

correct_answer: B. Starting urate-lowering therapy can trigger a flare as crystal deposits are mobilised
why_correct: When urate-lowering therapy is started, falling serum urate destabilises existing crystal deposits in the joints, which can provoke acute flares in the early months. Patients should be warned about this in advance, and allopurinol should be continued during a flare while the flare itself is treated. Prophylaxis, such as low-dose colchicine, is usually offered while urate-lowering therapy is being started and titrated.
why_wrong: A. A flare soon after starting does not mean treatment failure, and stopping allopurinol is the wrong response. C. Allopurinol hypersensitivity presents with a rash, fever and possible organ involvement, not a single inflamed joint. D. Allopurinol lowers serum urate; it is the fall in urate that mobilises crystals. E. Allopurinol does not cause septic arthritis, and he is afebrile and well.
pearl: Warn every patient starting allopurinol or febuxostat that early flares can happen, keep the urate-lowering drug going through a flare, and consider colchicine cover during titration.
thinking: Recurrent gout, allopurinol started two weeks ago ↓ new typical flare in the big toe, systemically well ↓ falling urate destabilises existing crystal deposits ↓ continue allopurinol and treat the flare ↓ Starting urate-lowering therapy can trigger a flare as crystal deposits are mobilised
exam_trap: A, Allopurinol has failed and should be stopped — the timing tempts patients and doctors to blame and stop the drug, but early flares are expected and stopping it undermines long-term urate control.
takeaway: Early gout flares after starting allopurinol are expected: warn, give cover, and do not stop it.

stem: A 41-year-old man attends his GP with three months of pain in both hands and wrists. Each morning his hands are so stiff that he cannot do up his shirt buttons for about two hours, and they loosen with use. Several knuckles and middle finger joints on both hands are swollen and boggy, and squeezing across the knuckles is painful. He has no rash, nail changes, back pain or recent infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Symmetrical, persistent synovitis of the small joints of the hands and wrists, with prolonged early-morning stiffness that eases with activity and a positive metacarpophalangeal squeeze test, is the pattern of rheumatoid arthritis. Persistent synovitis warrants urgent referral to rheumatology, even if blood tests such as rheumatoid factor are normal.
why_wrong: B. Psoriatic arthritis is usually asymmetrical, often affects distal joints and is associated with skin or nail changes. C. Osteoarthritis causes brief morning stiffness and bony swelling of the distal joints and thumb base. D. Gout typically affects one joint acutely with severe pain and redness. E. Reactive arthritis follows an infection and usually affects large joints of the legs asymmetrically.
pearl: Symmetrical small-joint swelling with long morning stiffness and a positive squeeze test should prompt urgent rheumatology referral; do not wait for a positive rheumatoid factor.
thinking: Bilateral hand and wrist pain for three months ↓ prolonged morning stiffness easing with use ↓ boggy swelling of MCP and PIP joints, positive squeeze test ↓ symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis without skin or infective features ↓ Rheumatoid arthritis
exam_trap: B, Psoriatic arthritis — an inflammatory hand arthritis in a man may tempt towards psoriatic arthritis, but the symmetrical MCP and PIP pattern without skin, nail or distal joint involvement fits rheumatoid arthritis.
takeaway: Symmetrical small-joint synovitis with long morning stiffness: suspect RA and refer urgently.

stem: A 69-year-old woman tells her GP that for the past six weeks she has struggled to lift her arms to brush her hair and finds it hard to get up from a low chair. Her shoulders, neck and hips ache and are very stiff for about two hours each morning. On examination, power in her arms and legs is normal once she gets going. She has no headache, scalp tenderness, visual symptoms or jaw pain. Her ESR and CRP are raised and her creatine kinase is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and prolonged morning stiffness in an older adult, with normal muscle strength, raised inflammatory markers and a normal creatine kinase, is characteristic of polymyalgia rheumatica. It typically responds rapidly to low-dose oral prednisolone. Giant cell arteritis symptoms should be asked about at every review.
why_wrong: A. Polymyositis causes genuine proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase. B. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain with normal inflammatory markers. D. Frozen shoulder restricts movement at the shoulder and does not explain hip girdle stiffness or raised inflammatory markers. E. Hypothyroid myopathy can cause proximal aching but typically with raised creatine kinase and no rise in ESR or CRP.
pearl: PMR is pain and stiffness, not weakness: patients struggle because it hurts, but power is normal on testing. Always ask about headache, jaw claudication and visual symptoms.
thinking: Older woman with shoulder and hip girdle symptoms ↓ prolonged morning stiffness with normal power ↓ raised ESR and CRP but normal creatine kinase ↓ inflammatory girdle syndrome, not a myopathy ↓ Polymyalgia rheumatica
exam_trap: A, Polymyositis — difficulty lifting the arms and rising from a chair sounds like proximal weakness, but power is normal on testing and the creatine kinase is normal, which rules out an inflammatory myopathy.
takeaway: Girdle pain and morning stiffness with normal strength and raised ESR in an older adult is PMR.

stem: A GP receives a telephone call from a 70-year-old woman. Thirty minutes ago, while they were having breakfast, her husband suddenly could not lift his right arm and his speech became slurred and muddled. He is awake and breathing normally. She asks whether she should bring him to the surgery this afternoon. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Book an urgent same-day GP appointment
options.B: Give aspirin at home and arrange review tomorrow
options.C: Call 999 now for immediate transfer to a hyperacute stroke unit
options.D: Refer to the TIA clinic to be seen within 24 hours
options.E: Wait an hour to see if the symptoms resolve

correct_answer: C. Call 999 now for immediate transfer to a hyperacute stroke unit
why_correct: Sudden-onset arm weakness and speech disturbance that are still present indicate a suspected acute stroke. He is within the time window for reperfusion therapy, so an emergency ambulance should be called immediately for transfer to a hyperacute stroke unit for urgent brain imaging and consideration of thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
why_wrong: A. A GP appointment wastes time that matters for reperfusion treatment. B. Aspirin must not be given before brain imaging excludes haemorrhage. D. The TIA clinic is for symptoms that have fully resolved, not ongoing deficits. E. Waiting loses treatment time, and persisting symptoms must be treated as a stroke.
pearl: Ongoing focal deficit means stroke, not TIA: call 999 and go straight to a hyperacute stroke unit. No aspirin until imaging has excluded a bleed.
thinking: Sudden arm weakness and slurred speech ↓ symptoms ongoing, onset 30 minutes ago ↓ suspected acute stroke within the reperfusion window ↓ time-critical imaging and treatment needed ↓ Call 999 now for immediate transfer to a hyperacute stroke unit
exam_trap: D, Refer to the TIA clinic to be seen within 24 hours — this tempts because rapid TIA pathways are well known, but they apply only when symptoms have resolved, and his deficit is still present.
takeaway: Persisting sudden focal deficit: call 999 for a hyperacute stroke unit; no aspirin before imaging.

stem: A 34-year-old woman attends the emergency department after noticing in the mirror that the left side of her mouth droops and she dribbles when drinking. The day before she had an ache behind her left ear. Food tastes odd. On examination she cannot wrinkle the left side of her forehead or fully close her left eye. There are no vesicles in or around the ear, and limb power, sensation and speech are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute unilateral facial weakness involving the forehead indicates a lower motor neurone facial nerve lesion. With preceding ear pain and altered taste, and no vesicles, limb signs or parotid mass, this is Bell palsy. Oral prednisolone should be started within 72 hours of onset, together with eye protection using lubricants and taping the eye at night.
why_wrong: A. Ramsay Hunt syndrome causes a similar palsy but with a painful vesicular rash in the ear or palate, which is absent. C. A stroke causes an upper motor neurone pattern that spares the forehead, often with limb or speech involvement. D. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable, often bilateral weakness with ptosis and diplopia. E. A parotid tumour causes a gradually progressive palsy, usually with a palpable mass.
pearl: Forehead involved means lower motor neurone. Look in the ear for vesicles, check for a parotid mass, then start prednisolone within 72 hours and protect the eye.
thinking: Sudden one-sided facial droop ↓ forehead involved and eye cannot close = lower motor neurone lesion ↓ ear ache and altered taste, no vesicles, no mass, no limb signs ↓ idiopathic facial nerve palsy ↓ Bell palsy
exam_trap: C, Middle cerebral artery stroke — sudden facial droop prompts stroke thinking, but a stroke spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation, while here the whole half of the face is weak.
takeaway: Sudden facial weakness including the forehead, with no other signs, is Bell palsy: steroids and eye care.

stem: An 82-year-old woman is on a stroke ward four days after a left hemisphere infarct. The nurse reports that she coughs immediately whenever she takes sips of water, food collects in her right cheek, and some fluid comes back through her nose. After drinking, her voice sounds gurgly. She does not report food sticking behind the breastbone. What type of swallowing problem is most likely?
why_correct: Coughing at the moment of swallowing, food pooling in the mouth, nasal regurgitation and a wet voice indicate failure of the oral and pharyngeal phases of swallowing, typical of neurological causes such as stroke. This places her at high risk of aspiration. She should remain nil by mouth until a speech and language therapist has carried out a formal swallowing assessment.
why_wrong: A. Achalasia causes slowly progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation of undigested food, not immediate coughing. B. A stricture causes food sticking behind the sternum, mainly with solids. D. A pharyngeal pouch causes delayed regurgitation of old food, halitosis and gurgling in the neck. E. Globus is a lump-in-the-throat feeling without true difficulty swallowing.
pearl: Where the problem shows itself locates the level: coughing at the moment of swallowing and nasal regurgitation mean oropharyngeal dysphagia; food sticking behind the sternum means oesophageal.
thinking: Recent stroke ↓ immediate coughing on sips, food pooling in the cheek, nasal regurgitation ↓ wet voice after drinking = penetration towards the airway ↓ failure of the oral and pharyngeal phases ↓ Oropharyngeal dysphagia
exam_trap: D, Pharyngeal pouch — gurgling and regurgitation in an older patient tempt towards a pouch, but a pouch causes delayed regurgitation of old food, not immediate coughing and nasal regurgitation after a stroke.
takeaway: Coughing on swallowing, nasal regurgitation and wet voice after stroke means oropharyngeal dysphagia.

stem: An 81-year-old woman with long-standing Parkinson disease lives in a care home. She has been treated for three chest infections in four months, each affecting the right lower zone on chest X-ray. Carers say her eyes water and she splutters when drinking tea, she takes a long time to finish meals, and food stays in her mouth. She has never smoked. What is the most likely underlying cause of her recurrent infections?
correct_answer: D. Aspiration due to impaired swallowing
why_correct: Dysphagia is common in advancing Parkinson disease, and spluttering on fluids, slow meals and food pooling, together with repeated right lower zone infections, indicate recurrent aspiration. The right lower lobe is the usual site because of the anatomy of the right main bronchus. She needs a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment and a review of her Parkinson medication timing.
why_wrong: A. Bronchiectasis causes daily productive cough, and the swallowing features point to aspiration as the driver. B. Lung cancer is less likely in a never-smoker and does not explain choking on fluids. C. Levodopa does not cause immunosuppression. E. Pulmonary emboli cause pleuritic pain and breathlessness, not recurrent lobar infection with choking on drinks.
pearl: Recurrent right lower lobe chest infections in a patient with a neurodegenerative disease should prompt questions about coughing on eating and drinking, and a speech and language therapy referral.
thinking: Advanced Parkinson disease ↓ spluttering on fluids, slow meals, food pooling ↓ repeated right lower zone infections ↓ material entering the airway via the right main bronchus ↓ Aspiration due to impaired swallowing
exam_trap: A, Bronchiectasis — repeated chest infections tempt towards a structural lung disease, but the choking on fluids and the neurological background show that aspiration is the cause.
takeaway: Recurrent right lower lobe infections in Parkinson disease suggest aspiration: refer for swallow assessment.

stem: A 59-year-old woman sees her GP because her voice has been husky for two months and has not improved since a cold settled. Over the past month, meat and bread have started to feel as if they catch in her throat, and her clothes have become loose. She has smoked a pack a day since her teens and drinks heavily. There is no palpable neck mass. What diagnosis must be excluded urgently?

options.C: Head and neck or oesophageal cancer

correct_answer: C. Head and neck or oesophageal cancer
why_correct: Persistent unexplained hoarseness together with progressive dysphagia and weight loss in a heavy smoker and drinker are alarm features for malignancy of the larynx, pharynx or oesophagus. She needs referral on the suspected cancer pathway, for ENT assessment and urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, rather than empirical treatment.
why_wrong: A. Reflux may cause hoarseness but is a diagnosis made only after cancer has been excluded in someone with red flags. B. Vocal cord nodules occur in voice overuse and do not cause dysphagia or weight loss. D. Hypothyroidism may cause a hoarse voice but does not cause progressive dysphagia with weight loss. E. Candidiasis causes a sore mouth with white plaques, usually in immunosuppressed patients or inhaler users.
pearl: Hoarseness that persists after a cold settles, with dysphagia or weight loss in a smoker and drinker, needs suspected cancer referral; never treat it as reflux first.
thinking: Hoarseness persisting beyond the viral illness ↓ new progressive dysphagia to solids and weight loss ↓ heavy smoking and alcohol use ↓ red flags for upper aerodigestive malignancy ↓ Head and neck or oesophageal cancer
exam_trap: A, Laryngopharyngeal reflux — reflux is a common, benign cause of hoarseness and tempts as the reassuring option, but alarm features in a high-risk patient mean cancer must be excluded first.
takeaway: Persistent hoarseness with dysphagia in a smoker needs urgent cancer assessment, not antacids.

stem: A 61-year-old woman tells her GP that she felt a lump in her right breast while showering two weeks ago. Her last screening mammogram was 18 months ago and was normal. Examination shows a hard, non-tender lump in the upper outer quadrant with puckering of the overlying skin when she raises her arms. There is no nipple discharge and no fever. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Review after one month to see whether it resolves
options.B: Bring forward her next screening mammogram
options.C: Suspected cancer pathway referral to the breast clinic
options.E: Routine referral to the breast surgeons

correct_answer: C. Suspected cancer pathway referral to the breast clinic
why_correct: A new, hard, painless breast lump with skin tethering is suspicious for breast cancer, regardless of a previous normal screening mammogram. She should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway for triple assessment (clinical examination, imaging and biopsy) at a breast clinic.
why_wrong: A. Watchful waiting is not appropriate for a lump with suspicious features. B. Screening is for women without symptoms and cannot replace diagnostic assessment of a symptomatic lump. D. There are no signs of infection or abscess to justify antibiotics. E. A routine referral causes an unacceptable delay for a suspected cancer.
pearl: A symptomatic breast lump goes to the breast clinic for triple assessment; a recent normal screening mammogram never provides reassurance about a new lump.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman with a new breast lump ↓ hard, painless, with skin puckering ↓ features suspicious for malignancy ↓ needs triple assessment without delay ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral to the breast clinic
exam_trap: B, Bring forward her next screening mammogram — the recent normal screen tempts towards a screening-based solution, but screening is for asymptomatic women and a suspicious lump needs diagnostic triple assessment.
takeaway: A hard lump with skin tethering needs urgent breast clinic referral, whatever the last mammogram showed.

stem: A 66-year-old woman attends her GP because on two occasions this month her urine has been red. She has no dysuria, frequency or loin pain and is not taking anticoagulants. She worked for many years in a rubber factory and is an ex-smoker. Abdominal examination is normal. A urine sample sent for culture shows no infection. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Suspected cancer pathway referral to urology
options.C: Repeat urine dipstick in three months
options.E: Reassure and advise increased fluid intake

correct_answer: B. Suspected cancer pathway referral to urology
why_correct: Unexplained painless visible haematuria, with infection excluded, in an older adult with occupational exposure and a smoking history must be investigated for urological cancer, most commonly bladder cancer. She should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway for cystoscopy and upper tract imaging.
