why_wrong: A. Culture has excluded infection, so antibiotics are not indicated and would delay diagnosis. C. Repeat testing delays investigation of an alarm symptom. D. Nephrology suits haematuria with proteinuria or reduced kidney function, not painless visible bleeding in a high-risk patient. E. Reassurance is unsafe when malignancy has not been excluded.
pearl: Painless visible haematuria without infection is cancer until proven otherwise. Smoking and occupational exposure to dyes and rubber chemicals both raise bladder cancer risk.
thinking: Older woman with recurrent red urine ↓ painless, no urinary symptoms, culture negative ↓ smoking and rubber industry exposure ↓ unexplained visible haematuria = urological cancer risk ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral to urology
exam_trap: A, Prescribe a course of nitrofurantoin — urinary infection is the commonest cause of blood in the urine, but culture is negative and there are no urinary symptoms, so antibiotics only delay diagnosis.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria with no infection needs urgent urology referral for possible bladder cancer.

stem: A 78-year-old man is on an orthopaedic ward on the first day after a hip replacement. He has received regular morphine for pain. The nurse calls you because he has not passed urine for ten hours and is restless and uncomfortable. There is a tender, smooth mass arising from the pelvis that is dull to percussion and reaches halfway to the umbilicus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Inability to pass urine with lower abdominal discomfort and a tender, dull suprapubic mass in an older man after surgery, opioid analgesia and immobility indicates acute urinary retention. The diagnosis can be confirmed with a bladder scan, and the bladder should be drained with a urethral catheter.
why_wrong: A. Pre-renal kidney injury reduces urine production, so the bladder would be empty, not palpably distended. C. A lower urinary tract infection causes frequency and dysuria rather than a palpable bladder. D. Faecal impaction may contribute to retention but does not itself produce a dull, tender suprapubic mass. E. Ureteric colic causes severe loin to groin pain without bladder distension.
pearl: No urine output after surgery: feel and scan the bladder before assuming kidney injury. Opioids, anaesthesia, immobility and prostatic enlargement all predispose to retention.
thinking: Older man after surgery on morphine ↓ no urine for hours, restless and uncomfortable ↓ tender suprapubic mass dull to percussion = full bladder ↓ outflow failure, not reduced production ↓ Acute urinary retention
exam_trap: A, Pre-renal acute kidney injury — low urine output after surgery tempts towards dehydration and kidney injury, but a palpable, dull bladder shows the urine is being made and cannot be passed.
takeaway: No urine passed after surgery with a palpable, dull bladder is urinary retention: scan and catheterise.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends the emergency department. For two days she has had burning on passing urine and frequency. Since last night she has had shaking chills, a temperature of 39.2°C and a constant ache in her left side below the ribs. She has vomited twice. There is marked tenderness at the left renal angle. A urine pregnancy test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Lower urinary symptoms progressing to high fever, rigors, vomiting, flank pain and renal angle tenderness indicate infection that has ascended to the kidney. She needs a urine culture and antibiotics suitable for upper urinary tract infection, given intravenously if she cannot tolerate oral treatment, and should be assessed for sepsis.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes severe colicky pain radiating to the groin and is not usually accompanied by high fever and rigors unless the system is obstructed. B. A lower urinary tract infection does not cause high fever, rigors or renal angle tenderness. D. Appendicitis causes right iliac fossa pain, not left flank pain after dysuria. E. Pelvic inflammatory disease causes lower abdominal pain with discharge and cervical motion tenderness.
pearl: Systemic features such as rigors and vomiting, with flank or renal angle tenderness, mean the infection has reached the kidney; treat as pyelonephritis and screen for sepsis.
thinking: Dysuria and frequency for two days ↓ then high fever, rigors and vomiting ↓ left flank pain with renal angle tenderness ↓ ascending infection involving the kidney ↓ Acute pyelonephritis
exam_trap: B, Lower urinary tract infection — the urinary symptoms tempt towards simple cystitis, but rigors, high fever and renal angle tenderness show upper tract involvement needing different treatment.
takeaway: Urinary symptoms with rigors, fever and renal angle tenderness mean acute pyelonephritis.

stem: A 38-year-old man arrives in the emergency department with sudden, severe pain in his right flank that comes in waves and shoots down into his right groin and testicle. He cannot keep still and is pacing the cubicle. He is afebrile. The abdomen is soft and both testes are normal on examination. Urine dipstick shows blood only. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden, severe, wave-like loin pain radiating to the groin and testicle in a restless patient, with non-visible haematuria and normal testes, is classic for a ureteric stone. Management includes analgesia, usually an NSAID if not contraindicated, and non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder to confirm the stone.
why_wrong: B. Testicular torsion causes a tender, high-riding testis, whereas both testes are normal here. C. Pyelonephritis causes fever and constant loin pain rather than colicky pain with restlessness. D. Appendicitis causes pain that migrates to the right iliac fossa with localised tenderness and patients lie still. E. A leaking aneurysm is unlikely at 38 and typically causes shock in an older patient.
pearl: Patients with colic writhe and pace; patients with peritonitis lie still. Loin to groin pain with blood on dipstick in a restless patient is ureteric colic until CT shows otherwise.
thinking: Sudden severe colicky right flank pain ↓ radiates to groin and testis, patient restless ↓ afebrile, normal testes, haematuria on dipstick ↓ obstruction of the ureter by a stone ↓ Renal colic
exam_trap: B, Testicular torsion — pain felt in the testicle in a young man tempts towards torsion, but both testes are normal and the pain began in the flank, which is referred pain from the ureter.
takeaway: Restless patient with loin to groin colic and haematuria has renal colic until proven otherwise.

stem: A 22-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic with a week of bilateral lower abdominal pain, pain deep inside during intercourse and bleeding after sex. She has a new sexual partner and they do not use condoms. Her temperature is 37.9°C. On bimanual examination there is tenderness in both adnexa and pain on moving the cervix. A pregnancy test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding and low-grade fever in a young woman with a new partner, with adnexal and cervical motion tenderness, indicate ascending genital tract infection. Because the diagnosis is clinical, antibiotics should be started promptly after testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, with partner notification.
why_wrong: A. A negative pregnancy test makes ectopic pregnancy very unlikely. B. Endometriosis causes cyclical pain over months, not an acute febrile illness with a new partner. D. Appendicitis causes right-sided pain without postcoital bleeding or cervical motion tenderness. E. Ovarian torsion causes sudden severe unilateral pain, often with vomiting.
pearl: PID is a clinical diagnosis. A low threshold for treatment matters because delay increases the risk of infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.
thinking: Young woman with a new partner ↓ bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding, low-grade fever ↓ adnexal and cervical motion tenderness, pregnancy test negative ↓ ascending genital tract infection ↓ Pelvic inflammatory disease
exam_trap: A, Ectopic pregnancy — lower abdominal pain and bleeding in a young woman rightly raise ectopic pregnancy, but the negative pregnancy test excludes it and the infective picture fits PID.
takeaway: Pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness and a negative pregnancy test: treat as PID promptly.

stem: A 39-year-old woman tells her GP that over the past year her periods have become much heavier, with large clots and flooding through her clothes. Her abdomen feels bloated and she needs to pass urine more often. Periods are not especially painful. A pregnancy test is negative. Abdominal examination reveals a firm, non-tender, knobbly mass rising out of the pelvis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Increasingly heavy menstrual bleeding with pressure symptoms and a firm, irregular, non-tender pelvic mass arising from the uterus is typical of fibroids (leiomyomas). Assessment is with a full blood count and pelvic ultrasound. Treatment depends on symptoms, fibroid size and fertility wishes.
why_wrong: A. Adenomyosis causes a uniformly bulky, tender uterus with painful periods, not an irregular knobbly mass. C. Endometrial cancer more often presents with postmenopausal or intermenstrual bleeding and does not typically cause an irregular uterine mass. D. An ovarian cyst causes an adnexal mass, without heavy menstrual bleeding. E. Endometriosis causes cyclical pain and dyspareunia rather than a palpable irregular uterus.
pearl: Heavy periods plus pressure symptoms plus an irregular, non-tender uterus mean fibroids. A smooth, tender, bulky uterus with painful periods suggests adenomyosis instead.
thinking: Progressively heavy periods with clots ↓ bloating and urinary frequency = pressure effects ↓ firm, irregular, non-tender pelvic mass, pregnancy excluded ↓ benign smooth-muscle tumours distorting the uterus ↓ Uterine fibroids
exam_trap: A, Adenomyosis — it also causes heavy bleeding and an enlarged uterus, but it gives a smooth, tender, globular uterus with painful periods, not a knobbly non-tender mass.
takeaway: Heavy periods with pressure symptoms and an irregular enlarged uterus suggest fibroids.

stem: A 63-year-old woman whose periods stopped ten years ago tells her GP that she has twice noticed fresh blood spotting on her underwear in the past month. She has never used hormone replacement therapy. She has type 2 diabetes and a raised BMI. Abdominal examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen and review in three months
options.B: Arrange a cervical screening test only
options.C: Suspected cancer pathway referral for assessment of the endometrium
options.D: Reassure her that occasional spotting is normal after the menopause
options.E: Start continuous combined hormone replacement therapy

correct_answer: C. Suspected cancer pathway referral for assessment of the endometrium
why_correct: Any vaginal bleeding after the menopause is abnormal and must be investigated to exclude endometrial cancer. Obesity and diabetes increase her risk further. She should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway, where assessment usually starts with transvaginal ultrasound and proceeds to endometrial sampling or hysteroscopy if needed.
why_wrong: A. Vaginal atrophy is common, but treating it before excluding cancer may delay a malignant diagnosis. B. A cervical screening test does not assess the endometrium and is not a diagnostic test for bleeding. D. Postmenopausal bleeding is never normal. E. Starting HRT would cause further bleeding and confuse the picture.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding means endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Obesity, diabetes and unopposed oestrogen are classic risk factors.
thinking: Bleeding a decade after the menopause ↓ not on HRT ↓ obesity and diabetes increase endometrial cancer risk ↓ endometrial assessment needed urgently ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral for assessment of the endometrium
exam_trap: A, Prescribe vaginal oestrogen and review in three months — atrophic vaginitis is the commonest cause of postmenopausal bleeding and tempts as a treatable diagnosis, but cancer must be excluded first.
takeaway: Any postmenopausal bleeding needs suspected cancer referral to assess the endometrium.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant mentions at her antenatal appointment that she has had intense vulval itching and soreness for five days. She recently finished a course of antibiotics for a chest infection. There is a thick, white, curd-like discharge with no unpleasant smell. The vulva is red with small superficial fissures. She has no new sexual partner. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Itching and soreness with a thick, white, odourless curd-like discharge and vulval erythema is classic vulvovaginal candidiasis. Pregnancy and recent antibiotic use are both predisposing factors. In pregnancy, a topical imidazole such as a clotrimazole pessary is used, and oral fluconazole should be avoided.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial vaginosis causes a thin, grey, fishy-smelling discharge with little itching. B. Trichomoniasis causes a frothy, yellow-green, offensive discharge. D. Herpes causes painful ulcers or blisters rather than discharge. E. Chlamydia is often asymptomatic or causes intermenstrual bleeding or cervicitis, not intense vulval itching.
pearl: Thick white itchy discharge without odour is thrush. Pregnancy, antibiotics, diabetes and immunosuppression predispose to it. In pregnancy use topical treatment, not oral fluconazole.
thinking: Pregnant woman after antibiotics ↓ intense vulval itching and soreness ↓ thick white curd-like odourless discharge, red fissured vulva ↓ fungal overgrowth favoured by pregnancy and antibiotics ↓ Vulvovaginal candidiasis
exam_trap: A, Bacterial vaginosis — it is the commonest cause of abnormal discharge and is also linked to antibiotics, but it causes a thin fishy-smelling discharge without marked itching.
takeaway: Itchy thick white odourless discharge is thrush; in pregnancy treat topically, not with fluconazole.

stem: A 34-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic because of a sore on the shaft of his penis that appeared ten days ago. He had condomless sex with a new male partner about four weeks ago. The lesion is a single, firm, clean-based ulcer that does not hurt even when pressed. There are rubbery, non-tender enlarged nodes in both groins. He feels well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A single, indurated, painless, clean-based genital ulcer appearing a few weeks after exposure, with painless rubbery inguinal lymphadenopathy, is a chancre of primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Diagnosis is by swab from the lesion and syphilis serology, and the first-line treatment is benzathine penicillin, with partner notification.
why_wrong: B. Herpes causes multiple painful vesicles and shallow ulcers with tender nodes. C. Chancroid causes painful, ragged ulcers with tender, sometimes suppurating nodes. D. Lymphogranuloma venereum causes a transient papule followed by painful, matted inguinal lymphadenopathy. E. Behçet disease causes recurrent painful oral and genital ulcers.
pearl: Pain separates genital ulcers: painless indurated ulcer with painless nodes is syphilis; painful vesicles are herpes; painful ragged ulcers are chancroid.
thinking: New condomless sexual contact a few weeks ago ↓ single, firm, clean-based ulcer that is painless ↓ painless rubbery inguinal nodes ↓ chancre of Treponema pallidum ↓ Primary syphilis
exam_trap: B, Genital herpes simplex — herpes is the most common cause of genital ulcers in the UK, but it is painful and multiple, whereas this ulcer is single, indurated and painless.
takeaway: A single painless indurated genital ulcer with painless nodes is primary syphilis.

stem: A 24-year-old man sees his GP about several small lumps on the shaft of his penis that he noticed a month ago. They are painless, soft, skin-coloured and have a rough, cauliflower-like surface. They are not umbilicated and there are no ulcers. He has had two new sexual partners this year. Which organism is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Painless, soft, skin-coloured papules with a cauliflower-like surface on the genitals are anogenital warts, caused mainly by low-risk human papillomavirus types 6 and 11. Treatment options include topical podophyllotoxin or imiquimod, or cryotherapy. He should also be offered a full sexually transmitted infection screen.
why_wrong: A. Herpes simplex causes painful vesicles and ulcers, not warty growths. B. Molluscum contagiosum causes smooth, pearly, umbilicated papules. C. Treponema pallidum can cause flat, moist condylomata lata in secondary syphilis, but these are not cauliflower-like. E. Chlamydia causes urethritis or discharge and no skin lesions.
pearl: Cauliflower-like genital lumps are HPV warts; smooth umbilicated papules are molluscum. Always offer a full sexual health screen.
thinking: Young sexually active man ↓ painless soft skin-coloured genital lumps ↓ cauliflower surface, not umbilicated, no ulcers ↓ anogenital warts ↓ Human papillomavirus
exam_trap: B, Molluscum contagiosum virus — molluscum also causes painless genital papules in sexually active adults, but its lesions are smooth, pearly and umbilicated rather than cauliflower-like.
takeaway: Painless cauliflower-like genital lumps are warts caused by human papillomavirus.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. She has sudden severe left-sided lower abdominal pain and pain at the tip of her left shoulder. Her last period was six weeks ago and she has had some brown vaginal spotting. She has a copper intrauterine device. She is pale and clammy, with a pulse of 128/min and low blood pressure. The abdomen is tender with guarding. A urine pregnancy test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A positive pregnancy test with sudden unilateral pelvic pain, collapse, shoulder-tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm and signs of shock indicates intraperitoneal haemorrhage from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. An intrauterine device does not exclude it, and when pregnancy does occur with a device in place it is more likely to be ectopic. She needs immediate resuscitation and urgent gynaecology review for surgery.
why_wrong: B. Ovarian torsion causes sudden severe pain with vomiting but does not explain a positive pregnancy test with shoulder-tip pain and shock. C. An incomplete miscarriage causes cramping with heavy visible bleeding through an open cervix, and her scanty spotting does not explain her shock. D. A ruptured cyst can cause pain and some haemoperitoneum but is less likely given a positive test and six weeks of amenorrhoea. E. Appendicitis causes gradually worsening right-sided pain with fever.
pearl: In any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, check a pregnancy test. Shoulder-tip pain and shock with a positive test mean ruptured ectopic pregnancy: resuscitate and call gynaecology.
thinking: Six weeks of amenorrhoea with a positive pregnancy test ↓ sudden unilateral pelvic pain and spotting ↓ shoulder-tip pain, guarding, tachycardia and hypotension = haemoperitoneum ↓ intrauterine device increases the chance any pregnancy is ectopic ↓ Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
exam_trap: C, Incomplete miscarriage — bleeding and pain in early pregnancy tempt towards miscarriage, but the scanty spotting does not explain the shock, which comes from concealed intra-abdominal bleeding.
takeaway: Positive pregnancy test with pain, shoulder-tip pain and shock means ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

stem: A 42-year-old woman sees her GP because for six months her periods have been so heavy that she changes pads every hour on the first two days and has had to leave work. She becomes breathless climbing stairs and looks pale. Her cycle is regular and she has no other symptoms. A pregnancy test is negative. Which blood test should be done for every woman presenting like this?
why_correct: NICE guidance on heavy menstrual bleeding recommends a full blood count for all women with heavy menstrual bleeding, to detect anaemia that needs treatment. Her breathlessness and pallor make this especially relevant. Other blood tests are requested only when the history or examination suggests a specific cause.
why_wrong: B. Thyroid tests are only indicated when there are features of thyroid disease. C. Serum ferritin is not recommended as a routine test in heavy menstrual bleeding. D. A coagulation screen is reserved for heavy bleeding since menarche or a personal or family history suggesting a bleeding disorder. E. Female hormone testing does not help in managing heavy menstrual bleeding.
pearl: Heavy periods: full blood count for everyone; thyroid tests, coagulation screen and other tests only when the history points to them.
thinking: Heavy menstrual bleeding affecting daily life ↓ breathless and pale = possible anaemia ↓ regular cycle, no features of thyroid or bleeding disorder ↓ routine test recommended for all ↓ Full blood count
exam_trap: C, Serum ferritin — iron deficiency is the main concern so ferritin seems logical, but it is not a routine test here; a full blood count is what identifies anaemia that needs treatment.
takeaway: Every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding should have a full blood count.

stem: A 33-year-old woman who has followed a vegetarian diet for many years attends her GP with months of tiredness and breathlessness when walking uphill. Her nails have become brittle and spoon-shaped, and the corners of her mouth are cracked. Blood tests show a low haemoglobin, small red cells and a low ferritin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, and koilonychia and angular cheilitis are recognised clinical signs. Dietary insufficiency and menstrual losses are likely causes in this woman. She should be treated with oral iron, and the cause should be explored, including coeliac serology.
why_wrong: A. Thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis with a normal or high ferritin. B. Anaemia of chronic disease is usually normocytic with a normal or raised ferritin. D. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia. E. Sideroblastic anaemia is rare and the iron stores are high.
pearl: Low ferritin is the most specific marker of iron deficiency. A microcytic anaemia with normal ferritin should prompt consideration of thalassaemia trait or anaemia of chronic disease.
thinking: Tired and breathless on exertion ↓ koilonychia and angular cheilitis ↓ low haemoglobin, microcytosis, low ferritin ↓ depleted iron stores ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia
exam_trap: A, Thalassaemia trait — it is the other common microcytic anaemia, but its ferritin is normal, so a low ferritin settles the diagnosis as iron deficiency.
takeaway: Microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin is iron deficiency: treat it and find the cause.

stem: A 27-year-old woman who has eaten a strict vegan diet for five years, without supplements, sees her GP with tiredness, a sore red smooth tongue and pins and needles in both feet. She looks pale with a slight lemon tinge. Blood tests show an anaemia with large red cells. She drinks no alcohol and her thyroid function is normal. Which deficiency is most likely?
why_correct: A macrocytic anaemia with glossitis and peripheral sensory symptoms in a long-term vegan without supplements points to vitamin B12 deficiency, which affects rapidly dividing cells and the nervous system. B12 is found almost only in animal products. Neurological involvement makes prompt intramuscular replacement important, and B12 should be replaced before any folic acid is given.
why_wrong: A. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis and glossitis but not neuropathy, and a vegan diet is usually rich in folate. B. Iron deficiency causes a microcytic, not macrocytic, anaemia. D. Vitamin C deficiency causes gum bleeding and perifollicular haemorrhages. E. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and muscle weakness, not macrocytic anaemia.
pearl: Macrocytosis plus neurology means B12 until proven otherwise. Check B12 and folate together, and never give folic acid alone when B12 is low, as it can worsen neurological damage.
thinking: Long-term vegan without supplements ↓ glossitis and pale lemon-tinged skin with macrocytic anaemia ↓ pins and needles in the feet = neurological involvement ↓ deficiency that affects both marrow and nerves ↓ Vitamin B12 deficiency
exam_trap: A, Folate deficiency — it also causes macrocytic anaemia with a sore tongue, but it does not cause neuropathy, and a vegan diet is rich in folate.
takeaway: Macrocytic anaemia with glossitis and paraesthesia in a vegan is vitamin B12 deficiency.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis who takes methotrexate is admitted with a sore throat, mouth ulcers, nosebleeds and a fever. She feels exhausted. Her full blood count shows a low haemoglobin, a low neutrophil count and a low platelet count. Which term best describes her blood picture?
why_correct: A reduction in all three cell lines — red cells, white cells and platelets — is pancytopenia, here most likely due to methotrexate-induced bone marrow suppression. It explains her fatigue, infection with mouth ulcers and bleeding. Methotrexate should be stopped, she should be treated as possible neutropenic sepsis, and folinic acid rescue should be considered with specialist advice.
why_wrong: B. Agranulocytosis refers to an absence of neutrophils only, not a fall in all three lines. C. A leukaemoid reaction is a very high white cell count in response to stress or infection. D. Isolated thrombocytopenia affects platelets only. E. Polycythaemia is an increase in red cell mass.
pearl: Methotrexate toxicity can cause pancytopenia; a febrile patient taking it needs urgent full blood count and treatment as possible neutropenic sepsis.
thinking: Methotrexate user ↓ tiredness, infection with mouth ulcers, bleeding ↓ low haemoglobin, neutrophils and platelets ↓ all three cell lines reduced ↓ Pancytopenia
exam_trap: B, Agranulocytosis — fever and mouth ulcers tempt towards a neutrophil problem, but agranulocytosis describes one cell line only, whereas the anaemia and low platelets here show all three are affected.
takeaway: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together is pancytopenia; think drug-induced marrow suppression.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to his GP with three weeks of tiredness, aching legs that wake him at night and pallor. His mother has noticed small red spots on his legs and bruises she cannot explain. On examination he has scattered non-blanching petechiae, enlarged cervical lymph nodes and a palpable liver and spleen. A same-day full blood count shows anaemia, a low platelet count and a raised white cell count, and the blood film shows blast cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bone pain, pallor, bruising, petechiae, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly with anaemia, thrombocytopenia and blasts on the film point to acute leukaemia, most often acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in a child. Marrow infiltration explains the failure of normal blood cell production. He needs immediate referral for specialist assessment.
why_wrong: A. Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated low platelets in an otherwise well child, without anaemia, organomegaly or blasts. B. IgA vasculitis causes a palpable purpuric rash on the legs and buttocks with a normal platelet count. C. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia without blasts or organ enlargement. E. Glandular fever can cause lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly but shows atypical lymphocytes, not blasts.
pearl: Unexplained petechiae, bone pain, pallor or hepatosplenomegaly in a child need an urgent full blood count. Any combination with blasts on the film means immediate specialist referral.
thinking: Child with fatigue, pallor and night-time bone pain ↓ petechiae, bruising, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly ↓ anaemia, low platelets, raised white count with blasts ↓ marrow infiltration by malignant cells ↓ Acute leukaemia
exam_trap: A, Immune thrombocytopenia — petechiae and bruising in a child tempt towards ITP, but ITP leaves the child otherwise well with only low platelets, not anaemia, bone pain, organomegaly and blasts.
takeaway: Bone pain, petechiae, pallor and organomegaly in a child with blasts on the film is acute leukaemia.

stem: A 14-month-old boy who has just started walking is brought to the emergency department with a hot, swollen, painful right knee after a minor tumble. He has had large bruises after his immunisations. Clotting tests show a prolonged APTT with a normal prothrombin time, and his factor VIII level is low. His mother's brother had similar bleeding problems as a child; his mother and father are well. What is the inheritance pattern of his condition?
why_correct: Haemarthrosis after minor trauma, a prolonged APTT with normal prothrombin time and low factor VIII indicate haemophilia A, which is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner. Males with one affected X chromosome have the disease, while carrier females are usually unaffected, which is why it passes from an affected maternal uncle through an unaffected mother.
why_wrong: A. Autosomal dominant conditions such as most von Willebrand disease affect both sexes and usually appear in each generation. C. Autosomal recessive inheritance would not explain bleeding confined to males on the maternal side. D. X-linked dominant conditions affect females as well, often all daughters of affected fathers. E. Mitochondrial inheritance passes from mothers to all children of both sexes.
pearl: Affected males linked through unaffected females, such as a maternal uncle, is the signature of X-linked recessive inheritance. Haemophilia A and B both follow this pattern.
thinking: Young boy with haemarthrosis after minor trauma ↓ prolonged APTT, normal PT, low factor VIII = haemophilia A ↓ affected maternal uncle, unaffected mother ↓ transmission through carrier females to sons ↓ X-linked recessive
exam_trap: A, Autosomal dominant — von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and is usually autosomal dominant, but low factor VIII with haemarthrosis in a boy with an affected maternal uncle fits haemophilia A.
takeaway: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive: affected boys, carrier mothers, affected maternal uncles.

stem: A 27-year-old man sees his GP about a painless lump on the side of his neck that has been slowly enlarging for six weeks. He has drenching sweats that soak his sheets, generalised itching, and has lost weight without trying. He noticed the lump aches after drinking alcohol. There is a firm, rubbery, non-tender enlarged node in the left supraclavicular region. He has no cough, sore throat or recent travel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A persistent, enlarging, painless rubbery lymph node with drenching night sweats, weight loss and itch in a young adult is highly suggestive of lymphoma, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma, in which pain in the nodes after alcohol is a classic though uncommon feature. He needs urgent referral on the suspected cancer pathway for assessment and biopsy.
why_wrong: B. Reactive nodes are usually tender, follow an infection and settle within a few weeks. C. Tuberculous lymphadenitis is possible with sweats but there is no travel, contact or respiratory history and the node is not matted or discharging. D. Glandular fever causes sore throat, fever and tender nodes, settling within weeks. E. Sarcoidosis usually causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with cough, rash or eye involvement.
pearl: A painless, rubbery, persistent node with B symptoms needs urgent referral. Supraclavicular nodes and pain in a node after alcohol are red flags for lymphoma.
thinking: Young adult with painless, enlarging neck node over six weeks ↓ drenching sweats, weight loss, itch ↓ rubbery supraclavicular node, pain after alcohol ↓ no infective features ↓ Lymphoma
exam_trap: C, Tuberculous lymphadenitis — night sweats and weight loss with a neck node tempt towards TB, but there are no risk factors or chest symptoms, and the rubbery node with itch and alcohol pain points to lymphoma.
takeaway: A painless rubbery node with night sweats, weight loss and itch suggests lymphoma: refer urgently.

stem: A 71-year-old right-handed woman is admitted to the stroke unit with right arm and face weakness. She follows spoken commands such as 'close your eyes and lift your left hand' correctly, but when asked about her family she produces only a few slow, halting words with great effort and becomes visibly frustrated. She cannot repeat a short phrase. Which brain area is most likely damaged?
why_correct: Non-fluent, effortful, halting speech with preserved comprehension and awareness of the deficit indicates expressive (Broca) aphasia. It results from damage to the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant, usually left, hemisphere, which fits her right-sided face and arm weakness. Repetition is also impaired because speech production is affected.
why_wrong: A. Wernicke aphasia causes fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. C. Arcuate fasciculus damage causes conduction aphasia, with fluent speech and good comprehension but poor repetition. D. Right parietal damage in a right-handed person causes neglect rather than aphasia. E. Cerebellar damage causes slurred, ataxic speech (dysarthria), not a language disorder.
pearl: Broca's is broken speech: non-fluent and effortful but with good understanding and insight. Wernicke's is fluent speech with poor understanding.
thinking: Right-sided weakness = left hemisphere ↓ understands commands ↓ slow, effortful, halting speech with frustration ↓ expressive, non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension ↓ Broca area
exam_trap: C, Arcuate fasciculus — impaired repetition tempts towards conduction aphasia, but conduction aphasia has fluent speech, whereas her speech is slow and effortful.
takeaway: Non-fluent effortful speech with preserved comprehension localises to Broca area.

stem: A 26-year-old man on a surgical ward is given his first intravenous dose of co-amoxiclav. Within ten minutes he develops itchy raised wheals on his chest and arms, and his eyelids become puffy. He has no stridor or wheeze, his oxygen saturation is normal and his blood pressure is stable. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction best explains this?
why_correct: Urticaria and angioedema developing within minutes of a drug dose reflect IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation with histamine release, which is a type I hypersensitivity reaction. Here there is no airway, breathing or circulatory compromise. The drug should be stopped, the patient treated symptomatically and closely observed for progression to anaphylaxis, and the allergy clearly recorded.
why_wrong: A. Type II reactions are antibody-mediated cell destruction, such as drug-induced haemolytic anaemia. C. Type III reactions are immune-complex mediated, such as serum sickness, appearing days to weeks later. D. Type IV reactions are delayed and T-cell-mediated, appearing after 48 hours or more. E. Drug intolerance is a predictable non-immune side effect, not urticaria with angioedema.
pearl: Speed points to the mechanism: wheals and swelling within minutes of a dose are type I; an eczematous or maculopapular rash days later is usually type IV.
thinking: First dose of a beta-lactam ↓ urticaria and eyelid swelling within minutes ↓ rapid mast cell degranulation ↓ IgE-mediated, without ABC compromise ↓ Type I
exam_trap: D, Type IV — drug rashes are often type IV, which tempts by frequency, but type IV reactions are delayed by days, whereas this reaction appeared within minutes with angioedema.
takeaway: Urticaria and angioedema within minutes of a drug is a type I, IgE-mediated reaction.

stem: A 16-year-old girl attends her GP with itchy, red, weeping, scaly patches on both earlobes. She had her ears pierced and started wearing inexpensive metal earrings three days ago. The rash is confined to the areas in contact with the earrings. She has had a similar reaction under a metal belt buckle in the past. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is most likely?
why_correct: An itchy, eczematous rash appearing a few days after contact with metal jewellery, limited to the site of contact, with a previous similar reaction, is allergic contact dermatitis to nickel. This is a delayed, T-cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Management is allergen avoidance and a topical corticosteroid, with patch testing if needed.
why_wrong: A. Type I reactions are immediate, causing wheals or angioedema within minutes. B. Type II reactions involve antibodies against cells, as in haemolytic anaemia. C. Type III reactions are immune-complex mediated and cause systemic features. E. Irritant dermatitis is non-immune and depends on the dose of an irritant, whereas her repeated reaction to metal suggests sensitisation.
pearl: Nickel allergy is the classic type IV reaction: an eczematous rash under jewellery, buckles or watch backs one to several days after contact. Patch testing confirms it.
thinking: New metal earrings ↓ eczematous itchy rash after a delay of days ↓ confined to the contact area, previous similar reaction ↓ delayed T-cell-mediated sensitisation ↓ Type IV
exam_trap: E, Irritant (non-immune) reaction — contact dermatitis from a substance tempts towards irritant dermatitis, but metal is not a significant irritant, and the recurrence with buckles shows immune sensitisation.
takeaway: Eczematous rash under jewellery days after contact is a type IV nickel allergy.

stem: A 62-year-old man telephones his GP practice on the third day of a course of trimethoprim for a urinary infection. He has developed itchy raised blotches over his trunk and arms. A same-day review finds no swelling of his lips or tongue, no wheeze or difficulty breathing, and a normal blood pressure and oxygen saturation. His urinary symptoms have improved. What is the most appropriate management?

options.C: Stop trimethoprim and give an oral non-sedating antihistamine

correct_answer: C. Stop trimethoprim and give an oral non-sedating antihistamine
why_correct: An urticarial rash after starting an antibiotic, without airway, breathing or circulatory compromise, is managed by stopping the likely cause and giving a non-sedating oral antihistamine for symptom relief. The reaction should be recorded in his notes. If his infection still needs treatment, an unrelated antibiotic can be chosen, and he should be given safety-netting advice about symptoms of anaphylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis with airway, breathing or circulation problems, which he does not have. B. Intravenous steroids are not needed for uncomplicated urticaria. D. Salbutamol treats bronchospasm, and he has no wheeze. E. Continuing the drug risks worsening the reaction.
pearl: Match treatment to severity: urticaria alone means stop the drug and give an antihistamine; any airway, breathing or circulation problem means intramuscular adrenaline.
thinking: Itchy wheals after starting an antibiotic ↓ no lip or tongue swelling, no wheeze, normal BP and saturations ↓ uncomplicated urticaria, not anaphylaxis ↓ remove the trigger and relieve symptoms ↓ Stop trimethoprim and give an oral non-sedating antihistamine
exam_trap: A, Intramuscular adrenaline — a drug allergy tempts candidates to give adrenaline, but it is for anaphylaxis with ABC compromise, not isolated skin features.
takeaway: Drug urticaria without ABC compromise: stop the drug and give an oral antihistamine.

stem: A 63-year-old man is on the coronary care unit two hours after primary angioplasty for an inferior myocardial infarction. He becomes pale, clammy and lightheaded. His pulse is 38/min and regular, and his blood pressure is low. The ECG shows sinus bradycardia. Oxygen has been given and intravenous access is in place. Which drug should be given first?
why_correct: Bradycardia with adverse features such as hypotension and reduced perfusion is first treated with intravenous atropine, in line with the Resuscitation Council UK bradycardia algorithm. Atropine blocks vagal tone at the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, increasing heart rate. Inferior infarction commonly causes vagally mediated bradycardia, which often responds well to atropine.
why_wrong: A. Adenosine blocks atrioventricular conduction and is used for narrow-complex tachycardia, so it would worsen bradycardia. B. Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic for tachyarrhythmias and can slow the heart further. C. An isoprenaline infusion is a second-line option if atropine fails, alongside pacing. E. Digoxin slows the heart rate and is contraindicated here.
pearl: Bradycardia with adverse features: atropine first; if it does not work, move on to further atropine, an isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion, or transcutaneous pacing with expert help.
thinking: Inferior MI ↓ sinus bradycardia with hypotension and poor perfusion = adverse features ↓ excess vagal tone on the conducting system ↓ first-line drug in the bradycardia algorithm ↓ Atropine
exam_trap: C, Isoprenaline infusion — it does increase heart rate and appears in the bradycardia algorithm, but it is a second-line treatment after atropine has failed, not the first drug given.
takeaway: Bradycardia with adverse features: give intravenous atropine first.

stem: A 41-year-old man comes to the emergency department with sudden pounding palpitations that began an hour ago while he was lifting boxes. He has no chest pain, breathlessness or dizziness, and no history of asthma. Blood pressure is normal. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 180/min without visible P waves. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre has been performed correctly without effect. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
why_correct: A haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia that has not responded to vagal manoeuvres should be treated with a rapid intravenous bolus of adenosine, given with continuous ECG monitoring, in line with the Resuscitation Council UK tachycardia algorithm. Adenosine briefly blocks the atrioventricular node, terminating re-entry circuits. The patient should be warned about transient chest discomfort and flushing.
why_wrong: B. Synchronised cardioversion is reserved for patients with adverse features such as shock, syncope, ischaemia or heart failure. C. Amiodarone is not first line for a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia. D. Verapamil is an alternative only when adenosine is contraindicated, for example in asthma. E. Oral digoxin acts too slowly and is not used to terminate this arrhythmia.
pearl: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first, then rapid IV adenosine. Verapamil is for when adenosine is contraindicated, and cardioversion is for adverse features.
thinking: Sudden palpitations ↓ stable, no adverse features ↓ regular narrow-complex tachycardia, vagal manoeuvre failed ↓ AV nodal re-entry likely, terminate by blocking the AV node ↓ Intravenous adenosine
exam_trap: D, Intravenous verapamil — it can terminate a narrow-complex tachycardia and is in the algorithm, but it is the alternative when adenosine is contraindicated, and he has no asthma.
takeaway: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia after failed vagal manoeuvres: give IV adenosine.

stem: An 84-year-old man with heart failure has had his furosemide dose doubled two weeks ago because of ankle swelling. He now has painful leg cramps, constipation and episodes of palpitations. His ankle swelling has improved. The ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves. Which electrolyte disturbance is most likely?
why_correct: Loop diuretics increase delivery of sodium to the distal nephron, which increases potassium loss in the urine. Muscle cramps, constipation, palpitations and ECG changes of flattened T waves and U waves after a dose increase are typical of hypokalaemia. Potassium should be checked and replaced, and magnesium should also be checked as it is often low too.
why_wrong: A. Hyperkalaemia causes tall tented T waves, not U waves, and is more typical of potassium-sparing diuretics. C. Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion, so hypercalcaemia is not expected. D. Hyponatraemia can occur with diuretics but causes confusion and does not produce U waves. E. Loop diuretics cause magnesium loss, not excess.
pearl: Loop and thiazide diuretics lose potassium; spironolactone, amiloride and ACE inhibitors retain it. U waves and flat T waves point to low potassium.
thinking: Furosemide dose increased ↓ cramps, constipation, palpitations ↓ flattened T waves and U waves on ECG ↓ renal potassium loss from a loop diuretic ↓ Hypokalaemia
exam_trap: D, Hyponatraemia — diuretics commonly lower sodium and this tempts, but the U waves and flattened T waves are specific to low potassium.
takeaway: Cramps and U waves after a furosemide increase suggest hypokalaemia.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure and chronic kidney disease takes ramipril. Three weeks ago spironolactone was added to her treatment. She now feels generally weak and has had episodes of palpitations. Her ECG shows tall, peaked T waves and a slightly widened QRS complex. Which adverse effect is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that reduces potassium excretion, and combining it with an ACE inhibitor in a patient with chronic kidney disease significantly raises the risk of hyperkalaemia. Weakness, palpitations, peaked T waves and QRS widening indicate significant hyperkalaemia needing urgent treatment, including cardiac protection with intravenous calcium.
why_wrong: B. Hypokalaemia causes flattened T waves and U waves and is associated with loop or thiazide diuretics. C. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT interval and causes tetany and perioral tingling. D. Hypernatraemia causes thirst and confusion, not peaked T waves. E. Hypomagnesaemia is associated with arrhythmias and loop diuretics rather than spironolactone.
pearl: Spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker plus reduced kidney function is a high-risk combination for hyperkalaemia; check potassium soon after starting and regularly afterwards.
thinking: Spironolactone added to ramipril in chronic kidney disease ↓ weakness and palpitations ↓ peaked T waves and widened QRS ↓ reduced renal potassium excretion ↓ Hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: B, Hypokalaemia — patients with heart failure on diuretics often have low potassium, which tempts, but spironolactone is potassium-sparing and peaked T waves indicate a high potassium.
takeaway: Spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor in kidney disease causes hyperkalaemia: check potassium.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and protein in her urine was started on lisinopril two months ago. She returns to her GP with a persistent tickly, non-productive cough that keeps her awake. She has no fever, breathlessness or wheeze, she does not smoke, her chest is clear and a chest X-ray is normal. She asks why her new tablet could cause a cough. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.C: Blockade of beta-2 receptors in the airways
options.D: Direct histamine release from mast cells

why_correct: Angiotensin-converting enzyme also breaks down bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors cause bradykinin to accumulate in the airways, which sensitises the cough reflex and causes a dry, persistent cough. If the cough is troublesome, switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker is appropriate, because it does not affect bradykinin and preserves the kidney benefit.
why_wrong: B. ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II levels rather than increasing them. C. Beta-2 blockade is a mechanism of bronchospasm with non-selective beta blockers, not ACE inhibitors. D. Direct mast cell histamine release is not the mechanism of ACE inhibitor cough. E. Reduced aldosterone explains the potassium rise with ACE inhibitors, not cough.
pearl: ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema both come from bradykinin build-up. Switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker usually solves the cough because these drugs do not block bradykinin breakdown.
thinking: Recently started on an ACE inhibitor ↓ dry, persistent cough with a clear chest and normal X-ray ↓ ACE normally degrades bradykinin ↓ accumulating bradykinin sensitises the cough reflex ↓ Reduced breakdown of bradykinin
exam_trap: E, Reduced aldosterone secretion — it is a real effect of ACE inhibitors and tempts on that basis, but it explains hyperkalaemia, not the cough.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough is caused by bradykinin build-up; switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker.

stem: A 61-year-old woman who has taken atorvastatin for a year was prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection eight days ago. She now has aching and weakness in both thighs and upper arms and struggles to climb stairs. Her urine is normal in colour. She has no skin rash. Her creatine kinase is markedly raised, her thyroid function is normal and her ESR is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: New symmetrical proximal muscle pain and weakness with a markedly raised creatine kinase in a patient on a statin indicates statin-associated myopathy. Clarithromycin inhibits the enzyme that breaks down atorvastatin, raising statin levels and increasing the risk. The statin should be stopped, kidney function checked and she should be monitored for rhabdomyolysis.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes stiffness with raised ESR and a normal creatine kinase. C. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain with normal blood tests. D. Dermatomyositis also raises creatine kinase but is accompanied by a characteristic rash, which is absent, and the drug interaction explains this picture. E. Guillain–Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness with areflexia and a normal creatine kinase.
pearl: Clarithromycin and erythromycin increase levels of simvastatin and atorvastatin; the statin should usually be paused during a course to reduce the risk of myopathy.
thinking: Long-term atorvastatin, clarithromycin started recently ↓ symmetrical proximal muscle pain and weakness ↓ markedly raised creatine kinase, normal thyroid function and ESR ↓ drug interaction raising statin levels ↓ Statin-associated myopathy
exam_trap: A, Polymyalgia rheumatica — proximal aching in an older woman tempts towards PMR, but PMR does not raise creatine kinase and is not associated with true weakness.
takeaway: Muscle pain with a high CK on a statin, especially with clarithromycin, means statin myopathy.

stem: A 28-year-old man was started on carbamazepine for epilepsy three weeks ago. He attends his GP with two days of fever and aching, followed by a painful red rash on his face and trunk with dusky patches, some of which are blistering. His lips are crusted and bleeding, it hurts to swallow and his eyes are red and sore. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Stop carbamazepine immediately and arrange emergency hospital admission
options.B: Reduce the carbamazepine dose and review in one week
options.C: Switch to oxcarbazepine and review in one week
options.D: Continue carbamazepine and start oral prednisolone
options.E: Continue carbamazepine and prescribe an oral antihistamine

correct_answer: A. Stop carbamazepine immediately and arrange emergency hospital admission
why_correct: A febrile prodrome followed by a painful, dusky, blistering rash with mucosal involvement of the mouth and eyes, weeks after starting carbamazepine, is Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. This is a medical emergency. The drug must be stopped immediately and the patient admitted for specialist care, often in a burns or intensive care setting, with ophthalmology input.
why_wrong: B. Any continuation of the causative drug worsens the reaction and outcome. C. Oxcarbazepine is structurally related and can cross-react, and outpatient review is unsafe. D. Continuing the drug is dangerous, and steroids in primary care are not the appropriate management. E. An antihistamine does not treat a severe cutaneous adverse reaction.
pearl: Skin pain, blistering and mucosal involvement after a new drug signal SJS/TEN. Aromatic anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine are classic culprits, typically within the first two months.
thinking: Carbamazepine started three weeks ago ↓ febrile prodrome then painful dusky blistering rash ↓ oral, lip and eye involvement ↓ severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction ↓ Stop carbamazepine immediately and arrange emergency hospital admission
exam_trap: C, Switch to oxcarbazepine and review in one week — switching anticonvulsants seems sensible for seizure control, but oxcarbazepine can cross-react, and this emergency needs admission, not outpatient review.
takeaway: Painful blistering rash with mucosal involvement after carbamazepine: stop it and admit urgently.

stem: An 83-year-old man is seen in a falls clinic after two falls in a month, both soon after getting out of bed. He feels lightheaded and his vision greys out when he stands up. His blood pressure drops considerably when he moves from lying to standing. His regular medicines include atorvastatin, omeprazole, alendronic acid, paracetamol, amlodipine and doxazosin, the last of which was started recently. Which group of his medicines is most likely contributing to his falls?
why_correct: Postural lightheadedness and falls with a significant drop in blood pressure on standing in an older adult are commonly caused or worsened by antihypertensive medications. Alpha-blockers such as doxazosin and calcium channel blockers impair the normal vasoconstrictor response to standing. A structured medication review to reduce or stop these drugs is an important part of falls prevention.
why_wrong: A. Statins can cause muscle symptoms but do not lower blood pressure on standing. C. Proton pump inhibitors are linked with fractures and low magnesium, not postural hypotension. D. Bisphosphonates reduce fracture risk and do not cause postural hypotension. E. Paracetamol does not affect blood pressure.
pearl: In any older person who falls, measure lying and standing blood pressure and review medicines. Alpha-blockers, diuretics, vasodilators and other antihypertensives are common contributors.
thinking: Older man with falls after standing ↓ lightheadedness and visual greying out ↓ significant postural drop in blood pressure ↓ recently started alpha-blocker alongside a calcium channel blocker ↓ Antihypertensive medications
exam_trap: D, Bisphosphonates — they are linked with falls clinics because they protect against fractures, but they treat the consequence of falls rather than causing the postural blood pressure drop.
takeaway: Postural hypotension and falls in older adults: review antihypertensives, especially alpha-blockers.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is having a colonoscopy under intravenous midazolam. Partway through the procedure she stops responding to voice and her oxygen saturation keeps falling despite supplemental oxygen and a jaw thrust. She has been given no opioid, takes no regular sedatives and has no history of epilepsy. Which drug should be given to reverse her sedation?
why_correct: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor. Reversal of over-sedation during a procedure in a patient who is not benzodiazepine-dependent and has no seizure history is one of the safest settings in which to use it. Airway support continues alongside, and she needs monitoring afterwards because flumazenil is shorter acting than midazolam.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids, and she has received none. C. Atropine treats bradycardia and does not reverse sedation. D. Sugammadex reverses the neuromuscular blockers rocuronium and vecuronium, which are not used for endoscopic sedation. E. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin and has no effect on sedatives.
pearl: Flumazenil wears off sooner than most benzodiazepines, so re-sedation can occur; keep the patient monitored after reversal rather than returning them straight to an unobserved area.
thinking: Sedation with midazolam during endoscopy ↓ unresponsive with falling saturations, no opioid given ↓ benzodiazepine effect needs reversing, low seizure risk ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: A, naloxone — it is the reflex reversal agent in a sedated, hypoxic patient, but no opioid was given and naloxone does nothing at the benzodiazepine receptor.
takeaway: Midazolam over-sedation during a procedure is reversed with flumazenil, with monitoring for re-sedation.

stem: A 74-year-old woman on the surgical ward, two days after a bowel resection, is reviewed urgently by the night doctor. She is grey, clammy and drowsy, and her blood pressure is 76/40 mmHg. The cardiac monitor shows a narrow-complex tachycardia with a chaotic baseline, no visible P waves and varying R–R intervals. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.E: Intravenous amiodarone before any shock is attempted

why_correct: This is atrial fibrillation with adverse features: shock and a reduced conscious level. In a tachyarrhythmia with adverse features, Resuscitation Council UK guidance is synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation or anaesthesia, which restores rhythm faster and more reliably than any drug. Amiodarone is added if the shocks do not work.
why_wrong: B. Oral beta-blockade is too slow, and its negative inotropic effect is unsafe when she is already shocked. C. Digoxin works slowly and is not a treatment for unstable fast AF. D. Anticoagulation matters for stroke prevention but does nothing for the instability. E. Amiodarone is given after shocks that have not worked, not instead of cardioversion in a patient who is shocked.
pearl: Adverse features in tachyarrhythmia are shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia and heart failure; any one of them moves treatment from drugs to synchronised cardioversion.
thinking: Post-operative patient with irregular narrow-complex tachycardia ↓ hypotension, clamminess and drowsiness = adverse features ↓ unstable tachyarrhythmia needs the fastest, most reliable treatment ↓ Synchronised DC cardioversion
exam_trap: E, intravenous amiodarone — it feels safer than a shock, but in a shocked patient it is reserved for after cardioversion has not worked.
takeaway: AF with shock or a reduced conscious level needs synchronised cardioversion first, not rate-control drugs.

stem: A 27-year-old man who works as a graphic designer says that over the past four days red tones on his screen have looked washed out when he uses his left eye alone, and the vision on that side has become blurred. He describes a dull ache behind the left eye. Left visual acuity is reduced. When a torch is swung from the right eye to the left, both pupils dilate. The fundi look normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Visual loss developing over days in a young adult, with reduced colour vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect, points to optic nerve disease. A normal-looking disc fits retrobulbar inflammation, and the ache behind the eye supports optic neuritis. He needs urgent ophthalmology review and consideration of demyelinating disease.
why_wrong: A. Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden, painless loss with a pale retina and cherry-red spot, not a normal fundus. B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a red, very painful eye with haloes and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. D. Vitreous haemorrhage causes sudden floaters or loss of vision and a hazy fundal view, without loss of colour vision. E. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and a curtain-like field loss, with a visibly detached retina.
pearl: In optic neuritis the disc often looks normal at first because the inflammation is behind the globe; red desaturation and an afferent pupillary defect show it is the nerve.
thinking: Young adult, monocular visual blurring over days ↓ red desaturation + relative afferent pupillary defect ↓ normal fundus, so retinal causes are unlikely ↓ optic nerve inflammation ↓ Optic neuritis
exam_trap: A, central retinal artery occlusion — it also causes an afferent pupillary defect, but its onset is sudden, it is painless and the retina looks abnormal.
takeaway: Subacute monocular blur, red desaturation and an afferent pupillary defect with a normal disc suggest optic neuritis.

stem: A 19-year-old university hockey player sees her GP after finding a lump in her left breast in the shower. Examination shows a discrete, rubbery lump in the upper outer quadrant that moves freely away from the examining fingers. The overlying skin and nipple are normal, there is no axillary lymphadenopathy, and she has not noticed it change with her periods. Which is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: A well-defined, rubbery, very mobile lump in a woman in her teens or twenties, with normal skin, nipple and axilla, is typical of a fibroadenoma. These are the commonest benign breast lumps in young women. She should still be referred to a breast clinic for triple assessment.
why_wrong: A. Breast cysts are most common in women in their late thirties to forties and often feel fluctuant or vary with the cycle. B. Fat necrosis usually follows trauma or surgery and feels firm, irregular and sometimes tethered. C. Invasive carcinoma is rare at this age and tends to be hard, irregular and fixed, sometimes with skin or nipple changes. E. Intraductal papilloma usually causes nipple discharge rather than a mobile lump.
pearl: A breast lump in a young woman is very likely benign, but diagnosis still rests on triple assessment (examination, imaging and, where needed, biopsy), not on how the lump feels.
thinking: Woman in her late teens with a breast lump ↓ smooth, rubbery, highly mobile ↓ normal skin, nipple and axilla, no cyclical change ↓ Fibroadenoma
exam_trap: A, breast cyst — it is also smooth and benign, but cysts usually appear in women in their late thirties and forties, not at nineteen.
takeaway: A discrete, rubbery, freely mobile breast lump in a young woman is most likely a fibroadenoma.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after her flatmate found her beside an empty bottle of her mother's temazepam. She opens her eyes only to pain and her breathing is slow and shallow. Intravenous naloxone given en route produced no change. She does not take any regular medicines, there is no evidence of other substances, and her ECG shows normal QRS and QT intervals. Which drug specifically reverses the agent she has taken?
why_correct: Temazepam is a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil competitively blocks the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor, reversing sedation and respiratory depression. Airway support comes first, and flumazenil is considered only when the risk of seizures is low. Here she is not a regular user and the ECG gives no suggestion of a pro-convulsant co-ingestant such as a tricyclic.
why_wrong: A. Phytomenadione (vitamin K) reverses warfarin and has no sedative-reversing action. B. Naloxone has already failed, and more of it will not reverse a benzodiazepine. C. Activated charcoal does not reverse established sedation and is hazardous when the airway is not protected. D. Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, not benzodiazepine effects.
pearl: Before giving flumazenil, ask whether the patient is benzodiazepine-dependent or has taken a pro-convulsant such as a tricyclic; if either is likely, supportive care is safer.
thinking: Reduced consciousness and hypoventilation after temazepam ↓ no response to naloxone ↓ not a regular user, ECG gives no sign of a tricyclic ↓ benzodiazepine receptor antagonist ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: B, more naloxone — escalating the familiar antidote is tempting, but naloxone acts only at opioid receptors and has already failed.
takeaway: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, but only after checking for dependence and pro-convulsant co-ingestion.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with diabetic nephropathy has been under the renal clinic for several years, and her kidney function has fallen steadily. She now complains of aching in her hips and lower back. Her latest bloods show a low-normal calcium, a raised phosphate and a raised parathyroid hormone. Which process best explains these results?
why_correct: Failing kidneys retain phosphate and make less active vitamin D (calcitriol), which reduces calcium absorption and tends to lower serum calcium. The parathyroid glands respond by producing more PTH, which is secondary hyperparathyroidism. Over time this causes renal bone disease and bone pain.
why_wrong: A. Primary hyperparathyroidism gives a high calcium with a low or normal phosphate, the opposite of this pattern. C. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism develops after long-standing secondary disease, once the glands become autonomous, and calcium is then high rather than low-normal. D. Hypoparathyroidism has a low PTH, not a raised one. E. Paget's disease typically causes an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphate and PTH.
pearl: In hyperparathyroidism, calcium points to the type: high in primary, low or normal in secondary, high in tertiary. In CKD, phosphate is usually raised.
thinking: Progressive CKD ↓ phosphate retention and less calcitriol ↓ calcium driven down, PTH up in response ↓ low-normal calcium, high phosphate, high PTH ↓ Secondary hyperparathyroidism
exam_trap: C, tertiary hyperparathyroidism — the long renal history suggests it, but tertiary disease causes hypercalcaemia, and her calcium is low-normal.
takeaway: CKD with low-normal calcium, high phosphate and high PTH means secondary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A 29-year-old man and his partner are seen in a fertility clinic after two years of trying to conceive. His semen analysis shows no sperm. He mentions that he had breast development as a teenager that never fully settled. On examination he is tall with sparse body and facial hair, and both testes are small and firm. Which karyotype is most likely?
why_correct: Azoospermia, small firm testes, gynaecomastia, sparse androgen-dependent hair and tall stature in a man are the picture of Klinefelter syndrome, which is caused by an extra X chromosome. The testes fail, so testosterone is low and gonadotrophins are high. Many cases are first found during an infertility work-up.
why_wrong: A. 46,XY is a normal male karyotype and would not explain primary testicular failure with this body habitus. B. 45,X is Turner syndrome, which gives a female phenotype. C. 47,XYY men are often tall but usually have normal testicular function and no gynaecomastia. D. 47,XXX gives a female phenotype.
pearl: Klinefelter syndrome often goes unnoticed until adulthood. Consider it in any man with azoospermia and small testes, and check FSH, LH and testosterone before karyotyping.
thinking: Man with infertility and azoospermia ↓ small firm testes + gynaecomastia + sparse hair ↓ tall stature, primary hypogonadism ↓ extra X chromosome ↓ 47,XXY
exam_trap: C, 47,XYY — tall stature points that way, but XYY men usually have normal testes and fertility, without gynaecomastia.
takeaway: Azoospermia, small firm testes and gynaecomastia in a tall man suggest 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome).

stem: A 36-year-old woman who works as a lifeguard attends because her partner keeps remarking on a dark brown mole on the back of her calf. She has had it since her teens. Comparing it with holiday photographs from last summer, she and the GP agree it now looks bigger and has darkened on one side. It does not itch or bleed. Which feature of this lesion is most worrying?

options.A: It has been present since adolescence
options.B: It is located on the calf
options.C: Its appearance has altered over recent months

correct_answer: C. Its appearance has altered over recent months
why_correct: Evolution, meaning change in size, shape or colour, is one of the strongest warning signs of melanoma, and many melanomas arise in existing naevi. The photographs give objective evidence that the lesion is growing and its pigment is changing. This needs urgent referral for dermatological assessment.
why_wrong: A. Having a mole for a long time is reassuring in itself; it is the recent change that matters. B. The lower leg is a common site for melanoma in women, but location alone is not a warning feature. D. A dark brown colour on its own is common in benign naevi; it is uneven or changing colour that raises concern. E. Many melanomas cause no symptoms, so the lack of itch or bleeding offers no reassurance.
pearl: A long-standing mole that starts to change deserves the same suspicion as a new lesion; serial photographs are a simple, objective way to document evolution.
thinking: Pigmented lesion on a sun-exposed site ↓ photographs show growth and uneven darkening ↓ evolution is a major melanoma warning sign ↓ Its appearance has altered over recent months
exam_trap: A, presence since adolescence — an old mole feels benign, but melanoma can arise within an existing naevus, and the change is what matters.
takeaway: A pigmented lesion that changes over time needs urgent assessment for melanoma, even if it has been there for years.

stem: A 26-year-old man attends an urgent care centre wearing sunglasses indoors. For two days his left eye has ached and bright light has been unbearable. For the past year he has had low back stiffness that wakes him in the early hours and eases after a hot shower and moving around. The redness is most intense in a ring around the cornea, the left pupil is smaller than the right, and there is no discharge. What is the most likely eye diagnosis?
why_correct: A painful red eye with marked photophobia, redness concentrated around the cornea (ciliary flush) and a small pupil is the picture of anterior uveitis. His inflammatory back pain, worse at night and better with activity, suggests axial spondyloarthritis, the condition most strongly associated with acute anterior uveitis. He needs same-day ophthalmology assessment.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial conjunctivitis causes diffuse redness with purulent discharge and little photophobia or pain. B. Episcleritis causes a localised, mildly uncomfortable red patch without photophobia or a change in the pupil. C. Acute angle-closure glaucoma gives a fixed, mid-dilated pupil with haloes and often vomiting, not a small pupil. D. A subconjunctival haemorrhage is a painless, well-defined red patch with normal vision.
pearl: Uveitis may be the first manifestation of spondyloarthritis that brings a patient to a doctor; asking about inflammatory back pain in anyone with uveitis can lead to the underlying diagnosis.
thinking: Painful red eye with marked photophobia ↓ ciliary flush and small pupil, no discharge ↓ inflammatory back pain suggests spondyloarthritis ↓ Anterior uveitis
exam_trap: B, episcleritis — it is also linked to inflammatory disease, but it is only mildly uncomfortable, without photophobia or a change in the pupil.
takeaway: A photophobic red eye with ciliary flush in a young man with inflammatory back pain is anterior uveitis.

stem: A 64-year-old woman who takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension describes a year of separate attacks in which first her right ankle and later her left knee became hot, swollen and very painful, each settling completely within about ten days. Between attacks she is well. On examination there are several small, firm, chalky-white nodules on the rim of her right ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent, self-limiting attacks of acute monoarthritis with full recovery between episodes suggest a crystal arthropathy. A thiazide diuretic, which reduces renal urate excretion, and tophi on the ear point specifically to urate deposition. Joint aspiration showing needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals would confirm gout.
why_wrong: A. Calcium pyrophosphate disease also causes recurrent attacks, often in the knee of an older person, but it does not produce ear tophi and is not linked to thiazides. B. Rheumatoid arthritis is a persistent, symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis, not separate attacks that resolve fully. C. Septic arthritis does not keep recurring and resolving on its own in different joints over a year. E. Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genital infection and usually affects several lower-limb joints at once.
pearl: Thiazide and loop diuretics raise serum urate and are common precipitants of gout in older women; review the drug chart before starting long-term urate-lowering therapy.
thinking: Recurrent self-limiting acute monoarthritis ↓ well and fully recovered between attacks ↓ thiazide use + chalky ear nodules (tophi) ↓ urate crystal deposition ↓ Gout
exam_trap: A, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease — a recurrent hot knee in an older woman suggests it, but tophi and a thiazide point to urate.
takeaway: Recurrent self-limiting monoarthritis with tophi in a patient on a thiazide is gout.

stem: A 33-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic after noticing a sore on her vulva while shaving. It has been there for about a week and has never hurt. Examination shows a single clean-based ulcer with a firm, indurated edge on the left labium majus, and there are bilateral rubbery, non-tender inguinal lymph nodes. Which infection is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A single painless ulcer with an indurated edge and a clean base, together with non-tender rubbery regional lymph nodes, is the chancre of primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Because it does not hurt it is easily missed. Diagnosis is by serology, with dark-ground microscopy or PCR of the lesion where available, and she should have a full STI screen.
why_wrong: A. Genital herpes causes multiple painful vesicles or shallow ulcers, often with tender nodes. B. Chancroid causes painful, ragged ulcers with tender, sometimes suppurating, nodes. C. In lymphogranuloma venereum the ulcer is small and short-lived, and the main feature is painful, matted inguinal lymphadenopathy. E. Candidiasis causes itching, soreness and discharge rather than an indurated ulcer.
pearl: Pain helps tell genital ulcers apart: herpes and chancroid hurt, the syphilitic chancre does not. Test anyone with a genital ulcer for syphilis, even if herpes seems more likely.
thinking: Single genital ulcer, present a week ↓ painless with an indurated edge and clean base ↓ non-tender rubbery inguinal nodes ↓ Primary syphilis
exam_trap: A, genital herpes — it is the commonest cause of genital ulceration in the UK, but it hurts and usually gives multiple lesions.
takeaway: A single painless indurated genital ulcer with non-tender nodes is primary syphilis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 41-year-old woman is an inpatient on the gastroenterology ward being treated for a flare of ulcerative colitis. She asks for the curtains to be closed because the ward lighting hurts her right eye, which has ached for a day and now looks blurred. The redness is concentrated around the edge of the cornea and the right pupil is slightly irregular. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Pain, photophobia, blurred vision, redness around the cornea (ciliary flush) and an irregular pupil from posterior synechiae indicate anterior uveitis. It is a recognised extra-intestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease and does not necessarily follow bowel activity. She needs same-day ophthalmology review.
why_wrong: A. Episcleritis is also linked to inflammatory bowel disease, but it causes mild discomfort, with no photophobia, blurred vision or pupil change. C. Allergic conjunctivitis is itchy and usually affects both eyes, with diffuse redness and a normal pupil. D. Retinal detachment is painless, with flashes, floaters and a field defect, and the eye is white. E. A corneal abrasion follows trauma and causes a foreign-body sensation, with fluorescein uptake.
pearl: Both episcleritis and uveitis occur in inflammatory bowel disease; photophobia, blurred vision and an abnormal pupil identify uveitis, which threatens sight.
thinking: Inflammatory bowel disease ↓ painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision ↓ ciliary flush and irregular pupil ↓ Anterior uveitis
exam_trap: A, episcleritis — it is the IBD-related red eye that most often tracks disease activity, but it does not cause photophobia, blurred vision or an irregular pupil.
takeaway: In IBD, a photophobic red eye with blurred vision is anterior uveitis, not episcleritis.

stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the emergency department on crutches the morning after a wedding reception. Overnight the joint at the base of his left great toe became so tender that he could not bear to pull a sock over it. The joint is swollen, and the skin over it is shiny and dusky red. He is afebrile and otherwise well, with no history of injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden overnight onset of severe pain, swelling and shiny red skin over the first metatarsophalangeal joint, after an evening of likely heavy eating and drinking, is the classic picture of acute gout. The first MTP joint is the commonest site of a first attack. Joint aspiration for crystals confirms it, but the clinical picture here is typical.
why_wrong: B. Septic arthritis must be considered in any hot joint, but it usually affects a systemically unwell patient and the first MTP joint is an uncommon site. C. Cellulitis causes spreading redness of the skin and soft tissue rather than pain centred on the joint itself. D. Hallux valgus causes chronic deformity and pressure pain, not an acute inflammatory attack overnight. E. Calcium pyrophosphate disease mainly affects the knee and wrist of older adults.
pearl: Alcohol, particularly beer, and purine-rich meals can trigger acute gout; colchicine or an NSAID started early shortens the attack.
thinking: Sudden overnight acute monoarthritis ↓ first MTP joint, exquisite tenderness, shiny red skin ↓ heavy food and alcohol intake, afebrile and well ↓ Gout
exam_trap: B, septic arthritis — the joint is hot and exquisitely tender, but he is afebrile and well and the site is classic for gout; aspirate if any doubt remains.
takeaway: Sudden, exquisitely painful swelling of the big toe joint in a well man is acute gout until shown otherwise.

stem: A 66-year-old retired farmer is examined in the GP surgery for an unrelated reason, and the doctor notices several pigmented lesions on his back. His wife says she has been keeping an eye on them. Which lesion most warrants urgent referral for suspected melanoma?

options.A: A brown, warty, stuck-on plaque that has been present for years
options.B: A flat, evenly brown mole that looks unchanged in old photographs
options.C: A small, bright red, dome-shaped papule
options.D: A firm brown nodule that dimples inwards when pinched
options.E: A flat brown patch that his wife says has spread and become darker in recent months

correct_answer: E. A flat brown patch that his wife says has spread and become darker in recent months
why_correct: A pigmented lesion that is growing and darkening shows evolution, which is one of the most important warning features of melanoma. In an older man with long-term outdoor sun exposure, this needs urgent referral under the suspected cancer pathway. The other lesions have typical benign features.
why_wrong: A. A warty, stuck-on plaque present for years is a seborrhoeic keratosis, which is benign. B. A uniformly coloured, unchanged mole is reassuring. C.
