A small bright red dome-shaped papule is a cherry angioma, a benign vascular lesion. D. A firm nodule that dimples when pinched is a dermatofibroma, which is benign.
pearl: Seborrhoeic keratoses can be dark and numerous in older adults; their warty, stuck-on surface is the clue, and a lesion that is changing still needs assessment even if it looks like one.
thinking: Several pigmented lesions in an older man with high sun exposure ↓ most have typical benign features ↓ one is enlarging and darkening = evolution ↓ A flat brown patch that has spread and darkened
exam_trap: A, the warty stuck-on plaque — its dark colour and irregular surface look alarming, but these are typical of a benign seborrhoeic keratosis that has been stable for years.
takeaway: Of several pigmented lesions, the one that is changing is the one to refer urgently.

stem: A 10-year-old girl's teacher has noticed that she keeps leaving lessons to go to the toilet and refills her water bottle several times every morning. Her mother says she has recently started wetting the bed again after years of being dry, and her school uniform now hangs loosely on her. She seems tired but is alert and talking normally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Frequent urination, new bedwetting, excessive thirst, weight loss and tiredness in a child are typical of new-onset type 1 diabetes. Glucose in the urine causes an osmotic diuresis, and the lack of insulin leads to catabolism and weight loss. A capillary glucose should be checked immediately, and if it is raised she needs same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team.
why_wrong: A. Psychogenic polydipsia is rare in children and would not cause weight loss. B. A urinary tract infection may cause frequency and new bedwetting but does not explain marked thirst and weight loss. C. Cranial diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst but not the catabolic weight loss seen here. E. Hyperthyroidism can cause weight loss but does not usually cause marked polyuria and polydipsia.
pearl: New bedwetting in a previously dry child is a common way for type 1 diabetes to present, and a bedside glucose check takes seconds.
thinking: Child with frequent urination and new bedwetting ↓ excessive thirst ↓ weight loss and tiredness ↓ osmotic diuresis with insulin deficiency ↓ Type 1 diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: B, urinary tract infection — frequency and new bedwetting suggest it, but a UTI does not explain the thirst and weight loss.
takeaway: Thirst, frequent urination, new bedwetting and weight loss in a child suggest type 1 diabetes; check glucose that day.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with known acute intermittent porphyria is admitted under the surgical team with severe colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and a tachycardia. The attack began a few days after she started a combined oral contraceptive. The surgical doctor needs to prescribe analgesia and an antiemetic. Which approach to her prescribing is most appropriate?

options.A: Withhold opioid analgesia until the attack settles
options.B: Check every proposed medicine against a porphyria drug-safety resource before giving it
options.C: Keep her nil by mouth without intravenous glucose to rest the bowel
options.D: Prescribe from the hospital's standard surgical analgesia protocol

correct_answer: B. Check every proposed medicine against a porphyria drug-safety resource before giving it
why_correct: Many drugs induce hepatic haem synthesis and can start or worsen an acute porphyric attack. Each new medicine should therefore be checked against a recognised porphyria drug-safety list before it is given. Effective analgesia must still be provided; morphine is generally considered safe.
why_wrong: A. Opioids such as morphine are generally considered safe in acute porphyria, and leaving her in severe pain is not appropriate. C. Fasting can worsen an attack, so carbohydrate intake should be maintained rather than stopped. D. Standard protocols may include porphyrinogenic drugs, so prescribing without checking is unsafe. E. Oestrogen and progestogen can precipitate attacks, so the contraceptive should be stopped.
pearl: Common precipitants of acute porphyria attacks include hormonal contraceptives, some anticonvulsants, alcohol and fasting; haem arginate is the specific treatment for a severe attack.
thinking: Acute porphyria attack with severe pain ↓ likely triggered by a hormonal drug ↓ many medicines are porphyrinogenic ↓ Check each drug against a porphyria safety resource before giving it
exam_trap: A, withhold opioids — caution feels safe, but morphine is generally considered safe here and undertreated pain helps keep the attack going.
takeaway: In acute porphyria, check every new drug for porphyria safety, but do not withhold adequate analgesia.

stem: A 28-year-old man sees his GP about a sore on his lower lip that appeared roughly three weeks after he began a new relationship and has been present for ten days. It has never been tender. There is a single firm, clean-based ulcer on the lip, and a non-tender, rubbery submandibular lymph node can be felt on the same side. He has no history of cold sores. What is the most likely cause?

options.D: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip

why_correct: A chancre forms where Treponema pallidum entered, which can be the lips or mouth after oral sex as well as the genitals. A single firm, painless, clean-based ulcer appearing a few weeks after a new sexual contact, with a non-tender regional node, is typical. He needs syphilis serology, a full sexual health screen and partner notification.
why_wrong: B. Herpes labialis causes a painful cluster of vesicles that crust, often with a tingling prodrome. C. Aphthous ulcers are painful, shallow, and occur inside the mouth rather than as a firm lesion on the lip. D. Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip is a slowly growing lesion of older, sun-exposed adults and is unlikely to appear this quickly at 28. E. Impetigo causes honey-crusted superficial lesions, not an indurated ulcer.
pearl: Chancres outside the genitals, on the lips, mouth or anus, are easily mistaken for other ulcers; consider syphilis for any painless indurated ulcer after a new sexual contact.
thinking: Single ulcer a few weeks after a new sexual relationship ↓ painless, firm, clean-based ↓ non-tender regional node, no herpes history ↓ Primary syphilis
exam_trap: B, herpes labialis — a lip sore suggests a cold sore, but herpes is painful and vesicular, while this ulcer is painless and indurated.
takeaway: A painless indurated ulcer at the site of sexual contact, including the lip, is a syphilitic chancre until proven otherwise.

stem: A 29-year-old woman attends the emergency department with two days of central chest discomfort and palpitations. Ten days earlier she had a flu-like illness with aching muscles and a temperature. She is tachycardic with normal oxygen saturation. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with widespread T-wave inversion, troponin is raised, and echocardiography shows global reduction in left ventricular contraction. Urgent coronary angiography reveals no stenosis, occlusion or dissection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Chest pain, palpitations, a troponin rise and global left ventricular dysfunction soon after a viral illness, with normal coronary arteries, point to acute myocarditis. Cardiac MRI can confirm myocardial inflammation. Management is supportive, with treatment of heart failure or arrhythmia and avoidance of strenuous exercise during recovery.
why_wrong: A. A myocardial infarction needs a culprit coronary lesion, and angiography showed none. B. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy usually affects older women after emotional or physical stress and causes regional apical ballooning, not global dysfunction after a viral illness. C. Pulmonary embolism typically causes hypoxia and right ventricular strain rather than global left ventricular impairment. E. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection would be seen at angiography, which was normal.
pearl: When the troponin is raised but the coronary arteries are normal, think of myocarditis, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and embolic or vasospastic causes; cardiac MRI often distinguishes them.
thinking: Chest pain and palpitations after a febrile viral illness ↓ raised troponin with global LV dysfunction ↓ angiography excludes a coronary cause ↓ myocardial inflammation ↓ Acute myocarditis
exam_trap: B, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy — raised troponin with normal coronaries fits, but it typically follows stress in older women and causes apical ballooning, not global dysfunction after a viral illness.
takeaway: Raised troponin, global LV dysfunction and normal coronaries after a viral illness indicate acute myocarditis.

stem: A 23-year-old man with known C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency is brought in by ambulance. Over the past hour his lips and tongue have swollen markedly, his voice has become muffled and he is struggling to swallow his saliva. There is no rash or itch. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Oral cetirizine and observation in the department
options.B: Urgent airway assessment and management with senior anaesthetic help
options.C: Intravenous hydrocortisone and admission to a medical ward
options.E: Nebulised salbutamol and a chest radiograph

correct_answer: B. Urgent airway assessment and management with senior anaesthetic help
why_correct: Swelling of the tongue with a muffled voice and difficulty swallowing saliva shows an upper airway at risk of rapid obstruction. Securing the airway, with early senior anaesthetic and ENT involvement, comes before everything else. Specific treatment such as C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant is given alongside, without delaying airway care.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary angioedema is mediated by bradykinin, not histamine, so antihistamines do not work and the airway is threatened now. C. Corticosteroids are ineffective in hereditary angioedema, and a ward is not a safe place for a threatened airway. D. Outpatient review ignores an immediate threat to life. E. Salbutamol treats bronchospasm, not upper airway swelling, and imaging would delay airway management.
pearl: Hereditary angioedema causes swelling without urticaria and responds poorly to adrenaline, antihistamines and steroids; treat with C1-esterase inhibitor or icatibant while managing the airway.
thinking: Known C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency ↓ tongue swelling, muffled voice, drooling ↓ impending upper airway obstruction ↓ airway takes priority over everything else ↓ Urgent airway assessment and management with senior anaesthetic help
exam_trap: C, intravenous hydrocortisone and admission — this reflects standard allergy treatment, but steroids do not work in bradykinin-mediated swelling and the airway needs securing now.
takeaway: In hereditary angioedema with tongue swelling, secure the airway first and give specific treatment alongside.

stem: An 84-year-old woman attends the GP surgery after her third fall since the spring. Each time she got up from her armchair, felt light-headed and went down without losing consciousness. Her regular medicines are amlodipine, ramipril, furosemide, zopiclone and doxazosin, which was added two months ago. Her blood pressure falls noticeably when she stands, and her ECG shows sinus rhythm. What is the most appropriate initial step?

options.A: Arrange an MRI scan of the brain
options.D: Carry out a structured review of her medicines
options.E: Advise her to wear hip protectors and take no further action

correct_answer: D. Carry out a structured review of her medicines
why_correct: Falls on rising with light-headedness and a postural drop in blood pressure, in a woman taking several antihypertensives, a diuretic, an alpha-blocker and a hypnotic, point to a medication-related cause. A structured medicines review is part of a multifactorial falls assessment and targets the most reversible contributor here. Rationalising or stopping drugs such as the recently added doxazosin and the zopiclone can reduce her risk of further falls.
why_wrong: A. Brain imaging is not indicated for postural falls without focal neurology or head injury concerns. B. Fludrocortisone is not used before removing the drugs that are causing the postural drop. C. Ambulatory ECG is for suspected arrhythmia, whereas this history points to orthostatic hypotension. E. Hip protectors may reduce fracture risk but leave the reversible cause untreated.
pearl: In an older person with falls on standing, look first at the drug chart: alpha-blockers, diuretics, antihypertensives and sedatives commonly combine to cause postural hypotension.
thinking: Falls on getting up with light-headedness ↓ postural drop in blood pressure confirmed ↓ several hypotensive and sedative drugs, one newly added ↓ remove the reversible cause first ↓ Structured medicines review
exam_trap: B, Start fludrocortisone — it treats orthostatic hypotension, so it looks targeted, but adding a drug while the culprit medicines remain is the wrong order; deprescribing comes first.
takeaway: Postural falls in an older adult on multiple drugs: review and rationalise the medicines first.

stem: An 81-year-old man with mild Alzheimer's dementia lives alone. His son tells the GP that he has found tablets left in some blister strips and other strips emptied early in the week. The man takes nine different medicines, several of them three or four times a day. He wishes to stay independent at home. Which is the best next step?

options.B: Ask his son to make all treatment decisions from now on
options.C: Review and simplify his medicines, with practical support for taking them
options.D: Stop all his medicines until he is seen in the memory clinic
options.E: Increase the number of medicines to cover missed doses

correct_answer: C. Review and simplify his medicines, with practical support for taking them
why_correct: Both missed and extra doses suggest he cannot reliably manage a complex regimen. A medication review to stop unnecessary drugs and reduce dosing frequency, combined with practical support such as pharmacist input, a suitable adherence aid or carer prompts, directly reduces the risk of harm. This respects his wish to remain independent while addressing the safety concern.
why_wrong: A. A care home placement is disproportionate when the risk can be reduced with simpler measures. B. Mild dementia does not remove his right to make decisions he has capacity for, and the son cannot simply take over. D. Abruptly stopping all medicines could cause serious harm. E. Adding medicines increases complexity and the risk of error.
pearl: Both under- and over-dosing are warning signs of an unmanageable regimen. Fewer drugs, fewer daily doses and practical support are safer than adding treatment or removing independence.
thinking: Mild dementia, lives alone ↓ evidence of both missed and extra doses ↓ complex regimen with frequent dosing ↓ reduce complexity and add support while preserving independence ↓ Review and simplify his medicines
exam_trap: B, Ask his son to make all treatment decisions — involving family feels supportive, but a diagnosis of mild dementia does not mean he lacks capacity, and relatives cannot consent on his behalf without legal authority.
takeaway: Medication errors in cognitive impairment: simplify the regimen and add support before anything more drastic.

stem: A 58-year-old woman who has type 2 diabetes telephones her GP practice. She caught a stomach bug from her grandchildren and has been vomiting and passing watery stools for 24 hours. She cannot keep fluids down, feels dizzy and has passed very little urine today. She takes metformin twice daily and asks what to do about her tablets. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Withhold metformin until she is eating and drinking normally, and arrange same-day assessment
options.B: Continue metformin at the usual dose with small sips of water
options.C: Halve the metformin dose until the vomiting stops
options.D: Take an extra dose of metformin to compensate for the illness
options.E: Stop metformin permanently and start gliclazide

correct_answer: A. Withhold metformin until she is eating and drinking normally, and arrange same-day assessment
why_correct: Dehydrating illness can cause acute kidney injury, and metformin then accumulates and increases the risk of lactic acidosis. Standard sick day guidance is to pause metformin temporarily and restart once eating and drinking normally. Her reduced urine output and inability to keep fluids down mean she also needs prompt clinical assessment.
why_wrong: B. Continuing the full dose despite significant dehydration risks AKI-related harm. C. A reduced dose still carries the same risk while the kidneys are under threat. D. Extra doses are unsafe and do not treat the illness. E. A permanent switch is unnecessary because metformin is only paused during the illness.
pearl: Sick day guidance pauses metformin (along with drugs such as ACE inhibitors, diuretics and SGLT2 inhibitors) during dehydrating illness, restarting once eating and drinking normally.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes on metformin ↓ vomiting and diarrhoea with poor intake and reduced urine output ↓ risk of AKI and metformin accumulation ↓ temporarily withhold and assess ↓ Withhold metformin and arrange same-day assessment
exam_trap: C, Halve the metformin dose — a reduced dose sounds like a cautious compromise, but the danger comes from impaired renal clearance, so the drug should be paused entirely.
takeaway: Dehydrating illness on metformin: pause the drug, restart once eating and drinking normally, and assess.

presentation: Warfarin — Raised INR After New Drug
stem: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has had stable INR results on the same warfarin dose for over a year. Eight days ago she was prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection. At the anticoagulation clinic today her INR is well above her target range. She has no bleeding and says she has not changed her diet or missed any tablets. What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: A recent increase in green leafy vegetables in her diet
options.D: An interaction with the recently prescribed antibiotic
options.E: Laboratory error, as the INR cannot change this quickly

correct_answer: D. An interaction with the recently prescribed antibiotic
why_correct: Clarithromycin inhibits the hepatic enzymes that metabolise warfarin, increasing its anticoagulant effect and raising the INR. A previously stable INR that rises shortly after a new drug is started should always prompt consideration of an interaction. Many antibiotics, antifungals and other drugs interact with warfarin, so INR checks are advised when they are started.
why_wrong: A. Missing doses lowers the INR rather than raising it. B. Vitamin K-rich foods reduce warfarin effect and lower the INR. C. Resistance would lower, not raise, the INR. E. The INR can change within days after a new interacting drug, so this result is plausible.
pearl: Macrolides, fluconazole, metronidazole and several other drugs potentiate warfarin. Check the INR within a few days of starting any interacting drug.
thinking: Long-standing stable INR ↓ new drug started a week earlier ↓ INR now raised with no other change ↓ enzyme inhibition increases warfarin effect ↓ Interaction with the antibiotic
exam_trap: B, Increase in green leafy vegetables — dietary change is a well-known cause of INR instability, but vitamin K lowers the INR, the opposite of what is seen here.
takeaway: A rising INR after a new prescription on warfarin should prompt a check for a drug interaction.

stem: An 86-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation is admitted to the medical ward with acute kidney injury after several days of diarrhoea. She takes digoxin and bisoprolol. Two days later she is off her food, vomiting and muddled, and says everything looks tinged with yellow. Her pulse is irregular at around 45 beats/min. Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Digoxin is cleared by the kidneys, so acute kidney injury causes it to accumulate, and potassium loss from diarrhoea increases its toxicity further. Anorexia, vomiting, confusion, yellow-tinged vision and a slow irregular pulse are the classic features. She needs a digoxin level, electrolytes, an ECG and the drug withheld.
why_wrong: A. Uraemia can cause confusion and vomiting but does not explain the yellow vision. B. A posterior circulation stroke would usually produce focal signs such as ataxia or visual field loss, not colour change. C. Hyperkalaemia can cause bradycardia but not altered colour vision, and diarrhoea tends to lower potassium. D. Gastroenteritis would not cause visual disturbance or marked bradycardia.
pearl: Digoxin toxicity is precipitated by renal impairment, hypokalaemia and interacting drugs. Visual colour change with GI upset and bradyarrhythmia is the classic triad.
thinking: On digoxin with new AKI ↓ diarrhoea causing potassium loss ↓ nausea, confusion and yellow-tinged vision ↓ slow irregular pulse ↓ Digoxin toxicity
exam_trap: A, Uraemic encephalopathy — the AKI makes it tempting, but uraemia does not cause xanthopsia, and the kidney injury is the reason the digoxin has accumulated.
takeaway: On digoxin with AKI and low potassium, GI upset, confusion and visual change mean toxicity.

stem: A 67-year-old man has been on the surgical ward for six days receiving intravenous gentamicin for an intra-abdominal infection. He now reports a constant ringing in his ears and feels unsteady when walking. His creatinine has risen each day for the past three days. Which pair of adverse effects is he showing?
why_correct: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin damage both the inner ear, causing tinnitus, hearing loss and vestibular unsteadiness, and the renal tubules. Toxicity is more likely with prolonged courses and accumulation, which is why levels and renal function are monitored. A rising creatinine and new ear symptoms should prompt review of the drug and its levels.
why_wrong: A. Neuropathy and optic neuritis are linked with antituberculous drugs such as isoniazid and ethambutol. B. Tendon damage and QT prolongation are associated with fluoroquinolones. C. Cholestatic jaundice is a recognised effect of co-amoxiclav and flucloxacillin. E. Red man syndrome is associated with rapid vancomycin infusion.
pearl: Gentamicin toxicity affects the ear and kidney. Vestibular damage may show as unsteadiness rather than deafness, and can be permanent.
thinking: Several days of IV gentamicin ↓ tinnitus and unsteadiness ↓ rising creatinine ↓ aminoglycoside damage to inner ear and kidney ↓ Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity
exam_trap: E, Red man syndrome and thrombocytopenia — vancomycin is also a monitored, potentially nephrotoxic antibiotic, so it tempts, but this patient is on gentamicin and the ear symptoms are the key.
takeaway: Gentamicin can damage the ear and kidney: monitor levels and renal function, and act on new ear symptoms.

stem: A 63-year-old man with psoriatic arthritis takes weekly methotrexate. Five days ago an out-of-hours doctor prescribed trimethoprim for a urinary infection. He now attends the GP surgery with a painful sore mouth, a temperature and small purple spots on his shins. He has no cough or breathlessness. Which complication of his treatment is most likely?
why_correct: Mouth ulceration, fever and petechiae in a patient on methotrexate suggest pancytopenia from bone marrow suppression. Trimethoprim is also a folate antagonist and markedly increases this risk when combined with methotrexate. He needs an urgent full blood count, methotrexate withheld and assessment for neutropenic sepsis.
why_wrong: A. Pneumonitis presents with cough and breathlessness, which he does not have. B. Hepatotoxicity causes deranged liver tests rather than ulcers and petechiae. D. Stevens-Johnson syndrome causes widespread mucocutaneous blistering and skin detachment, not isolated petechiae. E. Trimethoprim can raise potassium but this does not explain fever, ulcers or bruising.
pearl: Methotrexate plus trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole is a dangerous combination for marrow suppression. Sore throat, ulcers, fever or bruising on methotrexate needs an urgent FBC.
thinking: Weekly methotrexate ↓ recent trimethoprim, another folate antagonist ↓ mouth ulcers, fever and petechiae ↓ suggests falling white cells and platelets ↓ Bone marrow suppression
exam_trap: A, Methotrexate pneumonitis — fever on methotrexate brings pneumonitis to mind, but there are no respiratory symptoms, whereas ulcers and petechiae point to the marrow.
takeaway: Ulcers, fever or bruising on methotrexate suggest marrow suppression, especially after trimethoprim.

stem: A 58-year-old man is on the surgical ward the day after a laparotomy, using a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump. A nurse calls you because he is difficult to rouse, his pupils are pinpoint and his breathing is slow and shallow. His oxygen saturations keep dropping despite supplemental oxygen and airway support. Which drug should be given?
why_correct: Reduced consciousness, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression in a patient receiving morphine indicate opioid toxicity. Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist that reverses this, given in titrated doses alongside airway support. Its effect can wear off before that of the opioid, so further doses or an infusion and close monitoring may be needed.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids. B. Doxapram is a respiratory stimulant and is not the specific treatment for opioid toxicity. C. Glucagon is used for beta-blocker toxicity or hypoglycaemia. E. Sugammadex reverses certain neuromuscular blocking drugs and would not explain pinpoint pupils a day after surgery.
pearl: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids, so patients can re-sedate. Stop the PCA, titrate naloxone and keep monitoring.
thinking: Post-operative morphine PCA ↓ drowsy with pinpoint pupils ↓ slow shallow breathing and falling saturations ↓ opioid toxicity needs specific reversal ↓ Naloxone
exam_trap: A, Flumazenil — it is the other well-known reversal agent for sedation, but it acts only on benzodiazepines and has no effect on morphine.
takeaway: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression on opioids: support the airway and give titrated naloxone.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by a friend after taking a whole packet of paracetamol following an argument. She took all the tablets at once, four and a half hours ago. She now feels completely well, has no abdominal pain, and her observations are normal. Which is the best next step?

options.A: Start acetylcysteine immediately without measuring a level
options.B: Give activated charcoal and discharge with GP follow-up
options.C: Measure a plasma paracetamol concentration now and base treatment on the result
options.D: Discharge home as she is well, with mental health follow-up
options.E: Repeat liver function tests in 24 hours before deciding on treatment

correct_answer: C. Measure a plasma paracetamol concentration now and base treatment on the result
why_correct: Paracetamol overdose is often asymptomatic early, even when serious liver injury is developing. For a single ingestion at a known time, a paracetamol level taken at least four hours after ingestion is plotted against the treatment line to decide whether acetylcysteine is needed. Baseline liver function, renal function and INR are taken at the same time, and she will need a psychosocial assessment.
why_wrong: A. Immediate acetylcysteine without a level is for staggered or uncertain-time ingestions or late presentations, not a single dose with a timed level available. B. Charcoal is only useful within about an hour of ingestion, and discharge would miss treatable toxicity. D. Feeling well does not exclude a dangerous overdose. E. Waiting for liver tests to become abnormal loses the window in which acetylcysteine works best.
pearl: Liver tests may stay normal for many hours after a toxic paracetamol dose. For a single timed ingestion, the timed level decides treatment, not symptoms.
thinking: Single paracetamol overdose at a known time ↓ more than four hours ago ↓ asymptomatic does not mean safe ↓ timed level guides acetylcysteine ↓ Measure the paracetamol concentration now
exam_trap: A, Start acetylcysteine immediately — treating first sounds safe, but with a single, timed ingestion beyond four hours the level is available now and decides whether treatment is needed.
takeaway: Single timed paracetamol overdose: take a level from four hours and treat according to the nomogram.

stem: An ambulance crew brings a 46-year-old man to the emergency department after he swallowed an unknown number of over-the-counter tablets. He is restless and sweaty, complains of a high-pitched buzzing in both ears, and is breathing deeply and rapidly. An arterial blood gas shows a low carbon dioxide level together with a reduced bicarbonate. Which type of poisoning is most likely?
why_correct: Tinnitus, sweating and hyperventilation after an overdose are characteristic of salicylate poisoning. Salicylates stimulate the respiratory centre, causing respiratory alkalosis, and also uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, producing a metabolic acidosis, giving the mixed picture on the gas. Management includes a salicylate level, correcting fluid and electrolyte losses, and urinary alkalinisation or haemodialysis in severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Tricyclic poisoning causes anticholinergic features, seizures and broad QRS complexes rather than tinnitus. B. Opioids depress breathing rather than stimulating it. D. Paracetamol poisoning is usually asymptomatic early and does not cause tinnitus. E. Ethylene glycol causes metabolic acidosis with deep breathing but not tinnitus, and is not taken as tablets.
pearl: Salicylate poisoning classically gives a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Tinnitus is a key bedside clue.
thinking: Overdose of over-the-counter tablets ↓ tinnitus and sweating ↓ deep rapid breathing ↓ gas shows low CO2 and low bicarbonate, a mixed picture ↓ Salicylate poisoning
exam_trap: E, Ethylene glycol poisoning — it also causes a metabolic acidosis with deep, rapid breathing, but it does not cause tinnitus and is not an over-the-counter tablet overdose.
takeaway: Overdose with tinnitus, sweating and hyperventilation suggests salicylate poisoning.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit having taken an overdose the previous evening. She has vomited repeatedly, is sweaty, and describes a constant buzzing in her ears with muffled hearing. A venous blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap. Which drug did she most likely take?
why_correct: Vomiting, sweating, tinnitus with reduced hearing and a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis after an overdose point to aspirin. Salicylates disrupt cellular metabolism, producing acid, and directly affect the inner ear. A salicylate level guides treatment such as urinary alkalinisation or haemodialysis in severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Amitriptyline causes drowsiness, anticholinergic signs, seizures and arrhythmias rather than tinnitus. B. Paracetamol causes delayed liver injury and does not cause tinnitus. C. Iron causes vomiting and acidosis but not tinnitus or hearing change. D. Lithium toxicity causes tremor, ataxia and confusion rather than tinnitus with acidosis.
pearl: Tinnitus or deafness after an overdose should prompt a salicylate level, even when the patient does not name the drug taken.
thinking: Overdose with repeated vomiting ↓ tinnitus and muffled hearing ↓ raised anion gap metabolic acidosis ↓ combination fits salicylate toxicity ↓ Aspirin
exam_trap: C, Iron sulfate — iron overdose also causes vomiting and a metabolic acidosis, but it does not affect hearing, which is the discriminating clue.
takeaway: Overdose with vomiting, acidosis and ear symptoms suggests aspirin: check a salicylate level.

stem: A 29-year-old man on an acute psychiatric ward received intramuscular haloperidol for severe agitation two days ago. He is now sweating heavily, has a high temperature and is drowsy. His limbs show uniform lead-pipe stiffness, and his blood pressure and heart rate fluctuate widely. Creatine kinase is markedly raised. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability and a raised creatine kinase after a dopamine antagonist are the hallmarks of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It typically develops over days after starting or increasing an antipsychotic. Management is to stop the antipsychotic, give supportive care with cooling and fluids, and seek urgent senior and critical care input.
why_wrong: A. An acute dystonic reaction causes sudden muscle spasms such as oculogyric crisis, without fever or autonomic instability. B. Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and causes clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead-pipe rigidity. C. Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium. D. Meningoencephalitis can cause fever and drowsiness but does not explain the rigidity and timing after haloperidol.
pearl: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slow reflexes. Serotonin syndrome evolves over hours with clonus and hyperreflexia.
thinking: Recent haloperidol ↓ fever, drowsiness and autonomic instability ↓ lead-pipe rigidity with high CK ↓ dopamine blockade syndrome ↓ Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
exam_trap: B, Serotonin syndrome — it shares fever, confusion and autonomic instability, but the trigger is serotonergic and the neuromuscular sign is clonus, not lead-pipe rigidity.
takeaway: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity and a high CK after an antipsychotic means neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has taken prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica over the past year. She ran out of tablets while on holiday and has not taken any for six days. She attends the emergency department with profound tiredness, nausea, abdominal discomfort and light-headedness on standing. Her blood pressure is low and her sodium is slightly reduced. Which condition is she most likely to have?

options.A: Adrenal insufficiency from abrupt steroid withdrawal
options.D: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

correct_answer: A. Adrenal insufficiency from abrupt steroid withdrawal
why_correct: Long-term glucocorticoids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so the adrenal glands cannot produce enough cortisol when the steroid is suddenly stopped. Fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, postural hypotension and hyponatraemia are typical. She needs steroid replacement promptly, with intravenous hydrocortisone if she is acutely unwell, and advice on never stopping steroids abruptly.
why_wrong: B. A relapse of polymyalgia causes shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, not hypotension and nausea. C. Autoimmune adrenal failure is possible but far less likely than axis suppression given the clear history of stopping prednisolone. D. SIADH causes hyponatraemia but not hypotension. E. Hypothyroidism develops gradually and does not explain an acute postural hypotensive illness after stopping steroids.
pearl: Patients on long-term steroids should carry a steroid emergency card, follow sick day rules and never stop suddenly. Withdrawal after prolonged use needs a gradual taper.
thinking: A year of prednisolone ↓ stopped suddenly ↓ fatigue, nausea, postural hypotension and low sodium ↓ suppressed adrenal axis cannot respond ↓ Adrenal insufficiency from steroid withdrawal
exam_trap: C, Autoimmune primary adrenal failure — the features overlap, but the abrupt stop after prolonged prednisolone makes suppression of the axis by far the likeliest cause.
takeaway: Stopping long-term steroids abruptly can cause adrenal insufficiency: taper, and replace urgently if unwell.

stem: A 38-year-old woman attends a pre-operative clinic before a planned laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The surgeon explains why the operation is advised, the chance of bile duct injury or conversion to open surgery, the option of managing her symptoms without an operation, and what might happen if she declines. She asks questions, repeats the key points back accurately and, without any pressure, decides to proceed. Which principle does this conversation best illustrate?
why_correct: Valid consent requires that the patient has capacity, is given the information material to her decision (benefits, risks, alternatives including doing nothing), understands it, and decides voluntarily. All these elements are shown here. GMC guidance describes consent as a dialogue tailored to what matters to the individual patient.
why_wrong: A. Beneficence is acting in the patient's best interests, but the conversation is about her own informed choice. C. Duty of candour concerns openness when something has gone wrong. D. Confidentiality concerns protecting patient information. E. Justice concerns fair allocation of resources and equitable treatment.
pearl: Consent is valid only if the patient has capacity, is adequately informed, understands, and decides voluntarily. Alternatives, including no treatment, must be discussed.
thinking: Purpose, material risks and alternatives explained ↓ patient demonstrates understanding ↓ decision made freely ↓ all elements of valid consent present ↓ Valid informed consent
exam_trap: A, Beneficence — the surgeon is acting for her good, so it sounds right, but the focus is on her informed, voluntary decision, which is the definition of consent.
takeaway: Capacity, information, understanding and voluntariness together make consent valid.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with diabetes has wet gangrene of her right foot. The vascular team advise a below-knee amputation and explain that without it the infection could spread and she may die. In her own words she describes what the operation involves, its possible complications and the other options, and she repeatedly declines it. Her son is distressed and asks the team to operate anyway. How should the doctor respond?

options.A: Proceed with the amputation in her best interests
options.B: Respect her decision and continue to offer other treatment and support
options.C: Ask her son to sign the consent form instead
options.D: Detain her under the Mental Health Act to allow surgery
options.E: Delay all further treatment until she agrees to surgery

correct_answer: B. Respect her decision and continue to offer other treatment and support
why_correct: An adult with capacity may refuse any treatment, even if refusal may lead to death, and the decision must be respected even if clinicians disagree. The doctor should document the discussion and her capacity, keep the door open to her changing her mind, and continue to offer alternatives such as antibiotics and palliation. Her son's wishes do not override her own decision.
why_wrong: A. Best-interests decisions apply only when a patient lacks capacity. C. Relatives cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant legal power, and even then not against a capacitous refusal. D. The Mental Health Act cannot be used to impose treatment for a physical condition. E. Withholding other care to pressure her is coercive and unethical.
pearl: Capacity is decision-specific and presumed. An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity, and a capacitous refusal must be respected and documented.
thinking: Adult understands and weighs the information ↓ capacity demonstrated ↓ refuses life-saving surgery ↓ family pressure does not change the legal position ↓ Respect her decision and keep offering care
exam_trap: A, Proceed in her best interests — the risk of death makes acting seem compelling, but best-interests decisions apply only when capacity is lacking, which it is not.
takeaway: A capacitous adult's refusal must be respected, even if it may lead to death.

stem: A ward pharmacist contacts a junior doctor because the enoxaparin dose the doctor prescribed yesterday evening is ten times higher than intended. The pharmacist noticed it during a chart check and no dose has yet been given. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Correct the prescription and report the event through the local incident reporting system
options.B: Correct the prescription and take no further action as no harm occurred
options.C: Ask the pharmacist to amend the chart without mentioning who wrote it
options.D: Rewrite the drug chart so the original error no longer appears
options.E: Tell the pharmacist that the nurse must have misread the chart

correct_answer: A. Correct the prescription and report the event through the local incident reporting system
why_correct: The error must be corrected immediately, and because it was intercepted before reaching the patient it is a near miss that should still be reported. Reporting allows the organisation to identify system factors and prevent future harm. GMC guidance expects doctors to be honest about errors and to contribute to learning from them.
why_wrong: B. Near misses reveal risks that could cause harm next time, so they should be reported even when no harm occurred. C. Hiding authorship undermines honesty and learning. D. Altering records to conceal an error is dishonest and a serious professional failing. E. Blaming another professional falsely is dishonest.
pearl: Near misses are valuable learning events. Correct, document openly and report, without altering records or shifting blame.
thinking: Dosing error identified by pharmacist ↓ not yet given, so no harm ↓ near miss still reveals a system risk ↓ correct it and report for learning ↓ Correct and report through incident reporting
exam_trap: B, Take no further action as no harm occurred — it feels proportionate, but near misses are exactly what reporting systems are designed to capture.
takeaway: A prescribing error caught before harm is a near miss: correct it and report it.

stem: A 30-year-old man attends the GP surgery with three days of sore throat, runny nose and a dry cough. He is afebrile with no tonsillar exudate or enlarged neck glands. He asks for antibiotics because he is going on holiday next week. The GP explains that this is most likely viral, so antibiotics would not shorten it, advises on self-care, and explains when to seek help. No prescription is issued. Which principle is the GP demonstrating?
why_correct: Antimicrobial stewardship means using antimicrobials only when they are likely to benefit the patient, to reduce resistance and avoid unnecessary adverse effects. Explaining that a self-limiting viral illness will not respond to antibiotics, giving self-care advice and safety-netting is a core stewardship approach in primary care. NICE guidance supports a no-antibiotic or back-up strategy for most respiratory tract infections.
why_wrong: A. Delayed prescribing involves issuing a back-up prescription to use if symptoms worsen, which did not happen here. C. Therapeutic duplication is prescribing overlapping drugs. D. Defensive practice is acting mainly to protect the clinician rather than to benefit the patient. E. Polypharmacy refers to the use of multiple medicines.
pearl: Most upper respiratory tract infections are viral and self-limiting. Explaining the expected course and safety-netting is as important as the decision not to prescribe.
thinking: Viral-sounding upper respiratory illness ↓ patient requests antibiotics ↓ GP explains no benefit and offers self-care with safety-netting ↓ responsible use of antimicrobials ↓ Antimicrobial stewardship
exam_trap: A, Delayed antibiotic prescribing — it is a stewardship tool and sounds similar, but it involves issuing a back-up prescription, and none was given here.
takeaway: Withholding antibiotics for viral illness, with explanation and safety-netting, is antimicrobial stewardship.

stem: A 41-year-old man attends the GP surgery with a tender swelling on the back of his shoulder that has enlarged over four days. There is a warm, red, fluctuant lump about the size of a plum, with a yellow point at its centre and a small rim of surrounding redness. He is afebrile and otherwise well. Which management is most appropriate?

options.E: Review in one month if it persists

why_correct: A fluctuant, pointing swelling is a collection of pus, and the definitive treatment of a skin abscess is incision and drainage. Antibiotics penetrate a walled-off collection poorly and are reserved for extensive surrounding cellulitis, systemic illness or higher-risk patients. Pus can be sent for culture at the time of drainage.
why_wrong: A. Topical antibiotics do not treat a deep collection. B. Antibiotics alone rarely resolve an established abscess. D. Excision biopsy is for suspected tumours, not infection. E. Delaying treatment allows the infection to extend and cause systemic illness.
pearl: Fluctuance means pus. If pus is present, it needs to be drained; antibiotics are an adjunct, not the main treatment.
thinking: Enlarging painful lump ↓ warm, red, fluctuant and pointing ↓ established abscess ↓ pus needs a route out ↓ Incision and drainage
exam_trap: B, Oral flucloxacillin alone — it covers the likely staphylococcal cause, but an antibiotic cannot reliably penetrate an established abscess, which needs drainage.
takeaway: A fluctuant skin abscess is treated by incision and drainage, not antibiotics alone.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends the emergency department with three days of throbbing pain beside her anus. The pain is constant, not just on opening her bowels, and she can no longer sit down. Her temperature is 38.4°C. There is a hot, red, tender, indurated swelling at the anal margin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A constant throbbing pain with a hot, red, tender swelling at the anal margin and fever indicates a perianal abscess, usually arising from infection of an anal gland. Diabetes increases the risk. Treatment is prompt surgical incision and drainage, with antibiotics in addition if there is systemic illness or significant surrounding cellulitis.
why_wrong: A. A thrombosed external haemorrhoid is a painful bluish lump but does not cause fever or a hot, indurated swelling. B. A pilonidal abscess arises in the natal cleft, not at the anal margin. C. A fissure causes pain on defecation and a visible split, not fever with a swelling. E. Rectal prolapse causes a mass protruding through the anus, usually without fever.
pearl: Fever with a hot, tender perianal swelling is an abscess until proved otherwise. Diabetes and Crohn's disease increase the risk.
thinking: Constant perianal pain, unable to sit ↓ fever ↓ hot, red, indurated swelling at the anal margin ↓ infected collection near the anus ↓ Perianal abscess
exam_trap: A, Thrombosed external haemorrhoid — it causes a painful perianal lump, but not fever, induration or spreading redness.
takeaway: A hot, tender perianal swelling with fever is a perianal abscess needing drainage.

stem: A 55-year-old taxi driver attends the GP surgery for review two weeks after a flare of gout in his right ankle, which has now settled. It is his third flare this year. He is overweight and asks what changes he can make himself to reduce further attacks. Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Replace water with fruit juice to stay hydrated
options.B: Reduce his alcohol intake, particularly beer
options.C: Lose weight quickly with a very low-calorie fasting diet
options.D: Increase his intake of offal and shellfish for protein
options.E: Avoid all physical activity to protect his joints

correct_answer: B. Reduce his alcohol intake, particularly beer
why_correct: Alcohol, particularly beer, raises serum urate and is a common trigger for gout flares, so reducing intake is recommended. Other helpful measures include gradual weight loss, regular exercise and staying well hydrated with water. With recurrent flares he should also be offered urate-lowering therapy.
why_wrong: A. Fructose-sweetened drinks, including some fruit juices, raise urate. C. Rapid weight loss or fasting can raise urate and provoke flares, whereas gradual loss is beneficial. D. Offal and shellfish are purine-rich and increase urate. E. Regular activity is encouraged and does not worsen gout.
pearl: Lifestyle advice in gout: limit alcohol (especially beer), avoid sugary drinks, lose weight gradually and keep active. Recurrent flares warrant urate-lowering therapy.
thinking: Recurrent gout flares ↓ asking about self-help ↓ identify factors that lower urate ↓ alcohol is a key modifiable trigger ↓ Reduce alcohol, particularly beer
exam_trap: C, Lose weight quickly with a very low-calorie fasting diet — weight loss helps gout, so it tempts, but rapid weight loss and fasting can raise urate and trigger attacks.
takeaway: Reducing alcohol, especially beer, is a key self-help measure to reduce gout flares.

stem: A 46-year-old man is seen in the rheumatology clinic with three months of painful, swollen hands. Squeezing across his knuckles is painful on both sides, and several finger joints are swollen. He feels stiff for well over an hour each morning. Hand X-rays are normal. Which antibody test is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
why_correct: Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis and support the diagnosis in a patient with symmetrical small-joint synovitis. A positive result also predicts a more erosive course. NICE recommends testing rheumatoid factor first in suspected rheumatoid arthritis and anti-CCP if rheumatoid factor is negative, but anti-CCP is the more specific test.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid factor is common in RA but is also found in other conditions and healthy older people, so it is less specific. B. ANA is sensitive for lupus but not specific for RA. D. HLA-B27 is a genetic marker associated with spondyloarthritis, not an antibody test for RA. E. Anti-dsDNA is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.
pearl: Rheumatoid factor is more widely used but less specific; anti-CCP is highly specific and predicts erosive disease. Normal early X-rays do not exclude RA.
thinking: Symmetrical small-joint swelling ↓ prolonged morning stiffness ↓ suspected rheumatoid arthritis ↓ choose the most specific antibody ↓ Anti-CCP antibody
exam_trap: A, Rheumatoid factor — it is the best known and is tested first in practice, but it is less specific than anti-CCP.
takeaway: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody test for rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 71-year-old man with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is seen in pre-assessment before an elective hip replacement. He mentions a few months of pain at the back of his head and upper neck, tingling in both hands and increasing clumsiness with buttons. Examination shows brisk reflexes in all four limbs and upgoing plantar responses. Which complication needs to be considered?
why_correct: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis can weaken the ligaments stabilising the atlantoaxial joint, allowing subluxation that compresses the upper cervical cord. Occipital and neck pain with upper motor neurone signs in all four limbs suggests cervical myelopathy from this cause. It needs urgent imaging and specialist review, and is particularly important before anaesthesia because neck manipulation during intubation can cause cord injury.
why_wrong: A. Nerve root compression causes lower motor neurone signs in one dermatome, not brisk reflexes in all limbs. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve sensory symptoms without upper motor neurone signs or neck pain. D. Mononeuritis multiplex causes patchy lower motor neurone deficits. E. Peripheral neuropathy reduces reflexes rather than making them brisk.
pearl: Neck pain with upper motor neurone signs in rheumatoid arthritis suggests atlantoaxial subluxation. Flag it before any general anaesthetic.
thinking: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis ↓ occipital and neck pain ↓ hand clumsiness with brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars ↓ high cervical cord compression ↓ Atlantoaxial subluxation
exam_trap: C, Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome — it is common in RA and causes tingling hands, but it cannot produce brisk reflexes or extensor plantars.
takeaway: Rheumatoid arthritis with neck pain and upper motor neurone signs suggests atlantoaxial subluxation.

stem: A 63-year-old woman who enjoys gardening has had an aching pain around the root of her left thumb for over a year. It is worse when pinching, turning keys and using secateurs, with stiffness after rest. There is squaring of the thumb base and pain with crepitus when the joint is compressed and rotated. There is no tenderness over the radial styloid. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint

correct_answer: D. Osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint
why_correct: Chronic thumb-base pain worse with pinch and grip, squaring of the joint and crepitus on the grind test are classic features of first carpometacarpal joint osteoarthritis. It is common in older women. Management includes analgesia, a splint, hand therapy and, if needed, a steroid injection or surgery.
why_wrong: A. De Quervain tenosynovitis causes tenderness over the radial styloid and pain on Finkelstein's test, which are absent. B. Trigger thumb causes catching or locking at the base of the thumb on the palm side. C. A scaphoid fracture follows a fall on an outstretched hand. E. Rheumatoid arthritis usually affects several joints symmetrically and is less likely to be isolated to one thumb base.
pearl: Squaring of the thumb base and a positive grind test suggest first CMC osteoarthritis. Radial styloid tenderness with a positive Finkelstein test suggests De Quervain's.
thinking: Chronic thumb-base pain ↓ worse with pinch and grip ↓ squaring and crepitus on grinding ↓ radial styloid not tender ↓ First CMC joint osteoarthritis
exam_trap: A, De Quervain tenosynovitis — it also causes radial-sided thumb pain with use, but it is a tendon problem over the radial styloid, which is not tender here.
takeaway: Thumb-base pain with squaring and a positive grind test suggests first CMC osteoarthritis.

stem: A 39-year-old man attends the GP surgery with two months of pain in the small joints of his hands and feet. The GP wants to judge whether this is more likely to be inflammatory or mechanical. Which additional feature of the history would most suggest an inflammatory arthritis?

options.A: Pain that is worse at the end of a working day
options.B: Stiffness on waking that lasts more than an hour and eases with activity
options.C: Brief stiffness after sitting that resolves within minutes
options.D: Pain that is relieved by resting the joints
options.E: Episodes of the joints locking or giving way

correct_answer: B. Stiffness on waking that lasts more than an hour and eases with activity
why_correct: Prolonged early morning stiffness that improves with use is a hallmark of inflammatory joint disease, reflecting synovitis that eases as the joints are moved. Along with joint swelling and symmetrical small-joint involvement, it should prompt urgent rheumatology referral. Mechanical problems tend to worsen with use and improve with rest.
why_wrong: A. Pain building up through the day with use suggests a mechanical or degenerative process. C. Short-lived stiffness after inactivity is typical of osteoarthritis. D. Inflammatory pain typically improves with movement, whereas rest relieves mechanical pain. E. Locking and giving way suggest a mechanical internal joint problem.
pearl: Inflammatory: prolonged morning stiffness, better with activity. Mechanical: brief stiffness, worse with use, better with rest.
thinking: Small-joint pain in hands and feet ↓ need to separate inflammatory from mechanical ↓ inflammatory pain eases with movement ↓ long morning stiffness is characteristic ↓ Prolonged morning stiffness easing with activity
exam_trap: D, Pain relieved by resting the joints — rest sounds like a sensible response to inflammation, but inflammatory symptoms worsen with immobility and improve with movement.
takeaway: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour and easing with activity suggests inflammatory arthritis.

stem: A 44-year-old woman is lunging for a shot during a squash match when she hears a snap and feels as though her opponent's racket has struck the back of her ankle. She can still walk with a limp. In the emergency department there is a palpable gap above the heel, and squeezing her calf while she kneels on a chair produces no movement of the foot. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A sudden snap during a push-off movement, with a sensation of being struck behind the ankle, a palpable gap and a positive Simmonds calf-squeeze test, indicates Achilles tendon rupture. Patients can often still walk and weakly plantarflex using other muscles, which can lead to the diagnosis being missed. Management is in a below-knee cast or boot in equinus, or surgery, after orthopaedic assessment.
why_wrong: A. A calf strain causes pain in the muscle belly, and the calf squeeze test still moves the foot. C. A lateral ankle sprain follows an inversion injury with lateral swelling and tenderness. D. A stress fracture develops gradually with repetitive loading. E. DVT causes gradual calf swelling and pain, not a sudden snap.
pearl: Being able to walk does not exclude Achilles rupture. Check for a palpable gap and use Simmonds' calf-squeeze test.
thinking: Sudden snap during a lunge ↓ felt like being struck behind the ankle ↓ palpable gap above the heel ↓ calf squeeze produces no foot movement ↓ Achilles tendon rupture
exam_trap: A, Gastrocnemius muscle strain — it also occurs during sudden push-off and causes calf pain, but the tendon is intact so the calf squeeze test is normal.
takeaway: A snap behind the ankle with a positive Simmonds test means Achilles rupture, even if she can walk.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has been training for her first half marathon. She describes a dull ache around the front of both knees that is worse going down stairs, squatting and after sitting through long car journeys. There has been no injury, swelling, locking or giving way. Pressing the patella against the femur reproduces her pain, and the rest of the knee examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Anterior knee pain after an increase in training load, worse on stairs, squatting and prolonged sitting, without injury or mechanical symptoms, is typical of patellofemoral pain syndrome. Pain on patellar compression supports the diagnosis. Treatment is activity modification and physiotherapy focusing on quadriceps and hip strengthening.
why_wrong: A. Osgood-Schlatter disease causes pain over the tibial tuberosity in adolescents during growth. B. A meniscal tear usually follows a twisting injury and causes joint line tenderness, locking or swelling. C. An ACL injury follows trauma with immediate swelling and instability. D. Prepatellar bursitis causes a fluctuant swelling in front of the kneecap.
pearl: Patellofemoral pain is worse with stairs, squatting and prolonged sitting. No trauma, no swelling and no mechanical symptoms point away from internal derangement.
thinking: Young runner increasing distance ↓ anterior knee pain on stairs, squatting and sitting ↓ no injury, swelling or locking ↓ pain on patellar compression ↓ Patellofemoral pain syndrome
exam_trap: A, Osgood-Schlatter disease — it causes activity-related anterior knee pain in sporty young people, but it affects adolescents during growth and causes tenderness over the tibial tuberosity.
takeaway: Overuse anterior knee pain worse on stairs and sitting, without trauma, suggests patellofemoral pain syndrome.

stem: A 48-year-old plasterer has had pain on the outer side of his right elbow for six weeks. It is worst when lifting a full bucket or turning a screwdriver. He is tender just below the bony prominence on the outer elbow, and resisted extension of his middle finger reproduces the pain. Elbow movement is full. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Lateral elbow pain with tenderness just distal to the lateral epicondyle, worse with gripping and reproduced by resisted wrist or middle finger extension, is lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow). It is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin, common in manual workers. Most cases settle with activity modification, analgesia and physiotherapy.
why_wrong: B. Medial epicondylitis causes pain over the inner elbow, worse with resisted wrist flexion. C. Olecranon bursitis causes a swelling over the point of the elbow. D. A radial head fracture follows trauma and restricts movement. E. Cubital tunnel syndrome causes ulnar nerve symptoms in the ring and little fingers.
pearl: Tennis elbow is lateral and extensor-related; golfer's elbow is medial and flexor-related. Both are overuse tendinopathies.
thinking: Manual worker with outer elbow pain ↓ worse with gripping and twisting ↓ tender just below lateral epicondyle ↓ pain on resisted finger extension ↓ Lateral epicondylitis
exam_trap: B, Medial epicondylitis — it is the mirror-image overuse condition, but it affects the inner elbow and flexor origin.
takeaway: Outer elbow pain reproduced by resisted wrist or finger extension is lateral epicondylitis.

stem: A 29-year-old man attends the GP surgery with nine months of crampy lower abdominal pain that eases after opening his bowels. He feels bloated as the day goes on, and his stools vary between hard and loose. His weight is stable, he has no rectal bleeding and no symptoms wake him at night. Full blood count, CRP, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Abdominal pain relieved by defecation, bloating and altered stool form over more than six months, without red flags and with normal baseline tests, fits irritable bowel syndrome. NICE supports making a positive diagnosis in this setting once basic tests, including coeliac serology and, in younger adults, faecal calprotectin, are normal. Management begins with dietary and lifestyle advice.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease is unlikely with negative serology while eating gluten. B. Crohn's disease is unlikely with a normal calprotectin, CRP and blood count and no nocturnal symptoms. D. Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhoea, typically in older adults. E. Colorectal cancer is unlikely in a young man without bleeding, weight loss or anaemia.
pearl: IBS is a positive diagnosis: pain linked to defecation, bloating and altered bowel habit, with no red flags and normal basic tests including coeliac serology.
thinking: Chronic pain relieved by defecation ↓ bloating and variable stool form ↓ no red flags ↓ normal bloods, coeliac serology and calprotectin ↓ Irritable bowel syndrome
exam_trap: B, Crohn's disease — a young adult with abdominal pain and altered bowels raises it, but a normal faecal calprotectin and inflammatory markers make inflammatory bowel disease unlikely.
takeaway: Pain relieved by defecation with altered bowel habit, no red flags and normal tests suggests IBS.

stem: A 31-year-old man was diagnosed with coeliac disease on duodenal biopsy a year ago. He still has bloating and loose stools most weeks. His tissue transglutaminase antibody level has remained raised rather than falling. He often eats in the staff canteen and regularly drinks beer with colleagues. Which initial step is most appropriate?

options.A: Repeat upper GI endoscopy with duodenal biopsies
options.B: Detailed dietary review with a specialist dietitian to identify gluten exposure
options.C: Start oral corticosteroids for refractory coeliac disease
options.D: Arrange CT of the abdomen to look for lymphoma

correct_answer: B. Detailed dietary review with a specialist dietitian to identify gluten exposure
why_correct: Continued gluten exposure, often unintentional, is the most common cause of persistent symptoms and raised antibodies in coeliac disease. Beer brewed from barley contains gluten, and canteen food carries a risk of hidden gluten and cross-contamination. A specialist dietitian review of adherence is the first step before investigating other causes.
why_wrong: A. Repeat biopsy belongs to the work-up of non-responsive disease once gluten exposure has been excluded. C. Refractory coeliac disease can only be considered after confirming strict adherence. D. Imaging for lymphoma is for true non-responders after adherence is confirmed. E. Pancreatic insufficiency is an uncommon cause and is not the first consideration here.
pearl: Persistently raised coeliac antibodies usually mean ongoing gluten intake. Barley-based beer, eating out and cross-contamination are common hidden sources.
thinking: Known coeliac disease ↓ ongoing symptoms ↓ antibodies still raised ↓ likely sources of gluten in beer and canteen food ↓ Dietitian review of gluten exposure
exam_trap: A, Repeat endoscopy with biopsies — it is part of investigating non-responsive coeliac disease, but it comes only after ongoing gluten intake has been addressed.
takeaway: Persistent coeliac symptoms with raised antibodies: check gluten exposure with a dietitian first.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with known gallstones attends the emergency department with several hours of constant, severe upper abdominal pain that bores through to her back. She has vomited repeatedly and finds the pain slightly easier when sitting forward. Her epigastrium is tender without rigidity. Serum amylase is markedly raised. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to the back, eased by sitting forward, with vomiting and a markedly raised amylase, is characteristic of acute pancreatitis. Gallstones and alcohol are the commonest causes in the UK. Management includes fluid resuscitation, analgesia, severity assessment and an ultrasound to look for gallstones.
why_wrong: A. A perforated ulcer causes sudden pain with a rigid abdomen, which is absent here. C. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain without a markedly raised amylase. D. Acute cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain and fever, not back pain with a very high amylase. E. An inferior MI can cause epigastric pain but would not explain a markedly raised amylase.
pearl: Gallstones and alcohol cause most acute pancreatitis. A markedly raised amylase or lipase with typical pain confirms the diagnosis.
thinking: Known gallstones ↓ severe epigastric pain boring through to the back ↓ vomiting, easier sitting forward ↓ markedly raised amylase ↓ Acute pancreatitis
exam_trap: D, Acute cholecystitis — the gallstone history tempts, but cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain and does not markedly raise amylase.
takeaway: Epigastric pain through to the back with a markedly raised amylase is acute pancreatitis.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department from her care home with rigors and new confusion. Staff noticed her eyes looked yellow this morning and her urine has been dark. Her temperature is 39.1°C, and she winces when her right upper abdomen is palpated. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Carcinoma of the head of pancreas

why_correct: Fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot's triad), with confusion and a dilated common bile duct, indicates infection above an obstructed bile duct, usually from a stone. This is acute ascending cholangitis, which can rapidly progress to septic shock. Treatment is sepsis management with intravenous antibiotics and fluids, followed by biliary drainage, usually by ERCP.
why_wrong: A. Acute cholecystitis causes fever and right upper quadrant pain, but jaundice and a dilated bile duct are not typical. B. Viral hepatitis does not cause a dilated bile duct or rigors. C. Pyelonephritis causes loin pain and urinary symptoms, not jaundice. E. Pancreatic head cancer typically causes painless jaundice without fever.
pearl: Charcot's triad is fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Adding confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) signals severe cholangitis needing urgent drainage.
thinking: Older woman with rigors and confusion ↓ jaundice and dark urine ↓ right upper quadrant tenderness ↓ dilated common bile duct ↓ Acute ascending cholangitis
exam_trap: A, Acute cholecystitis — fever and right upper quadrant pain fit, but jaundice and a dilated common bile duct point to infection in an obstructed duct.
takeaway: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain with a dilated bile duct means cholangitis.

stem: A 49-year-old man attends the emergency department with 18 hours of constant pain under his right ribs that began after a takeaway meal. The pain has not eased. He has a low-grade fever, and he catches his breath on deep inspiration when the examiner presses below the right costal margin. His white cell count is raised and his bilirubin is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent right upper quadrant pain lasting many hours, with fever, a raised white cell count and a positive Murphy's sign, indicates inflammation of the gallbladder. The normal bilirubin makes bile duct obstruction less likely. Ultrasound confirms the diagnosis, and management includes antibiotics, analgesia and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
why_wrong: B. Biliary colic usually settles within a few hours and lacks fever and raised inflammatory markers. C. Cholangitis would typically cause jaundice and a raised bilirubin. D. Pneumonia can cause right upper quadrant pain but would usually cause cough and breathlessness. E. A perforated ulcer causes sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen.
pearl: Biliary colic is short-lived without fever; cholecystitis is persistent with fever, raised white cells and a positive Murphy's sign; add jaundice and think cholangitis.
thinking: Constant right upper quadrant pain for many hours ↓ fever and raised white cells ↓ positive Murphy's sign ↓ bilirubin normal ↓ Acute cholecystitis
exam_trap: B, Biliary colic — the post-meal right upper quadrant pain fits, but colic settles within hours and does not cause fever or raised inflammatory markers.
takeaway: Persistent right upper quadrant pain with fever and Murphy's sign is acute cholecystitis.

stem: A 58-year-old woman who takes naproxen daily for osteoarthritis develops abrupt, severe upper abdominal pain an hour before arriving in the emergency department. She is lying completely still, and any movement worsens the pain. Her abdomen is board-like with guarding throughout and absent bowel sounds. She is tachycardic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden severe abdominal pain with a board-like abdomen, generalised guarding and a patient lying still are signs of generalised peritonitis. In a patient taking an NSAID, a perforated peptic ulcer is the likely cause. She needs resuscitation, an erect chest X-ray or CT, and urgent surgical review.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain but rarely a truly board-like abdomen with such a sudden onset. B. Biliary colic causes colicky pain without peritonism. C. Gastritis causes epigastric discomfort without peritonitis. D. An inferior MI can cause epigastric pain but not a rigid abdomen.
pearl: Board-like rigidity with a patient lying still means peritonitis. NSAIDs and steroids increase the risk of peptic ulcer perforation.
thinking: Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ lying still, rigid abdomen ↓ generalised peritonitis ↓ NSAID use suggests ulcer perforation ↓ Perforated abdominal viscus
exam_trap: A, Acute pancreatitis — it also causes severe upper abdominal pain with tenderness, but sudden onset and board-like rigidity point to perforation.
takeaway: Sudden pain with a rigid abdomen means peritonitis: suspect perforation and get urgent surgical review.

stem: A 27-year-old woman sees her GP about bloating, wind and loose stools that come on within a few hours of drinking milky coffee or eating ice cream. She tolerates small amounts of hard cheese and has no problems with bread or pasta. She has no rash, lip swelling or wheeze after dairy, and coeliac serology is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bloating, flatulence and diarrhoea a few hours after foods high in lactose, with tolerance of low-lactose hard cheese, suggest lactase deficiency. Undigested lactose is fermented in the colon, producing gas and drawing water into the bowel. Management is reducing lactose intake or using lactose-free products while maintaining calcium intake.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease is triggered by gluten, and her serology is negative. B. Milk protein allergy in adults typically causes allergic features such as urticaria, swelling or wheeze. C. Giardiasis usually follows travel or contaminated water and is not consistently linked to dairy. E. IBS is not consistently triggered by lactose-containing foods with tolerance of hard cheese.
pearl: Hard cheeses contain little lactose, so tolerance of cheese with intolerance of milk is a useful clue to lactose intolerance rather than milk allergy.
thinking: Bloating, wind and loose stools after milk and ice cream ↓ hard cheese tolerated ↓ no allergic features ↓ coeliac serology negative ↓ Lactose intolerance
exam_trap: B, Cow's milk protein allergy — dairy is the trigger, but allergy causes allergic features and would not spare hard cheese.
takeaway: GI symptoms after milk but not hard cheese, without allergic features, suggest lactose intolerance.

stem: An 80-year-old woman is sent from her care home to the emergency department with three days of colicky abdominal pain. Her abdomen has become swollen and tense, she has vomited several times, and staff report she has not passed wind for two days. On auscultation the bowel sounds are high-pitched and tinkling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Colicky pain, abdominal distension, vomiting and absolute constipation are the cardinal features of intestinal obstruction. High-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds indicate a mechanical obstruction. She needs fluid resuscitation, nasogastric decompression, imaging to find the level and cause, and surgical review.
why_wrong: B. Paralytic ileus causes distension and absent flatus, but bowel sounds are absent and pain is not usually colicky. C. Diverticulitis causes left iliac fossa pain and fever rather than this picture. D. Gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea rather than failure to pass flatus. E. Urinary retention causes suprapubic swelling and discomfort but not vomiting with absolute constipation.
pearl: Colicky pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation suggest obstruction. Tinkling bowel sounds suggest mechanical obstruction; silence suggests ileus or late obstruction.
thinking: Colicky abdominal pain ↓ distension and vomiting ↓ no flatus for two days ↓ tinkling bowel sounds ↓ Intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: B, Paralytic ileus — it also causes distension and absent flatus, but bowel sounds are absent rather than tinkling, and colicky pain is unusual.
takeaway: Colicky pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation indicate intestinal obstruction.

stem: A 44-year-old man attends the emergency department with a day of colicky central abdominal pain and repeated bilious vomiting. He has not opened his bowels or passed wind since yesterday. He had a laparotomy after a road traffic collision ten years ago and has a healed midline scar. His hernial orifices are normal. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated central loops of small bowel. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Colicky central pain, early bilious vomiting, absolute constipation and dilated small bowel loops indicate small bowel obstruction. In a patient with previous abdominal surgery and normal hernial orifices, adhesions are by far the most likely cause. Many cases settle with conservative management (nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression and fluids), but signs of strangulation need urgent surgery.
why_wrong: A. Hernias are a common cause of small bowel obstruction, but his hernial orifices are normal. C. Sigmoid volvulus causes large bowel obstruction, usually in older adults with chronic constipation. D. Colorectal cancer causes large bowel obstruction and is less likely at his age. E. Gallstone ileus is rare and occurs mainly in older women.
pearl: In small bowel obstruction, look for a scar and examine the hernial orifices: adhesions after previous surgery and hernias are the commonest causes.
thinking: Colicky central pain with bilious vomiting ↓ absolute constipation ↓ dilated small bowel loops ↓ previous laparotomy, hernial orifices normal ↓ Adhesional small bowel obstruction
exam_trap: A, Obstructed inguinal hernia — hernias are a leading cause of small bowel obstruction, but his hernial orifices are normal and he has had previous surgery.
takeaway: Small bowel obstruction after previous abdominal surgery is most likely due to adhesions.

stem: An 82-year-old man with Parkinson's disease and long-standing constipation is brought in from his care home with marked abdominal distension and a day of not passing wind. An abdominal X-ray shows a large, inverted U-shaped loop of dilated colon arising from the pelvis, consistent with sigmoid volvulus. Which complication is the main reason urgent decompression is needed?

options.E: Malignant change in the bowel wall

correct_answer: C. Ischaemia of the twisted bowel
why_correct: In volvulus the bowel twists around its mesentery, creating a closed loop and compromising its blood supply. Without prompt decompression this can progress to ischaemia, gangrene and perforation. Sigmoid volvulus is usually decompressed endoscopically with a flatus tube, with surgery if there are signs of ischaemia or recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Aspiration is a risk with vomiting but is not the main danger of the twist itself. B. Urinary retention can occur with distension but is not the critical complication. D. Electrolyte disturbance may occur but is not the reason for urgent decompression. E. Volvulus does not cause malignant change.
pearl: Volvulus creates a closed loop with mesenteric twisting. Pain out of proportion, peritonism or a raised lactate suggests ischaemia and needs surgery.
thinking: Older man with chronic constipation ↓ distension and absolute constipation ↓ X-ray shows sigmoid volvulus ↓ mesenteric twist threatens blood supply ↓ Ischaemia of the twisted bowel
exam_trap: A, Aspiration pneumonia — it is a genuine risk in a frail patient with distension and vomiting, but the danger that makes this an emergency is loss of blood supply to the bowel.
takeaway: Volvulus threatens the bowel's blood supply, so it needs urgent decompression.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped her apixaban two weeks ago because of nosebleeds. She now attends the emergency department with sudden, severe central abdominal pain. She is writhing and distressed, yet her abdomen is soft with only mild tenderness and no guarding. Her lactate is raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings in a patient with atrial fibrillation, particularly one who has stopped anticoagulation, strongly suggests embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery. A raised lactate supports bowel ischaemia, although a normal lactate does not exclude it. Urgent CT angiography and surgical or vascular intervention are needed.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with marked epigastric tenderness. B. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain without a raised lactate. D.
