why_correct: Fever, lower abdominal pain, offensive lochia and a tender uterus after delivery are typical of postpartum endometritis. Caesarean section, especially after prolonged labour, is the main risk factor. She should be assessed for sepsis and started on broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, with an ultrasound if retained products are suspected.
why_wrong: A. Mastitis causes a painful, red, firm area of breast, and her breasts are normal. B. The wound is clean and dry, so a wound infection does not explain her signs. C. Pyelonephritis causes loin pain and urinary symptoms rather than uterine tenderness and offensive lochia. D. DVT causes leg swelling and pain, and her calves are normal.
pearl: Postpartum fever has a short list of sources: uterus, wound, breasts, urinary tract, chest and legs; offensive lochia with a tender uterus localises it to the endometrium.
thinking: Postnatal fever after caesarean section ↓ lower abdominal pain with offensive lochia ↓ bulky, tender uterus ↓ wound, breasts and legs normal ↓ Endometritis
exam_trap: B, Surgical wound infection — fever after a caesarean tempts towards the wound, but it is clean and dry, while offensive lochia and uterine tenderness point to the endometrium.
takeaway: Postnatal fever with offensive lochia and a tender uterus is endometritis.

stem: An 83-year-old man is admitted from his care home to the orthopaedic ward with a fractured neck of femur. He arrives with a bag of medicine boxes, some dispensed via his GP and some via a hospital cardiology clinic. The care home's medicines chart lists a different dose of one of his heart tablets from that printed on the box. You are the foundation doctor writing his inpatient drug chart. What should you do first to reduce the risk of a medication error?

options.A: Prescribe each medicine exactly as printed on the boxes he brought
options.B: Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
options.C: Withhold all his regular medicines until after surgery
options.D: Copy the care home chart onto the drug chart
options.E: Ask the patient to recall each medicine and dose

correct_answer: B. Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
why_correct: Medicines reconciliation means compiling an accurate list of what the patient is actually taking by comparing several sources, such as the GP record, care home chart, medicine labels and specialist letters, and resolving any discrepancies. It identifies omissions, duplications and dose errors at transfer of care, when errors are most common. Pharmacy teams should be involved soon after admission.
why_wrong: A. Labels may be out of date and already conflict with another source, so they cannot be used alone. C. Stopping all medicines can cause harm, for example from omitting cardiac drugs or anticoagulants. D. The care home chart is only one source and already conflicts with another. E. Recall by a frail, injured older patient is unreliable as the only source.
pearl: Transfers of care are high-risk points for medication errors; reconcile using at least two sources and document what was checked and any changes made.
thinking: Admission from a care home after a fall ↓ medicines from several prescribers with a dose discrepancy ↓ transfer of care is a high-risk point for errors ↓ compare several reliable sources and resolve differences ↓ Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
exam_trap: D, Copy the care home chart onto the drug chart — the care home chart looks authoritative, but it already conflicts with the boxes, so relying on it alone could carry an error forward.
takeaway: On admission, reconcile medicines from more than one reliable source before prescribing.

stem: A 37-year-old woman was started on lamotrigine for epilepsy by her neurologist three weeks ago. She now has a widespread blistering rash with painful mouth ulcers and sore eyes, and she is admitted to hospital. Once she is receiving appropriate treatment, the ward doctor wants to report the suspected drug reaction. Which route should be used?

options.A: The local incident reporting system only
options.B: Notification to the UK Health Security Agency
options.C: A letter to the drug manufacturer only
options.D: Referral to the General Medical Council

why_correct: Suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK are reported to the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency through the Yellow Card scheme. Serious reactions, such as suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome, should always be reported, even if causality is uncertain. Any health professional, and patients themselves, can submit a report.
why_wrong: A. Local incident systems record safety events within a trust but do not replace national adverse reaction reporting. B. UKHSA receives notifications of specified infectious diseases, not drug reactions. C. Contacting the manufacturer alone does not feed into the national monitoring system. D. The GMC regulates doctors and is not involved in reporting drug reactions.
pearl: Report any suspected serious adverse reaction to any medicine through the Yellow Card scheme, and all suspected reactions to products under additional monitoring (black triangle).
thinking: New antiepileptic started weeks ago ↓ blistering rash with mucosal involvement, a serious reaction ↓ suspected adverse drug reaction ↓ national reporting system run by the MHRA ↓ The Yellow Card scheme
exam_trap: A, The local incident reporting system only — hospital doctors are used to filing incident reports, but a suspected adverse drug reaction must be reported nationally through the Yellow Card scheme.
takeaway: Report suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

presentation: Police Request For Records Without Consent
stem: A police officer telephones the emergency department asking for details of a man treated overnight for a facial injury, saying they are investigating an assault. The patient has capacity and, when asked, refuses to allow any information to be shared. The officer does not have a court order. How should the doctor respond?

options.A: Send the officer a copy of the full clinical record as requested
options.B: Refuse and explain that confidentiality can never be broken
options.C: Consider whether disclosure is required by law or justified in the public interest, and if so share only the minimum necessary
options.D: Disclose once the officer emails the request on police headed paper
options.E: Seek consent from the patient's next of kin instead

correct_answer: C. Consider whether disclosure is required by law or justified in the public interest, and if so share only the minimum necessary
why_correct: Confidentiality is the default, but GMC guidance allows disclosure without consent when it is required by law or justified in the public interest, for example to prevent or detect a serious crime. The doctor should weigh this carefully, seeking senior or Caldicott Guardian advice if unsure, and if disclosure is justified share only the minimum relevant information. The decision and reasons should be documented and the patient usually informed.
why_wrong: A. Releasing the whole record without assessment breaches confidentiality and the minimum-necessary principle. B. Confidentiality is not absolute and can be set aside when legally required or justified in the public interest. D. A written request does not by itself create a legal basis for disclosure. E. Next of kin cannot consent on behalf of an adult with capacity.
pearl: Without consent, ask two questions before disclosing to police: is there a legal requirement or a genuine public interest justification, and what is the least information needed to meet it?
thinking: Police request for clinical information ↓ patient with capacity refuses consent ↓ confidentiality is the default but not absolute ↓ judge the legal or public interest basis, then limit disclosure ↓ Consider whether disclosure is required by law or justified in the public interest, and if so share only the minimum necessary
exam_trap: D, Disclose once the officer emails the request on police headed paper — formal paperwork feels like authority, but a written request is not a legal requirement to disclose; the doctor must still judge the justification.
takeaway: Police requests without consent need a judged legal or public interest basis and minimal disclosure.

stem: An 87-year-old woman with advanced heart failure has a completed DNACPR form after discussion with her and her family. She is admitted with a urinary tract infection and sepsis. She is alert, has capacity and says she would like the infection treated. A nurse asks whether the DNACPR decision means intravenous antibiotics and fluids should not be given. What is the correct response?

options.A: Yes, a DNACPR decision means only comfort care should be provided
options.B: No, the decision covers CPR only; other treatment is decided on its own merits
options.C: Only if her family agree to the antibiotics
options.D: Only oral antibiotics should be used
options.E: She should be transferred to a hospice instead

correct_answer: B. No, the decision covers CPR only; other treatment is decided on its own merits
why_correct: A DNACPR decision applies only to cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest. It does not mean withholding other appropriate treatment such as antibiotics, fluids or other active care, which should be decided individually with the patient. Many hospitals record wider treatment escalation plans, for example using the ReSPECT process, but these are separate decisions.
why_wrong: A. DNACPR is not a do-not-treat order and does not mean comfort care only. C. She has capacity, so the decision is hers with her clinicians, not her family's. D. The route of antibiotics should be based on clinical need, not on resuscitation status. E. Hospice transfer is not indicated simply because a DNACPR decision exists.
pearl: Misreading DNACPR as do-not-treat is a recognised cause of harm; every other treatment decision should be made on its own merits and discussed with the patient.
thinking: Valid DNACPR decision in place ↓ new treatable illness, sepsis from a urinary source ↓ patient has capacity and wants treatment ↓ DNACPR covers only CPR in cardiac arrest ↓ No, the decision covers CPR only; other treatment is decided on its own merits
exam_trap: A, Yes, a DNACPR decision means only comfort care should be provided — frailty and a DNACPR form tempt staff to assume palliation, but the form is limited to resuscitation and she wants active treatment.
takeaway: DNACPR applies only to CPR; antibiotics and other treatments are still given when appropriate.

stem: A 66-year-old man at a GP review asks about a new drug to prevent hip fracture. The leaflet he has read states that, in a large trial, the relative risk of hip fracture with the drug compared with placebo was 0.5. He asks you what this means. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: His own risk of fracture will fall by 50 percentage points
options.B: Half of all patients who take the drug will be protected from fracture
options.C: The number needed to treat to prevent one fracture is 2
options.D: The drug doubles the risk of fracture compared with placebo
options.E: People taking the drug had half the risk of hip fracture of those taking placebo

correct_answer: E. People taking the drug had half the risk of hip fracture of those taking placebo
why_correct: Relative risk is the risk of the outcome in the treated group divided by the risk in the control group. A value of 0.5 means the risk among people taking the drug was half that of those taking placebo, a 50% relative risk reduction. On its own it does not tell you the absolute benefit, which depends on the patient's baseline risk.
why_wrong: A. A fall in percentage points describes absolute risk reduction, which cannot be derived from the relative risk alone. B. The relative risk does not mean that half of patients are protected. C. The number needed to treat depends on the absolute risk reduction, not the relative risk. D. A relative risk below 1 indicates reduced, not increased, risk.
pearl: When explaining benefit to patients, pair relative risk with absolute figures: halving a small risk gives a much smaller absolute benefit than halving a large one.
thinking: Relative risk is risk in the treated group divided by risk in the control group ↓ a value below 1 means reduced risk ↓ 0.5 means the treated group's risk is half the control group's ↓ absolute benefit needs the baseline risk ↓ People taking the drug had half the risk of hip fracture of those taking placebo
exam_trap: A, His own risk of fracture will fall by 50 percentage points — it confuses a relative reduction with an absolute one; a baseline risk of 4% would fall to 2%, not by 50 points.
takeaway: A relative risk of 0.5 means the outcome risk is halved relative to control, not an absolute 50% fall.

stem: A journal club discusses a study that recruited 400 people with bladder cancer and 400 matched people without it, then compared how often each group had previously worked in the dye industry. For this exposure, the paper quotes 3.0 as the odds ratio. A trainee is asked to interpret this figure. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The odds of previous dye-industry work were three times higher among people with bladder cancer than among controls
options.B: The study measured the incidence of bladder cancer in dye workers as three times that in other workers
options.C: 3% of dye workers will develop bladder cancer
options.D: Dye-industry work causes a third of all bladder cancers
options.E: Dye-industry work reduces the odds of bladder cancer by a third

correct_answer: A. The odds of previous dye-industry work were three times higher among people with bladder cancer than among controls
why_correct: A case-control study starts with people who have the disease (cases) and people without it (controls) and looks back at their exposures. The odds ratio compares the odds of exposure in cases with the odds in controls, so a value of 3 means cases had three times the odds of past dye-industry work. When a disease is rare the odds ratio approximates the relative risk, but a case-control design cannot measure incidence directly.
why_wrong: B. Case-control studies select participants by disease status, so they cannot measure incidence. C. An odds ratio is a ratio, not the percentage of people affected. D. The proportion of cases due to an exposure is the attributable fraction, not the odds ratio. E. An odds ratio above 1 indicates a positive association, not a reduction.
pearl: Match the measure to the design: case-control studies give odds ratios, while cohort studies and trials can measure incidence and give relative risks.
thinking: Case-control design selects by disease status ↓ exposure history compared between cases and controls ↓ odds ratio is the odds of exposure in cases divided by the odds in controls ↓ a value of 3 indicates a positive association ↓ The odds of previous dye-industry work were three times higher among people with bladder cancer than among controls
exam_trap: B, The study measured the incidence of bladder cancer in dye workers as three times that in other workers — this reads the odds ratio as a cohort relative risk, but a case-control study cannot measure incidence.
takeaway: In a case-control study, the odds ratio compares exposure odds between cases and controls; it does not measure incidence.

presentation: Interpreting A Confidence Interval Crossing The Null
stem: A randomised trial compares a new antihypertensive drug with standard treatment. For stroke, it reports a risk ratio of 0.85 and a 95% CI of 0.70 to 1.04. A GP reading the paper wonders what conclusion can be drawn about stroke. Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: The new drug significantly reduces stroke risk
options.B: The trial proves the two drugs are equally effective
options.C: The result is compatible with no difference in stroke risk between treatments
options.D: The new drug increases stroke risk
options.E: The p-value for this result is below 0.05

correct_answer: C. The result is compatible with no difference in stroke risk between treatments
why_correct: For a ratio measure, the value representing no difference is 1. Because the 95% confidence interval runs from below 1 to above 1, the data are compatible with a reduction, no effect or a small increase, so the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level. This does not prove the drugs are equivalent; the trial may simply lack the precision to detect a difference.
why_wrong: A. Statistical significance would require the whole interval to lie below 1. B. Failing to show a difference is not proof of equivalence. D. The point estimate suggests a reduction, and the interval includes both benefit and harm. E. An interval that crosses 1 corresponds to a p-value above 0.05.
pearl: For ratios (relative risk, odds ratio, hazard ratio) the null value is 1; for differences (mean difference, risk difference) it is 0. Check whether the interval crosses the right line.
thinking: Ratio measure, so the null value is 1 ↓ the 95% interval runs from 0.70 to 1.04 ↓ it includes 1 ↓ not statistically significant, but not proof of equivalence ↓ The result is compatible with no difference in stroke risk between treatments
exam_trap: A, The new drug significantly reduces stroke risk — the point estimate below 1 tempts towards benefit, but the interval crosses 1, so a true reduction has not been demonstrated.
takeaway: A confidence interval crossing the null value means the result is compatible with no difference, not proof of none.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with vitiligo and hypothyroidism tells her GP she has had pins and needles in both feet and hands for several months, along with tiredness and a sore, smooth red tongue. Her blood count shows a raised mean cell volume and her vitamin B12 level is low. Which examination finding is most likely?

options.D: Reduced vibration sense in the feet with absent ankle jerks

correct_answer: D. Reduced vibration sense in the feet with absent ankle jerks
why_correct: Vitamin B12 deficiency, here probably due to autoimmune pernicious anaemia, causes a peripheral sensory neuropathy and can affect the dorsal columns, producing loss of vibration and joint position sense with reduced or absent ankle reflexes. Neurological damage can become permanent if treatment is delayed. Treatment is with intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, given more frequently at first when neurological features are present.
why_wrong: A. Lower motor neurone facial weakness is typical of Bell palsy, not B12 deficiency. B. A resting pin-rolling tremor suggests Parkinson disease. C. Bitemporal hemianopia suggests a pituitary lesion compressing the optic chiasm. E. Tongue fasciculation is a feature of motor neurone disease.
pearl: Absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars is a classic combination in B12 deficiency, reflecting peripheral neuropathy together with subacute combined degeneration of the cord.
thinking: Woman with other autoimmune conditions ↓ sore smooth tongue, tiredness, macrocytosis and low B12 ↓ suggests pernicious anaemia ↓ symmetrical distal tingling indicates peripheral nerve and dorsal column involvement ↓ Reduced vibration sense in the feet with absent ankle jerks
exam_trap: E, Fasciculation of the tongue — a sore tongue in the history draws the eye to this option, but fasciculation is a motor neurone sign, whereas B12 deficiency causes a symmetrical sensory neuropathy.
takeaway: B12 deficiency causes a sensory peripheral neuropathy with loss of vibration sense, alongside macrocytic anaemia.

stem: A 30-year-old woman sees her GP because friends have noticed that her eyes look yellow. She has felt increasingly tired and breathless on the stairs for two weeks. Her results show a low haemoglobin, a raised reticulocyte count, a raised unconjugated bilirubin, a raised LDH and a haptoglobin below the reference range. Her ALT and alkaline phosphatase are normal. Which process best explains these results?
why_correct: Anaemia with a raised reticulocyte count, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, raised LDH and low haptoglobin indicates increased red cell destruction. Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin released from lysed cells, so it is consumed and falls. The next steps include a blood film and a direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test to look for an immune cause.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis raises the ALT markedly and causes mixed or conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. B. Biliary obstruction raises the alkaline phosphatase and conjugated bilirubin. C. Gilbert syndrome causes isolated unconjugated bilirubin without anaemia or a low haptoglobin. D. Iron deficiency causes anaemia with a low reticulocyte response and no jaundice.
pearl: The haemolysis screen is raised unconjugated bilirubin, raised LDH, raised reticulocytes and low haptoglobin; follow it with a blood film and a direct antiglobulin test.
thinking: Jaundice with symptoms of anaemia ↓ unconjugated bilirubin and LDH raised, haptoglobin low ↓ reticulocytes raised, so the marrow is responding ↓ normal liver enzymes exclude a hepatic or obstructive cause ↓ Haemolysis
exam_trap: C, Gilbert syndrome — a young woman with isolated unconjugated jaundice tempts towards Gilbert, but Gilbert causes no anaemia, reticulocytosis or low haptoglobin.
takeaway: Anaemia with raised unconjugated bilirubin and LDH, raised reticulocytes and low haptoglobin is haemolysis.

stem: A 22-year-old man notices that the whites of his eyes turn slightly yellow during a bout of flu and again while fasting during Ramadan. Between episodes he feels well. He does not drink alcohol and takes no medicines. His GP finds a mildly raised bilirubin, which is almost entirely unconjugated. ALT, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, full blood count and reticulocyte count are all normal, and there is no bilirubin in the urine. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia brought on by fasting or intercurrent illness, with normal liver enzymes, blood count and reticulocytes, is Gilbert syndrome. It results from reduced activity of the enzyme that conjugates bilirubin and is benign. Once haemolysis and liver disease are excluded, reassurance is the main management and no treatment or follow-up is needed.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis would cause anaemia and a raised reticulocyte count. C. Crigler-Najjar syndrome causes severe unconjugated jaundice from the neonatal period. D. Hepatitis A causes a marked rise in ALT with systemic symptoms. E. Dubin-Johnson syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, with bilirubin in the urine.
pearl: Unconjugated bilirubin is not water-soluble, so it does not appear in urine; jaundice with dark urine suggests a conjugated cause.
thinking: Young man with episodes of mild jaundice ↓ triggered by illness and fasting ↓ unconjugated bilirubin only, with no bilirubinuria ↓ normal liver enzymes, blood count and reticulocytes ↓ Gilbert syndrome
exam_trap: A, Haemolytic anaemia — unconjugated jaundice tempts towards haemolysis, but a normal blood count and reticulocyte count exclude it.
takeaway: Recurrent mild unconjugated jaundice with fasting or illness and otherwise normal bloods is Gilbert syndrome.

stem: A 34-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is found to have iron deficiency anaemia on routine blood tests. He mentions intermittent loose stools and bloating over the past year. He eats bread and pasta most days. His GP wants to test him for coeliac disease. Which test should be requested first?

options.A: Upper GI endoscopy with duodenal biopsy
options.C: Total IgA with IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody

correct_answer: C. Total IgA with IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody
why_correct: NICE recommends IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody as the first-line test for suspected coeliac disease, with total IgA measured at the same time because IgA deficiency can cause a false-negative result. The person must be eating gluten regularly for several weeks before testing. In adults, a positive result is followed by referral for endoscopy and duodenal biopsy.
why_wrong: A. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis but follows positive serology rather than being the first test. B. HLA typing is mainly used to rule out coeliac disease in selected cases, as many people without the disease carry these genes. D. Calprotectin helps distinguish inflammatory bowel disease from functional symptoms, not coeliac disease. E. Anti-gliadin antibodies are no longer recommended because of poor accuracy.
pearl: Type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease and unexplained iron deficiency are all reasons to offer coeliac serology; make sure the patient is still eating gluten before testing.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes with unexplained iron deficiency ↓ bloating and loose stools ↓ coeliac disease suspected while he is eating gluten ↓ serology first, with total IgA to avoid false negatives ↓ Total IgA with IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody
exam_trap: A, Upper GI endoscopy with duodenal biopsy — biopsy confirms the diagnosis in adults, which tempts, but it follows positive serology rather than replacing it as the first test.
takeaway: Test suspected coeliac disease with IgA tTG plus total IgA while the patient is eating gluten.

stem: A 41-year-old man was diagnosed with coeliac disease on duodenal biopsy 18 months ago. He tells his GP he still has bloating and loose stools most weeks. His IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody level fell after diagnosis but remains above the normal range. He eats out at work most lunchtimes. What should be done first?

options.B: Review his gluten intake with a specialist dietitian

correct_answer: B. Review his gluten intake with a specialist dietitian
why_correct: The commonest reason for persistent symptoms in treated coeliac disease is continued gluten exposure, often inadvertent through cross-contamination or eating out. A persistently raised tTG antibody supports ongoing gluten intake. A detailed dietary review with a specialist dietitian is the first step before investigating other causes or refractory disease.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy may be considered for other causes such as microscopic colitis, but only after dietary adherence is checked. C. Steroids are reserved for confirmed refractory coeliac disease under specialist care. D. Repeat biopsy is considered if symptoms persist despite confirmed strict adherence. E. Pancreatic insufficiency is a less common cause and is investigated after gluten exposure has been addressed.
pearl: Coeliac serology falls on a strict gluten-free diet and is useful for monitoring adherence; persistently raised antibodies usually mean ongoing gluten exposure.
thinking: Established coeliac disease ↓ persistent bloating and loose stools ↓ tTG still raised and frequently eats out ↓ ongoing gluten exposure is the commonest cause ↓ Review his gluten intake with a specialist dietitian
exam_trap: D, Repeat the duodenal biopsy — persistent symptoms tempt towards re-examining the gut, but checking for dietary gluten comes first, especially when antibodies remain raised.
takeaway: Persistent symptoms in treated coeliac disease mean checking gluten-free diet adherence first.

stem: A 26-year-old woman telephones her GP surgery two days after getting back from a fortnight in Thailand. Since yesterday she has opened her bowels about six times a day with loose, watery stool. There has been no blood or mucus, she feels mildly warm but not unwell, and she is managing to drink and is passing urine normally. What should be the first priority in her care?

options.A: A three-day course of oral ciprofloxacin
options.B: Oral rehydration with fluids and oral rehydration salts
options.E: Avoid all oral intake until the diarrhoea settles

correct_answer: B. Oral rehydration with fluids and oral rehydration salts
why_correct: Acute watery diarrhoea after travel is usually a self-limiting infective illness, and the main danger is dehydration. In a patient who is drinking, passing urine and not systemically unwell, oral fluids supplemented with oral rehydration salts are the cornerstone of management. Advice on hand hygiene and safety-netting for blood in the stool, high fever or signs of dehydration should accompany this.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not routinely needed for uncomplicated watery traveller's diarrhoea and add side effects and resistance. C. She is drinking and passing urine, so intravenous fluids and admission are not required. D. Giardiasis typically causes prolonged, bloating, foul-smelling diarrhoea rather than an acute two-day illness. E. Withholding fluids or food worsens dehydration and is not recommended.
pearl: Most acute traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting. Rehydration comes first; antibiotics are reserved for specific indications such as dysentery, systemic illness or immunosuppression.
thinking: Recent travel with acute watery stools, no blood ↓ likely self-limiting infective gastroenteritis ↓ main risk is fluid and electrolyte loss ↓ drinking and passing urine, so oral route is adequate ↓ Oral rehydration with fluids and oral rehydration salts
exam_trap: A, A three-day course of oral ciprofloxacin — it tempts because the illness followed foreign travel, but routine antibiotics do not address the main risk of dehydration and are not indicated for uncomplicated watery diarrhoea.
takeaway: In acute watery diarrhoea without red flags, rehydrate first; antibiotics are rarely the priority.

stem: An 81-year-old man is on day six of an admission for pneumonia, treated with intravenous co-amoxiclav and then a cephalosporin. Over the last 24 hours he has had five episodes of foul-smelling, loose stool with lower abdominal cramps. He has not vomited, no other patients on the bay are unwell, and his white cell count has risen. Which cause is most likely?
why_correct: New diarrhoea in a hospitalised older adult receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics such as cephalosporins or co-amoxiclav is the classic setting for Clostridioides difficile infection. Antibiotics disrupt the normal colonic flora and allow toxin-producing overgrowth. He should be isolated, have a stool sample sent for C. difficile testing, and have the precipitating antibiotics reviewed.
why_wrong: A. Campylobacter is a community food-borne infection, usually from poultry, not a hospital-acquired illness during an antibiotic course. B. Norovirus usually causes prominent vomiting and spreads quickly to other patients and staff. C. Ischaemic colitis typically presents with sudden pain and bloody diarrhoea in a patient with vascular risk factors. E. Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhoea and would not appear acutely during an antibiotic course.
pearl: Suspect C. difficile in any patient with new diarrhoea during or after antibiotics, especially in hospital. Isolate first, test the stool, and stop or rationalise the causative antibiotic.
thinking: Older inpatient on broad-spectrum antibiotics ↓ new diarrhoea with cramps and rising white cells ↓ no vomiting, no outbreak on the bay ↓ antibiotic-associated colitis ↓ Clostridioides difficile infection
exam_trap: B, Norovirus gastroenteritis — it tempts because diarrhoea on a hospital ward suggests an outbreak, but norovirus causes prominent vomiting and spreads to others, whereas here the key link is recent broad-spectrum antibiotics.
takeaway: New diarrhoea during antibiotic therapy is C. difficile until proven otherwise: isolate and test.

stem: A 19-year-old man attends the emergency department with fever, crampy periumbilical pain and diarrhoea which became bloody this morning. Three days earlier he cooked chicken skewers on a barbecue at a party and admits some were pink in the middle. Two friends from the party have similar symptoms. Which organism is the likeliest cause?
why_correct: Campylobacter jejuni is the commonest bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in the UK and is strongly linked with undercooked poultry. After an incubation of a few days it causes fever, cramping abdominal pain and diarrhoea that is often bloody. Management is usually supportive, with stool culture and antibiotics reserved for severe or prolonged illness.
why_wrong: B. Staphylococcal toxin causes vomiting within hours of eating, not bloody diarrhoea days later. C. Bacillus cereus is linked with reheated rice and causes rapid-onset vomiting or watery diarrhoea. D. Norovirus causes vomiting and watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. E. Giardia causes prolonged, non-bloody, bloating diarrhoea, usually after travel or contaminated water.
pearl: Undercooked chicken, a few days' incubation, fever and bloody diarrhoea point to Campylobacter. Most cases settle with fluids alone.
thinking: Undercooked poultry ↓ incubation of a few days ↓ fever, cramps and bloody diarrhoea ↓ invasive bacterial enteritis ↓ Campylobacter jejuni
exam_trap: B, Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin — it tempts because a group became ill after shared food, but preformed toxins cause vomiting within hours, not bloody diarrhoea after several days.
takeaway: Undercooked poultry followed days later by fever and bloody diarrhoea suggests Campylobacter.

stem: A 38-year-old man is seen in the dermatology clinic with an intensely itchy rash on his buttocks and the front of his knees. Most lesions are excoriated, but a few small, clustered blisters remain intact. On questioning he mentions bloating and loose, pale stools for a year, and a recent blood test showed iron deficiency anaemia. Which underlying condition is most likely?
why_correct: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely itchy, clustered vesicular rash on extensor surfaces and buttocks, and it is a cutaneous manifestation of coeliac disease. Malabsorptive bowel symptoms and iron deficiency anaemia support the diagnosis. Coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA) should be checked while he is still eating gluten.
why_wrong: A. Crohn disease is associated with erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum, not grouped itchy blisters. B. Ulcerative colitis typically causes bloody diarrhoea and is not linked with dermatitis herpetiformis. D. Chronic pancreatitis causes steatorrhoea but has no characteristic blistering rash. E. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause iron deficiency anaemia or a blistering rash.
pearl: Dermatitis herpetiformis is essentially coeliac disease of the skin. Anyone with it should be tested for coeliac disease, and both respond to a strict gluten-free diet.
thinking: Very itchy grouped blisters on extensor surfaces and buttocks ↓ dermatitis herpetiformis ↓ bloating, pale stools and iron deficiency ↓ gluten-sensitive enteropathy ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: A, Crohn disease — it tempts because it is an inflammatory bowel disease with skin associations and malabsorption, but its skin signs are erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum, not grouped itchy vesicles.
takeaway: An intensely itchy, blistering extensor rash with malabsorption points to coeliac disease.

stem: A 47-year-old woman who has worn strong glasses for short-sightedness since childhood attends eye casualty. Yesterday she noticed a shower of black specks and brief flickering lights in her left eye. This morning a shadow has appeared in the lower part of her vision in that eye and is creeping upwards. The eye is white and painless. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Photopsia and a sudden shower of floaters followed by an advancing shadow or field defect are the warning features of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. High myopia is a recognised risk factor. This is a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day ophthalmology assessment, particularly before the macula becomes involved.
why_wrong: A. Posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters but does not produce a progressive field defect. B. Vitreous haemorrhage causes floaters or hazy vision but not the preceding flashes with a spreading shadow from one edge. C. Migraine aura is usually bilateral, lasts minutes and resolves fully. D. Central retinal artery occlusion causes abrupt, profound painless loss of vision without preceding flashes or floaters.
pearl: Flashes and floaters alone may be posterior vitreous detachment; once a shadow or curtain appears, assume retinal detachment and refer the same day.
thinking: Myopic patient with new flashes and floaters ↓ followed by a spreading shadow in one eye ↓ peripheral retina has lifted away ↓ painless, white eye ↓ Retinal detachment
exam_trap: A, Posterior vitreous detachment — it tempts because it also causes new flashes and floaters, but it does not cause a field defect; the advancing shadow means the retina itself has detached.
takeaway: Flashes plus floaters plus an advancing shadow equals retinal detachment until proven otherwise.

stem: A 46-year-old accountant visits his optometrist because over the past year he has struggled to read his phone and restaurant menus, especially in dim light, and now finds himself stretching his arm out to bring text into focus. His distance vision while driving is unchanged and he has no eye pain or glare. Which explanation is most likely?
why_correct: Presbyopia is the gradual, age-related loss of the lens's ability to accommodate for near objects, usually becoming noticeable in the mid-forties. Patients hold reading material further away and need better lighting, while distance vision is preserved. It is corrected with reading glasses or varifocal lenses.
why_wrong: A. Cataract usually causes glare and blurring at all distances rather than a selective near-focus problem. B. Myopia causes blurred distance vision with good near vision, the opposite of this pattern. C. Open-angle glaucoma is asymptomatic early and affects peripheral fields, not reading focus. E. Macular degeneration distorts central vision at all distances and typically affects older patients.
pearl: Near vision worsening in the mid-forties with normal distance vision is presbyopia. Holding text at arm's length is the classic clue.
thinking: Mid-forties ↓ difficulty only with near tasks ↓ holds text further away, distance vision normal ↓ reduced lens accommodation ↓ Presbyopia
exam_trap: A, Cataract — it tempts because it is a common age-related cause of reduced vision, but it blurs vision at all distances and causes glare rather than a pure loss of near focusing.
takeaway: Gradual near-vision difficulty with normal distance vision in middle age is presbyopia.

stem: A 24-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic. Three days after unprotected sex with a new partner he developed stinging on passing urine, and since yesterday a thick, yellow-green discharge has been staining his underwear. He has no genital ulcers, rash or fever. Which organism is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Symptomatic gonococcal urethritis in men typically appears within a few days of exposure, with dysuria and a copious purulent urethral discharge. Diagnosis is confirmed with nucleic acid amplification testing and microscopy and culture, and culture is important for antimicrobial sensitivity. He should be treated according to current BASHH guidance, with partner notification and testing for other infections.
why_wrong: A. Chlamydia is often asymptomatic or causes a scanty, clear or mucoid discharge rather than a copious purulent one. C. Trichomonas is usually asymptomatic in men and is less likely than gonorrhoea to cause this picture. D. Genital herpes causes painful ulcers and blisters rather than a purulent discharge. E. Syphilis presents with a painless chancre, not urethral discharge.
pearl: Short incubation with a thick, purulent urethral discharge favours gonorrhoea; chlamydia is commonly silent or causes a scanty discharge. Always test for both.
thinking: Man with dysuria after unprotected sex ↓ short incubation of a few days ↓ copious purulent urethral discharge ↓ gonococcal urethritis ↓ Neisseria gonorrhoeae
exam_trap: A, Chlamydia trachomatis — it tempts because it is the commonest bacterial STI in the UK, but it is usually silent or causes a scanty mucoid discharge rather than a copious purulent one.
takeaway: A thick purulent urethral discharge soon after exposure in a man suggests gonorrhoea.

presentation: Carcinoma Of The Head Of Pancreas
stem: A 71-year-old woman sees her GP because her family noticed her eyes turning yellow. She has had generalised itching for two weeks, her urine looks like strong tea and her stools have become pale. Her clothes have become loose over the last few months. She has had no abdominal pain or fever. On examination a smooth, non-tender mass is felt below the right costal margin. Which cause is most likely?

options.D: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas

correct_answer: D. Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
why_correct: Painless obstructive jaundice with pruritus, dark urine, pale stools and weight loss in an older adult strongly suggests a malignant obstruction of the distal bile duct, most often a pancreatic head tumour. A palpable, non-tender gallbladder supports this (Courvoisier sign). She needs urgent assessment and imaging on a suspected cancer pathway.
why_wrong: A. A duct stone usually causes biliary-type pain and often fever, and the gallbladder is typically fibrosed rather than palpable. B. Hepatitis A causes a prodromal illness and is not associated with months of weight loss. C. Primary biliary cholangitis is a slowly progressive condition mainly of middle-aged women with itch and fatigue, not rapid painless obstruction. E. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated jaundice with normal urine and stool colour.
pearl: In painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder, stones are unlikely and malignancy is likely. Weight loss raises suspicion further.
thinking: Painless jaundice with pale stools and dark urine ↓ obstructive (post-hepatic) picture ↓ weight loss and palpable non-tender gallbladder ↓ malignant distal bile duct obstruction ↓ Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
exam_trap: A, Common bile duct stone — it tempts because it is the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice, but stones usually cause pain and a fibrosed gallbladder, while painless jaundice, weight loss and a palpable gallbladder suggest malignancy.
takeaway: Painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss in an older adult suggests pancreatic head cancer.

stem: A 68-year-old man who smokes and drinks heavily tells his GP that for three months food has been sticking behind his breastbone. At first it was only bread and meat, but he now struggles with soup and has lost a noticeable amount of weight. He has had longstanding heartburn. Which diagnosis is of greatest concern?
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia, first for solids and then for liquids, with weight loss in an older smoker and drinker indicates an enlarging obstructing lesion and is highly suspicious of oesophageal cancer. Longstanding reflux adds a risk of adenocarcinoma. NICE recommends urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for dysphagia.
why_wrong: B. Achalasia typically causes difficulty with both solids and liquids from the outset, often in younger patients, with regurgitation. C. A pharyngeal pouch causes high dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis. D. A benign stricture from reflux can cause solid dysphagia but rarely progresses so quickly with significant weight loss. E. Oesophageal candidiasis causes painful swallowing, usually in immunosuppressed patients.
pearl: Dysphagia that progresses from solids to liquids with weight loss is malignant until proven otherwise. Any new dysphagia warrants urgent endoscopy.
thinking: Older smoker and drinker with reflux ↓ dysphagia worsening from solids to liquids ↓ weight loss ↓ progressive mechanical obstruction ↓ Oesophageal carcinoma
exam_trap: B, Achalasia — it tempts because it also involves difficulty with liquids, but in achalasia solids and liquids are affected from the start, whereas a solids-then-liquids progression with weight loss points to a growing tumour.
takeaway: Progressive solids-to-liquids dysphagia with weight loss needs urgent endoscopy for cancer.

stem: A 69-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, who stopped his anticoagulant a month ago because of nosebleeds, comes to the emergency department three hours after the abrupt onset of severe pain in his right calf. The right foot is white and cold to touch, he has pins and needles in his toes, and no pulses can be felt below the femoral artery. The left leg is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Sudden pain, pallor, coldness, paraesthesia and absent pulses describe acute arterial occlusion. Atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation makes an embolus the likely source. This is a vascular emergency: give analgesia, start heparin and seek urgent vascular surgical review to save the limb.
why_wrong: A. A deep vein thrombosis makes the leg swollen, warm and red, with pulses preserved. B. A ruptured Baker cyst causes calf pain and swelling but does not abolish pulses or make the foot white and cold. C. Nerve root pain does not cause pallor, coldness or absent pulses. D. Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia develops over weeks to months with rest pain or tissue loss, not abrupt onset over hours.
pearl: Sudden onset is the key discriminator: atrial fibrillation plus a pale, cold, pulseless limb suggests embolism and needs immediate vascular referral.
thinking: Abrupt severe limb pain ↓ pale, cold, pulseless foot with paraesthesia ↓ untreated atrial fibrillation as embolic source ↓ sudden arterial occlusion ↓ Acute limb ischaemia
exam_trap: D, Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia — it tempts because it also involves poor arterial supply, but the onset over hours and the embolic source define this as acute ischaemia, which needs emergency treatment.
takeaway: A suddenly pale, cold, pulseless limb is acute limb ischaemia: heparin and urgent vascular review.

stem: A 64-year-old man is reviewed at the practice nurse leg clinic with a shallow, sloughy wound just above the inner ankle that has been present for four months. He has prominent varicose veins, the skin around the ankle is hard, eczematous and stained brown, and his legs ache by the end of the day. Both foot pulses are easily felt. Which type of ulcer is this?
why_correct: Venous ulcers occur in the gaiter area, often over the medial malleolus, and are shallow with sloping edges. Surrounding haemosiderin staining, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis and varicose veins reflect chronic venous hypertension. An ankle-brachial pressure index should be checked before starting compression therapy.
why_wrong: A. Arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out, on the foot or toes, with absent pulses. C. Neuropathic ulcers occur on pressure points of the sole in a numb foot. D. Malignant change is possible in a long-standing ulcer but is not the likeliest cause given these classic venous features. E. Pyoderma gangrenosum produces a rapidly enlarging, painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined edge.
pearl: Gaiter area, sloping edge, brown staining and varicose veins indicate a venous ulcer. Always check arterial supply before compression.
thinking: Chronic shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus ↓ haemosiderin staining, eczema and hardened skin ↓ varicose veins with palpable pulses ↓ chronic venous hypertension ↓ Venous ulcer
exam_trap: A, Arterial ulcer — it tempts because it is the other main cause of chronic leg ulcers, but arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out, on the foot and occur with absent pulses.
takeaway: A shallow gaiter-area ulcer with brown staining and varicose veins is venous: check ABPI, then compress.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends her annual diabetic review. The nurse finds a painless, round ulcer surrounded by thick callus on the sole beneath the ball of her right big toe. She was unaware of it. She cannot feel the monofilament at several sites on either foot, but her feet are warm and the foot pulses are bounding. Which mechanism best explains the ulcer?

options.A: Loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy
options.B: Critical ischaemia from peripheral arterial disease

correct_answer: A. Loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy
why_correct: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy removes protective sensation, so repeated pressure over a bony prominence such as the first metatarsal head goes unnoticed and causes callus and then ulceration. The ulcer is painless and the foot is warm with good pulses. She needs same-day referral to the diabetic foot protection or multidisciplinary foot service.
why_wrong: B. Ischaemic ulcers are usually painful, on the toes or heel, with a cool foot and weak or absent pulses. C. Venous ulcers occur around the ankle, not under the forefoot. D. Gouty tophi lie over joints and are rarely the cause of a plantar pressure ulcer. E. Vasculitic ulcers are usually painful, multiple and accompanied by purpura.
pearl: A painless plantar ulcer with callus in a warm, numb foot with good pulses is neuropathic. Diabetic foot ulcers need urgent specialist foot team referral.
thinking: Diabetes with loss of monofilament sensation ↓ painless ulcer with callus under a pressure point ↓ warm foot with bounding pulses, so circulation intact ↓ unnoticed repetitive pressure ↓ Loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy
exam_trap: B, Critical ischaemia from peripheral arterial disease — it tempts because arterial disease is common in diabetes, but the warm foot with bounding pulses and a painless callused ulcer point to neuropathy.
takeaway: Painless, callused plantar ulcer in a warm, numb diabetic foot is neuropathic.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department three weeks after a caesarean section. This morning she developed a sharp pain in the right side of her chest that catches when she breathes in, together with sudden breathlessness. Her pulse is 112/min and oxygen saturation is lower than expected on air. Breath sounds are normal and equal on both sides, and she has no cough or fever. Which condition is the leading concern?
why_correct: The postpartum period, especially after caesarean section, carries a high risk of venous thromboembolism. Sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness, tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest are typical of pulmonary embolism. She should be assessed promptly, with anticoagulation started while awaiting imaging unless contraindicated.
why_wrong: A. A pneumothorax would usually reduce breath sounds on the affected side. B. Pericarditis causes central pain eased by sitting forward, usually without hypoxia. D. Pneumonia would usually cause fever, cough and focal chest signs. E. Costochondritis causes reproducible chest wall tenderness without tachycardia or hypoxia.
pearl: In a postpartum woman, sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness, tachycardia and hypoxia but a clear chest is pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise.
thinking: Recent caesarean section, a strong thrombotic risk ↓ sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness ↓ tachycardia and hypoxia ↓ clear chest with equal breath sounds ↓ Pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: A, Spontaneous pneumothorax — it tempts because of sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness, but breath sounds are equal and normal, and the postpartum state points to thromboembolism.
takeaway: Postpartum sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness and hypoxia with a clear chest suggests pulmonary embolism.

stem: A 72-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after suddenly being unable to get his words out at breakfast and dropping his cup from his right hand. Examination shows right arm and facial weakness with expressive dysphasia. His pulse is irregularly irregular and he takes no regular medication. A CT scan of the head shows no haemorrhage. By what process has this event probably occurred?

options.E: Embolism of thrombus from the left atrium

correct_answer: E. Embolism of thrombus from the left atrium
why_correct: In atrial fibrillation, disorganised atrial contraction allows blood stasis and thrombus formation, particularly in the left atrial appendage. Thrombus can embolise to a cerebral artery, producing a sudden cortical deficit such as dysphasia with arm and face weakness. Untreated atrial fibrillation is a major, preventable cause of ischaemic stroke.
why_wrong: A. Lacunar infarcts cause pure motor or pure sensory deficits without cortical signs such as dysphasia. B. Haemorrhage has been excluded on CT. C. Carotid dissection is more typical in younger patients, often with neck pain or Horner syndrome after trauma. D. Todd paresis follows a seizure, and none was described.
pearl: Cortical signs such as dysphasia plus an irregularly irregular pulse suggest a cardioembolic stroke. Secondary prevention includes anticoagulation once safe.
thinking: Sudden focal deficit with dysphasia ↓ cortical, territorial stroke ↓ no haemorrhage on CT ↓ irregularly irregular pulse, untreated ↓ Embolism of thrombus from the left atrium
exam_trap: A, Lacunar infarction from small-vessel disease — it tempts because it is common in older people with vascular risk, but lacunar strokes do not cause cortical signs such as dysphasia, and atrial fibrillation points to embolism.
takeaway: Stroke with cortical signs in untreated atrial fibrillation is cardioembolic until proven otherwise.

stem: A 66-year-old woman telephones her GP surgery. An hour ago, while watching television, the vision in her right eye went dark as if a light had been switched off. Her left eye is unaffected. She has no eye pain, redness or headache, and she has never had anything similar. How should the GP handle this call?

options.A: Book a routine optometrist appointment this week
options.B: Arrange immediate same-day emergency eye assessment
options.C: Offer a routine GP appointment next week
options.E: Advise rest and to call back if not better in two days

correct_answer: B. Arrange immediate same-day emergency eye assessment
why_correct: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye may be due to central retinal artery occlusion, giant cell arteritis, vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment, all of which threaten sight. She needs immediate assessment by emergency eye services, and an arterial occlusion should also be treated as a stroke-equivalent event needing vascular work-up.
why_wrong: A. A routine optometry review delays assessment of a potentially sight-threatening emergency. C. Waiting a week risks permanent visual loss and misses a possible vascular event. D. Antibiotic drops treat conjunctivitis, which does not cause visual loss. E. Watching and waiting is unsafe for sudden visual loss.
pearl: Sudden painless monocular visual loss is an emergency. Think retinal artery occlusion, giant cell arteritis, retinal detachment and vitreous haemorrhage, and refer the same day.
thinking: Sudden loss of vision in one eye ↓ painless, white eye ↓ possible retinal vascular occlusion or other sight-threatening cause ↓ time-critical ↓ Arrange immediate same-day emergency eye assessment
exam_trap: A, Book a routine optometrist appointment this week — it tempts because optometrists see many eye problems, but sudden visual loss needs emergency specialist assessment, not a routine check.
takeaway: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye always needs same-day emergency assessment.

stem: A 79-year-old man is brought to the GP by his daughter, who says the television is always too loud and he struggles to follow family conversations at restaurants. He feels his hearing has slowly declined over several years in both ears equally. He has no ear pain, discharge or dizziness. Otoscopy shows clear canals and normal eardrums, Rinne testing is positive on both sides and the Weber test is central. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Presbycusis is age-related, bilateral, symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss that usually affects high frequencies first. Patients struggle most with speech against background noise. Tuning fork tests are consistent with sensorineural loss, and management is referral for audiology assessment and hearing aids.
why_wrong: A. Otosclerosis causes conductive loss, usually in younger adults, with a negative Rinne test. B. Earwax would be seen on otoscopy and causes conductive loss. D. A vestibular schwannoma typically causes unilateral or asymmetrical hearing loss with tinnitus. E. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss.
pearl: Gradual, symmetrical hearing loss in an older adult, worst in background noise, with normal otoscopy is presbycusis. Asymmetrical loss needs further investigation.
thinking: Older adult with gradual hearing loss ↓ bilateral and symmetrical ↓ normal otoscopy, tuning fork tests suggest sensorineural loss ↓ no vertigo or unilateral features ↓ Presbycusis
exam_trap: B, Impacted earwax — it tempts because it is a common, treatable cause of hearing loss in older people, but the canals are clear on otoscopy and the tuning fork findings indicate sensorineural loss.
takeaway: Slowly progressive, symmetrical hearing loss in older age with normal ears is presbycusis.

stem: An 84-year-old care home resident is found on the floor of her bathroom. She has severe pain in her left groin and cannot lift her left leg from the trolley. The left foot points outwards and the left leg looks shorter than the right. There is no deformity at the knee or ankle. Which injury is most likely?
why_correct: A fall in an older person followed by groin pain, inability to raise the leg, and shortening with external rotation is the classic presentation of a proximal femoral fracture. She needs analgesia, including consideration of a nerve block, hip radiographs, and early orthogeriatric and surgical input, ideally with surgery within a day of admission.
why_wrong: A. A pubic ramus fracture causes groin pain after a fall but does not usually produce shortening and external rotation. B. Posterior hip dislocation shortens the leg but rotates it internally and usually follows high-energy trauma or hip replacement. C. Trochanteric bursitis causes lateral hip pain without deformity or inability to lift the leg. E. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute shortening and rotation after a fall.
pearl: Shortened and externally rotated after a fall indicates a hip fracture; shortened and internally rotated suggests posterior dislocation.
thinking: Older patient after a fall ↓ groin pain, unable to lift leg ↓ shortened, externally rotated limb ↓ fracture of the proximal femur ↓ Proximal femoral (hip) fracture
exam_trap: A, Pubic ramus fracture — it tempts because it also causes groin pain after a fall in older people, but it does not usually cause leg shortening and external rotation.
takeaway: Fall plus shortened, externally rotated leg in an older person means hip fracture.

stem: A 58-year-old publican, who has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for forty years, sees his GP because his voice has been croaky and rough for over a month. He had no cold beforehand, has no sore throat and the hoarseness has not improved. Examination of the neck is normal. What should the GP do next?

options.A: A course of oral amoxicillin and review
options.B: A trial of a proton pump inhibitor for reflux
options.C: Referral on the suspected cancer pathway to ENT
options.E: Voice rest and review in three months

correct_answer: C. Referral on the suspected cancer pathway to ENT
why_correct: Persistent, unexplained hoarseness in an older adult, especially a smoker, is a red-flag symptom for laryngeal cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance supports urgent referral to ENT so that the larynx can be examined directly. Early diagnosis greatly improves outcomes and the chance of preserving the voice.
why_wrong: A. There is no evidence of infection, and antibiotics would delay diagnosis. B. Treating presumed reflux would delay investigation of a red-flag symptom. D. A routine referral is too slow for possible cancer. E. Prolonged voice rest delays the diagnosis of a possible laryngeal tumour.
pearl: Hoarseness that persists without explanation in an older smoker needs urgent ENT assessment to visualise the larynx.
thinking: Older heavy smoker ↓ persistent hoarseness with no preceding infection ↓ red flag for laryngeal malignancy ↓ needs direct laryngeal examination quickly ↓ Referral on the suspected cancer pathway to ENT
exam_trap: B, A trial of a proton pump inhibitor for reflux — it tempts because reflux is a common cause of hoarseness, but in an older smoker with persistent symptoms an empirical trial delays urgent exclusion of cancer.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in an older smoker needs an urgent suspected cancer referral.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother. Yesterday evening he had a vague ache around his navel, but overnight it became a sharp pain in the right lower abdomen, made worse by coughing and by bumps during the car journey. He has not wanted to eat and has vomited once. His temperature is 37.9°C, he is tender with guarding in the right iliac fossa, and examination of the testes is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Visceral periumbilical pain that migrates to the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed, with anorexia, vomiting, low-grade fever and localised guarding, is the classic presentation of acute appendicitis. Pain worsened by coughing or movement reflects peritoneal irritation. He needs surgical review, analgesia and appropriate investigations.
why_wrong: B. Mesenteric adenitis usually follows a viral illness, with less localised tenderness and no guarding. C. Testicular torsion can refer pain to the abdomen, but the testes are normal. D. Gastroenteritis causes diarrhoea and generalised cramps without migrating localised pain and guarding. E. Meckel diverticulitis is rare and much less likely than appendicitis with this classic pattern.
pearl: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with anorexia is appendicitis. Always examine the testes in boys with lower abdominal pain.
thinking: Vague periumbilical pain ↓ shifts to right iliac fossa and worsens with movement ↓ anorexia, vomiting, low-grade fever ↓ localised peritonism ↓ Acute appendicitis
exam_trap: B, Mesenteric adenitis — it tempts because it mimics appendicitis in young people, but it usually follows a viral illness and lacks the migrating pain and localised guarding seen here.
takeaway: Central pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with anorexia and guarding means appendicitis.

stem: A 45-year-old man attends his GP with a painless swelling of the left side of his scrotum which has slowly enlarged over several months. The swelling is smooth and fluctuant, the examiner can get above it, and no separate testis is palpable within it. It glows brightly when a pen torch is held against it. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: A hydrocele is fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis, so the testis cannot be felt separately and the swelling transilluminates. Being able to get above it shows it is confined to the scrotum. Ultrasound is advised in adults to exclude an underlying testicular cause.
why_wrong: A. An epididymal cyst also transilluminates, but it lies separate from and usually above the testis, which can be felt distinctly. B. An inguinal hernia extends from the groin, so the examiner cannot get above it, and it does not usually transilluminate. C. A varicocele feels like a bag of worms and does not transilluminate. D. A testicular tumour is a firm, solid mass that does not transilluminate.
pearl: Transilluminates and testis not separately palpable indicates hydrocele; transilluminates and testis separate suggests epididymal cyst. Scan new hydroceles in adults.
thinking: Painless scrotal swelling ↓ can get above it, so confined to scrotum ↓ transilluminates, so fluid-filled ↓ testis not separately palpable ↓ Hydrocele
exam_trap: A, Epididymal cyst — it tempts because it also transilluminates, but an epididymal cyst lies separate from the testis, which can be felt distinctly.
takeaway: A transilluminating scrotal swelling surrounding an impalpable testis is a hydrocele.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with three children is seen in the gynaecology clinic with periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful over two years. Bimanual examination finds a symmetrically bulky, soft and tender uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows diffuse thickening of the myometrium with a heterogeneous texture, but no discrete masses. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium, typically in parous women in their late thirties and forties. It causes heavy, painful periods and a diffusely enlarged, boggy, tender uterus. Ultrasound shows diffuse, heterogeneous myometrial thickening rather than well-defined fibroids.
why_wrong: A. Fibroids cause an irregularly enlarged, firm uterus and appear as discrete, well-defined masses on ultrasound. B. Endometrial cancer typically presents with postmenopausal or intermenstrual bleeding, not progressive painful periods with a uniformly bulky uterus. C. Endometriosis causes cyclical pain and dyspareunia, usually with a normal-sized uterus. E. A polyp causes intermenstrual bleeding and is seen within the cavity, not as diffuse myometrial change.
pearl: Bulky, boggy, tender, symmetrically enlarged uterus in a parous woman with heavy painful periods suggests adenomyosis; discrete masses suggest fibroids.
thinking: Parous woman in her forties ↓ progressive heavy, painful periods ↓ uniformly bulky, tender uterus ↓ diffuse myometrial thickening without discrete masses ↓ Adenomyosis
exam_trap: A, Uterine fibroids — it tempts because fibroids are the commonest cause of heavy bleeding with an enlarged uterus, but they appear as discrete masses and make the uterus irregular rather than diffusely bulky and tender.
takeaway: Heavy painful periods with a diffusely bulky, tender uterus is adenomyosis.

presentation: Suspected Non-Accidental Injury In An Infant
stem: A 7-month-old baby is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a cold. While examining him the doctor notices several bruises on both cheeks and on the upper arms. The parents say he must have knocked himself against the cot bars. He is not yet rolling over or crawling and otherwise appears well. Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Reassure the parents and discharge with cold advice
options.B: Ask the health visitor to review him next week
options.C: Follow local safeguarding procedures, involving a senior and the safeguarding team
options.D: Tell the parents that you believe they have hurt him
options.E: Check a clotting screen and discharge if it is normal

correct_answer: C. Follow local safeguarding procedures, involving a senior and the safeguarding team
why_correct: Bruising in a baby who is not yet mobile is uncommon and should raise concern about physical abuse, especially on the face and arms with an implausible explanation. The doctor should document findings carefully, discuss with a senior and the safeguarding lead, and follow local child protection procedures, which may include referral to children's social care. Medical causes of bruising are considered as part of that assessment, not instead of it.
why_wrong: A. Discharging an infant with unexplained bruising may leave him at risk of further harm. B. Deferring to a later health visitor review delays safeguarding action. D. Confronting the parents with an accusation is inappropriate and may increase the risk to the child. E. Clotting tests may form part of the assessment, but discharging on a normal result ignores the safeguarding concern.
pearl: Bruising in a non-mobile infant is a red flag. Those who don't cruise rarely bruise: escalate through safeguarding procedures.
thinking: Infant who is not yet mobile ↓ bruises on face and arms ↓ explanation does not fit his development ↓ possible non-accidental injury ↓ Follow local safeguarding procedures, involving a senior and the safeguarding team
exam_trap: E, Check a clotting screen and discharge if it is normal — it tempts because a bleeding disorder is a valid differential, but a normal result does not remove the safeguarding concern, and investigations should be part of a safeguarding assessment, not a substitute.
takeaway: Any bruising in a non-mobile baby requires escalation through local safeguarding procedures.

presentation: Refusal Of Treatment By A Patient With Capacity
stem: A 54-year-old man on the surgical ward has had several admissions with gallstone pain and is offered a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. After a full discussion he declines surgery. He can explain the likely risks of further attacks, weighs them against his fear of operations and gives a consistent answer on two occasions. His wife is upset and asks the team to go ahead anyway. Which is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Ask his wife to sign the consent form on his behalf
options.B: Respect his decision, document the discussion and keep the option open
options.C: Proceed with surgery in his best interests
options.D: Apply to the Court of Protection to authorise surgery
options.E: Delay his discharge until he agrees to the operation

correct_answer: B. Respect his decision, document the discussion and keep the option open
why_correct: An adult with capacity can refuse treatment, even when the decision seems unwise to the team. The doctor should ensure he has the information he needs, document the discussion and his capacity, explain the warning signs that should prompt him to seek help, and make clear that he can change his mind. Relatives cannot consent for an adult who has capacity.
why_wrong: A. Relatives have no authority to consent for an adult with capacity. C. Best-interests decisions apply only when a patient lacks capacity. D. Court involvement is not needed when a capacitous adult has made a clear decision. E. Holding him in hospital to coerce agreement is unlawful and unethical.
pearl: Capacity is decision-specific and presumed in adults. An unwise decision is not proof of incapacity, and a capacitous refusal must be respected.
thinking: Adult offered elective surgery ↓ understands, retains, weighs and communicates his choice ↓ has capacity for this decision ↓ capacitous refusal is binding ↓ Respect his decision, document the discussion and keep the option open
exam_trap: C, Proceed with surgery in his best interests — it tempts because the team believes surgery would help, but best interests apply only to a person who lacks capacity, which he does not.
takeaway: An adult with capacity may refuse treatment; respect it, document it and leave the door open.

stem: A foundation doctor on a night shift is asked to review a 70-year-old woman's drug chart. He realises that because of a transcription error she was given an extra dose of amlodipine this evening. She is alert, comfortable and her blood pressure is satisfactory. How should he respond?

options.A: Take no further action as she has come to no harm
options.B: Rewrite the chart so the error is no longer visible
options.C: Ask the nurse who gave the dose to complete the incident report
options.D: Tell the patient only if she later develops symptoms
options.E: Ensure she is safe, inform a senior, be open with her, document and report the incident

correct_answer: E. Ensure she is safe, inform a senior, be open with her, document and report the incident
why_correct: When a medication error is found, the first step is to make sure the patient is safe and monitored, then correct the chart. GMC guidance on openness means the patient should be told what happened and offered an apology, a senior should be informed, the event documented accurately, and a report made through the local incident system so that the trust can learn from it, even when no harm has occurred.
why_wrong: A. Errors without harm should still be reported, as they reveal system weaknesses. B. Altering records to conceal an error is dishonest and a serious probity breach. C. The doctor who identified the error shares responsibility for reporting it rather than passing it on. D. Patients should be told about errors that could have harmed them, not only those that do.
pearl: For any medication error: patient safety first, then tell a senior, be honest with the patient, document accurately and file an incident report.
thinking: Medication error identified ↓ check and secure patient safety ↓ escalate to a senior ↓ be open and document ↓ Ensure she is safe, inform a senior, be open with her, document and report the incident
exam_trap: D, Tell the patient only if she later develops symptoms — it tempts because she appears unharmed and disclosure may seem to cause needless worry, but openness applies to errors that could have caused harm, not only to those that did.
takeaway: Medication errors, even harmless ones, need patient safety, honesty, escalation, documentation and reporting.

stem: A 62-year-old woman attends the emergency department with swelling of her lower lip and the left side of her tongue that developed over a few hours this morning. It is not itchy and there is no rash or wheeze. Her voice is normal and oxygen saturation is normal on air. She has hypertension treated with ramipril, which she has taken for 18 months, and has never had swelling before. Which is the most likely cause?

options.A: Angioedema due to her ACE inhibitor
options.D: Allergic contact dermatitis from a lip product

correct_answer: A. Angioedema due to her ACE inhibitor
why_correct: ACE inhibitors reduce the breakdown of bradykinin, which can cause non-itchy angioedema of the lips, tongue and face without urticaria. It can appear at any time, even after months or years of treatment. The ACE inhibitor must be stopped permanently, the airway monitored closely and the reaction recorded, as antihistamines and adrenaline often work less well than in allergic angioedema.
why_wrong: B. Anaphylaxis usually has a trigger exposure with rapid onset and features such as urticaria, wheeze or hypotension. C. Hereditary angioedema usually presents in childhood or adolescence with a family history. D. Contact dermatitis causes an itchy, eczematous rash rather than deep tongue swelling. E. Ludwig angina is a floor-of-mouth infection with fever, pain and dental sepsis.
pearl: ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, without itch or wheals, and can start years into treatment. Stop the drug permanently and watch the airway.
thinking: Lip and tongue swelling ↓ no itch, urticaria or wheeze ↓ bradykinin rather than histamine mechanism ↓ long-term ACE inhibitor use ↓ Angioedema due to her ACE inhibitor
exam_trap: B, Anaphylaxis — it tempts because facial and tongue swelling suggests an allergic emergency, but there is no urticaria, wheeze or haemodynamic compromise, and the non-itchy swelling in a patient on ramipril indicates bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
takeaway: Non-itchy lip or tongue swelling in a patient on an ACE inhibitor suggests drug angioedema.

stem: A 54-year-old woman is on day one after a hip replacement and has a morphine patient-controlled analgesia device. She also has chronic kidney disease. A nurse calls the doctor because she is very difficult to rouse. Her respiratory rate is 7/min, her pupils are pinpoint and her oxygen saturation is falling. Her airway is being supported and she is receiving oxygen. Which drug is now needed without delay?
why_correct: Reduced consciousness, a slow respiratory rate and pinpoint pupils in a patient receiving morphine indicate opioid toxicity, made more likely by reduced renal clearance of morphine metabolites. Alongside airway support and oxygen, the opioid antagonist naloxone should be given intravenously in titrated doses, and the analgesia device stopped. Because naloxone is short-acting, she needs continued monitoring and possibly repeated doses or an infusion.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids. C. Atropine treats bradycardia or organophosphate poisoning, not opioid respiratory depression. D. Activated charcoal is for recent oral ingestion and is unsafe with a reduced level of consciousness. E. Sodium bicarbonate is used in tricyclic antidepressant toxicity, not opioid toxicity.
pearl: Pinpoint pupils, drowsiness and slow breathing indicate opioid toxicity. Give naloxone, and remember that renal impairment allows morphine metabolites to accumulate.
thinking: Drowsy patient receiving morphine ↓ pinpoint pupils and slow breathing ↓ renal impairment causing accumulation ↓ opioid toxicity ↓ Naloxone
exam_trap: A, Flumazenil — it tempts because it is another reversal agent for sedation, but it only antagonises benzodiazepines and has no effect on opioid respiratory depression.
takeaway: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression after opioids: support the airway and give naloxone.

stem: A 36-year-old man started carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia three weeks ago. He telephones his GP surgery and is seen at home: for two days he has had a high temperature and sore, red eyes, then painful ulcers on his lips and inside his mouth. Today dusky red patches have spread across his chest and back, and some areas are blistering, with skin peeling when touched. What should the GP do now?

options.A: Continue carbamazepine and start oral prednisolone
options.B: Apply a potent topical steroid and review in one week
options.C: Switch to phenytoin and review in a few days
options.D: Start oral aciclovir for herpetic stomatitis
options.E: Stop carbamazepine and arrange emergency hospital admission

correct_answer: E. Stop carbamazepine and arrange emergency hospital admission
why_correct: Fever, conjunctivitis, painful mucosal ulceration and spreading dusky lesions with blistering and skin detachment soon after starting carbamazepine indicate Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single most important step, followed by urgent admission for specialist dermatology, ophthalmology and supportive care, often in a burns or intensive care setting. The reaction should be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.
why_wrong: A. Continuing the culprit drug allows the reaction to progress, and oral steroids are not a substitute for admission. B. This is a life-threatening skin failure that cannot be managed with topical treatment in the community. C. Phenytoin is another aromatic anticonvulsant that can cross-react and cause the same reaction. D. Herpes does not explain the widespread blistering rash with skin detachment, and delaying admission is dangerous.
pearl: Fever, mucosal erosions and blistering skin with peeling after a new drug indicates SJS or TEN. Stop the drug and admit urgently; aromatic anticonvulsants are common culprits.
thinking: Recently started carbamazepine ↓ fever and sore eyes, then mouth ulcers ↓ spreading dusky lesions with blistering and skin detachment ↓ severe cutaneous drug reaction ↓ Stop carbamazepine and arrange emergency hospital admission
exam_trap: D, Start oral aciclovir for herpetic stomatitis — it tempts because painful mouth ulcers suggest herpes, but the conjunctivitis, widespread blistering and skin peeling after a new drug indicate SJS or TEN.
takeaway: Suspected SJS or TEN: stop the culprit drug at once and admit as an emergency.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy is started on carbamazepine by the neurology team. She has used the combined pill for several years and is in a stable relationship.
