She asks her GP whether she needs to think about anything regarding her pill. What is the key issue to discuss?

options.A: Her pill will raise carbamazepine to toxic levels
options.B: Carbamazepine will cause her periods to stop permanently
options.C: Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
options.D: Her pill will lower carbamazepine levels and worsen seizure control
options.E: There is no clinically relevant interaction

correct_answer: C. Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
why_correct: Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes, which speed up the metabolism of oestrogen and progestogen and reduce the contraceptive effectiveness of the combined pill. She should be advised to use a method unaffected by enzyme inducers, such as a copper or levonorgestrel intrauterine device or the progestogen-only injection, in line with FSRH guidance. Pre-pregnancy counselling about antiseizure medicines is also important.
why_wrong: A. The pill does not significantly increase carbamazepine levels. B. Carbamazepine does not cause permanent amenorrhoea. D. Combined pills reduce lamotrigine levels, not carbamazepine levels. E. The interaction is clinically important and can lead to unplanned pregnancy.
pearl: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception. Intrauterine methods or the progestogen-only injection remain reliable.
thinking: Combined pill user ↓ starts carbamazepine ↓ hepatic enzyme induction ↓ faster metabolism of contraceptive hormones ↓ Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
exam_trap: D, Her pill will lower carbamazepine levels and worsen seizure control — it tempts because combined pills do lower lamotrigine levels, but with carbamazepine the problem is the other way round: the antiseizure drug weakens the pill.
takeaway: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs make the combined pill unreliable; switch to an unaffected method.

stem: An 18-year-old woman visits her practice nurse before moving into university halls of residence. Her records show she was absent from school on the day of the Year 9 meningococcal immunisation and has never had it since. She is otherwise fully immunised. She asks which vaccine will protect her against the meningococcal groups covered by the routine teenage programme. Which vaccine should be offered?
why_correct: The routine UK adolescent programme includes the MenACWY conjugate vaccine, which protects against meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y and reduces carriage in teenagers. Those who missed it remain eligible for a catch-up dose up to their 25th birthday, and first-time university entrants are specifically encouraged to have it. She should be offered MenACWY now.
why_wrong: A. MenB vaccine is given in the infant programme and does not protect against groups A, C, W or Y. B. Hib/MenC covers only group C, and is not the adolescent vaccine. C. HPV vaccine protects against human papillomavirus, not meningococcal disease. E. Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine protects against pneumococcus and is used mainly for older and at-risk groups.
pearl: MenACWY is the routine teenage meningococcal vaccine, and people who missed it can catch up until their 25th birthday. Encourage it before university.
thinking: Teenager who missed the school meningococcal dose ↓ moving into shared university accommodation ↓ adolescent vaccine covers groups A, C, W and Y ↓ catch-up eligibility applies ↓ MenACWY conjugate vaccine
exam_trap: A, MenB vaccine — it tempts because group B is an important cause of meningococcal disease, but MenB is part of the infant schedule and does not cover the groups in the adolescent programme.
takeaway: Missed the teenage meningococcal dose? Offer MenACWY catch-up, especially before university.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the GP because he has been limping on and off for six weeks and sometimes complains that his left knee aches after football. He has had no injury, fever or recent illness. He looks well and is afebrile. Examination of the knee is normal, but internal rotation and abduction of the left hip are reduced and uncomfortable. Which condition best explains his symptoms?
why_correct: Perthes disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head, most common in boys of primary school age. It typically causes an insidious limp with hip, thigh or referred knee pain in a well child, with reduced internal rotation and abduction of the hip. Hip radiographs should be arranged with referral to paediatric orthopaedics.
why_wrong: A. Transient synovitis develops acutely, often after a viral illness, and settles within days to a couple of weeks. B. A slipped capital femoral epiphysis is typical of overweight adolescents rather than a young child. C. Septic arthritis presents acutely with fever, an unwell child and refusal to bear weight. D. Osgood-Schlatter disease causes tibial tuberosity pain in adolescents, with abnormal knee examination findings.
pearl: Knee pain in a child may come from the hip, so always examine the hip. An insidious limp in a well child of primary school age suggests Perthes disease.
thinking: Primary school-aged boy ↓ weeks of intermittent limp, knee pain with normal knee ↓ well and afebrile ↓ restricted internal rotation and abduction of the hip ↓ Perthes disease
exam_trap: A, Transient synovitis — it tempts because it is the commonest cause of a limp in a well young child, but it is acute and short-lived, whereas six weeks of symptoms with restricted hip movement suggest Perthes disease.
takeaway: Weeks of limp and referred knee pain in a well young boy point to Perthes disease: examine the hip.

presentation: Contraception For A Competent Young Person
stem: A 15-year-old girl attends her GP alone and asks to start the contraceptive pill. She is in a relationship with a boyfriend of similar age and says the relationship is consensual, with no signs of pressure or exploitation. She understands the benefits, risks and how to take the pill, but despite encouragement she does not want her parents to know. She is likely to continue having sex without contraception. Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Refuse to prescribe without parental consent
options.B: Prescribe, but inform her parents after the consultation
options.C: Advise her to return when she reaches 16
options.D: Provide contraception confidentially, having assessed her competence and the Fraser criteria
options.E: Make a safeguarding referral for all sexual activity under 16

correct_answer: D. Provide contraception confidentially, having assessed her competence and the Fraser criteria
why_correct: Young people under 16 can consent to their own treatment if they have sufficient maturity and understanding (Gillick competence). For contraception, the Fraser guidelines also apply: she understands the advice, cannot be persuaded to involve her parents, is likely to continue having sex, her health may suffer without contraception, and treatment is in her best interests. Confidentiality should be respected, while remaining alert to safeguarding concerns such as exploitation or a large age gap.
why_wrong: A. Parental consent is not required for a competent young person meeting the Fraser criteria. B. Informing her parents breaches confidentiality without justification. C. Delaying contraception exposes her to the risk of unplanned pregnancy. E. Sexual activity at this age does not automatically require referral when there are no safeguarding concerns, though every case needs assessment.
pearl: Under 16s can consent to contraception if Gillick competent and the Fraser criteria are met. Always assess for exploitation, and note that sexual activity under 13 always requires safeguarding action.
thinking: Young person under 16 requesting contraception ↓ understands and weighs the information ↓ declines parental involvement, will continue sex ↓ no safeguarding concerns identified ↓ Provide contraception confidentially, having assessed her competence and the Fraser criteria
exam_trap: E, Make a safeguarding referral for all sexual activity under 16 — it tempts because she is under the age of consent, but referral depends on an individual risk assessment, and a consensual relationship with a peer of similar age without exploitation does not automatically need one.
takeaway: A competent under-16 meeting the Fraser criteria can receive confidential contraception.

presentation: Disclosure Of Abuse By A Young Person
stem: A 13-year-old girl attends the emergency department with a wrist injury she says happened when she fell. While the doctor is applying a splint, she says quietly that her stepfather hits her when he has been drinking and that he caused the injury. She pleads for it to be kept secret because things will get worse at home. How should the doctor respond?

options.A: Explain that this cannot be kept secret and follow local safeguarding procedures
options.B: Keep the disclosure confidential, as she has asked
options.C: Telephone the stepfather to hear his account
options.D: Discharge with a leaflet and ask her GP to follow up
options.E: Take action only if she repeats the allegation later

correct_answer: A. Explain that this cannot be kept secret and follow local safeguarding procedures
why_correct: A disclosure of physical abuse means the child may be at risk of serious harm, which justifies sharing information without consent. The doctor should listen, reassure her that telling was right, explain honestly that this information must be shared to keep her safe, document her words, and follow local safeguarding procedures with the safeguarding lead and children's social care. Immediate safety must be considered before she is discharged.
why_wrong: B. Confidentiality can be overridden when a child is at risk of serious harm. C. Contacting the alleged abuser may increase the danger to her and compromise any investigation. D. Discharging her to the home where the abuse is reported leaves her at risk. E. Waiting for her to repeat the disclosure delays protection and may mean it is never repeated.
pearl: Never promise a child confidentiality about abuse. Listen, reassure, document their exact words and share through safeguarding procedures.
thinking: Child discloses physical abuse ↓ ongoing risk of serious harm ↓ protection outweighs confidentiality ↓ be honest that information must be shared ↓ Explain that this cannot be kept secret and follow local safeguarding procedures
exam_trap: B, Keep the disclosure confidential, as she has asked — it tempts because respecting a young person's confidentiality is usually important, but risk of serious harm justifies sharing information to protect her.
takeaway: When a child discloses abuse, never promise secrecy; act through local safeguarding procedures.

stem: A GP is part of a regional working group preparing comments for the UK National Screening Committee on a proposal to introduce population screening for a cancer. The proposal lists several features of the cancer and of the suggested test. Which feature would most strongly support introducing a screening programme?

options.A: The cancer is very rare in the target population
options.B: Treatment is equally effective whenever it is started
options.C: The only available test is invasive, painful and costly
options.D: The cancer causes rapid death before any symptom-free stage
options.E: It has a detectable symptom-free stage at which treatment improves outcome

correct_answer: E. It has a detectable symptom-free stage at which treatment improves outcome
why_correct: Screening is only worthwhile if a condition has a recognisable latent or early symptomless stage, and if treating it at that stage leads to better outcomes than treating it once symptoms appear. This is central to the Wilson and Jungner principles used by the UK National Screening Committee. Other requirements include an important health problem, an acceptable and accurate test, and benefits outweighing harms.
why_wrong: A. A very rare condition generally gives too few true positives to justify population screening. B. If early treatment is no better than later treatment, early detection gives no benefit. C. A screening test must be acceptable to the population, so an invasive, painful test is unsuitable. D. With no detectable symptomless phase, there is nothing for screening to find early.
pearl: Screening works only if there is a detectable early phase and early treatment changes the outcome. Otherwise it just adds anxiety, cost and overdiagnosis.
thinking: Purpose of screening is earlier detection ↓ needs a detectable symptomless stage ↓ early treatment must improve outcome ↓ otherwise no benefit ↓ It has a detectable symptom-free stage at which treatment improves outcome
exam_trap: B, Treatment is equally effective whenever it is started — it tempts because effective treatment sounds desirable, but if timing makes no difference, detecting the disease early gives no benefit.
takeaway: Screening needs a detectable early stage where earlier treatment improves outcome.

stem: A GP practice audits a rapid throat swab test for group A streptococcus in patients with sore throats. Of those tested, 50 had a positive rapid test, and throat culture confirmed streptococcal infection in 45 of these 50. What does the figure of 45 out of 50 (90%) represent?
why_correct: The positive predictive value is the proportion of people with a positive test result who truly have the condition: true positives divided by all positive results. Here 45 of the 50 positive tests were confirmed, giving a positive predictive value of 90%. It answers the patient's question: given a positive result, how likely is it that I have the disease?
why_wrong: A. Sensitivity is the proportion of all people with the disease who test positive, so its denominator is everyone with the disease. B. Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. D. Negative predictive value is the proportion of negative results that are truly disease-free. E. A likelihood ratio combines sensitivity and specificity and is not a simple proportion of positives.
pearl: Predictive values start from the test result; sensitivity and specificity start from disease status. Predictive values also change with how common the disease is.
thinking: Denominator is all positive test results ↓ numerator is those confirmed to have disease ↓ true positives divided by all positives ↓ probability of disease given a positive test ↓ Positive predictive value
exam_trap: A, Sensitivity — it tempts because both measures involve true positives, but sensitivity divides by everyone with the disease, whereas here the denominator is everyone who tested positive.
takeaway: PPV is true positives divided by all positive results: the chance a positive is correct.

stem: A 71-year-old man sees his GP with two days of constant pain low in the left side of his abdomen and loose stools. He has had milder episodes like this before that settled. His temperature is 38.1°C, and there is localised tenderness in the left iliac fossa without guarding elsewhere. He has passed no blood and is otherwise stable. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Acute diverticulitis is inflammation of colonic diverticula, most often in the sigmoid colon, so it presents in older adults with constant left iliac fossa pain, fever and a change in bowel habit. Previous similar episodes support the diagnosis. NICE advises that uncomplicated cases in well patients may be managed in the community, with antibiotics only when clinically indicated, and referral if systemically unwell or complications are suspected.
why_wrong: B. Sigmoid volvulus causes marked abdominal distension and absolute constipation rather than fever with localised tenderness. C. Ischaemic colitis usually causes sudden pain followed by bloody diarrhoea. D. Ulcerative colitis causes bloody diarrhoea with urgency, usually in younger patients. E. Ureteric colic causes severe colicky loin-to-groin pain, often with haematuria, not fever with loose stools.
pearl: Diverticulitis is often described as left-sided appendicitis: constant left iliac fossa pain, fever and altered bowel habit in an older adult.
thinking: Older adult ↓ constant left iliac fossa pain with loose stools ↓ fever and localised tenderness ↓ previous similar episodes ↓ Acute diverticulitis
exam_trap: C, Ischaemic colitis — it tempts because it also causes left-sided pain in older adults, but it typically produces sudden pain with bloody diarrhoea rather than recurrent febrile episodes with localised tenderness.
takeaway: Older adult with fever and constant left iliac fossa pain most likely has diverticulitis.

stem: A 66-year-old woman tells her GP that for two months her stools have been looser and more frequent, and she has seen dark red blood mixed in with them. She feels tired, and a blood count shows an iron deficiency anaemia. She has no anal pain. Abdominal and rectal examination are unremarkable. What should the GP do?

options.A: Reassure her that haemorrhoids are the likely cause
options.B: Prescribe loperamide and review if symptoms persist
options.D: Urgent suspected cancer referral for colorectal assessment
options.E: Start ferrous sulfate and recheck her blood count in three months

correct_answer: D. Urgent suspected cancer referral for colorectal assessment
why_correct: A persistent change in bowel habit, blood mixed with the stool and iron deficiency anaemia in an older adult are red-flag features for colorectal cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance uses a faecal immunochemical test to guide urgent referral in symptomatic patients, and she should be assessed on the suspected cancer pathway. Iron replacement can be started, but must not delay investigation.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause bright red blood on the paper, not blood mixed in the stool with anaemia. B. Treating the symptom without investigation risks missing a cancer. C. A routine referral is too slow for these red-flag features. E. Treating the anaemia alone delays diagnosis of its likely cause.
pearl: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in an older adult is a colorectal or upper GI cancer until proven otherwise; combined with altered bowel habit and blood in the stool, refer urgently.
thinking: Older adult with change in bowel habit ↓ blood mixed with stool ↓ iron deficiency anaemia ↓ red flags for colorectal cancer ↓ Urgent suspected cancer referral for colorectal assessment
exam_trap: E, Start ferrous sulfate and recheck her blood count in three months — it tempts because the anaemia needs treating, but iron replacement without investigating the cause delays a possible cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Changed bowel habit, blood in the stool and iron deficiency in an older adult need urgent referral.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with known gallstones, who is awaiting elective surgery, is brought to the emergency department with shaking chills and a temperature of 39.2°C. She has pain under the right ribs, and her daughter noticed that the whites of her eyes have turned yellow since yesterday. Her blood pressure is low-normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fever with rigors, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice (Charcot triad) in a patient with gallstones indicate ascending cholangitis, a bacterial infection of an obstructed common bile duct. It can rapidly progress to sepsis. Management includes sepsis care with fluids, intravenous antibiotics and early biliary drainage, usually by ERCP.
why_wrong: A. Acute cholecystitis causes fever and right upper quadrant pain, but jaundice is not usual because the bile duct is not obstructed. C. Biliary colic is pain without fever or jaundice. D. Hepatitis A is not linked to gallstones and rarely causes rigors with sepsis. E. Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back, and jaundice with rigors points to cholangitis.
pearl: Fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice form the Charcot triad of cholangitis. Add confusion and hypotension and it becomes Reynolds pentad, an emergency.
thinking: Known gallstones ↓ rigors and high fever ↓ right upper quadrant pain ↓ new jaundice, so bile duct obstruction ↓ Ascending cholangitis
exam_trap: A, Acute cholecystitis — it tempts because it also causes fever and right upper quadrant pain in gallstone disease, but jaundice indicates common bile duct obstruction, which suggests cholangitis.
takeaway: Gallstones plus fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice is ascending cholangitis.

stem: A 49-year-old woman who takes ibuprofen regularly for knee arthritis collapses at home after vomiting a large amount of blood. In the emergency department she is pale, cold and clammy, with a heart rate of 125/min and blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg. She passed black, tarry stool this morning. What must happen first?

options.A: Arrange endoscopy before any fluids are given
options.B: Oral proton pump inhibitor and observation on the ward
options.D: Stop ibuprofen and start oral iron
options.E: Resuscitation with large-bore access, fluids and blood products

correct_answer: E. Resuscitation with large-bore access, fluids and blood products
why_correct: Haematemesis and melaena with tachycardia, hypotension and peripheral shutdown indicate a major upper gastrointestinal bleed with shock. The first priority is an ABCDE approach: wide-bore intravenous access, bloods including crossmatch, fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion according to the major haemorrhage protocol. Endoscopy follows once she is resuscitated, and NICE recommends it immediately after resuscitation in unstable patients.
why_wrong: A. Endoscopy is needed, but only after resuscitation; scoping a shocked patient first is unsafe. B. Oral treatment and ward observation are inadequate for a shocked patient. C. CT angiography may be used for some bleeding sources but does not take priority over resuscitation. D. Stopping the NSAID and giving iron are later measures, not the immediate priority.
pearl: In any shocked GI bleed, resuscitate first. Endoscopy follows promptly once the patient is resuscitated.
thinking: Haematemesis and melaena on an NSAID ↓ tachycardia, hypotension and cold peripheries ↓ haemorrhagic shock ↓ ABCDE comes before diagnosis ↓ Resuscitation with large-bore access, fluids and blood products
exam_trap: A, Arrange endoscopy before any fluids are given — it tempts because endoscopy finds and treats the bleeding source, but a shocked patient must be resuscitated first.
takeaway: Shocked upper GI bleed: resuscitate with access, fluids and blood before endoscopy.

stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a day of colicky central abdominal pain, repeated green vomiting and a swollen abdomen. He has not passed wind since last night. Ten years ago he had a laparotomy for a perforated duodenal ulcer. Bowel sounds are high-pitched and tinkling. Both groins and the laparotomy scar have no lumps. Abdominal imaging shows dilated small bowel loops. Which cause is most likely?
why_correct: Adhesions from previous abdominal surgery are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in the UK, and they can cause obstruction many years after the operation. Colicky pain, bilious vomiting, distension, absolute constipation and tinkling bowel sounds with dilated small bowel fit mechanical obstruction. Many cases settle with conservative management (nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids), with surgery needed if there are signs of strangulation or failure to resolve.
why_wrong: A. Hernias are the next most common cause, but none was found on examination of the groins or scar. B. Colorectal cancer causes large bowel obstruction with gradual change in bowel habit. D. Gallstone ileus is rare, typically in older women with gallstone disease. E. Crohn strictures usually occur with known inflammatory bowel disease and chronic symptoms.
pearl: Adhesions cause most small bowel obstruction in patients with previous abdominal surgery; always examine hernial orifices and scars for the second commonest cause.
thinking: Colicky pain, bilious vomiting and distension ↓ dilated small bowel, so small bowel obstruction ↓ previous laparotomy ↓ no hernia on examination ↓ Postoperative adhesions
exam_trap: A, Obstructed inguinal hernia — it tempts because hernias are a major cause of small bowel obstruction, but none was found and the previous laparotomy makes adhesions far more likely.
takeaway: Small bowel obstruction after previous abdominal surgery is most often due to adhesions.

stem: An 82-year-old care home resident with Parkinson disease and longstanding constipation is admitted because his abdomen has become hugely swollen over two days and he has passed no stool or wind. He is uncomfortable but not peritonitic. An abdominal radiograph shows a massively dilated, inverted U-shaped loop of large bowel rising from the pelvis towards the right upper quadrant, resembling a coffee bean. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Sigmoid volvulus occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery, typically in elderly, institutionalised patients with chronic constipation and neurological or psychiatric conditions. It causes marked distension and absolute constipation, and the radiograph shows a large inverted U or coffee-bean loop arising from the pelvis. Initial management in a patient without peritonitis is usually endoscopic decompression with a flatus tube.
why_wrong: A. Pseudo-obstruction causes diffuse colonic dilatation without a single twisted loop. C. Caecal volvulus produces a dilated loop arising in the right iliac fossa and pointing towards the left upper quadrant. D. Faecal impaction causes constipation but not a single massively dilated twisted loop. E. Toxic megacolon occurs with colitis, causing bloody diarrhoea and systemic toxicity.
pearl: Elderly, constipated and institutionalised patients with massive distension and a coffee-bean loop from the pelvis have sigmoid volvulus; decompress endoscopically if there is no peritonitis.
thinking: Elderly institutionalised patient with chronic constipation ↓ massive distension and absolute constipation ↓ coffee-bean loop arising from the pelvis ↓ twisted sigmoid colon ↓ Sigmoid volvulus
exam_trap: A, Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction — it tempts because it also occurs in frail elderly patients with distension, but it shows diffuse dilatation rather than a single twisted coffee-bean loop.
takeaway: Coffee-bean loop from the pelvis in a frail constipated older patient indicates sigmoid volvulus.

stem: A 41-year-old man with known peptic ulcer disease, who stopped his omeprazole months ago, arrives in the emergency department with sudden severe upper abdominal pain that has spread across his whole abdomen over two hours. He lies completely still and says any movement hurts. His temperature is 38.0°C and his pulse is 118/min. The abdomen is rigid like a board, with pain on light percussion. What do these examination findings indicate?
why_correct: Board-like rigidity, percussion tenderness and a patient lying still to avoid movement are signs of peritoneal irritation, and when they extend across the abdomen they indicate generalised peritonitis. In a man with peptic ulcer disease, sudden pain spreading across the abdomen suggests perforation. He needs resuscitation, analgesia, antibiotics, an erect chest radiograph or CT, and an urgent surgical opinion.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes colicky loin pain with restlessness and a soft abdomen. B. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain without generalised rigidity. C. Gastritis causes epigastric discomfort but not board-like rigidity or percussion tenderness. E. Irritable bowel syndrome is a chronic functional disorder without fever or peritonism.
pearl: Patients with peritonitis lie still; those with colic writhe. Board-like rigidity after sudden pain in a patient with ulcer disease suggests a perforated viscus.
thinking: Sudden severe pain spreading across abdomen ↓ lies still, fever and tachycardia ↓ board-like rigidity and percussion tenderness ↓ inflamed parietal peritoneum throughout ↓ Generalised peritonitis
exam_trap: C, Acute gastritis — it tempts because of his known ulcer disease and upper abdominal pain, but gastritis does not cause board-like rigidity, which indicates peritoneal inflammation from perforation.
takeaway: Board-like rigidity and a patient lying still indicate generalised peritonitis: get urgent surgical help.

stem: A 16-year-old boy sees his GP about a dragging ache in the left side of his scrotum that is worse after football and towards the end of the day. Standing, there is a soft, irregular swelling above the left testis that feels like a collection of worm-like strands; it becomes much less obvious when he lies flat. It does not transilluminate, and both testes feel normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A varicocele is a dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus. It is much more common on the left because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle. It feels like a bag of worms above the testis, is more prominent on standing and empties when lying down, and causes a dragging ache. Most need only reassurance, but referral is considered for pain, testicular growth concerns or subfertility.
why_wrong: B. A hydrocele is a smooth swelling surrounding the testis that transilluminates. C. An epididymal cyst is a smooth, discrete, transilluminating lump separate from the testis. D. A hernia extends from the groin, so the examiner cannot get above it, and it often has a cough impulse. E. Torsion causes sudden severe pain with a tender, high-riding testis, not a chronic dull ache.
pearl: Left-sided bag of worms that empties lying down is a varicocele. A new right-sided varicocele, or one that does not empty, needs imaging to exclude a retroperitoneal or renal mass.
thinking: Dull dragging scrotal ache ↓ soft worm-like swelling above the left testis ↓ prominent standing, reduces lying flat ↓ does not transilluminate ↓ Varicocele
exam_trap: D, Indirect inguinal hernia — it tempts because it can also reduce on lying down, but a hernia extends from the groin, so the examiner cannot get above it, whereas this soft swelling of worm-like strands lies above the testis within the scrotum.
takeaway: A left-sided bag of worms above the testis that empties on lying down is a varicocele.

stem: A 34-year-old man sees his GP because his partner noticed that his left testicle feels harder and slightly bigger than the right. He has no pain, fever or urinary symptoms. On examination there is a hard, non-tender irregularity arising from the body of the left testis. The epididymis feels normal and the swelling does not transilluminate. How should he be managed?

options.A: Reassure and review in six weeks
options.D: Refer on a suspected cancer pathway to urology
options.E: Advise scrotal support and simple analgesia

correct_answer: D. Refer on a suspected cancer pathway to urology
why_correct: A hard, painless swelling arising from the body of the testis is testicular cancer until proven otherwise. NICE suspected cancer guidance supports a suspected cancer pathway referral for a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis. Scrotal ultrasound and tumour markers follow, and outcomes are excellent when it is caught early.
why_wrong: A. Watchful waiting delays the diagnosis of a likely malignancy. B. There is no pain, fever or urinary symptom to suggest infection, and antibiotics would only delay assessment. C. Semen analysis has no role in assessing a testicular mass. E. Supportive measures treat inflammation, not a suspicious solid lump.
pearl: Location is the key: a lump you cannot separate from the testis is suspicious, whereas a lump separate from it (epididymal cyst) or one that transilluminates (hydrocele) is usually benign.
thinking: Young man with a new testicular change ↓ Painless, hard, arising from the testis itself ↓ No transillumination, epididymis normal ↓ Treat as testicular cancer until proven otherwise ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral to urology
exam_trap: B, doxycycline for epididymo-orchitis — it tempts because it is the commonest cause of scrotal swelling in young men, but there is no pain, fever or urinary symptom, and treating a tumour with antibiotics wastes valuable weeks.
takeaway: A painless, hard lump within the testis needs urgent urology referral, not antibiotics or reassurance.

stem: An 81-year-old man on an orthopaedic ward, two days after a hip hemiarthroplasty, becomes agitated and restless overnight. The nurse reports that he has not passed urine for 10 hours although he has been drinking normally. On examination there is a tender mass rising from the pelvis towards the umbilicus that is dull to percussion. Which action should be taken now?

options.B: Oral tamsulosin and review in the morning

why_correct: A tender, dull suprapubic mass with no urine output in an older man after surgery is acute urinary retention. The bladder needs prompt decompression with a urethral catheter, which relieves the pain and often the agitation. The residual volume should be recorded and causes such as constipation, opioids and anticholinergic drugs reviewed.
why_wrong: A. He is not dehydrated; the urine is being made but cannot be voided. B. An alpha-blocker may help a later trial without catheter but does not relieve retention now. C. Sedating him treats the symptom and ignores a painful, distended bladder. E. A diuretic adds more urine to a bladder that cannot empty.
pearl: New confusion or agitation in an older patient should prompt a check of the bladder and bowels; painless or painful retention is a common, easily reversed cause of post-operative delirium.
thinking: Older man after surgery, agitated ↓ No urine for many hours despite drinking ↓ Tender, dull mass arising from the pelvis ↓ Acute urinary retention ↓ Decompress with a urethral catheter
exam_trap: C, oral haloperidol — agitation in an elderly post-operative patient looks like delirium, but the cause here is a distended bladder, and sedation leaves the real problem untreated.
takeaway: Agitation plus a palpable, dull bladder means retention: catheterise first, then look for the cause.

stem: A 63-year-old woman phones her GP surgery because she has seen blood in her urine on three occasions over the past fortnight. She has no pain, frequency or burning, and is not taking any anticoagulant. A urine dipstick at the surgery is negative for nitrites and leucocytes. She is otherwise well. Which condition is the priority to exclude?
why_correct: Unexplained visible haematuria in an older adult, with no evidence of infection, must be investigated to exclude bladder or kidney cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance supports a suspected cancer pathway referral to urology in this situation. Assessment usually includes cystoscopy and upper tract imaging.
why_wrong: A. Overactive bladder causes urgency and frequency, not blood in the urine. C. A negative dipstick for nitrites and leucocytes with no symptoms makes infection unlikely. D. Atrophic vaginitis may cause spotting but does not explain repeated frank haematuria, and must not delay urology assessment. E. Glomerulonephritis is possible but much less likely in this age group and is not the priority to exclude.
pearl: Never accept painless visible haematuria as harmless in an older adult; even a single episode without infection deserves urological investigation, and anticoagulants do not explain it away.
thinking: Older woman with repeated visible haematuria ↓ No dysuria or frequency, dipstick negative for infection ↓ Not anticoagulated ↓ Unexplained painless haematuria ↓ Exclude urinary tract cancer
exam_trap: C, lower urinary tract infection — infection is the commonest cause of haematuria in women, but there are no urinary symptoms and the dipstick does not suggest infection, so treating with antibiotics would delay a cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Unexplained visible haematuria in an older adult is urinary tract cancer until urology says otherwise.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is admitted from her care home with three days of diarrhoea and very little to eat or drink. She is drowsy, her tongue is dry, her pulse is 108 bpm and her blood pressure is 96/58 mmHg. Her creatinine is about double the normal value recorded at her annual review two months ago, and her urine output has fallen. What best explains her kidney injury?
why_correct: Fluid losses with poor intake, a dry tongue, tachycardia and low blood pressure show hypovolaemia, which reduces renal perfusion and causes a pre-renal acute kidney injury. The rise in creatinine over a short period against a recent normal baseline confirms an acute process. Management is fluid resuscitation, review of nephrotoxic and antihypertensive drugs, and close monitoring of urine output.
why_wrong: B. Interstitial nephritis is usually drug-triggered and may cause rash, fever or eosinophilia, none of which is described. C. Obstruction is less likely in a woman and there is no palpable bladder. D. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis presents with haematuria, proteinuria and often systemic features, not dehydration. E. A recent normal baseline shows this is a new, acute change.
pearl: Always compare creatinine with a previous baseline; a recent normal result turns an isolated abnormal value into clear evidence of acute kidney injury.
thinking: Diarrhoea and poor intake ↓ Dry mucosa, tachycardia, low blood pressure ↓ Creatinine doubled from a recent baseline, low urine output ↓ Reduced renal perfusion from hypovolaemia ↓ Pre-renal acute kidney injury
exam_trap: E, progression of chronic kidney disease — an elderly patient with a raised creatinine is easily labelled as having CKD, but a normal result two months earlier shows this is an acute change driven by fluid loss.
takeaway: Fluid loss with tachycardia, hypotension and a fresh creatinine rise points to pre-renal AKI.

stem: A 52-year-old man is on the surgical ward the day after a total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goitre. He reports pins and needles in his fingertips and around his lips. When a blood pressure cuff is inflated on his arm, his wrist flexes and his fingers draw together. Which blood result is most likely?
why_correct: During thyroidectomy the parathyroid glands can be bruised, devascularised or removed, causing hypoparathyroidism and a fall in serum calcium. Perioral and fingertip paraesthesia with carpal spasm on cuff inflation (Trousseau sign) are classic features of hypocalcaemia. Calcium should be checked urgently and replaced, intravenously if severe.
why_wrong: A. Hyperkalaemia causes weakness and arrhythmias, not tetany. B. Raised calcium causes thirst, constipation and confusion rather than paraesthesia and spasm. C. Hyponatraemia causes confusion and seizures, not carpal spasm. D. Hypoglycaemia causes sweating, tremor and confusion, not Trousseau sign.
pearl: Trousseau sign (carpal spasm with a cuff) and Chvostek sign (facial twitch on tapping the facial nerve) both point to hypocalcaemia; after neck surgery, think parathyroid injury first.
thinking: Day after total thyroidectomy ↓ Perioral and fingertip tingling ↓ Carpal spasm on cuff inflation ↓ Parathyroid injury causing low calcium ↓ Hypocalcaemia
exam_trap: B, hypercalcaemia — the link between parathyroids and calcium makes it tempting, but tetany and paraesthesia are features of low calcium; parathyroid damage lowers, not raises, serum calcium.
takeaway: Tingling and carpal spasm after thyroid surgery mean hypocalcaemia from parathyroid injury.

stem: A 47-year-old man noticed a lump on the left side of the front of his neck while shaving. It moves upwards when he swallows. He has had no change in weight, no palpitations, no heat or cold intolerance and no change in his voice. Which blood test should be performed first as part of his assessment?
why_correct: A neck lump that moves on swallowing is thyroid in origin, and thyroid function tests (TSH, with free T4 if abnormal) are the first blood test for any thyroid nodule. The result shapes the next steps: a suppressed TSH suggests a hot nodule that may need a radionuclide scan, whereas a normal TSH leads on to ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration if indicated. Red flags such as rapid growth, hoarseness or stridor need an urgent suspected cancer referral.
why_wrong: A. Calcitonin is a marker for medullary thyroid cancer and is not a routine first test. C. Thyroid antibodies help diagnose autoimmune thyroid disease but do not assess a nodule. D. Thyroglobulin is used to monitor for recurrence after treatment of thyroid cancer, not to diagnose it. E. Calcium is relevant to parathyroid disease, not to an initial thyroid nodule assessment.
pearl: A thyroid lump moves on swallowing; a thyroglossal cyst also moves on tongue protrusion. TSH first, then ultrasound decides whether fine-needle aspiration is needed.
thinking: Neck lump that rises on swallowing ↓ Arises from the thyroid ↓ Need to know whether the nodule is functioning ↓ First blood test is TSH-based ↓ Thyroid function tests
exam_trap: D, serum thyroglobulin — it sounds like a thyroid cancer test, but thyroglobulin is used for surveillance after thyroidectomy, not for diagnosing a nodule.
takeaway: Every thyroid nodule starts with thyroid function tests; imaging and cytology follow the result.

stem: A 66-year-old man who spent 30 years working in a rubber tyre factory attends an urgent treatment centre after passing red urine with small clots for two days. He has no loin pain, fever or burning on micturition. Abdominal examination is unremarkable and digital rectal examination reveals a smooth, normal-sized prostate. Which diagnosis is most important to rule out?
why_correct: Painless visible haematuria in an older man is bladder cancer until proven otherwise. Occupational exposure to aromatic amines in the rubber, dye and chemical industries is a recognised risk factor, alongside smoking, the most important one. He needs a suspected cancer pathway referral for cystoscopy and upper tract imaging.
why_wrong: A. A ureteric stone usually causes severe colicky loin-to-groin pain. B. Prostatitis causes fever, perineal pain and a tender prostate. D. IgA nephropathy typically affects younger adults with haematuria soon after an upper respiratory infection. E. There are no urinary symptoms or fever to suggest infection.
pearl: Bladder cancer risk factors to recognise: smoking, aromatic amines (rubber, dyes, leather), previous pelvic radiotherapy, cyclophosphamide and, worldwide, schistosomiasis.
thinking: Older man with frank haematuria and clots ↓ Painless, no infective features ↓ Occupational exposure to aromatic amines ↓ Urothelial malignancy is the key risk ↓ Rule out bladder cancer
exam_trap: A, ureteric calculus — clots and blood suggest a stone to many, but stones cause severe colicky pain; painless haematuria points to a tumour.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria plus rubber or dye industry work: think bladder cancer and refer urgently.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is brought by ambulance to the emergency department 50 minutes after her husband saw her slump at the breakfast table. She has a left facial droop, cannot lift her left arm and her speech is slurred. Her capillary glucose is normal. Thrombolysis and thrombectomy are being considered. Which investigation is needed immediately?
correct_answer: C. Non-contrast CT of the head
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficit within the treatment window needs immediate brain imaging, usually a non-contrast CT head, to exclude intracerebral haemorrhage before any reperfusion treatment. Hypoglycaemia, a key stroke mimic, has already been excluded. CT angiography is added when thrombectomy is being considered.
why_wrong: A. Carotid imaging is part of the later work-up for secondary prevention, not the first test. B. Echocardiography looks for a cardiac source of embolism after the acute phase. D. Ambulatory ECG to detect atrial fibrillation is a later investigation. E. Lumbar puncture has no role in acute stroke and is contraindicated before imaging.
pearl: Time is brain: check glucose, then image immediately. Reperfusion treatment can never be given until a scan has excluded bleeding.
thinking: Sudden unilateral face and arm weakness with dysarthria ↓ Within the reperfusion window ↓ Glucose normal, mimic excluded ↓ Must exclude haemorrhage before treatment ↓ Immediate non-contrast CT head
exam_trap: A, carotid duplex ultrasound — carotid disease is a common cause of stroke, but carotid imaging guides later prevention and must not delay the CT that decides on reperfusion.
takeaway: In suspected acute stroke, image the brain immediately to exclude bleeding before reperfusion.

stem: A 58-year-old man attends the emergency department with a painful, swollen left leg. He had a knee arthroscopy 10 days ago and has spent most of the time since on the sofa. His left calf is visibly larger than the right, with pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins. He has no chest symptoms. A clinical prediction score indicates that DVT is likely. Which investigation should be arranged?

options.B: D-dimer, with imaging only if the result is raised

why_correct: When DVT is likely on a clinical prediction score, NICE recommends a proximal leg vein ultrasound, ideally within a few hours. If the scan cannot be done promptly, a D-dimer is taken and interim anticoagulation started while waiting. Recent surgery and immobility are strong provoking factors here.
why_wrong: B. Starting with a D-dimer is the pathway when DVT is unlikely; a negative result cannot safely exclude DVT when clinical probability is high. C. CTPA investigates pulmonary embolism and he has no chest symptoms. D. ABPI assesses arterial disease, not venous thrombosis. E. A knee radiograph does not show a venous clot.
pearl: The clinical probability decides the first test: likely DVT goes straight to ultrasound, unlikely DVT starts with a D-dimer. A positive D-dimer is non-specific, especially after surgery.
thinking: Unilateral leg swelling with deep vein tenderness ↓ Recent surgery and immobility ↓ Prediction score says DVT likely ↓ D-dimer cannot rule it out at this probability ↓ Proximal leg vein ultrasound
exam_trap: B, D-dimer first — it is the familiar first step, but D-dimer is a rule-out test for low-probability patients; with a likely DVT and recent surgery it adds nothing and delays diagnosis.
takeaway: Likely DVT goes straight to proximal leg ultrasound; D-dimer first only when DVT is unlikely.

stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to her GP because her teacher has noticed that she switches off many times a day, sometimes in the middle of a sentence, with her eyelids fluttering. Each episode lasts only seconds, she does not fall, and she carries on with her task straight afterwards with no drowsiness. An episode is triggered in clinic when she is asked to breathe deeply and quickly for a few minutes. What kind of seizure is she most likely having?
why_correct: Very brief, frequent episodes of staring with eyelid flutter, abrupt recovery and no post-ictal drowsiness in a school-age child are typical of absence seizures. Hyperventilation is a classic trigger, and the EEG shows generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges. She should be referred to a paediatric specialist for diagnosis and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Focal impaired awareness seizures usually last longer, often with automatisms and post-ictal confusion. C. Atonic seizures cause sudden loss of tone and falls. D. Myoclonic seizures are brief jerks of the limbs, without staring spells. E. Tonic seizures cause stiffening of the body, not quiet staring.
pearl: Hyperventilation in clinic is a simple bedside way to provoke an absence; teachers often first notice the episodes as poor concentration or daydreaming.
thinking: School-age child with many daily staring spells ↓ Seconds long, eyelid flutter, instant recovery ↓ Provoked by hyperventilation ↓ No post-ictal phase ↓ Absence seizure
exam_trap: A, focal impaired awareness seizure — it also causes staring and reduced awareness, but episodes last longer, often include lip-smacking or fiddling, and are followed by confusion.
takeaway: Seconds-long staring spells with instant recovery, triggered by hyperventilation, mean absence seizures.

stem: A 72-year-old retired teacher is brought to his GP by his wife, who says his handwriting has become tiny and he now takes a long time to get dressed. He takes no regular medication. On examination his right hand shakes while resting in his lap but settles when he reaches for a pen. He has a reduced arm swing on the right when walking, and there is cogwheel stiffness at the right wrist. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: An asymmetrical rest tremor that improves with movement, slowness of movement (micrographia, difficulty dressing, reduced arm swing) and cogwheel rigidity are the core features of Parkinson disease. With no drug that could cause parkinsonism, idiopathic Parkinson disease is most likely. NICE advises referral, before starting treatment, to a specialist for diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Essential tremor is a postural and action tremor, usually symmetrical, without rigidity or slowness. B. Normal pressure hydrocephalus causes gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline. D. Motor neurone disease causes weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs, not rest tremor. E. A cerebellar lesion causes an intention tremor and ataxia of sudden onset.
pearl: Parkinson tremor is worse at rest and often starts on one side; essential tremor is worse when holding a posture or drinking from a cup and often improves with alcohol.
thinking: Older man, gradual slowing and small handwriting ↓ Unilateral tremor at rest that settles with action ↓ Reduced arm swing and cogwheel rigidity ↓ No causative drugs ↓ Parkinson disease
exam_trap: A, essential tremor — it is the commonest tremor in older adults, but it is an action tremor and does not cause rigidity, slowness or reduced arm swing.
takeaway: Asymmetric rest tremor plus bradykinesia and rigidity means Parkinson disease; refer before treating.

stem: A 31-year-old man is referred to the emergency department by his optometrist. For a month his eyelids have drooped more as each day goes on, and by the evening he sees double while watching television. His jaw tires when he chews tough food. He feels much better on waking. His pupils are normal and his tendon reflexes are preserved. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Ptosis, diplopia and jaw fatigue that worsen as the day goes on and recover after rest are typical of fatigable weakness in myasthenia gravis. Pupils are spared and reflexes are normal. The diagnosis is supported by acetylcholine receptor antibodies, and swallowing and breathing must be monitored for myasthenic crisis.
why_wrong: B. A third nerve palsy is constant rather than fatigable and may involve the pupil. C. Lambert-Eaton syndrome mainly affects proximal limbs, improves briefly with exertion and reduces reflexes. D. MS can cause diplopia but not a daily pattern of fatigable ptosis and jaw weakness. E. Horner syndrome causes mild ptosis with a small pupil and no diplopia.
pearl: Fatigability is the hallmark of myasthenia: symptoms worsen with repeated use and through the day. Bulbar symptoms or breathlessness raise concern for crisis; check FVC, not oxygen saturation.
thinking: Young adult with ptosis and diplopia ↓ Worse in the evening, better on waking ↓ Jaw fatigue on chewing ↓ Pupils and reflexes normal ↓ Myasthenia gravis
exam_trap: C, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — the name sounds similar, but it is often paraneoplastic, causes proximal leg weakness, reduced reflexes and autonomic symptoms, and strength briefly improves with effort.
takeaway: Ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day with normal pupils point to myasthenia gravis.

stem: A 36-year-old man attends the emergency department because over five days he has found it increasingly difficult to climb stairs, and now his grip is weak too. He has tingling in both feet. Three weeks ago he had a bout of food poisoning after a barbecue. His knee and ankle reflexes cannot be elicited, and there is no sensory level on the trunk. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Weakness that spreads from the legs to the arms over days, with distal tingling and lost reflexes, after a gastrointestinal infection (often Campylobacter) is typical of Guillain-Barre syndrome. This is an immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy. Forced vital capacity must be monitored because respiratory muscle weakness can develop quickly.
why_wrong: A. Transverse myelitis produces a sensory level and sphincter disturbance. B. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with normal reflexes and often ocular involvement. C. Periodic paralysis causes episodic weakness over hours, without sensory symptoms. E. Motor neurone disease progresses over months, has no sensory symptoms and often brisk reflexes.
pearl: In Guillain-Barre syndrome, serial FVC is the key safety measurement; oxygen saturation stays normal until late and is falsely reassuring.
thinking: Weakness spreading upwards over days ↓ Distal tingling, absent reflexes ↓ No sensory level ↓ Preceding gastroenteritis ↓ Guillain-Barre syndrome
exam_trap: A, acute transverse myelitis — bilateral leg weakness and sensory symptoms suggest the cord, but there is no sensory level, and weakness now involving the hands with lost reflexes fits a peripheral neuropathy.
takeaway: Ascending weakness with areflexia weeks after gastroenteritis is Guillain-Barre: monitor the FVC.

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to his GP by his mother. For two months he has stayed in his bedroom, convinced that newsreaders on television are sending coded instructions meant only for him. He describes a man's voice that talks about him in the third person, narrating what he is doing. A urine drug screen is negative and he has no medical history. Which term best describes this group of symptoms?
why_correct: A fixed false belief that broadcasts carry personal messages (delusions of reference) and a voice giving a running commentary in the third person (an auditory hallucination) are psychotic symptoms. Third-person running commentary is a first-rank symptom that is particularly characteristic of schizophrenia. A first presentation of psychosis should be referred urgently to an early intervention in psychosis service.
why_wrong: A. Obsessional thoughts are recognised by the person as their own and resisted, unlike delusions. B. Depersonalisation is a feeling of being detached from oneself, without false beliefs or voices. C. Overvalued ideas are strongly held but understandable beliefs, not bizarre and fixed. D. Confabulation is filling memory gaps with false memories, as in Korsakoff syndrome.
pearl: Hallucinations and delusions together define psychosis; voices discussing the patient in the third person or giving a running commentary are first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia.
thinking: Young man, social withdrawal ↓ Belief that television sends messages to him ↓ Voice describing his actions in the third person ↓ Delusions plus hallucinations, drug screen negative ↓ Psychotic symptoms
exam_trap: C, overvalued ideas — they are also strongly held beliefs, but they are understandable within the person's culture and background; a belief that newsreaders send personal coded messages is a delusion.
takeaway: Delusions plus hallucinations, such as third-person running commentary, are psychotic symptoms.

stem: A 41-year-old man on the medical ward develops itchy, raised red blotches over his trunk and arms 30 minutes after his first dose of intravenous co-amoxiclav. His lips and tongue are normal, he has no wheeze, his voice is normal, his oxygen saturation is unchanged and his blood pressure is stable. The infusion has been stopped. Which treatment should he receive?

options.C: Restart the infusion at a slower rate

why_correct: Urticaria alone, without airway, breathing or circulation problems, is a mild allergic reaction rather than anaphylaxis. After stopping the drug, an oral non-sedating antihistamine relieves the itch and wheals. He should be observed for progression, the penicillin allergy clearly documented, and a non-penicillin alternative chosen.
why_wrong: A. Adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis with airway, breathing or circulation compromise. B. Salbutamol treats bronchospasm, and he has no wheeze. C. Re-exposing him to the suspected allergen is unsafe. D. His blood pressure is stable, so fluid resuscitation is not needed.
pearl: Anaphylaxis needs skin or mucosal features plus an airway, breathing or circulation problem; skin features alone are treated with antihistamine, but watch for progression.
thinking: New itchy wheals soon after an antibiotic ↓ Drug stopped ↓ Airway, breathing and circulation all normal ↓ Mild allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis ↓ Oral non-sedating antihistamine
exam_trap: A, intramuscular adrenaline — any allergic reaction to an antibiotic prompts fear of anaphylaxis, but with no airway, breathing or circulation compromise adrenaline is not indicated.
takeaway: Urticaria without airway, breathing or circulation problems: stop the drug and give an antihistamine.

stem: A 59-year-old publican who has smoked since his teens and drinks heavily tells his GP that his voice has been rough and croaky for the past two months. He had no cold beforehand, and voice rest has not helped. He has no stridor and no difficulty swallowing. Which action is most appropriate?

options.B: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor and review in three months
options.C: Refer on a suspected cancer pathway to ENT
options.D: Refer to speech and language therapy
options.E: Arrange a chest radiograph and reassure if normal

correct_answer: C. Refer on a suspected cancer pathway to ENT
why_correct: Persistent, unexplained hoarseness in a middle-aged smoker who drinks heavily is a red flag for laryngeal cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance supports a suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT so that the larynx can be examined directly with laryngoscopy. Early laryngeal cancer is highly treatable.
why_wrong: A. There is no infection, and antibiotics do not treat persistent hoarseness. B. Reflux laryngitis is a diagnosis of exclusion and a three-month trial would delay a cancer diagnosis. D. Voice therapy may follow ENT assessment but must not replace it. E. A chest radiograph may look for lung cancer affecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve, but a normal film does not exclude laryngeal cancer.
pearl: Smoking and alcohol multiply the risk of head and neck cancer. Hoarseness lasting weeks without an infection needs the larynx visualised.
thinking: Smoker and heavy drinker ↓ Hoarse for weeks, not after a cold ↓ No improvement with voice rest ↓ Red flag for laryngeal cancer ↓ Suspected cancer referral to ENT
exam_trap: B, PPI trial — reflux is a common cause of hoarseness, but in a high-risk patient a long empirical trial delays laryngoscopy and possible cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in a smoker needs urgent ENT referral, not trial treatments.

stem: A 26-year-old competitive swimmer attends her GP with a three-day history of a painful, itchy left ear and a small amount of discharge. Pressing on the tragus makes her wince. Otoscopy shows a red, swollen ear canal containing debris; the eardrum, where visible, looks normal. She is not diabetic and is otherwise well. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Ear pain and itch with tragal tenderness, a red swollen canal and debris, in someone whose ears are often wet, is otitis externa. It is an infection or inflammation of the external ear canal and is usually treated with topical acidic, antibiotic or steroid drops after cleaning. In people with diabetes or immunosuppression, severe pain should raise concern for necrotising otitis externa.
why_wrong: A. A perforated drum would be seen, and pain typically eases once the drum perforates; tragal tenderness is not a feature. B. Cholesteatoma causes painless, foul-smelling discharge and hearing loss over months. C. Mastoiditis causes swelling and tenderness behind the ear with fever. D. Ramsay Hunt syndrome causes ear pain with vesicles and facial nerve palsy.
pearl: Pain on moving the pinna or pressing the tragus localises the problem to the ear canal; swimming, eczema and cotton bud use are common triggers.
thinking: Swimmer with an itchy, painful ear ↓ Pain on pressing the tragus ↓ Red, swollen canal with debris ↓ Normal-looking drum ↓ Otitis externa
exam_trap: A, acute otitis media with perforation — discharge suggests a burst drum, but the drum looks normal and tragal tenderness places the problem in the canal.
takeaway: Tragal tenderness and a swollen, red ear canal mean otitis externa, not middle ear infection.

stem: A 30-year-old man who works in a residential care home attends his GP with three weeks of itching that keeps him awake at night. There are small papules and short, wavy greyish tracks on the sides of his fingers and the front of his wrists, and some itchy papules on his penis. Several residents he looks after have also been scratching. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Intense itch worse at night, burrows on the fingers and wrists, genital papules and itching in close contacts are classic features of scabies, an infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei. It spreads through prolonged skin contact and outbreaks are common in care homes. Treatment is permethrin cream applied to the whole body and repeated after a week, with all close contacts treated at the same time.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis follows exposure to an irritant or allergen and does not spread between people. B. Lichen planus causes purple, flat-topped papules on the wrists but no burrows and is not contagious. D. Dermatitis herpetiformis causes grouped vesicles on the elbows, knees and buttocks, linked with coeliac disease. E. Pompholyx causes deep-seated blisters on the palms and fingers, without burrows or spread to contacts.
pearl: Burrows are the diagnostic sign of scabies. Treat every close contact at the same time, even without symptoms, and warn that itch can persist for weeks after successful treatment.
thinking: Night-time itch for weeks ↓ Burrows on fingers and wrists, genital papules ↓ Close contacts also itching ↓ Contagious infestation ↓ Scabies
exam_trap: A, contact dermatitis — a care worker's hands are often exposed to gloves and soaps, but burrows, genital lesions and itching residents point to an infestation spreading between people.
takeaway: Night itch, finger web burrows and itchy contacts mean scabies: treat everyone at once.

stem: A 17-year-old boy attends his GP surgery with an itchy rash that started this morning. He shows photographs on his phone of raised, pale-centred pink swellings on his thigh that disappeared within a few hours, while new ones appeared on his back and arms. Today's lesions blanch and fade without leaving bruising or marks. He has no lip swelling or breathing difficulty and is otherwise well. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Itchy wheals that each last less than a day, appear in new places as old ones fade and leave no mark are typical of urticaria. It results from mast cell release of histamine and is often triggered by infection, food or drugs, though frequently no cause is found. A non-sedating antihistamine is first-line treatment.
why_wrong: B. Erythema multiforme causes fixed target lesions lasting days, mainly on the hands and feet. C. Urticarial vasculitis causes lesions lasting more than a day that are often painful and leave bruising. D. Erythema nodosum causes tender, red nodules on the shins. E. Pityriasis rosea causes a herald patch followed by a scaly rash on the trunk that lasts weeks.
pearl: Individual urticarial wheals fade within 24 hours without trace; lesions that last longer, burn or leave bruising suggest urticarial vasculitis and need further assessment.
thinking: Itchy raised wheals ↓ Each fades within hours as new ones appear ↓ No marks or bruising left ↓ No angioedema or airway features ↓ Urticaria
exam_trap: B, erythema multiforme — pale-centred lesions can look target-like, but erythema multiforme lesions are fixed for days, whereas these move and fade within hours.
takeaway: Itchy wheals that come and go within hours and leave no mark are urticaria.

stem: A 69-year-old woman attends her GP with burning pain under her left breast and around to her back that began three days ago. Yesterday a band of clustered blisters on a red base appeared in the same area. The rash stops sharply at the front of her chest in the middle. She had chickenpox as a child. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Pain in a band around one side of the chest followed by clustered vesicles in the same dermatome, stopping at the midline, is shingles. It is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus that has stayed dormant in a sensory ganglion since chickenpox. Oral antivirals are most useful when started early, particularly in older people, and analgesia is important.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis follows the area of contact with an allergen and is itchy rather than painful in a dermatomal band. B. Bullous pemphigoid causes large, tense, itchy blisters spread widely, often on the limbs. C. Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions, usually on the face, without preceding nerve pain. E. Dermatitis herpetiformis causes symmetrical itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces.
pearl: Pain often comes before the rash in shingles and can be mistaken for cardiac, pleural or abdominal disease; involvement of the tip of the nose suggests ophthalmic zoster needing urgent eye assessment.
thinking: Older woman with unilateral burning chest pain ↓ Vesicles appear in the same band ↓ Rash stops at the midline ↓ Dermatomal varicella-zoster reactivation ↓ Herpes zoster
exam_trap: B, bullous pemphigoid — it is a common blistering disease in older people, but its blisters are large, tense and widespread, not a painful band that respects the midline.
takeaway: Painful vesicles in a single dermatome that stop at the midline are shingles.

stem: A 19-year-old man attends a walk-in centre with a rash on the backs of his hands and on his palms that appeared over 48 hours. The lesions are round, with a dusky centre, a paler ring and an outer red rim. A week ago he had a crop of cold sores on his upper lip. His mouth, eyes and genitals are unaffected and he feels well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Target lesions with three zones on the hands, appearing about a week after herpes simplex, are classic erythema multiforme. It is an immune reaction, most often triggered by herpes simplex virus, and is usually self-limiting. Treatment is supportive, with antiviral prophylaxis considered for frequent recurrences.
why_wrong: B. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is usually drug-induced and causes widespread blistering with mucosal involvement and systemic illness. C. Urticarial wheals fade within hours and do not form fixed three-zone targets. D. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes small oval vesicles with mouth ulcers, mainly in young children. E. Secondary syphilis causes non-itchy copper-coloured macules on the palms and soles, not target lesions.
pearl: Herpes simplex is the commonest trigger for erythema multiforme; drugs are the commonest trigger for Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which always involves the mucosae.
thinking: Young man with lesions on the hands ↓ Fixed target lesions with three zones ↓ Cold sores a week earlier ↓ No mucosal involvement, systemically well ↓ Erythema multiforme
exam_trap: B, Stevens-Johnson syndrome — targets raise fear of SJS, but there is no mucosal involvement, no blistering or skin pain, and the trigger was herpes simplex rather than a drug.
takeaway: Target lesions on the hands a week after a cold sore, with no mucosal disease, mean erythema multiforme.

stem: A 47-year-old landscape gardener asks his GP to look at several marks on his skin because his wife says one of them looks different from the others. The GP examines each of the lesions carefully. Which finding would most strongly suggest melanoma?

options.A: A round, evenly brown mole that has been unchanged for 20 years
options.B: A brown lesion with a ragged, notched edge that has recently changed shape
options.C: A soft, raised, flesh-coloured mole with hairs growing from it
options.D: A waxy, brown plaque with a greasy, stuck-on surface
options.E: A firm pink-brown papule on the leg that dimples when pinched

correct_answer: B. A brown lesion with a ragged, notched edge that has recently changed shape
why_correct: An irregular, notched border and a recent change in shape are major warning features of melanoma in both the ABCDE approach and the weighted seven-point checklist used in UK primary care. A lesion with these features should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway to dermatology. Change in an existing lesion is particularly important.
why_wrong: A. A symmetrical, evenly coloured mole that has not changed for years is reassuring. C. A soft, flesh-coloured hairy lesion is typical of a benign intradermal naevus. D. A waxy, stuck-on lesion is a seborrhoeic keratosis, which is benign. E. A firm papule that dimples on pinching is a dermatofibroma, which is benign.
pearl: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter and Evolution are the warning features; change in size, shape or colour carries the greatest weight in the UK seven-point checklist.
thinking: Patient worried about a mole that looks different ↓ Compare features against melanoma warning signs ↓ Irregular, notched border ↓ Recent change in shape ↓ Most suspicious for melanoma
exam_trap: D, the waxy, stuck-on plaque — seborrhoeic keratoses can be dark and alarming, but their greasy, stuck-on surface is characteristic of a benign lesion.
takeaway: An irregular border and a recent change in shape are the features that most raise concern for melanoma.

stem: A 58-year-old man with hereditary haemochromatosis, managed with regular venesection, presents to the emergency department with a hot, swollen right knee that came on overnight. There has been no injury. He is apyrexial and otherwise well. A knee radiograph shows fine linear calcification within the joint cartilage. Which condition is most likely?
correct_answer: E. Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout)
why_correct: Haemochromatosis is a recognised cause of calcium pyrophosphate deposition, and cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis) on the radiograph supports it. An acute hot knee in this setting is most likely pseudogout. The knee should still be aspirated to exclude infection; the fluid shows weakly positively birefringent, rhomboid crystals.
why_wrong: A. Gout more often affects the first toe joint and does not cause chondrocalcinosis. B. Septic arthritis must always be excluded by aspiration, but he is apyrexial and the radiograph and history favour crystal arthritis. C. Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genital infection, which is not described. D. Haemarthrosis is usually caused by trauma or anticoagulation, neither of which is present.
pearl: Think of metabolic causes when pseudogout presents in a younger patient: haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia are the classic associations.
thinking: Acute hot, swollen knee ↓ History of haemochromatosis ↓ Chondrocalcinosis on radiograph ↓ No fever, trauma or infection history ↓ Pseudogout, still aspirate to exclude sepsis
exam_trap: A, gout — it is the commonest crystal arthritis, but haemochromatosis and cartilage calcification point specifically to calcium pyrophosphate disease.
takeaway: Haemochromatosis with an acute hot knee and chondrocalcinosis points to pseudogout; still aspirate.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her flatmate. For the past week she has slept two or three hours a night yet says she has never felt better. She talks rapidly, jumping between topics, and has spent all her savings on designer clothes and a business plan that she says will make her a millionaire. She has lost her job after arguing with her manager. A urine drug screen is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Elevated mood with little need for sleep, pressured speech with flight of ideas, grandiose plans and reckless spending, causing severe disruption such as job loss, define a manic episode. A negative drug screen makes a substance-induced cause less likely. Mania usually indicates bipolar affective disorder and needs urgent psychiatric assessment.
why_wrong: A. Generalised anxiety causes persistent worry and tension, not elevated mood or grandiosity. C. Delirium causes fluctuating confusion and inattention, usually with a medical cause. D. Emotionally unstable personality disorder causes long-standing, rapidly shifting emotions rather than a distinct episode of elation. E. ADHD is a lifelong pattern of inattention and impulsivity, not a new episode with reduced need for sleep.
pearl: A reduced need for sleep without tiredness is one of the most useful signs of mania; ask about it whenever someone presents with unusual energy or spending.
thinking: Week of very little sleep without fatigue ↓ Elevated mood, rapid speech, flight of ideas ↓ Grandiose plans and reckless spending ↓ Marked social and work disruption, drug screen negative ↓ Manic episode
exam_trap: D, emotionally unstable personality disorder — impulsive spending and conflict tempt this answer, but personality disorders are long-standing patterns, whereas this is a distinct episode with elevated mood and reduced sleep.
takeaway: Elevated mood, little need for sleep, grandiosity and reckless spending causing disruption mean mania.

stem: A 66-year-old woman sees her GP with three months of tiredness, two chest infections needing antibiotics and new bruises on her shins. She is pale, and there is no lymphadenopathy or palpable spleen. Her full blood count shows a low haemoglobin, a low white cell count and a low platelet count. Which is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: A fall in red cells, white cells and platelets together (pancytopenia) explains her tiredness, infections and bruising, and with no enlarged spleen points to failure of the bone marrow to produce cells. Causes include aplastic anaemia, myelodysplasia, leukaemia and marrow infiltration. She needs an urgent blood film and haematology referral, usually followed by bone marrow examination.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency causes anaemia, often with a normal or raised platelet count, not pancytopenia. B. Immune thrombocytopenia lowers only the platelet count. C. Anaemia of chronic disease affects the red cells only. E. Scurvy causes bruising and gum bleeding but does not cause pancytopenia.
pearl: Match the symptoms to the cell lines: anaemia causes tiredness, low white cells cause infections and low platelets cause bruising; all three together suggest a marrow problem.
thinking: Tiredness, recurrent infections and bruising ↓ All three cell lines low ↓ No splenomegaly to suggest hypersplenism ↓ Marrow not producing cells ↓ Bone marrow failure
exam_trap: B, immune thrombocytopenia — the bruising fits low platelets, but ITP spares the red and white cells, whereas she has infections and anaemia as well.
takeaway: Anaemia, infections and bruising with all cell lines low suggest bone marrow failure: refer urgently.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who takes the combined oral contraceptive pill attends her GP 10 days after a two-day coach journey across Europe. She is worried she may have a blood clot in her leg. Which examination finding would most support a diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis?

options.A: Swelling of both ankles that settles overnight
options.B: Swelling of one calf with tenderness along the deep veins
options.D: Calf pain that comes on after walking a set distance
options.E: Itchy, scaly skin above the inner ankle

correct_answer: B. Swelling of one calf with tenderness along the deep veins
why_correct: A clot in the deep veins obstructs drainage from one leg, causing unilateral calf swelling with tenderness along the course of the deep veins. Combined with risk factors such as oestrogen-containing contraception and prolonged sitting during travel, this makes DVT likely. A clinical prediction score then guides whether she needs an ultrasound or a D-dimer first.
why_wrong: A. Swelling of both ankles that settles overnight suggests dependent oedema, not a clot. C. Bilateral varicose veins reflect superficial venous disease and do not suggest acute DVT. D. Calf pain on walking a set distance suggests claudication. E. Itchy, scaly skin at the ankle is venous eczema from chronic venous insufficiency.
pearl: Unilateral is the key word: DVT almost always affects one leg. Bilateral leg swelling points towards systemic causes such as heart failure, low albumin or drugs.
thinking: Woman on oestrogen after prolonged travel ↓ Concern about a clot ↓ DVT obstructs one leg's deep veins ↓ Look for unilateral swelling and deep vein tenderness ↓ One swollen, tender calf
exam_trap: C, varicose veins — they are a venous problem and a minor risk factor, but they reflect chronic superficial disease and do not indicate an acute deep clot.
takeaway: Unilateral calf swelling with deep vein tenderness is the finding that most supports a DVT.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, who smoked for 40 years, tells her GP that a cramping ache in her right calf forces her to stop each time she walks to the post office. Standing still for a minute or two eases it, and she can then carry on. She has no pain at rest and her skin is intact. Her right foot pulses are weak. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Cramping calf pain that comes on with walking a consistent distance and eases quickly on standing still, with weak foot pulses, is intermittent claudication. It is caused by peripheral arterial disease, for which diabetes and smoking are major risk factors. The ankle-brachial pressure index confirms the diagnosis, and management starts with smoking cessation, supervised exercise and cardiovascular risk reduction.
why_wrong: B. Spinal stenosis pain is relieved by sitting or bending forwards, not simply by standing still, and pulses are normal. C. Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia causes rest pain, ulceration or gangrene. D. Venous insufficiency causes aching, swelling and skin changes that are worse after standing, not pain on walking. E. A ruptured Baker cyst causes sudden calf pain and swelling resembling a DVT.
pearl: Claudication eases with standing still; neurogenic claudication from spinal stenosis needs sitting or leaning forwards and is often worse walking downhill.
thinking: Smoker with diabetes ↓ Calf cramp on walking a set distance ↓ Relief within minutes on standing still ↓ Weak foot pulses, no rest pain ↓ Intermittent claudication
exam_trap: B, lumbar spinal stenosis — it also causes leg pain on walking in older people, but it needs sitting or bending forward to ease and the pulses are normal.
takeaway: Calf pain on walking eased by standing still, with weak pulses, is intermittent claudication.

stem: A 63-year-old man who has smoked about a packet a day since his teens sees the practice nurse because he gets breathless walking up hills. He has coughed up white sputum most winter mornings for several years. He never had childhood wheeze or hay fever, and his symptoms change little from day to day.
