exam_trap: B, thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis — also causes pain near the thumb base in this age group, but it is felt at the joint with a positive grind test rather than along the tendons.
takeaway: Radial wrist pain reproduced by Finkelstein's test is De Quervain tenosynovitis.

stem: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who drinks heavily notices that he can no longer lay his right hand flat on a table. His little finger is drawn into flexion at the knuckle and cannot be straightened, even passively. There are firm, painless nodules in the palm along the line of the finger. Sensation in the hand is normal. Which condition is responsible?
why_correct: Painless palmar nodules and cords with a fixed flexion deformity of the little or ring finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint are typical of Dupuytren disease, caused by fibrosis of the palmar fascia. Diabetes, alcohol excess, smoking and family history are risk factors. Inability to place the hand flat (a positive tabletop test) is a common prompt for surgical referral.
why_wrong: B. Trigger finger causes catching and locking, and the finger can be straightened, sometimes with a click. C. Ulnar nerve palsy causes clawing with sensory loss and weakness of the small hand muscles, not palmar cords. D. Mallet finger affects the fingertip, with inability to extend the distal joint. E. Flexor tendon rupture causes loss of active flexion, not a fixed flexion contracture.
pearl: Dupuytren contracture limits passive as well as active extension; a finger that straightens passively points to a different problem.
thinking: Fixed flexion of the little finger ↓ painless palmar nodules and cords ↓ normal sensation, risk factors present ↓ Dupuytren disease
exam_trap: C, ulnar nerve palsy — clawing of the little finger looks similar, but palpable palmar cords with normal sensation point to Dupuytren disease.
takeaway: Palmar cords with a fixed flexion contracture of the ring or little finger mean Dupuytren disease.

stem: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes reports that his right ring finger gets stuck in a bent position, especially first thing in the morning. He has to straighten it with his other hand and it then snaps straight painfully. There is a tender nodule in the palm at the base of the finger, which moves as he bends it. Which condition does he have?
why_correct: A finger that catches in flexion and then releases painfully, with a tender nodule at the base of the finger that moves with the flexor tendon, is trigger finger. Thickening of the tendon and narrowing of its sheath at the A1 pulley prevent smooth gliding. Diabetes is a recognised risk factor, and corticosteroid injection or surgical release are effective treatments.
why_wrong: A. Dupuytren disease causes a fixed, painless contracture without catching or snapping. C. Mallet finger is a loss of active extension at the distal joint after injury. D. Osteoarthritis causes joint pain and stiffness with bony swelling, not catching and release. E. A flexor sheath ganglion is a small firm lump that does not usually cause locking.
pearl: Triggering is often worst in the morning; a nodule that moves with the tendon over the A1 pulley at the palmar crease is the classic finding.
thinking: Finger catches in flexion ↓ painful snap on straightening ↓ tender mobile nodule at the finger base ↓ trigger finger
exam_trap: A, Dupuytren disease — both cause palmar nodules and share risk factors such as diabetes, but Dupuytren causes a fixed painless contracture, not catching and snapping.
takeaway: Catching and painful release of a finger with a palmar nodule is trigger finger.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has had a painful right shoulder for four months. The pain wakes her at night and she struggles to fasten her bra or reach her back pocket. On examination, external rotation is markedly reduced both when she moves the arm herself and when the examiner moves it. A shoulder X-ray is normal. Which diagnosis best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Global restriction of shoulder movement, particularly external rotation, that is equally limited actively and passively, with a normal X-ray, is the hallmark of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder). Diabetes is a strong risk factor. It typically passes through painful, stiff and recovery phases over many months and is managed with analgesia, physiotherapy and sometimes intra-articular steroid.
why_wrong: A. A rotator cuff tear reduces active movement and strength, but passive range is usually preserved. B. Impingement causes a painful arc on abduction with preserved passive movement. C. Glenohumeral osteoarthritis also restricts passive movement but would show joint space loss and osteophytes on X-ray. D. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness in older adults with raised inflammatory markers.
pearl: Loss of passive external rotation with a normal X-ray is the key clinical finding separating frozen shoulder from cuff disease and arthritis.
thinking: Painful stiff shoulder in a person with diabetes ↓ active and passive external rotation both reduced ↓ normal X-ray excludes arthritis ↓ adhesive capsulitis
exam_trap: C, glenohumeral osteoarthritis — it also limits passive movement, but the normal X-ray excludes it; frozen shoulder is a capsular, not bony, problem.
takeaway: Equal active and passive loss of external rotation with a normal X-ray means frozen shoulder.

stem: A 26-year-old netball player twisted her right knee while pivoting with her foot planted. She carried on playing, but the knee swelled gradually over the following day. Since then it has intermittently become stuck partly bent, and she has to wiggle it to free it. There is tenderness along the medial joint line. Which structure has she probably damaged?
why_correct: A twisting injury on a weight-bearing knee, followed by gradual swelling, joint-line tenderness and true locking, is typical of a meniscal tear. A displaced fragment of meniscus can jam in the joint and block full extension. MRI confirms the diagnosis, and a knee that is locked and cannot be freed needs urgent orthopaedic referral.
why_wrong: A. An ACL rupture usually causes an audible pop, rapid swelling from haemarthrosis and instability rather than locking. B. An MCL injury follows a valgus force and causes medial pain and laxity, but not mechanical locking. D. A patellar tendon injury impairs active knee extension, with pain below the patella. E. A lateral collateral injury follows a varus force and causes lateral rather than medial pain.
pearl: Swelling within an hour or so suggests haemarthrosis (ACL tear or fracture); swelling developing over the next day, with locking, suggests a meniscal tear.
thinking: Twisting on a planted foot ↓ delayed swelling ↓ intermittent locking and joint-line tenderness ↓ meniscal tear
exam_trap: A, anterior cruciate ligament — pivoting injuries in sport bring the ACL to mind, but ACL tears swell rapidly and cause giving way rather than locking.
takeaway: Twisting injury, delayed swelling, joint-line tenderness and locking suggest a meniscal tear.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the emergency department after coming off his bicycle and landing on his palm with the wrist bent back. He has pain on the thumb side of the wrist. Pushing along the thumb towards the wrist causes pain, and the scaphoid tubercle is tender. Wrist X-rays are reported as showing no fracture. Which injury must be presumed?
why_correct: A fall onto the extended wrist with radial-sided pain, tenderness of the scaphoid tubercle and pain on axial loading of the thumb should be treated as a scaphoid fracture, even when the initial X-rays are normal. Scaphoid fractures are often not visible at first and, if missed, risk non-union and avascular necrosis. He should be immobilised and have further imaging, usually MRI, or fracture clinic follow-up.
why_wrong: A. A Colles fracture is a distal radius fracture that would usually be visible on X-ray, with dorsal deformity. B. Lunate dislocation produces an obvious abnormality on a lateral X-ray and may cause median nerve symptoms. C. Diagnosing a sprain without excluding a scaphoid fracture risks serious complications. E. A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture at the thumb base, usually visible on X-ray.
pearl: Snuffbox tenderness, scaphoid tubercle tenderness and pain on thumb compression are the clinical signs of scaphoid fracture; a normal first X-ray does not exclude it.
thinking: Fall onto an extended wrist ↓ radial wrist pain with scaphoid tenderness ↓ normal initial X-ray does not exclude fracture ↓ suspect scaphoid fracture and immobilise
exam_trap: C, simple wrist sprain — the normal X-ray tempts reassurance, but scaphoid fractures are often occult at first and must be managed as fractures until excluded.
takeaway: Scaphoid tenderness after a fall needs immobilisation and further imaging, even with a normal X-ray.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with osteoporosis trips on a kerb and puts her hand out to save herself. Her wrist has a 'dinner fork' appearance. X-ray shows a fracture of the radius just above the wrist joint, with the distal fragment tilted and shifted towards the back of the hand. What is this fracture called?
why_correct: A Colles fracture is an extra-articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement and angulation of the distal fragment, producing the dinner fork deformity. It typically follows a fall onto an outstretched hand, especially in older women with osteoporosis. A fragility fracture like this should also prompt assessment of bone health.
why_wrong: B. A Smith fracture has volar (palmar) displacement of the distal fragment, often after a fall onto a flexed wrist. C. A Barton fracture is intra-articular, involving the rim of the distal radius with carpal subluxation. D. A Galeazzi fracture is a radial shaft fracture with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint. E. A Monteggia fracture is an ulnar shaft fracture with dislocation of the radial head.
pearl: Any low-trauma wrist fracture in an older adult is a fragility fracture and should trigger fracture risk assessment and consideration of bone protection.
thinking: Older woman with osteoporosis ↓ fall onto the hand ↓ distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement, dinner fork deformity ↓ Colles fracture
exam_trap: B, Smith fracture — also a distal radius fracture, but its fragment displaces towards the palm, the reverse of a Colles fracture.
takeaway: Distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement (dinner fork deformity) is a Colles fracture.

stem: A 45-year-old woman jammed her middle finger while tucking in a bed sheet. The tip of the finger now droops. She can straighten it fully when she pushes it up with her other hand, but cannot hold it straight on her own. The other finger joints move normally. Which injury has she sustained?
why_correct: A drooping fingertip after a forced flexion injury, with full passive but no active extension of the distal interphalangeal joint, is a mallet finger. It results from disruption of the terminal extensor tendon, sometimes with a small avulsion fracture. Treatment is continuous splinting of the distal joint in extension for several weeks, with an X-ray to look for a fracture.
why_wrong: A. Boutonnière deformity follows central slip injury, causing flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint with hyperextension at the distal joint. B. Jersey finger is avulsion of the deep flexor tendon, causing loss of active distal flexion. C. Trigger finger causes catching and locking in flexion, not a drooping tip after injury. E. Swan-neck deformity, often in rheumatoid arthritis, involves hyperextension at the proximal joint and flexion at the distal joint.
pearl: Mallet splints must be worn continuously; letting the fingertip drop even briefly during treatment can undo the healing.
thinking: Forced flexion injury to the fingertip ↓ drooping distal phalanx ↓ passive but no active extension of the DIP joint ↓ mallet finger
exam_trap: B, jersey finger — another fingertip tendon injury, but it involves the flexor tendon and causes loss of flexion, not extension.
takeaway: Inability to actively extend the DIP joint after a fingertip injury is mallet finger.

stem: A 67-year-old man has a routine blood test before starting a new medicine. It shows a low haemoglobin with small red cells and a low ferritin. He eats a varied diet including red meat, takes no regular medicines and has not noticed any bleeding or change in bowel habit. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give oral iron and recheck in 12 months without further tests
options.D: Refer for a bone marrow biopsy

correct_answer: E. Refer urgently for gastrointestinal investigation
why_correct: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in an adult, especially a man or a postmenopausal woman, should be presumed to be due to gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, including from colorectal or gastric cancer. He should be referred urgently for upper and lower gastrointestinal investigation and have coeliac serology checked, while iron replacement is started.
why_wrong: A. Iron alone without investigation may mask a gastrointestinal cancer. B. Transfusion is not indicated for a stable patient and does not address the cause. C. Haemoglobin electrophoresis investigates haemoglobinopathies, not a low ferritin. D. Bone marrow biopsy is unnecessary when a low ferritin already confirms iron deficiency.
pearl: A low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; in men and postmenopausal women without an obvious cause, look for gastrointestinal blood loss with upper and lower endoscopy.
thinking: Microcytic anaemia with low ferritin ↓ adequate diet and no obvious bleeding ↓ occult gastrointestinal loss must be excluded ↓ urgent gastrointestinal investigation
exam_trap: A, oral iron and recheck — correcting the anaemia seems sensible, but iron without investigation can hide a bleeding cancer while the haemoglobin improves.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in an adult needs investigation for gastrointestinal blood loss.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is referred with painless yellowing of her skin that has developed over three weeks. She has lost weight, her urine has become very dark and her stools are pale. On examination she has a smooth, non-tender mass in the right upper quadrant. Which pattern of hyperbilirubinaemia is expected?

options.B: Conjugated, due to obstruction of bile flow
options.D: Unconjugated, due to reduced hepatic uptake
options.E: Normal bilirubin with raised urobilinogen only

correct_answer: B. Conjugated, due to obstruction of bile flow
why_correct: Painless progressive jaundice with weight loss, dark urine, pale stools and a palpable gallbladder suggests obstruction of the common bile duct, for example by a tumour of the pancreatic head. Conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the bowel, so stools become pale, and because it is water-soluble it is excreted in the urine, making it dark. Urgent imaging and a suspected cancer referral are needed.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, which is not water-soluble, so the urine colour is normal. C. Gilbert syndrome causes mild intermittent unconjugated jaundice, typically with illness or fasting. D. Reduced hepatic uptake raises unconjugated bilirubin and would not cause pale stools or dark urine. E. Urobilinogen falls rather than rises when bile cannot reach the bowel.
pearl: Dark urine in jaundice means conjugated bilirubin is present; pale stools mean bile is not reaching the gut — together they indicate obstruction or cholestasis.
thinking: Painless jaundice with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder ↓ dark urine and pale stools ↓ bile cannot reach the bowel, water-soluble bilirubin in urine ↓ conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
exam_trap: A, unconjugated due to haemolysis — candidates link jaundice with haemolysis, but unconjugated bilirubin cannot enter the urine, so dark urine points the other way.
takeaway: Jaundice with dark urine and pale stools means conjugated (obstructive) hyperbilirubinaemia.

stem: A 55-year-old woman reports feeling tired and itchy for several months. She does not drink alcohol and has no pain. Her liver function tests show an ALP several times the upper limit of normal, a raised GGT and an ALT that is only slightly elevated. Bilirubin and albumin are normal. Which pattern of liver injury do these results indicate?

options.C: Bone disease such as Paget disease

why_correct: A predominant rise in ALP, confirmed as hepatic in origin by a raised GGT, with only a modest rise in transaminases, indicates a cholestatic pattern. Itch and fatigue in a middle-aged woman with this pattern raise the possibility of primary biliary cholangitis. An ultrasound to exclude duct obstruction and autoantibody testing are appropriate next steps.
why_wrong: A. A hepatocellular pattern shows transaminases rising much more than ALP. C. Bone disease raises ALP but leaves GGT normal. D. Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and LDH rather than ALP and GGT. E. Gilbert syndrome causes isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal liver tests.
pearl: GGT helps localise a raised ALP: a raised GGT suggests a liver source, a normal GGT suggests bone. Itch is a hallmark symptom of cholestasis.
thinking: ALP raised far more than ALT ↓ GGT also raised, so ALP is hepatic ↓ itch and fatigue ↓ cholestatic pattern
exam_trap: C, bone disease such as Paget disease — a raised ALP in middle age tempts this, but bone disease does not raise GGT.
takeaway: Raised ALP with raised GGT and only a modest transaminase rise indicates a cholestatic pattern.

stem: A 24-year-old man sees his GP with three months of loose stools, abdominal cramps and occasional urgency. He has no rectal bleeding, and his blood tests, including coeliac serology, are normal. The GP sends a stool sample for faecal calprotectin to help decide whether he needs referral. A raised result would mainly indicate which of the following?
correct_answer: A. Inflammation of the bowel wall
why_correct: Calprotectin is a protein released by neutrophils, so a raised faecal level indicates intestinal inflammation. In primary care it helps distinguish inflammatory bowel disease, which needs specialist referral, from irritable bowel syndrome, in which calprotectin is normal. It is not specific and can also be raised by gastrointestinal infection and NSAID use.
why_wrong: B. Pancreatic insufficiency is assessed with faecal elastase, not calprotectin. C. Coeliac disease is tested with serology, which has already been checked. D. Calprotectin is not a cancer test, and a normal result does not exclude colorectal cancer when red flags are present. E. Lactose intolerance does not cause mucosal inflammation.
pearl: Use faecal calprotectin in adults with lower gastrointestinal symptoms when IBD versus IBS is the question and cancer is not suspected; red flags need a suspected cancer referral instead.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea in a young adult ↓ need to separate IBD from IBS ↓ calprotectin comes from neutrophils in the gut ↓ raised level means intestinal inflammation
exam_trap: B, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency — another stool test is used for chronic diarrhoea, but that is faecal elastase; calprotectin reflects neutrophilic inflammation.
takeaway: Raised faecal calprotectin indicates intestinal inflammation and helps separate IBD from IBS.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Her husband found her at breakfast with a drooping face, slurred speech and a weak right arm; she had been seen well less than an hour earlier. Her capillary glucose is normal and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.B: Arrange an immediate non-contrast CT head as part of urgent stroke team assessment
options.D: Admit to a general medical ward for observation
options.E: Request an MRI head within the next 24 hours

correct_answer: B. Arrange an immediate non-contrast CT head as part of urgent stroke team assessment
why_correct: Sudden facial weakness, dysarthria and arm weakness with a recent known onset is an acute stroke until proven otherwise. She needs immediate assessment by the stroke team and urgent brain imaging, usually non-contrast CT, to exclude haemorrhage and decide on thrombolysis or thrombectomy. These treatments are time-critical, so imaging must not be delayed.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin must not be given until haemorrhage has been excluded by imaging. C. Carotid imaging is part of later work-up for anterior circulation events, not the immediate priority. D. Observation on a general ward delays time-critical treatment. E. Waiting for MRI would miss the window for reperfusion treatment.
pearl: Check glucose early in suspected stroke, as hypoglycaemia can mimic it; then image immediately, because every minute of delay to reperfusion costs brain tissue.
thinking: Sudden unilateral face and arm weakness with dysarthria ↓ recent known onset, glucose normal ↓ must exclude haemorrhage before reperfusion ↓ immediate stroke assessment and CT head
exam_trap: A, give aspirin straight away — antiplatelet therapy is part of ischaemic stroke care, but giving it before imaging risks worsening an intracerebral haemorrhage.
takeaway: Suspected acute stroke needs immediate stroke team assessment and brain imaging before any antithrombotic.

presentation: Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms
stem: A 71-year-old man presents to his GP with three weeks of a new headache over his right temple, scalp tenderness when combing his hair and aching in his jaw when he chews. This morning, the vision in his right eye went grey for a few minutes before recovering. Which complication is the most urgent concern?
why_correct: New temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication in an older adult suggest giant cell arteritis. Transient monocular visual loss is a warning that the arteries supplying the optic nerve are affected, and without immediate high-dose corticosteroids this can progress to irreversible blindness, sometimes in both eyes. He needs same-day steroids and urgent specialist assessment, without waiting for biopsy or imaging.
why_wrong: A. Aortic aneurysm is a recognised late complication that develops over years, not the immediate threat. B. Stroke can occur but is much less common than visual loss, and his symptom specifically affected one eye. D. Scalp necrosis is a rare complication. E. Steroid-induced diabetes is a treatment side effect to monitor, not a reason to delay treatment.
pearl: In suspected giant cell arteritis, visual symptoms raise the urgency: start high-dose steroids immediately and arrange same-day ophthalmology or rheumatology review.
thinking: Older adult with temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication ↓ giant cell arteritis ↓ transient monocular visual loss ↓ imminent risk of permanent blindness
exam_trap: A, thoracic aortic aneurysm — a true complication of giant cell arteritis, but it develops late; the urgent threat after transient visual loss is permanent blindness.
takeaway: Visual symptoms in giant cell arteritis threaten permanent blindness: give steroids immediately.

stem: A 66-year-old man describes several weeks of sudden spinning lasting under a minute whenever he lies back in bed or tilts his head up to reach a high shelf. He feels nauseated during attacks but is well between them. His hearing is normal and neurological examination is unremarkable. Which bedside test should be used to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Brief episodes of rotatory vertigo triggered by changes in head position, with normal hearing and neurology, are typical of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. The Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre is the diagnostic test: it reproduces the vertigo and a torsional nystagmus when the affected ear is lowered. Once confirmed, it is treated with a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley manoeuvre.
why_wrong: A. The head impulse test is used in acute continuous vertigo to help separate peripheral from central causes. C. The Epley manoeuvre treats posterior canal BPPV once diagnosed rather than confirming it. D. Rinne and Weber tests assess hearing loss, which he does not have. E. Romberg's test assesses proprioception and balance, not positional vertigo.
pearl: BPPV vertigo lasts seconds and is provoked by position; continuous vertigo lasting days suggests vestibular neuronitis or a central cause.
thinking: Short spinning episodes ↓ triggered by lying back or looking up ↓ normal hearing and neurology ↓ BPPV, confirmed with Dix–Hallpike
exam_trap: C, Epley manoeuvre — closely linked with BPPV, but it is the treatment; the diagnostic test is the Dix–Hallpike.
takeaway: Positional vertigo lasting seconds suggests BPPV: diagnose with Dix–Hallpike, treat with Epley.

stem: A 45-year-old woman attends the emergency department with a sore throat that has worsened rapidly over six hours. Her voice is muffled, she cannot swallow her saliva and is spitting into a bowl. She is leaning forward with her hands on her knees and has soft inspiratory stridor. What should be done first?

options.A: Examine her throat with a tongue depressor
options.B: Lie her flat for a lateral neck X-ray
options.C: Insert a cannula and take blood cultures before anything else
options.D: Give oral antibiotics and arrange GP follow-up
options.E: Call senior anaesthetic and ENT help urgently to secure the airway, keeping her upright

correct_answer: E. Call senior anaesthetic and ENT help urgently to secure the airway, keeping her upright
why_correct: Rapidly progressive sore throat with a muffled voice, inability to swallow saliva, a tripod posture and stridor suggests acute epiglottitis with impending airway obstruction. The priority is to keep her calm and upright and call senior anaesthetic and ENT help immediately so the airway can be secured in a controlled setting. Intravenous antibiotics and steroids follow once the airway is safe.
why_wrong: A. Examining the throat with a tongue depressor can provoke complete airway obstruction. B. Lying her flat or sending her to radiology risks sudden airway loss away from airway expertise. C. Cannulation and cultures are needed but must not delay summoning airway help, and distress can worsen obstruction. D. Oral antibiotics and discharge would be dangerous with signs of airway compromise.
pearl: In suspected epiglottitis, do not lie the patient down, do not examine the throat and do not leave them alone; get the most experienced airway help available.
thinking: Rapid sore throat with drooling and muffled voice ↓ tripod posture and stridor ↓ impending upper airway obstruction ↓ urgent senior airway help, keep upright
exam_trap: C, cannula and blood cultures first — it feels like proactive sepsis care, but anything that delays airway help or distresses the patient can precipitate complete obstruction.
takeaway: Drooling, stridor and a tripod posture: keep upright and call senior airway help before anything else.

stem: A 34-year-old woman tells her GP that when she takes food from the freezer or walks to work on a chilly morning, several fingers suddenly turn pale and numb. They then become dusky purple and, on rewarming, flush and throb. Between episodes her hands look normal, and there are no ulcers, rashes or joint symptoms. What is this called?
why_correct: Episodic, cold-triggered colour change of the fingers from white (vasospasm) to blue (deoxygenation) to red (reactive hyperaemia) is Raynaud phenomenon. Normal hands between attacks with no ulcers, rash or joint symptoms suggest the primary form. Management is keeping the whole body and hands warm and stopping smoking, with nifedipine if symptoms are troublesome.
why_wrong: A. Chilblains are itchy or painful red-purple swellings that persist for days after cold exposure. B. Acrocyanosis is persistent, painless blue discolouration rather than episodic colour change. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes tingling in the median nerve distribution without colour change. E. Frostbite follows prolonged freezing exposure and causes tissue injury, not brief reversible episodes.
pearl: Features suggesting secondary Raynaud include onset later in life, digital ulcers, asymmetry, abnormal nailfold capillaries and symptoms of connective tissue disease.
thinking: Episodic cold-triggered finger changes ↓ white then blue then red ↓ normal between attacks ↓ Raynaud phenomenon
exam_trap: A, chilblains — also cold-related and affecting the fingers, but they are persistent inflammatory swellings rather than brief colour changes.
takeaway: Cold-triggered white-blue-red colour change of the fingers is Raynaud phenomenon.

stem: A 52-year-old man has noticed over four months that he struggles to lift his arms to shave and to get up from a low sofa. His thigh and upper arm muscles ache slightly. There is no rash, double vision or drooping of the eyelids, and sensation and reflexes are normal. He takes no regular medicines. His creatine kinase is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradually progressive, symmetrical weakness of the shoulder and hip girdle muscles with a markedly raised creatine kinase and normal sensation suggests an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis. The absence of rash argues against dermatomyositis. Further assessment includes myositis antibodies, EMG, muscle MRI or biopsy, and screening for an underlying malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes pain and stiffness rather than true weakness, with a normal creatine kinase. C. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, often with ptosis and double vision, and a normal creatine kinase. D. Guillain–Barré syndrome causes rapidly ascending weakness with lost reflexes over days. E. Motor neurone disease causes mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs such as fasciculations and brisk reflexes, without a markedly raised creatine kinase.
pearl: True proximal weakness with a high creatine kinase points to myopathy; stiffness with normal strength and a normal creatine kinase points to polymyalgia rheumatica.
thinking: Progressive difficulty lifting arms and rising from a seat ↓ symmetrical proximal weakness ↓ markedly raised creatine kinase, normal sensation, no rash ↓ polymyositis
exam_trap: A, polymyalgia rheumatica — also affects the shoulders and hips in older adults, but it causes stiffness rather than true weakness and does not raise creatine kinase.
takeaway: Symmetrical proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase suggests an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis.

stem: A 58-year-old man attends his GP because over two months he has struggled to lift his arms to hang out washing and to get up from a low car seat. There is no ptosis or double vision, and the weakness does not worsen with repeated effort. Tendon reflexes and sensation in all limbs are normal. His serum creatine kinase is many times the upper limit of normal. Where is the primary pathology most likely to lie?
why_correct: Symmetrical proximal weakness with intact sensation and reflexes points to a myopathic process, and a markedly raised creatine kinase confirms damage to the muscle fibres themselves. This pattern fits an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis, which needs further assessment including screening for an associated malignancy in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Neuromuscular junction disorders cause fatigable weakness, often with ptosis or diplopia, and a normal creatine kinase. B. Anterior horn cell disease produces wasting and fasciculations with only a modest creatine kinase rise. D. Sensory nerve disease causes numbness and reflex loss, which are absent here. E. Corticospinal tract lesions give upper motor neurone signs such as brisk reflexes and spasticity.
pearl: A markedly raised creatine kinase localises weakness to muscle; neurogenic and junctional causes leave it normal or only mildly raised. Proximal symmetrical weakness plus high CK means myopathy until proven otherwise.
thinking: Proximal symmetrical weakness ↓ no fatigability, normal sensation and reflexes ↓ markedly raised creatine kinase signals muscle breakdown ↓ Skeletal muscle fibres
exam_trap: A, Neuromuscular junction — proximal weakness is also typical of myasthenia gravis, so it tempts; but myasthenia is fatigable, often affects the eyes, and does not raise creatine kinase.
takeaway: Proximal weakness with intact sensation and a high creatine kinase localises to skeletal muscle.

stem: A 36-year-old man sees his GP with a two-year history of attacks in which his feet, and sometimes his hands, become intensely red, hot and burning. Attacks are brought on by exercise, warm rooms or a hot bath, and he gets relief only by standing on a cold tiled floor or soaking his feet in cold water. Between attacks the skin looks normal and foot pulses are easily felt. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Episodic burning pain with redness and warmth of the extremities, triggered by heat and relieved by cooling, is the classic picture of erythromelalgia. It may be primary or secondary to conditions such as myeloproliferative disorders, so a full blood count is a sensible first test.
why_wrong: A. Raynaud phenomenon is triggered by cold and causes pallor then cyanosis, the opposite of this picture. B. Complex regional pain syndrome usually follows injury and is persistent rather than heat-triggered and fully resolving. C. Acute gout affects a single joint with swelling and is not provoked by warmth in both feet. E. Chilblains develop after cold exposure and present as itchy purple lesions on the toes.
pearl: Think of erythromelalgia as reverse Raynaud: heat brings on red, hot, burning extremities and cold relieves them. Check a full blood count to look for an underlying myeloproliferative disorder.
thinking: Recurrent red, hot, burning feet ↓ triggered by warmth and exercise ↓ relieved by cooling, normal between attacks with good pulses ↓ Erythromelalgia
exam_trap: A, Raynaud phenomenon — an episodic colour change in the extremities brings Raynaud to mind, but Raynaud is cold-triggered with white and blue phases, whereas this is heat-triggered redness.
takeaway: Heat-triggered red, hot, burning extremities relieved by cooling indicate erythromelalgia.

stem: A 34-year-old man attends the emergency department with a week of tiredness, breathlessness on climbing stairs and dark urine. His sclerae are yellow and the spleen tip is just palpable. Investigations reveal a low haemoglobin with a normal mean cell volume, an elevated reticulocyte count, a raised unconjugated bilirubin and a raised lactate dehydrogenase. Liver enzymes are normal. Which process best explains his anaemia?

options.A: Impaired DNA synthesis in red-cell precursors

why_correct: A raised reticulocyte count shows that the marrow is responding vigorously, while raised unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase reflect red cells being broken down. Together with jaundice, dark urine and splenomegaly, this indicates haemolysis, and a direct antiglobulin test and blood film are the next useful investigations.
why_wrong: A. Impaired DNA synthesis from B12 or folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia with a low reticulocyte count. B. Reduced erythropoietin, as in chronic kidney disease, gives a normocytic anaemia with a poor reticulocyte response. D. Marrow infiltration suppresses production, so the reticulocyte count is low and the film may be leucoerythroblastic. E. Iron-restricted production causes a microcytic anaemia without reticulocytosis or jaundice.
pearl: Separate anaemias by the reticulocyte count: high means loss or destruction, low means underproduction. Add raised unconjugated bilirubin and LDH and you have haemolysis.
thinking: Normocytic anaemia ↓ reticulocytes raised, so marrow is working hard ↓ raised unconjugated bilirubin and LDH with jaundice and dark urine ↓ Increased red-cell destruction
exam_trap: B, Reduced erythropoietin production — a normocytic anaemia often points to chronic disease or renal causes, but these underproduction states have a low reticulocyte count and no jaundice.
takeaway: Normocytic anaemia with reticulocytosis and raised unconjugated bilirubin means haemolysis.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a hot, swollen, painful right knee after a minor fall at nursery. His mother says her brother had a bleeding problem. The platelet count and prothrombin time are normal, but the activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged. Factor VIII activity is low and von Willebrand factor antigen is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Haemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII, so it typically affects boys with a maternal family history and causes deep bleeding such as haemarthrosis after trivial injury. A prolonged APTT with normal platelets and prothrombin time, low factor VIII and normal von Willebrand factor confirm the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding and would show low von Willebrand factor, which is normal here. B. Immune thrombocytopenia lowers the platelet count and causes petechiae rather than joint bleeds. C. Haemophilia B is due to factor IX deficiency, whereas factor VIII is low here. E. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time first, which is normal here.
pearl: Deep bleeding into joints and muscles suggests a clotting factor defect, while mucosal and skin bleeding suggests a platelet or von Willebrand problem. Isolated prolonged APTT in a boy with a maternal uncle affected is haemophilia until proven otherwise.
thinking: Haemarthrosis after minor injury in a boy ↓ maternal male relative affected, so X-linked ↓ isolated prolonged APTT with low factor VIII and normal von Willebrand factor ↓ Haemophilia A
exam_trap: A, Von Willebrand disease — it also lowers factor VIII and prolongs the APTT, so it tempts; but von Willebrand factor is normal here and the bleeding pattern is deep rather than mucosal.
takeaway: Low factor VIII with normal von Willebrand factor and haemarthrosis in a boy means haemophilia A.

stem: A 63-year-old woman is seen in fracture clinic after breaking her proximal humerus when she tripped on a kerb while walking. She went through the menopause at 46 and smokes. She has no history of cancer and is otherwise well. The consultant asks you to arrange a test to measure her bone mineral density. Which investigation is most appropriate?

options.A: Plain radiograph of the lumbar spine

why_correct: A low-trauma fracture after a fall from standing height is a fragility fracture and should prompt assessment for osteoporosis. DXA scanning of the hip and spine is the standard method of measuring bone mineral density and is used alongside a fracture risk assessment to guide treatment.
why_wrong: A. Plain radiographs show fractures and gross bone thinning but cannot reliably measure bone density. C. An isotope bone scan detects areas of increased bone turnover such as metastases, not bone density. D. Alkaline phosphatase is usually normal in osteoporosis and does not quantify bone density. E. MRI is used to assess marrow, cord and soft tissue, not to measure bone mineral density.
pearl: Every fragility fracture is a prompt to think osteoporosis: assess risk and measure bone density with DXA. Early menopause and smoking are classic risk factors to spot in the history.
thinking: Fracture after a fall from standing height ↓ fragility fracture with risk factors for osteoporosis ↓ need to measure bone mineral density ↓ DXA scan
exam_trap: A, Plain radiograph of the lumbar spine — radiographs can show osteopenia or vertebral fractures, so they seem relevant, but they are insensitive and cannot quantify bone mineral density.
takeaway: Bone mineral density after a fragility fracture is measured with a DXA scan.

stem: An 81-year-old man has had three episodes over the past year of a hot, swollen knee or wrist, each settling over about a week. He is now seen on the medical admissions unit with a swollen left knee. A knee radiograph shows a thin line of calcification running through the cartilage and menisci, parallel to the joint surface. Synovial fluid Gram stain shows no organisms. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Calcification within articular cartilage and menisci (chondrocalcinosis) is the radiographic hallmark of calcium pyrophosphate deposition, which causes recurrent acute attacks of large-joint inflammation known as pseudogout, typically in the knee or wrist of older adults. Polarised microscopy of the aspirate would show weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.
why_wrong: B. Gout classically affects the first toe joint and causes punched-out erosions rather than cartilage calcification. C. Reactive arthritis affects younger adults after a gut or genital infection. D. Septic arthritis is a single acute infection, not recurrent self-limiting episodes, and a negative Gram stain with chondrocalcinosis favours crystals, although culture is still needed. E. Osteoarthritis causes chronic mechanical pain with joint-space narrowing and osteophytes, not acute hot joints with chondrocalcinosis.
pearl: Chondrocalcinosis on an X-ray of an older person with recurrent hot knees or wrists points to calcium pyrophosphate disease. Always send the aspirate for culture, as infection and crystals can coexist.
thinking: Recurrent self-limiting hot large joints in an older man ↓ knee and wrist involvement ↓ linear calcification within cartilage on X-ray ↓ Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
exam_trap: B, Gout — recurrent acute monoarthritis suggests gout, but gout favours the first toe joint and does not cause linear cartilage calcification.
takeaway: Recurrent hot knees or wrists with chondrocalcinosis indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

stem: A 52-year-old man noticed a lump at the front of his neck while shaving. On examination there is a nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid that moves on swallowing. He feels otherwise well and thyroid function is normal. Which additional finding would most raise concern that the nodule is malignant?

options.A: A soft nodule present and unchanged for ten years
options.D: A hard nodule with an enlarged ipsilateral cervical lymph node
options.E: Several small nodules throughout an enlarged gland

correct_answer: D. A hard nodule with an enlarged ipsilateral cervical lymph node
why_correct: A hard, solitary thyroid nodule with an enlarged cervical lymph node on the same side suggests malignancy with nodal spread. An unexplained thyroid lump should be referred urgently on a suspected cancer pathway for ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration.
why_wrong: A. A soft nodule that has been stable for years is reassuring. B. Tremor and palpitations suggest hyperthyroidism, and hyperfunctioning nodules are usually benign. C. A family history of hypothyroidism points to autoimmune thyroid disease, not cancer. E. A multinodular goitre is usually benign, and a single dominant nodule is more concerning.
pearl: Thyroid red flags include a hard or fixed nodule, rapid growth, cervical lymphadenopathy, hoarseness and stridor. Male sex and extremes of age also raise the risk in a solitary nodule.
thinking: Thyroid nodule moving on swallowing ↓ look for features of malignancy ↓ hardness plus same-side cervical node suggests spread ↓ Hard nodule with ipsilateral lymphadenopathy
exam_trap: E, Several small nodules throughout an enlarged gland — more nodules can sound more worrying, but a multinodular goitre is usually benign, whereas a solitary hard nodule carries the higher cancer risk.
takeaway: A hard thyroid nodule with cervical lymphadenopathy needs urgent assessment for cancer.

stem: A 68-year-old man tells his GP that for six weeks his voice has been weak and breathy, and he gets short of breath when talking for long. He also has a hard, enlarging swelling in the left side of his thyroid gland. He has no difficulty swallowing and his tongue moves normally. Involvement of which structure best explains his voice change?

options.D: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the posterior thyroid and supplies most of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles, so invasion by a thyroid cancer causes vocal cord palsy with a weak, breathy voice. New hoarseness with a thyroid mass is a red flag that needs urgent referral and laryngoscopy.
why_wrong: A. Phrenic nerve involvement paralyses the diaphragm rather than altering the voice. B. Sympathetic chain involvement causes Horner syndrome, not voice change. C. Hypoglossal nerve damage causes tongue weakness and deviation, and his tongue is normal. D. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve affects pitch and vocal stamina but does not usually cause a breathy voice from cord paralysis.
pearl: Hoarseness with a thyroid lump suggests local invasion of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The left nerve has a longer course, looping under the aortic arch, so it is also vulnerable to chest pathology.
thinking: Hard enlarging thyroid mass ↓ new weak, breathy voice ↓ suggests vocal cord palsy from local invasion ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
exam_trap: D, External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve — it also lies close to the thyroid and affects the voice, but damage mainly reduces pitch and vocal stamina rather than paralysing the cord.
takeaway: New hoarseness with a thyroid mass suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion.

stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted to the ward breathless with bibasal crackles and pitting oedema to her knees. Echocardiography shows a reduced ejection fraction. She is given intravenous furosemide, passes a large volume of urine over the next few hours and her breathing improves. How does furosemide produce this effect?

options.A: It inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
options.B: It blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
options.C: It antagonises aldosterone in the collecting duct
options.D: It blocks sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, increasing sodium and water excretion
options.E: It directly increases the force of myocardial contraction

correct_answer: D. It blocks sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, increasing sodium and water excretion
why_correct: Furosemide inhibits the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This causes a powerful loss of sodium and water in the urine, reducing circulating volume, pulmonary congestion and peripheral oedema in heart failure.
why_wrong: A. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition is the action of acetazolamide, a weak diuretic. B. Blocking the distal sodium-chloride cotransporter is the action of thiazides such as bendroflumethiazide. C. Aldosterone antagonism is the action of spironolactone and eplerenone. E. Loop diuretics relieve symptoms through fluid loss, not by increasing contractility.
pearl: Loop diuretics relieve congestion and symptoms in heart failure but do not improve survival on their own. Monitor urea, electrolytes and weight while giving them.
thinking: Fluid overload from heart failure ↓ furosemide produces a brisk diuresis ↓ acts on the thick ascending limb transporter ↓ Increased sodium and water excretion
exam_trap: B, Thiazide action in the distal tubule — both are sodium-wasting diuretics, so they are easy to confuse, but furosemide acts on the loop of Henle and is far more potent.
takeaway: Loop diuretics block sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, offloading salt and water.

stem: An 82-year-old woman who takes furosemide for heart failure is brought to the emergency department after three days of diarrhoea. She feels weak and has leg cramps. Her blood tests show a low potassium concentration with normal sodium and renal function. Which complication of her electrolyte disturbance is most important to anticipate and monitor for?
why_correct: Low potassium alters myocardial repolarisation and increases excitability, predisposing to ectopics, atrial fibrillation and potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias, especially in older patients with heart disease. An ECG and cardiac monitoring are needed while potassium is replaced, and magnesium should also be checked.
why_wrong: A. Hypoglycaemia is not a recognised result of hypokalaemia. B. Seizures are more typical of severe hyponatraemia or hypocalcaemia. D. Acute pancreatitis is associated with hypercalcaemia and hypertriglyceridaemia rather than low potassium. E. Cerebral oedema follows rapid sodium shifts, not potassium depletion.
pearl: Hypokalaemia from diuretics, vomiting or diarrhoea can cause U waves, flattened T waves and dangerous arrhythmias. Correct magnesium too, or potassium may not stay up.
thinking: Loop diuretic plus diarrhoea ↓ potassium loss with weakness and cramps ↓ low potassium destabilises cardiac repolarisation ↓ Cardiac arrhythmia
exam_trap: B, Generalised seizures — electrolyte disturbances are often linked with seizures, but these are typical of sodium or calcium abnormalities, whereas potassium mainly threatens the heart.
takeaway: The key danger of significant hypokalaemia is cardiac arrhythmia, so get an ECG.

stem: A 46-year-old woman attends a health check with the practice nurse. Her blood pressure is raised on two readings taken during the visit, but she feels well and has no history of heart disease, diabetes or kidney problems. The nurse asks how to confirm whether she truly has hypertension. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.D: Repeat clinic blood pressure in five years

why_correct: NICE recommends confirming a raised clinic blood pressure with out-of-office readings, preferably ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, before diagnosing hypertension. This avoids treating white-coat hypertension; home monitoring is an alternative if ambulatory monitoring is unsuitable or not tolerated.
why_wrong: B. Treatment should not start before the diagnosis is confirmed unless blood pressure is severely raised or there are features of an emergency. C. Echocardiography assesses target organ damage in selected patients but does not confirm hypertension. D. Waiting five years leaves sustained hypertension untreated. E. Plasma metanephrines are only used when phaeochromocytoma is suspected from paroxysmal symptoms.
pearl: Clinic readings alone can overestimate blood pressure because of the white-coat effect. Confirm with ambulatory or home readings, then assess cardiovascular risk and target organ damage.
thinking: Raised clinic readings in a well patient ↓ white-coat effect must be excluded ↓ need out-of-office measurement ↓ Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
exam_trap: B, Start amlodipine today — repeatedly raised readings make treatment seem urgent, but without severe readings or emergency features the diagnosis must be confirmed first.
takeaway: Confirm suspected hypertension with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring before treating.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has confirmed hypertension on home monitoring. Her GP advises lifestyle changes and recommends starting an antihypertensive. She says she feels perfectly fit and asks why she should take a tablet every day. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: It will stop the headaches that raised blood pressure causes
options.B: Lowering her blood pressure reduces her future risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease
options.C: Once her blood pressure is normal the tablets can be stopped for good
options.D: Taking tablets means she no longer needs to cut down on salt
options.E: It will prevent her developing type 2 diabetes

correct_answer: B. Lowering her blood pressure reduces her future risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease
why_correct: Hypertension is usually symptomless but steadily damages arteries, the heart, brain and kidneys over years. Treatment aims to reduce the long-term risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure and chronic kidney disease, which is why it is offered even to people who feel well.
why_wrong: A. Hypertension rarely causes headaches, so symptom relief is not the reason to treat. C. Hypertension is usually a lifelong condition, and stopping treatment allows blood pressure to rise again. D. Lifestyle measures such as salt reduction remain important alongside medication. E. Antihypertensives do not prevent type 2 diabetes, and some can slightly worsen glucose control.
pearl: Explain hypertension as a silent risk factor: the benefit of treatment is fewer strokes, heart attacks and kidney problems in the future, not feeling better now.
thinking: Confirmed hypertension in a symptomless patient ↓ raised pressure damages vessels and organs over time ↓ treatment lowers future events ↓ Reduced cardiovascular and renal risk
exam_trap: C, Once normal the tablets can be stopped — patients often expect a cure, but essential hypertension is usually lifelong and stopping treatment allows the risk to return.
takeaway: We treat silent hypertension to reduce future stroke, heart attack and kidney disease.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department after a 20-minute episode of fast, regular palpitations that began and ended abruptly while she was dancing. She is now well, and her heart rate is 76 bpm. Her resting 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with a PR interval shorter than normal and a slightly broad QRS complex whose initial deflection is slurred. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
why_correct: A short PR interval with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) in sinus rhythm indicates ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory pathway. Combined with paroxysmal tachycardia, this is Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, which should be referred to cardiology, as catheter ablation is often curative.
why_wrong: A. Atrioventricular nodal re-entry causes similar palpitations, but the resting ECG is normal with no delta wave. B. Brugada syndrome shows coved ST elevation in V1 to V2, not a short PR interval. C. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes left ventricular hypertrophy patterns and deep Q waves, not pre-excitation. D. Lown–Ganong–Levine syndrome has a short PR interval but a normal QRS with no delta wave.
pearl: Delta wave plus short PR equals pre-excitation. In pre-excited atrial fibrillation, avoid AV nodal blockers such as verapamil, adenosine or digoxin, which can speed conduction down the accessory pathway.
thinking: Paroxysmal regular palpitations in a young adult ↓ resting ECG: short PR and slurred QRS upstroke ↓ delta wave means an accessory pathway ↓ Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome
exam_trap: A, Atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia — it is the commonest cause of paroxysmal regular palpitations in young people, but its resting ECG lacks a delta wave.
takeaway: Short PR with a delta wave in a patient with palpitations indicates Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome.

stem: A 39-year-old woman is on the surgical ward the day after a total thyroidectomy. She complains of numbness around her lips and pins and needles in her fingers. Her adjusted calcium is low. Which neuromuscular finding is most likely to be present?

options.E: Ptosis that worsens through the day

why_correct: Low calcium lowers the threshold for nerve firing, causing perioral and peripheral paraesthesia, muscle cramps and tetany such as carpopedal spasm, which can be provoked by inflating a blood pressure cuff (Trousseau sign). After thyroidectomy this usually reflects parathyroid damage, and symptomatic patients need calcium replacement with ECG monitoring.
why_wrong: A. Intention tremor indicates cerebellar disease. B. Flaccid areflexic weakness is more typical of severe hypokalaemia or Guillain–Barré syndrome, not the hyperexcitability of low calcium. D. Tongue fasciculations suggest motor neurone disease. E. Fatigable ptosis is a feature of myasthenia gravis.
pearl: Low calcium makes nerves irritable: perioral tingling, cramps, carpopedal spasm and Chvostek and Trousseau signs. Watch for laryngospasm, seizures and a prolonged QT interval.
thinking: Day one after total thyroidectomy ↓ perioral and finger paraesthesia with low calcium ↓ hypocalcaemia increases neuromuscular excitability ↓ Carpopedal spasm
exam_trap: B, Flaccid weakness with absent reflexes — electrolyte disturbances commonly cause weakness, but low calcium causes hyperexcitability and spasm rather than flaccid paralysis.
takeaway: Hypocalcaemia causes perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm from neuromuscular hyperexcitability.

stem: A 71-year-old man with known squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is admitted from home because he has become drowsy and muddled over a week. His wife says he has been passing urine frequently and drinking a lot. His serum calcium is raised. Which other symptom is most in keeping with this electrolyte disturbance?
why_correct: Hypercalcaemia reduces smooth muscle and neuromuscular excitability, typically causing constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, polyuria, thirst, lethargy and confusion. In a patient with squamous cell lung cancer it is often due to PTH-related peptide, and initial management is intravenous fluid rehydration followed by a bisphosphonate.
why_wrong: A. Perioral tingling is a sign of low calcium, not high. C. Carpopedal spasm reflects the neuromuscular hyperexcitability of hypocalcaemia. D. Hypercalcaemia slows the gut and does not cause profuse diarrhoea. E. High calcium tends to cause hypotonia and reduced reflexes rather than increased tone.
pearl: Bones, stones, groans and psychic moans: bone pain, renal stones, abdominal pain with constipation, and confusion or low mood. Polyuria and thirst lead to dehydration, which worsens the hypercalcaemia.
thinking: Raised calcium in a man with lung cancer ↓ polyuria, thirst and confusion ↓ high calcium slows smooth muscle and the gut ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: A, Perioral tingling — it is the best-known calcium symptom, but it belongs to hypocalcaemia, the opposite disturbance.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia causes constipation, thirst, polyuria and confusion; tingling belongs to low calcium.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with long-standing anorexia nervosa is admitted with a very low body weight. Nasogastric feeding is started at a high rate. On the third day she becomes weak, breathless and confused, and develops ankle swelling. Her blood tests show low phosphate, potassium and magnesium. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

why_correct: After prolonged starvation, reintroducing carbohydrate triggers insulin release, which drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and causes sodium and fluid retention. The resulting low phosphate causes muscle weakness, respiratory and cardiac failure and confusion, which is refeeding syndrome; feeding should be slowed and electrolytes and thiamine replaced.
why_wrong: B. Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and eye signs but does not explain low phosphate and oedema. C. SIADH causes low sodium with euvolaemia rather than low phosphate, potassium and magnesium. D. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and low potassium but not low phosphate after feeding. E. Diabetic ketoacidosis requires hyperglycaemia and ketosis, which are not described.
pearl: Feed high-risk malnourished patients slowly, give thiamine before and during feeding, and check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily in the first days.
thinking: Severe malnutrition ↓ feeding restarted at a high rate ↓ insulin surge shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells ↓ Refeeding syndrome
exam_trap: B, Wernicke encephalopathy — confusion in a malnourished patient after carbohydrate loading suggests thiamine deficiency, and thiamine should be given, but it does not explain the low phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
takeaway: Weakness and low phosphate soon after feeding a starved patient indicate refeeding syndrome.

stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol dependence is admitted to the medical ward after eating almost nothing for two weeks. He is thin and has lost a lot of weight. The dietitian plans to start oral nutritional supplements and asks which blood test needs particularly close monitoring over the first few days of feeding. Which test is most important?
why_correct: Prolonged poor intake and alcohol dependence put him at high risk of refeeding syndrome, in which feeding drives phosphate into cells and causes a dangerous fall in serum phosphate. Phosphate, together with potassium and magnesium, should be checked before feeding and monitored closely during the first days, alongside thiamine replacement.
why_wrong: A. Amylase is used to diagnose pancreatitis, not to monitor refeeding. C. Albumin changes slowly and mainly reflects inflammation, so it is not a guide to refeeding risk. D. Ferritin assesses iron stores and does not change acutely with feeding. E. Urate is not affected in a clinically important way by refeeding.
pearl: Low phosphate is the defining abnormality of refeeding syndrome. Risk factors include little or no intake for several days, low BMI, rapid weight loss, alcohol misuse and low electrolytes before feeding.
thinking: Alcohol dependence with prolonged poor intake ↓ high risk of refeeding syndrome ↓ feeding shifts phosphate into cells ↓ Monitor serum phosphate
exam_trap: C, Serum albumin — it sounds like a nutritional marker, but albumin reflects inflammation and changes too slowly to detect refeeding complications.
takeaway: Monitor phosphate closely when restarting nutrition in a malnourished patient.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 26 weeks of her second pregnancy attends the antenatal clinic. She was offered a glucose tolerance test because her body mass index is raised and her first baby was large. Her booking HbA1c was normal, she has no previous history of diabetes, and both the fasting and 2-hour glucose values on the test are now raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hyperglycaemia first detected in the second or third trimester in a woman with a normal booking HbA1c and no prior diabetes is gestational diabetes. It results from pregnancy-related insulin resistance, is first managed with diet and exercise, and needs postnatal glucose testing because of a raised lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes.
why_wrong: A. A normal booking HbA1c makes pre-existing type 2 diabetes unlikely. C. Maturity-onset diabetes of the young is a monogenic diabetes with a strong family history, and is not suggested here. D. Although insulin resistance rises in pregnancy, an abnormal glucose tolerance test is not normal. E. Type 1 diabetes presents with weight loss, polyuria and ketosis rather than an abnormal screening test.
pearl: Risk factors for gestational diabetes include a raised BMI, a previous large baby, previous gestational diabetes, a family history of diabetes and certain ethnic backgrounds. Recheck glucose after delivery.
thinking: Glucose tolerance test offered for risk factors ↓ raised values at 26 weeks ↓ normal booking HbA1c and no previous diabetes ↓ Gestational diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: A, Pre-existing type 2 diabetes — her risk factors overlap with type 2 diabetes, but the normal booking HbA1c shows the hyperglycaemia arose during pregnancy.
takeaway: Hyperglycaemia first found in later pregnancy after a normal booking HbA1c is gestational diabetes.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has a telephone consultation with her GP. Over the past eight months her cycles have lengthened to every six to nine weeks, and she wakes drenched in sweat most nights. She feels irritable and tired. Her last bleed was five weeks ago. She is otherwise well. Which term best describes her situation?
why_correct: Changing cycle length with vasomotor symptoms such as night sweats, while periods are still occurring, describes the perimenopause. NICE advises that in women over 45 with typical symptoms this can be diagnosed clinically without measuring FSH.
why_wrong: A. Premature ovarian insufficiency refers to loss of ovarian function before the age of 40. B. Postmenopause is diagnosed only after 12 months without a period, and she bled five weeks ago. D. Hypothyroidism causes tiredness but not night sweats with lengthening cycles in this pattern. E. Polycystic ovary syndrome causes long-standing irregular cycles from early adulthood, often with hirsutism, not new vasomotor symptoms in the late forties.
pearl: Over 45 with irregular periods and vasomotor symptoms: perimenopause is a clinical diagnosis. Remind her that contraception is still needed until menopause is confirmed.
thinking: Woman in her late forties ↓ lengthening cycles but still bleeding ↓ night sweats and mood change ↓ Perimenopause
exam_trap: B, Postmenopause — vasomotor symptoms suggest menopause, but postmenopause requires a full year without periods.
takeaway: Irregular but continuing periods with vasomotor symptoms over 45 indicate perimenopause.

stem: A 17-year-old girl who plays rugby for her school has a week of fever, a very sore throat and swollen glands at the back of her neck. A heterophile antibody (Monospot) test is positive. She feels a little better and asks her GP whether she can play in a match next weekend. What is the main reason to advise her against this?

options.B: Risk of airway obstruction from enlarged tonsils
options.E: Risk of passing the infection to teammates

why_correct: Infectious mononucleosis commonly causes splenic enlargement, even when the spleen cannot be felt, and a blow to the abdomen can rupture it with life-threatening bleeding. Contact sport and heavy lifting should therefore be avoided for several weeks after the illness.
why_wrong: B. Severe tonsillar swelling can rarely threaten the airway, but this is unrelated to playing sport. C. Myocarditis is a rare complication and is not the specific reason to avoid contact sport in glandular fever. D. Liver enzymes often rise mildly, but liver failure is very rare and not linked to sport. E. Transmission is through saliva, so sport is not the main concern.
pearl: Glandular fever enlarges the spleen in most patients, so advise avoiding contact sport and heavy lifting for several weeks. Avoid amoxicillin, which often causes a widespread rash.
thinking: Young person with glandular fever ↓ splenomegaly is common, even if not palpable ↓ contact sport risks abdominal trauma ↓ Splenic rupture
exam_trap: C, Risk of viral myocarditis — advice to avoid exercise after viral illness is often about myocarditis, but in glandular fever the specific danger of contact sport is splenic rupture.
takeaway: Avoid contact sport for several weeks after glandular fever because of splenic rupture.

stem: A 66-year-old man sees his GP with two days of burning pain followed by clusters of blisters on the left side of his forehead and scalp. On examination there are also vesicles on the side of the tip of his nose. His visual acuity is currently normal. Which complication is this distribution particularly associated with?

options.D: Ocular involvement such as keratitis or uveitis

correct_answer: D. Ocular involvement such as keratitis or uveitis
why_correct: Shingles in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve is herpes zoster ophthalmicus, and vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson sign) show involvement of the nasociliary branch, which also supplies the eye. This strongly predicts corneal and intraocular inflammation, so oral antivirals should be started promptly and the eye assessed urgently, with same-day ophthalmology referral if there are eye signs.
why_wrong: A. Facial palsy with ear vesicles is Ramsay Hunt syndrome, which involves the facial nerve rather than the ophthalmic division. B. Hearing loss also belongs to Ramsay Hunt syndrome. C. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock pains and is not a recognised result of this rash pattern. E. Bacterial meningitis is not a typical complication of shingles.
pearl: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose in forehead shingles signal nasociliary involvement and a high risk of eye disease. Start antivirals and get the eye examined urgently, even if vision seems normal.
thinking: Shingles in the ophthalmic dermatome ↓ vesicles on the side of the nose tip ↓ nasociliary branch also supplies the eye ↓ Ocular involvement such as keratitis or uveitis
exam_trap: A, Lower motor neurone facial palsy — facial shingles brings Ramsay Hunt syndrome to mind, but that involves the ear and facial nerve, not the forehead and nose.
takeaway: Forehead shingles with nose-tip vesicles predicts eye involvement and needs urgent eye assessment.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to his GP a few days after returning from a summer camp where he swam daily in an outdoor pool. Several other children are unwell. He has a fever, a sore throat, and both eyes are red and watery without pus. There are tender lymph nodes in front of both ears and in the neck. There is no rash. Which organism is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Fever, pharyngitis and bilateral follicular conjunctivitis with preauricular and cervical lymphadenopathy form pharyngoconjunctival fever, classically caused by adenovirus. Outbreaks are linked to swimming pools and close contact, and management is supportive with good hand and eye hygiene.
why_wrong: B. Epstein–Barr virus causes pharyngitis with marked lymphadenopathy but conjunctivitis is not a typical feature. C. Group A Streptococcus causes tonsillitis with exudate but not conjunctivitis. D. Herpes simplex conjunctivitis is usually unilateral, often with vesicles on the eyelids. E. Coxsackie A causes herpangina or hand, foot and mouth disease, with oral vesicles rather than conjunctivitis.
pearl: Sore throat plus red, watery eyes plus preauricular nodes suggests adenovirus. Adenoviral conjunctivitis is highly contagious, so advise against sharing towels.
thinking: Fever and sore throat ↓ bilateral watery conjunctivitis with preauricular nodes ↓ swimming pool cluster ↓ Adenovirus
exam_trap: B, Epstein–Barr virus — sore throat with tender cervical nodes in a young person suggests glandular fever, but EBV does not usually cause bilateral watery conjunctivitis.
takeaway: Fever, pharyngitis and bilateral watery conjunctivitis point to adenovirus.

stem: A 17-year-old is referred to the adolescent gynaecology clinic because she has never had a period. She is tall, with well-developed breasts, but has very scanty hair in the axillae and pubic area. There is a small, firm swelling in each groin. Pelvic ultrasound shows no uterus. Which diagnosis is most probable?
why_correct: In complete androgen insensitivity a 46,XY individual has testes, often in the groin or abdomen, that produce testosterone which the tissues cannot respond to. Testosterone is converted to oestrogen, giving breast development, while lack of androgen effect causes scanty body hair, and anti-Müllerian hormone from the testes prevents a uterus forming.
why_wrong: A. Müllerian agenesis also causes an absent uterus with normal breasts, but pubic and axillary hair are normal because androgen action is intact. B. Turner syndrome causes short stature and absent breast development from ovarian failure. C. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes androgen excess with virilisation, not scanty hair. E. Kallmann syndrome causes absent puberty with poor breast development and loss of smell.
pearl: Primary amenorrhoea with breasts but no uterus: check body hair. Scanty hair means androgen insensitivity; normal hair means Müllerian agenesis. Confirm with karyotype.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea with good breast development ↓ absent uterus ↓ scanty pubic and axillary hair plus groin swellings that are likely testes ↓ Androgen insensitivity syndrome
exam_trap: A, Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome — it shares primary amenorrhoea, normal breasts and an absent uterus, but body hair is normal because the patient is 46,XX with normal androgen response.
takeaway: Breasts, no uterus and scanty body hair point to androgen insensitivity syndrome.

stem: A 17-year-old attends her GP because she has not started her periods. She has no cyclical pelvic pain. She has normal height, normal breast development and normal pubic and axillary hair. Pelvic ultrasound shows two normal-looking ovaries, but no uterus can be seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome (Müllerian agenesis) is failure of the uterus and upper vagina to develop in a 46,XX individual. Because the ovaries function normally, breast development and pubic and axillary hair are normal, but there is primary amenorrhoea with an absent uterus.
why_wrong: A. Androgen insensitivity also causes an absent uterus with breasts, but pubic and axillary hair are scanty and gonads are testes, not ovaries. B. Turner syndrome causes short stature and poor breast development from ovarian failure. C. An imperforate hymen causes cyclical pain with a normal uterus filled with blood. E. Constitutional delay produces delayed breast and hair development, not complete puberty with an absent uterus.
pearl: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with primary amenorrhoea suggest an anatomical cause. Absent uterus with normal hair and ovaries is Müllerian agenesis.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea with normal breasts and normal body hair ↓ ovaries present, so ovarian and androgen function intact ↓ uterus absent ↓ Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome
exam_trap: A, Androgen insensitivity syndrome — breasts with an absent uterus suggest it, but normal pubic and axillary hair and visible ovaries rule it out.
takeaway: Primary amenorrhoea with normal hair and ovaries but no uterus indicates Müllerian agenesis.

stem: A 44-year-old woman attends the emergency department with right loin-to-groin pain, rigors and vomiting. She has a high fever, a fast pulse and low blood pressure. Non-contrast CT shows a stone at the right vesicoureteric junction with hydronephrosis above it. Blood cultures are taken and intravenous antibiotics are started. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Tamsulosin and await spontaneous stone passage
options.B: Urgent drainage of the kidney by nephrostomy or ureteric stent
options.C: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy within 24 hours
options.D: Switch to oral antibiotics and discharge with urology follow-up

correct_answer: B. Urgent drainage of the kidney by nephrostomy or ureteric stent
why_correct: A ureteric stone with fever and signs of sepsis means an infected obstructed kidney, a urological emergency that can rapidly cause septic shock and loss of the kidney. Alongside resuscitation and antibiotics, the collecting system must be urgently decompressed by percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent, with definitive stone treatment deferred until the infection has resolved.
why_wrong: A. Medical expulsive therapy is only suitable for uncomplicated stones without infection. C. Lithotripsy is contraindicated during active infection and does not relieve obstruction quickly. D. A septic patient with an obstructed kidney cannot be safely discharged. E. Delayed ureteroscopy is appropriate only after drainage and recovery, not as the immediate step.
pearl: Stone plus fever equals emergency drainage. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus trapped behind an obstruction.
thinking: Renal colic with fever, tachycardia and hypotension ↓ obstructing stone with hydronephrosis ↓ infected obstructed kidney, a source of sepsis ↓ Urgent nephrostomy or stent
exam_trap: A, Tamsulosin and await passage — it is standard for many ureteric stones, but in the presence of infection waiting allows sepsis to progress.
takeaway: An infected obstructed kidney needs urgent decompression alongside antibiotics.

stem: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who takes gliclazide is seen on the ward because he has become sweaty, shaky and anxious before lunch. A finger-prick glucose reads 2.8 mmol/L. He is alert, talking normally and able to swallow safely. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.A: Fast-acting carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or fruit juice by mouth
options.D: A sandwich or other starchy snack only
options.E: Omit his next gliclazide dose and recheck glucose in an hour

correct_answer: A. Fast-acting carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or fruit juice by mouth
why_correct: A conscious patient with symptomatic hypoglycaemia who can swallow safely should be given fast-acting oral carbohydrate first, with glucose rechecked after 10 to 15 minutes and treatment repeated if still low. Once glucose has recovered, a longer-acting carbohydrate is given; sulfonylurea-related hypoglycaemia can recur, so monitoring continues.
why_wrong: B. Intramuscular glucagon is for patients who cannot safely take oral treatment, and it is less effective after sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia. C. Intravenous glucose is reserved for patients who are drowsy, unconscious or unable to swallow. D. Starchy food is absorbed too slowly to correct hypoglycaemia and is used only after recovery. E. Delaying treatment risks further deterioration.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia ladder: alert and swallowing means oral fast-acting glucose; drowsy or unable to swallow means IV glucose or IM glucagon. Follow up with a starchy snack once recovered.
thinking: Symptomatic low glucose on a sulfonylurea ↓ patient alert and swallowing safely ↓ oral route is quickest and safest ↓ Fast-acting oral carbohydrate
exam_trap: B, Intramuscular glucagon — it is a familiar hypoglycaemia rescue treatment, but it is for patients unable to take oral glucose, not alert ones.
takeaway: Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate first in conscious hypoglycaemic patients who can swallow.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with severe asthma has needed oral prednisolone almost continuously for the past year. She attends the respiratory clinic with weight gain around her abdomen, purple stretch marks, thin skin that bruises easily and difficulty getting up from a squat. Her blood glucose is mildly raised. Which condition accounts for her presentation?

options.B: Cushing disease due to a pituitary adenoma

why_correct: Prolonged high-dose oral glucocorticoid treatment is the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome, producing central obesity, purple striae, skin thinning, easy bruising, proximal myopathy and hyperglycaemia. Management is to reduce the steroid to the lowest effective dose using steroid-sparing treatment, never stopping abruptly because of adrenal suppression.
why_wrong: A. Addison disease causes weight loss, fatigue, hypotension and pigmentation, the opposite of these features. B. Cushing disease is caused by a pituitary tumour and should not be assumed when there is a clear exogenous steroid source. D. Hypothyroidism causes weight gain and fatigue but not purple striae, bruising or hyperglycaemia. E. Ectopic ACTH is usually caused by a tumour such as small cell lung cancer and typically causes rapid weight loss, pigmentation and low potassium.
pearl: Always check the drug history before investigating Cushing syndrome; exogenous steroids are by far the commonest cause. Long-term steroids must be tapered, not stopped suddenly.
thinking: Cushingoid features with proximal myopathy ↓ near-continuous oral prednisolone for a year ↓ excess glucocorticoid from medication ↓ Exogenous (iatrogenic) Cushing syndrome
exam_trap: B, Cushing disease due to a pituitary adenoma — it produces the same appearance, but with a clear steroid exposure the drug is the cause.
takeaway: Cushingoid features on long-term oral steroids indicate iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.
