stem: An 81-year-old man in a care home takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Staff found him on the floor of his room this morning with a small cut on his scalp. Since then he has vomited twice and become increasingly drowsy. His capillary glucose is normal. Which diagnosis is the priority to rule out?
why_correct: Anticoagulation greatly increases the risk of intracranial bleeding after even minor head injury, and vomiting with increasing drowsiness suggests rising intracranial pressure. He needs urgent CT of the head, an INR check and rapid reversal of anticoagulation if bleeding is confirmed.
why_wrong: B. Vasovagal syncope may explain a fall but not progressive drowsiness and vomiting afterwards. C. Concussion is a diagnosis of exclusion and is unsafe to assume in an anticoagulated patient with worsening consciousness. D. Delirium from infection is common in older people but must not distract from a possible bleed after a head injury. E. Positional vertigo causes brief dizziness but not drowsiness.
pearl: Head injury on an anticoagulant warrants CT even when the injury seems minor; vomiting or falling consciousness makes it urgent.
thinking: Older man on warfarin ↓ unwitnessed fall with a scalp wound ↓ vomiting and increasing drowsiness ↓ Intracranial haemorrhage
exam_trap: D, Urinary tract infection causing delirium — confusion in a care home resident is often blamed on infection, but after a head injury on warfarin a bleed must be excluded first.
takeaway: Head injury on warfarin with drowsiness needs urgent CT to exclude intracranial bleeding.

stem: A 72-year-old woman on warfarin for a previous pulmonary embolism has a routine INR test at the anticoagulation clinic. Her INR is 9.1, having been in range for months. She started a course of clarithromycin five days ago for a chest infection. On telephone review she has no bleeding or bruising and feels well. How should this be managed?

options.A: Admit for intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
options.B: Continue warfarin unchanged and repeat the INR next week
options.C: Reduce the warfarin dose slightly and continue
options.D: Stop warfarin permanently and start aspirin
options.E: Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K (phytomenadione)

correct_answer: E. Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K (phytomenadione)
why_correct: A markedly raised INR without bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin and giving a small dose of oral vitamin K (phytomenadione), as set out in the BNF, then rechecking the INR and restarting warfarin once it has fallen back towards range. Clarithromycin inhibits warfarin metabolism and is the likely cause of the rise.
why_wrong: A. Intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate is for major bleeding. B. Continuing unchanged leaves her at high risk of bleeding. C. A small dose reduction without withholding warfarin does not lower a very high INR quickly enough. D. She still needs anticoagulation for her clot history, and aspirin is not an adequate substitute.
pearl: Match warfarin reversal to bleeding: no bleeding means withhold, plus oral vitamin K if the INR is very high; major bleeding means IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate. Check for interacting drugs such as macrolides.
thinking: Very high INR on warfarin ↓ no bleeding, so no emergency reversal needed ↓ withhold the drug and lower the INR safely ↓ Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K
exam_trap: A, Intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate — a very high INR feels like an emergency, but full reversal is reserved for major bleeding and would over-correct a well patient.
takeaway: Very high INR without bleeding: withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K.

stem: A 29-year-old man with a known peanut allergy eats a cereal bar at work. Within minutes he develops swollen lips, widespread urticaria, a hoarse voice and wheeze, and he feels faint. His blood pressure is low. He is given intramuscular adrenaline by paramedics and improves. What underlies his reaction?

options.C: Antibodies against cell-surface antigens (type II) hypersensitivity
options.D: Allergen cross-linking IgE on mast cells and basophils, causing degranulation

correct_answer: D. Allergen cross-linking IgE on mast cells and basophils, causing degranulation
why_correct: Anaphylaxis to food is a type I hypersensitivity in which the allergen cross-links specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine, tryptase and other mediators within minutes. This causes urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm and vasodilatation with hypotension, which is why intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment.
why_wrong: A. Type IV reactions are T-cell mediated and develop over days, as in contact dermatitis. B. Immune-complex reactions occur days after exposure, as in serum sickness. C. Type II reactions involve antibodies against cell surfaces, as in haemolytic transfusion reactions, not urticaria and wheeze within minutes. E. C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema without urticaria or wheeze and does not respond well to adrenaline.
pearl: Anaphylaxis is a rapid IgE-mediated mast cell release. Take a mast cell tryptase sample once resuscitation is under way, and refer to an allergy clinic.
thinking: Known peanut allergy ↓ urticaria, angioedema, wheeze and hypotension within minutes ↓ immediate allergen-specific reaction ↓ IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation
exam_trap: E, Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor — lip swelling suggests hereditary angioedema, but that causes swelling without urticaria or wheeze and is not triggered by a specific food allergen.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis results from IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation.

stem: A 52-year-old man on the medical ward is on day four of intravenous antibiotics for pneumonia. He develops an itchy, red, blotchy rash over his trunk and limbs. His lips, mouth and eyes are not affected, and his skin is not blistering or peeling. He has no facial swelling or wheeze, and his observations are stable. Which type of reaction is most likely?
why_correct: A widespread itchy rash appearing several days into a new drug, without mucosal involvement, skin loss or features of anaphylaxis, is typical of a delayed T-cell-mediated (non-IgE) drug reaction. The suspected drug should usually be stopped and replaced, and the reaction documented clearly in the notes and allergy record.
why_wrong: A. IgE-mediated reactions occur within minutes to an hour and cause urticaria, angioedema or bronchospasm. C. Stevens–Johnson syndrome involves mucous membranes with blistering and skin detachment, which are absent. D. Serum sickness-like reactions usually cause fever and joint pains alongside the rash. E. Hereditary angioedema causes swelling without an itchy rash and is not drug-induced.
pearl: Timing guides drug reactions: minutes suggest IgE-mediated; days suggest T-cell-mediated. Always check for mucosal involvement, blistering, fever and organ involvement to spot severe reactions.
thinking: New antibiotic started several days ago ↓ widespread itchy rash ↓ no mucosal signs, blistering, airway or circulatory compromise ↓ Delayed T-cell-mediated drug hypersensitivity
exam_trap: A, Immediate IgE-mediated reaction — any drug rash suggests allergy, but immediate reactions occur within an hour, not days later.
takeaway: A rash days into a new drug, without severe features, is a delayed T-cell drug reaction.

stem: A 24-year-old woman attends the emergency department with sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. She is tachycardic. A CT pulmonary angiogram shows a pulmonary embolus. She does not smoke and has not travelled or had surgery recently. She runs three times a week, takes cetirizine for hay fever, a vitamin D supplement and a combined oral contraceptive pill, and uses an emollient for eczema. Which factor in her history is most relevant to this event?
why_correct: The oestrogen in combined hormonal contraception increases clotting factor production and is a well-established risk factor for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. After a venous thromboembolism, oestrogen-containing contraception should be stopped and a non-oestrogen method such as a copper or levonorgestrel intrauterine device, implant or progestogen-only pill offered.
why_wrong: A. Regular exercise does not increase venous thromboembolism risk. B. Cetirizine is not associated with thrombosis. C. Vitamin D supplementation has no recognised link with clotting. E. Topical emollients have no systemic effect on clotting.
pearl: Oestrogen raises venous clot risk; progestogen-only methods and intrauterine devices do not significantly raise it and are suitable after a clot.
thinking: Young woman with pulmonary embolism ↓ no surgery, travel or smoking ↓ oestrogen increases clotting tendency ↓ Combined oral contraceptive pill
exam_trap: A, Running three times a week — exertion and dehydration can seem relevant to clotting, but regular exercise does not increase venous thromboembolism risk.
takeaway: Oestrogen-containing contraception is a key risk factor for venous thromboembolism.

stem: An 84-year-old man is seen in the falls clinic after two falls when getting out of bed at night. He feels light-headed on standing. He takes amlodipine, ramipril, doxazosin and furosemide for hypertension, and tamsulosin for his prostate. His lying blood pressure is 150/84 mmHg and after three minutes standing it is 118/70 mmHg, with symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Review his medications and reduce or stop those lowering his blood pressure
options.C: Increase ramipril because his lying blood pressure is raised
options.D: Advise fluid restriction to reduce night-time urination

correct_answer: A. Review his medications and reduce or stop those lowering his blood pressure
why_correct: Symptomatic postural hypotension in an older person is very often driven by medication, and he takes several drugs that lower blood pressure, including two alpha-blockers. The first step is a structured medication review to rationalise them, alongside advice on adequate fluid intake and getting up slowly; drug treatment is considered only if symptoms persist.
why_wrong: B. Midodrine is considered only after reversible causes have been addressed. C. Adding more antihypertensive treatment would worsen the postural drop and falls risk. D. Fluid restriction reduces circulating volume and worsens postural hypotension. E. A pacemaker treats bradyarrhythmias, not a drug-related postural blood pressure drop.
pearl: In an older person who falls, check lying and standing blood pressure and review drugs. Alpha-blockers, diuretics, vasodilators and some antidepressants are common culprits.
thinking: Falls with light-headedness on standing ↓ significant postural blood pressure drop ↓ several drugs that lower blood pressure, including two alpha-blockers ↓ Medication review
exam_trap: C, Increase ramipril — the lying blood pressure looks high, but increasing treatment would worsen the symptomatic drop on standing.
takeaway: Start postural hypotension management with a review of blood pressure-lowering drugs.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes wakes with weakness of the left side of her face, her left arm and her left leg, all affected to a similar degree. Her speech content and understanding are normal, her visual fields are full and she has no neglect of the left side. Sensation is intact. Which type of stroke is most likely?
why_correct: A pure motor deficit affecting the face, arm and leg equally, without cortical signs such as dysphasia, visual field loss or neglect, is typical of a lacunar infarct. These small deep infarcts in the internal capsule or pons result from small-vessel disease, for which hypertension and diabetes are major risk factors.
why_wrong: A. A total anterior circulation infarct needs weakness plus both a higher cortical deficit and a visual field defect. B. A partial anterior circulation infarct includes a cortical feature such as dysphasia or neglect. D. Posterior circulation strokes cause cerebellar, brainstem or isolated visual field signs. E. A spinal cord lesion cannot cause facial weakness.
pearl: Lacunar strokes are pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor or ataxic hemiparesis syndromes without cortical signs. Cortical signs such as dysphasia, neglect or field loss point to an anterior circulation stroke.
thinking: Sudden one-sided weakness of face, arm and leg equally ↓ no dysphasia, field loss or neglect ↓ small-vessel risk factors ↓ Lacunar infarct
exam_trap: B, Partial anterior circulation infarct — dense one-sided weakness suggests a larger stroke, but without any cortical sign it does not meet the definition.
takeaway: Equal face, arm and leg weakness without cortical signs indicates a lacunar infarct.

stem: A 31-year-old nursery teacher phones her GP practice. Her right eye became red and watery three days ago and her left eye has now started. Both feel gritty, but there is no real pain, her vision is normal, and bright light does not bother her. She had a cold last week, and several children in her class have had red eyes. There is a tender lump in front of her right ear. Which diagnosis is most probable?
why_correct: A watery, gritty red eye spreading to the other eye after a cold, with contacts affected and a tender preauricular node, is typical of viral (usually adenoviral) conjunctivitis. It is self-limiting, so management is hygiene advice, lubricants and avoiding sharing towels, with review if pain, light sensitivity or reduced vision develop.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial conjunctivitis causes a sticky purulent discharge rather than a watery one. B. Allergic conjunctivitis is mainly itchy, often with hay fever, and does not cause preauricular lymphadenopathy. D. Angle-closure glaucoma causes severe pain, haloes, reduced vision and vomiting. E. Anterior uveitis causes pain, photophobia and reduced vision, usually in one eye.
pearl: Red eye red flags are pain, photophobia, reduced vision and a fixed or abnormal pupil. Without them, watery discharge with preauricular nodes suggests viral conjunctivitis.
thinking: Bilateral sequential red, watery, gritty eyes ↓ recent cold and affected contacts ↓ no pain, photophobia or visual loss, tender preauricular node ↓ Viral conjunctivitis
exam_trap: A, Bacterial conjunctivitis — infectious spread among children suggests bacteria, but a watery discharge with a preauricular node points to a viral cause.
takeaway: Watery gritty red eyes with a preauricular node and no red flags suggest viral conjunctivitis.

stem: A 69-year-old man slipped on a wet bathroom floor and fell from standing onto his right side. In the emergency department he cannot bear weight and an X-ray shows a fractured neck of femur. He has never had cancer, has not lost weight and had no bone pain beforehand and is otherwise well. Which term best describes this fracture?
why_correct: A fragility fracture results from a force that would not normally break a healthy bone, such as a fall from standing height or less. Recognising it should prompt assessment of bone health, including fracture risk and bone density, and treatment to prevent further fractures.
why_wrong: B. Stress fractures result from repeated loading, such as long-distance running, rather than a single fall. C. A metastatic fracture is possible but there are no features of cancer, and it is a diagnosis to exclude rather than the default. D. A fall from standing height is low-energy trauma. E. Avulsion fractures occur when a tendon or ligament pulls off a fragment of bone.
pearl: A fall from standing height or less that causes a fracture means fragility fracture. Men get osteoporosis too, so assess bone health in both sexes.
thinking: Hip fracture after a fall from standing ↓ low-energy force that should not break healthy bone ↓ no features of malignancy ↓ Fragility fracture
exam_trap: C, Pathological fracture from bone metastasis — any low-trauma fracture can raise the possibility of tumour, but without cancer features the correct term is fragility fracture.
takeaway: A fracture from a fall at standing height or less is a fragility fracture and needs bone health review.

stem: A 64-year-old man has taken hydralazine for resistant hypertension for 14 months. He now has three weeks of low-grade fever, aching and swelling of his hands and wrists, and sharp chest pain on deep breathing. Antinuclear antibody is positive, anti-double-stranded DNA is negative, and renal function and urinalysis are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hydralazine is a classic cause of drug-induced lupus, which typically presents after months of treatment with fever, arthralgia and serositis such as pleurisy, but rarely with renal or neurological disease. ANA is positive and anti-histone antibodies are typical, while anti-dsDNA is usually negative; symptoms resolve after the drug is stopped.
why_wrong: A. Idiopathic lupus is more common in younger women, often with anti-dsDNA and renal involvement, and the clear drug trigger is more likely here. C. Rheumatoid arthritis does not usually cause fever and pleurisy with a positive ANA as its main features. D. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, not wrist swelling and pleurisy. E. Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genital infection and affects lower limb joints.
pearl: Common causes of drug-induced lupus include hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline and anti-TNF agents. Anti-histone antibodies support the diagnosis, and stopping the drug is the treatment.
thinking: Months of hydralazine ↓ fever, arthritis and pleurisy ↓ ANA positive, anti-dsDNA negative, kidneys spared ↓ Drug-induced lupus
exam_trap: A, Systemic lupus erythematosus — the features are lupus-like, but a recognised causative drug with negative anti-dsDNA and no renal disease points to drug-induced lupus.
takeaway: Lupus-like features after months of hydralazine, without renal disease, suggest drug-induced lupus.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis at a sexual health clinic and prescribed a seven-day course of oral metronidazole. She mentions she is going to a wedding at the weekend and asks whether she can drink. How should you advise her?

options.A: Alcohol is fine in moderation with this antibiotic
options.B: Take the tablets in the morning so that drinking in the evening is safe
options.C: Avoid alcohol only on the first day of the course
options.D: Avoid dairy products around each dose instead
options.E: Avoid alcohol during the course and for 48 hours after finishing it

correct_answer: E. Avoid alcohol during the course and for 48 hours after finishing it
why_correct: Metronidazole can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, producing flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache and palpitations. Patients should avoid alcohol throughout the course and for 48 hours after the last dose.
why_wrong: A. Even moderate amounts of alcohol can trigger the reaction. B. The drug remains active throughout the day, so timing the dose does not prevent the interaction. C. The risk lasts for the whole course and shortly afterwards, not just the first day. D. Dairy restriction applies to some tetracyclines, not to metronidazole.
pearl: Metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction: flushing, vomiting, headache and palpitations. Advise avoiding alcohol during the course and for 48 hours afterwards.
thinking: Metronidazole prescribed ↓ patient plans to drink ↓ risk of disulfiram-like reaction lasting beyond the last dose ↓ Avoid alcohol during and for 48 hours after the course
exam_trap: B, Take the tablets in the morning — separating the dose from drinking seems logical, but the drug acts throughout the day and the reaction can still occur.
takeaway: No alcohol on metronidazole, and for 48 hours after the course ends.

stem: A 58-year-old man with COPD is prescribed doxycycline for an infective exacerbation. He tells the community pharmacist that he usually takes his medicines just before getting into bed. What advice best reduces his risk of oesophageal injury from this drug?

options.A: Chew the capsule before swallowing to help it dissolve
options.B: Swallow it with a full glass of water while sitting or standing, and stay upright afterwards
options.C: Take it at bedtime as usual, lying flat straight afterwards
options.D: Take it with an indigestion remedy to protect the gullet
options.E: Swallow it without water so it is absorbed faster

correct_answer: B. Swallow it with a full glass of water while sitting or standing, and stay upright afterwards
why_correct: Doxycycline can lodge in the oesophagus and cause painful ulceration. It should be swallowed whole with plenty of water while sitting or standing, and the patient should not lie down immediately afterwards, so it should not be taken just before going to bed.
why_wrong: A. Chewing the capsule releases the drug in the mouth and oesophagus, increasing irritation. C. Lying flat soon after a dose is the main risk factor for oesophageal ulceration. D. Antacids contain metals that bind doxycycline and reduce its absorption. E. Taking it without water greatly increases the chance of it sticking in the oesophagus.
pearl: Doxycycline counselling: plenty of water, stay upright, avoid taking just before bed, separate from antacids and iron, and protect skin from strong sunlight.
thinking: Doxycycline can lodge in and ulcerate the oesophagus ↓ risk is highest when swallowed dry or lying down ↓ water and gravity help it pass ↓ Full glass of water and stay upright
exam_trap: D, Take it with an indigestion remedy — protecting the gullet sounds sensible, but antacids bind doxycycline and stop it working.
takeaway: Take doxycycline with plenty of water and stay upright afterwards.

stem: A 26-year-old woman who takes a combined oral contraceptive pill is prescribed a seven-day course of flucloxacillin for cellulitis of her leg. She has no vomiting or diarrhoea and takes no other medicines. She has heard that antibiotics stop the pill working and asks what she should do. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: No additional contraceptive precautions are needed
options.B: Use condoms during the course and for seven days afterwards
options.C: Stop the pill until the antibiotic course has finished
options.D: Take two pills a day during the antibiotic course
options.E: Switch to the progestogen-only pill straight away

correct_answer: A. No additional contraceptive precautions are needed
why_correct: Antibiotics that do not induce liver enzymes, such as flucloxacillin, do not reduce the effectiveness of combined hormonal contraception, so no additional precautions are needed. Extra precautions are needed only with enzyme-inducing drugs such as rifampicin or rifabutin, or if vomiting or severe diarrhoea affect absorption of the pill.
why_wrong: B. Advice to use condoms after any antibiotic is outdated and not supported by current guidance. C. Stopping the pill would leave her unprotected. D. Doubling the dose is unnecessary and increases side effects. E. Changing method is unnecessary because her current pill remains effective.
pearl: Only enzyme-inducing antibiotics, mainly rifampicin and rifabutin, reduce the effectiveness of combined hormonal contraception. Vomiting or severe diarrhoea can also reduce absorption of the pill.
thinking: Combined pill plus antibiotic ↓ flucloxacillin is not an enzyme inducer ↓ no vomiting or diarrhoea ↓ No additional precautions needed
exam_trap: B, Use condoms during the course and for seven days afterwards — this reflects old, widely held advice, but current guidance says non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics do not affect the pill.
takeaway: Non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics do not reduce combined pill efficacy, so no extra precautions are needed.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her sister. For ten days she has barely slept but says she is full of energy. She talks rapidly, jumping between topics, believes she has been chosen to launch a global business, and has spent her savings on two cars. She is irritable when interrupted. Two years ago she was treated for a severe depressive episode. A urine drug screen is negative and thyroid function is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Elevated or irritable mood with reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiosity and reckless spending that severely impair functioning describe a manic episode. A manic episode, especially with a previous depressive episode, indicates bipolar affective disorder once organic and substance causes have been excluded.
why_wrong: A. Schizophrenia causes psychotic symptoms without a sustained elevation of mood, energy and reduced need for sleep. C. Cyclothymia involves milder, persistent mood swings that do not reach full mania. D. Recurrent depressive disorder does not include manic episodes. E. Generalised anxiety disorder causes persistent worry, not elevated mood and grandiosity.
pearl: One manic episode is enough to diagnose bipolar disorder. Grandiose beliefs during mania are mood-congruent psychotic features, not a separate diagnosis of schizophrenia.
thinking: Reduced need for sleep with high energy ↓ pressured speech, grandiosity and reckless spending ↓ previous depressive episode, organic causes excluded ↓ Bipolar affective disorder
exam_trap: A, Schizophrenia — the grandiose belief sounds psychotic, but it occurs within a clear manic episode with elevated mood and reduced need for sleep.
takeaway: Mania with reduced need for sleep and grandiosity indicates bipolar affective disorder.

stem: A 23-year-old man is assessed by the home treatment team. He says the newsreader on television has been sending him personal coded instructions, and he is certain of this despite his family's reassurance. When alone in his flat he hears two men talking about him and commenting on what he is doing, although nobody else is there. What is he describing?
correct_answer: C. A delusion and auditory hallucinations
why_correct: A fixed, false belief held with certainty despite contrary evidence and out of keeping with the person's background is a delusion, here a delusion of reference. Hearing voices with no external source is an auditory hallucination, and voices discussing him in the third person or giving a running commentary are characteristic of schizophrenia.
why_wrong: A. Obsessions are intrusive thoughts recognised as the person's own, and compulsions are repetitive acts to relieve anxiety. B. Illusions are misinterpretations of real stimuli, and overvalued ideas are not held with delusional certainty. D. Depersonalisation and derealisation are feelings of unreality, with insight preserved. E. Confabulation fills memory gaps, and thought blocking is a sudden interruption of thought, neither of which is described.
pearl: A hallucination is a perception without a stimulus; an illusion is a misperception of a real one. A delusion is held with certainty despite evidence; an overvalued idea is not.
thinking: Belief in personal messages from the television, unshakeable ↓ fixed false belief, so a delusion ↓ voices heard with nobody present ↓ A delusion and auditory hallucinations
exam_trap: B, Illusions and overvalued ideas — the television is a real stimulus, which suggests illusion, but his voices have no source and his belief is held with total certainty.
takeaway: Fixed false beliefs are delusions; perceptions without stimuli are hallucinations.

stem: A 22-year-old man was given intramuscular haloperidol in the emergency department last night for severe agitation. This morning his eyes are fixed upwards, his neck is twisted painfully to one side and his jaw is clenched. He is fully alert, his temperature is normal and his limbs are not generally rigid. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
why_correct: Painful sustained muscle spasms such as oculogyric crisis, torticollis and trismus within hours to days of starting a dopamine-blocking drug are typical of acute dystonia. It is more common in young men and with high-potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol, and responds quickly to an anticholinergic drug such as procyclidine.
why_wrong: A. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome causes fever, generalised rigidity, altered consciousness and autonomic instability. B. Tardive dyskinesia develops after months to years and causes involuntary writhing or lip-smacking movements. C. Akathisia is a subjective inner restlessness with an inability to keep still, not fixed spasm. D. Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and causes clonus, hyperreflexia and agitation.
pearl: Antipsychotic movement effects by timing: dystonia within hours to days, akathisia and parkinsonism over days to weeks, tardive dyskinesia after months to years.
thinking: Recent high-potency antipsychotic ↓ upward eye deviation, torticollis and jaw spasm within hours ↓ alert, afebrile, no generalised rigidity ↓ Acute dystonic reaction
exam_trap: A, Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — severe muscle symptoms after haloperidol raise this fear, but there is no fever, rigidity or reduced consciousness.
takeaway: Painful spasms within hours of an antipsychotic indicate acute dystonia; treat with procyclidine.

stem: A 59-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years attends her annual diabetes foot check. She says both feet tingle and feel numb, as though she is walking on cotton wool, and are worse at night. Ankle reflexes are absent on both sides and she cannot feel the monofilament on either sole. Muscle power in her legs is normal. Which pattern of nerve damage best fits?
why_correct: Long-standing diabetes typically damages the longest nerves first, giving symmetrical sensory loss, paraesthesia and burning in a stocking distribution with reduced ankle reflexes. Loss of protective sensation on monofilament testing places her at increased risk of foot ulceration, so she needs foot protection education and podiatry follow-up.
why_wrong: B. Mononeuritis multiplex affects several separate named nerves asymmetrically. C. Diabetic amyotrophy causes painful proximal thigh weakness and wasting, not distal sensory loss. D. Radiculopathy follows a dermatome, usually with back pain, and is rarely symmetrical. E. Tarsal tunnel syndrome is a focal entrapment affecting one sole, not a symmetrical stocking pattern.
pearl: Diabetic neuropathy is length-dependent: toes first, then a stocking distribution. Loss of monofilament sensation means loss of protective sensation and a high risk of foot ulcers.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes ↓ symmetrical distal tingling and numbness ↓ absent ankle reflexes and lost monofilament sensation on both feet ↓ Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy
exam_trap: C, Diabetic amyotrophy — it is a diabetes-specific neuropathy, so it tempts, but it causes proximal painful weakness rather than distal symmetrical sensory loss.
takeaway: Symmetrical stocking sensory loss in diabetes is distal symmetrical polyneuropathy.

stem: A 61-year-old man with prostate cancer that has spread to bone phones the acute oncology service. For two days he has had a band-like pain around his chest, his legs feel heavy and unsteady, and he is struggling to pass urine. On arrival at hospital he has brisk knee reflexes and reduced sensation below the level of his umbilicus. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
why_correct: Band-like radicular pain, bilateral leg weakness with upper motor neurone signs, a sensory level on the trunk and urinary retention in a man with bone metastases indicate metastatic spinal cord compression. He needs urgent whole-spine MRI, high-dose dexamethasone and urgent oncology and spinal surgical input to preserve function.
why_wrong: A. Cauda equina syndrome affects nerve roots below the cord, so it causes lower motor neurone signs and saddle anaesthesia rather than a thoracic sensory level and brisk reflexes. C. Guillain–Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness with absent reflexes and no sensory level. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes distal glove-and-stocking loss without a sensory level or retention. E. Mechanical back pain does not cause neurological deficit.
pearl: In a patient with cancer, new back pain with leg weakness, sensory change or sphincter problems is cord compression until MRI proves otherwise. Act on symptoms before deficits become permanent.
thinking: Known bone metastases ↓ band-like thoracic pain with heavy legs and urinary retention ↓ brisk reflexes and a sensory level on the trunk ↓ Spinal cord compression
exam_trap: A, Cauda equina syndrome — leg weakness with retention suggests it, but a thoracic sensory level and brisk reflexes place the lesion in the cord itself.
takeaway: Sensory level, leg weakness and retention in cancer means spinal cord compression: urgent MRI.

presentation: Metastatic spinal cord compression – urgent action
stem: A 67-year-old woman treated for breast cancer three years ago telephones her GP surgery. For ten days she has had a band-like pain around her mid-back that is worse when she coughs or lies flat. Since yesterday her legs feel heavy and she has tripped twice on the stairs. How should this be managed?

options.A: Prescribe a stronger analgesic and review her in a fortnight
options.B: Request a non-urgent MRI of the lumbar spine
options.D: Immediate referral to the acute oncology/MSCC team for urgent whole-spine MRI
options.E: Arrange an outpatient isotope bone scan

correct_answer: D. Immediate referral to the acute oncology/MSCC team for urgent whole-spine MRI
why_correct: New thoracic spinal pain that is band-like and worse on coughing or lying flat, followed by leg weakness, in someone with a cancer history is metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise. With neurological symptoms this is an emergency: contact the MSCC coordinator or acute oncology team immediately and arrange urgent MRI of the whole spine. Delay risks permanent paralysis and loss of sphincter control.
why_wrong: A. Escalating analgesia and waiting allows irreversible cord damage. B. Imaging is needed urgently, not routinely, and the whole spine must be scanned because disease is often multilevel. C. Physiotherapy delays emergency diagnosis. E. A bone scan does not show the cord and is not the urgent test.
pearl: Breast, prostate and lung cancers commonly metastasise to the spine. Pain with a band-like radiation or worse on lying flat or straining is a warning sign even before weakness appears.
thinking: Previous breast cancer ↓ new thoracic band-like pain worse lying flat or coughing ↓ new leg heaviness and falls ↓ suspected MSCC with neurology = emergency ↓ immediate MSCC referral and urgent whole-spine MRI
exam_trap: B, non-urgent lumbar MRI — it tempts because MRI is the right test, but the urgency is wrong and the lumbar spine alone could miss a thoracic lesion.
takeaway: Cancer history plus new spinal pain and limb weakness needs same-day MSCC referral and whole-spine MRI.

stem: A 59-year-old woman attends the vascular clinic with cramping pain in her right calf that comes on after walking about 100 metres and settles with rest. Her ankle–brachial pressure index is reduced. She already takes atorvastatin and clopidogrel. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Which lifestyle measure will most reduce her risk of cardiovascular events and amputation?

options.C: Avoiding walking whenever the calf pain starts

why_correct: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for progression of peripheral arterial disease, critical limb ischaemia, amputation, myocardial infarction and stroke. Complete cessation, supported with behavioural support and pharmacotherapy, gives the greatest risk reduction. It should be offered alongside a supervised exercise programme and secondary prevention medicines.
why_wrong: B. Compression stockings can harm an ischaemic limb and are not used to treat arterial disease. C. Walking through to near-maximal pain is encouraged, as exercise improves claudication distance. D. Fish oil supplements have no proven benefit for limb or cardiovascular outcomes here. E. Low-tar cigarettes do not reduce vascular risk meaningfully.
pearl: In intermittent claudication, offer smoking cessation support and a supervised exercise programme first; consider referral for revascularisation if symptoms remain limiting.
thinking: Claudication with reduced ABPI = peripheral arterial disease ↓ already on statin and antiplatelet ↓ ongoing heavy smoking ↓ biggest modifiable risk factor ↓ stop smoking completely
exam_trap: E, switching to low-tar cigarettes — it sounds like harm reduction, but smokers compensate by inhaling more deeply and vascular risk stays high.
takeaway: In peripheral arterial disease, stopping smoking is the single most effective lifestyle change.

stem: A 63-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends the diabetic foot clinic. Under the head of her first metatarsal there is a punched-out ulcer surrounded by thick callus. She was unaware of it until her daughter noticed blood on her sock. The foot is warm, the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily felt, and she cannot detect a 10 g monofilament. What type of ulcer is this?
why_correct: A painless ulcer over a weight-bearing area, surrounded by callus, in a warm foot with good pulses and loss of protective sensation is a neuropathic ulcer. Repeated unnoticed pressure on an insensate foot causes callus and then breakdown. Management includes offloading, debridement, infection and vascular assessment, and urgent referral to the multidisciplinary foot service.
why_wrong: A. Venous ulcers sit around the gaiter area with oedema and pigmentation, not under the metatarsal head. B. Arterial ulcers are painful, in a cold foot with weak or absent pulses. D. Malignancy is considered for a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled or everted edges. E. Pyoderma gangrenosum is a painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined edge, usually with inflammatory bowel or joint disease.
pearl: Diabetic foot ulcers are often mixed. Always check pulses and consider an ABPI or toe pressures, remembering calcified vessels can falsely raise the ABPI.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ painless ulcer under metatarsal head with callus ↓ warm foot, good pulses ↓ cannot feel monofilament ↓ neuropathic ulcer
exam_trap: B, arterial ulcer — diabetes predisposes to arterial disease and both can look punched out, but this foot is warm with palpable pulses and the ulcer is painless.
takeaway: Painless ulcer at a pressure point in a warm, numb foot with pulses present is neuropathic.

stem: A 66-year-old man who had a deep vein thrombosis in his left leg ten years ago sees his GP about itchy, scaly skin above his left ankle. His leg aches and feels heavy by the evening. There is brown staining of the lower calf, pitting oedema, and the skin just above the ankle feels hard and woody. Foot pulses are present. What is the underlying cause?
why_correct: Previous DVT can damage venous valves, leading to sustained venous hypertension in the leg. This produces aching and heaviness, oedema, haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema and lipodermatosclerosis, and later venous ulceration. The unilateral picture on the side of the old DVT fits post-thrombotic chronic venous insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis is acute, hot and spreading, often with fever, not a chronic itchy pigmented change. B. Arterial disease causes cold, pale, hairless skin with weak pulses, not pigmentation and oedema. C. Heart failure causes bilateral oedema without unilateral pigmentation and woody induration. E. Necrobiosis lipoidica gives shiny yellow-brown plaques on the shins in diabetes.
pearl: Before compression therapy for venous disease, check the ABPI to exclude significant arterial disease, which makes strong compression unsafe.
thinking: Old DVT on same side ↓ aching heavy leg by evening ↓ haemosiderin staining, eczema, woody induration ↓ post-thrombotic venous hypertension ↓ chronic venous insufficiency
exam_trap: A, cellulitis — red-brown, itchy skin changes are often mislabelled as infection, but this is chronic, non-febrile and accompanied by classic venous signs.
takeaway: Pigmentation, eczema and woody induration above the ankle signal chronic venous insufficiency.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is reviewed in the cardiology clinic three months after an anterior myocardial infarction. Echocardiography shows a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction. Which of the following features points most specifically to failure of the left side of the heart?
why_correct: Left ventricular failure raises pulmonary venous pressure. On lying flat, venous return to the heart increases and fluid shifts into the lungs, causing breathlessness that is relieved by sitting up (orthopnoea). Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and bibasal crackles have the same origin.
why_wrong: A. Ankle oedema reflects systemic venous congestion and is non-specific. B. A raised JVP reflects right-sided filling pressure. D. Hepatic congestion results from right-sided failure. E. Ascites is a feature of right-sided or congestive failure.
pearl: Ask how many pillows the patient sleeps on and whether they wake breathless at night: both point to pulmonary congestion from left ventricular dysfunction.
thinking: Anterior MI with reduced ejection fraction ↓ left ventricle fails ↓ pulmonary venous congestion ↓ breathless when lying flat ↓ orthopnoea
exam_trap: A, bilateral ankle swelling — it is the most familiar heart failure feature, but it reflects systemic venous congestion and has many non-cardiac causes.
takeaway: Orthopnoea and nocturnal breathlessness reflect left-sided failure; oedema, JVP and liver signs reflect the right.

stem: A 77-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction phones the community heart failure nurse. He records his weight each morning, and his scales show he has gained a couple of kilograms over the past few days. His trousers feel tight around the waist and his ankles are puffier, although his appetite has been poor. What is the most likely explanation for the weight change?
why_correct: A rapid rise in weight over a few days in heart failure reflects salt and water retention, not a change in tissue mass. Increasing oedema and abdominal fullness support early decompensation. Daily weights are taught so patients can report this early, allowing diuretic adjustment before breathlessness worsens.
why_wrong: A. Muscle cannot be gained this quickly, especially without increased activity. B. Fat gain over days is implausible, particularly with a reduced appetite. C. Constipation does not explain worsening ankle oedema or a gain of this size. E. Dehydration causes weight loss, not gain.
pearl: Patients with heart failure are advised to weigh themselves daily at the same time and seek advice promptly if their weight rises quickly, as this often precedes breathlessness.
thinking: Heart failure ↓ weight up quickly over days ↓ more ankle swelling, abdominal fullness, poor appetite ↓ tissue gain impossible this fast ↓ fluid retention
exam_trap: B, increase in body fat — weight gain is commonly attributed to diet, but fat cannot accumulate over days and his appetite is actually reduced.
takeaway: Rapid weight gain in heart failure means fluid retention until proven otherwise.

stem: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin attends the emergency department with two weeks of fevers, night sweats and lethargy. There are linear splinter haemorrhages under several fingernails and tender red nodules on the pulps of two fingers. A pansystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal edge that was not documented at a visit six months ago. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever with a newly documented regurgitant murmur and vascular or immunological signs such as splinter haemorrhages and Osler nodes is infective endocarditis until proven otherwise. Injecting drug use classically causes right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis, often with Staphylococcus aureus. Take at least three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics and arrange echocardiography.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatic fever follows a streptococcal throat infection and causes migratory arthritis, carditis and skin signs, not Osler nodes in an injecting drug user. B. Lupus can cause fever and sterile valve lesions but this context and the infective picture favour endocarditis. D. Local cellulitis would not explain a new murmur or peripheral embolic signs. E. Polyarteritis nodosa causes vasculitic features but not a new valvular murmur.
pearl: Use the modified Duke criteria: positive blood cultures with a typical organism and evidence of valve involvement on echocardiography are the two major criteria.
thinking: Injecting drug use ↓ prolonged fever and night sweats ↓ splinter haemorrhages and Osler nodes ↓ newly documented murmur at left lower sternal edge ↓ infective endocarditis
exam_trap: A, acute rheumatic fever — fever with a murmur may trigger it, but there is no preceding sore throat and the peripheral signs and injecting history point to infection.
takeaway: Fever plus a new murmur, especially in someone who injects drugs, is endocarditis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who smokes has been taking carbimazole for hyperthyroidism for four months. Her optometrist refers her because her eyes feel gritty and look prominent, her upper lids are retracted so that white sclera shows above the iris, and she sees double when looking upwards. Visual acuity and colour vision are normal and she is afebrile. Which condition best explains her eye findings?
why_correct: Graves disease can cause autoimmune inflammation of the orbital fat and extraocular muscles, producing grittiness, proptosis, lid retraction and restricted eye movements with diplopia. Smoking strongly increases the risk and severity. She needs referral to an ophthalmology or joint thyroid eye clinic, smoking cessation and lubricants, with urgent review if vision or colour vision deteriorates.
why_wrong: A. Orbital cellulitis is usually unilateral, painful and febrile with eyelid swelling. C. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ptosis and diplopia, not proptosis or lid retraction. D. Allergic conjunctivitis causes itch and redness without proptosis or restricted movement. E. A sixth nerve palsy causes horizontal diplopia on looking laterally, without proptosis.
pearl: Reduced visual acuity, colour desaturation or a relative afferent pupillary defect in thyroid eye disease suggests optic nerve compression and needs emergency ophthalmology review.
thinking: Treated hyperthyroidism, smoker ↓ gritty prominent eyes ↓ lid retraction and upgaze diplopia ↓ orbital autoimmune inflammation ↓ thyroid eye disease
exam_trap: C, myasthenia gravis — it causes diplopia and is associated with autoimmune thyroid disease, but it gives ptosis rather than lid retraction and never proptosis.
takeaway: Proptosis, lid retraction and restricted gaze in Graves disease mean thyroid eye disease.

stem: A 55-year-old woman collapses on the orthopaedic ward while walking to the toilet four days after a total hip replacement. She is acutely breathless, pale and sweaty, with a heart rate of 128/min, blood pressure 78/50 mmHg and cold peripheries. Her neck veins are distended. The trachea is central, breath sounds are equal on both sides and the wound is dry. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden collapse with breathlessness, shock and distended neck veins after major orthopaedic surgery indicates acute right ventricular failure from a large pulmonary embolus obstructing outflow. A clear chest with equal breath sounds argues against tension pneumothorax. High-risk PE with haemodynamic instability needs immediate senior help and consideration of thrombolysis.
why_wrong: B. Haemorrhage causes shock with flat, not distended, neck veins. C. Tension pneumothorax would cause unilateral absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation. D. Vasovagal syncope recovers quickly and does not cause persistent shock or raised venous pressure. E. Pneumonia develops over days with fever and focal chest signs.
pearl: Obstructive shock with raised JVP has a short differential: massive PE, tension pneumothorax and cardiac tamponade; examination of the chest and heart sounds helps separate them.
thinking: Recent hip replacement ↓ sudden collapse with breathlessness ↓ hypotension, cold peripheries, distended neck veins ↓ equal breath sounds and central trachea ↓ massive PE
exam_trap: B, postoperative haemorrhage — shock after surgery prompts thoughts of bleeding, but bleeding empties the veins, whereas this patient has distended neck veins.
takeaway: Post-operative collapse with shock and raised JVP but a clear chest suggests massive PE.

stem: A 48-year-old man sees his GP with three days of rigors, an ache deep in his perineum and rectum, burning on passing urine and a weak stream. Both testes are non-tender. On digital rectal examination the prostate is swollen, warm and exquisitely tender. There is no loin tenderness. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Systemic features with perineal pain, lower urinary tract symptoms and an exquisitely tender, warm, swollen prostate indicate acute bacterial prostatitis, usually from Gram-negative organisms. Send a mid-stream urine for culture, avoid vigorous prostatic examination, and give an extended course of an appropriate antibiotic per local guidance, admitting if septic or in retention.
why_wrong: A. Pyelonephritis gives fever with loin pain and renal angle tenderness, and the prostate is not tender. C. Epididymo-orchitis causes scrotal pain and a tender testis or epididymis. D. Benign prostatic hyperplasia is painless and non-febrile with a smooth enlarged gland. E. A stricture causes a poor stream without fever or a tender prostate.
pearl: Acute prostatitis can cause acute urinary retention; check for a palpable bladder and consider suprapubic rather than urethral catheterisation if needed.
thinking: Rigors ↓ perineal and rectal ache with dysuria ↓ normal testes, no loin tenderness ↓ warm, very tender swollen prostate ↓ acute bacterial prostatitis
exam_trap: A, acute pyelonephritis — fever plus urinary symptoms suggests upper tract infection, but there is no loin pain and the tenderness localises to the prostate.
takeaway: Fever, perineal pain and a very tender prostate on rectal examination indicate acute prostatitis.

presentation: Helicobacter pylori and peptic ulcer disease
stem: A 39-year-old woman tells her GP she has had a gnawing pain in her upper abdomen for two months. It often wakes her in the early hours and eases when she eats or drinks milk. She has no weight loss, vomiting or anaemia. A stool antigen test is positive for Helicobacter pylori. Which condition is this infection most likely to have caused?
why_correct: H. pylori causes chronic gastritis, increases acid output and damages the mucosal defence, making it a leading cause of peptic ulceration, particularly duodenal ulcers. Night-time epigastric pain that eases with food is typical of a duodenal ulcer. Eradication therapy with a proton pump inhibitor and two antibiotics heals ulcers and reduces recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Barrett oesophagus results from long-standing acid reflux, not H. pylori. C. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is allergic, causing dysphagia and food bolus impaction. D. Coeliac disease is immune-mediated gluten sensitivity unrelated to H. pylori. E. Gallstones cause postprandial right upper quadrant pain and are not linked to H. pylori.
pearl: Before H. pylori testing, stop proton pump inhibitors for two weeks and antibiotics for four weeks to avoid false negatives. H. pylori is also linked to gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma.
thinking: Epigastric pain waking her at night ↓ eased by food ↓ no alarm features ↓ positive H. pylori stool antigen ↓ duodenal ulcer
exam_trap: A, Barrett oesophagus — it is linked with upper GI symptoms and cancer risk, but it arises from reflux, not H. pylori infection.
takeaway: H. pylori is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease, especially duodenal ulcers.

stem: A 66-year-old woman who went through the menopause fifteen years ago sees her GP because of tiredness. Her stools have been looser and more frequent for two months and her clothes have become loose. Blood tests show a microcytic anaemia with low ferritin. She eats a normal diet. Which diagnosis is most important to investigate for?
why_correct: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman, with a persistent change in bowel habit and weight loss, is a red-flag combination for colorectal cancer, especially right-sided tumours that bleed occultly. She needs referral on a suspected cancer pathway, with faecal immunochemical testing used to guide referral where available. Coeliac serology is usually checked as well, but cancer must be excluded first.
why_wrong: A. IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion and new symptoms after middle age with anaemia and weight loss are alarm features. B. Coeliac disease can cause iron deficiency and loose stools but does not take priority over excluding cancer. C. Haemorrhoids cause bright red bleeding, not occult iron deficiency with weight loss. D. Microscopic colitis causes watery diarrhoea but not iron-deficiency anaemia or weight loss.
pearl: Right-sided colon cancers often present with anaemia and fatigue rather than visible bleeding or obstruction, so iron deficiency without an obvious cause needs lower GI evaluation.
thinking: Older postmenopausal woman ↓ change in bowel habit with weight loss ↓ iron-deficiency anaemia without dietary cause ↓ occult GI blood loss ↓ colorectal cancer
exam_trap: B, coeliac disease — it is a genuine cause of iron deficiency and loose stools, but at this age with weight loss, malignancy must be excluded first.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency with change in bowel habit in an older adult needs urgent colorectal cancer investigation.

stem: A 71-year-old man who had an open appendicectomy and later a laparotomy for a perforated ulcer attends the emergency department with waves of central abdominal pain since the morning. He has vomited green fluid several times. The abdomen is mildly distended and diffusely tender without guarding, and tinkling bowel sounds are heard. He last passed wind a few hours ago. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Colicky central pain, early bilious vomiting, distension and tinkling bowel sounds indicate mechanical small bowel obstruction. Previous abdominal surgery makes adhesions the most likely cause in the UK. Initial management is drip and suck with fluid and electrolyte correction, analgesia and CT, with surgery if there are signs of strangulation.
why_wrong: B. Sigmoid volvulus causes gross distension with late vomiting in a large bowel pattern. C. Pancreatitis causes constant epigastric pain radiating to the back, not tinkling bowel sounds. D. Biliary colic is right upper quadrant pain without distension. E. Ileus causes absent or quiet bowel sounds and usually follows recent surgery or metabolic upset.
pearl: Adhesions are the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction in adults with previous abdominal surgery; hernias are the next to check, so always examine the groins.
thinking: Previous laparotomies ↓ colicky central pain with early bilious vomiting ↓ distension with tinkling bowel sounds ↓ mechanical obstruction of proximal bowel ↓ adhesional small bowel obstruction
exam_trap: E, paralytic ileus — distension and vomiting occur in both, but ileus has silent bowel sounds and no colic, whereas tinkling sounds mean mechanical obstruction.
takeaway: Colicky pain, early vomiting and tinkling bowel sounds after previous surgery suggest adhesional small bowel obstruction.

stem: A 38-year-old woman sees her GP with aching all over her body for over a year. She wakes unrefreshed, struggles to concentrate at work and feels exhausted. She is tender to light pressure at many sites across her trunk and limbs, but her joints look normal and muscle power is full. Full blood count, CRP, ESR, creatine kinase, thyroid function and calcium are all normal. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic widespread pain with unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, cognitive difficulty and widespread tenderness, with normal examination of the joints and normal inflammatory and muscle markers, is typical of fibromyalgia. Management focuses on explanation, graded exercise, sleep hygiene and psychological approaches such as CBT.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica affects people over 50 with shoulder and hip girdle stiffness and raised inflammatory markers. B. Hypothyroidism is excluded by normal thyroid function. D. Lupus usually causes inflammatory joint signs, rashes or abnormal blood tests. E. Polymyositis causes proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase.
pearl: Fibromyalgia is a clinical diagnosis, but a short set of tests including inflammatory markers, thyroid function and creatine kinase is reasonable to exclude mimics.
thinking: Widespread pain over a year ↓ unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, poor concentration ↓ normal joints and muscle power ↓ normal inflammatory, thyroid and muscle tests ↓ fibromyalgia
exam_trap: A, polymyalgia rheumatica — widespread aching suggests it, but she is too young, has no girdle stiffness and her inflammatory markers are normal.
takeaway: Chronic widespread pain, fatigue and poor sleep with normal tests points to fibromyalgia.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years attends the rheumatology clinic. She has noticed several painless rubbery lumps along the back of her forearm just below the elbow. They are firm, not fluctuant, mobile under normal overlying skin, and range from pea- to grape-sized. She smokes and takes methotrexate. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Firm, painless subcutaneous nodules over extensor surfaces and pressure points, particularly the proximal ulnar border of the forearm, are the commonest extra-articular feature of rheumatoid arthritis. They are associated with seropositive, long-standing disease and smoking, and methotrexate can increase nodule formation.
why_wrong: B. Olecranon bursitis is a single fluctuant fluid-filled swelling directly over the olecranon. C. Lipomas are soft and doughy rather than firm and are not linked to rheumatoid arthritis. D. Epidermoid cysts arise in the skin, often with a punctum. E. Ganglion cysts typically occur at the wrist or hand, arising from a joint or tendon sheath.
pearl: Rheumatoid nodules usually need no treatment, but they can ulcerate or become infected and occasionally occur in the lungs, where they may mimic other lesions on imaging.
thinking: Long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis ↓ smoker on methotrexate ↓ firm painless non-fluctuant lumps ↓ extensor forearm below elbow ↓ rheumatoid nodules
exam_trap: B, olecranon bursitis — it occurs at the same site and is common in rheumatoid arthritis, but it is a single fluctuant swelling, not several firm nodules.
takeaway: Firm, painless lumps on the extensor forearm in seropositive RA are rheumatoid nodules.

stem: A 27-year-old man of Greek Cypriot heritage was prescribed nitrofurantoin for a lower urinary tract infection two days ago. He now presents to the emergency department with lethargy, yellow eyes and urine the colour of cola. Blood tests show a low haemoglobin, a raised reticulocyte count, raised unconjugated bilirubin and raised LDH. The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative. Which condition most likely predisposed him to this reaction?
why_correct: G6PD deficiency is an X-linked enzyme defect, common in people of Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern and Asian descent, that leaves red cells unable to withstand oxidative stress. Oxidant drugs such as nitrofurantoin, some sulfonamides and primaquine, as well as fava beans or infection, can trigger acute intravascular haemolysis with jaundice and dark urine. The Coombs test is negative and the blood film may show bite and blister cells.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary spherocytosis causes chronic haemolysis with spherocytes and is not typically triggered by a drug. B. Autoimmune haemolysis would give a positive direct antiglobulin test. D. Gilbert syndrome raises unconjugated bilirubin but does not cause anaemia or haemolysis. E. Beta-thalassaemia trait causes mild stable microcytosis, not acute haemolysis.
pearl: G6PD levels can be falsely normal during an acute haemolytic episode because young red cells have more enzyme; repeat testing a few months later if the result is unexpectedly normal.
thinking: Mediterranean man ↓ oxidant drug started ↓ acute jaundice and dark urine with anaemia ↓ haemolysis with negative Coombs test ↓ G6PD deficiency
exam_trap: B, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia — drugs can trigger immune haemolysis, but the negative direct antiglobulin test rules it out.
takeaway: Acute Coombs-negative haemolysis after an oxidant drug suggests G6PD deficiency.

stem: A 14-year-old girl who has sickle cell disease (HbSS) is brought to the emergency department after an afternoon swimming in the cold sea. She has severe pain in both thighs and her lower back. She has not been injured and her temperature is normal. Her haemoglobin is close to her usual baseline and her reticulocyte count is raised as usual. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

options.E: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

why_correct: Sudden severe pain in several bones after a trigger such as cold exposure, dehydration or infection, without fever or injury, is a painful vaso-occlusive crisis. Sickled cells occlude small vessels in bone marrow causing ischaemia. Treatment is prompt strong analgesia (often opioids), hydration, oxygen if hypoxic, and monitoring for complications.
why_wrong: A. Aplastic crisis, usually from parvovirus B19, causes a sudden fall in haemoglobin with low reticulocytes rather than bone pain. C. Osteomyelitis usually affects one site with fever and raised inflammatory markers. D. Splenic sequestration causes a rapidly enlarging spleen with a fall in haemoglobin and shock. E. Avascular necrosis causes gradual hip pain, not acute pain in multiple sites.
pearl: NICE advises that people with sickle cell disease in an acute painful episode should receive analgesia promptly after arriving in hospital, with regular reassessment of pain.
thinking: Sickle cell disease ↓ cold exposure trigger ↓ severe pain in thighs and back ↓ afebrile, no injury, haemoglobin at baseline ↓ vaso-occlusive crisis
exam_trap: C, osteomyelitis — bone infection is more common in sickle cell disease, but she is afebrile with pain at several sites after a classic cold trigger.
takeaway: Multi-site bone pain after cold or dehydration in sickle cell disease is a vaso-occlusive crisis.

stem: A 23-year-old man who has sickle cell disease was admitted two days ago with a painful crisis in his legs and is using a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump. Overnight he develops a temperature of 38.4°C, a cough and pleuritic chest pain. His respiratory rate is 28/min and oxygen saturation has fallen to 89% on air. He is alert and his pupils are normal in size. A chest X-ray shows new consolidation in the right lower zone. Which complication has occurred?
why_correct: Acute chest syndrome is a new pulmonary infiltrate with respiratory symptoms, chest pain, fever or hypoxia in sickle cell disease. It often develops during admission for a painful crisis, partly from hypoventilation due to pain and opioids. It is a leading cause of death and needs urgent oxygen, antibiotics, analgesia, incentive spirometry and early haematology and critical care input, including consideration of transfusion.
why_wrong: B. Opioid toxicity causes a slow respiratory rate, drowsiness and small pupils, not fever, tachypnoea and new consolidation. C. Fluid overload causes bilateral crackles and congestion, not fever with focal consolidation. D. Splenic sequestration presents with an enlarging spleen, falling haemoglobin and shock. E. Costochondritis does not cause fever, hypoxia or radiological change.
pearl: Patients admitted with a painful crisis should be monitored for acute chest syndrome, and incentive spirometry helps prevent it by reducing atelectasis.
thinking: Sickle cell disease admitted with painful crisis ↓ on opioid PCA ↓ new fever, cough, pleuritic pain, hypoxia ↓ new consolidation on X-ray ↓ acute chest syndrome
exam_trap: B, opioid-induced respiratory depression — falling saturation on a morphine pump tempts, but he is tachypnoeic, alert and febrile with a new infiltrate.
takeaway: Fever, chest symptoms, hypoxia and a new infiltrate in sickle cell disease mean acute chest syndrome.

stem: A 61-year-old man with COPD who still smokes 30 cigarettes a day has routine blood tests at his GP surgery. His haemoglobin is 185 g/L (reference range 130–170 g/L) and haematocrit is raised. White cell and platelet counts are normal. He has no itching, his spleen is not palpable, and his oxygen saturation on air is 88%. He is drinking normally and his urea is normal. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic hypoxia from COPD and carbon monoxide from smoking stimulate erythropoietin release, raising red cell mass. An isolated rise in haemoglobin and haematocrit with normal white cells and platelets, no splenomegaly and documented hypoxia fits secondary (appropriate) polycythaemia. Management centres on smoking cessation and treating the underlying lung disease.
why_wrong: A. Polycythaemia vera often raises white cells and platelets, causes splenomegaly and aquagenic itch, and is JAK2-positive. C. Relative polycythaemia follows reduced plasma volume, which is unlikely with normal hydration and urea. D. Chronic myeloid leukaemia causes a high white cell count and splenomegaly. E. Essential thrombocythaemia raises the platelet count, not the haemoglobin.
pearl: When the cause of a raised haemoglobin is unclear, a JAK2 mutation test helps separate polycythaemia vera from secondary causes such as hypoxia or an EPO-secreting tumour.
thinking: Raised haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ normal white cells and platelets, no splenomegaly ↓ heavy smoker with COPD and low saturation ↓ hypoxia drives erythropoietin ↓ secondary polycythaemia
exam_trap: A, polycythaemia vera — any raised haemoglobin brings it to mind, but the other cell lines are normal, there is no splenomegaly and an obvious hypoxic cause exists.
takeaway: Isolated raised haemoglobin in a hypoxic smoker is usually secondary polycythaemia.

stem: A 49-year-old woman is ten days into a cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer. She calls the oncology helpline with a temperature of 38.3°C and is asked to attend. Her full blood count shows haemoglobin and platelets within the reference range, but a neutrophil count of 0.3 × 10^9/L (reference range 2.0–7.5 × 10^9/L). Which term best describes this blood result?
why_correct: Neutropenia is a neutrophil count below the reference range, and this result is severely low. Neutrophils are the main defence against bacterial and fungal infection, so fever in a neutropenic patient after chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise. She needs urgent assessment and empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics without waiting for culture results.
why_wrong: A. Lymphopenia refers to low lymphocytes, not neutrophils. C. Pancytopenia requires reduction of red cells, white cells and platelets, but her haemoglobin and platelets are normal. D. Leucocytosis is a raised white cell count. E. Eosinophilia is a raised eosinophil count.
pearl: In suspected neutropenic sepsis, NICE advises giving empirical antibiotics urgently, within one hour of arrival, rather than waiting for the neutrophil count.
thinking: Chemotherapy ten days ago ↓ fever ↓ haemoglobin and platelets normal ↓ only the neutrophil count is below range ↓ neutropenia
exam_trap: C, pancytopenia — chemotherapy suppresses the marrow so all lines may fall, but here only the neutrophils are below range.
takeaway: A low neutrophil count is neutropenia; with fever after chemotherapy treat it as neutropenic sepsis.

stem: An 18-month-old boy who has just started walking is brought to the emergency department with a hot, swollen, painful right knee after a minor fall. His mother says he bruises easily, and her brother had a bleeding problem needing regular injections. Platelet count and prothrombin time are normal, but the APTT is longer than the reference range. Which inherited condition best explains these findings?
why_correct: Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and B (factor IX deficiency) are X-linked, so they affect boys and pass through carrier mothers to their sons, such as a maternal uncle. Deficiency of these intrinsic pathway factors prolongs the APTT with a normal PT and platelet count. Deep tissue and joint bleeding (haemarthrosis), often appearing as a child starts to walk, is typical.
why_wrong: A. Von Willebrand disease is autosomal and usually causes mucocutaneous bleeding such as nosebleeds and gum bleeding rather than haemarthrosis. C. Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia causes nosebleeds and telangiectasia with normal clotting tests. D. Sickle cell disease causes painful crises and haemolysis, not a prolonged APTT. E. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis and jaundice, not bleeding.
pearl: In any child with unexplained bruising, check clotting and the family history, but also remember safeguarding; a bleeding disorder and non-accidental injury can coexist.
thinking: Boy with haemarthrosis after minor trauma ↓ affected maternal uncle = X-linked pattern ↓ normal platelets and PT ↓ prolonged APTT = intrinsic factor deficiency ↓ haemophilia
exam_trap: A, von Willebrand disease — it is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder and can prolong the APTT, but it is autosomal and joint bleeds are unusual.
takeaway: Haemarthrosis in a boy with an isolated prolonged APTT and an affected maternal uncle suggests haemophilia.

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her first pregnancy, at 40 weeks and 3 days, attends the midwife-led unit. Yesterday she had irregular tightenings that came and went. Now the contractions are strong, regular and last about a minute each, and she has to stop and breathe through them. Her membranes are intact and there is no vaginal bleeding. On vaginal examination the cervix is fully effaced and has dilated further since an examination two hours earlier, but it is not yet fully dilated. What best describes her current situation?
correct_answer: D. Established first stage of labour
why_correct: The established first stage of labour is defined by regular painful contractions together with progressive cervical dilatation. Her earlier irregular tightenings were the latent phase, and the change in her cervix between examinations confirms she has progressed into established labour. Progress, maternal observations and fetal heart rate are now monitored regularly.
why_wrong: A. Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular, usually painless and produce no cervical change. B. Her membranes are intact. C. Abruption causes constant pain, a tense tender uterus and often bleeding. E. The second stage starts only once the cervix is fully dilated.
pearl: Women in the latent phase are usually supported at home if well, with advice to return when contractions become regular and strong or if waters break, bleeding occurs or fetal movements reduce.
thinking: Term pregnancy ↓ irregular tightenings yesterday = latent phase ↓ now strong regular contractions ↓ progressive cervical dilatation, not yet full ↓ established first stage of labour
exam_trap: A, Braxton Hicks contractions — tightenings at term can be dismissed as practice contractions, but these are regular, painful and changing the cervix.
takeaway: Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical dilatation mean established first-stage labour.

stem: A 37-year-old woman having her fourth baby delivers vaginally after a long labour augmented with an oxytocin infusion. The placenta and membranes are delivered and checked as complete, and the perineum is intact. Twenty minutes later there is brisk vaginal bleeding. On abdominal palpation the fundus is above the umbilicus and feels soft, but it firms up when rubbed. Which is the likeliest cause of the bleeding?
why_correct: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage. A soft, high fundus that contracts with rubbing confirms the uterus is failing to contract to compress the placental bed vessels. Risk factors here include multiparity and a prolonged oxytocin-augmented labour. Management includes calling for help, uterine massage, uterotonics and resuscitation.
why_wrong: B. Retained tissue is less likely as the placenta and membranes were checked and complete. C. Trauma causes bleeding despite a well-contracted uterus, and her perineum is intact. D. Coagulopathy is uncommon without risk factors such as abruption, pre-eclampsia or massive transfusion. E. Uterine inversion causes sudden shock with the fundus absent or dimpled on palpation.
pearl: Remember the 4 Ts of postpartum haemorrhage: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin. Tone is by far the commonest.
thinking: Brisk bleeding soon after delivery ↓ placenta complete, perineum intact ↓ soft, high fundus that firms when rubbed ↓ uterus not contracting ↓ uterine atony
exam_trap: B, retained placental tissue — it is a common cause of PPH, but the placenta and membranes were checked as complete and the uterus responds to massage.
takeaway: A soft, high uterus with heavy bleeding after birth means atony, the commonest cause of PPH.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends her GP because she plans to stop her combined contraceptive pill next month to try for a baby. She is healthy, takes no medicines, has a normal BMI and no family history of birth defects. She asks which supplement will reduce her baby's risk of spina bifida. Which supplement should she be advised to take?
why_correct: Folic acid taken from before conception until the end of the first trimester reduces the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly. The neural tube closes very early, often before a woman knows she is pregnant, so starting before conception is important. A standard low dose is advised for women without additional risk factors.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin D is recommended in pregnancy for bone health, not to prevent neural tube defects. B. Iron is given for anaemia, not neural tube defect prevention. D. High-dose vitamin A should be avoided in pregnancy because it is teratogenic. E. Iodine is important for fetal brain development but does not prevent neural tube defects.
pearl: A higher dose of folic acid is advised for women at increased risk, for example with a previous neural tube defect, diabetes, obesity, sickle cell disease or taking antiepileptic drugs.
thinking: Planning pregnancy ↓ wants to prevent spina bifida ↓ neural tube closes in early first trimester ↓ supplement must start before conception ↓ folic acid
exam_trap: A, vitamin D — it is also routinely recommended in pregnancy in the UK, but its role is bone health, not neural tube protection.
takeaway: Start folic acid before conception and continue through the first trimester to prevent neural tube defects.

stem: A 27-year-old woman tells her GP that most evenings she eats huge quantities of food quickly and alone, continuing until she is uncomfortably full even though she is not hungry. She feels disgusted and ashamed afterwards. She has never made herself sick, used laxatives, fasted or exercised excessively to make up for it. Her BMI is in the obese range. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Binge-eating disorder is defined by recurrent episodes of eating unusually large amounts with a sense of loss of control and marked distress, without regular compensatory behaviours. It is commonly associated with obesity. NICE recommends a binge-eating-disorder-focused guided self-help programme as the first psychological treatment.
why_wrong: A. Bulimia nervosa requires regular compensatory behaviours such as vomiting, laxatives, fasting or excessive exercise. C. Anorexia nervosa requires a significantly low body weight. D. Night eating syndrome involves eating after waking at night or excessive evening eating without the large, loss-of-control binges described. E. Pica is the eating of non-food substances.
pearl: Weight loss programmes alone are not a treatment for binge-eating disorder; addressing the binge cycle psychologically comes first.
thinking: Recurrent large binges with loss of control ↓ distress and shame afterwards ↓ no vomiting, laxatives, fasting or exercise ↓ not underweight ↓ binge-eating disorder
exam_trap: A, bulimia nervosa — binges with loss of control occur in both, but bulimia needs compensatory behaviours, which she denies.
takeaway: Binges with loss of control and distress but no compensation indicate binge-eating disorder.

stem: A 72-year-old man with lung cancer receiving palliative care is visited at home by his GP. Over three days he has become unsteady and both legs feel numb from his navel downwards. He has a mid-back pain that is worse when he coughs. He has not passed urine since the morning and a tender, distended bladder is palpable. He is fully orientated. Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
why_correct: Back pain worse on coughing with progressive leg symptoms, a sensory level on the trunk and urinary retention in a patient with cancer are features of spinal cord compression. Lung cancer frequently spreads to the spine. Even in palliative care, prompt recognition matters because urgent treatment can preserve mobility and continence and improve quality of life.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, thirst, constipation and fatigue, not a sensory level. C. Brain metastases cause headache, seizures or focal weakness, not a sensory level with retention in an orientated patient. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes glove-and-stocking sensory loss, not a truncal level or retention. E. Opioids can cause retention but do not explain leg numbness with a sensory level.
pearl: A sensory level on the trunk localises the problem to the spinal cord. A level at the umbilicus corresponds to the T10 dermatome, and because cord segments lie higher than their matching vertebrae, the compressing lesion is at or above that level and often at a higher vertebral level than expected.
thinking: Known lung cancer ↓ mid-back pain worse on coughing ↓ leg numbness with a truncal sensory level ↓ urinary retention ↓ metastatic spinal cord compression
exam_trap: E, opioid-induced urinary retention — palliative patients on opioids often retain urine, but this does not explain the sensory level and unsteadiness.
takeaway: A sensory level with leg weakness and retention in cancer means spinal cord compression.

stem: A 41-year-old woman attends the gynaecology clinic with six months of bleeding between periods and periods that are heavier than before. Pelvic examination is normal and a cervical screening test is up to date and negative. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal-sized uterus with uniform myometrium and a small, well-circumscribed echogenic lesion within the endometrial cavity. Both ovaries are normal. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Endometrial polyps are localised overgrowths of endometrium projecting into the uterine cavity. They typically cause intermenstrual and heavy menstrual bleeding and appear as a focal, well-defined echogenic lesion within the cavity on ultrasound.
