Hysteroscopic removal confirms the diagnosis histologically and usually treats the bleeding.
why_wrong: B. Adenomyosis causes a diffusely bulky, tender uterus with heterogeneous myometrium, often with painful periods. C. Hyperplasia causes diffuse thickening of the endometrium rather than a focal lesion. D. Cervical ectropion can cause postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding but is seen on the cervix, not within the uterine cavity. E. PCOS causes irregular periods with multiple ovarian follicles, and her ovaries are normal.
pearl: Polyps are usually benign but can harbour hyperplasia or cancer, particularly in postmenopausal women or those with abnormal bleeding, so removed polyps are sent for histology.
thinking: Intermenstrual and heavy bleeding ↓ normal uterine size and myometrium ↓ focal well-defined echogenic lesion within the cavity ↓ normal ovaries ↓ endometrial polyp
exam_trap: C, endometrial hyperplasia — abnormal bleeding with an endometrial abnormality suggests it, but hyperplasia is diffuse thickening, not a discrete lesion.
takeaway: A focal, well-defined lesion in the uterine cavity causing intermenstrual bleeding suggests an endometrial polyp.

stem: A 41-year-old man arrives in the emergency department at 4 am with sudden severe pain in his left loin that comes in waves and spreads to his left groin. He is pacing around the cubicle, unable to get comfortable, and has vomited twice. His temperature is normal and the abdomen is soft. Urine dipstick shows blood but no nitrites or leucocytes. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden severe colicky loin-to-groin pain with restlessness, vomiting and microscopic haematuria is typical of a ureteric stone. NICE advises an NSAID as first-line analgesia if not contraindicated and urgent non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder to confirm the diagnosis. Fever with obstruction would need emergency decompression.
why_wrong: B. Pyelonephritis causes fever, constant loin pain and usually leucocytes or nitrites in the urine. C. Appendicitis causes right-sided pain and patients lie still. D. A leaking aneurysm should be considered in older patients, especially over 60, presenting with loin pain, but is unlikely at this age. E. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain with a tender, high-riding testis.
pearl: Patients with renal colic writhe and cannot settle, whereas patients with peritonitis lie still; this simple observation helps separate them.
thinking: Sudden severe colicky loin pain ↓ radiation to the groin ↓ restless, vomiting ↓ haematuria without infection signs ↓ renal colic
exam_trap: B, acute pyelonephritis — loin pain with blood in the urine suggests it, but he is afebrile with no infection markers and the pain is colicky.
takeaway: Colicky loin-to-groin pain in a restless patient with haematuria is renal colic.

stem: A district nurse asks a GP to review a 70-year-old woman with a leg ulcer that has been present for four months. It lies just above her left medial malleolus, is shallow with irregular sloping edges and a moist sloughy base, and is only mildly painful. Around it there is brown staining, small dilated veins at the ankle and tortuous veins on the calf. Her foot is warm and the pedal pulses are easily felt. What is the likeliest underlying cause?
why_correct: A shallow, irregular, mildly painful ulcer in the gaiter area above the medial malleolus, with haemosiderin pigmentation, ankle venous flare and varicose veins, is a venous ulcer from chronic venous hypertension. With an ABPI confirming adequate arterial supply, compression bandaging is the mainstay of treatment, and referral to vascular services should be considered.
why_wrong: B. Arterial ulcers are deep, punched out and painful, usually on the toes or lateral foot, with absent pulses. C. Neuropathic ulcers occur on pressure points of the sole in a numb foot. D. Vasculitic ulcers are often multiple, painful and associated with palpable purpura or systemic disease. E. Pressure injuries occur over bony prominences such as heels and sacrum in immobile patients.
pearl: Venous ulcers are the commonest type of leg ulcer in the UK; an ulcer that fails to heal after months of good compression needs specialist review and possibly biopsy.
thinking: Shallow irregular ulcer above medial malleolus ↓ pigmentation, ankle flare, varicose veins ↓ warm foot with good pulses ↓ venous hypertension ↓ chronic venous insufficiency
exam_trap: B, peripheral arterial disease — leg ulcers in older people often raise vascular concerns, but this foot is warm with palpable pulses and the ulcer is shallow.
takeaway: A shallow gaiter-area ulcer with venous skin changes is a venous ulcer; check the ABPI before compression.

stem: Paramedics bring a 66-year-old man with known ischaemic heart disease to the emergency department at 3 am. He woke suddenly fighting for breath and has been sitting bolt upright since. He is sweaty, tachypnoeic and coughing up frothy, pink-tinged sputum. There are fine crackles over both lungs up to the mid zones and a quiet wheeze. A chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar shadowing with upper lobe venous diversion. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden nocturnal breathlessness, frothy pink sputum and bilateral crackles in a patient with ischaemic heart disease indicate acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. The X-ray changes reflect fluid in the interstitium and alveoli. Immediate management includes sitting upright, oxygen if hypoxic, intravenous furosemide, and consideration of nitrates and non-invasive ventilation, while seeking the cause such as acute coronary syndrome.
why_wrong: B. Asthma causes wheeze without frothy pink sputum or crackles, and he has no asthma history. C. Pneumonia develops over days with fever and focal rather than bilateral perihilar changes. D. Pneumothorax gives unilateral reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance. E. COPD exacerbations cause wheeze and purulent sputum, not frothy pink sputum.
pearl: Wheeze in pulmonary oedema (so-called cardiac asthma) can mislead; bilateral crackles, frothy sputum and a cardiac history point to the heart.
thinking: Ischaemic heart disease ↓ sudden nocturnal breathlessness, sitting upright ↓ frothy pink sputum ↓ bilateral crackles, perihilar shadowing ↓ acute pulmonary oedema
exam_trap: B, acute asthma — the wheeze tempts, but there is no asthma history and the frothy sputum and widespread crackles indicate pulmonary oedema.
takeaway: Sudden breathlessness with frothy pink sputum and bilateral crackles is acute pulmonary oedema.

stem: A GP visits an 82-year-old woman who has heart failure at home. She stopped taking her furosemide a week ago because it made her rush to the toilet while out. Since then she has become breathless walking around the house, needs extra pillows at night and her shoes no longer fit. She is afebrile. There is pitting oedema to the knees and fine crackles at both lung bases, and her daughter reports her weight has gone up. What best explains her deterioration?

options.A: Fluid retention from decompensated heart failure

correct_answer: A. Fluid retention from decompensated heart failure
why_correct: Stopping a loop diuretic in heart failure allows salt and water to accumulate, causing weight gain, peripheral oedema and pulmonary congestion with orthopnoea and basal crackles. Management includes restarting and possibly increasing the diuretic, discussing timing of doses to fit her routine, and considering hospital admission if she is significantly unwell.
why_wrong: B. Pneumonia causes fever, cough and focal crackles, and would not explain weight gain and leg oedema. C. Dehydration causes weight loss and postural dizziness, not oedema. D. Anaemia worsens breathlessness but does not cause weight gain and crackles. E. Thyrotoxicosis causes weight loss, tremor and palpitations.
pearl: Diuretic non-adherence is common because of urinary urgency; adjusting the timing of doses can help patients keep taking them.
thinking: Known heart failure ↓ stopped furosemide ↓ worse breathlessness, orthopnoea, leg oedema ↓ weight gain and basal crackles, afebrile ↓ fluid retention from decompensation
exam_trap: B, community-acquired pneumonia — breathlessness with crackles in an older person suggests infection, but she is afebrile, the crackles are bilateral and weight and oedema have increased.
takeaway: Stopping diuretics in heart failure leads to fluid retention with weight gain, oedema and breathlessness.

stem: A 19-month-old girl whose parents declined MMR vaccination is brought to the GP. She has had a low-grade temperature and a faint pink rash that started on her face and spread to her trunk over a day. She is otherwise playful. There are tender enlarged lymph nodes behind her ears and at the back of her neck. Her aunt, who looks after her daily, is 9 weeks pregnant and unsure of her own vaccination history. Which infection is most likely, and of most concern for the aunt's pregnancy?
why_correct: A mild illness with a pink maculopapular rash spreading from the face downwards and postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy in an unvaccinated child suggests rubella. Infection in early pregnancy carries a high risk of congenital rubella syndrome, including deafness, cataracts and heart defects. Rubella is notifiable, and the pregnant contact needs urgent assessment and serology.
why_wrong: A. Roseola causes high fever for several days followed by a rash as the fever settles, and carries no recognised fetal risk. B. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash with sore throat and strawberry tongue. D. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes mouth ulcers and vesicles on the hands and feet. E. Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) causes slapped cheeks followed by a lacy rash on the limbs, and its fetal risk is anaemia and hydrops rather than malformations.
pearl: Any pregnant woman exposed to a rash illness should have her immune status checked urgently, as management depends on the likely infection and her stage of pregnancy.
thinking: Unvaccinated child ↓ mild fever, pink rash spreading from face downwards ↓ postauricular and suboccipital nodes ↓ pregnant contact at risk of congenital infection ↓ rubella
exam_trap: E, erythema infectiosum — parvovirus also endangers a pregnancy, but it gives slapped cheeks and a lacy limb rash, and its risk is fetal anaemia rather than malformation.
takeaway: Rash with postauricular nodes in an unvaccinated child suggests rubella; urgently assess any pregnant contact.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who is breastfeeding her three-week-old baby phones her GP surgery. Since yesterday a wedge-shaped area in the upper outer part of her left breast has become red, hot and tender, and she feels achy and shivery with a temperature of 38.2°C. She has been missing some feeds on that side because of nipple soreness. A same-day review finds no fluctuant swelling. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: A painful, red, wedge-shaped area of one breast with fever and flu-like symptoms during breastfeeding is lactational mastitis, usually caused by milk stasis that may become infected. Missed feeds and nipple damage are typical triggers. She should continue breastfeeding or expressing from the affected side, use analgesia, and receive an antibiotic such as flucloxacillin if symptoms are severe, infection is likely or they fail to settle.
why_wrong: A. An abscess presents as a fluctuant, tender lump, which is absent here. B. Inflammatory breast cancer causes diffuse redness and peau d'orange without fever, and should be considered if redness does not resolve. D. A galactocele is a painless milk-filled cyst. E. Engorgement is usually bilateral and generalised, without a focal red wedge and fever.
pearl: Stopping breastfeeding from the affected breast increases milk stasis and the risk of abscess; continued feeding is safe for the baby.
thinking: Breastfeeding, missed feeds on one side ↓ wedge-shaped red, hot, tender area ↓ fever and flu-like symptoms ↓ no fluctuant lump ↓ lactational mastitis
exam_trap: A, breast abscess — fever with a hot, tender breast raises concern for pus, but there is no fluctuant swelling and abscesses usually follow untreated mastitis.
takeaway: A red, tender breast wedge with fever during breastfeeding is mastitis; keep feeding from that side.

stem: A 63-year-old woman attends the emergency department with two days of constant pain and tenderness in the left iliac fossa and a temperature of 37.9°C. She is eating and drinking and her observations are otherwise normal. Her CRP is raised. CT shows multiple sigmoid diverticula with thickening of the sigmoid wall and stranding of the surrounding fat, with no fluid collection, no free gas and no fistula. Which term best describes her condition?
why_correct: Inflammation of colonic diverticula with wall thickening and fat stranding, but without abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction or bleeding, is acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. In patients who are systemically well, NICE supports managing this without antibiotics initially, with analgesia such as paracetamol, safety-netting and re-review, using antibiotics if systemically unwell or immunosuppressed.
why_wrong: A. Diverticulosis means diverticula without inflammation or symptoms. B. An abscess would appear as a fluid collection, which is absent. C. Ischaemic colitis typically causes sudden pain with bloody diarrhoea in older patients with vascular disease, often at the splenic flexure. E. Perforation would show free gas on CT and cause peritonitis.
pearl: NICE advises avoiding NSAIDs and opioids for diverticulitis pain where possible, because they may increase the risk of perforation.
thinking: Left iliac fossa pain with low-grade fever ↓ raised CRP ↓ CT: sigmoid diverticula with inflammation ↓ no abscess, perforation or fistula ↓ acute uncomplicated diverticulitis
exam_trap: A, diverticulosis — diverticula are present on the scan, but wall thickening and fat stranding show active inflammation, which makes it diverticulitis.
takeaway: Inflamed diverticula without abscess, perforation or fistula is acute uncomplicated diverticulitis.

stem: An 81-year-old woman attends the emergency department with 24 hours of colicky abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. She has not opened her bowels for two days. There is a tense, tender lump in her right groin, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, with reddened overlying skin. It has no cough impulse and cannot be reduced. Her abdomen is distended with tinkling bowel sounds. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
correct_answer: D. Strangulated hernia causing bowel obstruction
why_correct: A tense, tender, irreducible groin lump with overlying erythema, no cough impulse and features of bowel obstruction indicates a hernia that has trapped bowel and compromised its blood supply. The position below and lateral to the pubic tubercle in an older woman suggests a femoral hernia, which has a narrow neck and a high strangulation risk. She needs resuscitation and emergency surgery.
why_wrong: A. A saphena varix is soft, has a cough impulse and disappears on lying down, without obstruction. B. Lymphadenitis causes tender nodes but not bowel obstruction. C. A psoas abscess causes fever, back or hip pain and a fluctuant swelling, not obstruction. E. An aneurysm is pulsatile and does not cause vomiting and distension.
pearl: In any patient with bowel obstruction, examine the hernial orifices carefully; a small femoral hernia in an older woman is easily missed.
thinking: Groin lump below and lateral to pubic tubercle ↓ tense, tender, red, irreducible, no cough impulse ↓ vomiting, distension, no bowel motion ↓ trapped bowel with compromised supply ↓ strangulated hernia, emergency surgery
exam_trap: B, inguinal lymphadenitis — a red, tender groin lump suggests infected nodes, but it would not cause vomiting, distension and absent bowel motions.
takeaway: An irreducible, tender groin lump with bowel obstruction is a strangulated hernia needing emergency surgery.

stem: A 78-year-old man is admitted under the surgical team with colicky lower abdominal pain and increasing abdominal swelling over four days. CT shows a stricturing tumour of the sigmoid colon with dilated bowel proximal to it. The team needs to judge whether the bowel lumen is completely blocked. Which feature in his history would best indicate that the obstruction is complete?
why_correct: Absolute constipation, the inability to pass either faeces or flatus, indicates that nothing can pass the obstruction, which strongly suggests complete obstruction. In partial obstruction some flatus or liquid stool often still passes. Complete large bowel obstruction carries a risk of caecal perforation, especially with a competent ileocaecal valve, and needs urgent surgical decision-making.
why_wrong: A. Vomiting occurs in both partial and complete obstruction and is often late in large bowel obstruction. B. Distension is present in both partial and complete obstruction. C. Loss of appetite is non-specific. E. High-pitched bowel sounds indicate mechanical obstruction but do not distinguish partial from complete.
pearl: Ask specifically about passing wind, not just stool, because patients with partial obstruction may still pass flatus or liquid stool despite feeling constipated.
thinking: Sigmoid tumour with proximal dilatation ↓ question is partial or complete ↓ most features occur in both ↓ nothing passing at all, not even flatus ↓ absolute constipation
exam_trap: B, abdominal distension — it reflects obstruction and is striking, but it is seen in partial obstruction too and does not prove the lumen is fully blocked.
takeaway: Failure to pass both stool and flatus suggests complete bowel obstruction.

stem: A 68-year-old man sees his GP because he has been itching all over for three weeks and his wife has noticed his eyes are yellow. His urine looks like strong tea and his stools have become pale and putty-coloured. Liver blood tests reveal a raised bilirubin, mainly conjugated, with markedly raised alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT and only a mild rise in ALT. Which process best explains these findings?
why_correct: Itching, dark urine and pale stools with a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and a disproportionate rise in ALP and GGT indicate cholestasis, meaning impaired bile flow. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and passes into the urine, while less bilirubin reaches the gut so stools pale, and retained bile salts cause pruritus. An ultrasound to look for biliary dilatation is the next step.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal-coloured stools and no bilirubin in the urine. B. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without pale stools or itching. D. Hepatocellular injury would show transaminases raised far more than ALP. E. Ineffective erythropoiesis raises unconjugated bilirubin.
pearl: Painless obstructive jaundice in an older adult raises concern for pancreatic or biliary cancer; NICE advises suspected cancer referral for people aged 40 and over with jaundice.
thinking: Itching with yellow eyes ↓ dark urine, pale stools ↓ conjugated bilirubin raised ↓ ALP and GGT much higher than ALT ↓ cholestasis
exam_trap: D, hepatocellular injury — any abnormal liver tests with jaundice tempt it, but the ALP and GGT dominate while the ALT is only mildly raised.
takeaway: Pale stools, dark urine and an ALP-predominant conjugated jaundice indicate cholestasis.

stem: A 19-year-old man attends the emergency department five hours after swallowing around thirty paracetamol tablets at once following an argument. He has no symptoms, examination is normal and he says he now regrets it and wants to go home. Which statement best guides his management?

options.A: Normal liver function tests now exclude significant liver injury
options.B: Activated charcoal is the main treatment at this stage
options.C: He can be discharged because he has no symptoms
options.D: The decision to give acetylcysteine is based on the timed paracetamol level, not on symptoms
options.E: He should be referred for liver transplant assessment immediately

correct_answer: D. The decision to give acetylcysteine is based on the timed paracetamol level, not on symptoms
why_correct: Paracetamol poisoning is often asymptomatic for the first day, while liver damage is developing. For a single acute ingestion with a known time, a paracetamol level taken at least four hours after ingestion is plotted on the treatment nomogram, and acetylcysteine is given if it is on or above the treatment line. If the timing is uncertain or the overdose was staggered, acetylcysteine is started without waiting for the level.
why_wrong: A. Liver tests are often normal early and do not exclude later hepatotoxicity. B. Activated charcoal is only useful within about an hour of ingestion. C. Absence of symptoms is expected early and is not reassuring. E. Transplant referral is considered for established acute liver failure with specific criteria, not in a well patient at presentation.
pearl: Every patient after self-poisoning needs a psychosocial assessment before discharge, and a capacity assessment if they wish to leave before treatment is complete.
thinking: Single paracetamol overdose with known time ↓ asymptomatic at five hours ↓ symptoms appear late, after liver injury ↓ take a timed level and plot it ↓ treat according to the level, not symptoms
exam_trap: A, normal liver function tests — they seem reassuring, but transaminases rise only after a day or more, so early normal results do not exclude damage.
takeaway: In paracetamol overdose, treat on the timed level and history, never on the absence of symptoms.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a night out with crushing central chest pain radiating to her jaw for 40 minutes. She is restless and sweaty, with a heart rate of 124/min, blood pressure 172/104 mmHg and widely dilated pupils. She admits to snorting cocaine two hours earlier. She has no known medical history. Which serious condition must be excluded first?
why_correct: Cocaine causes intense sympathetic stimulation, coronary vasospasm, increased myocardial oxygen demand and a prothrombotic state, so it can cause myocardial ischaemia and infarction even in young people without risk factors. Crushing pain radiating to the jaw needs an immediate ECG and troponin. Benzodiazepines help control agitation, tachycardia and hypertension, and nitrates and aspirin are used for ischaemia.
why_wrong: A. Panic attacks can cause chest pain and sweating, but panic is a diagnosis of exclusion after cocaine use. C. Pneumothorax causes pleuritic pain and breathlessness with chest signs, not crushing pain to the jaw. D. Reflux causes burning retrosternal pain related to meals or lying down. E. Costochondritis causes localised chest wall tenderness without sympathetic features.
pearl: Beta-blockers are generally avoided acutely in cocaine toxicity because they may worsen coronary vasospasm; benzodiazepines are first line for sympathetic features.
thinking: Recent cocaine use ↓ crushing chest pain radiating to jaw ↓ tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils = sympathomimetic toxicity ↓ vasospasm and thrombosis ↓ exclude acute coronary syndrome
exam_trap: A, panic attack — a young, restless, sweaty woman with chest pain may be labelled as anxious, but cocaine can cause genuine myocardial infarction.
takeaway: Chest pain after cocaine use is acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise, whatever the patient's age.

stem: A 44-year-old woman sees her GP in December with several weeks of morning headaches, nausea and feeling muddled. Her two teenage children have similar headaches, and the family dog has become lethargic. Her symptoms ease during the day at work and return in the evenings. They use an old gas fire in the living room. Her oxygen saturation on a pulse oximeter is 99%. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Headache, nausea and confusion affecting several household members and a pet, improving away from home and returning there, with a gas appliance in use, is the classic pattern of chronic carbon monoxide exposure. Pulse oximetry is falsely normal because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so carboxyhaemoglobin should be measured on a blood gas. Treat with high-flow oxygen and ensure the appliance is not used until checked by a registered engineer.
why_wrong: A. Tension-type headache does not affect a whole household and pets at once. B. Gastroenteritis is a short illness with diarrhoea, not weeks of headaches that ease away from home. C. Medication overuse headache would not affect her children and dog simultaneously. D. Migraine is episodic and individual, not linked to being at home.
pearl: A normal pulse oximetry reading does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning; always measure carboxyhaemoglobin on a venous or arterial blood gas.
thinking: Several family members and a pet affected ↓ headache, nausea, confusion ↓ better away from home ↓ gas fire in winter ↓ carbon monoxide poisoning
exam_trap: B, viral gastroenteritis — nausea in several family members suggests an infection, but symptoms have lasted weeks, ease away from home and affect the dog.
takeaway: Household-wide headaches that improve away from home suggest carbon monoxide poisoning.

stem: An 84-year-old woman is admitted to the medical assessment unit after two falls and increasing drowsiness and muddled speech over five days. Her GP started bendroflumethiazide for hypertension three weeks ago. Blood tests show sodium 119 mmol/L (reference range 135–145 mmol/L), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (reference range 3.5–5.0 mmol/L), and normal calcium and glucose. Which electrolyte disturbance best explains her confusion?
why_correct: Her sodium is well below the reference range, and marked hyponatraemia causes cerebral swelling with confusion, drowsiness, unsteadiness and falls, particularly in older people. Thiazide diuretics are a common cause in older women. Management includes stopping the thiazide, assessing fluid status and correcting sodium slowly with close monitoring.
why_wrong: A. Her potassium is only marginally low and mild hypokalaemia causes weakness or arrhythmias rather than confusion. B. Calcium is normal. D. Her sodium is low, not high. E. Magnesium was not measured and is not suggested by the clinical picture.
pearl: Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly, because overly rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination syndrome.
thinking: Older woman with new confusion and falls ↓ recent thiazide ↓ sodium far below range, potassium only marginally low ↓ low sodium explains neurological features ↓ hyponatraemia
exam_trap: A, hypokalaemia — thiazides lower potassium and her level is slightly low, but this mild drop does not explain confusion and drowsiness.
takeaway: Thiazides commonly cause hyponatraemia in older people, presenting with confusion and falls.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department from a music festival. She took ecstasy (MDMA) and then drank large volumes of water because she was worried about overheating. She has a headache, has vomited and is becoming confused. Her serum sodium is very low. Which development would most strongly indicate life-threatening cerebral oedema needing immediate treatment?
why_correct: Acute severe hyponatraemia causes water to shift into brain cells, producing cerebral oedema. Seizures, reduced consciousness or coma indicate severe symptoms and a risk of brain herniation and death. These require immediate treatment with hypertonic saline in a monitored setting, with senior input and careful limits on the rate of rise of sodium.
why_wrong: A. A dry mouth is non-specific and expected with MDMA use. C. Cramps can occur with electrolyte disturbance but do not indicate cerebral oedema. D. Mild nausea is an early, less severe symptom. E. Tachycardia is a common sympathomimetic effect of MDMA and does not reflect raised intracranial pressure.
pearl: MDMA causes hyponatraemia both by stimulating ADH release and by prompting excessive water intake; young women appear particularly vulnerable.
thinking: MDMA plus large water intake ↓ acute severe hyponatraemia ↓ water moves into brain cells ↓ cerebral oedema ↓ seizure signals life-threatening severity
exam_trap: E, tachycardia — it is an abnormal sign, but in this context it reflects the stimulant effect of MDMA rather than cerebral oedema.
takeaway: Seizures in acute hyponatraemia signal cerebral oedema and need immediate hypertonic saline.

stem: During a heatwave, a GP visits an 81-year-old woman who lives alone. Her neighbour says she has barely eaten or drunk for three days. She is drowsy, her tongue and mouth are dry, and her daughter says she has passed very little urine. Which examination finding would most support reduced circulating volume?

options.E: A fall in blood pressure on standing

correct_answer: E. A fall in blood pressure on standing
why_correct: Fluid depletion reduces circulating volume and venous return, so blood pressure falls when moving from lying to standing (postural hypotension), often with dizziness and a compensatory rise in heart rate. Other supporting signs include a low JVP, tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill and reduced urine output. She needs fluid replacement, and admission should be considered given her drowsiness.
why_wrong: A. A raised JVP suggests fluid overload or right heart strain, not depletion. B. Volume loss usually causes tachycardia rather than bradycardia. C. Bibasal crackles suggest pulmonary oedema or infection, not dehydration. D. Hypovolaemia tends to lower, not raise, blood pressure.
pearl: Older people on beta-blockers may not mount a tachycardia when dehydrated, so a postural blood pressure drop can be a more reliable sign of volume depletion.
thinking: Older woman, heatwave, poor intake ↓ dry mouth, drowsy, low urine output ↓ reduced circulating volume ↓ venous return falls on standing ↓ postural hypotension
exam_trap: B, bradycardia — older patients may not become tachycardic, which can tempt, but bradycardia itself is not a sign of volume depletion.
takeaway: Postural hypotension is a key sign of reduced circulating volume in dehydration.

stem: A 48-year-old woman is on the surgical ward on the first day after a total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goitre. She tells the nurse that her fingertips and the skin around her lips feel numb and prickly. When her blood pressure is measured, her hand goes into spasm with the wrist flexed and the fingers extended. Her voice is normal. Which of the following best accounts for her symptoms?
why_correct: Damage to or devascularisation of the parathyroid glands during total thyroidectomy commonly causes a fall in serum calcium in the first few days after surgery. Low calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, producing perioral and fingertip paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm. Spasm provoked by inflating a blood pressure cuff is Trousseau's sign, so serum calcium should be checked urgently and replaced.
why_wrong: A. Hyperventilation can cause tingling, but after thyroidectomy with a positive Trousseau's sign, hypocalcaemia is far more likely. C. Hypercalcaemia reduces neuromuscular excitability and causes lethargy and constipation, not spasm. D. Hypokalaemia causes flaccid weakness and cramps, not perioral tingling with carpal spasm. E. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness or stridor, and her voice is normal.
pearl: After thyroid or parathyroid surgery, check calcium routinely. Tap over the facial nerve for Chvostek's sign and inflate a cuff for Trousseau's sign; severe or symptomatic cases need intravenous calcium gluconate.
thinking: Day 1 after total thyroidectomy ↓ Perioral and fingertip paraesthesia ↓ Carpal spasm on cuff inflation (Trousseau's sign) ↓ Parathyroid injury lowers calcium ↓ Hypocalcaemia causing tetany
exam_trap: A, anxiety with hyperventilation — respiratory alkalosis also causes perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm, but the postoperative setting after total thyroidectomy makes parathyroid-related hypocalcaemia the diagnosis to confirm and treat.
takeaway: Tingling and carpal spasm after thyroidectomy means hypocalcaemia until proven otherwise.

stem: A 61-year-old woman who completed treatment for breast cancer two years ago sees her GP because she has felt exhausted for a month. She has been opening her bowels only twice a week, is drinking large amounts of water, gets up several times at night to pass urine and has felt low and muddled. She also describes a new ache in her lower back. Which biochemical abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Constipation, thirst, polyuria, low mood, confusion and bone pain together are the classic picture of hypercalcaemia. In a woman with previous breast cancer and new back pain, malignancy-related hypercalcaemia from bone metastases or tumour-secreted PTH-related peptide is a key concern. Serum calcium, renal function and imaging of the spine should be arranged promptly.
why_wrong: A. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion but does not cause thirst with polyuria or constipation. B. Hypokalaemia may cause constipation and weakness but does not explain thirst, polyuria and bone pain together. C. Hyperglycaemia causes thirst and polyuria but not constipation and bone pain. E. Hypocalcaemia causes paraesthesia and tetany, the opposite picture.
pearl: Remember the pattern of bones, stones, abdominal groans and psychic moans. In a patient with a cancer history, hypercalcaemia with new bone pain should prompt a search for metastases.
thinking: Previous breast cancer, new back pain ↓ Constipation, thirst and polyuria ↓ Low mood and confusion ↓ Classic hypercalcaemia cluster ↓ Hypercalcaemia
exam_trap: C, hyperglycaemia — thirst and polyuria immediately suggest diabetes, but constipation, low mood and bone pain alongside them point to raised calcium.
takeaway: Thirst, polyuria, constipation and confusion together point to hypercalcaemia.

stem: A 66-year-old right-handed woman is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after her husband noticed her face drooping on the left and that she could not lift her left arm. She also reports reduced feeling in the left hand. She speaks fluently and follows commands correctly. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
why_correct: Motor and sensory pathways from the cerebral hemispheres cross the midline, so weakness and sensory loss affecting the left face, arm and hand localise to the right cerebral hemisphere. Preserved fluent speech and comprehension fit sparing of the dominant (left) hemisphere in a right-handed person. She needs immediate stroke assessment and brain imaging.
why_wrong: A. A left hemisphere lesion would cause right-sided weakness and, in a right-handed person, often dysphasia. C. A cerebellar lesion causes ataxia and incoordination rather than facial and arm weakness. D. A cervical cord lesion would not cause facial droop. E. A brachial plexus lesion would not affect the face and would not come on suddenly without trauma.
pearl: Facial involvement places the lesion above the spinal cord. Contralateral face and arm weakness with dysphasia suggests the dominant hemisphere; with neglect or inattention, think of the non-dominant hemisphere.
thinking: Sudden left face and arm weakness ↓ Left-sided sensory loss ↓ Pathways cross, so lesion is contralateral ↓ Speech preserved, dominant hemisphere spared ↓ Right cerebral hemisphere
exam_trap: A, left cerebral hemisphere — candidates sometimes localise to the same side as the symptoms, forgetting that the corticospinal and sensory pathways decussate.
takeaway: One-sided face and arm weakness localises to the opposite cerebral hemisphere.

stem: An 11-year-old boy is seen by the practice nurse because he has a night-time cough and wheezes when he runs in the cold. He had eczema in the creases of his elbows as an infant, and every summer he sneezes and has itchy, watery eyes. His father has hay fever. Which underlying predisposition best links these problems?
why_correct: Atopy is an inherited tendency to produce IgE antibodies against common environmental allergens. It underlies the clustering of eczema, allergic rhinitis and asthma in the same person and family. Nocturnal cough and wheeze with seasonal rhinoconjunctivitis and a history of infantile eczema fit this allergic background well.
why_wrong: A. Cystic fibrosis causes chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections and poor growth rather than seasonal allergic symptoms. B. Primary ciliary dyskinesia causes chronic wet cough, sinusitis and ear disease from early life, not seasonal itch and sneezing. D. IgA deficiency predisposes to recurrent infections and does not explain eczema and hay fever. E. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early emphysema and liver disease in adults, not childhood atopic disease.
pearl: Ask about eczema, hay fever and family history in any child with wheeze; a personal or family history of atopy makes asthma more likely.
thinking: Night cough and exercise wheeze ↓ Infantile eczema ↓ Seasonal sneezing and itchy eyes ↓ Family history of hay fever ↓ Atopy
exam_trap: A, cystic fibrosis — it is a classic cause of respiratory symptoms in children, but it gives a chronic wet cough and infections, not seasonal allergic features with eczema.
takeaway: Eczema, hay fever and asthma clustering in one child reflect an atopic predisposition.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with asthma attends the emergency department with acute wheeze and chest tightness that began about an hour after she took ibuprofen for back pain. She has no rash, her lips and tongue are not swollen and her blood pressure is normal. For several years she has had a constantly blocked nose and has lost her sense of smell. Anterior rhinoscopy shows grey, glistening, insensate masses in both nostrils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: The combination of asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and bronchospasm triggered by aspirin or other NSAIDs is aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter's triad). Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase shifts arachidonic acid metabolism towards leukotriene production, causing bronchoconstriction. She should be advised to avoid aspirin and other NSAIDs.
why_wrong: A. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis causes poorly controlled asthma with fleeting infiltrates and bronchiectasis, not NSAID-triggered wheeze with polyps. C. Anaphylaxis would usually involve skin, mucosal or circulatory features, which are absent. D. EGPA causes asthma and polyps but with marked eosinophilia and vasculitic features such as neuropathy or rash. E. Cystic fibrosis can cause nasal polyps but presents with chronic infection from childhood, not a drug-triggered asthma attack.
pearl: Ask every adult with asthma about reactions to aspirin or NSAIDs, especially if they have nasal polyps or anosmia. Paracetamol is the usual safer alternative for pain.
thinking: Asthma with wheeze after ibuprofen ↓ No skin or circulatory features ↓ Chronic blocked nose and anosmia ↓ Bilateral nasal polyps ↓ Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
exam_trap: C, anaphylaxis to ibuprofen — a drug followed by wheeze suggests anaphylaxis, but the absence of skin, mucosal or circulatory involvement and the polyps point to a non-allergic COX-inhibitor reaction.
takeaway: Asthma, nasal polyps and NSAID-triggered bronchospasm make up aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

stem: A 38-year-old man sees his GP because both sides of his nose have felt blocked for most of the past six months. He has thick yellow-green mucus running down the back of his throat, a dull pressure across his cheeks and forehead that worsens when he bends forward, and food tastes bland. He has no nosebleeds, and examination of the nose shows swollen, inflamed mucosa on both sides. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Long-standing bilateral nasal obstruction with discoloured discharge, facial pressure and reduced smell or taste is the typical picture of chronic rhinosinusitis. The persistence over many months distinguishes it from an acute sinusitis. First-line management is usually saline nasal irrigation and an intranasal corticosteroid, with ENT referral if symptoms persist.
why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis causes clear watery discharge, sneezing and itch rather than purulent discharge with facial pressure. B. Acute sinusitis follows a cold and settles over a few weeks rather than persisting for months. C. Malignancy typically causes unilateral obstruction, bleeding or cranial nerve signs rather than symmetrical bilateral symptoms. E. A dental abscess causes localised tooth pain and swelling, not months of bilateral nasal obstruction.
pearl: Bilateral, persistent symptoms suggest inflammatory sinus disease; unilateral obstruction, bleeding or facial numbness are red flags that need urgent ENT assessment.
thinking: Bilateral blockage for months ↓ Purulent postnasal discharge ↓ Facial pressure worse on bending ↓ Reduced taste and smell ↓ Chronic rhinosinusitis
exam_trap: B, acute bacterial sinusitis — the purulent discharge and facial pain fit sinus infection, but symptoms lasting most of six months make it chronic rather than acute.
takeaway: Months of bilateral blockage, purulent discharge and facial pressure indicate chronic rhinosinusitis.

stem: A 63-year-old retired carpenter attends his GP with three months of a blocked left nostril. He has noticed blood-stained mucus coming from the left side only and, over the past fortnight, a numb patch over his left cheek. The right side of his nose is clear. Which diagnosis must be excluded?
why_correct: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction with unilateral blood-stained discharge is a red flag for a sinonasal tumour, and new facial numbness suggests infiltration of the infraorbital nerve. Long-term occupational exposure to wood dust is a recognised risk factor for sinonasal adenocarcinoma. He needs urgent ENT referral for endoscopic examination and imaging.
why_wrong: A. Simple nasal polyps are usually bilateral and do not cause facial numbness. B. Allergic rhinitis is bilateral with sneezing and clear discharge. C. A deviated septum causes long-standing obstruction without bleeding or new numbness. D. Chronic rhinosinusitis is usually bilateral and does not cause cranial nerve signs.
pearl: Unilateral nasal symptoms in an adult, especially with bleeding, facial swelling, numbness or eye signs, should be treated as possible malignancy until examined by ENT.
thinking: Older man, wood dust exposure ↓ Unilateral nasal obstruction ↓ Unilateral blood-stained discharge ↓ New cheek numbness from nerve involvement ↓ Sinonasal malignancy
exam_trap: A, nasal polyps — they commonly cause obstruction, but polyps are typically bilateral, and unilateral bleeding with facial numbness signals a tumour.
takeaway: Unilateral nasal blockage with bleeding or facial numbness needs urgent exclusion of cancer.

stem: A 34-year-old man was started on lamotrigine for epilepsy two weeks ago. He attends the emergency department after several days of fever and aching, followed by a painful dusky red rash on his chest and back with some flaccid blisters. His lips are crusted and ulcerated, he can hardly eat because his mouth is so sore, and both eyes are red and gritty. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A painful dusky rash with blistering and involvement of two or more mucosal sites, developing within weeks of starting a high-risk drug such as lamotrigine, is typical of Stevens–Johnson syndrome. A flu-like prodrome often precedes the skin changes. The suspected drug must be stopped immediately and the patient managed urgently with specialist dermatology and ophthalmology input.
why_wrong: A. Erythema multiforme usually follows herpes simplex infection, with target lesions on the limbs and little or mild mucosal involvement. B. Bullous pemphigoid affects older adults with tense blisters and rarely involves mucosa. D. Scalded skin syndrome mainly affects young children and spares the mucous membranes. E. Chickenpox causes crops of small itchy vesicles and is not linked to starting a drug.
pearl: Drugs commonly linked to SJS include anticonvulsants such as lamotrigine and carbamazepine, allopurinol, sulfonamides and some NSAIDs. Early withdrawal of the culprit improves outcome.
thinking: New lamotrigine two weeks ago ↓ Flu-like prodrome ↓ Painful dusky rash with blisters ↓ Oral and ocular mucosal involvement ↓ Stevens–Johnson syndrome
exam_trap: A, erythema multiforme — it can involve the mouth and causes similar lesions, but it is usually triggered by herpes infection and lacks this extensive painful mucosal disease after a new drug.
takeaway: New drug, painful blistering rash and mucosal involvement mean Stevens–Johnson syndrome: stop the drug.

stem: An 8-year-old girl is seen in a paediatric allergy clinic. At a birthday party she ate a biscuit containing peanut, and within 15 minutes her lips swelled, she developed raised itchy weals over her neck, vomited twice and started coughing. Her symptoms settled after treatment by paramedics. Which immunological mechanism best explains this reaction?
correct_answer: D. IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation (type I)
why_correct: Rapid onset of multisystem symptoms within minutes of eating a specific food is typical of type I hypersensitivity. Allergen cross-links specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and other mediators that cause urticaria, angioedema, vomiting and bronchospasm. She should have allergy testing and an adrenaline auto-injector plan.
why_wrong: A. Type II reactions involve antibodies against cell-surface antigens, as in haemolytic transfusion reactions, not immediate food reactions. B. Type III reactions cause vasculitis, arthritis or nephritis hours to days after exposure. C. Type IV reactions are delayed by 48 to 72 hours, as in contact dermatitis. E. Food intolerance such as lactase deficiency causes gut symptoms without urticaria, angioedema or cough.
pearl: Immediate reactions within minutes with skin, gut or airway involvement suggest IgE-mediated allergy; delayed gut-only symptoms point to non-IgE allergy or intolerance.
thinking: Specific food trigger ↓ Onset within minutes ↓ Urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting, cough ↓ Mast cell mediator release ↓ IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity
exam_trap: C, type IV delayed reaction — non-IgE food allergy exists, but it causes delayed symptoms over hours to days, not a reaction within 15 minutes.
takeaway: Food reactions within minutes involving skin, gut and airway are IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity.

stem: A 30-year-old woman attends an urgent treatment centre with itchy raised weals that appeared over her arms and trunk an hour after a prawn curry. Her eyelids look slightly puffy. She is talking in full sentences, has no stridor or wheeze, and her pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation are normal. Which treatment should be given first?
why_correct: Urticaria with mild facial swelling but no airway, breathing or circulation problem is not anaphylaxis. An oral non-sedating antihistamine such as cetirizine is the appropriate first treatment, with advice to seek urgent help if breathing or swallowing becomes difficult. She should be observed briefly and given information about avoiding the suspected trigger.
why_wrong: B. Intramuscular adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis with airway, breathing or circulatory compromise, which is absent. C. Intravenous steroids are not needed for uncomplicated urticaria and are not first-line. D. Salbutamol treats bronchospasm, and she has no wheeze. E. Topical steroid cream does not help urticaria, which is a histamine-driven dermal swelling.
pearl: Anaphylaxis needs a life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation problem; skin and mild mucosal features alone are treated with an oral non-sedating antihistamine.
thinking: Weals after seafood ↓ Mild eyelid swelling ↓ No airway, breathing or circulation compromise ↓ Not anaphylaxis ↓ Oral non-sedating antihistamine
exam_trap: B, intramuscular adrenaline — swelling after a food allergen alarms candidates into treating it as anaphylaxis, but with normal airway, breathing and circulation adrenaline is not indicated.
takeaway: Urticaria without airway, breathing or circulation compromise is treated with an oral antihistamine.

stem: A 16-year-old boy who has type 1 diabetes is found sitting on the touchline after a school football match. He is pale and clammy, his hands are trembling, his speech is slurred and he is irritable and uncooperative. He had his usual morning insulin but skipped lunch. Capillary ketones are negative. Which diagnosis best fits this picture?
why_correct: Insulin, a missed meal and strenuous exercise together put a person with type 1 diabetes at high risk of hypoglycaemia. Sweating, pallor and tremor reflect the adrenergic response, while slurred speech and irritability reflect neuroglycopenia. A capillary glucose should be checked and, if he can swallow safely, fast-acting oral glucose given immediately.
why_wrong: A. DKA develops over hours with vomiting, abdominal pain and deep breathing, and ketones would be raised. C. Heat exhaustion causes headache and weakness but would not explain tremor and slurred speech in this setting. D. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state develops over days, usually in older people with type 2 diabetes. E. Vasovagal syncope causes brief loss of consciousness with rapid recovery, not ongoing confusion.
pearl: In anyone with diabetes who is confused, sweaty or behaving oddly, check capillary glucose first. Exercise increases insulin sensitivity, and the risk persists for hours afterwards.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes on insulin ↓ Exercise and missed meal ↓ Sweating, pallor, tremor ↓ Slurred speech and irritability ↓ Hypoglycaemia
exam_trap: A, diabetic ketoacidosis — any unwell young person with type 1 diabetes prompts thoughts of DKA, but the rapid onset after exercise, missed food and negative ketones point to low glucose.
takeaway: Insulin plus exercise and a missed meal causing sweating and confusion means hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 44-year-old woman was diagnosed with high blood pressure at the age of 40. Despite taking three antihypertensive drugs, none of them a diuretic, her home readings remain high. Repeated blood tests show a low serum potassium with normal renal function. She mentions muscle weakness and getting up at night to pass urine. She has no Cushingoid features and no episodes of palpitations or sweating. Which underlying cause is most likely?
why_correct: Hypertension that is difficult to control together with unexplained low potassium, particularly when not on a diuretic, should prompt screening for primary hyperaldosteronism. Autonomous aldosterone production from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia causes sodium retention and potassium loss. The first test is an aldosterone-to-renin ratio, which would show high aldosterone with suppressed renin.
why_wrong: B. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic headache, palpitations and sweating rather than persistent hypokalaemia. C. Cushing's syndrome can cause hypertension and low potassium but would usually show central obesity, striae or bruising. D. Renal artery stenosis can raise blood pressure but usually affects renal function, especially after starting an ACE inhibitor. E. Addison's disease causes low blood pressure and high potassium, the opposite picture.
pearl: Think of primary hyperaldosteronism in young or resistant hypertension, or hypertension with low potassium. Screen with an aldosterone-to-renin ratio, ideally with potassium corrected first.
thinking: Early-onset hypertension ↓ Resistant to three drugs ↓ Low potassium without a diuretic ↓ Weakness and nocturia from hypokalaemia ↓ Primary hyperaldosteronism
exam_trap: D, renal artery stenosis — it is a classic secondary cause of resistant hypertension and can also lower potassium, but normal renal function and no other vascular clues make primary aldosterone excess more likely.
takeaway: Resistant hypertension with unexplained low potassium: screen for primary hyperaldosteronism.

stem: A 58-year-old woman telephones her GP surgery. Twice this week she has noticed that her urine looked like rosé wine. She has no pain, no burning on passing urine and no increased frequency. She is postmenopausal, has smoked for 35 years and previously worked in a dye factory. A urine dipstick at the surgery shows blood but is negative for leucocytes and nitrites. Which action is most appropriate now?

options.A: Prescribe nitrofurantoin and review in one week
options.B: Repeat the urine dipstick in six weeks
options.C: Reassure her that this is probably menopausal
options.D: Refer urgently via the suspected cancer pathway to urology
options.E: Advise increased fluid intake and review if it recurs

correct_answer: D. Refer urgently via the suspected cancer pathway to urology
why_correct: Unexplained painless visible haematuria in an adult in her late fifties, without evidence of urinary infection, is a red flag for urological cancer. Smoking and occupational exposure to dyes are major risk factors for bladder cancer. She should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway for cystoscopy and upper tract imaging.
why_wrong: A. There are no symptoms or dipstick findings of infection, so antibiotics would only delay diagnosis. B. Repeating the dipstick in six weeks delays investigation of a red-flag symptom. C. The menopause does not cause visible haematuria, and attributing it to the menopause would miss a possible cancer. E. Watchful waiting is not appropriate for unexplained visible haematuria.
pearl: Painless visible haematuria is bladder cancer until proven otherwise, especially in smokers and people exposed to aromatic amines in dye, rubber or chemical industries.
thinking: Painless visible blood in urine ↓ No infection on history or dipstick ↓ Smoker with dye exposure ↓ Red flag for urothelial cancer ↓ Urgent suspected cancer referral
exam_trap: A, nitrofurantoin — haematuria in a woman suggests cystitis, but she has no urinary symptoms and a dipstick without leucocytes or nitrites, so treating as infection would delay cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Unexplained painless visible haematuria in an adult needs urgent suspected cancer referral.

stem: A 34-year-old woman in her third pregnancy is on the antenatal ward at 39 weeks with an unstable lie. Shortly after her waters break spontaneously, the CTG shows a prolonged fetal bradycardia. On vaginal examination the midwife feels a soft, pulsating loop in the vagina below the presenting part. There is no vaginal bleeding. Which emergency has occurred?
why_correct: A pulsating loop felt below the presenting part after rupture of the membranes, with sudden fetal bradycardia, is umbilical cord prolapse. An unstable lie and multiparity are recognised risk factors because the presenting part does not fill the pelvis. It is an obstetric emergency: call for help, relieve pressure on the cord by elevating the presenting part or positioning the mother knees-to-chest, and arrange urgent delivery.
why_wrong: A. Abruption causes abdominal pain, a tense uterus and often bleeding rather than a palpable loop of cord. B. Vasa praevia causes fresh bleeding at membrane rupture with fetal compromise, and there is no bleeding. D. Uterine rupture causes severe pain, maternal collapse and loss of the presenting part, usually with a previous caesarean scar. E. Shoulder dystocia occurs after delivery of the head.
pearl: Avoid handling the cord to reduce vasospasm; keep it in the vagina, elevate the presenting part and consider filling the bladder while arranging the quickest safe delivery.
thinking: Unstable lie, multiparous ↓ Spontaneous rupture of membranes ↓ Sudden fetal bradycardia ↓ Pulsating loop below presenting part ↓ Umbilical cord prolapse
exam_trap: B, vasa praevia — fetal compromise immediately after membrane rupture suggests it, but vasa praevia presents with bleeding, and here a loop of cord is felt.
takeaway: Fetal bradycardia after membrane rupture with a palpable cord is cord prolapse: relieve compression.

stem: A 29-year-old woman sees her GP 10 days after a vaginal delivery because her bleeding has become heavier, with clots, instead of settling. The delivery notes record that the placenta appeared incomplete. On examination the uterus is larger than expected for this stage and mildly tender, and the cervical os is open. Which underlying problem best explains her bleeding?

options.B: Uterine atony from a full bladder

why_correct: Heavy bleeding that increases rather than settling after delivery, with a bulky uterus, an open os and an incomplete placenta at delivery, indicates retained products of conception. Retained tissue prevents normal involution and is a common cause of secondary postpartum haemorrhage, often with associated endometritis. She needs same-day obstetric review, ultrasound and antibiotics, with surgical evacuation if indicated.
why_wrong: B. Atony is a cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage in the first 24 hours rather than at 10 days. C. Trauma typically causes bleeding immediately after delivery with a well-contracted uterus. D. A coagulopathy would usually cause bleeding from the start, often with other bleeding sites. E. Normal lochia gradually lessens and becomes paler, rather than becoming heavier with clots.
pearl: Check the placenta and membranes for completeness after every delivery. Secondary postpartum haemorrhage is usually due to retained products or infection.
thinking: Bleeding increasing 10 days postpartum ↓ Placenta incomplete at delivery ↓ Bulky tender uterus ↓ Open cervical os ↓ Retained placental tissue
exam_trap: B, uterine atony — it is the commonest cause of postpartum haemorrhage overall, but it causes bleeding in the first day; late bleeding with an incomplete placenta points to retained tissue.
takeaway: Postpartum bleeding with an incomplete placenta and open os suggests retained products.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who gave birth to her first baby three days ago is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed fit with jerking of all four limbs. Earlier that day she complained of a severe frontal headache and flashing lights. She has no history of seizures. Her blood pressure is markedly raised and urinalysis shows protein. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A generalised seizure in a woman in the postnatal period with severe hypertension, proteinuria, headache and visual disturbance is eclampsia. Eclampsia can occur for several days after delivery, not only during pregnancy. Treatment is intravenous magnesium sulfate to control and prevent seizures, with blood pressure control.
why_wrong: A. A first seizure with severe hypertension and proteinuria after delivery should not be attributed to epilepsy. C. Venous sinus thrombosis is a postpartum cause of headache and seizure, but it does not explain proteinuria with marked hypertension. D. Hypoglycaemia should be checked but does not explain the hypertension and proteinuria. E. Vasovagal episodes are brief and do not cause a prolonged tonic-clonic seizure with hypertension.
pearl: Eclampsia can occur before, during or after delivery. Magnesium sulfate is first-line for eclamptic seizures, and calcium gluconate reverses magnesium toxicity.
thinking: Three days postpartum ↓ Headache and visual disturbance ↓ Generalised seizure ↓ Severe hypertension with proteinuria ↓ Eclampsia
exam_trap: C, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — a postpartum woman with headache and seizure fits, but marked hypertension with proteinuria is the hallmark of eclampsia.
takeaway: Seizure with hypertension and proteinuria after delivery is eclampsia: give magnesium sulfate.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is seen in the fracture clinic after slipping on a kitchen step and landing on her outstretched hand. An X-ray shows a distal radius fracture. She went through the menopause at 42, has a low body weight and her mother broke a hip in her seventies. She has no bone pain and feels otherwise well. Which underlying condition should now be assessed?
why_correct: A fracture from a fall from standing height or less is a fragility fracture, and in a postmenopausal woman it strongly suggests osteoporosis. Early menopause, low body weight and a parental hip fracture are additional risk factors. She should have a fracture risk assessment and bone density scan, with bone-protective treatment considered.
why_wrong: A. Osteomalacia causes bone pain and proximal muscle weakness and is less likely without these features. B. Paget's disease usually causes bone pain and deformity with a raised alkaline phosphatase. C. Myeloma causes pathological fractures with bone pain, anaemia or renal impairment, which are absent. E. Metastatic fractures usually occur through painful lytic lesions in someone with known or suspected cancer.
pearl: Every low-trauma fracture in an older adult should trigger a fracture risk assessment. Distal radius, vertebral and hip fractures are the classic fragility fractures.
thinking: Fall from standing height ↓ Distal radius fracture ↓ Postmenopausal with early menopause and low weight ↓ Parental hip fracture ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: A, osteomalacia — it also weakens bone and causes fractures, but without bone pain, muscle weakness or deficiency risk factors, osteoporosis is far more likely.
takeaway: A low-trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman should prompt osteoporosis assessment.

stem: A 58-year-old man with mild asthma, previously well controlled on a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, was started on propranolol for essential tremor by a locum a week ago. He now reports a night-time cough, chest tightness and needing his reliever inhaler several times a day. He has no fever or ankle swelling. Which mechanism best explains his deterioration?
correct_answer: A. Bronchoconstriction from beta-2 receptor blockade
why_correct: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that blocks beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, opposing bronchodilation and triggering bronchospasm in people with asthma. Worsening wheeze and reliever use soon after starting it is typical. Non-selective beta-blockers should be avoided in asthma, and the drug should be stopped.
why_wrong: B. Bradykinin-related cough is a side effect of ACE inhibitors, not beta-blockers. C. Drug-induced fibrosis develops over months and causes progressive breathlessness with crackles. D. There is no oedema or other evidence of heart failure. E. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows exposure to organic antigens such as birds or mould, not beta-blockers.
pearl: Avoid non-selective beta-blockers, including propranolol and some eye drops such as timolol, in asthma; cardioselective agents carry lower but not zero risk.
thinking: Asthma previously controlled ↓ New propranolol ↓ Cough, tightness, more reliever use ↓ Non-selective blockade of bronchial beta-2 receptors ↓ Beta-blocker bronchoconstriction
exam_trap: B, bradykinin cough — drug-induced cough is classically linked with ACE inhibitors, but the wheeze and tightness after propranolol reflect beta-2 blockade.
takeaway: Non-selective beta-blockers can trigger bronchospasm in asthma and should be avoided.

stem: A 36-year-old woman who smokes and uses a combined hormonal pill for contraception is brought to the emergency department an hour after she suddenly dropped her cup and could not stand. She has weakness of the left arm and leg, a left facial droop and slurred speech. She has no history of migraine, and her capillary blood glucose is normal. What diagnosis must be urgently considered?
why_correct: Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit, with face, arm and leg weakness and dysarthria, is a stroke until proven otherwise, whatever the patient's age. Smoking and combined hormonal contraception both raise the risk of ischaemic stroke. She needs immediate brain imaging so that thrombolysis or thrombectomy can be considered if appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Hemiplegic migraine is a diagnosis of exclusion, usually with a history of similar attacks and headache, and should not delay stroke assessment. B. Bell's palsy affects only the face and does not cause limb weakness. C. A functional disorder cannot be assumed before structural causes are excluded. E. Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke, but her glucose is normal.
pearl: Young age does not exclude stroke. Always check glucose first, then image urgently. Combined hormonal contraception, smoking and migraine with aura add to stroke risk.
thinking: Sudden onset symptoms ↓ Face, arm and leg weakness on one side ↓ Dysarthria ↓ Glucose normal, no migraine history ↓ Acute stroke
exam_trap: A, hemiplegic migraine — a young woman with focal weakness tempts a migraine diagnosis, but with no migraine history and sudden deficit, stroke must be excluded first.
takeaway: Sudden focal neurological deficit is stroke until proven otherwise, even in the young.

stem: An 81-year-old man is brought to his GP by his daughter. Over the past two years he has repeatedly asked the same questions, has got lost driving to familiar places and has forgotten to pay bills. He is alert during the consultation and his performance has not changed from day to day. He sleeps well and says his mood is good. Blood tests are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A gradual, progressive decline in memory and other cognitive abilities over years, severe enough to affect daily activities such as driving and managing money, is dementia. His normal alertness and stable performance distinguish it from delirium. He should have a structured cognitive assessment and be referred to a memory service.
why_wrong: A. Delirium has an acute onset with fluctuating attention and conscious level. C. Depression can cause poor concentration, but his mood and sleep are normal. D. Normal ageing may slow recall but does not stop someone from managing familiar tasks such as finances or driving. E. Late-onset schizophrenia presents with delusions and hallucinations rather than progressive memory loss.
pearl: Key questions in cognitive impairment are timeline and attention: years with clear attention suggests dementia; hours to days with fluctuating attention suggests delirium.
thinking: Gradual decline over two years ↓ Memory and orientation problems ↓ Impact on daily function ↓ Alert with stable attention ↓ Dementia
exam_trap: A, delirium — confusion in an older person often prompts it, but delirium is acute and fluctuating, while this is slow and steady.
takeaway: Slow progressive cognitive decline affecting daily life, with clear attention, is dementia.

stem: A 33-year-old man on a psychiatric ward had his haloperidol dose increased three days ago. Staff report that he has become drowsy and confused. His temperature is 39.4°C, he is sweating heavily and his blood pressure is fluctuating. His limbs are stiff with uniform resistance throughout the range of movement, and reflexes are normal. Creatine kinase is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered consciousness and autonomic instability developing days after starting or increasing an antipsychotic are typical of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. A markedly raised creatine kinase reflects muscle breakdown and supports the diagnosis. The antipsychotic must be stopped and supportive care given urgently, as there is a risk of renal failure from rhabdomyolysis.
why_wrong: B. Serotonin syndrome develops within hours of a serotonergic drug and causes clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead-pipe rigidity with normal reflexes. C. Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium during anaesthesia. D. Acute dystonia causes sustained muscle spasms such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis without fever. E. Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry, hot skin and dilated pupils rather than heavy sweating and rigidity.
pearl: Differentiate NMS from serotonin syndrome: NMS is slower with rigidity and normal or reduced reflexes; serotonin syndrome is rapid with clonus, hyperreflexia and diarrhoea.
thinking: Recent haloperidol increase ↓ High fever and sweating ↓ Lead-pipe rigidity with normal reflexes ↓ Confusion and raised CK ↓ Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
exam_trap: B, serotonin syndrome — fever, confusion and autonomic instability overlap, but the trigger is an antipsychotic, onset is over days and there is rigidity without clonus.
takeaway: Fever, rigidity and confusion after an antipsychotic is neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is on the orthopaedic ward two days after an elective hip replacement. She has taken temazepam every night for many years, but it was not written up on her drug chart. She is now restless, tremulous, sweating, anxious and unable to sleep, although she is fully orientated. She drinks no alcohol, her observations are otherwise normal and her wound looks healthy. Which explanation best fits?
why_correct: Abrupt cessation of a benzodiazepine taken regularly for a long time causes rebound CNS hyperexcitability with anxiety, tremor, sweating and insomnia, and can progress to seizures. The omission from her drug chart on admission is the clear trigger. Her usual dose should be restarted and any future reduction made gradually.
why_wrong: A. She does not drink alcohol, so alcohol withdrawal is unlikely. B. Delirium causes disturbed attention and orientation, and she is fully orientated. D. Opioid toxicity causes drowsiness, small pupils and slow breathing rather than agitation and tremor. E. Thyrotoxicosis would not start suddenly two days after surgery with this clear drug trigger.
pearl: Always take an accurate drug history on admission, including sleeping tablets. Long-term benzodiazepines must never be stopped abruptly because withdrawal seizures can occur.
thinking: Long-term nightly temazepam ↓ Omitted on admission ↓ Anxiety, tremor, sweating, insomnia ↓ Orientated, no alcohol, no infection ↓ Benzodiazepine withdrawal
exam_trap: B, postoperative delirium — an agitated older patient after surgery suggests it, but she is fully orientated, and the missed temazepam explains the picture.
takeaway: Agitation, tremor and insomnia after omitting long-term benzodiazepines is withdrawal: restart the drug.

stem: A 27-year-old woman phones her GP surgery while on holiday. She ran out of her paroxetine three days ago and could not get more. She now feels dizzy and nauseated, is irritable, and describes brief electric jolts through her head when she moves her eyes. She has no fever, diarrhoea or muscle twitching, and her mood was good until she ran out. What best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Abruptly stopping an SSRI, particularly one with a short half-life such as paroxetine, commonly causes dizziness, nausea, irritability and electric-shock sensations within a few days. These symptoms are distinctive for discontinuation syndrome. Restarting the drug usually resolves them, and any future stopping should be done by gradual tapering.
why_wrong: A. Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonin, not stopping a drug, and causes fever, clonus and diarrhoea. B. Depressive relapse develops more slowly and does not cause dizziness or electric-shock sensations. C. Vestibular neuronitis causes severe vertigo but not irritability or electric jolts. E. Migraine aura causes visual or sensory symptoms followed by headache, not shock-like sensations on eye movement.
pearl: Paroxetine and venlafaxine have short half-lives and cause the most discontinuation symptoms; fluoxetine causes the fewest. Taper antidepressants rather than stopping abruptly.
thinking: Paroxetine stopped abruptly ↓ Symptoms within days ↓ Dizziness, nausea, irritability ↓ Electric-shock sensations ↓ SSRI discontinuation syndrome
exam_trap: B, relapse of depression — irritability after stopping an antidepressant suggests it, but relapse is slower and does not cause dizziness or electric jolts.
takeaway: Dizziness and electric-shock sensations after abruptly stopping an SSRI mean discontinuation syndrome.

stem: A 68-year-old man with polymyalgia rheumatica has taken prednisolone daily for 18 months. He attends pre-operative assessment before an elective bowel resection, and the anaesthetist plans to give intravenous hydrocortisone at induction and continue it after surgery. What is the main reason for this plan?

options.A: To prevent a flare of polymyalgia rheumatica
options.B: To reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting
options.E: His adrenal response to surgical stress may be suppressed

correct_answer: E. His adrenal response to surgical stress may be suppressed
why_correct: Long-term glucocorticoid treatment suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so the adrenal glands may be unable to produce the extra cortisol needed during the stress of major surgery. Without supplementation he could develop an adrenal crisis with hypotension and collapse. Additional hydrocortisone cover is therefore given around the time of surgery, and his usual steroid should not be omitted.
why_wrong: A. Preventing a PMR flare is not why extra steroid is given; his usual dose already controls the disease. B. Dexamethasone is sometimes used as an antiemetic, but that is not the reason for perioperative hydrocortisone cover. C. Corticosteroids impair rather than improve wound healing. D. Corticosteroids raise blood glucose rather than preventing hyperglycaemia.
pearl: Patients on long-term steroids should carry a steroid emergency card and need extra steroid cover during surgery or serious illness; abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal crisis.
thinking: Long-term prednisolone ↓ HPA axis suppressed ↓ Major surgery needs extra cortisol ↓ Risk of adrenal crisis ↓ Perioperative hydrocortisone cover for adrenal suppression
exam_trap: A, prevent a PMR flare — it sounds plausible because he takes steroids for PMR, but the extra cover is about adrenal suppression and the stress response, not the underlying disease.
takeaway: Long-term steroids suppress the adrenals, so major surgery needs supplementary steroid cover.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with Crohn's disease has needed high-dose prednisolone for most of the past six months because of repeated flares. At clinic she says her face has become rounder, she has wide purple stretch marks on her abdomen, a fatty hump has appeared between her shoulders and she bruises easily. Her blood pressure and blood glucose have risen. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Cushing's disease from a pituitary adenoma

why_correct: Prolonged high-dose glucocorticoid treatment is by far the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome. Moon face, purple striae, a dorsocervical fat pad, easy bruising, hypertension and hyperglycaemia are classic features of glucocorticoid excess. Management involves using the lowest effective steroid dose and steroid-sparing treatment for her Crohn's disease, without stopping prednisolone abruptly.
why_wrong: A. Cushing's disease is a rare endogenous cause and is unlikely when there is clear exposure to high-dose steroids. B. Hypothyroidism causes weight gain and fatigue but not striae, bruising or a dorsocervical fat pad. D. PCOS causes weight gain and hirsutism but not striae with bruising and hypertension. E. Adrenal insufficiency causes weight loss and low blood pressure, the opposite picture.
pearl: Always ask about steroid use, including inhaled, topical and injected forms, before investigating for endogenous Cushing's syndrome.
thinking: Months of high-dose prednisolone ↓ Moon face, striae, buffalo hump ↓ Easy bruising ↓ Hypertension and hyperglycaemia ↓ Iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome
exam_trap: A, Cushing's disease — the clinical features are identical, but exogenous steroid exposure is far commoner and explains the picture without a pituitary tumour.
takeaway: Cushingoid features in someone on long-term steroids are iatrogenic until proven otherwise.

stem: At her booking appointment, a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is found to be blood group O RhD-negative with no red cell antibodies. Her partner is RhD-positive. The midwife explains that she will be offered routine anti-D immunoglobulin in the third trimester. What is the main purpose of this treatment?

options.B: To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
options.C: To prevent ABO incompatibility in the newborn
options.D: To reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.E: To neutralise anti-D antibodies she already has

correct_answer: B. To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
why_correct: If an RhD-negative woman is exposed to RhD-positive fetal red cells, she may produce anti-D antibodies that cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, mainly in later pregnancies. Anti-D immunoglobulin clears fetal red cells from her circulation before her immune system responds. Routine antenatal prophylaxis, together with doses after sensitising events and after birth if the baby is RhD-positive, greatly reduces this risk.
why_wrong: A. Anti-D is preventive and does not treat fetal anaemia, which needs specialist fetal medicine care. C. Anti-D has no effect on ABO incompatibility. D. Anti-D does not affect the risk of pre-eclampsia. E. Anti-D cannot reverse sensitisation once a woman has formed her own antibodies.
pearl: Give anti-D after potentially sensitising events such as abdominal trauma, bleeding after 12 weeks, external cephalic version and amniocentesis, in addition to routine prophylaxis.
thinking: RhD-negative mother, RhD-positive partner ↓ Fetus may be RhD-positive ↓ Fetal cells entering maternal circulation ↓ Anti-D clears them before an immune response ↓ Prevents maternal sensitisation
exam_trap: A, treat existing fetal anaemia — anti-D is associated with haemolytic disease, but it is prophylactic and only works before the mother has been sensitised.
takeaway: Anti-D prevents RhD-negative mothers from becoming sensitised to fetal RhD-positive cells.

stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the GP because several children at her nursery have been unwell. She has had a mild fever for two days and very itchy spots that started on her scalp and chest. On examination there are red papules, clear fluid-filled blisters and crusted lesions side by side, mostly on the trunk, with a few shallow ulcers inside her mouth. Her palms and soles are spared. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chickenpox causes intensely itchy crops of lesions that progress from papules to vesicles to crusts, so lesions at different stages are seen together. The rash is concentrated on the trunk, scalp and face and may involve the mouth. Management is usually supportive, with advice on keeping her away from nursery until all lesions have crusted.
why_wrong: A. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes mouth ulcers with vesicles on the hands and feet, which are spared here. B. Measles causes a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears, with cough, conjunctivitis and coryza. C. Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions, usually around the nose and mouth, not widespread vesicles. E. Scarlet fever causes a fine sandpaper-like rash with a strawberry tongue and sore throat.
pearl: Lesions at different stages concentrated on the trunk point to chickenpox. Avoid NSAIDs in chickenpox because of the association with severe skin infection.
thinking: Nursery outbreak, mild fever ↓ Very itchy rash starting on scalp and chest ↓ Papules, vesicles and crusts together ↓ Truncal distribution, palms spared ↓ Chickenpox
