Fluorescein dye is taken up where the corneal epithelium is missing and fluoresces green under cobalt blue light, confirming the abrasion and showing its size. The upper lid should also be everted to look for a retained foreign body. Treatment is usually a topical antibiotic such as chloramphenicol with analgesia, and review if symptoms do not settle quickly.
why_wrong: A. Tonometry measures intraocular pressure and is used for glaucoma, not surface defects. B. Fundoscopy examines the retina and will not show an epithelial defect. C. Orbital X-ray is for suspected metallic intraocular foreign body after a high-velocity injury, which is absent. D. A swab is for suspected infective conjunctivitis or keratitis, not acute minor trauma.
pearl: Contact lens wearers with a painful red eye need same-day ophthalmology review to exclude microbial keratitis, and should not wear lenses until healed.
thinking: Minor trauma to the eye ↓ Pain, watering, photophobia and grittiness ↓ Normal acuity, no high-velocity injury ↓ Suspected epithelial defect ↓ Fluorescein staining under blue light
exam_trap: C, Plain X-ray of the orbits — imaging seems thorough after eye trauma, but it is only indicated for suspected high-velocity metallic foreign bodies, not a fingernail scratch.
takeaway: Suspected corneal abrasion is confirmed by fluorescein staining under blue light.

stem: A 64-year-old Black British woman is referred by her optometrist after a routine eye test. She has no symptoms and no eye pain. Intraocular pressures are raised in both eyes, the optic discs show enlarged cups with thinning of the neuroretinal rim, and visual field testing reveals defects in the periphery that she had not noticed. The anterior chambers are of normal depth. Which diagnosis best fits these findings?
why_correct: Primary open-angle glaucoma is a chronic, painless optic neuropathy with characteristic disc cupping and peripheral field loss, usually associated with raised intraocular pressure. It is often detected at routine optometry checks because central vision is preserved until late. Risk factors include older age, Black African or Caribbean heritage and a family history. She needs referral to ophthalmology, where treatment aims to lower the pressure; NICE now recommends selective laser trabeculoplasty as the first treatment for many patients, with pressure-lowering eye drops such as a prostaglandin analogue as the alternative.
why_wrong: B. Acute angle closure causes a painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes and a shallow anterior chamber. C. Ocular hypertension is raised pressure without optic disc damage or field loss, whereas she has both. D. Normal-tension glaucoma has disc and field changes with normal pressures. E. Macular degeneration affects central vision and does not cause disc cupping.
pearl: First-degree relatives of people with glaucoma aged 40 or over are at higher risk and are eligible for free NHS sight tests; encourage them to have regular checks.
thinking: Asymptomatic, detected at a routine eye test ↓ Raised intraocular pressure ↓ Optic disc cupping with peripheral field loss ↓ Painless, normal anterior chamber depth ↓ Primary open-angle glaucoma
exam_trap: C, Ocular hypertension — raised pressure is present, but ocular hypertension by definition has no disc damage or field loss, and she has both.
takeaway: Painless peripheral field loss with disc cupping and raised pressure is primary open-angle glaucoma.

stem: Nursery staff notice that a 4-year-old girl's left eye seems to drift outwards, especially when she is tired. At her GP appointment the reflection of a pen torch sits in the centre of the right pupil but towards the inner edge of the left pupil. When her right eye is covered, the left eye moves to take up fixation. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: An asymmetric corneal light reflex and movement of the deviating eye on the cover test confirm a true ocular misalignment, which is strabismus (squint), here an outward-turning eye. Any child with a suspected squint should be referred to orthoptics or paediatric ophthalmology, as untreated strabismus can lead to amblyopia. A red reflex check is also needed to exclude serious underlying causes.
why_wrong: B. In pseudostrabismus the corneal reflexes are symmetrical and the cover test shows no movement. C. A refractive error can contribute to squint but does not by itself produce a displaced light reflex with a corrective movement. D. A sixth nerve palsy causes an inward-turning eye with failure of abduction, not an outward drift. E. Retinoblastoma may present with squint, but the key sign is an absent or white red reflex, which is not described.
pearl: A child with a squint and an abnormal or white red reflex needs urgent ophthalmology referral to exclude retinoblastoma.
thinking: Child with an eye that drifts ↓ Asymmetric corneal light reflex ↓ Deviated eye moves on cover test ↓ True ocular misalignment ↓ Strabismus
exam_trap: B, Pseudostrabismus due to epicanthic folds — common in young children and often reassured, but it has symmetrical light reflexes and a normal cover test, unlike this child.
takeaway: An asymmetric light reflex with movement on cover test confirms strabismus; refer to prevent amblyopia.

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is on the labour ward at term. Her membranes ruptured more than a day ago and labour is being induced. She now has a high temperature and a fast pulse. Her uterus is tender between contractions and the draining liquor has become offensive-smelling. The CTG shows a rising fetal baseline heart rate. There is no vaginal bleeding. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Maternal fever and tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor and fetal tachycardia after prolonged rupture of membranes indicate intrauterine infection (chorioamnionitis). It can lead to maternal sepsis and neonatal infection. Management follows the sepsis pathway with blood cultures and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, expediting delivery and informing the neonatal team.
why_wrong: A. Abruption causes pain, a tense uterus and often bleeding, but not fever or offensive liquor. B. Pyelonephritis causes fever with loin pain and urinary symptoms rather than uterine tenderness and offensive liquor. D. Epidural-related fever is usually low grade, does not cause uterine tenderness or offensive liquor, and no epidural is mentioned. E. Endometritis occurs after delivery, and she has not yet delivered.
pearl: Prolonged rupture of membranes, repeated vaginal examinations and group B streptococcus colonisation increase the risk of chorioamnionitis; the baby may need assessment and antibiotics after birth.
thinking: Prolonged rupture of membranes ↓ Maternal fever and tachycardia ↓ Uterine tenderness and offensive liquor ↓ Fetal tachycardia ↓ Chorioamnionitis
exam_trap: A, Placental abruption — uterine tenderness and fetal compromise are shared features, but abruption does not cause fever or offensive liquor.
takeaway: Fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia after prolonged membrane rupture mean chorioamnionitis.

stem: A 63-year-old woman tells her GP she has to rush to the toilet many times a day and twice at night. When she gets home she often leaks before she can get her key in the door, and once the feeling starts she cannot hold on. She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes or lifts. Urine dipstick is negative and a bladder scan after voiding leaves very little urine behind. Which type of incontinence does she have?
why_correct: Urgency, frequency, nocturia and leakage before reaching the toilet, often triggered by cues such as arriving home, describe overactive bladder with urge incontinence, caused by involuntary detrusor contractions. The negative dipstick and small residual volume exclude infection and retention. NICE recommends lifestyle advice such as reducing caffeine and bladder training first, followed by drug treatment if needed.
why_wrong: A. Stress incontinence causes leakage with coughing, sneezing or exertion, which she denies. B. Overflow incontinence occurs with a large post-void residual from obstruction or an underactive bladder. C. Mixed incontinence needs both stress and urge components, and she has no stress leakage. D. Functional incontinence is due to mobility or cognitive problems preventing toilet access, which are not described.
pearl: Antimuscarinic drugs for overactive bladder add to anticholinergic burden and can worsen cognition in older people; take this into account when choosing treatment.
thinking: Urgency, frequency and nocturia ↓ Leakage before reaching the toilet ↓ No leakage on coughing or exertion ↓ Negative dipstick and small residual ↓ Urge urinary incontinence
exam_trap: C, Mixed urinary incontinence — common in older women and a frequent default, but she specifically has no leakage on coughing, sneezing or lifting, so there is no stress component.
takeaway: Sudden urgency with leakage before reaching the toilet is urge incontinence; start with bladder training.

stem: A 66-year-old Black man attends his GP with nocturia and a weaker stream over the past year. On rectal examination the prostate is asymmetrical, with a hard nodule in the right lobe, and the central groove cannot be felt. He has no fever and the gland is not tender. Which diagnosis needs to be considered?
why_correct: A hard, nodular, asymmetrical prostate with loss of the median sulcus on rectal examination is suspicious of prostate cancer. NICE advises referral on a suspected cancer pathway when the prostate feels malignant, whatever the PSA result, although PSA is usually checked as well. Black men have a higher risk of prostate cancer and tend to present younger.
why_wrong: A. Benign hyperplasia produces a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, rubbery gland with a preserved median sulcus. B. Chronic prostatitis causes pelvic pain and a boggy or tender gland rather than a hard nodule. C. A urethral stricture causes a poor stream but does not change the prostate on examination. E. A prostatic abscess causes fever, severe pain and a fluctuant, very tender gland.
pearl: Lower urinary tract symptoms do not distinguish cancer from benign enlargement; examination findings and PSA guide referral.
thinking: Older man with lower urinary tract symptoms ↓ Rectal examination performed ↓ Hard, asymmetric nodule with loss of the central groove ↓ Not tender, no fever ↓ Prostate cancer
exam_trap: A, Benign prostatic hyperplasia — it is the commonest cause of his urinary symptoms, but it produces a smooth, symmetrical gland, not a hard nodule with loss of the sulcus.
takeaway: A hard, irregular prostate on rectal examination needs suspected cancer referral.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for many years and also has background diabetic retinopathy. At her annual review her urine albumin:creatinine ratio is raised on repeated samples, and her eGFR has fallen slowly over several years. Her urine shows no blood or casts, and a renal ultrasound shows two normal-sized kidneys with no hydronephrosis. Which condition best explains her kidney disease?
why_correct: Persistent albuminuria with a slow decline in eGFR in someone with long-standing diabetes and another microvascular complication such as retinopathy is typical of diabetic nephropathy. Bland urine and normal-sized, unobstructed kidneys support this. Management includes an ACE inhibitor or ARB, an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate, and control of blood pressure, glucose and cardiovascular risk.
why_wrong: B. Renal artery stenosis typically causes asymmetric kidney sizes, resistant hypertension and little albuminuria. C. IgA nephropathy usually causes visible or microscopic haematuria, often after infections. D. Membranous nephropathy usually presents with nephrotic syndrome, heavy proteinuria and oedema. E. Obstruction is excluded by an ultrasound showing no hydronephrosis.
pearl: Features suggesting a cause other than diabetes include haematuria, a rapidly falling eGFR, heavy proteinuria without retinopathy or a short history of diabetes; these warrant nephrology referral.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes with retinopathy ↓ Persistent albuminuria ↓ Gradual fall in eGFR ↓ Bland urine and normal, unobstructed kidneys ↓ Diabetic nephropathy
exam_trap: B, Renal artery stenosis — vascular disease is common in diabetes, but stenosis gives asymmetric kidneys and minimal albuminuria rather than this picture.
takeaway: Albuminuria with slowly falling eGFR in long-standing diabetes with retinopathy is diabetic nephropathy.

stem: A 31-year-old man has had high blood pressure for a year. Despite taking an ACE inhibitor, a calcium-channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic at full doses, his clinic and home readings both remain well above target. Pharmacy records and pill counts show he takes his medicines reliably, and he eats a low-salt diet and drinks little alcohol. Which explanation should be considered first?

options.E: Essential hypertension needing no further investigation

why_correct: Blood pressure that stays uncontrolled despite three drugs at optimal doses, with confirmed adherence and raised out-of-clinic readings, is resistant hypertension, and in a young adult this strongly suggests a secondary cause. Causes include primary hyperaldosteronism, renal disease, renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma and drugs. He should be referred for specialist assessment, with initial tests such as electrolytes, renal function and urinalysis.
why_wrong: A. White-coat hypertension is excluded because home readings are also raised. B. Adherence has been checked with pharmacy records and pill counts. C. He already follows a low-salt diet and drinks little, so lifestyle does not explain the resistance. E. Accepting essential hypertension without investigation would miss a treatable cause in a young man.
pearl: Primary hyperaldosteronism is the commonest secondary cause of hypertension; check potassium, but remember that a normal potassium does not exclude it.
thinking: Young adult with hypertension ↓ Uncontrolled on three drugs at full doses ↓ Adherence confirmed and home readings raised ↓ Resistant hypertension at a young age ↓ Secondary hypertension
exam_trap: A, White-coat hypertension — a common reason for apparently resistant readings, but his home measurements are also high, so it has already been excluded.
takeaway: Resistant hypertension with confirmed adherence, especially in the young, needs a search for a secondary cause.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who runs for her university athletics team has had no periods for eight months; her cycles were previously regular. She trains twice a day and has lost weight this season. Urine hCG is negative. Blood tests show low LH, FSH and oestradiol, with normal prolactin and thyroid function. She has no acne or excess hair growth. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Intense exercise, weight loss and low energy availability suppress hypothalamic GnRH release, causing low LH, FSH and oestrogen and secondary amenorrhoea. Normal prolactin and thyroid function exclude other common endocrine causes. The low-oestrogen state risks bone loss, so management focuses on restoring energy balance, often with dietetic and psychological support, and screening for disordered eating.
why_wrong: A. Polycystic ovary syndrome causes oligomenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism and normal or raised LH, not low gonadotrophins. B. Premature ovarian insufficiency causes high FSH with low oestrogen. D. A prolactinoma would cause raised prolactin. E. Asherman's syndrome follows uterine instrumentation and causes amenorrhoea with normal hormone levels.
pearl: Amenorrhoea in athletes may be part of relative energy deficiency in sport, which also affects bone health and performance; consider bone density assessment if amenorrhoea is prolonged.
thinking: Secondary amenorrhoea with a negative pregnancy test ↓ Heavy training and weight loss ↓ Low LH, FSH and oestradiol ↓ Prolactin and thyroid normal ↓ Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea
exam_trap: B, Premature ovarian insufficiency — it also causes low oestrogen and amenorrhoea in a young woman, but FSH is high because the ovaries have failed, whereas here gonadotrophins are low.
takeaway: Amenorrhoea with low gonadotrophins after weight loss and heavy exercise is hypothalamic.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends the emergency department with three days of increasing pain and swelling on the right side of her vulva, and she now finds it hard to sit or walk. She is afebrile. On examination there is a hot, very tender, fluctuant swelling in the lower part of the right labium majus, posterolateral to the vaginal entrance. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: The Bartholin's glands lie posterolaterally on either side of the vaginal entrance, and blockage of a duct causes a cyst that can become infected to form a painful, fluctuant abscess. Treatment is drainage, commonly with Word catheter insertion or marsupialisation, with antibiotics if there is surrounding cellulitis or systemic upset. A new Bartholin's swelling in an older woman should be biopsied to exclude malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Sebaceous cysts arise in hair-bearing skin, are usually small and are not specifically sited beside the introitus. B. Skene's glands lie beside the urethral opening anteriorly, not at the back of the vaginal entrance. C. Gartner's duct cysts lie within the anterolateral vaginal wall and are usually painless. E. An inguinal hernia extending into the labium arises from the groin and has a cough impulse.
pearl: Bartholin's abscesses often recur after simple incision, which is why Word catheter insertion or marsupialisation is preferred to keep the duct open.
thinking: Painful, enlarging vulval swelling ↓ Fluctuant and tender ↓ Lower labium, posterolateral to the introitus ↓ Site of the Bartholin's gland ↓ Bartholin's gland abscess
exam_trap: B, Skene's duct abscess — another paravaginal gland abscess, but Skene's glands sit beside the urethra at the front, not at the back of the vaginal entrance.
takeaway: A tender, fluctuant swelling posterolateral to the vaginal entrance is a Bartholin's abscess.

stem: A 66-year-old woman who has had four vaginal deliveries tells her GP she can feel something 'coming down' that is worse at the end of the day. She sometimes has to push the lump back to finish emptying her bladder, and has had two urinary infections this year. On examination with a Sims speculum, the front wall of the vagina bulges downwards when she strains, while the cervix stays high. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Descent of the anterior vaginal wall on straining is a cystocele, the bladder bulging into the vagina through weakened pelvic support. Incomplete emptying, needing to push the bulge back to void and recurrent urinary infections are typical. Vaginal birth, age, menopause and obesity are risk factors, and management ranges from pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessaries to surgical repair depending on symptoms and wishes.
why_wrong: A. A rectocele is a posterior wall bulge causing difficulty with bowel emptying. C. In uterine prolapse the cervix descends, but here it stays high. D. An enterocele is small bowel herniating through the upper posterior vaginal wall or vault, usually after hysterectomy. E. A urethral diverticulum gives a tender anterior mass with post-void dribbling and discharge, not a bulge on straining.
pearl: Use a Sims speculum with the patient in the left lateral position to examine the anterior and posterior walls separately, and ask her to strain to reveal prolapse.
thinking: Sensation of a vaginal lump ↓ Older woman after several vaginal births ↓ Bladder emptying problems and recurrent infections ↓ Anterior wall descends on straining, cervix high ↓ Cystocele
exam_trap: C, Uterine prolapse — the commonest image of prolapse, but the cervix remains high and the bulge comes from the anterior wall, so the bladder is the organ prolapsing.
takeaway: Anterior vaginal wall descent with bladder symptoms is a cystocele.

presentation: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lip
stem: A 72-year-old retired fisherman attends his GP with a sore that has slowly grown on the lower lip over four months. It has a hard, raised edge with a central ulcer, and it bleeds when he shaves or eats. He has smoked a pipe for most of his life. There is a small, firm lymph node under his chin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A slowly enlarging, indurated, ulcerated lesion on the lower lip of an older man with long-term sun exposure and pipe smoking is typical of squamous cell carcinoma. The lower lip receives the most sun, and lip SCC can spread to submental and submandibular nodes. He should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway for biopsy and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Actinic cheilitis is a premalignant dry, scaly change of the lip without a hard ulcerated lesion or lymphadenopathy. B. Basal cell carcinoma usually affects facial skin and the upper lip rather than the lower lip vermilion, and rarely spreads to nodes. C. A mucocele is a soft, bluish, fluid-filled swelling that does not ulcerate and bleed. D. Herpes labialis causes recurrent short-lived vesicles that heal within days.
pearl: Cutaneous SCC can metastasise, unlike most basal cell carcinomas, so always examine the regional lymph nodes when assessing a suspicious lesion on the lip or ear.
thinking: Older man with outdoor work and pipe smoking ↓ Lower lip lesion growing over months ↓ Indurated edge, ulceration and bleeding ↓ Regional lymph node enlargement ↓ Squamous cell carcinoma
exam_trap: A, Actinic cheilitis — it occurs on the same sun-damaged lip and can progress to SCC, but it is a flat scaly change, not an indurated ulcer with a palpable node.
takeaway: An enlarging, indurated ulcer on the lower lip of a sun-exposed older adult is SCC until proven otherwise.

presentation: Unexplained Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Older Adult
stem: A 67-year-old man sees his GP because he has felt increasingly tired and breathless on the stairs over three months. He has no abdominal pain, change in bowel habit or visible bleeding, and does not take aspirin, NSAIDs or anticoagulants. His full blood count reveals anaemia that was not present previously, and his ferritin is low. Coeliac serology is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start oral iron and recheck the blood count in three months
options.B: Refer urgently for upper and lower gastrointestinal investigation
options.D: Advise dietary changes to increase iron intake
options.E: Arrange a chest X-ray and spirometry

correct_answer: B. Refer urgently for upper and lower gastrointestinal investigation
why_correct: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in an older adult should be presumed to be due to occult gastrointestinal blood loss, including colorectal or gastric cancer, until proven otherwise, even without gut symptoms. He should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway for lower GI investigation (colonoscopy or CT colonography) and upper GI endoscopy. Oral iron can be started alongside but must not replace investigation.
why_wrong: A. Treating with iron alone may correct the blood count but misses the underlying cause. C. Marrow biopsy is not indicated when the picture is clearly iron deficiency. D. Dietary deficiency is an unlikely explanation in an older man and does not exclude malignancy. E. His breathlessness is explained by anaemia, and chest tests do not investigate the source of iron loss.
pearl: Absence of gut symptoms does not exclude bowel cancer; right-sided colon cancers in particular often present with iron deficiency anaemia alone.
thinking: Older man with new anaemia ↓ Low ferritin: iron deficiency ↓ No obvious source or drug cause, coeliac excluded ↓ Occult GI blood loss, including cancer, must be excluded ↓ Urgent upper and lower GI investigation
exam_trap: A, Oral iron with a repeat count — it treats the anaemia and seems reasonable, but it delays the diagnosis of a possible bowel or gastric cancer.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in an older adult needs urgent upper and lower GI investigation.

stem: A 38-year-old man is referred to the bone clinic after his third metatarsal stress fracture in two years. He describes aching muscles and joints, and his mother recalls that as a toddler he lost several baby teeth with the roots still attached. His calcium, vitamin D and PTH are normal, phosphate is at the upper end of normal, and alkaline phosphatase is repeatedly below the reference range. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hypophosphatasia is an inherited deficiency of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, so a persistently low ALP is its biochemical hallmark. Defective mineralisation causes stress fractures, bone and muscle pain and early loss of baby teeth with intact roots. Recognising it matters because bisphosphonates may worsen it, and enzyme replacement therapy is available through specialist centres.
why_wrong: A. Osteomalacia causes a raised ALP with low vitamin D, calcium or phosphate. C. Paget's disease causes a markedly raised ALP and usually affects older adults. D. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes raised calcium with raised or inappropriately normal PTH. E. Osteogenesis imperfecta causes fractures, often with blue sclerae and hearing loss, but ALP is normal.
pearl: A low ALP is easily overlooked on a bone profile. Other causes include hypothyroidism, zinc or magnesium deficiency and malnutrition, but persistent unexplained low ALP with fractures suggests hypophosphatasia.
thinking: Recurrent low-trauma fractures and musculoskeletal pain ↓ Early loss of baby teeth with roots ↓ Normal calcium, vitamin D and PTH ↓ Persistently low ALP ↓ Hypophosphatasia
exam_trap: A, Osteomalacia — bone pain and fractures fit, but osteomalacia raises ALP with abnormal vitamin D or minerals, whereas here ALP is low and vitamin D normal.
takeaway: Fractures with a persistently low alkaline phosphatase suggest hypophosphatasia.

stem: An FY2 doctor on a surgical ward realises that she wrote up a patient's insulin dose incorrectly yesterday. The patient became hypoglycaemic overnight, needed intravenous glucose and has now fully recovered. The patient does not know that a mistake caused this. What is the most appropriate action regarding the patient?

options.A: Say nothing unless the patient asks why it happened
options.B: Tell her consultant and leave the decision about informing the patient to them
options.C: Apologise for the hypoglycaemia but avoid admitting the error because of legal risk
options.D: Explain to the patient what happened, apologise and report it through the incident system
options.E: Correct the drug chart so that it shows the intended dose

correct_answer: D. Explain to the patient what happened, apologise and report it through the incident system
why_correct: The professional duty of candour requires doctors to be open and honest with patients when something goes wrong with their care that causes, or could cause, harm. She should promptly tell the patient what happened, apologise, explain what is being done to put things right and prevent recurrence, and report the incident locally. She should also inform her seniors, but this does not remove her own responsibility to be honest.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for the patient to ask breaches the duty to be proactively open. B. Seniors should be informed, but the doctor involved should not simply hand over her own duty of candour. C. An apology is not an admission of legal liability, and withholding the explanation is dishonest. E. Altering records to hide an error is dishonest and could lead to serious regulatory action.
pearl: Joint GMC and NMC guidance makes clear that saying sorry is not an admission of legal liability, and that patients should hear about errors promptly from an appropriate person.
thinking: Prescribing error by this doctor ↓ Patient harmed: hypoglycaemia needing treatment ↓ Duty of candour applies ↓ Be open, apologise and explain to the patient ↓ Report through the incident system
exam_trap: B, Telling the consultant and leaving it to them — escalating is correct, but it does not discharge her personal duty to be open and honest with the patient.
takeaway: When your error harms a patient, tell them, apologise and report it.

stem: A GP receives a telephone call from a man whose father died at home last month. He wants to understand his father's final months and asks the GP to send him a copy of his father's entire medical record, including mental health consultations. The GP cannot confirm the caller's identity, and the notes contain no record of who the patient was happy to share information with. Which principle should guide the GP's response?

options.A: A son is automatically entitled to the complete record as next of kin
options.B: Confidentiality ends when the patient dies
options.C: The duty of confidentiality continues after the patient's death
options.D: Records can only be released after death by a court order
options.E: The record becomes available to anyone once the death has been registered

correct_answer: C. The duty of confidentiality continues after the patient's death
why_correct: The duty of confidentiality continues after a patient dies. Information can still be shared in some circumstances, for example sensitively with those close to the patient to help them understand the death, unless the patient had objected, or through a formal application by the personal representative or someone with a claim arising from the death. The GP should not release the whole record over the telephone, but can explain the process and offer to talk once identity and entitlement are confirmed.
why_wrong: A. Being next of kin does not by itself give a legal right to the entire record. B. Confidentiality does not end at death. D. A court order is not the only route, as statutory applications and sensitive disclosure to relatives are possible. E. Registering a death does not make the medical record public.
pearl: Access to a deceased person's health records is governed by the Access to Health Records Act 1990 rather than data protection law, which protects only living people.
thinking: Request for information about a deceased patient ↓ Confidentiality continues after death ↓ Caller's identity and entitlement uncertain ↓ Share sensitively or through the formal access route ↓ Duty of confidentiality continues after death
exam_trap: A, Automatic entitlement as next of kin — it feels natural that a close relative should have access, but next of kin status alone gives no automatic right to the whole record.
takeaway: Confidentiality persists after death; relatives have no automatic right to the full record.

presentation: Valid Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment
stem: A 74-year-old man with motor neurone disease is admitted unconscious with aspiration pneumonia and worsening respiratory failure. A year ago, while he had capacity, he signed a witnessed written advance decision stating that he refuses invasive ventilation even if his life is at risk. The document clearly covers this situation and there is no evidence that he changed his mind. His son asks the team to ventilate him anyway. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Ventilate him because his son is next of kin and can override the document
options.B: Apply to the Court of Protection before making any decision
options.C: Ventilate temporarily until he regains capacity and can be asked again
options.D: Treat the document as a DNACPR order only and proceed with ventilation
options.E: Respect the advance decision and do not start ventilation, while continuing other care and comfort measures

correct_answer: E. Respect the advance decision and do not start ventilation, while continuing other care and comfort measures
why_correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment has the same force as a refusal made at the time by a patient with capacity. For life-sustaining treatment it must be written, signed, witnessed and state that it applies even if life is at risk, which this does. Clinicians must respect it while continuing other treatment and symptom control, and should explain this sensitively to the family.
why_wrong: A. Relatives cannot override a valid advance decision; next of kin has no legal power to consent on an adult's behalf. B. Court involvement is only needed if there is genuine doubt about validity or applicability, which there is not here. C. Ventilating him would give exactly the treatment he has validly refused. D. The document specifically refuses ventilation and cannot be reinterpreted as a DNACPR order.
pearl: An advance decision can only refuse treatment; it cannot demand specific treatments, and it does not prevent basic comfort care such as warmth, hygiene and offering food and drink by mouth.
thinking: Patient now lacks capacity ↓ Written, signed, witnessed advance refusal of ventilation ↓ States it applies even if life is at risk and covers this situation ↓ Valid and applicable, so legally binding ↓ Respect it and continue other care
exam_trap: B, Applying to the Court of Protection — it seems a cautious safeguard, but it is only needed when validity or applicability is genuinely in doubt, and the delay here would lead to unwanted treatment.
takeaway: A valid, applicable advance refusal of treatment must be respected, even against the family's wishes.

stem: A 34-year-old man is seen in the emergency department 20 minutes after sharing a takeaway curry containing cashew nuts. His lips have become itchy, he has crampy central abdominal pain with two episodes of loose stool, and a wheeze is audible on auscultation. He has never had symptoms like this before. Which mechanism best explains his reaction?

options.A: Non-immune enzyme deficiency causing carbohydrate malabsorption
options.B: T-cell mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten
options.C: Functional bowel disturbance worsened by dietary triggers
options.D: IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity to a food

correct_answer: D. IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity to a food
why_correct: Symptoms began within minutes of eating a tree nut and affect more than one system: oral itching, gastrointestinal cramps with diarrhoea, and bronchospasm. This rapid, multi-system pattern is typical of an IgE-mediated (type I) reaction, in which allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and triggers histamine release. Wheeze means he should be assessed for anaphylaxis and managed accordingly.
why_wrong: A. Enzyme deficiency such as lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea but never wheeze or lip itching. B. Coeliac disease is a delayed, gluten-driven enteropathy rather than a reaction within minutes. C. Irritable bowel syndrome is chronic and does not cause bronchospasm. E. Bacterial toxin food poisoning causes vomiting and diarrhoea but not oral itching or wheeze, and others who ate the meal would usually be affected.
pearl: Food-triggered IgE reactions typically start within minutes to two hours of ingestion; involvement of the airway or circulation means anaphylaxis, treated first with IM adrenaline.
thinking: Symptoms within minutes of eating nuts ↓ Skin/mucosal, gut and respiratory systems all involved ↓ Rapid multi-system reaction suggests mast cell degranulation ↓ Mechanism is IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity ↓ Wheeze raises concern for anaphylaxis
exam_trap: A, Enzyme deficiency causing malabsorption — the diarrhoea and cramps after a meal make an intolerance tempting, but intolerance cannot explain oral itching or wheeze.
takeaway: Rapid multi-system symptoms after eating a specific food point to IgE-mediated food allergy.

stem: Paramedics are called to the home of an 84-year-old widow whose daughter found her on the kitchen floor in the morning, having fallen during the night in a house where the heating had broken. She is drowsy and slow to answer questions, her skin is cold to touch, and she is shivering. A low-reading thermometer confirms a reduced core temperature. Blood glucose is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: She has lain on a cold floor for hours in an unheated house and now has a reduced core temperature with shivering and drowsiness. Environmental cold exposure with a low core temperature defines accidental hypothermia, and older people living alone after a long lie are at particular risk. A normal glucose excludes hypoglycaemia as the cause of her confusion.
why_wrong: B. Heat exhaustion follows heat exposure and causes a raised, not lowered, temperature. C. Meningitis can cause drowsiness but does not explain prolonged cold exposure with a low core temperature. D. Her blood glucose is normal, so hypoglycaemia is not the explanation. E. Myxoedema coma can cause hypothermia, but there is no history of thyroid disease and a clear environmental cause is present.
pearl: Shivering usually stops as hypothermia becomes more severe, so its absence in a cold, drowsy patient does not reassure.
thinking: Long lie on a cold floor in an unheated house ↓ Cold skin, shivering and drowsiness ↓ Low core temperature confirmed ↓ Glucose normal, no thyroid history ↓ Accidental hypothermia
exam_trap: E, Hypothyroid myxoedema coma — it does cause low temperature and drowsiness in older women, but a clear environmental cause is present and there is nothing to suggest thyroid disease.
takeaway: An older person found after a long lie in a cold house with a low core temperature has accidental hypothermia until proven otherwise.

stem: An 11-year-old boy is brought to the GP surgery by his father because his asthma has worsened since he caught a cold. He is sitting forward, wheezy, and can manage only a few words between breaths. His oxygen saturation is above the level that would require admission on its own. Which drug should be given first?

options.B: Higher dose of his regular preventer inhaler
options.C: Salbutamol via a spacer, repeated as needed

correct_answer: C. Salbutamol via a spacer, repeated as needed
why_correct: He is unable to complete sentences, which indicates at least a severe asthma attack. The immediate priority is rapid bronchodilation with a short-acting beta-2 agonist, given through a spacer (or nebulised with oxygen if hypoxic), repeated according to response, alongside an oral corticosteroid and arrangements for transfer to hospital. Other preventer and add-on therapies have no role in reversing acute bronchospasm.
why_wrong: A. Montelukast is a maintenance add-on and does not relieve acute bronchospasm. B. Increasing the preventer dose takes days to work and does not treat an attack. D. Long-acting beta-2 agonists have a slower onset and are not used as rescue treatment in this way. E. Antihistamines have no role in an acute asthma attack.
pearl: In acute asthma in children, a short-acting beta-2 agonist via spacer is as effective as a nebuliser unless the child needs oxygen.
thinking: Known asthma with a viral trigger ↓ Too breathless to complete sentences ↓ Severe attack ↓ Needs immediate bronchodilation ↓ Short-acting beta-2 agonist via spacer, plus oral steroid and escalation
exam_trap: B, Higher dose of his regular preventer inhaler — stepping up preventer therapy sounds sensible for worsening control, but inhaled steroids do not reverse acute bronchospasm.
takeaway: Treat an asthma attack first with a short-acting beta-2 agonist, then assess severity and escalate.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 40 minutes after her husband noticed her speech became slurred and her left arm fell limply off the arm of her chair while she was watching television. She takes no anticoagulants. Thrombolysis is being considered. Which investigation is needed first?

options.B: Non-contrast CT scan of the head
options.C: Duplex ultrasound of the carotid arteries

correct_answer: B. Non-contrast CT scan of the head
why_correct: She has a sudden focal neurological deficit, so acute stroke is the working diagnosis. Urgent non-contrast CT of the head is the first investigation because it rapidly excludes intracerebral haemorrhage, which must be ruled out before thrombolysis or thrombectomy can be offered. It is quick and widely available, so it does not delay time-critical reperfusion treatment.
why_wrong: A. Lumbar puncture has no role in acute stroke assessment and is unsafe before imaging. C. Carotid imaging is part of secondary prevention after an ischaemic stroke or TIA, not the first test. D. An EEG is for suspected seizures and does not distinguish ischaemia from haemorrhage. E. Spinal MRI does not image the brain and would not explain slurred speech with arm weakness.
pearl: In suspected stroke, imaging should be immediate if thrombolysis or thrombectomy might be indicated, the patient is anticoagulated, or there is reduced consciousness.
thinking: Sudden slurred speech and unilateral arm weakness ↓ Acute stroke suspected ↓ Haemorrhage must be excluded before reperfusion ↓ Fastest test to do this is non-contrast CT head ↓ Image immediately
exam_trap: C, Duplex ultrasound of the carotid arteries — carotid disease is a common cause of stroke, but carotid imaging guides secondary prevention and is not the first test in the acute phase.
takeaway: Suspected acute stroke needs an immediate non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage before reperfusion.

stem: A 77-year-old man phones NHS 111 and is directed to the emergency department. For several years he has had a weak stream and frequent night-time voiding, and since this afternoon he has not been able to pass any urine at all. He is in obvious distress, and a tender, dull mass is felt rising out of the pelvis. What should be done first?

options.A: Start an alpha-blocker and review in the morning
options.C: Pass a urethral catheter to drain the bladder
options.D: Advise him to drink less and wait to see if he voids
options.E: Request a renal tract ultrasound before any intervention

correct_answer: C. Pass a urethral catheter to drain the bladder
why_correct: He has painful acute urinary retention on a background of prostatic symptoms, with a palpable distended bladder. The immediate treatment is to decompress the bladder with a urethral catheter (suprapubic if urethral passage fails), which relieves pain and protects the kidneys. The residual volume is recorded, and an alpha-blocker may then be started before a trial without catheter.
why_wrong: A. An alpha-blocker is used alongside catheterisation to improve the chance of a successful trial without catheter, not instead of draining the bladder. B. Outpatient follow-up leaves a painful, obstructed bladder untreated. D. Fluid restriction does nothing for an obstructed outlet. E. Imaging does not need to come before relieving the obstruction.
pearl: Record the volume drained after catheterisation; a large residual volume, or rising creatinine, suggests chronic retention and needs monitoring for post-obstructive diuresis.
thinking: Long history of obstructive voiding symptoms ↓ Sudden inability to pass urine with pain ↓ Palpable tender bladder ↓ Acute urinary retention ↓ Decompress immediately with a catheter
exam_trap: A, Start an alpha-blocker — it is part of the management plan, but it does not relieve an acutely distended bladder and is given after drainage.
takeaway: Painful acute urinary retention is treated first by catheterising the bladder.

stem: On a respiratory ward, a 58-year-old woman with COPD who is receiving non-invasive ventilation suddenly becomes agitated and grey. Her blood pressure is falling, her right chest is moving poorly with no breath sounds, and the trachea is displaced towards the left. What is the next step?

options.A: Book a CT thorax for the next morning
options.B: Request a routine chest radiograph and wait for the report
options.C: Perform urgent decompression of the right chest
options.D: Measure spirometry to assess airflow obstruction
options.E: Start oral antibiotics for an infective exacerbation

correct_answer: C. Perform urgent decompression of the right chest
why_correct: A sudden collapse on positive-pressure support with an absent breath sound on one side, contralateral tracheal shift and hypotension indicates tension pneumothorax. This is diagnosed clinically and treated straight away by decompressing the affected side, followed by a chest drain. Delaying for any test risks cardiac arrest.
why_wrong: A. A delayed CT is wholly inappropriate in a peri-arrest patient. B. Waiting for a routine film delays life-saving treatment. D. Spirometry has no place in an acutely shocked patient. E. Antibiotics do not address the life-threatening mechanical problem.
pearl: Non-invasive and invasive positive-pressure ventilation both increase the risk of pneumothorax in patients with emphysematous lungs.
thinking: Sudden deterioration on positive-pressure ventilation ↓ Unilateral absent breath sounds with tracheal shift ↓ Hypotension indicates obstructive shock ↓ Tension pneumothorax ↓ Decompress the right chest now
exam_trap: B, Request a routine chest radiograph — in a COPD patient bullae can mimic pneumothorax on film, which tempts confirmation, but the shock makes immediate decompression the priority.
takeaway: A clinically obvious tension pneumothorax needs decompression before any imaging.

stem: A pharmacy assistant attends a first-aid training session and is taught a simple community tool to help recognise a possible stroke and call 999 quickly. Which of the following is one of the features this tool asks people to check?

options.D: Drooping of one side of the face

correct_answer: D. Drooping of one side of the face
why_correct: The FAST tool asks people to check the Face for drooping, the Arms for weakness, and Speech for slurring, and reminds them that it is Time to call 999. Facial drooping is therefore one of the core features. It is designed to be simple so the public can act quickly.
why_wrong: A. Neck stiffness suggests meningism and is not part of FAST. B. Chest pain is not part of FAST and suggests a cardiac or aortic cause. C. Visual loss can occur in stroke but is not one of the FAST checks, which is why some strokes are missed by it. E. Fever is not part of FAST.
pearl: FAST misses some posterior circulation strokes, which can present with vertigo, imbalance or visual disturbance; BE-FAST adds Balance and Eyes.
thinking: Community stroke recognition tool ↓ FAST stands for Face, Arms, Speech, Time ↓ Face check looks for one-sided drooping ↓ Facial droop is a FAST feature ↓ Any positive check means call 999
exam_trap: C, Blurred vision in one eye — visual symptoms can occur in stroke, but they are not part of FAST and are covered only in extended versions such as BE-FAST.
takeaway: FAST checks Face, Arms and Speech, and stresses that it is Time to call 999.

stem: On the acute medical unit, a 45-year-old woman admitted with loin pain and rigors becomes drowsy over the next hour. She is now cold and clammy with a falling blood pressure and a rising heart rate, and she has not passed urine since admission. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Arrange a CT of the urinary tract and start fluids once the scan is reported
options.B: Take blood cultures and hold antibiotics until the organism is known
options.C: Switch her to oral antibiotics and plan discharge with GP follow-up
options.D: Book outpatient renal imaging and a clinic review
options.E: Activate the sepsis pathway, taking cultures and starting time-critical treatment without delay

correct_answer: E. Activate the sepsis pathway, taking cultures and starting time-critical treatment without delay
why_correct: She has a probable urinary source with drowsiness, shock and reduced urine output, so she is at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis. Cultures should be taken, but intravenous antibiotics, fluid resuscitation and senior review must start immediately rather than waiting for results or imaging. Source imaging, which may show an obstructed kidney needing drainage, is arranged in parallel.
why_wrong: A. Fluid resuscitation must not wait for imaging in a shocked patient. B. Waiting for culture results delays life-saving antibiotics by days. C. Oral antibiotics and discharge are wholly inappropriate for a deteriorating patient. D. Outpatient investigations ignore an acute emergency.
pearl: An infected, obstructed kidney is a urological emergency; antibiotics alone are not enough and the system needs urgent decompression.
thinking: Loin pain and rigors suggest pyelonephritis ↓ Drowsiness, hypotension and tachycardia ↓ No urine output ↓ High-risk suspected sepsis ↓ Sepsis pathway: cultures plus immediate antibiotics and fluids
exam_trap: A, Arrange a CT of the urinary tract — looking for obstruction is important, but resuscitation and antibiotics come first and imaging runs alongside.
takeaway: In high-risk sepsis, take cultures but never let investigations delay antibiotics and fluids.

stem: A 70-year-old man arrives at the emergency department feeling generally unwell, with a productive cough and fever for three days. The triage nurse wants to use the tool that NICE recommends in acute hospital settings to stratify his risk of severe illness or death from suspected sepsis. Which tool should be used?
why_correct: NICE recommends NEWS2 to stratify the risk of severe illness or death from suspected sepsis in adults who are not pregnant and are assessed in acute hospital settings, including emergency departments. It aggregates respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, oxygen use, blood pressure, pulse, consciousness or new confusion, and temperature. It is used alongside clinical judgement and other risk factors.
why_wrong: A. CURB-65 assesses pneumonia severity, not overall sepsis risk. B. qSOFA is not the tool NICE recommends for sepsis risk stratification in the UK. C. The Glasgow Coma Scale measures only conscious level. D. The Wells score estimates probability of venous thromboembolism.
pearl: NEWS2 is not validated for pregnancy or children; separate risk criteria and early warning tools are used for these groups.
thinking: Suspected infection in an adult ↓ Assessed in an acute hospital ↓ Not pregnant ↓ NICE recommends a single physiological aggregate score ↓ Use NEWS2
exam_trap: A, CURB-65 score — the history suggests pneumonia, so a pneumonia severity tool is tempting, but it is not the recommended tool for stratifying sepsis risk.
takeaway: In acute hospital settings, NICE uses NEWS2 to stratify sepsis risk in non-pregnant adults.

stem: An 81-year-old care home resident is admitted to the emergency department with a suspected chest infection. She is confused, hypotensive and tachypnoeic, and she has been assessed as being at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis. Blood cultures have been taken. When should antibiotics be given?

options.B: Intravenous antibiotics once she becomes more hypotensive
options.C: Oral antibiotics with review within 24 hours
options.E: After blood culture results are available

correct_answer: A. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour
why_correct: NICE advises that adults with suspected sepsis who are at high risk of severe illness or death should receive broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics at the maximum recommended dose within 1 hour, alongside senior review and fluids. Each hour of delay in high-risk patients is associated with worse outcomes. Cultures should be taken first only if this does not delay treatment.
why_wrong: B. Waiting for further deterioration is dangerous; she is already high risk. C. Oral antibiotics are inappropriate for a high-risk, shocked patient. D. A 3-hour window applies to lower-risk groups, not to her. E. Waiting for cultures delays treatment by days.
pearl: Antibiotic choice should follow local guidelines based on the likely source, with review at 48 hours to de-escalate or stop.
thinking: Suspected chest infection ↓ Confusion, hypotension and tachypnoea ↓ High risk of severe illness or death ↓ Cultures taken ↓ Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
exam_trap: D, Within 3 hours — this timescale exists for moderate-risk patients, which makes it look familiar, but it does not apply to someone at high risk.
takeaway: High-risk suspected sepsis needs intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.

stem: A 63-year-old man recovering on an orthopaedic ward after a hip replacement is reviewed by a foundation doctor at the request of a nurse. Since the morning he has become breathless with a climbing respiratory rate, his blood pressure is drifting down, and he no longer knows where he is. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Document the observations and ask for a repeat set at the end of the shift
options.B: Give oral haloperidol to settle his confusion
options.C: Encourage him to drink more and check his blood pressure later
options.D: Hand over to the team for review on tomorrow's ward round
options.E: Treat this as acute deterioration: assess him now with ABCDE and escalate to a senior

correct_answer: E. Treat this as acute deterioration: assess him now with ABCDE and escalate to a senior
why_correct: A rising respiratory rate, falling blood pressure and new confusion are warning signs of acute deterioration, for example from sepsis, pulmonary embolism or bleeding. He needs immediate ABCDE assessment, calculation of his NEWS2, prompt treatment of problems found and escalation to a senior according to local policy. Delay increases the risk of cardiac arrest.
why_wrong: A. Deferring repeat observations ignores clear signs of deterioration. B. Sedating new confusion without finding the cause is dangerous and masks the problem. C. Oral fluids do not address a potentially life-threatening cause. D. Waiting until tomorrow is unsafe.
pearl: Respiratory rate is often the earliest vital sign to change in a deteriorating patient and is the one most frequently missed.
thinking: Post-operative patient ↓ Rising respiratory rate and falling blood pressure ↓ New confusion ↓ Signs of acute deterioration ↓ Immediate ABCDE assessment and escalation
exam_trap: B, Give oral haloperidol — agitation and confusion after surgery tempt treatment as delirium, but new confusion with abnormal vital signs is a sign of physiological deterioration until proven otherwise.
takeaway: New confusion with worsening vital signs is acute deterioration and needs immediate assessment and escalation.

presentation: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem: Transferred from a mental health unit where she is prescribed fluoxetine and haloperidol, a 41-year-old woman is febrile, agitated and drenched in sweat. Two drug-induced hyperthermic emergencies are on the differential. On examination, which sign would point most strongly towards excess serotonergic activity?

options.C: Generalised lead-pipe rigidity with slowed reflexes
options.D: Inducible ankle clonus with brisk reflexes

correct_answer: D. Inducible ankle clonus with brisk reflexes
why_correct: Neuromuscular hyperactivity, particularly inducible or spontaneous clonus and hyperreflexia, is the hallmark of serotonin toxicity and is part of the Hunter criteria. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome instead causes bradykinesia with severe lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes. Fever, confusion and autonomic instability occur in both.
why_wrong: A. Altered consciousness occurs in both conditions. B. Severe hyperthermia can occur in both. C. Lead-pipe rigidity with sluggish reflexes favours neuroleptic malignant syndrome. E. A very high creatine kinase is more typical of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
pearl: Serotonin syndrome usually develops within hours of a drug change, whereas neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days.
thinking: Fever, agitation and sweating on two candidate drugs ↓ Both syndromes share fever, confusion and autonomic instability ↓ Look at neuromuscular signs ↓ Clonus and hyperreflexia indicate serotonin toxicity ↓ Rigidity with slow reflexes indicates NMS
exam_trap: E, Markedly raised creatine kinase — it signals muscle injury in both conditions, but very high levels point more towards neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
takeaway: Clonus and hyperreflexia favour serotonin syndrome; lead-pipe rigidity favours neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

presentation: Serotonin syndrome after recreational drug use
stem: A 22-year-old woman is brought from a music festival to the emergency department by her friends, who say she took several ecstasy tablets a few hours earlier. She is restless and shaking, her skin is flushed and drenched in sweat, her pupils are large, and her temperature is high. Her reflexes are very brisk and tapping the ankle produces repeated beats of clonus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: MDMA (ecstasy) releases large amounts of serotonin, and the combination of agitation, tremor, sweating, mydriasis, hyperthermia, hyperreflexia and inducible clonus developing within hours is classic serotonin toxicity. Management is supportive with cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation and specialist advice from TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service.
why_wrong: A. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotic exposure and causes rigidity with reduced reflexes over days. C. Opioid toxicity causes pinpoint pupils, sedation and respiratory depression. D. Benzodiazepine overdose causes drowsiness, not agitation and clonus. E. Anticholinergic toxicity causes hot, dry skin and normal reflexes without clonus.
pearl: Severe MDMA toxicity can also cause dangerous hyponatraemia from excess water intake and inappropriate ADH release.
thinking: Recent ecstasy use ↓ Agitation, tremor, sweating and dilated pupils ↓ Hyperthermia ↓ Hyperreflexia with inducible clonus ↓ Serotonin syndrome
exam_trap: E, Anticholinergic toxicity — dilated pupils, agitation and fever overlap, but anticholinergic patients have dry skin and no clonus, whereas she is sweating heavily.
takeaway: Agitation, sweating, hyperthermia and clonus after ecstasy indicate serotonin syndrome.

stem: In a GP surgery, a 31-year-old woman collapses minutes after a first dose of an injected antibiotic. She has stridor, widespread urticaria and a weak pulse. The practice nurse gave IM adrenaline 5 minutes ago and an ambulance is on its way, but she has not improved. What should be done now?

options.A: Give a second dose of IM adrenaline
options.B: Give oral cetirizine and wait for the ambulance crew
options.C: Give hydrocortisone as the priority treatment
options.D: Use a salbutamol inhaler instead of more adrenaline
options.E: Lie her flat and observe until paramedics arrive

correct_answer: A. Give a second dose of IM adrenaline
why_correct: She has anaphylaxis with airway and circulation involvement that has not responded to the first dose. Resuscitation Council UK guidance is to repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if there is no improvement, while maintaining the airway, positioning her appropriately and giving oxygen if available. If two doses fail, specialist help for an adrenaline infusion is needed.
why_wrong: B. Oral antihistamines act too slowly and do not treat airway or circulatory compromise. C. Corticosteroids are no longer routinely recommended in the initial emergency treatment and are not life-saving. D. Salbutamol does not treat stridor or shock and cannot replace adrenaline. E. Observation alone is unsafe when she has not responded.
pearl: Patients in anaphylaxis should not suddenly stand or sit up, as this can cause fatal cardiovascular collapse; lie them flat with legs raised unless breathing is easier sitting.
thinking: Rapid reaction after a drug with stridor, urticaria and weak pulse ↓ Anaphylaxis ↓ One IM adrenaline dose without improvement ↓ 5 minutes have passed ↓ Repeat IM adrenaline
exam_trap: C, Give hydrocortisone as the priority treatment — steroids were traditionally given, but they are not life-saving and must not delay repeat adrenaline.
takeaway: Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes if anaphylaxis is not improving.

stem: A 66-year-old man on the intensive care unit has had no urine at all draining from his catheter over the past 12 hours. The catheter has been flushed and is patent, a bladder scan shows an empty bladder, and his fluid status has been optimised. Which term best describes his urine output?
why_correct: Anuria is the absence, or near-absence, of urine production. Because the catheter is patent and the bladder is empty, there is no lower urinary tract obstruction, so he is genuinely not producing urine. This suggests severe acute kidney injury or, less commonly, obstruction of both upper tracts.
why_wrong: B. Oliguria means a reduced but measurable urine output, whereas he has produced none. C. Polyuria means an abnormally large urine volume. D. Dysuria is pain or burning on passing urine. E. Nocturia is waking at night to pass urine.
pearl: Sudden complete anuria in a catheterised patient should first prompt a check of the catheter for blockage before assuming renal failure.
thinking: No urine over 12 hours ↓ Catheter patent and bladder empty ↓ No lower tract obstruction ↓ Kidneys are not producing urine ↓ Anuria
exam_trap: B, Oliguria — it also describes low urine output in acute kidney injury, but it implies some urine is still being produced, whereas he has produced none.
takeaway: Anuria means essentially no urine production and points to severe kidney injury or complete obstruction.

stem: A 57-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the emergency department after a sudden tearing pain began in the front of his chest and moved between his shoulder blades. He is pale and sweating. The systolic pressure in his right arm is substantially higher than in his left. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
why_correct: Abrupt, severe tearing chest pain radiating or migrating to the back in a hypertensive man, with a significant blood pressure difference between the arms, is highly suggestive of acute aortic dissection. The arm difference reflects involvement of the aortic branches. He needs urgent CT aortography, blood pressure and heart rate control, and immediate discussion with cardiothoracic or vascular surgery.
why_wrong: A. Pericarditis causes sharp pain eased by sitting forward, without an inter-arm blood pressure difference. B. Oesophageal spasm can mimic cardiac pain but does not cause unequal arm pressures or shock. D. Pulmonary embolism causes breathlessness and pleuritic pain rather than tearing pain to the back with pulse asymmetry. E. Chest wall pain is reproducible on palpation and does not cause pallor, sweating or unequal pressures.
pearl: Thrombolysis given for a presumed myocardial infarction can be fatal in aortic dissection, so always consider dissection before reperfusion therapy.
thinking: Sudden tearing chest pain moving to the back ↓ Hypertensive man, pale and sweating ↓ Significant difference in arm blood pressures ↓ Aortic branch involvement ↓ Acute aortic dissection
exam_trap: D, Pulmonary embolism — sudden chest pain with distress raises it, but tearing pain moving to the back with unequal arm pressures points to the aorta.
takeaway: Tearing chest pain to the back with unequal arm blood pressures is aortic dissection until proven otherwise.

presentation: Acute cauda equina or cord compression
stem: A 44-year-old warehouse worker felt something give in her lower back while lifting a heavy box this morning. By the evening she attends the emergency department because both legs feel weak and numb, she has lost feeling around her bottom when wiping, and she has been unable to start a urine stream. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give analgesia and advise her to keep active
options.B: Refer for physiotherapy and review in the GP surgery
options.C: Request a routine lumbar spine MRI in the next few weeks
options.D: Insert a catheter and treat for a urinary tract infection
options.E: Arrange an emergency MRI of the spine

correct_answer: E. Arrange an emergency MRI of the spine
why_correct: Acute back pain followed by bilateral leg weakness and numbness, saddle sensory loss and urinary hesitancy are red flags for cauda equina syndrome or spinal cord compression. These require an emergency MRI of the spine and urgent referral to the spinal surgical team, because outcome depends on how quickly compression is relieved. Bladder dysfunction must not be attributed to infection.
why_wrong: A. Simple analgesia and keeping active is appropriate only for uncomplicated mechanical back pain without red flags. B. Physiotherapy delays urgent investigation of neurological compromise. C. A routine scan is far too slow for a surgical emergency. D. The urinary symptoms are neurological, not infective.
pearl: Outcomes in cauda equina syndrome are much better if decompression occurs before painless urinary retention with overflow develops.
thinking: Acute back pain after lifting ↓ Bilateral leg weakness and numbness ↓ Saddle anaesthesia and urinary hesitancy ↓ Red flags for cauda equina or cord compression ↓ Emergency MRI spine
exam_trap: D, Catheterise and treat for a urinary tract infection — difficulty passing urine suggests a urinary cause, but with saddle numbness and leg weakness it is neurological until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Back pain with bilateral leg symptoms, saddle anaesthesia or bladder change needs an emergency MRI of the spine.

stem: During a GP home visit, a 58-year-old woman treated for breast cancer three years ago describes a band of pain around her chest that has kept her awake for two weeks. Since yesterday she has stumbled several times and says her legs feel numb. Which diagnosis is most important to exclude urgently?
why_correct: Breast cancer commonly spreads to the spine, and band-like thoracic pain with night pain followed by leg numbness and unsteadiness strongly suggests metastatic spinal cord compression, even years after treatment. She needs immediate referral for an MRI of the whole spine and specialist management, because outcome depends on her ability to walk when treatment starts.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, thirst, constipation and abdominal pain, not a sensory level with leg numbness. B. Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness, usually after an infection, without band-like spinal pain. C. Lumbar stenosis causes leg pain on walking eased by bending forward, not band-like thoracic pain with acute numbness. D. Shingles can cause band-like pain but not leg numbness and stumbling.
pearl: Band-like (radicular) pain around the chest or abdomen in a patient with cancer can be an early sign of spinal metastases before any weakness.
thinking: Previous breast cancer ↓ Band-like thoracic pain, worse at night ↓ New leg numbness and stumbling ↓ Spinal metastasis compressing the cord ↓ Exclude metastatic spinal cord compression urgently
exam_trap: D, Shingles affecting a thoracic dermatome — band-like pain fits shingles, which tempts, but it does not explain new leg numbness and falls.
takeaway: Cancer history plus band-like spinal pain and new leg symptoms needs urgent investigation for metastatic spinal cord compression.

stem: A 69-year-old ex-smoker with lung cancer is admitted to a hospice for symptom control. The nursing team report that his upper back pain has become much more severe over a few days and he now needs help to stand because his legs have become weak. What diagnosis must be considered urgently?
why_correct: Worsening spinal pain followed by progressive leg weakness in a patient with lung cancer, which often metastasises to bone, is a red flag for metastatic spinal cord compression. Even in palliative settings this needs urgent recognition, MRI where appropriate, and treatment such as dexamethasone and radiotherapy to preserve mobility and continence.
why_wrong: B. Steroid myopathy causes gradual proximal weakness without severe new back pain. C. Opioids can cause drowsiness but not focal leg weakness with escalating spinal pain. D. Degenerative disease does not cause rapidly progressive pain with weakness over days. E. Coughing strain does not explain neurological deficit.
pearl: Preserving the ability to walk is a key goal: most patients who are walking at the start of treatment for cord compression remain able to walk afterwards.
thinking: Lung cancer with likely bone spread ↓ Rapidly worsening upper back pain ↓ New progressive leg weakness ↓ Cord compression by metastasis ↓ Urgent assessment and treatment even in palliative care
exam_trap: C, Opioid-induced drowsiness and unsteadiness — hospice patients often take opioids, but they do not cause escalating spinal pain with objective leg weakness.
takeaway: In a patient with cancer, worsening back pain and leg weakness are metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise.

stem: Care home staff ask the GP to see a 76-year-old resident with prostate cancer. Over the last ten days he has complained of new aching pain in his back and has gone from walking with a frame to barely being able to get from bed to chair. Which diagnosis should be considered urgently?
why_correct: New back pain with a rapid decline in mobility in a man with prostate cancer, which commonly spreads to the spine, is a warning pattern for metastatic spinal cord compression. NICE advises immediate referral to the local acute oncology or MSCC coordinator and an MRI of the whole spine when neurological symptoms are present. Early treatment aims to preserve walking.
why_wrong: B. Spinal stenosis causes chronic, posture-related leg symptoms rather than rapid loss of mobility. C. Osteoporotic collapse causes sudden localised pain but does not explain a progressive loss of mobility over days in a man with known cancer. D. Mechanical pain does not cause progressive inability to walk. E. Guillain-Barré syndrome is an ascending neuropathy, usually post-infective, and is far less likely with new spinal pain and known cancer.
pearl: In older people, a sudden decline in mobility may be the main clue to cord compression, as they may not report weakness specifically.
thinking: Prostate cancer ↓ New back pain ↓ Rapidly worsening mobility over days ↓ Possible spinal metastasis compressing the cord ↓ Consider metastatic spinal cord compression urgently
exam_trap: C, Osteoporotic vertebral collapse — common in older men on hormone therapy, it tempts as a cause of back pain, but progressive loss of walking points to cord compression.
takeaway: In a patient with cancer, new back pain with declining mobility needs urgent assessment for metastatic spinal cord compression.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with known metastatic breast cancer rings the acute oncology helpline. For a week she has had worsening pain in the middle of her back that wakes her at night and wraps around her chest like a band. Since yesterday her legs have felt heavy and she has stumbled twice at home. Which diagnosis must be urgently excluded?

options.A: Osteoporotic vertebral wedge fracture without neural involvement

why_correct: Breast cancer commonly metastasises to the spine, and thoracic pain that is progressive, worse at night and radicular (band-like) is a red flag for metastatic spinal cord compression. New leg heaviness and falls indicate evolving neurological deficit. This is an oncological emergency needing same-day assessment, whole-spine MRI and early treatment to preserve mobility and continence.
why_wrong: A. A simple wedge fracture may be painful but does not explain new bilateral leg weakness. B. Muscle strain does not cause night pain in a known cancer patient or neurological signs in the legs. D. Chemotherapy neuropathy is usually gradual, sensory and glove-and-stocking, not acute leg heaviness with spinal pain. E. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, thirst, constipation and fatigue rather than localised spinal pain with leg weakness.
pearl: Neurological outcome in spinal cord compression depends mainly on function at the time treatment starts, so patients who are still walking must be treated before they lose that ability.
thinking: Known malignancy with spinal metastatic potential ↓ Progressive thoracic pain, worse at night, band-like ↓ New leg heaviness and falls ↓ Red flags for cord compression ↓ Urgent whole-spine MRI and acute oncology involvement
exam_trap: E, Hypercalcaemia of malignancy — it is a common emergency in breast cancer and can cause weakness, but it does not produce band-like spinal pain with focal leg symptoms.
takeaway: New neurological symptoms with spinal pain in someone with cancer are metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise.

presentation: Major bleeding on a direct oral anticoagulant
stem: A care home resident aged 79, who takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation, is brought to the emergency department after vomiting fresh blood twice and passing black, tarry stools. She is pale with cool hands, a fast pulse and a low blood pressure. What should be the immediate priority?

options.A: Book a gastroscopy on the next routine list
options.B: Continue apixaban and start a high-dose oral proton pump inhibitor
options.C: Change apixaban to aspirin to reduce bleeding risk
options.D: Resuscitate, withhold apixaban and address its anticoagulant effect
options.E: Give oral vitamin K and arrange GP follow-up

correct_answer: D. Resuscitate, withhold apixaban and address its anticoagulant effect
why_correct: She has a major upper gastrointestinal bleed with signs of shock while anticoagulated. The priority is ABCDE resuscitation with large-bore access, blood products as needed and stopping the anticoagulant, with specialist advice on reversal. Urgent endoscopy follows once she is resuscitated.
why_wrong: A. An unstable upper GI bleed needs emergency assessment and endoscopy after resuscitation, not a routine list. B. Continuing an anticoagulant during life-threatening bleeding worsens the haemorrhage. C. Antiplatelet drugs also increase bleeding and do nothing for the acute problem. E. Vitamin K does not reverse apixaban and discharge would be unsafe in a shocked patient.
pearl: Vitamin K reverses warfarin but not factor Xa inhibitors; for life-threatening bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban, specific reversal with andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate may be given on haematology advice, and idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
thinking: Haematemesis and melaena ↓ Pale, cool, tachycardic, hypotensive ↓ Major bleed while on apixaban ↓ Resuscitate first and stop the anticoagulant ↓ Seek reversal advice, then urgent endoscopy
exam_trap: E, Oral vitamin K — it is the familiar reversal agent, but it acts only on warfarin and does nothing for a factor Xa inhibitor or for shock.
takeaway: In major bleeding on an anticoagulant, resuscitate, stop the drug and manage its anticoagulant effect.

stem: A 31-year-old woman on a trekking holiday has ascended rapidly to high altitude. On her third day she develops a dry cough that becomes frothy, and she is now breathless even at rest, with blue-tinged lips and crackles in both lungs. She is fully orientated and can walk heel-to-toe normally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rapid ascent, a dry cough progressing to frothy sputum, breathlessness at rest, cyanosis and crackles a few days after arrival are characteristic of high-altitude pulmonary oedema. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causes uneven pulmonary hypertension and capillary leak. Normal orientation and gait make cerebral oedema less likely.
why_wrong: A. Cerebral oedema causes confusion, ataxia and drowsiness, and her mental state and gait are normal. B. Acute mountain sickness causes headache, nausea and fatigue, not breathlessness at rest with crackles. C. Tuberculosis has a chronic course with fever, weight loss and night sweats. E. Pneumonia is less likely given the timing with rapid ascent and the absence of focal signs or high fever.
pearl: Descent is the definitive treatment for high-altitude pulmonary oedema; oxygen and nifedipine can be used as adjuncts.
thinking: Rapid ascent ↓ Cough, then frothy sputum ↓ Breathless at rest with cyanosis and crackles ↓ Orientation and gait normal ↓ High-altitude pulmonary oedema, so descend
exam_trap: A, High-altitude cerebral oedema — it is the other serious altitude illness, but it presents with confusion and ataxia rather than lung signs.
takeaway: Breathlessness at rest with crackles after rapid ascent is high-altitude pulmonary oedema until proven otherwise.

stem: An hour after a subclavian central venous catheter is placed on a surgical ward, a 58-year-old man becomes acutely breathless and his blood pressure drops. The trachea is pushed away from the side of the line, that hemithorax is hyper-resonant with no breath sounds, and his neck veins are distended. What is the key principle of management?

options.C: Remove the line and wait for a check chest X-ray
options.D: Observe, as procedure-related pneumothoraces are small

why_correct: Subclavian line insertion can puncture the pleura. Shock with tracheal deviation, a silent hyper-resonant hemithorax and distended neck veins indicate tension pneumothorax. Immediate decompression is needed, followed by a chest drain.
why_wrong: B. There is no wheeze, and bronchodilators do not relieve raised intrapleural pressure. C. Removing the line does not treat the pneumothorax, and waiting for an X-ray delays life-saving treatment. D. Iatrogenic pneumothoraces can progress to tension, and this one already has. E. There is no rash, wheeze or exposure to suggest anaphylaxis, and the signs are one-sided.
pearl: Current trauma teaching favours decompression in the fourth or fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line in adults, as the chest wall is thinner there than in the second intercostal space.
thinking: Recent subclavian line ↓ Sudden breathlessness and hypotension ↓ Tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds ↓ Tension pneumothorax ↓ Immediate decompression then chest drain
exam_trap: C, Remove the line and wait for an X-ray — it targets the cause, but the trapped air is already compressing the heart and needs releasing now.
takeaway: Tension pneumothorax is an emergency that needs immediate decompression.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer comes to the emergency department because her breathing has become steadily more laboured through the day. She now feels faint and is hypotensive. Her jugular venous pressure is markedly raised, her heart sounds are quiet and distant, her lungs are clear and her systolic pressure falls noticeably on inspiration. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Hypotension, a raised JVP and muffled heart sounds form Beck's triad, and an exaggerated fall in systolic pressure on inspiration (pulsus paradoxus) supports it. Malignancy is a common cause of a pericardial effusion that can accumulate until it compresses the heart. Urgent echocardiography and pericardiocentesis are needed.
why_wrong: B. Tension pneumothorax also causes shock with a raised JVP, but with absent breath sounds on one side and tracheal deviation, whereas her lungs are clear. C. Constrictive pericarditis develops over months with chronic right heart failure, not acute shock with quiet heart sounds. D. Massive pulmonary embolism causes shock and a raised JVP but does not muffle the heart sounds. E. Asthma causes wheeze and does not raise the JVP or muffle the heart sounds.
pearl: Bedside echocardiography confirms tamponade by showing a pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right-sided chambers.
