thinking: Known malignancy ↓ Progressive breathlessness and hypotension ↓ Raised JVP with quiet heart sounds and clear lungs ↓ Pulsus paradoxus ↓ Cardiac tamponade needing urgent drainage
exam_trap: D, Massive pulmonary embolism — cancer raises the risk and it causes shock with a high JVP, but it does not muffle the heart sounds, and quiet heart sounds with pulsus paradoxus point to fluid around the heart.
takeaway: Hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds should prompt urgent assessment for cardiac tamponade.

stem: On a cardiology ward, a 69-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and severely impaired left ventricular function tells the nurse he feels light-headed. He is clammy and his blood pressure is low. The monitor shows a fast, regular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, and there is no earlier ECG to compare it with. Which rhythm should be assumed until proven otherwise?

options.E: Atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block

why_correct: In a patient with structural heart disease, particularly previous infarction and poor ventricular function, a regular broad-complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia in the great majority of cases. It should be treated as such until proven otherwise, and here the low blood pressure makes it an emergency needing synchronised cardioversion.
why_wrong: B. Aberrant supraventricular tachycardia is possible but far less likely with ischaemic heart disease, and wrongly assuming it can lead to dangerous treatment. C. Sinus tachycardia usually has narrow complexes unless a pre-existing bundle branch block is known. D. Atrial flutter usually conducts with narrow complexes, and there is no evidence of an existing conduction defect. E. Atrial fibrillation would give an irregularly irregular rhythm, not a regular one.
pearl: Giving verapamil to someone with ventricular tachycardia mistaken for supraventricular tachycardia can cause profound hypotension and cardiac arrest.
thinking: Ischaemic cardiomyopathy with poor ventricular function ↓ Fast, regular, wide-complex rhythm ↓ No previous ECG showing bundle branch block ↓ Structural heart disease makes VT most likely ↓ Treat as VT; shock adverse features mean cardioversion
exam_trap: B, Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy — it can look identical, but assuming it in a patient with ischaemic heart disease risks giving harmful drugs.
takeaway: A regular broad-complex tachycardia in a patient with heart disease is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise.

stem: A 50-year-old man is rescued from a warehouse fire in which plastics and foam furniture were burning. Despite high-flow oxygen through a reservoir mask, he becomes drowsy, hypotensive and has a seizure. A blood gas shows severe lactic acidosis and only a modestly raised carboxyhaemoglobin. Which toxin should be suspected?
why_correct: Burning plastics, foam and other synthetic materials release hydrogen cyanide. Cyanide blocks mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, so cells cannot use oxygen despite good delivery, producing severe lactic acidosis with cardiovascular collapse, seizures and reduced consciousness. A carboxyhaemoglobin level too low to explain the picture adds to the suspicion.
why_wrong: A. Methanol causes acidosis with visual disturbance after a latent period and is not linked to smoke. C. Salicylate poisoning causes tinnitus, hyperventilation and a mixed acid-base disturbance, and there is no ingestion history. D. Benzodiazepines cause sedation but not lactic acidosis with cardiovascular collapse. E. Paracetamol causes delayed liver injury and is usually asymptomatic early.
pearl: Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote of choice for suspected cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation, as it binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin.
thinking: Enclosed fire with burning synthetics ↓ Collapse, seizure and hypotension despite oxygen ↓ Severe lactic acidosis ↓ Carboxyhaemoglobin too low to explain it ↓ Cyanide poisoning, give hydroxocobalamin
exam_trap: A, Methanol — it also causes a severe metabolic acidosis, but it comes from ingestion, not smoke, and has a delayed onset.
takeaway: Collapse with lactic acidosis despite oxygen after a house fire suggests cyanide poisoning.

stem: Firefighters bring a 58-year-old man out of a burning caravan. In the emergency department he has reddened skin on his face, black material around his lips and nose, and his voice sounds husky. Which complication needs the most urgent attention?
why_correct: A small enclosed space fire, facial burns, soot around the mouth and nose and a husky voice all suggest inhalational injury. The upper airway can swell rapidly and obstruct, so airway protection is the immediate priority following an ABCDE approach.
why_wrong: B. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain and is unrelated to fire exposure. C. Otitis media does not explain soot or voice change. D. There are no abdominal features of appendicitis. E. Thrombosis may be a later risk with immobility but is not the immediate threat to life.
pearl: Stridor, hoarseness, carbonaceous sputum and full-thickness facial or neck burns are all indications for early specialist airway assessment.
thinking: Rescued from an enclosed fire ↓ Facial burns and soot around lips and nose ↓ Husky voice ↓ Suspected inhalational injury ↓ Airway is the immediate priority
exam_trap: E, Deep-vein thrombosis — immobile burns patients are at risk, but it is not a threat in the first hours, unlike airway swelling.
takeaway: Soot and a voice change after a fire mean the airway comes first.

stem: A 37-year-old factory worker has extensive scalds over his trunk and legs. Over the next few hours he becomes thirsty and tachycardic, his blood pressure falls and his urine output drops. Which physiological process mainly accounts for these changes?

options.D: Loss of intravascular fluid into the tissues

correct_answer: D. Loss of intravascular fluid into the tissues
why_correct: Major burns trigger a systemic inflammatory response that makes capillaries leaky, so plasma moves from the circulation into the burned and unburned tissues. This leads to hypovolaemia, which explains his thirst, tachycardia, hypotension and falling urine output, and is why early, carefully titrated fluid resuscitation is needed.
why_wrong: A. Capillary permeability increases, not decreases, after burns. B. Thyroid storm is unrelated to burn injury. C. Loss of protein-rich fluid lowers, rather than raises, plasma oncotic pressure. E. Red-cell production does not increase acutely, and haemoconcentration reflects plasma loss.
pearl: Fluid resuscitation in major burns is guided by a formula initially but then titrated to urine output and clinical response.
thinking: Extensive burns ↓ Inflammatory mediators increase capillary permeability ↓ Plasma leaks out of the circulation ↓ Hypovolaemia: thirst, tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria ↓ Needs early fluid resuscitation
exam_trap: C, Rise in plasma oncotic pressure — haemoconcentration may suggest this, but protein is lost with the fluid and oncotic pressure falls.
takeaway: Major burns cause hypovolaemia through leakage of plasma from the circulation into the tissues.

stem: A 61-year-old woman is helped out of her smoke-filled kitchen after a chip-pan fire. She has superficial burns on her face and there is soot on her lips. The emergency department nurse asks which feature would most suggest that she has injured her airway. What is the best answer?
why_correct: Hoarseness after smoke exposure means the larynx and upper airway have been affected by heat or irritants. It warns of progressive airway oedema and should prompt early senior airway assessment, ideally before the swelling worsens.
why_wrong: B. Ankle swelling is not linked to acute inhalational injury. C. Loose stools are unrelated to airway injury. D. Wrist pain may reflect a fall but says nothing about the airway. E. Abdominal discomfort is not a sign of airway injury.
pearl: Other warning features of inhalational injury include stridor, singed nasal hair, carbonaceous sputum and burns inside the mouth.
thinking: Smoke exposure in a confined room ↓ Facial burns and soot on lips ↓ Look for airway warning signs ↓ Hoarseness indicates laryngeal involvement ↓ Early airway assessment
exam_trap: B, Mild ankle swelling — oedema is relevant in burns, but swelling in the ankles tells you nothing about the airway.
takeaway: Hoarseness after smoke exposure is a red flag for inhalational airway injury.

stem: Ten days after a right total knee replacement, a 58-year-old woman sees her GP with a dull ache in her right calf. She is otherwise well. Which examination finding would most strongly suggest a deep vein thrombosis?

options.A: Calf pain on walking that settles after a few minutes' rest
options.C: Swelling of the right calf, which is clearly wider than the left
options.D: Absent pulses in the right foot
options.E: A cold, pale right foot with slow capillary refill

correct_answer: C. Swelling of the right calf, which is clearly wider than the left
why_correct: Unilateral calf swelling, with the affected calf measurably larger than the other, is one of the Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis. Together with recent major orthopaedic surgery, it makes deep vein thrombosis likely, and she should have a proximal leg vein ultrasound.
why_wrong: A. Pain on walking relieved by rest is intermittent claudication from arterial disease. B. Bilateral ankle oedema suggests a systemic cause such as heart failure or low albumin. D. Absent pulses point to arterial disease or acute limb ischaemia. E. A cold, pale foot with slow refill suggests arterial insufficiency, not venous obstruction.
pearl: Calf circumference is measured about 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity and compared with the other leg when applying the Wells score.
thinking: Recent knee replacement increases venous thrombosis risk ↓ Unilateral calf ache ↓ Look for venous rather than arterial signs ↓ Asymmetrical calf swelling supports deep vein thrombosis ↓ Wells score and ultrasound
exam_trap: E, Cold, pale foot — it suggests a vascular emergency, but one of arterial, not venous, origin.
takeaway: Unilateral calf swelling is the examination finding that most supports a deep vein thrombosis.

stem: A 47-year-old man collapses during a five-a-side football match at a leisure centre. A team-mate has started chest compressions. The receptionist brings the wall-mounted defibrillator but says she has never had any training and is worried about using it. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Keep it in its case until a doctor or paramedic arrives
options.B: Carry on with compressions only and do not analyse the rhythm
options.C: Only use it if someone with formal training can be found
options.D: Use it only once the ambulance service confirms there is no pulse
options.E: Switch it on promptly, apply the pads and follow its voice instructions

correct_answer: E. Switch it on promptly, apply the pads and follow its voice instructions
why_correct: Automated external defibrillators are designed for use by anyone, with spoken and visual prompts guiding pad placement and shocks. Early defibrillation greatly improves survival from a shockable arrest, so the device should be used at once while compressions continue around it.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for professionals delays defibrillation and reduces survival. B. Without rhythm analysis a shockable rhythm will be missed. C. No training is needed to use an AED safely. D. Waiting for confirmation delays treatment; the AED itself decides whether a shock is required.
pearl: For every minute without CPR and defibrillation in a shockable arrest, the chance of survival falls substantially.
thinking: Sudden collapse during sport ↓ CPR started ↓ AED available ↓ Device guides any user and decides on shocks ↓ Use it immediately alongside CPR
exam_trap: C, Wait for someone trained — it feels responsible, but AEDs are built for untrained users and delay costs lives.
takeaway: Anyone can and should use an AED immediately in cardiac arrest.

stem: A 47-year-old lorry driver who has had episodes of low back pain for years sees his GP. Since yesterday he has struggled to start passing urine, and when he wipes after the toilet the skin around his anus and between his legs feels numb. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Refer immediately for emergency assessment and MRI for suspected cauda equina syndrome
options.B: Prescribe oral nitrofurantoin for a presumed urinary tract infection
options.C: Give analgesia and review him in six weeks
options.D: Request a routine outpatient MRI of the lumbar spine
options.E: Make a routine referral to urology for voiding difficulty

correct_answer: A. Refer immediately for emergency assessment and MRI for suspected cauda equina syndrome
why_correct: New urinary hesitancy with saddle sensory loss in someone with back pain are red flags for cauda equina syndrome. Compression of the sacral nerve roots can cause permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction if not decompressed promptly, so he needs immediate referral for emergency MRI and specialist spinal assessment.
why_wrong: B. There are no infective symptoms, and treating as infection would delay a time-critical diagnosis. C. Delay risks permanent loss of sphincter function. D. Suspected cauda equina needs emergency, not routine, imaging. E. Voiding difficulty with saddle numbness is neurological and needs emergency spinal assessment.
pearl: Outcomes in cauda equina syndrome are best when surgery happens before painless urinary retention with overflow develops.
thinking: Chronic back pain with new symptoms ↓ Urinary hesitancy ↓ Saddle numbness ↓ Red flags for cauda equina syndrome ↓ Immediate referral for emergency MRI
exam_trap: B, Nitrofurantoin — urinary symptoms tempt a diagnosis of infection, but saddle numbness points to nerve root compression.
takeaway: Urinary disturbance with saddle anaesthesia needs immediate referral for suspected cauda equina syndrome.

stem: A 22-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed crash. Within minutes of arrival he is struggling to breathe, his saturations are dropping and he is hypotensive. The left hemithorax is silent. Which management principle applies?

options.A: Get a chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis first
options.B: Give high-flow oxygen and reassess in half an hour
options.C: Give a large crystalloid bolus for haemorrhagic shock alone
options.D: Request a CT scan of the chest before any procedure
options.E: Treat as tension pneumothorax with immediate decompression, then a chest drain

correct_answer: E. Treat as tension pneumothorax with immediate decompression, then a chest drain
why_correct: Respiratory distress, hypoxaemia, hypotension and a silent hemithorax after major trauma should be treated as tension pneumothorax. It is a clinical diagnosis; immediate decompression by needle or finger thoracostomy is followed by a chest drain, and imaging must not delay it.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for an X-ray delays life-saving treatment. B. Oxygen alone does not relieve the pressure, and reassessment later is too late. C. Fluids do not reverse obstructive shock, though bleeding should also be looked for. D. Moving to CT in an unstable patient is unsafe.
pearl: Finger thoracostomy is preferred over needle decompression in ventilated trauma patients, as needles may be too short or kink.
thinking: High-energy trauma ↓ Rapid respiratory distress and hypoxaemia ↓ Hypotension ↓ Silent hemithorax ↓ Decompress immediately, then chest drain
exam_trap: A, Chest X-ray first — it seems to confirm the diagnosis, but tension pneumothorax is clinical and the delay can lead to arrest.
takeaway: Suspected tension pneumothorax after trauma is decompressed immediately without waiting for imaging.

stem: A 74-year-old retired publican who drinks heavily is brought to his GP by his daughter. Over the past month he has become forgetful, drowsy in the day and unsteady on his feet. Some weeks ago he banged his head on a kitchen cupboard but did not seek help. A CT scan shows a crescentic collection over the left hemisphere that crosses suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines is typical of a subdural haematoma, caused by tearing of bridging veins between the dura and arachnoid. Older people and those with alcohol excess have brain atrophy that stretches these veins, so even minor trauma can cause a slowly enlarging chronic bleed with fluctuating confusion.
why_wrong: B. An extradural haematoma is lens-shaped, limited by sutures and usually follows significant trauma with a lucid interval. C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with sudden severe headache, and blood lies in the subarachnoid spaces. D. Ischaemic stroke causes sudden focal deficits, not a crescentic extra-axial collection. E. A cerebral abscess is a ring-enhancing lesion within the brain, often with fever.
pearl: Chronic subdural haematoma should be considered in any older person with gradually fluctuating confusion, particularly with alcohol excess or anticoagulant use.
thinking: Older man with alcohol excess ↓ Minor head injury weeks ago ↓ Gradual confusion, drowsiness and unsteadiness ↓ Crescentic collection crossing sutures ↓ Chronic subdural haematoma
exam_trap: B, Extradural haematoma — it is the other classic traumatic bleed, but it is lens-shaped and does not cross sutures.
takeaway: A crescentic collection after minor trauma in an older person is a subdural haematoma.

stem: A 57-year-old woman who has been largely confined to bed on a medical ward for a week with a severe chest infection complains of abrupt breathlessness and pleuritic pain, then faints while walking to the toilet. She is grey and clammy, her systolic blood pressure is 75 mmHg despite a fluid bolus, her neck veins are distended and she needs high-flow oxygen. A bedside echo shows a dilated right ventricle. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Send a D-dimer and start anticoagulation only if it is raised
options.B: Start an oral anticoagulant and book a CT pulmonary angiogram for tomorrow
options.C: Manage as high-risk pulmonary embolism: resuscitate, call senior and critical care help now and consider immediate thrombolysis
options.D: Wait for troponin and BNP results to grade severity before any treatment
options.E: Request a ventilation-perfusion scan on the next available routine list

correct_answer: C. Manage as high-risk pulmonary embolism: resuscitate, call senior and critical care help now and consider immediate thrombolysis
why_correct: She has suspected pulmonary embolism with persistent hypotension and right ventricular strain, which defines a high-risk (massive) PE. This is an emergency: resuscitation and immediate senior, critical care and medical input are needed, and NICE advises considering thrombolysis for PE with haemodynamic instability. Routine diagnostic sequencing would waste the time she does not have.
why_wrong: A. D-dimer has no role when the clinical probability is high and the patient is shocked. B. Delayed imaging and an oral agent are for stable patients, not those in obstructive shock. D. Biomarkers help stratify stable patients but must not delay treatment of a shocked one. E. A routine V/Q scan is far too slow and needs a stable patient.
pearl: In suspected PE with haemodynamic instability, bedside echocardiography showing right ventricular dilatation can support the decision to thrombolyse if CT pulmonary angiography cannot be done safely; where thrombolysis is contraindicated (for example after recent major surgery), catheter-directed or surgical embolectomy is considered.
thinking: Immobile inpatient with sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain and syncope ↓ Persistent hypotension despite fluid ↓ Raised JVP and dilated right ventricle suggest obstructive shock ↓ This is high-risk PE ↓ Resuscitate, escalate now and consider thrombolysis
exam_trap: B, Oral anticoagulant and next-day CTPA — this is the correct pathway for a stable patient, so it feels like standard practice, but shock changes the urgency completely.
takeaway: Suspected PE with shock is an immediate emergency needing resuscitation, senior input and consideration of thrombolysis, not routine work-up.

stem: You are off duty in a supermarket when a middle-aged man near you drops to the floor. When you shake his shoulders and speak loudly to him he makes no response. The area around him is safe. What should you do first?

options.A: Place him in the recovery position and recheck him in ten minutes
options.B: Shout for help, open his airway and check for normal breathing, calling 999 and starting CPR if he is not breathing normally
options.C: Feel for a carotid pulse for at least one minute before doing anything else
options.D: Find someone with a glucose meter and check his blood sugar before calling for help
options.E: Wait for the ambulance crew to arrive before touching him further

correct_answer: B. Shout for help, open his airway and check for normal breathing, calling 999 and starting CPR if he is not breathing normally
why_correct: An unresponsive person after sudden collapse may be in cardiac arrest. Resuscitation Council UK guidance is to shout for help, open the airway and look for normal breathing; if breathing is absent or abnormal (including occasional gasps), call 999 and start chest compressions, sending for an AED. Every minute of delay reduces the chance of survival.
why_wrong: A. The recovery position is only for someone who is breathing normally, and he has not been assessed yet. C. A prolonged pulse check delays CPR; lay rescuers rely on breathing assessment and even trained rescuers should take no more than 10 seconds. D. Checking glucose before getting help or assessing breathing delays life-saving action. E. Waiting for the ambulance without starting assessment or CPR loses critical minutes.
pearl: Agonal gasping is common in the first minutes after cardiac arrest and should be treated as absent breathing, so CPR should start.
thinking: Sudden collapse, unresponsive ↓ Scene safe ↓ Shout for help, open airway ↓ Check for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds ↓ Not breathing normally: call 999, start CPR, get an AED
exam_trap: A, Recovery position — it feels like a safe first-aid step, but it is only appropriate once normal breathing is confirmed and can hide a cardiac arrest.
takeaway: After sudden unresponsive collapse, get help and check breathing at once, starting CPR if it is not normal.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency is brought to the emergency department the day after she fractured her wrist in a cycling accident. Because she was in pain and felt nauseated she did not take her medication or adjust her doses. She now has cramping abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, a systolic blood pressure of 72 mmHg that barely responds to fluid, and she is drowsy and muddled. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: In a person with known primary adrenal insufficiency, a physical stressor plus missed glucocorticoid doses can precipitate an adrenal crisis. The picture of abdominal pain, vomiting, refractory hypotension and impaired consciousness fits acute cortisol deficiency. Treatment is immediate parenteral hydrocortisone and IV fluids, without waiting for confirmatory results.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes abdominal pain and vomiting but does not explain the known adrenal history and fluid-refractory shock as well. B. HHS develops over days in people with diabetes, with marked hyperglycaemia. D. Thyroid storm causes fever, tachycardia and agitation rather than this pattern in someone with adrenal failure. E. Myxoedema coma occurs in severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia and bradycardia.
pearl: People with adrenal insufficiency should carry a steroid emergency card and an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit, and follow sick-day rules to increase their dose during illness or injury.
thinking: Known primary adrenal insufficiency ↓ Stressor (injury) plus missed glucocorticoids ↓ Vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion ↓ Hypotension unresponsive to fluid ↓ Adrenal crisis: give hydrocortisone now
exam_trap: A, Acute pancreatitis — abdominal pain with vomiting and shock suggests an abdominal cause, but the known adrenal disease and missed doses make cortisol deficiency the unifying diagnosis.
takeaway: Collapse with vomiting and refractory hypotension in someone with adrenal insufficiency is an adrenal crisis until proven otherwise.

stem: An 84-year-old woman who lives alone is found by her carer on the kitchen floor in the early morning after a fall overnight. The heating had broken and the house is very cold. She is drowsy and slow to answer, her skin is pale and cold to touch, she is not shivering and her pulse is slow. A low-reading thermometer shows a core temperature of 31°C. There is no focal neurological deficit. Which diagnosis best explains her condition?
why_correct: A core temperature below 35°C defines hypothermia, and older people who fall and lie for hours in a cold environment are at particular risk. Drowsiness, bradycardia and loss of shivering suggest it is at least moderate. She needs careful handling, gradual active rewarming and cardiac monitoring.
why_wrong: A. A stroke is not supported when there is no focal deficit, and it would not explain the low core temperature. B. Serotonin syndrome causes hyperthermia, agitation and clonus. C. DKA causes vomiting, dehydration and deep rapid breathing, not this picture. E. Heatstroke is the opposite problem, with a very high core temperature.
pearl: Shivering often stops as hypothermia deepens, so an absence of shivering in a cold, drowsy patient is a warning sign rather than reassurance.
thinking: Long lie after a fall in a cold house ↓ Drowsy, cold, not shivering ↓ Slow pulse ↓ Core temperature below 35°C ↓ Accidental hypothermia
exam_trap: A, Ischaemic stroke — a fall and reduced consciousness in an older person suggest a stroke, but the cold environment, low core temperature and no focal signs explain everything.
takeaway: An older person after a long lie in the cold with low core temperature and drowsiness has accidental hypothermia.

stem: An NHS 111 call handler speaks to a woman worried about her 86-year-old mother, who lives in a top-floor flat with the windows shut. The country is in the middle of a heatwave. Today her mother has been talking nonsense, does not know what day it is and feels burning hot, with dry skin. What is the most concerning diagnosis?
why_correct: Confusion with a very high body temperature and hot skin during a heatwave suggests heatstroke, a life-threatening emergency. Older people in poorly ventilated homes are especially vulnerable. She needs an emergency ambulance and cooling while help arrives.
why_wrong: B. A viral cold does not cause confusion and severe hyperthermia. C. Anxiety does not cause disorientation with hot dry skin. D. Mild dehydration does not explain confusion and very high temperature. E. Hypothyroidism causes cold intolerance and slowing, not hyperthermia.
pearl: While waiting for the ambulance, move the person somewhere cool, remove excess clothing and cool the skin with water and fanning.
thinking: Heatwave, older woman in a hot flat ↓ New confusion ↓ Burning hot dry skin ↓ Hyperthermia with neurological change ↓ Heatstroke: call 999 and start cooling
exam_trap: D, Mild dehydration only — dehydration is common in hot weather, but new confusion with burning skin indicates heatstroke.
takeaway: In a heatwave, an older person who is confused and very hot has heatstroke until proven otherwise.

stem: An 80-year-old woman in a care home was started on oral amoxicillin by her GP two days ago for a chest infection. She arrives in the emergency department much sleepier than usual and not making sense, which her daughter says is new. She is breathing fast, her blood pressure is low and her venous lactate is raised. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Treat as sepsis: urgent senior review, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within the hour and IV fluid resuscitation
options.B: Continue the oral antibiotic, encourage drinks and review her tomorrow
options.C: Hold antibiotics until blood culture results are available
options.D: Attribute the confusion to dementia and refer to the memory service
options.E: Change to a different oral antibiotic and arrange follow-up with her GP

correct_answer: A. Treat as sepsis: urgent senior review, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within the hour and IV fluid resuscitation
why_correct: She has a known infection with new confusion, tachypnoea, hypotension and a raised lactate, which places her at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis. NICE advises immediate senior review, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour and IV fluids. Cultures should be taken, but must not delay treatment.
why_wrong: B. Oral treatment and next-day review ignore clear signs of organ dysfunction. C. Waiting for cultures delays antibiotics that should be given within the hour. D. The confusion is new and acute, so it should be treated as delirium from serious illness, not dementia. E. Oral treatment with community follow-up is unsafe in someone who is shocked.
pearl: In older people, new or worsening confusion may be the earliest or only sign of sepsis, so take a family member's report of change seriously.
thinking: Known chest infection failing oral treatment ↓ New confusion ↓ Tachypnoea and hypotension ↓ Raised lactate ↓ High risk sepsis: antibiotics and fluids within an hour, senior review
exam_trap: D, Attributing confusion to dementia — older care-home residents often have cognitive impairment, but an acute change with abnormal observations is sepsis-related delirium.
takeaway: Infection plus new confusion, hypotension and raised lactate is high-risk sepsis needing IV antibiotics within the hour.

stem: You are the night FY1. A nurse on a medical ward bleeps you about a 74-year-old woman admitted two days ago after a fall. She has become muddled and agitated over the past hour, she is breathing rapidly and her blood pressure is much lower than earlier in the day. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Prescribe haloperidol for agitation and review her if it continues
options.B: Ask the nurse to repeat the observations in four hours
options.C: Document the change and hand it over to the day team in the morning
options.D: Attend immediately, assess her using an ABCDE approach and escalate to a senior
options.E: Leave her for review on the next consultant ward round

correct_answer: D. Attend immediately, assess her using an ABCDE approach and escalate to a senior
why_correct: New confusion, tachypnoea and hypotension are signs of acute serious illness such as sepsis, bleeding or pulmonary embolism. She needs immediate bedside assessment with a structured ABCDE approach, treatment of problems as they are found and early escalation to a senior. Delay risks further deterioration or cardiac arrest.
why_wrong: A. Sedating an agitated patient before finding the cause can mask deterioration and worsen hypotension. B. Four-hourly observations are far too infrequent for a patient with these changes. C. Handing over to the day team delays urgent assessment by hours. E. Waiting for a ward round leaves an unstable patient unassessed.
pearl: Abnormal physiology often precedes in-hospital cardiac arrest by several hours, which is the rationale for track-and-trigger systems such as NEWS2.
thinking: Acute change in a ward patient ↓ New confusion, tachypnoea, hypotension ↓ Possible sepsis, bleeding or PE ↓ See now with ABCDE ↓ Treat and escalate early
exam_trap: A, Haloperidol for agitation — it addresses the behaviour the nurse reports, but treats a symptom of serious illness while ignoring its cause.
takeaway: New confusion with abnormal vital signs on the ward needs immediate ABCDE assessment and escalation.

stem: A GP makes a home visit to a 46-year-old man who has had a red, hot, spreading area on his lower leg for three days. His wife says he has become confused this afternoon. He is breathing quickly, his skin is mottled and his blood pressure is low. What should this presentation prompt?

options.A: Increase the dose of his oral antibiotic and review in 48 hours
options.B: Reassure him that cellulitis takes time to settle
options.C: Emergency ambulance transfer to hospital for immediate assessment and treatment of possible sepsis
options.D: Advise rest and fluids as for a viral illness
options.E: Send a wound swab and decide on treatment when the result returns

correct_answer: C. Emergency ambulance transfer to hospital for immediate assessment and treatment of possible sepsis
why_correct: A suspected infection with new confusion, tachypnoea, hypotension and mottling indicates high risk of severe illness from sepsis. NICE advises urgent emergency transfer to hospital, alerting the receiving team, and giving antibiotics before transfer if the delay would be long and the GP can do so. Community review is not safe.
why_wrong: A. Adjusting oral treatment and reviewing in two days ignores signs of organ dysfunction. B. Reassurance is unsafe when he is confused, hypotensive and mottled. D. This is not a viral illness and needs urgent hospital care. E. Waiting for a swab result delays emergency management.
pearl: In the community, NICE advises that people at high risk of sepsis should be sent to hospital by blue-light ambulance with a pre-alert to the emergency department.
thinking: Skin infection as the source ↓ New confusion ↓ Tachypnoea, hypotension and mottled skin ↓ High risk of sepsis ↓ Emergency transfer for immediate treatment
exam_trap: A, Increasing the oral antibiotic — escalating treatment at home seems proactive, but signs of organ dysfunction mean he needs hospital treatment now.
takeaway: Suspected infection with confusion, hypotension and mottling in the community requires emergency hospital transfer for sepsis.

stem: The husband of a 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide calls an ambulance because she has suddenly developed slurred speech, seems muddled and cannot lift her right arm. On arrival the paramedic notes that she is sweaty. Which bedside test should be done first?
why_correct: Hypoglycaemia can cause focal neurological signs such as hemiparesis and dysphasia that closely mimic a stroke, especially in people taking sulfonylureas or insulin. A capillary glucose is quick, done at the bedside and changes management immediately. Stroke assessment tools require hypoglycaemia to be excluded first.
why_wrong: A. Cholesterol is a long-term vascular risk marker and does not alter immediate care. B. A urine dipstick will not explain or treat an acute neurological deficit. D. Visual acuity testing does not identify a reversible cause. E. HbA1c reflects long-term control, not her glucose now.
pearl: Sulfonylureas such as gliclazide can cause prolonged hypoglycaemia, so patients may need observation after correction.
thinking: Diabetic on a sulfonylurea ↓ Sudden focal neurology and confusion ↓ Sweating suggests hypoglycaemia ↓ Bedside glucose excludes a reversible stroke mimic ↓ Check capillary glucose first
exam_trap: A, Serum cholesterol — it relates to stroke risk, so it sounds relevant, but it does nothing to identify a treatable cause right now.
takeaway: Always check capillary glucose first in anyone with sudden neurological signs, especially if they have diabetes.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing heavy alcohol use is admitted with acute pancreatitis. On her second day on the ward she becomes disorientated, walks with a wide-based unsteady gait and has nystagmus with weakness of lateral gaze in both eyes. Deficiency of which vitamin should be suspected?
why_correct: Confusion, ataxia and eye signs such as nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia in someone with alcohol dependence suggest Wernicke encephalopathy, caused by thiamine deficiency. Vomiting and poor intake from pancreatitis make deficiency more likely. Treat urgently with parenteral thiamine (for example Pabrinex) before giving glucose where possible.
why_wrong: A. B12 deficiency causes anaemia, neuropathy and subacute cord degeneration over months, not acute ophthalmoplegia. B. Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia rather than this acute triad. C. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding problems. D. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and muscle weakness.
pearl: Only a minority of patients show the full classic triad, so NICE advises a low threshold for parenteral thiamine in anyone with alcohol misuse and unexplained confusion, ataxia or eye signs.
thinking: Alcohol dependence with poor intake ↓ Acute confusion ↓ Ataxia ↓ Nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia ↓ Thiamine deficiency: Wernicke encephalopathy
exam_trap: A, Vitamin B12 — it is the vitamin most often linked to neurological problems, but it causes a slow neuropathy rather than acute eye signs and ataxia.
takeaway: Confusion, ataxia and eye-movement abnormalities in alcohol misuse mean Wernicke encephalopathy and need urgent parenteral thiamine.

stem: Paramedics are called to a house party where a 17-year-old with type 1 diabetes cannot be woken. Friends say he injected his usual insulin, drank alcohol and has not eaten. He is breathing, has a pulse and his capillary glucose meter reads well below normal. Which treatment is appropriate?

options.A: Give an additional dose of long-acting insulin
options.B: Pour a sugary drink into his mouth
options.C: Place him in the recovery position and let him sleep it off
options.D: Give glucose immediately by a parenteral route, such as IV glucose or IM glucagon
options.E: Restrict his carbohydrate intake for the next 24 hours

correct_answer: D. Give glucose immediately by a parenteral route, such as IV glucose or IM glucagon
why_correct: He has severe hypoglycaemia with impaired consciousness, which is an emergency. Because he cannot swallow safely, glucose must be given without relying on the oral route: IV glucose (typically 10%) if access is available, or IM glucagon if not. Once he is awake he needs oral carbohydrate to prevent recurrence.
why_wrong: A. More insulin would deepen the hypoglycaemia. B. Fluids by mouth in an unconscious patient risk aspiration. C. Leaving him to sleep allows ongoing neuroglycopenia and risks brain injury. E. Restricting carbohydrate is the opposite of what he needs.
pearl: Alcohol suppresses hepatic glucose production, so glucagon may be less effective after heavy drinking and IV glucose is preferred where possible.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes, insulin plus alcohol, no food ↓ Unrousable ↓ Very low capillary glucose ↓ Cannot swallow safely ↓ Parenteral glucose or IM glucagon now
exam_trap: B, Sugary drink — oral glucose is the right treatment for a conscious patient, but in someone who cannot be woken it risks aspiration.
takeaway: Severe hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness needs immediate IV glucose or IM glucagon, not oral treatment.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother with a high fever after a cold last week. Today he refuses food and drink, is drooling, holds his neck stiffly and will not turn his head, and his breathing has become noisy. There is fullness at the back of the throat on gentle inspection. What is the most important immediate concern?

options.D: A retropharyngeal (deep neck space) abscess threatening the airway

correct_answer: D. A retropharyngeal (deep neck space) abscess threatening the airway
why_correct: Fever, drooling, refusal to swallow, neck stiffness and noisy breathing after an upper respiratory infection in a young child suggest a retropharyngeal abscess. This deep neck infection can compress the airway. Priority is airway protection with senior anaesthetic and ENT input, keeping the child calm, followed by imaging, IV antibiotics and drainage if needed.
why_wrong: A. Simple pharyngitis does not cause drooling, neck stiffness and noisy breathing. B. Reactive nodes may be present but do not explain the threatened airway. C. Muscle spasm would not explain fever, drooling and noisy breathing. E. Aphthous ulcers cause local pain only.
pearl: Retropharyngeal abscess is most common in children under 5 because retropharyngeal lymph nodes are prominent at that age and regress later.
thinking: Young child after a recent URTI ↓ High fever, drooling, refusing to swallow ↓ Neck stiffness and noisy breathing ↓ Deep neck space infection ↓ Airway first: senior anaesthetic and ENT help
exam_trap: B, Reactive lymphadenopathy — swollen neck nodes are common with throat infections, but drooling and noisy breathing signal a deep infection compromising the airway.
takeaway: Drooling, neck stiffness and noisy breathing with fever after a throat infection mean a deep neck abscess threatening the airway.

stem: A 59-year-old woman with pyelonephritis has been on the ward for six hours after receiving IV antibiotics and a fluid bolus. The nurse reports that she is now more confused than on admission, her blood pressure has continued to fall and her breathing is faster. What should happen?

options.A: Carry on with the current plan and review her at the four-hour mark
options.B: Urgent bedside reassessment by a senior clinician with escalation, including critical care review
options.C: Give a sedative to settle her confusion
options.D: Increase her observations to every four hours
options.E: Wait for blood culture results before altering treatment

correct_answer: B. Urgent bedside reassessment by a senior clinician with escalation, including critical care review
why_correct: Worsening confusion, hypotension and tachypnoea despite initial treatment suggest progressive sepsis and possible septic shock. She needs immediate senior reassessment of fluids, antibiotics and source control (for example an obstructed infected kidney), with early critical care involvement for possible vasopressors. NEWS2 and NICE sepsis guidance both call for urgent escalation.
why_wrong: A. Continuing unchanged ignores clear deterioration. C. Sedation masks her conscious level and can worsen hypotension. D. Four-hourly observations are too infrequent for a deteriorating patient. E. Culture results take time and do not justify delaying review.
pearl: In urosepsis that fails to respond, image the urinary tract early to look for obstruction, because an infected obstructed kidney needs urgent drainage.
thinking: Sepsis already treated ↓ Worsening confusion, hypotension, tachypnoea ↓ Not responding ↓ Senior reassessment of fluids, antibiotics and source ↓ Escalate to critical care
exam_trap: D, Increasing observation frequency — more monitoring feels like a response, but she already shows deterioration that needs action now.
takeaway: A patient who worsens despite sepsis treatment needs immediate senior reassessment and escalation, not more waiting.

stem: A 37-year-old man with diabetes is waiting in the emergency department with an infected foot ulcer. At triage he was alert, but two hours later his heart rate has climbed steeply, his blood pressure has dropped and he is now unsure where he is. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Recognise that he may be developing sepsis and escalate urgently for immediate senior review
options.B: Encourage oral fluids and repeat his observations in four hours
options.C: Continue his current oral antibiotics as the infection is already being treated
options.D: Give haloperidol to calm him and review on the next ward round
options.E: Check his observations hourly and mention him at handover

correct_answer: A. Recognise that he may be developing sepsis and escalate urgently for immediate senior review
why_correct: New tachycardia, hypotension and confusion in a patient with infection are high-risk features of sepsis. NICE advises immediate senior assessment, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour and IV fluids. Recognising the change and escalating it at once is the essential step.
why_wrong: B. Oral fluids and four-hourly checks are inadequate for a patient showing signs of shock. C. Being on oral antibiotics does not mean the infection is controlled. D. Sedating him ignores the cause of his confusion. E. Hourly checks and handover delay urgent action.
pearl: Diabetic foot infections can progress rapidly and may involve deep tissue or bone, so look for a collection or necrotising infection needing surgery.
thinking: Known infection source ↓ New tachycardia and hypotension ↓ New confusion ↓ High-risk sepsis criteria ↓ Escalate urgently for IV antibiotics and fluids
exam_trap: E, Hourly observations and handover — it sounds attentive, but monitoring without escalation leaves a deteriorating patient untreated.
takeaway: Tachycardia, hypotension and new confusion with infection mean possible sepsis and need urgent escalation.

presentation: Clinical concern despite a low NEWS2 score
stem: An 88-year-old man with a urinary catheter is on a rehabilitation ward. His NEWS2 score this afternoon is low, but his granddaughter tells the nurse he is not himself and is far more confused than yesterday, and the nurse notices new mottling over his knees and cool hands. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Repeat his observations in four hours as the score is low
options.B: Continue routine monitoring according to the NEWS2 trigger
options.C: Wait for the score to rise before escalating
options.D: Reassess him urgently and escalate despite the low score
options.E: Treat the confusion as delirium with a sedative

correct_answer: D. Reassess him urgently and escalate despite the low score
why_correct: NEWS2 supports clinical judgement but does not replace it. New mottling, cool peripheries and worsening confusion suggest poor perfusion, possibly from catheter-associated sepsis, even if the score is low. Concern from relatives or staff should trigger urgent review and escalation.
why_wrong: A. A low score does not exclude serious illness when there are other worrying signs. B. Routine monitoring ignores the clinical signs of hypoperfusion. C. Waiting for the score to rise may let him deteriorate further. E. Sedation masks his mental state and does not address the likely cause.
pearl: Older adults and people on beta-blockers may not mount a tachycardia or fever, so their NEWS2 can underestimate how unwell they are.
thinking: Low NEWS2 score ↓ Worsening confusion reported by family ↓ New mottling and cool hands ↓ Possible hypoperfusion from sepsis ↓ Escalate on clinical grounds
exam_trap: C, Waiting for the score to rise — it follows the trigger system to the letter, but scores are aids and clinical signs of hypoperfusion override them.
takeaway: Clinical concern such as mottling or new confusion needs urgent escalation even when the NEWS2 score is low.

presentation: Sepsis not responding within an hour
stem: A 50-year-old woman with a suspected urinary source is assessed as high risk for sepsis. Within the first hour she has received IV antibiotics and an IV fluid bolus, but she remains hypotensive, her lactate has not fallen and she is still drowsy. What is the appropriate next step?

options.A: A senior clinical decision-maker should attend in person, critical care should be involved and the consultant informed
options.B: Continue the current plan and review on the next ward round
options.C: Change to oral antibiotics and observe on the ward
options.D: Wait for blood culture results before further escalation

correct_answer: A. A senior clinical decision-maker should attend in person, critical care should be involved and the consultant informed
why_correct: NICE advises that if a person at high risk from sepsis does not respond within one hour of any intervention, the senior clinical decision-maker should attend in person, critical care should be asked to review and the responsible consultant should be told. Persistent hypotension and lactate after fluid suggest septic shock, which may need vasopressors.
why_wrong: B. Waiting for a ward round ignores a lack of response to initial treatment. C. Oral antibiotics are inappropriate in septic shock. D. Culture results take time and should not delay escalation. E. Deferring the lactate until tomorrow wastes the window for treating shock.
pearl: Hypotension persisting despite adequate fluid resuscitation, needing vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure, defines septic shock.
thinking: High risk sepsis ↓ Antibiotics and fluid within the first hour ↓ No response: still hypotensive with high lactate ↓ Possible septic shock ↓ Senior in person, critical care involved, consultant informed
exam_trap: D, Waiting for cultures — targeting therapy sounds sensible, but culture results take days while she needs escalation now.
takeaway: High-risk sepsis that does not respond within an hour needs senior attendance in person and critical care involvement.

stem: Back from a backpacking trip, a 26-year-old woman sees her GP because she has passed profuse watery stools for three days and nearly blacks out whenever she gets out of bed. On examination, which sign would best indicate that she has lost a clinically important amount of fluid from her circulation?

options.E: A fall in blood pressure on standing with light-headedness

correct_answer: E. A fall in blood pressure on standing with light-headedness
why_correct: Fluid losses from profuse diarrhoea reduce circulating volume, so blood pressure drops when she stands and she feels light-headed. A postural drop is one of the most useful bedside signs of hypovolaemia. She needs oral or IV rehydration depending on severity and stool testing given her travel history.
why_wrong: A. Ankle oedema suggests fluid overload or low albumin, not depletion. B. A raised JVP indicates fluid overload or right heart failure. C. Crackles suggest pulmonary oedema or infection. D. Shifting dullness indicates ascites.
pearl: Measure lying and standing blood pressure; a postural drop with symptoms on standing indicates hypovolaemia in a patient losing fluid.
thinking: Profuse watery diarrhoea ↓ Faint on standing ↓ Postural drop indicates low circulating volume ↓ Other options suggest overload ↓ Postural hypotension
exam_trap: B, Raised JVP — it is a key marker of fluid status, but it points to overload; in depletion the JVP is low.
takeaway: Postural hypotension with symptoms is a strong bedside sign of significant volume depletion.

stem: During a norovirus outbreak in his care home, an 81-year-old man has been vomiting and having watery stools for two days. He cannot keep sips down, his tongue is dry, his eyes look sunken and staff say he has passed only a little dark urine. What is the most likely problem?
why_correct: Ongoing vomiting and diarrhoea with inability to take fluids, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes and reduced dark urine indicate fluid depletion. Older adults are particularly vulnerable to dehydration and acute kidney injury. He needs fluid replacement, often IV, plus monitoring of renal function and electrolytes.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary oedema causes breathlessness and crackles, not losses from the gut. B. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and proteinuria. D. Fluid overload is the opposite of this picture. E. Hyperthyroidism may cause loose stools but does not explain acute vomiting and fluid loss in an outbreak.
pearl: Norovirus spreads rapidly in closed settings such as care homes and hospitals; alcohol hand gel is less effective against it than soap and water.
thinking: Outbreak of vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ Cannot keep fluids down ↓ Dry tongue, sunken eyes, low dark urine ↓ Fluid losses exceed intake ↓ Dehydration
exam_trap: D, Fluid overload — older patients are often at risk of overload, but every clue here points to depletion.
takeaway: Vomiting and diarrhoea with dry mucosa and low urine output in an older person means dehydration.

stem: A 24-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant attends the early pregnancy unit after several days of vomiting most of what she eats and drinks. She is tachycardic, feels dizzy when she stands up and has passed very little urine today. What should these findings prompt?

options.C: Assessment for dehydration and hypovolaemia, with fluid replacement

correct_answer: C. Assessment for dehydration and hypovolaemia, with fluid replacement
why_correct: Tachycardia, postural dizziness and oliguria after persistent vomiting indicate dehydration and hypovolaemia. In early pregnancy this suggests hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs assessment including ketones, electrolytes and renal function, plus fluid replacement and antiemetics. RCOG guidance supports ambulatory or inpatient IV fluids depending on severity.
why_wrong: A. Fluid restriction would worsen hypovolaemia. B. Transient biochemical hyperthyroidism can occur with hyperemesis but does not explain these signs and rarely needs treatment. D. Pulmonary oedema causes breathlessness and crackles. E. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and heavy proteinuria.
pearl: In hyperemesis gravidarum, give thiamine to women with prolonged vomiting to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
thinking: Early pregnancy with persistent vomiting ↓ Tachycardia ↓ Postural dizziness ↓ Reduced urine output ↓ Dehydration and hypovolaemia: assess and replace fluids
exam_trap: B, Hyperthyroidism — raised hCG can cause biochemical thyrotoxicosis in hyperemesis, but the signs here reflect fluid loss.
takeaway: Tachycardia, postural dizziness and low urine output after vomiting mean hypovolaemia and need fluid replacement.

stem: A 14-year-old boy was pulled out of a river by friends after going under for a short time. He seemed fine at first, but a few hours later in the emergency department he has a persistent cough, increasing shortness of breath and crackles at both lung bases. Which complication is the main immediate concern?

options.C: Respiratory compromise from aspiration-related lung injury

correct_answer: C. Respiratory compromise from aspiration-related lung injury
why_correct: After submersion, aspiration of water damages surfactant and the alveolar-capillary membrane, causing hypoxia, pulmonary oedema and sometimes acute respiratory distress syndrome. Persistent cough, worsening breathlessness and crackles indicate evolving lung injury. He needs oxygen, monitoring and observation in hospital.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa can follow swimming but is not an immediate threat. B. Muscle cramp does not explain cough, crackles and breathlessness. D. Conjunctivitis is a minor eye problem. E. Appendicitis has no link to submersion.
pearl: Patients who are symptomatic after submersion, even if initially well, need observation because lung injury can develop over several hours.
thinking: Submersion with initial recovery ↓ Hours later: cough and breathlessness ↓ Bibasal crackles ↓ Aspiration lung injury ↓ Oxygen and hospital monitoring
exam_trap: A, Otitis externa — it is linked to water exposure, but it is trivial compared with evolving lung injury.
takeaway: Cough and breathlessness after submersion signal respiratory compromise from aspiration lung injury.

stem: A coastguard team recovers a 67-year-old fisherman from cold harbour water. He is unresponsive, has a palpable pulse and is breathing slowly and shallowly. There is no history of a fall or dive. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Arrange a cervical spine X-ray before any intervention
options.B: Rewarm him fully before assessing his airway and breathing
options.C: Perform abdominal thrusts to expel inhaled water
options.D: Open and support his airway and breathing, ventilating with oxygen
options.E: Obtain a chest X-ray before deciding on treatment

correct_answer: D. Open and support his airway and breathing, ventilating with oxygen
why_correct: Drowning causes hypoxia, so the immediate priority is to open the airway and support breathing, giving oxygen and assisted ventilation as needed. Hypothermia should also be managed, but it does not take precedence over airway and breathing. Cervical spine precautions are only needed if trauma is suspected.
why_wrong: A. Imaging the cervical spine delays resuscitation and is not indicated without a history of trauma. B. Rewarming is important but must not delay airway and breathing support. C. Abdominal thrusts do not clear aspirated water and delay ventilation. E. A chest X-ray should not delay immediate airway management.
pearl: Routine cervical spine immobilisation is not needed after drowning unless there is a history of diving, trauma or other injury.
thinking: Recovered from water ↓ Unresponsive with a pulse ↓ Breathing inadequate ↓ Hypoxia is the core problem ↓ Airway and breathing support with oxygen first
exam_trap: B, Rewarming first — cold water makes hypothermia salient, but hypoxia kills faster and airway and breathing come first.
takeaway: After drowning with inadequate breathing, support the airway and ventilation with oxygen before anything else.

stem: During a summer storm, a group of hikers sheltering under a tree are struck by lightning. Several are dazed with minor burns, but a 52-year-old man in the group is found lying motionless and unresponsive. Which consequence is most important to address first when assessing him?
correct_answer: A. Cardiac arrest and neurological injury
why_correct: Lightning delivers a massive brief current that can cause immediate cardiac arrest, usually asystole, and respiratory arrest from injury to the brainstem respiratory centre. An unresponsive victim needs immediate assessment of airway, breathing and circulation and prompt CPR if he is in arrest, along with recognition of neurological injury.
why_wrong: B. Kidney stones are not an immediate consequence of lightning. C. Chronic liver failure develops over years and is unrelated. D. Appendicitis is not caused by lightning or blunt trauma in this way. E. Stress ulcer perforation is not an immediate concern at the scene.
pearl: At a lightning strike with several casualties, use reverse triage: those who appear dead are treated first, because prolonged ventilation and CPR can save victims whose heart restarts but whose breathing does not.
thinking: Lightning strike, multiple casualties ↓ He is unresponsive and motionless ↓ Lightning causes cardiac and respiratory arrest ↓ Neurological injury is common ↓ Assess ABC and start CPR if needed
exam_trap: E, Perforated stress ulcer — critical illness can cause stress ulceration, but this is a later complication and not what threatens his life in the first minutes.
takeaway: After a lightning strike, the immediate threats are cardiac arrest and neurological injury, so start with airway, breathing and circulation.

stem: A 61-year-old woman with heart failure, taking spironolactone and ramipril, is admitted feeling weak. Her serum potassium is markedly raised and her ECG shows broad QRS complexes with loss of P waves. Before measures to lower her potassium can take effect, which treatment should be given first to stabilise the heart?
why_correct: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, intravenous calcium stabilises the cardiac cell membrane within minutes and reduces the risk of fatal arrhythmia. It does not lower the serum potassium, so it must be followed by treatments that shift potassium into cells and remove it from the body. Her spironolactone and ramipril should also be stopped.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol shifts potassium into cells but does not protect the myocardium directly. B. Magnesium is used for torsades de pointes and hypomagnesaemia, not membrane stabilisation in hyperkalaemia. C. Potassium binders act over hours and remove potassium rather than protect the heart. D. Furosemide can increase potassium loss in some patients but is neither rapid nor cardioprotective.
pearl: Repeat the ECG after calcium and give further doses if changes persist; its protective effect lasts only around 30 to 60 minutes.
thinking: Spironolactone plus ACE inhibitor ↓ Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ ECG changes present ↓ Protect the heart before lowering potassium ↓ Give intravenous calcium
exam_trap: A, Nebulised salbutamol — it is part of acute hyperkalaemia treatment and works quickly, but it lowers serum potassium by shifting it rather than stabilising the cardiac membrane.
takeaway: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, intravenous calcium comes first to protect the heart.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is admitted with rhabdomyolysis after being found on the floor at home following a prolonged lie. Her potassium is dangerously high. The registrar explains that one treatment lowers blood potassium within about 15 to 30 minutes by driving it into cells, without removing any from the body. Which treatment is being described?
correct_answer: B. Intravenous soluble insulin with glucose
why_correct: Insulin stimulates the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, moving potassium from the blood into cells and lowering the serum level within minutes. Glucose is given with it to prevent hypoglycaemia, and capillary glucose must be monitored for several hours. Because total body potassium is unchanged, definitive removal still has to follow.
why_wrong: A. Haemodialysis removes potassium from the body rather than shifting it. C. Calcium protects the heart but does not change the potassium level. D. Potassium binders remove potassium through the gut and act more slowly. E. Furosemide increases renal excretion rather than shifting potassium into cells.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia is a common harm after insulin-glucose therapy, particularly in patients with kidney impairment, so check blood glucose regularly for several hours.
thinking: Rhabdomyolysis releases potassium ↓ Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ Need a rapid temporary fall ↓ Insulin drives potassium into cells ↓ Give insulin with glucose and monitor glucose
exam_trap: C, Intravenous calcium gluconate — it is the other drug given early in the emergency, but it protects the myocardium without lowering serum potassium at all.
takeaway: Insulin with glucose temporarily lowers serum potassium by shifting it into cells.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department from a music festival. She took ecstasy (MDMA) and then drank large volumes of water. Over a few hours she became muddled and vomited, and she has just had a tonic-clonic seizure. Her serum sodium is very low. What is the main mechanism underlying her neurological features?

options.C: Shrinkage of brain cells from dehydration
options.E: Water moving into brain cells, causing cerebral oedema

correct_answer: E. Water moving into brain cells, causing cerebral oedema
why_correct: When serum sodium falls rapidly, the extracellular fluid becomes hypotonic relative to brain cells and water moves into them. The brain has had no time to adapt by losing solutes, so cerebral oedema develops, causing headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures and potentially herniation. MDMA promotes ADH release and is often combined with heavy water intake.
why_wrong: A. Hyperviscosity is not caused by low sodium. B. Peripheral demyelination does not explain seizures and confusion. C. Brain cell shrinkage occurs with hypernatraemia, not acute hyponatraemia. D. Red cell production is not relevant.
pearl: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination, whereas symptomatic acute hyponatraemia with seizures needs urgent hypertonic saline under specialist guidance.
thinking: MDMA plus large water intake ↓ Sodium fell over hours ↓ Plasma becomes hypotonic ↓ Water enters brain cells ↓ Cerebral oedema causes seizures
exam_trap: C, Brain cell shrinkage from dehydration — it reverses the direction of water movement, which is the mechanism in hypernatraemia rather than hyponatraemia.
takeaway: Acute hyponatraemia causes neurological symptoms through cerebral oedema.

stem: On the renal ward, routine bloods for a 79-year-old man show severe hyperkalaemia, confirmed on a repeat sample. He is now bradycardic, and his ECG shows wide QRS complexes. The registrar asks for a drug that acts within minutes to protect the heart but does not itself reduce the potassium level. Which drug is needed?
why_correct: Intravenous calcium antagonises the effect of high potassium on the cardiac cell membrane, reducing the risk of arrhythmia within minutes. It does not lower serum potassium, so insulin with glucose and measures to remove potassium must follow. The ECG should be repeated, and further calcium given if changes persist.
why_wrong: A. Oral calcium is far too slow and is not used for cardioprotection. B. Iron has no role in hyperkalaemia. C. Hydroxocobalamin treats vitamin B12 deficiency and cyanide poisoning. D. Insulin should be given intravenously with glucose, and it lowers potassium rather than protecting the membrane.
pearl: Calcium chloride contains about three times as much calcium as the same volume of calcium gluconate but is more irritant to veins, so it is often reserved for cardiac arrest or central access.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia confirmed ↓ Bradycardia and broad QRS ↓ Imminent risk of arrhythmia ↓ Need rapid membrane stabilisation ↓ Intravenous calcium gluconate
exam_trap: D, Insulin without glucose — insulin belongs in hyperkalaemia treatment, but it shifts potassium rather than protecting the heart, and omitting glucose risks hypoglycaemia.
takeaway: Intravenous calcium protects the heart in hyperkalaemia but does not lower potassium.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes takes an ACE inhibitor and was recently given trimethoprim for a urinary infection. She visits her GP with generalised muscle weakness and is sent to the emergency department, where her potassium is severely raised and her ECG is abnormal. Which treatment is needed urgently to protect her heart?
why_correct: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes risks fatal arrhythmia, and intravenous calcium stabilises the myocardium within minutes. Trimethoprim reduces renal potassium excretion and adds to the effect of an ACE inhibitor. After calcium, she needs insulin with glucose, review of her medicines and treatment to remove potassium.
why_wrong: A. Fluid restriction does not protect the heart and may worsen kidney function. C. Binders act over hours and are not an emergency cardioprotective measure. D. Vitamin B12 has no role in hyperkalaemia. E. Iron has no role in hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Trimethoprim acts like the potassium-sparing diuretic amiloride on the distal tubule, so it can cause hyperkalaemia, especially with ACE inhibitors or kidney impairment.
thinking: ACE inhibitor plus trimethoprim ↓ Muscle weakness ↓ Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes ↓ Risk of arrhythmia ↓ Intravenous calcium to protect the heart
exam_trap: C, Oral patiromer on its own — binders are part of hyperkalaemia management, but they are slow and do nothing to protect the heart in the emergency.
takeaway: When hyperkalaemia causes ECG changes, give intravenous calcium first.

stem: A 49-year-old man on haemodialysis missed two sessions while away on holiday. At the dialysis unit he feels weak, and a blood gas shows a high potassium. His ECG shows tall, narrow-based T waves. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Low-potassium dietary advice and repeat bloods next week
options.B: Review at his next routine renal clinic
options.C: Increase his diuretic dose and recheck bloods tomorrow
options.D: Treat the hyperkalaemia urgently as an emergency
options.E: Start oral sodium bicarbonate and review him in clinic

correct_answer: D. Treat the hyperkalaemia urgently as an emergency
why_correct: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes can progress without warning to ventricular arrhythmia or asystole. It needs emergency treatment now: intravenous calcium, insulin with glucose and, for a dialysis patient, urgent dialysis to remove potassium. Delaying for dietary or outpatient measures risks cardiac arrest.
why_wrong: A. Dietary advice matters long term but does nothing for an immediate risk. B. Outpatient review is far too slow. C. Many dialysis patients pass little urine, and diuretics are too slow and unreliable here. E. Bicarbonate is not a first-line emergency treatment and clinic review is too slow.
pearl: In patients on haemodialysis, missed sessions are a common cause of severe hyperkalaemia, and dialysis is the definitive treatment.
thinking: On haemodialysis, missed sessions ↓ Weakness ↓ High potassium on blood gas ↓ ECG changes present ↓ Emergency treatment now
exam_trap: A, Dietary advice and repeat bloods — reducing potassium intake is sensible for the future, but it ignores the immediate arrhythmia risk shown by the ECG.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is an emergency needing immediate treatment.

stem: A 17-year-old girl falls from a horse and strikes the right side of her head at the temple. She is briefly dazed but then chats normally in the emergency department for an hour before becoming increasingly drowsy, with a dilating right pupil. Non-contrast CT shows a lens-shaped hyperdense collection between the skull and the brain that does not cross the suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A blow to the temple can fracture the thin squamous temporal bone and tear the middle meningeal artery, producing an arterial bleed between the skull and dura. Because the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, the blood forms a convex lens shape that does not cross them. A period of apparent recovery followed by rapid deterioration is classic and needs urgent neurosurgical evacuation.
why_wrong: A. A subdural haematoma is crescent-shaped and can cross suture lines. B. Subarachnoid blood lies in the sulci and basal cisterns rather than forming a lens-shaped collection. C. Intracerebral haemorrhage lies within the brain tissue rather than outside it. E. Ischaemic stroke does not cause an extra-axial collection and appears hypodense or normal early on.
pearl: The pterion is the weakest point of the skull and lies directly over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
thinking: Blow to the temple ↓ Lucid interval then drowsiness ↓ Pupil on the injured side dilating ↓ Lens-shaped collection not crossing sutures ↓ Extradural haematoma
exam_trap: A, Acute subdural haematoma — it is the commonest traumatic extra-axial bleed, but it is crescent-shaped and crosses sutures rather than forming a biconvex lens.
takeaway: A lens-shaped extra-axial bleed after a temporal blow, often with a lucid interval, is an extradural haematoma.

stem: An 81-year-old man taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a brisk nosebleed that has not stopped despite pinching his nose at home. Blood is running down the back of his throat and he looks pale and clammy. What should be done first?

options.A: Reverse his anticoagulation before attempting any first aid
options.B: Assess airway, breathing and circulation and resuscitate while acting to stop the bleeding
options.C: Insert an anterior nasal pack and discharge him home
options.D: Arrange an urgent ENT outpatient appointment
options.E: Give oral tranexamic acid and observe him at home

correct_answer: B. Assess airway, breathing and circulation and resuscitate while acting to stop the bleeding
why_correct: He has heavy ongoing bleeding with signs of shock, so the priority is an ABCDE approach: protect the airway, gain intravenous access, send blood for count, clotting and group and save, and give fluids or blood as needed. At the same time, first-aid pressure and local measures such as packing should be used to control the bleeding. Decisions about anticoagulant reversal follow alongside this, not before.
why_wrong: A. Reversal may be needed, but it must not delay resuscitation and simple measures to control bleeding. C. A shocked patient with brisk bleeding cannot be sent home. D. Outpatient review ignores an active emergency. E. Home observation is unsafe in someone pale, clammy and still bleeding.
pearl: Posterior epistaxis is more common in older patients and those on anticoagulants; blood running into the throat despite anterior pressure suggests a posterior source.
thinking: Elderly, on a DOAC ↓ Heavy ongoing nosebleed ↓ Pale and clammy, so shocked ↓ ABCDE resuscitation first ↓ Control bleeding at the same time
exam_trap: A, Reversing the anticoagulant first — the anticoagulant is clearly contributing, but resuscitation and direct control of bleeding come first and reversal must not delay them.
takeaway: Heavy ongoing epistaxis is managed with ABCDE resuscitation alongside direct control of bleeding.

stem: In the school canteen, a 15-year-old girl bites into a dessert containing cashew nuts, which she has never eaten before. Within minutes her lips and tongue begin to swell and she says her mouth feels tight. What is the most concerning associated complication?
correct_answer: C. Obstruction of the upper airway
why_correct: Swelling of the tongue and lips soon after a food allergen suggests an IgE-mediated reaction that may form part of anaphylaxis. The swelling can spread to the pharynx and larynx and block the airway, so she needs urgent assessment and IM adrenaline if there are airway, breathing or circulation problems.
why_wrong: A. Kidney injury is not a direct complication of lip and tongue swelling. B. Cataract is unrelated. D. Urinary retention is unrelated. E. Renal colic is unrelated.
pearl: Tree nuts and peanuts are among the commonest causes of fatal food anaphylaxis in young people, and coexisting asthma increases the risk.
thinking: New food, tree nuts ↓ Rapid lip and tongue swelling ↓ Allergic reaction, possibly anaphylaxis ↓ Swelling may spread to larynx ↓ Airway obstruction is the main danger
exam_trap: A, Acute kidney injury — prolonged shock from anaphylaxis can affect the kidneys, but it is not the immediate threat from tongue swelling.
takeaway: Tongue and lip swelling after a food allergen threatens the airway.

stem: A 50-year-old woman is having her first infusion of intravenous iron in a day unit. Within a few minutes her face becomes swollen, she starts to wheeze and her blood pressure falls. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: An expected side effect of the infusion

why_correct: Sudden airway or breathing problems with circulatory compromise after exposure to a trigger fulfil the criteria for anaphylaxis. The infusion should be stopped and IM adrenaline given immediately, following the Resuscitation Council UK algorithm, with high-flow oxygen and intravenous fluids.
why_wrong: A. Facial swelling, wheeze and hypotension are life-threatening and not an expected effect. B. The speed of onset after drug exposure does not fit a viral illness. D. A vasovagal episode causes bradycardia and pallor without wheeze or facial swelling. E. Intolerance does not cause wheeze, swelling and hypotension.
pearl: Intravenous iron should only be given where staff and equipment for treating anaphylaxis are immediately available, with observation for at least 30 minutes afterwards.
thinking: Intravenous drug started ↓ Minutes later facial swelling ↓ Wheeze plus hypotension ↓ Airway, breathing and circulation involved ↓ Possible anaphylaxis
exam_trap: D, A vasovagal faint — the fall in blood pressure can make this tempting, but a faint does not cause wheeze or facial swelling.
takeaway: Swelling, wheeze and hypotension soon after a drug should be treated as anaphylaxis.

stem: A 58-year-old man was started on lisinopril three weeks ago. He attends an urgent treatment centre because his tongue and the floor of his mouth have swollen over the last few hours. He is now struggling to speak clearly and feels breathless. What is the most important concern?
why_correct: ACE inhibitors reduce the breakdown of bradykinin and can cause angioedema of the tongue, floor of the mouth and larynx. Difficulty speaking and breathlessness suggest the airway is becoming compromised, which is a life-threatening emergency needing immediate transfer and senior airway support.
why_wrong: B. Reflux does not cause acute swelling of the tongue. C. Thrush causes white plaques, not acute swelling. D. Dry mouth does not cause objective swelling or breathlessness. E. Panic does not cause measurable swelling of the tongue.
pearl: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema responds poorly to adrenaline, antihistamines and steroids, so early airway planning is vital.
thinking: Recently started an ACE inhibitor ↓ Tongue and floor of mouth swelling ↓ Speech difficulty and breathlessness ↓ Airway at risk ↓ Angioedema compromising the airway
exam_trap: E, Panic attack — anxiety and breathlessness can coexist, but panic does not explain objective swelling of the tongue.
takeaway: Tongue swelling with breathlessness on an ACE inhibitor is airway-threatening angioedema.

stem: At a birthday party, a 13-year-old boy eats chicken satay. Within minutes his face swells, he becomes wheezy and he says he cannot get his breath. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Satay sauce is made with peanuts, and a sudden reaction causing facial swelling, wheeze and breathing difficulty within minutes is anaphylaxis. He needs IM adrenaline into the outer thigh straight away, with an ambulance called.
why_wrong: A. Hay fever causes sneezing and a runny nose, not facial swelling with breathing difficulty. C. A viral infection does not begin within minutes of eating. D. Urticaria alone does not cause wheeze or breathing problems. E. Contact dermatitis is a delayed skin reaction.
pearl: Anyone treated for anaphylaxis should be observed after treatment, referred to an allergy service and, where appropriate, given two adrenaline auto-injectors with training.
thinking: Peanut exposure in satay ↓ Onset within minutes ↓ Facial swelling ↓ Wheeze and breathlessness ↓ Anaphylaxis
exam_trap: D, Urticaria alone — skin features are common in allergy, but wheeze and breathing difficulty mean this is more than a skin reaction.
takeaway: Facial swelling with wheeze and breathing difficulty soon after an allergen is anaphylaxis.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has taken perindopril for many years without problems. She wakes with a swollen tongue and lips, and on arrival in the emergency department her breathing is noisy. She has no rash, no itch and no family history of similar swelling. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Hereditary angioedema presenting for the first time
options.C: Angioedema caused by her ACE inhibitor, putting her airway at risk
options.D: Allergic contact dermatitis of the lips

correct_answer: C. Angioedema caused by her ACE inhibitor, putting her airway at risk
why_correct: ACE inhibitor angioedema can occur at any point in treatment, including after many years. Swelling of the tongue and lips without urticaria, together with noisy breathing, indicates the upper airway is involved, so this needs immediate airway assessment and senior help. The ACE inhibitor must be stopped permanently.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary angioedema usually starts in childhood or adolescence, often with a family history. B. Sialadenitis causes painful swelling of one salivary gland, not tongue swelling. D. Contact dermatitis causes itchy, inflamed skin rather than deep swelling with airway compromise. E. A lichenoid eruption causes a chronic rash, not acute swelling.
pearl: Angiotensin receptor blockers can occasionally cause angioedema too, so switching to one after ACE inhibitor angioedema needs caution and specialist advice.
thinking: Long-term ACE inhibitor ↓ Tongue and lip swelling ↓ No urticaria or itch ↓ Noisy breathing, so airway involved ↓ ACE inhibitor angioedema threatening the airway
