exam_trap: A, First presentation of hereditary angioedema — swelling without urticaria fits, but onset in older age without a family history makes the drug the far likelier cause.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor angioedema can appear after years of uneventful treatment and can threaten the airway.

stem: A 63-year-old man with lymphoma had his last cycle of chemotherapy eight days ago. He rings the acute oncology helpline because he feels hot and shivery, and his wife has measured a fever. He is asked to attend, and his blood count shows a severely low neutrophil count. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Wait for blood culture results before deciding on antibiotics
options.B: Reassure him that fever is common after chemotherapy
options.C: Treat this as an emergency with urgent assessment and intravenous antibiotics
options.D: Give paracetamol and review him in clinic in two days
options.E: Start G-CSF alone and recheck his blood count

correct_answer: C. Treat this as an emergency with urgent assessment and intravenous antibiotics
why_correct: Fever around a week after chemotherapy with severe neutropenia is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise. Infection can progress rapidly without the usual signs because there are few neutrophils to mount a response. NICE advises treating suspected neutropenic sepsis as an acute medical emergency and starting empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for cultures delays life-saving treatment. B. Fever with neutropenia must never be dismissed as an expected effect. D. Paracetamol may mask fever and delay treatment. E. G-CSF is not a substitute for antibiotics.
pearl: The neutrophil nadir after most chemotherapy regimens occurs around 7 to 14 days after treatment.
thinking: Recent chemotherapy ↓ Fever and shivering ↓ Severe neutropenia ↓ Neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise ↓ Urgent assessment and IV antibiotics
exam_trap: E, G-CSF alone — growth factors can shorten neutropenia, which makes this seem logical, but they do not treat the infection.
takeaway: Fever after chemotherapy with neutropenia is an emergency needing immediate intravenous antibiotics.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with known severe idiopathic neutropenia, followed up by the haematology clinic, attends the emergency department with fever and shivering. Her blood count confirms a very low neutrophil count. She looks flushed but is alert and talking. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours
options.B: Start G-CSF and repeat the blood count tomorrow
options.D: Take blood cultures and wait for the results before treating

correct_answer: C. Urgent empirical intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
why_correct: Fever in someone with significant neutropenia from any cause should be treated as neutropenic sepsis. She may deteriorate quickly despite looking well, so cultures should be taken and empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics started without delay.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics with delayed review is not safe initial management for fever with severe neutropenia. B. G-CSF does not treat infection and delays antibiotics. D. Cultures are important but must not delay treatment. E. Discharge without treatment risks rapid deterioration.
pearl: Looking well on arrival does not reassure in neutropenic fever; only after senior risk assessment and initial treatment can selected low-risk patients be considered for oral step-down.
thinking: Known severe neutropenia ↓ New fever and shivering ↓ Looks well but risk is high ↓ Treat as neutropenic sepsis ↓ Urgent empirical IV antibiotics
exam_trap: D, Take cultures and await results — cultures are part of the work-up, but waiting for them delays treatment of a potentially fatal infection.
takeaway: Fever with severe neutropenia from any cause needs urgent empirical intravenous antibiotics.

stem: A 37-year-old man having chemotherapy for testicular cancer arrives at the acute oncology unit with a fever. A rapid blood count shows severe neutropenia, and blood cultures have already been taken. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: G-CSF alone with review in 24 hours
options.B: Empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately, within the first hour
options.C: Wait for blood culture results before starting antibiotics
options.D: Oral antibiotics and a haematology review the next day

correct_answer: B. Empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately, within the first hour
why_correct: Suspected neutropenic sepsis is an acute medical emergency. NICE advises giving empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately, and within an hour of arrival for anyone at high risk of sepsis; with cultures already taken there is no reason to delay. Local protocols usually recommend piperacillin with tazobactam.
why_wrong: A. G-CSF does not treat infection and is not a substitute for antibiotics. C. Waiting for cultures delays urgent treatment. D. Oral therapy with next-day review is unsafe at presentation. E. Platelets and paracetamol do not treat infection.
pearl: Do not wait for the neutrophil count if neutropenic sepsis is suspected clinically; start antibiotics on suspicion.
thinking: Chemotherapy, now febrile ↓ Severe neutropenia ↓ Cultures already taken ↓ Neutropenic sepsis is an emergency ↓ Immediate empirical IV antibiotics
exam_trap: C, Wait for culture results — targeting therapy seems sensible, but untreated neutropenic sepsis can be fatal within hours, so antibiotics come first.
takeaway: In suspected neutropenic sepsis, start empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately.

stem: A 66-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for ovarian cancer is admitted with rigors and a fever, and neutropenic sepsis is suspected. Intravenous antibiotics are being prepared. Which investigation should be taken first, as long as it does not delay the antibiotics?
why_correct: Blood cultures taken before antibiotics give the best chance of identifying the organism and its sensitivities, so treatment can later be targeted. In a patient with a central line, cultures should be taken from the line and peripherally. They must not delay starting antibiotics in suspected neutropenic sepsis.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy is not part of the emergency work-up and is risky in neutropenia. B. A DXA scan measures bone density and is irrelevant. C. Skin-prick testing is for allergy and irrelevant here. E. An exercise test is for coronary disease and inappropriate in sepsis.
pearl: Other initial investigations include a full blood count, kidney and liver tests, CRP, lactate and cultures from any suspected source, such as urine.
thinking: Chemotherapy with fever and rigors ↓ Suspected neutropenic sepsis ↓ Antibiotics must start without delay ↓ Cultures before antibiotics if no delay ↓ Blood cultures
exam_trap: A, Colonoscopy — searching for a gut source might seem thorough, but invasive procedures are not part of the emergency work-up and are hazardous in neutropenia.
takeaway: Take blood cultures before antibiotics in suspected neutropenic sepsis, but never let them delay treatment.

stem: A care home nurse telephones the GP about an 83-year-old resident who has become muddled and sleepy since yesterday. She has developed a new wet cough and feels hot to touch. The nurse adds that she is breathing quickly and that her blood pressure is lower than her usual readings. Which condition is most important to recognise?

options.A: Progression of her known vascular dementia

why_correct: A probable chest infection with new confusion, a raised respiratory rate and low blood pressure indicates a dysregulated host response to infection, which is sepsis. Each of these features is a high-risk marker in NICE sepsis risk stratification, so she needs urgent face-to-face assessment and likely emergency admission for antibiotics and fluids.
why_wrong: A. Dementia progresses gradually and does not cause fever, cough or hypotension over a day. C. Constipation can trigger delirium but would not explain fever, tachypnoea and low blood pressure. D. A TIA causes transient focal deficits, not fever and global drowsiness. E. Polymyalgia causes proximal girdle pain and stiffness, not acute confusion and shock.
pearl: In older people, new confusion or a change in behaviour may be the only early sign of sepsis, and fever can be absent.
thinking: New cough and feeling hot suggest infection ↓ Acute confusion and drowsiness ↓ Fast breathing and low blood pressure ↓ Organ dysfunction from infection ↓ Sepsis needing emergency treatment
exam_trap: C, Hypoactive delirium caused by constipation — delirium is common in care home residents, but it ignores the infective source and the haemodynamic compromise that mark this as sepsis.
takeaway: In an older person, infection plus new confusion, tachypnoea or hypotension should be treated as sepsis until proven otherwise.

stem: Over an NHS 111 call, a mother describes her 16-year-old son, who woke with a high temperature, aching legs and a headache. In the last hour she has noticed dark red spots on his chest that do not fade when she presses a glass tumbler against them. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Treat as a medical emergency for suspected meningococcal disease and send an emergency ambulance
options.B: Advise paracetamol and fluids and ask her to call back if he worsens
options.C: Book a routine GP appointment for tomorrow morning
options.D: Recommend an oral antihistamine for a presumed allergic rash
options.E: Reassure her that this is most likely a viral rash

correct_answer: A. Treat as a medical emergency for suspected meningococcal disease and send an emergency ambulance
why_correct: Fever with a non-blanching rash in a young person must be treated as meningococcal disease until proven otherwise, because septicaemia can progress to shock within hours. The correct action is immediate emergency transfer to hospital, with parenteral benzylpenicillin given beforehand if a clinician can do so without delaying transport.
why_wrong: B. Home care with a safety-net wastes time in a potentially rapidly fatal illness. C. Waiting until the next day is unsafe. D. An allergic rash typically blanches and is not accompanied by fever and limb pain. E. A non-blanching rash with fever cannot be assumed to be benign.
pearl: Leg pain, cold hands and feet and abnormal skin colour are early features of meningococcal septicaemia that often appear before the classic rash.
thinking: Fever and headache in a teenager ↓ Limb pain as an early warning feature ↓ Rash that does not fade under a glass ↓ Possible meningococcal septicaemia ↓ Emergency ambulance now
exam_trap: E, Reassuring her that it is viral — many feverish rashes are viral, but a non-blanching rash changes the risk completely and must never be dismissed over the phone.
takeaway: Fever plus a non-blanching rash means emergency treatment for suspected meningococcal disease.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who lives in a shared university residence is brought to the emergency department by her flatmate. Since this morning she has had rigors, an intense headache and pain on bending her neck forwards. A few purple spots that do not fade under pressure are seen around her ankles. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: The combination of an abrupt febrile illness, meningism and a non-blanching petechial rash in a young adult living in close-contact accommodation points to invasive meningococcal disease. It requires immediate parenteral antibiotics and senior input, and close contacts will need public health follow-up.
why_wrong: A. Subarachnoid haemorrhage causes a thunderclap headache and neck stiffness but not rigors or a petechial rash. B. Migraine does not cause fever, meningism or purpura. C. Viral meningitis causes headache and neck stiffness but not a non-blanching rash. E. IgA vasculitis causes a palpable purpuric rash on the legs but not meningism or rigors.
pearl: Close contacts of a confirmed case are offered antibiotic prophylaxis, usually a single dose of ciprofloxacin, arranged with the UKHSA health protection team.
thinking: Young adult in shared accommodation ↓ Rigors and severe headache ↓ Neck stiffness indicates meningism ↓ Non-blanching petechiae ↓ Meningococcal disease
exam_trap: C, Viral meningitis — it explains the headache and neck stiffness, but a non-blanching rash points to bacterial meningococcal infection.
takeaway: Meningism with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.

stem: An 18-month-old girl is carried into the resuscitation area by her father. She has been feverish since the night and is now floppy, only briefly opening her eyes to a painful stimulus. Scattered petechiae and larger purple patches are seen on her trunk and legs. Intravenous access has just been obtained. Which treatment should be given now?

options.B: Paracetamol and review in an hour
options.C: Antibiotics deferred until a lumbar puncture has been done

why_correct: A febrile toddler with a purpuric rash and reduced consciousness has presumed meningococcal septicaemia, and the priority alongside resuscitation is immediate intravenous antibiotics. A third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone is the recommended empirical choice in this age group and must not be delayed for investigations.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics are inadequate and unreliable in a critically ill child. B. Antipyretics do not treat the infection and delay is dangerous. C. Lumbar puncture should not delay antibiotics and is contraindicated in a child who is shocked or has reduced consciousness. E. Steroids are not a substitute for antibiotics.
pearl: In children younger than 3 months, NICE advises adding amoxicillin to cover Listeria in suspected bacterial meningitis.
thinking: Fever in a toddler ↓ Purpuric, non-blanching rash ↓ Responds only to pain ↓ Presumed meningococcal septicaemia ↓ Intravenous ceftriaxone without delay
exam_trap: C, Deferring antibiotics until after a lumbar puncture — it seems to secure a diagnosis, but it delays treatment and lumbar puncture is unsafe in a child with impaired consciousness.
takeaway: In suspected meningococcal disease, give intravenous antibiotics immediately and investigate afterwards.

presentation: Suspected meningococcal disease in primary care
stem: An out-of-hours GP visits a 7-year-old boy at home. His mother says he has been hot and listless since lunchtime and has refused his tea. On examination there are several pinpoint and blotchy purple lesions on his thighs that remain visible when the skin is pressed. What should the GP do?

options.A: Take blood for a full blood count and decide once the result is back
options.B: Give parenteral benzylpenicillin and arrange emergency hospital transfer
options.C: Prescribe oral antibiotics and review tomorrow
options.D: Advise antipyretics and give safety-netting advice
options.E: Refer to the next paediatric outpatient clinic

correct_answer: B. Give parenteral benzylpenicillin and arrange emergency hospital transfer
why_correct: A febrile, listless child with a non-blanching rash must be managed as suspected meningococcal disease. In primary care NICE advises giving intramuscular or intravenous benzylpenicillin as soon as possible, provided this does not delay transfer, and arranging an emergency ambulance to hospital.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for blood results delays life-saving treatment. C. Oral antibiotics and next-day review are inadequate for invasive bacterial infection. D. Treating the fever alone ignores a life-threatening cause. E. An outpatient referral is far too slow.
pearl: If benzylpenicillin is unavailable or contraindicated in the community, transfer to hospital must still not be delayed.
thinking: Child with fever and lethargy ↓ Rash that does not blanch ↓ Suspected meningococcal disease ↓ Benzylpenicillin if it does not delay transfer ↓ Emergency ambulance to hospital
exam_trap: A, Taking blood and deciding once the result is back — it feels thorough, but a normal blood count does not exclude meningococcal disease and the delay is dangerous.
takeaway: In the community, give benzylpenicillin and transfer urgently for a feverish child with a non-blanching rash.

stem: A 34-year-old man with acute myeloid leukaemia is on the haematology ward a week after induction treatment. During the night he becomes hot and has a shaking episode. His most recent blood count showed almost no neutrophils. He is alert and talking. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give paracetamol and recheck his temperature in a few hours
options.B: Assess him urgently and give intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics without delay
options.C: Take blood cultures and start antibiotics only if they grow an organism
options.D: Give granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and observe
options.E: Discuss him at the next haematology team meeting

correct_answer: B. Assess him urgently and give intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics without delay
why_correct: A fever with rigors in a profoundly neutropenic patient is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise, even if he looks well. Infection can progress to septic shock very quickly without neutrophils, so he needs urgent clinical assessment, cultures and empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately rather than after results.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol masks fever and delays treatment of a potentially fatal infection. C. Culture results take days and waiting for them is unsafe. D. G-CSF does not treat established infection. E. Deferring review to a meeting is an unacceptable delay.
pearl: Patients who are neutropenic may not mount typical signs of infection, so the absence of localising features does not reduce the urgency.
thinking: Recent intensive chemotherapy ↓ Almost no neutrophils ↓ New fever and rigor ↓ Neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise ↓ Immediate empirical intravenous antibiotics
exam_trap: D, Giving G-CSF and observing — it targets the low neutrophil count, but it does not treat the infection and leaves him without antibiotics.
takeaway: A neutropenic patient with fever needs empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately.

stem: A 67-year-old man with small-cell lung cancer attends the acute oncology unit eight days after his most recent cycle of treatment, feeling shivery and hot. Today's full blood count shows profound neutropenia. Blood cultures have been taken. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Start empirical intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam immediately
options.C: Withhold antibiotics until culture sensitivities are known
options.D: Give oral co-amoxiclav and discharge with review in clinic

correct_answer: A. Start empirical intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam immediately
why_correct: Fever after chemotherapy with a very low neutrophil count is neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency. NICE recommends starting empirical intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam promptly once suspected, then reviewing the regimen in light of cultures and the patient's risk.
why_wrong: B. Transfusing red cells does nothing for infection in neutropenia. C. Waiting for sensitivities risks rapid deterioration. D. Oral antibiotics and discharge are not appropriate initial management for a high-risk patient. E. G-CSF does not treat established infection and is not routine first-line therapy.
pearl: Aminoglycosides should not be added routinely to initial empirical treatment of neutropenic sepsis unless there are specific local or patient indications.
thinking: Recent chemotherapy ↓ Fever and rigors ↓ Profoundly low neutrophils ↓ Neutropenic sepsis ↓ Empirical intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam now
exam_trap: C, Withholding antibiotics until sensitivities are known — it sounds like good stewardship, but delay in neutropenic sepsis is associated with death.
takeaway: Start empirical intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam promptly for suspected neutropenic sepsis.

stem: A 58-year-old woman telephones the acute oncology helpline. She had her second cycle of chemotherapy for ovarian cancer nine days ago and since this afternoon has felt shivery, weak and generally unwell, and her thermometer at home shows a raised temperature. Which serious diagnosis must be assumed until proven otherwise?
why_correct: Fever and feeling unwell about a week to ten days after chemotherapy coincide with the expected nadir of the neutrophil count. She must be assumed to have neutropenic sepsis and asked to attend hospital immediately for assessment and empirical antibiotics, without waiting for a blood count.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia causes thirst, confusion and constipation rather than fever and rigors. B. Tumour lysis typically occurs within days of starting treatment for bulky, chemosensitive tumours and does not cause fever. C. Nausea alone does not explain fever and shivering. E. Pulmonary embolism is a risk in cancer but does not usually cause rigors and fever as the dominant features.
pearl: Patients on chemotherapy are given a 24-hour helpline number and an alert card so that fever is acted on as an emergency wherever they present.
thinking: Chemotherapy nine days ago ↓ Expected neutrophil nadir ↓ Fever, rigors and feeling unwell ↓ Assume neutropenic sepsis ↓ Immediate hospital assessment
exam_trap: E, Pulmonary embolism — cancer and chemotherapy do raise thrombotic risk, but fever with rigors at the neutrophil nadir points to infection first.
takeaway: Fever around the neutrophil nadir after chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 41-year-old man is given intravenous midazolam for sedation during an endoscopy. Shortly afterwards he cannot be roused and his breathing becomes slow and shallow despite airway support. He takes no regular medicines and has never had a seizure. Which drug specifically reverses this effect?
why_correct: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor. Reversing over-sedation from procedural benzodiazepines in a patient with no seizure history or benzodiazepine dependence is the situation in which flumazenil is most appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids, not benzodiazepines. B. Atropine treats bradycardia and cholinergic excess. D. Protamine reverses heparin. E. Glucagon is used for beta-blocker toxicity and hypoglycaemia.
pearl: Flumazenil has a shorter duration of action than many benzodiazepines, so re-sedation can occur and patients need continued monitoring.
thinking: Intravenous midazolam given ↓ Unrousable with respiratory depression ↓ Benzodiazepine over-sedation ↓ No seizure history or dependence ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: A, Naloxone — opioids are often co-administered for endoscopy, but naloxone has no effect on benzodiazepine-induced sedation.
takeaway: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and is safest in procedural over-sedation without seizure risk.

stem: After being stranded overnight on a snowy fell walk, a 29-year-old man is brought into the emergency department. Several of his toes are hard, white and numb, and the skin over them feels wooden to the touch. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Exposure to sub-zero temperatures has frozen the tissue, producing hard, white, insensate digits, which is frostbite. Management includes treating any hypothermia first, then rapid rewarming in warm water with analgesia and avoidance of refreezing.
why_wrong: A. Trench foot follows prolonged exposure to cold, wet conditions above freezing and the tissue does not freeze solid. C. Raynaud phenomenon causes episodic colour change that resolves, not frozen tissue. D. Chilblains are itchy red-purple swellings after damp cold, not hard white digits. E. Cellulitis causes warm, red, swollen skin.
pearl: Frozen tissue should not be rubbed or rewarmed if there is a risk of it refreezing, as this worsens tissue damage.
thinking: Prolonged sub-zero exposure ↓ Distal digits affected ↓ Hard, white, wooden and numb skin ↓ Tissue has frozen ↓ Frostbite
exam_trap: A, Non-freezing cold injury — it is also a cold injury of the feet, but it occurs above freezing in wet conditions and does not make the tissue hard and wooden.
takeaway: Hard, white, numb digits after freezing exposure indicate frostbite.

stem: A 79-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who takes warfarin is brought in by ambulance after passing large amounts of black, tarry stool and fainting at home. He is grey and clammy, with a low blood pressure and a fast pulse. His INR is above his target range. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Omit tonight's dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
options.B: Give oral vitamin K and observe on the ward
options.D: Resuscitate, reverse warfarin with intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate, and arrange urgent endoscopy
options.E: Give fresh frozen plasma alone and book a routine endoscopy

correct_answer: D. Resuscitate, reverse warfarin with intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate, and arrange urgent endoscopy
why_correct: This is a major, life-threatening bleed in an anticoagulated patient. Management runs in parallel: ABCDE resuscitation, immediate reversal of warfarin with intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate, and urgent endoscopy for definitive control once he has been resuscitated.
why_wrong: A. Omitting a dose is for a raised INR without major bleeding. B. Oral vitamin K acts too slowly and is not enough for haemodynamic compromise. C. Endoscopy in an unresuscitated, shocked patient is unsafe. E. Fresh frozen plasma is less effective than prothrombin complex concentrate and routine endoscopy is too slow.
pearl: Prothrombin complex concentrate reverses warfarin within minutes, while intravenous vitamin K is needed alongside it to sustain reversal.
thinking: Melaena and collapse ↓ Shocked ↓ On warfarin with a raised INR ↓ Major life-threatening bleed ↓ Resuscitate, reverse and arrange urgent endoscopy
exam_trap: E, Giving fresh frozen plasma alone — it contains clotting factors, but it reverses warfarin more slowly and less completely than prothrombin complex concentrate.
takeaway: Major bleeding on warfarin needs resuscitation, intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate, and urgent source control.

presentation: Bleeding on a direct oral anticoagulant
stem: A 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who takes apixaban attends the emergency department after vomiting dark blood twice this morning. She feels light-headed when she stands up. Which is the most important first step?

options.A: Give her usual apixaban dose so that her stroke risk stays covered
options.B: Start a proton pump inhibitor and arrange outpatient endoscopy
options.C: Arrange a CT of the abdomen before any other assessment
options.E: Assess airway, breathing and circulation and resuscitate as needed

correct_answer: E. Assess airway, breathing and circulation and resuscitate as needed
why_correct: She has a significant gastrointestinal bleed while anticoagulated, and postural symptoms suggest volume loss. The first step is structured ABCDE assessment and resuscitation, with the anticoagulant withheld and reversal considered according to the severity of bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Further apixaban would worsen the bleeding. B. Outpatient management is inappropriate for a symptomatic anticoagulated bleed. C. Imaging must not take priority over assessment and resuscitation. D. Changing anticoagulant does nothing for an active bleed.
pearl: Ask about the time of the last anticoagulant dose, as this guides whether specific reversal is likely to be needed.
thinking: Vomiting dark blood ↓ On apixaban ↓ Postural light-headedness suggests volume loss ↓ Potentially serious bleed ↓ ABCDE assessment and resuscitation first
exam_trap: A, Giving her usual apixaban dose — protecting against stroke sounds sensible, but continuing anticoagulation during an active bleed is dangerous.
takeaway: In any significant bleed on anticoagulation, assess and resuscitate first and withhold the anticoagulant.

stem: A man in his fifties on the cardiology ward, two days after a coronary stent and now taking dual antiplatelet therapy, suddenly vomits a large volume of bright red blood. Shortly afterwards his blood pressure falls. What is the immediate priority?

options.B: Give high-dose oral omeprazole and observe closely
options.C: Assess and stabilise his airway, breathing and circulation
options.D: Give tranexamic acid as the first measure
options.E: Arrange discharge if bleeding settles, with outpatient endoscopy

correct_answer: C. Assess and stabilise his airway, breathing and circulation
why_correct: A large haematemesis followed by hypotension shows a significant upper gastrointestinal bleed with haemodynamic compromise. The airway is also at risk from ongoing vomiting of blood, so ABCDE assessment and resuscitation come first, with urgent endoscopy and a senior cardiology discussion about antiplatelets once he is stabilised.
why_wrong: A. Endoscopy in an unresuscitated, hypotensive patient is unsafe. B. Oral omeprazole does not address shock or airway risk. D. Tranexamic acid is not recommended for gastrointestinal bleeding and does not replace resuscitation. E. Discharge is inappropriate for a bleed causing hypotension.
pearl: Stopping antiplatelet therapy soon after coronary stenting risks stent thrombosis, so decisions should be shared between gastroenterology and cardiology.
thinking: Recent stent on two antiplatelets ↓ Large bright red haematemesis ↓ Falling blood pressure ↓ Unstable upper GI bleed with airway risk ↓ ABC stabilisation first
exam_trap: D, Giving tranexamic acid first — it seems a quick way to stop bleeding, but trial evidence shows no benefit in gastrointestinal bleeding and it delays resuscitation.
takeaway: Haematemesis with hypotension demands airway, breathing and circulation stabilisation before anything else.

stem: An 82-year-old care home resident is sent to the emergency department after staff found blood in her vomit and noticed jet-black, sticky stools. She says she feels faint whenever she sits up. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Give oral omeprazole and arrange an outpatient endoscopy
options.B: Arrange endoscopy before any fluid resuscitation
options.C: Resuscitate her and start the upper GI bleeding pathway
options.D: Give tranexamic acid and observe on the ward
options.E: Discharge her if her haemoglobin is stable

correct_answer: C. Resuscitate her and start the upper GI bleeding pathway
why_correct: Haematemesis with melaena and postural faintness indicates a significant upper gastrointestinal bleed. She needs resuscitation and entry into the acute upper GI bleeding pathway, with formal risk scoring such as the Glasgow–Blatchford score and endoscopy within the recommended timeframe after resuscitation.
why_wrong: A. Outpatient management ignores a significant active bleed. B. Fluid resuscitation must come before endoscopy. D. Tranexamic acid is not recommended in gastrointestinal bleeding. E. A single haemoglobin can be falsely reassuring early in acute haemorrhage.
pearl: Melaena indicates bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz in most cases, and iron tablets can also cause black stools, which can be confused with it.
thinking: Blood in vomit ↓ Black, sticky stools ↓ Faint on sitting up ↓ Significant upper GI bleed ↓ Resuscitate and start the bleeding pathway
exam_trap: E, Discharging her if the haemoglobin is stable — a normal early haemoglobin does not reflect acute blood loss in an older person with postural symptoms.
takeaway: Haematemesis with melaena needs resuscitation, risk scoring and endoscopy through the upper GI bleeding pathway.

stem: A 30-year-old woman attends after a night of heavy drinking and repeated retching, followed by several episodes of vomiting fresh red blood. In triage she feels dizzy, her systolic pressure is low and her heart rate is fast. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Calculate the Glasgow–Blatchford score before doing anything else
options.D: Oral omeprazole and observation in the waiting area

why_correct: Although retching followed by haematemesis suggests a Mallory–Weiss tear, which often settles, she is now haemodynamically compromised. Any upper gastrointestinal bleed with hypotension and tachycardia needs immediate ABCDE assessment and resuscitation before scoring or endoscopy.
why_wrong: A. Risk scoring is useful but must not delay resuscitation in an unstable patient. C. Endoscopy should follow resuscitation. D. Oral treatment and waiting do not address shock. E. Tranexamic acid is not recommended for gastrointestinal bleeding.
pearl: Most Mallory–Weiss tears stop bleeding spontaneously, but the presence of shock should prompt consideration of other causes such as varices or ulcers.
thinking: Heavy drinking and retching ↓ Fresh haematemesis ↓ Dizzy, hypotensive and tachycardic ↓ Unstable upper GI bleed ↓ ABCDE resuscitation first
exam_trap: A, Calculating the Glasgow–Blatchford score first — scoring is part of the pathway, but it guides later decisions and must not delay treating shock.
takeaway: Whatever the likely cause, an unstable upper GI bleed is managed with immediate ABCDE resuscitation.

stem: A 64-year-old taxi driver with a past peptic ulcer is found by his family on the bathroom floor beside blood-stained vomit. In the emergency department he is light-headed, his radial pulse is rapid and thready and his blood pressure is well below normal. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Start oral iron and arrange GP follow-up
options.B: Resuscitate and assess his haemodynamic status
options.D: Start oral omeprazole and review in clinic
options.E: Arrange CT of the abdomen and pelvis before other treatment

correct_answer: B. Resuscitate and assess his haemodynamic status
why_correct: Collapse with haematemesis, a thready tachycardia and hypotension indicates haemorrhagic shock from an upper gastrointestinal source, most likely a recurrent peptic ulcer. Resuscitation and assessment of his circulation come first, with urgent endoscopy after stabilisation.
why_wrong: A. Iron replacement is irrelevant during acute haemorrhage. C. Outpatient endoscopy is far too slow. D. Oral omeprazole and clinic review ignore shock. E. Imaging must not delay resuscitation and is not the first-line investigation.
pearl: In upper GI bleeding, blood transfusion should be guided by the full clinical picture, avoiding both under-transfusion and over-transfusion.
thinking: Previous peptic ulcer ↓ Blood-stained vomit and collapse ↓ Thready tachycardia and hypotension ↓ Haemorrhagic shock ↓ Resuscitate first
exam_trap: E, CT of the abdomen and pelvis first — imaging seems to locate the source, but moving a shocked patient to the scanner before resuscitation is dangerous.
takeaway: Shock from haematemesis is treated with immediate resuscitation before any investigation.

stem: Three days after a total knee replacement, a 72-year-old woman becomes suddenly breathless and collapses on the orthopaedic ward. Her systolic pressure stays low despite fluids, her neck veins are distended and a bedside echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle. Clot is later confirmed in the main pulmonary arteries. How should this event be classified?
why_correct: Pulmonary embolism with sustained hypotension and obstructive shock is classified as high-risk or massive, regardless of other markers. It carries a high early mortality and is the main indication for systemic thrombolysis, unless contraindicated.
why_wrong: A. Low-risk embolism has normal blood pressure and no right ventricular strain. B. Intermediate-high risk shows right ventricular strain but the patient remains normotensive. C. Intermediate-low risk has limited markers of strain and a stable blood pressure. D. Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension develops over months after unresolved emboli.
pearl: Recent surgery is a relative rather than absolute contraindication to thrombolysis, so the bleeding risk must be weighed against the high mortality of massive PE.
thinking: Recent joint replacement ↓ Sudden breathlessness and collapse ↓ Persistent hypotension with raised neck veins ↓ Right ventricular dilatation and obstructive shock ↓ High-risk (massive) PE
exam_trap: B, Intermediate-high-risk embolism — right ventricular dilatation tempts this choice, but sustained hypotension automatically places the event in the high-risk category.
takeaway: Pulmonary embolism with persistent hypotension or shock is high-risk (massive) PE.

stem: A 17-year-old rugby player is struck on the side of the head by an opponent's knee and is knocked out for about a minute. He then chats normally on the touchline. Two hours later his parents notice he is confused and drowsy, and one pupil is becoming larger than the other. Which injury is most likely?
why_correct: A blow to the temple with brief unconsciousness, a lucid interval and then rapid deterioration with a dilating pupil is the classic pattern of an extradural haematoma, usually from middle meningeal artery bleeding. It is a neurosurgical emergency because arterial bleeding expands quickly and causes herniation.
why_wrong: A. Acute subdural haematoma usually causes a reduced conscious level from the outset rather than a lucid interval. B. Chronic subdural haematoma develops over weeks, typically in older people. C. Traumatic subarachnoid blood causes headache and meningism rather than this pattern. E. Diffuse axonal injury causes immediate and prolonged coma.
pearl: On CT, an extradural haematoma is lens-shaped (biconvex) and does not cross suture lines.
thinking: Blow to the side of the head ↓ Brief loss of consciousness ↓ Lucid interval ↓ Rapid decline with unequal pupils ↓ Extradural haematoma
exam_trap: A, Acute subdural haematoma — it is also a traumatic bleed causing deterioration, but it rarely produces a clear lucid interval in a young person.
takeaway: Brief unconsciousness, a lucid interval and then rapid decline suggests an extradural haematoma.

stem: A 26-year-old netball player was struck on the head by another player's elbow during a match last weekend. She did not lose consciousness. Since then she has had a dull headache, feels foggy and is struggling to focus at work. Neurological examination is normal and she has no red-flag features. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Headache, mental fogginess and poor concentration after a minor head injury, with a normal examination and no red flags, fit concussion, a mild traumatic brain injury. Management is a short period of relative rest followed by a graded return to work and sport, with safety-netting for deterioration.
why_wrong: B. Extradural haematoma causes rapid neurological deterioration, not persistent mild symptoms. C. Post-traumatic epilepsy presents with seizures. D. Bacterial meningitis causes fever and meningism. E. Chronic subdural haematoma usually affects older people and causes progressive or fluctuating neurological signs.
pearl: UK grassroots sport guidance advises that anyone with suspected concussion should be removed from play and not return on the same day.
thinking: Minor head impact ↓ No loss of consciousness ↓ Headache, fogginess and poor concentration ↓ Normal examination, no red flags ↓ Concussion
exam_trap: E, Chronic subdural haematoma — it can follow minor trauma, but it typically affects older or anticoagulated people and causes evolving neurological signs.
takeaway: Transient cognitive and physical symptoms after a minor head injury with a normal examination suggest concussion.

stem: Two older sisters who share a cottage heated by an old solid-fuel stove both see their GP after a week of dull headache, tiredness and queasiness. Neither has a fever or loose stools, and both felt better after spending a day at their niece's home. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Shared symptoms in people living together, linked to a solid-fuel stove and improving away from home, without fever or diarrhoea, suggest carbon monoxide poisoning rather than infection. They need removal from exposure, carboxyhaemoglobin testing and an urgent check of the appliance and ventilation.
why_wrong: A. Influenza usually causes fever and myalgia and does not improve with a change of location. B. Staphylococcal food poisoning causes abrupt vomiting within hours of eating and settles quickly. D. Viral gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea. E. Hypothyroidism develops slowly in one person and would not resolve after a day away.
pearl: Solid-fuel appliances, blocked flues and poorly ventilated rooms are common sources of domestic carbon monoxide, so a working alarm is recommended near any fuel-burning appliance.
thinking: Two people sharing a home ↓ Headache, fatigue and nausea ↓ No fever or diarrhoea ↓ Better away from the house with a solid-fuel stove ↓ Carbon monoxide poisoning
exam_trap: A, Influenza — it can affect several people at once, but the absence of fever and improvement away from home point to an environmental cause.
takeaway: Non-specific symptoms shared by people in one household that ease away from home suggest carbon monoxide poisoning.

stem: A 31-year-old woman phones NHS 111 from a ski resort abroad. She flew in yesterday and took a cable car straight up to a mountain hut, where she is spending her first night with two friends, who feel well. Over the last few hours she has developed a throbbing headache, light-headedness, nausea and poor sleep. She is fully alert, walking normally and not breathless at rest. Which condition best explains her symptoms?

options.D: Carbon monoxide poisoning from the hut stove

why_correct: Headache with nausea, light-headedness and disturbed sleep within a day of a rapid gain in altitude is the typical picture of acute mountain sickness. She has no confusion or ataxia to suggest high-altitude cerebral oedema and no breathlessness at rest to suggest high-altitude pulmonary oedema. Management is rest, no further ascent, simple analgesia and descent if symptoms worsen.
why_wrong: A. There is no fever, rash, neck stiffness or reduced consciousness to suggest meningitis. B. Migraine with aura has focal visual or sensory features and does not explain the clear link to rapid ascent. C. Pulmonary embolism presents with breathlessness, pleuritic pain or collapse rather than headache and nausea at altitude. D. Carbon monoxide can cause headache and nausea, but the timing with rapid ascent and her companions in the same hut being well point to altitude illness.
pearl: Confusion, ataxia or breathlessness at rest at altitude signal high-altitude cerebral or pulmonary oedema, which require immediate descent and oxygen.
thinking: Rapid ascent to altitude ↓ Headache plus nausea and poor sleep within 24 hours ↓ No ataxia or confusion ↓ No breathlessness at rest ↓ Acute mountain sickness
exam_trap: D, Carbon monoxide poisoning from the hut stove — headache and nausea overlap, but the clear trigger here is the abrupt altitude gain and her friends sharing the hut are well.
takeaway: Headache with nausea after rapid ascent is acute mountain sickness until features of cerebral or pulmonary oedema appear.

stem: During a summer heatwave, an 84-year-old woman is found by her carer slumped in a chair in her top-floor flat with the windows shut. She is muddled, does not recognise the carer and is drowsy. Paramedics find her skin flushed and burning to the touch, with a rapid pulse. She takes bendroflumethiazide. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.C: Postural hypotension due to her diuretic
options.E: Delirium due to a urinary tract infection

why_correct: Heatstroke is a core temperature that has risen to dangerous levels with central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion, drowsiness or seizures. Older people living alone in hot, poorly ventilated rooms, especially those on diuretics, are at particular risk of this classical non-exertional form. It is an emergency requiring rapid active cooling.
why_wrong: A. Heat exhaustion causes weakness, headache and nausea with preserved mental state; confusion and drowsiness mean heatstroke. B. Her skin is burning hot, the opposite of hypothermia. C. Postural hypotension causes dizziness on standing, not persistent confusion with hot skin. E. Infection can cause delirium in older people, but the heatwave exposure and burning skin make heatstroke the best fit.
pearl: Treat heatstroke by rapid cooling as soon as it is suspected; do not wait for a core temperature reading before starting.
thinking: Prolonged heat exposure in a vulnerable older person ↓ Burning hot skin ↓ Confusion and drowsiness ↓ Central nervous system dysfunction present ↓ Heatstroke rather than heat exhaustion
exam_trap: A, Heat exhaustion — it is part of the same spectrum, but any altered mental state with high body temperature means the more dangerous diagnosis of heatstroke.
takeaway: Hyperthermia plus confusion is heatstroke and needs immediate cooling.

stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on ramipril and spironolactone is admitted to the medical ward feeling weak. His blood results show severe hyperkalaemia, and a 12-lead ECG shows peaked T waves. The registrar asks you which drug should be given first to protect his heart from arrhythmia while other measures are arranged. Which treatment is most appropriate?
why_correct: Intravenous calcium (gluconate or chloride) stabilises the myocardial cell membrane within minutes and is given first when hyperkalaemia is accompanied by ECG changes. It does not lower the serum potassium, so it must be followed by treatments that shift potassium into cells and remove it from the body. His ramipril and spironolactone should also be stopped.
why_wrong: A. Insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells but does not protect the myocardium directly; it follows calcium. B. Salbutamol is an adjunct to shift potassium and does not stabilise the membrane. D. Potassium binders remove potassium slowly over hours and do nothing for the immediate arrhythmia risk. E. Furosemide may increase renal potassium loss but is slow and does not protect the heart.
pearl: The effect of intravenous calcium lasts only about 30 to 60 minutes, so the ECG should be repeated and further doses given if changes persist.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ ECG changes present ↓ Immediate risk is arrhythmia ↓ Stabilise the myocardium first ↓ Intravenous calcium, then shift and remove potassium
exam_trap: A, Intravenous insulin with glucose — it is essential and lowers potassium quickly, but it does not protect the heart and should follow calcium.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: give intravenous calcium first to stabilise the heart.

stem: Paramedics bring in a 66-year-old woman who takes gliclazide. Her husband found her slurring her words and unable to lift her left arm about 40 minutes ago. A stroke alert has been called. On arrival her capillary blood glucose is very low. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Request an urgent CT head before any other treatment
options.D: Correct the low blood glucose and reassess her neurology
options.E: Arrange a swallow assessment before giving anything

correct_answer: D. Correct the low blood glucose and reassess her neurology
why_correct: Hypoglycaemia is a well-recognised stroke mimic and can cause focal weakness and dysarthria, especially in people taking sulfonylureas. It is quickly reversible, so it should be treated immediately and the neurological examination repeated. Many patients recover fully once glucose is restored; if deficits persist, the stroke pathway continues.
why_wrong: A. Imaging is important for suspected stroke, but a reversible metabolic cause should be corrected first. B. Aspirin is not given before haemorrhage is excluded and does not address the low glucose. C. Thrombolysis is contraindicated until hypoglycaemia is corrected and stroke is confirmed. E. A swallow assessment matters for oral intake, but intravenous glucose can be given without delay.
pearl: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia can recur for many hours, so these patients need observation and repeated glucose monitoring after correction.
thinking: Acute focal deficit ↓ On a sulfonylurea ↓ Capillary glucose very low ↓ Treat reversible mimic first ↓ Reassess neurology after correction
exam_trap: A, Request an urgent CT head before any other treatment — speed matters in stroke, but scanning first delays a simple, reversible treatment.
takeaway: Always check and correct glucose in suspected stroke, because hypoglycaemia can mimic it.

stem: A 61-year-old man is admitted from the GP surgery with pyelonephritis. In the emergency department he has received intravenous antibiotics and two fluid boluses, but his mean arterial pressure remains low, his peripheral skin is mottled and he has passed very little urine. What does this persisting picture most likely represent?

options.B: Dehydration that will settle with oral fluids
options.C: Cardiogenic shock from an acute myocardial infarction
options.E: An adverse effect of the antibiotics

why_correct: Septic shock is sepsis with circulatory failure that persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation, typically needing vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure. Ongoing hypotension, mottled skin and poor urine output after fluids indicate this. He needs urgent senior and critical care review.
why_wrong: A. Uncomplicated infection does not cause refractory hypotension and oliguria. B. Simple dehydration responds to fluid; persistent hypotension after boluses does not. C. There are no cardiac features, and the infective source points to sepsis. E. Antibiotic reactions do not explain persistent circulatory failure in a septic patient.
pearl: Patients with septic shock need early critical care referral for vasopressors, usually noradrenaline, when hypotension persists after fluids.
thinking: Known infection ↓ Antibiotics and fluid boluses given ↓ Hypotension persists ↓ Signs of hypoperfusion ↓ Septic shock needing escalation
exam_trap: B, Dehydration that will settle with oral fluids — dehydration contributes, but failure to respond to intravenous fluid points to septic shock.
takeaway: Hypotension that persists after fluid resuscitation in sepsis is septic shock and needs critical care.

stem: A 79-year-old care home resident with a two-day cough is reviewed by the visiting GP. Staff say she has become much sleepier and muddled today. Her blood pressure has dropped well below her usual level, she is breathing fast and her hands feel cold. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Start oral amoxicillin and review at the next weekly visit
options.B: Arrange emergency transfer to hospital for immediate sepsis assessment and treatment
options.C: Wait for a chest X-ray and blood results before deciding
options.D: Give a dose of haloperidol for her confusion and observe
options.E: Increase her fluid intake and recheck observations tomorrow

correct_answer: B. Arrange emergency transfer to hospital for immediate sepsis assessment and treatment
why_correct: New confusion, low blood pressure and a raised respiratory rate in someone with a likely chest infection are high-risk features of sepsis. She needs emergency transfer for senior assessment, blood cultures, lactate, intravenous antibiotics within an hour and fluid resuscitation. Delay increases mortality.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics with delayed review are unsafe in a patient showing high-risk features. C. Investigations should not delay transfer and treatment of suspected sepsis. D. Sedation masks the confusion and does not treat the cause. E. Waiting until tomorrow risks further deterioration and death.
pearl: In suspected sepsis, new altered mental state, low systolic blood pressure or a high respiratory rate are each high-risk criteria in NICE guidance.
thinking: Probable infection ↓ New confusion and drowsiness ↓ Low blood pressure and fast breathing ↓ High-risk sepsis features ↓ Emergency transfer and immediate treatment
exam_trap: E, Increase her fluid intake and recheck observations tomorrow — it feels proportionate in a frail resident, but high-risk sepsis needs treatment within the hour.
takeaway: A deteriorating patient with suspected sepsis needs immediate assessment and treatment, not observation.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after her thigh was cut deeply by a fallen sheet of glass. Bystanders applied pressure but a large amount of blood was lost at the scene. She is cool, clammy and anxious, with a fast pulse and a low blood pressure. Which category of shock best describes her state?
why_correct: Haemorrhage reduces the circulating volume, lowering venous return and cardiac output, which is hypovolaemic shock. Compensatory sympathetic activity causes tachycardia, cool clammy skin and anxiety. Treatment is control of bleeding and replacement of blood.
why_wrong: A. Distributive shock arises from widespread vasodilatation, as in sepsis or anaphylaxis, usually with warm peripheries. C. Cardiogenic shock is pump failure, not volume loss. D. Obstructive shock results from blocked flow, such as tension pneumothorax or tamponade. E. Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury and typically causes hypotension with bradycardia.
pearl: Haemorrhagic shock should be treated with blood products early rather than large volumes of crystalloid.
thinking: Major external bleeding ↓ Cool clammy skin and tachycardia ↓ Hypotension ↓ Reduced circulating volume ↓ Hypovolaemic shock
exam_trap: E, Neurogenic shock — it is also caused by trauma, but it needs a spinal cord injury and typically gives warm skin with a slow pulse.
takeaway: Shock after major blood loss is hypovolaemic.

stem: Firefighters pull a 45-year-old man from a smoke-filled flat. In the emergency department he is coughing up black-flecked sputum, his eyebrows are singed and his voice has become croaky over the past half hour. His oxygen saturation is currently acceptable on high-flow oxygen. What should the team be most concerned about?

options.B: Inhalation injury with progressive airway swelling
options.E: Allergic contact dermatitis of the face

correct_answer: B. Inhalation injury with progressive airway swelling
why_correct: Carbonaceous sputum, singed facial hair and a voice that is becoming hoarse after smoke exposure indicate thermal and chemical injury to the airway. Swelling can progress rapidly over hours and close the airway, so early senior anaesthetic review and consideration of early intubation are needed. Normal saturations do not exclude this.
why_wrong: A. Carbon dioxide retention does not explain singed hair, soot or a changing voice. C. There is no history of chest trauma. D. Asthma causes wheeze, not progressive hoarseness after a fire. E. Contact dermatitis is a slow skin reaction and does not threaten the airway.
pearl: Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, so check carboxyhaemoglobin on a blood gas in anyone exposed to smoke.
thinking: Enclosed space smoke exposure ↓ Soot in sputum and singed facial hair ↓ Hoarseness getting worse ↓ Airway oedema developing ↓ Early airway protection
exam_trap: D, Acute asthma attack — smoke can trigger bronchospasm, but worsening hoarseness points to upper airway injury, which is the life threat.
takeaway: Hoarseness, soot and singed hair after a fire mean inhalation injury and an airway at risk.

stem: A 55-year-old woman in the intensive care unit has faecal peritonitis after a perforated sigmoid colon. She is on noradrenaline, her peripheries are cold and mottled and her arterial blood gas shows a low pH, a low bicarbonate and a high anion gap. Her lactate is greatly elevated. Which process best explains her acid-base disturbance?

options.A: Loss of bicarbonate through a high-output stoma
options.B: Accumulation of ketones from insulin deficiency
options.C: Anaerobic glycolysis caused by inadequate tissue oxygen delivery
options.D: Retention of carbon dioxide from hypoventilation
options.E: Accumulation of uraemic acids from chronic renal failure

correct_answer: C. Anaerobic glycolysis caused by inadequate tissue oxygen delivery
why_correct: In septic shock, poor perfusion and impaired cellular oxygen use force cells into anaerobic glycolysis. Pyruvate is converted to lactate, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. The degree of lactate rise reflects the severity of hypoperfusion.
why_wrong: A. Bicarbonate loss from the gut gives a normal anion gap acidosis without a lactate rise. B. Ketoacidosis needs insulin deficiency and would not explain the high lactate. D. Carbon dioxide retention produces a respiratory, not metabolic, acidosis. E. Chronic renal failure is not described and would not account for a markedly raised lactate.
pearl: Falling lactate on repeated measurement is a useful marker that resuscitation is restoring tissue perfusion.
thinking: Septic shock on vasopressors ↓ Cold mottled peripheries ↓ High anion gap metabolic acidosis ↓ Markedly raised lactate ↓ Anaerobic metabolism from hypoperfusion
exam_trap: A, Loss of bicarbonate through a high-output stoma — bowel surgery suggests it, but that gives a normal anion gap and does not raise lactate.
takeaway: Lactic acidosis in septic shock reflects anaerobic metabolism from poor tissue perfusion.

stem: An 82-year-old man is seen in the emergency department with fever and new confusion three days after a urinary catheter change. Blood cultures are sent and a venous gas shows a lactate above the normal range. The foundation doctor asks what this result tells the team. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Bacteria have been confirmed in the bloodstream
options.C: Organs and tissues may not be receiving enough oxygen

correct_answer: C. Organs and tissues may not be receiving enough oxygen
why_correct: A raised lactate in suspected sepsis is a marker of possible tissue hypoperfusion and physiological stress. It is used alongside clinical features to judge risk and guide escalation, and a raised value in a patient with sepsis increases the urgency of treatment. It says nothing on its own about the organism or the source.
why_wrong: A. Only blood cultures can confirm bacteraemia. B. Lactate accumulation produces a metabolic, not respiratory, acidosis. D. Lactate does not indicate chronic kidney disease. E. Diabetic ketoacidosis needs raised ketones and glucose, not lactate.
pearl: Lactate is a non-specific marker; it can also rise with seizures, liver failure, metformin and salbutamol, so interpret it in context.
thinking: Suspected urinary sepsis ↓ Venous lactate raised ↓ Lactate reflects anaerobic metabolism ↓ Suggests inadequate tissue perfusion ↓ Escalate care
exam_trap: A, Bacteria have been confirmed in the bloodstream — lactate is part of the sepsis work-up, but it measures perfusion, not infection.
takeaway: In suspected sepsis, a raised lactate signals possible tissue hypoperfusion.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with cellulitis of the leg is assessed using the NICE sepsis risk criteria. She meets moderate-to-high risk criteria only, with no high-risk features, and her blood pressure and heart rate are within normal limits. Her venous lactate comes back clearly above the normal range, and her renal function is normal. How should this result change her management?

options.A: Continue moderate-risk care, as lactate only matters once she becomes hypotensive
options.B: Downgrade her to low risk because her observations are normal
options.C: Manage her as high risk, as the raised lactate suggests hypoperfusion
options.D: Repeat the lactate tomorrow before deciding on antibiotics
options.E: Investigate for a myocardial cause, as lactate reflects cardiac ischaemia

correct_answer: C. Manage her as high risk, as the raised lactate suggests hypoperfusion
why_correct: In NICE sepsis guidance, a person at moderate-to-high risk who has evidence of hypoperfusion, such as a raised lactate or acute kidney injury, is managed as high risk. That means senior review and intravenous antibiotics within an hour, with fluids as needed. Normal blood pressure and heart rate do not cancel out the significance of a raised lactate.
why_wrong: A. A raised lactate can reveal hypoperfusion before blood pressure falls, so it should not be ignored until hypotension develops. B. Normal observations do not outweigh biochemical evidence of hypoperfusion. D. Waiting a day delays time-critical antibiotics. E. Lactate is not a marker of myocardial ischaemia here; it reflects tissue perfusion.
pearl: Hidden hypoperfusion can occur with normal blood pressure, which is why lactate is measured in moderate-risk patients.
thinking: Suspected sepsis ↓ Moderate-to-high risk only ↓ Lactate raised ↓ Evidence of hypoperfusion ↓ Treat as high risk
exam_trap: A, Continue moderate-risk care, as lactate only matters once she becomes hypotensive — her reassuring blood pressure is tempting, but a raised lactate is itself evidence of hidden hypoperfusion and warrants escalation.
takeaway: A raised lactate moves a moderate-risk sepsis patient into high-risk management.

presentation: Prognostic meaning of lactate in septic shock
stem: On the critical care outreach round, you review a 68-year-old man with pneumonia who needs vasopressors to maintain his blood pressure. His lactate is several times the upper limit of normal and has not fallen after fluid resuscitation. His daughter asks what this blood result means. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: His tissues are not getting enough oxygen, and this indicates a more severe illness
options.B: The pneumonia has been proven to be bacterial
options.C: He has had a heart attack that is causing the shock
options.D: An underactive thyroid is slowing removal of lactate
options.E: It is an expected finding that does not affect his outlook

correct_answer: A. His tissues are not getting enough oxygen, and this indicates a more severe illness
why_correct: A high lactate in septic shock reflects tissue hypoperfusion and impaired oxygen use. A higher level, and one that fails to clear with resuscitation, is linked to greater illness severity and higher mortality. It is used to guide escalation and monitor response.
why_wrong: B. Lactate does not identify the type of organism. C. Lactate is not a marker of myocardial infarction. D. Hypothyroidism does not explain a markedly raised lactate in septic shock. E. A persistently high lactate carries prognostic weight and should not be dismissed.
pearl: Lactate clearance after resuscitation is associated with better survival than a persistently high level.
thinking: Septic shock on vasopressors ↓ Very high lactate ↓ Not clearing after fluids ↓ Ongoing tissue hypoperfusion ↓ Greater severity and worse prognosis
exam_trap: E, It is an expected finding that does not affect his outlook — raised lactate is common in shock, but its level and clearance strongly predict outcome.
takeaway: A high, non-clearing lactate in septic shock indicates hypoperfusion and a worse prognosis.

stem: In theatre, a 26-year-old man is having an open reduction of a fractured ankle under general anaesthesia with sevoflurane. Twenty minutes in, the anaesthetist notes a sustained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide despite increased ventilation, a climbing heart rate and jaw and limb stiffness, followed by a steep rise in temperature. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Malignant hyperthermia is an inherited disorder of skeletal muscle calcium handling triggered by volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium. Uncontrolled muscle metabolism produces rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, tachycardia, rigidity and then hyperthermia. The trigger agent must be stopped and dantrolene given.
why_wrong: A. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotic use and develops over days. B. Anaphylaxis causes hypotension, bronchospasm and rash rather than rigidity and rising carbon dioxide. D. Thyroid storm needs underlying thyrotoxicosis and does not cause rigidity. E. Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and causes clonus and hyperreflexia.
pearl: Rising end-tidal carbon dioxide is often the earliest sign; fever may be a late feature.
thinking: Volatile anaesthetic exposure ↓ Rising end-tidal carbon dioxide ↓ Tachycardia and muscle rigidity ↓ Rapid temperature rise ↓ Malignant hyperthermia
exam_trap: A, Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — rigidity and fever overlap, but onset is over days after antipsychotics, not minutes into anaesthesia.
takeaway: Rigidity, rising carbon dioxide and hyperthermia under volatile anaesthesia is malignant hyperthermia.

stem: A 54-year-old man on the surgical ward is given his first dose of intravenous co-amoxiclav. Within ten minutes he says his throat feels tight and he feels faint. He has hives over his trunk, his lips are swelling and there is audible wheeze. Which diagnosis best accounts for this?
why_correct: Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapid-onset hypersensitivity reaction with airway, breathing or circulatory problems, usually with skin or mucosal changes. Throat tightness, wheeze and faintness alongside hives and lip swelling minutes after a new antibiotic fit this exactly. The antibiotic should be stopped and intramuscular adrenaline given.
why_wrong: A. A vasovagal episode does not cause hives, lip swelling or wheeze. B. Panic does not produce objective urticaria and angioedema. C. Urticaria alone does not explain the airway and breathing features. D. Asthma would not cause hives and lip swelling after a drug.
pearl: Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment and can be repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement.
thinking: New drug given ↓ Minutes later skin and mucosal changes ↓ Throat tightness and wheeze ↓ Feels faint ↓ Anaphylaxis
exam_trap: D, Asthma exacerbation — wheeze is prominent, but hives and lip swelling after a new drug indicate a systemic allergic reaction.
takeaway: Skin features plus airway, breathing or circulatory compromise after a trigger is anaphylaxis.

stem: An 80-year-old man with known gallstones is brought to the emergency department by his wife. Since yesterday he has had rigors and pain under his right ribs, and today his eyes have turned yellow. He is now disorientated, his blood pressure is low and his peripheries are cool. What should be the immediate priority?

options.A: Start the sepsis pathway now, with intravenous antibiotics and fluids, and arrange urgent biliary drainage
options.B: Book an MRCP and start antibiotics once the result is known
options.D: Discharge with oral antibiotics and GP review
options.E: List him for a cholecystectomy on the next elective list

correct_answer: A. Start the sepsis pathway now, with intravenous antibiotics and fluids, and arrange urgent biliary drainage
why_correct: Rigors, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice point to ascending cholangitis, and confusion with hypotension show it has progressed to septic shock. He needs immediate resuscitation with intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, followed by urgent biliary decompression, usually by ERCP. Delay in source control increases mortality.
why_wrong: B. Imaging must not delay antibiotics and resuscitation in a shocked patient. C. Outpatient imaging is unsafe in someone with septic shock. D. Oral antibiotics at home are inadequate for a hypotensive, confused patient. E. Elective surgery does not address the immediate septic emergency or the obstructed duct.
pearl: Severe cholangitis needs urgent biliary drainage, usually by ERCP, once the patient is resuscitated.
thinking: Rigors, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice ↓ Ascending cholangitis ↓ Confusion and hypotension ↓ Biliary sepsis with shock ↓ Resuscitate, antibiotics, then drainage
exam_trap: B, Book an MRCP and start antibiotics once the result is known — confirming obstruction seems sensible, but waiting for imaging delays life-saving treatment.
takeaway: Cholangitis with shock needs immediate sepsis treatment and urgent drainage.

stem: A 64-year-old woman who had an episode of biliary colic last year presents with a 24-hour history of shaking chills and pain under her right rib cage. Her sclerae are now yellow. On assessment she is drowsy and confused and her blood pressure is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice form Charcot's triad of ascending cholangitis. The addition of confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) indicates severe disease with septic shock. This follows stone obstruction of the common bile duct with infected bile.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis typically causes epigastric pain radiating to the back rather than jaundice with rigors. B. Biliary colic is self-limiting pain without fever or jaundice. D. Viral hepatitis may cause jaundice, but not rigors with septic shock. E. Cholecystitis causes fever and right upper quadrant pain, but jaundice with shock points to duct infection.
pearl: Reynolds' pentad (Charcot's triad plus confusion and hypotension) indicates severe cholangitis with high mortality without urgent drainage.
thinking: Gallstone history ↓ Rigors, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice ↓ Charcot's triad ↓ Confusion and hypotension added ↓ Severe acute cholangitis
exam_trap: E, Acute calculous cholecystitis — it shares fever and right upper quadrant pain, but jaundice and shock mean the duct is infected.
takeaway: Charcot's triad with confusion and hypotension is severe acute cholangitis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman on a diving holiday develops blotchy skin over her chest, aching in her knees and weakness and pins and needles in her legs a couple of hours after an ascent that was faster than planned. She is otherwise alert. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Carbon monoxide poisoning from a contaminated air cylinder

why_correct: Ascending too quickly lets nitrogen form bubbles in tissues, producing joint aches, skin mottling and spinal cord symptoms such as limb weakness and paraesthesia. The timing within hours of a fast ascent is typical. She needs 100 percent oxygen and urgent referral for hyperbaric recompression.
why_wrong: A. Contaminated air causes headache and drowsiness, not joint pain and skin mottling. C. Heat stroke causes hyperthermia and confusion. D. Hypothermia causes shivering, drowsiness and bradycardia rather than joint pain. E. Guillain-Barré syndrome develops over days, usually after an infection.
pearl: Flying soon after diving can trigger or worsen decompression sickness because of the lower cabin pressure.
thinking: Recent dive ↓ Faster than planned ascent ↓ Joint aches and skin mottling ↓ Leg weakness and paraesthesia ↓ Decompression sickness
exam_trap: A, Carbon monoxide poisoning from a contaminated air cylinder — it is a real diving hazard, but it does not explain joint pain, skin mottling and spinal symptoms after ascent.
takeaway: Rapid ascent followed by joint pain and neurological symptoms means decompression sickness.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes grazed her shin on a garden step two days ago. She now attends the emergency department in agony from the wound, which looks only mildly red with dusky purple patches spreading at the edges. She is tachycardic, febrile and feels very unwell. Strong analgesia barely helps. Which diagnosis must be urgently excluded?
why_correct: Pain far greater than the visible skin changes, dusky discolouration and systemic toxicity after a minor wound are warning signs of necrotising fasciitis. It is a rapidly spreading infection of the fascia that needs urgent surgical debridement and intravenous antibiotics. Diabetes is a recognised risk factor.
why_wrong: B. Superficial thrombophlebitis causes a tender cord along a vein without systemic toxicity. C. Cellulitis is the main differential, but pain out of proportion and dusky patches suggest deeper necrotising infection. D. Contact dermatitis is itchy and does not cause systemic illness. E. Pretibial myxoedema is a painless thyroid-related skin change.
pearl: Do not wait for imaging if necrotising fasciitis is suspected clinically; urgent surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
thinking: Minor wound ↓ Pain out of proportion to skin findings ↓ Dusky discolouration spreading ↓ Fever and tachycardia ↓ Necrotising fasciitis needing surgery
exam_trap: C, Simple cellulitis — redness and fever fit, but severe pain with dusky skin and toxicity mean a deeper, life-threatening infection.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion to the skin findings with systemic toxicity suggests necrotising fasciitis.

stem: A 39-year-old man attends the urgent treatment centre two days after returning from Australia, a journey with over 20 hours of flying. His left calf has become tense, warm and painful and his ankle is visibly puffier than the right. He has no breathlessness or chest pain. Which diagnosis should be excluded first?
why_correct: Unilateral calf pain and swelling after prolonged immobility on a long-haul flight is the classic setting for a deep vein thrombosis. It must be excluded promptly because of the risk of pulmonary embolism. Assessment uses the Wells score with D-dimer or proximal leg vein ultrasound.
why_wrong: A. A ruptured Baker's cyst can mimic a clot, but is less likely without knee disease and DVT must be excluded first. B. There is no history of exertion or injury to suggest muscle strain. D. Cellulitis causes redness and warmth, but the travel history makes a clot the priority to exclude. E. Varicose veins cause chronic symptoms, not acute calf swelling.
pearl: Long-haul travel, recent surgery, cancer, pregnancy and oestrogen therapy are major provoking factors for venous thromboembolism.
thinking: Long-haul flight ↓ Prolonged immobility ↓ Acute unilateral calf pain and swelling ↓ Risk of pulmonary embolism ↓ Exclude deep vein thrombosis first
exam_trap: D, Cellulitis of the lower leg — warmth suggests infection, but the travel history makes a clot the dangerous diagnosis to exclude first.
takeaway: Unilateral calf swelling after a long flight is a DVT until proven otherwise.

stem: A 61-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for ovarian cancer telephones her GP practice. Over the last day her right calf has become sore and her right leg looks thicker than the left, with pitting at the ankle. She has not had any injury. What diagnosis should the GP suspect?
why_correct: Acute pain and swelling of one leg in a patient with active cancer strongly suggests deep vein thrombosis. Cancer and chemotherapy create a prothrombotic state. She needs same-day assessment with a Wells score and imaging.
why_wrong: A. Claudication causes calf pain on walking relieved by rest, without swelling. B. Lymphoedema develops gradually and is usually painless, not over a day. C. Osteoarthritis affects the joint, not the whole calf. D. Achilles rupture follows sudden force and causes heel pain with loss of push-off.
pearl: Active cancer scores a point on the two-level Wells score and is one of the strongest risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
thinking: Active cancer on chemotherapy ↓ Acute unilateral calf pain ↓ One leg more swollen than the other ↓ No injury ↓ Suspect deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: B, Lymphoedema from her cancer — cancer can cause leg swelling, but painful swelling developing over a day is acute and thrombotic.
takeaway: Acute painful unilateral leg swelling suggests deep vein thrombosis, especially with cancer.

stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with a swollen, tender right calf that started two days after a long coach journey. She is not breathless and has no chest pain. What is the most appropriate approach to investigating a possible deep vein thrombosis?

options.C: Perform contrast venography of the right leg
options.D: Calculate a two-level Wells score to direct D-dimer testing or proximal leg vein ultrasound
options.E: Record an ECG to look for right heart strain

correct_answer: D. Calculate a two-level Wells score to direct D-dimer testing or proximal leg vein ultrasound
why_correct: NICE recommends assessing clinical probability with the two-level DVT Wells score. If a DVT is likely, a proximal leg vein ultrasound is arranged; if unlikely, a D-dimer is done, with ultrasound if it is positive. This structured approach avoids unnecessary scans and missed clots.
why_wrong: A. CT pulmonary angiography looks for pulmonary embolism, and she has no chest symptoms. B. A chest X-ray cannot diagnose a leg clot. C. Contrast venography is invasive and no longer first-line. E. An ECG does not diagnose a deep vein thrombosis.
pearl: If ultrasound cannot be done within 4 hours for a likely DVT, interim anticoagulation is started while waiting.
thinking: Suspected DVT ↓ No chest symptoms ↓ Assess clinical probability with Wells score ↓ Likely: ultrasound; unlikely: D-dimer first ↓ Structured pathway
exam_trap: A, Request a CT pulmonary angiogram — it seems thorough, but it investigates pulmonary embolism, not a leg clot, and she has no chest symptoms.
takeaway: Investigate suspected DVT with a two-level Wells score guiding D-dimer and ultrasound.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the walk-in centre by his friend after eating a cake that may have contained nuts. His upper lip has swollen up over the past 20 minutes. He is speaking in full sentences, has no stridor or wheeze, and his blood pressure and oxygen saturation are normal. What should be the main focus of the initial assessment?

options.A: Prescribe a course of oral antibiotics
options.B: Reassure him and discharge, as his breathing is normal
options.D: Watch closely for signs that the reaction is progressing to involve the airway or circulation
options.E: Advise him to take paracetamol at home

correct_answer: D. Watch closely for signs that the reaction is progressing to involve the airway or circulation
why_correct: Isolated lip swelling after a likely food allergen may be the start of an evolving reaction. Even with normal observations, airway, breathing and circulation must be reassessed repeatedly, as anaphylaxis can develop. Intramuscular adrenaline should be given at once if any airway, breathing or circulatory feature appears.
why_wrong: A. This is an allergic reaction, not infection. B. Normal breathing now does not exclude later progression. C. A lumbar puncture has no role. E. Paracetamol does not address an allergic reaction or the risk of progression.
pearl: Antihistamines can ease skin and mucosal symptoms but do not treat anaphylaxis; intramuscular adrenaline is the treatment once airway, breathing or circulation are affected.
thinking: Possible food allergen ↓ Lip swelling only ↓ Observations normal now ↓ Reaction can progress ↓ Reassess airway, breathing and circulation closely
exam_trap: B, Reassure him and discharge, as his breathing is normal — it seems reasonable while he is stable, but allergic reactions can progress over minutes.
takeaway: Isolated lip swelling after food needs close observation for progression to anaphylaxis.

stem: A 30-year-old motorcyclist is brought in by ambulance after being thrown from his bike at speed. He is complaining of severe pain in his hips and groin, his skin is pale and sweaty, his pulse is fast and his blood pressure is low. He has no external bleeding. Which complication is the most pressing concern?
why_correct: High-energy trauma with severe pelvic pain and shock suggests a pelvic fracture, which can cause massive haemorrhage from pelvic veins, arteries and fracture surfaces.
