A pelvic binder, activation of the major haemorrhage protocol and early blood products are needed. Haemorrhage is the leading preventable cause of death after trauma.
why_wrong: A. Fat embolism usually appears 24 to 72 hours after long-bone fractures. B. Urethral injury can occur with pelvic fractures but does not explain shock. D. Compartment syndrome causes severe limb pain, not this degree of shock. E. Peptic ulcer perforation is unrelated to the trauma.
pearl: A pelvic binder should be applied early in suspected pelvic fracture with shock; do not spring the pelvis to test stability.
thinking: High-speed trauma ↓ Severe pelvic pain ↓ Shock without external bleeding ↓ Suspected pelvic fracture ↓ Major internal haemorrhage
exam_trap: B, Urethral injury — it is a known pelvic fracture complication, but it does not threaten life in the way that shock from bleeding does.
takeaway: Shock with a suspected pelvic fracture means major internal bleeding until proven otherwise.

stem: A 63-year-old man with myasthenia gravis attends the emergency department two days after starting a course of clarithromycin for a chest infection. He has increasing weakness, double vision and difficulty clearing his secretions, and he is now breathless when lying flat. His speech is becoming nasal. What is the best interpretation of his deterioration?

options.A: Usual daily variation in his myasthenia
options.E: Myasthenic crisis needing urgent assessment of respiratory function

correct_answer: E. Myasthenic crisis needing urgent assessment of respiratory function
why_correct: Myasthenic crisis is a severe exacerbation with respiratory or bulbar muscle weakness that can lead to respiratory failure. Infection and drugs such as macrolide antibiotics are common triggers. He needs serial forced vital capacity, early critical care involvement and treatment such as intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.
why_wrong: A. Breathlessness and bulbar weakness are not normal fluctuation. B. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a separate disorder with ascending weakness and areflexia, not deterioration of known myasthenia. C. Steroid myopathy develops gradually and does not cause bulbar or respiratory failure. D. Lambert-Eaton syndrome improves with exertion and is usually paraneoplastic.
pearl: Oxygen saturation falls late in neuromuscular respiratory failure; monitor forced vital capacity rather than relying on pulse oximetry.
thinking: Known myasthenia gravis ↓ Recent infection and macrolide ↓ Bulbar weakness and poor secretion clearance ↓ Breathlessness ↓ Myasthenic crisis
exam_trap: B, Guillain-Barré syndrome — it causes respiratory failure too, but in known myasthenia with a trigger, crisis is far more likely.
takeaway: Respiratory or bulbar deterioration in myasthenia gravis is a crisis needing urgent respiratory monitoring.

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father, who saw her push a small round watch battery up her right nostril an hour ago. She is settled and breathing comfortably, with a little clear discharge from that side. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Arrange outpatient ENT review next week
options.B: Arrange urgent removal of the battery
options.C: Give a nasal decongestant and wait for it to fall out
options.E: Flush the nostril with saline repeatedly

correct_answer: B. Arrange urgent removal of the battery
why_correct: Button batteries in the nose cause rapid tissue injury through electrical current, leakage and pressure necrosis, with septal perforation possible within hours. They must be removed as an emergency by an experienced clinician. Delay worsens the damage even if the child seems well.
why_wrong: A. Outpatient review allows ongoing mucosal and septal damage. C. Waiting for the battery to fall out risks severe injury. D. Antibiotics do not remove the battery or prevent necrosis. E. Irrigation may increase current flow and spread caustic material.
pearl: A swallowed button battery in the oesophagus is an even greater emergency, as it can erode into major vessels.
thinking: Nasal foreign body ↓ Identified as button battery ↓ Rapid electrical and chemical injury ↓ Risk of septal perforation ↓ Urgent removal
exam_trap: E, Flush the nostril with saline repeatedly — it seems a gentle option, but fluid can worsen battery current injury and does not remove it.
takeaway: Button batteries in the nose need emergency removal.

stem: A 41-year-old woman on a diving holiday has a regulator failure at depth and makes a rapid, breath-held ascent. Within a few minutes of being pulled onto the boat she becomes confused, her speech is slurred and she cannot lift her left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Carbon monoxide poisoning from a contaminated air cylinder

why_correct: A rapid ascent while holding the breath lets expanding gas rupture alveoli and enter the pulmonary veins, from where bubbles pass to the cerebral arteries. The result is a stroke-like picture that begins within minutes of surfacing, exactly as here. Treatment is high-flow oxygen, lying flat and urgent transfer for hyperbaric recompression.
why_wrong: A. Contaminated air causes headache and drowsiness rather than abrupt focal weakness linked to a rapid ascent. B. Heat exhaustion causes malaise and dizziness, not sudden lateralising deficits. C. Hypoglycaemia should be checked but would not explain the timing tied to an uncontrolled ascent. D. Nitrogen narcosis occurs at depth and resolves on ascent rather than starting after surfacing.
pearl: Arterial gas embolism typically presents within about 10 minutes of surfacing, whereas decompression sickness usually develops more gradually over the following hours.
thinking: Uncontrolled breath-held ascent ↓ Expanding gas ruptures alveoli ↓ Bubbles enter the arterial circulation ↓ Focal neurology within minutes of surfacing ↓ Arterial gas embolism needing oxygen and recompression
exam_trap: D, Nitrogen narcosis — it is the best-known diving 'brain' problem, but it happens at depth and clears as the diver ascends.
takeaway: Sudden focal neurology within minutes of a rapid ascent is arterial gas embolism until proven otherwise.

stem: Paramedics are called to a homeless hostel where a 46-year-old woman with a history of heroin use is barely rousable. A used syringe lies beside her, her breaths are shallow and infrequent, and her pupils are tiny. Which drug should be given to reverse the cause of her breathing problem?
why_correct: Reduced consciousness, slow shallow breathing and very small pupils in a person who injects heroin point to opioid toxicity. Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that reverses respiratory depression within minutes, given alongside airway support and oxygen.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil antagonises benzodiazepines and has no effect on opioid receptors. C. Atropine is used for symptomatic bradycardia and cholinergic poisoning. D. Glucagon is used in beta-blocker toxicity and hypoglycaemia. E. Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest, not opioid-induced hypoventilation.
pearl: Naloxone wears off sooner than many opioids, so patients need observation and may need repeat doses or an infusion, especially after methadone or other long-acting opioids.
thinking: Known heroin use with a syringe nearby ↓ Reduced consciousness ↓ Slow shallow respirations ↓ Pinpoint pupils ↓ Opioid toxicity, so give naloxone
exam_trap: A, Flumazenil — it is also an overdose antidote, but it reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and may provoke seizures.
takeaway: The opioid triad of coma, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils is reversed with naloxone.

stem: A 34-year-old man calls NHS 111 at midday. He says that early that morning, after an argument with his partner, he swallowed a whole packet of paracetamol. He feels fine now and asks whether he can just stay at home and sleep it off. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Go to the emergency department now for urgent assessment and consideration of antidote treatment
options.B: Stay at home and attend only if vomiting or yellowing of the skin develops
options.C: Buy activated charcoal from a pharmacy and rest at home
options.D: Book a GP appointment tomorrow for liver blood tests
options.E: Attend in 24 hours so that a single blood level can guide treatment

correct_answer: A. Go to the emergency department now for urgent assessment and consideration of antidote treatment
why_correct: A deliberate paracetamol overdose needs same-day hospital assessment even when the person feels well, because liver injury develops silently and acetylcysteine works best when started early. In hospital the timing, amount and blood results guide whether treatment is needed, and his mental health and safety also need assessment.
why_wrong: B. Vomiting and jaundice are late signs, by which time liver damage is established. C. Charcoal is only useful within about an hour of ingestion and home care is unsafe. D. Waiting until tomorrow delays possible antidote treatment. E. Levels are interpreted from 4 hours after ingestion and treatment should not be postponed for a day.
pearl: Acetylcysteine is almost completely protective against liver injury when started within 8 hours of a single acute paracetamol overdose.
thinking: Deliberate paracetamol overdose some hours ago ↓ Currently asymptomatic ↓ Liver injury can be silent early on ↓ Antidote is time-critical ↓ Urgent ED assessment today
exam_trap: B, Attend only if symptoms develop — he sounds well, but symptoms appear only once serious liver damage has already occurred.
takeaway: Any deliberate paracetamol overdose needs urgent hospital assessment, however well the person feels.

stem: Staff at a care home find a 78-year-old woman sleepy but rousable and realise she has taken several days' supply of her prescribed temazepam. In the emergency department she responds to voice, her airway is clear, her breathing is regular with normal oxygen saturation, and her pulse and blood pressure are normal. No other substances are suspected. What is the main approach to her management?

options.A: Intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation
options.C: Supportive care with observation of airway, breathing and conscious level
options.E: Elective intubation to protect the airway

correct_answer: C. Supportive care with observation of airway, breathing and conscious level
why_correct: Isolated benzodiazepine overdose usually causes sedation with little cardiorespiratory compromise, and most people recover with supportive care alone. She is protecting her airway and breathing adequately, so the priority is monitoring her airway, breathing, oxygen saturation and conscious level until the drug wears off.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil is not routine because it can precipitate seizures and withdrawal, and she is not in danger. B. Gastric lavage is no longer recommended for this type of poisoning. D. Benzodiazepines are highly protein bound and not removed by dialysis. E. Intubation is not needed while she maintains her own airway and breathing.
pearl: Older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines and may stay sedated for longer, so observation periods are often extended.
thinking: Known benzodiazepine overdose only ↓ Rousable with patent airway ↓ Breathing and circulation stable ↓ Antidote risks outweigh benefits ↓ Supportive care and monitoring
exam_trap: A, Flumazenil — a specific antidote feels like the active choice, but it carries a seizure risk and is unnecessary when breathing is adequate.
takeaway: Stable isolated benzodiazepine overdose is managed supportively, not with a routine antidote.

stem: A 50-year-old man who takes amitriptyline at night for chronic back pain is brought in by his wife, who found the empty packets beside him. He is drowsy, with dilated pupils, dry flushed skin and a fast pulse. Which investigation should be performed first to identify the most dangerous complication?
why_correct: Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac sodium channels, causing QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmias and hypotension, which are the main causes of death. An early 12-lead ECG, followed by continuous cardiac monitoring, identifies those who need sodium bicarbonate and close observation.
why_wrong: A. A chest X-ray may later show aspiration but does not detect the life-threatening conduction effects. B. Head imaging is not the priority when the drowsiness is explained by the ingestion. C. Amylase does not assess tricyclic toxicity. D. A urine screen adds little when the drug is known and does not measure severity.
pearl: A QRS duration above 100 ms after tricyclic overdose predicts seizures, and above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmias.
thinking: Known amitriptyline overdose ↓ Anticholinergic features present ↓ Sodium channel blockade is the main killer ↓ Look for QRS widening and arrhythmia ↓ 12-lead ECG first
exam_trap: D, Urine drug screen — it seems a natural toxicology test, but the drug is already known and the screen tells you nothing about cardiac risk.
takeaway: In tricyclic overdose, get an ECG early and look closely at the QRS width.

stem: At a GP surgery, the mother of a 17-year-old boy says he admitted last night that he had taken a large number of paracetamol tablets at once. This morning he is eating breakfast and says nothing hurts, so she wonders whether hospital is really necessary. Which statement best explains why he needs urgent hospital assessment?

options.A: Feeling well the next morning means the drug has been safely cleared
options.B: Treatment is needed only once jaundice appears
options.C: Hospital is needed only if abdominal pain develops
options.D: Serious liver damage can be developing while he still feels well
options.E: A single overdose rarely harms the liver

correct_answer: D. Serious liver damage can be developing while he still feels well
why_correct: In the first day after a paracetamol overdose people often have mild nausea or no symptoms at all, yet a toxic metabolite is already damaging liver cells. Pain, jaundice and confusion appear later, when the opportunity for fully effective acetylcysteine treatment has passed. He therefore needs urgent ED assessment, including blood tests and a review of his safety.
why_wrong: A. Feeling well gives no reassurance because liver injury is silent early. B. Waiting for jaundice means treatment starts after damage is established. C. Abdominal pain is a late sign. E. A single large overdose can cause fatal liver failure.
pearl: When a significant paracetamol overdose was taken more than 8 hours earlier, acetylcysteine is started immediately rather than waiting for the blood results.
thinking: Large single paracetamol overdose last night ↓ Now looks well ↓ Toxic metabolite injures the liver silently ↓ Symptoms appear late ↓ Urgent hospital assessment now
exam_trap: A, Feeling well means it has cleared — a well-looking teenager is reassuring, but paracetamol toxicity is typically silent until liver damage is advanced.
takeaway: Looking well after a paracetamol overdose never rules out serious liver injury.

stem: A 62-year-old man is found by his daughter with empty packets of clomipramine. In the emergency department his conscious level is reduced and he is hypotensive, and his ECG shows a sinus tachycardia with a markedly broadened QRS complex. Which treatment is most important for his cardiac toxicity?
why_correct: A broad QRS and hypotension after tricyclic overdose reflect sodium channel blockade in the heart. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate alkalinises the blood and supplies sodium, reducing channel blockade, narrowing the QRS and improving blood pressure. Airway support, fluids and cardiac monitoring are given alongside.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil can provoke seizures in tricyclic poisoning and is contraindicated. B. Acetylcysteine is for paracetamol poisoning. D. Amiodarone further prolongs conduction and is avoided in tricyclic-induced arrhythmias. E. Naloxone reverses opioids and will not correct a sodium channel effect.
pearl: Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics and amiodarone are avoided in tricyclic poisoning because they worsen sodium channel blockade or prolong the QT interval.
thinking: Clomipramine overdose ↓ Reduced consciousness and hypotension ↓ Broad QRS on ECG ↓ Cardiac sodium channel blockade ↓ Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
exam_trap: D, Intravenous amiodarone — it treats many broad-complex rhythms, but in tricyclic poisoning it worsens conduction and can be harmful.
takeaway: Broad QRS after a tricyclic overdose calls for intravenous sodium bicarbonate.

presentation: Paracetamol overdose: timed level in a teenager
stem: In the paediatric emergency department, a 15-year-old girl admits to taking a large number of paracetamol tablets at about lunchtime after falling out with friends. Her father brought her in that evening, roughly six hours later. She has no symptoms. Which blood test is essential to judge her risk of liver damage?

options.E: Paracetamol concentration timed from the ingestion

correct_answer: E. Paracetamol concentration timed from the ingestion
why_correct: After a single acute paracetamol ingestion at a known time, the plasma concentration measured at least 4 hours after ingestion is plotted on the treatment nomogram to decide on acetylcysteine. The same approach applies to adolescents as to adults, and safeguarding and mental health assessment follow once she is medically safe.
why_wrong: A. Salicylate levels are often checked in unclear overdoses but do not measure paracetamol risk. B. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. C. Amylase is used for pancreatitis, not paracetamol toxicity. D. Creatine kinase measures muscle damage.
pearl: Young people who self-harm should have a psychosocial assessment by the child and adolescent mental health team before discharge.
thinking: Single paracetamol overdose with a known time ↓ About six hours ago ↓ Asymptomatic teenager ↓ Risk must be quantified ↓ Timed paracetamol concentration on the nomogram
exam_trap: A, Salicylate concentration — it is often requested in overdose screens, so it feels relevant, but it does not tell you anything about paracetamol hepatotoxicity.
takeaway: A timed paracetamol concentration is the key test after a single known-time paracetamol overdose.

stem: A 26-year-old woman who is prescribed propranolol for anxiety deliberately takes her whole supply. In the emergency department her pulse is very slow and she is hypotensive, and neither intravenous fluids nor repeated atropine has helped. Which drug is commonly used next for severe toxicity of this kind?
why_correct: Beta-blockers stop catecholamines from raising intracellular cyclic AMP in cardiac cells, causing bradycardia and low cardiac output. Glucagon acts on its own receptor to raise cyclic AMP independently of beta-receptors, improving heart rate and contractility. It is a recognised treatment for severe beta-blocker poisoning when atropine and fluids fail, alongside expert advice from TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity. B. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines. C. Acetylcysteine is the paracetamol antidote. D. Digoxin-specific antibody fragments treat digoxin toxicity, which is not involved here.
pearl: Propranolol is particularly dangerous in overdose because it also blocks sodium channels and crosses into the brain, causing seizures and broad QRS complexes.
thinking: Propranolol overdose ↓ Bradycardia and hypotension ↓ Fluids and atropine ineffective ↓ Bypass the blocked beta-receptor ↓ Glucagon raises cyclic AMP
exam_trap: D, Digoxin-specific antibody fragments — they are the classic antidote for drug-induced bradycardia, but only when the cause is digoxin.
takeaway: Glucagon is used in severe beta-blocker poisoning because it raises cyclic AMP independently of beta-receptors.

stem: A 55-year-old man who takes modified-release verapamil for angina deliberately swallows a large number of his tablets. He arrives in resus pale and clammy with a very slow pulse, a low blood pressure and a raised blood glucose. Which treatment is used early in severe toxicity of this kind?
why_correct: Verapamil blocks L-type calcium channels in the heart and vessels, causing bradycardia, heart block, vasodilatation and hypotension, and it also reduces insulin release, hence the hyperglycaemia. Intravenous calcium increases extracellular calcium to partly overcome the blockade and improve contractility and blood pressure. It is given early, with fluids, atropine and specialist poisons advice, and high-dose insulin therapy may follow in severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin K reverses warfarin anticoagulation. B. Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning. C. Naloxone reverses opioids. D. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
pearl: Hyperglycaemia in a bradycardic, hypotensive overdose patient is a useful clue to calcium-channel blocker poisoning and correlates with its severity.
thinking: Verapamil overdose ↓ Bradycardia and hypotension ↓ Hyperglycaemia from reduced insulin release ↓ Calcium channels blocked ↓ Give intravenous calcium
exam_trap: C, Naloxone — reduced consciousness in overdose often prompts a trial of naloxone, but it has no effect on calcium-channel blockade.
takeaway: Severe calcium-channel blocker poisoning is treated early with intravenous calcium alongside specialist support.

presentation: Paracetamol overdose in pregnancy: timed level
stem: A 31-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant attends the maternity assessment unit and tells the midwife that she took a large quantity of paracetamol at breakfast after a row at home. It is now mid-afternoon. She feels well and fetal movements are normal. Which investigation is most important for deciding whether she needs treatment?

options.B: Plasma paracetamol concentration related to the time of ingestion

correct_answer: B. Plasma paracetamol concentration related to the time of ingestion
why_correct: For a single acute paracetamol ingestion at a known time more than 4 hours ago, the plasma paracetamol level plotted on the nomogram decides whether acetylcysteine is needed. Pregnancy does not change this approach, and acetylcysteine is safe in pregnancy and protects both mother and fetus.
why_wrong: A. Salicylate levels assess aspirin poisoning rather than paracetamol risk. C. Creatine kinase reflects muscle injury. D. A qualitative urine screen shows presence, not the amount or risk of liver injury. E. These electrolytes do not predict paracetamol hepatotoxicity.
pearl: Pregnant women with paracetamol overdose are managed with the same treatment thresholds as other adults, because untreated maternal liver failure poses the greatest risk to the fetus.
thinking: Single paracetamol ingestion at breakfast ↓ More than 4 hours have passed ↓ Pregnancy does not alter thresholds ↓ Need to quantify toxicity ↓ Timed plasma paracetamol concentration
exam_trap: D, Qualitative urine drug screen — it feels thorough in a possible overdose, but it only shows that a drug is present and cannot guide antidote treatment.
takeaway: Pregnant or not, a timed plasma paracetamol level guides treatment after a single known-time overdose.

stem: A 47-year-old man is transferred from a minor injuries unit after telling the nurse practitioner that he swallowed most of a large tub of paracetamol at around 9 o'clock that morning. It is now early afternoon. He has no abdominal pain, his observations are normal and he is otherwise healthy. Which blood test is most useful in estimating his risk of liver damage?

options.C: Paracetamol concentration measured at a known interval after the ingestion

correct_answer: C. Paracetamol concentration measured at a known interval after the ingestion
why_correct: His ingestion was a single episode at a known time more than 4 hours ago, so the plasma paracetamol concentration can be plotted on the treatment nomogram. A level on or above the treatment line indicates the need for acetylcysteine, while liver tests, INR and renal function provide a baseline.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury, which is not a feature of paracetamol overdose. B. Salicylate concentration assesses aspirin poisoning. D. Ferritin and iron are relevant to iron poisoning or iron status. E. Amylase does not assess hepatotoxicity.
pearl: Liver tests are often normal in the first hours after a toxic paracetamol dose, so they cannot be used on their own to decide against treatment.
thinking: Single ingestion at a known time ↓ More than 4 hours ago ↓ Asymptomatic with normal observations ↓ Quantify the risk ↓ Plot the timed paracetamol level on the nomogram
exam_trap: B, Salicylate concentration — it is part of many overdose screens, but it measures aspirin exposure and says nothing about paracetamol liver risk.
takeaway: Measure paracetamol at a known time after a single ingestion to estimate hepatotoxicity risk.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with severe dental anxiety is having a tooth extracted under intravenous midazolam sedation in a community dental clinic. She becomes unrousable and her breathing becomes shallow, although she is not a regular user of sedatives. Which drug specifically reverses the sedative drug she has been given?
why_correct: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil competitively antagonises benzodiazepines at the GABA-A receptor, reversing sedation within minutes. Iatrogenic over-sedation in a person who does not take benzodiazepines regularly is an appropriate use, combined with airway support and oxygen.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids and does not affect benzodiazepine sedation. B. Glucagon is used for hypoglycaemia and beta-blocker toxicity. C. Vitamin K reverses warfarin. D. Atropine treats bradycardia and excess secretions but does not reverse sedation.
pearl: Flumazenil is avoided in mixed overdoses and in regular benzodiazepine users because it can precipitate seizures and withdrawal.
thinking: Intravenous midazolam given ↓ Over-sedation with shallow breathing ↓ Not a regular sedative user ↓ Benzodiazepine-specific antagonist required ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: A, Naloxone — it is the best-known reversal drug, but it only acts on opioid receptors and will not wake a patient sedated with midazolam.
takeaway: Flumazenil specifically reverses benzodiazepines such as midazolam.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted two days after taking a large amount of paracetamol, which she had not told anyone about. She now has pain under her right ribs, persistent vomiting and yellowing of her eyes, and her INR is raised. Which organ is mainly affected by this poisoning?
why_correct: Paracetamol is normally conjugated safely, but in overdose more is converted to NAPQI, which damages hepatocytes once glutathione runs out. Right upper quadrant pain, vomiting, jaundice and a raised INR one to three days later indicate acute liver injury, which can progress to liver failure.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis is not the typical consequence of paracetamol overdose. B. The spleen is not a target of paracetamol toxicity. C. Gallbladder disease would not explain a raised INR after an overdose. D. The stomach is not significantly injured by paracetamol, unlike with aspirin or NSAIDs.
pearl: Patients with severe paracetamol liver injury should be discussed with a liver unit, using criteria such as acidosis, INR, creatinine and encephalopathy to guide transplant referral.
thinking: Large paracetamol overdose two days ago ↓ Right upper quadrant pain and vomiting ↓ Jaundice and raised INR ↓ NAPQI damages hepatocytes ↓ Liver is the target organ
exam_trap: C, Gallbladder — right upper quadrant pain and jaundice suggest biliary disease, but a raised INR after paracetamol overdose points to liver cell injury.
takeaway: Paracetamol overdose mainly damages the liver.

stem: A 50-year-old man attends a walk-in centre with a cut hand. While it is being dressed, he mentions that about six hours earlier he took 'a lot' of paracetamol because he could not cope. He has no symptoms and his observations are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge him with advice to return if he becomes jaundiced
options.B: Give activated charcoal and send him home
options.C: Arrange liver tests at the GP surgery in 24 hours and treat if abnormal
options.D: Transfer him urgently to the emergency department for assessment under the paracetamol overdose pathway
options.E: Prescribe oral acetylcysteine and arrange GP review tomorrow

correct_answer: D. Transfer him urgently to the emergency department for assessment under the paracetamol overdose pathway
why_correct: A potentially toxic paracetamol ingestion needs prompt hospital assessment even when the person is symptom-free, because liver injury is silent early and acetylcysteine is most effective when given within 8 hours. In the ED, the timing and amount, blood levels and liver tests guide treatment, and his suicidal intent must also be assessed.
why_wrong: A. Jaundice is a late sign of established liver damage. B. Charcoal is of little value six hours after ingestion and discharge is unsafe. C. Waiting a day for liver tests delays time-critical treatment. E. Acetylcysteine is given intravenously in hospital, not as an outpatient oral course.
pearl: Intravenous acetylcysteine is licensed as a three-bag infusion over 21 hours, and many UK hospitals now use a two-bag regimen over about 12 hours; either way, blood tests are repeated before the infusion ends to decide whether to continue.
thinking: Deliberate paracetamol ingestion six hours ago ↓ Asymptomatic ↓ Antidote most effective within 8 hours ↓ Needs blood tests and risk assessment ↓ Urgent ED transfer
exam_trap: E, Oral acetylcysteine and GP review — it sounds like a pragmatic plan, but treatment is given intravenously in hospital with blood monitoring and a mental health assessment.
takeaway: A possibly toxic paracetamol overdose needs same-day hospital assessment, regardless of symptoms.

stem: A 39-year-old man is brought by ambulance after his sister found several empty, unlabelled medicine pots in his flat. He is awake but anxious and cannot say what or how much he took. What should be done first?

options.A: Arrange a psychiatric assessment before any medical treatment
options.B: Wait for toxicology results before examining him
options.C: Reassure him that most unknown ingestions are harmless and discharge him
options.D: Ask his sister to find the original packets before starting treatment
options.E: Assess and stabilise his airway, breathing and circulation

correct_answer: E. Assess and stabilise his airway, breathing and circulation
why_correct: Any patient who may have been poisoned is first assessed with an ABCDE approach, because airway compromise, respiratory depression, arrhythmias and seizures can develop quickly. Once he is stable, a history, ECG, glucose, paracetamol and salicylate levels, and advice from TOXBASE guide further care, followed by a mental health assessment.
why_wrong: A. Psychiatric assessment is important but follows medical stabilisation. B. Toxicology results take time and treatment should not wait for them. C. Unknown ingestions may be dangerous and premature discharge is unsafe. D. Collateral information is helpful but must not delay initial assessment.
pearl: In every unknown overdose, check capillary glucose, an ECG and paracetamol and salicylate levels, because these are common, treatable and often silent.
thinking: Possible ingestion of unknown drugs ↓ Toxic effects may evolve quickly ↓ Information is incomplete ↓ Life-threats come first ↓ ABCDE assessment and stabilisation
exam_trap: A, Psychiatric assessment first — the context suggests self-harm, but medical stabilisation must come before mental health review.
takeaway: In any suspected poisoning, start with airway, breathing and circulation.

stem: Friends bring a 24-year-old man to the emergency department after he took several alprazolam tablets bought online. He is slumped in a wheelchair and slurring his words. Which pattern is most typical of this type of drug toxicity?

options.A: Sedation with slurred speech and unsteadiness, often with near-normal vital signs
options.D: Agitation with hypertension and dilated pupils
options.E: Ringing in the ears with rapid deep breathing

correct_answer: A. Sedation with slurred speech and unsteadiness, often with near-normal vital signs
why_correct: Alprazolam is a benzodiazepine, and toxicity mainly causes central nervous system depression: drowsiness, slurred speech and ataxia. In isolated benzodiazepine poisoning, breathing and blood pressure are usually only mildly affected, so marked respiratory depression should prompt a search for co-ingested opioids or alcohol.
why_wrong: B. Fever with rigidity suggests neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin toxicity. C. Salivation, diarrhoea and wheeze are cholinergic features of organophosphate poisoning. D. Agitation, hypertension and mydriasis indicate stimulant toxicity. E. Tinnitus and hyperventilation are typical of salicylate poisoning.
pearl: Illicit 'benzodiazepine' tablets bought online or on the street are often counterfeit and may contain potent novel benzodiazepines or even opioids, causing deeper sedation than expected.
thinking: Alprazolam ingestion ↓ Benzodiazepine enhances GABA ↓ Brain depression ↓ Drowsiness, slurred speech, ataxia ↓ Vital signs usually preserved
exam_trap: D, Agitation with dilated pupils — tablets bought online raise suspicion of stimulants, but this man is sedated and slurring, which fits a benzodiazepine.
takeaway: Benzodiazepine toxicity looks like sedation and ataxia with largely preserved vital signs.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who takes sertraline for depression was started on tramadol for back pain a few days ago. She attends the emergency department restless, sweating and shaking, with diarrhoea, a raised temperature and a fast pulse. Her reflexes are brisk and there is sustained clonus at both ankles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Combining a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor with tramadol, which also increases serotonin, can cause serotonin syndrome. The triad of altered mental state, autonomic instability (sweating, fever, tachycardia, diarrhoea) and neuromuscular excitability, especially hyperreflexia and inducible or sustained clonus, is characteristic. Management is to stop serotonergic drugs and give supportive care, with benzodiazepines and specialist advice if severe.
why_wrong: A. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotic use and develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes. C. Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry skin, urinary retention and reduced bowel activity rather than sweating and diarrhoea. D. Malignant hyperthermia occurs during general anaesthesia with volatile agents or suxamethonium. E. Alcohol withdrawal causes tremor and sweating but not clonus, and there is no alcohol history here.
pearl: Clonus and hyperreflexia, most marked in the lower limbs, are the most useful signs separating serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
thinking: Sertraline plus newly started tramadol ↓ Agitation, sweating, diarrhoea, fever ↓ Hyperreflexia and ankle clonus ↓ Serotonergic excess ↓ Serotonin syndrome
exam_trap: A, Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — fever and autonomic instability overlap, but it needs antipsychotic exposure and causes rigidity with sluggish rather than brisk reflexes.
takeaway: Fever, agitation and clonus after combining serotonergic drugs indicate serotonin syndrome.

presentation: Opioid toxicity: airway support and naloxone
stem: An 81-year-old man with chronic kidney disease was started on oral morphine by his GP after a painful fall. Two days later his carer finds him unrousable in bed, breathing very slowly, with small pupils and oxygen saturation that keeps dropping. The ambulance crew arrive. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Give high-flow oxygen and wait for him to wake
options.B: Support the airway and ventilation with a bag-valve-mask and give naloxone
options.C: Give flumazenil to reverse the respiratory depression
options.D: Obtain a urine drug screen before giving any treatment
options.E: Give intravenous fluids and reassess in 30 minutes

correct_answer: B. Support the airway and ventilation with a bag-valve-mask and give naloxone
why_correct: Reduced kidney function lets morphine and its active metabolites accumulate, causing opioid toxicity. Life-threatening hypoventilation needs immediate airway opening and assisted ventilation with oxygen, with naloxone given in titrated doses to restore adequate breathing. Oxygen alone does not correct the failure to ventilate.
why_wrong: A. Oxygen without ventilatory support leaves carbon dioxide rising and does not treat the cause. C. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids. D. Testing delays life-saving treatment and adds nothing when the cause is clear. E. Fluids do not address respiratory depression and a 30-minute delay is dangerous.
pearl: In older adults and those on regular opioids, naloxone is given in small titrated doses to restore breathing without causing acute withdrawal or severe pain.
thinking: New morphine with kidney impairment ↓ Accumulation of active metabolites ↓ Unrousable with slow breathing and small pupils ↓ Failing ventilation ↓ Support the airway and breathing and give naloxone
exam_trap: A, High-flow oxygen and wait — oxygen improves the saturation reading, but it does nothing for the inadequate ventilation, so carbon dioxide continues to rise.
takeaway: Opioid respiratory depression needs airway and ventilatory support plus naloxone without delay.

presentation: Scald first aid in a young child
stem: A mother rings NHS 111 a few minutes after her 4-year-old daughter pulled a kettle off the worktop. The girl is crying and has a red, painful, blistering patch on the front of her thigh, but is alert and breathing normally. The call handler wants to give the most useful advice for what to do right now at home. What should the mother be told to do first?

options.A: Hold an ice pack firmly against the scald
options.B: Smear butter or a greasy cream over the area
options.C: Prick the blisters with a clean needle to release the fluid
options.D: Run cool tap water over the scald for a prolonged period
options.E: Seal the area with a sticky plaster or adhesive tape

correct_answer: D. Run cool tap water over the scald for a prolonged period
why_correct: Prompt cooling with cool or lukewarm running water limits the depth of a thermal injury and eases pain, and it remains useful for some time after the scald. It is the single most important first-aid step before covering the area loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy dressing and seeking assessment. A blistering scald in a young child also needs face-to-face review.
why_wrong: A. Ice causes vasoconstriction and can add a cold injury to damaged skin. B. Butter and greasy home remedies trap heat, raise infection risk and hinder assessment. C. Deliberately breaking blisters exposes the wound to infection and adds pain. E. Adhesive material stuck to burnt skin tears the surface when removed.
pearl: After cooling, cling film laid loosely over a burn (not wrapped round a limb) makes a clean, non-adherent covering that lets clinicians see the wound.
thinking: Child with a fresh hot-water scald ↓ Airway and breathing fine, so first aid is the priority ↓ Aim is to stop ongoing tissue damage and relieve pain ↓ Cool running water does both safely ↓ Avoid ice, grease, blister bursting and adhesives
exam_trap: A, Holding an ice pack against the scald — it sounds like stronger cooling, but ice constricts vessels and can deepen the injury.
takeaway: The first thing to do for a fresh scald is cool it with running water, not ice or home remedies.

stem: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his brother, who found empty packets of paracetamol in his kitchen. The man admits swallowing a lot of tablets at some point today after an argument, but is vague about details. He has no nausea or pain, is alert, and his observations and examination are normal. Which approach to his poisoning is most appropriate?

options.A: Reassure him that being symptom-free shows a harmless ingestion
options.B: Allow home once a mental health review is complete, with advice to return if vomiting starts
options.C: Hold off antidote treatment until his liver enzymes start to rise
options.D: Establish the timing and amount taken, then use a timed paracetamol level and the treatment line to guide acetylcysteine, starting it at once if the timing cannot be established
options.E: Give activated charcoal as the definitive treatment and then observe

correct_answer: D. Establish the timing and amount taken, then use a timed paracetamol level and the treatment line to guide acetylcysteine, starting it at once if the timing cannot be established
why_correct: Paracetamol poisoning is typically silent for the first day even when the liver is at serious risk, so the way he looks does not reflect the danger. Management depends on when and how much was taken: a level taken at or after four hours is plotted on the treatment nomogram, but because his timing is vague and may be staggered, acetylcysteine should be started immediately rather than waiting for a level. Acetylcysteine is most protective when given early, so it should not wait for abnormal liver tests.
why_wrong: A. Lack of symptoms early on gives no reassurance about liver injury. B. Sending him home before risk assessment could miss the window for effective antidote treatment. C. Raised transaminases mean damage is already under way; acetylcysteine works best before this. E. Charcoal only helps within about an hour of ingestion and is never the main treatment hours later.
pearl: If the time of ingestion cannot be established, or tablets were taken over more than an hour, start acetylcysteine without waiting for the blood level.
thinking: Deliberate paracetamol overdose, currently well ↓ Early phase is often symptom-free despite liver risk ↓ Establish time and quantity ↓ Timed level against the treatment line, or treat at once if timing unclear ↓ Acetylcysteine early, plus psychosocial assessment
exam_trap: A, Reassurance because he feels well — his normal appearance is exactly what makes early paracetamol toxicity easy to underestimate.
takeaway: In paracetamol overdose, timing and amount, not symptoms, decide treatment.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is seen at an out-of-hours GP centre with four days of worsening sore throat, now worse on the right. She has a muffled voice, drools, and can only open her mouth a little. Examination shows a tense bulge above and lateral to the right tonsil, and her uvula sits pushed over towards the left side. What is the explanation for the position of her uvula?

options.B: Weakness of the tongue from hypoglossal nerve injury
options.C: Pus collecting beside the tonsil pushing the soft palate and uvula across
options.D: Palsy of the facial nerve on the right
options.E: Downward traction on the larynx from neck swelling

correct_answer: C. Pus collecting beside the tonsil pushing the soft palate and uvula across
why_correct: A peritonsillar abscess forms in the space between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles. As pus accumulates it bulges the soft palate forward and medially, mechanically shoving the uvula to the opposite side. Together with trismus and a muffled voice, this mass effect is characteristic of quinsy and needs urgent ENT drainage.
why_wrong: A. Temporomandibular dislocation causes an open, fixed jaw rather than a displaced uvula. B. The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue and does not position the uvula. D. The facial nerve does not supply the palatal muscles. E. The larynx sits well below the oropharynx and does not move the uvula.
pearl: Quinsy is usually managed by needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus intravenous antibiotics, with ENT input; trismus helps distinguish it from simple tonsillitis.
thinking: Severe one-sided sore throat with trismus and muffled voice ↓ Bulge above and lateral to one tonsil ↓ Uvula displaced to the other side ↓ Mechanical push from a collection of pus ↓ Peritonsillar abscess needing urgent ENT drainage
exam_trap: B, Hypoglossal nerve weakness — tongue deviation is a familiar cranial nerve sign, but it affects the tongue, not the uvula, and the cause here is a mass.
takeaway: In quinsy, the uvula is pushed away from the abscess by the swelling itself.

stem: A GP sees three members of the same family on one winter morning. All describe headaches and nausea that ease when they are out of their rented flat and return each evening at home. Their cat has also been lethargic. The GP suspects carbon monoxide exposure and asks about appliances in the flat. Which household item is the most likely source?
why_correct: Carbon monoxide is produced by incomplete combustion of carbon-based fuel, so faulty or badly ventilated gas, oil, coal or wood-burning appliances are the classic household sources. Symptoms shared by several people (and pets) in one building that improve away from home are a strong pointer. A poorly serviced boiler is the item on this list that burns fuel.
why_wrong: A. A microwave heats food electrically and produces no combustion gases. C. An electric heater warms air without burning fuel. D. A fridge freezer does not burn fuel. E. Plug-in air fresheners release fragrance, not carbon monoxide.
pearl: Clustered symptoms in a household, improvement on leaving the building and worse symptoms when heating is on are key clues; advise the gas emergency line and fitting of an audible carbon monoxide alarm.
thinking: Several household members with headache and nausea ↓ Better away from home ↓ Suggests an environmental toxin indoors ↓ Carbon monoxide comes from incomplete combustion ↓ Fuel-burning appliance such as a gas boiler
exam_trap: C, Electric fan heater — any heater sounds suspicious in winter, but only fuel-burning appliances generate carbon monoxide.
takeaway: Carbon monoxide comes from faulty fuel-burning appliances such as gas boilers.

stem: A 40-year-old man is brought in by ambulance from a car repair workshop where colleagues saw him drink from a bottle of screen-wash or coolant some hours earlier. He is now drowsy with deep, rapid breathing, and a venous blood gas shows a severe metabolic acidosis. The exact substance is not known. What is the most appropriate overall approach?

options.A: Treat as a medical emergency with ABC resuscitation and urgent specialist poisons advice
options.B: Give activated charcoal and observe on the ward for six hours
options.C: Admit to the ward and repeat blood tests only if he deteriorates
options.D: Wait until visual or renal complications appear before starting specific treatment
options.E: Discharge once he is more alert, with a leaflet on the dangers of solvents

correct_answer: A. Treat as a medical emergency with ABC resuscitation and urgent specialist poisons advice
why_correct: Methanol and ethylene glycol cause toxicity through their metabolites, so a sick patient with an unexplained acidosis after possible ingestion needs immediate resuscitation and early specific treatment. TOXBASE and the National Poisons Information Service guide use of fomepizole or ethanol to block alcohol dehydrogenase, and haemodialysis may be needed. Waiting for end-organ damage loses the chance to prevent blindness and kidney failure.
why_wrong: B. Activated charcoal does not bind alcohols and observation alone delays antidote therapy. C. He is already severely acidotic, so passive observation is unsafe. D. Visual loss and kidney injury may be permanent once established; treatment should prevent them. E. A drowsy, acidotic patient after toxic ingestion is not safe for discharge.
pearl: Fomepizole (or ethanol if unavailable) inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, stopping conversion of methanol and ethylene glycol to their toxic acids.
thinking: Possible ingestion of screen-wash or coolant ↓ Drowsy with Kussmaul-type breathing ↓ Severe metabolic acidosis ↓ Toxic alcohol until proven otherwise ↓ Resuscitate and seek urgent poisons advice for antidote and dialysis
exam_trap: B, Activated charcoal with observation — it is a familiar poisoning step, but alcohols are not adsorbed and the delay allows toxic metabolites to accumulate.
takeaway: A seriously ill patient after suspected toxic alcohol ingestion needs emergency care and immediate poisons advice.

stem: A 47-year-old man is admitted from a homeless shelter after staff found him confused, having drunk a sweet-tasting liquid from an unlabelled container. Over the next day he develops a severe metabolic acidosis, falling urine output and a rising creatinine. His serum calcium is low, urine microscopy shows crystals, and he has no visual complaints. Which substance is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Ethylene glycol is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acids, causing a high anion gap acidosis. Oxalate binds calcium, producing hypocalcaemia and calcium oxalate crystals that deposit in the kidneys, leading to acute kidney injury. Its sweet taste is why it is sometimes drunk accidentally or as an alcohol substitute.
why_wrong: A. Methanol typically causes visual toxicity rather than oxalate crystalluria and kidney injury. B. Isopropyl alcohol causes ketosis and drowsiness without a marked acidosis. C. Ethanol causes intoxication without this acidosis or crystal deposition. E. Paracetamol is not an alcohol and primarily injures the liver.
pearl: Calcium oxalate crystals in the urine and hypocalcaemia are the hallmark clues for ethylene glycol.
thinking: Ingestion of a sweet unknown liquid ↓ Severe metabolic acidosis ↓ Acute kidney injury with low calcium ↓ Urinary crystals, no visual symptoms ↓ Oxalate from ethylene glycol
exam_trap: A, Methanol — the other classic toxic alcohol causing acidosis, but it targets the eyes rather than causing oxalate crystal kidney injury.
takeaway: Acidosis with kidney injury, hypocalcaemia and urinary crystals points to ethylene glycol.

stem: A 33-year-old farm worker is brought to the emergency department after spraying crops in an enclosed shed. He is sweating heavily, drooling and vomiting, has very small pupils, a wet bubbly chest with wheeze, and a heart rate of 40 per minute. Which drug is the mainstay for reversing these features?
why_correct: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates and over-stimulates muscarinic receptors, causing bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, salivation and miosis. Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic receptors and is given in repeated, escalating doses until the chest is dry and heart rate adequate. Drying of bronchial secretions is the main treatment target.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids, which cause small pupils but not secretions and sweating. C. Flumazenil antagonises benzodiazepines. D. Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning. E. Vitamin K reverses warfarin and has no effect on cholinergic toxicity.
pearl: Decontaminate the patient (remove clothing, wash skin) and protect staff, because organophosphates are absorbed through the skin.
thinking: Exposure to crop spray ↓ Sweating, salivation, small pupils ↓ Bronchorrhoea and bradycardia ↓ Cholinergic excess from acetylcholinesterase inhibition ↓ Atropine titrated to a dry chest
exam_trap: A, Naloxone — pinpoint pupils suggest opioids, but the profuse secretions, sweating and bradycardia point to cholinergic poisoning.
takeaway: Atropine is the key treatment for the muscarinic effects of organophosphate poisoning.

stem: An elderly couple are brought to the emergency department after a chimney sweep found their wood-burner flue blocked. Both had headaches and confusion, which settle with high-flow oxygen. Their son asks how the fumes starved their tissues of oxygen when their breathing had seemed normal. What is the main mechanism?

options.A: Binding to haemoglobin far more avidly than oxygen, displacing it and impairing its release
options.B: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at nerve endings
options.C: Blockade of insulin receptors on cell membranes
options.E: Direct obstruction of the renal tubules

correct_answer: A. Binding to haemoglobin far more avidly than oxygen, displacing it and impairing its release
why_correct: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with roughly two hundred times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity. It also shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left, so the remaining oxygen is released less readily to tissues. It additionally impairs mitochondrial respiration, adding to cellular hypoxia despite normal breathing.
why_wrong: B. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is the mechanism of organophosphate poisoning. C. Carbon monoxide has no effect on insulin receptors. D. Platelet destruction is not a feature of carbon monoxide toxicity. E. Carbon monoxide does not obstruct the renal tubules.
pearl: High-flow oxygen shortens the half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin considerably compared with breathing air.
thinking: Blocked flue on a fuel-burning stove ↓ Headache and confusion improving with oxygen ↓ Carbon monoxide exposure ↓ Forms carboxyhaemoglobin with very high affinity ↓ Less oxygen carried and less released to tissues
exam_trap: B, Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase — another classic poisoning mechanism, but it belongs to organophosphates, not carbon monoxide.
takeaway: Carbon monoxide causes tissue hypoxia by binding haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is admitted after drinking from an unlabelled bottle at a car repair workshop. About a day later she complains that bright light hurts and her vision has become misty. Fundoscopy shows swollen, hyperaemic optic discs, and an arterial blood gas confirms a metabolic acidosis. Which alcohol is most characteristically linked to this pattern of eye damage?
why_correct: Methanol is converted by alcohol dehydrogenase and then aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid, which is directly toxic to the retina and optic nerve. This produces blurred vision, photophobia, optic disc swelling and potentially permanent blindness, alongside a metabolic acidosis. The latent period before symptoms reflects the time needed to form the toxic metabolite.
why_wrong: A. Ethanol causes intoxication but does not characteristically damage the optic nerve. B. Isopropanol causes drowsiness and ketosis without optic toxicity. C. Propanol is not a classic cause of toxic optic neuropathy. D. Butanol is not recognised for this presentation.
pearl: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and is the preferred antidote for methanol, often combined with haemodialysis in severe cases.
thinking: Unknown liquid drunk at a workshop ↓ Delayed onset of symptoms ↓ Photophobia, misty vision, swollen optic discs ↓ Metabolic acidosis ↓ Formic acid toxicity from methanol
exam_trap: B, Isopropanol — a toxic alcohol that is also found in workshops, but it causes ketosis and sedation rather than optic nerve damage.
takeaway: Methanol is the toxic alcohol that damages the eyes.

presentation: Pulse oximetry in carbon monoxide poisoning
stem: A 50-year-old man is rescued from a smoke-filled house fire and brought to the emergency department. He is drowsy, has a pounding headache and is vomiting. A finger probe shows oxygen saturation of 99% on room air, and the nurse suggests oxygen is not needed. Why is this reading unreliable?

options.A: Finger probes measure blood pressure rather than oxygen content
options.B: The probe cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so it overestimates true saturation
options.C: Carbon monoxide converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin
options.D: Carbon monoxide markedly reduces arterial oxygen tension
options.E: Pulse oximetry readings are independent of haemoglobin

correct_answer: B. The probe cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so it overestimates true saturation
why_correct: Standard two-wavelength pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin because they absorb light similarly, so the displayed saturation is falsely normal. Arterial oxygen tension is also usually normal, which adds to false reassurance. He needs high-flow oxygen immediately and carboxyhaemoglobin measured by co-oximetry.
why_wrong: A. Pulse oximeters estimate haemoglobin oxygen saturation, not blood pressure. C. Carbon monoxide forms carboxyhaemoglobin rather than methaemoglobin. D. Dissolved oxygen tension is typically preserved despite tissue hypoxia. E. Pulse oximetry relies entirely on light absorption by haemoglobin.
pearl: Give 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask to anyone with suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, regardless of the saturation reading.
thinking: Smoke inhalation with headache, vomiting and drowsiness ↓ Saturation reads near normal ↓ Oximeter reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxygenated ↓ True oxygen content is reduced ↓ Treat with high-flow oxygen and check co-oximetry
exam_trap: D, Carbon monoxide markedly reduces arterial oxygen tension — it sounds logical, but the arterial tension usually stays normal, which is why the numbers mislead.
takeaway: A normal pulse oximeter reading does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning.

stem: A 76-year-old man on warfarin is sent from his care home with a nosebleed. Anterior nasal packing has been placed in the emergency department and no blood now appears at his nostrils, yet he keeps swallowing and spitting fresh clots from the back of his mouth and is becoming pale. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Bleeding that continues down the back of the throat despite effective anterior control suggests a posterior source, often from branches of the sphenopalatine artery. It is more common in older adults with hypertension or on anticoagulants and can cause significant blood loss. It needs urgent ENT involvement, posterior packing or a balloon device, and correction of anticoagulation where appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis causes sneezing and rhinorrhoea, not heavy ongoing bleeding. C. Haemoptysis is coughed up from the chest, whereas this blood is coming from the nasopharynx. D. Polyps cause obstruction and anosmia, rarely brisk bleeding. E. Otitis externa affects the ear canal and is unrelated.
pearl: Most nosebleeds arise anteriorly from Little's area; posterior bleeds are less common but heavier and harder to control.
thinking: Nosebleed in an older anticoagulated man ↓ Anterior packing stops visible bleeding ↓ Fresh blood still running into the throat ↓ Source lies further back in the nose ↓ Posterior epistaxis needing urgent ENT care
exam_trap: C, Haemoptysis from the lungs — blood in the mouth can suggest a chest source, but here it trickles from the nasopharynx after a nosebleed rather than being coughed up.
takeaway: Persistent bleeding into the throat after anterior control suggests posterior epistaxis.

stem: A 66-year-old man phones his GP surgery. Three weeks ago he started allopurinol for gout. Over the past two days he has developed a widespread red rash, his face has become puffy and he feels feverish and generally unwell. What is the most important immediate consideration?

options.A: Continue the tablets unchanged without further review
options.B: Treat it as dry skin with emollients
options.C: Reassure him that drug rashes are always harmless
options.D: Arrange routine review in several weeks
options.E: A possibly serious drug reaction needing urgent assessment and the drug stopping

correct_answer: E. A possibly serious drug reaction needing urgent assessment and the drug stopping
why_correct: A new widespread rash with facial swelling and systemic upset after starting a drug suggests a serious hypersensitivity reaction, such as DRESS or a severe cutaneous reaction, which can involve the liver, kidneys and blood. Allopurinol is a well-recognised culprit. The drug should be stopped and he needs same-day assessment for airway compromise, blood tests and features of skin failure.
why_wrong: A. Continuing the drug can worsen a potentially life-threatening reaction. B. Dry skin does not cause facial swelling, fever and malaise. C. Many drug rashes are mild, but these systemic features demand urgent review. D. Delay risks progression of organ involvement or skin failure.
pearl: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms typically appears two to eight weeks after starting the culprit drug, with fever, facial swelling, rash and organ involvement.
thinking: New drug started recently ↓ Widespread rash with facial swelling ↓ Fever and feeling unwell ↓ Systemic hypersensitivity reaction possible ↓ Stop the drug and assess urgently
exam_trap: B, Treat as dry skin — rashes are common and often benign, but facial swelling and fever after a new drug signal a serious reaction.
takeaway: A rash with facial swelling after a new drug needs urgent assessment, not reassurance.

stem: A 34-year-old man eating at a restaurant notices, within half an hour of a prawn starter, raised itchy pale blotches across his chest and arms and puffiness of his eyelids. He is speaking in full sentences with no stridor or wheeze, his blood pressure and heart rate are normal, and he feels otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rapid-onset itchy wheals with swelling of the deeper tissues around the eyes shortly after a likely food allergen is acute urticaria with angioedema. There are no airway, breathing or circulation problems, so the criteria for anaphylaxis are not met. He should still be monitored for progression and given a non-sedating antihistamine.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary angioedema causes swelling without wheals or itch and is not triggered by food in this way. B. Contact dermatitis is an eczematous reaction at the site of contact developing over days. C. Cellulitis is a localised, tender, spreading infection with warmth. E. Erythema multiforme causes target lesions, often after herpes simplex infection.
pearl: Angioedema with urticaria suggests a histamine-mediated process; angioedema without wheals raises the possibility of bradykinin causes such as ACE inhibitors or hereditary angioedema.
thinking: Food trigger with rapid onset ↓ Itchy wheals plus periorbital swelling ↓ No airway, breathing or circulatory compromise ↓ Not anaphylaxis ↓ Acute urticaria with angioedema
exam_trap: A, Hereditary angioedema — swelling around the face fits, but it lacks itchy wheals and is not an acute food reaction.
takeaway: Wheals plus swelling after food, without ABC compromise, is urticaria with angioedema.

stem: A 48-year-old man takes the first tablet of co-amoxiclav prescribed by his GP while still in the pharmacy. Within fifteen minutes he develops an itchy blotchy rash spreading across his body, becomes short of breath and has an audible wheeze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapidly developing systemic hypersensitivity reaction with airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually with skin changes. Sudden widespread rash plus breathlessness and wheeze within minutes of a penicillin-based antibiotic fits this. Treatment is intramuscular adrenaline without delay and an emergency ambulance.
why_wrong: A. Viral exanthems develop over days with fever and are not linked to wheeze within minutes of a drug. B. Cellulitis is localised infection of the skin, not a generalised rash with bronchospasm. C. Psoriasis causes chronic scaly plaques. E. Tinea corporis is a slowly enlarging fungal ring lesion.
pearl: Skin features are absent in a minority of anaphylaxis cases, so airway, breathing or circulation problems after a trigger should prompt adrenaline even without a rash.
thinking: Penicillin-type antibiotic just taken ↓ Rapid widespread itchy rash ↓ Breathlessness and wheeze ↓ Skin plus breathing involvement ↓ Anaphylaxis
exam_trap: A, Viral exanthem — a widespread rash suggests a viral cause, but the sudden onset with wheeze minutes after a drug indicates anaphylaxis.
takeaway: A sudden rash with wheeze after a drug is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise.

stem: During a CT scan, a 62-year-old woman is given intravenous iodinated contrast. Within a few minutes she says her chest feels tight, becomes wheezy, her eyelids and cheeks swell and she feels faint. She is cold and clammy, her pulse is fast and her blood pressure is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A sudden reaction minutes after a known trigger with bronchospasm, facial swelling and hypotension involves breathing and circulation, which defines anaphylaxis. Contrast media are a recognised cause in radiology departments. Immediate intramuscular adrenaline, oxygen, fluids and calling for help are needed.
why_wrong: B. Vasovagal syncope causes bradycardia and pallor without wheeze or facial swelling. C. Panic attacks do not cause hypotension or angioedema. D. An asthma attack would not explain the facial swelling and low blood pressure. E. Simple urticaria lacks breathing or circulatory compromise.
pearl: Tachycardia with hypotension helps distinguish anaphylaxis from a vasovagal episode, which typically causes bradycardia.
thinking: Intravenous contrast just given ↓ Wheeze and chest tightness ↓ Facial swelling ↓ Hypotension with fast pulse ↓ Anaphylaxis requiring intramuscular adrenaline
exam_trap: B, Vasovagal syncope — feeling faint during a procedure is common, but a vasovagal episode slows the pulse and does not cause wheeze or swelling.
takeaway: Wheeze, swelling and hypotension minutes after a drug is anaphylaxis.

stem: A school nurse is called to a 15-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes who collapsed after a PE lesson. He is unresponsive, his fingerprick glucose is very low, and nobody present can place an intravenous cannula. An ambulance has been called. Which treatment can be given now?
why_correct: In severe hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness, oral treatment is unsafe because of aspiration risk. Glucagon given intramuscularly or subcutaneously mobilises hepatic glycogen and raises blood glucose without needing intravenous access. Once he is awake and can swallow, he should have oral carbohydrate to prevent recurrence.
why_wrong: B. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia further. C. Furosemide is a diuretic with no role in hypoglycaemia. D. Omeprazole reduces stomach acid and does not treat low glucose. E. Warfarin is an anticoagulant and is irrelevant here.
pearl: Glucagon may be less effective when liver glycogen is depleted, for example after prolonged fasting, heavy alcohol use or sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia.
thinking: Known type 1 diabetes ↓ Collapse after exercise with very low glucose ↓ Unresponsive, so nothing by mouth ↓ No intravenous access ↓ Intramuscular glucagon
exam_trap: B, Subcutaneous insulin — it is the familiar diabetes drug, but giving more insulin to a hypoglycaemic patient is dangerous.
takeaway: Intramuscular glucagon treats severe hypoglycaemia when intravenous access is unavailable.

stem: Paramedics attend a 38-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes who has collapsed at her office desk. She groans but does not follow commands and has a weak gag reflex. Her fingerprick glucose is very low. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.A: Rub glucose gel onto her gums
options.E: Give intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon

correct_answer: E. Give intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon
why_correct: In a hypoglycaemic patient who cannot safely swallow, glucose must be delivered by a parenteral route. Intravenous glucose works quickly if access can be obtained, and intramuscular glucagon is the alternative if it cannot. Once alert, she needs oral long-acting carbohydrate and review of the cause.
why_wrong: A. Gel on the gums risks aspiration in someone with impaired swallowing and absorbs unreliably. B. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia. C. Hydrocortisone treats adrenal crisis, not insulin-induced hypoglycaemia. D. Tablets cannot be swallowed safely with reduced consciousness.
pearl: In adults, 10% glucose is preferred to 50% for intravenous treatment because it is less irritant to veins and causes less extravasation injury.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes with collapse ↓ Very low capillary glucose ↓ Reduced consciousness and weak gag ↓ Nothing by mouth ↓ Intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon
exam_trap: A, Rub glucose gel onto her gums — it feels safer than drinking, but with a weak gag it can still be aspirated and absorption is unreliable.
takeaway: Unconscious hypoglycaemia needs intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon.

stem: Police bring a 30-year-old woman to the emergency department after finding her slumped in a bus shelter. She can barely be roused, takes only occasional shallow breaths and her pupils are pinpoint. Both forearms show old needle track marks. Which drug class is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Pinpoint pupils, profoundly reduced consciousness and depressed breathing form the opioid toxidrome, and track marks suggest intravenous drug use such as heroin. Management is airway support, bag-valve-mask ventilation if needed and naloxone. Naloxone has a shorter duration than many opioids, so observation for re-sedation is required.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotic overdose causes sedation, hypotension and arrhythmias but not pinpoint pupils with apnoea. B. Stimulants cause agitation, tachycardia and dilated pupils. C. Beta-blocker overdose causes bradycardia and hypotension rather than this picture. D. SSRIs typically cause serotonin toxicity with agitation and dilated pupils.
pearl: Naloxone can precipitate acute withdrawal in dependent users, so titrate the dose to adequate breathing rather than full wakefulness.
thinking: Found collapsed in public ↓ Barely rousable ↓ Very slow, shallow breathing ↓ Pinpoint pupils with track marks ↓ Opioid toxicity, give naloxone
exam_trap: B, Stimulants — they are also used by injecting drug users, but stimulants dilate the pupils and cause agitation rather than sedation.
takeaway: Reduced consciousness, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils means opioids until proven otherwise.

stem: A 19-year-old woman's flatmate calls an ambulance after finding her unresponsive beside an empty unlabelled pill bottle. In the emergency department her breathing is very slow and shallow, her pupils are constricted to pinpoints, and she is not sweating. Which drug class is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Marked respiratory depression with pinpoint pupils and coma is characteristic of opioid toxicity, from prescription or illicit sources. Benzodiazepines alone usually cause sedation with relatively preserved breathing and normal pupils. Naloxone, with airway and ventilatory support, is the immediate treatment.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines cause sedation but usually with normal-sized pupils and milder respiratory depression. C. Amphetamines cause agitation, hyperthermia and dilated pupils. D. Cocaine causes sympathetic overactivity with dilated pupils. E. Tricyclic overdose causes dilated pupils, tachycardia and anticholinergic features.
pearl: A combined overdose with opioids and benzodiazepines greatly increases the risk of fatal respiratory depression.
thinking: Unresponsive after unknown tablets ↓ Very slow, shallow breathing ↓ Pinpoint pupils ↓ No features of sympathetic or anticholinergic excess ↓ Opioid overdose
exam_trap: A, Benzodiazepines — they also cause unresponsiveness after an overdose, but pupils are usually normal and breathing less depressed.
takeaway: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression after an overdose indicates opioids.

stem: On a surgical ward, a 74-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on insulin has been nil by mouth since midnight awaiting an operation. At mid-morning she is found unresponsive and her capillary glucose is very low. She already has a working cannula in her forearm. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: She cannot swallow safely, so oral treatment is excluded, and because intravenous access is already available, intravenous glucose is the quickest and most reliable way to correct the glucose. Insulin regimens need adjusting during fasting periods to prevent this. Once she recovers, she needs repeat glucose checks and a review of her peri-operative diabetes plan.
why_wrong: A. Tablets cannot be taken by an unconscious patient. C. More insulin would deepen the hypoglycaemia. D. Metformin is an oral glucose-lowering drug and cannot raise the glucose. E. Iron has no role in hypoglycaemia.
pearl: When a patient with diabetes is nil by mouth before surgery, a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion with glucose-containing fluids may be needed.
thinking: Insulin-treated and fasting before surgery ↓ Unresponsive with very low glucose ↓ Cannot take anything by mouth ↓ Cannula already in place ↓ Intravenous glucose
exam_trap: A, Oral glucose tablets — they are first-line for a conscious patient, but not for someone who is unresponsive.
takeaway: An unconscious hypoglycaemic patient with venous access needs intravenous glucose.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing back pain is found collapsed by her daughter after a long hot bath. She is barely rousable, breathing slowly and shallowly, and her pupils are tiny. Several skin patches are stuck on her upper back. Which type of poisoning is most likely?
why_correct: Slow breathing, reduced consciousness and pinpoint pupils indicate opioid toxicity. Transdermal opioid patches such as fentanyl can release more drug when the skin is heated, for example by a hot bath, causing accidental overdose. Remove the patches, support breathing and give naloxone, remembering that absorption from the skin depot continues.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol overdose does not cause early coma with pinpoint pupils. B. Salicylate toxicity causes rapid breathing and tinnitus. D. Iron poisoning causes vomiting, diarrhoea and gastrointestinal bleeding. E. Cocaine causes agitation, tachycardia and dilated pupils.
pearl: Heat (fever, hot baths, heat pads) increases absorption from transdermal fentanyl patches and can cause toxicity.
thinking: Chronic pain with skin patches ↓ Collapse after a hot bath ↓ Barely rousable with slow breathing ↓ Pinpoint pupils ↓ Opioid toxicity, remove patches and give naloxone
exam_trap: B, Salicylate toxicity — another analgesic overdose, but it causes rapid breathing and agitation rather than respiratory depression and miosis.
takeaway: Heat can increase opioid absorption from patches and cause toxicity.

stem: A 29-year-old man is in the resuscitation room after accidentally eating peanut. He has had high-flow oxygen and two doses of intramuscular adrenaline five minutes apart, but remains hypotensive with cool peripheries and a rapid pulse, although his wheeze is improving. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give further intramuscular adrenaline, a rapid intravenous fluid bolus and get urgent critical care help
options.B: Give intravenous chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone and then observe
options.C: Give nebulised salbutamol as the next priority
options.D: Send mast cell tryptase before any further treatment
options.E: Watch closely for six hours before more adrenaline

correct_answer: A. Give further intramuscular adrenaline, a rapid intravenous fluid bolus and get urgent critical care help
why_correct: Persistent shock despite two doses of intramuscular adrenaline is refractory anaphylaxis. Resuscitation Council UK advises giving further intramuscular adrenaline every five minutes, a rapid intravenous crystalloid bolus and early critical care input so that an adrenaline infusion can be started. Antihistamines and steroids do not treat shock.
why_wrong: B. Antihistamines and steroids are not life-saving and must not replace adrenaline and fluids. C. Salbutamol helps bronchospasm, but hypotension is the problem now. D. Tryptase helps later diagnosis but should not delay treatment. E. Waiting while he remains shocked risks cardiac arrest.
pearl: Refractory anaphylaxis is persistent airway, breathing or circulation problems despite two appropriate doses of intramuscular adrenaline.
thinking: Anaphylaxis after peanut ↓ Two doses of intramuscular adrenaline given ↓ Still hypotensive and shocked ↓ Refractory anaphylaxis ↓ More adrenaline, fluid bolus and critical care for infusion
exam_trap: B, Chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone then observe — they are traditional anaphylaxis drugs, but do not treat shock and can delay life-saving therapy.
takeaway: Persistent shock after two doses of intramuscular adrenaline needs further adrenaline, fluids and critical care.

stem: A 50-year-old welder working with his sleeve pushed up is caught by a flash of flame. Only the dorsal side of his left upper limb, shoulder to fingertips, has blistered; the palm side and the rest of his skin are untouched. The ED registrar is estimating the extent for referral, applying the Wallace method for a grown man. How much of his body has been burnt?
why_correct: In the adult rule of nines, each whole upper limb is 9% of total body surface area. When only the front or back surface of the limb is involved, half of that applies, giving about 4.5%. Accurate estimates matter because they guide fluid resuscitation and referral decisions.
why_wrong: A. One per cent is the patient's palm with fingers, not half an arm. B. Nine per cent is the whole limb, front and back. D. Eighteen per cent is a whole lower limb or front or back of the trunk. E. Forty-five per cent is far too large for a single limb surface.
pearl: For small or patchy burns, the patient's palm and fingers represents roughly 1% of their body surface area; in children, the Lund and Browder chart is more accurate.
thinking: Burn to one upper limb only ↓ Whole arm is 9% ↓ Only the back surface affected ↓ Half of the arm ↓ About 4.5%
exam_trap: B, 9% — it is the arm value in the rule of nines, but that covers both surfaces, not just the back.
takeaway: One surface of one arm is about 4.5% of body surface area in an adult.

stem: An 81-year-old man who smokes collapses while gardening. His wife calls an ambulance; he complains of severe pain in his left loin and lower back. In the emergency department he is grey and sweaty, with a fast pulse and low blood pressure. An ill-defined pulsatile mass is felt above the umbilicus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden severe back or loin pain with collapse and shock in an older male smoker, plus a pulsatile abdominal mass, is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise. He needs immediate vascular surgical review, permissive hypotension and activation of major haemorrhage protocols. Imaging should not delay transfer if he is unstable.
why_wrong: A. Diverticulitis causes left iliac fossa pain with fever developing over days. B. Ureteric colic causes loin pain but not shock or a pulsatile mass. D. Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back without a pulsatile mass. E. A perforated ulcer causes sudden peritonitis with a rigid abdomen, not a pulsatile mass.
pearl: In an older man presenting with first-time renal colic, consider a leaking aneurysm before settling on a stone.
thinking: Older male smoker ↓ Sudden loin and back pain with collapse ↓ Shock ↓ Pulsatile abdominal mass ↓ Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
exam_trap: B, Left ureteric colic — loin pain makes stones tempting, but shock and a pulsatile mass in an older man indicate a ruptured aneurysm.
takeaway: Back or loin pain with shock and a pulsatile mass in an older man is a ruptured aneurysm.
