exam_trap: A, Similar faints since her teens — a long history of blackouts may seem worrying, but recurrent typical vasovagal episodes are reassuring rather than suggestive of heart disease.
takeaway: Syncope during exertion should be treated as cardiac until proven otherwise.

stem: A 58-year-old builder is brought in by ambulance with an hour of crushing central chest pain spreading to his jaw. He is sweaty and pale, and the paramedic ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which pathological process underlies this presentation?

options.E: Sudden thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery

correct_answer: E. Sudden thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery
why_correct: ST elevation in a coronary territory with ongoing ischaemic pain indicates transmural myocardial ischaemia. This is usually caused by rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with thrombus completely blocking a coronary artery, here most likely the right coronary artery supplying the inferior wall. That is why urgent reperfusion with primary PCI is the priority.
why_wrong: A. Pericarditis causes widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation and pleuritic, positional pain, not territorial changes. B. Aortic valve calcification causes aortic stenosis with exertional symptoms, not acute ST elevation. C. Pulmonary embolism may cause right heart strain but not inferior ST elevation from coronary occlusion. D. Bronchospasm causes wheeze and does not cause ST elevation.
pearl: Inferior STEMI is usually due to right coronary artery occlusion; record right-sided leads to look for right ventricular involvement, which makes patients sensitive to nitrates.
thinking: Ongoing ischaemic chest pain ↓ ST elevation in a coronary territory ↓ Transmural ischaemia ↓ Plaque rupture with occlusive thrombus ↓ Urgent reperfusion
exam_trap: A, Inflammation of the pericardium — pericarditis also causes ST elevation, but it is widespread rather than territorial, and the pain is pleuritic and positional.
takeaway: STEMI usually reflects acute thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery and needs urgent reperfusion.

stem: A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her partner, who says she has had two days of worsening headache and has become muddled this evening. Her blood pressure is 226/134 mmHg, and fundoscopy reveals swollen optic discs bilaterally. How should this presentation be classified?
why_correct: Very high blood pressure combined with evidence of acute organ injury, here confusion suggesting encephalopathy and papilloedema, defines a hypertensive emergency. It needs admission, usually to a high-dependency setting, for controlled intravenous blood pressure reduction. Lowering pressure too fast risks cerebral and myocardial ischaemia.
why_wrong: B. White-coat hypertension is a clinic-only effect in a well person, not a cause of confusion and papilloedema. C. Her readings are far above the stage 1 range. D. Both systolic and diastolic pressures are markedly raised. E. Confusion and papilloedema are signs of acute target-organ damage, so this label does not apply.
pearl: In a hypertensive emergency, blood pressure is usually reduced gradually, by no more than about a quarter in the first hours, unless there is aortic dissection.
thinking: Markedly raised blood pressure ↓ New confusion ↓ Bilateral papilloedema ↓ Acute target-organ damage ↓ Hypertensive emergency needing controlled IV treatment
exam_trap: E, Severe hypertension without target-organ damage — the readings are in the severe range, but confusion and papilloedema show acute organ injury, making this an emergency.
takeaway: Severe hypertension with acute organ damage such as encephalopathy or papilloedema is a hypertensive emergency.

stem: A 34-year-old man who injects drugs is admitted with fever and a new heart murmur, and blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. On examination there are flat, non-tender, red-purple macules on the soles of his feet and the thenar eminences of his hands. What are these lesions called?
why_correct: Janeway lesions are painless, flat haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles, caused by septic microemboli. They are typical of acute endocarditis, particularly due to Staphylococcus aureus. The fact that they are non-tender distinguishes them from Osler nodes.
why_wrong: A. Osler nodes are painful, raised nodules on the finger and toe pads, thought to be immune-mediated. C. Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with pale centres seen on fundoscopy. D. Splinter haemorrhages are linear streaks under the nails. E. Erythema nodosum causes tender red nodules on the shins.
pearl: Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis in people who inject drugs often causes septic pulmonary emboli, presenting with cough and multiple cavitating lung lesions.
thinking: Fever, new murmur, positive cultures ↓ Infective endocarditis ↓ Flat lesions on palms and soles ↓ Painless, so not Osler nodes ↓ Janeway lesions
exam_trap: A, Osler nodes — they are also peripheral signs of endocarditis on the hands and feet, but they are painful raised nodules on the finger pads.
takeaway: Painless macules on the palms and soles in endocarditis are Janeway lesions; painful finger pad nodules are Osler nodes.

stem: A 79-year-old woman living in a care home is found to have an irregularly irregular pulse, and an ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. Bisoprolol has now settled her heart rate. Her daughter phones the GP to ask why apixaban is also being recommended. What is the main purpose of this treatment?

options.A: To convert her heart back to sinus rhythm
options.B: To slow her heart rate further
options.D: To reduce her risk of an embolic stroke

correct_answer: D. To reduce her risk of an embolic stroke
why_correct: In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract effectively, so blood stagnates, particularly in the left atrial appendage, and clots can form and travel to the brain. Anticoagulation substantially reduces this risk of embolic stroke. The decision is based on stroke risk assessment balanced against bleeding risk, and rate control alone does not remove the clot risk.
why_wrong: A. Apixaban has no effect on rhythm; cardioversion or antiarrhythmic drugs are used for that. B. Rate control is achieved by her beta-blocker, not anticoagulation. C. Anticoagulants do not lower blood pressure. E. Apixaban has no effect on cholesterol; statins are used for that.
pearl: Aspirin is not recommended by NICE for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation; a direct oral anticoagulant is usually first choice.
thinking: Atrial fibrillation confirmed ↓ Rate now controlled ↓ Stagnant atrial blood forms clots ↓ Clots embolise to the brain ↓ Anticoagulate to prevent stroke
exam_trap: B, To slow her heart rate further — rate control is the most visible part of AF management, but anticoagulants do not affect heart rate; their role is stroke prevention.
takeaway: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is given to prevent embolic stroke, not to control rate or rhythm.

presentation: Stroke risk assessment in atrial fibrillation
stem: A GP is reviewing a 67-year-old man whose paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was first flagged by his smartwatch and then confirmed on Holter monitoring. To decide whether he should be offered an anticoagulant, which tool should be used to estimate his risk of stroke?
correct_answer: A. CHA₂DS₂-VA (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) atrial fibrillation stroke-risk score
why_correct: Stroke risk in atrial fibrillation is estimated with the CHA₂DS₂ family of scores, which count heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, previous stroke or TIA and vascular disease. The newer CHA₂DS₂-VA version simply drops the sex category of the older CHA₂DS₂-VASc; the other components are unchanged, and for this man the two give the same result. The score applies to paroxysmal as well as persistent AF, and the decision to anticoagulate is shared with the patient alongside an assessment of bleeding risk.
why_wrong: B. CURB-65 assesses the severity of community-acquired pneumonia. C. The Wells score estimates the probability of pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis. D. ABCD2 was used to assess stroke risk after TIA and is not used for AF. E. QRISK3 estimates 10-year cardiovascular risk to guide statin use, not anticoagulation in AF.
pearl: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation carries a stroke risk similar to persistent AF, so it is assessed in the same way; female sex on its own is no longer regarded as a reason to anticoagulate, which is why the sex category was dropped to give CHA₂DS₂-VA.
thinking: Atrial fibrillation confirmed ↓ Paroxysmal AF still carries stroke risk ↓ Use an AF-specific stroke-risk score ↓ CHA₂DS₂-VA (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) ↓ Balance against bleeding risk and decide with the patient
exam_trap: D, ABCD2 score — it is a stroke-risk tool, so it sounds right, but it was designed for patients after a TIA, not for atrial fibrillation.
takeaway: Stroke risk in atrial fibrillation of any pattern is assessed with an AF-specific stroke-risk score (CHA₂DS₂-VA or its predecessor CHA₂DS₂-VASc) to guide anticoagulation.

stem: An 81-year-old man in a care home has fallen twice this week after feeling light-headed, and on one occasion he briefly lost consciousness. The visiting GP finds a regular but very slow pulse. He takes no rate-limiting medicines and his capillary glucose is normal. What is the key clinical concern?

options.A: A benign vasovagal finding that needs no action
options.B: An athletic heart that needs reassurance
options.E: The slow rate is likely reducing his cardiac output and causing his symptoms

correct_answer: E. The slow rate is likely reducing his cardiac output and causing his symptoms
why_correct: Light-headedness, falls and syncope in a patient with a very slow pulse suggest that the bradycardia is reducing cardiac output and cerebral perfusion. Causes such as high-grade heart block or sinus node disease need urgent ECG assessment and often pacing. Adverse features such as syncope mark the bradycardia as high risk.
why_wrong: A. Bradycardia causing syncope and falls is not benign and needs urgent assessment. B. An athletic heart is unlikely in a frail 81-year-old with symptoms. C. Hyperventilation does not explain a very slow pulse. D. His glucose is normal, so hypoglycaemia is excluded.
pearl: Under the Resuscitation Council UK bradycardia algorithm, adverse features are shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia and heart failure; atropine is the first-line drug treatment if any are present.
thinking: Very slow pulse ↓ Light-headedness, falls, syncope ↓ Low cardiac output from bradycardia ↓ Exclude drugs and metabolic causes ↓ Urgent ECG and assessment for pacing
exam_trap: A, A benign vasovagal finding that needs no action — slow pulses are common in reflex syncope, but a persistently slow pulse with recurrent symptoms in an older man suggests conduction disease.
takeaway: Bradycardia with syncope or dizziness suggests haemodynamic compromise and needs urgent assessment.

stem: A 16-year-old girl collapses halfway through a cross-country race at school and comes round within a minute. Her PE teacher thinks she was probably just overheated. Her GP arranges an urgent cardiology assessment. Why does this event warrant urgent investigation?

options.D: Collapse during exertion may indicate an underlying heart condition
options.E: Collapse during exercise is always benign

correct_answer: D. Collapse during exertion may indicate an underlying heart condition
why_correct: Syncope during physical effort can be the first sign of conditions such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, inherited arrhythmia syndromes or congenital coronary anomalies, which can cause sudden death. NICE recommends urgent cardiovascular assessment, within 24 hours, for anyone with syncope during exertion. She should avoid strenuous exercise until assessed.
why_wrong: A. Anxiety cannot be diagnosed from an exertional collapse, and assuming it risks missing heart disease. B. Dehydration may contribute, but a collapse does not prove it and does not exclude a cardiac cause. C. A single collapse with rapid recovery does not confirm epilepsy. E. Exertional syncope is a red flag, not a benign event.
pearl: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes; ask about a family history of sudden unexplained death.
thinking: Collapse during exercise ↓ Rapid recovery ↓ Exertion is a cardiac red flag ↓ Consider HCM and inherited arrhythmias ↓ Urgent cardiology assessment
exam_trap: B, It proves she was dehydrated — heat and exertion make dehydration seem obvious, but this assumption can miss a life-threatening cardiac cause.
takeaway: Collapse during exertion warrants urgent cardiac assessment because it may signal serious heart disease.

stem: A 27-year-old man of South-East Asian origin is seen in the cardiology clinic after his wife found him gasping and briefly unresponsive in bed one night. His older brother died suddenly in his sleep at the age of 30. His resting ECG shows coved ST elevation in V1 and V2 with a pattern resembling right bundle branch block. Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: Brugada syndrome is an inherited sodium channelopathy, more common in young men of South-East Asian origin. It causes coved ST elevation in the right precordial leads and ventricular arrhythmias, often at rest or during sleep, leading to nocturnal syncope or sudden death. Management includes avoiding triggering drugs and treating fever promptly, with an implantable defibrillator for high-risk patients.
why_wrong: A. Long QT syndrome causes a prolonged QT interval rather than coved right precordial ST elevation. B. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy typically causes left ventricular hypertrophy and exertional symptoms. C. Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome shows a short PR interval and delta wave. E. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy typically shows T-wave inversion and epsilon waves in the right precordial leads.
pearl: The Brugada pattern may only appear intermittently and can be unmasked by fever or by an ajmaline or flecainide challenge.
thinking: Nocturnal syncope in a young man ↓ Family history of sudden death in sleep ↓ Coved ST elevation in V1 and V2 ↓ Inherited sodium channelopathy ↓ Brugada syndrome
exam_trap: E, Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — it also affects the right precordial leads and causes sudden death, but it shows T-wave inversion and epsilon waves rather than coved ST elevation.
takeaway: Coved ST elevation in V1 to V2 with nocturnal syncope or a family history of sudden death suggests Brugada syndrome.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department after collapsing while reaching for a shelf in a supermarket. A witness says she dropped to the floor with no warning, looked pale for a few seconds and then came round fully alert. She reports no sweating, nausea or light-headedness beforehand. Which cause is most important to exclude?
why_correct: Sudden loss of consciousness with no warning and rapid, complete recovery is the typical pattern of an arrhythmia, where cardiac output stops abruptly and returns. Absence of a prodrome is a red flag for cardiac syncope. She needs a 12-lead ECG and, if unexplained, prolonged rhythm monitoring.
why_wrong: A. Vasovagal syncope usually has a prodrome of warmth, sweating or nausea and a clear trigger. B. Migraine rarely causes loss of consciousness and would be accompanied by headache. D. Hypoglycaemia does not resolve within seconds without treatment and often has warning symptoms. E. Panic attacks build up with anxiety and rarely cause true loss of consciousness.
pearl: NICE advises cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours for blackouts with an abnormal ECG, heart failure, onset during exertion, a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40, new breathlessness or a murmur, and to consider it for people over 65 who collapse without any prodrome.
thinking: Sudden collapse ↓ No warning symptoms ↓ Rapid full recovery ↓ Pattern suggests abrupt loss of cardiac output ↓ Exclude cardiac arrhythmia
exam_trap: A, Vasovagal syncope — it is the commonest cause of fainting, but the lack of any prodrome or trigger makes it less likely and an arrhythmia must be excluded.
takeaway: Syncope without prodrome should prompt assessment for a cardiac arrhythmia.

stem: A 66-year-old man passes out briefly in church after standing up to sing. His wife says he went grey, slumped to the floor and came round within about 20 seconds, immediately aware of where he was. He had felt dizzy and his vision dimmed just before. Which term best describes this episode?
why_correct: Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness from reduced cerebral perfusion, with rapid, spontaneous and complete recovery. A prodrome of dizziness and dimming vision, pallor and immediate return to normal orientation are typical. The cause, such as reflex, orthostatic or cardiac, should then be determined with a history, examination, lying and standing blood pressure and an ECG.
why_wrong: A. A TIA causes focal neurological deficits and rarely causes loss of consciousness. B. Seizures are usually followed by a period of confusion, and there may be tongue biting or prolonged jerking. D. A migraine aura causes visual or sensory symptoms, not loss of consciousness with rapid recovery. E. Delirium is a fluctuating confusional state lasting hours to days, not a brief blackout.
pearl: Brief jerks can occur in syncope and should not be mistaken for a seizure; prolonged post-event confusion is the more reliable sign of a seizure.
thinking: Brief loss of consciousness ↓ Prodrome of dizziness and dimming vision ↓ Rapid recovery without confusion ↓ Cerebral hypoperfusion ↓ Syncope
exam_trap: B, Epileptic seizure — sudden collapse can suggest a fit, but the immediate return to full orientation is typical of syncope rather than a seizure.
takeaway: Brief loss of consciousness with a prodrome and rapid, complete recovery is syncope.

stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department with sudden pounding palpitations that started while he was lifting boxes at work. He is talking comfortably and denies chest pain, breathlessness or dizziness, and his blood pressure is normal. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. What should be tried first?

options.B: Vagal manoeuvres such as a modified Valsalva manoeuvre
options.E: Oral bisoprolol and discharge with follow-up

correct_answer: B. Vagal manoeuvres such as a modified Valsalva manoeuvre
why_correct: He has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no adverse features (no shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or heart failure), so the Resuscitation Council UK algorithm starts with vagal manoeuvres. Raising vagal tone slows AV nodal conduction and can break a re-entry circuit that depends on the AV node. The modified Valsalva, with leg elevation after the strain, is more successful than the standard technique and avoids drug side effects.
why_wrong: A. Adenosine is the next step if vagal manoeuvres fail, not the first. C. Electrical cardioversion is reserved for tachycardia with adverse features. D. Amiodarone is used for broad-complex or refractory tachycardia, not as first-line for stable SVT. E. Discharging him while still in tachycardia without trying to terminate it is inappropriate.
pearl: In the modified Valsalva manoeuvre the patient strains semi-recumbent for about 15 seconds and is then laid flat with the legs raised, which roughly doubles the conversion rate compared with the standard method.
thinking: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia ↓ Check for adverse features: none present ↓ Stable SVT pathway applies ↓ First step is non-drug vagal manoeuvres ↓ Adenosine only if this fails
exam_trap: A, Adenosine — it is the drug most associated with SVT, so it is tempting to reach for it straight away, but in a stable patient vagal manoeuvres come first.
takeaway: In stable narrow-complex SVT, start with vagal manoeuvres before giving adenosine.

presentation: Infection as a precipitant of delirium
stem: A nurse at a residential care home telephones the GP about an 87-year-old resident who, since yesterday, has been restless, muddled about where she is and refusing her meals. Until this week she chatted happily with staff and recognised everyone. She has several long-term conditions, all unchanged for years. Which of the following should be specifically looked for as a likely trigger of this change?

options.A: Her stable hypothyroidism on an unchanged dose of levothyroxine
options.C: Her hip replacement performed ten years ago
options.D: Her chronic open-angle glaucoma treated with eye drops
options.E: A new infection, for example of the urinary or respiratory tract

correct_answer: E. A new infection, for example of the urinary or respiratory tract
why_correct: A sudden change in cognition and behaviour in an older person who was previously well suggests delirium, and infection is one of the commonest triggers. Urinary and chest infections in particular should be actively sought through history, observations and examination. The other conditions are stable and long-standing, so they do not explain an acute change.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid disease on an unchanged, stable dose would not cause an abrupt deterioration. B. Well-controlled hypertension does not precipitate acute confusion. C. A joint replacement from a decade ago is not an acute trigger. D. Stable glaucoma on eye drops does not cause sudden delirium.
pearl: In older people infection may present with delirium, falls or reduced eating rather than fever or localising symptoms, so a normal temperature does not rule it out.
thinking: Previously well resident ↓ Abrupt change in cognition and behaviour ↓ Suggests delirium ↓ Look for an acute precipitant ↓ Infection is among the commonest causes
exam_trap: A, Stable hypothyroidism — thyroid disease can cause cognitive change, so it seems relevant, but a well-controlled condition on an unchanged dose does not explain an abrupt deterioration.
takeaway: When an older person suddenly becomes confused, actively look for a new infection.

presentation: Medication as a precipitant of delirium
stem: His wife asks the GP to make a home visit because her 79-year-old husband has been drowsy and muddled on and off for four days. He was recently discharged after treatment for shingles with codeine and amitriptyline for nerve pain, and a urologist has also started oxybutynin for urinary urgency. Before this he managed the household finances. What is the most important consideration?

options.A: He has developed Alzheimer disease and needs memory clinic referral
options.B: This represents expected cognitive slowing for his age
options.C: The newly started medicines may be precipitating delirium
options.D: He is most likely depressed after his recent illness
options.E: This is a first presentation of late-onset schizophrenia

correct_answer: C. The newly started medicines may be precipitating delirium
why_correct: Fluctuating drowsiness and confusion developing over days point to delirium rather than a chronic disorder. He has recently started three drugs with sedative or anticholinergic effects (codeine, amitriptyline and oxybutynin), which together create a high anticholinergic and sedative burden. A medication review with reduction or withdrawal of the culprits is central to assessment.
why_wrong: A. Alzheimer disease develops gradually over months to years, not over days with fluctuation. B. Acute confusion is never a normal part of ageing. D. Depression does not usually cause fluctuating drowsiness and disorientation. E. A new primary psychotic illness would not explain fluctuating consciousness after new drugs.
pearl: Opioids, tricyclic antidepressants and bladder antimuscarinics all add to anticholinergic or sedative burden, which is strongly linked to delirium and falls in older people.
thinking: Fluctuating confusion over days ↓ Previously cognitively intact ↓ Likely delirium ↓ Three new sedating or anticholinergic drugs ↓ Consider medication as the precipitant
exam_trap: A, Alzheimer disease — confusion in an older man prompts thoughts of dementia, but the short fluctuating course after new medicines points to delirium.
takeaway: New confusion in an older person after recent prescribing changes should prompt a review of the medicines as a cause.

stem: Three days after an elective knee replacement, a 77-year-old retired teacher is noticed by the night staff to be talking to people who are not in the room. In the morning she is calm and answers questions correctly, but by late afternoon she cannot keep track of a conversation and keeps drifting off. Her husband says she ran her own affairs without difficulty before surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: She developed confusion over a short period after surgery, with attention that varies through the day and perceptual disturbance, on a background of normal function. Acute onset, fluctuation and inattention are the core features of delirium. Postoperative patients are at high risk because of pain, opioids, anaesthesia, dehydration and infection.
why_wrong: A. Alzheimer disease develops insidiously over years and does not fluctuate hour to hour. B. A primary psychosis would not explain inattention and fluctuating alertness after surgery. C. Depression may affect concentration but would not cause an abrupt fluctuating confusional state. E. Charles Bonnet syndrome causes visual hallucinations with preserved insight and normal attention in people with visual loss.
pearl: Delirium can be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed; the hypoactive form, with quiet drowsiness, is the most often missed.
thinking: Acute change after surgery ↓ Previously independent ↓ Attention fluctuates through the day ↓ Hallucinations at night ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: E, Charles Bonnet syndrome — the hallucinations suggest it, but it does not cause inattention or fluctuating awareness.
takeaway: Acute onset with fluctuating attention in a hospital patient indicates delirium until proven otherwise.

stem: A 90-year-old man is admitted after his daughter found him disorientated at home. He has been drinking very little for several days, has dry mucous membranes, a fever and new burning on passing urine. The admitting team diagnoses delirium. What should management include?

options.A: Rehydration and antibiotics for the urinary infection, with supportive care such as reorientation, glasses, hearing aids and good sleep
options.B: Regular oral haloperidol and referral to the memory clinic
options.C: Lorazepam at night to settle his confusion
options.D: Antibiotics with fluid restriction to reduce incontinence
options.E: Raised bed rails and a lap belt to prevent falls

correct_answer: A. Rehydration and antibiotics for the urinary infection, with supportive care such as reorientation, glasses, hearing aids and good sleep
why_correct: NICE guidance on delirium centres on identifying and treating the underlying causes, here dehydration and a urinary infection. This is combined with non-drug supportive measures: clear communication, reorientation, sensory aids, adequate hydration and nutrition, mobilisation and protection of sleep. Delirium is often reversible once the precipitants are corrected.
why_wrong: B. Antipsychotics are only for short-term use when a patient is distressed or a risk to themselves or others and non-drug measures have failed; memory clinic referral is inappropriate during acute delirium. C. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium unless it is due to alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. D. Restricting fluids would worsen his dehydration. E. Bed rails and restraint increase agitation and the risk of injury.
pearl: Every patient with delirium should be screened for common reversible causes: infection, dehydration, drugs, pain, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia and electrolyte disturbance.
thinking: Acute disorientation in an older man ↓ Dehydration and urinary infection found ↓ Delirium with clear precipitants ↓ Treat the causes ↓ Add supportive non-drug care
exam_trap: B, Regular haloperidol — it seems to target the confusion directly, but antipsychotics do not treat the cause and are reserved for short-term use in severe distress or risk.
takeaway: Manage delirium by treating its causes and providing supportive care, not by sedating the patient.

presentation: Acute confusion: delirium until proven otherwise
stem: Over a single afternoon, an 84-year-old man admitted to a cardiology ward with heart failure becomes muddled and is intermittently sleepy and hard to rouse, then alert again. The nurse who looked after him this morning says he was fully orientated and chatting. What should be considered first?

options.A: Sundowning caused by the unfamiliar ward environment
options.B: Normal ageing made worse by being in hospital
options.C: Delirium with an acute medical cause that needs to be found
options.D: Previously unrecognised dementia that has now become apparent
options.E: A first episode of late-onset psychosis

correct_answer: C. Delirium with an acute medical cause that needs to be found
why_correct: A change in cognition over hours with fluctuating alertness is delirium until proven otherwise. It should prompt an urgent search for an acute cause, such as infection, electrolyte disturbance from diuretics, hypoxia, medicines or urinary retention. Assuming a benign or chronic explanation risks missing a treatable and potentially serious illness.
why_wrong: A. Sundowning is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not explain drowsiness developing over hours. B. Acute confusion is not part of normal ageing. D. Dementia develops gradually; an abrupt change suggests delirium, which may be superimposed. E. Psychosis does not cause fluctuating consciousness.
pearl: Hypoactive delirium with drowsiness carries a worse prognosis than the hyperactive form and is more often missed.
thinking: Orientated this morning ↓ Confused and drowsy by afternoon ↓ Acute onset with fluctuating alertness ↓ Delirium ↓ Search for the medical cause
exam_trap: A, Sundowning — evening confusion in hospital is common, so it is tempting, but it cannot be assumed when there is an acute change in alertness.
takeaway: New confusion over hours in an older inpatient is delirium until proven otherwise.

stem: A 76-year-old woman is brought to her GP by her son, who says she has become forgetful and muddled over the past week. Since a hospital outpatient appointment last month several tablets have been added to her repeat list, and she also buys sleeping tablets from the pharmacy. What is an appropriate part of the initial assessment?

options.A: Stop all her medicines straight away until she improves
options.B: Review all prescribed and bought medicines for recent changes that could be contributing
options.C: Refer her to the memory clinic as the first step
options.D: Add zopiclone to improve her sleep
options.E: Reassure her son that medicines are unlikely to be relevant

correct_answer: B. Review all prescribed and bought medicines for recent changes that could be contributing
why_correct: Confusion developing over a week after new prescriptions suggests delirium, and medicines are a common reversible cause. A structured review of everything she takes, including over-the-counter products such as sedating antihistamine sleep aids, identifies likely contributors. Culprit drugs can then be reduced or stopped in a planned way.
why_wrong: A. Stopping everything abruptly risks withdrawal effects and loss of essential treatment. C. Memory clinic referral is not appropriate while an acute, potentially reversible cause is being investigated. D. Adding another sedative may worsen confusion. E. Recent medication changes are one of the most likely explanations.
pearl: Many over-the-counter sleep aids contain sedating antihistamines such as diphenhydramine or promethazine, which have anticholinergic effects that can cause confusion in older people.
thinking: Confusion over a week ↓ New prescriptions and bought sleeping tablets ↓ Possible drug-induced delirium ↓ Review every medicine taken ↓ Targeted changes
exam_trap: C, Memory clinic referral — confusion in an older woman suggests dementia, but a short history after new medicines needs an acute review first.
takeaway: In an older person with new confusion, review every medicine, including those bought over the counter.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with no previous memory problems is admitted with pyelonephritis. Her daughter is worried because her mother keeps losing the thread of conversations and seems fine one moment and lost the next. Which feature of her presentation would most support a diagnosis of delirium?

options.A: Onset over hours with attention that varies through the day
options.B: Slowly progressive forgetfulness noticed over two years
options.C: Mild learning disability present since childhood
options.D: Cognitive test scores unchanged from those recorded last year
options.E: Isolated difficulty recalling names for some time

correct_answer: A. Onset over hours with attention that varies through the day
why_correct: Delirium is defined by an acute onset, a fluctuating course and disturbed attention and awareness. In this woman the change developed over hours during an acute infection, with attention that comes and goes. These features separate delirium from chronic cognitive disorders.
why_wrong: B. Gradual decline over years suggests dementia. C. A lifelong learning disability is a developmental condition, not an acute change. D. Unchanged scores indicate stable cognition rather than an acute disturbance. E. Long-standing isolated word or name recall difficulty suggests a chronic process.
pearl: The 4AT is a quick bedside screening tool for delirium that assesses alertness, orientation, attention (months backwards) and acute change or fluctuation.
thinking: Previously normal cognition ↓ Acute infection ↓ Change over hours ↓ Fluctuating attention ↓ Supports delirium
exam_trap: B, Slowly progressive forgetfulness — memory loss is a familiar feature of confusion, but a gradual course points to dementia, not delirium.
takeaway: Acute onset and fluctuating inattention are the hallmarks of delirium.

presentation: Acute confusion in hospital: find the cause
stem: During the ward round, a nurse reports that a 68-year-old man admitted two days ago with an exacerbation of COPD has become disorientated overnight and is shouting at staff, which is completely new. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Look for and treat underlying causes such as hypoxia, hypercapnia, infection or drug effects
options.B: Discharge him home where his surroundings are familiar
options.C: Record a new diagnosis of dementia in his notes
options.D: Start donepezil to improve his cognition
options.E: Give intramuscular haloperidol and continue the ward round

correct_answer: A. Look for and treat underlying causes such as hypoxia, hypercapnia, infection or drug effects
why_correct: New confusion in a hospital inpatient should be treated as delirium until proven otherwise. In a man with COPD, hypoxia or rising carbon dioxide from oxygen therapy, infection, steroids and other drugs are important causes to check with examination, blood gases and a medication review. Treating the precipitant is the priority.
why_wrong: B. Discharge is unsafe while an acute and possibly serious cause is unidentified. C. Dementia cannot be diagnosed during an acute confusional state. D. Cholinesterase inhibitors treat dementia, not delirium. E. Sedation does not address the cause and may mask a deteriorating patient.
pearl: In COPD, new confusion or drowsiness should prompt an arterial blood gas to look for type 2 respiratory failure, particularly if oxygen has been given.
thinking: Inpatient with COPD ↓ New confusion overnight ↓ Delirium until proven otherwise ↓ Consider hypoxia, hypercapnia, infection and drugs ↓ Investigate and treat the cause
exam_trap: E, Intramuscular haloperidol — the shouting makes rapid sedation appealing, but it ignores the cause and may hide worsening respiratory failure.
takeaway: New confusion in an inpatient demands a search for its cause before anything else.

stem: In a community hospital, a 75-year-old man is started on promethazine at night because he is sleeping poorly. Within two days he is muddled, unsure where he is and mistaking staff for relatives. Before this his cognition was normal. What should be considered in his assessment?

options.A: The new sedating drug as a possible precipitant of delirium
options.B: Cognitive change expected with normal ageing

correct_answer: A. The new sedating drug as a possible precipitant of delirium
why_correct: His confusion started within days of a new sedating drug with anticholinergic effects. Medicines are among the most common and most reversible contributors to delirium, so promethazine should be reviewed and ideally stopped. Other causes should still be screened for at the same time.
why_wrong: B. Acute confusion is not part of normal ageing. C. Alzheimer disease develops gradually and should not be diagnosed during an acute change. D. Misidentifying staff during an acute confusional state after a new drug suggests delirium, not a primary psychosis. E. An abrupt change after a new drug should not be attributed to underlying dementia without excluding reversible causes.
pearl: Sedating antihistamines such as promethazine and chlorphenamine are on lists of potentially inappropriate medicines for older people because of anticholinergic effects.
thinking: Normal cognition before ↓ New sedating antihistamine started ↓ Confusion within two days ↓ Drug-induced delirium likely ↓ Review and stop the culprit
exam_trap: E, Progression of unnoticed dementia — undiagnosed dementia is common, but an abrupt change straight after a new drug points to delirium.
takeaway: Always consider recently started sedating or anticholinergic drugs as a cause of acute confusion.

stem: A 70-year-old woman recovering on the gynaecology ward after an abdominal hysterectomy is found by the evening nurse to be drowsy and disorientated. She had been fully orientated and reading a book that morning. Which principle should guide the initial response?

options.A: Diagnose dementia and refer her to the memory clinic
options.B: Start regular haloperidol and review again in a week
options.C: Attribute it to the effects of being in hospital
options.D: Restrict oral fluids overnight to reduce incontinence
options.E: Search for an underlying precipitant such as infection, pain, urinary retention or medication

correct_answer: E. Search for an underlying precipitant such as infection, pain, urinary retention or medication
why_correct: An acute change from normal cognition after surgery is delirium, which almost always has one or more precipitating causes. Postoperative opioids, infection, urinary retention, constipation, electrolyte disturbance and bleeding should all be considered. Finding and treating the cause is the key to recovery.
why_wrong: A. Dementia cannot be diagnosed during an acute confusional state. B. Regular antipsychotics do not treat the cause and are only for short-term use in severe distress or risk. C. Blaming the environment risks missing a serious postoperative complication. D. Fluid restriction can cause dehydration and worsen delirium.
pearl: Urinary retention and constipation are easily overlooked causes of delirium after surgery; a bladder scan and abdominal examination are simple checks.
thinking: Normal cognition in the morning ↓ Drowsy and disorientated by evening ↓ Post-operative delirium ↓ Consider pain, opioids, infection, retention ↓ Find and treat the cause
exam_trap: C, Attribute to hospital surroundings — unfamiliar wards can unsettle older people, but this excuse may hide a serious postoperative complication.
takeaway: Delirium nearly always has a cause, and finding it is the first priority.

stem: Care home staff ask for a review of an 86-year-old resident with known Alzheimer disease. Usually settled, over the last day she has become far more muddled, is seeing insects crawling on the walls, has a temperature and is passing urine very frequently. What is the most likely explanation for the change?

options.A: Expected progression of her Alzheimer disease
options.B: Charles Bonnet syndrome due to poor eyesight
options.E: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia with no other cause

why_correct: A sudden worsening over a day, with new visual hallucinations, in someone with dementia who has signs of infection indicates delirium on top of the dementia. People with dementia are particularly vulnerable to delirium. The urinary symptoms and fever suggest an infection that needs assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Alzheimer disease progresses gradually and does not cause an abrupt change over a day. B. Charles Bonnet syndrome causes visual hallucinations without confusion or fever. C. There is no history of a primary psychotic illness, and fever with acute confusion suggests a medical cause. E. Behavioural symptoms of dementia should only be considered once delirium and its causes have been excluded.
pearl: Delirium superimposed on dementia is common and is easily missed because staff may attribute changes to the dementia itself; any acute change from baseline should be assessed.
thinking: Known dementia, usually settled ↓ Abrupt worsening over a day ↓ New hallucinations ↓ Fever and urinary frequency ↓ Delirium superimposed on dementia
exam_trap: E, Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia — agitation and hallucinations do occur in dementia, but an abrupt change with fever points to delirium.
takeaway: An abrupt deterioration in a person with dementia should be treated as delirium until proven otherwise.

presentation: Delirium in dementia: treat the precipitant
stem: A GP is asked to see an 80-year-old man with moderate vascular dementia in a nursing home. Over two days he has become restless, shouts at staff and has tried to hit a carer, which is unlike him. He has a new cough producing green sputum and feels hot. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Start regular risperidone to control his aggression
options.B: Assess for and treat an acute medical precipitant such as the chest infection
options.C: Restrict his fluids to reduce wandering to the toilet
options.D: Accept that his dementia has progressed
options.E: Arrange transfer to an inpatient mental health unit

correct_answer: B. Assess for and treat an acute medical precipitant such as the chest infection
why_correct: A sudden change in behaviour in a man with dementia, alongside cough, sputum and fever, suggests delirium triggered by a chest infection. The first step is clinical assessment and treatment of the precipitant, with supportive care. Behaviour usually settles as the infection resolves.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotics carry stroke and mortality risks in dementia and do not treat the cause. C. Restricting fluids risks dehydration and worsening delirium. D. Dementia does not deteriorate this abruptly; an acute cause must be sought. E. This is a medical problem needing medical assessment, not psychiatric admission.
pearl: Antipsychotics in people with dementia increase the risk of stroke and death, so they should only be used short term when there is severe distress or risk of harm.
thinking: Vascular dementia, usually calm ↓ New aggression over two days ↓ Cough, sputum and fever ↓ Delirium from chest infection ↓ Treat the precipitant
exam_trap: A, Regular risperidone — aggression invites a drug to control behaviour, but it ignores the infection and carries significant harm in dementia.
takeaway: Sudden behavioural change in dementia should prompt a search for an acute medical cause.

stem: A 92-year-old woman admitted to a medical ward because she was struggling to mobilise at home becomes disorientated and agitated on her third day. The ward team draws up a list of possible triggers to check. Which of the following is a common precipitant of delirium that should be on that list?

options.C: Infection, such as a urinary or chest infection

correct_answer: C. Infection, such as a urinary or chest infection
why_correct: Infection is one of the commonest precipitants of delirium in older people, particularly urinary and respiratory infections, including those acquired in hospital. The other options are stable chronic conditions that would not explain an acute change. Observations, examination and targeted tests help identify an infection.
why_wrong: A. Presbyopia is a stable age-related change in near vision and does not precipitate delirium. B. Stable osteoarthritis does not cause acute confusion, although uncontrolled pain could. D. Chronic psoriasis is not a recognised precipitant. E. Well-controlled thyroid disease does not cause an acute change.
pearl: Hospital-acquired infection, dehydration, new medicines, pain and urinary catheters are all frequent triggers of delirium that begins after admission.
thinking: Very elderly inpatient ↓ New confusion on day three ↓ Delirium likely ↓ List reversible triggers ↓ Infection is among the commonest
exam_trap: B, Stable osteoarthritis — pain can trigger delirium, so it may tempt, but stable, controlled arthritis does not cause an acute change.
takeaway: Infection is a leading precipitant of delirium in older inpatients.

stem: A 74-year-old man on a urology ward has developed a catheter-associated urinary infection and is now confused, especially at night, when he becomes restless and frightened. A diagnosis of delirium is made. Which management approach is appropriate?

options.A: Regular haloperidol to control the confusion
options.C: Bed rails and hand mittens to prevent him pulling at the catheter
options.D: Lorazepam each night to help him sleep
options.E: Treat the infection and provide supportive care such as reorientation, good lighting and sleep protection

correct_answer: E. Treat the infection and provide supportive care such as reorientation, good lighting and sleep protection
why_correct: Delirium is driven by an underlying illness, here a catheter-associated infection, so treating it, and reviewing whether the catheter is still needed, is central. Non-drug measures such as reorientation, involving family, sensory aids, adequate lighting by day and quiet at night help recovery. Medicines are avoided unless there is severe distress or risk.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotics are only for short-term use when non-drug measures fail and he is distressed or a risk. B. Delirium is an acute disorder and is not treated with dementia drugs. C. Restraint and bed rails increase agitation and the risk of injury. D. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium in older people.
pearl: Urinary catheters are themselves a risk factor for delirium, so the need for a catheter should be reviewed daily and it should be removed as soon as possible.
thinking: Catheter-associated infection ↓ Night-time confusion and restlessness ↓ Delirium ↓ Treat infection and review catheter ↓ Supportive non-drug care
exam_trap: D, Lorazepam at night — poor sleep and restlessness make a sedative tempting, but benzodiazepines can worsen delirium in older people.
takeaway: Treat the cause of delirium and use supportive care before considering drugs.

stem: On the trauma ward the night after admission with a fractured neck of femur, an 88-year-old woman who lives independently becomes disorientated, insists she is at a bus station and keeps trying to leave. In the morning she is quieter but still struggles to attend to questions. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Acute, fluctuating confusion with poor attention during an acute illness or hospital admission is typical of delirium. Hip fracture is a classic high-risk setting because of pain, opioids, blood loss, surgery and dehydration. She should be assessed for causes and managed with supportive care.
why_wrong: A. Personality disorder is a long-standing pattern and does not cause acute fluctuating confusion. B. Dementia develops gradually and cannot arise overnight. D. Schizophrenia does not typically appear as acute disorientation in an older woman with an acute injury. E. A specific learning difficulty is a lifelong developmental condition.
pearl: NICE recommends that people with hip fracture are assessed for delirium, and orthogeriatric input reduces its incidence and severity.
thinking: Independent beforehand ↓ Hip fracture admission ↓ Disorientated at night ↓ Poor attention next morning ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: B, Dementia developing overnight — confusion in an older woman suggests dementia, but dementia never starts abruptly.
takeaway: New confusion after hip fracture is delirium until proven otherwise.

stem: Nursing notes for a 78-year-old woman with an exacerbation of bronchiectasis record that she was muddled on Tuesday night, chatty and orientated on Wednesday morning, and drowsy again by Wednesday evening. Her family are unsure what she is like normally. Which aspect of her history would most point towards delirium rather than a long-standing condition?

options.B: Persistent low mood for some months
options.D: A personality change that has been stable for years
options.E: A level of attention that comes and goes over the day

correct_answer: E. A level of attention that comes and goes over the day
why_correct: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that characteristically fluctuates, so a patient may be alert and attentive at one time and unable to focus at another. Fluctuating attention is therefore a strong pointer. The other options describe chronic conditions.
why_wrong: A. Gradual decline over years suggests dementia. B. Persistent low mood suggests depression. C. Obsessional rituals suggest obsessive-compulsive disorder. D. A long-standing personality change is not a feature of delirium.
pearl: Because delirium fluctuates, a single normal assessment does not exclude it; information from nurses and relatives about the previous 24 hours is essential.
thinking: Confusion since admission ↓ Delirium or chronic problem ↓ Delirium is acute and fluctuating ↓ Attention varies through the day ↓ Supports delirium
exam_trap: A, Gradual deterioration over years — cognitive decline is a familiar cause of confusion, but a slow course describes dementia.
takeaway: Fluctuating attention is a hallmark of delirium.

stem: In the early hours, a nurse calls the on-call doctor about an 81-year-old man recovering from pneumonia, already diagnosed with delirium. He is swinging his legs over the side of the bed, looks scared and keeps asking whether this is his home. His daughter has been phoned and is coming in. What should be done now?

options.A: Raise the bed rails so he cannot climb out
options.C: Calmly reassure and reorientate him in a quiet, adequately lit setting, with his daughter and familiar objects nearby
options.D: Move him alone to a darkened side room
options.E: Physically restrain him in the bed

correct_answer: C. Calmly reassure and reorientate him in a quiet, adequately lit setting, with his daughter and familiar objects nearby
why_correct: Frightened, disorientated patients with delirium respond best to calm reassurance, clear explanation and reorientation. A familiar person, glasses and hearing aids, and a quiet but not dark environment reduce fear and agitation. These measures are first-line before any medication.
why_wrong: A. Bed rails can increase injury when a confused patient climbs over them; a low bed is safer. B. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and are not first-line. D. Isolation and darkness increase disorientation and fear. E. Restraint increases agitation and the risk of harm.
pearl: Keeping the same staff and involving family or carers in reorientation are simple measures that reduce the duration of delirium.
thinking: Frightened, disorientated patient ↓ Delirium already diagnosed ↓ Try non-drug measures first ↓ Reassure, reorientate, familiar people ↓ Calm environment, not dark or isolated
exam_trap: A, Raising the bed rails — they seem protective, but a confused patient may climb over them and fall from a greater height.
takeaway: Reassurance, reorientation and a calm, familiar environment come first in agitated delirium.

presentation: Delirium superimposed on dementia: distinguishing feature
stem: An 80-year-old man with Alzheimer disease, which his wife says has worsened slowly over four years, is admitted with a chest infection. Since yesterday he has been much more muddled than usual. Which feature most clearly points to delirium on top of his dementia?

options.B: Needing more help with dressing over the past year
options.C: A sudden change with attention fluctuating through the day
options.D: Word-finding problems that have progressed over years

correct_answer: C. A sudden change with attention fluctuating through the day
why_correct: Dementia worsens gradually, so a sudden deterioration with fluctuating attention indicates superimposed delirium. The chest infection is a likely precipitant. The other options describe the chronic features of his existing dementia.
why_wrong: A. Problems with finances reflect long-standing executive and cognitive impairment. B. Gradually increasing dependence fits dementia progression. D. Progressive word-finding difficulty is a chronic feature of neurodegenerative disease. E. Poor short-term memory over a long period is typical of Alzheimer disease.
pearl: Collateral history about the person's usual baseline is essential to recognise delirium in someone with dementia.
thinking: Alzheimer disease with slow decline ↓ Chest infection ↓ Much worse since yesterday ↓ Sudden change with fluctuating attention ↓ Delirium superimposed on dementia
exam_trap: E, Long-standing poor short-term memory — memory loss is prominent in Alzheimer disease, but it is a chronic feature and does not indicate a new delirium.
takeaway: In dementia, a sudden change with fluctuating attention signals superimposed delirium.

stem: Her husband phones the surgery about his 71-year-old wife, who has mild mixed dementia. Since tramadol was prescribed for back pain two days ago, she has become suddenly confused, cannot tell morning from evening and loses track of the television programme. Which principle is most important in managing her suspected delirium?

options.A: Keep her in a quiet, darkened room until she settles
options.B: Stop all her regular medicines regardless of their purpose
options.D: Identify and treat the underlying cause
options.E: Assume her dementia has suddenly progressed

correct_answer: D. Identify and treat the underlying cause
why_correct: Delirium is usually secondary to one or more precipitants, and here the newly started tramadol is a likely culprit, though infection, constipation and dehydration should also be considered. Management centres on finding and correcting the cause, for example by stopping or replacing the drug. Supportive care helps her recover.
why_wrong: A. Darkness and isolation increase disorientation; a calm, well-lit setting is better. B. Medicines should be reviewed and changed selectively, not all stopped. C. Fluid restriction risks dehydration and worsening delirium. E. Dementia does not deteriorate abruptly over days; an acute cause must be sought.
pearl: Tramadol can cause confusion and lowers the seizure threshold, and it interacts with serotonergic antidepressants, so it needs particular caution in older people.
thinking: Mild dementia at baseline ↓ New tramadol ↓ Acute confusion within days ↓ Suspected delirium ↓ Identify and treat the cause
exam_trap: B, Stop all regular medicines — removing drugs seems sensible when one has caused harm, but stopping everything risks withdrawal and loss of essential treatment.
takeaway: In suspected delirium, the key principle is to identify and treat its cause.

stem: A woman calls NHS 111 about her 73-year-old mother, who until yesterday was driving and doing her own shopping. Today her mother has a temperature, burning when passing urine, is saying odd things and does not know what day it is. Which term best describes the acute change in her mother's cognition?
why_correct: An abrupt change in cognition over a day, with disorientation and disordered speech, in the setting of a urinary infection is delirium. It reflects a physical illness affecting brain function and is usually reversible with treatment of the cause. She needs prompt medical assessment.
why_wrong: A. Anxiety does not cause acute disorientation. B. Depression does not usually cause abrupt confusion with fever. D. Dementia develops over months to years, not overnight. E. Schizophrenia is a chronic psychiatric disorder and would not be associated with fever and urinary symptoms.
pearl: Delirium can be the first or only sign of serious illness such as sepsis in older people, so new confusion needs urgent clinical assessment.
thinking: Independent until yesterday ↓ Fever and urinary symptoms ↓ New disorientation and odd speech ↓ Acute onset with physical illness ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: D, Dementia — confusion in an older woman prompts this label, but a change overnight with infection is delirium.
takeaway: Sudden confusion in an older person with an infection is delirium, not dementia.

presentation: Delirium in a previously well older adult
stem: A district nurse visiting a 79-year-old retired teacher finds him muddled about where he is and talking about events that did not happen. His wife says that yesterday he was doing the crossword, managing his own tablets and driving to the shops. Since this morning he keeps losing the thread of conversation and drifts off mid-sentence. Which diagnosis should be considered first?
why_correct: A change in cognition developing over hours, with poor attention in a man who was fully independent the day before, is the hallmark of delirium. The time course alone separates it from the neurodegenerative and primary psychiatric disorders. Delirium is a medical emergency that needs a search for an underlying cause such as infection, medicines, dehydration or urinary retention.
why_wrong: A. Anxiety can cause restlessness but does not produce disorientation and impaired attention over a few hours. B. Depression develops over weeks and does not usually cause sudden disorientation. C. Alzheimer's disease progresses over months to years, not overnight. E. Late-onset psychosis causes delusions and hallucinations with relatively preserved attention and develops more gradually.
pearl: The 4AT is a quick bedside screening tool for delirium that does not require special training and includes an attention test such as reciting the months backwards.
thinking: Previously independent and cognitively intact ↓ New confusion developing within a day ↓ Inattention and disorientation ↓ Acute time course points away from dementia and psychiatric illness ↓ Delirium until proven otherwise
exam_trap: C, Alzheimer's disease — confusion in an older man prompts thoughts of dementia, but dementia never appears overnight in someone who was managing complex tasks the day before.
takeaway: Acute onset of confusion with inattention in an older person is delirium until proven otherwise.

stem: On a night shift you are called to the orthopaedic ward because a 77-year-old woman, two days after a hip hemiarthroplasty, is shouting, pulling at her cannula and trying to walk out of the bay. She is known to have delirium. She is frightened and says she needs to get home to feed her cat. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Prescribe intramuscular lorazepam to calm her quickly
options.B: Ask staff to hold her in bed and raise the bed rails
options.C: Start haloperidol twice daily for the rest of her admission
options.D: Request an urgent transfer to the psychiatric unit
options.E: Calmly reassure and reorientate her while looking for and treating precipitating causes

correct_answer: E. Calmly reassure and reorientate her while looking for and treating precipitating causes
why_correct: Agitation in delirium is best handled first with calm verbal de-escalation, reorientation and looking for reversible drivers such as pain, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia, infection or medicines. Treating the cause is what ultimately resolves delirium. Drugs are reserved for severe distress or risk to herself or others after non-drug measures have failed, and only short term.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and increase falls, and are reserved for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. B. Physical restraint increases distress and injury risk and is not a routine measure. C. Antipsychotics are not first line and, if needed, should be used at the lowest dose for the shortest time. D. Delirium is a medical problem and is managed by treating its cause on a medical or surgical ward.
pearl: Post-operative delirium after hip fracture is common, and pain, opioids, constipation and urinary retention are frequent and treatable drivers.
thinking: Known delirium after hip surgery ↓ Frightened and agitated, not violent ↓ Use de-escalation and reorientation first ↓ Look for pain, retention, constipation, hypoxia, infection, drugs ↓ Medication only if severe distress or risk persists
exam_trap: C, Regular haloperidol — it looks like decisive control of agitation, but antipsychotics are only for severe distress or danger when other measures fail, and never as routine regular treatment.
takeaway: In agitated delirium, reassure and treat the cause before considering sedation.

stem: The daughter of an 81-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease asks how the ward can help her mother, who has become tearful and restless since being admitted with a fractured wrist. Her mother keeps asking what day it is and does not recognise the bay. Which measure is most likely to reduce her distress?

options.A: Take out her hearing aids so she hears less ward noise
options.B: Provide familiar objects, a visible clock and calendar, and regular reorientation
options.C: Transfer her to a busy assessment unit for closer watching
options.D: Keep the curtains closed during the day so she can rest

correct_answer: B. Provide familiar objects, a visible clock and calendar, and regular reorientation
why_correct: People with dementia cope poorly with unfamiliar settings, and simple environmental measures such as familiar belongings, clear orientation cues, consistent staff and involving family reduce confusion and distress. Making sure glasses and hearing aids are in use also helps. These measures come before any drug treatment.
why_wrong: A. Removing hearing aids worsens sensory deprivation and confusion. C. Noisy, busy areas increase disorientation and distress. D. Darkness in daytime disturbs the sleep-wake cycle. E. Antipsychotics are not first line for distress in dementia and increase the risk of stroke and death.
pearl: The 'This is me' document, completed with family, helps ward staff learn the person's routines, preferences and what calms them.
thinking: Dementia in an unfamiliar ward ↓ Disorientation and restlessness ↓ Non-drug environmental measures first ↓ Familiar items, orientation cues, sensory aids ↓ Avoid antipsychotics as first-line
exam_trap: E, Regular low-dose antipsychotic — it seems a quick way to settle her, but antipsychotics in dementia raise stroke and mortality risk and should not be first line.
takeaway: Familiar surroundings and orientation cues are the first step for distress in a person with dementia in hospital.

presentation: New agitation in dementia: look for delirium
stem: A 76-year-old woman with vascular dementia is three days into an admission for heart failure. The nurses report that since this morning she has been pacing, pushing at the fire doors and asking repeatedly why she is not at home. Her husband says she has never behaved like this before. What should be assessed first?

options.B: Need for referral for cataract surgery
options.D: Whether she now has a psychotic illness
options.E: Need for replacement of her hearing aids alone

correct_answer: A. Possible reversible causes of delirium
why_correct: An abrupt change in behaviour in a person with dementia should be treated as delirium until proven otherwise. In a heart failure admission, diuretics can cause dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and urinary retention, and infection, pain, constipation and new medicines are also common triggers. Identifying and treating these is the priority.
why_wrong: B. Cataract surgery does not address an acute change in behaviour. C. There is no evidence of depression and antidepressants will not treat an acute cause. D. A new primary psychotic illness is unlikely; acute change in an older person is more often delirium. E. Sensory aids help, but replacing hearing aids alone ignores possible medical causes.
pearl: Delirium is more common in people with dementia, and dementia is one of the strongest risk factors for developing it.
thinking: Background dementia ↓ New behaviour since this morning ↓ Family say this is not her usual self ↓ Suspect superimposed delirium ↓ Look for infection, drugs, electrolytes, retention, pain
exam_trap: D, New psychotic illness — the agitation can look psychiatric, but an acute change in an older woman with dementia during a medical admission is far more likely to be delirium.
takeaway: New agitation in someone with dementia should prompt a search for reversible causes of delirium.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with known Alzheimer's disease lives in a care home. Staff ring the GP because she has started shouting at night and has tried to leave the building. To decide whether this is delirium rather than a worsening of her dementia, which piece of history is most helpful?

options.A: She has had trouble remembering names for six years
options.B: Her ability to dress herself has slowly declined
options.C: She has struggled to find words for a long time
options.D: She has needed help with her finances for two years
options.E: The change in her behaviour began abruptly over the last 48 hours

correct_answer: E. The change in her behaviour began abruptly over the last 48 hours
why_correct: Delirium is defined by an acute onset, over hours to days, and a fluctuating course with impaired attention. Dementia progresses slowly over months to years. A sudden change over two days therefore points strongly to superimposed delirium, which needs a search for a cause.
why_wrong: A. Long-standing memory loss reflects her known dementia. B. Slow functional decline is typical of dementia progression. C. Chronic word-finding difficulty is part of established dementia. D. Gradual loss of financial skills is also a feature of chronic dementia.
pearl: Collateral history from carers or family about the person's usual baseline is the most valuable tool in detecting delirium on a background of dementia.
thinking: Dementia with new behaviour ↓ Key question: how fast did it start? ↓ Months to years suggests dementia ↓ Hours to days suggests delirium ↓ Abrupt onset over 48 hours
exam_trap: B, Gradual decline in dressing — functional decline is relevant to dementia care, but a slow change tells you nothing about a new acute process.
takeaway: Abrupt onset is the key feature that separates delirium from progression of dementia.

stem: An 87-year-old man is on day four of treatment for cellulitis of the leg. His daughter tells the ward doctor that he has hardly spoken today, is leaving his meals and keeps dozing off in the chair, which is unlike him. When woken he answers questions slowly and loses track halfway through. The nurses say he seems brighter at some times of day than others. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Hypoactive delirium presents with drowsiness, withdrawal, reduced movement and poor oral intake rather than agitation. The key clues are an acute change from his usual self, inattention and a fluctuating course during an acute illness. It is easily missed and has a worse prognosis than the agitated form.
why_wrong: B. Schizophrenia does not begin acutely in late life with drowsiness and inattention. C. Depression causes low mood and withdrawal but develops more slowly and does not cause fluctuating attention or drowsiness. D. These changes are acute and abnormal, not part of normal ageing. E. Alzheimer's disease does not change over days or fluctuate in this way.
pearl: Hypoactive delirium is common in older people and is often mistaken for depression or tiredness.
thinking: Acute change from usual self ↓ Quiet, sleepy, eating little ↓ Inattention and fluctuation ↓ Acute illness as a trigger ↓ Hypoactive delirium
exam_trap: C, Depressive episode — withdrawal and poor intake look like low mood, but the drowsiness, fluctuation and inattention developing over a day point to delirium.
takeaway: A quiet, drowsy, inattentive older patient may have hypoactive delirium.

presentation: Breathlessness in advanced illness: assessment first
stem: A palliative care nurse calls the GP about a 68-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer who is being cared for at home. Over the past three days she has become increasingly short of breath and is frightened by it. She has not been examined since the change began. What is the most appropriate initial step?

options.A: Start regular diazepam on the basis that this is anxiety
options.B: Arrange home oxygen before seeing her
options.C: Assess her for the cause of breathlessness and any reversible factors
options.D: Stop all her regular medicines to simplify her care
options.E: Set up a syringe driver with midazolam

correct_answer: C. Assess her for the cause of breathlessness and any reversible factors
why_correct: Even in advanced disease, new breathlessness may have a treatable cause, such as a pleural effusion, infection, anaemia, pulmonary embolism or heart failure. Assessing her first allows treatment that fits her goals and wishes, as well as symptom control. Drug and oxygen decisions should follow this assessment.
why_wrong: A. Anxiety may contribute, but assuming this without assessment could miss a treatable cause. B. Oxygen helps only if she is hypoxic and should not replace assessment. D. Stopping all medicines may remove useful treatments and does not address the symptom. E. Continuous sedation is for the last days of life or refractory distress, not a first step.
pearl: A malignant pleural effusion is a common, treatable cause of breathlessness in metastatic breast cancer and may respond to drainage or pleurodesis.
thinking: New breathlessness in advanced cancer ↓ Not yet assessed ↓ Consider effusion, infection, anaemia, PE, heart failure ↓ Treat reversible causes where appropriate ↓ Then tailor symptom control
exam_trap: A, Treat it as anxiety with diazepam — fear is obvious, but labelling the symptom as anxiety without assessing her risks missing a drainable effusion or other treatable cause.
takeaway: New breathlessness in advanced illness needs assessment for reversible causes before symptom control is chosen.

stem: A hospice doctor is reviewing a 64-year-old man with mesothelioma who has received all appropriate oncological treatment. He is now breathless when talking and finds it frightening. The team plan to start a low-dose oral opioid to ease the sensation of breathlessness. What is the main aim of this treatment?

options.A: Reducing the size of the tumour
options.C: Relieving the symptom and improving comfort
options.E: Stopping all future symptoms from developing

correct_answer: C. Relieving the symptom and improving comfort
why_correct: Low-dose opioids are used in palliative care to reduce the distressing sensation of breathlessness. The aim is comfort and quality of life, not treatment of the cancer. When titrated carefully, they do not cause dangerous respiratory depression at these doses.
why_wrong: A. Opioids have no anti-tumour effect. B. Blood pressure control is not the purpose of this treatment. D. Sedation to unconsciousness is not the goal of symptom control. E. No treatment can prevent all future symptoms; the aim is to manage current distress.
pearl: Simple non-drug measures, such as a hand-held fan directed at the face, breathing techniques and positioning, also reduce the sensation of breathlessness.
thinking: Advanced mesothelioma ↓ Disease-directed treatment complete ↓ Distressing breathlessness ↓ Low-dose opioid to ease the sensation ↓ Goal is comfort
exam_trap: D, Making him unconscious — fears about opioids lead some to see them as sedation, but carefully titrated low doses relieve breathlessness without aiming to reduce consciousness.
takeaway: In palliative care, opioids for breathlessness are given to relieve the symptom and improve comfort.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with heart failure and advanced lung cancer is at home under the community palliative care team. Her breathlessness has worsened over a week. Her GP has examined her, found no effusion, infection or other treatable cause, and confirmed that she does not want to go into hospital. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Avoid treating the breathlessness because her illness is advanced
options.B: Agree an individualised plan to relieve her breathlessness at home
options.C: Limit discussions with her and her family about the situation
options.E: Start antibiotics in case of hidden infection

correct_answer: B. Agree an individualised plan to relieve her breathlessness at home
why_correct: When no reversible cause is found and further hospital treatment is not wanted, breathlessness should be managed with an individual symptom plan. This may include a fan, breathing and positioning advice, low-dose opioids and anxiety management, along with support for her and her family. Her wishes about place of care should guide the plan.
why_wrong: A. Breathlessness is distressing and should always be treated, whatever the stage of illness. C. Open communication is central to palliative care. D. Supportive care continues and is often increased at this stage. E. Antibiotics without evidence of infection are not appropriate and do not relieve breathlessness.
pearl: Anticipatory medicines prescribed in advance allow community teams to manage breathlessness, pain and agitation quickly in the last days of life.
thinking: Advanced illness with worsening breathlessness ↓ Reversible causes excluded ↓ Wishes to stay at home ↓ Individual symptom plan ↓ Non-drug measures plus low-dose opioids as needed
exam_trap: E, Antibiotics just in case — giving something active feels like doing more, but with no sign of infection it adds harm without relieving her breathlessness.
takeaway: Breathlessness without a reversible cause in advanced illness should be managed with an individualised palliative plan.

presentation: Sepsis in frail older people: atypical presentation
stem: A care-home nurse phones NHS 111 about an 88-year-old woman with frailty who has had a cough for two days. Today she will not get out of her chair, is muddled and keeps refusing her drinks, which is very unlike her. The nurse is worried she is just having an off day. How should this new change be interpreted?

options.A: As a reason to be more alert to possible sepsis
options.B: As a reason to wait and reassess in a few days
options.C: As unlikely to be significant because the carer is not a doctor
options.D: As a sign that she now has dementia
options.E: As reassuring because sepsis is uncommon at her age

correct_answer: A. As a reason to be more alert to possible sepsis
why_correct: A new change in behaviour or mental state is a recognised risk feature for sepsis, and frail older people often present atypically, without fever. With a likely chest infection, this should increase concern and lead to prompt face-to-face assessment. Concerns from carers who know the person well are important warning signs.
why_wrong: B. Waiting risks delay in a time-critical condition. C. Carers notice subtle changes from baseline and their concerns should be taken seriously. D. An acute change points to illness or delirium, not new dementia. E. Older and frail people are at greater, not lower, risk of sepsis.
pearl: Older people with sepsis may have a normal or low temperature, so the absence of fever should not be reassuring.
thinking: Frail older woman with likely infection ↓ New confusion and change from usual behaviour ↓ Atypical presentation of sepsis is common ↓ Carer concern is a warning sign ↓ Urgent assessment for sepsis
exam_trap: B, Wait and reassess in a few days — an 'off day' seems minor, but a new change in behaviour with infection can be the only early sign of sepsis.
takeaway: A new change in behaviour in a frail older person with infection should raise suspicion of sepsis.

presentation: Visuospatial and recognition impairment in dementia
stem: A 77-year-old woman with a two-year history of memory problems is brought to the memory clinic by her son. He explains that she recently could not find her way home from the post office she has used for 30 years, and last week she picked up the television remote and did not know what it was for. Her speech and understanding are normal. Which cognitive domain is most likely impaired?
correct_answer: D. Visuospatial function and object recognition
why_correct: Getting lost in familiar places reflects impaired visuospatial skills, and failing to recognise a familiar object despite seeing it reflects a recognition deficit. These are usually due to parietal and temporal lobe involvement. Her normal speech and understanding argue against a language disorder.
why_wrong: A. Expressive language problems cause word-finding difficulty, not getting lost. B. Apraxia affects carrying out learned movements, not recognising objects. C. Social and behavioural change suggests frontal involvement. E. Her understanding of speech is preserved.
pearl: Prominent early visuospatial problems with relatively preserved memory may suggest posterior cortical atrophy, an atypical form of Alzheimer's disease.
thinking: Gets lost on a familiar route ↓ Visuospatial problem ↓ Cannot recognise a common object ↓ Recognition deficit ↓ Language intact, so visuospatial and recognition domain
exam_trap: B, Praxis — difficulty using the remote may suggest a problem with actions, but she failed to recognise what it was rather than how to use it.
takeaway: Getting lost and failing to recognise familiar objects reflect visuospatial and recognition impairment.

stem: A care-home worker tells a visiting GP that an 83-year-old man with advanced dementia has started to treat his wife of 60 years as a stranger when she visits. His eyesight was checked recently and is adequate, and he can describe her clothes and hair accurately. Which term best describes this problem?
why_correct: Agnosia is the inability to recognise people, objects or sounds despite intact basic sensation. He can see and describe his wife but cannot identify who she is, so this is a recognition failure. Difficulty recognising faces is a specific form called prosopagnosia.
why_wrong: B. Ataxia is a disorder of coordination. C. Dysarthria is a problem with articulating speech. D. Aphasia is a disorder of language production or understanding. E. Apraxia is the inability to carry out learned movements despite normal strength.
pearl: Agnosia, apraxia, aphasia and amnesia together are sometimes called the four As of cortical dementia.
thinking: Sees his wife clearly ↓ Can describe her appearance ↓ Cannot recognise who she is ↓ Intact sensation but failed recognition ↓ Agnosia
exam_trap: E, Apraxia — it sounds similar and is another cortical sign of dementia, but apraxia affects actions, not recognition.
