takeaway: Failure to recognise familiar people or objects despite normal vision is agnosia.

stem: An occupational therapist assesses a 78-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease at home. When asked to make a cup of tea she clearly understands the task and has normal power and coordination, and she picks up and correctly names the kettle and spoon, but she cannot work out how to use them in the right order, which she has done every day of her life. Which term best describes this difficulty?
why_correct: Apraxia is the inability to carry out learned, purposeful movements despite intact understanding, strength and coordination. She knows what she has been asked to do and has the physical ability, but cannot organise the movements. This commonly develops as dementia progresses and affects daily activities.
why_wrong: B. Agnosia is a failure of recognition rather than of performing actions. C. Ataxia is a coordination problem, which she does not have. D. Dysphonia is an abnormality of the voice. E. Aphasia is a language disorder, and her understanding is intact.
pearl: Dressing apraxia, difficulty putting on clothes correctly, is a common practical problem in dementia and often prompts occupational therapy input.
thinking: Understands the instruction ↓ Normal power and coordination ↓ Cannot carry out a familiar learned task ↓ Motor planning is the problem ↓ Apraxia
exam_trap: B, Agnosia — both are cortical signs, but she recognises the kettle and spoon; the problem is performing the actions.
takeaway: Inability to perform learned tasks despite normal strength and understanding is apraxia.

presentation: Acute confusion with hallucinations during infection
stem: A 79-year-old retired builder was admitted to the medical ward with cellulitis of the arm. On the third evening he becomes disorientated, picks at the bedsheets and says he can see insects crawling up the wall. By the morning ward round he is calmer and chatting, but by afternoon he is muddled again. His wife says he lived independently and managed his own finances. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Screen for delirium and look for and treat its causes
options.B: Plan discharge as soon as his inflammatory markers settle
options.C: Refer him to the memory service for a dementia work-up
options.D: Start an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor for possible Lewy body dementia
options.E: Prescribe regular haloperidol and carry on with current treatment

correct_answer: A. Screen for delirium and look for and treat its causes
why_correct: Visual hallucinations, disorientation and a fluctuating course arising during an acute illness in a previously independent man are typical of delirium. He should be formally screened, for example with the 4AT, and assessed for precipitants such as infection, medicines, dehydration, pain, constipation and urinary retention. When delirium and dementia cannot be separated, delirium should be treated first.
why_wrong: B. Discharge before the confusion is assessed and resolving risks harm and misses other causes. C. Dementia cannot be assessed reliably during an episode of delirium. D. An acute onset during infection in someone with normal cognition does not fit Lewy body dementia. E. Antipsychotics are not first line and regular use without assessing causes is inappropriate.
pearl: Visual hallucinations are common in delirium, and in an older person new visual hallucinations should prompt a search for delirium before a primary psychiatric diagnosis is considered.
thinking: Previously independent ↓ Acute confusion during infection ↓ Visual hallucinations and fluctuation ↓ Delirium ↓ Screen and treat precipitants
exam_trap: D, Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor for Lewy body dementia — hallucinations and fluctuation fit that diagnosis, but the acute onset during infection in a man with normal baseline cognition points to delirium.
takeaway: New fluctuating confusion and hallucinations during an acute illness should be managed as delirium, with treatment of its causes.

stem: A 78-year-old woman who takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation sees her GP because her husband is worried. Over the past three weeks she has had a dull headache that is getting worse, she has become forgetful and slow, and she seems drowsier. About a month ago she banged her head on a kitchen cupboard but did not lose consciousness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Older people on anticoagulants are at high risk of a subdural haematoma after even minor head injury, because bridging veins tear easily in the atrophic brain. A chronic subdural develops over weeks with headache, cognitive slowing, drowsiness or fluctuating confusion. She needs urgent CT of the head.
why_wrong: A. Migraine rarely starts in old age and does not cause progressive cognitive decline and drowsiness. B. Tension-type headache does not cause confusion or drowsiness. C. Giant cell arteritis causes headache with scalp tenderness and jaw claudication, not drowsiness after head injury. E. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief shooting facial pain.
pearl: A head injury in someone taking an anticoagulant calls for a low threshold for CT of the head, even when the injury seems minor.
thinking: Older woman on an anticoagulant ↓ Minor head injury weeks earlier ↓ Progressive headache ↓ Confusion and drowsiness ↓ Chronic subdural haematoma
exam_trap: C, Giant cell arteritis — new headache over 50 brings it to mind, but drowsiness and cognitive slowing after a head injury on an anticoagulant point to a subdural bleed.
takeaway: In an older person on an anticoagulant, headache and confusion weeks after a minor head injury suggest chronic subdural haematoma.

stem: An 86-year-old man with hearing loss and cataracts is admitted to a surgical ward for planned bowel surgery. The ward sister asks the foundation doctor which measures the team should put in place to reduce his chance of developing delirium. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Discourage family visits and conversation in the evening
options.B: Prescribe a nightly benzodiazepine to help him sleep
options.C: Carry out observations every hour through the night, waking him each time
options.D: Keep his glasses and hearing aids locked away to avoid loss
options.E: Support orientation, good fluid intake, use of his glasses and hearing aids, and undisturbed sleep

correct_answer: E. Support orientation, good fluid intake, use of his glasses and hearing aids, and undisturbed sleep
why_correct: Delirium can be prevented in many people by a package of measures that address risk factors. These include reorientation, adequate hydration and nutrition, making sure sensory aids are used, good sleep, early mobilisation, pain control and avoiding unnecessary medicines. He has sensory impairment, which makes his aids especially important.
why_wrong: A. Familiar visitors and conversation help orientation rather than harm it. B. Benzodiazepines increase the risk of delirium and falls. C. Unnecessary waking at night disturbs sleep and promotes delirium. D. Without his glasses and hearing aids, sensory deprivation increases the risk of delirium.
pearl: Age 65 or over, cognitive impairment, current hip fracture and severe illness are recognised risk factors for delirium on admission.
thinking: Older man having surgery ↓ Sensory impairment ↓ High risk of delirium ↓ Multicomponent prevention ↓ Orientation, hydration, sensory aids, sleep
exam_trap: B, Nightly benzodiazepine — it seems sensible to promote sleep, but sedatives are a well-known cause of delirium in older people.
takeaway: Multicomponent measures such as orientation, hydration, sensory aids and good sleep reduce the risk of delirium.

presentation: Infection as a precipitant of delirium
stem: A 91-year-old woman is admitted from home after her carer found her muddled and unable to follow instructions. Overnight she has become wet for the first time, her urine is cloudy and smells offensive, she winces when her lower abdomen is pressed and she feels hot to touch. She has long-standing knee arthritis and wears hearing aids. Which factor is most likely to have triggered her delirium?
why_correct: New incontinence, offensive urine, suprapubic tenderness and fever point to a urinary tract infection, which is a common acute trigger of delirium in older people. Delirium arises when an acute precipitant acts on a vulnerable person. Her chronic conditions make her more vulnerable but do not explain the acute change.
why_wrong: B. Long-standing arthritis is a chronic problem and has not changed. C. Hearing loss increases vulnerability but does not cause an acute change. D. Cataracts are a background risk factor rather than an acute trigger. E. Age increases risk but delirium always needs an acute precipitant to be looked for.
pearl: In people over 65, urine dipstick testing is unreliable for diagnosing urinary infection, so diagnosis should rely on symptoms and signs, with a urine culture sent.
thinking: Acute confusion ↓ Fever and suprapubic tenderness ↓ New incontinence and offensive urine ↓ Urinary infection ↓ Acute precipitant of delirium
exam_trap: C, Age-related hearing loss — sensory impairment is a genuine risk factor, but it is long-standing and does not explain why she became confused now.
takeaway: Infection is a common acute precipitant of delirium in older people.

stem: A 79-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer's disease is in hospital with a fractured neck of femur. Her daughter visits on the second day after surgery and says her mother, who normally chats and recognises her, is now staring blankly, cannot keep track of what is said and drifts in and out. What should be suspected?

options.A: Delirium on a background of dementia

correct_answer: A. Delirium on a background of dementia
why_correct: A sudden worsening of confusion, with inattention and a fluctuating level of awareness, in someone with known dementia suggests superimposed delirium. Surgery, pain, opioids, constipation and urinary retention are common triggers after hip fracture. It should be assessed and treated rather than accepted as part of her dementia.
why_wrong: B. Dementia progresses slowly and does not change over a day or two. C. There is no history of psychotic illness and the time course is acute. D. Depression does not cause fluctuating attention over hours. E. Her cognition has worsened, not improved.
pearl: Family members are often the first to notice subtle changes in a person with dementia, so their concerns should be taken seriously.
thinking: Known dementia ↓ Sudden change after surgery ↓ Inattention and fluctuation ↓ Not her usual baseline ↓ Delirium superimposed on dementia
exam_trap: B, Expected progression of dementia — it is tempting to attribute change to the known diagnosis, but dementia does not deteriorate over a single day.
takeaway: A sudden worsening in someone with dementia suggests superimposed delirium.

stem: A 75-year-old man becomes confused and disorientated on the third day after a transurethral resection of the prostate. He has started codeine and has not opened his bowels since admission. The team agree he has delirium. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Start regular haloperidol as first-line treatment
options.B: Refer him to the memory clinic as an urgent case
options.C: Use bed rails and restraint to stop him falling
options.D: Identify and treat contributing factors such as his medicines and constipation
options.E: Nurse him alone in a side room with minimal contact

correct_answer: D. Identify and treat contributing factors such as his medicines and constipation
why_correct: Delirium usually has one or more reversible causes, and in this man codeine, constipation, possible urinary retention or clot retention and infection should be looked for. Treating these, along with supportive care, is the main approach. Medicines that may contribute should be reviewed and reduced where possible.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotics are not first line and are only for severe distress or risk when other measures fail. B. Dementia assessment is not appropriate during acute delirium. C. Restraint and bed rails increase distress and the risk of injury. E. Isolation and reduced contact worsen disorientation.
pearl: Opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines and steroids are among the medicines most often linked to delirium.
thinking: Acute confusion after surgery ↓ Delirium ↓ New opioid and constipation ↓ Consider retention, infection too ↓ Treat contributing factors
exam_trap: A, Regular haloperidol — it seems to target the confusion directly, but it does not treat the cause and is not first-line management.
takeaway: Manage delirium by identifying and treating causes such as medicines and constipation.

stem: A 69-year-old man who drinks heavily is brought to the emergency department by his sister. For the past few weeks he has been increasingly forgetful and unsteady, and today he seems drowsy. She remembers that he fell outside a pub about six weeks ago and hit his head, but he refused to go to hospital. Which intracranial problem should be suspected?
why_correct: A chronic subdural haematoma develops over weeks after minor head trauma, particularly in older people and those who drink heavily, who have brain atrophy and frequent falls. It presents with gradual confusion, headache, unsteadiness or drowsiness. Urgent CT of the head will show a crescent-shaped collection.
why_wrong: A. An extradural haematoma follows significant trauma and deteriorates within hours, not weeks. B. Subarachnoid haemorrhage causes a sudden severe headache. D. Normal pressure hydrocephalus causes a slowly evolving triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline, not increasing drowsiness. E. Meningitis causes fever, headache and neck stiffness over hours to days.
pearl: On CT, a chronic subdural haematoma is typically a crescent-shaped collection that crosses suture lines and is darker than an acute bleed.
thinking: Head injury weeks earlier ↓ Heavy alcohol use and brain atrophy ↓ Gradual confusion and unsteadiness ↓ Increasing drowsiness ↓ Chronic subdural haematoma
exam_trap: A, Acute extradural haematoma — both follow head injury, but extradural bleeds cause rapid deterioration within hours rather than a slow decline over weeks.
takeaway: Gradual confusion weeks after a minor head injury suggests a chronic subdural haematoma.

stem: A 92-year-old woman living alone has lost weight over the past year, walks slowly with a frame and tires easily. She was independent until she developed a mild chest infection last week, after which she could no longer get to the toilet on her own and needed carers four times a day. Which term best describes her underlying state?
why_correct: Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve across several body systems, which makes a person vulnerable to a large decline after a minor stressor. Weight loss, slowness, weakness and exhaustion are typical, and a small infection causing a major loss of function is characteristic. Recognising frailty should prompt a comprehensive geriatric assessment.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism can cause weight loss but would not explain the marked loss of function after a minor illness. C. Hypertension does not cause weakness and loss of reserve. D. There are no psychotic features. E. Asthma is a respiratory disease and does not explain her overall decline.
pearl: The Clinical Frailty Scale is a simple tool, based on function and dependence, used to grade frailty in older people.
thinking: Weight loss, slowness, fatigue ↓ Reduced reserve ↓ Minor infection ↓ Disproportionate loss of function ↓ Frailty
exam_trap: A, Hyperthyroidism — unexplained weight loss points towards it, but it does not account for the large decline in function after a small illness.
takeaway: A large loss of function after a minor illness reflects the reduced reserve of frailty.

stem: At an annual review, the practice nurse sees an 87-year-old man whose daughter says he has become thinner and weaker over the past year. He now takes much longer to walk to the corner shop, needs help with bathing and has given up gardening. There is no single disease to explain the change. Which concept best describes this presentation?
why_correct: Frailty is a clinical syndrome of reduced reserve and resilience, often shown by unintentional weight loss, weakness, slow walking speed, low activity and growing dependence. It is not explained by a single disease. Identifying it allows targeted support, medicine review and planning of care.
why_wrong: A. Stable angina causes exertional chest pain rather than general decline. B. Migraine causes recurrent headaches. C. Hyperthyroidism can cause weight loss but there is no single disease here and no thyroid features. E. Appendicitis is an acute surgical illness.
pearl: Simple tools such as gait speed, the timed up and go test or the PRISMA-7 questionnaire can help identify frailty (NICE NG56).
thinking: Unintentional weight loss ↓ Weakness and slow walking ↓ Reduced activity ↓ Growing dependence with no single disease ↓ Frailty
exam_trap: C, Hyperthyroidism — weight loss can suggest it, but slowness, low activity and dependence without other thyroid features describe frailty.
takeaway: Weight loss, weakness, slowness and growing dependence together describe frailty.

stem: The daughter of a 70-year-old woman calls the GP surgery. Last week her mother was started on oxybutynin for an overactive bladder. Since then she has become muddled, restless and suspicious of neighbours, although at times she seems her normal self. There is no weakness or speech change. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A new, fluctuating confusion with restlessness developing soon after starting a drug points to delirium. Oxybutynin has strong anticholinergic effects that can precipitate delirium in older people. Stopping or switching the drug and checking for other causes is the next step.
why_wrong: A. Dementia develops gradually and does not fluctuate in this way. C. Mania causes elevated mood, overactivity and grandiosity rather than confusion. D. Depression does not cause fluctuating confusion. E. Schizophrenia does not begin acutely in late life after starting a new drug.
pearl: Anticholinergic burden from several medicines adds up, and reducing it can improve cognition in older people.
thinking: New anticholinergic drug ↓ Confusion within days ↓ Fluctuating course ↓ No focal signs ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: A, Dementia — confusion in an older woman suggests it, but the acute onset after a new medicine and the fluctuation point to delirium.
takeaway: Acute fluctuating confusion soon after starting a new medicine suggests drug-induced delirium.

stem: A 77-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a productive cough and fever. His son says that until yesterday he was living alone, cooking and walking his dog. Since last night he has not known what day it is and is struggling to follow simple questions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Confusion that has developed within a day in a previously independent man with a likely chest infection is typical of delirium. Infection is a common precipitant in older people. He needs assessment and treatment of the infection and screening for other contributors.
why_wrong: A. Dementia develops gradually over months to years. B. Schizophrenia does not present acutely in late life with a medical illness. C. Learning disability is lifelong and present from childhood. E. Depression does not cause acute disorientation over a day.
pearl: Delirium is common in older people with community-acquired pneumonia and is part of the CURB-65 score as new confusion.
thinking: Previously independent ↓ Chest infection with fever ↓ Disorientation since last night ↓ Acute onset with acute illness ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: A, Dementia — confusion in an older man brings dementia to mind, but a change overnight during an infection is delirium.
takeaway: New confusion over a day during an acute illness is delirium.

stem: An 86-year-old woman with mild dementia and poor hearing is transferred to the orthopaedic ward after fixation of a hip fracture. The nursing team recognises that she has several risk factors for acute confusion and asks what should be put in place from the start of her stay. Which measure is most appropriate?

options.A: Give a hypnotic such as zopiclone each night so that she sleeps through
options.B: A multicomponent plan with reorientation, her hearing aids, encouraged fluids, early mobilisation and protected night-time sleep
options.C: Move her to a quiet side room and keep the curtains drawn during the day
options.D: Ask her family to keep away so that she is not overstimulated
options.E: Start regular low-dose haloperidol at bedtime as prophylaxis

correct_answer: B. A multicomponent plan with reorientation, her hearing aids, encouraged fluids, early mobilisation and protected night-time sleep
why_correct: NICE recommends that people at risk of delirium on admission receive a tailored multicomponent intervention addressing cognition and orientation, sensory impairment, dehydration, immobility, sleep, pain, infection and medicines. Restoring her hearing aids, keeping her oriented, encouraging drinking and getting her moving early tackle the risk factors she has. This approach reduces the incidence of delirium, whereas drugs do not prevent it.
why_wrong: A. Hypnotics are deliriogenic in older people and increase falls. C. Isolation in a darkened room removes orientation cues and worsens disorientation. D. Familiar visitors help with orientation and reassurance. E. Antipsychotics are not recommended for preventing delirium and carry significant risks in older people with dementia.
pearl: Delirium after hip fracture is common, and a structured prevention bundle delivered by a trained multidisciplinary team reduces its incidence.
thinking: Older woman after hip fracture ↓ Dementia and sensory impairment are delirium risk factors ↓ Prevention needs to address modifiable risks ↓ Drugs do not prevent delirium ↓ Multicomponent non-drug bundle
exam_trap: E, Bedtime haloperidol — it sounds proactive, but antipsychotic prophylaxis does not prevent delirium and adds risks of sedation, falls and stroke in dementia.
takeaway: Delirium is prevented with a multicomponent non-drug package, not sedatives or antipsychotics.

stem: Staff at a nursing home ask the GP to review Albert, an 89-year-old man with Parkinson's disease who takes codeine for knee pain. For the past week his pads have been repeatedly soiled with loose brown fluid, yet the carers say he has not passed a proper formed motion for well over a week. He is mildly uncomfortable, his abdomen is slightly distended but soft and non-tender, and he is afebrile. What is the most likely cause of his loose stools?
why_correct: Reduced mobility, Parkinson's disease and an opioid all promote constipation, and a long gap without a formed stool followed by frequent leakage of liquid stool is the typical picture of overflow around impacted faeces. He is afebrile with a soft, non-tender abdomen, which argues against an inflammatory or infective colitis. Rectal examination and treatment of the impaction, with review of the codeine, are the next steps.
why_wrong: A. C. difficile usually follows antibiotics and causes frequent diarrhoea with systemic upset, not a background of no formed stool. B. Ischaemic colitis presents with sudden pain and bloody diarrhoea. C. Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorptive diarrhoea and would not explain the preceding constipation. D. Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhoea without a history of failure to pass stool.
pearl: In a frail older person, new loose stools should prompt a digital rectal examination before any antidiarrhoeal is given, because loperamide would worsen an impaction.
thinking: Frail older man on codeine with Parkinson's disease ↓ No formed stool for over a week ↓ Frequent leakage of liquid stool ↓ Afebrile, soft abdomen ↓ Liquid stool bypassing impacted faeces
exam_trap: A, Clostridioides difficile infection — loose stools in a care home resident trigger infection concerns, but there is no antibiotic exposure or systemic upset, and the preceding constipation points to overflow.
takeaway: Loose stool in a constipated older person is overflow from faecal impaction until proved otherwise.

stem: On a stroke rehabilitation ward, a 91-year-old woman who is largely immobile and receiving oral morphine is noted by nurses to be leaking small volumes of liquid stool several times a day. She has had hard, infrequent bowel actions for months. Digital rectal examination reveals a rectum packed with a large, hard faecal mass. What best explains the liquid stool?

options.C: Liquid stool passing around impacted faeces

correct_answer: C. Liquid stool passing around impacted faeces
why_correct: The finding of a rectum filled with hard faeces in an immobile woman on morphine confirms faecal impaction. Proximal liquid stool seeps around the obstructing mass, which produces apparent diarrhoea and incontinence. Treatment is disimpaction with suppositories or enemas and then regular laxatives.
why_wrong: A. C. difficile colitis would not produce a rectum loaded with hard stool. B. Laxative overuse produces an empty rectum with loose stool, not a hard faecal mass. D. Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhoea with a normal rectal examination. E. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause a palpable faecal mass and is rarely a new diagnosis at this age.
pearl: Opioids, immobility, dehydration and anticholinergic drugs are the main contributors to faecal impaction in older inpatients.
thinking: Immobile, on morphine ↓ Long history of hard, infrequent stool ↓ New small-volume liquid leakage ↓ Rectum packed with hard faeces ↓ Overflow around impaction
exam_trap: B, Excessive stimulant laxatives — loose stool in someone with constipation makes laxative excess tempting, but a hard faecal mass in the rectum shows the bowel is still obstructed by stool.
takeaway: A rectum full of hard stool plus liquid leakage means overflow from faecal impaction.

stem: A GP visits an 84-year-old housebound man who has had hard, infrequent motions for years. His son reports that over the last few days he has had cramping lower abdominal pain and has been unable to control frequent watery stool. On examination there is an indentable mass in the left iliac fossa, and the rectum contains hard stool. There is no blood on the glove. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A long history of constipation, an indentable left-sided abdominal mass and hard stool on rectal examination indicate heavy faecal loading. The new watery stool is overflow leaking past the impacted faeces rather than true diarrhoea. Management is disimpaction followed by a regular laxative regimen and review of constipating factors.
why_wrong: A. Ulcerative colitis causes bloody diarrhoea with urgency and would not produce hard stool in the rectum. B. Diverticular bleeding presents with painless fresh rectal bleeding, which is absent. C. Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorptive diarrhoea, not acute overflow around hard stool. D. Gastroenteritis would not explain years of constipation with faecal loading.
pearl: A faecal mass is typically indentable on palpation, which helps distinguish it from a colonic tumour.
thinking: Years of constipation ↓ New watery stool and incontinence ↓ Indentable abdominal mass ↓ Hard stool in rectum ↓ Overflow from impaction
exam_trap: D, Infective gastroenteritis — watery stool and cramps suggest infection, but it does not account for the chronic constipation and the hard faecal mass found on examination.
takeaway: New incontinence of liquid stool with faecal loading on examination is overflow from impaction.

stem: A 76-year-old woman attends her GP surgery because for the past month she has felt faint within seconds of getting up from her armchair, which settles if she sits back down. Over recent months amlodipine, ramipril and indapamide have been added to her treatment. Lying and standing blood pressure readings show a substantial drop on standing that reproduces her symptoms. She has no spinning sensation and no symptoms on turning her head. What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: Orthostatic hypotension caused by her antihypertensive treatment

correct_answer: B. Orthostatic hypotension caused by her antihypertensive treatment
why_correct: Symptoms that come on immediately after standing, settle on sitting and are reproduced by a measured postural drop indicate orthostatic hypotension. The timing alongside the addition of three blood pressure lowering drugs, including a diuretic, makes medication the most likely cause. Her treatment should be reviewed and rationalised.
why_wrong: A. Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is provoked by neck pressure or head turning, not by standing. C. Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as prolonged standing, pain or emotion with a prodrome, rather than occurring immediately on rising. D. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief rotational vertigo with head movement, not a pre-syncopal feeling. E. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency causes transient brainstem symptoms and would not explain a measured postural blood pressure drop.
pearl: Antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blockers, nitrates, tricyclics and dopaminergic drugs are common culprits for orthostatic hypotension in older people.
thinking: Faintness immediately on standing ↓ Settles on sitting ↓ Postural drop measured and symptomatic ↓ Several recently added antihypertensives ↓ Drug-induced orthostatic hypotension
exam_trap: A, Carotid sinus hypersensitivity — it is a classic cause of dizziness in older people, but it is triggered by neck stimulation, and here the symptoms are tied to posture and new drugs.
takeaway: Postural faintness with a measured drop in someone on several antihypertensives is medication-related orthostatic hypotension.

stem: A daughter brings her 80-year-old father to the GP surgery. Two weeks ago doxazosin was added to his blood pressure treatment, and since then he has felt woozy and unsteady each morning when he gets out of bed, although he has not fallen. He is otherwise well and examination of his heart and nervous system is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Stop all of his regular tablets straight away
options.B: Advise him to cut back his fluid intake
options.C: Add a further antihypertensive to smooth his blood pressure control
options.D: Measure lying and standing blood pressure and review the newly started drug
options.E: Reassure him that unsteadiness is expected at his age

correct_answer: D. Measure lying and standing blood pressure and review the newly started drug
why_correct: New dizziness on rising soon after an alpha-blocker is started strongly suggests drug-induced postural hypotension. The first step is to confirm it with lying and standing blood pressure and then review the new drug, reducing or stopping it if the drop is significant. Doxazosin is a recognised cause of first-dose and ongoing postural hypotension.
why_wrong: A. Stopping every medicine abruptly risks rebound hypertension and withdrawal effects; review should be targeted. B. Fluid restriction would worsen postural hypotension. C. A further antihypertensive would deepen the postural drop. E. Postural symptoms after a drug change need assessment, not reassurance.
pearl: Alpha-blockers such as doxazosin can cause a marked first-dose postural drop, so they are started at a low dose and titrated, with advice to rise slowly.
thinking: Older man ↓ New alpha-blocker two weeks ago ↓ Dizziness on getting out of bed ↓ Suspect drug-induced postural hypotension ↓ Confirm with postural blood pressure and review the drug
exam_trap: A, Stopping all tablets — it seems a quick fix, but abrupt withdrawal of everything is unsafe and unnecessary when one recently added drug is the likely culprit.
takeaway: Dizziness on standing after a new antihypertensive needs postural blood pressure and a review of that drug.

stem: Carers at a residential home report that an 85-year-old woman grips the furniture and says her head swims each time she gets up from a chair. Her medication chart lists bisoprolol, amlodipine, lisinopril and bendroflumethiazide, and her recent blood pressure readings have been at the low end of normal. She has had no chest pain or palpitations. What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.A: Review the medicines that may be lowering her blood pressure

correct_answer: A. Review the medicines that may be lowering her blood pressure
why_correct: Her symptoms on rising, low-normal blood pressure and four blood pressure lowering drugs point to medication-related orthostatic hypotension. The first step is a structured medication review, aiming to reduce or stop drugs whose harms now outweigh their benefits. Postural blood pressure should be measured as part of that assessment.
why_wrong: B. There is no indication such as atrial fibrillation for anticoagulation, and it would increase bleeding risk if she falls. C. Another antihypertensive would worsen her symptoms. D. Nothing suggests depression, and some antidepressants can themselves cause postural hypotension. E. Fluid restriction reduces circulating volume and worsens orthostatic symptoms.
pearl: Deprescribing antihypertensives in frail older people with postural symptoms reduces dizziness and falls without a clear increase in cardiovascular events.
thinking: Head swims on rising ↓ Low-normal blood pressure ↓ Four antihypertensive drugs ↓ Likely medication-related orthostatic hypotension ↓ Review and reduce contributing medicines
exam_trap: C, Adding another antihypertensive — treatment targets can tempt escalation, but her pressure is already low and further lowering would worsen her symptoms.
takeaway: Postural symptoms in a frail person on several antihypertensives call for a medication review first.

stem: A 79-year-old retired builder is brought to the emergency department after collapsing briefly while shaving the side of his neck with an electric razor. He came round within seconds without confusion. He recalls nearly passing out twice before, once while looking back over his shoulder to reverse the car and once after fastening a tight shirt collar. There was no tongue biting and no spinning sensation. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent pre-syncope or syncope provoked by pressure on the neck or by head turning in an older man is characteristic of carotid sinus hypersensitivity. Stimulation of the carotid baroreceptors triggers an exaggerated reflex causing bradycardia, vasodilatation or both. It is confirmed by carotid sinus massage with ECG and blood pressure monitoring, and pacing may be considered for the cardioinhibitory form.
why_wrong: A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief spinning vertigo with head movement, not loss of consciousness. B. Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as pain, fear or prolonged standing rather than neck pressure. C. A vertebrobasilar TIA causes focal brainstem symptoms and rarely isolated, quickly recovered syncope. E. Temporal lobe seizures are not provoked by neck pressure and are usually followed by confusion.
pearl: Carotid sinus massage should not be performed in patients with a carotid bruit or a recent stroke or TIA.
thinking: Older man ↓ Brief collapse while shaving the neck ↓ Previous episodes with head turning and a tight collar ↓ Rapid recovery without confusion ↓ Reflex syncope from carotid sinus stimulation
exam_trap: B, Vasovagal syncope — it is the commonest reflex syncope, but the specific neck triggers in an older man point to carotid sinus hypersensitivity.
takeaway: Syncope triggered by neck pressure or head turning in an older person suggests carotid sinus hypersensitivity.

stem: An 83-year-old man is recovering on a medical ward after an admission with heart failure, during which his furosemide dose was increased and tamsulosin was started for urinary retention. The physiotherapist notes that he becomes pale and light-headed each time he stands to walk, with a clear drop in blood pressure on standing. He is keen to go home. Which action is most appropriate?

options.B: Prescribe a night sedative to help him rest
options.D: Advise bed rest until the symptoms settle
options.E: Review the recently changed medicines that may be causing the postural drop

correct_answer: E. Review the recently changed medicines that may be causing the postural drop
why_correct: Symptomatic postural hypotension after recent medication changes should prompt a review of drugs that lower blood pressure, such as diuretics and alpha-blockers. Adjusting the furosemide dose to his fluid status and considering whether tamsulosin can be reduced or stopped address the likely cause while keeping necessary treatment. This should be done before discharge to reduce his risk of falls at home.
why_wrong: A. More antihypertensive treatment would worsen the drop. B. Sedatives increase falls risk and do nothing for the blood pressure. C. Stopping everything would risk decompensation of his heart failure; review should be targeted. D. Bed rest causes deconditioning and worsens orthostatic intolerance.
pearl: Alpha-blockers used for urinary symptoms, such as tamsulosin, are an often-forgotten cause of postural hypotension in older men.
thinking: Recent diuretic increase and new alpha-blocker ↓ Symptomatic postural drop on mobilising ↓ Likely drug-related ↓ Targeted review rather than stopping everything ↓ Adjust contributing medicines before discharge
exam_trap: C, Stopping every regular medicine — it removes all culprits, but abrupt withdrawal of heart failure treatment is dangerous and review should be selective.
takeaway: Symptomatic postural hypotension after medication changes needs a targeted review of the drugs responsible.

stem: A 64-year-old woman phones her GP because she often feels her vision grey out when she jumps out of bed in the morning or stands quickly from the sofa. The feeling eases within a minute if she sits back down. She has had no falls, and examination and an ECG are normal. Which simple advice is most likely to reduce her symptoms?

options.A: Cut down on how much she drinks during the day
options.B: Stay standing until the feeling passes
options.C: Get up in stages, sitting on the edge of the bed or chair before standing
options.E: Stand up quickly so the episode is brief

correct_answer: C. Get up in stages, sitting on the edge of the bed or chair before standing
why_correct: Her symptoms are typical of postural hypotension, which is worse with rapid changes of position. Changing posture slowly, for example sitting on the edge of the bed for a short time before standing, gives the baroreflex time to compensate. Other helpful measures include adequate fluid intake and avoiding large meals and hot environments.
why_wrong: A. Reducing fluid intake lowers circulating volume and worsens symptoms. B. Remaining upright while symptomatic risks fainting and injury; she should sit or lie down. D. Regular activity helps maintain vascular tone, and avoiding it causes deconditioning. E. Rising abruptly is the trigger for her symptoms.
pearl: Physical counter-manoeuvres such as leg crossing and tensing the leg muscles can abort an episode of postural pre-syncope.
thinking: Greying vision on rising quickly ↓ Eases on sitting ↓ Postural hypotension pattern ↓ Rapid postural change is the trigger ↓ Advise rising slowly in stages
exam_trap: A, Cutting down on fluids — it may seem sensible if she is worried about nocturia or fluid balance, but dehydration worsens postural hypotension.
takeaway: Rising slowly in stages is a simple, effective measure for postural hypotension.

stem: During a heatwave, an 88-year-old man with advanced dementia who relies entirely on care home staff to offer him drinks becomes increasingly drowsy. He keeps reaching for cups and has a dry tongue and reduced skin turgor. Blood tests show a raised serum sodium with a raised urea. What is the most likely underlying problem?

options.E: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

correct_answer: C. A deficit of free water
why_correct: Hypernatraemia in a dependent older person with limited access to fluid usually reflects loss of free water greater than loss of sodium. Hot weather increases insensible losses, and his dementia stops him from getting drinks for himself despite thirst. Treatment is gradual replacement of water, orally if possible or with hypotonic fluids, avoiding rapid correction.
why_wrong: A. Dietary calcium does not raise serum sodium. B. Hypokalaemia alone does not cause hypernatraemia or the dehydration seen here. D. B12 deficiency causes anaemia and neurological problems, not hypernatraemia. E. SIADH causes water retention and hyponatraemia, the opposite of this picture.
pearl: Older people have blunted thirst and reduced renal concentrating ability, so those dependent on others for fluids are at particular risk of hypernatraemia.
thinking: Dependent on others for drinks ↓ Hot weather increases losses ↓ Thirst, dry tongue, raised urea ↓ Raised sodium ↓ Free water deficit
exam_trap: E, SIADH — it is a familiar sodium disorder in older people, but it causes low sodium through water retention, not high sodium.
takeaway: Hypernatraemia in a frail, dependent older person usually means they have not had enough water.

stem: After a large stroke, a 90-year-old woman with an unsafe swallow is kept nil by mouth over a weekend, and her intravenous fluid prescription lapses. On Monday she is drowsier, and her blood tests show a markedly raised serum sodium. What does the raised sodium concentration most likely reflect?

options.B: Loss of free water that has not been replaced

correct_answer: B. Loss of free water that has not been replaced
why_correct: Serum sodium is a measure of the balance between sodium and water, so a high value usually means there is too little water relative to sodium rather than too much sodium. With no oral intake and no fluid prescribed, ongoing insensible and urinary losses have left her short of free water. Correction should be with water or hypotonic fluid and should be gradual to avoid cerebral oedema.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis raises potassium and bilirubin, not sodium. C. Potassium excess is a separate disturbance and does not explain a high sodium. D. Iron deficiency causes anaemia, not hypernatraemia. E. Calcium intake has no direct effect on serum sodium.
pearl: Hypernatraemia is mostly a disorder of water balance, and it should be corrected slowly because rapid lowering of sodium risks cerebral oedema.
thinking: Nil by mouth after stroke ↓ No intravenous fluids ↓ Ongoing insensible and urinary losses ↓ High serum sodium ↓ Relative water deficit
exam_trap: A, Excess haemolysis — it is a well-known cause of spurious electrolyte results, but it affects potassium, not sodium.
takeaway: A raised serum sodium usually indicates a relative deficit of water.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is receiving chemotherapy. Her oncology nurse suggests a referral to the palliative care team because of bone pain and fatigue. She becomes tearful and says she thought this meant the doctors were giving up on her treatment. How is palliative care best explained to her?

options.A: It replaces chemotherapy and other treatment aimed at the cancer
options.B: It begins only once there are no further treatment options
options.C: It means her oncology follow-up will pass to her GP
options.D: It is provided mainly as inpatient care in a hospice
options.E: It focuses on symptoms and wellbeing and can be given alongside her chemotherapy

correct_answer: E. It focuses on symptoms and wellbeing and can be given alongside her chemotherapy
why_correct: Palliative care aims to improve quality of life by addressing physical symptoms and psychological, social and spiritual needs for people with life-limiting illness. It can be introduced early and delivered alongside disease-directed treatment such as chemotherapy. Explaining this addresses her misconception and supports her to accept help with her pain and fatigue.
why_wrong: A. Palliative care complements rather than replaces anticancer treatment. B. Early involvement improves symptom control and is not reserved for when treatment options are exhausted. C. Her oncology care continues; the palliative team works alongside it. D. Most palliative care is delivered in the community, clinics and hospitals, not only in hospices.
pearl: Early integration of specialist palliative care with oncology treatment improves quality of life and mood in advanced cancer.
thinking: Advanced cancer on chemotherapy ↓ Troublesome symptoms ↓ Misconception that palliative means stopping treatment ↓ Palliative care addresses symptoms and wider needs ↓ It runs alongside active treatment
exam_trap: B, Begins only when treatment options run out — this reflects a common public belief, but palliative care can and should start early alongside disease-directed treatment.
takeaway: Palliative care is about symptoms and quality of life and can run alongside active treatment.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with pancreatic cancer wishes to die at home. Her GP prescribes a small supply of injectable drugs for pain, nausea, agitation and noisy breathing, which is kept in her house with an authorisation chart so that district nurses can give a dose promptly if a symptom arises out of hours. What are these medicines commonly called?
why_correct: Anticipatory, or just in case, medicines are prescribed in advance for people approaching the end of life so that common symptoms such as pain, nausea, agitation, breathlessness and respiratory secretions can be treated without delay. They are usually given subcutaneously because swallowing often fails in the last days. Having them in the home avoids distressing waits and unwanted admissions.
why_wrong: A. Thrombolytic medicines dissolve clots in conditions such as stroke or pulmonary embolism. B. Depot antipsychotics are long-acting injections for chronic psychotic illness. C. Disease-modifying drugs alter the course of conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or multiple sclerosis. E. Vaccines prevent infection and have no role in end-of-life symptom control.
pearl: Typical anticipatory medicines cover four symptoms: pain (an opioid), nausea (an antiemetic), agitation (a benzodiazepine such as midazolam) and secretions (an antimuscarinic such as hyoscine butylbromide).
thinking: Wishes to die at home ↓ Symptoms may arise suddenly out of hours ↓ Injectable drugs prescribed in advance ↓ Kept in the home with an authorisation chart ↓ Anticipatory medicines
exam_trap: B, Depot antipsychotic medicines — the injectable form and the inclusion of a drug for agitation may mislead, but depot preparations are long-term treatments for psychosis, not as-needed symptom relief.
takeaway: Anticipatory medicines are prescribed in advance so end-of-life symptoms can be treated quickly.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with end-stage COPD has been treated on the respiratory ward for pneumonia for five days but continues to deteriorate despite intravenous antibiotics. The team and her family agree that she is dying and that her care should now focus on comfort. She can no longer manage tablets and is becoming breathless and restless. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Stop all symptom-relief medicines as she can no longer swallow
options.B: Refer to intensive care for intubation and ventilation
options.C: Prescribe subcutaneous anticipatory medicines for breathlessness, agitation, pain and secretions
options.D: Continue intravenous antibiotics until her breathing improves
options.E: Hold off symptom control until she becomes unconscious

correct_answer: C. Prescribe subcutaneous anticipatory medicines for breathlessness, agitation, pain and secretions
why_correct: Once it is recognised that a person is dying and care is focused on comfort, symptoms should be anticipated and treated promptly. Because she can no longer swallow, anticipatory medicines should be prescribed by the subcutaneous route, for example an opioid for breathlessness and pain, midazolam for agitation and an antimuscarinic for secretions. A syringe pump can be used if repeated doses are needed.
why_wrong: A. Loss of the oral route is a reason to change route, not to withhold symptom relief. B. Intubation is not consistent with the agreed focus on comfort and would not reverse her dying. D. Antibiotics have not altered her course and are unlikely to relieve her distress. E. Delaying symptom control leaves her distressed unnecessarily.
pearl: In the last days of life, regular oral medicines should be reviewed and those not contributing to comfort stopped, while symptom control is switched to the subcutaneous route.
thinking: Deteriorating despite treatment ↓ Recognised as dying, comfort focus agreed ↓ Unable to swallow ↓ Breathless and restless ↓ Subcutaneous anticipatory medicines
exam_trap: D, Continuing antibiotics until breathing improves — it feels like not giving up, but she is dying despite treatment and her distress needs direct symptom control.
takeaway: When a dying patient cannot swallow, give symptom relief by the subcutaneous route with anticipatory medicines.

stem: A 56-year-old man with mesothelioma has had his pleural effusion drained, but he still feels increasingly short of breath at rest. He tells his GP that he understands his cancer cannot be cured and asks whether there is any point in treating his breathlessness. Which principle of palliative care best guides the response?

options.A: Avoid opioids because dependence is inevitable
options.B: Relieve distressing symptoms even when the illness cannot be cured
options.C: Treat symptoms only once they become life-threatening
options.D: Stop symptom treatment to avoid side effects
options.E: Avoid discussing symptoms because the illness is terminal

correct_answer: B. Relieve distressing symptoms even when the illness cannot be cured
why_correct: Palliative care aims to maximise quality of life, and symptom relief remains worthwhile even when cure is impossible. For breathlessness, this includes non-drug measures such as a handheld fan, breathing techniques and positioning, and low-dose oral opioids where appropriate. Explaining this gives him hope of feeling better without false hope of cure.
why_wrong: A. Low-dose opioids are safe and effective for breathlessness in advanced illness, and dependence is not a reason to withhold them. C. Waiting until symptoms are life-threatening leaves him suffering needlessly. D. Side effects are managed by careful titration, not by abandoning treatment. E. Open discussion of symptoms is central to good palliative care.
pearl: A handheld fan directed at the face is a simple, evidence-based measure that reduces the sensation of breathlessness.
thinking: Incurable cancer ↓ Persistent breathlessness after treating the effusion ↓ Asks if treatment is worthwhile ↓ Quality of life is the goal ↓ Relieve symptoms despite no cure
exam_trap: A, Avoid opioids because of dependence — fear of addiction is common, but carefully titrated opioids are appropriate and effective for breathlessness in advanced illness.
takeaway: Distressing symptoms should be treated even when the underlying illness cannot be cured.

presentation: Anticipatory prescribing in the last days of life
stem: An 84-year-old man with advanced dementia in a nursing home has stopped eating and can no longer swallow safely. His GP judges that he is in the last days of life, and the family agree that he should stay in the home. Staff are worried about how they will manage pain, distress and noisy breathing over the coming weekend. What should the GP arrange?

options.B: Stopping all medicines, including those for symptom relief
options.C: Admission to hospital for nasogastric feeding
options.D: Prescription of anticipatory medicines for pain, agitation and secretions
options.E: Referral to physiotherapy for an exercise programme

correct_answer: D. Prescription of anticipatory medicines for pain, agitation and secretions
why_correct: In the last days of life, symptoms such as pain, agitation and respiratory secretions are common and can arise suddenly. Prescribing anticipatory medicines by the subcutaneous route, with clear instructions and the means to give them, allows staff to respond promptly without a hospital admission. This supports his family's wish for him to stay in his home.
why_wrong: A. Screening investigations have no place in the last days of life. B. Non-essential medicines can be stopped, but symptom relief must continue by an alternative route. C. Artificial feeding does not prolong life or improve comfort in advanced dementia and transfer conflicts with the agreed plan. E. An exercise programme is inappropriate for a person who is dying.
pearl: Noisy respiratory secretions near death are often more distressing to relatives than to the patient; repositioning and explanation come first, with an antimuscarinic if needed.
thinking: Advanced dementia, no longer swallowing ↓ Recognised as dying ↓ Wish to stay in nursing home ↓ Pain, agitation and secretions likely ↓ Prescribe anticipatory medicines
exam_trap: C, Admission for nasogastric feeding — it can feel like doing something active, but tube feeding does not benefit people dying with advanced dementia and goes against the agreed plan.
takeaway: Anticipatory medicines let symptoms in the last days of life be managed promptly where the person wishes to be.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with advanced heart failure has been admitted three times in the past four months. At her cardiology clinic appointment the consultant believes she is likely to be in the last months of her life, and she says she would like to talk about what lies ahead. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Discuss only the treatments that could reverse her heart failure
options.B: Explore what matters most to her and her preferences and goals for future care
options.C: Wait until she loses consciousness before discussing care
options.D: Make decisions with her family without involving her
options.E: Avoid mentioning deterioration in case it upsets her

correct_answer: B. Explore what matters most to her and her preferences and goals for future care
why_correct: Advance care planning is a voluntary conversation in which a person with capacity explores their values, wishes and priorities for future care, including where they would like to be cared for. She has capacity and has invited the discussion, so the clinician should explore what matters to her and record her preferences. This allows future decisions to reflect her wishes if she later loses capacity.
why_wrong: A. Focusing only on curative options gives a misleading picture and misses her wider goals. C. Discussions should happen while she can take part, not once she cannot. D. She has capacity and must be central to decisions about her care. E. Withholding honest information prevents her from planning and is not what she has asked for.
pearl: Frequent admissions with advanced heart failure are a recognised trigger for starting advance care planning conversations.
thinking: Advanced heart failure with repeated admissions ↓ Likely last months of life ↓ She has capacity and wants to talk ↓ Advance care planning ↓ Explore her values, preferences and goals
exam_trap: E, Avoid mentioning deterioration — it can feel kind, but she has asked to talk and honest discussion allows her to plan.
takeaway: Advance care planning starts by exploring what matters most to the patient while they can still take part.

stem: A 66-year-old man with lung cancer is looked after at home by the community palliative care team. Over the last week he has become noticeably more breathless, and his nurse finds he is paler than usual. He still wants treatment that might help him feel better and stay at home. What is the most appropriate general principle?

options.A: Look for and treat reversible causes in line with his wishes while relieving his symptoms
options.B: Withhold any further treatment because his illness is terminal
options.C: Give antibiotics routinely for any increase in breathlessness
options.D: Stop all regular medicines to reduce his tablet burden
options.E: Limit discussion with him to avoid causing distress

correct_answer: A. Look for and treat reversible causes in line with his wishes while relieving his symptoms
why_correct: Even in advanced illness, a new deterioration may have a treatable cause, such as anaemia, a pleural effusion, infection or pulmonary embolism. Where investigation and treatment fit his goals and are not burdensome, these should be considered, alongside direct relief of breathlessness. Decisions should be shared with him and reflect what he wants.
why_wrong: B. Terminal illness does not mean that reversible problems or symptoms should be left untreated. C. Antibiotics are only appropriate when infection is likely and treatment fits his goals. D. Medicines should be reviewed individually rather than stopped wholesale. E. Open communication is essential to shared decisions in palliative care.
pearl: Anaemia is a common, readily treatable contributor to breathlessness and fatigue in advanced cancer.
thinking: Advanced cancer at home ↓ New increase in breathlessness and pallor ↓ Possible reversible cause such as anaemia ↓ He wants treatment to stay well at home ↓ Treat reversible causes and relieve symptoms
exam_trap: B, Withholding further treatment — terminal illness can make any intervention seem futile, but a reversible cause treated in line with his wishes may improve his remaining time.
takeaway: In palliative care, look for reversible causes that fit the patient's goals while also relieving symptoms.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with end-stage COPD tells her GP that she wants to remain at home for the rest of her illness. She is increasingly troubled by breathlessness, anxiety and poor sleep despite optimised inhaled treatment, and she asks whether there is a team that could help her manage these symptoms at home. Which service is most appropriate to involve?
why_correct: Specialist palliative care teams provide expert symptom control and psychological, social and spiritual support for people with advanced, life-limiting illness, including non-cancer conditions such as COPD. Community palliative care services can support her to stay at home in line with her wishes. Palliative care is based on need, not diagnosis or prognosis alone.
why_wrong: A. A memory clinic assesses cognitive impairment, which she does not have. B. A falls clinic addresses falls risk, not breathlessness and anxiety in advanced lung disease. D. Ophthalmology manages eye conditions. E. Orthopaedic surgery treats musculoskeletal problems.
pearl: People with advanced non-malignant disease such as COPD and heart failure have symptom burdens comparable to cancer but are less often referred to palliative care.
thinking: End-stage COPD ↓ Wants to stay at home ↓ Breathlessness, anxiety and poor sleep despite treatment ↓ Needs specialist symptom control and support ↓ Specialist palliative care team
exam_trap: B, Falls clinic — a frail older patient with breathlessness may seem at risk of falls, but her needs are symptom control and support, which is what palliative care provides.
takeaway: Specialist palliative care supports symptom control at home in advanced illness, including non-cancer conditions.

stem: On a respiratory ward, an 81-year-old woman with end-stage pulmonary fibrosis is expected to die within days. Assessment has found nothing new that could be corrected, such as infection, effusion or a clot. She is frightened by episodes of air hunger, and her daughter keeps asking whether more scans should be done. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Focus on relieving her breathlessness and talk openly with her and her daughter about her goals of care
options.B: Request CT pulmonary angiography to search for another cause
options.C: Withhold morphine because of the risk of respiratory depression
options.E: Avoid any discussion of prognosis to protect her from distress

correct_answer: A. Focus on relieving her breathlessness and talk openly with her and her daughter about her goals of care
why_correct: When no reversible cause is present and death is expected within days, care should focus on comfort and communication. Breathlessness can be eased with carefully titrated opioids, a benzodiazepine if anxiety is prominent, positioning and a fan. Honest conversations with her and her daughter about what to expect and what matters to her help align care with her wishes and reduce pressure for unhelpful tests.
why_wrong: B. Reversible causes have already been sought, and further imaging would add burden without benefit. C. Low-dose, titrated opioids relieve breathlessness and are appropriate at the end of life. D. There is no evidence of infection, and antibiotics would not ease her distress. E. Avoiding prognosis undermines shared decisions and leaves the family unprepared.
pearl: Anxiety and breathlessness feed each other at the end of life, so treating panic, for example with a low-dose benzodiazepine, can ease the sensation of air hunger.
thinking: Expected to die within days ↓ No reversible cause found ↓ Distressing air hunger ↓ Family seeking more tests ↓ Symptom relief and open discussion of goals
exam_trap: B, CT pulmonary angiography — the family's request and the thought of missing a clot make it tempting, but reversible causes have been considered and further scans would not change her care.
takeaway: At the end of life without a reversible cause, prioritise symptom relief and honest discussion over further tests.

stem: A daughter phones her mother's GP surgery. Her mother, a 74-year-old widow who lives alone, has been found on the kitchen floor twice in the past two months. She was unhurt both times and insists she simply lost her footing. What should the GP offer?

options.A: Stopping all of her regular medicines straight away
options.B: Bed rest at home until she feels steadier
options.C: Reassurance that falls are a normal part of getting older
options.E: No further action because she has not been injured

correct_answer: D. A multifactorial falls risk assessment
why_correct: More than one fall in a year identifies an older person at increased risk who should be offered a multifactorial falls risk assessment. This looks at gait and balance, strength, medicines, postural blood pressure, vision, cognition, continence, footwear and home hazards, and leads to an individualised plan. The absence of injury does not lower her risk of future harm.
why_wrong: A. Medicines should be reviewed selectively; abruptly stopping all of them may cause harm. B. Bed rest causes deconditioning and increases falls risk. C. Falls are not an inevitable part of ageing and often have modifiable causes. E. Uninjured falls still predict further falls and injury.
pearl: Lying on the floor for a long time after a fall is associated with pressure damage, dehydration and rhabdomyolysis, so people who live alone may benefit from a personal alarm.
thinking: Older woman living alone ↓ Two falls in two months ↓ No injury, but recurrent ↓ High risk of further falls ↓ Multifactorial falls risk assessment
exam_trap: E, No action as she was not injured — the lack of harm is reassuring, but recurrent falls signal risk regardless of injury.
takeaway: Recurrent falls in an older person warrant a multifactorial falls risk assessment, even without injury.

stem: At an annual long-term condition review, a practice nurse learns that an 85-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis has gone over three times since the spring, and on one occasion lay on the floor for an hour before her neighbour found her. She mentions it only in passing and says it is just her age. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.B: Arrange a comprehensive multifactorial falls assessment
options.C: Advise her to avoid physical activity
options.D: Reassure her that falls are expected at her age
options.E: Investigate only if she has another fall

correct_answer: B. Arrange a comprehensive multifactorial falls assessment
why_correct: Recurrent falls, especially with a long lie, mark her as high risk and should trigger a comprehensive multifactorial assessment. This includes gait, balance and muscle strength, her osteoarthritis and pain, medicines, postural blood pressure, vision, cognition, continence and environmental hazards. The findings guide interventions such as strength and balance training and home modification.
why_wrong: A. There is nothing to suggest infection. C. Inactivity weakens muscles and increases falls risk; strength and balance exercise reduces falls. D. Falls are not an inevitable part of ageing. E. Waiting for another fall delays intervention and risks serious injury.
pearl: Strength and balance training programmes are among the most effective single interventions for reducing falls in older people living in the community.
thinking: Three falls in a few months ↓ Long lie on one occasion ↓ Patient minimises it as age ↓ High risk of injury ↓ Comprehensive multifactorial assessment
exam_trap: D, Reassurance about her age — she frames it this way herself, but falls usually have modifiable causes and warrant assessment.
takeaway: Recurrent falls should never be dismissed as normal ageing; they need a comprehensive falls assessment.

stem: An 82-year-old man is seen in the falls clinic after several falls this year. He explains that he keeps misjudging the edge of the kerb and does not notice steps, particularly in poor light. He has not had his eyes tested for many years and his glasses are scratched and old. Which assessment is particularly relevant?
why_correct: Visual impairment is a common, modifiable risk factor for falls, and his description of missing kerbs and steps suggests that poor vision is contributing. Assessment of acuity and referral for an eye test may identify a need for new glasses or treatment of cataract, which can reduce falls. Vision should be checked as part of every multifactorial falls assessment.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid antibodies have no role in assessing his falls. B. Spirometry assesses lung function, which is not relevant to his symptoms. D. Stool culture investigates infective diarrhoea. E. Serum amylase is used in suspected pancreatitis.
pearl: Cataract surgery on the first eye reduces falls, and multifocal glasses can increase falls on stairs and kerbs by blurring the lower field of view.
thinking: Recurrent falls ↓ Misjudges kerbs and steps ↓ Worse in poor light ↓ Old glasses, no recent eye test ↓ Assess vision
exam_trap: B, Spirometry — breathlessness can contribute to falls in older people, but nothing in his story suggests a respiratory problem, whereas his visual clues are specific.
takeaway: Visual impairment is a modifiable falls risk factor that should be assessed in anyone with recurrent falls.

stem: An 80-year-old woman lives alone in a terraced house. She tells her GP that she has caught her foot on a frayed hall rug and on the worn stair carpet several times, and that the landing light has not worked for months. She has no dizziness, and her gait and strength are reasonable for her age. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.A: Advise her to stay in one downstairs room as much as possible
options.B: Prescribe hip protectors to wear at home
options.C: Refer her for a bone density scan
options.D: Arrange a home hazard assessment and modification by an occupational therapist

correct_answer: D. Arrange a home hazard assessment and modification by an occupational therapist
why_correct: Her trips are clearly linked to hazards in her home, such as loose rugs, worn carpet and poor lighting. A home hazard assessment, usually by an occupational therapist, with removal or repair of hazards and better lighting, reduces falls in people with these environmental risks. It also allows fitting of aids such as rails if needed.
why_wrong: A. Restricting her movement leads to deconditioning and isolation. B. Hip protectors may reduce fracture if she falls but do nothing to stop the trips. C. A bone density scan assesses fracture risk rather than preventing falls. E. Vitamin D supplementation alone does not address the environmental cause of her falls.
pearl: Home hazard interventions are most effective when delivered by an occupational therapist to people at higher risk of falls.
thinking: Repeated trips at home ↓ Loose rug, worn carpet, poor lighting ↓ No dizziness, reasonable gait ↓ Environmental cause is dominant ↓ Home hazard assessment and modification
exam_trap: C, Bone density scan — falls in older women make fracture risk assessment relevant, but it does not address why she is tripping.
takeaway: When falls are caused by home hazards, arrange an occupational therapy home hazard assessment.

stem: A night carer at a nursing home reports that an 86-year-old man has been found on the floor three times in the past two months, each time at night and with no clear reason. His drug chart includes zopiclone, amitriptyline for neuropathic pain and amlodipine. As part of assessing his falls, what is particularly important?

options.B: Stopping all his medicines at once
options.D: A structured review of his medicines

correct_answer: D. A structured review of his medicines
why_correct: Hypnotics, tricyclic antidepressants and antihypertensives can all contribute to falls through sedation, impaired balance, confusion and postural hypotension. A structured medication review, with planned reduction or withdrawal of falls-risk drugs where possible, is a core part of multifactorial falls assessment. Night-time falls in someone taking zopiclone and amitriptyline make this especially important.
why_wrong: A. Restricting mobility causes deconditioning and increases falls risk. B. Abrupt withdrawal of all medicines can cause harm, including withdrawal effects, and review should be planned. C. Assuming a cause risks missing reversible contributors. E. Medicines are among the commonest modifiable causes of falls.
pearl: Z-drugs such as zopiclone carry a falls risk similar to benzodiazepines in older people and should be tapered rather than stopped abruptly after long-term use.
thinking: Recurrent unexplained falls at night ↓ On a hypnotic, a tricyclic and an antihypertensive ↓ Sedation and postural hypotension likely ↓ Medicines are modifiable risk factors ↓ Structured medication review
exam_trap: B, Stopping all medicines at once — it removes every possible culprit, but sudden withdrawal can cause harm and review should be planned and selective.
takeaway: A structured medication review is a core part of assessing recurrent falls.

stem: An 84-year-old woman is referred to a geriatric outpatient clinic after her third fall this year, which left her with bruising but no fracture. She takes lisinopril, doxazosin, mirtazapine and a nightly temazepam. She walks with a stick and lives with her husband. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Stop all her blood pressure tablets and sedatives from today
options.B: Undertake a multifactorial falls assessment that includes a review of her medicines
options.C: Arrange a CT head to look for an intracranial cause
options.D: Refer for a DXA scan as the main intervention
options.E: Provide a walking frame and hip protectors without further review

correct_answer: B. Undertake a multifactorial falls assessment that includes a review of her medicines
why_correct: Recurrent falls in an older person should lead to a multifactorial falls assessment covering gait and balance, strength, vision, cognition, continence, postural blood pressure, home hazards and medicines. Her medicines include several that increase falls risk, so a medication review is an important part of this assessment. The findings then guide a tailored plan of interventions.
why_wrong: A. Stopping several drugs abruptly risks rebound hypertension and benzodiazepine withdrawal; changes should be planned. C. A CT head is not routinely needed for falls without head injury or focal neurological signs. D. Bone health assessment is useful but does not reduce falls on its own. E. Aids without assessment miss the modifiable causes of her falls.
pearl: Benzodiazepines, antidepressants, antipsychotics and antihypertensives are the drug classes most strongly associated with falls in older people.
thinking: Third fall this year ↓ Several falls-risk medicines ↓ Needs assessment of all contributing factors ↓ Medication review is one part ↓ Multifactorial falls assessment
exam_trap: A, Stopping her blood pressure tablets and sedatives today — it targets the obvious culprits, but abrupt withdrawal is unsafe and other contributing factors would be missed.
takeaway: Recurrent falls need a multifactorial assessment, with medication review as one key component.

stem: Paramedics attend a 79-year-old man who has fallen at home for the second time this month. He is uninjured and declines to go to hospital, so they pass his details to his GP, who sees him the next day. His observations are normal and he is keen to stay independent. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Arrange a hip X-ray and reassure him if no fracture is seen
options.B: Stop all his regular medicines immediately
options.C: Carry out a multifactorial falls risk assessment
options.D: Prescribe antibiotics in case an infection caused the falls
options.E: Advise bed rest at home until his mobility improves

correct_answer: C. Carry out a multifactorial falls risk assessment
why_correct: Two falls in a short period identify him as at high risk of further falls. A multifactorial falls risk assessment looks at medicines, gait and balance, cardiovascular causes, vision, cognition, footwear and home hazards, and leads to targeted interventions that help him stay independent. Paramedic referral after a non-conveyed fall is a common route into this assessment.
why_wrong: A. He has no injury or hip pain, and a normal X-ray would not address why he is falling. B. Medicines should be reviewed selectively; stopping everything abruptly is unsafe. D. Antibiotics are inappropriate without evidence of infection. E. Bed rest leads to deconditioning and makes falls more likely.
pearl: Many ambulance services refer older people who have fallen but are not taken to hospital to community falls services for assessment.
thinking: Second fall this month ↓ Uninjured, not taken to hospital ↓ Wishes to stay independent ↓ High risk of further falls ↓ Multifactorial falls risk assessment
exam_trap: A, Hip X-ray and reassurance — imaging feels thorough after a fall, but he has no injury and reassurance would leave the causes of his falls unaddressed.
takeaway: An older person with recurrent falls needs a multifactorial assessment, not just exclusion of fracture.

stem: In a community falls clinic, an 81-year-old woman describes the room going dim when she gets up from bed, and she has fallen three times since January. She takes eight regular medicines prescribed by different specialists. She has a few bruises but no fractures. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: No further action, as she has not fractured anything
options.B: Advise bed rest with a bedside commode to avoid walking
options.C: Stop all her regular medicines and review her in a month
options.D: Arrange a CT head and an outpatient EEG as first investigations
options.E: Multifactorial falls assessment, including a medication review and lying and standing blood pressure

correct_answer: E. Multifactorial falls assessment, including a medication review and lying and standing blood pressure
why_correct: Recurrent falls with symptoms on standing suggest that orthostatic hypotension may be contributing, and polypharmacy makes medicines a likely cause. A multifactorial assessment should include lying and standing blood pressure and a structured medication review, together with gait, balance, vision and home assessment. This identifies modifiable factors and directs targeted treatment.
why_wrong: A. Falls without fracture still indicate a high risk of future injury. B. Bed rest causes deconditioning and worsens orthostatic intolerance. C. Stopping all medicines at once is unsafe; changes should be selective and planned. D. Neuroimaging and EEG are not first-line without features of head injury, seizures or focal neurology.
pearl: Postural blood pressure should be measured after lying for at least five minutes and then at one and three minutes after standing.
thinking: Three falls this year ↓ Vision dims on standing ↓ Eight regular medicines ↓ Possible drug-related orthostatic hypotension ↓ Multifactorial assessment with postural blood pressure and medication review
exam_trap: C, Stopping all medicines and reviewing in a month — polypharmacy invites a clean sweep, but sudden withdrawal can be dangerous and other causes would remain unassessed.
takeaway: Recurrent falls with postural symptoms need a multifactorial assessment that includes postural blood pressure and medication review.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted to the medical assessment unit after a fall at home, her second in a month. She says she feels faint whenever she stands. A nurse records her blood pressure as 146/82 mmHg after lying for five minutes and 118/70 mmHg after three minutes of standing, when she again feels light-headed. What is the most likely explanation for her falls?
why_correct: A sustained fall in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg (or diastolic of at least 10 mmHg) within three minutes of standing, with reproduction of her symptoms, confirms orthostatic hypotension. Her systolic pressure falls by 28 mmHg on standing, explaining her faintness and falls. The next step is to look for causes such as medicines, dehydration or autonomic dysfunction.
why_wrong: A. Essential hypertension does not cause symptomatic drops in pressure on standing. B. Thyrotoxicosis causes tachycardia, weight loss and tremor rather than a postural blood pressure fall. C. Raised intracranial pressure causes headache, vomiting and reduced consciousness, often with a rising blood pressure. D. Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as pain or prolonged standing, rather than a consistent drop each time she stands.
pearl: Orthostatic hypotension in older people is frequently caused by medicines and volume depletion, but autonomic failure, for example in Parkinson's disease or diabetes, should also be considered.
thinking: Recurrent falls ↓ Faint on standing ↓ Systolic fall of 28 mmHg within three minutes ↓ Symptoms reproduced ↓ Orthostatic hypotension
exam_trap: D, Vasovagal syncope — faintness and falls suggest reflex syncope, but the consistent, measured drop on standing points to orthostatic hypotension.
takeaway: A symptomatic fall in blood pressure on standing in an older person who falls is orthostatic hypotension.

stem: Care home staff ask the visiting GP to see Albert, an 81-year-old widower. Three weeks ago an out-of-hours doctor prescribed zopiclone because he was sleeping poorly after his wife died. Since then he has twice been found on his bedroom floor in the early hours, unhurt but muddled for a short while. His observations and examination today are unremarkable. Which step should come first to lower his risk of further falls?

options.A: Add melatonin so that the zopiclone dose can stay the same
