options.B: Increase the zopiclone so that he sleeps through the night
options.C: Raise bed rails each night to keep him in bed
options.D: Arrange a CT scan of his head
options.E: Review the zopiclone and reduce or stop it

correct_answer: E. Review the zopiclone and reduce or stop it
why_correct: The falls began soon after a sedative hypnotic was started, so the drug is the most likely and most easily reversible cause. Z-drugs cause night-time confusion, impaired balance and hangover sedation in older people, so the first step is to review the prescription and reduce or stop it, with sleep hygiene and bereavement support instead.
why_wrong: A. Adding melatonin leaves the causative sedative in place and adds another drug. B. A higher dose would increase sedation and the chance of further falls. C. Bed rails are a restraint and can lead to more serious falls when people climb over them. D. He has no head injury or focal signs, and imaging does not address the cause.
pearl: Hypnotics such as benzodiazepines and Z-drugs are among the medicines most strongly linked to falls and hip fracture in older adults and should be prescribed only for short courses, if at all.
thinking: Falls began after a new hypnotic ↓ No injury or new neurological findings ↓ Z-drugs impair balance and alertness at night ↓ Most reversible cause is the drug itself ↓ Review and reduce or stop the zopiclone
exam_trap: C, Raising bed rails — it looks like a simple safety measure, but rails are a form of restraint, people with confusion often climb over them, and they do nothing about the sedative causing the falls.
takeaway: When falls start after a new sedative, review and withdraw the sedative first.

presentation: Medicines as a falls risk factor
stem: An 86-year-old retired builder is brought to the emergency department after tripping at home. He has a graze but no fracture. His regular medicines are doxazosin, furosemide and amitriptyline for neuropathic foot pain, and his wife says this is his third fall since the spring. Which element should be included in assessing the cause of his falls?

options.A: A CT scan of the head, as for every older person who falls
options.B: Explaining that falls are an unavoidable part of growing old
options.C: Stopping all his regular tablets on discharge
options.D: A review of his medicines for drugs causing sedation or low blood pressure
options.E: Advice to avoid walking until he is seen in clinic

correct_answer: D. A review of his medicines for drugs causing sedation or low blood pressure
why_correct: Doxazosin and furosemide can both lower blood pressure on standing, and amitriptyline adds sedation and postural hypotension. A review of each medicine for its contribution to falls is a core part of a multifactorial falls assessment and can identify drugs to reduce, switch or stop.
why_wrong: A. Head imaging is guided by head injury criteria, not used routinely for every fall. B. Recurrent falls have modifiable causes and need assessment. C. Stopping everything at once is unsafe; medicines should be reviewed one by one. E. Prolonged inactivity worsens strength and balance and increases future falls.
pearl: Alpha-blockers, diuretics, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics and sedatives are classic fall-risk-increasing drugs in older people.
thinking: Third fall in a few months ↓ Takes an alpha-blocker, a diuretic and a tricyclic ↓ All can cause postural hypotension or sedation ↓ Medicines are a modifiable risk factor ↓ Include a medication review in the falls assessment
exam_trap: C, Stopping all his tablets — it seems decisive, but abrupt withdrawal can cause harm and some medicines may still be needed; each should be reviewed against its benefit.
takeaway: Every falls assessment should include a review of medicines that cause sedation or hypotension.

stem: Edna, aged 88, is on the orthogeriatric ward with a pubic ramus fracture after slipping in her kitchen. Nurses notice she is intermittently confused, she has lost weight over the last few months and she says she has stopped going upstairs at home. She lives alone and is assessed as moderately frail. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Manage the fracture pain and discharge her once she can walk
options.B: Put the confusion and weight loss down to her age
options.C: Comprehensive geriatric assessment by the multidisciplinary team
options.D: Arrange permanent care home placement directly from the ward
options.E: Plan her future care with her family without involving her

correct_answer: C. Comprehensive geriatric assessment by the multidisciplinary team
why_correct: She has several interacting problems: confusion, weight loss, declining mobility and a fragility fracture, on a background of frailty. Comprehensive geriatric assessment looks at medical, functional, cognitive, nutritional, medication, social and psychological needs together and agrees goals with the patient, which improves outcomes such as returning home.
why_wrong: A. Treating the fracture alone misses the other problems that caused and will follow the fall. B. Confusion and weight loss are not normal ageing and need assessment. D. Long-term placement should only be decided after assessment and rehabilitation, with her involvement. E. Her views and goals must be central to planning, and capacity should be assessed rather than assumed absent.
pearl: Comprehensive geriatric assessment of frail older inpatients increases the chance of being alive and living in their own home at follow-up.
thinking: Frail older woman admitted after a fall ↓ New confusion, weight loss and reduced mobility ↓ Problems are multiple and interlinked ↓ Needs holistic multidisciplinary assessment ↓ Comprehensive geriatric assessment
exam_trap: A, Managing the fracture and discharging when mobile — it fits a single-problem model of care, but in frailty the fall is a marker of wider decline that will lead to readmission if not addressed.
takeaway: A frail older person admitted after a fall needs comprehensive geriatric assessment, not just treatment of the injury.

stem: A 77-year-old man with heart failure attends his GP after two falls. He takes bisoprolol, ramipril and furosemide, and a fortnight ago pregabalin was added for shingles pain. Since then he has felt unsteady and woozy, particularly in the mornings. Which part of his falls assessment is most likely to identify a modifiable cause?
why_correct: His unsteadiness began soon after pregabalin was added to several drugs that lower blood pressure. A structured medication review weighs the benefit and harm of each medicine and is the step most likely to find a cause that can be changed quickly, such as reducing or stopping the pregabalin and checking for postural hypotension.
why_wrong: A. A DXA scan assesses fracture risk, not why he is falling. B. An echocardiogram helps manage heart failure but will not explain the recent change. C. Brain imaging is not indicated without focal neurological signs. E. B12 deficiency is a rare cause of unsteadiness and does not fit the clear timing with a new drug.
pearl: Gabapentinoids cause dizziness, somnolence and ataxia, and the risk is higher when combined with other sedating drugs or in reduced kidney function.
thinking: Two falls with new unsteadiness ↓ Started pregabalin two weeks ago ↓ Also on several blood pressure-lowering drugs ↓ Drug effects are the most likely modifiable cause ↓ Structured medication review
exam_trap: B, Echocardiogram — heart failure makes a cardiac cause tempting, but nothing suggests a change in his heart, whereas the timing with a new sedating drug points to the medicines.
takeaway: Look first at recently started or changed medicines when an older person begins to fall.

stem: At a flu vaccination appointment, an 85-year-old man mentions to the practice nurse that he has fallen three times this year. He was not hurt, but his wife has started to worry when he goes out alone. Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Reassure him that falling is a normal part of getting older
options.B: Suggest he uses a wheelchair whenever he leaves the house
options.C: Offer a multifactorial falls risk assessment to find modifiable causes
options.D: Arrange a DXA scan and take no further action
options.E: Provide a pendant alarm instead of any further assessment

correct_answer: C. Offer a multifactorial falls risk assessment to find modifiable causes
why_correct: Older people who report recurrent falls should be offered a multifactorial falls risk assessment. This looks at causes such as medicines, gait and balance, vision, postural hypotension, continence, cognition, footwear and home hazards, so that targeted interventions can be offered to prevent further falls.
why_wrong: A. Falls are common in later life but are not inevitable, and many causes can be modified. B. A wheelchair would reduce activity and worsen strength and balance. D. Bone health matters, but a DXA scan alone does nothing to reduce falls. E. An alarm helps summon help after a fall but does not prevent one.
pearl: Strength and balance training is one of the most effective single interventions for preventing falls in older people living at home.
thinking: Three falls this year ↓ Recurrent falls mean increased future risk ↓ Many causes are modifiable ↓ Multifactorial assessment identifies them ↓ Offer targeted interventions
exam_trap: E, A pendant alarm — it is a sensible addition and reassures relatives, but it only shortens time on the floor after a fall and leaves the causes unaddressed.
takeaway: Recurrent falls warrant a multifactorial assessment for modifiable risk factors.

stem: A care home nurse is reviewing a 90-year-old resident who has fallen four times in two months. Staff have not witnessed the falls and no clear cause has been found. She is on several regular tablets. Which bedside test is most useful to look for a common, treatable contributor?
correct_answer: D. Lying and standing blood pressure
why_correct: Orthostatic hypotension is a common and often reversible cause of falls in older people, frequently due to medicines or dehydration. Measuring blood pressure lying and then standing is a simple bedside test that can reveal it and guide changes such as reducing antihypertensives.
why_wrong: A. Peak flow assesses airflow obstruction, not falls. B. Grip strength reflects frailty but does not identify a specific treatable cause. C. Resting oxygen saturation is unlikely to explain recurrent unexplained falls. E. Body mass index helps assess nutrition but does not reveal a cause of falling.
pearl: Postural blood pressure should be measured after the person has been lying down for at least five minutes and repeated after standing for one and three minutes.
thinking: Recurrent unexplained falls ↓ Takes several regular medicines ↓ Postural hypotension is common and treatable ↓ Detected by a simple bedside test ↓ Lying and standing blood pressure
exam_trap: B, Hand grip strength — it is a validated marker of frailty and sounds relevant, but it does not point to a specific reversible cause the way a postural drop does.
takeaway: Measure lying and standing blood pressure in every older person with unexplained falls.

stem: Margaret, 84, is recovering on a trauma ward after surgery for a hip fracture sustained in a fall at home. Her drug chart lists tramadol, diazepam, amlodipine, bendroflumethiazide and lisinopril, along with several other medicines. Which medication-related problem should be the focus of her falls review?

options.C: Combined adverse effects of several sedating and blood pressure-lowering drugs
options.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency caused by her medicines

correct_answer: C. Combined adverse effects of several sedating and blood pressure-lowering drugs
why_correct: She takes an opioid and a benzodiazepine, which cause sedation and impaired balance, plus three drugs that lower blood pressure, which can cause postural hypotension. Together these adverse effects greatly increase falls risk, so the review should target polypharmacy and reduce or stop the drugs contributing most.
why_wrong: A. Constipation is a real side effect of tramadol but is not the main way her medicines cause falls. B. There is no suggestion that diazepam has been stopped; the problem is its ongoing sedation. D. B12 deficiency is not a recognised effect of these drugs. E. Lisinopril with a thiazide is unlikely to cause hyperkalaemia and this would not be the main falls mechanism.
pearl: The more medicines an older person takes, the higher the falls risk, and combinations of sedatives with antihypertensives are particularly hazardous.
thinking: Fall leading to hip fracture ↓ On an opioid and a benzodiazepine ↓ Also on three antihypertensive drugs ↓ Additive sedation and postural hypotension ↓ Focus on polypharmacy and adverse effects
exam_trap: B, Diazepam withdrawal — benzodiazepine withdrawal can cause falls, but she is still taking it, so its sedative effect, not withdrawal, is the concern.
takeaway: Polypharmacy with sedating and blood pressure-lowering drugs is a major modifiable cause of falls.

stem: An 82-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after falling on his way to the bathroom at night. His regular medicines are alendronic acid, clopidogrel, lansoprazole, an emollient cream and amitriptyline, which was recently started for poor sleep. Which of his medicines is most likely to have contributed to the fall?
why_correct: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant with sedative, anticholinergic and alpha-blocking effects, causing drowsiness, confusion and postural hypotension. It is a recognised fall-risk-increasing drug, especially at night in older people, and should be reviewed and ideally stopped.
why_wrong: A. Alendronic acid reduces fracture risk and does not cause falls. B. Clopidogrel increases bleeding if he falls but does not make falling more likely. D. Lansoprazole is not associated with sedation or postural hypotension. E. A topical emollient has no systemic effects that cause falls, although spilt emollient can make floors slippery.
pearl: Antidepressants of all classes, including SSRIs, are associated with falls in older people, partly through hyponatraemia as well as sedation.
thinking: Night-time fall in an older man ↓ Recently started a tricyclic antidepressant ↓ Tricyclics cause sedation and postural hypotension ↓ Other medicines do not cause falls ↓ Amitriptyline is the likely contributor
exam_trap: B, Clopidogrel — antiplatelets are often flagged after a fall, but they affect the consequences of a fall (bleeding), not the likelihood of falling.
takeaway: Antidepressants, particularly tricyclics, are fall-risk-increasing drugs that should be reviewed after a fall.

stem: During a telephone consultation, the wife of a 79-year-old man tells his GP he fell in the garden yesterday and seems unsteady most mornings. He has taken temazepam every night for many years for insomnia and has a few other regular medicines. He was not injured. What is the most appropriate first step to reduce his risk of falling again?

options.A: A medication review with a plan to gradually withdraw the temazepam
options.B: Advice to stay indoors until his balance improves

correct_answer: A. A medication review with a plan to gradually withdraw the temazepam
why_correct: Morning unsteadiness in an older man on a long-term benzodiazepine strongly suggests hangover sedation and impaired balance. A medication review should address the temazepam with a planned, gradual reduction, because abrupt withdrawal after years of use can cause rebound insomnia, anxiety or seizures.
why_wrong: B. Staying indoors reduces activity and worsens strength and balance. C. Hip protectors may reduce fracture risk but do not prevent falls. D. Z-drugs carry a similar falls risk to benzodiazepines. E. Bone health assessment is useful but does not reduce falls.
pearl: Long-term benzodiazepines should be tapered gradually over weeks to months rather than stopped abruptly.
thinking: Fall plus morning unsteadiness ↓ Long-term nightly benzodiazepine ↓ Hangover sedation impairs balance ↓ Drug is a modifiable cause ↓ Medication review with gradual withdrawal
exam_trap: D, Switching to zopiclone — it seems like moving to a gentler hypnotic, but Z-drugs have similar effects on balance and falls risk.
takeaway: Review and gradually withdraw long-term sedatives in older people who fall.

stem: A 70-year-old woman sees her GP two weeks after discharge from hospital, where several changes were made to her tablets. Since getting home she has fallen twice and feels lightheaded when she gets up. Which part of her history is most likely to reveal a reversible cause of the falls?

options.D: Her current prescribed and over-the-counter medicines

correct_answer: D. Her current prescribed and over-the-counter medicines
why_correct: New falls and lightheadedness on standing that began after medication changes point strongly to an adverse drug effect, such as postural hypotension from a new or increased antihypertensive. Taking an accurate medicines history, including anything bought over the counter, identifies drugs that can be adjusted.
why_wrong: A. A family history of dementia does not explain new falls after discharge. B. Age at menopause affects bone health, not the cause of falling. C. Smoking history is relevant to vascular risk but not to this recent change. E. Occupation does not explain falls that began after medication changes.
pearl: Medicines reconciliation after hospital discharge is a key point to catch new drugs, dose changes and duplications that cause harm.
thinking: New falls after hospital discharge ↓ Tablets were changed in hospital ↓ Lightheaded on standing ↓ Suggests an adverse drug effect ↓ Take a full medicines history
exam_trap: A, Family history of dementia — cognitive impairment is a real falls risk factor, but nothing here suggests it and the timing fits the medication changes.
takeaway: Always take a full medication history, including recent changes, in someone with new falls.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with chronic low back pain and depression has fallen twice in a month. She takes gabapentin, codeine and mirtazapine, and also buys promethazine from the pharmacy to help her sleep. She describes feeling drowsy and slow during the day. What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.A: Add zopiclone to improve her sleep
options.B: Advise bed rest until the drowsiness settles
options.C: Review her medicines and reduce the sedating drugs
options.E: Provide a walking frame and make no other changes

correct_answer: C. Review her medicines and reduce the sedating drugs
why_correct: She takes four drugs with sedative effects, including an over-the-counter antihistamine, and her daytime drowsiness explains her falls. A medication review can reduce or stop the sedating drugs in a planned way, while still managing her pain and mood.
why_wrong: A. Another hypnotic would add to the sedative burden. B. Bed rest causes deconditioning and does not address the cause. D. Stopping everything abruptly risks withdrawal and uncontrolled pain or depression. E. A walking aid does not deal with the drugs making her drowsy.
pearl: Sedating antihistamines bought over the counter, such as promethazine, are easily missed in a medication history unless asked about directly.
thinking: Recurrent falls in a younger adult ↓ Several sedating drugs including over-the-counter promethazine ↓ Daytime drowsiness ↓ Additive sedation is the likely cause ↓ Planned medication review
exam_trap: D, Stopping all her medicines — it removes the problem drugs, but abrupt withdrawal of gabapentin, codeine and mirtazapine can cause withdrawal effects and leave pain and depression untreated.
takeaway: Falls are not just a problem of old age; sedative polypharmacy should be reviewed at any age.

stem: A community matron visits a 90-year-old woman in sheltered housing who has had several falls recently. She takes lorazepam for anxiety, ramipril, indapamide and a number of other regular medicines. Her mobility is otherwise reasonable and she wants to stay independent. What is the most important initial intervention?

options.A: Advise her to stay in her chair for most of the day
options.B: Stop all her medicines at once
options.C: Medication review focusing on the lorazepam and her blood pressure tablets
options.E: Increase the lorazepam to help her anxiety about falling

correct_answer: C. Medication review focusing on the lorazepam and her blood pressure tablets
why_correct: A benzodiazepine causes sedation and impaired balance, and ramipril with indapamide can cause postural hypotension, so her medicines are likely contributors. A medication review that targets these drugs, with gradual benzodiazepine reduction, is a key initial step and supports her wish to stay independent.
why_wrong: A. Prolonged sitting leads to deconditioning and more falls. B. Abrupt withdrawal of lorazepam can cause rebound anxiety or seizures, and some medicines may be needed. D. Admission is not needed for medication review and can cause harm through deconditioning. E. More lorazepam would increase sedation and falls risk.
pearl: Indapamide and other thiazide-like diuretics can cause hyponatraemia in older women, which itself increases the risk of falls.
thinking: Recurrent falls in a very old woman ↓ On a benzodiazepine and two antihypertensives ↓ Sedation plus postural hypotension ↓ Modifiable drug causes ↓ Targeted medication review
exam_trap: E, Increasing the lorazepam — fear of falling is real and distressing, but more sedative would make further falls more likely.
takeaway: In recurrent falls, start by reviewing sedatives and blood pressure-lowering drugs.

stem: A 69-year-old man is seen in a GP surgery after two falls in three weeks. He was recently started on tamsulosin for urinary symptoms, and at about the same time his amlodipine dose was increased. He says he feels faint when he first stands up in the morning. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Advise him to stay in bed until the faintness passes each morning
options.B: Review his medicines and check lying and standing blood pressure
options.D: Refer him for an MRI of the brain
options.E: Reassure him that dizziness is common at his age

correct_answer: B. Review his medicines and check lying and standing blood pressure
why_correct: Faintness on standing after starting an alpha-blocker and increasing a calcium channel blocker suggests drug-induced postural hypotension. Measuring lying and standing blood pressure confirms this, and reviewing the new and changed medicines allows the likely culprit to be adjusted.
why_wrong: A. Staying in bed reduces activity and does not treat the cause. C. Stopping everything is unnecessary and may cause harm. D. There are no neurological features to justify brain imaging. E. New dizziness with falls after drug changes needs assessment, not reassurance.
pearl: Alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin and doxazosin commonly cause postural hypotension, especially when first started or combined with other vasodilating drugs such as calcium channel blockers.
thinking: Falls after new tamsulosin and higher amlodipine ↓ Faint on standing ↓ Suspect drug-induced postural hypotension ↓ Confirm with lying and standing blood pressure ↓ Review and adjust the medicines
exam_trap: D, MRI of the brain — dizziness can prompt thoughts of a central cause, but postural symptoms after new vasodilating drugs point to the medicines, not the brain.
takeaway: Postural dizziness after medicine changes needs a postural blood pressure check and a medication review.

stem: An 86-year-old man with COPD, type 2 diabetes, heart failure and osteoarthritis takes thirteen regular medicines. His carer tells the GP that he has had dizzy spells for a few weeks and has fallen twice, with no injury. Examination shows no new focal findings. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: A structured review of his medicines for adverse effects and interactions
options.B: Stop his heart failure medicines today
options.C: Add a sleeping tablet to improve his night-time rest
options.D: Reassure him and review at his annual check
options.E: Advise him to rest in his chair and limit walking

correct_answer: A. A structured review of his medicines for adverse effects and interactions
why_correct: With thirteen medicines and several conditions, adverse effects and interactions are a likely cause of his dizziness and falls. A structured medication review, ideally shared with him, can identify drugs causing hypotension, hypoglycaemia or sedation and agree which to change or stop.
why_wrong: B. Heart failure medicines have prognostic benefit and should be adjusted after review, not stopped abruptly. C. A sleeping tablet adds sedation and falls risk. D. New dizziness with falls needs prompt assessment. E. Inactivity worsens strength and balance.
pearl: Tools such as the STOPP/START criteria help identify potentially inappropriate medicines in older people.
thinking: Thirteen regular medicines ↓ New dizziness and two falls ↓ Adverse effects and interactions are likely ↓ Some drugs carry important benefits ↓ Structured medication review
exam_trap: B, Stopping his heart failure drugs today — they may be lowering his blood pressure, but stopping them all abruptly could precipitate decompensation; a considered review is needed.
takeaway: In polypharmacy with falls, a structured medication review comes first.

stem: An 81-year-old woman is found on the kitchen floor by her son. She says she went giddy as soon as she got up quickly from the sofa and then fell, without losing consciousness. She takes several regular medicines. Which group of medicines is most often responsible for this type of fall?
why_correct: Giddiness immediately on standing suggests orthostatic hypotension. Antihypertensives, including diuretics, ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers and alpha-blockers, reduce the body's ability to maintain blood pressure on standing and are a common cause of falls in older people.
why_wrong: A. Inhaled corticosteroids do not lower blood pressure. C. Topical antifungals have negligible systemic absorption. D. Proton pump inhibitors are not associated with postural hypotension. E. Emollients have no systemic effect on blood pressure.
pearl: Other drug causes of orthostatic hypotension include nitrates, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics and levodopa.
thinking: Fall after standing up quickly ↓ Giddiness without loss of consciousness ↓ Suggests orthostatic hypotension ↓ Commonly caused by blood pressure-lowering drugs ↓ Antihypertensives
exam_trap: D, Proton pump inhibitors — they are often flagged in reviews of polypharmacy, but they do not cause postural hypotension.
takeaway: Antihypertensives are a common cause of orthostatic hypotension and falls.

stem: A 72-year-old retired teacher has fallen twice this month. He takes nine prescribed medicines and has recently been buying a sedating antihistamine from the supermarket to help him sleep. He has no injuries. What is the most important first step in reducing his risk of further falls related to medication?

options.B: Advise him to stay in bed in the mornings
options.C: Stop all of his tablets at once

correct_answer: D. Medication review, including over-the-counter products
why_correct: He has polypharmacy plus a sedating over-the-counter antihistamine, both of which can contribute to falls. A medication review that includes non-prescribed products can identify sedative and hypotensive drugs to stop or reduce, which is the key first step in tackling medication-related falls.
why_wrong: A. Fluid restriction can cause dehydration and postural hypotension. B. Staying in bed reduces activity and worsens balance. C. Abruptly stopping everything is unsafe. E. A stronger hypnotic would increase sedation and falls risk.
pearl: Always ask specifically about over-the-counter sleep aids and antihistamines, as patients often do not consider them to be medicines.
thinking: Two falls in a month ↓ Nine prescribed medicines ↓ Also taking a sedating antihistamine ↓ Medicines are a modifiable cause ↓ Full medication review
exam_trap: C, Stopping all his tablets — it seems to remove every possible culprit, but it risks withdrawal and loss of benefit from essential medicines.
takeaway: A medication review, including over-the-counter products, is the first step in medication-related falls.

stem: An 83-year-old man with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse at his annual review that he misjudged a kerb and fell last week, and also tripped over a step at home last month. He finds it hard to read and has not had his eyes checked for several years. Which intervention is most likely to reduce his falls related to poor vision?

options.A: Arrange a vision assessment with an optometrist
options.B: Advise him to wear varifocal glasses when walking outdoors
options.C: Prescribe a sedative to improve his sleep
options.D: Advise him to stop going outside
options.E: Keep his home lighting dim at night to aid sleep

correct_answer: A. Arrange a vision assessment with an optometrist
why_correct: Poor vision is a modifiable risk factor for falls. A vision assessment can identify correctable problems such as refractive error, cataract or diabetic eye disease, leading to new glasses or referral for treatment.
why_wrong: B. Varifocal and bifocal lenses blur the lower field of view and increase the risk of trips when walking outdoors. C. A sedative increases falls risk. D. Stopping outdoor activity reduces strength and independence. E. Dim lighting makes trips more likely, especially at night.
pearl: Expedited cataract surgery for the first eye has been shown to reduce falls in older people with visual impairment.
thinking: Two trips over kerbs and steps ↓ Difficulty reading and no recent eye check ↓ Diabetes increases eye disease risk ↓ Poor vision is modifiable ↓ Arrange a vision assessment
exam_trap: B, Varifocal glasses outdoors — they seem convenient, but multifocal lenses distort the lower visual field and increase trips on steps and kerbs.
takeaway: Check vision in older people who fall, and treat any correctable cause.

stem: An 87-year-old man is brought by ambulance after falling in a supermarket. He has a large bruise on his thigh and some bruising on his arm. He cannot remember the names of his tablets but says he takes a blood thinner. What is an important part of his initial assessment?

options.A: Confirm exactly which medicines he takes, including the anticoagulant and dose
options.B: Give aspirin for the pain from the bruising
options.C: Discharge him with reassurance that bruising is common in older people
options.D: Stop all his regular medicines permanently
options.E: Leave assessment for bleeding to his GP

correct_answer: A. Confirm exactly which medicines he takes, including the anticoagulant and dose
why_correct: An anticoagulant increases the risk of serious bleeding after a fall, including intracranial or soft tissue haemorrhage. Establishing an accurate medication history, including the drug, dose and timing, guides assessment of bleeding, the need for imaging, blood tests and reversal, and later review.
why_wrong: B. Aspirin would further increase bleeding risk and is a poor analgesic choice here. C. Bruising on anticoagulation may signal significant bleeding and needs assessment. D. Medicines should be reviewed, not all stopped permanently. E. Bleeding must be assessed now, not deferred.
pearl: Anticoagulation lowers the threshold for CT head imaging after a head injury in an older person, even when no other indication for a scan is present.
thinking: Fall in an older man ↓ Bruising and takes a blood thinner ↓ Anticoagulants increase bleeding after falls ↓ Need drug, dose and timing to guide care ↓ Accurate medication history
exam_trap: C, Discharging with reassurance — bruising often is minor in older people, but on an anticoagulant it may indicate significant bleeding.
takeaway: After a fall, always establish whether the person takes an anticoagulant.

stem: A carer at a residential home asks the GP to see an 80-year-old woman who has fallen once and has been dizzy for a few days. A week ago she was started on oxybutynin for urge incontinence, and she takes several other regular medicines. She has no fever or urinary symptoms beyond her usual frequency. What should be considered as part of her assessment?

options.A: Antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection
options.D: Diagnosis of Parkinson's disease and starting levodopa

why_correct: New dizziness and a fall soon after starting an anticholinergic drug suggest an adverse drug effect. Oxybutynin can cause dizziness, blurred vision and confusion in older people, so a medication review is needed, often switching to an alternative with less anticholinergic burden.
why_wrong: A. Without fever or new urinary symptoms, antibiotics are not indicated and can cause harm. C. Cataract surgery would only be considered after an eye assessment showed it was needed. D. Parkinson's disease cannot be diagnosed from a single fall without features such as bradykinesia. E. Dental review does not address dizziness or falls.
pearl: The total anticholinergic burden of a person's medicines is associated with falls, confusion and cognitive decline in older people.
thinking: New fall and dizziness ↓ Recently started oxybutynin ↓ Anticholinergic drugs cause dizziness and confusion ↓ No signs of infection ↓ Review her medicines
exam_trap: A, Antibiotics for a presumed urinary infection — infection is often assumed in care home residents who fall, but she has no new symptoms, and the timing points to the new drug.
takeaway: New falls or dizziness after a new medicine should prompt a medication review.

stem: A 74-year-old woman on a medical ward reports feeling faint each time she gets out of bed, and she fell yesterday when walking to the toilet. She was recently started on doxazosin. Her blood pressure is measured lying and then after standing for a few minutes, and shows a reproducible, marked drop on standing that brings back her symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A sustained, reproducible fall in blood pressure within a few minutes of standing that reproduces her symptoms is the defining feature of orthostatic hypotension. The recent start of an alpha-blocker is a likely cause.
why_wrong: B. Vasovagal syncope is triggered by pain, emotion or prolonged standing and does not cause a reproducible drop on simply standing up. C. Hypertensive emergency involves very high blood pressure with organ damage. D. Pulmonary embolism causes breathlessness and tachycardia rather than a consistent postural drop. E. Hyperthyroidism causes tachycardia and weight loss, not postural hypotension.
pearl: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing.
thinking: Faint on getting out of bed ↓ Recently started doxazosin ↓ Reproducible drop in standing blood pressure ↓ Symptoms reproduced on standing ↓ Orthostatic hypotension
exam_trap: B, Vasovagal syncope — it is the commonest cause of fainting overall, but it depends on a trigger, whereas her drop happens every time she stands.
takeaway: A reproducible fall in blood pressure on standing with symptoms is orthostatic hypotension.

stem: A physiotherapist asks you to see an 81-year-old man recovering on the ward from pneumonia. He nearly collapses each time he stands, and lying and standing readings confirm a large postural drop. His medicines include bisoprolol, ramipril, furosemide and tamsulosin. His mucous membranes are dry and he has been eating and drinking poorly. What is the most appropriate initial step?

options.A: Reassure him that postural drops are common at his age
options.B: Add doxazosin to improve his blood pressure control
options.C: Review his medicines and look for reversible causes such as dehydration
options.D: Restrict his fluids to prevent fluid overload
options.E: Start a hypnotic to help him rest

correct_answer: C. Review his medicines and look for reversible causes such as dehydration
why_correct: His postural hypotension is likely to have several reversible causes: four blood pressure-lowering drugs and dehydration after acute illness with poor intake. The first step is to review and hold or reduce the contributing drugs and correct his fluid deficit, while watching his heart failure status if relevant.
why_wrong: A. A large symptomatic postural drop is not normal and needs management. B. Adding an alpha-blocker would worsen postural hypotension. D. Fluid restriction would worsen his dehydration. E. A hypnotic adds sedation and falls risk.
pearl: Acute illness often makes previously tolerated antihypertensives excessive, so they should be reviewed during and after hospital admissions.
thinking: Near-collapse on standing ↓ Confirmed postural drop ↓ On four drugs that lower blood pressure ↓ Dehydrated after pneumonia ↓ Review medicines and correct reversible causes
exam_trap: D, Restricting fluids — furosemide suggests a fluid-sensitive condition, but he is clinically dry and restriction would worsen his postural drop.
takeaway: In postural hypotension, review blood pressure-lowering drugs and correct dehydration first.

stem: Doreen, 85, is reviewed on a medical ward. Her daughter mentions that she has been taking promethazine every night to help her sleep and is very drowsy until late morning. She has had two recent falls at home. Which adverse effect of this medicine is of greatest concern?
why_correct: Promethazine is a sedating antihistamine with anticholinergic effects. Persistent daytime drowsiness and impaired alertness increase her falls risk, which is the most relevant adverse effect given her recent falls, and the drug should be stopped.
why_wrong: A. Promethazine does not cause hyperglycaemia. B. It does not affect clotting or platelets. C. It is not associated with reduced bone density. D. It does not affect potassium.
pearl: First-generation antihistamines are listed as potentially inappropriate in older adults because of sedation, confusion and anticholinergic effects.
thinking: Older woman with two falls ↓ Nightly sedating antihistamine ↓ Daytime drowsiness ↓ Sedation impairs balance and reactions ↓ Increased falls risk
exam_trap: C, Reduced bone density — it would make fractures after falls more likely, but promethazine does not cause it; the real concern is sedation causing falls.
takeaway: Sedating medicines increase falls risk in older people and should be stopped where possible.

stem: At his annual diabetes review, a 79-year-old man mentions he has fallen twice in the last month, both times indoors. He was not hurt. He lives with his daughter and remains independent with personal care. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Multifactorial assessment of reversible risks, including medicines, vision, gait, balance and the home
options.B: Advise hip protectors alone, since some falls are expected with age
options.C: Arrange a DXA scan only and reassess if he fractures
options.D: Prescribe a night-time hypnotic to improve sleep and alertness
options.E: Advise him to walk less until a walking aid is provided

correct_answer: A. Multifactorial assessment of reversible risks, including medicines, vision, gait, balance and the home
why_correct: Two falls in a month should prompt a multifactorial falls risk assessment. In a man with diabetes this includes checking for hypoglycaemia, neuropathy and visual problems as well as medicines, postural hypotension, gait, balance and home hazards, so that targeted interventions can follow.
why_wrong: B. Hip protectors may reduce fracture risk but do not prevent falls, and falls are not an expected part of ageing. C. Bone health is important but a DXA scan alone does not reduce falls. D. Hypnotics increase falls risk. E. Walking less causes deconditioning and more falls.
pearl: In older people with diabetes, overly tight glucose control with insulin or sulfonylureas can cause hypoglycaemia and falls.
thinking: Two falls in one month ↓ Recurrent falls need assessment ↓ Diabetes adds neuropathy, vision and hypoglycaemia risks ↓ Look for all modifiable factors ↓ Multifactorial falls assessment
exam_trap: C, A DXA scan only — bone health matters after falls, but this addresses fracture risk, not why he is falling.
takeaway: Recurrent falls need a multifactorial assessment of reversible risk factors.

stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and an enlarged prostate was started on doxazosin by the urology team, and his GP recently increased his amlodipine. He now feels light-headed when stepping out of the bath and has fallen twice. His blood pressure falls noticeably when he stands. What is the most appropriate initial step?

options.A: Advise him to stop having baths
options.D: Stop all his tablets at once
options.E: Review his medicines, particularly the recent changes

correct_answer: E. Review his medicines, particularly the recent changes
why_correct: His postural hypotension and falls began after an alpha-blocker was added and a calcium channel blocker increased. Reviewing these recent changes, and reducing or switching the culprits, is the first step before considering drugs to raise blood pressure.
why_wrong: A. Avoiding baths does not address the cause and his symptoms occur on standing generally. B. A higher dose would worsen postural hypotension. C. Fludrocortisone is only considered after reversible causes have been addressed. D. Stopping everything may cause uncontrolled hypertension or urinary retention.
pearl: Doxazosin and amlodipine together have an additive vasodilating effect, making postural hypotension more likely.
thinking: Two falls with light-headedness on standing ↓ Recent alpha-blocker and higher amlodipine ↓ Postural drop confirmed ↓ Drug changes are the likely cause ↓ Review the medicines first
exam_trap: C, Fludrocortisone — it is a treatment for orthostatic hypotension, but adding a drug before removing the cause is the wrong order.
takeaway: Review recent medicine changes before treating postural hypotension with new drugs.

stem: An 80-year-old man with glaucoma attends the falls clinic after two falls in six weeks. He says he keeps catching his foot on steps he did not see, and he takes several regular medicines. He has no injuries. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Multifactorial assessment of his modifiable falls risks
options.C: Bed rest until his confidence returns
options.D: A hypnotic to improve his sleep
options.E: Reassurance that falls are expected at his age

correct_answer: A. Multifactorial assessment of his modifiable falls risks
why_correct: He has at least two modifiable risk factors, poor vision and several medicines, and there may be others such as gait or home hazards. A multifactorial assessment identifies all of these so that targeted interventions, including eye review, medication changes and home modification, can be offered.
why_wrong: B. Hip protectors do not prevent falls or address causes. C. Bed rest causes deconditioning and increases falls. D. Hypnotics increase falls risk. E. Falls are not an inevitable part of ageing.
pearl: Home hazard assessment and modification by an occupational therapist reduces falls, especially in people with visual impairment.
thinking: Two falls in six weeks ↓ Glaucoma with trips on unseen steps ↓ Several medicines ↓ Multiple potentially modifiable factors ↓ Multifactorial falls assessment
exam_trap: B, Hip protectors — they may lessen injury, but they do nothing to find or treat why he is falling.
takeaway: Falls with visual problems and polypharmacy need a full multifactorial assessment.

stem: An 88-year-old man is about to be discharged from the frailty unit after a fall at home. He walks by holding on to furniture, takes nine regular medicines and lives with his wife, who has dementia. Which intervention is most likely to reduce his chance of falling again?

options.A: Night sedation to stop him getting up at night
options.B: Multifactorial falls assessment with medication review and tailored interventions
options.C: Advice to stay indoors to avoid trip hazards outside
options.D: A period of bed rest to recover from the fall
options.E: A walking stick and hip protectors alone

correct_answer: B. Multifactorial falls assessment with medication review and tailored interventions
why_correct: His falls are likely to have several causes, including impaired gait, polypharmacy and home factors. A multifactorial assessment with medication review, followed by tailored interventions such as strength and balance training, home hazard modification and changes to medicines, is the most effective way to reduce further falls.
why_wrong: A. Sedation increases falls risk. C. Staying indoors reduces activity and does not address the main risks. D. Bed rest leads to deconditioning. E. A stick and hip protectors may help but alone do not address the underlying causes.
pearl: Furniture walking is a sign of impaired balance and a strong predictor of further falls.
thinking: Fall in a frail older man ↓ Unsteady gait and nine medicines ↓ Falls are multifactorial ↓ Assess all modifiable factors ↓ Multifactorial assessment with tailored interventions
exam_trap: E, A walking stick and hip protectors — they are practical aids, but without assessing why he falls they will not prevent further falls.
takeaway: Multifactorial assessment with tailored interventions is the best way to prevent further falls.

stem: A 76-year-old woman is referred to the falls clinic after two falls this month. She has atrial fibrillation and osteoarthritis and takes digoxin, diltiazem, co-codamol and amitriptyline at night. She feels drowsy in the mornings. Which is an important initial part of her falls assessment?
why_correct: Several of her medicines can contribute to falls: amitriptyline and codeine cause sedation, and diltiazem with digoxin can cause bradycardia or hypotension. Reviewing her medicines is an important early part of falls assessment and may reveal drugs to reduce or stop.
why_wrong: A. Serum amylase investigates pancreatitis, not falls. B. A chest X-ray is not indicated without respiratory symptoms. C. An EEG is used when seizures are suspected, which nothing here suggests. D. Abdominal ultrasound has no role in falls assessment.
pearl: Digoxin toxicity in older people can present with confusion, nausea, visual changes and falls, especially with reduced kidney function.
thinking: Two falls this month ↓ On sedating drugs and rate-controlling drugs ↓ Morning drowsiness ↓ Medicines are a modifiable factor ↓ Review her medicines
exam_trap: C, Electroencephalogram — unexplained falls can raise concern about seizures, but nothing here suggests them, while her drug list offers obvious causes.
takeaway: Review medicines early in every falls assessment.

presentation: Falls and anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation
stem: An 82-year-old woman on a community hospital ward is found to have atrial fibrillation. Her stroke risk is high and her bleeding risk has been assessed. She had two falls last year without injury. Her daughter asks whether the falls mean she should not take a blood thinner. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Offer anticoagulation, addressing modifiable bleeding and falls risks rather than withholding it
options.B: Offer aspirin as a safer alternative for someone who falls
options.C: Withhold anticoagulation because her falls risk outweighs the benefit
options.D: Delay anticoagulation until a falls clinic has fully assessed her
options.E: Avoid anticoagulation because she is over 80

correct_answer: A. Offer anticoagulation, addressing modifiable bleeding and falls risks rather than withholding it
why_correct: NICE advises not to withhold anticoagulation solely because of age or risk of falls. Her high stroke risk means the benefit of anticoagulation is likely to outweigh the bleeding risk from falls, so it should be offered, with falls risk factors and modifiable bleeding risks addressed.
why_wrong: B. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation and still carries bleeding risk. C. A person would need to fall very often for the bleeding risk to outweigh the stroke benefit. D. Delay leaves her exposed to stroke risk, and falls assessment can happen in parallel. E. Age alone is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation, and older people gain more benefit.
pearl: A direct oral anticoagulant is usually preferred to warfarin in atrial fibrillation, with dosing adjusted for kidney function, age and weight.
thinking: New atrial fibrillation with high stroke risk ↓ History of falls ↓ Falls alone are not a reason to withhold ↓ Benefit outweighs bleeding risk ↓ Offer anticoagulation and address falls risks
exam_trap: C, Withholding anticoagulation because of falls — it seems protective, but the stroke risk far outweighs the risk of a serious bleed from falls.
takeaway: Do not withhold anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation because of falls or age alone.

stem: An 86-year-old woman with moderate frailty has symptomatic severe aortic stenosis and is being considered for transcatheter aortic valve implantation. She has capacity and lives with her son. Which principle should guide the decision?

options.A: Base the decision mainly on her age
options.B: Proceed because the procedure is indicated for her valve disease
options.C: Weigh her goals, frailty, likely benefits and burdens in shared decision-making
options.D: Ask her son to decide for her
options.E: Decline the procedure because she is frail

correct_answer: C. Weigh her goals, frailty, likely benefits and burdens in shared decision-making
why_correct: Decisions about invasive treatment in frail older people should be individualised. Frailty affects the risks and likely recovery, but the decision should balance her priorities, the expected benefits and burdens of treatment and the alternatives, through shared decision-making with her.
why_wrong: A. Age alone is a poor guide to outcome. B. A clinical indication does not mean the procedure is in her interests without considering her frailty and goals. D. She has capacity, so the decision is hers. E. Frailty informs risk but is not on its own a reason to refuse treatment.
pearl: Frailty is a better predictor than age of complications and functional decline after surgery or invasive procedures.
thinking: Frail older woman considered for an invasive procedure ↓ She has capacity ↓ Frailty affects risk and recovery ↓ Her goals and values matter ↓ Shared decision weighing benefits and burdens
exam_trap: E, Declining because she is frail — frailty increases risk, but some frail people benefit greatly and the decision must be individual.
takeaway: Invasive treatment decisions in frailty should weigh goals, benefits and burdens, not age or frailty alone.

stem: An 86-year-old woman sees her GP after her third fall this year. She lives alone, takes eleven regular medicines, and her daughter has noticed she is eating less and seems low in mood. A Clinical Frailty Scale assessment places her in the moderately frail category. What is the most appropriate next step in her care?

options.A: Request an echocardiogram and cardiology opinion
options.B: Prescribe calcium and vitamin D as the main intervention
options.C: Arrange a comprehensive geriatric assessment with an individualised care plan
options.E: Admit her to hospital for intensive inpatient rehabilitation

correct_answer: C. Arrange a comprehensive geriatric assessment with an individualised care plan
why_correct: Frailty is a multidimensional state, and her falls, polypharmacy, poor intake, low mood and isolation each need attention. A comprehensive geriatric assessment brings together medical, functional, psychological, social and environmental review by a multidisciplinary team. It produces a shared, individualised plan, such as medicine rationalisation, strength and balance work and support at home.
why_wrong: A. A cardiac work-up addresses only one possible cause of falls and ignores her other needs. B. Bone supplements may form part of the plan but do not assess the many contributing problems. D. Placement decisions should follow assessment of her needs and wishes, not replace it. E. She is not acutely unwell, and admission carries its own risks of deconditioning and delirium.
pearl: Older people with frailty tolerate minor stressors poorly, so a new infection or medicine change can cause a sudden fall, delirium or loss of mobility.
thinking: Recurrent falls, polypharmacy, poor intake, low mood ↓ Moderate frailty confirmed on a validated scale ↓ Problems span medical, functional, psychological and social areas ↓ Needs a holistic multidisciplinary review ↓ Comprehensive geriatric assessment and personalised plan
exam_trap: D, Arranging care home placement — repeated falls in someone living alone can make placement seem the safe option, but it pre-empts assessment, ignores her preferences and misses reversible contributors.
takeaway: An older person identified as frail should have a comprehensive geriatric assessment rather than a single-system intervention.

stem: A practice nurse is contacted by the carer of an 88-year-old man. Over the past year he has walked more slowly to the local shop, lost weight without trying, complains of constant tiredness and now needs help with cleaning and shopping that he used to manage himself. A recent examination and routine blood tests were unremarkable. Which clinical syndrome best describes his presentation?
why_correct: Slow walking speed, unintentional weight loss, exhaustion and declining ability to manage daily tasks are the core features of frailty. It reflects a loss of physiological reserve across several body systems, leaving him vulnerable to minor stressors. Normal investigations make an alternative single disease less likely.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism can cause weight loss but would usually show tremor, tachycardia or abnormal thyroid tests, and does not explain the overall picture. C. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness with raised inflammatory markers. D. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention, not a decline over a year. E. Migraine causes episodic headaches and does not explain global decline.
pearl: Fried's frailty phenotype uses five features: weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking speed and low physical activity.
thinking: Gradual decline over a year ↓ Slow walking, weight loss, exhaustion ↓ Loss of independence in daily tasks ↓ Normal examination and bloods ↓ Reduced reserve across systems: frailty
exam_trap: A, Hyperthyroidism — weight loss and tiredness can suggest it, but normal bloods and the absence of thyroid features point to a global loss of reserve rather than an endocrine disorder.
takeaway: Slowing, weight loss, exhaustion and loss of function in an older person should prompt recognition of frailty.

stem: A 69-year-old retired teacher is brought to the memory clinic by his wife. Over eight months his steps have become short and wide-based, he struggles to start walking, he has begun wetting himself before he can reach the toilet, and he has become slow in his thinking and apathetic. A CT scan of the head shows dilated ventricles that are disproportionate to any sulcal widening. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Gait disturbance, urinary urgency or incontinence and cognitive slowing together with ventricular enlargement out of proportion to atrophy point to normal pressure hydrocephalus. Gait problems usually come first and are most likely to improve with treatment. It matters because it is a potentially treatable cause of cognitive and mobility decline, sometimes helped by ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
why_wrong: A. Parkinson's disease causes tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia with a narrow-based gait and does not produce ventriculomegaly. B. Multiple sclerosis usually presents earlier in life with relapsing focal neurological episodes. D. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an acute ascending peripheral neuropathy developing over days to weeks. E. Lambert–Eaton syndrome causes proximal weakness and autonomic symptoms without cognitive decline or hydrocephalus.
pearl: A large-volume lumbar puncture that temporarily improves gait supports the diagnosis and helps predict who will benefit from shunting.
thinking: Gait problem developing over months ↓ Urinary urgency and incontinence ↓ Cognitive slowing and apathy ↓ Ventricles enlarged out of proportion to atrophy ↓ Normal pressure hydrocephalus
exam_trap: A, Parkinson's disease — shuffling steps and difficulty initiating walking can mimic parkinsonism, but the wide base, early incontinence and disproportionate ventriculomegaly point elsewhere.
takeaway: Gait disturbance, incontinence and cognitive decline with enlarged ventricles should prompt consideration of normal pressure hydrocephalus, a treatable cause.

stem: An 83-year-old man attends a pre-operative clinic before cataract surgery. He gives muddled replies and answers questions he was not asked. His records note severe bilateral hearing loss, and today he has left his hearing aids at home. What should the doctor do first?

options.A: Ask his son to answer the questions on his behalf
options.B: Record that he lacks capacity to consent to surgery
options.C: Raise your voice and keep the appointment as brief as possible
options.D: Request a dementia screen before continuing
options.E: Optimise communication, for example a quiet room, facing him, written prompts or an amplifier, then check his understanding

correct_answer: E. Optimise communication, for example a quiet room, facing him, written prompts or an amplifier, then check his understanding
why_correct: Apparent confusion in someone with severe hearing loss may simply reflect that he cannot hear the questions. The Mental Capacity Act requires all practicable steps to help a person communicate and understand before any conclusion about capacity is reached. Removing background noise, facing him, using written information or a portable amplifier and checking understanding should come first.
why_wrong: A. Talking to a relative instead excludes him from decisions about his own care. B. Capacity cannot be judged until communication barriers have been addressed. C. Shouting distorts speech and rushing reduces understanding further. D. A cognitive screen done without adequate hearing support will give misleading results.
pearl: Untreated hearing loss in midlife and later life is one of the largest potentially modifiable risk factors for dementia.
thinking: Muddled answers in a consultation ↓ Known severe hearing loss, aids not worn ↓ Hearing deficit can mimic confusion ↓ Remove communication barriers first ↓ Then reassess understanding and capacity
exam_trap: D, Requesting a dementia screen — muddled replies suggest cognitive impairment, but testing without adequate hearing support produces falsely abnormal results.
takeaway: Address sensory and communication barriers before concluding that an older person is confused or lacks capacity.

stem: An 84-year-old man slips on his kitchen floor and is admitted to the orthopaedic ward with an intracapsular fracture of the right femoral neck. He is awaiting hemiarthroplasty and is expected to have limited mobility for several days. Which complication of his admission is most important to assess for and actively prevent from the outset?
why_correct: Hip fracture combines major lower limb trauma, surgery and immobility, which together put him at high risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. NICE advises VTE risk assessment on admission and pharmacological prophylaxis, such as low molecular weight heparin, unless bleeding risk outweighs benefit, with mechanical prophylaxis if drugs are contraindicated, alongside early mobilisation after surgery. Pulmonary embolism is an important preventable cause of death after hip fracture.
why_wrong: A. Cataract develops slowly and is not a complication of admission. C. Reflux is not a major preventable threat in this setting. D. Gout flares can occur in hospital but are not the priority complication. E. Otitis externa has no link to fracture or immobility.
pearl: After hip fracture, surgery on the day of or day after admission and early mobilisation reduce complications, including VTE, pressure ulcers and delirium.
thinking: Femoral neck fracture after a fall ↓ Surgery planned and prolonged immobility ↓ Trauma plus surgery plus immobility raises clotting risk ↓ Assess VTE risk on admission ↓ Prophylaxis and early mobilisation
exam_trap: C, Gastro-oesophageal reflux — bed rest and medicines can cause indigestion, but it is not a life-threatening complication in the way that pulmonary embolism is.
takeaway: Every patient admitted with a hip fracture needs VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis from the start.

stem: A 70-year-old woman on the stroke unit has a dense left hemiplegia and cannot turn herself in bed. Her skin is intact, but a risk assessment shows she is at high risk of skin breakdown. Which measure will most reduce her risk?

options.A: Massage over her heels and sacrum each shift
options.B: Inspect her skin weekly when other dressings are changed
options.C: Use a ring cushion when she sits out in a chair
options.D: Keep her sitting upright with the head of the bed at 60 degrees
options.E: Reposition her on a regular schedule and provide a pressure-redistributing mattress

correct_answer: E. Reposition her on a regular schedule and provide a pressure-redistributing mattress
why_correct: She cannot relieve pressure herself, so scheduled repositioning and a pressure-redistributing mattress directly reduce the duration and intensity of pressure on bony prominences. This is the core of NICE guidance on pressure ulcer prevention for high-risk adults. Frequent skin inspection, nutrition and continence care support this plan.
why_wrong: A. Massage can damage fragile tissue and is not recommended. B. High-risk patients need skin inspection much more often than weekly. C. Ring cushions concentrate pressure on the surrounding tissue and reduce blood flow. D. A steep head-up position increases shear and pressure over the sacrum.
pearl: Shear and friction, as when a patient slides down the bed, add to pressure damage, so positioning and handling technique matter as well as frequency.
thinking: Unable to move independently after stroke ↓ High risk on assessment, skin still intact ↓ Damage comes from sustained pressure ↓ Relieve and redistribute pressure ↓ Regular repositioning and suitable mattress
exam_trap: A, Massaging bony prominences — it sounds like it would improve circulation, but rubbing damages already vulnerable tissue.
takeaway: For a high-risk immobile patient, regular repositioning and pressure-redistributing equipment are central to prevention.

presentation: Pressure ulcer prevention in spinal cord injury
stem: A 58-year-old man with a complete thoracic spinal cord injury is admitted to a rehabilitation ward. He has no sensation below the level of his umbilicus and is intermittently incontinent of urine and faeces. Which plan best protects his skin?

options.A: Reposition him only when he reports discomfort
options.B: Restrict his fluid intake to reduce episodes of incontinence
options.C: Frequent skin inspection, scheduled repositioning and a high-specification pressure-redistributing mattress
options.D: Weekly skin checks with barrier cream applied to all pressure areas
options.E: Rub any reddened areas firmly to restore blood flow

correct_answer: C. Frequent skin inspection, scheduled repositioning and a high-specification pressure-redistributing mattress
why_correct: Without sensation he will not feel the warning discomfort of prolonged pressure, so prevention cannot rely on him reporting it. He needs frequent skin inspection, a repositioning schedule and a high-specification pressure-redistributing surface, with attention to continence and nutrition, in line with NICE CG179.
why_wrong: A. He has no sensation over the areas at risk, so he will not report discomfort. B. Dehydration worsens skin health and does not prevent incontinence damage safely. D. Barrier cream protects against moisture but does not relieve pressure, and weekly checks are too infrequent. E. Massaging reddened skin can worsen tissue injury.
pearl: Non-blanching redness over a bony prominence is a category 1 pressure ulcer and signals that the prevention plan needs immediate review.
thinking: Complete spinal cord injury with sensory loss ↓ Cannot sense pressure or move freely ↓ Incontinence adds moisture damage ↓ Prevention must be proactive ↓ Inspection, repositioning, pressure-redistributing surface
exam_trap: A, Repositioning only when he reports discomfort — this works for people with normal sensation but fails completely when pressure cannot be felt.
takeaway: Patients with sensory loss need a proactive schedule of skin checks and repositioning rather than waiting for symptoms.

stem: An 81-year-old widow who lived alone and did her own shopping is recovering on a medical ward after treatment for pneumonia. Nurses report that she now needs help from two staff to wash and dress and cannot make herself a drink. Her son asks whether she should go straight into a nursing home. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.B: Assess her functional needs and rehabilitation potential with the multidisciplinary team
options.C: Discharge her home with her previous level of support once she is medically stable
options.D: Set up a care package on the basis that her dependency is permanent
options.E: Wait to see whether she recovers on her own before any assessment

correct_answer: B. Assess her functional needs and rehabilitation potential with the multidisciplinary team
why_correct: New dependency after an acute illness is often partly reversible, especially when deconditioning is the main cause. A multidisciplinary assessment by doctors, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and social care can identify her needs and her potential for rehabilitation, for example through reablement or intermediate care. Long-term decisions should follow this assessment and take her own wishes into account.
why_wrong: A. Committing to placement now assumes she will not recover and ignores her views. C. Sending her home without the extra help she now needs is unsafe. D. Planning for permanent dependency underestimates her chance of recovery. E. Delaying assessment wastes the window for active rehabilitation and prolongs her stay.
pearl: Hospital-acquired deconditioning develops quickly in older people, so early mobilisation and getting dressed during admission help preserve function.
thinking: Previously independent ↓ Acute illness followed by loss of daily skills ↓ Decline may be reversible ↓ Multidisciplinary functional assessment ↓ Rehabilitation before long-term decisions
exam_trap: A, Arranging nursing home placement — the family's worry and her current dependency make this tempting, but it overlooks her rehabilitation potential.
takeaway: Loss of function after acute illness in an older person calls for assessment of needs and rehabilitation potential before any long-term decisions.

stem: A 75-year-old retired accountant comes to the surgery with his daughter. Over the last eighteen months he has missed appointments, left the hob on several times and can no longer follow the card games he used to enjoy. During the consultation he is alert and attentive, and his daughter says the problems have crept up steadily rather than coming and going. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: A slowly progressive decline in memory and other thinking skills that interferes with everyday activities, with normal alertness, points to dementia. The time course over many months and the lack of fluctuation distinguish it from delirium. He should be assessed for reversible contributors and referred to a memory service.
why_wrong: B. Delirium develops over hours to days with fluctuating attention, unlike this steady course. C. Panic disorder causes episodes of intense anxiety, not progressive cognitive loss. D. Acute psychosis is marked by delusions or hallucinations with a rapid onset. E. Migraine causes episodic headache and does not produce progressive cognitive decline.
pearl: Dementia and delirium often coexist, and an older person with dementia is at greatly increased risk of delirium during acute illness.
thinking: Gradual onset over many months ↓ Memory and executive skills affected ↓ Daily activities impaired ↓ Alert, no fluctuation ↓ Dementia
exam_trap: B, Delirium — confusion in an older person often brings delirium to mind, but his attention is normal and the decline is slow and steady.
takeaway: Insidious, progressive cognitive decline that impairs daily function with preserved alertness suggests dementia.

stem: On a care home visit, a GP is asked about an 87-year-old resident. Staff describe a slow, steady loss of memory and self-care skills since she moved in three years ago. Her alertness and ability to concentrate in conversation have stayed the same throughout, and there has been no sudden deterioration. Which diagnosis best fits this history?
why_correct: A gradual, progressive decline in memory and function over years with preserved attention and conscious level is the pattern of dementia. Delirium, in contrast, has an acute onset, fluctuates and is defined by impaired attention. The long time course and stable alertness make an acute cause very unlikely.
why_wrong: A. Delirium starts over hours to days with fluctuating attention, not a steady decline over years. B. Hypoglycaemia causes acute episodes of confusion that resolve with glucose. C. Meningitis presents acutely with fever, headache and neck stiffness. D. Syncope is a brief loss of consciousness with full recovery, not progressive cognitive loss.
pearl: Attention is the key differentiating domain: it is impaired early in delirium but usually preserved until later stages in most dementias.
thinking: Decline over three years ↓ Memory and self-care both affected ↓ Attention and alertness stable ↓ No acute change or fluctuation ↓ Chronic progressive picture: dementia
exam_trap: A, Delirium — confusion in a care home resident is often due to delirium, but the absence of acute onset or fluctuating attention argues strongly against it.
takeaway: A gradual decline over years without fluctuating attention fits dementia rather than delirium.

stem: A 68-year-old man books a GP appointment because his wife thinks his memory has been slipping for about a year. He has not seen a doctor for several years, and no examination or blood tests have been done. Which is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Diagnose dementia on the basis of his wife's account
options.B: Take a full history, examine him and arrange blood tests to look for reversible or treatable causes
options.C: Start donepezil as a therapeutic trial
options.D: Refer for an MRI scan before any examination or blood tests
options.E: Tell him he has Alzheimer's disease and signpost him to support groups

correct_answer: B. Take a full history, examine him and arrange blood tests to look for reversible or treatable causes
why_correct: Memory problems have many possible contributors, including depression, hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, medicines, alcohol and hearing loss. NICE recommends a history from the patient and an informant, a physical examination, a cognitive assessment and appropriate blood tests before referral to a memory service. This identifies treatable problems and avoids a premature label.
why_wrong: A. A diagnosis of dementia needs a structured assessment, not an informant history alone. C. Drug treatment should only follow specialist diagnosis of the dementia subtype. D. Imaging is part of specialist assessment and should not replace basic examination and bloods. E. Assuming Alzheimer's disease without assessment risks missing a reversible cause.
pearl: Routine initial bloods for suspected dementia usually include full blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, glucose or HbA1c, thyroid function and vitamin B12 and folate.
thinking: Memory concerns raised by spouse ↓ No previous assessment ↓ Several reversible causes possible ↓ History, examination, cognitive test and bloods ↓ Then refer to memory service if needed
exam_trap: C, Starting donepezil — it is a familiar dementia treatment, but starting it before assessment and diagnosis is inappropriate.
takeaway: Before diagnosing dementia, carry out a basic assessment to exclude reversible or treatable causes.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with hypothyroidism, recurrent depression and an overactive bladder treated with oxybutynin is referred by her practice nurse after scoring poorly on a cognitive screening test. Her husband says she has found cooking and paying bills harder over the past year. Which principle should guide her work-up before dementia is diagnosed?

options.A: Medicines are unlikely to contribute, so they need not be reviewed
options.B: Assume her decline is irreversible and plan for long-term care
options.C: Start an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor while awaiting tests
options.D: Look for and address reversible or contributing factors such as medicines, mood and thyroid function
options.E: Diagnose Alzheimer's disease from the screening score alone

correct_answer: D. Look for and address reversible or contributing factors such as medicines, mood and thyroid function
why_correct: Several of her problems can impair cognition: oxybutynin has strong anticholinergic effects, depression can cause marked cognitive symptoms, and poorly controlled hypothyroidism slows thinking. NICE NG97 advises excluding reversible causes and reviewing medicines that may impair cognition before making a diagnosis of dementia. Treating these may improve her function considerably.
why_wrong: A. Anticholinergic medicines such as oxybutynin are a well-recognised cause of cognitive impairment in older people. B. Labelling the decline as irreversible may lead to missed treatable causes. C. Drug treatment should not start before assessment and diagnosis. E. A screening test cannot diagnose dementia or its subtype on its own.
pearl: Cumulative anticholinergic burden from several medicines is linked to cognitive decline and falls, so it should be reviewed in any older person with memory concerns.
thinking: Cognitive decline over a year ↓ Anticholinergic drug, depression, thyroid disease ↓ Each can impair cognition ↓ Review medicines and treat contributors ↓ Diagnose dementia only after this
exam_trap: E, Diagnosing Alzheimer's disease from the screening score — a low score feels conclusive, but screening tools cannot exclude other causes or confirm a subtype.
takeaway: Always search for reversible or contributing causes, especially medicines, before diagnosing dementia.

stem: A 77-year-old woman's husband reports that for two years she has asked the same questions about family plans and forgets conversations within minutes, while her personality and walking are unchanged. More recently she has struggled to find words and has been unable to work out how to use the washing machine. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Early, prominent loss of recent episodic memory followed by gradual involvement of language and practical skills is the typical pattern of Alzheimer's disease. Personality and gait are often preserved in the early stages. It is the most common cause of dementia in the UK.
why_wrong: B. Frontotemporal dementia usually begins with personality or behaviour change or language problems, with memory relatively spared early. C. Dementia with Lewy bodies features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism. D. Delirium is acute and fluctuating, not a decline over two years. E. A stroke causes sudden focal deficits rather than slowly progressive memory loss.
pearl: Short-term memory is affected early in Alzheimer's disease because the hippocampus and medial temporal lobes are involved first.
thinking: Insidious onset over two years ↓ Recent memory affected first ↓ Later language and practical skills decline ↓ Personality and gait preserved ↓ Alzheimer's disease
exam_trap: B, Frontotemporal dementia — word-finding difficulty may suggest it, but the early memory loss and preserved personality are typical of Alzheimer's disease.
takeaway: Gradual loss of recent memory followed by wider cognitive decline suggests Alzheimer's disease.

stem: A 70-year-old man who still volunteers at a charity shop has, over three years, become unable to remember the names of new colleagues or what he did the day before, and he now gets muddled when giving change at the till. Neurological examination shows no tremor, rigidity, involuntary movements or focal deficit. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A slowly progressive illness that begins with difficulty learning and recalling new information and then spreads to other cognitive skills, such as handling money, is characteristic of Alzheimer's disease. The normal neurological examination makes conditions with prominent early motor features unlikely.
why_wrong: A. Huntington's disease typically starts in mid-adulthood with chorea and psychiatric symptoms, often with a family history. B. Parkinson's disease presents with tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia, and any dementia develops later. C. Delirium is acute and fluctuating rather than a steady decline over years. D. Multiple sclerosis usually starts in young adults with focal relapsing neurological episodes.
pearl: In Alzheimer's disease, recall is not helped much by cues, because new information was never properly stored in the first place.
thinking: Three-year gradual decline ↓ Recent memory affected first ↓ Spreads to other domains such as calculation ↓ No early movement disorder ↓ Alzheimer's disease
exam_trap: B, Parkinson's disease — it can cause dementia, but this usually comes after years of motor symptoms, and he has none.
takeaway: Progressive memory loss followed by wider cognitive decline without early motor features points to Alzheimer's disease.

stem: An 80-year-old man attends his GP surgery with his son, who now opens his post because several bills had gone unpaid and his father had been muddling the tablets in his dosette box. The son describes a slowly worsening forgetfulness for recent events over about four years. His father concentrates normally throughout the consultation and there has been no sudden change. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A slowly progressive decline in recent memory over years that now affects managing finances and medicines indicates dementia. His preserved concentration and the lack of sudden change make delirium unlikely. He needs assessment for reversible contributors and referral to a memory service.
why_wrong: A. Dissociative disorder involves disruption of identity or memory linked to psychological stress, not a steady decline over years. B. Panic disorder causes episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms. C. Delirium has an acute onset and fluctuating attention. D. Acute psychosis presents with hallucinations or delusions over a short time.
pearl: Difficulty managing money and medicines is often one of the first signs of dementia noticed by families.
thinking: Four years of gradual decline ↓ Recent memory loss ↓ Bills and medicines now mismanaged ↓ Normal attention, no sudden change ↓ Dementia
