options.D: Arrange an urgent CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
options.E: Formal nutritional assessment with a dietitian and a nutritional support plan

correct_answer: E. Formal nutritional assessment with a dietitian and a nutritional support plan
why_correct: Poor intake and falling weight after hip fracture surgery are common and strongly linked to delayed recovery, infection and pressure damage. NICE advises that inpatients identified as malnourished or at risk should have a nutritional assessment and a support plan, such as food fortification and oral nutritional supplements. Treating this now will help her mobilise and rehabilitate.
why_wrong: A. Prophylactic dosing may be appropriate after hip surgery, but therapeutic anticoagulation is not a response to poor intake. B. Fluid restriction has no indication here and would worsen her overall intake. C. Delaying action prolongs undernutrition, slows rehabilitation and increases complications. D. Reduced intake after major surgery in a frail patient does not by itself warrant cancer imaging.
pearl: Oral nutritional supplements after hip fracture surgery reduce complications and are a standard part of orthogeriatric care.
thinking: Frail woman after hip surgery ↓ Leaving most meals ↓ Weight falling on the ward ↓ Fatigue limiting rehabilitation ↓ Assess nutrition and start a support plan
exam_trap: C, Waiting until discharge — it seems sensible to let her recover first, but untreated undernutrition is itself delaying her recovery.
takeaway: Hospital patients with poor intake and weight loss need prompt nutritional assessment and support, not observation.

presentation: Undernutrition in a care home resident
stem: At the monthly weight review in a nursing home, staff ask the visiting GP to see a 90-year-old man with advanced dementia. He often refuses food or falls asleep during meals, his cheeks and temples look hollow, and his grip is noticeably weaker than six months ago. His BMI is now below the healthy range. He has no fever, abdominal pain or bowel change. Which condition best explains these findings?
why_correct: Reduced intake, low BMI, visible temporal wasting and declining muscle strength together point to malnutrition. Feeding difficulty is common in advanced dementia and is a frequent cause of undernutrition in care homes. He needs a nutritional assessment and a care plan that considers eating support and his wishes.
why_wrong: A. Thyrotoxicosis causes weight loss with increased appetite, tremor and tachycardia rather than food refusal. B. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, not wasting from poor intake. C. Acute cholecystitis presents with right upper quadrant pain and fever. D. Hypercalcaemia can cause anorexia but would usually bring confusion, constipation and thirst and is not suggested here.
pearl: Temporal wasting and reduced grip strength are useful bedside signs of loss of muscle and fat stores.
thinking: Advanced dementia ↓ Refusing or sleeping through meals ↓ Low BMI and temporal wasting ↓ Reduced grip strength ↓ Malnutrition
exam_trap: A, Thyrotoxicosis — it is a classic cause of weight loss, but it raises appetite and causes adrenergic features, none of which are present.
takeaway: Low BMI, muscle wasting and poor intake in a frail older person indicate malnutrition.

presentation: Unintentional weight loss in older age
stem: A daughter books a telephone appointment for her 81-year-old mother, Brenda, who has been widowed for eight months. The daughter reports that Brenda has gone off her food and that her clothes now hang off her; the practice records show a fall in weight of over a stone since her last review. Brenda says she simply is not hungry these days and thinks it is because she is getting old. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Reassure them that a lower appetite is expected at her age
options.B: Start mirtazapine to improve her appetite
options.C: Advise her to cut down on snacks and eat only at mealtimes
options.D: Prescribe nutritional drinks and review her in twelve months
options.E: Arrange a full assessment for physical, psychological, medication-related and social causes

correct_answer: E. Arrange a full assessment for physical, psychological, medication-related and social causes
why_correct: Losing more than a stone without trying is clinically significant at any age. In an older person causes include cancer, chronic disease, medication effects, dental or swallowing problems, depression after bereavement, cognitive decline and social factors such as isolation. She needs a structured face-to-face assessment with history, examination and baseline tests before treatment is chosen.
why_wrong: A. Significant unintentional weight loss should never be put down to normal ageing. B. Treating with a drug before establishing a cause risks missing depression, cancer or other disease, and may not be appropriate. C. Restricting eating occasions would reduce her intake further. D. Supplements alone with a year's delay could miss serious disease and leaves the cause unaddressed.
pearl: Bereavement, depression and loneliness are common and treatable contributors to weight loss in older people.
thinking: Unintentional weight loss over months ↓ Recent bereavement ↓ Patient attributes it to age ↓ Ageing is not an explanation ↓ Assess medical, psychological, drug and social causes
exam_trap: A, Reassurance — the patient herself blames her age, but significant weight loss always needs a cause sought.
takeaway: Significant unintentional weight loss in an older adult needs a broad assessment of medical, psychological and social causes.

stem: A 70-year-old retired lorry driver with Parkinson's disease is reviewed in the movement disorders clinic. Since his wife went into hospital he has been living on toast because his tremor makes cooking and cutting food difficult and he cannot get to the shops. His belt is two notches tighter, his arms look thin and he feels weak. Swallowing is normal and he has no abdominal symptoms. Which problem is most likely?
why_correct: He has a clear reduction in the quantity and variety of food because of physical and social barriers, together with weight loss, muscle wasting and weakness. These are the features of malnutrition. Management should include nutritional screening, dietetic input, practical support with meals and a social care assessment.
why_wrong: A. A ureteric stone causes acute colicky loin pain, not gradual wasting. B. Coeliac disease can cause weight loss but usually with diarrhoea, bloating or anaemia, and his intake problem is already explained. C. Graves' disease causes weight loss with a good appetite, tremor and eye signs, and his tremor is due to Parkinson's. E. Cluster headache causes severe periorbital pain attacks and does not explain weight loss.
pearl: Practical barriers such as tremor, poor dexterity, isolation and lack of transport are major causes of malnutrition in people with chronic neurological disease.
thinking: Parkinson's disease ↓ Cannot cook or shop since wife admitted ↓ Monotonous, inadequate diet ↓ Weight loss, thin arms, weakness ↓ Malnutrition
exam_trap: C, Graves' disease — tremor and weight loss tempt a thyroid diagnosis, but his tremor is from Parkinson's and his appetite is not increased.
takeaway: Inadequate intake from practical or social barriers, with weight loss and wasting, should be recognised as malnutrition.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with COPD is admitted to the acute medical unit with an infective exacerbation. During the admission clerking she mentions that her dentures no longer fit and that she has been eating mainly soup for months; her daughter thinks she has lost a lot of weight. Her oxygen saturation is now on target with treatment. Alongside management of the exacerbation, which assessment is most appropriate?

options.D: Nutritional screening and assessment of her dietary intake

correct_answer: D. Nutritional screening and assessment of her dietary intake
why_correct: She has had a long period of poor and restricted intake with apparent weight loss, which places her at high risk of malnutrition. NICE recommends nutritional screening of all hospital inpatients on admission, and undernutrition is particularly harmful in COPD because it weakens the respiratory muscles. Screening should lead to dietetic input and a dental review for her ill-fitting dentures.
why_wrong: A. Audiometry tests hearing and does not address her weight loss. B. Visual-field testing assesses the visual pathways and is not relevant. C. Skin-prick testing looks for IgE-mediated allergy and is not indicated. E. Sleep studies investigate sleep-disordered breathing, which is not the concern here.
pearl: A low BMI is an independent predictor of poor outcome in COPD, so nutritional support is part of COPD care.
thinking: COPD exacerbation admission ↓ Ill-fitting dentures and a soup-only diet ↓ Apparent weight loss ↓ High malnutrition risk ↓ Screen and assess nutrition
exam_trap: E, Overnight polysomnography — respiratory disease may make sleep studies seem relevant, but they do nothing for her clear nutritional problem.
takeaway: All hospital admissions should be screened for malnutrition, especially when intake has been poor.

stem: A 25-year-old man attends the clinical genetics clinic because his sister was recently diagnosed with acute intermittent porphyria after attacks of abdominal pain and limb weakness following a crash diet. Their father has a confirmed pathogenic variant but has never had symptoms. The man asks how the condition is passed on in families. Which inheritance pattern applies?
correct_answer: E. Autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance
why_correct: Acute intermittent porphyria is caused by a single pathogenic variant in the HMBS gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Penetrance is low, so many carriers such as the father never have attacks. His sister's attack was triggered by fasting, a recognised precipitant. He has a 50% chance of carrying the variant and can be offered predictive testing.
why_wrong: A. X-linked recessive conditions mainly affect males, and the gene involved in AIP lies on an autosome. B. Mitochondrial disorders pass only from mother to child, but here the variant came from the father. C. Autosomal recessive conditions need two pathogenic alleles; AIP needs only one. D. Y-linked disorders affect only males, yet his sister is affected.
pearl: Most people carrying an AIP variant never have an attack; triggers include fasting, alcohol, progestogens and enzyme-inducing drugs.
thinking: Sister affected, father an asymptomatic carrier ↓ One variant from father is enough ↓ Male-to-female transmission excludes Y-linked and mitochondrial ↓ Silent carrier implies reduced penetrance ↓ Autosomal dominant
exam_trap: C, Autosomal recessive — an unaffected parent makes recessive inheritance look likely, but the father carries the variant and has simply not expressed it.
takeaway: Acute intermittent porphyria is autosomal dominant with low penetrance.

stem: A 39-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his partner after two days of severe, poorly localised abdominal pain that began after a weekend of heavy drinking and almost no food. He is tachycardic and hypertensive, his abdomen is soft despite the pain, and a CT scan and serum amylase are normal. Over the next day he becomes agitated and hallucinates, develops weakness of his upper arms and his sodium falls. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination and normal imaging, together with autonomic features, neuropsychiatric change, a motor neuropathy and hyponatraemia, is the classic picture of an acute porphyria attack. Alcohol and fasting are well-known precipitants. A fresh urine sample should be sent urgently for porphobilinogen, and haem arginate is the specific treatment.
why_wrong: A. A normal amylase and CT make acute pancreatitis unlikely, and it does not cause proximal motor weakness. C. Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness but not severe abdominal pain with psychiatric features. D. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause hyponatraemia, autonomic instability or neurological deficits. E. Withdrawal can cause agitation, hallucinations and tachycardia but not motor neuropathy with severe abdominal pain.
pearl: Many common drugs can worsen an acute porphyria attack, so always check prescribing against a porphyria-safe drug list.
thinking: Abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging ↓ Triggered by alcohol and fasting ↓ Tachycardia and hypertension ↓ Hallucinations, proximal weakness, low sodium ↓ Acute porphyria
exam_trap: E, Alcohol withdrawal delirium — the drinking history and hallucinations fit, but withdrawal does not explain the neuropathy and the dominant abdominal pain.
takeaway: Unexplained severe abdominal pain with neuropsychiatric features and hyponatraemia should prompt testing for acute porphyria.

stem: A 24-year-old trainee electrician has a routine health check at work and is told his cholesterol is very high; repeat fasting bloods at his GP surgery show a markedly raised LDL cholesterol with normal triglycerides. He has thickened Achilles tendons. His father had a heart attack at 46 and his paternal uncle needed coronary stents at 50. His thyroid and liver function and glucose are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A very high LDL cholesterol in a young adult, tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease in first- and second-degree relatives strongly suggest familial hypercholesterolaemia. Secondary causes have been excluded. NICE recommends using the Simon Broome or Dutch Lipid Clinic criteria, referral to a specialist lipid service for genetic testing, and cascade testing of relatives.
why_wrong: A. His thyroid function is normal, so hypothyroidism is excluded. B. Nephrotic syndrome raises cholesterol but presents with oedema and proteinuria, and does not explain the family history. C. Metabolic syndrome features raised triglycerides, central obesity and insulin resistance rather than isolated very high LDL. E. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes very high triglycerides and pancreatitis, not isolated high LDL.
pearl: Tendon xanthomata in the patient or a relative make a diagnosis of definite familial hypercholesterolaemia under the Simon Broome criteria when combined with raised cholesterol.
thinking: Young adult with very high LDL ↓ Achilles tendon xanthomata ↓ Premature coronary disease in father and uncle ↓ Secondary causes excluded ↓ Familial hypercholesterolaemia
exam_trap: A, Hypothyroidism — it is the classic secondary cause to exclude, but his thyroid tests are normal and the family history points to an inherited cause.
takeaway: Very high LDL with premature family coronary disease suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia and warrants specialist and cascade testing.

stem: A 9-year-old girl is referred to the paediatric growth clinic because, over several years, her height has drifted down from the 25th centile to well below the 2nd, although both parents are of average height. She has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, a low posterior hairline, short fourth metacarpals and numerous pigmented moles. A chromosome analysis is sent. Which result is most likely?
why_correct: Short stature that falls away from the expected centile despite average-height parents is the commonest presenting feature of Turner syndrome in childhood. A shield chest, low hairline, short fourth metacarpals and multiple naevi support the diagnosis. Turner syndrome is most often caused by complete loss of one X chromosome, giving a 45,X karyotype, although mosaic forms also occur, and growth hormone treatment improves final height.
why_wrong: A. Trisomy 21 is usually recognised at birth by hypotonia and characteristic facial features. B. 46,XY is the typical male karyotype. D. Trisomy X tends to cause tall rather than short stature. E. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome in a male and causes tall stature.
pearl: Any girl with unexplained short stature should have a karyotype to look for Turner syndrome, as dysmorphic features can be subtle.
thinking: Girl with height falling across centiles ↓ Parents of average height ↓ Shield chest and low hairline ↓ Short fourth metacarpals and many naevi ↓ Turner syndrome, 45,X
exam_trap: D, 47,XXX — an abnormal number of X chromosomes in a girl sounds plausible, but trisomy X causes tall stature with few physical features.
takeaway: Turner syndrome is classically 45,X and often presents in childhood with unexplained short stature.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is referred by her GP to the adolescent endocrine clinic because she has never had a period and her breasts have not developed. She has always been the smallest in her class and needed grommets for repeated ear infections as a child. She has a low hairline and her elbows angle outwards. Blood tests show high FSH and LH with low oestradiol. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

why_correct: Primary amenorrhoea with absent breast development and raised gonadotrophins indicates primary ovarian failure. Combined with lifelong short stature, recurrent otitis media, a low posterior hairline and an increased carrying angle, this points to Turner syndrome with gonadal dysgenesis. A karyotype confirms the diagnosis and oestrogen replacement is used to induce puberty.
why_wrong: A. Kallmann syndrome causes low, not high, gonadotrophins and is linked to a poor sense of smell. B. Androgen insensitivity usually gives normal breast development with absent pubic hair, and patients are not short. C. Constitutional delay causes low gonadotrophins for age and does not cause dysmorphic features. D. Anorexia nervosa causes low gonadotrophins and weight loss rather than lifelong short stature.
pearl: Recurrent middle ear disease and hearing loss are common in Turner syndrome and need lifelong audiology follow-up.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea and no breast development ↓ High FSH and LH means ovarian failure ↓ Lifelong short stature ↓ Recurrent otitis media, low hairline, wide carrying angle ↓ Turner syndrome
exam_trap: C, Constitutional delay — it is the commonest cause of late puberty, but it gives low gonadotrophins and no dysmorphic features.
takeaway: Short stature with primary amenorrhoea and raised gonadotrophins in a girl suggests Turner syndrome.

stem: A woman and her husband attend a preconception counselling appointment. Cascade testing, offered because her nephew has cystic fibrosis, has shown that she carries a CFTR variant, and her husband has since been found to carry a different disease-causing CFTR variant. Neither has any symptoms. They want to know, for any pregnancy, the chance that their baby would be healthy but carry a variant just like them. What is the answer?
why_correct: When both parents are heterozygous for the same autosomal recessive condition, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child, a 2 in 4 chance of an unaffected carrier and a 1 in 4 chance of an unaffected non-carrier. The two different CFTR variants still behave as alleles of the same gene. So the chance of a healthy carrier child is 50%.
why_wrong: A. Each parent passes on their variant half the time, so carrier children are expected. B. 25% is the chance of an affected child, or of a child with no variant at all. C. 75% is the chance that a child is unaffected, which includes both carriers and non-carriers. E. Each child inherits only one of each parent's two alleles, so not every child will be a carrier.
pearl: Cystic fibrosis can be caused by two different pathogenic CFTR variants (compound heterozygosity), so partners with different variants still have a 25% risk per pregnancy of an affected child.
thinking: Both parents carry CFTR variants ↓ Autosomal recessive ↓ Cross gives 1 affected : 2 carriers : 1 non-carrier ↓ Healthy carrier is 2 in 4 ↓ 50%
exam_trap: C, 75% — this is the chance of an unaffected child, and it is easy to give that figure when the question asks only about unaffected carriers.
takeaway: For two carrier parents, half of children are expected to be healthy carriers.

stem: A health visitor sees a family whose first baby was diagnosed with sickle cell disease on the newborn blood spot test. Both parents are well and have now been confirmed to have sickle cell trait. The mother is 10 weeks pregnant again and asks what the chance is that this new baby will also have sickle cell disease. What is the correct risk?
why_correct: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive. With both parents carrying the trait, every pregnancy carries an independent 1 in 4 chance that the baby inherits the variant from both and is affected. Having already had an affected child does not change this risk. The couple should be offered referral for counselling and prenatal diagnosis if they wish.
why_wrong: B. 50% is the chance this baby will have sickle cell trait, like the parents. C. 75% is the chance the baby will not have the disease. D. Two carriers can clearly have an affected child, as their first baby shows. E. Each pregnancy is independent, and only one in four is expected to be affected.
pearl: Couples who are both carriers of a haemoglobin disorder should be offered prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis.
thinking: Affected first child ↓ Both parents have the trait, so both are carriers ↓ Autosomal recessive ↓ Each pregnancy independent ↓ 25% chance of an affected baby
exam_trap: B, 50% — this is the chance of the baby being a carrier, not of having the disease.
takeaway: Two carrier parents have a 25% chance of an affected child in every pregnancy.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who drinks very little alcohol is seen in the hepatology clinic after ultrasound showed a cirrhotic liver. Viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune liver screen are negative, and her ferritin and caeruloplasmin are normal. She mentions she has become breathless climbing stairs, and spirometry shows airflow obstruction. Her older brother needed a lung transplant in his forties. Which inherited disorder is most likely?
why_correct: Cirrhosis without alcohol or another cause, early-onset airflow obstruction and a sibling with severe early lung disease point to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Abnormal protein accumulates in hepatocytes causing liver damage, while lack of circulating enzyme inhibitor allows unopposed neutrophil elastase to destroy alveoli. The diagnosis is made by measuring serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotype.
why_wrong: B. Wilson's disease causes liver and neuropsychiatric disease, not emphysema, and her caeruloplasmin is normal. C. Haemochromatosis causes liver disease, diabetes and arthropathy but not early emphysema, and her ferritin is normal. D. Cystic fibrosis causes bronchiectasis and pancreatic insufficiency, usually diagnosed in childhood. E. Gilbert's syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and never cirrhosis or lung disease.
pearl: Emphysema in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is typically panacinar and worst at the lung bases.
thinking: Cirrhosis with a negative liver screen ↓ Early airflow obstruction ↓ Sibling with severe early lung disease ↓ Liver plus lung disease ↓ Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
exam_trap: B, Wilson's disease — it is the classic cause of unexplained liver disease in young adults, but it does not cause emphysema and her caeruloplasmin is normal.
takeaway: Unexplained liver disease with early emphysema should prompt testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with Turner syndrome, diagnosed in childhood, transfers from paediatric to adult care. Her blood pressure is raised in the right arm, her femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared with the radial pulse, and there is a systolic murmur heard best between the shoulder blades. Which cardiovascular abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Turner syndrome is strongly associated with left-sided heart lesions, particularly bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta. Upper limb hypertension, radio-femoral delay and an interscapular murmur are the classic signs of coarctation. Women with Turner syndrome need lifelong cardiac imaging because of the added risk of aortic dilatation and dissection.
why_wrong: B. Mitral stenosis is usually rheumatic, causes a diastolic murmur and does not cause radio-femoral delay. C. Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanotic heart disease, usually repaired in infancy, and is not a Turner association. D. Ebstein's anomaly is linked to maternal lithium exposure and affects the tricuspid valve. E. Patent ductus arteriosus causes a continuous machinery murmur and bounding pulses.
pearl: Women with Turner syndrome have a raised risk of aortic dissection, especially in pregnancy, so cardiac MRI is advised before any planned pregnancy.
thinking: Turner syndrome ↓ Arm hypertension ↓ Weak, delayed femoral pulses ↓ Interscapular murmur ↓ Coarctation of the aorta
exam_trap: E, Patent ductus arteriosus — it is another congenital lesion with a murmur, but it causes bounding pulses and a continuous murmur, not radio-femoral delay.
takeaway: Coarctation of the aorta is a key cardiovascular association of Turner syndrome.

stem: At the antenatal clinic, a 38-year-old woman has been told that her combined first-trimester screening shows a higher chance of Down syndrome, and she is considering diagnostic testing. Her partner asks what chromosome change most often underlies the condition. What should he be told?

options.E: An extra X chromosome in a male

why_correct: About 95% of Down syndrome is due to free trisomy 21, usually from non-disjunction in maternal meiosis, which becomes more likely with increasing maternal age. A smaller proportion is due to a Robertsonian translocation or mosaicism. Translocation cases matter because a parent may be a balanced carrier with a high recurrence risk.
why_wrong: A. An extra chromosome 13 causes Patau syndrome. C. Loss of an X chromosome causes Turner syndrome. D. An extra chromosome 18 causes Edwards syndrome. E. An extra X chromosome in a male causes Klinefelter syndrome.
pearl: If Down syndrome is due to a translocation, both parents should be offered karyotyping because a balanced carrier parent greatly raises recurrence risk.
thinking: Higher-chance screening result ↓ Question is about the usual chromosomal cause ↓ Most cases are non-disjunction ↓ Extra free chromosome 21 ↓ Trisomy 21
exam_trap: D, An extra chromosome 18 — combined screening also reports chances for trisomies 18 and 13, so the numbers are easily confused.
takeaway: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by free trisomy 21.

stem: A 20-week anomaly scan in a 41-year-old woman shows a fetus that is small for dates, with a strawberry-shaped skull, hands that stay persistently clenched with the index finger overlapping the middle finger, and feet with a rounded, convex sole. A ventricular septal defect is also seen. Which chromosomal condition is most likely?
why_correct: Growth restriction, a strawberry-shaped skull, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet and cardiac defects together suggest trisomy 18, Edwards syndrome. The risk rises with maternal age. Prognosis is very poor, with most affected babies dying in the first year, and the parents should be offered diagnostic testing and counselling.
why_wrong: A. Down syndrome is suggested by soft markers such as nuchal thickening and duodenal atresia rather than clenched overlapping fingers. B. Turner syndrome is suggested by cystic hygroma and fetal hydrops. C. Fragile X syndrome has no specific prenatal ultrasound features. D. Klinefelter syndrome is usually invisible on antenatal scans.
pearl: Edwards syndrome features: small for dates, overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, prominent occiput and heart defects.
thinking: Older mother ↓ Growth-restricted fetus ↓ Clenched hands with overlapping fingers ↓ Rocker-bottom feet and VSD ↓ Trisomy 18
exam_trap: A, Down syndrome — it is the most familiar trisomy and is also linked to cardiac defects, but its features are different.
takeaway: Clenched overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet point to Edwards syndrome.

stem: A paediatric registrar is called to the delivery suite to see a baby boy with a bilateral cleft of the lip and palate, an extra digit on the ulnar side of each hand and small, close-set eyes. There is also a sharply defined area of absent skin on the scalp. An echocardiogram shows a congenital heart defect. Which karyotype is most likely?
why_correct: Midline defects such as cleft lip and palate, microphthalmia or close-set eyes, postaxial polydactyly, scalp skin defects (cutis aplasia) and heart defects are characteristic of trisomy 13, Patau syndrome. These babies often have holoprosencephaly. Most die within the first weeks of life.
why_wrong: A. Trisomy 18 causes overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet, not polydactyly with scalp defects. B. 45,X is Turner syndrome and is seen in phenotypic females. C. Trisomy 21 causes hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease. E. Klinefelter syndrome is not apparent at birth in this way.
pearl: Cutis aplasia of the scalp with polydactyly and midline facial clefts is a strong pointer to Patau syndrome.
thinking: Newborn with cleft lip and palate ↓ Postaxial polydactyly ↓ Small close-set eyes ↓ Scalp skin defect and heart defect ↓ Trisomy 13
exam_trap: A, Trisomy 18 — both are severe trisomies with heart defects, but polydactyly and midline clefts favour trisomy 13.
takeaway: Cleft lip and palate, polydactyly and scalp defects suggest Patau syndrome, trisomy 13.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the gynaecology ward with severe abdominal pain that started a week after a progestogen-only implant was fitted. A urine sample was clear when passed, but the nurse notices that after sitting in the sluice room in daylight for several hours it has turned a deep reddish-brown. Acute porphyria is suspected. What causes the urine to darken?

options.C: Oxidation of porphobilinogen and porphyrins to coloured pigments

correct_answer: C. Oxidation of porphobilinogen and porphyrins to coloured pigments
why_correct: In an acute porphyria attack large amounts of the colourless haem precursors porphobilinogen and aminolaevulinic acid are excreted. On standing, particularly in light, porphobilinogen oxidises to porphobilin and related porphyrins, which are reddish-brown. Progestogens are a recognised trigger. The diagnosis is confirmed by a raised urinary porphobilinogen, and samples should be protected from light.
why_wrong: A. Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis is dark on passing rather than darkening on standing. B. Conjugated bilirubin causes dark urine in cholestasis, with pale stools and jaundice. D. Haemoglobinuria is dark when passed and is a feature of haemolysis, not porphyria. E. Urobilinogen rises in haemolysis or liver disease rather than porphyria, and its oxidation on standing gives only a mild orange tint, not the deep reddish-brown of porphyrins.
pearl: Urine for porphobilinogen should be sent fresh and protected from light; a normal result during symptoms effectively excludes an acute attack.
thinking: Suspected acute porphyria ↓ Urine clear when fresh ↓ Darkens after standing in light ↓ Colourless precursors oxidise ↓ Porphobilinogen converted to coloured pigments
exam_trap: D, Free haemoglobin — red urine suggests blood, but haemoglobinuria is coloured on passing and does not appear only after standing.
takeaway: Urine in acute porphyria darkens on standing because porphobilinogen oxidises to coloured pigments.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the GP by his mother, who is worried about his breast development. He is the tallest in his year with long legs, has sparse facial and body hair and finds schoolwork harder than his peers. Both testes are small and firm. Blood tests show low testosterone with raised LH and FSH. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Tall stature with long legs, gynaecomastia, poor virilisation, mild learning difficulty and small firm testes with low testosterone and raised gonadotrophins indicate primary testicular failure. This is the classic picture of Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY. A karyotype confirms the diagnosis, and testosterone replacement supports puberty and bone health.
why_wrong: A. Prader-Willi syndrome causes short stature, obesity and hyperphagia. B. Fragile X syndrome is associated with large testes after puberty, not small ones. C. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature but normal pubertal development and testes. D. Pubertal gynaecomastia is common but occurs with normal testes and normal hormones.
pearl: Klinefelter syndrome is the commonest cause of primary hypogonadism in males and is often underdiagnosed.
thinking: Tall adolescent boy ↓ Gynaecomastia and poor virilisation ↓ Small firm testes ↓ Low testosterone with high LH and FSH ↓ Klinefelter syndrome
exam_trap: D, Physiological pubertal gynaecomastia — breast tissue in teenage boys is usually benign, but small testes and abnormal hormones make this pathological.
takeaway: Tall stature, gynaecomastia and small firm testes with raised gonadotrophins suggest Klinefelter syndrome.

stem: A 32-year-old man and his wife attend the fertility clinic after two years of trying to conceive. Two semen analyses show no sperm. He shaves only every few days, and examination shows small, firm testes and a little breast tissue. His FSH is markedly raised. A chromosome analysis is requested. Which karyotype is most likely?
why_correct: Non-obstructive azoospermia with small firm testes, reduced virilisation, gynaecomastia and a high FSH indicate primary testicular failure. Klinefelter syndrome is the most common chromosomal cause of male infertility, and the classic karyotype is 47,XXY. Some men can father children with surgical sperm retrieval and assisted conception.
why_wrong: A. 46,XX testicular disorder of sex development can also cause azoospermia but is far rarer, and affected men are usually of short or average height. B. 47,XYY usually causes tall stature with normal fertility and testes. C. 45,X is Turner syndrome in females. D. Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome with characteristic features recognised from birth.
pearl: Men with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia should have a karyotype as part of their infertility assessment.
thinking: Male infertility ↓ Azoospermia ↓ Small firm testes and gynaecomastia ↓ Raised FSH, primary testicular failure ↓ 47,XXY
exam_trap: B, 47,XYY — an extra sex chromosome in a man sounds similar, but XYY men usually have normal testes and fertility.
takeaway: Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY, is a leading chromosomal cause of azoospermia.

stem: A 46-year-old man breaks his wrist after tripping on a kerb, and a DXA scan arranged by the fracture liaison service shows osteoporosis. He has never needed to shave daily, has little chest hair and fathered no children despite trying. On examination he is tall with long legs, has mild gynaecomastia and small, firm testes. Testosterone is low and FSH and LH are high. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Lifelong poor virilisation, infertility, tall stature, gynaecomastia and small firm testes with raised gonadotrophins indicate primary hypogonadism present since puberty. This is the typical adult presentation of undiagnosed Klinefelter syndrome. Long-standing testosterone deficiency explains his osteoporosis and low-trauma fracture, and testosterone replacement should be considered.
why_wrong: A. Cushing's syndrome causes osteoporosis but with central obesity, striae and proximal myopathy rather than lifelong hypogonadism. B. Hyperprolactinaemia causes secondary hypogonadism with low or normal gonadotrophins. C. Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadism with low gonadotrophins and anosmia. D. Haemochromatosis usually causes secondary hypogonadism from pituitary iron deposition, with acquired rather than lifelong features.
pearl: Many men with Klinefelter syndrome are not diagnosed until adulthood, through infertility, osteoporosis or hypogonadism.
thinking: Low-trauma fracture with osteoporosis in a man ↓ Lifelong poor virilisation and infertility ↓ Tall with gynaecomastia ↓ Small firm testes, high LH and FSH ↓ Klinefelter syndrome
exam_trap: C, Kallmann syndrome — it also causes lifelong hypogonadism, but gonadotrophins are low and the testes are not firm.
takeaway: Klinefelter syndrome can present late in adult men with osteoporosis and primary hypogonadism.

stem: A 19-year-old man books a GP appointment because his voice has not broken and he has almost no facial or pubic hair. He mentions that he has never been able to smell gas or burning food, which his family jokes about. He is of normal height for his family, his testes are small, and blood tests show low testosterone with low LH and FSH. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

why_correct: Absent puberty with low testosterone and inappropriately low gonadotrophins means hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. Combined with lifelong anosmia, this is Kallmann syndrome, caused by failed migration of GnRH neurones and olfactory neurones during development. Treatment with testosterone, or gonadotrophins when fertility is wanted, induces puberty.
why_wrong: A. Klinefelter syndrome causes primary testicular failure with high LH and FSH and a normal sense of smell. B. Constitutional delay would normally have resolved by 19 and does not cause anosmia. C. Prader-Willi syndrome causes hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity and learning difficulty. E. Androgen insensitivity results in a female phenotype with high testosterone.
pearl: Anosmia with delayed puberty is the hallmark of Kallmann syndrome; formal smell testing helps confirm it.
thinking: Absent puberty at 19 ↓ Low testosterone ↓ LH and FSH low, so central cause ↓ Lifelong inability to smell ↓ Kallmann syndrome
exam_trap: A, Klinefelter syndrome — small testes and hypogonadism fit, but Klinefelter gives raised gonadotrophins and normal smell.
takeaway: Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism with anosmia is Kallmann syndrome.

stem: A health visitor reviews a 10-month-old boy whose family recently moved to the UK from a country without a newborn screening programme. He was well in his early months but cannot yet sit unsupported. He has very fair hair and skin compared with his siblings, an eczematous rash and a musty smell to his urine. Which inherited metabolic disorder, caused by a build-up of phenylalanine, is most likely?
why_correct: Phenylketonuria is an autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, so phenylalanine accumulates and tyrosine is reduced. Untreated babies appear normal at first, then develop developmental delay, eczema, a musty odour and pale hair and skin from reduced melanin. In the UK it is detected by newborn blood spot screening and treated with a low-phenylalanine diet.
why_wrong: B. Alkaptonuria causes accumulation of homogentisic acid, dark urine and later arthropathy, not infant developmental delay. C. Maple syrup urine disease involves branched-chain amino acids, gives a sweet smell and presents acutely in the newborn period. D. Homocystinuria causes lens dislocation, marfanoid habitus and thrombosis. E. Galactosaemia presents in the newborn with feeding problems, jaundice and liver dysfunction after milk feeds.
pearl: Reduced tyrosine in phenylketonuria lowers melanin production, giving fair hair, fair skin and blue eyes.
thinking: Infant missed newborn screening ↓ Normal early months then delayed development ↓ Fair hair and skin, eczema ↓ Musty urine odour ↓ Phenylketonuria
exam_trap: B, Alkaptonuria — it is another disorder of the phenylalanine-tyrosine pathway with abnormal urine, but it does not cause developmental delay.
takeaway: Untreated phenylketonuria causes developmental delay, fair colouring and a musty odour.

stem: A 4-year-old girl is seen in the community paediatric clinic. She says no words, walks with a jerky, wide-based gait with her arms held up and bent at the elbows, and is fascinated by water. Her parents describe her as constantly smiling and bursting into laughter at unexpected moments. Her development has been slow since early infancy with no loss of skills she had gained. She had her first seizure at the age of two and her head circumference is small. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Severe developmental delay with absent speech, an ataxic gait with raised arms, a happy demeanour with frequent laughter, fascination with water, microcephaly and seizures form the characteristic picture of Angelman syndrome. It is caused by loss of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene on chromosome 15, most often through a maternal deletion of 15q11-q13.
why_wrong: A. Prader-Willi syndrome causes neonatal hypotonia followed by hyperphagia and obesity, not ataxia and inappropriate laughter. B. Rett syndrome causes regression after normal early development with stereotyped hand-wringing. D. Fragile X syndrome causes learning disability with autistic features, a long face and large ears. E. Williams syndrome causes an overly friendly personality with good expressive language and supravalvular aortic stenosis.
pearl: The same 15q11-q13 deletion causes Angelman syndrome when maternal and Prader-Willi syndrome when paternal, an example of genomic imprinting.
thinking: Severe delay with no speech ↓ Ataxic gait with raised arms ↓ Happy demeanour and inappropriate laughter ↓ Microcephaly and seizures ↓ Angelman syndrome
exam_trap: A, Prader-Willi syndrome — both involve chromosome 15q11-q13 and imprinting, but the clinical pictures are very different.
takeaway: Severe delay, absent speech, ataxia and a happy, laughing demeanour suggest Angelman syndrome.

stem: A 13-year-old boy is referred to the paediatric neurology clinic because his school grades have dropped, he has become irritable and inattentive, and he has had two recent seizures. His mother explains that a heel-prick test soon after birth found a condition for which he has had special low-protein foods and an amino acid supplement ever since. Over the last year he has been eating normal meals with friends. Which condition is he most likely to have?
why_correct: Phenylketonuria is detected on newborn blood spot screening and treated with a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet using restricted natural protein and a phenylalanine-free amino acid supplement. Stopping the diet allows phenylalanine levels to rise, causing poor concentration, mood change, declining school performance and sometimes seizures. He needs urgent review by the metabolic team to restore control.
why_wrong: A. Congenital hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine, not a low-protein diet. B. Cystic fibrosis is managed with physiotherapy, enzymes and a high-calorie diet, not protein restriction. C. MCAD deficiency is managed by avoiding fasting, not with lifelong protein restriction and amino acid supplements. E. Sickle cell disease is managed with penicillin prophylaxis and vaccination, not dietary restriction.
pearl: Treatment for phenylketonuria is now advised for life, and strict control is vital before and during pregnancy to prevent fetal harm.
thinking: Condition found on newborn heel-prick test ↓ Low-protein diet with amino acid supplement ↓ Diet abandoned in the last year ↓ Cognitive decline and seizures ↓ Phenylketonuria
exam_trap: C, MCAD deficiency — it is also on the newborn screening panel and managed with diet, but by avoiding fasting rather than restricting protein.
takeaway: Phenylketonuria needs a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet, and loss of control causes neurocognitive problems.

stem: A 26-year-old woman sees her GP because, since starting a combined oral contraceptive pill four months ago, she has had several episodes of firm swelling of her eyelids and cheek that last two to three days. Two of the episodes came with crampy abdominal pain and vomiting. The swellings are not itchy, there are no wheals, and antihistamines have not helped. Her mother and maternal uncle have had similar attacks. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent non-itchy angioedema without urticaria, lasting days and unresponsive to antihistamines, with abdominal attacks and an affected mother and uncle, suggests hereditary angioedema due to C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency. It is bradykinin-mediated and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, and oestrogen is a recognised trigger. A low C4 is a useful screening test, and the oestrogen-containing pill should be stopped.
why_wrong: A. Chronic spontaneous urticaria causes itchy wheals and responds to antihistamines. B. Contact dermatitis causes an itchy eczematous rash at the site of contact. D. Orbital cellulitis is a single acute infection with fever, pain on eye movement and redness. E. Lupus can rarely be linked to acquired angioedema, but this family pattern and the lack of systemic features favour an inherited cause.
pearl: Hereditary angioedema does not respond to antihistamines, steroids or adrenaline; acute attacks are treated with C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant.
thinking: Recurrent non-itchy swelling, no wheals ↓ Abdominal attacks ↓ Started after an oestrogen-containing pill ↓ Affected mother and uncle ↓ Hereditary angioedema
exam_trap: A, Chronic spontaneous urticaria — it is the commonest cause of recurrent swelling, but the absence of wheals and antihistamine failure argue against it.
takeaway: Recurrent angioedema without urticaria and a family history suggests hereditary angioedema.

stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a football hit him in the face; a few hours later his upper lip has become grossly swollen and tense. It is uncomfortable but not itchy, and there is no rash anywhere on his body. His airway is clear. His mother says he has had three similar lip or hand swellings since starting secondary school, each settling over about three days, and an antihistamine did nothing. He takes no regular medicines. Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent, non-itchy swelling of the lips and hands lasting days, without urticaria and not responding to antihistamines, is typical of hereditary angioedema. Minor trauma, including dental work, is a well-known trigger, and symptoms often worsen around puberty. A family history may be absent because a quarter of cases arise from new mutations. A C4 level is the screening test.
why_wrong: A. Chronic spontaneous urticaria typically causes itchy wheals and responds to antihistamines. B. A haematoma would not explain the earlier spontaneous episodes affecting the hands. C. Orofacial granulomatosis causes persistent painless lip swelling rather than self-limiting attacks at different sites. D. Food allergy usually causes itch and urticaria soon after eating the trigger food and responds to antihistamines.
pearl: Before dental surgery, people with hereditary angioedema may need short-term prophylaxis with C1 inhibitor concentrate.
thinking: Recurrent non-itchy swelling of lips and hands ↓ No urticaria ↓ No response to antihistamine ↓ Triggered by minor trauma, starting around puberty ↓ Hereditary angioedema
exam_trap: B, Haematoma of the lip — the blow to the face makes this tempting, but it cannot explain the earlier spontaneous swellings.
takeaway: Recurrent angioedema without wheals or itch, sometimes triggered by trauma, suggests hereditary angioedema even without a family history.

stem: A 5-year-old boy is assessed by the community paediatrician for delayed speech, poor eye contact and hand-flapping. He has a long face, prominent ears and very flexible finger joints. His mother developed early menopause at 36, and her brother has a learning disability. DNA testing confirms a CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. Which inheritance pattern best describes this condition?

options.B: X-linked, with expansion of the repeat through the generations

correct_answer: B. X-linked, with expansion of the repeat through the generations
why_correct: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. A premutation carried by a woman tends to expand into a full mutation when passed to her children, so severity increases in later generations, which is anticipation. The mother's early menopause suggests she carries a premutation, which causes fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. The FMR1 gene is on the X chromosome and the disease depends on repeat expansion. C. Mitochondrial conditions affect all children of an affected mother and are not caused by FMR1 repeat expansion. D. Fragile X is not autosomal, and many carriers are unaffected or mildly affected. E. Y-linked disorders pass from father to son only, and here the condition comes through the mother's family.
pearl: Fragile X premutation carriers can develop premature ovarian insufficiency in women and a late-onset tremor-ataxia syndrome, mainly in men.
thinking: Boy with learning disability and autistic features ↓ Long face, large ears, lax joints ↓ Affected maternal uncle, mother with early menopause ↓ FMR1 CGG repeat expansion ↓ X-linked with anticipation
exam_trap: D, Autosomal dominant — affected people in two generations suggest dominance, but the gene is on the X chromosome and expansion occurs through female transmission.
takeaway: Fragile X syndrome is X-linked and shows anticipation through maternal CGG repeat expansion.

stem: A neurologist is assessing a 30-year-old woman with myotonic dystrophy type 1, whose grip is slow to release and who has bilateral ptosis. Her mother was only diagnosed in her sixties after cataract surgery, while her own newborn son was floppy at birth and needed help with breathing. Genetic testing shows a larger CTG repeat in each successive generation. Which genetic phenomenon is illustrated?
why_correct: Anticipation is earlier onset or greater severity of a disorder in successive generations. It is characteristic of trinucleotide repeat disorders because unstable repeats tend to lengthen during transmission. In myotonic dystrophy type 1 the CTG repeat in DMPK expands especially through the mother, which explains mild late disease in the grandmother, classic adult disease in the woman and congenital disease in her son.
why_wrong: A. Germline mosaicism explains affected children of an apparently unaffected parent, not worsening severity over generations. B. Imprinting describes a parent-of-origin effect on gene expression, not progressive repeat lengthening. C. Incomplete penetrance means some carriers never show the condition, whereas here every generation is affected. D. Variable expressivity describes differences in severity, but alone it does not explain the consistent earlier and more severe onset with growing repeats.
pearl: Congenital myotonic dystrophy is almost always inherited from an affected mother.
thinking: Three generations affected ↓ Mild late onset in grandmother ↓ Adult onset in mother ↓ Severe congenital form in son ↓ Expanding CTG repeat, so anticipation
exam_trap: D, Variable expressivity alone — severity does vary, but the consistent worsening with a lengthening repeat defines anticipation.
takeaway: Anticipation is earlier or more severe disease in successive generations, typical of repeat expansion disorders.

presentation: Recurrence risk after an affected child
stem: Seen at her GP surgery with her husband, a 29-year-old woman explains that their 18-month-old son was diagnosed last month with spinal muscular atrophy by the regional neuromuscular team. They hope to have another baby next year and want to know how likely it is that the condition could happen again and what options might be open to them. Which service should they be referred to?

options.C: Health visiting team for developmental advice
options.E: Routine antenatal booking with a community midwife

why_correct: The couple's question is about inheritance, recurrence risk and reproductive choices after an affected child, which is exactly what the regional clinical genetics service provides. Genetic counsellors and clinical geneticists confirm the diagnosis and inheritance pattern, discuss carrier testing and explain options such as prenatal diagnosis or preimplantation genetic testing before the next pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. Occupational health deals with fitness for work and workplace hazards, not inherited disease. B. Physiotherapy supports their son's mobility but cannot assess recurrence risk. C. Health visitors support child development and family well-being but do not provide genetic risk assessment. E. Antenatal booking is for an established pregnancy and would come too late to plan reproductive options.
pearl: Referral to clinical genetics is best made before the next pregnancy, so that carrier testing and choices such as preimplantation genetic testing or early prenatal diagnosis can be planned in time.
thinking: Child already diagnosed with an inherited condition ↓ Parents planning a further pregnancy ↓ Question is about recurrence risk and reproductive options ↓ This needs specialist inheritance assessment ↓ Refer to clinical genetics before conception
exam_trap: E, Routine antenatal booking with a community midwife — it feels relevant because the topic is pregnancy, but booking happens after conception and cannot provide preconception carrier testing or a full discussion of reproductive options.
takeaway: Couples with an affected child who are planning another pregnancy should be referred to clinical genetics before conceiving.

presentation: Relative with a confirmed inherited cancer syndrome
stem: A 27-year-old man books a GP appointment after his older brother, aged 34, was treated for bowel cancer and then found on genetic testing to carry a pathogenic mismatch repair gene variant consistent with Lynch syndrome. The man is well, has no bowel symptoms and a normal abdominal examination. He wants to know what he should do. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure him that he needs nothing until bowel screening is offered in later life
options.B: Request a carcinoembryonic antigen level to assess his risk
options.C: Refer him on the suspected cancer pathway for urgent colonoscopy
options.D: Refer him to clinical genetics to discuss predictive testing
options.E: Advise him that only female relatives are at risk in this condition

correct_answer: D. Refer him to clinical genetics to discuss predictive testing
why_correct: His brother has a confirmed pathogenic variant, so he has a 1 in 2 chance of carrying the same variant. Clinical genetics can offer predictive testing for the known familial variant, and if he is a carrier he will be offered regular colonoscopic surveillance from an early age. He has no symptoms, so this is a risk-assessment pathway rather than an urgent cancer referral.
why_wrong: A. Lynch carriers need colonoscopic surveillance well before population screening age, so waiting would be unsafe. B. Tumour markers such as CEA are not used to assess inherited risk or screen for cancer. C. The suspected cancer pathway is for people with symptoms or signs, and he has neither. E. Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant and affects men and women; women also carry endometrial and ovarian risk.
pearl: Once a familial pathogenic variant is known, relatives can be offered a targeted predictive test for that exact variant, which is quicker and more definitive than testing an affected person for the first time.
thinking: Brother has a confirmed pathogenic variant ↓ Autosomal dominant condition gives a 1 in 2 risk to siblings ↓ He has no symptoms ↓ Needs predictive testing and planned surveillance ↓ Refer to clinical genetics
exam_trap: C, Suspected cancer pathway referral — a family member with bowel cancer makes this feel urgent, but he has no symptoms and what he needs is genetic assessment and planned surveillance, not a two-week-wait colonoscopy.
takeaway: A well relative of someone with a confirmed inherited cancer syndrome should be referred to clinical genetics for predictive testing.

stem: Her mother was recently found to carry a pathogenic BRCA1 variant after treatment for ovarian cancer, and a 34-year-old primary school teacher now attends her first appointment at the regional genetics clinic. She has no breast symptoms. At the start of the consultation she asks what this appointment is actually for. Which of the following best describes the main purpose of genetic counselling?

options.A: To examine her breasts and arrange mammography today
options.B: To book her for risk-reducing surgery
options.C: To find out whether she currently has breast or ovarian cancer
options.D: To explain her inherited risk, the testing available and what results could mean for her and her family
options.E: To remove the need for any future breast surveillance

correct_answer: D. To explain her inherited risk, the testing available and what results could mean for her and her family
why_correct: Genetic counselling is a communication process that helps a person understand the chance that they carry a familial variant, the pros and cons of predictive testing and what a positive or negative result would mean for screening, surgery options, insurance and relatives. It supports an informed, voluntary decision about testing rather than delivering a set treatment.
why_wrong: A. Clinical examination and imaging belong to diagnosis or surveillance, not counselling itself. B. Risk-reducing surgery may be discussed later, but counselling informs the choice rather than booking it. C. Counselling assesses inherited risk; it does not diagnose current cancer. E. Even with counselling and testing, carriers usually need enhanced surveillance.
pearl: Genetic counselling is non-directive: the counsellor explains options and consequences but does not tell the person whether to have the test or which preventive option to choose.
thinking: Mother carries a known BRCA1 variant ↓ Daughter is asymptomatic and attending genetics ↓ Main task is understanding risk and testing choices ↓ Includes implications for her and her relatives ↓ Counselling supports an informed, voluntary decision
exam_trap: B, Booking risk-reducing surgery — surgery is often mentioned with BRCA1, but counselling only informs that choice and it is never the starting point before testing and discussion.
takeaway: Genetic counselling explains inherited risk, testing options and their implications so that the person can make an informed choice.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is referred from a university sports medical by a doctor who noticed a soft mitral murmur. She is 1.86 m tall, her arm span is greater than her height, her fingers are long and slender, and she has a pectus excavatum. She is of normal intelligence. Her maternal uncle died suddenly in his thirties from a tear in his aorta. Which inherited disorder is most likely?
why_correct: Tall stature with an arm span exceeding height, arachnodactyly, chest wall deformity and a mitral valve murmur point to a connective tissue disorder of fibrillin-1. A relative dying suddenly from aortic dissection fits the autosomal dominant pattern of Marfan syndrome, which needs echocardiographic assessment of the aortic root.
why_wrong: A. Turner syndrome causes short stature in females, not tall stature. C. Noonan syndrome is associated with short stature and pulmonary stenosis. D. Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism with a poor sense of smell. E. Homocystinuria also causes a tall, long-limbed build, but typically with learning disability, downward lens dislocation and venous thrombosis, and it is autosomal recessive rather than causing familial aortic dissection.
pearl: In Marfan syndrome the main threat to life is aortic root dilatation leading to dissection, so regular echocardiography and blood pressure control (often with a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker) are central to care.
thinking: Tall with long limbs and fingers ↓ Pectus excavatum and mitral murmur ↓ Relative died of aortic dissection ↓ Fibrillin-1 connective tissue disorder, autosomal dominant ↓ Marfan syndrome
exam_trap: E, Homocystinuria — it mimics the tall, long-fingered Marfanoid build, but she has normal intelligence and the family history of aortic dissection fits autosomal dominant Marfan syndrome, not a recessive metabolic disorder that causes thrombosis.
takeaway: Tall stature, arachnodactyly and a family history of aortic dissection suggest Marfan syndrome.

stem: During a contraception review at her GP surgery, a 37-year-old woman mentions that her younger sister was diagnosed with breast cancer at 36 and her mother at 44. She has no breast lumps or other symptoms and asks the GP whether she might have inherited a higher risk. No genetic testing has been done in the family. What is the most appropriate initial response?

options.A: Arrange a CA 15-3 blood test to estimate her inherited risk
options.B: Take a detailed family history across generations and consider referral for familial risk assessment
options.D: Make a suspected cancer referral to the breast clinic today
options.E: Reassure her that she should simply wait for routine NHS breast screening

correct_answer: B. Take a detailed family history across generations and consider referral for familial risk assessment
why_correct: Two first-degree relatives with breast cancer at young ages raise the possibility of an inherited predisposition. NICE guidance on familial breast cancer advises taking a detailed family history across at least two generations, including ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancers and ages at diagnosis, and then referring to secondary care or genetics according to the estimated risk.
why_wrong: A. Tumour markers do not estimate inherited risk and are not used for screening. C. Risk-reducing surgery is only considered after formal risk assessment and counselling. D. She has no symptoms, so a suspected cancer referral is not indicated. E. Her family history may qualify her for earlier or more frequent surveillance than routine screening.
pearl: In familial breast cancer assessment, cancers on both the maternal and the paternal side matter, and a relative with ovarian cancer or male breast cancer markedly increases concern.
thinking: Asymptomatic woman ↓ Two close relatives with early breast cancer ↓ Possible inherited predisposition ↓ First step is a detailed family history ↓ Refer according to estimated risk
exam_trap: D, Suspected cancer referral — worry about cancer tempts an urgent referral, but this pathway is for symptoms and she has none; her need is familial risk assessment.
takeaway: An asymptomatic woman with a worrying family history needs a detailed family history and referral for risk assessment, not an urgent cancer referral.

stem: A 22-year-old woman has had intermittent bright red blood mixed with her stools and looser motions for three months. Her father had his whole colon removed in his thirties, though she does not know why. Colonoscopy shows the colon and rectum carpeted with hundreds of small adenomatous polyps. Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: Hundreds of adenomas throughout the colon in a young adult is the defining feature of familial adenomatous polyposis, an autosomal dominant condition caused by APC gene variants. A parent who needed colectomy at a young age supports this, and without surgery the lifetime risk of colorectal cancer approaches certainty.
why_wrong: A. Ulcerative colitis causes continuous mucosal inflammation, not hundreds of adenomas. C. Lynch syndrome increases cancer risk but usually with only a few adenomas. D. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome causes hamartomatous polyps, mainly in the small bowel, with lip pigmentation. E. Juvenile polyposis produces hamartomatous rather than adenomatous polyps.
pearl: Children of a person with FAP are usually offered predictive APC testing in early adolescence and, if positive, regular colonoscopy until prophylactic colectomy.
thinking: Young adult with rectal bleeding ↓ Hundreds of adenomatous polyps ↓ Parent had early colectomy ↓ Autosomal dominant APC disorder ↓ Familial adenomatous polyposis
exam_trap: C, Lynch syndrome — it is the commonest inherited bowel cancer syndrome, but it does not cause a carpet of hundreds of adenomas; it is non-polyposis.
takeaway: Hundreds of colonic adenomas in a young person indicate familial adenomatous polyposis.

stem: At the gynaecology oncology clinic, a 38-year-old woman is told that her endometrial biopsy shows endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Taking her family history, the registrar learns that her father was treated for bowel cancer at 45 and her paternal aunt died of bowel cancer in her forties. Immunohistochemistry on her tumour shows loss of a mismatch repair protein. Which inherited syndrome is most likely?

options.B: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome

why_correct: Early-onset endometrial cancer, two relatives with young-onset colorectal cancer across generations and loss of a mismatch repair protein in the tumour are all features of Lynch syndrome. It is an autosomal dominant mismatch repair disorder that also raises the risk of ovarian, gastric, urinary tract and other cancers.
why_wrong: A. FAP causes hundreds of colonic adenomas and is not typically linked with endometrial cancer. B. BRCA-related syndromes cause breast and ovarian cancers, not mismatch repair loss. C. Peutz-Jeghers causes hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation. D. Li-Fraumeni (TP53) causes sarcomas, early breast cancer, brain tumours and adrenocortical cancers.
pearl: NICE recommends that all colorectal and endometrial cancers are tested for mismatch repair deficiency to help identify people with Lynch syndrome.
thinking: Endometrial cancer at a young age ↓ Young-onset colorectal cancers in relatives ↓ Tumour shows mismatch repair protein loss ↓ Autosomal dominant mismatch repair disorder ↓ Lynch syndrome
exam_trap: A, Familial adenomatous polyposis — bowel cancer in the family brings FAP to mind, but FAP is defined by hundreds of polyps and is not associated with endometrial cancer or mismatch repair loss.
takeaway: Endometrial cancer with a family history of young-onset bowel cancer should prompt consideration of Lynch syndrome.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after twisting his ankle at nursery; X-ray shows a fracture of the distal tibia. It is his third fracture after minor falls. His sclerae look distinctly grey-blue, his teeth are discoloured and translucent, and his mother reports she has needed hearing aids since her twenties and also broke bones easily as a child. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent low-energy fractures with blue-grey sclerae, abnormal translucent teeth (dentinogenesis imperfecta) and a parent with fragile bones and early hearing loss point to osteogenesis imperfecta. Most cases are autosomal dominant defects of type I collagen. Safeguarding must still be considered in any child with multiple fractures, but these features strongly support an inherited cause.
why_wrong: A. Rickets causes bowed legs, widened wrists and delayed growth from poor mineralisation, not blue sclerae. B. Achondroplasia causes disproportionate short stature, not bone fragility. C. Osteopetrosis produces abnormally dense bones and can cause marrow failure, but not blue sclerae or dentinogenesis imperfecta. E. Duchenne causes progressive proximal weakness; fractures are not the main feature.
pearl: Children with osteogenesis imperfecta are often treated with bisphosphonates to reduce fracture frequency and should have audiology review because conductive and sensorineural hearing loss is common.
thinking: Several fractures after minor trauma ↓ Blue-grey sclerae ↓ Abnormal teeth ↓ Parent with fragile bones and early deafness ↓ Type I collagen disorder: osteogenesis imperfecta
exam_trap: A, Rickets — it also weakens bones in young children, but it causes bowing and metaphyseal changes, not blue sclerae, dental abnormality or a parent with early deafness.
takeaway: Fragile bones with blue sclerae and a family history of early hearing loss suggest osteogenesis imperfecta.

presentation: Recurrence risk when the diagnosis is not yet confirmed
stem: On the neonatal unit, a baby boy born yesterday has short limbs and a narrow chest, and the paediatric team suspects a skeletal dysplasia. Results of the genetic tests sent this morning will take several weeks. His parents, who are not affected, ask the registrar what the chance is that a future baby would have the same condition. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Quote a 25% recurrence risk because both parents are unaffected
options.B: Tell them it was a one-off event that cannot happen again
options.C: Explain that the risk depends on the exact diagnosis and arrange genetic counselling once results are available
options.D: Advise them to avoid any further pregnancies
options.E: Tell them family history is not relevant to the risk

correct_answer: C. Explain that the risk depends on the exact diagnosis and arrange genetic counselling once results are available
why_correct: Skeletal dysplasias can be autosomal dominant (often new variants with low recurrence), autosomal recessive (high recurrence) or follow other patterns, so no accurate figure can be given before the exact condition is known. The right approach is to be honest about this uncertainty and ensure they are seen by clinical genetics to discuss the confirmed diagnosis, recurrence risk and options.
why_wrong: A. A recessive risk cannot be assumed; many skeletal dysplasias arise from new dominant variants with a low recurrence risk. B. Recurrence is possible for several types, including recessive conditions and parental mosaicism. D. Reproductive choices are theirs to make after accurate information. E. Family history is a key part of assessing inheritance.
pearl: Even when a condition appears to be a new dominant variant in a child, parents are usually given a small recurrence risk because of possible germline mosaicism in one parent.
thinking: Baby with a suspected but unconfirmed genetic condition ↓ Parents unaffected ↓ Inheritance pattern unknown until diagnosis confirmed ↓ No accurate figure can be given yet ↓ Arrange genetic counselling with the result
exam_trap: A, Quoting a 25% recurrence risk — unaffected parents of an affected child suggests recessive inheritance, but many skeletal dysplasias are new dominant variants, so this figure could be badly wrong.
takeaway: Recurrence risk depends on the exact diagnosis, so parents should be offered genetic counselling rather than an early guessed figure.

stem: A 26-year-old woman attends a preconception clinic. Her brother has severe haemophilia A, and testing has now confirmed that she carries the same F8 variant. She has never had abnormal bleeding. Her husband has no bleeding disorder. She asks what this means for any children they have. Which statement is correct?

options.A: All of her sons will have haemophilia
options.B: Her daughters cannot inherit the variant
options.C: None of her sons can be affected because her husband is healthy
options.D: Each son has a 1 in 2 chance of having haemophilia
options.E: Every daughter will have severe haemophilia

correct_answer: D. Each son has a 1 in 2 chance of having haemophilia
why_correct: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive. Each son inherits one of his mother's two X chromosomes, so each son has a 1 in 2 chance of receiving the affected X and having haemophilia. Daughters receive their father's normal X, so they will not have severe disease, but each has a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier.
why_wrong: A. A son receives only one of her two X chromosomes, so not every son is affected. B. Each daughter has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting the variant as a carrier. C. Sons take their X from their mother, so the father's health does not protect them. E. Daughters get a normal X from their unaffected father, so severe haemophilia would not be expected.
pearl: Some female carriers of haemophilia have low factor VIII levels and bleed abnormally, so carriers should have their factor levels checked, especially before surgery or delivery.
thinking: Brother affected and she is a confirmed carrier ↓ X-linked recessive condition ↓ Sons receive one maternal X ↓ Half of her X chromosomes carry the variant ↓ Each son has a 1 in 2 chance of being affected
exam_trap: C, None of her sons can be affected — it seems logical because the father is healthy, but a son's X chromosome always comes from his mother.
takeaway: Each son of a female carrier of an X-linked recessive condition has a 1 in 2 chance of being affected.

presentation: Carrier couple for an autosomal recessive condition
stem: A 24-year-old woman at 9 weeks of gestation has just been told through the antenatal screening programme that she has sickle cell trait. Her partner has since been tested and also carries sickle cell trait. They are worried and ring the screening midwife to ask what happens next. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure them that the baby will be unaffected because they are both healthy
options.B: Tell them the baby will definitely have sickle cell disease
options.C: Offer prompt genetic counselling, including discussion of prenatal diagnosis
options.D: Advise them that no further information can be obtained until birth
options.E: Arrange a repeat of both parents' screening test at the end of pregnancy

correct_answer: C. Offer prompt genetic counselling, including discussion of prenatal diagnosis
why_correct: When both partners carry sickle cell trait, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of sickle cell disease, a 1 in 2 chance of carrier status and a 1 in 4 chance of being unaffected. The NHS sickle cell and thalassaemia screening programme aims to offer the couple prompt counselling and, if they wish, prenatal diagnosis early enough to allow informed choices.
why_wrong: A. Two healthy carriers can still have an affected child. B. The risk of an affected baby is 1 in 4, not certain. D. Prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis is available during pregnancy. E. Repeating screening adds nothing and wastes time when decisions are time-sensitive.
pearl: Antenatal screening for sickle cell and thalassaemia should be offered by 10 weeks of pregnancy so that, if both parents are carriers, prenatal diagnosis can be offered early.
thinking: Mother found to carry sickle cell trait ↓ Partner also a carrier ↓ Autosomal recessive: 1 in 4 risk per pregnancy ↓ Time-sensitive decisions in early pregnancy ↓ Offer counselling and prenatal diagnosis
exam_trap: A, Reassuring them because both are healthy — healthy parents feel reassuring, but two carriers of a recessive condition have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child in every pregnancy.
takeaway: A carrier couple for an autosomal recessive condition should be offered prompt genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis.

presentation: Purpose of genetic testing in a newborn
stem: A baby boy born at 39 weeks is small for his gestational age. The neonatal team notices clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rounded soles of the feet and a loud heart murmur, and they ask the parents for consent to send a blood sample for urgent chromosome analysis. His mother asks why a blood test is needed when the doctors can already see what is wrong. What is the main purpose of the test?

options.A: To avoid the need for a full newborn examination
options.B: To predict his intelligence in adulthood
options.C: To decide whether he can have the routine childhood immunisations
options.D: To work out how tall he will be as an adult
options.E: To confirm the diagnosis and guide his management and the family's counselling

correct_answer: E. To confirm the diagnosis and guide his management and the family's counselling
why_correct: These features suggest a chromosomal disorder such as trisomy 18, but appearance alone is not proof, and the result has major consequences. Confirming the diagnosis and its type (for example a full trisomy, mosaicism or an unbalanced translocation) guides decisions about cardiac and surgical care, informs honest discussion of prognosis and determines the recurrence risk for the parents.
why_wrong: A. Genetic testing complements, rather than replaces, a full clinical examination. B. Testing cannot predict an individual's future intelligence. C. Children with chromosomal disorders follow the routine immunisation schedule. D. A karyotype does not determine an individual's adult height.
pearl: When a chromosomal disorder is due to an unbalanced translocation rather than a standard trisomy, one parent may carry a balanced translocation, which raises the recurrence risk in future pregnancies.
thinking: Newborn with features of a chromosomal disorder ↓ Clinical suspicion is not confirmation ↓ Test confirms diagnosis and type ↓ Guides care, prognosis and parental counselling ↓ Main purpose is diagnosis and management
exam_trap: B, Predicting adult intelligence — parents often hope a test will show how their child will develop, but genetic tests confirm a diagnosis and cannot predict individual ability.
takeaway: Genetic testing in a newborn with suspected chromosomal features confirms the diagnosis and guides management and family counselling.

presentation: Implications of genetic testing for relatives
stem: A 46-year-old man attends an inherited cardiac conditions clinic after his father died suddenly and post-mortem examination showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Genetic testing of stored tissue has found a pathogenic variant, and the man is considering a predictive test. He has two teenage children and a younger sister. He asks whether his own result could matter to anyone else. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: His result will be sent to his relatives automatically by the clinic
options.B: He has a legal duty to tell his sister and children his result
options.C: His children and sister must be tested before he can be
options.D: His result may carry important information for his blood relatives
options.E: His result only becomes relevant to others if he develops symptoms

correct_answer: D. His result may carry important information for his blood relatives
why_correct: Genetic variants are shared within families, so his result could change the risk estimate and screening needs of his children and sister. Clinicians should explain this before testing, encourage him to share relevant information and offer support such as a family letter, while respecting his confidentiality.
why_wrong: A. Results are confidential and are not shared with relatives without consent, except in rare circumstances. B. There is no legal duty to inform relatives, although he will be encouraged to do so. C. He can be tested independently; there is no need for relatives to go first. E. Implications for relatives come from the shared variant, whether or not he has symptoms.
pearl: GMC guidance allows disclosure of genetic information to a relative without consent only in exceptional cases where the risk of serious harm to them outweighs the patient's right to confidentiality.
thinking: Familial pathogenic variant found ↓ He is considering predictive testing ↓ Genetic information is shared by blood relatives ↓ Result may change their risk and screening ↓ Discuss family implications before testing
