exam_trap: B, A legal duty to tell relatives — it seems right because relatives may benefit, but sharing is encouraged rather than legally required.
takeaway: Before a genetic test, explain that the result may have implications for blood relatives.

stem: A mother brings her 16-year-old son to the GP because he has become self-conscious about breast swelling that has lasted over a year. He is the tallest in his year, shaves very rarely and has been struggling with schoolwork. On examination there is bilateral gynaecomastia, his limbs are long, and both testes are small and firm. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Tall stature with long limbs, persistent gynaecomastia, poor facial hair growth and small firm testes in an adolescent male are characteristic of Klinefelter syndrome (usually 47,XXY). The testes fail, so testosterone is low and gonadotrophins are high, and mild learning difficulties are common.
why_wrong: B. Kallmann syndrome causes delayed puberty with a reduced or absent sense of smell; the testes are small and soft (prepubertal) and gonadotrophins are low, not high. C. Complete androgen insensitivity gives a female external appearance. D. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature but normal testes and no gynaecomastia. E. Hyperthyroidism can cause gynaecomastia but not small firm testes and poor virilisation.
pearl: Klinefelter syndrome is confirmed by karyotype; testosterone replacement helps virilisation and bone health, and sperm may sometimes be retrieved surgically for assisted conception.
thinking: Tall adolescent male ↓ Persistent gynaecomastia ↓ Poor facial hair ↓ Small firm testes ↓ Primary testicular failure from an extra X: Klinefelter syndrome
exam_trap: B, Kallmann syndrome — it also causes poor virilisation and can give long limbs, but it is a central (hypogonadotrophic) problem, typically with anosmia and soft prepubertal testes rather than small firm testes with gynaecomastia.
takeaway: Tall stature, gynaecomastia and small firm testes in a male suggest Klinefelter syndrome.

presentation: Congenital heart disease in Down syndrome
stem: A baby girl delivered at 38 weeks has features consistent with trisomy 21, later confirmed on rapid testing. She is feeding slowly, and on day two a soft murmur is heard. An echocardiogram is arranged before discharge from the postnatal ward. Which cardiac abnormality is most characteristically associated with her condition?
why_correct: About half of babies with Down syndrome have congenital heart disease, and the most characteristic lesion is an atrioventricular (endocardial cushion) septal defect. Because a large defect may be silent in the first days, all babies with Down syndrome should have an echocardiogram in the neonatal period.
why_wrong: B. Coarctation of the aorta is classically associated with Turner syndrome. C. Transposition is linked with maternal diabetes rather than Down syndrome. D. Hypoplastic left heart is not a characteristic association. E. Bicuspid aortic valve is associated with Turner syndrome and coarctation.
pearl: Ventricular septal defect is also common in Down syndrome, but the atrioventricular septal defect is the lesion most specifically linked with it.
thinking: Newborn with trisomy 21 ↓ Heart defects common in this condition ↓ Endocardial cushion development affected ↓ All need neonatal echocardiography ↓ Atrioventricular septal defect
exam_trap: B, Coarctation of the aorta — it is a classic syndrome-associated lesion, but it belongs to Turner syndrome, not Down syndrome.
takeaway: The congenital heart defect most characteristic of Down syndrome is an atrioventricular septal defect.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attending a contraception review is found to have a raised blood pressure on three separate readings. She has had a dull ache in both flanks for some months. Her mother started dialysis at 55, though she is unsure of the cause. Ultrasound shows both kidneys to be enlarged with numerous cysts, and there are also several cysts in the liver. Which condition is most likely?

options.E: Simple renal cysts related to age

correct_answer: C. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
why_correct: Bilateral enlarged kidneys with many cysts, liver cysts, early hypertension, flank pain and a parent who needed dialysis in middle age are typical of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. It is caused mainly by PKD1 or PKD2 variants and is the commonest inherited cause of kidney failure.
why_wrong: A. Fibromuscular dysplasia causes renovascular hypertension but does not produce kidney or liver cysts. B. Medullary sponge kidney causes small medullary cysts and stones, not enlarged cystic kidneys with a family history of kidney failure. D. Alport syndrome causes haematuria, kidney failure and hearing loss without multiple cysts. E. Simple cysts are common in older adults but do not enlarge both kidneys or explain the family history.
pearl: Hypertension in ADPKD often appears before kidney function declines, and good blood pressure control is a key part of slowing progression.
thinking: Young woman with hypertension ↓ Flank pain ↓ Parent on dialysis in middle age ↓ Enlarged cystic kidneys plus liver cysts ↓ Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
exam_trap: E, Simple age-related cysts — cysts are common incidental findings, but not multiple bilateral cysts enlarging both kidneys in a 31-year-old with a parent on dialysis.
takeaway: Enlarged kidneys with multiple bilateral cysts, hypertension and a family history of kidney failure indicate ADPKD.

stem: A 27-year-old man with cystic fibrosis tells the nurse specialist at his adult CF clinic that he and his partner have been trying for a baby for 14 months. His semen sample was of low volume and contained no sperm, but his testes are of normal size and his testosterone and gonadotrophin levels are normal. He asks why his condition has caused this. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.A: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
options.C: Primary testicular failure with absent sperm production

correct_answer: A. Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
why_correct: Almost all men with cystic fibrosis have congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, so sperm cannot reach the ejaculate even though spermatogenesis in the testes is usually normal. This explains low-volume azoospermic semen with normal testicular size and normal hormones. Sperm can often be retrieved surgically from the testis or epididymis for assisted conception.
why_wrong: B. Normal gonadotrophins and testosterone exclude pituitary failure. C. Normal testicular size and hormones indicate that sperm production is preserved. D. Retrograde ejaculation is associated with diabetes or prostate surgery and would show sperm in post-ejaculation urine, not a CF-related cause. E. Torsion is not a feature of cystic fibrosis, and his testes are of normal size.
pearl: Because sperm production is usually normal, many men with cystic fibrosis can become biological fathers using surgical sperm retrieval with ICSI; the partner should be offered CFTR carrier testing first.
thinking: Man with cystic fibrosis ↓ Low-volume semen with no sperm ↓ Normal testes and hormones ↓ Sperm made but cannot leave ↓ Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
exam_trap: C, Primary testicular failure — azoospermia suggests the testes are not working, but normal size and normal hormones show production is intact and the problem is obstruction.
takeaway: Male infertility in cystic fibrosis is usually obstructive, from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.

stem: A 44-year-old man is referred to the endocrine clinic after a wrist fracture from a fall at standing height, with a DXA scan showing osteoporosis. He is tall, has always had sparse body hair and never fathered children. His testes are small, his testosterone is low and his LH and FSH are markedly raised. A karyotype is requested. Which result is most likely?
why_correct: The combination of tall stature, small testes, infertility, low testosterone with high gonadotrophins (primary hypogonadism) and osteoporosis from long-standing androgen deficiency fits Klinefelter syndrome. It is classically caused by one extra X chromosome, giving the 47,XXY karyotype, and is often diagnosed late in adult life.
why_wrong: B. 45,X is Turner syndrome, which affects females. C. 47,XYY men are often tall but usually have normal testicular function. D. Trisomy 21 is Down syndrome. E. A normal karyotype would not explain primary testicular failure with this phenotype.
pearl: Klinefelter syndrome is under-diagnosed; many men are only identified when investigated for infertility, low testosterone or early osteoporosis.
thinking: Tall man with sparse body hair and infertility ↓ Small testes ↓ Low testosterone with high LH and FSH ↓ Primary hypogonadism with osteoporosis ↓ Extra X chromosome: 47,XXY
exam_trap: C, 47,XYY — tall stature points here too, but men with an extra Y usually have normal testosterone and testes, unlike this man.
takeaway: Klinefelter syndrome is classically caused by a 47,XXY karyotype.

stem: A 30-year-old woman attends a genetics clinic because her brother has moderate learning disability and has just been diagnosed with fragile X syndrome. Her own son is 2 years old and talking less than expected. She asks how the condition is passed on in families. Which description of its inheritance is most accurate?

options.C: Y-linked inheritance from father to son
options.D: Autosomal dominant inheritance from a single parent
options.E: X-linked inheritance of a CGG repeat expansion that can grow when passed on by a mother

correct_answer: E. X-linked inheritance of a CGG repeat expansion that can grow when passed on by a mother
why_correct: Fragile X syndrome is caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. A premutation carried by a woman can expand to a full mutation when she passes it to her children. Males, with a single X chromosome, are usually more severely affected, while females with a full mutation are often more mildly affected because of their second X. Her son should be offered testing.
why_wrong: A. FMR1 lies on the X chromosome, not an autosome, and carriers can be affected. B. It is a nuclear gene, not mitochondrial DNA. C. It is not carried on the Y chromosome, so it does not pass from father to son. D. The gene is on the X chromosome, so autosomal dominant inheritance does not describe it.
pearl: Female premutation carriers have a raised risk of premature ovarian insufficiency, and older male premutation carriers can develop fragile X-associated tremor ataxia syndrome.
thinking: Brother has fragile X ↓ FMR1 gene is on the X chromosome ↓ Caused by a CGG repeat expansion ↓ Repeat can expand when transmitted by a mother ↓ X-linked trinucleotide repeat inheritance
exam_trap: D, Autosomal dominant inheritance — females with a full mutation can be affected, which looks dominant, but the gene is on the X chromosome and the pattern is X-linked.
takeaway: Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked trinucleotide repeat disorder that can expand through maternal transmission.

stem: A 33-year-old man with Becker muscular dystrophy comes to the GP with his partner, who is 20 weeks pregnant with a boy. She is not a carrier. He is anxious that his son will inherit his condition from him. The GP reassures him that his son cannot inherit it from him. What is the reason for this?

options.A: A son receives his father's Y chromosome, not his X
options.B: The condition is carried on an autosome
options.C: Fathers pass no chromosomes to their sons
options.D: A son receives two X chromosomes from his parents
options.E: A son receives his father's X chromosome, which is protected

correct_answer: A. A son receives his father's Y chromosome, not his X
why_correct: Becker muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive. A father passes his Y chromosome to every son and his X chromosome to every daughter, so male-to-male transmission of an X-linked condition does not occur. All of his daughters, however, will be obligate carriers.
why_wrong: B. The dystrophin gene is on the X chromosome, not an autosome. C. Fathers contribute half of every child's chromosomes, including the Y to sons. D. Typical males have one X and one Y chromosome. E. Sons do not receive their father's X chromosome at all.
pearl: Absence of male-to-male transmission in a family tree is a key clue to X-linked inheritance; seeing it rules out an X-linked pattern.
thinking: Father has an X-linked recessive condition ↓ Fathers give their Y to sons ↓ Fathers give their X to daughters ↓ Son cannot inherit it from him ↓ All his daughters are obligate carriers
exam_trap: E, A son receives his father's X chromosome — confusing which sex chromosome a father passes to a son is common, but sons always receive the paternal Y.
takeaway: Fathers cannot pass X-linked conditions to their sons because sons inherit the paternal Y chromosome.

stem: An 18-year-old man with sudden painless loss of central vision in both eyes over several weeks has been diagnosed in the eye clinic with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy caused by a mitochondrial DNA variant. His mother's brother had the same problem. He asks whether he could pass the condition to children he may have in the future. Which statement best describes how such conditions are inherited?

options.A: They pass only from fathers to their children
options.B: They are always carried on the X chromosome
options.C: Both parents must be affected for a child to inherit them
options.D: Only male children can inherit them
options.E: They pass down through the maternal line

correct_answer: E. They pass down through the maternal line
why_correct: Mitochondria, and their DNA, come almost entirely from the egg, so mitochondrial disorders are passed on by mothers to children of both sexes. An affected man does not transmit mitochondrial DNA to his children, so his own offspring would not inherit the condition from him, whereas his sisters could pass it on.
why_wrong: A. Fathers do not normally transmit mitochondrial DNA. B. Mitochondrial DNA is separate from the nuclear X chromosome. C. Inheritance comes from the mother alone. D. Children of both sexes can inherit mitochondrial DNA variants, although Leber optic neuropathy shows more often in males.
pearl: Because cells contain a mixture of normal and abnormal mitochondria (heteroplasmy), severity varies widely between family members carrying the same mitochondrial variant.
thinking: Mitochondrial DNA variant identified ↓ Mitochondria come from the egg ↓ Mothers pass it to sons and daughters ↓ Affected fathers do not transmit it ↓ Maternal-line inheritance
exam_trap: D, Only male children can inherit them — Leber optic neuropathy is commoner in males, which tempts this, but both sexes inherit the variant from their mother.
takeaway: Mitochondrial disorders are inherited through the maternal line.

stem: A 29-year-old woman at her 12-week antenatal appointment says her husband, aged 38, has just been diagnosed with Huntington disease by the neurology team after developing jerky movements and irritability. She is not affected and has no family history. She asks the midwife what the chance is that the baby has inherited the faulty gene from him. What is the approximate risk?
why_correct: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant, and an affected person almost always carries one expanded and one normal copy of the HTT gene. Each child therefore has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting the expanded allele, regardless of sex. Referral to clinical genetics allows discussion of prenatal testing options.
why_wrong: A. 25% is the risk of an affected child when both parents carry an autosomal recessive condition. B. Only one of his two alleles is passed on, so transmission is not certain. C. 10% is not a Mendelian figure for this situation. D. 75% does not apply to a single heterozygous parent.
pearl: Huntington disease shows anticipation: the CAG repeat tends to expand, especially when passed on by the father, leading to earlier onset in the next generation.
thinking: Father diagnosed with Huntington disease ↓ Autosomal dominant inheritance ↓ He is heterozygous ↓ Each pregnancy receives one of his two alleles ↓ 50% risk
exam_trap: A, 25% — a quarter is a familiar inheritance figure, but it applies to two carrier parents in recessive conditions, not one affected parent with a dominant condition.
takeaway: A child of a parent with Huntington disease has a 50% chance of inheriting the expanded gene.

stem: A 33-year-old man with neurofibromatosis type 1, who has many cafe-au-lait macules and cutaneous neurofibromas, attends a dermatology follow-up appointment. He and his partner, who is unaffected, are planning to start a family. He asks what the chance is that each of their children will inherit his condition. What is the approximate risk?
why_correct: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is autosomal dominant, caused by a pathogenic variant in one copy of the NF1 gene. Each child inherits one of his two alleles, so each has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting the condition, although the severity can vary greatly even within a family.
why_wrong: A. 75% does not correspond to a single heterozygous parent. B. 25% is the risk for a child of two carriers of a recessive condition. C. He passes on only one of his two alleles to each child, so transmission is not certain. D. 10% is not a Mendelian risk.
pearl: About half of people with NF1 have a new variant with no family history, but once they have the condition they pass it on with the usual 1 in 2 risk.
thinking: Parent affected by NF1 ↓ Autosomal dominant condition ↓ One faulty and one normal allele ↓ Each child receives one allele ↓ 1 in 2 chance per child
exam_trap: B, 25% — this figure is often remembered for inherited conditions, but it applies to two carrier parents with a recessive condition.
takeaway: An affected heterozygous parent passes an autosomal dominant condition to each child with a 50% chance.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes), who has diabetes and hearing loss, attends a preconception appointment at the neurology clinic. Her husband is healthy. She asks which of her future children could inherit the condition. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Only her daughters could inherit it, as it is X-linked
options.B: Her husband would have to carry it for a child to be affected
options.C: Both her sons and her daughters could inherit it from her
options.D: Each child has exactly a 25% risk
options.E: Her children are not at risk because it skips a generation

correct_answer: C. Both her sons and her daughters could inherit it from her
why_correct: MELAS is caused by a mitochondrial DNA variant, and mitochondrial DNA is passed on through the egg. An affected mother can therefore transmit it to children of either sex. Because of heteroplasmy, the proportion of affected mitochondria and the severity in each child cannot be predicted precisely, so specialist genetic counselling is important.
why_wrong: A. Mitochondrial disorders are not X-linked, and sons can inherit them from their mother. B. Fathers do not contribute mitochondrial DNA. D. A fixed 25% risk describes an autosomal recessive pattern, not mitochondrial inheritance. E. Mitochondrial inheritance does not skip generations in a fixed way; her children are at risk.
pearl: Mitochondrial disorders commonly combine diabetes, sensorineural deafness, myopathy and neurological features, because tissues with high energy demand are most affected.
thinking: Mother with a mitochondrial disorder ↓ Mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg ↓ Passed to children of both sexes ↓ Severity varies with heteroplasmy ↓ Sons and daughters at risk
exam_trap: D, A 25% risk — a fixed Mendelian figure feels precise, but mitochondrial disorders do not follow Mendelian ratios and the risk depends on heteroplasmy.
takeaway: An affected mother can pass a mitochondrial disorder to both sons and daughters.

stem: A 44-year-old woman who has never smoked is seen in the respiratory clinic with progressive breathlessness. CT shows panacinar emphysema mainly in the lower lobes, and blood tests confirm a low alpha-1 antitrypsin level with the PiZZ phenotype. She asks whether any other organ could be affected so that it can be monitored. Which organ is most characteristically affected in this condition besides the lungs?
why_correct: In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency the abnormal Z protein is made in hepatocytes but cannot be secreted, so it accumulates in the liver and can cause hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Lack of circulating protein allows unopposed neutrophil elastase to damage the lungs, giving basal panacinar emphysema. Liver function tests and liver imaging should be part of her follow-up.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatic damage is characteristic of cystic fibrosis, not alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. C. The thyroid is not affected by this condition. D. The adrenal glands are not a recognised target. E. Cardiac disease is not a characteristic manifestation.
pearl: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can present in infancy with prolonged neonatal jaundice from cholestatic liver disease, long before any lung problem.
thinking: Never-smoker with early emphysema ↓ Lower-lobe panacinar pattern ↓ Low alpha-1 antitrypsin, PiZZ ↓ Abnormal protein trapped in hepatocytes ↓ Liver disease is the other main target
exam_trap: A, Pancreas — inherited lung disease with another organ affected brings cystic fibrosis to mind, but that is a different condition; in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency the liver is the second organ.
takeaway: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency affects the liver as well as the lungs.

stem: A 36-year-old man with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and well-controlled hypertension attends his annual renal clinic review. He explains that his mother, who also had ADPKD, survived a subarachnoid haemorrhage last year. He wants to know which condition affecting the brain he is at increased risk of because of his kidney disease. Which condition is it?
why_correct: ADPKD is associated with saccular (berry) intracranial aneurysms, which can rupture to cause subarachnoid haemorrhage. The risk is higher in people with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage, as here, so screening with MR angiography is often offered in that group even though it is not routine for every person with ADPKD.
why_wrong: A. Multiple sclerosis has no link with ADPKD. C. Myasthenia gravis is autoimmune and not associated with ADPKD. D. Motor neurone disease is not associated with ADPKD. E. Normal pressure hydrocephalus is not a recognised association.
pearl: Other extrarenal features of ADPKD include liver cysts, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula and abdominal wall hernias.
thinking: Man with ADPKD ↓ Mother with ADPKD had a subarachnoid haemorrhage ↓ ADPKD linked with berry aneurysms ↓ Family history of haemorrhage raises his risk ↓ Intracranial aneurysm
exam_trap: A, Multiple sclerosis — a young adult asking about a brain condition may prompt this, but it has no association with polycystic kidney disease.
takeaway: ADPKD is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms, particularly when relatives have had a subarachnoid haemorrhage.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is reviewed by a community paediatrician because of global learning difficulties and poor eye contact. His teacher reports hand-flapping and that he becomes very distressed by noise. On examination he has a long narrow face, prominent ears and very flexible finger joints. His maternal uncle also needed special schooling. Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: Learning disability with autistic features, a long face, large prominent ears and joint hypermobility in a boy suggest fragile X syndrome. An affected maternal uncle supports an X-linked condition passed through the female line. It is the commonest inherited cause of learning disability, and DNA testing for the FMR1 repeat expansion confirms it.
why_wrong: A. NF1 causes cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, which are not described. B. Down syndrome has a different facial appearance with upslanting eyes and a flat face, and is rarely inherited from a maternal uncle's line. D. Klinefelter syndrome usually causes milder learning problems with tall stature and small testes, mostly recognised at puberty. E. Tuberous sclerosis causes seizures, ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas.
pearl: Macro-orchidism is a classic feature of fragile X syndrome but usually only becomes obvious after puberty, so its absence in a young boy does not exclude the diagnosis.
thinking: Boy with learning disability ↓ Autistic features ↓ Long face, large ears, hypermobile joints ↓ Affected maternal uncle suggests X-linked inheritance ↓ Fragile X syndrome
exam_trap: D, Klinefelter syndrome — it is another sex chromosome condition linked with learning difficulty in boys, but it does not cause this facial appearance or a maternal-line family pattern.
takeaway: Learning disability, autistic features, a long face and large ears in a boy suggest fragile X syndrome.

stem: The parents of a 3-week-old baby boy receive a phone call from the specialist team because his newborn blood spot test showed a raised immunoreactive trypsinogen and a result suggesting cystic fibrosis. He is feeding well and gaining weight. His mother asks the GP the next morning whether this means her son definitely has the condition. What is the most accurate explanation?

options.A: Yes, the blood spot test confirms the diagnosis
options.B: Treatment should begin straight away without any further tests
options.C: The blood spot test should simply be repeated when he is one year old
options.D: Further diagnostic testing, such as a sweat test, is needed to confirm or exclude it
options.E: A positive screening result means his disease will be severe

correct_answer: D. Further diagnostic testing, such as a sweat test, is needed to confirm or exclude it
why_correct: Newborn screening identifies babies at higher likelihood of a condition, but a positive screen is not a diagnosis. For cystic fibrosis, babies with a positive screen are referred quickly to a specialist centre for a sweat test, which confirms or excludes the diagnosis, and some screen-positive babies turn out to be carriers or unaffected.
why_wrong: A. A screening test is not diagnostic and has false positives. B. Treatment decisions follow diagnostic confirmation at the specialist centre. C. Waiting a year would delay care for a condition that benefits from early treatment. E. A positive screen gives no information about severity.
pearl: Screening tests are designed to be highly sensitive so that few cases are missed, which means some positive results will be false positives that need confirmatory testing.
thinking: Baby has a positive newborn blood spot result ↓ Screening estimates likelihood, not diagnosis ↓ False positives and carriers occur ↓ Confirm with a diagnostic test ↓ Sweat test at the specialist centre
exam_trap: A, The blood spot confirms the diagnosis — parents and clinicians often treat a positive screen as final, but screening only selects who needs a diagnostic test.
takeaway: A positive newborn screening result needs confirmatory diagnostic testing before a diagnosis is made.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is seen by a physiotherapist after her third shoulder dislocation this year, each one occurring with minimal force. She mentions that small cuts on her shins leave wide, thin, papery scars and that she bruises after the slightest knock. Her skin can be pulled well away from the forearm and springs straight back. She is of average height and has never broken a bone. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
why_correct: Recurrent dislocations from joint hypermobility, soft hyperextensible skin, easy bruising and wide atrophic scars together point to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a group of inherited collagen disorders. The combination of joint, skin and tissue-fragility features is the key, rather than any one finding alone. Normal height and no fractures make the main alternatives less likely.
why_wrong: A. Marfan syndrome causes hypermobility with tall stature and long limbs, but not markedly stretchy skin with papery scars. B. Systemic sclerosis makes the skin thick and tight, the opposite of what is seen here. C. Osteogenesis imperfecta presents with recurrent fractures and blue sclerae, and she has never broken a bone. D. Rheumatoid arthritis causes inflammatory synovitis and stiffness, not lax joints and fragile skin.
pearl: The vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1) carries a risk of arterial, bowel and uterine rupture, so thin translucent skin with visible veins and severe bruising should prompt specialist referral.
thinking: Recurrent low-energy dislocations ↓ Hyperextensible skin that recoils ↓ Easy bruising and wide atrophic scars ↓ Normal height, no fractures ↓ Inherited collagen disorder: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
exam_trap: A, Marfan syndrome — hypermobility is the shared feature, but Marfan is defined by tall stature, aortic root disease and lens problems, not stretchy skin and papery scars.
takeaway: Hypermobile joints plus stretchy, fragile skin with poor scarring suggests Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after splitting his chin on a playground step. The wound gapes widely, and the nurse notices several thin, shiny scars on his knees from earlier falls. His joints bend well beyond the normal range, and he bruises easily. His father, who came with him, says he has always been 'double-jointed' and also scars badly. Into which broad group of disorders does this picture most likely fall?
why_correct: Generalised joint laxity, easy bruising and wounds that gape and heal with thin scars all reflect weak collagen-containing tissues. A parent with the same lifelong features suggests an inherited cause. Together these place him in the group of heritable connective tissue disorders, such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Primary immunodeficiency causes recurrent or unusual infections, not lax joints and poor scarring. B. An eye disorder alone cannot explain joint, skin and wound-healing features. D. A nutritional deficiency would not give lifelong identical features in father and son. E. Functional disorders do not produce objective joint laxity, gaping wounds or abnormal scars.
pearl: Unexplained bruising in a child always needs safeguarding to be considered, but a consistent lifelong pattern of tissue fragility with a similarly affected parent supports an inherited connective tissue cause.
thinking: Gaping wound and thin shiny scars ↓ Generalised joint laxity ↓ Easy bruising ↓ Father has the same lifelong features ↓ Heritable connective tissue disorder
exam_trap: A, Primary immunodeficiency — a child presenting repeatedly to hospital may suggest an underlying immune problem, but nothing here points to infection.
takeaway: Lax joints, easy bruising and poor scarring running in a family suggest a heritable connective tissue disorder.

stem: A 34-year-old woman attends her antenatal booking visit at 10 weeks. The midwife notices several bruises on her thighs, which she says appear after very minor bumps and always have. She can touch the floor with her palms flat and bend her thumbs back to her forearms. Her mother has the same flexibility and also bruises easily. A full blood count and clotting screen taken today are normal. Which type of disorder is most likely?
why_correct: Lifelong easy bruising with generalised joint hypermobility and an affected mother suggests a heritable connective tissue disorder. Normal blood count and clotting point away from a platelet or coagulation problem, so the bruising is better explained by fragile tissues and blood vessels. Recognising this in pregnancy matters for planning delivery and wound care.
why_wrong: A. Immune thrombocytopenia would show a low platelet count and does not cause hypermobility. B. Scurvy causes bruising and gum bleeding from poor diet, not lifelong familial joint laxity. C. Acute leukaemia would usually produce an abnormal blood count and systemic illness. E. Inflammatory arthritis causes painful, stiff, swollen joints rather than increased range of movement.
pearl: Bruising with normal platelets and clotting should make you think of vessel or connective tissue fragility, including inherited conditions such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
thinking: Lifelong easy bruising ↓ Marked generalised hypermobility ↓ Mother similarly affected ↓ Normal platelets and clotting ↓ Heritable connective tissue disorder
exam_trap: A, Immune thrombocytopenia — bruising in pregnancy commonly prompts thoughts of low platelets, but her count is normal and ITP does not explain the joints or the family pattern.
takeaway: Familial hypermobility with easy bruising and normal blood tests suggests a heritable connective tissue disorder.

stem: A 14-month-old boy is brought to the GP because his right knee became hot, tense and swollen the day after he tumbled while learning to walk. He cries when the leg is moved. A large firm bruise developed on his thigh after his routine immunisations. His mother says her brother 'bleeds for days' after any injury and her maternal grandfather had a similar problem. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: A bleed into a joint after trivial trauma, deep bruising after an intramuscular injection and affected males on the mother's side suggest an X-linked clotting factor deficiency. Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is the commonest and classically presents when a boy starts crawling or walking. It causes deep tissue and joint bleeding rather than the skin petechiae seen with platelet problems.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency anaemia causes pallor and tiredness, not bleeding into joints. C. Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive and causes painful vaso-occlusive crises, such as dactylitis, rather than haemarthrosis. D. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis with jaundice and anaemia, not joint bleeds. E. Immune thrombocytopenia causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding and does not affect male relatives in an X-linked pattern.
pearl: In haemophilia the APTT is prolonged while the platelet count and PT are normal; intramuscular injections should be given carefully and joint bleeds treated promptly with factor replacement.
thinking: Haemarthrosis after trivial fall ↓ Deep bruise after injection ↓ Affected maternal male relatives ↓ X-linked clotting factor deficiency ↓ Haemophilia A
exam_trap: E, Immune thrombocytopenia — it is a common cause of bruising in toddlers, but it causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding, not joint bleeds, and has no X-linked family pattern.
takeaway: A boy with a haemarthrosis and affected maternal uncles most likely has haemophilia.

stem: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the memory clinic by her husband. Over two years she has become irritable and disorganised, and she now has restless, flowing, purposeless movements of her face and hands that she seems unaware of. Her mother died in a nursing home in her sixties after a similar illness. Which pattern of inheritance does the most likely condition follow?
why_correct: Chorea, personality change and cognitive decline in mid-life with an affected parent fits Huntington disease. It is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant way, so each child of an affected person has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it. Both sexes are affected and it can pass from either parent.
why_wrong: A. Mitochondrial disorders pass only through the mother but typically cause myopathy, deafness or stroke-like episodes, not adult-onset chorea with dementia. B. X-linked recessive disorders mainly affect males and are not passed from mother to daughter as an illness. C. Autosomal recessive conditions usually skip generations and affected parents are uncommon. E. Y-linked inheritance would affect only males.
pearl: Huntington disease shows anticipation: the CAG repeat tends to expand when passed on, especially through the father, causing earlier onset in later generations.
thinking: Mid-life chorea ↓ Behavioural change and cognitive decline ↓ Affected parent, female patient ↓ Huntington disease ↓ Autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion
exam_trap: A, Mitochondrial — the illness came through her mother, which tempts maternal inheritance, but Huntington disease can be passed on by either parent.
takeaway: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant: each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk.

stem: A baby girl is admitted to the neonatal unit shortly after birth because she is very small for her gestational age and feeding poorly. Examination shows a prominent back of the head, a small jaw, fists held tightly with the index finger overlapping the middle finger, and soles that are rounded rather than flat. A loud murmur suggests a ventricular septal defect. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Growth restriction, a prominent occiput, micrognathia, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet and a heart defect are the classic findings of Edwards syndrome. It results from trisomy 18 and carries a very poor prognosis, with most babies dying in the first year. The overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet are the most specific clues.
why_wrong: A. Trisomy 21 gives hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease rather than clenched overlapping fingers. B. Trisomy 13 typically causes cleft lip and palate, scalp defects, small eyes and extra digits. C. 45,X causes Turner syndrome with lymphoedema of the hands and feet and a webbed neck. E. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, which affects males and is rarely recognisable at birth.
pearl: Edwards syndrome is screened for in the first trimester combined test alongside Down and Patau syndromes in the NHS fetal anomaly screening programme.
thinking: Growth restriction and poor feeding ↓ Prominent occiput, small jaw ↓ Clenched hands, overlapping fingers ↓ Rocker-bottom feet and VSD ↓ Trisomy 18
exam_trap: B, Trisomy 13 — it is the other severe trisomy and also causes heart defects, but its hallmarks are midline defects such as cleft lip and extra digits.
takeaway: Clenched hands with overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet suggest trisomy 18.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is reviewed by a community paediatrician because of rapid weight gain. His parents now lock the kitchen cupboards because he searches for food at night. As a newborn he was so floppy and weak at sucking that he needed tube feeding for several weeks. He has small hands and feet, almond-shaped eyes and had bilateral undescended testes corrected surgically. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Severe neonatal hypotonia with feeding difficulty, followed in early childhood by an insatiable appetite and obesity, is the classic two-phase course of Prader-Willi syndrome. Small hands and feet, almond-shaped eyes and hypogonadism such as undescended testes add support. It results from loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-13.
why_wrong: A. Klinefelter syndrome causes tall stature and small testes in adolescence, not infant hypotonia followed by hyperphagia. B. Fragile X causes learning difficulty, a long face and large ears, but not this feeding pattern. C. Turner syndrome affects girls. D. Marfan syndrome produces tall stature and connective tissue features rather than obesity.
pearl: Prader-Willi syndrome is usually due to deletion of the paternal 15q11-13 region or maternal uniparental disomy; the same region lost from the mother causes Angelman syndrome.
thinking: Floppy newborn needing tube feeds ↓ Later uncontrolled food seeking ↓ Obesity ↓ Small hands, almond eyes, undescended testes ↓ Prader-Willi syndrome
exam_trap: B, Fragile X syndrome — it is the commonest inherited cause of learning difficulty in boys, but it does not give early hypotonia followed by hyperphagia.
takeaway: Floppy feeding problems in infancy followed by insatiable appetite suggests Prader-Willi syndrome.

stem: Two weeks after his sister was treated for ovarian cancer and found to have a BRCA1 fault, a 39-year-old builder agreed to be tested too. The result confirms he shares it. He has no symptoms and has two young daughters. Sitting in the clinical genetics department, he wants to understand the implications. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: He cannot pass the variant on because it is only significant in women
options.B: He definitely has a cancer that has not yet been found
options.C: Each of his children has a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting it
options.D: It raises his inherited risk of some cancers but does not mean he will develop cancer
options.E: It mainly raises his risk of bowel cancer

correct_answer: D. It raises his inherited risk of some cancers but does not mean he will develop cancer
why_correct: A pathogenic BRCA1 variant increases lifetime risk of certain cancers but is not a diagnosis of cancer and does not make cancer inevitable. In men it modestly raises the risk of breast and prostate cancer. It is autosomal dominant, so he can pass it to sons and daughters, each with a 1 in 2 chance.
why_wrong: A. Men can carry and transmit BRCA1 variants to children of either sex. B. Carrying a variant is a risk factor, not evidence of current cancer. C. Autosomal dominant inheritance gives each child a 1 in 2 chance, not 1 in 4. E. BRCA1 mainly affects breast, ovarian and prostate cancer risk rather than bowel cancer.
pearl: Male BRCA carriers have an increased risk of male breast cancer and prostate cancer, and their daughters should be offered genetic counselling and testing when they reach adulthood.
thinking: Carrier result on predictive testing ↓ He is currently well ↓ Variant means increased risk, not certainty ↓ Autosomal dominant, either sex passes it on ↓ Each child 1 in 2
exam_trap: A, He cannot pass the variant on because it is only significant in women — BRCA is linked in many minds with breast and ovarian cancer in women, but men carry and transmit it just as often.
takeaway: A pathogenic BRCA1 variant raises cancer risk in either sex and can be passed on by fathers as well as mothers.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has a routine blood test at her GP surgery before starting the combined pill and is found to have a very high LDL cholesterol. She is slim, does not smoke and eats a healthy diet. She has a pale ring around the edge of both irises. Her mother died suddenly of a heart attack at 46, and her maternal aunt had coronary stents at 50. Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: A very high LDL cholesterol in a young, lean, healthy adult with premature coronary disease in first-degree relatives points to familial hypercholesterolaemia. Corneal arcus at a young age is a supportive sign. It is usually an autosomal dominant defect of the LDL receptor pathway, and NICE advises using the Simon Broome or Dutch Lipid Clinic criteria and offering cascade testing of relatives.
why_wrong: A. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can cause sudden death in families but does not raise LDL cholesterol. B. Marfan syndrome causes aortic root dilatation and dissection, not hyperlipidaemia. D. Haemophilia A is an X-linked bleeding disorder unrelated to lipids. E. Addison disease causes adrenal insufficiency and does not explain very high LDL.
pearl: Familial hypercholesterolaemia should be treated with high-intensity statin from diagnosis and first-degree relatives offered cascade testing, as early treatment largely removes the excess coronary risk.
thinking: Very high LDL in a lean young adult ↓ Corneal arcus under 45 ↓ Premature coronary events in mother and aunt ↓ Dominant family pattern ↓ Familial hypercholesterolaemia
exam_trap: A, Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — a parent's sudden cardiac death at a young age suggests an inherited cardiac condition, but HCM does not explain the very high LDL.
takeaway: Very high LDL with premature coronary disease in close relatives suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia.

stem: A 30-year-old man with acute intermittent porphyria, diagnosed after his sister had the same condition, attends the GP surgery for advice on preventing further attacks. His last admission involved severe abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion and leg weakness. He wants to know which factor he should be most careful about in day-to-day life. Which of the following is a recognised precipitant of acute attacks?
why_correct: Acute intermittent porphyria attacks are precipitated by factors that increase hepatic haem synthesis, through induction of ALA synthase. Many medicines do this, which is why every new drug should be checked against a porphyria-safe drug list. Other triggers include alcohol, fasting, hormonal changes, infection and stress.
why_wrong: A. Sunlight causes skin blistering in the cutaneous porphyrias, but acute intermittent porphyria has no skin involvement. B. Fava beans trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. C. Carbohydrate intake is protective and glucose is used to treat mild attacks, whereas fasting is the trigger. D. Cold precipitates Raynaud phenomenon and cold agglutinin haemolysis, not porphyria attacks.
pearl: Attacks are treated with intravenous haem arginate, and carbohydrate loading is used for mild attacks, because both suppress ALA synthase.
thinking: Known acute intermittent porphyria ↓ Attacks follow increased hepatic haem demand ↓ ALA synthase induction ↓ Many drugs induce it ↓ Certain medicines are a key precipitant
exam_trap: A, Exposure to strong sunlight — porphyria is strongly associated with photosensitivity, but that applies to the cutaneous types, not acute intermittent porphyria.
takeaway: Certain medicines, alcohol and fasting can precipitate acute porphyria attacks; check every new drug against a safety list.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department with severe central abdominal pain, vomiting, dark urine and weakness of both arms. She also seems anxious and briefly hallucinated overnight. Acute intermittent porphyria is suspected and the ward team is writing her drug chart. Which of the following should be avoided?

options.D: A medicine listed as porphyrinogenic, such as certain anticonvulsants

correct_answer: D. A medicine listed as porphyrinogenic, such as certain anticonvulsants
why_correct: Porphyrinogenic medicines induce hepatic ALA synthase and can worsen or prolong an acute attack, so they must be avoided. Many anticonvulsants, some antibiotics and hormonal preparations fall into this group, and the UK porphyria drug database should be checked before prescribing. Opioids, paracetamol and intravenous glucose are generally regarded as safe.
why_wrong: A. Glucose suppresses ALA synthase and is part of supportive treatment. B. Morphine is considered safe and is commonly needed for the severe pain. C. Paracetamol is considered safe in acute porphyria. E. Sodium chloride is safe and may be needed because hyponatraemia is common in attacks.
pearl: Hyponatraemia from SIADH is common in acute porphyria attacks and can cause seizures; managing these is challenging because many anticonvulsants are themselves porphyrinogenic.
thinking: Abdominal pain, dark urine, motor neuropathy ↓ Psychiatric symptoms ↓ Suspected acute porphyria ↓ Drugs that induce ALA synthase worsen attacks ↓ Avoid porphyrinogenic medicines
exam_trap: B, Morphine for pain — opioids feel risky in someone with neuropsychiatric symptoms, but they are considered safe in porphyria and adequate analgesia is essential.
takeaway: In suspected acute porphyria, check every medicine against a porphyria-safe list and avoid porphyrinogenic drugs.

stem: A 9-year-old girl of Turkish heritage is reviewed in the paediatric outpatient clinic. Since the age of four she has had attacks every few weeks of high fever with sharp pain in one side of her chest or across her abdomen, each settling on its own within two to three days. Between attacks she is completely well and her inflammatory markers return to normal. Her parents are related, and her older brother has had similar attacks. Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: Short, self-limiting episodes of fever with serositis such as pleurisy or peritonitis, complete recovery between attacks and normal inflammatory markers in between suggest familial Mediterranean fever. It is an autosomal recessive autoinflammatory disease (MEFV gene), more common in Turkish, Armenian, Arab and Sephardic Jewish populations. Consanguineous parents and an affected sibling fit recessive inheritance.
why_wrong: A. Crohn disease causes ongoing gut symptoms, weight loss and growth failure rather than brief febrile attacks with full recovery. B. Hereditary angioedema causes afebrile swelling and abdominal pain, not fever with pleurisy. C. Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome does not cause fever or chest pain. E. Ulcerative colitis presents with bloody diarrhoea rather than episodic fever and serositis.
pearl: Daily colchicine prevents attacks and, importantly, protects against AA amyloidosis, the main long-term cause of kidney failure in familial Mediterranean fever.
thinking: Recurrent fever lasting 2 to 3 days ↓ Pleuritic or abdominal serositis ↓ Fully well between attacks ↓ Turkish heritage, consanguinity, affected sibling ↓ Familial Mediterranean fever
exam_trap: B, Hereditary angioedema — it also causes recurrent abdominal pain and runs in families, but attacks are afebrile swellings, not fever with serositis.
takeaway: Recurrent short febrile attacks of serositis in a child of Mediterranean ancestry suggest familial Mediterranean fever.

stem: A 34-year-old man attends the emergency department the morning after a dental extraction with marked swelling of his face and tongue. There is no itch and no rash. He has had several previous episodes of painless swelling of his hands and one admission with severe abdominal pain, and treatment with antihistamines made no difference. His mother has had similar swellings. He takes no regular medicines. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent non-itchy swelling without urticaria, abdominal attacks, poor response to antihistamines and an affected parent suggest hereditary angioedema. It is usually due to an autosomal dominant deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor, causing bradykinin-mediated swelling. Dental procedures and minor trauma are classic triggers, and airway swelling can be life-threatening.
why_wrong: B. Chronic spontaneous urticaria causes itchy wheals that respond to antihistamines. C. Allergic contact dermatitis causes an itchy eczematous rash, not deep swelling. D. Anaphylaxis would be rapid in onset with urticaria, wheeze or hypotension, and does not run in families with recurrent abdominal attacks. E. Haemochromatosis causes iron overload, not episodic swelling.
pearl: Screen with a serum C4 level, which is low during and usually between attacks; acute attacks are treated with C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant, not adrenaline or antihistamines.
thinking: Swelling after dental work ↓ No itch or urticaria ↓ Previous limb and abdominal attacks ↓ No response to antihistamines, mother affected ↓ Hereditary angioedema
exam_trap: D, Anaphylaxis to latex — dental work involves gloves, but anaphylaxis brings urticaria and rapid onset, and does not explain years of familial swelling episodes.
takeaway: Recurrent non-itchy swelling and abdominal pain unresponsive to antihistamines with a family history suggests hereditary angioedema.

stem: An 11-year-old girl is referred to the dermatology clinic with small, firm, pinkish bumps across her nose and cheeks that have not improved with acne treatment. She had spasms as a baby that were treated in hospital, still has occasional seizures, and attends a special school. On examination there are also flesh-coloured growths beside several toenails. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Facial angiofibromas over the nose and cheeks, periungual fibromas, epilepsy beginning with infantile spasms and learning difficulty are classic features of tuberous sclerosis. It is an autosomal dominant condition caused by TSC1 or TSC2 variants, causing benign hamartomas in many organs. The facial papules are often mistaken for acne.
why_wrong: A. Sturge-Weber syndrome causes seizures with a facial port-wine stain, not angiofibromas. B. Down syndrome causes learning difficulty but not facial angiofibromas or nail-fold fibromas. C. Fragile X causes learning difficulty with a long face and large ears but no skin hamartomas. D. Neurofibromatosis type 1 causes café-au-lait macules, freckling and neurofibromas.
pearl: Tuberous sclerosis also causes renal angiomyolipomas and cardiac rhabdomyomas; the latter may be the first sign on antenatal scans.
thinking: Facial papules not responding to acne treatment ↓ Periungual fibromas ↓ Infantile spasms and ongoing epilepsy ↓ Learning difficulty ↓ Tuberous sclerosis
exam_trap: D, Neurofibromatosis type 1 — it is the best-known neurocutaneous syndrome, but its skin signs are café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, not angiofibromas.
takeaway: Facial angiofibromas with epilepsy and learning difficulty suggest tuberous sclerosis.

stem: An 8-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents, who filmed him having clusters of sudden jerks in which he flexes his trunk and throws his arms out, several times a day. He has stopped babbling and is less interested in toys. Examination shows several pale, leaf-shaped patches on his back and legs, which are more obvious under a Wood's lamp. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Infantile spasms with developmental regression and several hypomelanotic 'ash-leaf' macules, best seen under a Wood's lamp, suggest tuberous sclerosis. These pale patches are often the earliest skin sign, appearing before facial angiofibromas. Tuberous sclerosis is one of the commonest identifiable causes of infantile spasms.
why_wrong: A. Sturge-Weber syndrome causes seizures with a port-wine stain on the face, not pale macules. C. Neurofibromatosis type 1 gives darker café-au-lait macules rather than pale patches. D. Down syndrome has characteristic facial features and does not cause hypomelanotic macules. E. Vitiligo produces depigmented patches but does not cause seizures or regression.
pearl: Vigabatrin is the first-line treatment for infantile spasms caused by tuberous sclerosis.
thinking: Clusters of flexor spasms ↓ Developmental regression ↓ Pale leaf-shaped macules ↓ Enhanced by Wood's lamp ↓ Tuberous sclerosis
exam_trap: E, Vitiligo — pale patches on the skin bring vitiligo to mind, but it does not cause infantile spasms, and the leaf shape is typical of tuberous sclerosis.
takeaway: Infantile spasms with ash-leaf macules suggest tuberous sclerosis.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is referred to the adolescent clinic by her GP because she has never had a period. She is well below her mother's and sister's height. As a baby she had puffy feet and had surgery for narrowing of the aorta. Breast development has not begun, and she has a low hairline at the back of the neck. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Short stature, primary amenorrhoea and absent breast development from ovarian failure, with neonatal lymphoedema and coarctation of the aorta, are typical of Turner syndrome. It affects girls with a missing or abnormal X chromosome. Gonadotrophins are raised because the ovaries fail, and karyotyping confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Klinefelter syndrome affects males and causes tall stature. B. Fragile X syndrome mainly causes learning difficulties and does not cause ovarian failure with coarctation. C. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature and normal puberty. D. Down syndrome has characteristic facial features and learning difficulty, not this pattern of gonadal failure.
pearl: Girls with Turner syndrome need lifelong cardiac surveillance because of bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation and a risk of aortic dissection, especially in pregnancy.
thinking: Short for family ↓ Primary amenorrhoea and no breast development ↓ Neonatal lymphoedema ↓ Repaired coarctation ↓ Turner syndrome
exam_trap: A, Klinefelter syndrome — it is the other common sex chromosome disorder causing hypogonadism, but it occurs in males and causes tall stature.
takeaway: Short stature with absent puberty, coarctation and neonatal lymphoedema suggests Turner syndrome.

stem: On the postnatal ward, a midwife asks for a review of a newborn girl because her hands and feet are puffy and swollen. The baby has loose skin folds at the side of the neck and her femoral pulses are hard to feel. Turner syndrome is suspected. Which karyotype is most typical of this condition?
why_correct: Turner syndrome results from complete or partial loss of one X chromosome, most classically giving the karyotype 45,X. In the newborn it may present with lymphoedema of the hands and feet and neck webbing, and weak femoral pulses suggest coarctation of the aorta. Some girls are mosaic, for example 45,X/46,XX, and have milder features.
why_wrong: A. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, which affects males. B. Trisomy 18 causes Edwards syndrome with clenched hands and rocker-bottom feet. C. 47,XXX is triple X syndrome, often with tall stature and few physical signs. E. Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome with hypotonia and characteristic facial features.
pearl: Turner syndrome is a sex chromosome monosomy; it is the only monosomy compatible with life.
thinking: Newborn girl with lymphoedema of hands and feet ↓ Neck skin folds ↓ Weak femoral pulses, likely coarctation ↓ Turner syndrome ↓ 45,X
exam_trap: C, 47,XXX — it is also a sex chromosome abnormality in girls, but having an extra X usually causes few physical signs.
takeaway: Turner syndrome is classically 45,X, a missing X chromosome.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is seen by his GP for a routine review. His head is large with a prominent forehead and a flattened nasal bridge, and his arms and legs are noticeably short, especially the upper arms and thighs, while his trunk is of normal length. His hands are short with a gap between the middle and ring fingers. His development is otherwise normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Disproportionate short stature with short proximal limbs, a normal-length trunk, macrocephaly with frontal bossing and trident-shaped hands is classic achondroplasia. It is caused by a gain-of-function variant in FGFR3, which impairs endochondral bone growth. It is autosomal dominant but most cases arise from new variants with unaffected parents.
why_wrong: A. Turner syndrome causes proportionate short stature in girls. B. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature with long limbs. C. Down syndrome causes hypotonia, learning difficulty and characteristic facial features, not short-limbed disproportionate short stature. E. Osteogenesis imperfecta causes fragile bones with fractures and blue sclerae.
pearl: Infants with achondroplasia are at risk of foramen magnum narrowing, which can cause compression of the brainstem and sleep apnoea, so they need monitoring.
thinking: Short limbs, normal trunk ↓ Proximal limb shortening ↓ Large head with frontal bossing ↓ Trident hands, normal development ↓ Achondroplasia
exam_trap: A, Turner syndrome — it is a classic cause of short stature, but it affects girls and the shortening is proportionate.
takeaway: Short-limbed disproportionate short stature with macrocephaly suggests achondroplasia.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the GP because his mother is worried about the number of light-brown flat patches on his body. There are eight of them, several larger than a 5p coin, and he also has clusters of small brown freckles in both groins. He is otherwise healthy, with normal development and no early signs of puberty. Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: Six or more café-au-lait macules with freckling in the axillae or groins are key diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1. It is an autosomal dominant disorder of the NF1 gene, which encodes neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor. Neurofibromas and Lisch nodules usually appear later in childhood.
why_wrong: A. Tuberous sclerosis gives pale ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas rather than café-au-lait patches with freckling. B. McCune-Albright syndrome causes a few large irregular patches with fibrous dysplasia and early puberty, not groin freckling. C. Down syndrome is not associated with multiple café-au-lait macules. D. Turner syndrome is a sex chromosome disorder of girls with short stature.
pearl: Children with NF1 need annual review including blood pressure, vision and development, as optic pathway gliomas and phaeochromocytoma can occur.
thinking: Multiple café-au-lait macules ↓ More than six, several large ↓ Inguinal freckling ↓ No precocious puberty ↓ Neurofibromatosis type 1
exam_trap: B, McCune-Albright syndrome — it also causes café-au-lait patches, but they are few, large and irregular, with fibrous dysplasia and precocious puberty.
takeaway: Multiple café-au-lait macules with axillary or groin freckling suggests neurofibromatosis type 1.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is treated in the emergency department for a spontaneous left pneumothorax. He is very tall and thin, his arm span is greater than his height, and he can wrap his thumb and little finger around his opposite wrist with them overlapping. He has a sunken sternum and does well at school. His paternal uncle died suddenly at 38 from a tear in the aorta. Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: Tall stature with long limbs, arachnodactyly shown by the wrist sign, pectus excavatum and spontaneous pneumothorax are typical of Marfan syndrome. A relative's early death from aortic dissection supports an autosomal dominant fibrillin-1 disorder. Normal intellect helps separate it from homocystinuria.
why_wrong: A. Klinefelter syndrome causes tall stature with small testes and hypogonadism, but not arachnodactyly or familial aortic dissection. B. Homocystinuria gives a similar body shape but usually with learning difficulty and thromboses, and is autosomal recessive. C. Turner syndrome causes short stature in girls. D. Fragile X causes learning difficulty and is not linked with aortic dissection.
pearl: Diagnosis of Marfan syndrome uses the revised Ghent criteria, in which aortic root dilatation and ectopia lentis carry the most weight.
thinking: Tall with arm span exceeding height ↓ Positive wrist sign, pectus excavatum ↓ Spontaneous pneumothorax ↓ Relative died of aortic dissection, normal intellect ↓ Marfan syndrome
exam_trap: B, Homocystinuria — the body shape is similar, but it typically brings learning difficulty and thromboses and is not inherited in a dominant pattern.
takeaway: Tall stature, long fingers and a family history of aortic dissection suggest Marfan syndrome.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome attends a pre-pregnancy counselling clinic because she and her partner hope to start a family. She is well and has a lens problem in one eye, treated in childhood. She wants to know which heart or vessel problem is the main concern for her during pregnancy and in the long term. Which complication is most important?
why_correct: The defining cardiovascular problem in Marfan syndrome is progressive dilatation of the aortic root, which can lead to aortic dissection or rupture. Pregnancy increases this risk because of haemodynamic and hormonal changes, so aortic root size is measured before conception and monitored throughout. Beta-blockers and planned surgical repair reduce the risk.
why_wrong: B. Venous thromboembolism risk rises in any pregnancy but is not the characteristic Marfan complication. C. Mitral stenosis is usually rheumatic; Marfan syndrome causes mitral valve prolapse instead. D. Coarctation is associated with Turner syndrome. E. A ventricular septal defect is a congenital defect not typical of Marfan syndrome.
pearl: In Marfan syndrome, mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation is common, but the life-threatening complication is aortic dissection.
thinking: Known Marfan syndrome ↓ Fibrillin defect weakens the aortic wall ↓ Progressive aortic root dilatation ↓ Pregnancy increases dissection risk ↓ Aortic root is the priority
exam_trap: B, Pulmonary embolism — pregnancy makes clotting a natural worry, but it is a general pregnancy risk rather than the specific danger in Marfan syndrome.
takeaway: In Marfan syndrome the key cardiovascular risk is aortic root dilatation leading to dissection.

stem: A 10-year-old girl with Marfan syndrome is referred by her optician because her vision has become blurred and fluctuates. On slit-lamp examination the edge of the lens can be seen through the pupil, displaced upwards and outwards, and the iris trembles slightly when she moves her eye. What is the name of this finding?
why_correct: A lens that has shifted from its normal central position is called ectopia lentis. In Marfan syndrome the zonular fibres holding the lens are weak, so it typically moves upwards and outwards. Trembling of the iris (iridodonesis) occurs because the lens no longer supports it.
why_wrong: A. A cataract is clouding of the lens, not displacement. C. Keratoconus is a conical thinning of the cornea. D. Retinal detachment involves the retina separating from the back of the eye, which is a recognised risk in Marfan syndrome but not this finding. E. Optic neuritis is inflammation of the optic nerve with painful loss of vision.
pearl: In Marfan syndrome the lens usually dislocates upwards and outwards, whereas in homocystinuria it tends to dislocate downwards and inwards.
thinking: Known Marfan syndrome ↓ Blurred, fluctuating vision ↓ Lens edge visible through the pupil ↓ Lens displaced up and out, iris trembling ↓ Ectopia lentis
exam_trap: D, Retinal detachment — it is genuinely more common in Marfan syndrome, but the finding here is a displaced lens, not a detached retina.
takeaway: Displacement of the lens, typically upward in Marfan syndrome, is called ectopia lentis.

presentation: X-linked recessive inheritance from a father
stem: A 32-year-old man with Becker muscular dystrophy attends genetic counselling with his wife, who has no family history of muscle disease. His own mother was found to be a carrier. They are planning children and ask which relatives could receive his altered X chromosome from him directly. Which of the following will always inherit it from him?
why_correct: A man has one X chromosome, which he passes to every daughter, while every son receives his Y chromosome. So all his daughters will be obligate carriers of the Becker variant, and none of his sons will be affected by it. His daughters' sons will then each have a 1 in 2 chance of being affected.
why_wrong: A. All of his daughters inherit his X chromosome. B. Sons receive his Y chromosome, so cannot inherit an X-linked variant from him. C. His nephew receives his X chromosome from his own mother, not from his uncle. D. A parent cannot inherit a variant from his child.
pearl: X-linked recessive conditions never pass from father to son; male-to-male transmission in a family excludes X-linked inheritance.
thinking: Affected man has one X chromosome ↓ Daughters receive his X ↓ Sons receive his Y ↓ So all daughters are carriers ↓ Sons unaffected by his variant
exam_trap: B, Any son he has — sons are the ones who show X-linked disease, so they seem at highest risk, but they inherit their father's Y, not his X.
takeaway: An affected man passes an X-linked variant to all his daughters and none of his sons.

stem: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and protein in her urine calls the GP surgery because of a tickly, dry cough that has kept her awake for several weeks. It began shortly after a new tablet was added for her blood pressure and kidneys. She has no fever, breathlessness or sputum and her chest sounds clear. Which drug is most likely responsible?
why_correct: A persistent dry cough is a well-known adverse effect of ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril, caused by accumulation of bradykinin. An ACE inhibitor is the expected choice for hypertension in type 2 diabetes with albuminuria because it protects the kidneys. If the cough is troublesome, NICE suggests switching to an angiotensin II receptor blocker.
why_wrong: A. Amlodipine typically causes ankle swelling, flushing and headache. B. Indapamide causes electrolyte disturbance such as hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia. C. Bisoprolol may cause tiredness, cold peripheries or bronchospasm in asthma, not a dry cough. D. Doxazosin causes postural hypotension.
pearl: Angiotensin II receptor blockers do not inhibit bradykinin breakdown, so they rarely cause cough and are the usual alternative.
thinking: Dry cough without infection ↓ Started after a new antihypertensive ↓ Diabetes with albuminuria suggests ACE inhibitor was chosen ↓ Bradykinin accumulation ↓ Lisinopril
exam_trap: C, Bisoprolol — beta-blockers are linked with breathing problems, but they cause bronchospasm in asthma, not a persistent dry cough.
takeaway: A new dry cough after starting an antihypertensive suggests an ACE inhibitor.

stem: A 58-year-old man is on the surgical ward two days after a bowel resection. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and dapagliflozin, which were continued around surgery. He is eating little, has vomited several times, has abdominal discomfort and is breathing deeply and rapidly. His blood pressure is normal, his abdomen is soft without peritonism, and his capillary glucose is only slightly raised. Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin can cause diabetic ketoacidosis with near-normal or only modestly raised glucose. Surgery, fasting, vomiting and acute illness are typical triggers, which is why these drugs should be stopped before surgery and during acute illness. Deep, rapid breathing reflects a metabolic acidosis, and blood ketones and a blood gas should be checked.
why_wrong: A. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state involves very high glucose and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis. B. Hypoglycaemia would show a low glucose and does not cause deep sighing breathing. C. An anastomotic leak should be considered after bowel surgery, but he is not shocked, the abdomen is soft, and the drug history with acidotic breathing and near-normal glucose points to ketoacidosis. D. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst, not acidosis.
pearl: Always check blood ketones in an unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor, even if the glucose is normal.
thinking: Taking an SGLT2 inhibitor ↓ Surgery, fasting and vomiting ↓ Deep, rapid breathing ↓ Only mildly raised glucose ↓ Euglycaemic DKA
exam_trap: A, Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — it is the other diabetic emergency in type 2 diabetes, but it needs very high glucose and has no marked ketoacidosis.
takeaway: An unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor can have DKA despite near-normal glucose.

stem: A 79-year-old woman in a care home takes warfarin for a previous deep vein thrombosis. She has been eating very little during a recent cold. The district nurse finds her INR is 6.4, well above her target range. She has no bruising, blood in the urine or stool, nosebleeds or other bleeding, and she feels well. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Give prothrombin complex concentrate to correct the INR
options.B: Give intravenous vitamin K straight away
options.C: Continue the usual dose and recheck in a week
options.D: Withhold warfarin and manage according to the INR and bleeding risk

correct_answer: D. Withhold warfarin and manage according to the INR and bleeding risk
why_correct: A high INR without bleeding is managed by stopping warfarin temporarily, finding the cause, and restarting at a lower dose once the INR falls, guided by the level and the patient's bleeding risk. Poor food intake during illness reduces vitamin K and is a common trigger. Very high INRs may also need a small oral dose of vitamin K, as set out in the BNF.
why_wrong: A. Prothrombin complex concentrate is for major bleeding. B. Intravenous vitamin K is reserved for bleeding; without bleeding, oral vitamin K is used only at very high INRs, and unnecessary reversal makes re-anticoagulation harder. C. Continuing the same dose leaves her at significant risk of bleeding. E. Fresh frozen plasma is not used without bleeding and is less effective than prothrombin complex concentrate.
pearl: Reduced food intake, intercurrent illness, alcohol and new interacting drugs are the commonest causes of an unexpectedly high INR.
thinking: High INR on warfarin ↓ No bleeding ↓ Reduced oral intake during illness ↓ Withhold warfarin, find cause ↓ Restart at adjusted dose when INR falls
exam_trap: A, Give prothrombin complex concentrate to correct the INR — it rapidly normalises the INR, but it is reserved for major bleeding and carries a thrombosis risk.
takeaway: A high INR without bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin and acting according to the INR and bleeding risk.

stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has taken warfarin for years with stable INRs. He has had a painful dental abscess, and his dentist prescribed a five-day antibiotic course. At his anticoagulation clinic visit a week later his INR is far above his usual range. Which antibiotic is most likely to have caused this?
why_correct: Metronidazole inhibits the hepatic enzymes (CYP2C9) that metabolise warfarin, so it markedly raises the INR and bleeding risk. It is commonly prescribed for dental infections, which makes this a frequent real-world interaction. The BNF advises avoiding it in patients on warfarin where possible, or monitoring the INR closely and adjusting the dose.
why_wrong: A. Phenoxymethylpenicillin is not a classic cause of a marked INR rise. B. Topical fusidic acid has minimal systemic absorption. C. Nitrofurantoin is used for urinary infection and is not a major warfarin interaction. D. Flucloxacillin, if anything, may lower the INR.
pearl: Other drugs that raise the INR include clarithromycin, erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, fluconazole and amiodarone.
thinking: Stable INR on warfarin ↓ Dental abscess treated with antibiotic ↓ INR rises sharply ↓ Enzyme inhibition of warfarin metabolism ↓ Metronidazole
exam_trap: A, Phenoxymethylpenicillin — it is also used for dental infections, but it is not a major cause of INR rise.
takeaway: Metronidazole strongly increases the effect of warfarin; check the INR or avoid it.

stem: A 58-year-old man had atorvastatin started for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease three months ago. His GP repeats his liver function tests as part of routine monitoring and finds that his ALT has risen above the upper limit of normal. He feels well, drinks alcohol most evenings and is not jaundiced. What is the most appropriate principle to follow?

options.A: Ignore the result unless he becomes jaundiced
options.B: Assess the size and cause of the abnormality before deciding about the statin
options.E: Change to a fibrate and repeat the tests in a year

correct_answer: B. Assess the size and cause of the abnormality before deciding about the statin
why_correct: Raised liver enzymes on a statin need assessment rather than reflex action. NICE advises checking liver tests at baseline, 3 months and 12 months, and not stopping a statin for minor rises; it should be stopped only if transaminases rise to over three times the upper limit of normal. Other causes such as alcohol or fatty liver must also be considered.
why_wrong: A. Abnormal results should be assessed even without symptoms. C. Mild rises are common and do not justify stopping a statin that reduces cardiovascular risk. D. Raising the dose without knowing the cause could be harmful. E. Fibrates are not recommended as an alternative for prevention and also affect the liver.
pearl: Statins are not contraindicated in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which is a common cause of mildly raised ALT in patients needing them.
thinking: Statin started 3 months ago ↓ ALT mildly raised ↓ Other causes possible, such as alcohol ↓ Assess the size and cause ↓ Stop only if markedly raised
exam_trap: C, Stop the statin permanently — stopping seems the safest response to abnormal liver tests, but minor rises are common and stopping removes important cardiovascular protection.
takeaway: Assess raised liver enzymes on a statin rather than stopping or continuing automatically.

stem: A 68-year-old woman has had Parkinson disease for nine years and takes co-careldopa. Her daughter brings her to the neurology clinic because she now has restless, twisting, flowing movements of her trunk and arms, which are worst about an hour after each dose. Her tremor and stiffness are well controlled at those times. She does not take any antipsychotic. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: After several years of levodopa, many patients develop dyskinesias, involuntary choreiform or writhing movements. They are typically peak-dose, occurring when plasma levodopa levels are highest, as in this case. Management includes adjusting the dose timing or size, or adding amantadine, guided by a specialist.
why_wrong: A. Essential tremor is an action tremor, not writhing movements linked to doses. B. Tardive dyskinesia follows long-term dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotics, which she does not take. C. A functional disorder should not be assumed when a known drug cause fits. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes sensory loss or weakness, not involuntary movements.
pearl: Motor complications of levodopa include wearing-off, on-off fluctuations and peak-dose dyskinesia; they are more likely with higher doses and younger age at onset.
thinking: Long-standing Parkinson disease ↓ Years of levodopa ↓ Writhing movements ↓ Peak about an hour after a dose ↓ Levodopa-induced dyskinesia
exam_trap: B, Tardive dyskinesia — it also causes involuntary writhing, but it follows dopamine-blocking drugs, not dopamine replacement.
takeaway: Involuntary writhing movements at peak levels after years of levodopa are levodopa-induced dyskinesia.

stem: On a day-surgery unit, a 17-year-old girl is given intravenous metoclopramide for vomiting after a laparoscopic appendicectomy. About forty minutes later her jaw clenches, her tongue keeps pushing forwards and her head is twisted to the left. She is fully alert and frightened, and her temperature, pulse and blood pressure are normal. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Tetanus from a contaminated surgical wound
options.D: Acute dystonic reaction to the antiemetic

correct_answer: D. Acute dystonic reaction to the antiemetic
why_correct: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the basal ganglia and can provoke an acute dystonic reaction within hours of a dose, especially in young women and adolescents. Sustained twisting of the neck, trismus and tongue protrusion in an alert patient with normal observations is the classic picture. It usually settles promptly with an anticholinergic such as procyclidine.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus develops days after a contaminated wound, not within an hour of a clean operation, and is accompanied by spasms triggered by stimuli. B. Hypocalcaemic tetany causes carpopedal spasm and perioral tingling rather than torticollis and tongue protrusion. C. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days with fever, generalised rigidity, autonomic instability and reduced consciousness. E.
