A focal seizure is brief and often alters awareness; it does not produce sustained posturing with preserved alertness after a new dopamine antagonist.
pearl: Under the MHRA advice, metoclopramide should be used only short term (up to 5 days) because of the risk of neurological adverse effects, and young patients are most susceptible to acute dystonia.
thinking: Recent intravenous dopamine antagonist ↓ Sustained involuntary muscle contraction of neck, jaw and tongue ↓ Alert, afebrile, normal observations ↓ Onset within an hour of the dose ↓ Acute dystonic reaction
exam_trap: C, Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — it is the dramatic dopamine-antagonist reaction everyone remembers, but it needs fever, rigidity and autonomic upset developing over days.
takeaway: Sudden twisting postures in an alert young person shortly after metoclopramide indicate an acute dystonic reaction.

stem: A 52-year-old man was started on levothyroxine after radioiodine treatment for Graves' disease. Over the past year his TSH has stayed above the reference range even though his GP has increased the dose twice. He says he never misses a tablet: he swallows it whole with a glass of water at the same time every morning, together with his breakfast of toast and coffee before driving to work. Which aspect of how he takes the tablet is most likely to explain his results?

options.A: Taking it alongside his breakfast and coffee
options.B: Taking it with a glass of water
options.C: Taking it at the same time each day
options.D: Swallowing it whole rather than chewing it
options.E: Taking it in the morning rather than at bedtime

correct_answer: A. Taking it alongside his breakfast and coffee
why_correct: Levothyroxine absorption from the small bowel is reduced by food and by coffee, so taking it with breakfast can leave the TSH persistently high despite good adherence and dose increases. It should be taken on an empty stomach, usually 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast or caffeine-containing drinks. Correcting the timing is preferable to repeatedly increasing the dose.
why_wrong: B. Water is the recommended drink to take levothyroxine with. C. A consistent time each day supports stable absorption. D. The tablet is designed to be swallowed whole. E. A morning dose before food is the standard advice; taking it in the morning is not the problem.
pearl: Other common causes of a raised TSH on stable levothyroxine include calcium, iron and antacids taken at the same time, coeliac disease and poor adherence.
thinking: TSH high despite dose increases ↓ Good adherence reported ↓ Ask exactly how the tablet is taken ↓ Taken with breakfast and coffee ↓ Food and caffeine reduce absorption ↓ Take on an empty stomach before breakfast
exam_trap: E, Taking it in the morning rather than at bedtime — some people do take it at night, which tempts, but morning dosing is perfectly correct as long as it is before food.
takeaway: Levothyroxine should be taken on an empty stomach, separated from food, coffee and mineral supplements.

stem: A carer at a residential home calls the GP about an 84-year-old woman whose thinking has become muddled over the last three days. She is drowsy in the mornings, agitated in the evenings and has been picking at her bedclothes. An out-of-hours doctor recently started promethazine at night for poor sleep. She has not passed urine since early morning and her mouth is very dry. Which property of the new medicine most likely explains this picture?
why_correct: Promethazine is a sedating antihistamine with strong antimuscarinic activity. In older people, blocking central muscarinic receptors readily causes fluctuating confusion (delirium), while peripheral effects give dry mouth and urinary retention. The new drug, the time course and the anticholinergic features point to this cause, and the medicine should be stopped.
why_wrong: A. Serotonergic excess causes agitation with clonus, sweating and hyperthermia, not dry mouth and urinary retention. C. Promethazine does not stimulate dopamine receptors; dopaminergic drugs cause hallucinations but not retention and a dry mouth. D. Enzyme induction alters the levels of other drugs and would not itself produce this syndrome. E. Promethazine has no mineralocorticoid effect, which would cause fluid retention and hypokalaemia rather than delirium.
pearl: Each additional anticholinergic medicine increases the cumulative anticholinergic burden, which is linked to delirium, falls and cognitive decline in older adults.
thinking: Acute fluctuating confusion in an older person ↓ New sedating antihistamine started ↓ Dry mouth and urinary retention ↓ Points to antimuscarinic toxicity ↓ Stop the drug and review the anticholinergic burden
exam_trap: A, Serotonergic activity — agitation and confusion after a new drug can suggest serotonin toxicity, but the dry mouth and urinary retention are antimuscarinic features.
takeaway: In older people with new delirium, look for medicines with anticholinergic activity.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with gout has been taking naproxen regularly for two weeks for a flare. She is admitted to the medical assessment unit after three days of vomiting and diarrhoea, and her creatinine is well above her baseline. Urine dipstick is bland and her CK is normal. Which mechanism best explains how the naproxen contributed to her kidney injury?

options.A: Efferent arteriolar dilatation from reduced angiotensin II activity
options.B: Precipitation of drug crystals within the renal tubules
options.E: Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation

correct_answer: E. Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation
why_correct: When circulating volume falls, as with vomiting and diarrhoea, the kidney depends on prostaglandins to dilate the afferent arteriole and maintain glomerular perfusion. NSAIDs such as naproxen block prostaglandin synthesis, so afferent flow and GFR fall, producing prerenal AKI. A bland urine and normal CK support a haemodynamic cause rather than glomerular disease or rhabdomyolysis.
why_wrong: A. Efferent arteriolar dilatation from reduced angiotensin II is the mechanism with ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. B. Crystal nephropathy is linked with drugs such as aciclovir and methotrexate. C. Immune-complex glomerulonephritis would give blood and protein on dipstick and is not the typical NSAID effect. D. Myoglobin injury requires rhabdomyolysis, which the normal CK excludes.
pearl: During acute illness with dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, diuretics and metformin should usually be paused until the patient is eating and drinking normally.
thinking: Regular NSAID use ↓ Volume depletion from gastroenteritis ↓ Kidney relies on prostaglandins to dilate the afferent arteriole ↓ NSAID removes this compensation ↓ GFR falls: haemodynamic AKI
exam_trap: A, Efferent arteriolar dilatation — it is the other well-known haemodynamic drug mechanism, but it belongs to ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, not NSAIDs.
takeaway: NSAIDs reduce GFR by blocking prostaglandin-driven afferent arteriolar dilatation, which matters most in volume-depleted patients.

presentation: ACE inhibitor and renal artery stenosis
stem: A 64-year-old woman had her left kidney removed for renal cell carcinoma several years ago. She now has hypertension that is difficult to control, and imaging shows a tight stenosis of the right renal artery. Ten days after her GP adds perindopril, her creatinine has risen sharply. How does the new drug cause this fall in kidney function?

options.A: Raised erythropoietin production increasing blood viscosity
options.B: Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction lowering glomerular pressure
options.C: Direct toxic injury to the tubular epithelium
options.D: Constriction of the afferent arteriole reducing renal blood flow
options.E: Obstruction of urine outflow at the bladder neck

correct_answer: B. Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction lowering glomerular pressure
why_correct: With a stenosed artery supplying her only kidney, glomerular filtration pressure is maintained by angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. An ACE inhibitor removes this constriction, so intraglomerular pressure and GFR fall abruptly. The same applies to bilateral renal artery stenosis, and the drug should be stopped.
why_wrong: A. ACE inhibitors tend to lower, not raise, erythropoietin and do not cause hyperviscosity. C. The injury is haemodynamic, not a direct tubular toxicity. D. Afferent arteriolar constriction is the NSAID mechanism, not the effect of ACE inhibition. E. ACE inhibitors do not cause bladder outflow obstruction.
pearl: A rise in creatinine of more than about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker should prompt review of the drug and a search for renovascular disease.
thinking: Solitary kidney with a stenosed renal artery ↓ GFR depends on efferent arteriolar tone ↓ Angiotensin II maintains that tone ↓ ACE inhibitor removes it ↓ Glomerular pressure and GFR fall
exam_trap: D, Afferent arteriolar constriction — it sounds logical when renal blood flow is reduced, but that is the NSAID story; ACE inhibitors act on the efferent side.
takeaway: In renal artery stenosis to a solitary kidney or both kidneys, ACE inhibitors drop GFR by removing efferent arteriolar constriction.

stem: At his annual diabetes review in general practice, a 63-year-old man who has taken metformin for eight years mentions tingling in both feet that has crept up to his ankles. His glycaemic control has been good. His full blood count shows a raised mean cell volume, and he drinks very little alcohol. Which deficiency should be checked for first?
why_correct: Long-term metformin reduces vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum, and deficiency can cause a peripheral neuropathy and macrocytosis. In a man with good glycaemic control, new sensory symptoms with a raised MCV should not simply be attributed to diabetic neuropathy. B12 should be measured and replaced if low.
why_wrong: A. Thiamine deficiency causes neuropathy and Wernicke encephalopathy but not macrocytosis, and is not linked to metformin. B. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis but not this neuropathy, and metformin is principally associated with B12 malabsorption. C. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and myopathy, not macrocytosis. E. Pyridoxine deficiency is linked to isoniazid and causes neuropathy with a microcytic, not macrocytic, picture.
pearl: MHRA advice is to check vitamin B12 in people on metformin who develop neuropathy or anaemia, and to consider periodic monitoring in those at risk, as the deficiency can mimic or worsen diabetic neuropathy.
thinking: Long-term metformin ↓ Ascending sensory symptoms in the feet ↓ Raised MCV ↓ Metformin impairs ileal B12 absorption ↓ Check vitamin B12
exam_trap: B, Folate — it also causes macrocytosis, but it does not explain the neuropathy and is not the deficiency classically caused by metformin.
takeaway: Neuropathy or macrocytosis in a patient on long-term metformin should prompt a vitamin B12 level.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with obesity began weekly semaglutide injections through a specialist weight management service two weeks ago. She reports mild queasiness, feeling full after only a few mouthfuls and occasional loose stools. She has no abdominal pain, fever or vomiting, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. What is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?

options.C: Expected gastrointestinal adverse effects of the new drug

correct_answer: C. Expected gastrointestinal adverse effects of the new drug
why_correct: GLP-1 receptor agonists slow gastric emptying and act centrally to reduce appetite, so nausea, early fullness and altered bowel habit are common, especially after starting or increasing the dose. Her symptoms are mild, began with the drug and come without pain or abnormal signs. They usually settle with time, smaller meals and slower dose escalation.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis is a rare adverse effect and presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. B. Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain, fever and tenderness. D. Gastric outlet obstruction causes persistent, often projectile vomiting of undigested food. E. Coeliac disease would not begin abruptly with a new medicine and the timing points to the drug.
pearl: Patients on GLP-1 receptor agonists should be told to seek urgent help for severe persistent abdominal pain, which may indicate pancreatitis.
thinking: New GLP-1 receptor agonist ↓ Mild nausea, early satiety, loose stools ↓ No pain, fever or abnormal signs ↓ Drug slows gastric emptying and suppresses appetite ↓ Expected gastrointestinal adverse effects
exam_trap: A, Acute pancreatitis — it is the serious warning attached to this drug class, but it causes severe abdominal pain, which she does not have.
takeaway: Mild nausea and early fullness after starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist are expected effects, while severe abdominal pain needs urgent assessment.

stem: A 60-year-old man with gastroparesis asks his GP whether he could try domperidone, which a friend found helpful. He has ischaemic heart disease and already takes citalopram. Which adverse effect is the most important to consider before prescribing it?
correct_answer: E. QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia
why_correct: Domperidone can prolong the QT interval and has been associated with serious ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. The risk is greater in older people, those with heart disease and those taking other QT-prolonging drugs such as citalopram. In this man it is likely to be contraindicated, and any use should be at the lowest dose for the shortest time.
why_wrong: A. Agranulocytosis is linked to drugs such as carbimazole and clozapine, not domperidone. B. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is a lithium effect. C. Pulmonary fibrosis is associated with amiodarone, methotrexate and nitrofurantoin. D. Sensorineural deafness is a recognised toxicity of aminoglycosides and loop diuretics.
pearl: The MHRA restricts domperidone to relief of nausea and vomiting, at the lowest effective dose for a short course, and contraindicates it in people with cardiac disease or conduction problems and in those taking QT-prolonging drugs.
thinking: Request for domperidone ↓ Background ischaemic heart disease ↓ Already on another QT-prolonging drug ↓ Domperidone prolongs QT ↓ Risk of ventricular arrhythmia
exam_trap: A, Agranulocytosis — a rare but serious blood reaction that comes to mind with many drugs, but it is not the safety concern with domperidone.
takeaway: Domperidone carries a risk of QT prolongation and sudden cardiac death, so check cardiac history and interacting drugs first.

stem: During pre-operative assessment for a hernia repair, a 55-year-old man says he cannot take codeine. After a dental extraction last year it made him feel sick and he vomited twice; he had no rash, lip or tongue swelling, wheeze or faintness. How should this be recorded in his notes?

options.A: As an allergy to all opioids
options.B: Not recorded, as it was a minor reaction
options.C: As anaphylaxis to codeine, to be cautious
options.D: As an intolerance (non-allergic side effect) to codeine, describing the reaction
options.E: As a contraindication to every opioid analgesic

correct_answer: D. As an intolerance (non-allergic side effect) to codeine, describing the reaction
why_correct: Nausea and vomiting are predictable, dose-related side effects of codeine, not an immune-mediated allergy. Recording it accurately as an intolerance, with the nature of the reaction, keeps the information available to prescribers without wrongly excluding useful analgesics. Clear documentation of both drug and reaction type is part of safe prescribing.
why_wrong: A. Labelling this as an opioid allergy is inaccurate and could deny him effective post-operative pain relief. B. Even minor reactions should be documented so future prescribers can make informed choices. C. Vomiting alone is not anaphylaxis, and an overstated label is misleading. E. A side effect of one drug does not contraindicate a whole class.
pearl: When recording a drug reaction, document the drug, the reaction, its timing and severity, and whether it was allergic or a side effect, as recommended by NICE guidance on drug allergy.
thinking: Previous reaction to codeine ↓ Nausea and vomiting only ↓ No skin, airway or circulatory features ↓ Predictable side effect, not allergy ↓ Record as intolerance with details
exam_trap: C, As anaphylaxis to be cautious — over-labelling feels safe, but it is inaccurate and can block appropriate treatment later.
takeaway: Record side effects as intolerances, not allergies, and describe exactly what happened.

presentation: Yellow Card reporting of suspected adverse reactions
stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the dermatology ward with widespread blistering, mucosal ulceration and skin peeling three weeks after starting lamotrigine for epilepsy. The drug is stopped and the team suspects Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The foundation doctor is unsure whether anything else needs to be done about the reaction. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Report it only once rechallenge has confirmed the drug as the cause
options.B: Report it to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme
options.C: Document it in the notes only, as the reaction is already known
options.D: Leave reporting to the manufacturer of the medicine
options.E: Ask the consultant to report it, as junior doctors cannot

correct_answer: B. Report it to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme
why_correct: Any suspected serious adverse drug reaction should be reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme, even if the reaction is already listed and causality is not proven. Reports from all healthcare professionals, and patients, feed national safety surveillance. The reaction should also be clearly recorded as an allergy in her notes.
why_wrong: A. Proof of causality is not needed, and rechallenge after Stevens-Johnson syndrome would be dangerous. C. Serious reactions should be reported even when they are known adverse effects. D. Healthcare professionals should report directly rather than rely on the manufacturer. E. Any healthcare professional, including doctors in training, can submit a Yellow Card.
pearl: Yellow Card reports are especially wanted for all suspected reactions to new medicines marked with a black triangle and for serious reactions to established medicines.
thinking: Serious suspected drug reaction ↓ Drug already stopped ↓ Causality need not be proven ↓ Any professional can report ↓ Submit a Yellow Card to the MHRA
exam_trap: A, Report once rechallenge confirms — it sounds rigorous, but suspicion is enough and rechallenge here could be fatal.
takeaway: Report any suspected serious adverse reaction via the Yellow Card scheme without waiting for proof.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and protein in her urine starts ramipril at the diabetes clinic. She feels well, but routine bloods taken a fortnight later show a clear rise in creatinine and a slightly higher potassium than before. She takes no other new medicines. Which recognised adverse effect of her new drug do these results show?

options.C: Acute kidney injury from reduced glomerular filtration

correct_answer: C. Acute kidney injury from reduced glomerular filtration
why_correct: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II-driven efferent arteriolar tone, lowering glomerular filtration pressure, so a rise in creatinine and potassium after starting them is a recognised effect. A small rise is expected, but a significant rise represents acute kidney injury and needs review of the dose and a search for causes such as renovascular disease or volume depletion. This is why U&E are checked before and one to two weeks after starting or increasing the dose.
why_wrong: A. Ototoxicity is associated with aminoglycosides and loop diuretics. B. Urinary retention is an anticholinergic effect, not an ACE inhibitor effect. D. Rhabdomyolysis is linked with statins and fibrates, and would cause muscle pain and a high CK. E. Hypercalcaemia is associated with thiazides, not ACE inhibitors.
pearl: Check renal function and potassium before starting an ACE inhibitor and again after starting or each dose increase.
thinking: New ACE inhibitor ↓ Creatinine and potassium rise within two weeks ↓ Lower efferent tone reduces glomerular pressure ↓ Recognised drop in GFR ↓ Review dose and look for a cause
exam_trap: B, Urinary retention — a creatinine rise may suggest obstruction, but retention is an anticholinergic effect and does not fit a new ACE inhibitor.
takeaway: A significant creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor is a recognised adverse renal effect that needs prompt review.

stem: Four months into treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica, a 66-year-old woman is told by her GP that she will probably need her steroid tablets for well over a year. She wants to know what protective treatment she should take alongside them. Which complication is the main reason for this added treatment?
why_correct: Glucocorticoids reduce bone formation and increase bone resorption, causing rapid bone loss and fracture risk, especially in the first months of treatment. Anyone expected to take oral steroids for three months or more should have their fracture risk assessed, and older people usually need bone protection with a bisphosphonate plus calcium and vitamin D. This woman fits that group.
why_wrong: B. Corticosteroids do not characteristically cause bradycardia. C. They raise blood glucose and can cause steroid-induced diabetes. D. They tend to raise the neutrophil count. E. Their mineralocorticoid effect causes potassium loss, not hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Steroid-induced fracture risk rises within the first three to six months of treatment, so bone protection should start at the same time as long-term steroids in high-risk patients.
thinking: Long-term oral prednisolone ↓ Older woman ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation and increase resorption ↓ High fracture risk ↓ Offer bone protection
exam_trap: C, Hypoglycaemia — steroids clearly affect glucose, but they cause hyperglycaemia, not low blood sugar.
takeaway: Prolonged corticosteroid treatment causes osteoporosis, so assess fracture risk and give bone protection early.

stem: A 42-year-old man started amitriptyline at night a month ago for chronic tension-type headache. At a community pharmacy medicines check he says his headaches are better, but his mouth feels parched, he is passing hard stools only every few days and he struggles to focus on small print. He has no other medical problems. What is the most likely explanation?
correct_answer: D. Antimuscarinic side effects of amitriptyline
why_correct: Amitriptyline blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing salivation, slowing gut motility and impairing accommodation of the eye. A parched mouth, constipation and difficulty focusing on near objects after starting it are typical anticholinergic effects. Lowering the dose or changing treatment can be discussed with him.
why_wrong: A. Sjögren's syndrome causes dry eyes and mouth but not constipation and blurred near vision, and is unlikely in a man with symptoms starting after a new drug. B. Serotonin syndrome causes agitation, tremor, clonus, sweating and hyperthermia. C. Hypothyroidism can cause constipation but not a dry mouth and accommodation problems. E. Autonomic neuropathy occurs in conditions such as long-standing diabetes, which he does not have.
pearl: Tricyclic antidepressants are among the drugs with the highest anticholinergic burden, and even low doses for pain can cause these effects.
thinking: New tricyclic antidepressant ↓ Dry mouth, constipation, blurred near vision ↓ All are muscarinic blockade effects ↓ No alternative condition ↓ Antimuscarinic side effects
exam_trap: A, Primary Sjögren's syndrome — the dry mouth tempts, but it does not explain constipation and blurred near vision appearing just after a new drug.
takeaway: Dry mouth, constipation and blurred vision after starting a tricyclic are antimuscarinic side effects.

stem: In the third week of treatment on the cardiology ward for enterococcal endocarditis, a 71-year-old man receiving amoxicillin and gentamicin says the room seems to jump about when he turns his head, and his wife notices he now has the television much louder. Which adverse effect of one of his antibiotics best explains this?
why_correct: Gentamicin, an aminoglycoside, damages the hair cells of the vestibular apparatus and cochlea, causing oscillopsia, imbalance and hearing loss that may be permanent. The risk rises with prolonged courses, older age and renal impairment, all relevant in endocarditis treatment. Levels should be monitored and the need for gentamicin reviewed urgently.
why_wrong: A. Gingival hyperplasia is linked with phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium-channel blockers. B. Hyperprolactinaemia follows dopamine antagonists. C. Pulmonary fibrosis is associated with drugs such as amiodarone and nitrofurantoin. E. Photosensitivity is typical of tetracyclines and amiodarone, not aminoglycosides or amoxicillin.
pearl: People with the mitochondrial m.1555A>G variant are at very high risk of aminoglycoside deafness even after a single dose, so testing is advised where it will not delay urgent treatment.
thinking: Prolonged aminoglycoside course ↓ Oscillopsia and reduced hearing ↓ Cochlear and vestibular hair-cell damage ↓ Cumulative dose-related toxicity ↓ Ototoxicity
exam_trap: E, Photosensitive skin rash — antibiotics commonly cause rashes, which tempts, but his symptoms are vestibular and auditory, the hallmark of aminoglycoside toxicity.
takeaway: Aminoglycosides cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, so monitor levels, hearing and renal function.

presentation: Oral NSAID risk in older people with CKD
stem: An 80-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease, who takes ramipril and furosemide, asks her pharmacist-led medication review whether she can start naproxen every day for painful knee osteoarthritis. Paracetamol has not helped much, and she has not tried a topical anti-inflammatory gel. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Start naproxen, as renal risk only matters in end-stage kidney disease
options.B: Start the highest licensed naproxen dose to get pain controlled quickly
options.C: Assess her renal, gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risk before any oral NSAID, and offer a topical NSAID first
options.D: Start naproxen with omeprazole, which protects both stomach and kidneys
options.E: Start naproxen and check her kidney function at next year's review

correct_answer: C. Assess her renal, gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risk before any oral NSAID, and offer a topical NSAID first
why_correct: Oral NSAIDs can cause acute kidney injury, gastrointestinal bleeding and cardiovascular events, and the risks are higher in older people with CKD. Combining an NSAID with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic (the triple whammy) particularly threatens renal function. NICE advises a topical NSAID first for knee osteoarthritis and assessing individual risk before any oral NSAID, which is likely to be unsuitable for her.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs can cause AKI at any stage of CKD, especially with an ACE inhibitor and diuretic. B. If used at all, NSAIDs should be at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time. D. A proton pump inhibitor reduces gastrointestinal risk but does nothing for the kidneys. E. Annual monitoring is far too infrequent given her renal risk.
pearl: An NSAID taken with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker plus a diuretic is a well-recognised cause of acute kidney injury in older people.
thinking: Older woman with CKD ↓ Already on ACE inhibitor and diuretic ↓ Oral NSAID would add renal, GI and cardiovascular risk ↓ Topical NSAID not yet tried ↓ Assess risk and offer topical treatment first
exam_trap: D, Naproxen with omeprazole — co-prescribing a PPI is correct practice for the stomach, which makes it feel safe, but it offers no renal protection.
takeaway: Before any oral NSAID in an older person with CKD, weigh renal, gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risk and prefer topical options.

presentation: Risk assessment before oral NSAIDs in osteoarthritis
stem: A 72-year-old man with osteoarthritis of the hands speaks to his GP by telephone. Paracetamol and a topical anti-inflammatory gel have given little relief, and he asks to try an anti-inflammatory tablet. He had indigestion a few years ago. Which factors should be assessed before an oral NSAID is offered?

options.A: Gastrointestinal risk only, as a proton pump inhibitor removes it
options.B: His weight and blood pressure, but not his kidney function
options.C: Pain severity and his preferred brand of tablet
options.D: Gastrointestinal, renal, liver and cardiovascular risk
options.E: His age only, as NSAIDs are low risk below 75

correct_answer: D. Gastrointestinal, renal, liver and cardiovascular risk
why_correct: NICE advises that before prescribing an oral NSAID for osteoarthritis, the person's gastrointestinal, liver and cardio-renal risk factors are considered, the lowest effective dose is used for the shortest time and a proton pump inhibitor is co-prescribed. His previous dyspepsia adds to gastrointestinal risk, and his age raises renal and cardiovascular risk. A full assessment guides whether an oral NSAID is appropriate at all.
why_wrong: A. A proton pump inhibitor lowers but does not remove gastrointestinal risk, and other organ risks remain. B. Kidney function is central, because NSAIDs can cause acute kidney injury. C. Pain severity and brand do not address safety. E. NSAID risks apply at every age and rise with age.
pearl: Topical NSAIDs are recommended first-line for knee osteoarthritis and should be considered for hand osteoarthritis before oral NSAIDs.
thinking: Osteoarthritis not controlled by first-line measures ↓ Oral NSAID being considered ↓ Past dyspepsia raises GI risk ↓ Older age raises renal and cardiovascular risk ↓ Assess GI, renal, liver and cardiovascular risk
exam_trap: A, Gastrointestinal risk only — PPI co-prescription is rightly emphasised, which tempts, but renal and cardiovascular harms are just as important.
takeaway: Before an oral NSAID, assess gastrointestinal, renal, liver and cardiovascular risk, and use the lowest dose for the shortest time with a PPI.

presentation: Safe opioid prescribing in opioid-naive patients
stem: A 67-year-old man with COPD and obstructive sleep apnoea is admitted to the surgical ward with three rib fractures after a fall from a ladder. He has never taken opioids, and the foundation doctor plans to prescribe morphine for his pain. Which approach is most important for safe prescribing?

options.A: Begin modified-release morphine twice daily as the first step
options.B: Add diazepam to settle his anxiety about breathing
options.C: Start at the maximum licensed dose for rapid relief
options.D: Prescribe both oral morphine and oxycodone for better control
options.E: Assess his respiratory reserve, renal function, sedation risk and other sedatives before choosing the dose

correct_answer: E. Assess his respiratory reserve, renal function, sedation risk and other sedatives before choosing the dose
why_correct: Opioids cause dose-related sedation and respiratory depression, and his COPD, sleep apnoea and lack of previous exposure all increase that risk. Reviewing his breathing, kidney function and any other sedating drugs allows a cautious starting dose of immediate-release opioid with monitoring. Regional anaesthesia may also be considered for rib fractures to spare opioids.
why_wrong: A. Modified-release opioids are unsuitable for starting acute pain relief in opioid-naive patients because they are harder to titrate and can accumulate. B. Benzodiazepines with opioids greatly increase respiratory depression. C. High starting doses are dangerous in opioid-naive patients with lung disease. D. Combining two strong opioids increases toxicity without benefit.
pearl: Naloxone should be prescribed and available when strong opioids are started in patients at high risk of respiratory depression.
thinking: Opioid-naive patient ↓ COPD and sleep apnoea ↓ High risk of respiratory depression ↓ Check renal function and other sedatives ↓ Cautious immediate-release dosing with monitoring
exam_trap: A, Modified-release morphine — it gives steady cover and sounds convenient, but in an opioid-naive patient it is hard to titrate and risks accumulation.
takeaway: Before prescribing strong opioids for acute pain, assess the patient's risk factors and start low with immediate-release preparations.

stem: At a nurse-led hypertension clinic, a 55-year-old man reports that both his ankles have become puffy by the end of each day since his amlodipine was increased to the maximum dose a month ago. He can lie flat without breathlessness, his jugular venous pressure is not raised, his calves are soft and equal and his urine dipstick shows no protein. What is the most likely explanation?
correct_answer: B. Dose-related vasodilator oedema from amlodipine
why_correct: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers dilate pre-capillary arterioles more than venules, raising capillary pressure and causing fluid to leak into dependent tissues. The swelling is dose related, appeared after the dose increase and comes without signs of heart failure or proteinuria. Diuretics work poorly; lowering the dose or switching drug is usually more effective.
why_wrong: A. DVT is usually unilateral with a tender, swollen calf. C. Nephrotic syndrome would show heavy proteinuria on dipstick. D. He has no orthopnoea and a normal JVP, which argues against heart failure. E. Cellulitis causes red, hot, tender skin and is rarely bilateral.
pearl: Adding an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker can reduce calcium-channel blocker oedema by dilating the venous side of the capillary bed.
thinking: Bilateral dependent ankle swelling ↓ Began after amlodipine dose increase ↓ No signs of heart failure ↓ No proteinuria, calves equal ↓ Calcium-channel blocker oedema
exam_trap: D, Congestive heart failure — bilateral ankle swelling in a hypertensive man suggests it, but he has no orthopnoea and a normal JVP.
takeaway: Ankle swelling after starting or increasing amlodipine, with no heart failure signs, is drug-related vasodilator oedema.

stem: A 63-year-old man with stable angina attends the cardiology clinic. Six weeks ago amlodipine was added to his bisoprolol because he was still getting chest tightness on hills. His angina is now much better, but he has noticed his socks leaving deep marks around both ankles. His chest is clear and he has no orthopnoea. He also takes atorvastatin, clopidogrel and a glyceryl trinitrate spray when needed. Which of his medicines is the most likely cause of the swelling?
why_correct: Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, commonly causes bilateral ankle oedema by dilating arterioles and raising capillary pressure. The timing after it was added, and the absence of heart failure features, make it the most likely cause. Options include lowering the dose or changing to another anti-anginal.
why_wrong: B. Bisoprolol can worsen decompensated heart failure but does not usually cause isolated ankle oedema, and he has taken it for longer. C. Atorvastatin is associated with myalgia, not ankle swelling. D. Clopidogrel causes bleeding and bruising rather than oedema. E. Occasional glyceryl trinitrate causes headache and flushing, not persistent ankle swelling.
pearl: Calcium-channel blocker ankle oedema responds poorly to diuretics because it is caused by capillary pressure, not salt and water overload.
thinking: New bilateral ankle swelling ↓ Started weeks after a new anti-anginal ↓ No signs of heart failure ↓ Dihydropyridines dilate arterioles and raise capillary pressure ↓ Amlodipine
exam_trap: B, Bisoprolol — beta-blockers are linked with heart failure, which tempts, but he has no failure signs and the swelling followed the amlodipine.
takeaway: Amlodipine is a common, dose-related cause of bilateral ankle oedema.

stem: A care home nurse asks the visiting GP to review an 83-year-old woman whose lower legs have become swollen over the past three weeks. After a recent hospital admission she was started on several new medicines: treatment for osteoporosis, an acid-suppressing drug, an antidepressant, a tablet for hay fever and a new blood pressure tablet. Her lungs are clear and she is not breathless lying flat. Which class of drug is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as amlodipine, felodipine and lercanidipine are among the commonest drug causes of peripheral oedema. Among her new medicines, the blood pressure tablet is the one most likely to be from this class and to cause swelling without heart failure. A medication review should identify it and consider an alternative.
why_wrong: A. Bisphosphonates cause oesophagitis and, rarely, osteonecrosis of the jaw, not ankle oedema. B. Proton pump inhibitors cause hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia and diarrhoea rather than oedema. D. SSRIs cause hyponatraemia and bleeding risk, not significant oedema. E. Non-sedating antihistamines are not a recognised cause of leg swelling.
pearl: Other drug classes that cause peripheral oedema include NSAIDs, corticosteroids, glitazones and gabapentinoids.
thinking: New bilateral leg swelling in an older woman ↓ Several new medicines ↓ No heart failure features ↓ Which class causes vasodilator oedema? ↓ Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker
exam_trap: D, Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor — antidepressants cause several adverse effects in older people, but oedema is not one of their typical ones.
takeaway: When an older person develops ankle swelling after medication changes, check for a newly started calcium-channel blocker.

stem: A 6-year-old boy develops an expanding red rash on his thigh a week after a family camping trip in the New Forest, and the GP diagnoses erythema migrans. His mother had doxycycline for the same problem last year and asks why her son is being given amoxicillin instead. What is the main reason tetracyclines are generally avoided at his age?

options.C: They harm cartilage in growing joints
options.D: They are deposited in developing teeth, causing permanent staining and enamel hypoplasia

correct_answer: D. They are deposited in developing teeth, causing permanent staining and enamel hypoplasia
why_correct: Tetracyclines such as doxycycline chelate calcium and are incorporated into developing teeth and bone. In young children whose permanent teeth are still forming, this can cause lasting yellow-brown discolouration and enamel hypoplasia. For this reason NICE recommends amoxicillin for Lyme disease in younger children, while doxycycline is used in older children and adults.
why_wrong: A. Ototoxicity is characteristic of aminoglycosides. B. Nephrotoxicity is not the main concern with tetracyclines in children. C. Cartilage damage in growing joints is a concern with fluoroquinolones. E. Grey baby syndrome is caused by chloramphenicol in neonates.
pearl: Tetracyclines are also avoided in pregnancy and generally while breastfeeding because of the same effects on developing teeth and bone.
thinking: Young child needing antibiotic for Lyme disease ↓ Tetracycline used for adults ↓ Tetracyclines bind calcium in developing teeth ↓ Permanent staining and enamel hypoplasia ↓ Use an alternative such as amoxicillin
exam_trap: C, Cartilage damage in growing joints — this is a real paediatric antibiotic concern, but it belongs to fluoroquinolones.
takeaway: Tetracyclines are generally avoided in young children because they permanently stain developing teeth.

stem: A 35-year-old teacher sees her GP after four days of a blocked nose, facial pressure and a mild temperature. The GP diagnoses acute sinusitis that is likely to be viral and advises self-care rather than antibiotics. She asks what harm there would be in taking a course just in case. Which answer best explains why unnecessary antibiotics should be avoided?

options.A: They weaken the immune system and slow recovery from viruses
options.B: The main concern is the cost of the medicines to the NHS
options.C: They make it more likely she will catch viral infections from others
options.D: They encourage resistant bacteria and can cause side effects without any benefit
options.E: They hide fever, so serious infections are diagnosed later

correct_answer: D. They encourage resistant bacteria and can cause side effects without any benefit
why_correct: Antibiotics do not help viral illness, so the only effects of an unnecessary course are harms. They select for resistant bacteria in her own body and the wider community, and cause adverse effects such as diarrhoea, thrush, allergic reactions and Clostridioides difficile infection. Most acute sinusitis resolves without antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not suppress the immune system. B. Cost is not the main reason; resistance and adverse effects are. C. Antibiotics do not increase the chance of catching viral infections. E. Antibiotics do not mask fever.
pearl: NICE suggests no antibiotic for acute sinusitis of up to 10 days, as most cases are viral and self-limiting.
thinking: Probable viral sinusitis ↓ Patient asks for antibiotics just in case ↓ No benefit against viruses ↓ Harms: resistance and adverse effects ↓ Explain and support self-care
exam_trap: B, Cost to the NHS — cost is a real factor, but the main reasons are antimicrobial resistance and harm to the patient.
takeaway: Unnecessary antibiotics give no benefit and cause harm through resistance and side effects.

presentation: Antimicrobial resistance as a public-health concern
stem: At a practice meeting, the prescribing data for a GP surgery show far more antibiotic prescriptions than neighbouring practices, mostly for coughs and sore throats. A new receptionist asks why the integrated care board is so concerned about this. What is the main public-health reason for limiting unnecessary antibiotic use?

options.A: Antibiotic use makes the population permanently immune to bacteria
options.B: Every antibiotic course leads to a future allergy
options.C: Antibiotic exposure selects for resistant bacteria that then spread in the community
options.E: Antibiotic use causes outbreaks of viral infection

correct_answer: C. Antibiotic exposure selects for resistant bacteria that then spread in the community
why_correct: Every antibiotic course kills susceptible bacteria and allows resistant strains to survive and multiply. These resistant organisms spread between people, so high prescribing in a community reduces how well antibiotics work for everyone. This is why prescribing rates are monitored and stewardship is a national priority.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not give immunity to bacteria. B. Allergy can occur but most courses do not cause one. D. Antibiotics do not stop vaccines from working. E. Antibiotics do not cause viral outbreaks.
pearl: Antimicrobial resistance is a major global threat to health, and the UK national action plan aims to reduce inappropriate antibiotic use in people and animals.
thinking: High antibiotic prescribing in a practice ↓ Mostly for self-limiting infections ↓ Antibiotics kill sensitive bacteria and leave resistant strains ↓ Resistant strains spread in the community ↓ Antimicrobial resistance
exam_trap: B, Future allergy — antibiotics can cause allergies, which tempts, but this is not the population-level concern and it does not follow every course.
takeaway: The main public-health reason to limit antibiotics is the spread of antimicrobial resistance.

presentation: Antimicrobial stewardship: treat only when indicated
stem: On a surgical ward, a 74-year-old man has a long-term urinary catheter after a hip replacement. He is eating well, apyrexial and has no abdominal pain or confusion. A routine catheter urine sample grows bacteria, and the nurse asks whether antibiotics should be started. Which prescribing principle applies?

options.A: Treat every positive urine culture to prevent sepsis
options.B: Start the broadest-spectrum antibiotic available to cover all organisms
options.C: Prescribe antibiotics only when there is a clinical indication, so asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated
options.D: Give antibiotics until the catheter is removed
options.E: Start antibiotics because his family has asked for them

correct_answer: C. Prescribe antibiotics only when there is a clinical indication, so asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated
why_correct: Bacteria are almost always found in urine from long-term catheters, and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria gives no benefit while increasing resistance, adverse effects and Clostridioides difficile infection. Antimicrobial stewardship means using antibiotics only when there is a genuine clinical indication, such as signs of infection. He is well, so antibiotics should not be started.
why_wrong: A. A positive culture without symptoms is not an indication in a catheterised patient. B. Broad-spectrum drugs should be reserved for situations that truly need them. D. Antibiotics for the duration of a catheter are not recommended and drive resistance. E. Requests from family are not a clinical indication.
pearl: Do not send catheter urine for culture unless there are features of infection, as a positive result in a well patient often leads to unnecessary treatment.
thinking: Long-term catheter ↓ Positive urine culture ↓ No symptoms or signs of infection ↓ Asymptomatic bacteriuria ↓ No antibiotic: treat only when indicated
exam_trap: A, Treat every positive culture — a positive result looks like a clear reason to act, but in a catheterised patient without symptoms it reflects colonisation.
takeaway: Antibiotics should be prescribed only when there is a real clinical indication, not for a positive culture alone.

stem: A 58-year-old woman on long-term warfarin after a pulmonary embolism is given a course of fluconazole by her dentist for oral thrush. At her next anticoagulation clinic check, her INR is far above her target range. She has no bruising or bleeding at present. What is the main risk from this result?
correct_answer: C. Serious bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage
why_correct: Fluconazole inhibits the liver enzymes that metabolise warfarin, raising its effect and the INR. A markedly raised INR means excessive anticoagulation, so the key danger is major bleeding, including gastrointestinal and intracranial haemorrhage, even when no bleeding is yet visible. Management follows BNF guidance based on the INR and whether bleeding is present.
why_wrong: A. A high INR reflects too much anticoagulation, which lowers rather than raises the risk of thrombosis. B. Skin necrosis is a rare complication when warfarin is started, linked to protein C deficiency, not to a raised INR. D. Osteoporosis is not an acute consequence of a high INR. E. Warfarin does not affect potassium.
pearl: Common enzyme-inhibiting drugs that raise the INR include clarithromycin, erythromycin, fluconazole, metronidazole and amiodarone.
thinking: Warfarin plus a new enzyme inhibitor ↓ INR well above target ↓ Excess anticoagulation ↓ No bleeding yet but high risk ↓ Major bleeding is the main concern
exam_trap: B, Warfarin-induced skin necrosis — it is a famous warfarin complication, but it occurs when warfarin is started and is not caused by a high INR.
takeaway: A markedly raised INR on warfarin means a high risk of serious bleeding and needs prompt action.

stem: An 81-year-old man in a nursing home takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. A neurologist starts carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia and writes to the GP asking for his INR to be monitored more closely over the coming weeks. Why is this medication review necessary?

options.A: Warfarin prevents the absorption of most other oral drugs
options.B: Warfarin is renally excreted and accumulates in older people
options.C: Warfarin is a strong inducer of liver enzymes
options.D: Warfarin speeds up the elimination of other medicines
options.E: Interacting medicines can raise or lower the INR

correct_answer: E. Interacting medicines can raise or lower the INR
why_correct: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic range and is metabolised by liver cytochrome P450 enzymes. Carbamazepine induces these enzymes, so warfarin is cleared faster and the INR may fall, increasing stroke risk; other drugs inhibit metabolism and raise the INR, increasing bleeding risk. Any new medicine, or stopping one, should prompt a check for interactions and closer INR monitoring.
why_wrong: A. Warfarin does not block absorption of other oral drugs. B. Warfarin is cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism, not the kidneys. C. Warfarin is not an enzyme inducer; its own metabolism is affected by inducers such as carbamazepine. D. Warfarin does not increase the elimination of other medicines.
pearl: Enzyme induction takes days to weeks to develop and wear off, so INR changes may appear late after starting or stopping an inducer.
thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ New enzyme-inducing drug started ↓ Warfarin metabolism speeds up ↓ INR may fall with stroke risk ↓ Interactions can move the INR either way
exam_trap: C, Warfarin is an enzyme inducer — enzyme induction is relevant here, which tempts, but it is carbamazepine that induces enzymes, not warfarin.
takeaway: Any new medicine in a patient on warfarin can change the INR, so check interactions and monitor more closely.

presentation: DOAC accumulation in acute kidney injury
stem: A 77-year-old man taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation is admitted with pneumonia and sepsis. His creatinine is several times his usual value and his urine output has fallen. He has no bleeding at present. What is the main concern about his anticoagulant?

options.A: Kidney injury makes dabigatran ineffective, so his stroke risk rises
options.B: Dabigatran must be continued unchanged to avoid stroke
options.C: The dose should be doubled to overcome reduced absorption
options.D: Reduced renal clearance increases dabigatran levels and bleeding risk
options.E: Dabigatran is cleared by the liver, so kidney function does not matter

correct_answer: D. Reduced renal clearance increases dabigatran levels and bleeding risk
why_correct: Dabigatran is mostly eliminated by the kidneys, so in acute kidney injury it accumulates, increasing anticoagulant effect and the risk of serious bleeding. It should be withheld and reviewed while renal function is impaired, with anticoagulation reconsidered as he recovers. A reversal agent, idarucizumab, is available if life-threatening bleeding occurs.
why_wrong: A. Accumulation increases, rather than reduces, the anticoagulant effect. B. Continuing unchanged ignores the bleeding risk from accumulation. C. Doubling the dose would greatly increase bleeding risk; absorption is not the problem. E. Dabigatran is the most renally dependent of the direct oral anticoagulants.
pearl: Of the direct oral anticoagulants, dabigatran relies most on renal excretion, while apixaban relies least.
thinking: Renally cleared anticoagulant ↓ Acute kidney injury from sepsis ↓ Reduced drug clearance ↓ Higher drug levels ↓ Increased bleeding risk: withhold and review
exam_trap: A, Dabigatran becomes ineffective — kidney injury changes drug handling, but it causes accumulation and over-anticoagulation, not loss of effect.
takeaway: In acute kidney injury, renally cleared anticoagulants accumulate and raise bleeding risk, so review them promptly.

presentation: DOAC review when renal function declines
stem: At her yearly review in general practice, a 69-year-old woman taking apixaban after recurrent deep vein thromboses is found to have much worse kidney function than last year, as her diabetic kidney disease has progressed. She feels well and has had no bleeding. What is the most appropriate action regarding her anticoagulant?

options.A: Increase the apixaban dose to keep the same level of protection
options.B: Continue the same dose and recheck kidney function next year
options.C: Switch her to aspirin as a safer option
options.D: Stop apixaban together with all her other regular medicines
options.E: Review the apixaban dose and whether it remains suitable for her current renal function

correct_answer: E. Review the apixaban dose and whether it remains suitable for her current renal function
why_correct: Direct oral anticoagulants are partly renally cleared, so their suitability, and for some drugs and indications their dose, depends on creatinine clearance. A significant fall in renal function means the dose and choice of drug should be reviewed using the BNF or product information, and kidney function monitored more often. Anticoagulation is still needed for recurrent venous thromboembolism.
why_wrong: A. Increasing the dose would raise drug levels and bleeding risk. B. A marked decline needs action now and more frequent monitoring, not another year at the same dose. C. Aspirin is not an adequate substitute for anticoagulation after recurrent DVT. D. Stopping all medicines is unsafe; each should be reviewed on its merits.
pearl: DOAC dosing should be based on creatinine clearance calculated with the Cockcroft-Gault equation using actual body weight, rather than eGFR alone.
thinking: DOAC for recurrent DVT ↓ Progressive decline in kidney function ↓ DOACs are partly renally cleared ↓ Dose and suitability depend on renal function ↓ Review the dose and monitor more often
exam_trap: C, Switch to aspirin — it feels gentler for someone with weaker kidneys, but it does not adequately prevent recurrent venous thromboembolism.
takeaway: When renal function declines on a DOAC, review the dose and suitability rather than continuing unchanged.

presentation: Warfarin and a newly prescribed interacting drug
stem: An 81-year-old care home resident with atrial fibrillation has been stable on warfarin for years. During a telephone consultation the GP decides she needs a course of oral fluconazole for oesophageal candidiasis, a medicine known to enhance the effect of warfarin markedly. What is the most appropriate approach to her anticoagulation?

options.A: Stop warfarin completely until the antifungal course is finished
options.B: Confirm the interaction in the BNF and arrange closer INR monitoring during and after the course
options.C: Keep her usual INR schedule, because antifungal interactions are rarely important
options.D: Increase the warfarin dose in advance to keep the INR stable
options.E: Halve the warfarin dose and recheck the INR at her next three-monthly check

correct_answer: B. Confirm the interaction in the BNF and arrange closer INR monitoring during and after the course
why_correct: Fluconazole inhibits the enzymes that metabolise warfarin, so her INR is likely to rise during the course. Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index, so the safe approach is to check the interaction, warn the care home and arrange INR checks within a few days of starting and after stopping the new drug. Any dose change should be guided by these INR results rather than made blindly.
why_wrong: A. Stopping warfarin leaves her unprotected against stroke when monitoring alone would manage the risk. C. Azole interactions with warfarin are clinically significant, so routine monitoring is not enough. D. Fluconazole enhances warfarin, so increasing the dose would make bleeding more likely. E. A blind dose cut with no INR check for months could cause either clotting or bleeding unnoticed.
pearl: Enzyme inhibitors such as macrolides, azoles and metronidazole raise the INR, whereas enzyme inducers such as rifampicin and carbamazepine lower it.
thinking: Stable on warfarin ↓ New drug that strongly enhances warfarin ↓ Narrow therapeutic index ↓ Check the interaction and inform those giving the medicine ↓ Closer INR monitoring, with dose changes guided by results
exam_trap: E, Halving the dose — it sounds proactive, but an empirical dose change without prompt INR checks can cause harm in either direction.
takeaway: When an interacting drug is started or stopped in someone on warfarin, check the interaction and monitor the INR more closely.

presentation: Raised INR on warfarin without bleeding
stem: A 58-year-old woman taking warfarin after a previous pulmonary embolism phones the anticoagulation clinic. She has had a week of poor appetite from a stomach upset, which has now settled. Her routine INR today is 6.4, well above her target. She has no bleeding, bruising or other symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Switch her to treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin
options.B: Continue her usual warfarin dose and recheck the INR next week
options.C: Arrange IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate today
options.D: Withhold one or two doses of warfarin and restart at a reduced maintenance dose
options.E: Give oral vitamin K now and continue her usual warfarin dose

correct_answer: D. Withhold one or two doses of warfarin and restart at a reduced maintenance dose
why_correct: Her INR is raised but below 8 and she is not bleeding. In this situation the BNF advises withholding one or two doses of warfarin, reducing the maintenance dose and rechecking the INR. Management is guided by the INR level and bleeding status, not by simply carrying on with her usual dose.
why_wrong: A. Adding heparin to someone who is already over-anticoagulated would increase bleeding risk. B. Continuing the same dose leaves her at risk of bleeding. C. IV vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate is for major bleeding. E. Oral vitamin K without bleeding is reserved for a higher INR, and the usual dose should not simply continue.
pearl: Reduced dietary vitamin K intake, illness, alcohol and interacting drugs are common causes of an unexpectedly high INR.
thinking: INR raised above target ↓ No bleeding ↓ INR below the level where vitamin K is used without bleeding ↓ Withhold one or two doses ↓ Reduce maintenance dose and recheck
exam_trap: E, Oral vitamin K with the usual dose — it seems a sensible fix, but vitamin K is not needed at this INR without bleeding, and continuing the same dose ignores the cause of the rise.
takeaway: Manage a high INR according to the level and any bleeding; without bleeding, withhold doses and reduce the maintenance dose.

stem: A 47-year-old man with a newly diagnosed deep vein thrombosis is starting warfarin. At the anticoagulation clinic he asks why the nurse has told him to keep his intake of green leafy vegetables steady rather than eating large amounts one week and none the next. Which vitamin does warfarin act against?
why_correct: Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, so less reduced vitamin K is available to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Green leafy vegetables are rich in vitamin K, so large swings in intake change how strongly warfarin works and make the INR unstable.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin B12 is needed for red cell and nerve function, not clotting factor activation. B. Vitamin C is involved in collagen synthesis. C. Vitamin E is an antioxidant with no central role in warfarin action. E. Vitamin D regulates calcium and bone metabolism.
pearl: Because factor VII has the shortest half-life, the INR rises within days of starting warfarin, but full anticoagulation takes longer, which is why heparin cover is needed at the start for acute thrombosis.
thinking: Starting warfarin ↓ Advised to keep leafy greens steady ↓ Leafy greens are rich in vitamin K ↓ Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling ↓ Fewer active factors II, VII, IX and X
exam_trap: C, Vitamin E — it is a fat-soluble vitamin like vitamin K and can mildly affect bleeding, but it is not the target of warfarin.
takeaway: Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist, so changes in dietary vitamin K alter its effect.

presentation: Antimicrobial stewardship in viral respiratory infection
stem: The mother of a 4-year-old boy brings him to the GP surgery after three days of runny nose, mild cough and a low-grade fever. She asks for antibiotics because his nursery wants him to get better quickly. He is alert, drinking well, and examination shows clear chest, normal breathing and no signs of ear or tonsil infection. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Prescribe a five-day course of amoxicillin to prevent a chest infection
options.B: Explain that antibiotics are unlikely to help, and give advice on symptom care and when to seek help
options.C: Prescribe amoxicillin and clarithromycin together to cover all likely organisms
options.D: Give a single dose of azithromycin to cover atypical bacteria
options.E: Prescribe phenoxymethylpenicillin because his sibling responded to it last month

correct_answer: B. Explain that antibiotics are unlikely to help, and give advice on symptom care and when to seek help
why_correct: This is a self-limiting viral upper respiratory tract infection in a well child with no features of bacterial infection. NICE advises against antibiotics here because they do not shorten the illness, cause side effects and drive resistance. The parent should be given advice on fluids, antipyretics, expected duration and clear safety-netting about red flags.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not prevent complications of viral colds in well children. C. Combined broad cover is unnecessary and increases resistance and side effects. D. A single macrolide dose has no role in a viral illness. E. Another person's response to an antibiotic is not an indication.
pearl: Uncomplicated colds usually last about one to two weeks, and a cough can persist for up to three weeks; telling families this reduces repeat consultations.
thinking: Well child with coryza and cough ↓ No signs of bacterial infection ↓ Viral and self-limiting ↓ Antibiotics give no benefit but cause harm and resistance ↓ Explain, give symptom advice and safety-net
exam_trap: A, Prescribing amoxicillin to prevent a chest infection — it seems protective and pleases the parent, but it does not reduce complications and adds harm.
takeaway: In a viral upper respiratory tract infection, explain why antibiotics will not help and give clear symptom and safety-net advice.

stem: A practice audit finds that a 30-year-old woman has received seven courses of antibiotics over two years from walk-in centres, mostly for short-lived coughs and sore throats with no documented signs of bacterial infection. The practice pharmacist is preparing a teaching session on this pattern of prescribing. Which public health problem does it most directly contribute to?

options.E: Rising prevalence of chronic kidney disease

why_correct: Each unnecessary course of antibiotics exposes bacteria to selective pressure, so resistant strains survive and spread. Repeated prescribing for self-limiting infections is a key driver of antimicrobial resistance, which UKHSA and NICE stewardship guidance aim to reduce.
why_wrong: A. Osteoporosis is not caused by short antibiotic courses. B. Vitamin D deficiency relates to sunlight and diet, not antibiotic use. C. Iron deficiency is not a population consequence of antibiotic overuse. E. Chronic kidney disease is not driven by short courses for minor infections.
pearl: Repeated antibiotic exposure also raises the individual's own risk of carrying resistant organisms and of Clostridioides difficile infection.
thinking: Repeated antibiotic courses ↓ No clear bacterial indication ↓ Selective pressure on bacteria ↓ Resistant organisms survive and spread ↓ Antimicrobial resistance
exam_trap: E, Chronic kidney disease — some antibiotics can harm the kidneys, but short courses for minor infections are not a recognised population cause of CKD.
takeaway: Unnecessary antibiotic prescribing drives antimicrobial resistance.

stem: A 62-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiac rehabilitation clinic six weeks after a myocardial infarction. He asks why he must keep taking low-dose aspirin for life when he no longer has chest pain. The nurse explains that aspirin stops platelets clumping together. Which enzyme does aspirin block to produce this effect?
why_correct: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclo-oxygenase (mainly COX-1) in platelets, preventing thromboxane A2 production. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts for the platelet's lifespan of about 7 to 10 days, reducing the risk of further arterial thrombosis.
why_wrong: A. HMG-CoA reductase is the target of statins. B. ACE is inhibited by drugs such as ramipril. C. Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate and trimethoprim. D. SGLT2 is blocked by gliflozins such as dapagliflozin.
pearl: Because the block is irreversible, aspirin's antiplatelet effect wears off only as new platelets are made, which is why it is often stopped about a week before some surgery when advised.
thinking: Post-MI secondary prevention ↓ Aspirin reduces platelet aggregation ↓ Platelets make thromboxane A2 via cyclo-oxygenase ↓ Aspirin irreversibly blocks this enzyme ↓ Less clumping for the platelet lifespan
exam_trap: A, HMG-CoA reductase — statins are also lifelong after an MI, so it is easy to mix up which enzyme each secondary prevention drug targets.
takeaway: Aspirin works by irreversibly inhibiting platelet cyclo-oxygenase, reducing thromboxane A2.

presentation: Aspirin and Reye syndrome in children
stem: At a community pharmacy, a father asks whether he can give aspirin to his 9-year-old daughter, who has chickenpox with fever and itchy spots. He takes aspirin himself for headaches and has some at home. The pharmacist advises against it. Which serious risk is the main reason?
why_correct: Aspirin given to children during viral illnesses, particularly chickenpox and influenza, is associated with Reye syndrome, a rare but life-threatening disorder causing acute encephalopathy and liver failure. For this reason aspirin is not recommended for children under 16 unless specifically prescribed by a specialist, for example in Kawasaki disease.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin does not cause appendicitis. B. Nephrotic syndrome is not a recognised risk of aspirin in children. D. Aspirin can worsen existing aspirin-sensitive asthma but does not cause asthma in every child, and this is not the main reason it is avoided. E. Congenital heart disease is present from birth and cannot be caused by aspirin in childhood.
pearl: Ibuprofen should also be avoided in chickenpox because of an association with severe skin and soft tissue infection, so paracetamol is the preferred antipyretic.
thinking: Child under 16 ↓ Viral illness with fever ↓ Parent wants to give aspirin ↓ Associated with Reye syndrome ↓ Advise paracetamol instead
exam_trap: D, New-onset asthma — aspirin can provoke bronchospasm in sensitive people, which makes this tempting, but Reye syndrome is the reason aspirin is avoided in children.
takeaway: Aspirin is avoided in children under 16 with viral illnesses because of the risk of Reye syndrome.

stem: A 19-year-old man is in the emergency department resuscitation bay with acute severe asthma. Over the past two hours he has received back-to-back nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium and oral prednisolone. His wheeze is easing, but the nurse notices new flattened T waves and U waves on his cardiac monitor. Which blood abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Beta-2 agonists such as salbutamol stimulate the sodium-potassium pump and drive potassium into cells, lowering serum potassium. Repeated high doses in acute asthma, often with corticosteroids, can cause significant hypokalaemia, and flattened T waves with U waves are typical ECG changes. Potassium should be monitored and replaced when needed.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol does not raise calcium. B. Sodium is not typically affected by nebulised salbutamol. C. Magnesium is used as a treatment in severe asthma but salbutamol does not raise it. D. Salbutamol does not cause raised bilirubin.
pearl: Hyperglycaemia, tachycardia, tremor and lactic acidosis are other recognised effects of high-dose beta-2 agonist therapy.
thinking: Acute severe asthma ↓ Repeated nebulised salbutamol ↓ Beta-2 stimulation shifts potassium into cells ↓ Flat T waves and U waves ↓ Hypokalaemia
exam_trap: C, Hypermagnesaemia — magnesium is part of severe asthma management, so it comes to mind, but it is not caused by salbutamol and does not produce U waves.
takeaway: Repeated beta-2 agonist doses can cause hypokalaemia, so check potassium in severe asthma.

stem: A 79-year-old woman attends her GP with several weeks of dizziness on standing and tiredness. Three months ago an ophthalmologist started timolol eye drops for open-angle glaucoma. She takes no other regular medicines. Her pulse is regular at 46 beats per minute and her blood tests are normal. Which adverse drug effect best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker, and enough is absorbed from eye drops to reduce sympathetic drive to the heart. This can slow the heart rate and cause light-headedness and fatigue, particularly in older people. Her slow pulse after starting the drops points to beta-blocker-induced bradycardia.
why_wrong: B. Beta-blockers mask features of hyperthyroidism rather than cause it, and her bloods are normal. C. Hyperglycaemia does not slow the pulse, and her blood tests are normal. D. Urinary retention is an antimuscarinic effect. E. Diarrhoea is not a typical beta-blocker effect.
pearl: Topical beta-blocker eye drops can also trigger bronchospasm in asthma, so always ask about eye drops when taking a drug history.
thinking: Dizziness and fatigue ↓ Recently started timolol drops ↓ Timolol is a beta-blocker absorbed systemically ↓ Pulse slow ↓ Beta-blocker-induced bradycardia
exam_trap: D, Urinary retention — eye drops for glaucoma can bring to mind anticholinergic effects, but timolol is a beta-blocker and slows the heart.
takeaway: Beta-blockers, including eye drops, can cause symptomatic bradycardia.

stem: A 63-year-old woman is on the general surgical ward after an emergency laparotomy and has been nil by mouth for four days. Her regular atenolol for hypertension and ischaemic heart disease has not been prescribed in any other form since admission. She now reports a pounding heartbeat and tightness in her chest when walking to the bathroom. Her pulse is 118 and regular. What is the most likely explanation?

options.E: Permanent loss of cardiac beta receptors

correct_answer: A. Rebound increase in sympathetic activity
why_correct: Long-term beta-blockade upregulates beta receptors, so when the drug is suddenly stopped, normal levels of adrenaline and noradrenaline produce an exaggerated response. This rebound causes tachycardia, palpitations, raised blood pressure and worsening angina, and can precipitate myocardial infarction. Beta-blockers should be continued around surgery where possible, or given by another route, and tapered rather than stopped abruptly.
why_wrong: B. Stopping a beta-blocker does not cause insulin deficiency. C. Beta-blocker withdrawal does not reduce thyroid hormone production. D. Red cell production is not affected within days of stopping a beta-blocker. E. Beta receptors are increased, not destroyed, by long-term blockade.
pearl: Ischaemic heart disease, rather than hypertension alone, carries the greatest risk from rebound after stopping a beta-blocker.
thinking: Long-term atenolol ↓ Suddenly omitted for several days ↓ Upregulated beta receptors ↓ Tachycardia and exertional chest tightness ↓ Rebound sympathetic activity
exam_trap: C, Reduced thyroid hormone production — palpitations suggest thyroid disease, but the timing after stopping atenolol points to rebound, and withdrawal would not lower thyroid output.
takeaway: Abrupt withdrawal of a beta-blocker can cause rebound tachycardia and angina, so avoid sudden omission.

presentation: Assessing anticoagulant effect in bleeding on warfarin
stem: A 69-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve presents to the emergency department with a hot, tense, painful swollen left knee that came on overnight without injury. Aspiration yields frank blood. He takes warfarin and has recently had a course of antibiotics. Which blood test best measures the effect of his anticoagulant?
why_correct: The international normalised ratio is a standardised form of the prothrombin time and is used to monitor warfarin. A spontaneous haemarthrosis in someone on warfarin, especially after an antibiotic, raises concern about over-anticoagulation, and the INR will guide how urgently and how far the anticoagulation needs reversing.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. B. TSH assesses thyroid function. D. HbA1c reflects glucose control over about three months. E. Amylase is used in suspected pancreatitis.
pearl: Spontaneous bleeding into a joint or muscle in someone on warfarin should always prompt an urgent INR check.
thinking: Spontaneous haemarthrosis ↓ Takes warfarin ↓ Recent antibiotic may have raised its effect ↓ Warfarin effect measured by prothrombin time ↓ INR
exam_trap: A, Troponin — he has a mechanical valve so a cardiac test feels relevant, but it says nothing about the level of anticoagulation.
takeaway: The INR is the test that measures the anticoagulant effect of warfarin.

stem: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who takes warfarin is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after vomiting fresh blood twice and passing black stools. He has been taking ibuprofen bought from a supermarket for back pain over the past fortnight. He is pale and clammy, with a pulse of 122 and a low blood pressure. What is the most appropriate approach to his anticoagulation?

options.A: Continue warfarin and start a high-dose proton pump inhibitor infusion
options.B: Assess severity, resuscitate, stop warfarin and urgently reverse it according to severity
options.C: Give IV protamine sulfate to neutralise the warfarin
options.D: Omit tonight's warfarin dose and repeat the INR tomorrow morning
options.E: Book a routine outpatient endoscopy once the INR is back in range

correct_answer: B. Assess severity, resuscitate, stop warfarin and urgently reverse it according to severity
why_correct: He has a major upper gastrointestinal bleed with signs of shock while anticoagulated. Priorities are ABC assessment, large-bore access, fluid and blood resuscitation, and stopping warfarin. Because the bleeding is major, the BNF advises urgent reversal with IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate, followed by urgent endoscopy.
why_wrong: A. Continuing warfarin during major bleeding will worsen it, even with acid suppression. C. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin. D. Omitting one dose does nothing for a life-threatening bleed already under way. E. A shocked patient needs urgent inpatient endoscopy, not a routine appointment.
pearl: NSAIDs combined with warfarin greatly increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, both by damaging the mucosa and by impairing platelet function.
thinking: Haematemesis and melaena ↓ Tachycardic and hypotensive ↓ On warfarin with NSAID use ↓ Major bleed ↓ Resuscitate, stop warfarin and reverse urgently
exam_trap: D, Omitting one dose and rechecking tomorrow — this is the right plan for a high INR without bleeding, but not for a shocked patient who is actively bleeding.
takeaway: Major bleeding on warfarin needs urgent assessment, resuscitation and reversal tailored to severity.

stem: A 66-year-old woman on the cardiology ward is on an intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion after a coronary angiogram for unstable angina. Two hours later the nurse finds a rapidly expanding haematoma at the femoral puncture site, and the woman becomes pale and hypotensive. The infusion has been stopped. Which drug specifically reverses the anticoagulant effect of this treatment?
why_correct: Protamine sulfate is a positively charged protein that binds the negatively charged heparin molecule and neutralises it. Unfractionated heparin has a short half-life, so stopping the infusion helps, but serious bleeding needs protamine, dosed according to the amount of heparin given recently.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin K reverses warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, not heparin. C. Idarucizumab is the specific antidote to dabigatran. D. Acetylcysteine is used for paracetamol poisoning. E. Naloxone reverses opioids.
pearl: Protamine fully reverses unfractionated heparin but only partly reverses low-molecular-weight heparin.
thinking: Heparin infusion ↓ Major bleeding from puncture site ↓ Stop infusion ↓ Need specific reversal agent ↓ Protamine sulfate
exam_trap: B, Vitamin K — it is the best-known reversal agent for anticoagulants, but it only works for vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin.
takeaway: Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent for unfractionated heparin.

presentation: Vitamin K in reversal of warfarin
stem: A 77-year-old woman with a previous stroke is seen in the ENT emergency clinic with a nosebleed that has continued despite nasal packing. She takes warfarin and her INR is 9.2. The registrar plans to give a vitamin by slow intravenous injection to help reverse the warfarin. Which vitamin is this?
why_correct: Warfarin prevents recycling of vitamin K, which is needed to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Giving vitamin K bypasses this block so the liver can make functional factors again. In bleeding with a markedly raised INR, warfarin is stopped and IV vitamin K is given, with prothrombin complex concentrate added if the bleeding is major.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin D is involved in calcium and bone metabolism. B. Vitamin B12 is used for deficiency anaemia and neuropathy. C. Vitamin C is used for scurvy. D. Vitamin E has no role in warfarin reversal.
pearl: IV vitamin K takes several hours to work, so prothrombin complex concentrate is needed for immediate reversal in life-threatening bleeding.
thinking: Persistent epistaxis ↓ Markedly raised INR on warfarin ↓ Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling ↓ Replace the missing cofactor ↓ IV vitamin K
exam_trap: D, Vitamin E — it is fat-soluble like vitamin K and is sometimes linked to bleeding tendency, but it does not reverse warfarin.
takeaway: Vitamin K reverses warfarin by restoring synthesis of active clotting factors.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation falls from a ladder while gardening and is brought to the major trauma centre with a reduced level of consciousness. A CT head shows an acute subdural haemorrhage. His wife brings in his medicines, which include dabigatran taken that morning. Which agent specifically reverses his anticoagulant?
why_correct: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, and idarucizumab is a humanised antibody fragment that binds it tightly and reverses its effect within minutes. In life-threatening bleeding such as an intracranial haemorrhage, it should be given urgently alongside neurosurgical review and supportive care.
why_wrong: B. Protamine reverses heparin, not dabigatran. C. Vitamin K reverses warfarin and has no effect on direct thrombin inhibitors. D. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines. E. Naloxone reverses opioids.
pearl: Idarucizumab acts only on dabigatran and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban or rivaroxaban; because dabigatran is mainly renally excreted, it can also be partly removed by haemodialysis.
thinking: Head injury with subdural haemorrhage ↓ Takes dabigatran ↓ Direct thrombin inhibitor ↓ Life-threatening bleed needs specific reversal ↓ Idarucizumab
