exam_trap: C, Vitamin K — it is the familiar anticoagulant reversal agent, but it only works against vitamin K antagonists, not DOACs.
takeaway: Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran.

stem: A 61-year-old man is seen in the emergency department three weeks after his GP started allopurinol for recurrent gout. He has a fever, a spreading dusky red rash with blisters on his trunk, and painful erosions on his lips and inside his mouth. His eyes are red and gritty. What is the main concern?
correct_answer: E. Severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction
why_correct: Blistering skin with involvement of two or more mucosal surfaces, fever, and onset a few weeks after starting a new drug strongly suggests Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Allopurinol is one of the commonest causes. The drug must be stopped immediately and he needs urgent specialist care, often in a burns or intensive care unit.
why_wrong: A. Bullous pemphigoid causes tense blisters in older people but rarely involves the mouth and is not linked to a new drug in this way. B. Urticaria causes itchy wheals without blistering or mucosal erosions. C. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes mild vesicles on the hands, feet and mouth, mainly in children. D. Scalded skin syndrome usually affects young children and spares the mucous membranes.
pearl: Common triggers of Stevens-Johnson syndrome include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfonamides and nevirapine, usually within the first eight weeks of treatment.
thinking: New drug started weeks ago ↓ Fever and blistering rash ↓ Painful oral and eye involvement ↓ Mucosal involvement suggests SJS/TEN ↓ Severe cutaneous drug reaction: stop drug and admit urgently
exam_trap: D, Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome — it also causes widespread blistering, but it typically affects young children and does not cause mucosal erosions.
takeaway: Blistering rash with mucosal involvement after a new drug is a severe cutaneous drug reaction until proven otherwise.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has needed oral prednisolone for most of the past five years. She visits her optometrist because of gradually worsening glare from car headlights at night and misty vision in both eyes. Her eyes are not red or painful, and the optometrist sees an opacity at the back of each lens. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Long-term corticosteroid use is a well-recognised cause of cataract, typically posterior subcapsular, which causes gradual blurring and glare, especially at night. The painless course and lens opacity on examination fit this, and she should be referred to ophthalmology.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and a field defect, not lens opacity. B. Optic neuritis causes painful eye movements and reduced colour vision. C. Conjunctivitis causes a red, sticky or itchy eye without lens change. D. A corneal abrasion is painful and usually follows trauma.
pearl: Long-term corticosteroids can also cause raised intraocular pressure and glaucoma, so people on prolonged treatment should have regular eye checks.
thinking: Years of oral prednisolone ↓ Gradual misty vision and glare ↓ Painless, white eyes ↓ Opacity at the back of the lens ↓ Steroid-induced cataract
exam_trap: B, Optic neuritis — it is linked with autoimmune disease and causes blurred vision, but it is painful and does not cause a lens opacity.
takeaway: Long-term corticosteroids can cause posterior subcapsular cataracts.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has taken amiodarone for 18 months to control recurrent ventricular tachycardia. She is referred to the respiratory clinic with several months of a non-productive cough and gradually worsening breathlessness on walking uphill. She has no fever, and fine bibasal crackles are heard. Which adverse drug effect should be suspected?

options.E: Pulmonary embolism caused by the drug

why_correct: Amiodarone can cause interstitial pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis, usually after months of treatment, presenting with dry cough, progressive exertional breathlessness and fine crackles. It is related to cumulative dose and needs chest imaging and lung function testing, with review of the drug by cardiology.
why_wrong: A. A pneumothorax causes sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness, not a gradual course with crackles. C. Tuberculosis usually causes fever, sweats and weight loss and is not a drug effect of amiodarone. D. Sinusitis causes facial pain and nasal symptoms. E. Amiodarone does not directly cause pulmonary embolism.
pearl: Before and during amiodarone treatment, baseline chest X-ray, thyroid and liver function tests are needed because of its lung, thyroid and liver toxicity.
thinking: Long-term amiodarone ↓ Months of dry cough ↓ Progressive exertional breathlessness ↓ Fine crackles, no fever ↓ Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity
exam_trap: E, Pulmonary embolism — breathlessness in a cardiac patient suggests it, but the slow course with fine crackles points to drug-induced lung disease, and amiodarone does not cause clots.
takeaway: Progressive breathlessness and dry cough on amiodarone should raise suspicion of pulmonary toxicity.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with end-stage idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is visited at home by the community palliative care nurse. She is too breathless to finish a sentence while dressing, although a fan, pacing techniques and treatment of a recent chest infection have been tried. Her oxygen saturation at rest is within her usual range. Which drug treatment is most appropriate to ease her symptoms?

options.D: A further course of oral antibiotics
options.E: Oxygen even though she is not hypoxic

why_correct: In advanced disease, once reversible causes have been treated and non-drug measures tried, low-dose oral opioids such as morphine can reduce the sensation of breathlessness. They are started at a low dose and titrated carefully, alongside continued fan use, breathing techniques and psychological support.
why_wrong: B. Bronchodilators help reversible airway obstruction, not fibrotic lung disease. C. There is no evidence of thromboembolism to justify anticoagulation. D. The infection has already been treated, and antibiotics do not relieve breathlessness from fibrosis. E. Oxygen offers no more benefit than air in patients who are not hypoxic.
pearl: A hand-held fan blowing air across the face is a simple, evidence-based measure that reduces the sensation of breathlessness.
thinking: Advanced lung disease ↓ Severe breathlessness despite non-drug measures ↓ Reversible causes treated ↓ Not hypoxic ↓ Low-dose oral morphine
exam_trap: E, Oxygen without hypoxia — it feels like the natural remedy for breathlessness, but it does not help more than air when saturations are adequate.
takeaway: Low-dose oral morphine can relieve refractory breathlessness in palliative care after reversible causes are treated.

stem: An 84-year-old woman with heart failure is on the orthopaedic ward two days after a hip fracture repair. Because her oral intake has been poor, she has been receiving continuous intravenous fluids. Overnight she becomes short of breath when lying flat, with crackles at both lung bases and new swelling of her ankles and sacrum. What is the most likely complication?
why_correct: Older people with heart failure tolerate intravenous fluid poorly. New orthopnoea, bilateral basal crackles and dependent oedema during continuous IV fluids indicate fluid overload with pulmonary oedema. The fluids should be stopped or reduced, the fluid balance reviewed and she should be assessed for treatment such as a diuretic.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration does not cause crackles and oedema. B. Hypoglycaemia causes sweating and confusion, not oedema and crackles. C. Renal colic causes severe loin to groin pain. E. Appendicitis causes abdominal pain and fever.
pearl: NICE advises daily review of fluid prescriptions and fluid balance in hospital, with particular caution in older people and those with heart or kidney disease.
thinking: Heart failure and older age ↓ Continuous IV fluids ↓ Orthopnoea, basal crackles, new oedema ↓ Too much fluid for the heart to handle ↓ Fluid overload
exam_trap: A, Severe dehydration — her poor oral intake was the reason for fluids, but her new signs show she now has too much fluid, not too little.
takeaway: New breathlessness, crackles and oedema during IV fluids suggest fluid overload, so review the fluids promptly.

presentation: Bruising after a new medicine in a patient on warfarin
stem: A 70-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve has had stable INR results on warfarin for two years. A cardiologist recently added amiodarone after an episode of fast atrial fibrillation. Ten days later she comes to her GP with large bruises on her arms and thighs that she cannot explain. What should the GP consider first?

options.A: That warfarin does not interact with heart medicines
options.B: That the amiodarone is not working
options.C: That she should double her warfarin dose
options.D: A drug interaction increasing the effect of warfarin
options.E: That the bruising shows iron deficiency

correct_answer: D. A drug interaction increasing the effect of warfarin
why_correct: Amiodarone inhibits the metabolism of warfarin and commonly raises the INR, often needing a lower warfarin dose. New unexplained bruising soon after starting it suggests over-anticoagulation from this interaction, so the GP should check the INR urgently, assess for other bleeding and adjust the dose with the anticoagulation service.
why_wrong: A. Amiodarone is one of the best-known drugs that interacts with warfarin. B. Bruising says nothing about whether amiodarone is controlling her rhythm. C. Doubling the dose would worsen over-anticoagulation. E. Iron deficiency does not cause unexplained bruising.
pearl: Amiodarone has a very long half-life, so its effect on the INR can persist for weeks to months after it is stopped.
thinking: Stable on warfarin ↓ Amiodarone recently added ↓ Unexplained bruising ↓ Amiodarone inhibits warfarin metabolism ↓ Interaction raising anticoagulant effect, so check INR
exam_trap: B, The amiodarone is not working — it focuses on the new drug, but the bruising points to an effect on warfarin rather than a failure of rhythm control.
takeaway: New bruising after starting a drug in someone on warfarin should prompt consideration of an interaction and an urgent INR.

presentation: Minor bleeding with a high INR on warfarin
stem: A 61-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who takes warfarin comes to the GP surgery after a week of heavy drinking at a family celebration. He has developed widespread bruises on his arms and legs without injury. A point-of-care INR is 7.8, well above his target. He has no other bleeding and is haemodynamically stable. What is the key principle of management?

options.A: Withhold warfarin and manage according to the INR level and extent of bleeding
options.B: Double the warfarin dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
options.C: Give IV protamine sulfate to reverse the warfarin
options.D: Continue warfarin and recheck the INR in a week
options.E: Add low-dose aspirin to protect against stroke

correct_answer: A. Withhold warfarin and manage according to the INR level and extent of bleeding
why_correct: His INR is markedly raised and he has minor bleeding in the form of bruising, likely related to acute alcohol excess. Warfarin should be withheld, and management depends on the INR and bleeding status; for minor bleeding with an INR above 5, the BNF advises IV vitamin K and restarting warfarin once the INR has fallen. He should also be advised about alcohol.
why_wrong: B. Increasing the dose would raise the INR even further. C. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin. D. Continuing at the same dose ignores the high INR and bleeding. E. Adding aspirin would increase bleeding risk.
pearl: Binge drinking tends to raise the INR by inhibiting warfarin metabolism, whereas chronic heavy drinking can lower it through enzyme induction.
thinking: On warfarin ↓ Binge drinking ↓ Spontaneous bruising ↓ INR markedly raised, no major bleeding ↓ Withhold warfarin and treat according to INR and bleeding
exam_trap: D, Continue and recheck in a week — he is stable and only bruised, which can tempt a wait-and-see plan, but a high INR with bleeding needs warfarin withheld now.
takeaway: With a high INR and minor bleeding on warfarin, withhold it and manage according to the INR and bleeding.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with three fractured ribs after a fall from her horse is seen by her GP a few days later. Paracetamol and naproxen have not controlled her pain, so the GP decides to start regular codeine phosphate four times a day for a few weeks. She asks whether the new tablets will cause any problems. Which medicine should be prescribed with the codeine to prevent a common adverse effect?
why_correct: Opioids such as codeine reduce gut motility and increase fluid absorption, causing constipation in most people taking them regularly. Unlike nausea or drowsiness, tolerance to this effect does not develop. A laxative, typically a stimulant with or without a softener, should be co-prescribed when regular opioids are started, alongside advice on fluids and fibre.
why_wrong: A. Antihistamines do not prevent constipation and can make it worse. C. A proton pump inhibitor protects the stomach but does not treat opioid constipation. D. An antacid alone has no effect on gut motility. E. There is no indication for anticoagulation.
pearl: Bulk-forming laxatives such as ispaghula are not recommended for opioid-induced constipation because they can worsen symptoms when motility is reduced.
thinking: Starting regular opioid ↓ Opioids slow gut motility ↓ Constipation is very common and persistent ↓ Tolerance does not develop ↓ Co-prescribe a laxative
exam_trap: C, A proton pump inhibitor — she is also on naproxen, so gastroprotection is tempting, but it does not prevent the main problem caused by codeine.
takeaway: When regular opioids are started, a laxative should be prescribed to prevent constipation.

stem: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson's disease has long-standing constipation, which is common in his condition. He takes senna tablets at night, and at a medication review with the practice pharmacist he asks how they actually work. What is the main action of this type of laxative?
why_correct: Senna is a stimulant laxative. It stimulates the nerves of the colonic wall to increase peristalsis and also increases water and electrolyte secretion into the bowel. Its effect usually begins 8 to 12 hours after a dose, which is why it is taken at night.
why_wrong: A. Suppressing acid is the action of proton pump inhibitors and H2 antagonists. B. Laxatives do not work by reducing bile production. D. Stimulant laxatives increase, rather than stop, bowel activity. E. Laxatives do not affect insulin secretion.
pearl: Stimulant laxatives such as senna and bisacodyl can cause abdominal cramping, and should be avoided in suspected bowel obstruction.
thinking: Chronic constipation ↓ Takes senna ↓ Stimulant laxative ↓ Stimulates the colonic nerves ↓ Increased intestinal motility
exam_trap: D, They paralyse the colon — the old worry that long-term use damages the colon can mislead, but the immediate action is to increase motility.
takeaway: Stimulant laxatives such as senna work by increasing intestinal motility.

stem: A GP visits a care home to review a 79-year-old man who was started on a low-strength buprenorphine patch for chronic back pain two weeks ago. His pain is now well controlled and he is walking with his frame again. Staff report that he passes hard stools only every few days and strains. Examination is unremarkable and he is not obstructed. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Start ispaghula husk and limit his fluid intake
options.B: Start a regular laxative, such as a stimulant with or without an osmotic agent, and keep the patch
options.C: Remove the patch and switch him to regular codeine
options.D: Increase the strength of the patch

correct_answer: B. Start a regular laxative, such as a stimulant with or without an osmotic agent, and keep the patch
why_correct: Constipation is an expected adverse effect of every opioid, including buprenorphine, and tolerance to it does not develop. As the opioid is working well, the right step is to keep it and treat the bowel effect with a regular laxative, usually a stimulant such as senna with or without an osmotic agent such as a macrogol. Good fluid intake and mobility also help.
why_wrong: A. Bulk-forming laxatives are not recommended for opioid-induced constipation and fluid restriction would make stools harder. C. Codeine is also an opioid and is very constipating. D. A higher opioid dose would worsen constipation and his pain is already controlled. E. An antispasmodic slows gut motility and does nothing for hard stool.
pearl: Unlike nausea and drowsiness, tolerance to opioid constipation does not develop, so laxatives are usually needed for as long as the opioid continues.
thinking: Effective opioid started recently ↓ New hard, infrequent stools ↓ No features of obstruction ↓ Constipation is a persistent opioid effect ↓ Keep the opioid and add a regular stimulant or osmotic laxative
exam_trap: C, Switching to codeine — it sounds like a step down to a weaker drug, but codeine is itself an opioid and causes as much or more constipation.
takeaway: Treat opioid-induced constipation with a regular stimulant or osmotic laxative while continuing an effective opioid.

stem: At a hospice outpatient appointment, a 52-year-old woman with bone metastases from breast cancer is about to begin modified-release morphine twice daily for pain that has not settled with paracetamol and an NSAID. Her bowels currently open daily and she is eating well. What should be prescribed or advised at the same time to protect her bowel function?

options.A: Regular loperamide to keep the bowel settled
options.B: A bulk-forming laxative only if constipation develops later
options.C: Reduce fluid intake to limit nausea
options.D: Stop the morphine if her bowels open less than daily
options.E: A regular laxative from the outset, with monitoring of bowel habit

correct_answer: E. A regular laxative from the outset, with monitoring of bowel habit
why_correct: Almost everyone taking regular strong opioids becomes constipated, so NICE advises prescribing a laxative routinely when strong opioids are started for pain in palliative care. Starting it from the first dose and checking bowel habit at each review prevents distressing constipation and avoids loss of good pain control.
why_wrong: A. Loperamide is itself a peripherally acting opioid and would cause constipation. B. Waiting until constipation appears is reactive, and bulk-forming agents are not preferred in opioid-induced constipation. C. Reducing fluids hardens stools and worsens constipation. D. Analgesia should not be withdrawn because of a manageable, predictable side effect.
pearl: Patients starting strong opioids should also be told that nausea and drowsiness often settle within days, whereas constipation persists.
thinking: Starting regular strong opioid ↓ Constipation is almost universal and persistent ↓ Prevention is better than treatment ↓ Co-prescribe a regular laxative ↓ Monitor bowel habit at each review
exam_trap: B, A bulk-forming laxative if constipation develops — it seems a cautious, minimal approach, but it waits for a predictable problem and uses a laxative type that is unhelpful with opioids.
takeaway: Prescribe a regular laxative whenever regular strong opioids are started.

stem: A 23-year-old woman calls NHS 111 at breakfast. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and has just found that yesterday's tablet, from the second week of her current strip, is still in the packet. Every other pill this month has been taken on time, and she has no vomiting or diarrhoea. She wants to know what to do now. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Discard the forgotten pill and use condoms for the next seven days
options.B: Stop this strip now and take a seven-day break
options.C: Take emergency contraception today and then continue the strip
options.D: Take two pills every day until the strip is finished
options.E: Take the forgotten pill now, take today's pill at the usual time even if that is two in one day, and finish the strip as normal

correct_answer: E. Take the forgotten pill now, take today's pill at the usual time even if that is two in one day, and finish the strip as normal
why_correct: One missed combined pill, with less than 48 hours since the last one should have been taken, does not reduce contraceptive cover. FSRH advice is to take the most recent missed pill as soon as possible, carry on with the rest of the strip at the usual time and keep the normal hormone-free interval. No extra precautions or emergency contraception are needed.
why_wrong: A. The missed pill should be taken, and condoms are not required after one missed pill. B. Starting an early break lengthens the hormone-free interval and increases the risk of ovulation. C. Emergency contraception is not indicated after a single missed pill. D. Doubling up for the rest of the strip is not recommended and only adds side effects.
pearl: The highest-risk time to miss combined pills is at the start or end of a strip, because this extends the hormone-free interval.
thinking: Combined pill, one tablet missed ↓ Less than 48 hours late, no other missed pills ↓ Cover is maintained ↓ Take it now, continue strip ↓ No extra precautions or emergency contraception
exam_trap: C, Emergency contraception — it feels like the safest option after any missed pill, but a single missed combined pill does not reduce protection, so it is unnecessary.
takeaway: After one missed combined pill, take it as soon as remembered and continue the strip without extra precautions.

stem: After a condom split 30 hours ago, a 31-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic. She is offered an intrauterine device but declines it and asks for a tablet instead. The nurse explains that the tablet chosen works mainly by preventing or postponing ovulation rather than by acting on the lining of the womb. Which emergency contraceptive is being described?
why_correct: Oral levonorgestrel emergency contraception acts chiefly by inhibiting or delaying ovulation, so it does not work if ovulation has already occurred. It is licensed for use up to 72 hours after unprotected intercourse and is suitable for this woman, who wants an oral method and is within that window.
why_wrong: B. The copper device works by being toxic to sperm and ova and preventing implantation, and she has declined it. C. Mifepristone is an antiprogestogen used for medical abortion and is not used as emergency contraception in the UK. D. Misoprostol is a prostaglandin analogue used in medical abortion and miscarriage management. E. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic used for heavy menstrual bleeding.
pearl: The copper intrauterine device is the most effective emergency contraception and can be fitted up to 5 days after intercourse or up to 5 days after the earliest expected ovulation.
thinking: Oral emergency contraception requested ↓ Mechanism is delaying ovulation ↓ Copper device works differently ↓ Abortifacients and haemostatics are not contraceptives ↓ Levonorgestrel
exam_trap: B, Copper intrauterine device — it is the best-known emergency contraceptive, but it works mainly through toxicity to gametes and preventing implantation, not by delaying ovulation.
takeaway: Oral levonorgestrel emergency contraception works by delaying or preventing ovulation.

stem: At a cardiac rehabilitation session, a 70-year-old woman who had a myocardial infarction two months ago mentions a tickly, non-productive cough that started a few weeks after discharge. Her medicines include aspirin, a statin, bisoprolol and perindopril. She has no wheeze, fever or sputum, and her chest is clear. Which mechanism most likely explains her cough?

options.A: Increased angiotensin II in the airways
options.B: Histamine release from airway mast cells
options.C: Beta-2 receptor blockade in the bronchi

why_correct: Angiotensin-converting enzyme also breaks down bradykinin. When perindopril inhibits the enzyme, bradykinin builds up in the airways and sensitises the cough reflex, producing a dry, persistent cough. The timing after starting her secondary prevention drugs and the absence of chest signs fit this.
why_wrong: A. ACE inhibitors reduce, not increase, angiotensin II. B. Mast cell histamine release is the mechanism of allergic reactions, not this cough. C. Beta-blockade can cause bronchospasm with wheeze, not an isolated dry cough with a clear chest. E. ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone production.
pearl: Angiotensin II receptor blockers do not affect bradykinin breakdown, which is why they rarely cause cough.
thinking: Dry cough after starting secondary prevention ↓ Clear chest, no infection ↓ Perindopril is an ACE inhibitor ↓ ACE also degrades bradykinin ↓ Bradykinin accumulation
exam_trap: C, Beta-2 receptor blockade — she is on bisoprolol, which tempts, but beta-blocker airway effects cause wheeze and bronchospasm rather than a dry tickly cough with a clear chest.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough is caused by accumulation of bradykinin.

presentation: Alternative to ACE inhibitor after cough
stem: A 49-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and persistent albuminuria returns to his GP. Ramipril was started for kidney protection, but for the last two months he has had a dry cough that disturbs his sleep. His chest examination is normal and he has no reflux symptoms. He would like to stop the cough but keep protecting his kidneys. What is the most appropriate change?

options.B: Continue ramipril and add codeine linctus
options.C: Switch to an angiotensin II receptor blocker such as losartan

correct_answer: C. Switch to an angiotensin II receptor blocker such as losartan
why_correct: A troublesome dry cough is a class effect of ACE inhibitors. An angiotensin II receptor blocker gives the same renin-angiotensin blockade, including the renal benefit in diabetic kidney disease with albuminuria, without causing bradykinin-related cough. Swapping to an ARB is the recommended option when an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated.
why_wrong: A. Another ACE inhibitor will cause the same cough. B. A cough suppressant masks the symptom and leaves the cause in place. D. Amlodipine lowers blood pressure but lacks the antiproteinuric benefit he needs. E. There is no reflux, and a PPI does not treat ACE inhibitor cough.
pearl: The cough can take weeks to settle after the ACE inhibitor is stopped, so patients should be warned not to expect immediate improvement.
thinking: Dry cough on ramipril ↓ No other cause on examination ↓ Class effect of ACE inhibitors ↓ Still needs renin-angiotensin blockade for albuminuria ↓ Switch to an ARB
exam_trap: A, Changing to lisinopril — it seems like trying a different drug, but cough is a class effect and will recur with any ACE inhibitor.
takeaway: When an ACE inhibitor causes cough, switch to an angiotensin II receptor blocker.

stem: A 63-year-old man with heart failure is referred to a respiratory clinic with a dry cough that has persisted for several months. He has never smoked. His chest radiograph and spirometry are normal and there are no crackles or wheeze. Since a cardiology admission last year he has taken enalapril, bisoprolol and furosemide. Which adverse drug effect most likely explains his symptoms?

options.C: Drying of airway secretions from anticholinergic activity
options.E: Cough as an adverse effect of the ACE inhibitor

correct_answer: E. Cough as an adverse effect of the ACE inhibitor
why_correct: A persistent dry cough with a normal chest radiograph, normal spirometry and no chest signs in someone taking enalapril strongly suggests ACE inhibitor cough. It affects a significant minority of patients and can begin weeks or months after starting. Switching to an angiotensin II receptor blocker usually resolves it while keeping the prognostic benefit in heart failure.
why_wrong: A. Interstitial lung disease causes crackles and an abnormal radiograph and is linked to drugs such as amiodarone and methotrexate. B. Bronchospasm would cause wheeze and obstructive spirometry. C. None of his medicines has significant anticholinergic activity. D. He takes no opioids.
pearl: Always review the medication list before investigating a chronic cough further; ACE inhibitors are a common and reversible cause.
thinking: Chronic dry cough ↓ Normal radiograph, spirometry and examination ↓ Takes enalapril ↓ Recognised ACE inhibitor effect ↓ Consider switch to an ARB
exam_trap: B, Beta-blocker-induced bronchospasm — he takes bisoprolol, but bronchospasm causes wheeze and reduced spirometry, both absent here.
takeaway: A chronic dry cough with normal investigations in a patient on an ACE inhibitor is usually drug-induced.

stem: A 58-year-old man with severe plaque psoriasis has taken weekly methotrexate from the dermatology clinic for four months. He presents to the medical assessment unit with two weeks of low-grade fever, a non-productive cough and breathlessness that is now present when he walks across a room. There are fine bibasal crackles and his oxygen saturation falls on exertion. He has no leg swelling or chest pain. Which drug-related complication should be considered first?
why_correct: Methotrexate can cause a hypersensitivity pneumonitis, usually within the first year, with subacute dry cough, breathlessness, fever, crackles and exertional desaturation. It is potentially fatal, so methotrexate should be withheld and the patient assessed urgently with imaging and exclusion of infection, including opportunistic infection.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary embolism is usually more abrupt, often with pleuritic pain, and is not a recognised direct effect of methotrexate. C. Bronchiectasis causes chronic productive cough over months to years. D. Pneumothorax causes sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness, without fever or crackles. E. There are no features of heart failure such as oedema or orthopnoea, and the fever points elsewhere.
pearl: Patients on methotrexate should be told to report new cough or breathlessness promptly, as well as sore throat, bruising and mouth ulcers.
thinking: Weekly methotrexate for months ↓ Subacute dry cough, fever, breathlessness ↓ Crackles and exertional desaturation ↓ No cardiac or thromboembolic features ↓ Suspect methotrexate pneumonitis and withhold the drug
exam_trap: E, Left ventricular failure — crackles and breathlessness suggest it, but there is no oedema or cardiac history, and the fever and dry cough fit drug pneumonitis.
takeaway: New cough, fever and breathlessness on methotrexate should prompt consideration of methotrexate pneumonitis.

stem: A 61-year-old woman with hypertension, treated with ramipril and indapamide, bought naproxen from a pharmacy a week ago for a painful flare of gout and has taken it at full dose since. At a GP review her joint is settling, but routine bloods show a creatinine considerably higher than her usual baseline, with a reduced urine output over the past two days. Which adverse effect of the anti-inflammatory drug best explains these results?

options.C: Acute kidney injury from reduced renal perfusion

correct_answer: C. Acute kidney injury from reduced renal perfusion
why_correct: NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, and prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole to maintain glomerular filtration. With an ACE inhibitor reducing efferent tone and a diuretic reducing circulating volume, losing this prostaglandin effect can sharply cut filtration and cause acute kidney injury. The naproxen should be stopped and renal function rechecked.
why_wrong: A. Bleeding is a major NSAID risk but would not explain a rising creatinine with falling urine output. B. Hepatitis is an uncommon NSAID effect and does not explain the renal results. D. Bronchospasm occurs in aspirin- or NSAID-sensitive asthma and is unrelated to these bloods. E. Aseptic meningitis is a rare NSAID reaction causing headache and neck stiffness.
pearl: The combination of an NSAID, a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor or ARB is sometimes called the triple whammy because of its high risk of acute kidney injury.
thinking: Recent full-dose NSAID ↓ Also on ACE inhibitor and diuretic ↓ Rising creatinine and low urine output ↓ Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation ↓ NSAID-related acute kidney injury
exam_trap: A, Upper gastrointestinal bleeding — it is the most famous NSAID harm, but nothing here suggests blood loss and it does not explain the renal picture.
takeaway: NSAIDs can precipitate acute kidney injury, especially alongside ACE inhibitors and diuretics.

stem: At a diabetes clinic, a 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has a new tablet added to his metformin. The consultant explains that it blocks reabsorption of filtered glucose in the proximal tubule, so that excess glucose is passed in the urine, and warns him about genital hygiene. To which drug class does the new tablet belong?
why_correct: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin and empagliflozin block the sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 in the proximal convoluted tubule, so less filtered glucose is reabsorbed and more is excreted in urine. They also offer cardiac and renal benefits, which is why they suit this man with heart failure. Glycosuria explains the increased risk of genital fungal infection.
why_wrong: A. DPP-4 inhibitors prolong the action of endogenous incretins to boost glucose-dependent insulin secretion. B. Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release from beta cells. D. Thiazolidinediones such as pioglitazone increase insulin sensitivity and can worsen heart failure. E. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors slow carbohydrate digestion in the gut.
pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause diabetic ketoacidosis with only modestly raised glucose, so they should be paused during acute illness, surgery or fasting.
thinking: Drug acts on proximal tubule ↓ Blocks glucose reabsorption ↓ Causes glycosuria and genital infection risk ↓ Also benefits heart failure ↓ SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_trap: D, Thiazolidinediones — they are another add-on tablet to metformin, but they act on insulin sensitivity and cause fluid retention, which makes them unsuitable in heart failure.
takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose by increasing urinary glucose excretion.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and obesity is reviewed by the practice nurse six weeks after starting a once-weekly subcutaneous injection alongside metformin. She reports feeling full after small meals and some nausea, and she has lost weight. Her blood glucose has improved without any hypoglycaemic episodes. Which drug class is she most likely taking?
why_correct: GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and dulaglutide mimic incretin hormones, increasing glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppressing glucagon, slowing gastric emptying and reducing appetite via central effects. This gives early satiety, nausea and weight loss with a low risk of hypoglycaemia, and weekly injectable forms are common.
why_wrong: A. DPP-4 inhibitors are oral, weight-neutral and have little effect on gastric emptying or appetite. B. Insulin tends to cause weight gain and carries a risk of hypoglycaemia. C. SGLT2 inhibitors are oral and act on the kidney. D. Sulfonylureas are oral, cause weight gain and can cause hypoglycaemia.
pearl: GLP-1 receptor agonists have been linked with acute pancreatitis, so severe persistent abdominal pain on treatment should prompt stopping the drug and assessment.
thinking: Weekly injection added to metformin ↓ Early satiety and nausea ↓ Weight loss without hypoglycaemia ↓ Slowed gastric emptying and reduced appetite ↓ GLP-1 receptor agonist
exam_trap: B, Long-acting basal insulin — it is also injected, but it causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia rather than satiety and weight loss.
takeaway: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying, promoting weight loss.

stem: A 34-year-old man phones his GP surgery on the fourth day of a course of clarithromycin prescribed for a chest infection. His cough is improving, but he has developed loose stools a few times a day with mild cramping. He has no blood in the stool, no fever and no vomiting, and he is eating and drinking normally. He has not travelled recently. What is the most likely cause of his diarrhoea?
why_correct: Mild, non-bloody diarrhoea that starts during an antibiotic course in a patient who is otherwise well is most often simple antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, caused by disruption of normal gut flora. Macrolides can also increase gut motility. Management is fluids and safety-netting, with stool testing for Clostridioides difficile if symptoms worsen, become severe or persist.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease causes chronic symptoms, not diarrhoea that starts abruptly during an antibiotic course. B. Appendicitis causes progressive abdominal pain, anorexia and fever. C. Crohn disease is a chronic condition, usually with weight loss and systemic features. D. Irritable bowel syndrome is a long-term diagnosis that cannot explain a new, clearly drug-linked change.
pearl: Advise patients to seek review if diarrhoea becomes bloody, frequent, or is accompanied by fever or abdominal pain, as this may indicate Clostridioides difficile infection.
thinking: New loose stools during an antibiotic course ↓ No blood, fever or systemic illness ↓ Clear temporal link ↓ Disturbed gut flora and macrolide prokinetic effect ↓ Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea
exam_trap: C, Crohn disease — abdominal cramps and diarrhoea in a young adult bring it to mind, but the acute onset during an antibiotic course in a well man points to a drug effect.
takeaway: Mild diarrhoea during antibiotic treatment in a well patient is usually simple antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

stem: An 81-year-old man with Parkinson disease dementia was started on rivastigmine patches by the memory service. His daughter reports that since the dose was stepped up he has had nausea, occasional vomiting and frequent loose stools, without fever or blood. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. Which mechanism best explains these symptoms?

options.A: Activation of opioid receptors in the gut wall
options.D: Blockade of muscarinic receptors in the gut
options.E: Increased acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors in the gut

correct_answer: E. Increased acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors in the gut
why_correct: Rivastigmine, like donepezil and galantamine, inhibits acetylcholinesterase so that acetylcholine accumulates. Besides the intended central effect, extra acetylcholine stimulates muscarinic receptors in the gut, increasing motility and secretions and causing nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly after dose increases.
why_wrong: A. Opioid receptor activation slows gut transit and causes constipation. B. Prostaglandin inhibition is the action of NSAIDs and causes gastric mucosal injury, not this pattern. C. D2 blockade is how antiemetics work and would reduce nausea rather than cause it. D. Muscarinic blockade is an anticholinergic effect that causes constipation, the opposite of what is seen.
pearl: Cholinesterase inhibitors can also cause bradycardia and syncope through increased vagal tone, so ask about falls and check the pulse.
thinking: Recent rivastigmine dose increase ↓ Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ Acetylcholinesterase is inhibited ↓ Excess acetylcholine stimulates gut muscarinic receptors ↓ Cholinergic gastrointestinal effects
exam_trap: D, Blockade of muscarinic receptors — it names the right receptor, but blocking it is anticholinergic and would cause constipation, not diarrhoea.
takeaway: Cholinesterase inhibitors cause diarrhoea and nausea through increased cholinergic stimulation of the gut.

stem: Ten days after starting metformin for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, a 47-year-old woman returns to her GP complaining of bloating, a metallic taste and loose stools. She feels otherwise well, has no vomiting, blood in the stool or weight loss, and her abdomen is soft. Her capillary glucose is lower than at diagnosis. What is the most likely explanation?

options.E: Common gastrointestinal side effect of metformin

correct_answer: E. Common gastrointestinal side effect of metformin
why_correct: Gastrointestinal upset, including bloating, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea and a metallic taste, is the most common adverse effect of metformin and typically appears soon after starting or increasing the dose. It often settles with slower titration, taking tablets with food, or switching to a modified-release preparation.
why_wrong: A. Lactic acidosis is rare and causes a systemically unwell patient, usually with renal impairment or acute illness. B. Coeliac disease does not appear abruptly within days of a new drug. C. She has had no antibiotics or hospital exposure, and she is well. D. Ketoacidosis causes vomiting, dehydration and a high glucose, whereas her glucose has fallen.
pearl: Long-term metformin can reduce vitamin B12 absorption, so consider checking B12 if anaemia or neuropathy develops.
thinking: Metformin started ten days ago ↓ Bloating, loose stools, metallic taste ↓ Patient well, glucose improving ↓ No features of serious illness ↓ Expected gastrointestinal intolerance
exam_trap: A, Lactic acidosis — it is the feared metformin complication, but it is rare and produces a seriously ill patient rather than mild bowel upset.
takeaway: Gastrointestinal upset is the commonest side effect of metformin and often settles with slow titration or a modified-release form.

stem: A father brings his 6-year-old daughter to a community pharmacy. She is on day three of co-amoxiclav prescribed for a skin infection after an animal bite, and since yesterday she has had softer, more frequent stools. She is playing normally, drinking well and has no fever, abdominal pain or blood in her stools. What is the most likely explanation for her bowel change?
why_correct: Co-amoxiclav is one of the antibiotics most likely to cause diarrhoea, through disruption of normal bowel flora and a direct effect of clavulanic acid on gut motility. In a well, playful child with no blood, pain or fever and a clear link to the antibiotic, this is the most likely cause. Advice is to keep up fluids, finish the course and return if she becomes unwell or the stool contains blood.
why_wrong: B. Intussusception causes episodes of severe colicky pain, pallor, vomiting and sometimes redcurrant-jelly stools, usually in younger children. C. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome follows bloody diarrhoea and causes pallor, reduced urine output and illness. D. Coeliac disease causes chronic symptoms and poor growth, not an acute change during antibiotics. E. Toddler diarrhoea affects children under about five and is chronic, not linked to a new medicine.
pearl: The clavulanic acid component of co-amoxiclav makes it more likely to cause diarrhoea than amoxicillin alone.
thinking: Soft frequent stools during co-amoxiclav ↓ Child well, playing, drinking ↓ No blood, pain or fever ↓ Disruption of gut flora by antibiotic ↓ Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea
exam_trap: E, Toddler diarrhoea — loose stools in a young child bring it to mind, but it is a chronic pattern in under-fives and does not start during a course of antibiotics.
takeaway: A well child with mild diarrhoea during co-amoxiclav most likely has antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

stem: A foundation doctor on a cardiology ward is preparing the discharge of a 77-year-old woman after admission with fast atrial fibrillation. During the stay she was started on warfarin, her insulin doses were changed, and her digoxin was stopped. She lives alone and her INR will need checking within a few days. Which step is most important for her safe transfer home?

options.A: Pause INR monitoring until her routine GP review in three months
options.B: Send a clear discharge summary to the GP and patient listing every medicine change, the doses, required monitoring and follow-up
options.C: Let the GP practice work out the changes from the inpatient drug chart
options.D: Give her the new medicines without a written list to avoid confusion
options.E: Tell her to resume all the medicines she was taking before admission

correct_answer: B. Send a clear discharge summary to the GP and patient listing every medicine change, the doses, required monitoring and follow-up
why_correct: Moving between hospital and home is a high-risk point for medication errors, especially with anticoagulants and insulin. A complete, clear discharge summary that states what was started, stopped and changed, why, the doses, the monitoring needed and who is responsible ensures the GP, community pharmacist and patient all act on the same information.
why_wrong: A. Warfarin needs early INR checks after starting, and delaying monitoring risks bleeding or clotting. C. The GP does not see the inpatient chart and cannot be expected to reconstruct changes from it. D. A written list helps patients, especially older people living alone, take medicines correctly. E. Restarting pre-admission medicines could reintroduce the stopped digoxin and old insulin doses.
pearl: Many hospitals refer patients on high-risk medicines to their community pharmacy at discharge via the Discharge Medicines Service so that changes are reconciled.
thinking: Several high-risk medicine changes in hospital ↓ Transfer of care is an error-prone step ↓ GP and patient need accurate information ↓ Include changes, doses, monitoring and follow-up ↓ Clear written discharge communication
exam_trap: E, Telling her to resume her pre-admission medicines — it sounds simple and familiar for her, but it would undo deliberate changes such as stopping digoxin.
takeaway: At discharge, communicate every medicine change, dose, monitoring need and follow-up clearly to the GP and patient.

stem: A 37-year-old man attends a TB nurse clinic two weeks into treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. He is worried because his urine has turned orange and his soft contact lenses have become stained the same colour. He feels well, his appetite is good and he has no abdominal pain or muscle aches. What is the most likely explanation?

options.C: Expected, harmless discolouration of body fluids caused by rifampicin

correct_answer: C. Expected, harmless discolouration of body fluids caused by rifampicin
why_correct: Rifampicin is a red-orange compound that is excreted in urine, sweat and tears, colouring them orange-red and permanently staining soft contact lenses. This is expected and harmless, and patients should be warned about it before treatment starts. His wellbeing and the involvement of his tears make other causes unlikely.
why_wrong: A. Haematuria from a stone causes colicky loin pain and would not stain contact lenses. B. Pyrazinamide hepatotoxicity causes jaundice, malaise and dark urine, not orange tears. D. Rhabdomyolysis causes muscle pain and dark brown urine, and tears are unaffected. E. Interstitial nephritis is rare and causes renal impairment, rash or fever rather than orange tears.
pearl: Rifampicin is a potent liver enzyme inducer and makes hormonal contraception, warfarin and many other drugs less effective.
thinking: Started rifampicin-containing regimen ↓ Orange urine and stained contact lenses ↓ Well, no pain or jaundice ↓ Drug pigment excreted in body fluids ↓ Harmless rifampicin discolouration
exam_trap: B, Drug-induced liver injury from pyrazinamide — liver toxicity is a real concern with TB drugs, but it causes jaundice and malaise and does not colour tears.
takeaway: Orange-red urine and tears on rifampicin are expected and harmless.

stem: Staff at a nursing home ask a GP to see an 80-year-old woman who was started on bisoprolol a fortnight ago for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. She has felt light-headed when walking to the dining room and nearly fell this morning. Her pulse is regular at 44 beats per minute, and she has no chest pain or breathlessness. Which adverse effect of her new medicine is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Beta-blockers slow conduction through the atrioventricular node and reduce sinus rate by blocking cardiac beta-1 receptors. In older people this can cause excessive slowing, leading to light-headedness, falls or syncope. A slow pulse with dizziness after starting bisoprolol should prompt an ECG and dose reduction or review.
why_wrong: A. Hypokalaemia is caused by loop and thiazide diuretics, not beta-blockers. B. Bronchospasm would cause wheeze and breathlessness, which she does not have. C. Hyperglycaemia is not the immediate cause of light-headedness with a slow pulse. D. Peripheral oedema is typical of calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine.
pearl: Beta-blockers can also mask the warning signs of hypoglycaemia, such as tremor and palpitations, in people with diabetes.
thinking: Bisoprolol recently started ↓ Light-headed and near-fall ↓ Pulse slow and regular ↓ Beta-1 blockade slows heart rate ↓ Drug-induced bradycardia
exam_trap: B, Bronchospasm — it is the best-known beta-blocker caution, but she has no wheeze or breathlessness and it does not explain a slow pulse.
takeaway: Symptomatic bradycardia is a common adverse effect of beta-blockers, particularly in older people.

stem: A 69-year-old man with lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic enlargement was started on a new tablet by his GP last week, which was also chosen because his blood pressure was high. Since then he has felt faint when getting out of bed at night to pass urine, and once had to sit back down. His blood pressure drops markedly when he stands. Which of his medicines is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Doxazosin blocks alpha-1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle as well as in the prostate, so it lowers blood pressure and relaxes the bladder outlet. Vasodilatation can cause marked postural hypotension, especially after the first doses, when standing up quickly or at night. Patients should be advised to rise slowly and take the first dose at bedtime.
why_wrong: A. Finasteride shrinks the prostate by blocking 5-alpha reductase and does not characteristically cause postural hypotension. B. Statins cause muscle aches rather than postural drops. D. Omeprazole is not associated with orthostatic hypotension. E. Levothyroxine in excess causes palpitations and tremor, not postural hypotension.
pearl: Alpha-blockers can cause floppy iris syndrome, so patients should tell their ophthalmologist before cataract surgery.
thinking: New tablet for prostate and blood pressure ↓ Faintness on standing, worse at night ↓ Postural drop on testing ↓ Alpha-1 blockade causes vasodilatation ↓ Doxazosin
exam_trap: A, Finasteride — it is also a prostate drug, but it works hormonally over months and does not lower blood pressure or cause postural drops.
takeaway: Alpha-1 blockers such as doxazosin commonly cause postural hypotension, especially when first started.

stem: After a stroke, a 72-year-old woman with epilepsy can no longer swallow tablets safely, and her regular carbamazepine is changed to the oral liquid. The speech and language therapist has cleared her for thickened liquids. The prescription is for 300 mg, and the bottle on the ward states 100 mg in 5 mL. How much liquid should the nurse measure for each dose?
why_correct: The liquid contains 100 mg in 5 mL, which is 20 mg per mL. A 300 mg dose therefore needs 300 divided by 20, which is 15 mL. Equivalently, 300 mg is three times 100 mg, so three times 5 mL is needed.
why_wrong: A. 1.5 mL contains only 30 mg, a tenth of the dose. B. 3 mL contains 60 mg, which confuses the number of 100 mg units with millilitres. D. 20 mL contains 400 mg, a third more than prescribed. E. 30 mL contains 600 mg, double the prescribed dose.
pearl: Always check whether the strength on a liquid label is per 5 mL or per mL, as misreading this is a common cause of tenfold or fivefold errors.
thinking: Prescribed dose 300 mg ↓ Concentration 100 mg per 5 mL ↓ Equals 20 mg per mL ↓ 300 divided by 20 ↓ 15 mL
exam_trap: B, 3 mL — it comes from noticing that three lots of 100 mg are needed but forgetting that each lot is in 5 mL, not 1 mL.
takeaway: Volume to give equals the dose required divided by the concentration per mL.

presentation: Checking a dose against renal function
stem: On a night shift, a doctor is asked to review an 83-year-old woman admitted that afternoon with a urinary infection. A full treatment dose of low molecular weight heparin was written up on admission before her blood results were available, and these now show acute kidney injury with markedly reduced renal function. The nurse says the next dose is due within the hour. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Withhold all of her regular medicines until the renal team can review her
options.B: Check the dose against her current renal function and the BNF or local guidance before it is given, and amend it with the prescriber if needed
options.C: Allow the dose to be given because the admitting doctor will have considered this
options.D: Give half the dose tonight and recheck her bloods tomorrow
options.E: Allow the dose and record the concern for the morning ward round

correct_answer: B. Check the dose against her current renal function and the BNF or local guidance before it is given, and amend it with the prescriber if needed
why_correct: Low molecular weight heparins are renally cleared and accumulate in significant renal impairment, increasing bleeding risk. When a dose seems inconsistent with current renal function, it must be checked against a reliable reference such as the BNF or local anticoagulation guidance and corrected, with the prescriber or senior if appropriate, before the next dose is given.
why_wrong: A. Stopping every medicine is disproportionate and may cause harm; the concern is about one drug. C. A prescription written before results were available may now be unsafe, and every clinician giving or approving a dose shares responsibility. D. Guessing a reduced dose without checking guidance may still be wrong. E. Giving a potentially excessive dose and raising it later does not prevent harm.
pearl: Many renally cleared high-risk drugs, such as low molecular weight heparins, gentamicin, digoxin and some DOACs, need dose adjustment based on current renal function rather than the admission prescription.
thinking: High-risk drug prescribed before bloods available ↓ New acute kidney injury ↓ Renally cleared drug may accumulate ↓ Check dose against renal function and reference before giving ↓ Amend prescription if needed
exam_trap: C, Giving the dose as prescribed — trusting the prescriber feels respectful, but the prescription predates the renal results and the person approving administration must check it.
takeaway: If a dose looks wrong for current renal function, check it against guidance and correct it before it is given.

stem: A care home nurse calls the out-of-hours GP about an 86-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease. Two days ago she started regular oral morphine for pain from rib fractures after a fall. This evening she is increasingly hard to wake, her breathing is slow and shallow, and her pupils are small. Her capillary glucose is normal and she has no new weakness of the face or limbs. Which serious complication is most likely?

options.A: Hypoactive delirium caused by a urinary infection

correct_answer: C. Opioid toxicity with respiratory depression
why_correct: Morphine and its active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide are renally excreted, so in chronic kidney disease they accumulate over the first few days of regular dosing. Increasing drowsiness, slow shallow breathing and small pupils are the classic picture of opioid toxicity, and respiratory depression is the life-threatening part. She needs urgent assessment, airway support and naloxone if breathing is compromised.
why_wrong: A. Delirium from infection does not explain small pupils and slow, shallow breathing developing on a new opioid. B. There are no focal neurological signs. D. Her glucose is normal. E. Serotonin syndrome causes agitation, fever, clonus and dilated pupils.
pearl: In significant renal impairment, opioids with less renal accumulation, such as oxycodone at reduced dose or fentanyl, are often preferred, and doses should start low and go slow.
thinking: New regular morphine ↓ Chronic kidney disease causes accumulation ↓ Drowsy, slow shallow breathing, small pupils ↓ Glucose normal, no focal signs ↓ Opioid toxicity with respiratory depression
exam_trap: A, Hypoactive delirium from infection — it is common in frail care home residents, but it does not account for pinpoint pupils and slowed breathing straight after starting morphine.
takeaway: Drowsiness, slow breathing and small pupils after starting an opioid indicate opioid toxicity, especially in renal impairment.

stem: In the emergency department resuscitation room, a 38-year-old motorcyclist with a fractured femur has received several intravenous doses of morphine over the past hour. A nurse now finds him unrousable to voice, with pinpoint pupils, a respiratory rate of 6 per minute and falling oxygen saturation. He has a patent cannula. What is the priority?

options.A: Open and support the airway, give oxygen and assist ventilation if needed, and give intravenous naloxone
options.C: Withhold further morphine and reassess in an hour
options.D: Let him rest, as he is likely exhausted after the injury
options.E: Give oral fluids and halve the next morphine dose

correct_answer: A. Open and support the airway, give oxygen and assist ventilation if needed, and give intravenous naloxone
why_correct: Unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils and a very low respiratory rate after repeated morphine indicate opioid toxicity with life-threatening respiratory depression. Following an ABCDE approach, the airway must be opened and supported, oxygen given with bag-valve-mask ventilation if needed, and naloxone given intravenously in titrated doses, then repeated or infused because its action is shorter than morphine's.
why_wrong: B. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids. C. Waiting an hour with this respiratory rate risks hypoxic arrest. D. Interpreting this as tiredness ignores a life-threatening emergency. E. Oral fluids are unsafe in an unrousable patient and dose reduction does not treat current toxicity.
pearl: In patients needing opioids for severe pain, naloxone can be titrated in small doses to restore breathing without completely reversing analgesia.
thinking: Repeated IV morphine ↓ Unrousable, pinpoint pupils ↓ Respiratory rate very low, saturations falling ↓ ABCDE: airway and breathing first ↓ Support ventilation and give naloxone
exam_trap: B, Flumazenil — it is a reversal agent that comes to mind for sedation, but it acts only on benzodiazepines and has no effect on opioid toxicity.
takeaway: Opioid respiratory depression needs immediate airway and breathing support plus naloxone.

presentation: Airway and breathing first in opioid respiratory depression
stem: During a night shift on an oncology ward, a nurse calls the doctor urgently about a 72-year-old woman with lung cancer. A fentanyl patch was started yesterday, and she has also taken several doses of oral morphine for breakthrough pain this evening. She is now very difficult to rouse and is breathing only about 6 times a minute. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Reduce the breakthrough morphine dose and review in an hour
options.B: Assess and support her airway and breathing immediately
options.C: Encourage her to take deep breaths and monitor oxygen saturation
options.D: Give flumazenil to reverse the sedation
options.E: Change to a different opioid at a lower dose

correct_answer: B. Assess and support her airway and breathing immediately
why_correct: A very low respiratory rate and severe drowsiness after combining a new fentanyl patch with breakthrough morphine indicate opioid toxicity with respiratory depression. The first priority is an ABCDE assessment with immediate airway and breathing support, including oxygen and ventilation if needed, followed by naloxone, removal of the patch and urgent senior help.
why_wrong: A. Adjusting future doses does nothing for the respiratory depression happening now. C. A patient who is hard to rouse cannot reliably follow instructions, and this does not treat hypoventilation. D. Flumazenil is the antidote for benzodiazepines; naloxone reverses opioids. E. Giving any further opioid now would deepen respiratory depression.
pearl: Transdermal fentanyl takes many hours to reach steady state and continues to release drug from a skin depot for many hours after removal, so prolonged monitoring is needed.
thinking: New fentanyl patch plus breakthrough morphine ↓ Very drowsy ↓ Respiratory rate about 6 per minute ↓ Life-threatening respiratory depression ↓ Airway and breathing support first
exam_trap: A, Reducing the breakthrough dose — it addresses the cause, but it ignores that she is hypoventilating right now and needs immediate support.
takeaway: In opioid respiratory depression, assess and support airway and breathing before anything else.

presentation: Opioid sedation in a child: urgent help
stem: On a paediatric ward, a 15-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is receiving a continuous morphine infusion for a painful vaso-occlusive crisis. At a routine check, the nurse finds him barely responsive to his name, with breathing that is slow and shallow. His mother is at the bedside and asks whether he is just catching up on sleep. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Give a further morphine bolus in case pain is causing exhaustion
options.B: Assess his airway and breathing straight away and call for urgent help
options.C: Reassure his mother and recheck observations in four hours
options.D: Give oral lorazepam to help him rest
options.E: Change the infusion to oral morphine at the same total dose and review later

correct_answer: B. Assess his airway and breathing straight away and call for urgent help
why_correct: Reduced responsiveness with slow, shallow breathing during a morphine infusion is opioid toxicity until proven otherwise. The immediate actions are to assess and support airway and breathing, stop the infusion and summon urgent help so that oxygen, ventilatory support and naloxone can be given without delay. In sickle cell disease, hypoventilation can also precipitate acute chest syndrome.
why_wrong: A. More opioid would deepen respiratory depression. C. Treating this as normal sleep and delaying review risks respiratory arrest. D. A benzodiazepine would add to the sedation and respiratory depression. E. Converting to oral morphine continues the same opioid load and does not address the current danger.
pearl: Patients on opioid infusions need regular sedation scores and respiratory rate checks, as rising sedation usually precedes respiratory depression.
thinking: Continuous morphine infusion ↓ Barely responsive ↓ Slow, shallow breathing ↓ Possible opioid toxicity, life-threatening ↓ Assess airway and breathing and get urgent help
exam_trap: C, Reassuring his mother and rechecking later — it seems kind and calm, but sleepiness with slow breathing on an opioid infusion is dangerous and must be acted on now.
takeaway: Reduced consciousness with slow breathing on opioids needs immediate airway and breathing assessment and urgent help.

stem: The wife of a 69-year-old man with pancreatic cancer receiving care at home phones the GP. Three days ago his modified-release morphine was increased because of worsening pain. Since then he has been dozing off mid-conversation and has had a few muddled moments, although his breathing seems normal to her and his pain is much better. He has been drinking less. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Arrange prompt assessment for opioid toxicity, including renal function, and review the morphine dose
options.B: Continue the current dose, as tolerance to drowsiness always develops
options.C: Double the dose to make sure his pain stays controlled
options.D: Add a second opioid for breakthrough pain
options.E: Add a benzodiazepine for the muddled episodes

correct_answer: A. Arrange prompt assessment for opioid toxicity, including renal function, and review the morphine dose
why_correct: New drowsiness and confusion after an opioid dose increase suggest excess opioid effect, which can progress to respiratory depression. Reduced fluid intake may have caused renal impairment and accumulation of morphine metabolites. He needs prompt review, with the dose reduced or the opioid changed if toxicity is confirmed, while maintaining comfort.
why_wrong: B. Mild initial sleepiness often settles, but increasing sedation and confusion are warning signs of toxicity and cannot be assumed to pass. C. Doubling the dose would worsen toxicity, and his pain is already improved. D. Adding another opioid without assessment increases the overall opioid load. E. A benzodiazepine would add sedation and could precipitate respiratory depression.
pearl: Myoclonic jerks, hallucinations and confusion are also signs of opioid toxicity, particularly with morphine in renal impairment.
thinking: Recent opioid dose increase ↓ New drowsiness and confusion ↓ Reduced fluid intake risks renal impairment ↓ Possible opioid toxicity ↓ Assess promptly and review the dose
exam_trap: B, Continuing the same dose because tolerance will develop — mild sedation often settles, but progressive drowsiness with confusion signals toxicity that needs action.
takeaway: New or increasing sedation after an opioid dose increase should prompt assessment for toxicity and dose review.

stem: A doctor on a surgical ward is about to give a 56-year-old woman her evening dose of prophylactic low molecular weight heparin, because the nurse looking after her is busy with an emergency. The patient has been on the ward for three days and greets the doctor by name. The pre-filled syringe has been taken from the ward stock. Which principle should guide the doctor before giving the injection?

options.A: Estimate the dose from the syringe size, as it is pre-filled
options.B: Any injection site is acceptable for this medicine
options.C: Patient identity checks can be skipped because she is well known to the staff
options.D: Check the right patient, drug, dose, route and time against the prescription chart and her identity band
options.E: The route does not need confirming because the syringe is designed for one route

correct_answer: D. Check the right patient, drug, dose, route and time against the prescription chart and her identity band
why_correct: Safe administration of any medicine requires checking the right patient, right drug, right dose, right route and right time against the current prescription, and confirming identity using the wristband and the patient's own details. Pre-filled syringes come in several strengths, and familiarity with a patient does not remove the risk of giving a drug to the wrong person.
why_wrong: A. Pre-filled syringes come in different strengths, so the dose must be checked against the chart, not estimated. B. The site must suit the medicine, for example the abdominal wall with rotation for heparin injections. C. Identity checks are mandatory every time, regardless of familiarity. E. Wrong-route errors can be fatal, so the route must always be checked.
pearl: Before giving anticoagulant injections, also check for active bleeding, a low platelet count and whether a dose has already been given that day.
thinking: Medicine to be given by injection ↓ Five rights: patient, drug, dose, route, time ↓ Check against current prescription ↓ Confirm identity with wristband ↓ Then administer
exam_trap: C, Skipping the identity check because she is known — familiarity feels reassuring, but wrong-patient errors often happen exactly when checks are skipped for familiar patients.
takeaway: Before any injection, check the right patient, drug, dose, route and time against the prescription.

stem: A 62-year-old man with pernicious anaemia attends the GP surgery for his regular intramuscular hydroxocobalamin injection. Since his last appointment he has been discharged from hospital after a heart attack with several new medicines. The practice nurse is unavailable, and a newly qualified GP is asked to give the injection. Which step is most important before giving it?

options.A: Confirm the drug, dose, route and his identity against the current prescription, and check for allergies and contraindications in light of his new medicines
options.B: Check the drug and dose only, as the route is decided by the pharmacy
options.C: Inject into the deltoid regardless of volume because it is less painful
options.D: Give the same dose as last time without checking the current prescription
options.E: Ask him to name the drug instead of checking the record

correct_answer: A. Confirm the drug, dose, route and his identity against the current prescription, and check for allergies and contraindications in light of his new medicines
why_correct: Before an intramuscular injection the clinician must confirm the drug, dose, route and patient identity against the current prescription, and check for allergies and contraindications. His new medicines since the heart attack must be reviewed first, because an anticoagulant in particular raises the risk of bleeding and haematoma at an intramuscular site and may need the technique or timing to be considered.
why_wrong: B. The administering clinician is responsible for checking the route, patient and contraindications, not just the drug and dose. C. The site must suit the drug and volume, and the deltoid only takes small volumes. D. The current prescription must be checked, as a previous dose may no longer be correct. E. The prescription and record, not the patient's memory, determine what is given.
pearl: Hydroxocobalamin for pernicious anaemia is given intramuscularly for life, typically every three months once loading is complete.
thinking: Regular intramuscular injection due ↓ New medicines since last dose ↓ Check drug, dose, route and identity ↓ Check allergies and contraindications in light of new medicines ↓ Then administer
exam_trap: D, Giving the same dose as last time — it seems efficient for a routine injection, but it skips checking whether his circumstances or prescription have changed.
takeaway: Before an intramuscular injection, confirm drug, dose, route, identity and any allergies or contraindications.

stem: On the acute medical unit, a doctor uses the hospital's electronic order set for community-acquired pneumonia to prescribe antibiotics for a 52-year-old man. A moment later, while reviewing his record, the doctor sees a coded entry stating anaphylaxis to penicillin, and the order set has generated oral amoxicillin. No dose has been given yet. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Leave the amoxicillin because the electronic system accepted it
options.B: Increase the dose so that the pneumonia is treated quickly
options.C: Remove the allergy entry because the system did not block the order
options.D: Allow the dose if he currently feels well
options.E: Cancel the amoxicillin and choose a suitable non-penicillin antibiotic before any dose is given

correct_answer: E. Cancel the amoxicillin and choose a suitable non-penicillin antibiotic before any dose is given
why_correct: Amoxicillin is a penicillin, and a documented history of anaphylaxis means it must not be given. The prescription should be stopped before administration and replaced with a non-penicillin antibiotic recommended by local guidance, and the allergy should be confirmed with the patient. Electronic systems and order sets reduce but do not eliminate errors.
why_wrong: A. Acceptance by an electronic system does not make an unsafe prescription safe. B. A higher dose would increase the danger. C. A documented allergy must not be deleted without proper review, and doing so falsifies the record. D. Feeling well now offers no protection against anaphylaxis on re-exposure.
pearl: When recording an allergy, document the drug, the nature of the reaction and when it happened, so that true allergy can be distinguished from intolerance.
thinking: Order set generated amoxicillin ↓ Record shows penicillin anaphylaxis ↓ Amoxicillin is a penicillin ↓ No dose given yet ↓ Cancel and choose a non-penicillin alternative
exam_trap: A, Leaving it because the system accepted it — electronic prescribing feels like a safety net, but it can miss allergies and the prescriber remains responsible.
takeaway: Stop and review any prescription that conflicts with a documented severe allergy before a dose is given.

presentation: Prescribing after severe immediate penicillin reaction
stem: A 28-year-old woman sees her GP with severe tonsillitis, and an antibiotic is felt to be indicated. The GP is about to prescribe phenoxymethylpenicillin when she mentions that, as a child, her lips and tongue swelled and she had difficulty breathing within minutes of a dose of amoxicillin, and she was treated in hospital. She has had no penicillins since. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Give a single test dose in the surgery and observe her before prescribing the full course
options.B: Avoid all penicillins and use a non-penicillin alternative unless allergy specialist assessment has shown penicillin is safe
options.C: Prescribe the penicillin with an oral antihistamine taken beforehand
options.D: Prescribe co-amoxiclav as it belongs to a different class
options.E: Prescribe the penicillin, because reactions in childhood are usually outgrown

correct_answer: B. Avoid all penicillins and use a non-penicillin alternative unless allergy specialist assessment has shown penicillin is safe
why_correct: Lip and tongue swelling with breathing difficulty within minutes of amoxicillin indicates a probable immediate, IgE-mediated allergy. NICE advises avoiding all penicillins in such patients and choosing an alternative, such as clarithromycin for tonsillitis, unless specialist allergy testing has shown it is safe. The allergy should be clearly recorded.
why_wrong: A. Re-challenge after a severe immediate reaction should only take place under allergy specialist supervision, not in general practice. C. Antihistamines do not prevent anaphylaxis. D. Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin and is a penicillin. E. Many people lose penicillin sensitivity over time, but this cannot be assumed without specialist testing after a severe reaction.
pearl: Most people labelled penicillin-allergic are not truly allergic, and specialist delabelling can safely widen their antibiotic options.
thinking: Antibiotic needed ↓ History of lip and tongue swelling with breathing difficulty ↓ Immediate, probably IgE-mediated ↓ Avoid all penicillins ↓ Non-penicillin alternative unless specialist clears
exam_trap: E, Assuming childhood reactions are outgrown — many penicillin labels are wrong, but after a severe immediate reaction only specialist testing can safely confirm this.
takeaway: After a severe immediate reaction to a penicillin, avoid all penicillins unless an allergy specialist has shown they are safe.

presentation: Penicillin allergy label with a non-allergic history
stem: During a routine medication review at his GP practice, a 58-year-old man is noted to have 'penicillin allergy' on his record. The practice pharmacist asks him about it. He explains that his mother told him he felt sick after a course of amoxicillin for an ear infection when he was about six. He never had a rash, lip or tongue swelling, wheeze or collapse, and he has not taken a penicillin since. What is the most appropriate way to handle this entry?

options.A: Leave the label as it is and code it as a severe allergy to all beta-lactams
options.B: Ask about and record the exact reaction he had, rather than accepting the label as a true allergy
options.C: Change the entry to anaphylaxis to amoxicillin as the safest option
options.D: Delete the label from his record without telling him
options.E: Prescribe a full course of amoxicillin next time without asking anything further

correct_answer: B. Ask about and record the exact reaction he had, rather than accepting the label as a true allergy
why_correct: The phrase 'penicillin allergy' is used for anything from nausea to anaphylaxis, so the history behind it must be taken and written down accurately. Nausea alone, with no skin, airway or circulatory features, describes a side effect rather than an immune reaction. Recording the actual reaction, drug and timing (as NICE advises) stops an inaccurate label from steering him away from first-line penicillins in future.
why_wrong: A. Coding a severe allergy overstates a history of nausea and needlessly excludes useful antibiotics. C. Recording anaphylaxis is factually wrong and would be dangerous misinformation in his record. D. Any change to an allergy entry should be discussed and agreed with the patient and documented clearly. E. Skipping enquiry altogether is unsafe; the history must still be clarified and recorded.
pearl: Around 1 in 10 people in the UK carry a penicillin allergy label, but most do not have a true allergy when properly assessed.
thinking: Allergy label found on record ↓ Ask what actually happened ↓ Nausea only, no rash, swelling or breathing problems ↓ Fits a side effect, not an immune reaction ↓ Document the true reaction accurately
exam_trap: A, Leaving it coded as severe allergy — it feels like the cautious choice, but a false severe label pushes patients towards broader-spectrum antibiotics with more resistance and C. difficile risk.
takeaway: Never take a penicillin allergy label at face value: find out and record exactly what the reaction was.

stem: A 45-year-old man attends his GP with a productive cough and fever, and community-acquired pneumonia is suspected. Before an antibiotic is chosen, he mentions that about ten years ago, within an hour of taking a penicillin tablet, he came out in itchy raised welts all over his body and his lips and eyelids swelled up. How should this history be interpreted?

options.A: As a gastrointestinal side effect that does not need recording
options.B: As a sign that his chest infection is likely to be penicillin-resistant
options.C: As a probable immediate, IgE-mediated allergy to penicillin
options.D: As a contraindication to every class of antibiotic
options.E: As a reason to re-challenge with amoxicillin under observation in the surgery

correct_answer: C. As a probable immediate, IgE-mediated allergy to penicillin
why_correct: Widespread urticaria with lip and eyelid swelling coming on within an hour of the drug is the classic pattern of an immediate (type I, IgE-mediated) reaction. NICE advises documenting this as a penicillin allergy and avoiding all penicillins. A non-penicillin antibiotic should be chosen now, and specialist allergy referral considered if penicillin might be needed in future.
why_wrong: A. Hives and angioedema are immune features, not a gastrointestinal side effect. B. Allergy is a host reaction and says nothing about bacterial resistance. D. Only penicillins (and possibly related beta-lactams) need to be avoided, not all antibiotics. E. A re-challenge with a known immediate reaction risks anaphylaxis and is only done in specialist allergy services.
