Ureteric colic is colicky loin-to-groin pain with restlessness and haematuria, without fever or iliac fossa guarding. D. Appendicitis causes right iliac fossa signs except in rare anatomical variants, so it is not the most likely cause here.
pearl: NICE advises that people with suspected uncomplicated acute diverticulitis who are systemically well may be managed without antibiotics, with paracetamol for pain and review if symptoms persist or worsen.
thinking: Older man with constant lower left abdominal pain ↓ Fever and new loose stools ↓ Localised left iliac fossa tenderness without peritonism ↓ Abdomen soft and not distended, so no obstruction ↓ Sigmoid diverticular inflammation fits best
exam_trap: D, Acute appendicitis — fever with localised tenderness and guarding sounds like appendicitis, but the signs are on the left, which points to the sigmoid colon.
takeaway: Left iliac fossa pain, fever and altered bowel habit in an older adult suggest acute diverticulitis.

stem: A 66-year-old man who has taken oral prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica for over a year is sent for bone densitometry. He has never broken a bone. The report gives a lumbar spine T-score of -3.1. Which term best describes his bone status?

options.C: Bone density within the normal range

why_correct: The WHO densitometric classification, applied to postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or over, defines osteoporosis as a T-score of -2.5 or lower. His T-score is well below this, so he has osteoporosis. Because he has had no fragility fracture, the label of established or severe osteoporosis does not apply.
why_wrong: A. Osteopenia describes a T-score between -1 and -2.5, which is higher than his result. B. Osteomalacia is defective mineralisation from vitamin D deficiency and is not diagnosed from a T-score. C. A normal result is a T-score of -1 or above. E. Established or severe osteoporosis requires a T-score in the osteoporotic range plus one or more fragility fractures, and he has none.
pearl: Long-term oral glucocorticoids are a major cause of secondary osteoporosis, and bone protection should be considered early in anyone expected to take them for three months or more.
thinking: Man over 50 on long-term steroids ↓ DXA T-score below -2.5 ↓ No previous fragility fracture ↓ Meets the WHO definition of osteoporosis ↓ Not severe, as there is no fracture
exam_trap: E, Established (severe) osteoporosis — a very low T-score in a man on steroids feels severe, but the term needs a fragility fracture as well, and he has never broken a bone.
takeaway: A T-score of -2.5 or lower without any fragility fracture is osteoporosis, not severe osteoporosis.

stem: A 24-year-old woman sees her GP with one day of mild discomfort low in the right side of her abdomen. She is eating, has no fever and has not vomited. There is slight tenderness in the right iliac fossa but no guarding or rebound, her urine dipstick is clear and a pregnancy test is negative. The GP thinks this is probably non-specific pain but cannot exclude early appendicitis. What is the most appropriate way to manage her?

options.A: Tell her confidently that nothing serious is going on so that she is not worried
options.B: Send her to the surgical assessment unit to be kept in until the cause is clear
options.C: Explain that the cause is uncertain, give specific advice on when to seek help and arrange a review
options.D: Request an extensive set of blood tests and imaging to rule out every serious cause
options.E: Give her the most probable diagnosis and advise that no further contact is needed

correct_answer: C. Explain that the cause is uncertain, give specific advice on when to seek help and arrange a review
why_correct: When a serious condition cannot yet be excluded but she is well enough to go home, safe practice is to share the uncertainty honestly, give clear safety-netting advice (for example worsening pain, fever, vomiting or pain on moving), say how and where to seek help, and arrange planned follow-up. This keeps her involved in decisions and creates a route back if the picture changes, in line with GMC Good medical practice.
why_wrong: A. False reassurance can delay her return if appendicitis is evolving and is not honest about uncertainty. B. She has no features needing admission now, and admitting every uncertain case is neither proportionate nor helpful. D. Scattergun testing is not proportionate, can give misleading results and does not replace safety-netting. E. Offering no follow-up removes the safety net that uncertainty requires.
pearl: Good safety-netting is specific: it names the warning symptoms, says how quickly to act and tells the person exactly where to go.
thinking: Mild right iliac fossa pain, systemically well ↓ Serious cause cannot be fully excluded ↓ No current need for admission ↓ Be honest about uncertainty ↓ Specific safety-net advice plus planned review
exam_trap: B, Admitting until the cause is clear — it feels like the safest option, but she has no features needing hospital care now and a clear safety net with review is the proportionate approach.
takeaway: When a diagnosis is uncertain in a well patient, explain the uncertainty, safety-net specifically and arrange follow-up.

presentation: Escalating a possible serious acute condition
stem: An FY1 doctor on night cover is called to a 31-year-old man on the orthopaedic ward two days after a hip fracture fixation. He has new sharp right-sided chest pain on breathing and a fast heart rate. The doctor is unsure whether this is a chest infection, a pulmonary embolism or post-operative pain. Which course of action is safest?

options.A: Give analgesia for musculoskeletal pain and ask the day team to see him in the morning
options.B: Assess and stabilise him, inform the registrar, arrange investigations and agree a plan for review
options.C: Wait until test results give a firm diagnosis before telling a senior colleague
options.D: Reassure him that pain after hip surgery is common and leave the notes unchanged
options.E: Record only the most likely diagnosis to avoid worrying the patient

correct_answer: B. Assess and stabilise him, inform the registrar, arrange investigations and agree a plan for review
why_correct: A serious condition such as pulmonary embolism cannot be excluded, so the priority is an ABCDE assessment and treatment of any immediate threat, early escalation to a senior and appropriate investigations. A clear documented plan, including when he will be reviewed again, makes sure the uncertainty is actively managed rather than left until the morning.
why_wrong: A. Treating for the most benign cause and deferring review risks missing a pulmonary embolism. C. Escalation must not wait for a definite diagnosis; uncertainty about a serious condition is itself a reason to involve a senior. D. Reassurance without assessment is unsafe and leaves no record of concern. E. The differential and uncertainty should be documented honestly so that others can act on it.
pearl: Seeking help when a problem is beyond your experience is a professional duty under GMC Good medical practice, not a sign of weakness.
thinking: Post-operative patient with pleuritic pain and tachycardia ↓ Pulmonary embolism cannot be excluded ↓ Assess and stabilise first ↓ Escalate early to a senior ↓ Investigate, document and plan review
exam_trap: A, Analgesia and review by the day team — post-operative pain is common, but tachycardia and pleuritic pain after orthopaedic surgery need a pulmonary embolism to be excluded tonight.
takeaway: If a serious acute diagnosis cannot be excluded, assess, escalate early, investigate and keep a clear plan.

presentation: Working safely with uncertainty as a new doctor
stem: A doctor in the first week of foundation training is clerking an 83-year-old woman sent to the acute medical unit from her care home. She has become more confused over a day, has vague abdominal discomfort and is mildly hypotensive, and her venous lactate is raised. He suspects something serious, possibly sepsis or an intra-abdominal catastrophe, but cannot decide on the cause. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Treat the least serious explanation so that she is not referred unnecessarily
options.B: Acknowledge the uncertainty, start initial resuscitation and escalate to a senior while continuing care
options.C: Hold off contacting a senior until scans have confirmed the diagnosis
options.D: Tell her family that a serious cause is unlikely so that they are not alarmed
options.E: Leave the uncertainty out of the notes so that the next team is not confused

correct_answer: B. Acknowledge the uncertainty, start initial resuscitation and escalate to a senior while continuing care
why_correct: An unwell older woman with hypotension and a raised lactate needs action even without a clear diagnosis. Recognising the limits of his experience, starting appropriate initial management such as fluids, cultures and antibiotics if sepsis is suspected, and calling a senior early is the safe approach. He should keep managing her while help arrives rather than waiting.
why_wrong: A. Choosing the least serious explanation is a form of diagnostic bias and could delay treatment of sepsis or ischaemia. C. Waiting for imaging before escalating loses valuable time in a deteriorating patient. D. False reassurance to relatives is dishonest and may later damage trust. E. Documenting uncertainty helps the next clinician; hiding it is unsafe.
pearl: Older people often present atypically with serious illness, and new confusion with a raised lactate should be treated as a red flag until shown otherwise.
thinking: Frail older woman with new confusion ↓ Hypotension and raised lactate ↓ Serious cause likely but unclear ↓ Start initial management now ↓ Escalate early and keep caring while help comes
exam_trap: C, Waiting for scans before escalating — confirming the diagnosis first feels thorough, but a hypotensive patient with a raised lactate needs senior input and treatment straight away.
takeaway: Uncertainty about a potentially serious diagnosis is a reason to act and escalate, not to wait.

stem: A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hypothyroidism attends the practice pharmacist clinic. Over the last few weeks he has had frequent queasiness, a bloated feeling in his abdomen and looser stools. He looks well and his abdomen is soft and non-tender. Which of his regular medicines is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Gastrointestinal upset, including nausea, bloating, abdominal discomfort and loose stools, is the most common adverse effect of metformin. It is dose related and often settles if the drug is taken with food, titrated more slowly or switched to a modified-release preparation.
why_wrong: A. Amlodipine typically causes ankle swelling, flushing and headache rather than nausea and loose stools. B. Atorvastatin can cause mild gastrointestinal upset, but muscle symptoms are its key concern and it is a much less likely cause. C. Levothyroxine at the correct dose rarely causes gut symptoms; excess dosing causes palpitations and weight loss. E. Ramipril is known for a dry cough, angioedema and hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Modified-release metformin can be tried when standard-release metformin is not tolerated because of gastrointestinal effects.
thinking: Well man with nausea, bloating and loose stools ↓ Normal examination ↓ Review his medicines for gut side effects ↓ Metformin is the commonest culprit ↓ Consider food, slower titration or modified release
exam_trap: B, Atorvastatin — statins do list gut upset as a side effect, but metformin causes it far more often and is the first drug to review.
takeaway: Nausea, bloating and loose stools in someone with type 2 diabetes should prompt review of metformin.

stem: A 38-year-old man who is overweight has had a burning feeling rising from the upper abdomen into his lower chest for several months. It comes on after large evening meals, when he bends to tie his shoes and when he goes to bed, and he sometimes wakes with a sour taste in his mouth. Over-the-counter antacids ease it. He has no difficulty swallowing, vomiting or weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Burning that rises behind the sternum and is provoked by large meals, bending and lying flat reflects acid reflux into the oesophagus, and the sour taste is regurgitation. Relief with antacids and absence of alarm symptoms such as dysphagia, weight loss or vomiting support uncomplicated reflux disease.
why_wrong: A. Duodenal ulcer pain is typically epigastric, occurs hours after eating and is often eased by food, without positional reflux. C. Gastric cancer is unlikely at his age without alarm features. D. Biliary colic is a severe right upper quadrant or epigastric ache lasting hours, not positional burning with regurgitation. E. Chronic pancreatitis causes boring epigastric pain into the back, often with steatorrhoea and weight loss, usually with heavy alcohol use.
pearl: Lifestyle measures for reflux include weight loss, smaller evening meals eaten well before bed, stopping smoking and raising the head of the bed.
thinking: Burning rising into the chest ↓ Worse after big meals, bending and lying down ↓ Sour regurgitation, eased by antacids ↓ No alarm features ↓ Typical reflux disease
exam_trap: A, Duodenal ulcer — epigastric burning and nocturnal symptoms suggest ulcer disease, but the positional trigger and sour regurgitation point to reflux.
takeaway: Burning heartburn worsened by bending or lying down, with regurgitation and no alarm features, is typical of GORD.

stem: Over the last two months, a 41-year-old bus driver who smokes has kept snacks in his cab because a hungry, gnawing ache under his breastbone tends to build up a couple of hours after lunch and settles once he eats something. Around 2am it often rouses him from sleep, and a glass of milk helps. His weight is steady and he has not been sick. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Pain that comes on hours after a meal, wakes the patient at night and is relieved by eating is the classic pattern of a duodenal ulcer. Food buffers acid and slows its arrival in the duodenum, while acid secretion without food overnight provokes the pain. His stable weight and lack of vomiting make a complicated or malignant cause less likely.
why_wrong: A. Gastric ulcer pain is classically made worse by eating and may cause weight loss. B. Reflux causes retrosternal burning and regurgitation, worse on lying down, rather than pain eased by food. C. Biliary colic is a severe constant pain after fatty meals, not relieved by eating. E. Chronic pancreatitis pain is boring, radiates to the back and is worsened by food.
pearl: Helicobacter pylori is the commonest cause of duodenal ulcers, so testing and eradication are central to management.
thinking: Gnawing epigastric pain ↓ Starts hours after meals ↓ Wakes him at night ↓ Relieved by food or milk ↓ Duodenal ulcer pattern
exam_trap: A, Gastric ulcer — both are peptic ulcers, but food usually worsens gastric ulcer pain whereas it eases duodenal ulcer pain.
takeaway: Epigastric pain relieved by eating and waking the patient at night suggests a duodenal ulcer.

stem: A 61-year-old woman tells her GP she has had three courses of treatment for vaginal thrush in two months. She has also been drinking more water than usual, getting up at night to pass urine and feeling tired all the time. A blood test shows an HbA1c of 52 mmol/mol. How should this result be interpreted?

options.C: A normal result for her age
options.D: Not diagnostic until confirmed with a repeat test
options.E: Likely to be falsely raised by iron deficiency

why_correct: An HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or more is diagnostic of diabetes. She has typical osmotic symptoms and recurrent candida infection, and in a symptomatic person a single raised value is enough to make the diagnosis. Her age and presentation make type 2 diabetes the likely type.
why_wrong: A. Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia lies below the diabetic range, and her value is above it. C. HbA1c does not have an age-adjusted normal range that would include this value. D. A repeat test is needed only when the person has no symptoms. E. There is nothing to suggest iron deficiency, and HbA1c should not be dismissed without a reason to doubt it.
pearl: HbA1c is unreliable for diagnosis in children, in pregnancy, when symptoms have developed rapidly and in conditions that change red cell turnover, where plasma glucose should be used instead.
thinking: Thirst, nocturia and tiredness ↓ Recurrent thrush ↓ HbA1c in the diabetic range ↓ Symptomatic, so one result is enough ↓ Diagnose type 2 diabetes
exam_trap: D, Repeat test needed — a second confirmatory test is required in people without symptoms, but she has classic symptoms, so one diagnostic result suffices.
takeaway: With typical symptoms, a single HbA1c in the diabetic range confirms diabetes.

stem: A 59-year-old woman who used to smoke has a CT scan of her abdomen and pelvis in the emergency department for suspected diverticulitis. The report notes, as an aside, a small solid nodule at the base of the right lung. She has no cough, breathlessness or weight loss. How should this finding be handled?

options.A: Assess the nodule's size and features against BTS guidance and arrange surveillance or referral as indicated
options.B: Refer her urgently to thoracic surgeons to have the nodule removed
options.C: Tell her it is probably lung cancer and refer her straight to oncology
options.D: Mention it to her GP to discuss at her next routine appointment if she attends
options.E: Reassure her that small nodules are always benign and need no further action

correct_answer: A. Assess the nodule's size and features against BTS guidance and arrange surveillance or referral as indicated
why_correct: Incidental lung nodules are common and most are benign, but some are early cancers. The British Thoracic Society recommends a structured assessment of nodule size, appearance and the patient's risk (such as smoking history), which then decides whether no action, CT surveillance or referral to the lung cancer team is needed. The finding must be communicated and acted on with a clear plan.
why_wrong: B. Most small nodules are benign, so immediate surgery without risk assessment would expose her to unnecessary harm. C. Labelling the nodule as cancer is premature and causes needless distress. D. Leaving an incidental finding for possible discussion at an unscheduled routine visit risks it being lost. E. Not all small nodules are benign, especially in a former smoker, so blanket reassurance is unsafe.
pearl: Incidental findings are a common source of missed diagnoses; whoever requested the scan is responsible for making sure the result is acted on or handed over clearly.
thinking: Incidental lung nodule on abdominal CT ↓ Former smoker, so some risk ↓ Most nodules benign, a few malignant ↓ Use BTS risk-based assessment ↓ Ensure follow-up is arranged and communicated
exam_trap: E, Reassure that small nodules are benign — most are, but a former smoker can have an early cancer, so the nodule needs structured assessment rather than dismissal.
takeaway: Incidental pulmonary nodules need risk-based assessment against guidelines, with a clear plan for follow-up.

stem: A 5-week-old boy is admitted with several days of forceful vomiting after every feed. He is dehydrated, and blood tests show a low chloride, low potassium and a raised bicarbonate in keeping with pyloric stenosis. Which change in his breathing would help to correct the acid-base disturbance?

options.A: Faster, deeper breathing to blow off carbon dioxide
options.B: Increased renal excretion of hydrogen ions
options.C: Slower, shallower breathing so that carbon dioxide accumulates
options.D: A rise in lactic acid production by the muscles

correct_answer: C. Slower, shallower breathing so that carbon dioxide accumulates
why_correct: Loss of gastric acid causes a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. The respiratory system compensates by hypoventilating, allowing carbon dioxide to rise, which increases carbonic acid and brings the pH back towards normal. This compensation is limited because hypoventilation also lowers oxygen levels.
why_wrong: A. Hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide and would worsen an alkalosis; it is the compensation for metabolic acidosis. B. Changes in renal acid handling are a metabolic, not respiratory, response, and in pyloric stenosis the kidney paradoxically excretes acid to conserve sodium. D. Lactate production is not a compensatory mechanism. E. Apnoea is a dangerous complication, not a useful compensation.
pearl: Infants with pyloric stenosis must have their alkalosis and dehydration corrected before pyloromyotomy, partly because uncorrected alkalosis increases the risk of post-operative apnoea.
thinking: Repeated vomiting of gastric acid ↓ Low chloride, raised bicarbonate ↓ Metabolic alkalosis ↓ Respiratory compensation retains carbon dioxide ↓ Achieved by hypoventilation
exam_trap: A, Faster, deeper breathing — a deep breathing pattern is often linked with compensation, but blowing off carbon dioxide corrects acidosis and would make his alkalosis worse.
takeaway: Metabolic alkalosis is compensated by hypoventilation and carbon dioxide retention.

stem: A 77-year-old woman with urosepsis on a medical ward is becoming drowsier. Her skin is mottled, her lips look blue and her hands are cold and clammy. The finger probe is displaying a saturation of 97% on room air, and the nurse says the reading must be fine. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Move the probe to another finger and act only if the number drops
options.B: Accept the reading because blue lips are a poor guide in ward lighting
options.C: Increase observations to hourly and review her later in the shift
options.D: Assess her clinically and obtain an arterial blood gas rather than relying on the oximeter
options.E: Reassure the nurse because a machine reading is more accurate than inspection

correct_answer: D. Assess her clinically and obtain an arterial blood gas rather than relying on the oximeter
why_correct: She is visibly cyanosed and deteriorating, which outweighs a single reassuring number. In shocked patients with poor peripheral perfusion the oximeter may lock on to a poor signal or display inaccurate values, and it can overestimate saturation in some groups. She needs an immediate ABCDE assessment, oxygen as indicated, an arterial blood gas and escalation.
why_wrong: A. Moving the probe still relies on a device that may be unreliable in this situation and delays action. B. Cyanosis in a deteriorating patient is a significant sign and should not be dismissed. C. Hourly observations and later review are too slow for a patient who is becoming drowsy and mottled. E. Oximeters have recognised limitations and should never override clear clinical signs of deterioration.
pearl: Pulse oximeters can overestimate oxygen saturation in people with darker skin, which is why MHRA advice stresses interpreting readings alongside clinical assessment.
thinking: Septic, drowsy, mottled and cyanosed ↓ Oximeter shows a normal reading ↓ Clinical signs outweigh a single number ↓ Poor perfusion makes oximetry unreliable ↓ Assess clinically and check an arterial gas
exam_trap: A, Re-siting the probe — checking the device seems sensible, but she is clearly deteriorating and needs direct clinical assessment and a blood gas now.
takeaway: When a patient looks unwell, trust the clinical picture and confirm oxygenation with an arterial blood gas.

stem: A 29-year-old woman attends a routine asthma review with the practice nurse. She has had no recent symptoms, is chatting comfortably and her breathing rate is normal. She is wearing dark gel nail varnish, and the finger probe shows an oxygen saturation of 89%. What should be done next?

options.A: Check the probe position and signal, try another site, and reassess her clinically
options.B: Arrange an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram
options.C: Accept the result and refer for a long-term oxygen assessment
options.D: Stop using the oximeter because she looks well
options.E: Recheck her saturation at her next annual review

correct_answer: A. Check the probe position and signal, try another site, and reassess her clinically
why_correct: A low reading that does not match a comfortable, well-looking patient suggests a measurement problem. Dark nail varnish or gel coatings can interfere with light transmission, so the probe and waveform should be checked, an unvarnished site such as the earlobe or another finger used, and the patient reassessed. If genuine hypoxaemia remains possible, it must then be investigated.
why_wrong: B. Imaging for pulmonary embolism is not justified by an isolated, probably artefactual reading in a well patient. C. Oxygen assessment requires confirmed, persistent hypoxaemia, not one doubtful reading. D. Oximetry is still useful once the source of error is corrected, and abandoning it could miss real hypoxaemia. E. Waiting a year leaves a possibly real abnormality unexplained.
pearl: Nail varnish, poor perfusion, movement, bright ambient light and a poorly fitting probe are common causes of spurious oximetry readings.
thinking: Well woman with normal breathing ↓ Low saturation reading ↓ Mismatch suggests artefact ↓ Dark nail coating can block the probe ↓ Check probe and signal, use another site and reassess
exam_trap: C, Long-term oxygen assessment — taking the number at face value seems thorough, but the reading does not fit a well patient and is most likely artefact.
takeaway: Always interpret an oximeter reading alongside the patient; when they do not match, check the device first.

stem: On a children's ward, a 6-year-old boy recovering from gastroenteritis keeps setting off the saturation alarm, which flashes 84%. He is sitting up playing a game on a tablet and swinging his arm about, he is pink and talking normally, and the trace on the monitor is irregular and low in amplitude. What is the most appropriate first action?

options.A: Start high-flow oxygen through a face mask
options.B: Request an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram
options.C: Take an arterial blood gas before looking at the probe
options.D: Check the probe position and signal quality, then reassess him
options.E: Switch off saturation monitoring as unreliable

correct_answer: D. Check the probe position and signal quality, then reassess him
why_correct: A pink, comfortable child with a poor, irregular trace almost certainly has movement artefact. The first step is to check the probe fit and waveform, keep the limb still or re-site the probe, and then reassess the child. Treatment should follow a confirmed reading, not an artefactual one.
why_wrong: A. Starting oxygen on the basis of an unreliable reading treats a number rather than the child. B. There is no clinical reason to suspect pulmonary embolism, and CT carries radiation risk in a child. C. An arterial stab is painful and unnecessary before the simple step of checking the probe. E. Monitoring should be corrected, not abandoned, in case he does become hypoxic.
pearl: A clean, regular plethysmograph waveform is the best sign that an oximeter reading can be trusted.
thinking: Well, pink, talking child ↓ Alarm reading is low ↓ Waveform irregular and weak ↓ Movement artefact likely ↓ Check probe and signal, then reassess
exam_trap: C, Arterial blood gas first — it gives a definitive answer, but it is painful and unnecessary before the quick check of probe position and signal quality.
takeaway: A poor waveform in a well child points to artefact; check the probe before acting on the number.

presentation: Irritable bowel syndrome: exclude coeliac disease
stem: A 27-year-old man sees his GP about cramping pain across his lower abdomen that has come and gone for 18 months. The pain eases after he opens his bowels, he often feels bloated by the evening, and his stools swing between loose and hard. He has not lost weight, has no blood in his stools and is not woken at night by symptoms. Examination is normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis, with the test that should be done before confirming it?

options.A: Irritable bowel syndrome; check coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase antibodies)
options.B: Crohn's disease; arrange ileocolonoscopy with biopsies
options.C: Bowel cancer; request urgent CT colonography
options.D: Lactose intolerance; arrange a hydrogen breath test
options.E: Diverticular disease; request CT of the abdomen and pelvis

correct_answer: A. Irritable bowel syndrome; check coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase antibodies)
why_correct: Long-standing abdominal pain relieved by defecation, bloating and alternating bowel habit in a young man without red flags fits irritable bowel syndrome. NICE advises that coeliac disease, which can mimic IBS closely, is excluded with serological testing, alongside a full blood count and inflammatory markers, before the diagnosis is made.
why_wrong: B. Crohn's disease usually causes weight loss, nocturnal or bloody diarrhoea and raised inflammatory markers, none of which he has. C. He has no red flags and is young, so urgent cancer investigation is not indicated. D. Lactose intolerance gives symptoms linked to dairy intake and does not explain alternating constipation. E. Diverticular disease is uncommon at his age and CT is not a first-line test for these symptoms.
pearl: Faecal calprotectin can help distinguish IBS from inflammatory bowel disease in adults with lower gastrointestinal symptoms when cancer is not suspected.
thinking: Chronic pain eased by defecation ↓ Bloating and alternating bowel habit ↓ Young, no red flags ↓ Fits irritable bowel syndrome ↓ Exclude coeliac disease with serology first
exam_trap: B, Crohn's disease with colonoscopy — chronic abdominal pain and loose stools in a young man raise this, but he has no weight loss, bleeding or night symptoms, so IBS is far more likely.
takeaway: Before diagnosing IBS, check coeliac serology, a full blood count and inflammatory markers.

stem: A GP is called by the nurse at a care home about an 84-year-old woman with heart failure who has been sitting in a draughty lounge all afternoon. Her fingers feel icy, and the finger probe shows 87%. When the GP arrives she is chatting, not breathless at rest and her chest sounds unchanged from her last review. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Start high-flow oxygen on the strength of the reading
options.B: Diagnose type 1 respiratory failure from the saturation
options.C: Arrange admission for a CT pulmonary angiogram
options.D: Assess her and check the reading's reliability, warming her hands or using an earlobe probe
options.E: Remove the oximeter because readings are useless in cold hands

correct_answer: D. Assess her and check the reading's reliability, warming her hands or using an earlobe probe
why_correct: Cold, vasoconstricted fingers reduce pulsatile blood flow, so the oximeter may give a falsely low value. Because she appears comfortable and unchanged, the GP should assess her clinically and check the reading by looking at the waveform, warming her hands or moving to a better perfused site such as the earlobe. Only a confirmed low saturation should drive treatment.
why_wrong: A. Giving oxygen based on a doubtful reading is unnecessary and may delay finding the true cause. B. Respiratory failure is diagnosed from arterial blood gases, not from a single peripheral reading. C. Nothing in her presentation suggests pulmonary embolism. E. Oximetry remains useful once perfusion is improved or a better site is used.
pearl: Earlobe or forehead probes are less affected by peripheral vasoconstriction than finger probes.
thinking: Elderly woman with cold fingers ↓ Low finger saturation ↓ Clinically comfortable and unchanged ↓ Poor perfusion likely causing artefact ↓ Assess her and recheck with warm hands or an earlobe probe
exam_trap: A, High-flow oxygen — a low number in an older woman with heart failure prompts quick treatment, but she is comfortable and the reading is probably false because her fingers are cold.
takeaway: Cold peripheries can give falsely low oximeter readings; assess the patient and recheck at a well-perfused site.

stem: A 46-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis is attending a rheumatology clinic in winter. Several of her fingertips are white and dusky from a Raynaud's attack. A finger probe reads an oxygen saturation of 86%, yet she is talking in full sentences, her respiratory rate is normal and she says her breathing is as usual. What should be considered first?

options.A: Ignore the reading because she looks well and is speaking normally
options.B: Start oxygen through a non-rebreather mask and arrange urgent CT pulmonary angiography
options.C: Diagnose pulmonary embolism and give treatment-dose heparin
options.D: Diagnose respiratory failure and refer her to critical care
options.E: Check the probe, signal and her clinical state before relying on the reading

correct_answer: E. Check the probe, signal and her clinical state before relying on the reading
why_correct: Vasospasm in Raynaud's phenomenon greatly reduces fingertip blood flow, so a finger oximeter is likely to under-read. The probe site, waveform quality and her clinical state should be checked, ideally using an earlobe probe or a warm finger. Because systemic sclerosis can involve the lungs, genuine hypoxaemia should be excluded with an arterial blood gas if any doubt remains.
why_wrong: A. Ignoring the reading risks missing interstitial lung disease or pulmonary hypertension, both associated with systemic sclerosis. B. Starting oxygen and arranging imaging is premature before the reading is confirmed. C. There is no clinical evidence of pulmonary embolism to justify anticoagulation. D. She has no clinical signs of respiratory failure that would justify critical care referral.
pearl: Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension are leading causes of death in systemic sclerosis, so true breathlessness or hypoxaemia in these patients must be taken seriously.
thinking: Fingertips white from Raynaud's attack ↓ Low finger saturation ↓ Clinically comfortable ↓ Vasospasm makes the probe under-read ↓ Check probe and signal, confirm before acting
exam_trap: A, Ignore the reading — the reading is probably false, but systemic sclerosis can affect the lungs, so it should be checked properly rather than dismissed.
takeaway: Oximeter readings from poorly perfused fingers should be checked, not simply accepted or ignored.

stem: A practice nurse is completing a health check for a 45-year-old man. He weighs 81 kg and is 1.8 metres tall. What is his body mass index?
why_correct: Body mass index is weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres. Here, 1.8 squared is 3.24, and 81 divided by 3.24 gives 25 kg/m². Remembering to square the height is the key step.
why_wrong: A. 20 kg/m² would need a weight of about 65 kg at this height. C. 30 kg/m² would need about 97 kg. D. 35 kg/m² would need about 113 kg. E. 45 kg/m² is what you get by dividing 81 by 1.8 without squaring the height.
pearl: NICE advises using lower BMI thresholds to trigger action in people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean family background, because their cardiometabolic risk rises at a lower BMI.
thinking: BMI equals weight divided by height squared ↓ Height squared is 3.24 ↓ 81 divided by 3.24 ↓ Result 25 kg/m² ↓ Check the height was squared
exam_trap: E, 45 kg/m² — dividing weight by height without squaring it is an easy slip and produces this much larger figure.
takeaway: BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.

presentation: Acute infective gastroenteritis in a traveller
stem: Three days after returning from a fortnight in Thailand, a 30-year-old woman calls NHS 111. Since yesterday she has had several episodes of vomiting, cramping abdominal pain and frequent watery stools with no blood. She is drinking, passing urine and feels only mildly feverish. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden vomiting and watery diarrhoea starting within days of returning from abroad is most likely acute infective gastroenteritis, such as enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli, Campylobacter or a virus. It is usually self-limiting and managed with oral rehydration, with stool testing and antibiotics reserved for severe, bloody or prolonged illness.
why_wrong: A. Giardiasis usually develops one to two weeks after exposure and causes prolonged bloating, flatulence and greasy stools rather than an abrupt vomiting illness. B. Typhoid presents with a rising fever, headache and malaise, often with constipation, rather than profuse watery diarrhoea. C. Ulcerative colitis is a chronic condition with bloody diarrhoea. E. Appendicitis causes localised abdominal pain and tenderness rather than profuse watery stools.
pearl: Travellers' diarrhoea is most often caused by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli; stool culture is indicated if there is blood, high fever, severe illness or symptoms persisting beyond a week or so.
thinking: Recent return from abroad ↓ Abrupt vomiting and watery diarrhoea ↓ No blood, mildly unwell ↓ Short incubation fits common enteric pathogens ↓ Acute infective gastroenteritis
exam_trap: A, Giardiasis — it is a classic travel-related cause of diarrhoea, but it has a longer incubation and a more chronic, bloating picture than this abrupt illness.
takeaway: Acute vomiting and watery diarrhoea soon after travel is usually infective gastroenteritis managed with rehydration.

stem: A 63-year-old man has blood tests before starting a statin. He feels well and has no symptoms of thyroid disease. The results include TSH 7.8 mU/L (reference 0.4–4.0) and free T4 15 pmol/L (reference 10–22). How should these thyroid results be classified?
why_correct: A raised TSH with a free T4 still inside the reference range is subclinical hypothyroidism. The pituitary is driving a thyroid that is starting to fail, but hormone output is maintained. Thyroid function should usually be repeated after a few months to confirm it before deciding on treatment.
why_wrong: A. The TSH is clearly above the reference range, so this is not normal. B. Secondary hypothyroidism gives a low or inappropriately normal TSH with a low free T4. D. Overt hypothyroidism requires a low free T4. E. Non-thyroidal illness occurs in acutely unwell people and typically shows low or normal TSH with low T3, not this pattern in a well man.
pearl: Hypothyroidism can raise LDL cholesterol and increase the risk of statin-related muscle symptoms, which is why thyroid function is checked before starting a statin.
thinking: Well man, routine pre-statin bloods ↓ TSH above the range ↓ Free T4 within the range ↓ Raised TSH plus normal T4 ↓ Subclinical hypothyroidism, repeat to confirm
exam_trap: A, Normal thyroid function — the free T4 is normal and he feels well, but the raised TSH shows the thyroid is under strain.
takeaway: Raised TSH with a normal free T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism.

stem: A 58-year-old man sees his GP with six weeks of tiredness, vague aches in his arms and legs and a reduced appetite. He is still working, has no fever, chest pain or breathlessness, and his examination is unremarkable. The symptoms do not point clearly to any one diagnosis and he is not acutely unwell. Which is the safest approach?

options.A: Avoid discussing uncertainty with him in case he becomes anxious
options.B: Consider the differential and red flags, arrange targeted first-line tests and safety-net with planned review
options.C: Pick the most likely cause and treat it without any further follow-up
options.D: Tell him that serious illness has been excluded because his examination is normal
options.E: Order every available investigation to rule out all possible causes at once

correct_answer: B. Consider the differential and red flags, arrange targeted first-line tests and safety-net with planned review
why_correct: Undifferentiated symptoms like this need a structured approach: thinking through important differentials such as anaemia, thyroid disease, diabetes, depression or malignancy, asking specifically about red flags such as weight loss or night sweats, and arranging proportionate first-line tests. Honest discussion, clear safety-netting and a planned review allow the picture to evolve safely.
why_wrong: A. Hiding uncertainty is not honest and makes it harder for him to know when to come back. C. Settling on one diagnosis without review risks missing a serious cause. D. A normal examination does not exclude conditions such as cancer, myeloma or polymyalgia rheumatica. E. Indiscriminate testing produces false positives and anxiety without improving safety.
pearl: Unexplained weight loss, night sweats or new symptoms in someone over 50 should prompt consideration of cancer pathways under NICE NG12.
thinking: Vague tiredness and aches in a man over 50 ↓ No single obvious diagnosis ↓ Not acutely unwell ↓ Consider differentials and red flags ↓ Targeted tests, safety-net and planned review
exam_trap: E, Investigating everything at once — broad testing feels thorough, but it is not proportionate and false positives can lead to further harm.
takeaway: Undifferentiated symptoms need a considered differential, targeted tests and a clear safety net.

stem: A 74-year-old retired farmer asks his GP about rough patches on his bald scalp and the backs of his hands. They feel like sandpaper, are easier to feel than to see and sometimes flake and come back. He never wore a hat or sunscreen while working outdoors. Several pink, scaly, flat lesions a few millimetres across are seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Multiple rough, scaly, pink macules on chronically sun-exposed skin of an older man with heavy outdoor exposure are typical of actinic (solar) keratoses. They result from cumulative ultraviolet damage and carry a small risk of progressing to squamous cell carcinoma.
why_wrong: A. Seborrhoeic keratoses are raised, waxy, stuck-on brown lesions, most often on the trunk, rather than flat, rough, pink sun-related patches. C. Discoid lupus causes scarring plaques with follicular plugging and pigment change, usually in younger adults. D. Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes greasy scaling in the scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds rather than discrete rough spots. E. Nodular BCC is a single pearly papule with rolled edges and telangiectasia, not multiple flat rough patches.
pearl: An actinic keratosis that becomes thick, tender, rapidly enlarging or ulcerated should raise suspicion of squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Older man with years of outdoor sun exposure ↓ Multiple rough, sandpaper-like patches ↓ On scalp and backs of hands ↓ Pink and scaly, flat ↓ Actinic keratoses
exam_trap: E, Nodular basal cell carcinoma — sun damage in an older man raises skin cancer, but BCC is usually a single pearly nodule rather than many rough flat patches.
takeaway: Rough, scaly patches on sun-damaged skin in older people are usually actinic keratoses.

stem: A 66-year-old man with COPD has finished a course of doxycycline for an exacerbation. He uses a high-dose steroid inhaler and admits he rarely rinses his mouth afterwards. He now complains of a sore mouth and an odd taste. Creamy white patches are seen on his tongue and inner cheeks, and they wipe away with a spatula to leave a raw red surface. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: White plaques that can be scraped off to reveal a red, raw base are characteristic of oral candidiasis. The recent antibiotic course and inhaled corticosteroid use without rinsing both encourage Candida overgrowth. Treatment is usually with an oral antifungal such as miconazole oral gel or nystatin, with inhaler technique and mouth rinsing addressed.
why_wrong: A. Leukoplakia is a white patch that cannot be wiped away and is potentially premalignant. B. Oral lichen planus produces lacy white striae that do not rub off. D. Aphthous ulcers are painful shallow ulcers with a yellow base and red rim, not white plaques. E. Oral hairy leukoplakia causes corrugated white patches on the sides of the tongue that cannot be removed and is linked to Epstein-Barr virus and immunosuppression.
pearl: Miconazole oral gel interacts significantly with warfarin, so nystatin is usually preferred in people taking warfarin.
thinking: Recent antibiotics ↓ Inhaled steroid without rinsing ↓ White plaques on tongue and cheeks ↓ Wipe off leaving a raw red base ↓ Oral candidiasis
exam_trap: A, Leukoplakia — both cause white patches in the mouth, but leukoplakia cannot be scraped off, whereas these lesions wipe away.
takeaway: White oral plaques that wipe off to leave red mucosa are candidiasis.

stem: Staff at a nursing home ask the visiting GP to see an 84-year-old man. For several weeks he has been scratching red, hive-like patches on his thighs and lower abdomen, and in the past few days large firm blisters filled with clear fluid have appeared on these areas. The blisters are intact and do not break easily, and his mouth is not affected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Tense, intact blisters on the limbs and trunk in an older person, often after a period of itchy urticarial plaques, with sparing of the mouth, are typical of bullous pemphigoid. It is an autoimmune disease with antibodies against the dermo-epidermal junction, so the blister roof is thick and resists rupture. He should be referred to dermatology for confirmation by biopsy and immunofluorescence.
why_wrong: B. Pemphigus vulgaris causes flaccid, fragile blisters and erosions that usually start in the mouth, in a slightly younger age group. C. Scabies causes intense itch with burrows in finger webs and genital papules, and blistering is uncommon in adults. D. Dermatitis herpetiformis produces small, very itchy vesicles over the elbows, knees and buttocks, linked to coeliac disease. E. Bullous impetigo gives fragile blisters that leave honey-coloured crusts, usually in children.
pearl: Bullous pemphigoid can be triggered by some medicines, including gliptins such as sitagliptin, so the drug history should be reviewed.
thinking: Older man in a nursing home ↓ Weeks of itchy urticarial patches ↓ Then large tense blisters ↓ Mouth spared, blisters hard to rupture ↓ Bullous pemphigoid
exam_trap: B, Pemphigus vulgaris — it is the other major autoimmune blistering disease, but it causes fragile blisters with early mouth involvement rather than tense blisters with oral sparing.
takeaway: Tense, itchy blisters in an older person with sparing of the mouth suggest bullous pemphigoid.

stem: A 58-year-old man attends the emergency department three weeks after starting allopurinol for gout. He felt feverish with a sore throat a few days ago, and now has a painful, spreading dusky red rash with blisters on his trunk. Areas of skin slide off with gentle pressure, and he has crusted lips, painful mouth ulcers and red, gritty eyes. Which condition should be suspected?

options.B: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

correct_answer: C. Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis
why_correct: A painful dusky rash with blistering and skin detachment, involvement of two or more mucous membranes and a recently started high-risk drug such as allopurinol point to Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. A flu-like prodrome is typical. The drug must be stopped at once and he needs urgent specialist care, often in a burns or intensive care setting.
why_wrong: A. Bullous pemphigoid causes tense itchy blisters in older people, usually without mucosal involvement or a drug-related painful skin loss. B. DRESS presents with a widespread rash, facial swelling, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and organ involvement, usually without extensive epidermal detachment. D. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome mainly affects young children and spares the mucous membranes. E. Pompholyx causes itchy deep-seated vesicles on the palms and soles without systemic illness.
pearl: Allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfonamides and nevirapine are among the drugs most often linked to Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
thinking: Recently started allopurinol ↓ Flu-like prodrome ↓ Painful dusky rash with blisters and skin sliding off ↓ Mouth and eye involvement ↓ Suspect SJS/TEN and stop the drug
exam_trap: B, DRESS — it is also a severe reaction to allopurinol and anticonvulsants, but it does not usually cause sheets of skin detachment with mucosal ulceration.
takeaway: Painful blistering with skin detachment and mucosal involvement after a new drug is SJS/TEN until proven otherwise.

stem: A 23-year-old man comes back from a week of skiing and books a GP appointment. Two days ago a sore, stinging patch appeared on the edge of his lower lip, and it has turned into a cluster of small clear blisters sitting on a red base. He has had similar spots after sunny holidays before. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A cluster of small vesicles on a red base at the vermilion border of the lip, recurring after exposure to strong sunlight, is herpes labialis. Ultraviolet light is a well-recognised trigger for reactivation of herpes simplex virus from the trigeminal ganglion. Lesions usually crust and heal within about ten days.
why_wrong: B. Angular cheilitis causes cracking and soreness at the corners of the mouth, not grouped vesicles. C. Bullous impetigo produces larger fragile blisters that leave honey-coloured crusts, without a recurring pattern after sun exposure. D. Actinic cheilitis is chronic dryness and scaling of the lower lip from long-term sun damage, usually in older people. E. Perioral dermatitis causes small red papules and pustules around the mouth, sparing the lip border.
pearl: Sun protection for the lips, such as a high-factor lip balm, can reduce sunlight-triggered recurrences of cold sores.
thinking: Young man after strong sun exposure ↓ Stinging patch on the lip border ↓ Grouped vesicles on a red base ↓ Similar episodes before ↓ Recurrent herpes simplex
exam_trap: D, Actinic cheilitis — sun exposure and the lower lip suggest it, but it is a chronic scaly change in older people, not an acute cluster of blisters.
takeaway: Grouped vesicles on a red base at the lip border, recurring after sun exposure, are cold sores.

stem: A 70-year-old man is on a medical ward being treated for pneumonia, which caused high fevers for the first two days. He tells the doctor that his upper lip began tingling and burning yesterday, and now a crop of small, painful vesicles has appeared at the same spot, where he says 'fever blisters' have come up occasionally over the years. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Shingles in the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve

why_correct: A tingling or burning prodrome followed by grouped painful vesicles at the same site on the lip, with past recurrences, is typical of herpes simplex reactivation. Fever and acute illness are classic triggers, which is why cold sores are also called fever blisters. Recurrent lesions usually heal without scarring.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes diffuse redness, swelling and warmth rather than a cluster of vesicles. B. Shingles causes a dermatomal band of vesicles across one side of the face, usually without repeated attacks at the same small spot. C. Candidiasis causes white plaques inside the mouth, not vesicles on the lip. D. Aphthous ulcers occur inside the mouth on non-keratinised mucosa and do not begin as vesicles.
pearl: Topical aciclovir has only a small benefit for recurrent cold sores and works best if started at the first tingle of the prodrome.
thinking: Acute febrile illness ↓ Tingling prodrome on the lip ↓ Then grouped painful vesicles ↓ Same site as previous episodes ↓ Recurrent herpes simplex
exam_trap: B, Shingles — vesicles on the face in an unwell older man suggest it, but shingles follows a dermatome and does not keep recurring at one spot on the lip.
takeaway: A tingling prodrome followed by grouped lip vesicles at a recurring site is herpes simplex.

stem: A 38-year-old woman asks a community pharmacist for advice about a sore spot near the corner of her upper lip. It appears most months in the days before her period, starts as a few small clustered blisters that weep and crust, and clears on its own within about a week. Today the blisters are on a red, tender base. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Clusters of small vesicles on a red base near the lip that crust and heal within a week, and recur at the same site in relation to a predictable trigger, are typical of recurrent herpes simplex. Hormonal changes around menstruation, like stress, illness and sunlight, are recognised triggers of reactivation.
why_wrong: A. Impetigo causes honey-coloured crusts that spread, without regular monthly recurrence. B. Shingles is usually a single episode in a dermatomal pattern, not monthly recurrences. C. Angular cheilitis causes cracking at the mouth corners, not clusters of blisters. E. Contact dermatitis causes itchy eczematous change wherever the product touches, rather than a single recurring blister cluster.
pearl: Herpes simplex is highly contagious while blisters are present, so people should avoid kissing and oral sex until lesions have healed.
thinking: Recurrent sore spot near the lip ↓ Linked to menstrual cycle ↓ Clustered vesicles on a red base ↓ Crusts and heals within a week ↓ Recurrent herpes simplex
exam_trap: A, Impetigo — weeping and crusting near the mouth suggest it, but impetigo does not recur monthly at one spot and typically spreads with golden crusts rather than healing within a week.
takeaway: Recurrent clustered vesicles at the same spot on the lip, with a predictable trigger, are herpes simplex.

stem: A 29-year-old woman visits the pharmacy-led minor illness clinic with an itchy, red, slightly weeping patch of skin just below her navel. It started about a week after she bought new jeans, and the patch exactly matches where the metal button presses against her skin. The rest of her skin is clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An itchy eczematous patch confined to the area in contact with a metal button points to allergic contact dermatitis, most often due to nickel sensitivity. The sharply defined outline matching the object is the key clue. Management is avoiding the allergen, for example by covering the button, with an emollient and a short course of topical corticosteroid.
why_wrong: B. Discoid eczema causes multiple coin-shaped patches, often on the limbs, unrelated to a contact object. C. Tinea causes an annular scaly lesion with an active edge and central clearing. D. Psoriasis gives well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and scalp. E. Scabies causes widespread itch with burrows in the finger webs and wrists.
pearl: Patch testing is the investigation of choice to confirm suspected allergic contact dermatitis and identify the allergen.
thinking: Itchy, weeping red patch ↓ Exactly where a metal button touches ↓ Started after new clothing ↓ Rest of skin clear ↓ Allergic contact dermatitis, likely nickel
exam_trap: B, Discoid eczema — a single eczematous patch could be discoid, but its outline matching the button shows an external contact cause.
takeaway: A rash precisely matching an object in contact with the skin is contact dermatitis.

presentation: Herpes zoster (shingles) of a thoracic dermatome
stem: A care home nurse asks the visiting GP to see a 79-year-old woman. For four days she has complained of a stinging ache under her right breast that staff put down to a muscle strain. This morning a strip of clustered blisters on a red base has appeared, running from beside her spine round to the front of her lower ribs. It stops sharply at the midline and the left side is clear. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Prodromal pain in one area followed by grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, confined to one dermatome and stopping at the midline, is the typical picture of varicella-zoster reactivation. Older age is the main risk factor. The pain often comes before the rash, which is why it was first mistaken for a muscular problem.
why_wrong: A. Bullous pemphigoid causes tense, itchy bullae that are widespread and usually on the limbs and flexures, not in a single band. B. Contact dermatitis follows the shape of an exposure, is itchy rather than painful and has no prodromal pain. C. Scabies causes widespread itchy papules and burrows, not a one-sided vesicular strip. D. Bullous impetigo gives flaccid blisters that leave honey-coloured crusts, without a dermatomal pattern or preceding nerve pain.
pearl: Starting oral aciclovir within 72 hours of rash onset is recommended for people over 50, and it may still be worth starting later in older or immunosuppressed patients while new lesions are appearing.
thinking: Several days of localised pain with nothing to see ↓ Then clustered vesicles on a red base ↓ Strictly one side, stopping at the midline ↓ Band-shaped, following one thoracic dermatome ↓ Older patient, so reactivation is likely: herpes zoster
exam_trap: A, Bullous pemphigoid — it is the classic blistering disease of older people in care homes, but its blisters are tense, itchy and widespread, not a painful one-sided band.
takeaway: Pain first, then a unilateral band of grouped vesicles that stops at the midline, means shingles.

stem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father. She has atopic eczema, which flared last week. Over the past 36 hours the eczema on her face and neck has become very painful, with crops of small, uniform blisters that break down into round, punched-out erosions. She has a temperature, is irritable and is feeding poorly. Her older brother had a cold sore a few days ago. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Rapidly spreading, painful, monomorphic vesicles and punched-out erosions concentrated on eczematous skin, together with fever and systemic upset, indicate widespread herpes simplex infection of eczema. The sibling's cold sore gives a likely source. This needs same-day treatment with aciclovir, and urgent ophthalmology review if lesions are near the eye.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial infection of eczema causes weeping and golden crusting, but not uniform punched-out erosions with marked pain and fever. B. Chickenpox spreads over the trunk in crops at different stages, rather than clustering on the areas of eczema. C. Contact dermatitis is itchy, follows an exposure and does not cause fever or punched-out erosions. D. Scalded skin syndrome causes tender widespread redness with superficial sheet-like peeling and a positive Nikolsky sign, not grouped vesicles.
pearl: Eczema herpeticum can spread quickly and be life-threatening in infants. Suspect it whenever eczema becomes suddenly painful and fails to respond to usual treatment, and start aciclovir without waiting for viral swab results.
thinking: Infant with known atopic eczema ↓ Sudden pain in the eczema rather than itch ↓ Uniform vesicles becoming punched-out erosions ↓ Fever and poor feeding, plus a recent herpes simplex contact ↓ Herpes simplex spread over eczema: eczema herpeticum
exam_trap: A, Staphylococcal infection of eczema — infected eczema is far more common and also causes a flare with crusting, but monomorphic punched-out erosions, marked pain and fever point to herpes simplex.
takeaway: A sudden painful flare of eczema with punched-out erosions and fever is eczema herpeticum until proven otherwise.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is seen at his GP surgery on the second day of a course of an oral antibiotic for a chest infection. About an hour after this morning's dose he became very itchy. Raised pale-pink swellings with red flares are now scattered over his trunk and thighs, and his mother has noticed that individual swellings fade within a few hours while new ones appear. His lips, mouth and eyes are normal, there are no blisters, and he is playing happily with normal observations. Which type of drug reaction is this?

options.B: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

why_correct: Itchy wheals with surrounding flare, coming on within an hour or so of a dose and with each lesion lasting only hours, describe acute urticaria. There is no mucosal disease, blistering or systemic upset to suggest a severe cutaneous reaction. The drug should be stopped, a non-sedating antihistamine given, and the reaction recorded as a suspected allergy.
why_wrong: A. A fixed drug eruption gives one or a few well-defined dusky plaques that recur at the same site each time the drug is taken. B. DRESS develops weeks after starting a drug, with fever, facial swelling, a widespread rash, eosinophilia and organ involvement. C. Stevens–Johnson syndrome causes painful skin with blistering, skin loss and mucosal erosions. E. A morbilliform eruption is a flat or slightly raised blotchy red rash that usually starts several days into a course and lasts days, not migrating wheals.
pearl: Urticarial lesions that each last less than 24 hours suggest ordinary urticaria; lesions that last longer, burn rather than itch, or leave bruising should raise concern about urticarial vasculitis.
thinking: New antibiotic taken shortly before the rash ↓ Itchy raised wheals with a red flare ↓ Each lesion fades within hours and new ones appear ↓ No mucosal involvement, blisters or systemic upset ↓ Simple drug-induced urticaria
exam_trap: E, Morbilliform drug eruption — it is the most common drug rash with antibiotics, but it is flat to papular, appears several days in and lasts days, whereas these lesions are transient wheals.
takeaway: Transient itchy wheals soon after a new drug, without mucosal or systemic features, are drug-induced urticaria.

stem: An out-of-hours GP is called to a nursing home to review an 84-year-old woman. Since yesterday she has had a cluster of painful blisters spreading over the left side of her forehead and scalp, and her left upper eyelid is now swollen and red. The rash does not cross the midline. Staff are giving regular paracetamol. Which complication most needs to be looked for and acted on urgently?
why_correct: A vesicular rash over the forehead and upper eyelid lies in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, so this is herpes zoster ophthalmicus. The main danger is involvement of the eye itself, such as conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis or retinitis, which can threaten vision. She needs prompt antiviral treatment and same-day ophthalmology assessment.
why_wrong: A. Ramsay Hunt syndrome affects the facial nerve via the geniculate ganglion, with ear vesicles and facial weakness, not a forehead rash. B. Postherpetic neuralgia is a later problem that matters but does not threaten sight right now. D. Bacterial infection of the lesions can occur but is not the most important threat in this distribution. E. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock pains and is not a complication of acute zoster.
pearl: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is an emergency for the eye even when vision is normal at presentation, because keratitis and uveitis can develop over the following days.
thinking: Painful unilateral vesicles on the forehead and scalp ↓ Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve ↓ Upper eyelid now involved ↓ The eye itself is at risk ↓ Antivirals and same-day eye assessment
exam_trap: B, Postherpetic neuralgia — it is the most common complication of shingles in older people, but it develops later and is not the urgent threat in a rash around the eye.
takeaway: Shingles in the ophthalmic division puts the eye at risk and needs urgent ophthalmology input.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant attends maternity triage. Three days ago she had tingling on the left side of her forehead, and now there are grouped blisters on her left forehead, along the margin of her upper eyelid and down the side of her nose. She had chickenpox as a child. She is worried about her baby. Fetal movements are normal. What is the most important concern in this presentation?

options.E: Allergic reaction to a new cosmetic

correct_answer: B. Possible involvement of the eye
why_correct: This is shingles of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and lesions on the side of the nose show the nasociliary branch is involved, which supplies the eye. The main concern is sight-threatening eye involvement, so she needs antiviral treatment and urgent ophthalmology review. Shingles in pregnancy carries little risk to the baby, because the mother already has antibodies.
why_wrong: A. Fetal varicella syndrome follows primary maternal chickenpox in early pregnancy, not shingles. C. Neonatal varicella is a risk when the mother has chickenpox close to delivery, not shingles at 30 weeks. D. Varicella pneumonia is a complication of primary chickenpox in adults, especially in pregnancy, not localised zoster. E. A cosmetic reaction would be itchy and follow the area of application, not a painful one-sided vesicular band.
pearl: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson sign) suggest nasociliary nerve involvement and a higher chance of eye complications in herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
thinking: Prodromal tingling, then unilateral grouped vesicles ↓ Forehead, eyelid margin and side of nose ↓ Ophthalmic division with nasociliary branch involved ↓ Shingles poses little risk to the fetus ↓ Main concern is the eye: urgent ophthalmology review
exam_trap: A, Fetal varicella syndrome — pregnancy draws attention to the baby, but that syndrome follows primary chickenpox in early pregnancy, and the real threat here is to the mother's eye.
takeaway: In ophthalmic shingles, even in pregnancy, the key concern is eye involvement.

stem: A 15-year-old girl returns to her GP about her acne. Over the past year she has used topical benzoyl peroxide with adapalene and has just completed a three-month course of oral lymecycline alongside it. She still has deep, painful lumps along her jawline and upper back, and small pitted marks and raised scars are now forming where earlier lesions have healed. She has no menstrual irregularity or excess hair growth. What is the main reason she should now be referred to a consultant dermatologist?

options.A: Her acne suggests polycystic ovary syndrome needing endocrine tests
options.B: Her nodular acne is already scarring, and effective treatment is needed to prevent further permanent scarring
options.C: Topical treatments are unsafe to continue at her age
options.D: A second antibiotic course is not allowed in primary care
options.E: Nodular acne at her age suggests an underlying malignancy

correct_answer: B. Her nodular acne is already scarring, and effective treatment is needed to prevent further permanent scarring
why_correct: Acne with deep nodules and cysts that is already leaving scars carries a high risk of permanent disfigurement. NICE advises referral to a consultant dermatologist-led team for acne with scarring or nodulocystic acne, and for acne that has not responded to an adequate course of topical plus oral antibiotic treatment. Specialist care allows access to oral isotretinoin, which can stop further scarring.
why_wrong: A. She has no features of hyperandrogenism, so an endocrine cause is not the reason for referral. C. Topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide are standard and safe in adolescents. D. Another course of a different treatment could be tried, but scarring makes specialist referral the priority. E. Acne is not a sign of malignancy.
pearl: Isotretinoin can only be started by a consultant dermatologist-led team, and for anyone who could become pregnant it requires a pregnancy prevention programme because it is highly teratogenic.
thinking: Teenager with persistent inflammatory acne ↓ Adequate trial of topical plus oral antibiotic has failed ↓ Deep nodules and cysts ↓ Scars already forming ↓ Refer to dermatology to prevent permanent scarring
exam_trap: A, Polycystic ovary syndrome — acne in a young woman tempts a hormonal work-up, but she has no other features, and the urgent issue is the scarring.
takeaway: Nodular acne that is scarring needs specialist referral to prevent permanent damage.

stem: A 47-year-old man asks a community pharmacist for cold sore cream. For two days he has had pricking pain on the right side of his face, and now there are small crusting blisters on the tip of his nose and patches of blisters on his right forehead. His eye feels normal. The pharmacist advises him to see a doctor the same day. Why is this pattern of rash particularly worrying?

options.A: It suggests impetigo that needs oral antibiotics
options.B: It means postherpetic neuralgia is now unavoidable
options.C: It indicates a first episode of herpes simplex
options.D: It suggests the nasociliary nerve is involved, so the eye is at risk
options.E: It indicates disseminated zoster needing hospital admission

correct_answer: D. It suggests the nasociliary nerve is involved, so the eye is at risk
why_correct: Painful one-sided vesicles on the forehead mean shingles in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) show that the nasociliary branch, which also supplies the cornea, is involved. This strongly predicts eye complications, so he needs antivirals and urgent assessment of the eye even though it feels normal.
why_wrong: A. The prodromal pain and dermatomal blisters indicate a viral cause, not a bacterial skin infection. B. Neuralgia risk rises with age and severity, but it is never certain and is not why the nose matters. C. Herpes simplex does not cause a dermatomal rash across the forehead after a painful prodrome. E. Disseminated zoster means lesions well beyond the dermatome, which he does not have.
pearl: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with Hutchinson sign needs same-day ophthalmology assessment, because keratitis and uveitis may develop before symptoms are noticed.
thinking: Painful prodrome, then unilateral vesicles ↓ Forehead lesions: ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve ↓ Nose tip involved: Hutchinson sign ↓ Nasociliary branch also supplies the eye ↓ High risk of eye involvement, so urgent review
exam_trap: C, A first episode of herpes simplex — he asked for cold sore cream, but the dermatomal spread over the forehead after nerve pain is shingles, and the nose tip lesion is a warning about the eye.
takeaway: Shingles vesicles on the tip of the nose signal a high risk of eye involvement.

stem: A 52-year-old man is referred to the dermatology clinic by his optometrist, who noticed red eyelid margins and dry, gritty eyes. He reports that his face has gone red easily for several years. Examination shows small red papules and pustules on his nose and both cheeks, with fine, dilated thread veins. The forehead is less affected. There are no blackheads or whiteheads and no scale. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.D: Malar rash of systemic lupus erythematosus

why_correct: Central facial redness with a history of flushing, telangiectasia and inflammatory papules and pustules in a middle-aged adult, with no comedones, is papulopustular rosacea. Blepharitis and gritty eyes are common in ocular rosacea and can be the first feature to be noticed. First-line options include topical ivermectin, azelaic acid or metronidazole, with an oral tetracycline for more extensive disease.
why_wrong: A. Acne vulgaris is defined by comedones, which are absent, and usually begins in adolescence. B. Seborrhoeic dermatitis gives greasy yellow scale in the nasolabial folds, eyebrows and scalp, without pustules. D. The lupus malar rash is a photosensitive erythema that does not cause pustules, and there are no systemic features of lupus. E. Perioral dermatitis clusters around the mouth and chin, often with a clear margin by the lips.
pearl: The absence of comedones is the key feature separating rosacea from acne, and eye symptoms such as blepharitis can occur in rosacea.
thinking: Middle-aged adult with a history of easy facial redness ↓ Central papules and pustules with telangiectasia ↓ No comedones ↓ Gritty eyes and blepharitis: ocular involvement ↓ Rosacea
exam_trap: A, Acne vulgaris — papules and pustules point people towards acne, but the lack of comedones, the telangiectasia and the age of onset fit rosacea.
takeaway: Facial papules and pustules with telangiectasia but no comedones in a middle-aged adult is rosacea.

stem: A 57-year-old woman attends the emergency department with shivering and a temperature. Two years ago she had breast cancer surgery with axillary node clearance, and her left arm has been swollen since. Since yesterday the left forearm has developed a shiny, bright red, hot, tender area. Its edge is raised and so clear that it can be traced with a finger. There is no crepitus, and the pain matches the appearance. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Erysipelas is a superficial streptococcal infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, producing a bright red, raised, sharply demarcated plaque with fever and rigors. Lymphoedema after axillary surgery is a major risk factor because lymphatic drainage is impaired. It is treated with an antibiotic that covers streptococci, given intravenously if she is systemically unwell.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis is itchy, follows an exposure and does not cause rigors or fever. B. Thrombophlebitis gives a tender cord along a superficial vein, not a broad plaque with a raised edge. C. Urticarial wheals come and go within hours and are itchy, not hot and tender with fever. D. Tinea gives a slowly spreading scaly ring with central clearing and no systemic illness.
pearl: Lymphoedema greatly increases the risk of recurrent erysipelas and cellulitis; people with repeated episodes may be offered antibiotic prophylaxis.
thinking: Fever and rigors with a hot tender red plaque ↓ Raised, sharply demarcated edge ↓ Superficial dermal and lymphatic infection ↓ Lymphoedema after axillary clearance is a risk factor ↓ Erysipelas
exam_trap: A, Allergic contact dermatitis — the sharp edge can suggest a contact reaction, but fever, rigors, heat and tenderness point to infection.
takeaway: A hot, bright red plaque with a raised, sharp edge and fever is erysipelas.

stem: A 39-year-old woman who works as a chef has a telephone consultation with her GP. For about two years her cheeks, nose and chin have flushed red within minutes of being in the hot kitchen, drinking coffee or having a glass of wine. Recently the redness over the centre of her face has stayed between flushes. She has no joint pains, mouth ulcers, scale or itch, and her periods are regular. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Episodes of facial flushing triggered by heat, hot drinks and alcohol, progressing to persistent central facial redness, are typical of rosacea. Her job exposes her to frequent heat triggers. Management starts with identifying and avoiding triggers, daily sun protection and gentle skin care, with topical or oral treatment depending on the features present.
why_wrong: A. Lupus causes a photosensitive malar rash with systemic features such as joint pain and mouth ulcers, not trigger-related flushing. B. Seborrhoeic dermatitis gives greasy scale in the nasolabial folds and eyebrows. D. Menopausal flushes involve the upper body as well as the face and occur with menstrual change; her cycles are regular. E. Contact dermatitis is itchy and follows an exposure, not heat or hot drinks.
pearl: Common rosacea triggers include heat, sunlight, hot drinks, spicy food and alcohol, and keeping a symptom diary helps patients identify their own triggers.
thinking: Recurrent facial flushing ↓ Triggered by heat, hot drinks and alcohol ↓ Now persistent central facial redness ↓ No systemic, scaly or itchy features ↓ Rosacea
exam_trap: A, Systemic lupus erythematosus — facial redness in a woman of this age makes people think of a malar rash, but trigger-related flushing without systemic features is rosacea.
takeaway: Facial flushing triggered by heat, hot drinks and alcohol, with persistent central redness, is rosacea.

stem: A 27-year-old woman sees her GP because of three episodes over the past six months of puffy swelling of her upper lip and both eyelids. Each episode develops over a few hours and takes about two days to settle. The swelling feels tight and slightly uncomfortable but not itchy, and there have never been raised red wheals on her skin. Between episodes she is well, she has no dental pain and she has not had a fever. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Angioedema is swelling of the deeper dermis, subcutaneous tissue or mucosa, and typically affects the lips, eyelids, tongue and genitals. It lasts longer than wheals, often up to two or three days, and is usually not itchy. Angioedema without wheals should prompt review of medicines such as ACE inhibitors and consideration of hereditary or acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency.
why_wrong: B. Cellulitis is a single, persistent, hot and tender area that does not come and go, and usually causes fever. C. Contact dermatitis is itchy with redness and scale where an allergen touched the skin. D. Urticaria causes superficial itchy wheals lasting less than 24 hours, which she has never had. E. A dental abscess causes tooth pain and continuous swelling, not recurrent eyelid and lip swelling.
pearl: Recurrent angioedema with no wheals and no medicine trigger should prompt a C4 level, which is low in hereditary angioedema.
thinking: Recurrent episodes of facial swelling ↓ Lips and eyelids affected ↓ Deep, non-itchy, lasting about two days ↓ No wheals, fever or dental cause ↓ Angioedema
exam_trap: D, Urticaria — urticaria and angioedema often occur together, but she has deep non-itchy swelling and has never had wheals.
takeaway: Recurrent deep, non-itchy swelling of the lips and eyelids without wheals is angioedema.

stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is seen in the community podiatry clinic. Over the past two years several of his toenails have become opaque and yellowish-white, much thicker than before and lifted from the nail bed at the free edge, with crumbly material packed underneath. The skin between his toes is white and scaly. His fingernails are normal and there are no skin plaques elsewhere. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Thickened, discoloured nails with onycholysis and subungual debris, together with tinea pedis between the toes, describe fungal nail infection, most often caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum. Diabetes and older age increase the risk. Nail clippings should be sent for microscopy and culture before starting oral antifungal treatment.
why_wrong: B. Nail psoriasis usually affects the fingernails too, with pitting and oil-drop discolouration, and is accompanied by skin plaques. C. Chronic paronychia affects the nail fold, causing swelling and loss of the cuticle, rather than subungual debris. D. Subungual melanoma usually affects a single nail with a pigmented band or nail destruction. E. Onychogryphosis is a markedly thickened, curved, ram's-horn nail, usually of one great toe after trauma or neglect, without white interdigital scale.
pearl: Confirm onychomycosis with nail clippings for microscopy and culture before starting oral terbinafine, because several other nail diseases look very similar.
