thinking: Several toenails slowly thickened and discoloured ↓ Onycholysis with crumbly subungual debris ↓ Scaly skin between the toes: tinea pedis ↓ Fingernails and skin otherwise normal ↓ Fungal nail infection
exam_trap: B, Nail psoriasis — it can cause thick nails with debris and onycholysis, but normal fingernails, no plaques and coexisting athlete's foot point to fungal infection.
takeaway: Thick, discoloured toenails with crumbly debris beneath, alongside athlete's foot, suggest onychomycosis.

presentation: Diffuse non-scarring hair loss in iron deficiency
stem: A 40-year-old woman with long-standing heavy menstrual bleeding is found to have a low ferritin. She also mentions that over the past few months she has been finding much more hair on her pillow and in the shower drain, and her ponytail is noticeably thinner. She has not noticed any bald spots, and her scalp is not itchy, sore or scaly. Which description best fits the hair loss she is most likely to have?

options.A: Round, smooth bald patches with exclamation-mark hairs
options.B: Loss of follicular openings with shiny scarred skin
options.C: A scaly patch with broken hairs and an enlarged neck node
options.D: Diffuse thinning across the scalp with intact follicles
options.E: Recession of the frontal hairline along the line of a tight hairstyle

correct_answer: D. Diffuse thinning across the scalp with intact follicles
why_correct: Iron deficiency is linked with diffuse, non-scarring hair shedding across the whole scalp rather than discrete patches. The follicles are preserved, so regrowth is expected once the cause is corrected. Treating the heavy bleeding and replacing iron are the key steps.
why_wrong: A. Smooth round patches with exclamation-mark hairs describe alopecia areata. B. Loss of follicular openings describes scarring alopecia, which is permanent. C. A scaly patch with broken hairs and lymphadenopathy suggests tinea capitis. E. Hairline loss from tight hairstyles is traction alopecia.
pearl: In diffuse hair loss, check for iron deficiency, thyroid disease and recent stressors such as illness, childbirth or new medicines.
thinking: Heavy periods with low ferritin ↓ Increased shedding over the whole scalp ↓ No discrete patches ↓ Scalp healthy, follicles preserved ↓ Diffuse non-scarring hair loss
exam_trap: A, Alopecia areata — it is the hair loss most people think of first, but it causes discrete bald patches, not diffuse thinning.
takeaway: Iron deficiency is associated with diffuse non-scarring hair shedding rather than patchy loss.

stem: A 55-year-old man attends his GP three months after a two-week intensive care admission with severe pneumonia. He is alarmed that handfuls of hair come out when he washes it and that it looks thin all over. Gentle pulling on several areas of the scalp easily removes a few hairs, each with a small white bulb at the root. The scalp skin looks entirely normal, with no patches, scale, redness or scarring. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A serious illness pushes many hair follicles into the resting (telogen) phase at once, and those hairs are shed around two to four months later. This causes diffuse shedding of club hairs with a positive pull test and a normal scalp. It is usually self-limiting, with regrowth over the following months once the trigger has passed.
why_wrong: A. Alopecia areata gives discrete smooth patches, often with exclamation-mark hairs. C. Androgenetic alopecia develops gradually in a pattern over years, not as sudden shedding after an illness. D. Tinea capitis causes scaly patches with broken hairs. E. Frontal fibrosing alopecia is a scarring process causing recession of the frontal hairline in older women.
pearl: Telogen effluvium typically appears two to four months after the trigger, such as severe illness, surgery, childbirth, crash dieting or starting a new medicine.
thinking: Diffuse shedding of hair ↓ Around three months after a severe illness ↓ Positive pull test with club hairs ↓ Normal scalp with no scarring ↓ Telogen effluvium
exam_trap: C, Androgenetic alopecia — he is a middle-aged man, but the sudden diffuse shedding after a major illness fits telogen effluvium, not a gradual patterned loss.
takeaway: Sudden diffuse hair shedding a few months after major illness is telogen effluvium.

stem: A 56-year-old woman, five years past the menopause, sees her GP because over several years the hair over the top of her head has become thinner, so that her centre parting looks wider and her scalp shows through under bright lights. Her frontal hairline is in the same place as always. There has been no sudden shedding, no bald spots and no itch. The scalp is healthy, the hair pull test is negative and close inspection shows many fine, short hairs on the crown. Her blood tests are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Gradual thinning over the crown with a widening central parting, preserved frontal hairline and miniaturised hairs is androgenetic (female-pattern) hair loss. It is non-scarring and becomes more common after the menopause. Topical minoxidil is the main treatment option.
why_wrong: A. Telogen effluvium causes sudden diffuse shedding with a positive pull test after a trigger. B. Alopecia areata gives discrete smooth bald patches. C. Traction alopecia affects the margins where hair is pulled tight, not the crown. E. Discoid lupus causes scarring, scaly, red patches with loss of follicles.
pearl: In women, androgenetic alopecia usually spares the frontal hairline and widens the parting, whereas in men it causes temporal recession and crown thinning.
thinking: Slow thinning over years ↓ Widening central parting, frontal hairline kept ↓ Miniaturised hairs and negative pull test ↓ Non-scarring, healthy scalp ↓ Female-pattern androgenetic alopecia
exam_trap: A, Telogen effluvium — diffuse thinning in a woman suggests shedding, but the slow course, negative pull test and miniaturised hairs mean androgenetic alopecia.
takeaway: Gradual crown thinning with a widening parting and a preserved hairline is androgenetic alopecia.

presentation: Irritant contact dermatitis of the hands
stem: A 45-year-old kitchen porter sees his GP with sore hands. For the last three months he has spent most of each shift washing dishes in hot soapy water without gloves. The backs of his hands and his fingers are dry, red and rough, with painful cracks over the knuckles, while the skin above his wrists is normal. The rash settled almost completely during a two-week holiday and returned within days of going back to work. There are no burrows and no blisters on the palms. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Repeated wet work with detergents strips the skin barrier and causes irritant contact dermatitis, the commonest occupational skin disease. It is confined to the exposed skin, improves away from work and recurs on return. Management includes protective gloves, soap substitutes and frequent emollients.
why_wrong: A. Pompholyx causes itchy deep-seated blisters on the palms and sides of the fingers. B. Scabies causes intensely itchy papules and burrows in the finger webs and elsewhere, with affected contacts. C. Tinea manuum is usually one-sided, with a scaly edge, often alongside tinea pedis. E. Palmar psoriasis gives thick, well-defined scaly plaques and does not clear on holiday.
pearl: Occupational hand dermatitis that persists despite glove use should prompt patch testing to look for an additional allergic contact dermatitis.
thinking: Prolonged wet work with detergents ↓ Dry, red, cracked skin limited to exposed areas ↓ Improves away from work, returns on return ↓ No burrows, palmar blisters or plaques ↓ Irritant contact dermatitis
exam_trap: A, Pompholyx eczema — it is a common hand eczema, but it causes deep itchy palmar blisters rather than dry cracking on the backs of the hands after wet work.
takeaway: Dry, cracked hands after repeated wet work that improve on holiday mean irritant contact dermatitis.

stem: A 30-year-old man attends a surgical follow-up clinic four months after an emergency laparotomy. His midline wound healed after a minor wound infection, but the scar is now thick, red, firm and itchy, standing up above the surrounding skin. It has not spread sideways: the raised tissue stays exactly within the line of the original incision, and he thinks it has started to soften slightly. There is no bulge on coughing and no discharge. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A hypertrophic scar is raised, red and sometimes itchy, but stays within the boundaries of the original wound and often improves gradually over months. Wound infection and tension, as in a midline abdominal wound, increase the risk. Silicone gel or sheeting and pressure can help.
why_wrong: A. A keloid extends beyond the original wound margins and does not regress. B. An incisional hernia gives a bulge beneath the scar that increases on coughing. C. A suture granuloma is a small, localised nodule, often discharging, at a stitch site. D. A seroma is a soft, fluctuant fluid collection in the early weeks after surgery.
pearl: Keloids are more common in people with darker skin and on the chest, shoulders and earlobes, and they may recur after excision.
thinking: Raised, red, firm, itchy scar ↓ Confined to the original incision ↓ Starting to soften with time ↓ No cough impulse or discharge ↓ Hypertrophic scar
exam_trap: A, Keloid scar — both are raised, but a keloid grows beyond the wound edges, whereas this scar stays within the incision.
takeaway: A raised scar that stays within the original wound boundaries is a hypertrophic scar.

stem: A 24-year-old nursery assistant sees her GP about a sore patch on her chin that appeared five days ago. It began as a red spot that wept and has now spread into a moist, red area covered with yellow-brown crusts, with two new spots nearby. She feels well. Over the past fortnight several of the toddlers in her room have had similar sores around the nose and mouth. She has never had cold sores. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial bacterial infection, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. It causes weeping lesions that form honey or yellow-brown crusts and spread to nearby skin. Close contact with affected young children explains how she caught it.
why_wrong: A. Cold sores start with tingling and grouped vesicles at the lip margin and tend to recur at the same site; she has no history of them. B. Scabies causes widespread itchy papules and burrows, not localised crusted erosions. C. Tinea faciei gives a slowly expanding scaly ring, not weeping crusts within days. E. Perioral dermatitis gives small papules and pustules around the mouth without honey-coloured crusts or contagious spread.
pearl: Hydrogen peroxide 1% cream is first line for localised non-bullous impetigo in people who are not systemically unwell, with topical fusidic acid if it is unsuitable and oral flucloxacillin for widespread disease.
thinking: Weeping red lesion spreading over days ↓ Yellow-brown crusts ↓ Close contact with children with similar sores ↓ Feels well, no previous cold sores ↓ Impetigo
exam_trap: A, Herpes simplex labialis — a crusted sore near the mouth makes people think of a cold sore, but the yellow-brown crusts, spread and outbreak among the children fit impetigo.
takeaway: Weeping, crusted lesions spreading among close contacts suggest impetigo.

stem: A 40-year-old man sees a nurse practitioner at a walk-in centre a week after a camping trip. He scratched several insect bites on both shins, and these have turned into shallow, moist erosions topped with honey-coloured crusts. New similar spots have appeared nearby over the past two days. There are no blisters, no deep ulcers, and the surrounding skin is not swollen, hot or tender. He is otherwise well with normal observations. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Honey-coloured crusts over superficial erosions that spread to nearby skin describe impetigo. Scratching broke the skin barrier over the bites and allowed secondary infection with Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. Because the lesions are superficial and he is systemically well, topical treatment is appropriate if the area is localised.
why_wrong: B. Cellulitis causes a spreading, hot, tender, swollen area of deeper infection, which he does not have. C. Ecthyma is a deeper infection that leaves punched-out ulcers with thick crusts, not shallow erosions. D. Discoid eczema gives itchy, coin-shaped, scaly or weeping plaques without honey-coloured crusts after bites. E. Tinea corporis gives a slowly spreading scaly ring with central clearing.
pearl: Impetigo often develops on skin already damaged by bites, scratches, eczema or scabies, and this is called secondary impetigo.
thinking: Scratched insect bites ↓ Shallow erosions with honey-coloured crusts ↓ Spreading to nearby skin ↓ No deep ulcers, heat or swelling ↓ Impetigo
exam_trap: C, Ecthyma — it is also a crusted streptococcal infection of the legs, but it causes deeper punched-out ulcers rather than superficial erosions.
takeaway: Honey-coloured crusts on scratched, broken skin indicate impetigo.

presentation: Scabies in a care home resident
stem: An 81-year-old woman with dementia lives in a nursing home. Over three weeks staff have noticed her scratching constantly, especially at night. On examination there are excoriated papules on the fronts of her wrists, between her fingers, around the waist and in the axillae, with a few short wavy lines in the finger webs. Two of the carers who help her wash now have itchy wrists. There are no blisters. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Night-time itch, papules in the finger webs, wrists, waist and axillae, burrows and itching in people who have close contact with her are typical of scabies. Care homes are a common setting for outbreaks. Treatment is permethrin 5% cream, applied to the whole body including the scalp and face in older people, and repeated after a week, with staff and contacts treated at the same time and the local health protection team informed of the outbreak.
why_wrong: A. Bullous pemphigoid can begin with an itchy rash in older people, but it does not spread to carers and later forms tense blisters. B. Asteatotic eczema gives dry, cracked crazy-paving skin on the shins, and is not contagious. C. Contact dermatitis follows an exposure and does not explain burrows or itch in carers. E. Drug-induced itch does not cause burrows or affect other people.
pearl: Older and immunosuppressed people may develop crusted scabies with thick scale and huge numbers of mites, which is very contagious and may need oral ivermectin.
thinking: Night-time itch ↓ Papules at the wrists, finger webs, waist and axillae ↓ Burrows in the finger webs ↓ Carers with close contact are itchy ↓ Scabies
exam_trap: A, Bullous pemphigoid — it is a classic cause of itch in older people, but it does not spread to carers and does not cause burrows.
takeaway: Itch with burrows that spreads to close contacts in a care home is scabies.

presentation: Urticaria after an opioid on the ward
stem: A 58-year-old man is on an orthopaedic ward the day after a hip replacement. Thirty minutes after his first dose of oral codeine he says he feels very itchy. The nurse sees raised, pale swellings with surrounding redness on his chest and arms, and some of them have disappeared within an hour while new ones have appeared on his back. His pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation are unchanged, his lips and tongue are not swollen, he has no wheeze, and there is no blistering or peeling. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Itchy, transient wheals with a flare that move around within hours, starting shortly after a drug, are urticaria. Opioids such as codeine can release histamine directly from mast cells. Normal observations and no airway, mucosal or skin-loss features exclude anaphylaxis and severe cutaneous reactions, so treatment is to stop the drug and give a non-sedating antihistamine.
why_wrong: A. Erythema multiforme gives fixed target lesions that last days, often after herpes simplex infection. B. DRESS starts weeks after the drug, with fever, facial swelling and organ involvement. C. Stevens–Johnson syndrome causes painful blistering and mucosal erosions. D. Cellulitis is a single hot, tender, spreading area of infection, not migrating itchy wheals.
pearl: Codeine and morphine can cause itch and wheals by direct histamine release, which is not always true allergy, but the reaction should still be documented.
thinking: Itch within minutes of a new drug ↓ Raised wheals with a flare ↓ Lesions fade within hours and appear elsewhere ↓ No airway, circulatory, mucosal or blistering features ↓ Urticaria
exam_trap: C, Stevens–Johnson syndrome — a widespread rash after a new drug raises fear of a severe reaction, but transient wheals with no mucosal involvement or blistering are urticaria.
takeaway: Transient itchy wheals after a new drug, without mucosal or systemic features, are urticaria.

stem: A health visitor asks the GP to see a 7-month-old boy who has been unsettled and scratching for three weeks, waking repeatedly at night. There are itchy red papules and small pustules on his palms and soles, the sides of his feet and his armpits. His mother and his 4-year-old sister both complain of an itchy rash on their hands and wrists that is worse in bed. He is feeding well and has no fever. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent itchy papules and pustules on the palms, soles and axillae of an infant, with itchy family members, are typical of scabies. In infants the palms, soles, face and scalp can be involved, unlike in adults. The whole household should be treated at the same time, and for babies under two months specialist advice is needed before treatment.
why_wrong: A. Infantile eczema usually affects the cheeks and extensor surfaces and is not shared by family members. B. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes short-lived oval vesicles on the hands and feet with mouth ulcers and fever, and it is not intensely itchy for weeks. C. Chickenpox causes a fever and crops of vesicles mainly on the trunk, resolving within about two weeks. E. Pompholyx gives deep blisters on the palms in older children and adults and does not spread to others.
pearl: In infants and older people, scabies treatment should also be applied to the scalp, neck, face and ears, avoiding the eyes and mouth.
thinking: Infant with weeks of itch, worse at night ↓ Papules and pustules on palms, soles and axillae ↓ Mother and sister also itchy ↓ Afebrile and feeding well ↓ Scabies
exam_trap: A, Infantile atopic eczema — it is the commonest itchy rash in babies, but it does not spread to family and rarely affects the palms and soles in this way.
takeaway: An itchy infant with palmar and plantar papules and itchy family members has scabies.

stem: A 29-year-old man consults the prison healthcare team four weeks after being moved to a shared cell. He has an itchy rash that keeps him awake at night. There are excoriated papules around his waistband, on his buttocks and on the inner thighs, and several firm red nodules on the shaft of his penis. Two of his cellmates have recently been seen for itching. No insects or eggs are visible in his pubic hair. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Intense night-time itch with papules in typical sites and itchy nodules on the genitals, in someone living in close quarters with others who are itchy, is scabies. Genital nodules are very suggestive of scabies in men. Shared living settings such as prisons are prone to outbreaks, so contacts should be treated at the same time and health protection informed.
why_wrong: A. Pubic lice cause itch in the pubic area with visible lice and eggs on the hair, which are absent here. B. Secondary syphilis typically causes a non-itchy rash, often including the palms and soles. C. Lichen planus gives flat, violaceous, polygonal papules on the wrists and mouth, and is not contagious. E. Atopic eczema does not suddenly appear in someone with no history or spread to cellmates.
pearl: Itchy nodules on the penis or scrotum are almost diagnostic of scabies, and patients with genital involvement should be offered sexual health screening.
thinking: Weeks of itch, worse at night ↓ Papules at waist, buttocks and thighs ↓ Itchy nodules on the penis ↓ Cellmates affected, no lice seen ↓ Scabies
exam_trap: A, Pubic lice — genital itch after close contact suggests lice, but there are no lice or eggs on the hair, and the waist, buttocks and penile nodules fit scabies.
takeaway: Night-time itch with genital nodules and affected close contacts is scabies.

presentation: Acute urticaria after food without anaphylaxis
stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to a walk-in centre by her friend about an hour after eating prawns at a birthday party. Itchy, raised, pale welts have appeared on her neck, arms and trunk. She is talking in full sentences, has no wheeze, no swelling of her lips or tongue, no difficulty swallowing, no abdominal pain and does not feel faint. Her observations are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Widespread itchy wheals soon after a food, without any airway, breathing, circulatory or gastrointestinal features, fit acute urticaria. This is a skin-only reaction, managed with a non-sedating antihistamine and advice to avoid the suspected trigger. She should be told to seek urgent help if she develops throat or breathing symptoms.
why_wrong: B. Anaphylaxis needs airway, breathing or circulation problems, which she does not have. C. Hereditary angioedema causes recurrent non-itchy deep swelling without wheals and does not respond to antihistamines. D. Contact dermatitis is an eczematous reaction at the site of skin contact over a day or two, not widespread wheals within an hour. E. Erythema multiforme gives fixed target lesions lasting days, often after herpes simplex infection.
pearl: Acute urticaria plus any airway, breathing or circulation problem is anaphylaxis, which needs intramuscular adrenaline first.
thinking: Food eaten shortly before ↓ Widespread itchy wheals ↓ No airway, breathing or circulation problems ↓ No gastrointestinal symptoms ↓ Acute urticaria, not anaphylaxis
exam_trap: B, Anaphylaxis — food and rapid-onset wheals tempt this, but there is no airway, breathing or circulation problem, so this is urticaria alone.
takeaway: Itchy wheals after food with no airway, breathing or circulation problems are acute urticaria.

stem: A 45-year-old man phones NHS 111. He came back four days ago from a week at a ski resort, where he shared a bunk room with three friends. Since then he has had an itchy rash over his arms, waist and hands that is worse at night, and two of the friends have messaged to say they are itching too. He has no fever, no breathing difficulty and no facial swelling, and he has eaten nothing unusual since returning. What is the most important consideration?

options.A: A shared food allergy is the most likely cause
options.B: A transmissible infestation such as scabies or bed bugs should be considered
options.C: An autoimmune blistering disease is the likely cause
options.D: Infection is excluded because he has no fever
options.E: Antihistamines alone are enough and no assessment is needed

correct_answer: B. A transmissible infestation such as scabies or bed bugs should be considered
why_correct: An itchy rash appearing in several people who shared sleeping quarters suggests a transmissible cause, so scabies or another infestation such as bed bugs must be considered. Scabies spreads through prolonged skin-to-skin contact and sometimes through shared bedding. He needs to be examined for burrows and bites, and if scabies is confirmed, all close contacts need treatment at the same time.
why_wrong: A. Food allergy causes urticaria within hours of eating, and they did not share a recent meal or symptom pattern. C. Autoimmune blistering diseases are not shared between friends at the same time. D. Infestations do not cause fever, so its absence excludes nothing. E. Antihistamines may ease the itch but would miss a transmissible cause that needs treatment of all contacts.
pearl: When several people sharing a home or sleeping space develop itch at the same time, think of scabies or bed bugs before an individual skin disease.
thinking: Itchy rash worse at night ↓ Started after sharing sleeping quarters ↓ Several roommates affected ↓ No systemic features or food link ↓ Consider a transmissible infestation
exam_trap: A, A shared food allergy — several people affected at once suggests a shared exposure, but food reactions occur within hours, and shared bedding points to infestation.
takeaway: Itch in several people who shared a room should raise suspicion of scabies or another infestation.

presentation: Allergic contact dermatitis to a metal stud
stem: A 23-year-old man sees his GP about an itchy patch just below his navel that has been there on and off for two months. It is red, slightly weeping and scaly, with a sharp margin, and is the size and shape of the metal stud on his jeans that rests against the skin there. It improves when he wears tracksuit trousers. There is no rash elsewhere and no ring with central clearing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: An eczematous, itchy rash that exactly matches the shape of something touching the skin, and improves when contact stops, is contact dermatitis. Nickel in jeans studs, belt buckles and jewellery is the commonest cause of allergic contact dermatitis. Patch testing can confirm the allergen, and he should avoid direct contact with the stud.
why_wrong: B. Tinea corporis forms an expanding ring with a scaly edge and central clearing and does not follow an object. C. Discoid eczema gives several coin-shaped patches, usually on the limbs, unrelated to contact. D. Pityriasis versicolor gives scaly pale or brown patches on the trunk that are usually only mildly itchy. E. Psoriasis gives silvery-scaled plaques on the extensor surfaces, not a weeping patch matching an object.
pearl: Nickel allergy is the commonest contact allergy in the UK, and patch testing is the investigation that confirms allergic contact dermatitis.
thinking: Itchy, sharply defined eczematous patch ↓ Matches the shape of a metal stud ↓ Improves when the stud is not worn ↓ No annular or psoriatic features ↓ Contact dermatitis to nickel
exam_trap: B, Tinea corporis — a sharply bordered red scaly patch on the trunk suggests ringworm, but it matches the stud and clears without it, which points to contact dermatitis.
takeaway: An itchy rash that matches the shape of an object touching the skin is contact dermatitis.

stem: A 5-year-old girl has been diagnosed with scabies at her GP surgery and prescribed permethrin cream. Her father asks why he, his wife and their teenage son must also apply the cream on the same day, as none of them is itching. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: The child's skin could become infected with bacteria unless everyone uses it
options.B: Scabies runs in families because of an inherited tendency
options.C: The mites can live for months on furniture and toys
options.D: Contacts may already be infested without itch, because symptoms take weeks to appear
options.E: The cream only works on the child if the rest of the family also uses it

correct_answer: D. Contacts may already be infested without itch, because symptoms take weeks to appear
why_correct: On first infestation it takes several weeks to become sensitised to the mites, so close contacts may be infested and infectious before they itch. Treating all household and close contacts at the same time, even without symptoms, prevents the infestation passing back and forth. Bedding, towels and clothing should be washed at a high temperature on the day of the first treatment.
why_wrong: A. Secondary bacterial infection is a complication of scabies, but it is not the reason for treating the family. B. Scabies is caused by a mite spread by close contact, not by inheritance. C. Mites survive only a few days away from human skin. E. Permethrin kills mites on the person treated; treating contacts prevents reinfestation rather than making the cream work.
pearl: Itch can persist for up to four to six weeks after successful scabies treatment, so persistent itch alone is not proof of treatment failure.
thinking: Child diagnosed with scabies ↓ Family members currently without itch ↓ First infestation takes weeks to cause symptoms ↓ Untreated contacts can reinfest others ↓ Treat all close contacts at the same time
exam_trap: C, Mites living for months on furniture — environmental spread seems plausible, but mites survive only a few days off the body, and the real reason is silent infestation in contacts.
takeaway: Treat all close contacts of scabies at the same time, because they may be infested before itching starts.

stem: A 63-year-old retired engineer has a telephone appointment with his GP and sends photographs. For ten days he has had repeated outbreaks of raised, pale pink, very itchy swellings on his arms, back and thighs. He drew round one with a pen in the evening and by the next morning it had gone completely, leaving normal skin, while fresh ones had appeared elsewhere. There are no blisters, no target-shaped spots and no bruising. He has started no new medicines. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Itchy wheals that move from place to place and resolve without a mark in less than 24 hours are the defining feature of urticaria. Drawing around a lesion is a simple way to show that each wheal is short-lived. Most acute urticaria has no identifiable trigger, and a non-sedating antihistamine is the first-line treatment.
why_wrong: A. Urticarial vasculitis gives lesions lasting longer than 24 hours that burn and leave bruising or staining. B. Erythema multiforme gives fixed target lesions that last for days. C. Bullous pemphigoid can start with fixed urticarial plaques in older people, but these last for days and later blister. D. Dermatitis herpetiformis gives intensely itchy small vesicles on the elbows, knees and buttocks, linked to coeliac disease.
pearl: Urticaria lasting more than six weeks is chronic; most cases are spontaneous, and a non-sedating antihistamine can be increased up to four times the standard dose (off-label) if symptoms are not controlled.
thinking: Recurrent itchy raised swellings ↓ A marked lesion gone within a day ↓ No marks, bruising or blisters left ↓ New lesions appearing elsewhere ↓ Urticaria
exam_trap: A, Urticarial vasculitis — it looks similar, but its lesions last longer than 24 hours and leave bruising, whereas these clear completely overnight.
takeaway: Itchy wheals that each clear without a trace within 24 hours are urticaria.

stem: A 38-year-old primary school teacher sees her practice nurse because the back of her neck and the skin behind her ears have been itching for two weeks. Detection combing of her wet hair with a fine-toothed comb brings out several small, moving, greyish-brown insects. There are also tiny oval white specks firmly stuck to the hair shafts close to the scalp, which cannot be brushed off. The scalp skin is otherwise normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Finding live lice on detection combing confirms an active head lice infestation, and the eggs and egg cases (nits) are cemented to the hair shafts. Itch on the nape and behind the ears is typical. Close contact with children is a common source. Treatment options include dimeticone lotion or repeated wet combing, with household contacts checked and treated only if live lice are found.
why_wrong: A. Seborrhoeic dermatitis flakes are loose and brush off easily, with no live insects. B. Scalp psoriasis gives well-defined, thick, silvery-scaled plaques along the hairline. D. Tinea capitis causes scaly patches with broken hairs and hair loss, mainly in children. E. Scabies affects the finger webs, wrists and body rather than the scalp in adults, and the mites are not visible on hair.
pearl: Only live lice confirm active head lice infestation; nits alone may be empty egg cases left over from a past infestation.
thinking: Itching at the nape and behind the ears ↓ Live insects found on wet combing ↓ Oval specks fixed to the hair shafts ↓ Scalp otherwise normal ↓ Head lice
exam_trap: A, Seborrhoeic dermatitis — white specks on the hair look like dandruff, but dandruff brushes off, whereas nits are firmly attached and live lice were seen.
takeaway: Live lice on detection combing, with nits stuck to the hair shafts, confirm head lice.

stem: The mother of a 4-year-old boy with mild atopic eczema on his elbows and knees asks the practice nurse what is most important for keeping his skin under control in the long term, including when it looks clear. He uses a mild topical corticosteroid only during flares. What should be the foundation of his everyday skin care?

options.A: A topical antibiotic cream applied daily
options.B: Liberal, regular emollients, also used as a soap substitute and continued when the skin is clear
options.C: A potent topical corticosteroid twice daily all year
options.D: A regular oral antihistamine every day

correct_answer: B. Liberal, regular emollients, also used as a soap substitute and continued when the skin is clear
why_correct: Emollients restore the damaged skin barrier, reduce dryness and itch, and lower how often eczema flares. NICE advises using them liberally and often, as a soap substitute too, and continuing them even when the skin is clear. Topical corticosteroids are added for flares on top of this.
why_wrong: A. Routine topical antibiotics encourage resistance and are only used briefly for localised infection. C. Long-term potent corticosteroids risk skin thinning and are not used continuously on mild eczema in a child. D. Oral antihistamines are not recommended routinely; a sedating one may help short term if sleep is badly disturbed. E. Regular washing with an emollient soap substitute is helpful; normal soaps and bubble baths should be avoided instead.
pearl: Children with eczema need large amounts of emollient; NICE suggests about 250 to 500 g a week, and the emollient should be applied in the direction of hair growth.
thinking: Atopic eczema reflects a faulty skin barrier ↓ Long-term control needs barrier repair ↓ Emollients are used liberally every day ↓ Continue when clear, and use as a soap substitute ↓ Steroids only for flares
exam_trap: C, Potent topical corticosteroid all year — steroids are effective for flares, but continuous potent use in a child causes skin thinning and is not the basis of maintenance care.
takeaway: Regular, liberal emollient use is the foundation of atopic eczema management.

stem: A 59-year-old woman had a mastectomy with axillary node clearance for breast cancer four years ago. Since then her right arm has been persistently swollen, and she is now attending the GP surgery with her third episode of hot, red, tender skin on that forearm in a year. She asks why infections keep affecting only the swollen arm. Which mechanism best explains her susceptibility?

options.A: Reduced arterial blood flow to the skin of the swollen limb, leading to tissue ischaemia
options.B: A generalised fall in circulating neutrophils caused by the previous cancer treatment
options.C: Toxins generated by the trapped protein-rich fluid itself
options.D: Poor lymph flow impairing immune cell trafficking and clearance of organisms in the affected tissue
options.E: A body-wide defect in neutrophil killing that predisposes to skin infection

correct_answer: D. Poor lymph flow impairing immune cell trafficking and clearance of organisms in the affected tissue
why_correct: Damaged lymphatics after axillary clearance leave protein-rich fluid pooled in the arm and slow the movement of antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes to regional nodes. Local immune surveillance and bacterial clearance are therefore impaired, so organisms entering through minor skin breaks establish infection more easily. This explains why repeated cellulitis is confined to the lymphoedematous limb.
why_wrong: A. Lymphoedema is a disorder of lymph drainage; arterial supply to the skin is normal. B. Chemotherapy-related neutropenia is transient and would not cause infections confined to one arm years later. C. Interstitial fluid does not generate bacterial toxins; it simply provides a favourable medium once bacteria enter. E. A systemic neutrophil defect would cause infections at many sites, not just the swollen limb.
pearl: People with lymphoedema and repeated episodes of cellulitis may be offered prophylactic antibiotics (penicillin V first line in UK guidance), alongside meticulous skin care and compression.
thinking: Chronic arm swelling after axillary node clearance ↓ Recurrent cellulitis limited to that limb ↓ Lymphatic damage causes stasis of protein-rich fluid ↓ Local immune cell trafficking and bacterial clearance are impaired ↓ Minor skin breaks lead to repeated infection
exam_trap: E, A body-wide neutrophil defect — the history of cancer treatment makes systemic immunosuppression feel plausible, but a global defect would not explain infections that only ever affect the swollen arm.
takeaway: Lymphoedema predisposes to cellulitis because impaired lymphatic drainage weakens local immune defence in the affected limb.

stem: A primary school teacher aged 26 rings her surgery's nurse triage line, back from a week of skiing at altitude. On Saturday a prickling, burning sensation began on the right side of her upper lip, where the red margin meets the skin; by Monday a crop of pinhead blisters filled with clear fluid had erupted there and is sore. This has occurred in the same place two or three times a year since her teens, often during busy school terms or after a cold. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.E: Irritant contact dermatitis from lip balm

why_correct: Prodromal tingling followed by a cluster of painful vesicles on the vermilion border is typical of reactivated herpes simplex virus. Recurrence at the same site, triggered by sunlight, stress or illness, reflects reactivation of latent virus in the trigeminal ganglion.
why_wrong: A. Angular cheilitis causes cracking and soreness at the corners of the mouth, not grouped blisters on the lip border. C. Impetigo typically gives honey-coloured crusts and does not recur in the same spot with a tingling prodrome. D. Molluscum causes painless pearly umbilicated papules, not painful vesicles. E. Contact dermatitis causes diffuse redness and scaling related to the product, not a recurring grouped vesicular cluster.
pearl: Topical aciclovir only modestly shortens a cold sore episode and works best if started during the prodrome; most episodes heal without treatment within about 10 days.
thinking: Prodromal tingling and burning ↓ Grouped painful vesicles on the lip border ↓ Recurs at the same site ↓ Triggered by sun, stress or illness ↓ Reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus
exam_trap: C, Bullous impetigo — impetigo also affects the face and can blister, but it crusts with a golden appearance, lacks a tingling prodrome and does not recur in an identical spot.
takeaway: Recurrent grouped painful vesicles on the lip border after a tingling prodrome are herpes simplex labialis.

stem: A 58-year-old retired lorry driver is at his annual diabetes review when the practice nurse notices a dark lesion on his left shoulder. His daughter took a photograph of it at a family barbecue last spring, and comparing the two images shows it has grown, its outline has become uneven and parts of it have darkened. He has had it for as long as he can remember. Which aspect of this history is most worrying for melanoma?

options.A: The lesion has been present for most of his life
options.B: Its location on a sun-exposed area of the upper body
options.D: Documented change in the lesion over recent months
options.E: The fact that it causes him no pain

correct_answer: D. Documented change in the lesion over recent months
why_correct: Change over time (evolution) in size, shape or colour is one of the most important warning signs for melanoma and is a major feature on the weighted 7-point checklist used in UK primary care. Photographic evidence of growth, an increasingly irregular outline and darkening in a lifelong mole makes melanoma a real concern and warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral.
why_wrong: A. Long-standing presence is generally reassuring; it is the recent change that matters here. B. Sun exposure raises risk, but site alone is far less discriminating than documented change. C. Diabetes does not meaningfully raise melanoma risk. E. Most early melanomas are painless, so absence of pain offers no reassurance.
pearl: In the weighted 7-point checklist, change in size, irregular shape and irregular colour each score 2 points; a total of 3 or more prompts a suspected cancer referral.
thinking: Long-standing mole ↓ Photographs show growth, uneven outline and darkening ↓ Evolution is a major warning sign ↓ Pain and duration are not reassuring ↓ Refer on the suspected cancer pathway
exam_trap: A, Present for most of his life — a lifelong mole sounds benign, but melanoma can arise in a pre-existing naevus and recent change outweighs its long history.
takeaway: Recent documented change in a pigmented lesion is a major warning sign of melanoma.

presentation: Melanoma warning features: asymmetry and colour
stem: While trimming a 61-year-old woman's hair, her hairdresser spots a dark mark on the crown of her scalp and advises her to get it checked. At the GP surgery the lesion is about the size of a fingernail; its two halves do not match, and it contains patches of black, tan and pinkish-grey. She cannot see the area herself and has no idea how long it has been there. Which finding should most raise concern for melanoma?

options.A: Its position on the scalp, where lesions are often overlooked
options.B: Her lack of awareness of the lesion
options.C: Hair growing normally through the lesion
options.D: The absence of any itch or bleeding
options.E: The mismatched halves and multiple colours within the lesion

correct_answer: E. The mismatched halves and multiple colours within the lesion
why_correct: Asymmetry and colour variation are two of the core ABCDE warning features of melanoma, and irregular pigmentation is a major criterion on the weighted 7-point checklist. A scalp lesion with uneven shape and several shades including black and grey therefore needs urgent referral, even without a known history of change.
why_wrong: A. The scalp is a site where melanoma presents late, but location itself is not the morphological warning sign. B. Not having noticed the lesion tells us nothing about its nature. C. Hair growth through a lesion is not a reliable sign either way. D. Absence of itch or bleeding does not exclude melanoma; these are minor features.
pearl: Scalp and neck melanomas tend to be thicker at diagnosis than those at other sites, partly because they are hidden from the patient.
thinking: Pigmented scalp lesion noticed by a third party ↓ Uneven halves indicate asymmetry ↓ Several colours including black and grey ↓ Core ABCDE warning features ↓ Urgent suspected cancer referral
exam_trap: D, Absence of itch or bleeding — symptoms feel like they should be needed for concern, but most melanomas are asymptomatic and itch or bleeding are only minor features.
takeaway: Asymmetry and multiple colours in a pigmented lesion are key warning features of melanoma.

stem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is seen in the community podiatry clinic. Over the past year both great toenails have become yellow, opaque and much thicker, with crumbly debris under the free edge, and they now split easily. He also has scaling between his toes. There is no pain, redness or swelling of the nail folds. What is the most likely cause of the nail changes?

options.A: Pseudomonas colonisation of the nail plate
options.B: Dermatophyte fungal infection of the nail
options.D: Human papillomavirus infection around the nail

correct_answer: B. Dermatophyte fungal infection of the nail
why_correct: Slowly progressive yellow thickening of the toenails with subungual debris and brittleness is typical of onychomycosis, which is most often caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum. Coexisting tinea pedis between the toes supports a fungal source, and diabetes and older age increase the risk. Nail clippings should be sent for microscopy and culture before starting oral antifungals.
why_wrong: A. Pseudomonas causes green-black discolouration, usually with onycholysis, rather than yellow crumbly thickening. C. Herpes simplex causes painful vesicles (whitlow), not chronic nail dystrophy. D. Warts produce rough papules at the nail fold rather than diffuse thickening of the nail plate. E. Shingles causes a painful dermatomal vesicular rash and does not cause chronic nail thickening.
pearl: Confirm onychomycosis with nail clippings for microscopy and culture before oral terbinafine, because treatment lasts months and other conditions, such as psoriasis, can look similar.
thinking: Older man with diabetes ↓ Yellow, thick, crumbly toenails with subungual debris ↓ Coexisting interdigital scaling ↓ No paronychia or pain ↓ Dermatophyte onychomycosis
exam_trap: A, Pseudomonas — it does discolour nails, but it produces a green-black hue rather than the yellow crumbly thickening and accompanying athlete's foot seen here.
takeaway: Thickened, discoloured, brittle toenails are most commonly due to dermatophyte onychomycosis.

stem: A 42-year-old man attends the rheumatology clinic with pain and swelling in the end joints of several fingers. He has had scaly plaques on his elbows and in his umbilicus for years. On the fingernails of both hands there are numerous tiny, punched-out depressions scattered across the nail plates, like the surface of a thimble. What is the name of this nail sign?
why_correct: Multiple small, punctate depressions in the nail plate are nail pitting, caused by psoriatic involvement of the proximal nail matrix that leaves defects as the nail grows. Nail changes are especially common in people with psoriatic arthritis, particularly with distal interphalangeal joint disease, as in this man.
why_wrong: A. Koilonychia is spoon-shaped, concave nails, classically with iron deficiency. B. Beau's lines are transverse grooves across the nail after a period of severe illness, not scattered pits. C. Onycholysis is separation of the nail from the nail bed; it occurs in psoriasis but is not described here. D. Clubbing is loss of the angle between nail and nail fold with bulbous fingertips, not surface depressions.
pearl: Nail disease in psoriasis is strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis; distal interphalangeal joint involvement and nail changes often occur together.
thinking: Long-standing plaque psoriasis ↓ Distal finger joint pain and swelling ↓ Tiny punched-out depressions in the nail plates ↓ Matrix involvement by psoriasis ↓ Nail pitting
exam_trap: C, Onycholysis — it is also a psoriatic nail sign, so it tempts, but it describes lifting of the nail from its bed rather than small surface depressions.
takeaway: Small scattered depressions in the nail plates are nail pitting, a classic sign of psoriasis.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the GP by her father because of stubborn 'dandruff' that has not improved with medicated shampoo. There are thick silvery scales extending just beyond the hairline behind her ears. While examining her hands, the GP notices several small dents on the surfaces of her fingernails. The nail folds are normal and she has no other symptoms. What does the fingernail finding most likely represent?

options.B: Fungal infection of the nail plate
options.C: Chronic bacterial infection of the nail fold

correct_answer: E. Psoriatic involvement of the nails
why_correct: Well-demarcated thick scaling at and beyond the hairline is typical of scalp psoriasis, and small surface dents in the fingernails are nail pitting from psoriatic involvement of the nail matrix. Recognising the nail sign supports the diagnosis of psoriasis rather than seborrhoeic dermatitis.
why_wrong: A. Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) are concave and do not show scattered pits. B. Fungal infection more often affects toenails and causes thickening, discolouration and debris rather than fine pits. C. Paronychia affects the nail fold with redness and swelling, which are absent here. D. Clubbing alters the nail angle and fingertip shape and does not cause dents.
pearl: Scalp psoriasis characteristically extends just beyond the hairline, which helps distinguish it from seborrhoeic dermatitis.
thinking: Resistant scalp scaling extending beyond the hairline ↓ Small dents on several fingernails ↓ Normal nail folds ↓ Suggests psoriasis of scalp and nails ↓ Nail pitting is psoriatic nail involvement
exam_trap: B, Fungal nail infection — nail changes often prompt thoughts of fungus, but fungal disease usually thickens and discolours toenails rather than producing fine pits in fingernails.
takeaway: Fingernail pitting in a patient with scaly skin points to psoriatic nail involvement.

stem: A 31-year-old administrative worker who habitually bites her nails presents to an urgent treatment centre with two days of throbbing pain beside the nail of her right index finger. The skin at the side of the nail is red, hot and swollen, and a yellow pocket of pus is visible beneath the nail fold. She is otherwise well and the rest of the finger is not tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: D. Acute paronychia with abscess formation
why_correct: Rapid onset of pain, redness and swelling of the lateral nail fold after minor trauma such as nail biting, with a visible collection of pus, is acute bacterial paronychia complicated by an abscess. It is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci, and a fluctuant collection needs incision and drainage.
why_wrong: A. Herpetic whitlow causes grouped painful vesicles with clear fluid, not a pus collection at the nail fold. B. Onychomycosis is a slowly progressive fungal infection of the nail plate without acute pain or pus. C. Chronic paronychia develops over weeks in people whose hands are often wet and lacks an acute abscess. E. A felon involves the fingertip pulp, which is not tender here.
pearl: Do not incise a herpetic whitlow; drainage of a viral lesion can spread infection, so look carefully for vesicles before draining.
thinking: Nail biting causes minor trauma ↓ Acute throbbing pain at the nail fold ↓ Red, hot swelling with visible pus ↓ Pulp not involved ↓ Acute paronychia with abscess, needs drainage
exam_trap: A, Herpetic whitlow — it also causes a painful finger near the nail, but it produces clear vesicles and should not be drained, whereas here there is frank pus.
takeaway: A painful, red nail fold with a pus collection after minor trauma is acute paronychia with an abscess.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is sent to her GP by her dentist. At a check-up a white plaque was seen on the inside of her left cheek; her ill-fitting denture was adjusted and the area was rechecked a month later, but the patch persists. It cannot be removed with gauze and is painless. She drinks heavily and used to smoke a pipe. There is no lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this lesion?

options.A: Oral candidiasis that will respond to antifungal treatment
options.B: A frictional change that can be ignored now the denture is fixed
options.C: Lichen planus that only needs topical steroid
options.D: Possible leukoplakia, a potentially malignant lesion needing specialist assessment
options.E: A recurrent aphthous ulcer that will heal spontaneously

correct_answer: D. Possible leukoplakia, a potentially malignant lesion needing specialist assessment
why_correct: A persistent white patch that cannot be wiped off and does not resolve after removing a source of friction is leukoplakia until proven otherwise. It is a potentially malignant disorder, and her alcohol and tobacco history increases the risk of dysplasia or squamous cell carcinoma. She needs referral to oral medicine or oral and maxillofacial surgery for assessment and biopsy rather than reassurance or empirical treatment.
why_wrong: A. Candidal plaques usually wipe off, leaving a red base. B. Frictional keratosis should settle once the cause is removed; persistence after adjustment is a red flag. C. Lichen planus usually has a lacy, bilateral pattern and still needs confirmation; it should not be assumed. E. An aphthous ulcer is a painful shallow ulcer, not a painless white plaque.
pearl: Erythroplakia (a red patch) carries a considerably higher risk of malignant change than leukoplakia.
thinking: Persistent white buccal patch ↓ Cannot be wiped off ↓ Persists after removing friction ↓ Alcohol and tobacco risk ↓ Potentially malignant leukoplakia, refer for biopsy
exam_trap: B, Frictional change — the denture was a plausible cause, but persistence after it was corrected removes that explanation and makes leukoplakia more likely.
takeaway: A persistent non-removable white oral patch is possible leukoplakia and needs specialist assessment.

stem: A 45-year-old man who started doxycycline for acne rosacea a fortnight ago attends a walk-in centre after a weekend spent gardening. He has a burning, itchy red rash on the backs of both hands, the forearms, the V of his neck and his forehead. The skin under his watch strap, beneath his chin and behind his ears is untouched. He is otherwise well. What is the best overall description of this rash?

options.B: Allergic contact dermatitis from garden plants

why_correct: A rash limited to light-exposed skin, with sharp sparing of shaded areas such as under a watch strap, below the chin and behind the ears, is the hallmark of a photosensitive eruption. Doxycycline is a well-recognised photosensitising drug, which explains the reaction after a weekend outdoors. He should avoid sun exposure and use high-factor sunscreen, and the drug may need to be reviewed.
why_wrong: B. Plant contact dermatitis follows the pattern of contact, often streaky, and would not spare shaded areas so neatly. C. Erythema multiforme causes target lesions, typically on the hands and feet, not a sun-distributed erythema. D. Cellulitis is usually unilateral, tender and spreading, not symmetrical across all exposed sites. E. Seborrhoeic dermatitis affects the scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds with greasy scale.
pearl: Shaded sites such as under the chin, behind the ears and the upper eyelids are characteristically spared in photosensitive rashes, and this is a useful clue.
thinking: Recently started doxycycline ↓ Rash after time outdoors ↓ Confined to exposed skin ↓ Sharp sparing of shaded areas ↓ Photosensitive eruption
exam_trap: B, Allergic contact dermatitis from plants — gardening suggests plant contact, but the neat sparing of shaded skin points to light, not contact, as the cause.
takeaway: A rash on sun-exposed skin with sparing of shaded areas is a photosensitive eruption.

presentation: Suspected melanoma in a care home resident
stem: A care assistant in a residential home tells the visiting GP that, while helping an 84-year-old man to wash, she has noticed a dark spot in the middle of his back that was not there when he moved in last year. On inspection it is lopsided in shape, its edge is notched and ragged, and it contains shades of dark brown, black and red. He has mild dementia and cannot say whether it is sore. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: A new pigmented lesion in an older adult that is asymmetrical, has an irregular notched border and several colours has the classic ABCDE features of melanoma. Its appearance within the last year adds the feature of evolution. He should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway, with appropriate support for decision-making given his dementia.
why_wrong: A. A lipoma is a soft, mobile subcutaneous lump with normal overlying skin, not pigmented. B. Warts are rough skin-coloured papules, not multicoloured flat pigmented lesions. C. Urticarial wheals are transient, itchy and fade within hours. D. Cellulitis produces spreading warm erythema rather than a discrete multicoloured lesion.
pearl: Melanoma in older men is most common on the back, a site they cannot see, so carers, partners and clinicians are often the first to notice it.
thinking: New pigmented lesion in an older man ↓ Asymmetrical with notched border ↓ Multiple colours including black and red ↓ Appeared within the last year ↓ Suspect melanoma and refer urgently
exam_trap: B, Viral wart — warts are common skin lumps in older people, but they are skin-coloured and rough rather than flat, irregular and multicoloured.
takeaway: A new, asymmetrical, irregularly bordered, multicoloured lesion should be treated as possible melanoma.

stem: At a pre-operative assessment clinic before an elective hernia repair, a 45-year-old builder mentions that a mark on his upper back has been 'changing' since last winter. Examination shows a brown-black lesion with an uneven outline, one half larger than the other and blotchy shades of brown, black and blue-grey. There is no surrounding redness or warmth. How should this lesion be interpreted?

options.A: A benign compound naevus that needs no further action
options.B: A lesion with features concerning for melanoma
options.C: A seborrhoeic keratosis with its typical stuck-on appearance
options.D: Localised cellulitis around a hair follicle

correct_answer: B. A lesion with features concerning for melanoma
why_correct: Asymmetry, irregular border, multiple colours including blue-grey, and recent change are the core warning features of melanoma. Nothing in the description suggests inflammation or a stuck-on warty surface. He should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway, and the timing of elective surgery can be discussed with the team.
why_wrong: A. Change with asymmetry and colour variation means a benign naevus cannot be assumed. C. Seborrhoeic keratoses have a waxy, warty, stuck-on surface and are usually multiple in older people. D. There is no redness, warmth or tenderness to suggest cellulitis. E. Discoid eczema forms itchy coin-shaped scaly plaques, not a pigmented irregular lesion.
pearl: A blue-grey or black colour within a pigmented lesion is a particularly concerning sign of deeper melanin.
thinking: Pigmented lesion changing over months ↓ Asymmetrical with irregular outline ↓ Several colours including blue-grey ↓ No inflammation ↓ Concerning for melanoma, refer urgently
exam_trap: C, Seborrhoeic keratosis — these are common, brown and can look irregular, but they are warty and stuck-on and do not show this pattern of recent change and blue-grey colour.
takeaway: A changing, asymmetrical, multicoloured pigmented lesion should be interpreted as possible melanoma.

stem: At her 20-week antenatal appointment, a 34-year-old woman asks the midwife about a mole on her right calf. It appeared in her early twenties but has altered since she became pregnant: one side now bulges outward, the edge is blurred and jagged, and it contains black and pinkish areas alongside the original brown. Her other moles have darkened slightly but remain uniform and symmetrical. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Pregnancy can cause uniform darkening of existing naevi, but it does not explain one lesion becoming asymmetrical with an irregular border and multiple colours. This 'ugly duckling' lesion with ABCDE features should be suspected as melanoma and referred on the suspected cancer pathway; pregnancy should not delay assessment.
why_wrong: B. Pregnancy-related darkening is symmetrical and affects moles uniformly, unlike this lesion. C. Dermatofibromas are firm papules that dimple when pinched and are usually uniform brown. D. Seborrhoeic keratoses are warty, stuck-on and uncommon at this age. E. A lipoma is a soft subcutaneous lump without pigmentation.
pearl: The 'ugly duckling' sign, a mole that looks different from the patient's other moles, is a useful clue to melanoma.
thinking: Pregnant woman with a changing calf mole ↓ Other naevi darkened uniformly ↓ This one is asymmetrical, irregular and multicoloured ↓ Ugly duckling lesion ↓ Suspect melanoma and refer without delay
exam_trap: B, Benign naevus darkened by pregnancy — hormonal darkening is real and reassuring in symmetrical moles, but it does not produce new asymmetry, irregular edges and several colours.
takeaway: Pregnancy does not explain a mole becoming asymmetrical and multicoloured; suspect melanoma.

presentation: Management of a suspicious pigmented lesion
stem: A 40-year-old man attends a minor injuries unit after twisting his ankle playing five-a-side football. While examining the leg, the nurse practitioner notices a pigmented lesion on his shin. He says it has grown over the summer, turned a darker and patchier colour, and its edge has become ragged. The ankle injury is a simple sprain. What is the most appropriate approach to the skin lesion?

options.A: Reassure him that pigmented lesions in young adults are almost always benign
options.B: Remove it by cryotherapy in the unit
options.C: Prescribe a topical antifungal and review if no improvement
options.D: Advise him to monitor it and return if it bleeds
options.E: Ensure urgent assessment for possible melanoma via the suspected cancer pathway

correct_answer: E. Ensure urgent assessment for possible melanoma via the suspected cancer pathway
why_correct: A pigmented lesion that has grown, darkened unevenly and developed an irregular border has features of melanoma and should be assessed urgently through a suspected cancer referral to dermatology, usually arranged by the GP. Incidental findings should be acted on and clearly communicated, even when the reason for attendance is unrelated.
why_wrong: A. Melanoma does occur in young adults; reassurance without assessment is unsafe. B. Destroying the lesion prevents histological diagnosis and staging. C. There is no suggestion of fungal infection. D. Waiting for bleeding delays diagnosis; change alone justifies urgent referral.
pearl: Suspicious pigmented lesions should not be removed in primary care by destructive methods or partial biopsy; they need excision with a margin and histology by an appropriate service.
thinking: Incidental finding during unrelated attendance ↓ Pigmented lesion growing, darkening, irregular edge ↓ Features of melanoma ↓ Do not destroy or ignore ↓ Urgent suspected cancer referral
exam_trap: D, Monitor and return if it bleeds — watchful waiting can seem proportionate in a well young man, but documented change already meets the threshold for urgent referral.
takeaway: A changing pigmented lesion needs urgent suspected cancer assessment, even when found incidentally.

stem: A 63-year-old Black British woman with type 2 diabetes attends her annual diabetic foot check. The podiatrist notes a dark brown-black flat patch on the sole of her left heel. Comparing it with a note from last year, it has spread and its edge has become irregular and blurred. She had not noticed it and it is painless. Which feature is most worrying for melanoma?

options.A: Its location on the sole, which is rarely exposed to sun
options.D: Recent enlargement with an increasingly irregular outline
options.E: Its dark brown-black colour, which is normal in darker skin

correct_answer: D. Recent enlargement with an increasingly irregular outline
why_correct: Spread and an increasingly irregular border over a year indicate evolution, the key warning sign of melanoma. Acral lentiginous melanoma on the palms and soles is the commonest subtype in people with darker skin and is often diagnosed late because it is not linked to sun exposure and is hidden from view. This lesion needs urgent suspected cancer referral.
why_wrong: A. Acral melanoma is not caused by sun exposure, so a sun-protected site does not reassure. B. Melanoma is typically painless. C. Diabetes does not raise melanoma risk; the foot check simply led to detection. E. Benign pigmentation on the sole can occur in darker skin, but dark colour alone is not as worrying as documented change.
pearl: Acral lentiginous melanoma, often on the sole or under a nail, is the commonest melanoma subtype in people of African and Asian heritage.
thinking: Pigmented patch on the sole ↓ Spread and irregular edge compared with last year ↓ Acral sites are not sun-related ↓ Evolution is the key warning sign ↓ Suspect acral lentiginous melanoma, refer urgently
exam_trap: A, Location on the sole — a sun-protected site sounds reassuring, but acral melanoma is unrelated to sun exposure and is often missed for this reason.
takeaway: Change in a pigmented lesion on the sole should raise concern for acral melanoma, especially in darker skin.

stem: A 32-year-old man visits a walk-in centre, worried about a rash. About ten days ago, shortly after a cold, he noticed one pink, slightly scaly, oval patch the size of a large coin on his flank. Since then dozens of smaller pink ovals with a fine fringe of scale just inside their edges have appeared over his trunk and upper arms, their long axes running obliquely along the ribs. His face, palms and soles are clear and the rash is mildly itchy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A single larger 'herald patch' followed days later by many smaller oval lesions with a collarette of scale, aligned along the skin cleavage lines of the trunk, is characteristic of pityriasis rosea. It often follows a viral illness, may be linked to human herpesvirus reactivation, and resolves spontaneously over around 6 to 12 weeks.
why_wrong: A. Guttate psoriasis gives small drop-like lesions after a streptococcal sore throat, without a herald patch. B. Pityriasis versicolor causes hypo- or hyperpigmented finely scaly patches without a herald patch or cleavage-line pattern. C. Tinea causes one or a few annular lesions with an active scaly edge, not a widespread eruption along skin lines. E. Secondary syphilis can mimic it but typically involves the palms and soles, which are clear here.
pearl: If a pityriasis rosea-like rash involves the palms and soles, or there are risk factors, test for syphilis; in pregnancy, pityriasis rosea may need obstetric discussion.
thinking: Recent viral illness ↓ Single larger herald patch ↓ Followed by many oval lesions with collarette scale ↓ Distributed along skin cleavage lines ↓ Pityriasis rosea, self-limiting
exam_trap: C, Tinea corporis — the herald patch resembles a ringworm lesion, but tinea does not produce a sudden widespread eruption following skin lines.
takeaway: A herald patch followed by smaller oval lesions along skin cleavage lines is pityriasis rosea.

stem: A 33-year-old woman of South Asian heritage, who has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill for three years, visits the GP about darkening of her facial skin. Over two summers, flat, evenly brown patches with irregular but well-defined edges have developed symmetrically over both cheeks, the bridge of her nose and her upper lip. They fade a little in winter. They do not itch and there is no scale. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Symmetrical, flat brown patches on the cheeks, nose and upper lip that worsen with sun exposure in a woman taking oestrogen-containing contraception are classic melasma. It is more common in darker skin types and is driven by hormones and ultraviolet light. Strict sun protection is the cornerstone of management.
why_wrong: A. Post-inflammatory pigmentation follows a preceding rash or injury, which she has not had. C. Lentigo maligna is usually a single, irregular, slowly growing pigmented patch on sun-damaged skin of older people. D. Pityriasis versicolor affects the trunk with fine scale and is uncommon on the face. E. Vitiligo causes loss of pigment, producing white patches.
pearl: Melasma is triggered by pregnancy, combined hormonal contraception and sunlight; it often improves when the hormonal trigger stops but may persist, and it recurs easily with sun exposure.
thinking: Woman on combined hormonal contraception ↓ Symmetrical brown facial patches ↓ Cheeks, nose and upper lip ↓ Worse in summer, no scale or itch ↓ Melasma
exam_trap: A, Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation — common in darker skin and easily confused, but it requires a preceding inflammatory rash and would not be so symmetrical.
takeaway: Symmetrical facial hyperpigmentation linked to hormones and sunlight is melasma.

stem: A 74-year-old retired postwoman with bunions and flattened forefeet sees the practice nurse because of pain when walking, 'like standing on a stone'. Under the ball of her right foot, beneath the second metatarsal head, there is a small, round, sharply circumscribed area of hard yellowish skin. When the surface is pared, a translucent central core is revealed, with no pinpoint black dots or bleeding. Pressing directly on it reproduces the pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A small, well-defined, painful area of hyperkeratosis over a pressure point that reveals a translucent central core on paring is a corn (heloma). Abnormal foot mechanics from bunions and a dropped forefoot concentrate pressure under the second metatarsal head. Offloading with appropriate footwear and podiatry is the mainstay of treatment.
why_wrong: B. Paring a verruca reveals black dots of thrombosed capillaries and pinpoint bleeding, and it is more painful when squeezed side to side. C. A callus is broader, more diffuse thickening without a central core. D. A foreign body granuloma usually follows a penetrating injury and may be red and inflamed. E. An ulcer is a break in the skin, usually painless in neuropathy, rather than intact hard skin.
pearl: Squeezing a plantar wart from side to side is painful, whereas direct pressure is more painful in a corn.
thinking: Forefoot deformity and abnormal pressure ↓ Small, well-defined hard skin under a metatarsal head ↓ Paring shows a translucent central core ↓ No black dots or pinpoint bleeding ↓ Corn
exam_trap: B, Plantar wart — a verruca also causes painful hard skin on the sole, but paring would show black dots and bleeding points rather than a translucent core.
takeaway: A small, painful hyperkeratotic lesion with a central core at a pressure point is a corn.

presentation: Scabies outbreak in a care home
stem: The manager of a nursing home asks the visiting GP for advice. Over three weeks, four residents on the same floor have become very itchy, scratching especially at night; one has crusted, thickened skin on her hands. Two care assistants who help those residents with personal care now report itching between their fingers and around their wrists. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Treat only the resident with crusted skin and observe the others
options.B: Prescribe oral antihistamines and review everyone in a month
options.C: Apply topical antibiotics to excoriated skin across the floor
options.D: Diagnose asteatotic eczema and start emollients for all residents
options.E: Confirm scabies and coordinate simultaneous treatment of cases and contacts, including staff, with local health protection advice

correct_answer: E. Confirm scabies and coordinate simultaneous treatment of cases and contacts, including staff, with local health protection advice
why_correct: Nocturnal itch spreading among residents and staff who have close skin contact is typical of a scabies outbreak, and crusted scabies in a frail resident is highly infectious. Control depends on confirming the diagnosis and treating all affected people and their contacts, including staff and, often, their households, at the same time, with environmental measures. The local UKHSA health protection team should be involved in institutional outbreaks.
why_wrong: A. Treating one person leaves others infested and allows ongoing transmission and reinfestation. B. Antihistamines relieve symptoms but do not eradicate mites, and delay lets the outbreak spread. C. Antibiotics only treat secondary infection and do nothing for the infestation. D. Dry skin does not spread from person to person, and staff are now affected too.
pearl: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies occurs in immunocompromised or frail people, carries huge numbers of mites and often drives outbreaks in care settings; it usually needs oral ivermectin with topical treatment and specialist input.
thinking: Clustered nocturnal itch in a care home ↓ Crusted skin in a frail resident ↓ Staff with finger-web and wrist itch ↓ Institutional scabies outbreak ↓ Simultaneous treatment of cases and contacts with health protection support
exam_trap: A, Treat only the crusted case — it seems to target the obvious source, but untreated contacts keep the outbreak going and will reinfest her.
takeaway: Institutional scabies outbreaks need simultaneous treatment of cases and contacts, including staff, with health protection advice.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is diagnosed with scabies at the GP surgery after a fortnight of night-time itching and burrows on his wrists. His mother, father and 18-month-old sister have no symptoms at all. His mother asks why the whole family, including the toddler, should be treated when only her son is itchy. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Treating the family stops the boy developing a secondary bacterial skin infection
options.B: Family members can be infested without symptoms for several weeks and can pass mites back to him
options.C: Family contacts often carry a fungal infection alongside scabies
options.D: Scabies mites are mainly spread through shared food and water
options.E: Relatives share a genetic tendency to attract mites

correct_answer: B. Family members can be infested without symptoms for several weeks and can pass mites back to him
why_correct: Itching in scabies results from a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that can take up to six to eight weeks to develop after a first infestation. Household contacts may therefore already carry mites while having no symptoms. Treating everyone at the same time, including young children with an appropriate product, prevents the infestation being passed back and forth.
why_wrong: A. Contact treatment does not prevent secondary infection in the index case. C. There is no link between scabies and fungal infection in contacts. D. Scabies spreads mainly through prolonged skin-to-skin contact, not food or water. E. Susceptibility is not inherited; exposure through close contact is what matters.
pearl: Permethrin 5% cream is applied to the whole body, including the scalp, face, neck and ears in young children and older adults, and repeated after seven days.
thinking: Index case confirmed ↓ Contacts symptom-free ↓ Itch from delayed hypersensitivity, so may take weeks to appear ↓ Asymptomatic contacts may still be infested ↓ Treat all household contacts at the same time
exam_trap: A, Preventing secondary infection — infection of scratched skin is a real complication, but treating relatives does not prevent it; the purpose is to stop reinfestation.
takeaway: Close contacts of scabies are treated because they may be infested before symptoms appear and can cause reinfestation.

stem: A school nurse sees a 7-year-old girl whose teacher has noticed her constantly scratching behind her ears and at the back of her neck. Close inspection of the hair shows many tiny greyish-white specks stuck to the hairs near the scalp that cannot be brushed or flicked off, unlike flakes of skin. The scalp itself has no scaling, bald patches or redness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Itching behind the ears and at the nape with small specks firmly glued to the hair shafts close to the scalp is typical of head lice, the specks being eggs (nits). Dandruff and other scale can be flicked off easily, whereas nits are cemented to the hair. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding a live louse with detection combing.
why_wrong: B. Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes greasy loose scale on the scalp that brushes off. C. Tinea capitis causes scaly patches with broken hairs or hair loss. D. Psoriasis produces thick silvery plaques on the scalp, not specks on the hair. E. Alopecia areata causes smooth bald patches without itching or specks.
pearl: Only treat head lice when a live louse is found; nits alone may be empty shells from a past infestation.
thinking: School-age child ↓ Itch behind the ears and nape ↓ Specks glued to hair shafts near the scalp ↓ Scalp normal ↓ Head lice
exam_trap: B, Seborrhoeic dermatitis — the white specks look like dandruff, but scale flakes off easily whereas nits are firmly attached to the hair shaft.
takeaway: An itchy scalp with specks firmly attached to hair shafts in a child is head lice.

stem: A 20-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic with three weeks of intense itching that keeps him awake. There are itchy reddish-brown nodules on his penis and scrotum and fine wavy tracks on the sides of his fingers. His girlfriend, with whom he shares a bed, has started itching around her waist. What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.A: Treat him and his girlfriend at the same time, even if her symptoms are mild
options.B: Treat him now and treat her only if her itch persists after his treatment
options.C: Prescribe oral antibiotics for both of them
options.D: Hot-wash bedding and clothes as the main treatment
options.E: Treat him and advise abstinence, without treating her

correct_answer: A. Treat him and his girlfriend at the same time, even if her symptoms are mild
why_correct: Nocturnal itch, burrows on the fingers and genital nodules are typical of scabies, which spreads through prolonged skin contact including sexual contact. Close contacts, including sexual partners, should be treated at the same time as the index case, whether or not they have symptoms, to prevent reinfestation. Washing bedding and clothing supports but does not replace treatment, and screening for other sexually transmitted infections is sensible.
why_wrong: B. Sequential treatment allows the untreated partner to reinfest him. C. Antibiotics do not kill scabies mites. D. Environmental measures are adjuncts; mites live on the skin and need a scabicide. E. Not treating a partner who is already itchy guarantees ongoing infestation.
pearl: Itchy nodules on the male genitalia are highly suggestive of scabies and can persist for weeks after successful treatment.
thinking: Severe nocturnal itch ↓ Finger burrows and genital nodules ↓ Partner now itching ↓ Scabies spread by close skin contact ↓ Simultaneous treatment of index case and partner
exam_trap: B, Treat her only if itch persists — it seems economical, but by the time she itches she may already have reinfested him.
takeaway: In scabies, treat the patient and all close contacts at the same time.

stem: A 55-year-old chef is admitted to a surgical ward with acute cholecystitis. While taking blood, the foundation doctor notices that several of his fingernails have many small surface depressions, and two nails show yellow-orange patches beneath the plate resembling a drop of oil. He has well-defined red plaques with silvery scale on both knees, which he has 'had for ages'. What is the most likely explanation for the nail changes?

options.B: Chronic candidal infection from wet work
